author: Mzi Velapi
title: ‘End hunger, stop climate harm’: protesters take demands to Parliament
content:
About 200 residents and activists marched through the streets of Cape Town on World Food Day, calling for the government to end hunger and stop climate harm. Organised by the Climate Justice Charter Movement (CJCM) and the South African Food Sovereignty Campaign and allied partners, the protesters handed the memorandum to parliament where they called for the adoption of the People’s Sovereignty Act No 1 of 2024, a People’s Sovereignty Policy and an immediate ban on pesticides.




At least 14 to 15 million people in South Africa live below the food poverty line and experience regular food insecurity, while 11,000 children die due to malnutrition every year, and 10-million tonnes of food go to waste every year, according to Unite Against Hunger. 




A recent report by the International Panel of Experts on Sustainable Food Systems (IPES-Food) found that nearly 1.4-billion people in the world work in the agrifood sector, including farmworkers. Despite their number and the vital role they play, they are among the most exploited workers in the world. 




Speaking to 

Elitsha

, Kara Mackay from Women on Farms Project said that women farmworkers bear the brunt of lack of access to food because of the unequal power relations that govern their relationship with farm owners. “The issue of poor wages and the high prices of food is linked to unequal power relations where the farmer is seen as the producer and the farmworkers as merely consumers,” she said.




Retired farmworker, Magrieta Prins from De Doorns said that farmers deny workers the opportunity to grow their own food by controlling their access to water. “Farmworkers do not have land to grow their own food but even in instances where they are allowed to do so, the farmer controls their use of water and in most times just deny them access to water,” Prins said.




A seasonal farmer from Ceres, Charmaine Lynx said that not having access to water impacts on their ability to produce their own food. “The social grants play a crucial role during off season. I have to look after my daughter and family during off season as I share my AllPay grant with them. Some have to resort to recycling as a means to put food on the table for their families,” said Prins.




One of the demands of the protesters is the implementation of the climate emergency social contract, that requires the government and the corporations which promote and profit from fossil fuels, pay the price.




Communities on the coastal areas of the Western Cape are experiencing severe weather that has impacted on their ability to feed their families. Fisher woman from Buffels Baai in the Southern Cape, Sarah Niemand said that the weather patterns have resulted in cold waters and fish migrating away. “For the past two months we struggled to get fish because they are scarce because of the bad weather,” she said.




Addressing the protesters outside of parliament, activist and academic, Vishwas Satgar said that southern Africa is heating at twice the global average rate, pushing the region toward an estimated 3°C of warming as global mitigation targets face severe shortfalls. “We are here to tell this government that we are not going to pay the price for their failure of leadership to prepare this country. Climate signs are telling us that El Niño is coming and the last El Niño resulted in collapsed food systems and pushed the food prices up as a result,” Satgar said.




Responding to the memorandum, Mfuneko Toyana said that the government will announce additional funding to respond to El Niño, when the minister of finance tables the Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement next week.




Satgar responded to this news: “It does not add up, this is the government that is squeezing the working class and the poor in this country. They are driving austerity meaures, and this is just a modest gesture given that the problem is big and El Niño is coming.”

author: Wanessa Celina
title: Locais de votação alterados e abstenção: estigma afasta eleitores da Maré das urnas
content:
No primeiro turno das 

eleições de 2026

, a alteração de locais de votação pelo Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Rio Janeiro (TRE-RJ) impactou mais da metade dos eleitores do Complexo da Maré, na zona norte da capital fluminense. A justificativa do tribunal é que as comunidades da Maré são uma “área de risco” pela dominação de facções e do tráfico de drogas.




“O Estado reconhece que aqui [na Maré] não é seguro para votar e coloca os moradores para votar do lado de fora. Qual o impacto disso? [Que a] gente está sempre no antagonismo”, afirma Tainá Alvarenga, coordenadora da organização Redes da Maré, no eixo direito à segurança pública e acesso à Justiça.




Para Alvarenga, várias instâncias do poder público utilizam a falta de segurança como argumento, mas acabam interferindo no acesso a direitos fundamentais dos moradores das comunidades

 como transporte, saúde, investigações de crimes e, entre eles, o de “não ter os espaços de votação mudados com o discurso da segurança pública”, declara à 

Agência Pública

. 




“A escola oferece menos dias de aula por causa da segurança, a defensoria não pode vir sem uma autorização por causa da segurança, o Ministério Público não pode vir porque é um território conflagrado, não pode ter perícia [pelo mesmo motivo]”, afirma a coordenadora.




Em um 

artigo

 publicado no Jornal O Globo, a diretora fundadora da organização Redes da Maré, Eliana Sousa Silva, explica que a Zona Eleitoral (ZE) 161ª é a mais representativa para a Maré porque cerca de 60% de suas seções estão localizadas dentro do território ou em seu entorno.




Um 

levantamento

 feito pelo Consultor Jurídico mostra que as nove zonas eleitorais do Rio de Janeiro com locais de votação alterados apresentaram um índice maior de abstenção. 

Nelas, a média de abstenção foi de 25,83% enquanto o índice nacional ficou em 21,08%. A 161ª ZE foi justamente a que teve o maior número de endereços trocados, segundo a pesquisa, e alcançou o maior índice de abstenção, 28,46%.




No total, 72 locais de votação do Rio de Janeiro foram alterados pelo TRE-RJ, atingindo 20 municípios do Estado e cerca de 200 mil eleitores, segundo Eliana Sousa Silva. No Complexo da Maré, eleitores foram remanejados para locais com até 7 quilômetros de distância do local original.




A fundadora da Redes Maré também aponta em seu artigo que na 161ª ZE, Lula venceu Flávio Bolsonaro por uma diferença de 14 pontos percentuais, alcançando quase 10 pontos a mais do que obteve na cidade do Rio. E, para governador, Eduardo Paes teve 8 pontos percentuais a mais do que a sua média no restante da capital. “Falta transparência sobre quais critérios justificam a retirada de algumas seções e a manutenção de outras na mesma região” avalia Silva.




“

Os locais transferidos funcionam em escolas municipais. Se esses prédios recebem crianças diariamente, por que seriam inadequados para adultos votarem por algumas horas?

 Sem critérios transparentes, a decisão reforça o estigma da favela como território perigoso e desconsidera a sua organização comunitária”, complementa.




Não é a primeira vez que o TRE-RJ transfere eleitores para outros lugares. Em 2024, a Redes da Maré calculou que 50,6% dos eleitores aptos do local foram impactados pelas mudanças de locais de votação. O estudo “Como vota a Maré”, realizado pela organização, ressalta que o alerta sobre o risco de abstenção em função das constantes alterações de endereço feitas pela Justiça eleitoral do estado já era feito na votação anterior.




Segundo a análise, os moradores da Maré que antes votavam dentro do território foram os que mais sofreram com as dificuldades de acessibilidade e mobilidade urbana. “A transferência pode significar aumento do tempo de caminhada, necessidade de atravessar grandes vias como a Avenida Brasil e Linha Amarela, ausência ou inadequação de transporte público, […] o que impacta desproporcionalmente jovens, mulheres chefes de família, pessoas com deficiência e pessoas idosas que vivem na Maré”, detalha.




A pesquisa ainda destaca que, por mais que o transporte público gratuito nos dias de votação seja “fundamental para reduzir barreiras econômicas ao voto”, não é o suficiente para garantir o direito ao voto. “

Gratuidade não significa, por si só, acessibilidade territorial

. Essa distinção é especialmente importante na Maré, onde o transporte coletivo se concentra nas grandes vias que margeiam o território”, avalia.




A Justiça Eleitoral, neste ano, incluiu a Maré no projeto “Seu Voto Importa”, destinado a auxiliar pessoas com mobilidade reduzida e pessoas com deficiência para se locomover até suas áreas de votação, em Bonsucesso.

author: Frida Garza
title: Trump Admin Just Effectively Killed a Popular Renewable Energy Program
content:
Solar panels can be an economic lifeline in the rural US — but now they’re going to be a lot harder to build.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Earlier this month, after a series of stops and starts, the U.S. Department of Agriculture announced changes to a long-running program that is supposed to help farmers and rural small businesses stand up renewable energy projects.

The new rules, set to go into effect today, October 16, effectively make any solar power development ineligible for funding through the Rural Energy for America Program, or REAP. It’s the latest of multiple rollbacks by the second Trump administration that advocates say are essentially making the program unusable.

Installing solar systems on farmland can cost tens of thousands of dollars upfront, which many agricultural producers may not have or may be reluctant to spend, given their low profit margins. REAP has long provided financial support to farmers to build out renewable energy systems on their land.

These projects often provide multiple benefits to participants. First, they can help lower utility bills for agricultural producers and rural businesses by providing their operations with additional power. But farmers and business owners are also able to sell excess energy back to the grid. By cutting costs or padding revenue, these systems can be a lifeline at a time when farmers are facing escalating costs for things like fertilizer, fuel, labor, and seeds, making it difficult to make ends meet.

Research shows investing in renewable energy can also be an economic driver in rural parts of the country. “All of these things lined up,” said Matt Russell, the executive director of the Iowa Farmers Union, an independent organization representing family farmers. So for the Trump administration to “shift away from those kinds of win-win-win investments is very disappointing,” he added.

The Iowa Farmers Union is one of the plaintiffs in a lawsuit filed last month against the USDA, alleging that previous changes to REAP were already harming rural communities by severely restricting solar development under the program. (The lawsuit was filed on September 28, just days before the agriculture department published its new rules.)

The lawsuit takes aim at changes made to REAP in August 2025, following an executive order by President Donald Trump the previous month stating that taxpayers would no longer “subsidize expensive and unreliable energy sources like wind and solar.” Although the executive order did not instruct the USDA to do anything in particular, the office within the agriculture department that administers REAP changed the criteria for applicants such that most solar projects would become ineligible for grants or loan guarantees.

Part of the plaintiffs’ argument is that such a move violates the REAP statute. Lawmakers created REAP in 2008 as part of that year’s farm bill by combining two existing programs that sought to develop renewable energy and increase energy efficiency. “Rather than complying” with this mandate, “the agency has decided to completely ignore what Congress told them to do,” said Michael Youhana, an attorney at Earthjustice, the nonprofit environmental law group representing the plaintiffs. “In fact,” he added, the USDA is doing “the opposite of what Congress told them to do” by promoting the use of fossil fuels over renewables.

The lawsuit also alleges that these anti-solar moves from the USDA violate the Administrative Procedure Act, which essentially requires agencies to show that regulatory decisions were made through careful consideration. The USDA says “that they’re taking this action to protect farmland from being gobbled up by solar systems,” said Youhana. “But farmers are voluntarily applying for REAP, and they’re doing it because solar gives them all kinds of really great financial benefits that the agency has completely ignored.”

The USDA told Grist it “will not comment on pending litigation.” In an email to energy news site Utility Dive, a representative for the USDA said that under the Biden administration, “fertile farmland that should be feeding America” was used instead to produce solar power. “Those days are over. USDA will not actively participate in repurposing farmland historically used to sustain this country’s abundant food supply.”

Grist has previously reported on how the USDA’s abrupt freeze of REAP grants in the early days of Trump’s second term created confusion and chaos for small farmers who had already spent tens of thousands of dollars on energy upgrades. In March 2025, the agency released that grant money but asked participants to voluntarily revise and resubmit their applications without any mention of climate change. That summer, the USDA announced the anti-solar policy over which Earthjustice, along with the Environmental Law and Policy Center, are suing.

But the switch-ups didn’t stop there. A year later, in March 2026, the USDA effectively paused REAP as a whole, announcing it would suspend further grant awards until the program rules were rewritten to comply with Trump’s executive order from the year before.

This month, on October 1, the department published its final rule changes. They state that solar or wind projects on cropland involving “any component made in a country named as a foreign adversary” are no longer eligible for funding through REAP. Because so many parts of solar power systems are manufactured in China, this effectively means an end to any new solar development on farms through the once-popular USDA program.

Another change drags out the timeline for receiving funding; applicants must now have energy systems up and running for one year in order to be considered eligible for reimbursement.

These changes “more deeply entrench the anti-solar policy we’ve challenged in our lawsuit,” said Youhana. While “federal investments in renewable energy projects could help to offset rising energy costs, making life more affordable for farmers and the broader American public alike,” he added, the USDA seems to be moving in the opposite direction.

Russell argued that further restricting funding sources like REAP will only lead to the further consolidation of the agricultural industry, where only the biggest, wealthiest operations can survive, and the little guys suffer without adequate public support.

“It’s like stacking the deck against family farms, and entrepreneurial businesses in small towns that are trying to bootstrap themselves,” he said. “It’s picking winners and losers, and the losers are the very kinds of farms and businesses and communities that I think the vast majority of American taxpayers think that they’re investing in.”

author: Ali Harb
title: “Democrats for Mike Rogers” PAC Is Funded by Republicans, Records Show
content:
The group has spent more than $4 million in an attempt to defeat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Democrats for Mike Rogers, a group that has spent millions of dollars to defeat Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, has received funds from Republican-aligned organizations, campaign finance records show.

Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings, made public on October 16, revealed that TFM, a super PAC that has been running commercials against El-Sayed under the “Democrats for Mike Rogers” name, was funded by two other PACs that back Republican candidates.

GLCF, a pro-Rogers group, gave TFM $50,000, while American Unity PAC, whose stated mission is to promote “Republicans who support LGBT freedom,” transferred $25,000 to the Michigan group.

Other donors include three individuals in Tennessee and one Michigan resident.

The name and place of residence of the Michigan donor — Michael Sandler, of West Bloomfield — matches those of a doctor who was appointed to the Central Michigan University board of trustees in 2017 by then-Gov. Rick Snyder, a Republican.

Friday’s quarterly filings cover up to September 30, offering only a partial picture of TFM’s finances. The group has spent more than $4 million to help defeat El-Sayed, suggesting that most of its donations came after the September 30 deadline and will not be made public until after the election on November 3.

Nonetheless, the records appear to back suspicions from El-Sayed’s supporters against the group that it may be a Republican-led operation trying to manufacture Democratic support for Rogers and paint the progressive Democrat as an extremist.

An X account associated with the group was created after the bruising Democratic primary ended in August, which pitted El-Sayed against pro-Israel Congresswoman Haley Stevens. It quickly amassed thousands of followers.

The Democrats for Mike Rogers account frequently shares and amplifies attacks against El-Sayed, including regularly questioning his medical credentials and painting him as untruthful.

Last week, the group released a TFM-funded ad, featuring several people who are supposedly Black voters in Michigan questioning El-Sayed’s commitment to Michigan and arguing that he cares more about Palestine.

“I think Abdul cares more about the West Bank than west Detroit,” one person says in the commercial — a message that is echoed by two other people.

“I’m a lifelong Democrat, and this year I’m voting for Mike Rogers,” another says.

El-Sayed is supportive of Palestinian rights and says U.S. taxpayer dollars should be spent improving the lives of Americans, not sent overseas to commit war crimes.

Rogers, a former member of Congress, is a staunch supporter of Israel and has pledged to “unconditionally support” what he calls “Israel’s right to defend itself.”

Israel — which leading human rights groups and United Nations investigators say is committing genocide in Gaza — receives at least $3.8 billion in U.S. military support annually.

U.S. support for Israel has become a key point of contention in the Senate race in Michigan.

TFM was established initially as Democrats for Mike Rogers on August 27 but later changed its name at the FEC’s behest because independent expenditure PACs cannot include a candidate’s name without authorization.

State Representative Karen Whitsett, who was elected as a Democrat but has aligned with Republicans for years, is the sole person listed on the TFM’s filings, serving as the group’s treasurer and custodian of records.

In 2020, Democrats in the Michigan House of Representatives censured Whitsett after she met with President Donald Trump and thanked him for promoting hydroxychloroquine, an unproven drug that she said helped with her recovery from COVID-19. Earlier this year, Whitsett announced she would not run for office again due to her faith. “For me, it is impossible to be a faithful follower of Jesus Christ while remaining a member of the Democratic Party as it exists today,” Whitsett said at the time. “I cannot reconcile that platform with Scripture.”

Prior reporting from Drop Site News has also found that several other people publicly associated with Democrats for Mike Rogers, are, in fact, not Democrats.

Truthout reached out to TFM through the email listed on its FEC records and did not get a response by the time of publication.

Whitsett also did not respond to Truthout’s request for comment.

The Senate race in Michigan is seen as one of the most important contests in the midterm election. It will be difficult for Democrats to regain control of the chamber if they lose in the Midwestern state.

The seat is currently held by retiring Democrat Gary Peters.

If El-Sayed wins, he would become the first Muslim senator. In recent weeks, Rogers and his allies have intensified their attacks on El-Sayed with accusations that he supports “terrorism” and has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood — allegations that Democrats say are unfounded and rooted in Islamophobia.

Last week, Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana), campaigning alongside Rogers, said El-Sayed goes to bed in an Osama bin Laden jersey.

The group Democrats for Mike Rogers has echoed such attacks, baselessly claiming that El-Sayed is “funded by the Muslim brotherhood and Iran lobby.” (Iran and the Muslim Brotherhood do not follow the same Islamic sect and are at odds politically and ideologically).

The group has also said that El-Sayed is “running to do the bidding of CAIR,” referring to the Council on American-Islamic Relations, a civil rights group.

El-Sayed has argued that Republicans want to distract from his policy ideas and Trump’s unpopularity by focusing on the Muslim candidate’s identity.

After the president misrepresented E-Sayed’s first name as “Mohammed” in an apparent effort to draw attention to his Muslim faith earlier this month, the Democratic nominee accused Trump of attacking all Michiganders.

“He thinks so low of us,” El-Sayed wrote in a social media post. “He thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor’s office. He thinks we don’t know any better. It’s time for change.”

author: Amy Goodman
title: Inside the Worker Resistance in Silicon Valley’s Tech Oligarchy
content:
Longtime tech worker organizers discuss early victories in the movement — and the repression that followed.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Longtime tech worker organizers Clarissa Redwine and JS Tan’s new book, Against Tech Oligarchy: Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry, draws on the authors’ experiences at major tech companies to chronicle the rise and fall of the tech worker movement, its early victories, and the repression and slide to corporate control that followed.

“Over the course of the 2010s, what we saw was that the tech industry wasn’t quite the industry that it had promised to its workers and to the public. Rather than making the world more open, more democratic, we saw it really be the culprit of misinformation,” says Tan, who was pushed out of Microsoft after raising objections to the company’s ties to fossil fuel companies.

Silicon Valley’s slide to the right was influenced by corporate backlash to labor’s demands, explains Redwine, who was fired from Kickstarter for union organizing. She says she hopes to inspire a new generation of tech workers to organize “within these tech oligarchs’ own empires, to stand up and push back.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman.

If you work in the tech industry, your boss might not want you to tune in to our next segment. It’s about a remarkable new book called Against Tech Oligarchy: Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry. It’s written by longtime tech worker organizers Clarissa Redwine and JS Tan. Drawing on their own experience organizing at high-tech companies, they chronicle the rise of the tech worker movement, its early victories, and the challenges it faces today as tech titans consolidate their economic and political power, while tech workers face mass layoffs.

Clarissa Redwine helped unionize Kickstarter, where she was fired amidst a union-busting campaign before workers went on to win union recognition. JS Tan is a former Microsoft software engineer who publicly challenged Microsoft’s work with the Pentagon, with ICE and with fossil fuel companies, including its use of cloud and AI technologies to help Chevron expand oil extraction.

Their new book comes as tech companies embrace artificial intelligence, workplace surveillance and increased automation. At Meta, for example, a new initiative will collect workers’ mouse movements, keystrokes and some screenshots to help train AI models to replace them in the future. In response, Meta workers reached out to United Tech and Allied Workers, a branch of the Communication Workers Union, to discuss unionization efforts and how best to resist.

Clarissa Redwine and JS Tan join us now.

We welcome you both to Democracy Now! It’s great to have you with us. Clarissa, let’s start with you. First of all, explain what Kickstarter is and how you got the experience you did, and then how you tried to unionize your workplace, though it ultimately did get unionized.

CLARISSA REDWINE: Yes, it did. Yeah. So, I joined the tech industry in a moment where there was a lot of optimism for what tech could do for society. And Kickstarter was especially idealistic, where the reason the platform exists is to give communities a tool for bringing projects to life, cultural projects, but also technology. And, you know, in 2016, when I joined, there was a moment where tech management and workers felt aligned and united against the Trump administration. But as the years went by, we saw, over and over, tech companies capitulating, becoming complicit in the rise of the alt-right. And there came a moment at Kickstarter where we had the same experience.

So, there was a moment where Breitbart wrote an article saying that a Kickstarter project was inciting violence. This project was a comic book called Always Punch Nazis, which they did not like. And management decided, rather than stand up to Breitbart and this push from the alt-right, that they would cancel the project. And I and my co-workers demanded that we keep this project on the site. And that moment of collective action was transformative for myself, but also my co-workers, where we saw the promise of collective action. And after that, we decided we wanted structural power in the workplace. We wanted lasting change. And we fought for a union, and we won.

AMY GOODMAN: And talk about where you went in that struggle.

CLARISSA REDWINE: Yeah, so, I was part of the core organizing group at Kickstarter, and when management was attempting to bust the union, they decided to fire a third of our organizing committee in the same week. And unfortunately, I was first to go. But it was all completely worth it. And the reason that Kickstarter is such a bright spot in the tech worker movement is because it showed tech workers across the industry that it was possible to win a union. And ever since, I’ve been organizing and building worker power.

AMY GOODMAN: And, JS Tan, talk about your experience at Microsoft.

JS TAN: Yeah, you know, so, I started in the tech industry in the mid-2010s, and my first job out of college was at Microsoft. And, you know, I think it was around that time where this idea that the tech sector, you know, with the rise of the internet especially, was going to be this place that could really push for a more open society, a more connected society, and even a more democratic society. And so, coming out of college, you know, myself and a lot of us coming out of these CS departments had these ideas that joining the tech industry and building these internet platforms would allow us to do just that. And so, that’s what happened to me when I went to Microsoft.

But, you know, I think over the course of the 2010s, what we saw was that the tech industry wasn’t quite — you know, wasn’t quite the industry that it had sort of promised to its workers and to the public, right? You know, rather than making the world more open, more democratic, we saw it really be the culprit of misinformation. You know, when I started at Microsoft, they were starting to get involved with military contracts with the Pentagon. And, you know, in particular at Microsoft, at that time when I was working there, there was this really strong messaging push from the bosses that Microsoft was going to be this place of — that was really going to push the agenda of sustainability and green technology. But, you know, from the inside, it was clear to me and many of my co-workers that, actually, they were collaborating with the oil and gas companies and, in many cases, helping them intensify the drilling that these companies were doing.

AMY GOODMAN: And how did they respond to those inside raising objections?

JS TAN: Yeah, I mean, compared to some of the other companies, they were a little bit more tactful and not sort of just outright firing a lot of the organizers. But in my case, you know, I had gone to Kazakhstan and had had sort of seen up close how Chevron wanted to use Microsoft cloud and AI technologies to drill and to extract even more oil. And, you know, I came back to the U.S. and wrote about it all in an essay, and that ended up getting me in some trouble, where I ended up getting pushed out of the company.

AMY GOODMAN: And what do you do now?

JS TAN: Well, now I’m a — I’m a graduate student at MIT, and I continue, with Clarissa, to continue to organize in the tech worker movement.

AMY GOODMAN: So, this latest news that we just included in the lede about Meta, Clarissa, a new initiative collecting workers’ mouse movements, keystrokes and some screenshots to help train AI models to replace them in the future, especially for the Luddites among us, if you can explain what exactly that means?

CLARISSA REDWINE: Yes, absolutely. So, you know, if you think about how a company operates, management is always trying to cut costs, cut corners. And the management at Meta saw that they had this very valuable resource, which was their employees and the work that their employees do every day. So, they decided to ingest all of this activity from their workers, every time that you click on your keyboard, every time you move your mouse, and they used all of that data to train an AI model that could actually do software engineering, could do some of the core work that these employees do every day.

And unfortunately, this news slipped in the company, and workers were enraged, not just because this felt like they didn’t give consent for their data to be used this way, there was a threat of automation, but also because management was doing this in a very insecure way, not following procedures within the company.

And luckily, I was embedded with some workers at Meta when they were pushing back, and got to see up close how they, you know, had this amazing open letter that gained traction, thousands of signatures seemingly overnight. They were speaking back to management and even organizing in more structural, strategic ways behind the scenes.

AMY GOODMAN: I mean, the Meta AI surveillance came as the company announced 8,000 layoffs —

CLARISSA REDWINE: Right. And that’s very convenient to announce layoffs right before you’re going to have this initiative that is very extractive of your workforce. You know, your workers want to keep their heads down and not make waves. But I’m very excited and really proud of the workers at Meta that did stand up in that moment.

AMY GOODMAN: Also from our headlines today, The Washington Post has revealed the names of private donors who’ve donated $330 million to help fund President Trump’s ballroom, the new White House ballroom. Tech giants Nvidia and Apple each gave $25 million. Other donors included Amazon and Microsoft. Your response? Well, actually, since you worked for Microsoft, JS Tan?

JS TAN: Yeah, you know, that’s a great question. And I think that really gets to the tip of this ice — the tip of the iceberg of what is a broader shift in the politics of Silicon Valley. You know, I’m sure your listeners know fully well that, you know, the tech elites have cozied up with Trump, and now they’re embracing the kind of politics that’s much more associated with MAGA. And tech workers know this well, as well. You know, in their own workplaces, they’re seeing a reduction in DEI initiatives, a crackdown on sort of the open culture that was once so celebrated in the tech industry.

And, you know, there are many ways to explain this shift. You know, we’ve seen in other reporting and other books that — you know, for instance, tracing key figures like Peter Thiel or Curtis Yarvin and how the spread of right-wing ideology permeated through Silicon Valley. You know, we’ve also sort of seen reporting that looks at why it was under the Biden administration that the tech elites essentially moved away from the Democratic Party, especially as they cracked down on monopoly-type patterns in the tech industry.

But, you know, to that list, our book adds one more, one more explanation, and that’s really about class struggle. You know, it’s really about how it was that the tech worker movement itself was central in the shifting politics of Silicon Valley. And I think, you know, to —

AMY GOODMAN: Explain that further.

JS TAN: Yeah, and, you know, I guess to really understand that, we have to go back to 2018, which was the beginning of the tech worker movement. And, you know, that was a period in which we saw, you know, tech workers from across the industry start participating in various kinds of activism, both labor activism and political activism, in the workplace. And, you know, for folks who remember the media cycle back then, that was a moment where we were seeing this type of activism happening in the news cycle on a weekly basis and, in fact, at both big and small companies alike.

And, you know, it was really quite a remarkable moment, I think, because that was a period in which the activism that was happening had fundamentally a progressive backing to it. Right? The folks who were — the folks who were, you know, participating in this activism were fighting over things like the collaboration with the Pentagon, right? So anti-militarism. They were fighting over things like I was involved with — right? — against the sort of collaborations with Big Oil, and also joining up with the #MeToo movement to fight rampant sexism in the workplace.

And so, you know, the way the bosses responded to that, initially, they tried to sort of double down on this progressive facade, you know, in some cases, putting more money into AI ethics, in some cases, ceding to worker demands. But eventually, you know, the bosses got fed up, right? They got fed up, and they didn’t want to continue listening to their employees.

AMY GOODMAN: JS Tan, you’re at school now. You’re at MIT. The technology of surveillance and repression is increasingly sophisticated. Are radicalized tech workers building liberatory code?

JS TAN: You know, I think right now, oftentimes they’re forced into a position where they cannot. Right? They’re forced into a position where their bosses are telling them that they have to do certain things or put their jobs on the line. And, you know, I think, in some cases also, tech workers themselves see the code that they’re building as not being — as not having a societal problem. But, you know, what’s really central in our book is that we realize that when tech workers participate in this collective action and participate in organizing against the boss, that transforms their politics, as well.

AMY GOODMAN: Clarissa, we have 15 seconds. The most important issue you feel you want conveyed in your new book, Against Tech Oligarchy?

CLARISSA REDWINE: Yeah. We hope this book inspires the workers within these tech oligarchs’ own empires to stand up and push back, like many of us did in the early days of the tech worker movement. And I think there’s a lot to learn from these struggles.

AMY GOODMAN: Clarissa Redwine and JS Tan, authors of the new book, Against Tech Oligarchy: Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry.

That does it for our show. Democracy Now! is currently accepting applications for an individual giving manager to support our fundraising team. Learn more and apply at democracynow.org.

I’ll be at Woodstock International Film Festival today at 2:30 — you can check our website — and California next week, USC on Monday. We’ll be screening Steal This Story, Please! I’ll be there with the film’s director. Also, next week, on Friday, I’ll be at Stanford University, and then in San Francisco and Marin, and then on to Colorado. Check our website. I’m Amy Goodman.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Washington Post Journalist Hospitalized After Israeli Settler Attack
content:
Netanyahu cast doubt on the journalists’ account of the attack just hours after it happened.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Israeli settlers conducting an assault on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank amid their autumn olive harvest also attacked a U.S. journalist on Friday, sending her to the hospital as she and other journalists were documenting the coordinated violent raid.

Heidi Levine, a veteran photojournalist for The Washington Post, was donning a “press” vest when settlers chased her and a group of other journalists away from the site of the raid on Palestinian families. They knocked her to the ground, stole her phone and cameras, and beat her.

“They just kept kicking me and kicking me, like probably 50 times,” Levine said. Video of the attack shows Levine on the ground being beaten by masked assailants.

Fellow U.S. journalist Jasper Nathaniel said that Levine was being prepared for surgery on Friday morning Eastern Time. Her “injuries are significantly worse than initially thought,” Nathaniel said, adding that she has a cracked rib and may have been stabbed. He also posted a picture of her bloodied hand, which showed that she had multiple stitches in at least one finger.

Nathaniel said that Israeli settlers and soldiers had opened fire with machine guns on Palestinian families attempting to conduct their olive harvest and that at least one Palestinian was shot. Multiple witnesses said Israeli forces arrived on the scene to help protect and enable the settler raid. Journalist Andrey Khrzhanovskiy, who also witnessed the attack, said that the presence of the Israeli soldiers actually emboldened the settlers.

As Nathaniel and Khrzhanovskiy came to Levine’s aid and they ran from the settlers toward the Palestinian medics, video taken by Nathaniel shows a battered Levine saying: “I can’t. Let me die. Let me die.”

The Post’s executive editor, Matt Murray, called for an investigation in response to the attack.

“This morning, a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, was attacked by Israeli settlers while reporting in the West Bank. She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist. While we are relieved that Heidi has received medical care and is safe, we are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities.”

Israel is notorious for opening supposed investigations into incidents of settler or soldier violence, and either never finishing the probe or clearing themselves of responsibility.

Indeed, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office already cast doubt on the journalists’ and witnesses’ accounts of the attack.

“The facts surrounding the confrontation near Abu Falah, during which Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was allegedly assaulted, remain unclear and are under investigation,” Netanyahu’s office said in a statement. “We will not allow disputed incidents to be exploited to demonize the hundreds of thousands of law-abiding Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria.”

Just a day before Levine was attacked, Nathaniel reported that another American, Haytham Taysir, was beaten by settlers in Ramallah.

The attacks come after a report last week found that the U.S. embassy in Israel has purposefully suppressed findings on nine Palestinian Americans who have been killed by Israeli forces and settlers in the West Bank in recent years.

author: Daron Letts
title: Blasting begins for new Ampere facility in Iqaluit
content:
Iqaluit’s Road to Nowhere is making space for a makerspace.




Manager Cole Tucker, left, and technician Bryce So work on a computer upstairs at Ampere as part of the Computers for Success Nunavut initiative on Thursday. The pair say they look forward to more space in a new facility being designed for the organization. (Photo by Daron Letts)




Tower Arctic Ltd. is preparing to blast rock starting this weekend for Ampere’s proposed Makerspace Economic Development Hub, which would allow the non-profit organization to allow more people to participate in its science and technology focused educational programming. Currently every program has a waitlist.




“We are looking forward to seeing this building come to fruition,” said Kevin Kelly, Ampere’s director of Nunavut operations, in an interview on Thursday.




Ampere provides people of all ages opportunities take part in media and online literacy activities and entrepreneurial skills training.




Programming runs throughout the week, including after school and on evenings and weekends.




Ampere staff also refurbish old laptops for free redistribution across the territory, as part of the organization’s Computers for Success Nunavut initiative.
















Ampere has outgrown its current space, said Cole Tucker, the tech program’s manager.




“We’re pretty cramped up here,” Tucker said. “In the new building we’re going to have a lot more space.”




Tucker supervises six staff who fix computers on the second floor. He said he can’t schedule the full team at one time due to the lack of space.




As for what the new structure would look like, that’s in part up to Iqalummiut.




Ampere secured a little over $1 million from the Canadian Northern Economic Development Agency in April to cover design and pre-construction work for a two-storey, 7,200-square-foot building. That’s more than double the size of the organization’s current location at 1412 Sikituuq Crt.




The nonprofit educational organization purchased the plot at 4120 Road to Nowhere from the city back in 2024. The site is located on the southwest corner of the intersection with Imiqtarviminiq Street.
















Ampere plans to host one of several community consultations as early as November to ask residents what they’d like to see in the space.




In the meantime, Ampere staff are informally seeking input from individual educators, students, small business owners, policy makers, families and anyone else they cross paths with, to solicit ideas for the new space, said Kent Driscoll, Ampere’s director of advocacy and strategic initiatives.




“We’re going to have the perspective of all members of the community on what they would like to see,” Driscoll said Thursday in an interview.




There is no timeline for the final design and construction of the new building, said Driscoll, adding the organization is still looking for funding.




Once Ampere’s new home is built, the organization will double its staff of 12 mostly full-time positions, Kelly said.
















The city issued a public service announcement earlier in the week that advised construction crews will remove a bedrock outcrop at the site from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. starting Friday. The work was scheduled to run until Oct. 26.




The city is asking residents to use caution in the area.

author: Halie Moses
title: The Z Factor: Young Voters and the 2026 Midterms
content:
Generation Z voters (aged 18-29) are predicted to make a significant impact on the upcoming 2026 Midterm elections. This has not always been the case, as student and youth voter turnout has historically remained low. Only 47% of Americans aged 18-29 voted in the 2024 election. This year, 50 million Gen Z Americans are eligible to vote.

In October, a report by UCLA’s William Institute examined the political priorities and voting intentions of Gen Z adults ahead of the 2026 midterms. The study found that nearly 74 percent of respondents said they were likely or certain to vote. These numbers come as no surprise to those who work with students, spend time organizing on college campuses, or identify as Gen Z during the Trump Administration. Rising living costs, ICE raids, attacks on reproductive rights access, sexual assault cases, climate change, and unwanted wars have directly impacted their lives and are driving them to the polls with a passion for change.

Leela Strong, Director of CIRCLE, who works to empower the youth vote, reflected: “Young people are sending us clear signals, not only of dissatisfaction with our politics and deep economic concerns, but also of a strong desire to take action and drive change.” Organizations such as When We All Vote are working to engage young people by connecting their priorities with the issues and candidates on their ballots. Opportunities to participate alongside friends and classmates can also encourage young people to become more involved in politics.

Campus organizing is another part of these efforts. The Feminist Majority Foundation’s Feminist Campus program is actively working to get the student vote out. Students can help their peers register to vote, understand their ballot, and march to the polls in solidarity. These efforts are particularly important for first-time voters, who may need guidance.

Not only are young people planning to vote, but they are also planning to vote overwhelmingly Democratic. In the September Economist/YouthGov Poll, when asked who they will cast their ballot for, 54% of 18-29-year-olds said the Democratic candidate, compared with 22% who said the Republican candidate. The same survey found a sentiment among youth that reflects that the Republican Party is too extreme. When asked, “Do you think the Republican Party is too extreme?” 65% of 18- 29-year-olds replied yes. In contrast, only 29% believe the Democratic Party is too extreme. These results reflect the views of respondents at the time of the survey and do not necessarily predict how young people will vote in November.

These numbers are significant and show promising signs that young people are empowered to change the course of our political and social reality. Voter registration, accessible election information, and campus organizing can help young people navigate the voting process and participate in decisions that affect their futures. To learn more, head to vote411.org/feminist.

author: David Swanson
title: The One Big Peace Conference and Open Borders
content:
Nonviolent Activism, What to do, Why End War, World

By David Swanson, World BEYOND War, October 16, 2026

Approximately once a day for forever, so approximately 365 times a year, someone proposes to me the same good idea. Hey, they suggest, I’d like to organize one big peace conference and create one big peace movement to unite everyone and be stronger instead of fractured.

I have several answers. First and foremost is: hell yeah, great idea, do it! do it! do it!

Another answer is: there are reasons the 364 other people who’ve said this to me this year have not actually done it, just like the 365 who thought of it last year. It costs lots of money. It’s harder to get people to a conference than to a rally or a protest. There are language barriers. Whoever is in charge of organizing it will be assumed by others to not be totally welcoming of their views. There will be at least some truth to that, since no two people completely agree on everything. If you have this one big conference for everyone in a physical location, as 90 percent of you with this idea want, it will be closer and easier to get to for some people than for others. Maybe we should attempt a regional one for some people. Etc. Etc.

But once a year, I like to focus on a different answer, this one: I don’t have time to do yours for you because I’m already doing it.

In 2014, a bunch of us created World BEYOND War to be one big global peace movement based only on Earth and nowhere more specific, to oppose every side of every war, to oppose every manufacturing of every weapon, to oppose every scrap of war propaganda and war culture no matter its origin, to abolish the entire war business in toto as a global nonviolent educational and activist movement collectively run by a global board. We now have a large and growing staff (14) and board (17) and advisory board (19) and list of active chapters (56) and affiliates (125) engaged in opposing war and promoting peace night-and-day, year-in and year-out. We’re not yet nearly what we need to be, but we are a good step forward from “Hey, I’ve got an idea!” And we have an annual conference online for everyone.

Of course, no conference will meet exactly the detailed vision of any single person. But you’re all invited to make this one yours. It is the reason I can’t stop and start over with your idea for one, so why not at least check it out? It’s a gathering and strategizing bonanza with dedicated activists from locations in dozens of countries, plotting as a global movement to abolish the most horrible thing humanity does to itself. Want to come?

Each year, we focus on a particular theme closely tied to ending all war. This year’s conference, which is coming up soon on October 23-25 on Zoom (Register here) is looking at borders, including how wars form them, what they do and do not prevent, how borders are militarized against the victims of war transforming them into enemies in a new sort of war, and how borders creep inward militarizing whole societies.

We’ll be considering the prospects for a world beyond war and borders. What would that mean? What would it look like? What steps are already being taken to get there?

The mythical world of “open borders” that rightwing politicians falsely accuse liberal politicians of favoring: what is that world in the words of people who actually do favor it, and why is it not frightening so much as enticing? This conference will include panel discussions, breakout rooms where we can all share, artistic performances, and the growing solidarity and power of one big growing peace movement. You should come.

If you select to make a recurring contribution of at least $15 per month, you may select a thank-you gift. We thank our recurring donors on our website.

title: Conectivas: First Time in (Por primera vez en) CADF
content:
A table of our own: Conectivas First Time in CADF.    

 




 




For many years, we have seen organizations that serve people with disabilities occupy spaces like the Central American Donors Forum (CADF); this year, thanks to WEI’s support, we were able to attend in person, make our voices heard, and become visible in places where we are usually invisible.   

 




We were not there to hear people speak about us; we went there to speak ourselves, for the first time and in first person – as an organization led by women with disabilities.   

 




What did we achieve?

  

 







We facilitated a networking table on women and disability.  

 










We offered support to WEI’s lighting talk on women with disabilities fighting back anti rights movements.   

 










We networked with different actors about how we see – from a human rights perspective- the backlashes in rights we are seeing globally and how we want to be included in the resistance.  

 







They still see us as something apart.

  

 




Most of the donors we engaged in conversations agreed that the disability movement needs funding but struggled to see how to include us into what they are already doing. 

Disability. Intersects democracy, protection and gender equality. 

Yes, we need specific resources and at the same time. Inclusion in the actions already put in place.   

 




Our accessibility is not enough. We could get there thanks to WEI’s support, but many other women are missing from the conversation. A

rriving is not enough: we need conditions to remain in those spaces

. To guarantee accessibility for women with disability the following spaces are also needed:   

 







Desstined spaces for rest  

 










Physical and menstrual hygiene accommodations  

 










Spaces where we can rest from noise and crowds  

 







To invest in the participation of the female disabled leaders is to invest in the movements: 

it strengthens the local networks that already exist to access resources, but also to weave alliances that survive the forum’s duration.   

 




Thank you to Women Enabled International for the technical assistance provided that opened up a space for us without occupying it. 

This time we had a table of our own: what comes next is that this stops being the exception.

  

 




In solidarity,  

 




Conectivas

 · October 2026. 

 







 




Una mesa propia: Conectivas por primera vez en CADF

  

 




 




Por muchos años hemos visto cómo organizaciones que prestan servicios a personas con discapacidad ocupan espacios como el Foro Centroamericano de Donantes (CADF) y este año gracias al apoyo de WEI pudimos estar en persona, poner nuestra propia voz y hacernos visibles donde solemos ser invisibles. 

 

 




No fuimos a que hablaran de nosotras; fuimos a hablar, por primera vez y en primera persona, como organización representativa de mujeres con discapacidad 

 

 




¿Qué logramos?

 

 

 







Facilitamos una mesa de networking sobre mujeres y discapacidad  

 

 










Apoyamos la charla relámpago de WEI sobre mujeres con discapacidad frente a movimientos antiderechos. 

 

 










Conversamos con distintos actores sobre cómo vemos, desde los derechos humanos, los retrocesos que estamos viviendo, y también sobre cómo queremos incluirnos. 

 

 







Nos siguen viendo como un punto a parte.

 

 

 




La mayoría de donantes con quienes conversamos dicen que necesitarían recursos específicos para discapacidad, pero no ven cómo incluirnos en lo que ya hacen. L

a discapacidad atraviesa la democracia, la protección y la igualdad

 de género. Sí, necesitamos recursos específicos y, a la vez, inclusión en las acciones que ya existen.  

 

 




Nuestra accesibilidad no es suficiente. Nosotras pudimos llegar gracias al apoyo de WEI, pero faltan muchas otras, y 

llegar no basta; necesitamos condiciones para quedarnos. 

Para garantizar la accesibilidad de mujeres con discapacidad también son necesarios espacios para: 

 

 







Descansar 

 

 










Higiene corporal y menstrual 

 

 










Aislamiento del ruido y de la multitud,  

 

 







Invertir en la participación de líderes feministas con discapacidad es invertir en movimientos: 

fortalece las redes locales que ya existen, tanto para acceder a recursos como para tejer alianzas que duren más que el foro. 

 

 




Gracias a WEI por una asistencia técnica que nos abrió espacio sin ocupar nuestro lugar. 

Esta vez tuvimos una mesa propia; lo que sigue es que deje de ser la excepción.

 

 

 




En solidaridad, 

 

 




Conectivas

title: Jineolojî Academy: Jineolojî should be at the heart of social organization
content:
In a message sent to the European Jineolojî Conference, the Jineolojî Academy Board reflected on 11 years of accumulated experience in Jineolojî activities and highlighted the tasks and responsibilities of the new period.




Stating that Jineolojî is rooted in the historical experience of struggle of the Kurdish Women’s Freedom Movement, the board emphasized that its activities should be developed on the basis of building a democratic society and advancing women’s freedom.




Stating that Jineolojî should not be confined to a single committee, the board emphasized that all institutions within the women’s movement should incorporate this perspective into their activities.




“Every individual, institution, organization, and structure working towards social transformation and revolution can achieve their political objectives only through a sound sociological approach,” the message stated.










https://1649452211.rsc.cdn77.org/20261016113503_2026-10-16-haelen-avrupa-jineoloji-konferansi-pajk-mesaji_1.mp4













‘Jineolojî should be organized under the umbrella of the Jineolojî Academy’




The message stressed the need for a new organizational model at the current stage of Jineolojî activities, highlighting the importance of transitioning from a committee structure to an academy model. It called for research, education, written studies, and academic activities to be organized under a common umbrella, urging the establishment of “a functional academy model worthy of its role as the science of the women’s revolution.”




The board emphasized the need to distinguish between integrating the Jineolojî perspective into all areas of work and the specific responsibilities of institutions specializing in Jineolojî. Highlighting the importance of coordination and joint planning among institutions, the message stressed the need to prevent confusion over duties and roles.




‘We must reach our own social base’




The message highlighted the significant international impact of Jineolojî activities in Europe, while identifying the failure to sufficiently strengthen ties with women from Kurdistan and the Middle East as one of the main shortcomings. “We must engage in self-criticism regarding our failure to reach and establish a meaningful presence within the social fabric of Kurdistan and the Middle East,” the board stated.




Drawing attention to the changing sociological realities of the Kurdish community living in Europe, the message emphasized that activities should move beyond an approach focused solely on supporting the struggle in Kurdistan. It highlighted the importance of organizing Jineolojî within its own social base and developing solutions to the problems faced by women and society.




‘Defending society must be a priority’




Addressing violence against women, the targeting of young people by prostitution and drug gangs, and the problems arising from nationalist and religious influences on society, the message stressed that Jineolojî activities must develop responses to these challenges.




The board pointed out that educational, research, and camp activities carried out within the framework of Jineolojî should strengthen social organization. “When determining the perspective, model, and planning of Jineolojî activities, the most important task must be to defend and organize society as a collective,” it said.




The message also warned against distorting the concept of Jineolojî by severing it from its historical roots. Emphasizing that Jineolojî is grounded in the experience of the struggle of the Kurdish Women’s Freedom Movement, the board called for the accumulated knowledge and experience to be brought together and further developed through a strategic perspective.

title: I giovani lo sanno.
content:
Oltre 40 città si sono mobilitate nella giornata di sciopero studentesco di venerdì 16 ottobre. Il tema è chiaro: contro la guerra e contro chi vuole mandarci in guerra. Una guerra che si traduce in crisi sociale e impoverimento a tutti i livelli, la scuola è uno di questi. 




Torino, Padova, Bologna, Roma, Cosenza, Campobasso sono solo alcune delle città che hanno visto decine di migliaia di studenti e studentesse manifestare insieme. La Polizia ha risposto con cariche a Bologna e con idranti e lacrimogeni a Torino nel tentativo di reprimere le proteste. Nei giorni scorsi si è scatenata un’ offensiva poliziesca contro le scuole in occupazione senza precedenti, con arresti e fermi all’interno degli istituti scolastici.




La chiarezza riguarda anche gli intenti: non ci potrà essere qualcun altro a decidere al posto dei giovani. Chi oggi è sceso in piazza, uscendo dalla propria scuola occupata, dai licei ai tecnici, ha vissuto passaggi epocali in questa fase storica. Prima una pandemia globale, poi la guerra sempre più vicina. Chiusura di prospettive e assenza di futuro, non solo dal punto di vista della valorizzazione delle proprie capacità ma di un futuro 

sostenibile

, nel più profondo senso del termine. Se va così è perché l’assenza di senso complessivo è totale, a partire dalle proprie aule scolastiche. A partire da ben prima dell’istruzione media superiore la perdita completa di un obiettivo comune, del perché si è lì ogni giorno su banchi sporchi e tra quattro mura scrostate, del motivo per il quale bisognerebbe stare a sentire qualcuno che a sua volta – molto spesso e non in tutti i casi – non sa perché si trovi lì, è un processo devastante. Non c’è nessun bisogno che qualcun altro, tendenzialmente adulto e incline a contribuire al fallimento generale, dica come è meglio fare. O come bisogna stare. 




Un mondo mediatizzato e ipercollegato permette di vedere che in Francia i ragazzi e le ragazze si sentono esattamente nello stesso modo. Permette un collegamento profondo tra chi si riconosce su delle istanze che hanno un significato politico intrinseco. Distruggere perché non c’è niente di riformabile. Ma anche riconquistare uno spazio in cui esserci, sentirsi collettività, imporsi, nella gioia e nella rabbia. 




Il ruolo del mediatico è evidentemente ambivalente e la narrazione dei giornali ha immediatamente assunto un piano banale e becero ossia la caccia “all’incappucciato” che non sarebbe studente (eppure giovane lo è) e che si infiltra nelle scuole o nei cortei per essere “violento”. Fioccano gli inviti di dirigenti (perché la scuola è un’azienda) a isolare i violenti, a tenere fuori gli esterni e a gestire gli infiltrati, il tutto con il supporto delle forze dell’ordine. Eppure, al di là dei titoli e di qualche video sensazionalistico, quel che si è visto oggi nelle piazze in tutta Italia è una gioventù che insieme ha partecipato a cortei con numeri e determinazione significativi. Si è visto la presenza di docenti e personale scolastico solidale. Si è visto che il rifiuto della divisione razzista portata dall’alto non passa tramite il buonismo moralista di sinistra ma dall’essere insieme con un sentire comune. 




Sarebbe inutile lanciarsi in immagini evocative che vogliono romanticizzare una realtà che invece porta con sé le sue contraddizioni. Ma la realtà è fatta di dati: una mobilitazione a macchia d’olio si sta diffondendo, scuole che mai avevano occupato prima d’ora oppure che lo avevano fatto per la prima volta con il Blocchiamo Tutto dell’autunno scorso lo hanno rifatto, l’insofferenza si traduce in moto collettivo. Non è poco in un tempo di frammentarietà e individualismo. Non è poco quando il governo italiano si trova a dover affrontare una crisi probabilmente recessiva nell’arco di pochi mesi, non è poco quando anche altri settori sociali decidono di mobilitarsi, come gli autotrasportatori e gli agricoltori. 




La coperta è corta e per capire che con i rapporti di forza è possibile anche vincere il passo è breve.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Chuck Schumer Hasn’t Said a Word About Trump’s Attempt to Deport Ilhan Omar
content:
Ethics lawyers say the raid violated the Hatch Act. The Democratic Senate minority leader has been silent.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Days after the Trump administration’s unprecedented raid of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-Minnesota) house just weeks before the midterm elections, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-New York) has not once publicly defended the progressive Democrat against the naked political prosecution.

The Democratic leader — one of the most powerful in the country — has not issued statements to the press or through his social media channels about the Homeland Security Investigations raid on Monday, nor has he done any media appearances to comment on the issue, which critics have described as a five alarm fire for the state of democracy in the U.S.

This is despite the fact that the Trump administration is waging an inter-agency effort to denaturalize and deport Omar, as reports have uncovered this week. The timing of the raid is also unprecedented, coming just 22 days before the midterm elections in which Omar is on the ballot; these elections should be of grave import to Schumer, since they’ll determine whether or not Democrats will have the power to follow through on their pledges to hold Donald Trump accountable for his escalating fascist authoritarianism.

Other top Democrats have spoken out in defense of Omar — but even those statements have been muted in relation to the magnitude of the attacks.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) and other House Democratic leaders issued a short statement following the raid that called it “deeply disturbing” and said that it “raises serious questions” about the Trump administration’s “weaponization of the federal government.”

The only mention of consequences in the statement, however, is a promise that the Democrats “will deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power from the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice.” There is no mention of what that “accountability” would entail.

Jeffries also addressed the issue in an interview on MS NOW about the elections. Throughout the 11-minute interview, Jeffries doesn’t bring up the attacks on Omar once — until he’s asked about them at the very end. In that answer, he simply says that the Department of Justice (DOJ) “is going to be held accountable” and rattles off a list of other people that Trump has tried to prosecute, including Republican Federal Reserve Governor Jerome Powell.

The Democratic Party has also been relatively mum. Chair Ken Martin’s statement about the raid was short, simply calling it a “new low for the Trump administration.”

By contrast, it was shorter than the post about the raid by far right former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, who said that she and Omar are “far apart” on beliefs but called the raid a distraction from real issues like gas and health insurance prices: “People are so sick and tired of the bullshit,” Greene said.

This is despite the fact that Democrats have many avenues to defend Omar. The Washington Post reported on Thursday that Trump administration officials had already tried to search Omar’s immigration records for evidence to take away her citizenship in 2019, but found insufficient evidence to mount a full investigation.

None of the top Democrats’ statements named Trump’s attacks on Omar as openly racist and Islamophobic, despite Trump having called Omar and other Somalis “garbage” for years. Meanwhile, a group of prominent ethics lawyers have said that they believe the actions of the DOJ and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) were actually illegal. The lawyers, including former counsels to the White House, said that the raid was a violation of the Hatch Act because of its timing in relation to the election.

“DOJ and DHS’s decision to instigate this raid at this very moment and for these alleged reasons is unexplainable — except for as a politically motivated use of power to influence the Minnesota congressional election in violation of the Hatch Act,” the lawyers wrote.

Critics say that Schumer’s silence may be explained by the simple fact that he does not ally himself with Omar, despite sharing a party with her. Omar is a vocal critic of Israel; Schumer is a vehement supporter of the genocidal state. In 2019, when Omar criticized the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC — one of the most powerful groups in Washington for decades — Schumer and then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-California) piled on to Omar, forcing her to apologize and smearing her as an antisemite.

“Schumer’s silence is hardly surprising,” wrote Jeet Heer for The Nation. “Because Omar has been outspoken in her criticism of Israel and the Israel lobby, establishment Democrats such as Schumer have often kept their distance from her.”

This and Omar’s other progressive viewpoints may also explain the relative media silence about the attacks. Media critic Adam Johnson compared legacy media’s coverage of the Omar raid to Trump’s raid on conservative John Bolton, which spawned an explosion of scathing columns and opinion pieces. By contrast, Johnson noted, the raid of Omar’s home has scarcely prompted any op-eds or columns in the legacy corporate media — only an Atlantic article that argued for both sides.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Chris Walker
title: HHS Demands Answers From Orgs Over Support for Youth Gender-Affirming Care
content:
Studies have demonstrated that gender-affirming care for transgender young people can be life-saving treatment.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) sent letters this week to multiple medical organizations, demanding they provide the department with a “clear, current statement” on their positions regarding gender-affirming care for transgender youth.

The organizations in question have expressed support for such care, with many noting that gender-affirming care is based on years of study and careful implementation.

Conversely, HHS framed the letters using non-medical terminology, asking the groups to “answer” for their support of so-called “sex-rejecting procedures for minors.”

The letters from HHS have been sent to the Endocrine Society, the American Psychiatric Association, the American Medical Association, the American Psychological Association, Columbia University trans health expert Asa Radix, and American Academy of Pediatrics CEO Mark Del Monte.

“HHS has asked these organizations for clear answers about their current positions, the evidence supporting their guidance, and whether they intend to change it,” HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in announcing the letters.

In a press release explaining why the letters were sent out, HHS stated it also wants “identification of any planned revisions to their respective guidance, and a timeline for those changes.” The department is giving the organizations 10 business days to respond.

Past statements from some of these organizations note that health care for transgender individuals — including trans children and teenagers — is beneficial, and that denial of such care when it’s warranted is harmful.

“We recognize health as a basic human right for every person, regardless of gender identity or sexual orientation,” reads a statement from the American Psychiatric Association published in 2021. “For gender-diverse individuals, including children and adolescents, this means access to gender-affirming care that is part of comprehensive primary care.”

“Physicians must be able to practice medicine that is informed by their years of medical education, training, experience, and the available evidence, freely and without threat of punishment,” the organization added. “Patients and their physicians, not policymakers, should be the ones to make decisions together about what care is best for them.”

The American Medical Association made a similar statement that same year, writing that:

Physicians are guided by their ethical duty to act in the best interest of their patients and must tailor recommendations about specific interventions and the timing of those interventions to each patient’s unique circumstances. Such decisions must be sensitive to the child’s clinical situation, nurture the child’s short- and long-term development, and balance the need to preserve the child’s opportunity to make important life choices autonomously in the future.

Dozens of other medical organizations, beyond those that HHS sent letters to, have also affirmed the need to preserve gender-affirming care, including for young trans patients.

Gender-affirming care is life-saving for many transgender and/or nonbinary individuals, including for young people. An observational study from late 2025, examining hundreds of trans patients between the ages of 12 and 20 from 2017-2024, found that suicidality rates for these patients dropped by 67 percent after they were given treatments that affirmed their gender identity.

Despite overwhelming evidence demonstrating the benefits of gender-affirming care, dozens of states across the U.S. have banned such treatment options for trans youth and young adults, often using misinformation to justify doing so.

President Donald Trump has also used blatantly false anti-trans talking points in an attempt to scare or anger people into backing Republicans in this year’s midterm elections. Meanwhile, some Democrats have also tried to appeal to voters by claiming they are skeptical of transgender rights, supporting, for example, unfounded bans on trans athletes, disallowing them to participate on teams corresponding to their correct genders.
