author: Admin101
title: Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense
content:
Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN) is excited to announce the publication of 

Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense

.




Drawing on organizing experiences of Black Rose/Rosa Negra members across the United States, this pamphlet explores how workers, neighbors, and communities are building collective resistance to ICE and defending their immigrant coworkers, classmates, and loved ones. By connecting struggles across workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods, the 

transversal organizing

 approach we prioritize builds solidarity across different sectors of society to confront the interconnected structures of domination that shape our lives.




You can find a downloadable PDF version of the pamphlet at the end of this text.







Two Years of Trump II: Immigrants in the Crosshairs, Resistance Under Attack




Upon returning to office, Donald Trump wasted little time fulfilling his white supremacist campaign pledge of “Mass Deportations Now.” Via a flurry of executive orders and congressional acts his administration reinstated the reviled “family separation” policy; directed virtually unlimited resources to stop a fictitious “invasion” of the country’s borders; and sought to end birthright citizenship. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents blitzed Los Angeles in June 2025 with spectacular raids, followed shortly by similar operations in dozens of cities across the country including New York City; Chicago, IL; New Orleans, LA; and Durham, NC. This “shock and awe” strategy culminated in Operation Metro Surge, a months-long invasion of the Minnesota Twin Cities that deported over 2,000 residents. 




Meanwhile, support for the deportation machine plummeted as collective action against it swelled. Everyday people covered their cars, lawns, and lips with the slogan “Abolish ICE;” as of July 2026, nearly 50% of US adults support such a measure. Both May Days since Trump’s second inauguration centered immigrant defense in their celebrations. Rapid-response networks that keep watch for ICE, document kidnappings, and sometimes disrupt them spread wildly. Know-your-rights training flourished at worksites and community centers. Millions of Red Cards–wallet-sized cards outlining the holder’s constitutional protections around interactions with ICE and other police–were distributed at schools, churches, restaurants, and municipal buildings. Children and their parents caged in concentration camps went on hunger strike as constituents bombarded politicians’ hotlines and town halls demanding humanitarian treatment and release outside their walls.




Popular responses in St. Paul and Minneapolis demonstrate the possibilities of mass resistance. Like the Los Angeles Tenant Union’s community defense centers that countered ICE’s Southern California invasion, organizers reactivated dormant neighborhood networks from the 2020 uprising and began building new ones when word spread that Commander-at-Large Greg Bovino was bringing his paramilitary forces to town. Once Operation Metro Surge launched, everyday Minnesotans refined sophisticated systems to track, delay, and disrupt arrests. ICE agents retaliated by killing rapid-responder Renée Good and shooting Julio C. Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan immigrant targeted for deportation. Instead of cowering from the naked clampdown, neighborhood networks coordinated with unions, churches, and other civil societal organizations to shut down their cities on January 23rd. In its wake, Trump ousted Bovino and immigration enforcement plummeted.




But July 2026 saw record high immigrant detentions since Trump’s return to office with little public opposition. What explains it? ICE’s tactical shifts undoubtedly played a role. Bovino replacement and “Border Czar” Tom Homan traded provocative street operations with quiet detainers at jails and prisons and “targeted operations” at sites protected from activist impediment like airports. Escalating repression has also raised the costs of resistance. ICE’s bevy of brutality has included intimidation, beatings, and shootings, culminating in murdering Good and rapid-responder Alex Pretti. Federal grand juries fish from the shadows for information about our movements, stoking fears of informants that slow our organizing. From the Prairieland defendants to the Minnesota 15 and more, indictments and convictions on flimsy charges could make prosecuting dissidents even easier. Evidentiary discovery in the Minnesota 15 case has even revealed how the Department of Homeland Security subpoenaed thousands of records from the local AFL-CIO, other unions, veterans organizations, and liberal non-profits to chill community defense. Although shootings by ICE agents still spark spontaneous protests, these momentary outbursts remain largely contained to their immediate locales.




In short, mass resistance briefly but seriously disrupted the administration’s campaign of ethnic cleansing that forced strategic shifts to cut its losses. How can we adapt to these changing conditions and renew blows to the state, its borders, and the machinery that upholds them?




Immigrant Defense as Transversal Struggle




Members of Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation have fiercely organized defense of our immigrant coworkers, neighbors, and classmates over the last several years. We have facilitated mass assemblies and built neighborhood councils to keep ICE out of the California Bay Area. In Austin, TX, we’ve brought workers and tenants together to fight for wages stolen from immigrant workers. Public school educators in Durham and Chicago forged ICE watches to protect themselves, their students, and their students’ caregivers. Healthcare workers even won added protections at their workplace that helped free patients from unlawful deportations.




We approach immigrant defense as a “transversal issue.” Pioneered by Chilean feminists to confront femicide in all its subtle and overt sexist manifestations, transversal issues span the sectors where we organize—the sites and actors of struggle we prepare to supplant bourgeois-statist institutions with our own mass organizations. Our movements come together at these intersections to wage a frontal assault on the structures of domination that run our lives.




Thus, we do not organize “immigrants” as a category of struggle unto itself. Especially in the wake of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrival (DACA), such framing has extended limited, primarily legal protections to “deserving” groups of immigrants while withholding them from “undeserving” ones. Instead, we defend our immigrant coworkers, neighbors, and classmates as one step in a broader fight for greater control of our workplaces, our communities, and our schools. 




This sectoral perspective critically allows us to cut across the multiple sources of domination immigrants face while concretely attending to their specific needs. Rooted mass organizations that enable immigrant self-determination, rather than solely relying on narrowly focused campaigns, organizations, and formations, can better maintain defense initiatives while empowering people to sustain and expand struggle across all sectors of the lives of dominated classes. 




Based on our own and related experiences defending immigrant coworkers and community members in the articles linked below, we share some lessons and strategic directions to get our movements off the ropes and keep them fighting back around this pivotal transversal issue.




1.

 

Defensive initiatives can spark movements; offensive campaigns can sustain them.




Righteous, reactive defensive efforts mobilized thousands to take on ICE. Take Northern California: organizers throughout the region grew neighborhood-based rapid-response networks, foot and car patrols, and more to prepare for ICE deployments. To their surprise, sustained preparation successfully thwarted a planned insurgency in October 2025. But without confrontational raids, it has been less readily useful and the wide pool of activated residents largely demobilized.




Conversely, offensive campaigns that sprouted from defensive initiatives have won measurable gains and sustained momentum. Shan in Durham, NC explains how collective bargaining by educators renewed protections for immigrant students and staff amidst Operation Charlotte’s Web. Morgan’s union colleagues in healthcare similarly seized protective policies from their hospital administrators that when paired with legal support freed a patient from an unlawful ICE detention. To be certain, these organizers will admit these victories are modest. Confronting the routine operations of ICE lay the groundwork for consistent, widespread participation.




2.

 

Cultural “herd immunity” alone will not protect us through repression. We must foster movement structures and practices that can widely inoculate against it.




Organizers tried to prepare activated participants for the realities of repression. For example, rapid-response, legal observer, and other direct-action training often explores some of the risks that participants should anticipate, and know-your-rights literature circulates widely. Repression has  undoubtedly chilled organizing, though. Outbursts to ICE’s murders of Good and Pretti were relatively short-lived. Mobilizations since the Prairieland verdicts have largely stalled, and rapid-response networks have slowed their vigilance.




Relying on a “herd immunity” of cultural diffusion that grows individual tolerance to withstand repression is not enough. As the state strategically mutates to repress our movements, we must build infrastructure that can inoculate against intimidation as well as fight off coordinated governmental attacks. Decentralized, federated defense committees that become bases for continued revolutionary activity point to how we might go beyond narrow, reactive vessels for legal support. Like with immigrant defense, we must tie together mass organizations in our workplaces, neighborhoods, schools, and sites of confinement into the social antibodies that can take on repression as the transversal plague it is.




3.

 

We must continue going beyond non-profits. In the short-term, though, we are unlikely to go completely without them.




In many urban centers, non-profit organizations dedicated to immigrant defense have played a limited but notable role against ICE. Across the country, the National Day Laborer Organizing Network (NDLON) published how-to guides and led training on “adopting corners” to watch for ICE while the Immigrant Legal Resource Center (ILRC) has distributed more than 10 million Red Cards since Trump’s reelection. Similar organizations have also affected on-the-ground initiatives. Overstretched immigrant support nonprofits in Austin, TX shepherded wage disputes to a budding solidarity network. Siembra NC in Durham similarly supported educators and parents of students to assemble ICE watches at schools. In Northern California, a network of liberal nonprofits mobilized hundreds of people to stop ICE from setting up a base of operations at a local Navy station. 




This diverges from their modus operandi since the social service boom in the 1970s, wherein nonprofits have been an effective counterinsurgent cudgel against social movements for liberation. But federal criminalization, popular discontent, and radical rhetoric have pushed many of these institutions to take a more confrontational posture than previous eras. We should acknowledge that opening for collaboration, drawing on the resources and networks they may be able to provide budding movements. Even if we don’t embrace their participation, at minimum we must brace for their interventions. If we are to build robust, independent movements, militants must prevent these law-fearing organizations from corralling discontent into tried-and-true avenues for demobilization and disorganization like election campaigning and deference to liberal leadership.




4.

 

Broaden and connect the struggle against immigration enforcement to policing more generally.




Immigration enforcement is both a mechanism for reasserting white supremacy and policing the working class in the United States and across its borders. For decades, Black residents, workers, and students have led struggles against the expanding carceral state, from confrontations with police to opposing jail construction and prison expansion. These arenas of struggle are one in the same, and yet the lessons from and relationships between these movements remain largely underdeveloped.




As more and more people are pushed into deportation proceedings by police arrests and custodial transfers, rooted social movements and mass organizations need to take on local police departments and county sheriffs. Every time a “false alarm” mistakenly identifies a different agency deploying into our communities as ICE is an opportunity to learn how to document, disrupt, and disorganize policing operations. Moreover, taking on policing and winning protections against a specific form of policing can encroach against all 

forms of it, as Heather in Chicago and Morgan in Northern California highlight. Making links between all-too-often disparate transversal struggles mutually expands their scopes and consolidates a pole of opposition to the central way the state is reasserting its might in our authoritarian era.




5.

 

Keep rooting movement democracy in independent, durable, and nimble mass organizations we can pivot on shifting terrain.




Defending one another is not solely about the correct tactical techniques or strategic steps. Defined at the broadest level, collective self-defense invites shared participation in our self-emancipation. In all of the cases below, you will read how rank-and-file workers and everyday neighbors collectively identified unique needs among their immigrant neighbors, coworkers, patients, and students, and devised plans to fulfill them. They dedicated lots of time, attention, and effort to make their struggles and victories possible; in some cases, these initiatives grew from organizing that stretches back years. 




Rather than a particular organization or even network of organizations working on our behalf, we can grow self-confidence, initiative, and popular power when we directly act around transversal issues like immigrant defense through our own organizations. Durable mass organizations like the labor unions, neighborhood assemblies, rapid-response teams, and solidarity networks create containers to learn from our defeats, build on our victories, and navigate shifting terrains of struggle towards a world where we can freely move and live.






















Download Pamphlet













If you enjoyed this article, we recommend reading our previous writing from which these lessons were distilled, such as: 

How Everyday Organizing Stopped Trump’s Bay Area ICE Surge

; 

“A Dense Web of Solidarity”: Chicago Public School Workers Defend Students Against ICE and the Feds

; and 

Healthcare Workers Freed a Patient from ICE – You Can Do the Same




The post 

Sanctuary as a Verb: Experiences and Directions from Transversal Organizing for Immigrant Defense

 appeared first on 

Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation

.

author: Francis Annagu
title: Nigeria has not decided how to regulate Chinese businesses. Who will decide?
content:
In mid-September 2026, traders in the auto spare parts section of the Lagos International Trade Fair Complex 

protested against Chinese traders who sell directly to customers

. One protester 

said

 the Chinese had ‘built warehouses, rented shops and are now selling as we do as retailers.’ Police called the protesters 

‘a few miscreants’

.




Nigeria already has rules for foreign businesses. But the government has not said what it wants from Chinese businesses, or who will carry out the policy. In the two weeks after the protest, the police, a market board, a minister’s aide and a governor all spoke. None said whether the rules will change. Mining shows the same gap. In both, a policy question is being handled as a policing problem.




Competition over one supply chain




Retailer John Chidebere 

told Premium Times

 that goods from China take two to three months to arrive and leave him little profit. Meanwhile, 

Chinese businesses can sell directly

 to local customers at wholesale prices. Nigeria imported 

N11.01 trillion

 of goods from China in the first half of 2026, nearly 40 per cent of its imports, according to National Bureau of Statistics data. 

SBM Intelligence

 says the trade deficit is ‘substantially a symptom of Nigeria’s broader industrial and macroeconomic environment, not a cause in itself.’ Commentator 

Martin Beck Nworah

 said: ‘once the wholesaler becomes the middleman, the retailer is edged out.’ So this is a fight inside one supply chain, not only Nigerians against Chinese competitors.




Protesters rally outdoors in Nigeria, October 2020




What the traders are asking for




Newsclick

 reported placards reading ‘The Chinese must go.’ But Chief Osigwe told Premium Times that Chinese traders should leave the market and trade elsewhere, 

not leave Nigeria

. Trader Clement Ebere said: ‘I’m not saying the Chinese should leave, but it should be negotiated.’ The association’s president, 

Nnamdi Ngozi Emechebe

, said asking the Chinese to leave Nigeria was not an option. 

Some of the Chinese wholesalers

 approached by Premium Times declined to comment. So the slogan and the demand did not match. The traders want Chinese businesses out of retail, not out of Nigeria.




The law allows it




A 

BusinessDay legal explainer

 says the Nigerian Investment Promotion Commission (NIPC) Act lets foreigners invest in most businesses. 

The Act’s short list of banned areas

 covers arms and ammunition, narcotic drugs, and military and paramilitary clothing, plus anything the Federal Executive Council adds. Retail is not on it. Foreigners still need visas, 

business permits and expatriate quotas

. So the legal question is whether these businesses have the right permits. The political question is bigger: does Nigeria want foreign companies in retail at all?




The 

Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise

 and a 

Daily Trust editorial

 of 2 October both ask for the rules on foreign retailers to be reviewed. Neither asks for a ban. The rules exist. What is missing is a decision on whether to change them.




Institutions have spoken, but no decision taken




Police Area Commander ACP Chike Oti said the protesters had 

been cautioned

 and arrests would follow, but 

no arrest had been reported

 in the coverage I found. Veronica Ndanusa, who heads the 

Lagos International Trade Fair Complex Management Board

, a body under the Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment, 

told traders to stay calm

 and said foreign investors who 

follow the law

 would be protected.




Ms Ndanusa spoke about investors, not about whether foreigners should be in retail. I found no public statement on that question, or on the protest, from the Nigerian Investment Promotion Commission, the trade ministry itself, or the Lagos State Government. The nearest Lagos voice was the governor’s new-media aide, Jubril Gawat, 

sharing a video of a police officer

 speaking about arrests.




Political comments filled the gap. Lere Olayinka, an aide to FCT Minister Nyesom Wike, 

mocked the protesters on X

. Abia Governor Alex Otti, on 29 September, said Igbo traders were 

‘moving from the market to manufacturing’

. Actor 

Joseph Okechukwu

 claimed the federal government brought Chinese people in to destroy Igbo businesses. The report quoting him gave no evidence.




The same gap in mining




Local gold miners at work in Kano State, Nigeria, August 2022.




On 3 September 2026, Premium Times reported that Niger State’s commissioner had asked 

four Chinese nationals at Maiya’aki

, in Lapai, to show their mining licences. They could not, and were arrested. Under the Minerals and Mining Act 2007, small-scale titles go only to Nigerian citizens, Nigerian companies or mining cooperatives, 

administered by a federal office

.




In Nasarawa State, the lines blur. In June 2024, leaders of Amba and Agwada 

said their communities were fully behind two Chinese companies

 and knew of no consent given to the firm TIMADIX. In December 2024, TIMADIX 

said state officials had unlawfully licensed Chinese nationals

 on the same site. The state commissioner replied that TIMADIX itself was operating illegally. After arrests on 16 May 2026, federal Mining Marshals of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) 

took 15 Chinese nationals and nine Nigerians to court

, reported on 1 June 2026, over alleged illegal mining on a site 

licensed to TIMADIX

.




In an interview reported on 20 September, Niger State Governor Umaru Bago told Channels Television he was 

‘in between the devil and the Red Sea’

. He said: ‘I cannot just go and order the police or military to start shooting people or arresting people.’ He asked for an executive order from the Presidency or the minerals ministry ‘to ban mining in certain locations’. Federal enforcement in his state is also under scrutiny. Thirty-seven suspected miners 

died in NSCDC custody on 17 September

. Survivors told 

Reuters

 the cell was overcrowded and guards sprayed an unidentified substance. Reuters could not independently verify this.




Official numbers differ too. In May, Minister of Solid Minerals Dele Alake gave 

327 arrests and 142 prosecutions

. The Mining Marshals’ commander, Attah Onoja, gave 

671 arrests and 397 charges

 in July, then 

over 600 and over 500

 in September.




The link between Chinese mining and violence is disputed. In February 2026, five Republican US lawmakers, including Riley Moore and Chris Smith, introduced a bill on religious freedom in Nigeria. As 

Premium Times reported

, it says Chinese nationals in illegal mining pay ‘protection money to Fulani militias’. 

SBM Intelligence and WikkiTimes

 had earlier reported Chinese-linked miners paying armed groups for access to sites. The Chinese embassy called the claims 

‘completely baseless’

. Separately, the NGO 

Renevlyn Development Initiative

 published Silent Conquest on 11 December 2025, linking Chinese mining to insecurity. The 

China Mining Federation of Nigeria

 called it ‘false, misleading and unsupported by evidence’. A 

Blueprint commentary

 says blaming Chinese firms oversimplifies a problem rooted in weak regulation.




Where are the politicians?




Senator Adams Oshiomhole has said some military generals are 

backing Chinese nationals

 in illegal mining, but named no one. Minister Alake has also accused politically connected people, but a 

2024 investigation

 reported he had not named or arrested anyone. This article names no politician as part of Chinese mining operations, because I found no published evidence for that claim.




Nigeria must choose




Nigeria can allow foreign retailers to trade, regulate them, limit them or ban them. The government must decide, say so openly, and hear traders, importers and Chinese business owners. Kenya has made its choice: 

President William Ruto ordered

 foreign nationals to stop running small retail shops and hawking from 7 September 2026, saying such trade should be reserved for Kenyans. In mining, Nigeria needs one agency in charge, public court results, and public records of who holds each licence and for how long. Until the authorities say what the rules are, and who has been arrested and why, rumours will fill the gap between answers and policy.




The post 

Nigeria has not decided how to regulate Chinese businesses. Who will decide?

 appeared first on 

African Arguments

.

author: Mag
title: Automatisierung in der Logistikbranche am Beispiel Amazon
content:
Dossier




„

Forscher der TU Berlin haben mit ihrem Roboter die „Picking Challenge“ des Onlinehändlers Amazon gewonnen. Was der Wettbewerb für die Zukunft des Online-Riesen und seine Angestellten bedeutet

. 

(…) Mit dem Wettbewerb verfolgt der Online-Händler ein ganz konkretes Ziel: Die möglichst vollständige Automatisierung seiner Logistik. Will Amazon mit der steigenden Zahl der Bestellungen und den wachsenden Anforderungen der Kunden mithalten, muss es die Abläufe in den Logistikzentren effizienter machen. Noch verfeinert der Konzern dazu vor allem das Einlagerungssystem und optimiert den Einsatz der Mitarbeiter – so weit, dass sich manche von ihnen schon als „Roboter“ fühlen

…“ 

Artikel von Andreas Menn und Stephan Happel vom 29. Mai 2015 in der Wirtschaftswoche online

 

 („Amazon: Roboter verändern die Zukunft des Onlinehandels“). Siehe dazu:







Indien, USA und Großbritannien…: Amazons Investitionen in die KI-Infrastruktur kosten massiven Stellenabbau und bei der Unfallquote den Mythos der „sicheren Automatisierung“ 







Amazon gegen seine Beschäftigten: Sieben internationale Konflikte zwischen Streiks, Gewerkschaftsbildung und Entlassungen




„

Der multinationale Konzern Amazon sieht sich mit sieben Arbeitskonflikten konfrontiert, die zeigen, wie seine Belegschaften versuchen, sich angesichts von Produktionsrhythmen, Untervergabe, mangelnder Anerkennung der Gewerkschaften und Entlassungen zu organisieren. In Italien hat eine neue Streikwelle begonnen; in den USA kommt es zu Arbeitsniederlegungen und Gewerkschaftskampagnen; in Deutschland und Großbritannien dauern langwierige Arbeitskämpfe an; und ein weiterer Personalabbau betrifft die USA, Indien und Großbritannien. Es handelt sich um unterschiedliche Konflikte mit unterschiedlichen Zeitpunkten, Forderungen und Situationen, die jedoch alle mit demselben Unternehmen in Verbindung stehen. (…)




USA, Indien und Großbritannien: eine weitere Entlassungswelle




Amazon bestätigte am 7. Oktober weitere Stellenstreichungen, vor allem in seiner Sparte „Stores“, die für einen Großteil des Online-Einzelhandelsgeschäfts verantwortlich ist. Nach Angaben von Reuters betrifft die Maßnahme weniger als 1.000 Verwaltungsstellen und betrifft Mitarbeiter in den USA, Indien und Großbritannien, unter anderem in den Bereichen Kundenservice und Dienstleistungen für Verkäufer. Die Stellenkürzungen folgen auf einen weitaus umfangreicheren Abbau von rund 30.000 Stellen, der im Jahr 2025 begann und bis Januar 2026 andauerte. Amazon führt die Veränderungen auf eine Neuorganisation seiner Teams und Prioritäten zurück. Die Betroffenen müssen mit dem Verlust ihres Arbeitsplatzes rechnen, während der Konzern einen Teil seiner Geschäftstätigkeit weiter umstrukturiert. Die Zahl von 30.000 bezieht sich auf die vorherige Entlassungsrunde und darf nicht so addiert werden, als wären all diese Entlassungen diese Woche angekündigt worden

…“ span. 

Beitrag vom 13. Oktober 2026 der Redaktion von Sindicalismo.org

 

 mit Ausführungen zu Italien, USA, Deutschland, Großbritannien (maschinenübersetzt)




Amazon veranstaltete in derselben Woche einen Ausverkauf und verschickte E-Mails über Entlassungen




„

Am 7. Oktober startete Amazons „Great Indian Festival“ für Prime-Mitglieder, während Mitarbeiter im Einzelhandel per E-Mail darüber informiert wurden, dass ihre Stellen gestrichen wurden. Amazon hat zu Beginn der großen Verkaufsaktionen weniger als 1.000 Stellen im Einzelhandel in Indien, den USA und Großbritannien abgebaut.




Was wirklich hinter den Kulissen vor sich geht




Das Unternehmen verband die Entlassungen mit Investitionen in die KI-Infrastruktur und behandelte beides als routinemäßige Umstrukturierungsmaßnahmen.




Das Fazit




Amazon führte die Verkaufsaktion und den Stellenabbau im selben Zeitraum durch, da beides mittlerweile lediglich operative Maßnahmen sind. (…)




Zeile für Zeile übersetzt:




– Im weiteren Sinne: weniger als 1.000 Arbeitsplätze im Einzelhandelsgeschäft in Indien, den USA und Großbritannien.


– Umstrukturierung: Betroffen waren der Kundenservice, verkaufsbezogene Bereiche, der Marktplatz-Support und die Entwicklungsteams.


– Neugestaltung der Teams: Die neue Struktur umfasst weniger Stellen.


– Aktuelle Prioritäten: Rund 220 Milliarden US-Dollar sind für Rechenzentren, Chips und die dazugehörige Infrastruktur vorgesehen

….“ engl. 

Beitrag vom 11. October 2026 von und bei The Corporate Joker

 

 (maschinenübersetzt)




„

1) Die Unfallquote in den Amazon-Lagern ist doppelt so hoch wie der Branchenstandard. Roboter und Automatisierung sollten das eigentlich ändern – haben es aber nicht getan.




2) Untersuchungen von @united4respect.bsky.social 

zeigen, dass Robotikanlagen zwar nur 13,5 % der Amazon-Fulfillment-Center ausmachen, jedoch 31 % der Fälle schwerer Verletzungen auf sie entfallen.




3) Die Arbeiter bewegen sich immer schneller, um mit ihren Roboter-„Kollegen“ Schritt zu halten – bis ihr Körper nicht mehr mitmacht.




4) Die einfacheren Aufgaben werden oft den Robotern übertragen, während Menschen die schwierigeren Bewegungen ausführen, die mit einem höheren Verletzungsrisiko verbunden sind.




5) Die Beschäftigten äußern diese Bedenken schon seit Jahren. Würde Amazon ihnen Gehör schenken, könnte das Unternehmen verhindern, dass Tausende von Menschen lebensverändernde Verletzungen davontragen

.“ engl. 

Post von Athena Coalition vom 13.10.2026 auf bsky

 




„

Aktuelle Erkenntnisse widerlegen den Mythos der sicheren Automatisierung bei Amazon. Wirst du dich während der Amazon Prime Days an die Seite der Beschäftigten stellen und dich für eine faire Zukunft und Technologien einsetzen, die FÜR die Mitarbeiter arbeiten und nicht gegen sie? Unterzeichne die „Tech for Respect“-Erklärung

!“ engl. 

Post von United for Respect vom 06.10.2026 auf bsky

 

 zu:





„Tech for Respect“-Verpflichtungserklärung




„

Angesichts des immer schnelleren Wandels am Arbeitsplatz durch künstliche Intelligenz ist es JETZT an der Zeit, die Rahmenbedingungen für eine gerechte Umgestaltung von Niedriglohnarbeit festzulegen.


Um eine mutige, von den Arbeitnehmern getragene Vision von Sicherheit, Würde und Gerechtigkeit in der KI-Wirtschaft voranzubringen:


–    Die Arbeitnehmer müssen ein maßgebliches Mitspracherecht dabei haben, wie KI am Arbeitsplatz gestaltet und eingesetzt wird.


–    KI sollte die Arbeit sicherer, einfacher und humaner machen – und nicht die Ausbeutung verschärfen oder die Rechenschaftspflicht außer Kraft setzen.


–    Die Arbeitnehmer haben ein Recht auf vollständige Transparenz darüber, wie KI-Systeme eingesetzt werden, um sie zu bewerten, zu überwachen und zu steuern.


–    Menschen sollten bei Entscheidungen am Arbeitsplatz stets eine zentrale Rolle spielen.


–    Die Privatsphäre der Arbeitnehmer*innen sollte geschützt werden, und sie sollten wissen, wie ihre personenbezogenen Daten am Arbeitsplatz erhoben und genutzt werden.


–    Invasive Überwachung, die Arbeitnehmer*innen auf unfaire Weise verfolgt und kontrolliert, muss verboten werden.


–    Menschliche Verbundenheit und Mitgefühl sollten weiterhin im Mittelpunkt unserer Arbeit und unserer Arbeitsplätze stehen.


„Tech for Respect“ bringt Arbeitnehmer und Aktivisten zusammen, um sich für arbeitnehmerorientierte Lösungen einzusetzen, während unsere Wirtschaft mit großen Schritten ins Zeitalter der KI vorstößt.


Unterzeichnen Sie noch heute die „Tech for Respect“-Erklärung und gestalten Sie gemeinsam mit uns eine Zukunft, in der jeder Arbeitnehmer sicher ist, respektiert wird und selbstbestimmt handeln kann

.“  engl. 

Erklärung von United for Respect

 

 zum Mitzeichnen (maschinenübersetzt)










Siehe auch das Dossier: 

[Nicht nur in USA] Amazons LagerarbeiterInnen wesentlich häufiger und schwerer verletzt – von Stress und Hitze nicht abgesehen










Nach 21 Jahren: Amazon schließt „Mechanical Turk“ – betroffen wohl weltweit Hunderttausende Clickworker




„

Auf „Mechanical Turk“ kann man Menschen dafür bezahlen, dass sie beispielsweise massenhaft Fotos klassifizieren. Nach mehr als zwei Jahrzehnten ist nun Schluss.




Nach fast 21 Jahren schließt Amazon die Plattform „Mechanical Turk“, auf der Menschen für Arbeiten bezahlt werden konnten, mit denen Computer lange überfordert waren oder für die Algorithmen zu lange brauchten. Das hat der US-Konzern 

auf der zugehörigen Internetseite

 

 publik gemacht. Dort heißt es, dass der Dienst am 30. September endgültig geschlossen wird. Als Begründung wird lediglich darauf verwiesen, dass Programme, Werkzeuge und Dienste regelmäßig überprüft würden, um „Anpassungen“ vorzunehmen. CNBC zitiert eine Expertin mit der Einschätzung, dass sich der Dienst schon lange im Niedergang befunden hat, zuletzt vor dem Hintergrund der zunehmenden Leistungsfähigkeit von KI-Modellen. Seit Juli wurden keine Neukunden mehr akzeptiert. (…)




Zwischenzeitlich haben mehr als 500.000 Menschen auf MTurk ihre Dienste angeboten, 

schreibt CNBC

 

. Je mehr Aufgaben dann doch KI-Modelle übernehmen konnten, desto weniger Ressourcen habe Amazon in die Weiterentwicklung gesteckt. In der Folge seien viele zu anderen Plattformen gewechselt, die ähnliche Dienste anbieten. Trotzdem gebe es noch immer Menschen, die in Vollzeit ihr Geld auf „Mechanical Turk“ verdienen, zitiert CNBC die Expertin: „Die machen sich jetzt Sorgen

.“ 

Artikel von Martin Holland vom 26.08.2026 in heise news

 

 („Nach 21 Jahren: Amazon schließt „Mechanical Turk““)







Griff nach mehr Kontrolle: Amazon schaltet Mechanical Turk ab




„

Datenarbeit: Nach 21 Jahren wird die Plattform Amazon Mechanical Turk eingestellt. Das heißt nicht, dass die menschliche Arbeit hinter der KI überflüssig wird (…)


Auf einen kurzen Dank für die »Mitgestaltung der Crowdsourcing-Welt« folgte die Aufforderung, die eigenen Zahlungsdaten bis zum Stichtag zu aktualisieren, da Auszahlungen nur noch bis Ende Oktober abgewickelt würden. Ein Statement von Amazon-Chef Jeff Bezos gibt es bislang nicht.


Die Abwicklung der größten Plattform für Datenarbeit und für menschliche Evaluierung von KI-Systemen trifft Hunderttausende Datenarbeiter in aller Welt, die trotz der schlechten Arbeitsbedingungen beinahe vollständig von Amazon Mechanical Turk abhängig sind. Der Missstand der Scheinselbständigkeit war wohlbekannt, wurde aber aufgrund der globalen Struktur der Plattform zugunsten der Auftraggeber toleriert, denen dadurch weitreichende Kontrolle über die Höhe und Auszahlung der Vergütung zukam. Camilla Salim Wagner, Forscherin beim Distributed AI Research Institute, berichtete vergangene Woche auf Nachfrage von junge Welt, dass sich die Datenarbeiter nicht nur Erfahrung, sondern auch Nutzerprofile erarbeitet haben, wobei »gute Quoten oft Zugang zu besser bezahlten Tasks ermöglichten«. »Wenn hier jetzt die Accounts geschlossen werden, müssen das viele der Arbeiterinnen und Arbeiter von null neu aufbauen«, sagte sie. Das zerschlage außerdem die Netzwerke und gegenseitigen Hilfsangebote der Beschäftigten. Da viele von ihnen auf andere Crowdsourcing-Plattformen umsiedeln werden, drohe sich die »Überausbeutung von Amazon Mechanical Turk zu wiederholen oder gar zu verschärfen«. (…)


Angesichts dieses Wettlaufs ist die Schließung von Amazon Mechanical Turk keine rein betriebliche Anpassung an das von Amazon verheißene Wunschdenken, dass KI-Modelle menschliche Datenarbeit bereits überflüssig gemacht hätten. Vielmehr ist es ein Versuch, partielle Kontrolle über den Datenmarkt zu erlangen. »Als Amazon Mechanical Turk eingeführt wurde, wurde es zwar als Produkt angeboten, war jedoch in erster Linie für Amazon konzipiert«, sagte Krystal Kaufmann, eine ehemalige Aktivistin bei Turkopticon, gegenüber jW. »So haben die Datenarbeiterinnen und -arbeiter neben den anonymen Anfragen besonders doppelte Einträge auf amazon.com bereinigt und Bilder beschriftet, die für die Entwicklung von ›intelligenten Produkten‹ wie Alexa verwendet wurden«.


Nach Kaufmanns Einschätzung ist der ausschlaggebende Grund für die Schließung, dass Amazon »den Dienstleister einfach nicht mehr benötigt« und der Konkurrenz, die ihrerseits auf der Plattform Aufträge vergeben hat, den Zugang zu qualitativ hochwertigen erschweren will. Und: Amazon hat Alternativen. Amazon Mechanical Turk werde zwar eingestellt, aber der Konzern bleibe über Dienste wie AWS Data Exchange, ein Marktplatz für Datensätze von Drittanbietern, und die Amazon Marketing Cloud in zentrale Infrastrukturen des Datenökosystems eingebunden. Hinzu komme, so Kaufmann, dass sich die Anforderungen an die Datenarbeit in den letzten Jahren »über die einfache Kennzeichnung hinaus« zu einer »immer weitreichenderen Spezialisierung« der Arbeiter entwickelt habe, was die Kosten für die Arbeitskraft erhöht hat. Wegen der nun noch umfassenderen Kontrolle könnte Amazon seine Dienste dabei überproportional verteuert anbieten

…“ 

Artikel von Laurenz Sachenbacher in der jungen Welt vom 29.09.2026

 










Ausbeutung bei Amazon: Flexibel in die Armut 


„

Neue Formen der Tagelöhnerei: Unter dem Vorwand der Modernisierung und Digitalisierung der Arbeitswelt treibt Amazon den Abbau der Rechte von Beschäftigten voran




Seit den 1990er Jahren lagern viele große Unternehmen wachsende Teile ihrer Arbeit an Fremdunternehmen mit geringeren Lohnkosten aus, was als »Outsourcing« bekannt ist. Amazon spitzte diese verstärkte Form der Ausbeutung weiter zu und verlagerte Teile seiner Entwicklungskosten online an einen Schwarm (»Crowdsourcing«) von Subunternehmen in Niedriglohnländern, selbstausbeuterische Startup-Unternehmen und selbst an freiwillige, völlig unbezahlte private Internetnutzer. Das gelang Amazon mit einer Plattform namens »Mechanical Turk« (M-Turk). Diese wurde als Entwicklungsplattform zur Abarbeitung von »Human Intelligence Tasks« (HITs, Programmieraufgaben) Ende 2005 ins Leben gerufen und erfreute sich innerhalb kürzester Zeit einer rasch ansteigenden Beachtung in der Entwicklerszene.¹ Mit Hilfe von künstlicher Intelligenz erledigen nicht etwa Maschinen die Aufgaben von Menschen, sondern Menschen arbeiten ihnen von Computern gestellte Aufgaben ab.² Amazon führte so eine digitale Tagelöhnerei ein und kombinierte finsterste Arbeitsbedingungen mit elektronischer Komplettüberwachung. Amazon verkauft online Mikrojobs für Cent-Beträge. Das bedeutet Arbeit auf Zuruf, für Hungerlohn, auf eigenes Risiko und ohne jegliche soziale Absicherung. Einen großen Teil seiner digitalen Tagelöhner, die sich selbst als »Turker« bezeichnen, setzt Amazon in der Eigenwerbung und Marktmanipulation ein (…) Neben der digitalen kehrte mit Amazon »Flex« auch die altbekannte Tagelöhnerei im Bereich der Paketdienste zurück. Die miesen Arbeitsverhältnisse werden von der Unternehmerseite als »Gig-Economy« beschönigt (…) Die Vermarktung dieser Scheinselbständigkeit als Flexibilität

⁵

 verschleiert, dass ihre Freiheit vor allem eine Freiheit von Absicherungen ist, die in regulären Beschäftigungsverhältnissen erkämpft und gesetzlich verankert worden sind: Kündigungsschutz, gesetzlicher Urlaub, Beiträge der Unternehmerseite zu Sozial- und Krankenversicherungen usw. Auch fallen den Lieferpartnerinnen und Lieferpartnern jede Menge Kosten an. (…) Anders verläuft die Prekarisierung der Arbeit über die Amazon-Lagerhäuser. Die überwältigende Mehrheit der rund 840.000 direkt bei Amazon beschäftigten Arbeiterinnen und Arbeiter übt eine schablonenhafte, monotone Tätigkeit aus und erhält die niedrigsten gesetzlich zulässigen sozialen Sicherheiten. Sie haben oftmals keinen Kündigungsschutz, entgrenzte Arbeitszeiten, extrem prekäre Bedingungen am Arbeitsplatz und keinerlei Betriebsräte oder gewerkschaftliche Mitbestimmung. (…) Bei den extrem prekären Stundenlöhnen und den immer wieder geschilderten verheerenden Arbeitsbedingungen sollen freie Getränke (Wasser, Kaffee, Tee) und erfolgsabhängige Prämien locken. Die Prämien im Falle »entsprechender Zielerreichung« bedeuten nichts anderes als Akkordarbeit. (…)Angriffe auf die psychische Gesundheit der Arbeiterinnen und Arbeiter und die Untergrabung ihrer gewerkschaftlichen Betätigung gehören zu den Grundlagen des Erfolgs und zum Kern der Strategie von Amazon. Seine Logistikzentren baut Amazon gezielt an Orten mit überdurchschnittlicher Arbeitslosigkeit, um so den Druck auf die Beschäftigten zu erhöhen. Kolleginnen und Kollegen berichten außerdem von einem Klima der Denunziation und der totalen Überwachung

…“ 

Ausschnitt des Dossiers von Niklas Hoves als Vorabdruck in der jungen Welt vom 21.12.2020

 







Siehe das Dossier: 

Internationaler ethecon Awards 2020: Dead Planet Award an Amazon – digitale Schmähung von Jeffrey Bezos am 21.11.2020










Kiva, Fetch und Freight. Die Automatisierung in der Logistikbranche schreitet voran. Es geht um Lagerkapazitäten, Kosteneffizienz – und die Zukunft von Beschäftigten


„

Amazon ist immer wieder wegen des Arbeitskampfes der Gewerkschaft ver.di um einen besseren Tarifvertrag in den Schlagzeilen. Auch die Arbeitsbedingungen beim Versandhändler sind oft ein Thema. Der Konzern ist allerdings auch, das hängt durchaus damit zusammen, wegen seiner Politik der Kostensenkung durch Automatisierung bekannt. Das klappt nicht immer und überall so, wie Amazon sich das wünscht. Aber die Entwicklung ist unaufhaltsam, welche Folgen das für die Beschäftigten hat, wird man sehen müssen

…“ 

Artikel von Vincent Körner vom 30.05.2015 in Neues Deutschalnd online

 

. Aus dem Text: „… 

Der Konzern sagt, es sei bisher kein Mitarbeiter wegen des Einsatzes von Robotern entlassen worden – die komplizierten Aufgaben könnten die maschinellen Kollegen nicht. Noch nicht, wie man mit Blick auf die »Picking Challenge« und Neuentwicklungen wie Fetch und Freight sagen könnte. In der Branche werde geschätzt, dass Roboter potenziell 25.000 menschliche Beschäftigte ersetzen könnten

…“










Sie nennen es Freizeit




„Vor zehn Jahren hat Amazon mit seiner Plattform Mechanical Turk eine neue Dynamik der Ausbeutung eingeleitet. Organisierter Widerstand kommt erst allmählich ins Rollen

…“ 

Artikel von Thomas Wagner in junge Welt vom 26.05.2015

 

. Aus dem Text: „… 

Der weltweit agierende Versandhandelskonzern stellte 2005 eine ganz besondere Website ins Netz. Sie heißt Mechanical Turk und sollte Amazon beim Handel mit CDs unterstützen. Da die damaligen Computer noch nicht in der Lage waren, die Produktangaben hinreichend effizient zu überprüfen, wurde menschliche Arbeitskraft als »Artificial Artificial Intelligence« (künstliche künstliche Intelligenz) eingesetzt. Daraus entwickelte sich eine Arbeitsplattform für solche Kleinjobs, sogenannte Human Intelligence Tasks (HIT), die nicht von Rechnern übernommen werden können. Die auf der mittlerweile etablierten Plattformen wie Mechanical Turk oder Clickworker vollzogene Art von Arbeitsvermittlung wird als Crowdsourcing bezeichnet. Arbeiter, die auf diese Weise ihren Lebensunterhalt bestreiten, nennen sich selbst Turker. Allein bei Amazon sollen es heute 500.000 Menschen aus 190 Ländern sein. Wer die angebotenen Microtasks übernimmt, löscht Pornofotos aus Bilddatenbanken, tippt Visitenkarten ab, testet Internetseiten oder übernimmt überschaubare Programmieraufgaben

…“




Crowdwork: Wie sich Klickarbeiter organisieren




„

Die Amazon-Plattform „Mechanical Turk“ ist das prominenteste Beispiel für Crowdwork. Das einzige ist es nicht. Auch in Deutschland verdienen Hunderttausende ihr Geld auf Plattformen im Netz. Ein Buch bringt jetzt die Debatte voran

…“ 

Artikel von Jeannette Goddar im Magazin Mitbestimmung Ausgabe 12/2014 der HBS

 







Siehe auch:

CrowdworkerInnen-Partizipation auf Crowdsourcing-Plattformen: eine Bestandsaufnahme




Clickworker, vereinigt euch. Die Arbeitswelt wird digital, viele erhoffen sich durch die neuen Technologien mehr Wachstum und Wohlstand. Doch sie gefährden die soziale Sicherheit







Der Beitrag 

Automatisierung in der Logistikbranche am Beispiel Amazon

 erschien zuerst auf

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: "Against Tech Oligarchy": Inside the Worker Resistance in the World's Most Powerful Industry
content:
Longtime tech worker organizers Clarissa Redwine and JS Tan’s new book, 

Against Tech Oligarchy: Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry

, draws on the authors’ experiences at major tech companies to chronicle the rise and fall of the tech worker movement, its early victories, and the repression and slide to corporate control that followed.




“Over the course of the 2010s, what we saw was that the tech industry wasn’t quite the industry that it had promised to its workers and to the public. Rather than making the world more open, more democratic, we saw it really be the culprit of misinformation,” says Tan, who was pushed out of Microsoft after raising objections to the company’s ties to fossil fuel companies.




Silicon Valley’s slide to the right was influenced by corporate backlash to labor’s demands, explains Redwine, who was fired from Kickstarter for union organizing. She says she hopes to inspire a new generation of tech workers to organize “within these tech oligarchs’ own empires, to stand up and push back.”

author: anred
title: «¡Son infiltrados!»: acusar y deslegitimar la autodefensa popular
content:
Imagen: Germán Romeo Pena (@germanromeopena)




Cada vez que una movilización responde a la represión con piedras, barricadas o acciones de resistencia, reaparece una explicación que parece resolverlo todo: «son infiltrados». No puede haber una respuesta automática: la presencia de agentes policiales de civil en las protestas es una realidad documentada, pero no alcanza para explicar todas las acciones de resistencia. Detrás de esa simplificación queda una pregunta: ¿por qué cuesta tanto reconocer que también hay sectores populares dispuestos a enfrentar la violencia estatal? 

Por ANRed.







La escena se repite. Una movilización multitudinaria reclama por sus derechos. La policía avanza con gases, balas de goma, golpes y detenciones. Un grupo de manifestantes responde con piedras, intenta levantar barricadas o enfrenta el avance de las fuerzas represivas. Inmediatamente, aparece la explicación: «son infiltrados, no son de los nuestros», como aseguró C5N toda la tarde y repitieron otros medios. La sospecha puede tener fundamento en determinadas circunstancias. Los servicios de inteligencia y las fuerzas de seguridad han utilizado históricamente agentes de civil y mecanismos de infiltración para vigilar, perseguir y desarticular organizaciones populares.




Imagen: Germán Romeo Pena (@germanromeopena).




 




El problema comienza cuando la hipótesis se convierte en una certeza sin pruebas y se aplica automáticamente a cualquier manifestación de resistencia. Es necesario no quedar atrapados entre dos explicaciones excluyentes: que toda acción violenta es una operación policial o que cualquier forma de resistencia debe reivindicarse sin discusión. Existe una tercera posibilidad que suele quedar fuera del debate: que haya militantes y manifestantes que decidan actuar por cuenta propia frente a una represión que consideran intolerable o, en este caso, el avance de la entrega total con medidas tales como el DNU 70/23, como se vio con grupos que también de forma colectiva y coordinada actuaban para ahogar los gases lanzados, en medio de una masiva protesta que mezcló el reclamo en defensa por la educación pública universitaria con el reclamo contra el desfinanciamiento en discapacidad y el abandono de las familias endeudadas, y las banderas por la soberanía de Malvinas, con banderas argentinas, palestinas y whipalas.




Guido Piotrkowski, fotógrafo de Página/12, registró cómo le apuntaban directo y tiraban desde la PFA. Le dieron en el pecho, y a un colega que estaba con él en las piernas. El país en el que Javier Milei asegura que «no odiamos demasiado a los periodistas».




La historia desmiente las explicaciones fáciles. Uno de los ejemplos más contundentes que recupera Pablo Solana es la Masacre de Avellaneda del 26 de junio de 2002, cuando en medio de una brutal represión, la Policía Bonaerense asesinó a Darío Santillán y Maximiliano Kosteki. Durante la resistencia popular hubo piedrazos contra la policía, barricadas, vehículos incendiados y otros hechos de enfrentamiento. En su reconstrucción de aquellos acontecimientos, Solana explica que, aunque se documentó la participación de policías de civil y de un expolicía que actuó como parapolicial, la investigación no encontró que las fuerzas de seguridad hubieran provocado la mayoría de los destrozos atribuidos a los manifestantes.




Choque entre organizaciones piqueteras y fuerzas policiales bonaerenses, el día de la Masacre de Avellaneda, el 26 de junio de 2002. Foto: Enrique Cabrera (Télam).




La diferencia es fundamental: comprobar que había agentes de civil no significa demostrar que cada acción de resistencia era una provocación. En aquel caso, la experiencia de investigación sobre los crímenes de Darío y Maxi llevó a una conclusión distinta de la que algunos sectores habían sostenido inicialmente: buena parte de los enfrentamientos había sido protagonizada por militantes que resistían el avance represivo.




Solana también recupera otros momentos de la historia argentina en los que la confrontación callejera fue parte de procesos de lucha popular. El Cordobazo de 1969, con barricadas y enfrentamientos que desbordaron la capacidad represiva de la dictadura de Onganía, es uno de ellos.




Imagen de la resistencia popular durante el Cordobazo.




También las jornadas de diciembre de 2001, cuando las protestas, los saqueos, las barricadas y los enfrentamientos acompañaron la caída del gobierno de Fernando de la Rúa.




20 de diciembre de 2001 en Buenos Aires.




Otro antecedente son las movilizaciones de diciembre de 2017 contra la reforma previsional impulsada por Mauricio Macri, que quedaron asociadas a las imágenes de las piedras arrojadas frente al Congreso.




La Policía de la Ciudad recibe una lluvia de piedras como respuesta popular a su accionar represivo en la protesta contra la reforma previsional de 2017 de Mauricio Macri.




En esos episodios, reducir toda acción de confrontación a una maniobra de los servicios de inteligencia habría impedido comprender la dimensión de los conflictos y la disposición de sectores sociales a desafiar el orden establecido, lo cual no significa que todas las acciones fueran iguales ni que sus consecuencias deban idealizarse.







Invitamos a leer las notas de Solana sobre el tema publicadas en ANRed:




Molotovs en el Congreso: la tercera hipótesis







Derecho a la rebelión







Punto de inflexión: 10 reflexiones sobre el 12M para planificar las resistencias que vendrán







Violencia ultraderechista y reacción popular: ¿Ninguna agresión sin respuesta?

author: Daron Letts
title: Esthetician prepares for New York Fashion Week
content:
Odette Wills wasn’t allowed to wear makeup as a teenager.




Now, the 26-year-old Iqaluit esthetician is preparing to work as a makeup artist backstage at New York Fashion Week, from Feb. 12 to 14.




“I still think I have a long way to go,” Wills said during an interview in her new home-based Authentic Glow Studio which opened in May, the product of a New Year’s resolution.




Wills travelled to New York City for a week in September, where she completed a course at Aimakeup Beauty Academy in Westside Manhattan’s Chelsea neighbourhood and 

befriended Instagram influencer Ipek.




“Odette is very talented,” said Aiyma, the school’s founder who goes by one name, in a phone interview Tuesday.




New York Fashion Week, held in February and September every year, features fashion industry shows throughout Manhattan and marks the debut of many international labels.




In the fall, Aiyma’s students (not including Wills) provided makeup for models working with brand labels such as Geo in Style, F&W and Amari Carter, among others. 

In December, Wills will learn what brands she will be working with, Aiyma said.
















After the course ended, Wills returned north with buoyed confidence, a suitcase packed with new supplies and a plan for expanding her business.




She has added exfoliating, cleansing, and non-medical facial massage to her studio’s services.




As her wait list grows, she said, so will she. She’s planning to take a manicure certification course next.

title: 20th Year of the Kurdish Conference releases final resolution
content:
The 20th conference was held on 14–15 October at the European Parliament in Brussels, organized by the European Union Turkey Civic Commission (EUTCC) in cooperation with The Left Group, the Greens/European Free Alliance (Greens/EFA), and the Progressive Alliance of Socialists and Democrats (S&D).




The final resolution, titled 

20 Years of EUTCC Conferences – 20 Demands for Peace and Democracy

, reads as follows:




"The Annual International Conference on the EU, Turkey, the Middle East and the Kurds, hosted by the EU Turkey Civic Commission (EUTCC) in cooperation with the Left Group, the Greens-European Free Alliance (GREENS/EFA) and the Progressive Alliance of Socialists and Democrats (S&D), was successfully held on 14th and 15th of October 2026 in the European Parliament in Brussels.




The 20th EUTCC Conference looks back on two decades of continuous work for democracy, human rights, the rule of law, a peaceful resolution of the Kurdish question and a European future for Türkiye. Founded in 2004 to provide critical monitoring of Turkey’s EU accession process, the EUTCC’s mission remains as relevant as ever twenty years on.




The conference notes that Turkey continues to face a fundamental democratic choice. At the same time, the current process aimed at ending the armed conflict and finding a political solution to the Kurdish question presents a historic opportunity. Abdullah Öcalan’s statement of February 2025, the subsequent developments surrounding the dissolution of the PKK and the call for a democratic society have opened up a new perspective. 




The EUTCC therefore calls on the European Union, its Member States, the Council of Europe and the Turkish institutions to implement the following 20 steps:




1.  Peace through political dialogue: The peace process must continue on a democratic and legally secure basis.




2.  An end to the isolation on Imralı: Unrestricted access to Abdullah Öcalan must be guaranteed.




3.  Freedom for Abdullah Öcalan: Abdullah Öcalan must be granted his fundamental political, legal and communication rights without delay. His free participation in the peace process is of central importance to its success.




4.  Implementation of the ECtHR judgments: Türkiye must implement all relevant judgments of the European Court of Human Rights fully and without delay, including the right to hope. 




5.  Removal of the PKK from the EU’s list of terrorist organisations: In order to strengthen a sustainable peace process, the European Union should review the inclusion of the PKK on ist list of terrorist organisations and remove the organisation from the list.




6.  Legal foundations for the peace process: The Turkish Government and Parliament must immediately establish the legal and constitutional conditions necessary for a lasting political solution.




7.  Release of political prisoners: All individuals who have been persecuted and imprisoned for carrying out political, journalistic or human rights activities must be released.




8.  Protection of democratic parties: The right to political organisation and parliamentary representation must be guaranteed. Parties must not be forced out of the political arena through bans, criminal proceedings or administrative measures.




9.  End to state-appointed trustees: Democratically elected mayors must be able to carry out their duties freely. The systematic appointment of state-appointed trustees must be brought to an end.




10. Strengthening the rule of law: The independence of the judiciary, fair trials, the separation of powers, and the independence of public prosecutors’ offices and courts must be restored.




11.  Democratic constitutional reform: Türkiye needs a new democratic social contract that guarantees the equality of all citizens, the plurality of society, and the political, cultural and linguistic rights of all population groups.




12.  Kurds as citizens with equal rights: Kurdish identity, language and culture must be fully recognised and protected. A lasting solution to the Kurdish question can only be based on equality.




13.  Women as agents of peace: Women must be involved on an equal footing at all levels of the peace and democratisation process. The conference particularly recognises the central role of Kurdish women in the region’s democratic and peace movements.




14.  Protection of civil society and the media: Journalists, academics, human rights defenders and civil society organisations must be able to work free from state repression.




15.  End to cross-border military presence: Türkiye must end its military presence in Syria, as well as in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, and fully respect international law.




16.  A democratic solution for Syria: The European Union should support a political process that recognises and safeguards pluralism and the participation of all sections of the population in Syria’s future political order.




17.  Recognising the Kurds as political actors: The EU and its Member States must involve the Kurds and their political representatives as legitimate actors in the search for peace and stability in the Middle East.




18.  A new European policy on Türkiye: The EU must not prioritise strategic interests – such as migration, trade, security or energy – over democracy and human rights. Relations with Türkiye must be conditional on tangible progress in the rule of law, human rights and democratic participation.




19.  Keeping the European perspective open: The EUTCC reaffirms its fundamental support for a democratic European future for Türkiye. A credible EU perspective remains an important lever for reform, peace and democratisation.




20.  European support for peace and democracy: To mark its 20th anniversary, the EUTCC calls on the European Union and the Council of Europe to support a comprehensive international initiative for peace, democracy and the rule of law in Türkiye and the Middle East.




20 years of the EUTCC – a commitment to the future




The conviction with which the EUTCC was founded twenty years ago has lost none of its significance. Today’s historic situation offers a new opportunity: decades of conflict can give way to a process of peace and democratic transformation. This requires political courage in Türkiye and an active, credible and principled European Union.




The 20th EUTCC Conference therefore calls on all democratic forces in Turkey, Europe and the Middle East to seize this historic opportunity together.




Peace requires dialogue. Democracy requires freedom."

title: Hasakah tensions: Are Kurds and Arabs being drawn into conflict?
content:
Rising tensions in Hasakah (Hesekê) in the first days of October 2026 have once again raised concerns about the future of Rojava. Clashes between security forces and protesters were reported in the city on 9 October, with several Kurdish youths reportedly injured. Around the same time, pro-government Arab demonstrators held protests against the Kurdish administration, while counter-protests followed attacks on Kurdish symbols.




The Governor of Hasakah blamed the incidents on groups opposed to the integration agreement. However, this statement does not mean that all those involved in the incidents, or their motives, have been conclusively identified.




To view these developments simply as a dispute that has arisen naturally between Arabs and Kurds would be to overlook their political dimensions.




Hasakah is a strategic city where Kurds, Arabs, Syriacs and other communities live together, and where the future of security and administrative structures is being debated. A large-scale conflict here might not remain confined to a single neighbourhood or city. It could directly affect Rojava's political future, relations between its peoples and the integration process with the Damascus administration.




The central issue, therefore, is not to deny the genuine problems that exist between communities, but to question who is exploiting these problems, under what political circumstances and for what purposes.




1. Why do Kurds face a new challenge whenever their political status is discussed?




Kurds in Syria faced serious discrimination concerning their identity, language and citizenship rights for many years under Ba'ath rule. The weakening of central authority following the outbreak of the civil war in 2011 created opportunities for new forms of political and social organisation to emerge under Kurdish leadership in North and East Syria.




During the struggle against ISIS, the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) became one of the international coalition's key local partners. Throughout this period, Kurds gained significant experience not only in military affairs but also in governance, women's participation in social life and the establishment of local institutions.




However, transforming the administrative authority established on the ground into a permanent political status guaranteed by the constitution has proved far more difficult.




The integration process between Damascus and the SDF in 2026 has therefore become a decisive stage. The process concerns not only the incorporation of armed forces into state institutions but also fundamental issues such as the powers of local administrations, security structures, language rights and the management of resources. Disagreements over these matters have heightened concerns within Kurdish society that the gains achieved could be lost.




The historical contradiction is clear: while the role played by Kurds in the struggle against ISIS has gained international recognition, how the political and social gains resulting from that struggle will be protected remains unresolved.




The Kurdish demand is not simply for recognition of their past struggle. The central issue is securing a political order in which they can continue to exist with their own language, identity and democratic institutions.




2. The historical background of Turkey's Rojava policy




 To understand Turkey's approach to Rojava, it is not enough to examine the issue solely through current statements concerning security. 




Ankara maintains that the Kurdish-led armed groups in northern Syria are linked to the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) and opposes their establishment as a permanent military and political force along its border. This approach has long been a defining element of Turkey's policy towards Syria. Turkey's military interventions and policies aimed at shaping local balances of power have also been guided by this position.




 However, the issue has broader implications for Kurds. 




The Kurdish question in Turkey and the issue of Kurdish political status in Syria are not legally identical. Nevertheless, developments in the two countries can influence one another. Progress towards peace and a democratic solution in Turkey cannot be considered independently of discussions concerning the future of Kurds in Syria. This creates a significant contradiction: on the one hand, there are efforts to end armed conflict and seek a political solution; on the other, there are serious disagreements over the future of the Kurdish political and military presence in Rojava. 




This contradiction creates the risk that Kurdish demands for political status will be overshadowed by regional security calculations. 




Nevertheless, concrete evidence would be needed to claim that every incident in Hasakah was planned by Turkey or that every escalation occurred on Ankara's direct orders. The convergence of political interests is not the same as the organisation of a particular incident. 




The strength of the analysis lies precisely here: it is possible to question the interests of political actors without presenting unproven allegations as established facts.




3. The ENKS question: Who benefits from divisions in Kurdish politics?




 The Kurdish National Council in Syria (ENKS) is one of the political actors in Rojava and holds political positions that differ from those of the SDF and the Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria. 




The ENKS leadership has openly stated that a federal system in Syria is among its preferred models for guaranteeing Kurdish rights. It would therefore be inaccurate to describe ENKS as an organisation entirely opposed to Kurdish political status, as this would not adequately reflect its current political positions. 




Nevertheless, it should not be overlooked that competition between Kurdish political movements creates opportunities for external actors to exert influence. 




The fundamental question is this: Will differences between Kurdish political actors develop into democratic competition based on shared rights and constitutional guarantees, or will they become a means of undermining one another? 




The fact that a political organisation holds talks with Ankara, Damascus or another regional power does not, in itself, make it a puppet. Such an assessment must consider the circumstances under which it makes decisions, the policies it supports and whether its actions ultimately serve to strengthen or weaken the collective rights of Kurds. 




Kurdish political unity does not mean that all parties must share the same views. However, different political movements must not allow Kurdish rights to language, identity, representation and local self-government to become bargaining chips. 




Any party that places its own political interests above those of the people should be criticised, regardless of the political tradition from which it comes.




4. Who benefits if Arabs and Kurds are turned against each other?




 One of Rojava's most important social realities is its multi-ethnic character. Different communities, particularly Kurds and Arabs, have legitimate demands concerning security, the economy and governance. 




The existence of these demands is not, in itself, a cause of conflict. The real danger lies in turning problems with public services, disagreements over local administration, security concerns and questions of identity into ethnic confrontation. It would be just as wrong to regard all Arab communities in Hasakah as supporters of the Damascus administration or any external power as it would be to identify all Kurds with a single political or military organisation. Nevertheless, the possibility that social sensitivities could be exploited for political purposes must be taken seriously.




 For example, blaming an entire community before those responsible for a security incident have been identified, spreading calls for retaliation or inciting mass anger over symbols could turn a local dispute into a large-scale conflict. 




Three consequences could emerge in such circumstances:




- Kurdish-Arab relations could be damaged. The experience of coexistence could give way to mutual distrust and social division.




- The political solution process could be weakened. Security concerns could be used to push local representation and administrative rights into the background.




- The scope for external intervention could expand. As social conflict deepens, different powers could find new opportunities to pursue their own interests. These consequences do not require all parties to have reached an agreement beforehand. A conflict can also escalate through the independent actions of different actors and their reactions to one another. The question, therefore, should not simply be, “Who started it?” Equally important are the questions: “Who benefits from escalating tensions, which institutions are being weakened, and which political demands are being pushed aside?”




5. The possibility of provocation: How can the motives behind an incident be understood? 




The possibility of provocation is an issue that must be investigated in relation to developments in Hasakah. However, examining the political consequences of an incident alone is not enough to determine whether it was a provocation.




 The fact that an incident serves a particular objective does not necessarily prove that it was planned with that objective in mind.




 Nevertheless, it is possible to examine the consequences of these developments. First, it is necessary to establish whether responsibility for a local incident has quickly been attributed to an entire community. Second, attention should be paid to who calls for the expansion of security powers, the dismantling of political institutions or the suspension of existing agreements in the aftermath of an incident. Third, verified information must be distinguished from allegations circulating on social media.




Statements have linked the tensions in Hasakah to groups opposed to the integration process. However, this alone does not prove that all the incidents were coordinated from a single centre or that a particular state was directly responsible. 




Even so, the political risk is clear: as tensions escalate, trust between the parties may diminish and the prospects for reaching an agreement may narrow. 




Preventing society from becoming vulnerable to provocation is therefore just as important as investigating the possibility of provocation itself.




6. Why is the prospect of Kurdish gains becoming a regional issue? 




The Kurdish pursuit of political status is not merely a debate about the model of governance in Rojava. The issue is directly linked to border security, the powers of the central state, the management of natural resources, international alliances and regional balances of power.




 The establishment of a permanent political status in Rojava could mean securing Kurdish rights through constitutional guarantees and protecting the powers of local administrations. This could also have significant implications for other Kurdish political movements in the region. 




However, military strength alone is not enough to make these gains permanent. Kurds must be able to manage political disagreements among themselves, establish democratic relations with Arabs and other communities, and defend their shared demands for rights in negotiations with international actors. Otherwise, internal divisions, alongside political and military pressure, could weaken their negotiating position. 




There is a historical lesson here: a people's struggle may coincide with the interests of international powers, but there is no guarantee that external support will continue in the same form when those interests change. Shifting balances of power in Syria and the progress of the integration process have once again demonstrated this reality. The future of Kurds will therefore be determined not only by what external actors want, but also by which rights Kurdish political actors recognise as shared and non-negotiable.




7. Is the solution another war or a shared political will?




 One of the greatest dangers facing Rojava is that political disagreements could turn into armed conflict and communities could be pitted against one another. Defending Kurdish rights does not require ignoring the legitimate demands of Arabs. Equally, defending Arab rights cannot serve as a justification for eliminating the historical identity, language and political representation of Kurds. A genuine solution requires the establishment of a political system that guarantees the rights of all communities. To achieve this:




- Kurdish rights to identity, language, political representation and local self-government must be constitutionally guaranteed.




- The political representation, security and economic rights of Arabs and other communities must also be protected.




- The terms of the integration process must be transparent, and uncertainties concerning the future of security institutions, the powers of local administrations and the distribution of resources must be resolved.




- The incidents in Hasakah must be investigated independently and transparently, and those responsible for attacks against civilians must be held accountable, regardless of who carried them out.




- Kurdish political actors must be able to act together to prevent the weakening of shared rights and prospects for a democratic solution, while maintaining their political differences. 




These are not merely political preferences, but necessary steps to prevent another social conflict. 




Conclusion: Rojava's future must not depend on turning communities against each other 




To view the events in Hasakah solely as a security issue would leave unanswered the broader questions shaping Rojava's future. Kurdish demands for political status are closely intertwined with questions about what kind of state Syria will become, how much influence local communities will have over their own futures and how regional powers will intervene in this process. 




Turkey's security policies towards Rojava, the Damascus administration's objective of re-establishing central authority, divisions among Kurdish political movements and the changing priorities of international powers must each be examined separately within this equation. Rather than assuming that individual actors control every development, it is necessary to identify where their interests converge and what consequences arise from that convergence.




 The real danger is that Kurds and Arabs will be turned into enemies and that this conflict will be used as a justification for eliminating Kurdish political status altogether, leaving no room for debate. Such an outcome would harm not only Kurds but all communities seeking to coexist in Rojava. 




Protecting Kurdish political gains depends not on deepening conflict with Arabs, but on strengthening a shared political will based on rights. Equally, lasting peace cannot be achieved through centralisation that disregards Kurdish identity and political demands.




 Rojava's future must not become a battleground where communities are incited against one another. Instead, it must be built on coexistence, with equal rights and democratic self-determination guaranteed for all. 




A people's future cannot be built upon the defeat of another people. And no political process can produce lasting peace by disregarding the will of the people.
