author: CNT Santander
title: Ni alquileres abusivos, ni sueldos de miseria
content:
La huelga es la mejor herramienta que tiene la clase trabajadora para conquistar derechos al sistema capitalista. Las mejoras laborales, las libertades y los avances sociales son fruto de la organización, la solidaridad y la lucha colectiva. Cuando nos unimos, tenemos la capacidad de detener la maquinaria que se alimenta de nuestro esfuerzo.




Desde CNT Santander nos unimos a la llamada del Sindicato de Inquilinas y el 11 de noviembre saldremos a la calle para reivindicar nuestros derechos como clase trabajadora.




Es por todo ello que:







Revindicamos un 

incremento salarial

 en todos los sectores, incluido el salario mínimo interprofesional, que nos permita poder asumir los costes de la vida sin sentir que nos ahogamos, sin incertidumbre ni pánico.




Necesitamos la 

reducción de la jornada laboral máxima

 a 30 horas semanales, sin merma salarial, de manera progresiva.




Lucharemos por 

un incremento de las pensiones públicas

, tanto contributivas como no contributivas.







La vivienda no es un lujo para especular, es un derecho innegociable que ha de ser respetado. Ninguna persona debería elegir entre pagar el alquiler, llenar la nevera y/o encender la calefacción este invierno. Ninguna familia debería vivir con miedo a perder su hogar mientras existen viviendas convertidas en mercancía para la especulación de los fondos buitre.




Exigimos una vivienda digna y asequible para todas las personas

, que se intervengan y regulen los precios, que no haya que destinar más del 30% a este fin, necesitamos que se ponga un límite a los alquileres abusivos que desestabilizan las economías familiares, la 

protección social frente a los desahucios

 y unas 

medidas directas y efectivas

 que pongan las necesidades humanas por delante del beneficio privado, sobre todo las de las personas más vulnerables.




Reclamamos una 

estabilidad en el empleo

 para no vivir con inseguridad, para poder tener planes de futuro y también una 

estabilidad en el arrendamiento de la vivienda

. Precisamos 

contratos de alquiler indefinidos

, no interrumpidos con la llegada del turismo masivo y acabar con la expulsión temporal.




¡A LA HUELGA GENERAL!

 se publicó primero en 

CNT Santander

.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: 2023 Operation Al-Aqsa Flood as resistance vs US-Israel
content:
“We cannot condemn the genocide in Palestine without also condemning the imperialist United States.”

Filipino activists remembered the Operation Al-Aqsa Flood three years ago as the day Palestinians amplified their stand against imperialism.

Led by the International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines, Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association (PPFA), and the Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan), activists marched on October 7 to the US Embassy to remember the historic operation against Israeli occupation after decades of Palestinian oppression.

Carrying the Palestinian flag and placards with images of slain journalists in Gaza, they marched along Kalaw Avenue in Ermita, Manila to condemn the Israeli attacks despite the ceasefire that supposedly took effect on October 10, 2025.

During the program, Amirah Lidasan, secretary-general of Moro Christian People’s Alliance and co-chairperson of Sandugo Movement of Moro and Indigenous Peoples for Self-Determination, said, “Gaza is not the land of another people. Gaza belongs to the Palestinians who are struggling.”

In 2025, US President Donald Trump introduced the Gaza peace plan, also known as the “Board of Peace,” which saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza. It also includes an agreement to end the war.

According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, Israeli attacks since the October 7, 2023 Operation Al-Aqsa Flood have killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children. The actual death toll may be higher, as official records rely on documented deaths and do not account for those still missing or buried under the rubble.

Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) Chairperson and former Bayan Muna Rep. Teddy Casiño highlighted the US role in Israel’s attacks on Palestine by continuing to provide unconditional financial and military support

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) rely heavily on imported arms from the US which accounts for 69 percent of Israel’s weapon imports from 2019-2023.

“We cannot condemn the genocide in Palestine without also condemning the imperialist United States. Not only has Israel committed genocide in Palestine, but the United States has also attached Venezuela, Iran and Yemen, and is now there is possibility to attack Cuba,” Casiño said.

On January 3, the United States abducted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his spouse, Cilia Flores, following months of US strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific that reportedly killed more than 100 people.

The Trump administration’s actions, which critics have condemned as violations of international law and Venezuela’s national sovereignty, reflect what the progressive groups describe as a longstanding pattern of US imperialism.

Despite the controversy surrounding the operation, the Trump administration insisted on its intention to “run the country,” further raising concerns over Venezuela’s sovereignty and the Venezuelan people’s right to self-determination.

Rev. Alan Sarte, secretary-general of the Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association stressed the determination of Palestinians to continue fighting for their freedom, calling on people around the world to oppose imperialism and defend national sovereignty.

“We will ensure that on the day of Donald Trump’s arrival, he is met by a massive protest from the Filipino people,” said Kilusang Mayo Uno Secretary-General Jerome Adonis. (AMU, DAA)

author: Oyunga Pala
title: When Baba Died: One Year Later
content:
Last October, two weeks before Baba died, I was returning to Nairobi after a two-year hiatus. The last time I was home was during the first-year memorial of my sister, Nyangi, who was now the prominent character in my book.




Home had changed in many ways, yet it had not, in a kind of same old but different way. The vibe was familiar, the actors younger, the pace faster. Roads once familiar were now dwarfed by high-rise towers sprouting around the city like wild mushrooms. The expressway from the airport straddling the city dominated the cityscape, a marker of a city in a hurry to grow up.




I used to wonder whether I would change. Would I be like the other diaspora Kenyans I had seen who lost all sense of belonging after just a few miserable winters abroad, and began to look down on their own? Stepping away seemed to have had the opposite effect on me.




This notion of belonging was immediately tested as I faced my former public self. When I announced that I had published a book and would be going on a book tour, the reception was warm. I was reminded of how big 

Mantalk

 was, the weekly national column in the Daily Nation that I laboured over for a decade and that has now become part of the country’s cultural landscape, a reference point to a bygone era, for many stuck in nostalgia. I was no longer the Mantalk guy. I had traveled far both within and without. I had grown up, but to many of my readers, I was still that guy, who showed up every Saturday, a mysterious figure who ruffled feathers. The man some female readers used to love to hate.




I had been part of several life journeys unwittingly. And like all fans of urban culture, I was a mascot for those bygone times. Yet here I was, older, perhaps wiser, certainly a lot humbler. I had just poured my soul into a book that detailed my own journey away from the glam and fame of the national spotlight and delved into trying not only to make sense of my unresolved grief but also the grief of a nation. The shift in persona was stark: From a young man who used to critique modern rules of chivalry to one sharing lessons on how to navigate the profound loss that follows the death of a loved one.




To reach these moments of connection, I first had to navigate the city itself. My first stop the night after my arrival was the Prestige Bookshop and Nairobi traffic- well, what has changed? The roads remained clogged, and nothing quite captures Nairobi’s class dynamics as the expressway, raised above, smooth and scenic, with arresting views of flashy high-rise buildings obscuring the reality of chaos that rules just underneath it, bottleneck traffic, matatu madness, and boda bodas that now make matatus appear quite tame. It became a metaphor in hindsight of how we process grief: stoic and contained on the surface, but underneath the facade, a bubbling volcano waiting to erupt.




I remember Prestige bookshop from another time, when the city centre was a little more serene, and Mama Ngina Street still had a taste of the bourgie back when 20th Century Plaza, the Hilton hotel and the International Life House were iconic landmarks in the city centre. Yvonne Adhiambo Owuor was launching her second novel, The DragonFly Sea, in the small bookshop. The shelves had been pushed to the side to create space for the fans, and I was the MC of the day, here to celebrate one of Kenya’s finest novelists. I looked at the bookshop now, wondering how we had pulled it off, for there seemed to be hardly any room to swing a cat.




When the people started to come through, I knew this was going to be special. Odd that despite 28 years of a public writing life, I had never signed an autograph. I remained struck that people would endure Nairobi traffic to meet over a book and demand my bad handwriting on their personal copies.




I didn’t know what to expect as a new world and role began to unfold for me. Lost connections revived. People I had gone to school with, names I hadn’t seen or heard from in years. Friends, family, acquaintances, total strangers, with entwined pasts and reminders of a time once spent in communion; between the firm handshakes and tight embraces, it took me a minute to realise what was happening.




I was being honoured and celebrated. When I went to Ukombozi Library to donate a copy of my book, I met Ogutu, who told me how the story of my father’s funeral process was also his story. At the United Kenya Club, I met Clifford Derrick, who had just buried his mother, and the book triggered his own spontaneous reflections on his moment of loss. At Nuria bookstore on Moi Avenue, I found my old schoolmate Omenge Nyamato, who was still grieving the recent loss of his mother, and he confessed my book would be a guide through grief that he was no longer interested in suppressing. I spoke to a man called Rollex, who pointed out that it was the death anniversary of his father and he wanted a particular chapter signed in dedication to his memory.




The collective sharing continued in Kisumu when I arrivedat the Text Book Centre at the United Mall. I met Sharon who told me that she had just gone through a season of loss, family members who had seemingly died in pairs, as if calling out to each other from the other side and it did not make sense until she found a page in 

Strength and Sorrow

 that precisely spoke to her unique grief. The next day in Kisumu I met a smart young man called Akal from Lolwe bookshop who filled a room with eager listeners, joining me in a conversation about death and funerary practices.




What had death taught us, and what was it continuing to teach us?




All the people I met had either recently gone through loss, were trying to make sense of a death from the past, or had come to the realisation of the inevitability of our mortality and were seeking the language to understand it. I realised that I was not just selling a book. I had opened the space for something deeper, through mere presence and perhaps holding a mirror to parts of themselves that they could not see or had forgotten existed.




In the various book stops I made, the meet-and-greets turned into spontaneous grief circles, and I found myself counseling strangers who found resonance in my reflections on loss. Together, we could broach pains that they were afraid to touch for fear of what would erupt.




I was here to hold space for people dealing with complicated and conflicted losses, the unresolved, the forgotten, and to share pathways for people looking back to fetch what had been lost. I was no longer that spirited young man who was grappling with the challenges of modern masculinity. Life had reconstructed me, and now I had returned almost in the mode of a death Douala.




Then, just as I concluded the book tour, this shared human inevitability was amplified on a national stage.




The second chapter of 

Strength and Sorrow,

 titled “Baba’s Gone,

”

 is dedicated to my own father.




The first line reads…




When Baba died, I became numb.




He had died of a heart attack….




Then, a national father figure, the one, the country fondly called Baba, the former Prime Minister of the Republic of Kenya and perhaps its most consequential leader, Raila Amolo Odinga, had died.




The same sinking feeling returned. I was numb.




As the phone calls started to come through, I recognized the emotion immediately.




It was…Shock!




My cousin described it precisely.




“I don’t know how I am feeling”.




I remember only ten days prior, sitting at the back of a boda, and just as I arrived at the city centre near the University Way, adjacent to the Uhuru Highway, I encountered a most unusual sight. A flight of bats had covered the sky above. I thought about this moment for a long time afterwards.




It seemed ominous. A bat is a creature that flies like a bird, active at night so its flight during the day is an anomaly. I immediately thought there must be some symbolic resonance to this sight. In esoteric traditions, the bat is a symbol of death and rebirth.




When I received the shocking news of the death of the Baba of the nation, Raila Odinga, I thought of those bats again and of the connections to the story of my father.




When Baba died, I became numb.




He died of a heart attack at eighty years of age. He collapsed in a modest clinic in Kerala India, one morning after his routine walk. They said his bodyguard and personal doctor tried to revive him with CPR and that his last-born daughter was there to hold him as he took his last breath. At my age, I had witnessed the passing of many national figures, but I’d never imagined that this one would feel so personal.




Baba had spent five decades as a political engineer, engineering a new vision for a better Kenya. He rose to the apex in his political career as the symbol of democratic reform and even though he was never elected president, he was the beloved people’s president. An elder statesman and a master bridge builder.




He first came to my attention as a political prisoner in the 80s, spending a total of 8 years in harsh detention conditions and surviving it to move out of his father’s shadow and build an illustrious career in political defiance, before becoming the ultimate pragmatist who always pulled the country from the brink with recurring political handshakes. His life was never quiet despite his advanced age and he continued to build, mentor, and raise the political consciousness of the nation.




He was the man everyone thought to call when the nation itself was burning.




Over the years, I had learnt how to see him as a man and not just as a political figure. He embodied the hopes of my generation, and he was the last of our second liberation heroes who remained relevant straight to our adulthood. Baba was a constant of our political reality, and for my parents’ generation who revered him, he stood like a lighthouse.




Baba was a complex character, and I didn’t always understand his political motivations. He broke my heart many times, but I never stopped admiring his ability to stay relevant and his impeccable sense of occasion. Baba embodied all our political disillusionment and hurts, our historical wounds of exclusion, the ethnic prejudice, and the elusive yearning for a just future.




Now, the biggest tree in the homestead had fallen, and the people were discombobulated.




When the news of Baba’s death arrived, I worried about how the country would react. He had died abroad, and the announcement came that Baba had to be buried in 72 hours. I had never felt such a seismic shift in the political atmosphere and my world was spinning, all I could see was darkness.




I knew my tears for Baba would come, and I braced for the tension of the wake. This was no time to be stoic, for our symbol of stoicism had breathed his last.




I watched the hysteria take over as his body arrived from India. Mourners overran the airport; unruly grief was on display, which degenerated into chaotic scenes at Kasarani Stadium, where the body was taken for a public viewing. I watched in dismay at the government’s irrational response of tear gassing and firing shots to contain overwhelmed mourners. It was heavy to bear.




The trigger-happy security forces, the ethnic profiling, the lack of empathy, and the denigration of the ordinary citizen’s grief.




I remember watching the next day as his body lay in state in Parliament, as the country’s political class got a chance to pay their last respects. I watched their faces, caught the performance, the bewilderment, the genuine grief that bared itself. He lay there, draped in an orange sash and black suit, an odd sight for a man remembered for his boundless energy. The ordinary people who truly loved him held nothing back when his remains were wheeled to Nyayo Stadium in Nairobi and later to Mamboleo Grounds in Kisumu. I thought about the millions watching it on livestream around the country and the world. We were all escorting Baba, united in our grief.




The country was steeped in pensive mourning in the days leading to his final interment in Bondo. That spirit combusted the moment the body arrived in Kisumu, where Baba was met with the deafening wailing of multitudes, crying out for a glimpse of 

Raila, Agwambo, Jakom, Tinga, Wo Nyalego, Wuod Mary.




It was in Kisumu, after the moving 

sigweya,

 the funeral dirge by the Luo elder Ajiki Koth Yamo, that my tears for Baba finally arrived, rolling freely down my cheeks. I knew then I wasn’t weeping alone; the elder’s sonorous chant was the nation’s permission to grieve.




I remembered the date of the state funeral was set for Sunday, four days after his death. The burial date would be on the 19th day of October, in Kang’o ka Jaramogi, in his ancestral homeland in Bondo where he would be laid next to his father’s mausoleum.




Funerals are also history classes, sites of memory where forgotten branches of the national family tree are traced. In the shadow of the coffin, the country revisits the archives of its pain and is forced to confront the unfinished lessons of its struggle and reform. Many were given a proper introduction to Baba’s extended national family and political networks that consisted of multiple generations, all claiming an intimate association.




I found it mildly amusing but mostly sad that the political class used the stage to immediately begin carving up the power vacuum, reasserting old rivalries and desperately laying claim as the rightful custodians of Baba’s legacy.




I knew the spectacle would soon be over and that the real mourning would begin after the cameras moved on and the flags went back up. First comes the shock of the loss, followed by the frenzy of the funeral, and once the deceased is buried under concrete, the second wave of grief kicks in after the adrenaline rush and numbness wears off.




Only then can one grasp the magnitude of the loss as the weeks, months, and years unfold. The listlessness and disorientation follow you everywhere, and the triggers erupt. The true grief work, the task we so love to avoid, can only begin then.




I knew this grief so well. It’s the kind that bangs on your door demanding entry, and when you claim that there are no chairs for it to sit in this house, it answers back coldly. 

“I brought my own stool.”




This was the silence of absence, the helplessness that dominates the thoughts of life after. For us, Baba was that parental figure whose death had never been factored into our reality. The signs could be right in front of you, but for a loss of this magnitude, you are never ready.




Chalgi ngero, thoo wuod Odinga, Chalgi ngero




The night before he was buried, I had my curated Baba playlist on repeat. Coster Ojwang, Musa Juma, Lady Maureen, Emma Jalamo, Prince Indah. I found myself clinging to the refrains, which served as an endless dirge. I needed the music to bear me through the darkness, finding my solace in the song, in the words I couldn’t, wouldn’t stop singing, resisting all attempts to return to normalcy.




How could they understand? We weren’t mourning a politician. This man had transcended that label. They knew him as the Right Honorable Raila Amolo Odinga, the party leader, Agwambo the Enigma, Tinga the Force, Jakom the General, Baba the Patriarch. But he was also Amolo, a human with all his fragilities.




The one who embodied our essence, 

kitwa,

 our nature. He was the epitome of sacrifice, yet he was the special one because he had been tried and tested like no other. He always rose again from the ashes like a phoenix, with that cheeky smile and sparkle in his eye. Amolo was a man whose humanity mirrored our highest hopes and deepest struggles, one who took his personal pain and forged it into purpose. He was our grief alchemist who turned suffering into a source of strength.




I met Amolo in close proximity twice, and both times were rather late in my life. The first time was at the United Kenya Club foyer in Nairobi. I stopped him on his way to the bathroom to share news of my cousin Adhiambo’s passing, knowing his acquaintance with her mother, my Aunty Raduodi. Raila had an incredible grasp of Luo genealogy, and all you needed was to mention a name, and he could trace your ancestry. He paused, remembered a moment from the past, and asked me to pass his sympathies. Just two men, talking briefly, sharing loss.




I stumbled into him the second time in my own village while visiting my cousin Bill Okwirry during Christmas. There was Amolo, amidst friends and family, listening to loud music, sharing laughter and whisky. It was an image of stunning normalcy for a man who, just months before, had suffered a humiliating election defeat after his fifth attempt at the presidency.




I met Amolo as Baba at many other funerals, and it was on those stages that I realised that he was also a historian and griot. At my late uncle Okeyo’s funeral, he arrived halfway through the ceremony, momentarily disrupting the proceedings. When he was given the mic, he regaled everyone with a history lesson, posing questions that reminded us of our shared ancestry.




“Who are these people called the Abasuba? Where did they come from?




This was a uniquely fatherly trait; he was a constant reminder that we are all family.




The true warrior dies on the battlefield. Death found Baba on the go. Even at eighty, he had refused to slow down. Now he rests, the storm has passed, and we continue to assess the loss.




This reckoning takes time, certainly years. You cannot know what you have lost until you have walked through the aftermath because that is when the real, inner pain is revealed, the kind that lingers despite the course of time because that love has nowhere to go.




His physical presence has left us; the 

Mbii

, his inner force, is now subject only to archive and memory. For his presence, our eyes search again.




Where do we find another, like him?




Lowo otero Amolo maa nyocha wa hero!




Baba was our crucible holding together our searing contradictions: the purity of a singular political dream against the murk of political pragmatism, and he was able to hold those contradictions without shattering.




In a recent paper, written by Bishop Francis Omondi, of the Anglican Diocese of Garissa, I found the language to express what I was struggling to explain. Omondi’s paper is on the legitimacy of Baba’s leadership and he opens it with a question that had shadowed Raila all his life: how did a man who never became president remain one of the most influential political figures in Kenya?




Omondi’s answer is insightful. He writes that Raila’s authority 

“emerged from sacrifice. Not from the exercise of power. But from resistance to the abuse of power”.




Presidents come and go, and power won at the ballot box rises and falls with each election, but power born of sacrifice finds its place in the collective memory of a people. Baba may have lost elections, but he never lost the people.




Omondi traces this legitimacy to three sources. The first is resistance in detention, and the price that Raila paid in his own body for opposing dictatorship. Then came reform, captured by the long fight for a new constitution and devolution, a gift that many have forgotten was bitterly fought for. And lastly, perhaps the most controversial, came the consensus, what we remember as handshakes, coalitions and reconciliations that pulled the country back from the brink of disaster. Those handshakes broke many hearts, mine included but Omondi reads them as part of a longer quest for inclusion and stability in a country too often at war with itself.




So one year on, we continue to grieve. His absence still weighs heavily. Depression might come knocking for some, as they come to terms with how dependent they were on the charisma of a single individual.




But we also celebrate because his spirit has finally been liberated from the limits of an earthly existence and all that he represented has been unleashed. This is a generational gift and his story will carry the nation through new seasons of trials. Like Winnie Mandela, he multiplied and we have to grow up and embody what he stood for.




There is no saviour coming. The desire is for another Baba but that same strength now belongs to the collective, who must find the power for their own becoming. Baba’s life’s work is incomplete: his legacy is a call to a generation to complete the work he started.




I return to my playlist, to Coster Ojwang’s tribute to Raila.




Baba’s gone and he is not coming back.




The brave one has left us.




Mayoo wee! Amolo osenindo




Chalgi ngero, thoo wuod Odinga, Chalgi ngero.

title: Αντιφασιστική διαδήλωση στο Περιστέρι, Παρασκευή 16/10, στις 19:00
content:
Αφίσες/Καλέσματα:




Προλεταριακό Αντιφασιστικό Μέτωπο Δυτικών Προαστίων




ΑΝΤΙΦΑΣΙΣΤΙΚΗ ΣΥΓΚΕΝΤΡΩΣΗ




ΠΑΡΑΣΚΕΥΗ 16 ΟΚΤΩΒΡΗ στις 19:00 πλατεία δημαρχείου (μετρό Περιστέρι)







ΦΑΣΙΣΤΕΣ ΤΟ ΜΕΛΛΟΝ ΣΑΣ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΠΡΟΔΙΑΓΕΓΡΑΜΜΕΝΟ




Η Δολοφονική επίθεση με μαχαίρι στον αντιφασίστα στην Ελευσίνα και η επίθεση με μπογιές και σπρέι στο στέκι της Αριστερής Κίνησης Περιστερίου θα απαντηθούν κοινωνικά και μαχητικά.




Καλούμε όλο το αντιφασιστικό κίνημα σε πλήρη συσπείρωση και μαχητική θέση ενάντια στους μαχαιροβγάλτες νοσταλγούς των ναζί.




Ο φασισμός δεν πέφτει από τον ουρανό. Γεννιέται μέσα στις αντιθέσεις της καπιταλιστικής κοινωνίας και αποτελεί την πιο ακραία και αντιδραστική μορφή υπεράσπισης της εξουσίας του κεφαλαίου. Όταν η κοινωνική οργή μεγαλώνει, ο φασισμός επιχειρεί να της δώσει άλλο στόχο. Να στρέψει τον εργαζόμενο ενάντια στον μετανάστη, τον φτωχό ενάντια στον φτωχότερο, τον έναν καταπιεσμένο ενάντια στον άλλο. Ο ρατσισμός και ο εθνικισμός είναι τα όπλα του για να διασπά την εργατική τάξη και να κρύβει τον πραγματικό ταξικό αντίπαλο.




Γινόμαστε εκ νέου μάρτυρες του ίδιου φαινομένου, σε μια εποχή πολέμων, ακρίβειας, φτώχειας και ανασφάλειας, η ακροδεξιά προσπαθεί ξανά να δηλητηριάσει την οξυμένη κοινωνική οργή με ρατσισμό, εθνικισμό και μίσος. Προσπαθεί να πείσει τον εργαζόμενο ότι για τη ζωή που του στερούν φταίει ο πρόσφυγας, ο μετανάστης, ο διαφορετικός. Να μετατρέψει την αγανάκτηση σε τυφλό μίσος και να αφήσει στο απυρόβλητο τις πραγματικές σχέσεις εκμετάλλευσης και εξουσίας.




Δεν υπάρχει πιο ειρωνική συγκυρία που να αποδεικνύει του λόγου το αληθές όταν την επόμενη της φασιστικής δολοφονικής επίθεσης στην εργατούπολη της Ελευσίνας δολοφονήθηκαν μερικά χιλιόμετρα πιο κάτω, ξανά από εργοδοτική αμέλεια, δυο εργάτες στην Motor Oil στους Αγίους Θεοδώρους. Το έγκλημα αυτό είναι ένα από τα πολλά των τελευταίων χρόνων και οι δύο εργάτες που έχασαν την ζωή τους είναι 2 από τους 142 (ΟΣΕΤΕΕ), μέχρι τώρα, εργαζομένους που έχασαν την ζωή τους εντός του 2026. Δεν είναι, λοιπόν, καθόλου τυχαίο ότι τέτοιες φασιστικές επιθέσεις πραγματοποιούνται σε ανθρώπους που μάχονται για έναν πιο δίκαιο κόσμο ή σε συλλογικότητες που επιδιώκουν να περιγράψουν μια άλλη κοινωνία χωρίς εκμετάλλευση ανθρώπου από άνθρωπο. Όπως δεν είναι τυχαίο ότι αυτά συμβαίνουν κατά βάση σε περιοχές που διαμένουν ή εργάζονται τα φτωχότερα κοινωνικά στρώματα, όπως είναι η Ελευσίνα, με βιωμένη την εργοδοτική αυθαιρεσία και την εγκληματική αμέλεια με σωρεία εργατικών ατυχημάτων και δυστυχημάτων.




Γι’ αυτό η αποφυλάκιση του Ηλία Κασιδιάρη και η δηλωμένη πρόθεσή του να επιστρέψει στην πολιτική δράση, δεν μπορούν να αντιμετωπίζονται με αδιαφορία. Η Χρυσή Αυγή δεν ήταν απλώς ένα ακροδεξιό κόμμα. Ήταν μια ναζιστική οργάνωση με τάγματα εφόδου, ξυλοδαρμούς και δολοφονικές επιθέσεις. Δεν ξεχνάμε τους Αιγύπτιους αλιεργάτες, τους συνδικαλιστές του ΠΑΜΕ, τον Σαχζάτ Λουκμάν. Δεν ξεχνάμε τον Παύλο Φύσσα. Και δεν πρόκειται να αφήσουμε τη μνήμη αυτών των εγκλημάτων να ξεθωριάσει για να παρουσιαστούν ξανά οι ίδιοι άνθρωποι και οι ίδιες ιδέες ως κάτι «καινούργιο» ή «αντισυστημικό».




Απέναντι σε αυτή την απειλή δεν χωρά εφησυχασμός. Ο φασισμός δεν αντιμετωπίζεται με σιωπή και αναμονή. Αντιμετωπίζεται πολιτικά και μαζικά, στους χώρους δουλειάς, στις σχολές και στις γειτονιές, με οργάνωση, ταξική αλληλεγγύη και συλλογική δράση. Η αντιφασιστική πάλη δεν είναι τελετουργία μιας επετείου. Είναι καθημερινό μέτωπο απέναντι στο φασισμό, στον ρατσισμό και στις κοινωνικές συνθήκες που τους επιτρέπουν να σηκώνουν ξανά κεφάλι.




ΦΑΣΙΣΤΕΣ ΘΑ ΠΕΡΑΣΟΥΜΕ ΑΠΟ ΠΑΝΩ ΣΑΣ







 Αριστερή Κίνηση Περιστερίου




 ΟΙ ΝΑΖΙ ΔΕΝ ΕΧΟΥΝ ΘΕΣΗ ΣΤΙΣ ΓΕΙΤΟΝΙΕΣ ΜΑΣ




[ 

 ΑΝΤΙΦΑΣΙΣΤΙΚΗ ΔΙΑΔΗΛΩΣΗ ΣΤΟ ΠΕΡΙΣΤΕΡΙ ]




 Παρασκευή 16/10 στις 19:00, στην πλατεία Δημαρχείου







 Την Πέμπτη 8/10, νεοναζί έστησαν ενέδρα και μαχαίρωσαν αντιφασίστα στην Ελευσίνα.




 Το βράδυ της Δευτέρας 5/10, φασιστοειδή γέμισαν την πρόσοψη του στεκιού της Αριστερής Κίνησης Περιστερίου με ναζιστικά σύμβολα.




 Τις τελευταίες μέρες, φασίστες βάφουν τα σχολεία των δυτικών προαστίων με σβάστικες.




Οι ναζί μαχαιροβγάλτες κλιμακώνουν την προσπάθειά τους να επαναφέρουν στους δρόμους τα τάγματα εφόδου, και αυτό δεν είναι τυχαίο. Συμβαίνει παράλληλα με την υπερπροβολή της αποφυλάκισης Κασιδιάρη από τα ΜΜΕ, αλλά και με το σταθερό άνοιγμα της κυβέρνησης Μητσοτάκη στην ακροδεξιά.




 Καλούμε όλο τον κόσμο της πόλης να σταθεί απέναντι στο τέρας που θέλει να πατήσει το πόδι του στις γειτονιές μας !




 Την Παρασκευή 16/10 στις 7 το απόγευμα διαδηλώνουμε μαζί στην πλατεία Δημαρχείου Περιστερίου!




 Ο φασισμός δεν έχει θέση στην πόλη μας!







☆ Δυτικός τομέας Ρουβίκωνα







 Την Πέμπτη 8/10, νεοναζί έστησαν ενέδρα μέρα μεσημέρι και μαχαίρωσαν, παρολίγο θανάσιμα, αντιφασίστα σύντροφο στην Ελευσίνα.




 Το βράδυ της Δευτέρας 5/10, φασιστοειδή γέμισαν την πρόσοψη του στεκιού της Αριστερής Κίνησης Περιστερίου με ναζιστικά σύμβολα.




 Τις τελευταίες μέρες, φασίστες βάφουν τα σχολεία των δυτικών προαστίων με σβάστικες.




Κάθε επίθεση είτε σε χώρους του κινήματος είτε σε συντρόφους και συντρόφισσες δεν θα πρέπει να μένει αναπάντητη.




Εδώ και αρκετό καιρό, οι φασίστες έχουν αρχίσει να διεκδικούν όχι μόνο την επάνοδό τους στην πολιτική σκηνή, αλλά και την εδραίωσή τους στον δρόμο. Αποτελεί, λοιπόν, καθήκον κάθε αντιφασίστα και αντιφασίστριας, και του ριζοσπαστικού κινήματος συνολικά, αυτά τα φαινόμενα να τα κόβει από τη ρίζα.




Τσακίζουμε τον φασισμό και το σύστημα που τον γεννά!




ΜΑΧΗΤΙΚΟΣ ΑΝΤΙΦΑΣΙΣΜΟΣ ΕΝΑΝΤΙΑ ΣΤΟΥΣ ΠΑΡΑΚΡΑΤΙΚΟΥΣ ΦΑΣΙΣΤΕΣ

content:
Nivîskar û bernamegerê Halk TVyê Bahadir Ozgurr duh(15ê Cotmehê) hatibû desteserkirin. 




Rêvebera Weşanê ya Giştî ya halktv.com.tryê Bengu Şap Babaekerê agahiya desteserkirinê li ser hesabê xwe yê Xê bi gotinên “Bahadir Ozgur tê desteserkirin” ragihand.




Ozgur îdîaya ku “nihêniya lêpirsîna fonê binpê kiriye” hat desteserkirin. Lêpirsîn ji aliyê Serdozgeriya Komarî ya Stenbolê ve tê birêvebirin.




Ozgur piştî karûbarên li Emniyetê îro ji bo Edliyeyê hat şandin. Dozgeriyê bi daxwaza şertê kontrola edlî û qedexeya derketina derve Ozgur sewqî dadgehê kir.




Dadgehê jî xwest ku Ozgur heftê de 2 caran li emniyetê îmzeyê bide û derketina derveyî welat lê qedexe kir û serbest berda.




Rojnameya Evrenselê nivîsî ku polîsan Ozgur birine Emniyeta Vatanê. Rojnameger Hakki Ozdal jî gotiye ku îfadeya Bahadir Ozgur a li emniyetê bi dawî bûye û dê di saetên sibehê de bibin adliyeyê.




Her weha hesabê Xê ê Bahadir Ozgur ku 163 hezar şopînerên wê hene (@bahadir_ozgr) hat astengkirin. Ev hesab hîn ji aliyê platforma Xê ve ji bo bikarhênerên li Tirkiyeyê nehatiye reş kirin.







Lîsteya di lêpirsînê de kiribû nûçe




Bahadir Ozgur di nûçeya xwe ya 13ê Cotmehê de diyar kiribû ku Serdozgeriya Komarî ya Stenbolê lîsteya tedbîrê ya mal û mulkên 141 kesan ku di nav wan de wezîra berê Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya û hevjînê wê İlyas Kaya jî hene, ji saziyên peywendîdar re şandiye.




Ozgurr nivîsîbû ku serdozgeriyê di 13ê Cotmehê de nivîseke nû şandiye û ragihandiye ku navên 29 kesan di lîsteyê de ‘bi xeletî’ cih girtine û diyar kiribû ku di nav van kesan de Enver Çevik û Kemal Akkaya jî hene.




Serdozgeriyê ragihand ku wan ev rewş bi nivîseke nû rast kiriye û tedbîrên li ser mal û mulkên 109 kesan berdewam dikin.

author: Unknown
title: Aksu: Ecology is better understood, but shallow approaches persist
content:
Ecological destruction and the plundering of nature are increasing day by day in Turkey and Kurdistan. As the environmental impact of projects carried out under the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government's “mega projects” is debated, the loss of forested areas continues.




Cemil Aksu of Polen Ecology spoke to ANF about the ecological destruction taking place in Turkey and Kurdistan, the causes of the plundering of nature and the struggle against it.




Aksu pointed out that 68 percent of forest destruction in Turkey has occurred under AKP rule and said: “The export-led growth strategy pursued by the AKP is turning Turkey into the West's Africa. Turkey's ecological problems began to escalate dramatically under AKP rule. The AKP started with ‘urban transformation’, ‘dual carriageways’, ‘megacities’ and ‘mega projects’, turning the entire country into a construction site. To supply the energy, cement and other raw materials needed for this construction site, it also turned rural areas, valleys and rivers across the country into sites for energy production, mining and other activities.




Global Forest Watch (GFW) data show that Turkey lost a total of 840,000 hectares of tree cover between 2001 and 2025, equivalent to approximately 8 percent of its tree cover area in 2000. In 2025 alone, 51,000 hectares of natural forest were lost. Professor Erdoğan Atmış's 2024 assessment is even more striking: the area legally or effectively deforested has exceeded 1.5 million hectares, and at least 68 percent of this resulted from land allocations made under AKP rule. Energy and mining rank first among the causes.




Over the past five or six years, a new wave of destruction has emerged. This new wave of extractivism is led by large-scale mining projects, including cyanide-based gold mining, oil and natural gas exploration using hydraulic fracturing, and rare earth element mining.




The government wants to turn the steps taken by the US-led Western imperialist bloc in its new struggle to divide up the world against Russia and China into an opportunity to transform the imperial legacy inherited by the Turkish bourgeoisie from the Ottoman Empire into a vision for the future. This neo-Ottomanism is not an AKP project; it is part of the historical consciousness of the Turkish bourgeoisie. The discourse of ‘the Turkish world from the Adriatic to the Great Wall of China’ predates the AKP and extends beyond it.




In the previous period, they made certain manoeuvres within the magnetic field between the US and Russia. But in the new phase that began with Russia's defeat in Syria, the government rapidly changed its position and became Trump's close ally. Over the past decade, particularly through advances in the arms industry, they have sought to secure a significant place in the emerging global system and gain an economic advantage over rivals of comparable strength. To achieve this, they are trying to benefit from the sanctions imposed on Russia and China by the US and other Western imperialist powers, positioning Turkey as a supply hub for certain essential intermediate goods and raw materials.




To this end, they are particularly seeking to expand the production of raw materials needed by digital technologies and the arms industry. This is also something Trump wants. It could even be said that the ‘super permit law’, passed by parliament last year and granting major advantages to mining companies, was enacted at Trump's direct request.




According to the Extractivism Report prepared by the Polen Ecology Collective, the areas allocated to companies over the past four years have exceeded one million hectares. In 2026 alone, an area larger than eight of the country's provinces was handed over to capital. A total of 266 districts where mining, oil and natural gas activities are concentrated were identified as ‘sacrifice zones’.




In Maraş, eight districts were included on the list: the central district, Göksun, Çağlayancerit, Onikişubat, Afşin, Elbistan, Pazarcık and Nurhak. In Gümüşhane, Torul, the central district, Kürtün, Kelkit and Şiran were identified as ‘sacrifice zones’, along with Küre, Bozkurt, Çatalzeytin, Taşköprü, the central district, Pınarbaşı and Tosya in Kastamonu.




In Kütahya, nine districts were included on the list: Emet, Gediz, Simav, Şaphane, Domaniç, Tavşanlı, the central district, Altıntaş and Aslanapa. The capital was not spared the expansion of mining either. Ankara's districts of Kızılcahamam, Çubuk, Haymana, Polatlı, Nallıhan, Mamak and Kahramankazan were also listed among the ‘sacrifice zones’.”




‘The government wants to turn Istanbul into an energy and logistics hub’




Aksu pointed to the enormous scale of the plundering of nature and ecological destruction in Istanbul, adding that the government wants to turn the city into an energy hub. He continued: “Turkey’s economy is financially and technologically dependent. That is why they constantly try to overcome domestic crises by borrowing from British bankers and lending institutions. To this end, the government continually comes up with mega investment projects. The Third Bridge, Third Airport, Northern Motorway, Canal Istanbul and Yenişehir projects are examples of this. Of these, only the Canal Istanbul project has not been realised, but the government has continued to support the construction sector and its allies through massive land speculation in the project area. They did this by removing Sazlıdere Lake, one of the few remaining water basins of the ‘megacity of Istanbul’, from its status as a water resource. However, these projects did not generate the financial resources on the scale the government had hoped for.




They are now trying to develop projects that would take advantage of the difficulties Iran’s control over the Strait of Hormuz has created for global oil and natural gas flows. They are seeking to attract global investors through measures such as announcing tax reductions to turn the concentration of buildings in Ataşehir into headquarters for global companies, as in Dubai, or through projects to connect the railway line beginning in Basra to Turkey’s railway network.




The government has long wanted to turn Istanbul and Thrace into an energy and logistics hub. These projects date back almost half a century. The Third Airport was also built for this purpose. They are now trying to take these plans further.




After the bridge, the Northern Marmara Motorway, Istanbul Airport and Canal Istanbul, they are rapidly moving forward with a new railway project that will further fragment the Northern Forests. The project route covers 12 districts, 10 in Istanbul and two in Kocaeli. The Ministry’s Review and Evaluation Commission met on 17 September. The first tender is scheduled for 14 October.




The approximately 127-kilometre project, planned to pass through 12 districts in Istanbul and Kocaeli, will cause further destruction in the Northern Forests and the basin of Ömerli Dam, another of Istanbul’s water catchment areas. According to the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) report, the project will affect approximately 281.7 hectares of land. Studies conducted along the route estimate that between 24,721 and 44,994 trees could be cut down.




The railway line will pass through four drinking water basins. Construction will generate approximately 30 million cubic metres of excavated material. The State Hydraulic Works (DSI) has warned that the impacts on water resources have not been adequately explained. Northern Forests Defence describes this project as the fifth major wave of destruction targeting the Northern Forests. The new railway line will further fragment the forests, increase pressure on Istanbul’s water basins and push urban development northwards.




The investment cost of this project, which aims to turn Thrace into a logistics hub, has been announced as 240 billion 281 million Turkish lira. This figure is approximately one-quarter of the 830 billion lira cited in the fund fraud scandal involving numerous members of the government. Such an enormous amount of public money will be transferred to capital at the cost of immeasurable ecological destruction, devastating the Northern Forests, water basins and agricultural land.”




‘

We cannot separate the ecological struggle from the broader social struggle’




Cemil Aksu said the ecological struggle cannot be considered separately from the broader social struggle, adding that the failure of the ecological movement to grow must be examined in the context of the failures of social movements. 




Aksu said: “Several women are murdered every day. More than half of the working class earns the minimum wage and cannot even exercise rights won at the cost of blood and lives, such as social security, union membership and an eight-hour working day. Farmers are constantly struggling between years of abundance and years of scarcity, while young people live on the brink of suicide, trapped in a cycle of hopelessness about the future. Under these conditions, we need to examine the situation not only of the ecological movement but also of the broader social opposition from multiple perspectives. This question can therefore be analysed at both global and local levels.




At this point, rather than focusing on the government's successes or its ability to emerge stronger from every development, we need to examine the failures of the social opposition in recent history. The social opposition had significant opportunities to make breakthroughs. There was the Gezi uprising, followed by the alliance formed around the Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP), which gained broad support in society and received 13 percent of the vote in the 2015 elections. The opposition's successes between 2010 and 2015 also contained the reasons for its inability to resist the state of emergency regime that emerged after 2015. This was a period marked by the crackdown on the HDP, the Suruç and Ankara massacres, and the destruction of many cities and towns, including Şırnak (Şirnex), Cizre, Silopi, Nusaybin, Sur and Yüksekova, by tanks.




This recent history is not being examined. The period that began with the AKP coming to power was also marked by ideological and political debates within the left, alongside efforts to establish alliances. The imperialist intervention in Syria and the resistance for self-government that developed in Rojava also created significant divisions within the socialist movement. Among some sections, approaches emerged that relegated the struggle in Turkey to a secondary position. They failed to anticipate how the war in Syria would shake global balances. We can now see more clearly that their approach was extremely short-sighted.




The shift in the balance of power in Syria in favour of the US and Israel, and the immediate alignment of the AKP-Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) government with them, also gave the government opportunities to pursue all kinds of repression and unlawful practices on the domestic front. The operations aimed at intimidating and dismantling the Republican People's Party (CHP) through İmamoğlu, who himself became a presidential candidate with the support of Western powers, the pressures and dilemmas created by the choice imposed on the Kurdish political movement between ‘becoming another Gaza or reaching a compromise’, and the already weakened socialist movement's inability to make a breakthrough capable of confronting the challenges of this period have created a climate of uncertainty, waiting and apparent resignation among the largely unorganised working masses.




The split between the CHP and the New Party, along with the constant defections of mayors and council members to the AKP, is deepening the crisis that has existed since 2016, when the leadership of the social movement was surrendered to these forces. Of course, we do not know when this crisis might reach the point of ‘suicide’.




Therefore, under these circumstances, it is ‘normal’ that the ecological struggle has been unable to grow and that resistance movements have not emerged on a scale matching the destruction. Nevertheless, over the past month or two, resistance has taken place in 38 to 40 locations, and some of these struggles are continuing. These are struggles born out of desperation and the instinct to survive. They are struggles waged by working peasants who refuse to become wage slaves in mines and organised industrial zones and who are fighting for a breath of clean air and a sip of clean water.”




‘Socialist movements have failed to approach the ecological struggle properly’




Cemil Aksu said socialist movements have failed to adopt the right approach to the ecological struggle. He said, “Parties that see themselves as the vanguard of society have not taken on the responsibility of understanding the class character and global significance of the ecological question, addressing the problems of the struggle in this field and developing theoretical and political solutions.”




Aksu continued: “The socialist movement, and I include the HDP and DEM Party in this, continues to relegate the ecological question to commissions. Over the past 20 to 30 years, ecology has become a recognised issue within the socialist movement. Many organisations and parties have established ecology commissions and organisations, but the shallow and pragmatist approaches seen in other areas have not been overcome here either. Parties that see themselves as the vanguard of society have not taken on the responsibility of understanding the class character and global significance of the ecological question, addressing the problems of the struggle in this field and developing theoretical and political solutions.




On the contrary, ecology activists and platforms are leading the parties. Activists within the ecological movement are trying to fulfil this responsibility themselves. This is also what we are trying to do as Polen Ecology. We are trying to fill the vacuum left by our parties.




Two weeks ago, the DEM Party organised a rally against cyanide-based gold mining in the Diyadin district of Ağrı, with the participation of one of its co-chairs. Are our co-chairs always going to speak only about the ‘solution process’, femicides, the economy and similar issues? Of course, a co-chair should also have knowledge and understanding of ecological issues, from climate change to extractivism, from industrial agriculture to speciesism.”




‘Those who want peace must struggle against the destruction of nature’




Cemil Aksu also addressed solutions to ecological problems, stressing the need for a complete transformation. 




Aksu said: “The solution to ecological problems is to consign capitalist barbarism to the dustbin of history. No other solution is possible. To achieve this, we must stand against capitalist barbarism wherever it attacks, organise to prevent it from carrying out its plans, push it back and wage an organised struggle.




At the beginning of our interview, I said the government was trying to turn Turkey into the West's Africa. At the same time, this government wants to turn Kurdistan into Turkey's Africa. Oil exploration activities in and around Diyarbakır (Amed), cyanide-based gold mining in Diyadin, mining projects that will destroy the Euphrates and Munzur basins, road and tourism projects that will destroy the Cilo glaciers. Approximately 80 of the 266 districts designated as sacrifice zones for mega mining projects are in Kurdish provinces.




The government and its allied business interests want to turn the ‘Peace and Democratic Society Process’ into an opportunity for plunder and exploitation in the region. Neither freedom nor peace will have any meaning in a barren land. That is why those who want peace, democracy and freedom must understand that they also have to struggle against capital's domination and destruction of nature.




As everyone is aware, we face a choice between destruction and construction. For capital, destruction means greater profits and economic gains. For us, construction means surviving and rebuilding life by establishing new organisations and movements against this destruction, guided by all the progressive, democratic and libertarian values and principles accumulated throughout human history.




Democratic principles, demands for equality, gender freedom, communal life... These must become the fundamental principles of our organisations, built on solid foundations. If the organisations we establish are flawed in these respects, it will be all too easy for those in power to incorporate us into their own strategy.




Acting with a sense of urgency leads to strategically mistaken steps. Contrary to the saying, ‘You cannot put the caravan in order once it is on the road.’ A button fastened incorrectly at the very beginning can sometimes lead to strategic defeat. That is why we need a complete transformation from top to bottom.”

title: No news of artist Jîna Ehmedî, arrested in Iran, for 10 days
content:
There has been no news for 10 days of artist Jîna Ehmedî, also known as Jîlemo, who was detained by Iranian regime forces in the city of Merîwan in Eastern Kurdistan.




According to Kolber News, Jîna Ehmedî, who is from the village of Nigil in the Merîwan area, was detained by Iranian regime forces at her home in Merîwan. She was subsequently taken to Sine Central Prison. Despite 10 days having passed since her detention, no information has been obtained about her health or whereabouts.




It has been reported that Ehmedî is being held in the women's ward of the prison and has been denied the right to meet with her lawyer, communicate by telephone, or meet with her family in person.




She provided art education to children




Jîna Ehmedî is known as the founder of Jîlemo Music House, which operates in Merîwan.




No explanation has been given for the reasons behind Ehmedî's detention. She founded the institution, which provides children with education in music, singing, painting, and cinema.

title: Namzeta Partiya Nû Ayşe Unluce weke Cîgira Serokê Yekîtiya Şaredariyên Tirkiyeyê hat hilbijartin
content:
Serokê Şaredariya Bajarê Mezin a Mersînê Vahap Seçer hatibû girtin û ji wezîfeyê hatibû dûrxistin. Meclîsa Yekîtiya Şaredariyên Tirkiyeyê (TBB), ji bo li şûna Seçer cîgirê serok hilbijêre, roja Pênşema 15ê Cotmehê li Enqereyê kom bû.




Dengdana nihênî çar tûr dom kir. Namzeta Partiya Nû û Şaredara Bajarê Mezin a Eskişehirê Ayşe Unluceyê, 48 deng ji namzetê Hevpeymaniya Cumhur, Şaredarê Bajarê Mezin ê Kocaeliyle yê AKPyî Tahir Buyukakin zêdetir girt.




Li gorî encamên nefermî ku saet di 20.55an de hatin aşkerekirin, Unluce 417 deng û Buyukakin jî 369 deng stendin.




Unluce piştî hat hilbijartin li ser kursî axivî û ev tişt gotin: 







“Ez ji bo cîgiriya Serokê me ê TBByê Vahap Seçer hatim hilbijartin. Heta ku ew bi lez azadiya xwe bi dest bixe û vegere ser erka xwe, ez soz didim ku ez ê vê erka xwe ji bo we bi awayekî wekhev û adil pêk bînim.”







CHPyê namzet nîşan neda, piştgirî da Unluceyê




Beriya hilbijartinê di navbera CHP, Partiya Nû û DEM Partiyê de li ser namzetê hevpar hevdîtin hatin kirin.Partiya Nû, Şaredara Bajarê Mezin a Eskişehirê Ayşe Unluce wekî namzeta xwe nîşan da.




Berdevkê CHPyê Muslim Sari di 14ê Cotmehê de daxuyaniyek da û diyar kir ku hewldanên partiya wan ên ji bo diyarikirina namzetê hevpar bêencam man. Tevî vê yekê, ji bo ku rêveberiya TBByê nekeve destê Hevpeymaniya Cumhur, ew ê piştgiriyê bidin Unluceyê.




Hefsengiyên siyasî yên di Meclîsê de




Beriya hilbijartina ku bi dengdana veşartî hat kirin, li gorî belavbûna partiyan a ku hatibû aşkerekirin, di Meclîsa TBByê de 304 endamên AKPê, 261 endamên CHPê, 131 endamên Partiya Nû, 57 endamên MHPê, 56 endamên DEM Partiyê, 9 endamên Yeniden Refah Partiyê û 3 endamên İYİ Partiyê hebûn.




Di vê dabeşkirinê de hiimara endamên CHP û Partiya Nû bi giştî 392 û yên AKP û MHPyê jî bi giştî 361 bûn.




417 dengên ku Unluceyê di tûra çarem de stendin, ji hijmara giştî ya kursiyên CHP û Partiya Nû 25 deng zêdetir bûn. Buyukakin jî ji jimara giştî ya AKP û MHPyê 8 deng zêdetir wergirtin.




(AEK/AY)

author: Ed Wanderley
title: Um jumento na filarmônica
content:
De orelhas sempre de pé e com uma zurra que ecoa por mais de 3 km entre a vegetação, talvez o jumento não seja a associação mais óbvia que se pense em relação ao universo da música. E, no entanto, aos 33 anos, Antonino Tertulino está mais do que habituado a preencher as caixas mais improváveis.




“Eu me considero um jumento. E eu tenho essa visão, pois nunca penso em ser uma peça de destaque. Aqueles que são muito presenteados, muito exigidos, e como o jumento é subestimado, passa despercebido, sabe?”

, conta o jovem magro de cabelos rareando, cujo talento diante de um contrabaixo acústico, já exibido perante ao menos três presidentes e dois papas, há muito, não o deixa passar tão despercebido quanto tenta se enxergar.




No dia 19 de julho, Antonino deixou a Áustria, onde integrava a Orquestra Filarmônica de Salzburgo, para uma semana de passeio pela memória, no Recife, onde nasceu, um compromisso que se tornou regular em seu calendário anual.




Entre as paredes do Teatro de Santa Isabel, templo cultural que, desde a metade do século 19, se fez palco nobre da sociedade pernambucana, ele foi um dos músicos a capitanear uma sequência de apresentações da Orquestra Criança Cidadã, formada por estudantes de 6 a 21 anos, na qual ele mesmo, vinte anos antes, teve sua iniciação no mundo da música. O trote silencioso de Antonino ecoa. O zurro é de gratidão, mas os olhares ao redor são mesmo aspiracionais. O contrabaixista tirou tempo para estar junto das crianças, conceder entrevistas e reencontrar amigos.




O ritual se deu antes dos preparativos para mudar de casa mais uma vez, agora para desbravar a Alemanha, onde acaba de assinar com a 

Niederbayerische Philharmonie

, de Landshut.

 “Uma das dezessete melhores do mundo”, diz uma das vozes contemplativas no interior do teatro, fazendo jus à megalomania pernambucana, sempre disposta a um ranking que nem sequer carece de fontes. 




A impressão dos que o acompanham é que a carreira de Antonino não tem um limite claro de até onde pode chegar e que segue em rota ascendente, sempre em frente, sem desvios. Quem é do interior, sabe: jumentos têm excelente senso de direção.










Antonino em 7 notas































































































































DO

is coelhos com uma cajadada







Fugir das aulas de física e química. Essa foi a primeira intenção de um Antonino de 13 anos, ainda em 2006, admite o hoje músico, em retrospecto. Aos alunos da Escola Nossa Senhora do Carmo, logo após a apresentação de um quinteto de cordas, foi oferecida a oportunidade de concorrer a uma das vagas do projeto Orquestra Criança Cidadã.




A escolha da unidade de ensino no Coque não foi por acaso. A região do bairro Joana Bezerra carecia de infraestrutura básica e tinha uma pobreza hostil que, muitas vezes, era retratada apenas pela face da violência.

 Não por menos, o discurso padrão era o de resgate, oferecendo atividades para que os alunos jovens não tivessem tempo de serem capturados pelo trabalho infantil ou cooptados pelo tráfico – e, entre os atrativos, estavam acompanhamento médico e odontológico, bem como refeições regulares.  




As aulas de música seriam no contraturno do calendário escolar, nas dependências do 7º Depósito de Suprimentos do Exército. Como incentivo, a atividade representaria horas de aula – o que, para o garoto, seria uma chance de se livrar das matérias que, àquela altura, já lhe causavam dor de cabeça. O impulso inicial, no entanto, deu lugar à admiração pelo novo mundo.




“Algo que me deixou bem curioso foi a comunicação entre os músicos, sem nenhuma comunicação verbal, sabe? Hoje, com colegas, eu faço isso no dia a dia, na orquestra, essa comunicação de gesto, de olhar, tudo. Mas aquilo teve um efeito “uau” pra mim, de como eles agiam como um time.”




As crianças da região, a partir dos seis anos, foram convidadas a realizar testes de aptidão musical facilitados. O desafio consistia em uma melodia de solfejo e em um método rítmico simplificado. Aprovados, eles seriam divididos entre os instrumentos – e as atenções se voltaram todas ao violino. 




“E eu dizia: ‘aquele ali, rapaz, pelo tamanho, vai ser difícil de controlar’. Se o violino é difícil, aquele ali é ainda mais difícil, pelo tamanho.’ E eu sempre fui franzino, assim, magrinho, né?”

, lembra Antonino. Desde então, a relação com o instrumento se fez como complemento de si mesmo e da própria imagem que tentava projetar.
















Do Recife para a Alemanha: músico acaba de assinar com a Niederbayerische Philharmonie, de Landshut




“Não é sobre volume, não é sobre 

show-off

, sobre se exibir. É sobre criar o piso, a base para que tudo aconteça. Por isso, sempre pensei ‘aquele ali é o instrumento’. E eu sempre fui muito tímido, porém, com o contrabaixo não tenho timidez. E ele tem essa virtude também, de não ser um instrumento exibicionista. É como se fosse [também] um jumento. Muitas vezes subestimado, porém ali, forte e necessitado, sabe? Pode ser veloz e bonito.”




E assim tem sido, há 20 anos.































































































































RE

cife e Carpina, a conexão que não se perde







Voltar para casa pode ser agridoce. O pai de Antonino, Antônio Tertuliano, mora em Carpina, na Mata Norte de Pernambuco. Comerciante, com ensino fundamental incompleto, vêm dele os costumes mais fortes que o músico mantém até hoje. “Meu pai brincava que, no dia em que desse 6h da manhã e ele ainda não tivesse acordado, não acordaria mais. Uma figura”, lembra. As visitas rápidas ao Recife nem sempre permitem vivenciar o estilo de vida do interior ou curtir a família vencendo a distância que se mantém ao longo de todo o ano.




No Recife, por outro lado, as diferenças gritam. Uma delas, que perpassa toda a cidade, o músico descreve apenas como “o barulho”. A poluição sonora, que os ouvidos locais normalizam e praticamente não sentem, salta aos sentidos de quem hoje vive outra realidade. 




Andar pelas ruas da comunidade onde cresceu também pode ser desafiador, até mesmo para a própria memória. No Coque, Antonino descreve ver, a cada visita, um processo de “desfavelamento”, com a remoção de barracos e a mudança da dinâmica da própria região, onde, conta, convivia com colegas de orquestra ao máximo durante as aulas porque, fora dela, os espaços possíveis de trânsito eram delimitados pela área onde cada um morava, em que cada trecho era reclamado por grupos diferentes ligados ao crime local.




A segurança acaba sendo um tema recorrente das reflexões inevitáveis ao comparar a realidade atual com as alternativas, caso suas escolhas fossem diferentes. E, ainda que o contexto de Israel envolva até mesmo a guerra, ele diz que regressar ao Recife “é outro tipo de terror”. 




“Ontem estávamos jantando a um quilômetro do hotel e ‘vamos pegar um Uber por segurança’. Isso é tirar a sua individualidade e sua independência. Apesar das guerras, eu digo que me sentia muito mais seguro em Tel Aviv do que na minha cidade. Isso é muito triste. De você poder fazer uma chamada de vídeo, uma, duas da manhã, caminhando na rua, e, no máximo, vai chegar alguém pedindo informação ou pedindo ajuda pra empurrar um carro, sabe? Mas a sensação de que alguém iria me roubar, ou fazer algo contra mim, nunca existiu. Eu falo que em Israel também eu aprendi a valorizar a vida. Porque aqui no Recife o perigo acontece, mas, de certa forma, também temos que viver com isso”, lamenta.































































































































MI

nha vez







Enquanto milhões de brasileiros se encaminham às urnas para as 

eleições de 2026

, os jovens da Orquestra Criança Cidadã estarão completando o primeiro aniversário de sua última incursão do outro lado do mundo, que começou no Parque Memorial da Paz, em Hiroshima, no Japão, um dos Concertos pela Paz. 




A cidade, assolada por uma bomba nuclear norte-americana durante a Segunda Guerra Mundial, foi uma das paradas da turnê promovida pelo projeto social do Recife, que abrangeu três países. 

A iniciativa reuniu músicos de áreas de conflito para tocarem junto com as crianças e envolveu, por exemplo, encontro da música clássica de artistas da Rússia e da Ucrânia no mesmo palco, um recado que excede qualquer limite imposto pelas guerras.




Após passarem pela Coreia do Sul, as crianças do projeto encerraram a sequência de shows no Vaticano, com uma performance na Praça de São Pedro, diante do Papa Leão 14. Não foi o primeiro Papa para quem o projeto se apresentou. Desde 2011, quando estava prestes a ser encerrado, após um apelo feito diretamente ao presidente Lula, o projeto recebeu patrocínio de um banco estatal, o que permitiu a estruturação da iniciativa e passou a viabilizar voos mais altos. 
















Evento do 5º Aniversário da Orquestra Criança Cidadã (OCC) com a presença de Lula




Ao longo desse período, os jovens se apresentaram para três presidentes, dois papas e tiveram comitivas tocando em países como Argentina, Itália, Japão, Estados Unidos e Portugal.

 Em 2010, foi reconhecida como boa prática de inclusão social pela Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU) e, em 2015, foi a segunda escola de música do mundo a integrar o Programa de Escolas Associadas da Unesco.































































































































FÁ

bulas e farpas







Cerca de 400 crianças e adolescentes, entre 6 e 21 anos, são atendidos pela Orquestra Criança Cidadã, sendo 250 no Coque, primeira sede do projeto, além de 120 em Camela (Ipojuca) e 30 em Chã de Cruz (Igarassu), ambos na Região Metropolitana do Recife.

 Além das aulas de música, o projeto previa a alimentação dos integrantes e, em geral, foi bem recebido pela comunidade.




A iniciativa não passa ilibada de críticas de organizações sociais que atuam no Coque, devido ao discurso de salvamento que sempre associou, na ponta contrária da atuação das crianças na música, à criminalidade. À época, a região foi escolhida para sediar a intervenção por ser uma das de menores índices de desenvolvimento humano na capital pernambucana e por ser frequentemente associada, na imprensa, a casos de violência urbana.




“Eu conheci o Coque quando fui assaltado nas suas imediações […] Tive sorte de não levar uma bala no crânio”. Com essa frase, um dos três idealizadores do projeto, e primeiro maestro da orquestra, Cussy de Almeida, apresentava a comunidade em rede nacional, durante a apresentação da OCC no antigo Domingão do Faustão, em 2008, à época, com 103 integrantes. 




Além de Almeida, também fizeram parte da concepção do projeto o desembargador Nildo Nery dos Santos, falecido, e o juiz João Rocha Targino, que também participou do projeto à época conclamando figuras políticas a escolherem “se quer[em] formar cidadãos como esses, ou se quer[em] formar presidiários”.
















Apresentação da Orquestra Cidadã no Domingão do Faustão em 2008




Frases ditas por Cussy na ocasião, como “Eles eram pequenos índios”, “estão arrodeados do crime”, “Eles sabem comer com o garfo na mão esquerda, a faca na mão direita, ele sabe escovar dente, passar fio dental, tem asseio, sabe entrar no banheiro sem deixar rastro” e “hoje em dia são meninos que você pode levar pra sua casa e passar um fim de semana” são, ainda hoje, citadas para criticar o discurso dos idealizadores quanto à manutenção de estigmas enfrentados pela comunidade. Na ocasião, o programa chegou a apresentar-se como uma iniciativa “que tira crianças da rua” e Fausto Silva chegou a usar a expressão “essa gente do Coque”. O maestro faleceu dois anos depois, aos 74 anos.




Questionado sobre o papel do discurso intervencionista da direção da Orquestra na manutenção de estereótipos que afetam a comunidade, o idealizador ainda à frente da OCC, o juiz João Rocha Targino, responde que acredita que “somos todos irmãos” e que o Coque “sempre foi visto” como palco de “marginalidade e prostituição, não igual a outros bairros do Recife”

, mas que acredita que a promoção de oportunidades e que a região tem pessoas “pobres de bens materiais, mas ricas de talento”.































































































































SOL

 sem céu







Antonino deixou o Coque para tocar na Orquestra Sinfônica de Goiânia, onde permaneceu por dois anos até dar início a um bacharelado em música em Tel Aviv. Foi quando a distância exigiu um preço maior. Com a mãe, Maria Denise, falava nas madrugadas, por videochamada. E lembra do desejo de apresentar o mundo da música que passou a desbravar.




“Antes era uma coisa muito simplória, muito singela. Depois, tudo se otimizou, cenário internacional, sabe? […] Se antes ela já ficava orgulhosa só de ir assistir às apresentações…”, conta.




Ao longo de cinco anos, Antonino estudava e se dedicava a um objetivo: integrar a Orquestra Filarmônica de Israel, uma das mais reconhecidas do mundo, dirigida pelo maestro indiano Zubin Mehta desde 1969.

 Foram cinco tentativas fracassadas. Em algumas, ninguém sequer chegou a ocupar a vaga oferecida. A filosofia era a de que apenas os mais preparados podiam integrar o grupo. 




O jogo virou em 2021, quando o contrato do posto de contrabaixista lhe foi oferecido. “Eu me lembro da primeira ligação após a audição. Foi pra minha mãe. Mesmo sem saber o que era a Filarmônica de Israel, ou quem era Zubin Mehta. Mas ela via a euforia na minha fala e então só dizia: ‘Poxa, estou tão orgulhosa de ti, quero muito te ver [se apresentando]’, lembra. Não viu.




Algumas semanas depois, no Recife, a doméstica Denise faleceu aos 64 anos, vítima de um mal súbito, e não chegou a testemunhar o filho em carreira internacional. “Foi muito precoce o falecimento da minha mãe. Foi algo muito súbito. Não teve um processo, não teve um… E foi quando eu tinha acabado de girar a chave pro profissionalismo, sabe? Foi algo assim que, ou eu desmorono com tudo aquilo que eu vinha construindo, ou utilizo isso como nutriente, pra minha música, pra minha trajetória”, avalia.










 




Eu vejo que as simplicidades que minha mãe tinha, a limitação que ela tinha para se expressar, sabe? Essa dificuldade que ela tinha de se expressar, de fazer o que ela sonhava, mas não era por ela não saber, era totalmente falta de conhecimento, falta de oportunidade, que ela não teve. Eu não tenho dúvida de que a mamãe estaria muito orgulhosa de ver esse momento.”




Antonino Tertulino

 

Contrabaixista

 





































































































































LÁ

 pro lado das Europas







O macarrão estava cozendo na água fervente quando o som de uma sirene tomou conta da vizinhança. Mais uma. Era o sistema antiaéreo de defesa antimísseis que alertava sobre possíveis ataques na área urbana de Tel Aviv. O ano era 2023, início do conflito com o Hamas, mas duas semanas já eram tempo suficiente para Antonino entender: “Eu não vim aqui pra isso. Essa não é a minha guerra”, resume o pensamento.




Foi assim, meio que às pressas e se recusando a normalizar a convivência com sirenes de guerra, que um plano engavetado do contrabaixista ganhou nova luz: aplicou para um mestrado na Mozarteum University Salzburg, na Áustria, foi aprovado e conseguiu antecipar o início das aulas. Assinou então com a Orquestra Filarmônica de Salzburgo até 2026, logo após voltar do reencontro com as crianças da OCC, quando se mudou para o norte da Alemanha, para um novo desafio: a Niederbayerische Philharmonie. 




“Eu ainda acredito que foi tudo muito precoce. As coisas, as oportunidades vieram, eu abracei as que pude, as que digo, as portas que eu abri, sabe? E eu continuo com fome de continuar essa caminhada.”































































































































SI

nfonia da gratidão







Mais de 700 crianças e adolescentes já passaram pelo projeto Orquestra Criança Cidadã – e ao menos 360 delas se revezaram no palco do Teatro de Santa Isabel, no Recife, no fim das férias de julho, para a apresentação dos 20 anos do projeto. Orquestras infantis, infantojuvenis e jovens revisitaram da música clássica aos sucessos regionais, com releituras próprias, algumas vezes acompanhadas de um coro infantil. 




Antonino, convidado de honra, se apresentou em destaque como a principal referência de sucesso da proposta, iniciada ainda em 2006.

 Repetiu o ritual de sempre: pouca salada, muita água e várias sessões de meditação ao longo do dia até subir ao palco. Dividiu os holofotes com colegas músicos, que convidou das orquestras europeias das quais participou, com o mesmo empenho e ares de showman que exibiu ao estar à frente dos pequenos talentos recifenses por duas noites consecutivas.




Apresentações da Orquestra Criança Cidadã no Teatro de Santa Isabel

Apresentações da Orquestra Criança Cidadã no Teatro de Santa Isabel

Apresentações da Orquestra Criança Cidadã no Teatro de Santa Isabel

Apresentações da Orquestra Criança Cidadã no Teatro de Santa Isabel

Apresentações da Orquestra Criança Cidadã no Teatro de Santa Isabel




Em frente a um público de 570 espectadores, com movimentos precisos, ele claramente se transportava a outro lugar, onde se encontrava em pleno conforto. Como se, de suas mãos, dependesse o mundo. Carrega ali arte, fardo, história e um tanto mais de expectativas ainda não alcançadas, que não divide.




Perguntado sobre estacionar e fazer carreira em uma única orquestra, em que possa ascender e encontrar zona de conforto, Antonino ri:

 “Não sou mustang, não sou manga larga [raças de cavalo]. Quero sempre ser a base, estar aprendendo, participar de algo que seja muito maior que eu”

, resume o contrabaixista que faz questão de descobrir os maiores verdes pastos que o mundo que anda desbravando ainda lhe possa ofertar. Você sabe, coisa de quem se diz jumento.

author: dialogocomospovos
title: II Raízes - A Gameleira  é Planta Sagrada!
content:
Cacique Juvenal Payayá fala sobre a gameleira, planta sagrada para seu povo. Ele explica que a gameleira é árvore própria da Caatinga, que sempre deu na beira das águas, e que seu significado sagrado é histórico. O local onde hoje acontece o encontro, na cabeceira do Rio Utinga, foi o palco da mais cruenta batalha que fomentou a chamada Guerra dos Bárbaros. Depois de massacrar os Payayá, os invasores deram um ponto final àquele nome. A região era habitada pelos Payayá, e a mata que existe ali já foi plantio deles.




Cacique Juvenal conta que, naquele lugar, havia um pé de gameleira. Para construir a barragem, derrubaram a árvore com machado — para ele, o último golpe no processo de apagamento histórico. As avós foram apanhadas, tiveram seus nomes trocados: tia Gita não se chamava Gita, avó Maria não se chamava Maria, avó Duninha não se chamava Duninha. Todas passaram a ser Ana, Maria, Francisca, nomes de santas. Elas resistiram e passaram a ser chamadas de gameleira, pela atenção que davam àquela árvore imensa, de raízes triangulares, mais altas que uma mão levantada, que seguravam um tronco maior.




Mesmo derrubada, logo ali na frente um novo pé de gameleira nasceu. O povo Payayá o cultiva com carinho e transformou a filha da gameleira em sua raiz sagrada.




Cacique Juvenal pede que guardem essa história e que pesquisadores a estudem: há muito ainda a ser descoberto. A gameleira que insiste em brotar é como a resistência do povo Payayá, o 15º povo indígena da Bahia.

title: Community care needs time
content:
Community care takes time and energy that rising rents and the cost of living leave people without. The speaker describes people working two and three jobs, and points to the idea of community care as something to pursue as far as possible: take care of each other and organize collectively, in solidarity. The ask that follows is to liberate our time and work less, so there is more time to care for friends and families.
