author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: Palawan farmers remain landless
content:
FILE PHOTO: Women farmers in Lupang Ramos (Photo by Carlo Manalansan / Bulatlat)

CORON, Palawan — For more than a decade, 38 families of farmers in Coron, Palawan faced possible eviction from a disputed property awarded to beneficiaries whom peasant groups stressed are not the actual tillers.

The Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP) and Katipunan ng Samahan ng mga Magbubukid sa Timog Katagalugan (KASAMA-TK) said that the decades-long dispute over 887.76 hectares of agricultural land in Barangay Decalachao exposes the failure of agrarian reform programs.

The groups referred to the unresolved dispute involving the Philippine Agri-Business Center Corporation (PACECO) and the former Yulo King Ranch (YKR) where farmers organized under Alyansa ng Magsasaka at Mamamayan sa Yulo King Ranch (ALMMA-YKR) remain excluded from portions of the land they cultivate.

“From PD 27 to CARP, farmers have been promised land reform for decades, yet actual tillers remain excluded from the land they cultivate,” said Danilo Ramos, KMP chairperson, referring to Presidential Decree 27 and the Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Program.

According to KASAMA-TK, farmers began clearing and cultivating portions of the property in November 2009. The dispute affects 38 families or more than 200 people.

In 2014, 361 individuals were given Certificates of Land Ownership Award (CLOAs) covering portions of the property. However, the group said that most of the beneficiaries were not the actual tillers occupying the land.

Some actual tillers were excluded from the awards while nine farmers received CLOAs containing technical descriptions that did not match the land they occupied. KASAMA-TK also reported that some beneficiaries who did not cultivate the property began selling their awarded land in 2016.

The farmers brought their complaints to the Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR) in 2020 and filed a petition for disqualification in 2021, seeking the cancellation of awards issued to allegedly unqualified beneficiaries.

The petition remains unresolved, according to a case briefer provided by the groups despite a 2022 directive for the local DAR office to report on the complaints.

Meanwhile, the farmers faced possible eviction and fabricated criminal charges for asserting their rights to the land.

For KMP and KASAMA-TK, the situation shows how agrarian reform can fail its intended beneficiaries when land distribution prioritizes the issuance of titles over the rights of those who cultivate the land.

The conflict is rooted in the Marcos Sr. administration’s declaration of 40,000 hectares in Coron and Busuanga as the Busuanga Pasture Reserve in 1975 through Proclamation No. 1387.

The area was operated by Yulo King Ranch, owned by Marcos associate Luis Yulo. PACECO later claimed 887.76 hectares within the former ranch area.

Although the disputed property was placed under the CARP’s coverage in 1993 and a Notice of Coverage was issued, farmers alleged that the DAR office in Coron withheld the notice.

The subsequent distribution of land titles, which reportedly excluded actual tillers, has left the farmers contesting awards that they say failed to recognize their longstanding cultivation of the property.

Renato Batocabe of KASAMA-TK said the dispute reflects the failure of existing agrarian reform measures to resolve the fundamental problem of landlessness.

“PD 27 and CARP have failed to resolve the fundamental problem of landlessness. The farmers of Yulo King Ranch deserve justice, not more broken promises,” Batocabe said.

He said that distributing land titles to individuals who do not cultivate the land, while excluding the farmers who do, does not constitute genuine agrarian reform.

The groups’ criticism centers on the gap between the government’s land distribution policies and the conditions faced by landless farmers. Despite decades of agrarian reform initiatives, the PACECO dispute remains unresolved, leaving farming families uncertain about their access to the land they till.

KASAMA-TK called on the DAR to immediately resolve the pending petition, review the CLOAs issued to allegedly unqualified beneficiaries, and cancel awards found to have been improperly issued through due process.

It also demanded a relocation survey to establish the boundaries of the land cultivated by qualified farmers and ensure that awards correspond to the areas they actually till.

The group further called for an end to the alleged filing of fabricated criminal cases against ALMMA-YKR farmers and leaders.

In January 2026, 4,600 hectares of YKR land were reportedly transferred to the DAR, while 726 hectares were distributed to 727 farmers. However, KMP and KASAMA-TK said that these developments do not erase the decades of unresolved land claims or address the exclusion of actual tillers in the PACECO property.

The groups said that the dispute must be resolved as part of a broader struggle for genuine agrarian reform, one that transfers land to landless farmers, dismantles land monopoly, and protects cultivators from eviction.

For the farmers of ALMMA-YKR, the unresolved petition is not merely a dispute over land titles. It is a struggle to secure the land they have cultivated for years, amid a land reform system that has yet to guarantee their rights. (RTS, DAA)

title: 6e assemblée anticarcérale paname et environs : 25 Octobre à la Parole Errante !
content:
La sixième Assemblée Anticarcérale Paname & Environs aura lieu le dimanche 25 Octobre à la parole errante (9 Rue François Debergue, Montreuil). Le lieu sera ouvert dès 15h30 pour s'installer, écrire ensemble des lettres à des prisonnier·es ou parcourir l'infokiosque, et l'assemblée même commencera à 16h. On conseille d'essayer autant que possible de venir sans téléphone (ou au pire, de l'éteindre en avance) pour réduire la surveillance que l'on s'impose à travers l'omniprésence des mouchards technologiques dans nos milieux. Il y aura aussi un coin et des activités pour les enfants, pour permettre aux personnes qui ont des enfants de pouvoir participer à l'assemblée.




 

 

 

 




L'assemblée anti carcérale paris & environs a pour vocation d'être un espace d'organisation ouvert se réunissant mensuellement afin d'agir collectivement en solidarité avec les mouvements des prisonnier.es et tisser des liens avec les prisonnier.es et leurs proches sans passer par des cadres partisans ou syndicaux.




Lors des dernières grosses révoltes qui ont eu lieu, la réalité sociale de la répression nous a laissé-es face à un constat amer : nous sommes bien loin d'avoir les outils nécessaires pour réagir correctement face à l'appareil d'État, ainsi qu'amplifier la voix des prisonnier·ères et de celleux qui font les frais du système carcéral.


Pourtant, les mouvements ne manquent pas d'inventivité pour s'opposer de front aux prisons, que ce soit par des actions telles que l'attaque de la prison de Fresnes lors des révoltes de 2023, les attaques répétées de comicos dans cette même révolte comme lors des gilets jaunes, ou encore les attaques et intimidations de matons à domicile comme lors de 

DDPF

.




Nous voulons nous en inspirer pour pousser nos luttes anti-carcérales plus loin, à la fois pour dépasser nos milieux anarchistes et adopter une position qui ne soit pas simplement défensive, en simple réaction à la répression.




La prison est — et sera toujours — l'un des symbole les plus éloquents de la puissance de l'État, de sa capacité à réprimer, enfermer et isoler l'ensemble des individu·es qui menacent son existence. La prison est au centre même de l'appareil colonial qui constitue l'État français : elle sert à mater et punir les révoltes des colonies comme récemment en Kanaky, Guadeloupe ou Martinique, à intensifier le tri aux frontières comme à Mayotte, et à tracer des frontières intérieures en incarcérant massivement les populations racisées, colonisées et les plus pauvres.




Attaquer les lieux d'incarcération - par les mots, la solidarité, le feu ou la bombe - c'est alors s'attaquer à ses outils privilégiés.




Rompre l'isolement des/avec les détenu·es est alors devenu rapidement pour les mouvements anticarcéraux un moyen d'affaiblir l'appareil carcéral et l'État colonial. En exposant la voix des personnes enfermé·es, on se donne le moyen de penser «

 

la prison

 

» (son fonctionnement, ses outils, etc.), mais aussi de la rendre moins «

 

extérieure à nos vies

 

». Des surgissements tels que 

DDPF

 ou les révoltes pour Nahel parviennent à la remettre au centre de l'attention en s'y attaquant ouvertement, créant des fissures dans lesquelles nous désirons nous engouffrer pour mettre fin à la trop commune realité de l'incarcération et des assassinats policiers.




Une des prouesse des États dits «

 

démocratiques

 

», est d'avoir réussi à faire de la notion d'enfermement un impensé pour toute une partie de la population. Une situation si lointaine que l'on ne prend même pas la peine de l'envisager, alors que c'est pourtant le quotidien de beaucoup de personnes...




Cette nécessité de destruction est d'autant plus présente dans une région parisienne qui concentre à elle seule une densité collossale d'institutions d'enfermements : que ce soit les taules, tribunaux, comicos, ou prisons pour sans-papiers, mineur-es, enfants, fols, tox, handi-es, animaux non-humains...




Pour nous, s'organiser signifie construire des nouvelles formes de lutte, de solidarité et de décision, par notre capacité collective à rompre avec l'ordre existant, à expérimenter, à créer, à inventer...




Depuis le début du 20

e

 siècle, les Anarchist Black Cross (

ABC

) et leurs réseaux ont cet avantage de se présenter sous une forme autonome et souple, fondée sur un internationalisme radicalement anti-carcéral, d'où notre envie de nous réaproprier cette forme et de s'inscrire dans un réseau pour abattre les prisons proches de chez nous comme à l'autre bout du monde, pour l'insurrection ailleurs comme ici. Loin de voir cette modalité comme une structure rigide et fermée, nous souhaitons, à partir du modèle des 

ABC

, créer un espace de discussion et d'échange, une assemblée libre où chacun·e pourrait partager et expérimenter, tout en s'inspirant des actions déjà existantes : lettres, cantines, parloirs, traductions, évènements...




Nik la taule et mort aux matons

 

!

author: Unknown
title: Demandez le programme ! Créer la brèche : construire et penser des perspectives révolutionnaires et antifascistes
content:
À la suite de la mort du néo-nazi Deranque, nous nous sommes retrouvé·es à quelques-un·es pour tenter de dépasser collectivement l'état de sidération face à la répression et la réaction de la classe politique et médiatique.




Nous constatons la place importante qu'occupe le milieu autonome à Lyon mais il nous semble nécessaire de le structurer afin de développer sa pleine puissance.




De ce fait, nous pensons qu'il faut s'organiser de manière collective et dans une perspective révolutionnaire. Notre volonté serait de dépasser l'agenda politique institutionnel, de proposer des espaces d'organisation laissant place à nos désaccords et à nos ambitions révolutionnaires tout en étant capables d'être à la hauteur des coups portés contre notre camp.




Pour cela, nous proposons un moment de discussion le week-end du 23, 24 et 25 octobre afin d'échanger ensemble pour penser les années à venir. Ces discussions suivront trois axes après un premier temps consacré au bilan de nos luttes et expériences révolutionnaires de ces dernières années :




 

Attaque

 : Les formes d'organisation possibles, leurs limites et leurs réussites

 

Défense

 : les possibilités de résistance et de solidarité concrètes

 

Propagande

 : Forces et limites de nos outils de diffusion des idées




Assemblée Antifasciste Autonome




Vendredi 23 octobre : Accueil




Rendez-vous à partir de 19h à l'Amicale du futur (31 rue Sébastien Gryphe, Lyon 7

e

) pour la soirée d'accueil du week-end. Tout le matériel des discussions seront mis à disposition à cette occasion.










Samedi 24 et dimanche 25 octobre




Rendez-vous à l'Ile Égalité (4 rue de l'Égalité à Villeurbanne, métro Cusset) pour les journées de discussion. Les discussions du matin démarrent à 9h et celles de l'après-midi à 14h. Nous vous invitons à rester en fin de journée pour un temps convivial. Il y aura une cantine et une buvette à prix libre (pas de 

CB

, que du cash).










Samedi matin : Bilan de ces dix dernières années




Pour démarrer le week-end et lancer les discussions, un premier temps est organisé pour revenir sur la séquence politique de 2014 à aujourd'hui afin de prendre du recul sur les réussites et les échecs de l'autonomie lyonnaise.




Samedi après-midi : Défense/Solidarités




On le constate tous les jours : c'est la merde. À l'international, les capitalistes nous précipitent dans une fuite en avant guerrière, impérialiste et écocide. L'Europe et l'Occident transformés en bunker ont globalement fait le pari du fascisme pour tenter de garder leur place historique en tête du classement mondial, à coup de guerres impérialistes pour l'énergie et les minerais, de répression dans les anciens territoires colonisés, en érigeant des murs et en massacrant les migrant.e.s aux frontières. Au national, les gouvernements se succèdent et se ressemblent tant et si bien que la chanson demeure toujours la même : austérité et renforcement autoritaire de l'état, surveillance de masse et répression à gogo, mesures antisociales profitant au patronat et décrets liberticides, racistes et islamophobes tandis que les médias mainstream fabriquent de toutes pièces des ennemis intérieur à abattre. État d'urgence, état policier... À Lyon, ces dernières années, les choses se sont corsées, entre les vagues de dissolution de collectifs et les expulsions de squats de logement et d'organisation, le milieu autonome s'est trouvé amputé de lieux d'organisations stratégiques et de forces d'appel larges. La peur de la répression, qui isole les personnes face au triptique police/justice/prison, mais aussi l'abattement des défaites politiques d'après les retraites et les révoltes pour Nahel ont favorisé le sentiment d'inertie et ont laissé un goût amer.




C'est pourquoi nous sommes tombé.e.s d'accord sur l'idée qu'il fallait nous renforcer, nous, nos outils, nos espaces, nos stratégies. Renforcer notre camp social en mettant en place des mesures d'autodéfense révolutionnaires et en faisant vivre concrètement la solidarité entre nous. D'abord, nous protéger de la répression, et tout particulièrement de la possibilité de la prison. À l'intérieur de laquelle nous souhaitons parler du soutien aux prisonnier.e.s en prison et en 

CRA

. Ensuite, il y a l'auto-défense physique, qui induit les pratiques de renforcements collectifs par le sport populaire, le fait de défendre un cortège face à la police, un quartier face aux fascistes, mais aussi le soin physique et psychique souvent éludé après les manifs, les vagues de répression, les blessures... Enfin, nous avons voulu aborder l'accès de plus en plus compliqué aux produits de premières nécessité, et à la bouffe, dans un contexte économique d'inflation généralisée et de précarisation grandissante.




Dimanche matin : Propagande




Lyon est une ville historique des médias libres et autonomes. Dès les années 70, c'est là que naissent le journal 

IRL

 (Informations Rassemblées à Lyon puis Journal d'expressions libertaires (1971-2002)) et Radio Canut, radio pirate puis libre, autogérée (1978-aujourd'hui). C'est aussi à Lyon que naît le premier site du réseau Mutu (réseau de sites internet collaboratifs d'informations anti-autoritaires), Rebellyon (2004-aujourd'hui). Le milieu autonome lyonnais dispose donc depuis longtemps de ses propres médias.




Les outils de propagande autogérés ne sont cependant pas les seuls que nous investissons. L'arrivée des réseaux sociaux et l'explosion de leur popularité à la fin des années 2000 a marqué un tournant dans les modes de communication auquel le milieu autonome a emboîté le pas. Les 

RS

 jouent un rôle central aujourd'hui, notamment pendant les mouvements sociaux. De manière connexe, au milieu des années 2010, les médias en ligne se sont beaucoup développés. Avec des lignes éditoriales peut-être plus souples que les revues papiers, et des médium d'expression audiovisuels plus populaires, ils sont largement investis et leurs productions consommées par nos milieux.




Cet état des lieux des outils développés et/ou investis par le milieu autonome à des fins de propagande, pose des questions. Autour de la portée des médias autogérés, et l'écueil de leur potentiel vieillissement : on peine parfois à atteindre les plus jeunes dont les pratiques se tournent plus vers les 

RS

 et les médias audiovisuels. Dans un même temps, les 

RS

 se heurtent à une problématique tant politique que stratégique : possédés par des géants capitalistes, voire fascistes, soumis à des algorithmes qu'on ne maîtrise pas et qui peuvent se retourner contre nous et nos luttes, ils sont des outils qui représentent un danger, en terme de censure comme de répression.




Enfin, les médias indépendants (qui passent notamment pas Youtube et Twich), très populaires, aux lignes éditoriales sociales-démocrates, sont parfois prêts à accueillir une parole qui émane de nos milieux : mais là aussi, à quel prix stratégique et politique, et sous quelles contraintes

 

?




Pour ce temps d'échange et de réflexion, avec plusieurs collectifs et camarades invité·es, on souhaite construire une discussion afin de déterminer quelles sont nos perspectives pour diffuser nos idées, à l'extérieur comme à l'intérieur de notre milieu politique. Peut-on atteindre une diffusion aussi large que les 

RS

 ou les médias indépendants

 

? Comment penser la complémentarité des médias pour construire et diffuser la propagande autonome

 

?




Dimanche après-midi : Attaque/Organisation




L'autonomie dans sa construction lyonnaise s'est toujours éloignée des grandes formes de structuration. L'expérience des partis politiques électoraux, les vieilles structures militantes ont fini d'enterrer la nécessité de s'organiser autour de structures établies. Pourtant en 10ans d'expérience autonome qu'avons nous construit

 

? Nous sommes nombreux et nombreuses à ne pas nous sentir à la hauteur de l'époque.




Ces dernières années la France et Lyon ont été traversé de mouvement sociaux et de révoltes puissantes, de la loi travail,au révolte de Nahel, des gilets jaunes au mouvement contre les retraites. Nous constatons que le mouvement autonome est très ancré à Lyon et qu'il existe de nombreux lieux et collectifs. Pourtant lors des différents moments de révoltes nos interventions ont surgi sous différentes formes sans pour autant réussir à maintenir sur le long terme, une poussée révolutionnaire. Nous sommes nombreux.ses à avoir pris part de manière disparate à ces évènements mais comment donner à toutes ces interventions une consistance nous permettant d'avoir une force collective

 

? Bien souvent à la fin du mouvement social, ou du lieu portant ce surgissement, les forces qui en émanaient se délitent et disparaissent. Trop longtemps bloqués dans ces logiques mouvementistes et à l'heure d'une potentielle victoire de l'extrême droite, nous souhaitons tenter un nouveau pari, celui de la structuration.




Nous aimerions partir d'exemples concrets pour étudier des formes de structures qui éclairent les questions qui nous traversent.




Quelles formes nouvelles d'organisation pouvons nous mettre en place pour décupler notre puissance d'agir

 

? Nous amener collectivement dans des perspectives révolutionnaires qui rendent capable cet horizon

 

? Comment pouvons nous prendre des décisions, ou comment résoudre des conflits lorsque les désaccords nous semble insurmontables, en maintenant le lien qui nous unis dans un même camps. Jusqu'où acceptons nous de faire certaines alliances.




Mais au-delà des questions formelles, réfléchir à une organisation c'est aussi réfléchir à ses modalités d'intervention dans les contextes sociaux et dans la rue. Comment adaptons nous nos pratiques au contexte et aux situations

 

? Enfin l'organisation nécessite des espaces physiques dans lesquels se réunir, et permettre à d'autres de nous rejoindre, mais aussi des moyens matériels pour pouvoir déployer nos ambitions. Quels en sont les avantages et leurs limites

 

? Comment acquérir ces bases logistiques et financières

 

?




Le programme du week-end en version imprimable recto/verso :

author: winter oak
title: For life and truth: his struggle was his success
content:
by Paul Cudenec, who reads the article 

here




Sigmund Kvaløy Setreng (1934-2014)

 was a philosopher and activist who was deeply opposed to what he termed the Industrial Growth Society – IGS.




We live, he 

warned

 in 1993, in “a global robber economy, a systematic plundering of the earth’s last resources at an exponential rate”.




“Like so many of my own generation in Norway, I have experienced a complete transformation of society in one lifetime – from an almost medieval, agricultural self-reliant society to a modern super industrialism, replete with computers, holidays at Mallorca, and complete dependency on world market forces…




“The industrial transformation was slow at first, and throughout the first half of this century people largely went along with the hydroprojects, feeling that electricity and industrialization would compensate for the river losses.




“But after World War II all that changed: the schemes grew out of all reasonable proportions and far beyond the needs of the people. That’s when Norwegian electricity finally became the bridgehead for modern international big industry”. [1]




This imperial pillaging obviously 

had

 a destructive impact on Norway’s magnificent landscape: “IGS tries to transform all mountainous areas and river sheds into gigantic cisterns for the production of industrial energy”. [2]










But Kvaløy Setreng also stressed the ill effects on the lives, culture and happiness of the Norwegian people. He wrote: “The deterioration of taste in half a generation coincides strikingly with the industrialization of the country. The state of aesthetic taste must somehow be the fruit of the transition to an IGS society”. [3]




And he 

added

 in 2007: “Small-scale farming and fishing is being replaced by a tourist economy where exotic folklore on abandoned farms is taking the place of food production and computer games are replacing real games.




“It should be of interest to note that exactly in parallel with this development the rate of suicides has grown tremendously in Norway, now being one of the highest in the world”. [4]




Kvaløy Setreng described how modern urban society is designed to serve the demands of the rapacious “techno-capitalist economy” which cannot function without treating human beings in a supposedly rational and entirely “quantitative” manner.




Stripped of meaningful work and reduced to the slave-like status of dependent and obedient employees, people “gradually and unnoticeably 

lose the ability

 to master their own situation and to take part in a conscious shaping of their society. In other words, we reach a state of affairs where people 

have

 to be governed from the outside and above… Society becomes ‘addicted to’ a continuation on the same course”. [5]










“We see today a great drive to centralize people from the rural communities and the small towns into the great metropolis. The planners are at work, creating vast suburbs from scratch, pouring people into the quickly finished product.




“It is not taken into consideration that these people come from different backgrounds and different kinds of communities, and that they arrive with their ‘roots in mother earth’s soil’ torn off…




“The majority inhabiting the bottom sector of the IGS power pyramid 

cannot be allowed

 to develop an ego-complexity anywhere nearly as strong as their leaders, because that would mean their effective refusal to function as quantities; then they could not be programmed, and statistical forecasts would break down all the time.




“The most functional citizen of IGS is one with no protruding edges – one who has the slippery shape of a simple disc – well suited to slide through the centrally designed pipe system of modern techno-society”. [6]




In contrast to this dehumanised industrial society, Kvaløy Setreng 

presented

 the idea of a “

livsnødvendighetssamfunnet

 (“life necessities society”, LNS) a society characterized by solidarity, autonomous small communities and the production of only the necessities of life. [7]










He 

explained

: “The top of the IGS pyramid, seen as a centralized social organization, may also be compared to the governing station of a machine – the single position from which you start and stop it and control all its functions.




“It is a basic characteristic of a machine to have just one such control center, while a 

living, organic

 process has many, or you might say, none: the whole is governing itself”. [8]




This is, of course, very much the vision of green anarchism and what I call organic radicalism – which is why a version of this profile has now been 

added

 to that mighty library of thinkers. [9]




Indeed, in his writing Kvaløy Setreng cited the influence of other organic radical inspirations such as 

E.F. Schumacher

, 

Mohandas Gandhi

, [10] 

Jacques Ellul

 

and

 

Theodore Roszak

. [11]




And I see close parallels to my own concept of 

withness

 [12] in this passage: “What became clear to me here was that it is a blockage of our understanding of a human being’s personality to draw limits around it as something trapped within the skin of one body.




“It is more fruitful to look upon the person’s full environment – all the things and events that are near to him – as elements that are being 

integrated into his personality

 as it matures and unfolds”. [13]










Rootedness was essential to this vision of natural belonging. The philosopher 

insisted

: “A basic, specifically human need is to grow and mature into a specific identity. That again means the living availability of a particular cultural tradition – a pattern of activity, thought and feeling that has emerged over many generations as the complex answer to the specific challenges nature offers in this culture’s place on the earth.




“These local challenges are the main reason why we have a variety of deeply different cultures around the world. A human identity worth the name presupposes an existence that extends in an unbroken manner far beyond an individual lifespan.




“Identity for the individual means a history and an inherited worldview containing everything that is necessary to deal with ‘survival-with-abundance’ in her own place.




“The catch-words here are 

self-sufficiency

 and 

self-reliance

. Without identities reflecting the eco-social histories of the many different landscapes that Gaia presents to human beings, there would be no individuals or societies with sufficient moral strength and inspiration to counter difficulties as they arise”. [14]




Kvaløy Setreng’s anti-industrial radicalism was thus combined with what another organic radical thinker, 

Edward Abbey

, described in 

The Monkey Wrench Gang

 as “the conservative instinct to keep things not as they are but as they should be… to keep it like it was”. [15]










This kind of outlook is, of course, anathema to the industrial mafia and their fascistic ideological thought police, who regard any objection to their foul imperial megamachine as “reactionary” or even, absurdly, “eco-fascist”.




Kvaløy Setreng defiantly declared: “What we stand for may seem archconservative and at the same time extremely radical. We will therefore strike in both directions, and we will be attacked from all sides”. [16]




One of the key distinctions he made was between the complexity of organic societies and the complication of the industrial world.




He explained: “By ‘complexity’ (CX) I mean the dynamic, irreversible, self-steering, goal-directed, conflict-fertilized manifoldness of nature and – as a particularly refined and intricate version of that – the human body/mind.




“By ‘complication’ (CC) I mean the static, reversible, externally steered, standardizing structure-intricacy of the machine. The computer is a particularly refined and intricate version of that…




“The propaganda of IGS tells us that LNS is a simple, primitive, and even standardized sort of society, while IGS is complex. One of my main points here is to show that it is actually the other way around. And there are many examples that most people will recognize that clarify the opposite view: that the complexity of IGS is just an appearance”. [17]




Here Kvaløy Setreng introduced a third concept to explain how it is that the static and standardising industrial world manages to pass itself off as more complex than the organic richness of “primitive” and natural ways of living.




“‘Pseudocomplexity’ (PCX) 

mimics

 CX; it is the human invention of various arrangements and activities designed to keep people occupied in a diverse manner, through mass media, hobbies, tourism, schools, and so on, but on the kind of shallow level that is exemplified by the amusement park – without offering training or development that equips them better for creative interaction with nature or with human society”. [18]










He also made an interesting distinction between organic and mechanical time: “Organic time is concrete; it has no existence separate from material-spiritual events (‘being-processes’ is one tentative word that might be useful to get away from the Cartesian split between matter and spirit). It cannot be ‘objectively’ measured, because any kind of measuring rod would change with it…




“Mechanical time is a human intellectual invention. It was historically prepared through the observation of the rhythmical pulses of day and night and the seasons, but came into consequential being as something different from organic time only with the invention of a reliable mechanical ‘time-keeper’ (a device that conserves time) – the clock.




“It is used to quantify natural time – or, rather, to substitute mechanical co-ordination for rhythmical living in approximation with the sun’s rising and setting, tides in the sea, and various rhythmical body functions.




“Mechanical time is regarded as being the same for all natural processes; it’s ‘objective’ not ‘subjective’, we speak as if we are ‘moving through it’, it is supposed to stretch out into the future (it is actually constituting the concept ‘future’ in Western civilization – a sheet of paper, a map, now a screen, on which the 

planners

 trace their lines), as if what has not yet happened is already ‘there’ ‘someplace'”. [19]




This idea of a future that has already been decided, which we are utterly powerless to change or challenge, is central to the industrialist brainwashing which always tells us that the advance of malignant and parasitical “progress” is not only beneficial to us but also 

inevitable

.




Kvaløy Setreng was a bit of an artist (

as readers might have noticed

) and liked to use pictures to get his message across, including the contrasting images of a pylon and the Mardøla waterfall which he and others fought (and failed) to save from the ravages of the hydroelectric industry.




He commented: “To put it in simple and strong colors: The pylon is a symbol of ‘life frozen to rigid death’; the natural waterfall symbolizes the unfathomable potentialities of the life process itself”. [20]










From the early 1970s, Kvaløy Setreng was heavily involved in the successful fight against Norway joining what is now the European Union – the 

EUSSR

 to some of us. [21] At the same time he was involved in non-violent resistance to the industrial empire of which the European entity is so clearly a part.




He was fascinated by the traditional way of life and thinking of the Sherpa people in the Himalayas and this led on to a considerable Buddhist influence on his outlook, but he did not promote the political passivity that often seems to be associated with that religion, at least in its Western form.




He argued: “Instead of that, we should learn the karma-yoga message of Gandhi: You have to step into the stream to be grabbed by something outside your private soul, 

something you do not control

.




“It’s then that you have a chance of being shaken so that you’re changed, and through that already contributing to changing the system. Instead of observing the river ‘scientifically’, from a safe distance, you step into the river, are – surprisingly – grabbed by the current, and are 

forced

 to learn how to swim.




“That’s when you learn to accept that nothing is permanent, that everything is time and that time is creativity. Only then will you have the initiative and ability to escape control by the powers above you in the pyramid…




“Gandhi tells us that the most important source of human knowledge is not to be found at some university or in meditation, but at the center of social and political conflict, the fight for Life and for Truth”. [22]










Kvaløy Setreng 

related

 how he and his fellow campaigners put Gandhi’s principles into practice in their efforts to defend their land from the empire of greed.




“

Innerdalen

, ‘The Inner-most Valley’, is (was, I now regret to say) a beautiful, extremely fertile mountain valley in Mid-Norway, that was to be completely inundated as a hydroelectric dam.




“In this valley we were finally able to stage a pure Gandhian action, plowing and harvesting crops, keeping cattle, producing milk, butter and cheese. We organized a ‘Green University’ and a ‘green factory workers occupation’, proclaiming the dam workers as ‘strike breakers’. The latter was to provoke discussion with the labor movement”. [23]




And this philosophy made them stronger and more determined in their long-term resistance to industrialism, with its emphasis on not being attached to outcomes, on not striving for the fruit of the action.




“We experienced something unexpected – invulnerability! Even if we lost a kindergarten to a four-lane road or a fishing ground to oil drilling, we didn’t feel beaten down and we didn’t stop acting. Having acted – with all our care and strength – was our success!” [24]




Kvaløy Setreng’s morale must also have been maintained by his conviction that industrial society, IGS, was bound to collapse and that part of the task in hand was to ensure that this happens “as a soft crash and not as a sudden, violent one accelerated by positive feedback”.  [25]




His philosophy and his activism represented one seamless whole – the action fuelled the philosophy and the philosophy fuelled the action. He wrote: “Ecophilosophy is a form of activity and a direction of thought that appears as something not freely chosen but as a necessity – a response required by the total system crisis we are experiencing in the world, challenging us to attempt a deep-level revision of the basic notions of our Euro-American civilization.




“In such an extraordinary situation, the limits of the academic tradition – value-neutral and strictly intellectual – must, at least for the present, be broken out of”. [26] For him, as for me, what was required was “a viable new paradigm, a new world picture, or rather a new mode of perceiving, thinking, and living, maybe a new myth”. [27]




Kvaløy Setreng saw the need in 

our righteous struggle

 [28] for “people with identity within their own culture, self-assuredness, inventiveness in the practical sphere, originality of approach, and willpower”. [29]




And he stressed the importance of those across the world “whose own skin is burnt by the heat of the industrial growth ovens”, those who find themselves physically in the way as the insatiable imperial bulldozer crashes on and on.




“It is from 

their

 angle we must rediscover the world. Their suffering, their anguish, the futility of their effort as long as IGS persists – these facts must tear the veil from our eyes and pull the plugs out of our ears.




“Their struggle to gain freedom must become our own struggle, and their direct, everyday toil to save morsels of soil and keep the earth green to sustain life lastingly must become our own point of departure into a new world”. [30]

author: Unknown
title: Groupe Révolutionnaire Charlatan - Will 1793 Take Place?
content:
Author

: Groupe Révolutionnaire Charlatan

Title

: Will 1793 Take Place?

Subtitle

: Destituent Remarks on the Chilean Uprising and the Yellow Vests

Date

: October 6

th

, 2026

Notes

: Translated by the authors and Ill Will

Source

: https://illwill.com/1793




 










 First published in French in August 2026, the present article argues that the 2018–19 Yellow Vests movement in France and the 2019 Chilean uprising form two instances of a single pattern. In each case, an insurrection begins with modest demands, such as a metro fare or a fuel tax only to then explode outward, outstripping its own stated goals, before ultimately being contained by constituent processes, referendums, and left-wing electoral projects. The authors treat the Constitution of 1793, with its famous article on the “duty of insurrection,” as the archetypal “act of capture” for such sequences: on the one hand, it was an attempt by ruling powers to absorb revolutionary energy into itself; at the same time, it served to embed a permanent insurrectionary principle into the political-legal system, one which the state has never been able to fully extirpate. Against the left’s push for new constitutional initiatives, the authors argue for a “revolution without power” grounded in the refusal of institutions and representation, crediting the Yellow Vests with developing new forms of assembly and fleeting affiliation in the absence of a distinct language or subject of its own. The key question, they suggest, is ultimately not whether 1793 will take place, but who will finish the job. 










 










 Then annihilate forever what may one day destroy your work. Consider that the fruit of your labors being reserved for your grandchildren only, duty and probity command that you bequeath them none of those seeds of disaster which could mean for your descendants a renewal of the chaos whence we have with so much trouble just emerged. At the present moment our prejudices are weakening; the people have already abjured the Catholic absurdities; they have already suppressed the temples, sent the relics flying, and agreed that marriage is a mere civil undertaking; the smashed confessionals serve as public meeting places; the former faithful, deserting the apostolic banquet, leave the gods of flour dough to the mice. […] One more effort; since you labor to destroy all the old foundations, do not permit one of them to survive, for let but one endure, ‘tis enough, the rest will be restored. And how much more certain of their revival must we not be if the one you tolerate is positively the source and cradle of all the others! —Marquis de Sade, 

Philosophy in the Bedroom

, 1795 










In Santiago as in Paris




 Chile, October 25

th

, 2020.

[1]

 After months of insurrectionary demonstrations, the government agrees to hold a referendum to elect a constituent assembly. The vote takes place on the 15

th

 and 16

th

 of May, 2021, and on July 4

th

 the assembly begins its work, which is to last for a period of one year. With the initiation of the constituent process, another quite distinct process draws to a close: the revolutionary process. The latter began on October 7, 2019 when groups of young people, dissatisfied with the rise in metro fares, decided to refuse to pay and to jump the ticket barriers en masse. Collective ingenuity, the joy of rebellion, the determination of the 

primera línea

 (frontline), the feeling of being on the verge of storming heaven, all gradually give way to self-serious protocols and democratic formalism. On two separate occasions, the newly drafted constitution is rejected in referendums and abandoned. The rest is history: the left wins the elections of November–December 2021 with an abstention rate of roughly 50 percent, taking power in March 2022. Yet the aftermath proves disappointing and, in December 2025, a far-right candidate, the son of a Nazi, is elected as the country’s leader against a backdrop of a spectacular rise in voter turnout (up thirty-eight percent in the first round, and twenty-nine in the second). Once again, hopes for a Chilean path towards a freer and more egalitarian society are dashed. Once again, counterrevolution succeeds in stifling the revolutionary process, by imposing upon it the timeframe and institutional forms of democratic power: the mirage of a referendum, a moment of national electoral unity, a left-wing government, and a breakthrough by the far right. 




 In France, the Chilean uprising enjoyed a certain resonance with the Yellow Vests movement. It was not the price of the metro ticket but rather the cost of fuel that sparked the unrest, dragging out into the open the aspirations and courage of hundreds of thousands of people confronting the rising cost of living, the unwavering contempt of those in power, constant disparagement in the media, and the extreme brutalization of law enforcement. The grievances of the Yellow Vests included the resignation of Macron, a reshuffling of government, and still more importantly, increased active participation among citizens in political life through the Citizens’ Initiative Referendum (RIC). In the absence of anything else to articulate, uprisings always begin with such demands. But the specific demands of the movement should not obscure the fact that, rather than simply opposing a particular tax or government, this was a struggle for the dignity of life. To put it another way, what the movement said did not fully reflect what it wanted. In the absence of a common language, its actions went further than its words, without ever truly finding a way to express its aims. This distinguishes it from the so-called Marxist revolutions, which inherited the language of their century, even though their substance may have differed from what their ideology implied (representative democracy, a mixed economy, parliamentarism, tax justice, agrarian reform, etc.). There is always a disconnect between the desires expressed and experienced during an uprising and what subsequently materializes: this “cunning of reason” is the crucible of the insurgents and their failed emancipation. 




...

title: Groupe Révolutionnaire Charlatan - Remarks on the Ongoing Student Revolt
content:
Author

: Groupe Révolutionnaire Charlatan

Title

: Remarks on the Ongoing Student Revolt

Date

: October 9

th

, 2026

Notes

: Translated by Ill Will

Source

: https://illwill.com/remarks-on-the-ongoing-student-revolt










 The following remarks, forged in the heat of battle during a wave of student unrest that is now spreading to Belgium and Italy, were posted to 

x.com

 on October 6, 2026. For a longer position piece by the same authors, see their recent article, “

Will 1793 Take Place?

” 










1.




 The student revolt is the spearhead of the movement announced for October 17. 




2.




 The “gangs” [bandes] of students from working-class neighborhoods constitute the actual driving force both within and against the current youth movement. In a sense, this force is less a part of the student movement than it is a continuation of the Nahel revolt. It has neither demands nor representatives; it does not conform to the codes of the Left and rejects bourgeois politeness. It wants revenge. 




3.




 The universities have followed the high schools and joined the dynamic of the blockades. They, in turn, could bring about a qualitative leap by, for example, launching an occupation that could be taken up and spread by other sectors of society—whether students or not. This hypothesis, however, is oppposed by the overwhelming dominance of student union organizations, which leave little room for group spontaneity, collective ingenuity, and self-subversive practices. 




4.




 When one speaks of “blockades” at high schools, one is already engaging in a form of reduction and simplification of the practices of the student revolt. There are acts of sabotage (doors set on fire, gates knocked down, “e-blockades” against distance learning) and acts of revenge (against the school hierarchy and the police outside), urban guerrilla tactics (barricades) and wildcat strikes (work stoppages during breaks and staggered blockades), and finally something akin to a game aimed at ridiculing authority (slogans about Macron and his teacher, superhero costumes in contrast to the oppressors’ uniforms). 




5.




 The unions cannot come to terms with the idea of October 17, as it reminds them too much of the Yellow Vests. They must pretend to join the movement in order to gain better control over it—both through their monopoly on negotiations and by dictating the timeline. If the inter-union coalition called for action on October 6 alongside the students, it was only to better defuse the call for October 17, which they wish to reduce to an interim date ahead of their mobilization on November 5. 




6.




 In high schools, the left differs from other political forces in form, but not in substance. In form, the left pushes students into the role of victims, thereby allowing itself to present as the “responsible adults.” Consider the human chains of parents and teachers, or elected officials denouncing the police’s use of LBD weapons. It is striking, however, that batons, shields, helmets, and other standard components of the arsenal of democracy are far less frequently called into question. 




7.




 In terms of substance, the left aligns itself with the other political forces in their efforts to restore peace. This is precisely what happens when it puts forward demands that are consistent with its platform, thereby helping to separate the “good” students (those with demands deemed legitimate) from the “bad” students (these “rioters” without ideas or genuine political motives). 




8.




 Unlike the left, we have neither flags to wave, nor a tempo to set, nor lessons to teach. 




9.




 How should we deal with the enthusiasm for “October 17” and the way certain segments of the youth present it as an echo of the Yellow Vests movement? Even if a new generation seems to invoke its symbolic power full of hope, it is by no means certain that reusing the object will help us rediscover its spirit. Nevertheless, perhaps that is precisely what is expected of us: to don it and see if it—even if only temporarily—embodies a sense of belonging with which others can identify and to which they can align themselves, without appropriating it in the process. At the risk of appearing ridiculous and anachronistic, and discarding it again swiftly. 




10.




 The spectacular actions of the student revolt are the work of bands or gangs [bandes] that organize themselves and make their identity known in this way. Wearing Under Armour outfits fools no one: only to the extent that we reconnect with our emotions and our gang-like instincts will our actions resonate and have an impact, both offensively and tactically (distribution of masks, Phy-Serum, Anrirep flyers, lists of lawyers, food, sound and lighting equipment). By acting in this way, we hope to prolong the time we have fought to open for encounters, discussion, and conspiracy.

author: greensyndic
title: Speed Kills: Snuff Capitalist Acceleration - Jeff Shantz
content:
The elimination of jobs at the workplace now coincides with the elimination of former workers outside the workplace under snuff capitalism. And this elimination too must be done in accelerating rates. Time, as always, is money from capital’s perspective. From Anarcho-Syndicalist Review, 95, Fall 2026.

Whether we like it or not, capital is accelerationist. Speed up is built right into the very engine of capitalism. Capital’s drive for accumulation, in competition with other capital for profit, means that it must always go faster, must always accelerate exploitation and value extraction. This is the drive behind the ceaseless, permanent, push for technological advance, from motors to assembly lines to robots to computers, to AI, and beyond.

Speed is the means by which capital beats its competitors in extracting value. More surplus value in an ever-shorter period of time. Any worker knows the tyranny of the clock in the capitalist workplace. Marx suggests that this surplus value extraction is either absolute, the lengthening of the working say, so we work longer beyond the point that we produce the value equivalent to our wages or relative, narrowing the time it takes us to produce the equivalent of our wages. Relative surplus value is the logic of the speed up—using technology to get us producing more and faster. Both forms of extraction, though, dominate the worker’s lifetime. Denying us rest, breaks, mealtimes, or even bathroom breaks. Stealing our life times—time away from family, from loved ones, from ourselves.

Speed also, significantly, overcomes obstacles—first and foremost among them the slowness built into human labor by the physical and mental limits and frailties of our bodies. Technological acceleration is therefore about overcoming the human element in labor. It is about controlling us too, taking initiative away from us.

Reducing and then replacing our numbers, and our capacities to resist or control the labor process. Fundamentally it is about rendering our human labor irrelevant, while doing the same to the embodiment of that labor itself—us.

Capital has used speed to overcome the limitations posed by workers on value extraction and accumulation. But under current and emerging conditions of accelerating electronicization (AI and its ilk are exemplars), capital is accelerating, not with workers, but without us. The working class becomes an obstacle to be overcome, not only at work but increasingly outside of work. The living bodies of the working class slow down the circuits of capital in distribution (consumption) as well as in production. Capital moves quickly from stealing our life times to stealing our life itself.

The elimination of jobs at the workplace now coincides with the elimination of former workers outside the workplace under snuff capitalism. And this elimination too must be done in accelerating rates. Time, as always, is money from capital’s perspective.

From Social Services to Snuff Services

Those expelled from production and (simultaneously) from consumption are too costly for capital, too much of an obstacle to accumulation. As capital becomes more desperate it increasingly sees any supports that might sustain the unemployed, such as welfare, unemployment insurance, social housing, health care, as a transfer of wealth by the state away from capital and to the unproductive and unnecessary. They are, from capital’s perspective, expendable. They must be eliminated. This is the impetus, and organizing principle, of snuff capitalism.

Like production and consumption themselves, this elimination must be done quickly, at accelerating speeds. Every day the unneeded are kept around is an impediment to accumulation, a drain on capital.

This elimination must at least keep pace with the elimination of jobs, of workers from work, of consumers from consumption. Time, as always for capital, is money. First and foremost.

This is driving expansion of and innovation in snuff industries, innovation and expansion of murder infrastructures, innovation and transformation of capital’s states from neoliberal tools (of crisis) to democidal weapons (of extermination).

This is made to happen through the dual spheres of the state as usual, through law (legality) and force (police). Increasingly it will happen through what were once called social services—health care as assisted suicide and coercive detention, social assistance as death camp labor and medical experimentation.

One focus of democidal states has been the removal of laws and regulations that would impede capital or slow its circulation, such as environmental or workplace protections. While writing this piece the US Supreme Court gave a decision protecting Bayer from lawsuits over cancer related to glyphosate, the active ingredient in the company’s Roundup weedkiller. Ominously, it protects capital from having to warn about deadly ingredients in their products. Why worry about warnings when death is the point?

Snuff capital cannot even wait for people to die before treating them as if they are dead—killing them legislatively. The same month it was learned that the Trump administration had plans to falsely declare 2.7 million people dead as part of the government’s mass deportation efforts. According to a whistleblower, the White House planned to have people’s names and Social Security numbers added to the Death Master File which tracks when a person has died in order to stop government benefits.

While this was not implemented (this time) it shows us a workable model for future democidal policy under snuff capitalism. It can be done that quickly—with the stroke of a pen you are legally dead. Then, of course, literally.

This is the mindset of snuff. We must not be mistaken in the false hope that these experiments, intentions, innovations will stay at the level of the snuff fantasies of madmen.

In the realm of state force, we have already seen the death squads of ICE in action. Rapid and mobile murder infrastructures. Organized state gangsterism, the mode of the democidal state.

The litany of atrocities, and the ever growing roster getting set to launch from the starting blocks, come at us faster than we can enumerate. Every day, new horrors are announced to a reeling public. And that is as intended. We are meant to recoil in horror. Acceleration is the point and the way. It cannot be otherwise for capital desperate to accumulate, despairing for still more. It will not slow down. From the perspective of capital, it must not.

Acceleration itself is an attack on life. Humans (and other living beings for that matter) are not meant to live our lives at ever increasing speed. We are not built for it. It breaks us down mentally and physically. We cannot process, integrate, and act at the speed capital requires. We are built to live according to celestial time, not capital time.

The toll on life built into capitalist accelerationism is expressed in growing levels of physical ailment and disability (which have long been linked to capitalist time, like heart disease) and in epidemics of mental health problems, such as depression and suicide.

We see it too in the severe negative impacts on health, including deaths, associated with capital’s great rush to return to business as (more than) usual before COVID was over with and while it is still killing people. Capital moved with a speed that led many to forget COVID already, to act as if it is no longer dealing death. But for snuff capital, dealing death is the order of the day, so what does it matter?

What some refer to, rather cynically, as compassion fatigue, is not really about compassion at all. It is a reflection of people being overwhelmed psychologically and emotionally by the waves in which atrocities are unleased against us. The rapid streams of horrors we are faced with, even only as images and reports overwhelm the senses. We cannot properly process them. Our capacities for understanding are flooded.

Acceleration confronts us with new disasters, crises, atrocities, while we are still trying to analyze those that have already trampled us. At the same time democidal states cynically refer to compassion fatigue in justifying cuts to social services that might benefit the working class, especially the excluded sectors of the working class. People are tired of tax dollars going to support the “unproductive” they tell us. We can no longer afford sympathy for programs to help those who will not help themselves. Far from reflecting compassion fatigue among the working class broadly, these reflect the views of capital. Though we may recognize that some workers, having bought into the dog-eat-dog priorities of capital and its states, turning to fascist survivalism in the false hope of buying themselves some time.

Creating Roadblocks to Capitalist Accelerationism

One outcome, of course, is fatalism, demoralization, defeatism—what some today call “doomersim” or the all pervading belief that we are all condemned, no matter what we do. We have to avoid doomerism, but at the same time be honest about what confronts us. These are the realities we must face, and against which we must be fierce. Unfortunately, movements (anarchist as well as leftist) are still moving at the speed of a glacier.

Movements are still oriented towards literal dead ends. Social democracy, electoralism, “green new deals,” symbolic protests, demonstrations, making moral appeals to the immoral. Slow march politics that do nothing to stop the fast march to the graveyard.

Snuff capital is not open to reform. It has no interest in bargaining. And why should it, given the current imbalance of power in its favor. It is fully dedicated to the path it is, with full awareness and intent, pursuing. There is no reforming a system operated by and according to those who have determined that their existence is predicated on our extermination. In any event, you do not reform snuff.

We must be clear too that we cannot pursue our aims through the dominant, traditional structures of working class organizing—most notably through mainstream trade unions. Unions have been vehicles for negotiation with capital—vehicles for capitulation, accommodation, and containment within contracturalism.

We have long seen union responses to earlier forms of mechanization and automation—negotiated layoffs and severance packages. Union will cling to hopes of bargaining with snuff right up until the last worker is out the door. An illusion that you can slow the culling, while still allowing the culling to occur.

We need to remember once-familiar militant working-class methods from slow downs to sit downs, strikes and occupations. These are the great (often literal) roadblocks to capitalist speed. The sabotage that derails and dismantles. These are the exploited and oppressed pulling the emergency break. Not asking for capital to take its foot off the gas pedal.

Revolutionary rank-and-file action will be key as part of this, while we still have access to workplaces that we could win control of away from capital. And shut down as necessary. Before our place as workers is eliminated. Syndicalism, which has always taken a class-wide approach, is necessary as are its preferred tactics of militant direct action against (not in negotiation with) capital. To end the labor-capital structure. To snuff out capitalism before it snuffs out us.

title: La surveillance fait sa rentrée, Technopolice Lyon aussi !
content:
L'État en pleine surenchère sécuritaire, après l'

adoption de la loi 

RIPOST

 , envoie des drones et des armes de guerre contre les lycéen·nes. Pendant ce temps 

la métropole

 s'en donne aussi à coeur joie côté sécurité (qui ne relève pourtant pas de sa compétence mais la compétence n'est pas spécialement leur fort), et nos municipalités continuent à déployer le parc de caméras de surveillance pour outiller la police.




Bref c'est la rentrée et 2027 sent le soufre

 

!




Le

On vous invite à la Luttine à des temps d'échange, de partage et d'autoformation sur ces questions :


> mercredi 4 novembre, 19H : Tour d'horizon des outils de la Technopolice, Surveillance, Contrôle et Fichage, et répertoire des moyens de luttes. On revoit les bases et on met à jour nos connaissances sur des sujets divers comme les caméras, la 

VSA

, qui gère quoi en matière de sécurité, surveillance des manifs ou des outils numériques... L'occasion de faire un point sur nos droits, les bonnes pratiques et les outils de lutte (veille, documenter, cartographier, visibiliser...)

!) : la Demande d'Accès aux Documents Administratifs. Que trouve-t-on en «

 

open data

 

»

 

? Que demander, à qui et comment

 

? Quels sont nos droits et nos recours

 

? Comment exploiter les documents reçus

author: Brian Hioe
title: Army Suicide Reminds of Recurring Issues with Bullying and Hazing in the Military
content:
A RECENT CASE in which a female Army first lieutenant committed suicide is being investigated as a potential case of bullying. The first lieutenant in question, surnamed Wang, jumped to her death from a building at the Army’s 206th Brigade base in Hsinchu County on September 30th. An audio recording that was posted on Threads on October 12th shows a man berating Wang for failing to heed instructions, leading to the bullying allegations.

The Ministry of National Defense has vowed that the case is being investigated and that Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo is attentive to its developments. This would not be the only case in recent years in which a suicide in the military has been linked to bullying.

In November 2020, a similar case emerged of a corporal surnamed Liu stationed in the Eighth Army Command’s 203rd Brigade in Danei District, Tainan, who died by hanging. Liu, too, was reportedly bullied by his superiors and peers.

The most famous case of a death in the military thought to have resulted from bullying in the military would be the death of cadet Hung Chung-chiu in July 2013. Hung is thought to have been bullied by his superiors and peers shortly before his discharge from mandatory military service, as a form of hazing or as retribution against him before his service ended. The lack of government transparency in the wake of the death, with allegations of a cover-up, led to the Citizen 1985 movement, one of the major predecessor movements of the 2014 Sunflower Movement.

The government is likely sensitive to the optics of bullying in the military. The Hung Chung-chiu case, as well as the military’s perceived lack of transparency, is thought to be a major factor in public distrust in the military. This proves an important issue for the government at a time when it seeks to boost recruitment numbers, so as to counter rising Chinese threats.

At the same time, one notes that the military was an authoritarian institution during the many decades of the White Terror. In the course of the White Terror, the military served as the enforcer of the KMT state, and it conducted many of the political killings during the purges that took place then. Deaths due to bullying or hazing, as well as the cover-up of such deaths, were a common occurrence during the authoritarian era. In fact, incidents such as the Hung Chung-chiu case were relatively common during the authoritarian era and were mostly covered up, such that a single death in post-authoritarian Taiwan would garner such attention.

To this extent, one notes that cases of workplace bullying in government that have resulted in suicides have received greater scrutiny. Cases in point include the suicide of a civil servant surnamed Wu who worked in the Ministry of Labor in 2024. After the death of deputy trade representative Yen Huai-hsing in March at age 53, allegations that Yen was bullied by her superiors also emerged. Though such issues regarding workplace bullying have not always been put in the same frame as deaths in the military, insofar as both are, in some sense, public sector workers

author: Peter Boyle
title: NSW Parliamentary Friends of the Kurdish people launched
content:
NSW Parliamentary Friends of the Kurdish People was launched in NSW Parliament House on October 13. It has an initial membership of 11 MPs, including co-chairs Abigail Boyd (Greens), Anthony D’Adam MLC (Labor) and secretary Tim James MP (Liberal).

Gulfer Olan, co-chair of the Federation of Democratic Kurdish Society Australia, said this was “an historical milestone”.

Boyd explained that it took seven years and the hard work of many people to get to the Parliamentary Friends of the Kurdish People officially established. “I resonate with the spirit of the Kurdish community, your commitment to grassroots democracy, your commitment to gender equality and economic equality, your love of nature, the environment.”

D’Adam said: “We are one in commitment to democracy and human rights, the right to self-determination and the right to cultural autonomy... [this is] another marker of the status that this community now holds in Australian society as an important part of our multicultural community.”

He added that it is “a very important thing to acknowledge our multicultural society where people aren’t asked to surrender their culture and become part of a monoculture”.

“We are all Australians and we’re able to maintain our cultural identity and that’s something that’s really important. It’s important that we defend that at this time when, as we know, there are dark forces rising in our community that are threatening those very values that we hold here.”

Parliamentary Friends of the Kurdish People

Federation of Democratic Kurdish Society Australia

author: Ella Gutteridge
title: Hundreds protest far-right conference in Brisbane
content:
High-profile racists and far-right leaders descended on the Brisbane showgrounds over the weekend of 10 and 11 October for the Conservative Political Action Conference.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson headlined the event. She was joined by Liberal leader Angus Taylor, far-right podcaster Karl Stefanovic, and one of Britain’s least successful politicians, former Prime Minister Liz Truss.

Inside, it was a carnival of reaction. The ABC reported that 

Hanson was greeted with 

rapturous applause

 as she harangued the Coalition for signing up to net-zero and creating an eSafety commissioner, which she pledged to abolish on the grounds of free speech.

The leader of the National Party, Matt Canavan, cosplayed as a blue-collar worker as he took to the stage to extol the virtues of Australian manufacturing. Despite earlier criticisms, Hanson said that she’d be willing to work with the Coalition to “

throw out this wretched and corrupt Labor government

”.

Outside, hundreds of irreverent high schoolers, trade union activists and community members rallied, waving homemade signs, chanting and drumming. The crowd was a sea of keffiyehs, rainbow flags and signs, with many commenting on Hanson’s close relationship with Australian billionaire Gina Rinehart (“Pauline works for Gina!”).

“Migrants are welcome, racists are not!” was a popular chant, echoing across the showgrounds while conferencegoers streamed out for their lunch break. One Nation recently unveiled 

its policy to cut Australia’s immigration intake

 by 750,000 people over three years, including plans to cut visas for the family members of skilled migrants and international students to zero.

“Pauline Hanson wants net zero immigration, but my parents are immigrants, my friends are immigrants, and without them this country would be nothing and fuck Pauline!”, Sam, a high school student, told 

Red Flag

.  

The rally heard from Dave Pullen, an Indigenous elder from Inala who ran against Hanson in Ipswich in 1996. Draped in an Indigenous flag, Pullen opened with an acknowledgement of country and of Hanson’s long record of racism towards Indigenous people.

National convenor of the Socialist Party and teacher unionist Rebecca Barrigos highlighted the importance of posing an alternative socialist vision to One Nation and the broader right:

“Today’s rally isn’t just about sending a signal to those inside the conference; it’s about saying we know what you’re doing. They’re fighting for a more competitive, more brutal, more pro-billionaire, anti-worker vision of society, and to that we say, fuck your vision of society! We have an alternative vision.”

There is a long way to go to realise that vision. 

Hanson is currently the preferred prime minister to Anthony Albanese

 and is polling at 36 percent in Queensland. While the right has momentum, it still faces opposition. People who oppose One Nation’s vision for the world should rally to our side and put up a fight.

author: Kodao Productions
title: Peso dives to new record low
content:
The Philippine Peso dove to a new record low on Thursday, breaching past the P63 threshold per US dollar for the first time in history. The Peso-Dollar exchange rate closed at P63.15 per US greenback. The previous record was P62.925 per US dollar set exactly a month ago on September 15.




The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) cited a stronger US dollar, shifting expectations around US Federal Reserve rate cuts, and regional market pressures brought about by the prolonged war in the Middle East as the reasons for the dive.




The Philippine currency had lost P5.21 to the US dollar since the US-Israel led war against Iran started in February 28.




The new record low happened as the BSP played conservative in defending the peso against the volatile foreign exchange market, choosing to preserve its reserves and intervening only when movements become sharp and disorderly.




The BSP primarily uses the country’s Gross International Reserves to stabilize the Philippine peso against foreign exchange volatility and to service foreign debt obligations.




The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), meanwhile, said electronic products and petroleum products, such as crude oil and refined fuel are two top importations that drain the country’s foreign exchange and import outlays.




Much of the country’s reserves come from remittances from its millions of workers abroad, such as 2.4 million overseas laborers in the Middle East. There are about a million Filipinos in the UAE alone, contributing approximately P380 billion or $6.06 billion every year.




Local economic think-tank Ibon Foundation said that a record-low Philippine peso paired with high global oil and import prices creates a “double whammy” that aggressively drives up domestic inflation and worsens economic strain for Filipino households.




The PSA recently reported that the inflation rate in the Philippines was at a whopping 7.2 per cent last September, a sharp increase from 6.1 per cent last August.




Philippine oil industry sources have already announced a gasoline price increase of up to P4.30 per liter next week. # 

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

Peso dives to new record low

author: To be a name
title: In Gaza, even thinking has become a struggle
content:
I have thought carefully about how to write about my life in Gaza. Even speaking about what we experience requires caution. How can I tell the truth about my reality without putting myself at risk?

This question alone says something about what it means to live here.

My days have become a series of moments. in which survival takes priority over everything else.

At night, the sound of surveillance drones makes it difficult to think about anything beyond the possibility that we could be next. Even when the sky grows quiet, peace feels unreal. At night, closing my eyes no longer feels different from opening them.

Our homes are destroyed, yet we still hope to recover even one small belonging from the rubble.

We want something to carry from our past into a future we cannot imagine.

Sometimes, the movement of rats among the ruins makes us wonder whether danger has returned. Even animals seek shelter in the remains of our homes, while we cannot safely retrieve the things that once made those homes ours.

Then comes the daily search for drinking water.

In 2026, finding clean water should not be the greatest problem occupying a person's mind. Yet we wait in line, hoping to receive enough to get through the day. We think about studying, working, resting and finding moments of happiness, but every ordinary activity competes with the demands of survival. Even water becomes a calculation.

After a bombing, another family may enter the records of the dead. Their loss might become a headline for a few seconds, or pass almost unnoticed.

But those who knew them will remember their names, their voices and the lives they lived. Human beings should never have to meet an unspoken threshold of tragedy before their deaths are considered worthy of attention.

I see people carrying grief that no words can fully express.

I see destroyed homes, displaced neighbours and parents trying to comfort hungry children. I see people who have lost their work, their security and loved ones, yet still find reasons to smile. Their smiles do not mean the suffering has disappeared.

Sometimes, they are simply a way of remaining human.

Then, from far beyond Gaza, we see people raising Palestinian flags and speaking out against oppression and genocide. Their solidarity reminds us that we are not alone. It gives us a moment to feel pride, connection and hope.

We do not ask the world merely to witness our deaths. We ask it to recognise our lives: Our right to study, to find clean water, to enjoy ordinary moments, to protect our families and to imagine a future without fear.

I write not only for myself, but for the millions whose daily struggles may never become headlines.

Thank you to those who have not forgotten us. Your solidarity cannot undo our losses, but it reminds us that humanity has not abandoned us — and that we are still here, trying to live.

author: Josh Richman
title: In Memoriam: Barry Steinhardt
content:
Barry Steinhardt, a lifelong privacy champion and an early leader in the battle for digital civil liberties who served as EFF’s president in 1998-99, died last week at age 73.

 




A Connecticut native, Steinhardt led the Vermont and Pennsylvania affiliates of the American Civil Liberties Union before becoming associate director of the national ACLU. There, he helped spearhead the fight to overturn much of the Communications Decency Act, resulting in the U.S. Supreme Court’s landmark 

Reno v. ACLU

 

ruling in 1997.

 




When the internet was still young, 

Steinhardt 

became one of 

the first 

attorneys to 

specialize in the intersection of technology and privacy

. 

In early 1998 he took a leave of absence from the ACLU to become EFF’s president, and then returned to the ACLU in 1999.

 




In 2002 he founded the ACLU’s Program on Technology and Liberty. After retiring from the ACLU, he continued on as a senior advisor to London-based 

Privacy International

.

 




Steinhardt chaired the 2003 Computer Freedom and Privacy Conference and served on a wide variety of significant panels and boards, including the Department of Transportation’s Negotiated Rule Making on national driver’s license standards, the Advisory Committee to the US Census, and the Blue Ribbon Panel on Genetics of the National Conference of State Legislatures. He also was selected to be a member of the US delegation to the G-8 Government and Private Sector Tokyo conference on Cyber Crime and served as an advisor to the Czech Helsinki Committee. 

 




“Barry led many critical technology and civil liberties fights and was an important mentor to me and others in the field,” said EFF Executive Director Nicole Ozer. “Barry’s influential work across strategy to defend and advance privacy rights and safeguard people against surveillance has made its mark on the law and policy of our digital world and protected the rights and safety of people across the United States and around the world.”
