title: İstanbul: Selde can kaybı 4'e yükseldi, 5 kişi de kayıp
content:
İstanbul Valisi Davut Gül, 15 Ekim akşamüstü yaptığı açıklamada 3 kişinin yaşamını yitirdiğini, 5 kişi için kayıp başvurusu yapıldığını bildirdi. Gül'ün açıklamasının ardından Beykoz'da işçi Faik Şentürk'ün ölüm haberi geldi. 




Vali Gül, kurtarma ve sağlık çalışmalarına ilişkin şu bilgileri paylaştı: 







“7 hemşehrimiz tedavisi bittikten sonra taburcu oldu, 5 kişiyle ilgili kayıp başvurusu yapıldı. Arama çalışmaları devam ediyor.”







Gül, kentin normalleşmeye başladığını, hasar tespit çalışmalarının sürdüğünü ve zarar gören yurttaşlara ödemelerin en geç pazartesi günü başlatılacağını söyledi. 




84 yılın yağış rekoru kırıldı, 3 bin 50 kişi kurtarıldı




İçişleri Bakanı Mustafa Çiftçi, İstanbul'da yağışın bazı bölgelerde metrekareye 

272 kilograma

 ulaştığını açıkladı. İstanbul Valisi Davut Gül ise kentin 1942'den bu yana kaydedilen en yoğun yağışla karşı karşıya kaldığını söyledi.




Vali Gül'ün akşam saatlerinde verdiği bilgiye göre selde mahsur kalan 3 bin 50 kişi kurtarıldı. Kurtarılmayı bekleyen kimse kalmadığını belirten Gül, kayıp başvurusu yapılan 5 kişinin aranmasına devam edildiğini bildirdi. 




İstanbul'da 16 Ekim Cuma günü de okullarda eğitime ara verilecek. Erdoğan, sağanağın devam edeceğine ilişkin tahminler nedeniyle yurttaşlardan resmi uyarıları izlemelerini istedi. 




838 sigortalı hasar ihbarı




Türkiye Sigorta Birliği (TSB), 15 Ekim itibarıyla İstanbul'da sel ve su baskınları nedeniyle sigorta şirketlerine 838 hasar ihbarı yapıldığını açıkladı. Bunların 776'sı yangın sigortası, 62'si kasko kapsamında kaydedildi.




TSB Başkanı Ahmet Yaşar, Bursa, Kocaeli ve Yalova'daki başvurularla birlikte toplam ihbar sayısının 897'ye ulaştığını belirterek şöyle dedi:







“Bunlar, henüz ilk bildirimler. Önümüzdeki günlerde yeni ihbarların gelmesi ve ekspertiz çalışmalarının ilerlemesiyle hasarın gerçek boyutu daha net ortaya çıkacaktır.”







İstanbul Valisi Davut Gül de hasar tespit çalışmalarının sürdüğünü, selden zarar gören yurttaşlara yapılacak ödemelerin mümkünse cuma öğleden sonra, en geç 19 Ekim Pazartesi başlayacağını bildirdi.




Barajlarda bir günde 7,16 puan doluluk artışı




İstanbul Su ve Kanalizasyon İdaresi'nin (İSKİ) 15 Ekim saat 09.14'te yayımladığı verilere göre, bir gün önce yüzde 38,06 olarak ölçülen kente su sağlayan barajlardaki ortalama doluluk oranı  yüzde 45,22'ye çıktı.




Elmalı Barajı yüzde 100 doluluğa ulaşırken, doluluk Istrancalar 'da yüzde 84,2, Alibey'de yüzde 68,13, Darlık'ta yüzde 67,74 ve Ömerli'de yüzde 62,17 seviyesine yükseldi.




Diğer barajlardaki doluluk oranları Terkos'ta yüzde 34,64, Büyükçekmece'de yüzde 29,02, Sazlıdere'de yüzde 27,47, Kazandere'de yüzde 8,28 ve Pabuçdere'de yüzde 3,41 olarak kaydedildi.




Yağış öncesinde Elmalı Barajı'nın doluluğu yüzde 77,79 olarak  ölçülmüştü.




Elmalı Barajı tamamen doldu: Taşkın tehlikesi var mı?




Elmalı Barajı'nın yüzde 100 dolması, barajın yıkılma veya denetimsiz taşma tehlikesi altında olduğu anlamına gelmez. Barajların olağan su tahliye sistemleri bulunuyor. Ancak güvenliğin değerlendirilmesi için doluluk oranının yanında baraja gelen su miktarı, dolusavak kapasitesi ve aşağı havzadaki akış koşullarının da bilinmesi gerekiyor.




(AEK)

author: Amy Goodman
title: Regulation Should Target AI’s Current Harms, Not Superintelligence Possibilities
content:
A mix of science fiction and delusion distracts from the real harms that we’re seeing, says tech journalist Paris Marx.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

We speak with tech journalist Paris Marx about his new book, Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires. In the book, Marx exposes the deceptive ways tech companies are taking resources from vulnerable communities in order to build massive AI data centers. “We have seen the tech companies that, back in 2019, 2020, wanted us to see them as climate leaders … completely throw their targets out the window in order to pursue generative AI and this data center buildout,” says Marx. He notes that after failing to connect to electrical grids in the locations where they were building data centers, some AI companies have pivoted to building “on-site gas plants,” further increasing dependency on fossil fuels.

Tech companies “want us to believe” that AI models are “starting to become so powerful that within 10 years they could decide that they want to wipe out humanity or a significant chunk of humanity,” says Marx. “That is a mix of science fiction and delusion … and it is also a very effective way to distract from the real harms that we’re seeing from these generative AI products.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now! I’m Amy Goodman, with Nermeen Shaikh.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: With the midterms less than three weeks away, we continue to look at how AI data centers have emerged as a political flashpoint.

AMY GOODMAN: We’re joined now by the Canadian journalist Paris Marx, host of the award-winning Tech Won’t Save Us podcast, writes the Disconnect newsletter, author of the new book Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires. He’s joining us from St. John’s, Newfoundland.

And we just talked to Justin Pearson, taking on Elon Musk’s xAI data centers in Memphis. In fact, though, the largest concentration of data centers is in northern Virginia, as you write about. And Nermeen and I are speaking to you from New York, which has the only state moratorium on the building of data centers. Can you give us — can you put that battle in Memphis in the global picture? Why northern Virginia, for example, is there this massive concentration of data centers? It’s not one of the poorest areas in the country.

PARIS MARX: No, certainly not. It’s much more for historical reasons, right? Because a lot of that early work on the internet was happening in northern Virginia, you know, obviously, a lot of military spending that went into that. And, of course, for that reason, a lot of infrastructure, a lot of, you know, fiber infrastructure, connectivity infrastructure, data centers, certainly, over time, were built out in that area. And that, you know, kind of — that legacy continues to this day.

And so, you know, the people who live there in northern Virginia have really felt the effects of all of these data centers having been built out. And especially, you know, they have had data centers for a long time — right? — but one of the things I try to get to in the book is really the shift from data centers as they used to be, you know, in industrial areas, maybe not so much larger than other tenants that would be in those, you know, kind of industrial parks and things like that, to the hyperscale data centers that are just on a whole other scale. You know, the resource demands are just immense, as, of course, you know, Representative Justin Pearson was just talking about in Memphis, where they have really been feeling this firsthand. And I think, you know, because Elon Musk was involved, this really brought it to the attention of a lot more people, seeing the effects that come with one of these major data centers. But, obviously, in northern Virginia, people are feeling a lot of that.

But as we have seen this significant escalation in the construction of these hyperscale data centers, particularly in the past four to five years, and certainly since the generative AI boom really started to take off in 2023, we have seen not just many more communities in the United States seeing data centers planned or being constructed next to them, and feeling, you know, what comes with that, whether that is the increases in their electricity prices, the pressures on their water system, or just, you know, kind of the noise and light pollution that can come from living next to one of these infrastructures, but many more communities around the world are feeling that, too. And I think that’s part of the reason why we’re seeing this kind of collective backlash, you know, throughout the United States, but in many other parts of the world, against these data centers.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: So, Paris, let’s just — you know, to give people a sense of the scale of these data centers, there are 3,000 — more than 3,000 operational data centers in the U.S. now and about 1,500 that are being planned. So, why don’t you explain, if you could, why? Why so many, and why so quickly?

PARIS MARX: Yeah, absolutely. So, you know, we need data centers to process the types of things that we do online, you know, the digital services that we use. You know, of course, I’m connected to you digitally. That is likely going through a data center somewhere, right? So, it’s not to say that we need absolutely no data centers; we need to get rid of them all. I think there have certainly been benefits from the digital technologies that have arisen over the past few decades. But we have seen this continued escalation in the amount of computing power that the tech companies and the tech industry are demanding, right? And they make the products that they’re offering to people more computationally intensive.

And so, the real reason, you know, one of the key reasons at least, that we have seen this significant escalation over the past few years in the construction of data centers, because we really saw this start to take off in 2023, 2024, which is why it has become such a political flashpoint over the past 12 to 18 months, is really because of generative AI — right? — because of the chatbots and image generators that companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, but also Google, Microsoft, Amazon, have been pushing for the past few years, because, you know, for regular people who are not really into the technical side of things, it might just be like, “Oh, OK, this is a new service that these companies are offering,” but the reality is that these are much more computationally intensive than what, you know, these companies were offering before.

It takes a lot more computation to kind of create, you know, kind of a text response to a prompt that you’re putting in, or to generate an image or a video based on some prompts that you’re putting into the system. And that has meant they have needed to build so many more data centers so much more quickly and make those data centers even larger than they have in the past, which, again, is why so many people are, you know, seeing data centers arrive in their communities, just because these tech companies are looking for so many places to be able to locate them, places that are willing to, you know, have them become their neighbors. And they’re finding that increasingly a lot of communities are saying no to that.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: Well, one of the chapters in your book, Paris, is devoted to the climate impacts, which we heard about earlier from Justin in Memphis. So, the question — you know, obviously, America, the U.S., has exponentially more data centers than any country in the world. Now, China, which is also building, you know, massively data centers, though, again, nowhere near the number of what the U.S. has, they have been attempting to employ renewable energy to diminish the climate impacts of these data centers. In your research, do you see any indication that these tech companies are looking for more sustainable sources of energy?

PARIS MARX: Not in any significant way, right? Like, if you listen to what the tech companies say, they will certainly tell you that they’re investing a lot of money in renewable energy. You know, in the past, you know, last year in particular, they made a big push into nuclear energy, which, obviously, is very debatable whether it can be considered clean. But in their ledger, they would claim it is — right? — which is part of their way to say, like, you know, “Look, we’re trying to do this efficiently. We’re trying to do this sustainably.” And, you know, they will certainly talk about how they will reduce kind of the intensity of water use at a data center — right? — so, you know, kind of the total quantity that a data center itself will use. But then, when you look across the total number of data centers that they’re building out, their water use and their electricity use, as well, is just absolutely soaring.

But the real story here, if you think about the climate impact, is really their dependence on fossil fuels and their dependence on natural gas, in particular. And so, you know, in kind of ’23, ’24, we saw this real push for them to try to get connections to the grid in the various places where they were building out these data centers, right? But in many of those places, they have now exhausted those connections, right? The demand on the grid was so great that it became much more difficult to connect a data center in the kind of amount of time that they would need to connect it for it to come online to, you know, benefit their generative AI ambitions.

And so, what we’ve seen over the past year is a real pivot toward building on-site gas plants. You know, obviously, when we look at Memphis, there was the use of a lot of generators on site in order to power the data center. We have seen other data centers using that model, as well. But now, of course, increasingly they’re moving toward actually just building dedicated gas plants for the data centers, such that there was a report out recently that it’s something like 189 gigawatts of new gas capacity is in the pipeline in the United States just to power these data centers, which is just staggering to imagine, right?

You know, we have already seen our governments roll back on their climate ambitions. We have seen the tech companies that, back in 2019, 2020, wanted us to see them as climate leaders and, you know, as though they cared about climate change and taking action on that, completely throw their targets out the window in order to pursue generative AI and this data center buildout, regardless of the consequences that come of that. And, of course, you know, those are consequences that will be felt by everybody through, you know, how it’s going to make climate change worse. But again, as Representative Pearson was saying, we also see very clearly the local impacts of local air pollution on the people who live next to these data centers, as the people in Memphis are feeling, but also in many other communities where this is happening.

AMY GOODMAN: Paris Marx, I want to ask you about your critique of the legislation Senator Bernie Sanders is putting forward, certainly seen as an AI critic, a deep concern about what’s happening, and what’s happening so fast. Senator Sanders and Congressmember Greg Casar announced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act to stop AI oligarchs from building machines humans cannot control. It would permanently ban the development and deployment of superintelligent AI and temporarily pause advanced AI development until a federal regulator has established safety rules. They would also direct the U.S. to pursue international agreements to prevent superintelligence from being developed anywhere in the world. You are critical of this approach.

PARIS MARX: Yeah, absolutely. You know, I certainly welcome Senator Sanders’ work on the data center moratorium and trying to move that forward on a national level. I think that’s very important. And, you know, even when we look at the kind of superintelligence legislation and, you know, the discussion of kind of limiting or rolling back the further development of these AI models, I would also be on board with that, as well, but probably not for the same reasons that are being laid out in this legislation.

And so, to me, this feels like a response to these narratives that we have had for the past couple months now about, you know, the power and the threat that these AI models can pose to humanity. Right? You know, we have seen these tech companies and people who work at them come out and talk about how they feel or they believe — and, you know, they want us to believe, as well — that these models are getting to a place that they are starting to learn on their own, and they’re starting to become so powerful that within 10 years they could decide that they want to wipe out humanity or a significant chunk of humanity, and that is a real threat to, you know, our collective species, right?

And to me, quite frankly, I feel that that is a mix of science fiction and delusion on the part of the people who are running these companies, and it is also a very effective way to distract from the real harms that we’re seeing from these generative AI products, from the chatbots and image generators today. You know, for me, I think that, you know, kind of this future-focused stuff is an attempt to make sure that regulation is not targeting the things that people are actually feeling and that would actually restrict what the chatbots and the AI companies are doing right now, and, you know, rather, having the discussion being about something that might happen 10 years down the line, that I would argue is actually very unlikely and doesn’t reflect how the technology really works.

You know, what I would like to see, from a regulatory perspective, is not this focus on the superintelligence stuff, but, you know, the effects that — you know, as we’re seeing more reports, the effects that dependence on chatbots can have on people’s mental health, where we see them have mental health spirals because they have become dependent on these technologies; you know, the kind of deepfake crisis that we have seen, and really saw very clearly on Elon Musk’s platform and with the Grok chatbot at the beginning of the year; the questions about what dependence on chatbots and use of chatbots means for people’s ability to learn, to think critically, to kind of have these cognitive skills and to develop them properly.

You know, we can even go beyond that to the environmental impact of the data centers themselves, or, you know, the various other ways that we have seen chatbots used for people to try to harm themselves or to harm others — of course, in the case that we’re seeing here in Canada, where the shooter out in British Columbia earlier this year, in one of the worst mass shootings in our history, was actually using ChatGPT for eight months to help plan violent scenarios in that attack in particular, right up until the morning of the attack, when the shooter asked the chatbot what time school shootings tend to occur, and then, of course, went to carry out that act of mass violence.

And so, these are the things that I think that regulation should really be targeting, not these kind of more fantastical ideas of superintelligence that, you know, I think are really the product of kind of delusional and deceptive tech people.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: So, Paris, would you say that there is a distinction between your critique, which is a political economic critique of the technology, in addition to, of course, these horrifying incidents that you’ve recounted of present-day harms, and the scientific and technological potential of this, say, generative artificial intelligence? Or do you think even that potential that has been touted to us is misleading or an exaggeration?

PARIS MARX: Yeah, in my view, I do think the potential is severely overstated. You know, I think that when we look especially at how the tech industry tends to operate, it it operates on exaggeration — right? — in order to drive investment, in order to drive hype cycles, to get people interested in its products, to, you know, get a lot of media attention on what it’s doing, which is not to say that, you know, at the end of a shakeout — of course, there’s a lot of talk of whether there is an AI bubble and whether there’s overinvestment into generative AI and into data centers right now, and what might happen when there is a kind of market correction, you know, in that sector.

And I think that what we’ll find is that a lot of the places where the tech industry said that generative AI would be useful is actually not going to pan out in the long run. I think that there will certainly be some instances where, you know, certain sectors, certain companies find that it’s useful to use generative AI products. And even then, I think their use of the products will look very different than what we have today. You know, there’s obviously a big reliance and push to use centralized tools like ChatGPT or Claude from Anthropic, but, actually, I think we’ll see much more kind of use of the open-weight models, the kind of smaller models that are targeted to certain use cases that are obviously also less resource-demanding, which I think is how things are going to shake out.

But even then, I would say that, you know, I think that the usefulness of generative AI as a technology has been overstated. I think that the pursuit of it comes out of certain kind of ideological ideas that the tech companies have. You know, they want to build this, you know, kind of human brain within the computer, and to do that, you need larger and larger models. But that’s not necessarily the best way to actually develop AI for, you know, kind of benefiting the public, right? And one of the things that I took away from Karen Hao’s work, who I know you’ve had on the show, as well, and her book, Empire of AI, is that there are a lot of other ways you can approach AI, right? But a lot of the money that goes into AI development right now is focused on generative AI rather than these, you know, many other techniques or approaches that could actually be much, much better for the public, you know, be using far less resources, but the industry is not very interested in that right now.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: And finally, if you could talk about — because it seems to me that a number of people in the medical profession are very hopeful about the changes that generative AI will make possible in many, many different fields, and already, you know, the discovery of Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which is considered one of the most significant scientific achievements in the history of artificial intelligence. We have 30 seconds. Your response?

PARIS MARX: I am quite skeptical of many of these claims. You know, I think that we have, actually, a history of thinking that new technologies are going to make big changes in medical advances, and then they don’t deliver. And I would just point to, you know, in Canada, the auditor general in Ontario looked into these AI medical scribes, you know, the tools that transcribe conversations between patients and doctors, and found that in over half of cases, they were inserting false information, recording the wrong drugs, you know. And if this is kind of the basis of, you know, how — a patient’s medical history, that can really have some significant effects on, you know, how they are treated going forward, if their medical file is filled with false information about their history. So, again, I’m a bit skeptical on that point, as well.

AMY GOODMAN: Paris Marx, we want to thank you so much for being with us, author of the new book Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires, host of the award-winning Tech Won’t Save Us podcast. He writes the Disconnect newsletter.

A very happy birthday to Juan González! Tomorrow, on Friday, I’ll be at the Woodstock International Film Festival moderating a panel at 2:00. On Monday, at the Eileen Norris Cinema Theater at USC, the University of Southern California, we’ll be screening Steal This Story, Please!, about Democracy Now! And on October 26th and 27th in Colorado, first at CU Boulder, then at Fort Collins. Check our website, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Nermeen Shaikh.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

title: The Encampment Movement against Evictions and Gentrification : A Report from Madrid and Barcelona
content:
On September 23, 2026, Spanish authorities violently evicted Maricarmen Abascal, a disabled 87-year-old woman, from her home in Madrid following her long judicial struggle with a real estate company named Urbagestión. She had lived there for 70 years, but could not afford the latest rent increases. In response, 10,000 people took the streets in protest that day. Three days later, a much larger demonstration established an encampment in the Puerta del Sol square, which had been the site of the 

15-M movement

 in 2011, itself the trigger for the 

Occupy

 movement in the United States.




Maricarmen Abascal passed away on October 7 as a consequence of the stress resulting from the eviction. Protesters have continued to occupy the squares in many cities across the Iberian Peninsula. A general strike has been called for November 11.




Here, our correspondents in Madrid and Barcelona offer a view from within the movement against evictions and gentrification that has spread across Spain and Catalunya.







 




Anti-fascists gather to defend the housing encampment in Madrid’s Plaza del Sol, 2026.













The housing movement in Spain has a long and complex history. For any period that we might choose as a point of departure, there always exists a prior precedent that could serve just as well—so where we begin depends on how we wish to make sense of what is happening today, how we wish to narrate this story that is still being written in the streets. What follows, then, is an attempt, however insufficient and incomplete, to tell this story, in hopes that you can learn or be inspired by something from it and, in this way, become part of this story and build upon it wherever you live.




We could perhaps begin with the 

15-M movement

, which erupted a decade and a half ago as part of the sequence of uprisings that unfolded across the globe in 2011. Encampments spread across Spain much as they have today, full of people clamoring for “

real democracy

.”




Whereas elsewhere, repression often put these movements to an unresolved end, in Spain, this movement culminated with the formation of several far-left political parties, including Podemos, as well as strong municipalist movements in Madrid, Barcelona, and other cities. Today, these parties lie in ruins, while the municipalists have largely lost whatever power they once held. Ultimately, much like 

Occupy Wall Street

 and the Arab Spring, the true legacy of this sequence remains ambiguous, contested, and open to interpretation. Perhaps the 15-M movement is not the beginning of the story we’re telling, but simply the ruins from which the current one is being told.







 




Riot police are covered in eggs and paint while attempting to evict a building in Barcelona, 2021.










The movement that is now swelling across Spain emerged as a result of strong and stable union-style organizations that operate apart from the official institutional structures that are otherwise so present and influential in political life here. These organizations were built to tackle the housing crisis using horizontal and grassroots power, while simultaneously driving widespread and popular mobilizations like those we are witnessing today. These unions are novel in that they don’t involve questions of work directly, but rather address the conditions in which we live. The movement’s most significant antecedents lie in the creation of organizations such as the PAH (Platform for People Affected by Mortgages), the first chapter of which was founded in Barcelona in 2009. Like the more recently created housing organizations, the PAH groups practice what we call “social unionism.”




The premise is simple: an individual problem like a person facing the threat of losing their home is transformed into a collective issue addressed through shared political action. A variety of union-style tactics soon began to emerge, leading to the halting of many imminent evictions.







A group of thirty or so people assembles in front of an apartment in the historic city center as the sun is rising. People cling to one another tightly, locked arm in arm, crowding in front of the door of the building’s entrance while several vans of riot police pull up and park nearby as scheduled. There’s an announcement from a police loudspeaker to the effect that people must disperse, but no one does. Eventually, the cops move in, struggling to pull each person away one by one, until finally everyone has been cleared. In the end, the eviction is successful, but it takes several dozen police and several hours, slowing the pace of evictions and making it ever more costly and difficult for the city to execute them.




Those who took part in the defense are members the neighborhood’s tenants’ union. Afterwards, they head their separate ways, but then see one another again soon at their next meeting, reflect upon how the defense went, and make plans for the next one. Occasionally, they hold public gatherings, putting out folding chairs in a circle in a plaza or street where people from the neighborhood are invited to take turns describing the problems that they experience with their landlords or reflecting on the broader challenges they face. These people are young and old. Some are radicals with a depth of experiences in various social movements; others simply live nearby and don’t want to see their neighbors kicked out of their homes.




Similar scenes are unfolding across Spain with increasing regularity. It is possible to come across eviction defense actions unexpectedly as one goes on a morning walk to buy bread. They are becoming a part of the fabric of everyday life.







 




Members of the Tenants’ Union block the front of an apartment building to halt an eviction.













The 2008 crisis shifted the terrain upon which housing organizations operated by drastically transforming the Spanish real estate market. While at first, housing disputes centered on those who had mortgage agreements, changes in legislation and property structures eventually caused struggles around rent to take center stage. Tenants’ unions were founded in Madrid and Catalonia in 2017, a period that also saw the emergence of numerous other housing groups and significant disputes between them. These unions developed new organizing strategies, such as the organization and mobilization of entire apartment buildings and neighborhoods; they focused on organic growth by inviting people to become formal members and attend regular meetings in radical social centers, bookstores, and public spaces. Eviction by eviction, dispute by dispute, block by block: the social explosion of recent weeks is, in reality, the result of this patient work that unfolded over years, addressing a social issue that was bound to erupt sooner or later.




The current housing mobilizations cannot be understood without recognizing the presence of these grassroots organizations, which are the product of a deliberate political strategy by social movement activists—particularly those who come from the autonomous, libertarian, and communist traditions that operate outside of the standard institutional frameworks, which are now widely considered a dead end. This most recent cycle of mobilizations arguably began with a massive demonstration on October 13, 2024 under the slogan “Enough is enough. Let’s lower rents!” The massive scale of that event took many by surprise, including the activists themselves. Since then, other major mobilizations and high-profile evictions have laid the groundwork for the recent social upheaval.







 




A housing protest takes place in Barcelona in 2024. Its scale surprised even the organizers.













Thousands upon thousands of people pour into the streets. Some carry large banners; others light smoke flares that illuminate the crowd in the evening light and cause them to cheer. Every so often, people take their keys out of their pockets and shake them above their heads, displaying what has come to be symbol of the movement while creating a discordant chorus of metal clanking upon metal. Small groups of people weave in and out of the march with flat pieces of cardboard and cans of spray paint in their hands, decorating the bus stops, bank windows, and walls of the city with messages against the financial “vultures” that prey upon the housing market.




People are awakening to the possibility that this could be something more, something bigger, something with force.







 




A protester holds up their apartment keys, the symbol of the movement, 2026.













In societies with relatively low economic productivity, such as ours, capital seeks to extract profit from financial markets such as the housing market. This is a systemic phenomenon; people across the globe feel the pressure of it in their daily lives. It takes various forms: neighborhoods rapidly changing, being forced to move because housing has become unaffordable, being compelled to allocate an ever-larger share of their wages to housing costs. One can see organizations similar to our local housing unions in many other countries, as conflict inevitably follows capital wherever it goes.




All of this is palpable in people’s everyday lives. There are other equally important issues, the causes of which can be traced back to capitalism but which may not be so clearly linked to people’s daily experiences—for instance, the rising food prices caused by wars taking place thousands of kilometers away. But being evicted from your home or seeing your neighbor evicted is something very palpable, as it has immediate and tangible consequences.




It is also easy to identify the culprits: everyone knows that they are the police who physically remove people from their homes, the companies or landlords who request such actions, the judges who issue the orders, and the politicians who have created the legal framework that enables this to happen. The key success lies in having framed this as a political and social issue, through housing organizations and the political networks in which they are embedded. A future challenge, though significant work has already been done in this regard, is to link the struggle for housing with other struggles and the various other problems that people face.




As the state recedes as a horizon of political possibility, the potential of another way from below becomes more legible—it can be felt as more attainable and real.







 




Members of the Tenants’ Union block the front of an apartment building to halt an eviction.













A squatted social center faces eviction under the socialist government in Barcelona, and there is a call to defend the space. It’s a cold January at the opening of the year 2025. Neighbors have used the space for several years as an autonomously organized gym, meeting space, and library, but because it is close to the tourist area of the city, the local politicians want to tear it down. The people who have been active in L’Antiga Massana, named after the art school which previously had its home there, call for a series of demonstrations aiming to halt the eviction, but the police arrive without warning one morning to seal the doors shut.




Large crowds mobilize in the evening in an attempt to take back the building, but armies of police block the way, and the gathering concludes with street fighting throughout the neighborhood with fireworks and flares, until everyone eventually feels like they must call it a night and disperse. Another squatted space is tragically lost, and the city is transformed an inch further into a place not for living, but for shopping and tourism—not for sharing, but for capital.







 




Protesters mobilize to defend the squatted social center L’Antiga Massana, 2025.













In these tumultuous times, our political landscape has changed completely. It has been a total U-turn, one we welcome with great joy and which gives us a new momentum to fight harder and more effectively. We were experiencing a period of relative paralysis, during which we watched helplessly as fascism gained ground in Spain and across Europe. Now, we see the emergence of a massive social force eager to change everything. Suddenly, we are preparing for a general strike, something this country hasn’t seen in over a decade.




This strike, however, is not taking place under the circumstances we had hoped for. Parliament has been dissolved after failing to pass housing relief, and elections will be held on November 29—elections that the progressive media and left-wing parties will seek to frame as a national referendum on housing. The right will try to take advantage of this situation, trying to present the encampments and the government as two sides of the same coin. The socialist PSOE party in power has played its cards well, as it is in a position to capitalize—at least in the eyes of part of the general public—on what was initially a strong wave of protests against the government’s housing policies.




The right and the far right may well win the upcoming elections, or the socialists may survive this moment once again, but all this has shown that regardless of what happens, they will face a mobilized opposition on the streets. An opposition mobilized notony against fascism and the failures of the state, but as an autonomous force intent on securing material improvements for our class.







 




The Tenants’ Union holds a public assembly to organize the neighborhood.













The tenants’ unions continue to develop and grow—organizing within each neighborhood and regularly calling for public meetings, developing forms of solidarity, and reflecting upon their evolving strategies and tactics. These unions draw people together from across the political spectrum, bringing together people from socialist youth groups, independentist political parties, anarchists, and people with less clear political affiliations.




Another flashpoint emerges in Barcelona around Casa Orsola, a large apartment building in the residential area of the city that is home to several families, as speculators attempt to evict it so that it can be converted into short-term rental units. Demonstrations are called in order to defend the space; this draws hundreds of neighbors onto the streets on the day the police are expected to arrive. People of all ages and backgrounds can be seen gathering. Grandparents stand alongside their children and grandchildren in front of the building’s doors, while masked figures dressed all in black stalk the rooftop, ready for whatever might come. After a standoff that lasts all morning, the local government halts the eviction and declares its intention to purchase the building and convert it into public housing.




The local government sides with the movement, for now, hoping thus to bring calm and redirect some of its energy back into institutional frameworks.







 




Neighbors gather to defend Casa Orsola, 2025.













As the general strike is organized, there are already several forces that seek to steer it in this or that direction. The CCOO (Comisiones Obreras) and UGT (Unión General de Trabajadores), unions that have historically functioned as state proxies and buffers to suppress social conflict, have already announced that they are supporting the general strike. As the largest unions, their backing was crucial for ensuring strong participation in the strike—though, to an extent, this support was wrested from them, as it is not their natural stance. At the same time, it is equally important to push beyond the pacifying role these unions have played. The CCOO and UGT will seek to channel the strike into forms of civic expression and frame it as “the people” closing ranks with the left wing of the state, a narrative which we must resist.




The encampment and any future mobilizations must struggle to maintain their original spirit of challenging the status quo by opposing the entire parliamentary system, while specifically highlighting the hypocrisy of the progressive government and opposing the housing business and all the capitalist interests that profit from it.







 




Protesters mobilize to defend the squatted social center L’Antiga Massana, 2025.













The encampments that have spread across the country continue to blossom, building community kitchens, establishing info points to inform people about upcoming events and demonstrations, holding regular meetings and skillshares throughout the day. Occasional threats from far-right fascist groups give rise to anti-fascist demonstrations that defend the camps. The number of tents grows, and grows, and grows.




Various organizations establish themselves in the encampments, but most only last a few days before withdrawing again, confirming the encampment’s autonomous and horizontal form. In Madrid, an eviction is successfully halted after people from the encampment drive the police away. Then, a series of incredibly large demonstrations take place across Spain to build upon the energy of the movement, filling the centers of most large cities. Chants such as “Here are the anti-fascists!” and “A, Anti, Anticapitalista!” and “Long live the struggle of the working class!” suggest a broader horizon than the tenants’ struggle. The demonstration in Barcelona ends in a confrontation with the police, leading to a street battle that involves the improvised assembly of flaming barricades and the liberation of nearby construction materials, which participants throw at riot police and their vans as they retreat.




In the aftermath, people look towards the general strike as a moment to expand the movement and sharpen its intensity. The various groups that had developed to capacity to regularly organize neighborhood meetings around eviction defense now put these skills to use again by holding regular meetings with neighbors to prepare for the strike.







 




People build barricades after riot police halt a housing demonstration in Barcelona, 2026.













Across Europe, there is new life in the streets. Across France, 

students are in revolt

 against a state that has abandoned them. Recently, this revolt has spread to Belgium, and there are early signs of it in Italy—now [Albania’s education ministry has caught fire], and it may go further still.




To break out of the pincer movement in which the progressive government and the CCOO and UGT have trapped us here in Spain, we must ensure that upcoming mobilizations, especially the general strike in November, do not turn out the way they want them to. The streets must not fall in line behind any government. Both our demands and our forms of action must outflank all of these actors from the left, placing them once again in an untenable position. We need to become unacceptable to the institutional left within the state apparatus once more. Otherwise, the window for mobilization that has opened up could close far too soon. The general strike must not become the end of this story, but only one additional chapter, one which we here must struggle to leap past and continue to push beyond.







 




People build barricades after riot police halt a housing demonstration in Barcelona, 2026.













Further Reading




On the current encampment movement:







The Destituent Question of the Encampments




And Suddenly, a Jolt: Notes on the Fly from the Puerta del Sol Encampment

 (in Spanish)







On tenants’ unions and rent strikes:







Picking Fights: Seventeen Years of Organizing in the Seattle Solidarity Network




Rent Strike? A Strategic Appraisal of Rent Strikes throughout History

author: Daron Letts
title: Taloyoak’s new Pangniq High School unveiled with public ceremony
content:
Metalshop students at Taloyoak’s new $90-million Pangniq High School crafted the qulliq that will be lit at an unveiling ceremony set for Friday. 




The school overlooks the community from atop a raised plot of ground next to the airport.




Its stature in the landscape is mirrored by its name —  pangniq, an Inuktitut term for the most prominent bull in a caribou herd. Students helped choose that name as part of a contest last year.




“The school is outstanding — state of the art,” said first-year principal Rodney Drover Wednesday in a phone interview.




The school’s 16 staff members and 200 students from grades 7 to 12 began their fall semester in the 3,300-square-metre facility for the first time since 

construction

, which was completed on schedule, began in 2023.




It’s the fifth school completed by Iqaluit-based general contractor Pilitak Enterprises Ltd., Winnipeg-based Accutech Engineering Inc., and Parkin Architects, which has offices in Ontario and B.C.




The building blends traditional learning with technology that includes smartboards, microphone systems, and screens in every classroom, Drover said.
















“There’s not much that we don’t have,” he said, adding that the

 science lab is “what you would expect to find in a university.”




There’s also a culinary training facility and processing room, in which elders can lead students through lessons in skinning and breaking down country food.




Early in the semester, students used the brand-new stoves to cook muskox recipes. On Wednesday, they prepared seal dishes to serve at Friday’s public event.




The shop, overseen by instructor Bill Akerly, is equipped for carpentry, electrical, welding and other trades.




The building is designed to accommodate more than 400 students.




Friday’s ceremony includes two bands, accordian jigs, throatsinging and drumdancing.
















The gymnasium at Taloyoak’s new Pangniq High School is set up in anticipation of Friday’s public unveiling, which Premier John Main is expected to attend. (Photo courtesy of Rodney Drover)




Those on Friday’s guest list, which will include Nunavut Premier John Main and other MLAs, will be greeted by the natural light that floods into the foyer through large banks of north- and east-facing windows. 




Guests will be led on a private tour before doors open to the public at 2 p.m. A community feast is scheduled to follow at 3:30 p.m.




“[The school is] a wonderful gift to the community and, more importantly, the students,” Drover said.

title: Cómplices: quiénes son los diputados peronistas y de otros bloques que salvaron a Milei y al DNU 70/23
content:
Este jueves finalmente no hubo quórum para tratar en Diputados el DNU 70/23, así como tampoco emergencia en dispacidad y endeudamiento. Conocé uno por uno quiénes fueron los diputados que resultaron claves para impedir esta sesión.

 Por La Izquierda Diario.







Cuando el reloj marcó las 14:30 hs, quedó claro que este jueves no habría quórum para tratar el DNU 70/23, emergencia en discapacidad y endeudamiento familiar. El decreto, en particular, fue una herramienta fundacional de La Libertad Avanza que avanzó con desregulaciones a favor del mercado en múltiples áreas y favorece desde hace casi 3 años al lloby inmobiliario, de las prepagas, farmaceúticas y otros, afectando gravemente la vida de las mayorías populares.




En ese horario se llegó apenas a 121 presentes. Faltaron apenas 8 para el quórum. Los faltazos que ayudaron al gobierno de Milei y al poder económico fueron transversales y comprometieron a varios gobernadores del PJ, de los ex Juntos por el Cambio y hasta integrantes de Unión por la Patria.




Uno por uno, los responsables claves de no haber dado quórum fueron los 3 tucumanos del PJ de Osvaldo Jaldo (Medina, Noguera y Fernández), 1 de Salta de Gustavo Sáenz (Vega), 1 de Córdoba de Llaryora (Torres) , 2 jujeños de la UCR de Sadir (Rizzotti y Zigarán), 1 misionero de Passalaqcua (Vancsik), 2 santafesinos que respoden a Pullaro (Scaglia y Núñez). author: Chris Walker
title: Trump Tells MAGA Audience Leakers Should “Be Shot”
content:
Trump has a long history of deriding leakers and the press, accusing those who publish leaked stories of “treason.”

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump said Wednesday that anyone leaking information out of his own White House should face execution, in an escalation of violent rhetoric against leakers and journalists.

“Somebody leaked, some sleazebag. They ought to go to jail or be shot,” Trump told the audience.

Speaking at a campaign rally in Arizona on Wednesday, Trump framed his remarks in terms of the start of the war with Iran, “when they leak what time you’re going to attack a country,” the president said. However, no such “leak” has been confirmed to have occurred at that point in time.

After the war began, a White House leak revealed assessments from U.S. Defense intelligence that contradicted the president’s public claims about the impacts of initial strikes on Iran.

“The leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly. … To me, they’re the scum of the Earth,” the president added at the rally.

Trump: "In my opinion, leakers should be shot. In the old days we used to shoot leakers."

Trump also directed his ire against the free press, expressing disdain for journalists over their reporting on leaks from the White House.

“They’re almost as bad as a leaker,” Trump said.

Trump has previously attacked leakers within his own administration, bemoaning the publication of previously hidden information that casts him or others in his orbit in a negative light. In April, he threatened reporters with jail for reporting on details of a rescue mission near the start of the war.

“We have to find that leaker, because that’s a sick person. … The person that did the story will go to jail if he doesn’t say,” Trump said at the time.

In August, Trump threatened “leakers” with treason charges, stating in a Truth Social post that “Long term jail sentences will be sought!”

Treason is a charge punishable by death.

Reporting on leaks is critical for holding government officials accountable. The Pentagon Papers case in the 1970s, for example, divulged how “lies were the foundation of U.S. policy” in the lead-up to and during the Vietnam War, according to an explainer from Freedom of the Press Foundation.

The Pentagon Papers leak established an important Supreme Court precedent on press freedom, ensuring that government entities had to overcome a “very heavy burden” to deny publications of their right to print leaks for the public to see, including in instances involving national security or wartime secrets. Trump’s suggestion that leakers (and the press) should be jailed or even shot for their actions infringes on the right guaranteed by that decades-old precedent.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Dyepeson Martins
title: Chefe da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro esteve no Senado mas não votou na 6×1
content:
Enquanto governistas discursavam a favor do projeto que estabelecia o fim da escala de trabalho 6×1, parlamentares da oposição se reuniam para debater estratégias e discursos da campanha do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) à Presidência da República. A reunião durou mais de três horas e aconteceu no gabinete do líder do PL no Senado Federal e chefe da campanha de Flávio, Rogério Marinho (RN), que não compareceu ao plenário nem participou da votação da proposta — 

aprovada na noite de quarta-feira (14), como mostrou a 

Agência Pública

.

 Procurado pela reportagem, Marinho não retornou até a publicação. 
















Discussão e votação, em primeiro turno, da proposta de emenda à Constituição que acaba com a escala 6×1




Outros dois aliados de Flávio também não votaram: os senadores Sérgio Moro (PL-PR) e Marcio Bittar (PL-AC). O presidente do Congresso Nacional, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), que presidiu a sessão, não votou. Pelas regras do regimento interno do Senado, o presidente não vota. Entretanto, a norma permite que o parlamentar entregue o comando da Casa a outro senador para que este participe da votação. O texto foi aprovado em dois turnos por 75 votos a favor e um voto contrário: o do ex-vice-presidente da República, Hamilton Mourão (Republicanos-RS). 
















O senador Hamilton Mourão (Republicanos-RS) foi o único parlamentar a votar contra a PEC que acaba com a escala de trabalho 6×1 no Senado




Rogério Marinho é autor da Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC), apresentada em maio deste ano, que prevê uma jornada por regime de horas trabalhadas — alternativa da oposição à PEC que estabeleceu o fim da escala 6×1. Flávio Bolsonaro e seus aliados sempre se posicionaram contra a redução da jornada de trabalho sem impacto nos salários, por considerarem que isso representaria prejuízos econômicos à indústria. No entanto, diante da campanha governista e da mobilização popular em favor da proposta, Flávio recuou e afirmou que votaria a favor da aprovação do texto. A mudança foi anunciada na terça-feira (13), após ele visitar o pai, o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, que cumpre prisão domiciliar por tentativa de golpe de Estado. 



















Flávio Bolsonaro trocou a votação sobre o fim da escala 6×1 no Senado por um ato de campanha em Porto Alegre







O novo discurso foi reforçado durante a reunião no gabinete de Rogério Marinho. Além dele, três correligionários do PL estavam no encontro: os senadores Magno Malta (ES), Carlos Portinho (RJ) e o eleito José Medeiros (MT). Também estavam presentes três congressistas do PP: a senadora e ex-ministra da Agricultura de Jair Bolsonaro, Tereza Cristina (MS); o senador eleito e ex-presidente da Câmara dos Deputados, Arthur Lira (AL); e o deputado federal Ricardo Barros (PR), ministro da Saúde na gestão de Michel Temer. 




“A gente não pode deixar a narrativa nas mãos do adversário”, declarou à 

Pública

, sob reserva, um dos membros da reunião a respeito da mudança no discurso da campanha a menos de duas semanas para o segundo turno das eleições. “Foi uma decisão do presidente [Flávio] e o Lira também concordou”, completou o parlamentar. 




Questionado pela 

Pública

 após sair da reunião, Lira afirmou que não foi ao gabinete para tratar da PEC em votação.




Flávio Bolsonaro votou à distância enquanto participava de um ato político em Porto Alegre, no Rio Grande do Sul. Ele subiu ao palanque ao lado dos governadores eleitos Luciano Zucco (PL-RS) e Sérgio Moro (PL-PR); e dos governadores reeleitos Jorginho Mello (PL-SC) e Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos-SP). Na ocasião, afirmou aos apoiadores que o governo terá que “pagar a conta” do novo modelo de trabalho para compensar empresários que, segundo ele, estariam “quebrados”.




Senado conservador: “não teremos medo de realizar todas as mudanças necessárias”




Aliados de Flávio confirmaram à 

Pública

 que a campanha se reuniu, ao longo do último mês, com empresários para discutir as possíveis consequências da implantação da nova jornada de trabalho. A transição de 44 para 40 horas semanais será gradual e começará a valer dois meses após a promulgação da PEC —  função do presidente do Congresso. Durante o primeiro ano da nova regra, a jornada terá um limite de 42 horas. Após esse período, o limite passará a ser oficialmente de 40 horas. 




Diante disso, Flávio sinalizou ao setor empresarial que, caso eleito, pretende aplicar medidas “compensatórias”; entre elas, propostas legislativas que revertam os efeitos do fim da escala 6×1. As ações seriam possíveis com o apoio dos parlamentares do PL no Congresso Nacional. Em 2027, a legenda terá a maior bancada das duas casas: 28 senadores e 121 deputados. “Com um Senado conservador, não teremos medo de realizar todas as mudanças necessárias”, disse uma parlamentar da extrema-direita à reportagem, sob condição de anonimato. 




Após a imprensa revelar a articulação com representantes da indústria, contudo, o discurso da campanha tornou-se mais cauteloso. O senador Carlos Portinho (PL-RJ) declarou que a medida estudada por uma possível nova gestão bolsonarista é a desoneração da folha de pagamento. O benefício já é garantido a 17 setores da economia. Com ele, há uma diminuição expressiva no percentual de impostos pagos pelas empresas, decorrente de uma tributação baseada na receita bruta total, em vez de uma taxa fixa sobre o salário dos funcionários. 




“Como a gente não tem os dados [de possíveis prejuízos com a aprovação], não pode avaliar, a gente entende que a proposta para o trabalhador é um benefício. Para o setor produtivo, a gente terá instrumentos no futuro para tentar mitigar, o que só empiricamente a gente vai poder comprovar se houve dano ou não. A única coisa que falei aqui é que isso vai ser avaliado durante a execução da lei e vai ter impactos, é lógico. E, para mitigar o setor produtivo, pode voltar a desoneração da folha para tentar equilibrar essa relação”, declarou Portinho. 




Na Câmara dos Deputados, a oposição se manifestou de forma mais incisiva contra o novo modelo de trabalho. Durante a discussão do texto no Senado, o líder do PL na Câmara, Sóstenes Cavalcante (RJ), frisou que o partido defende a aprovação, no ano que vem, de uma PEC sobre jornada de trabalho por horas trabalhadas. Conforme o parlamentar, a proposta dará a opção de escolha entre a contratação baseada na Consolidação das Leis de Trabalho (CLT) ou por meio do modelo de Microempreendedor Individual (MEI). 




Mesmo com os votos favoráveis da oposição em meio a pressão eleitoral, o plenário do Senado foi tomado pela base governista. Uma semana antes da votação, parlamentares do PL ainda acreditavam que a pauta poderia ser adiada com uma possível reavaliação por parte de Davi Alcolumbre, em meio a negociações para se reeleger presidente do Congresso. 




A proposta estava parada no Senado desde maio de 2026, quando foi aprovada na Câmara dos Deputados. Desde então, Alcolumbre fez várias declarações afirmando que não se renderia às “pressões” para votar em pleno ano eleitoral. A postura mudou após negociações com a campanha de Lula, sobretudo com a intensificação da disputa pelo Planalto e os resultados desfavoráveis a Alcolumbre no primeiro turno das eleições. Os dois candidatos apoiados por ele no Amapá foram derrotados: o governador Clécio Luís (União) e o senador Randolfe Rodrigues (PT).




Um dia antes da sessão, parlamentares do PT discutiam nos bastidores a possibilidade de o presidente Lula comparecer ao Congresso para comemorar o resultado. O presidente, por sua vez, comemorou por meio de um vídeo publicado nas redes sociais. “Quero parabenizar o povo que foi para a rua, quero parabenizar os senadores e senadoras que votaram favorável porque o povo merece respeito e conquistou esse respeito”.

title: Kurdish Conference: The Kurdish question must be placed at the center of EU relations
content:
A session titled “The European Union, Turkey and the Kurds: Between Strategic Partnership and Democratic Expectations” was held as part of a Kurdish conference at the European Parliament.




The session was moderated by Hişyar Özsoy, a former member of parliament for the HDP (Peoples’ Democratic Party).




Speakers at the session included Li Andersson, a Finnish Member of the European Parliament and member of The Left group; Pernando Barrena, a Spanish MEP from The Left group; Vladimir Prebilič, a Slovenian representative from the Greens/European Free Alliance; Raziye Öztürk of the Asrın Law Office; and Eleonora Scala, a member of the International Bar Association’s Human Rights Institute from the United Kingdom.




The full conference can be watched here 







https://left.eu/events/20th-international-conference-the-european-union-turkey-the-middle-east-and-the-kurds/

left.eu







Li Andersson, in her remarks, drew particular attention to the European Union’s silence and inaction in the face of authoritarian regimes, stressing that resolving the Kurdish issue must be placed at the center of EU–Turkey relations.




Eleonora Scala shared several observations on behalf of the Independent Legal Mission for the Peace Process in Turkey, of which she is a member.




The mission was established under the auspices of the European Association of Lawyers for Democracy and World Human Rights (ELDH) and the Association for Democracy and International Law (MAD).




Raziye Öztürk of the Asrın Law Office said, “We are going through a process of historic importance,” adding: “We are at a stage where we are discussing whether it is possible to bring an end to a conflict that has continued for many years and to resolve the Kurdish question through democratic and political means. Yet, despite this major change, unfortunately, we still have to talk about the right to hope and, in connection with it, Europe’s policy towards Turkey and the Kurds.




This is because, as I will explain shortly with concrete examples, it is almost impossible to say that Europe has made any changes to its approach towards the Kurds.”

author: Jim McIlroy
title: ‘Wall of Tears’ memorialises Gaza’s lost children
content:
The Wall of Tears exhibition, memorialising the 18,500 children officially recorded as killed by Israeli forces over two years in Gaza from October 7, 2023, opened at the Pitt Street Uniting Church, in Sydney, on October 9.

The exhibition is supported by Amnesty International Australia (AIA) and Palestinian Christians in Australia. The 15-metre-long artwork is on loan from Perth Doctors Medical Aid for Palestine and is open to the public until October 28.

The Wall of Tears lists the names of children killed in Gaza between October 7, 2023, and July 19, 2025, alongside photographs and stories.

Barbara Gorman, convenor of AIA's Pennant Hills Action Group, told Green Left that the exhibition “confronts us with the human reality behind the devastating number of children killed in Gaza. Every name on this Wall represents a child, a life, a family and a future.

“We hope that by bringing the Wall to Sydney, people will take the time to see those names, reflect on the scale of this loss and remember the children behind the numbers.”

Created by United States artist Phil Buehler, the Wall was first displayed in Brooklyn, New York, in January. A replica was later brought to Australia and has been displayed in Western Australia and on the lawns of Parliament House in Canberra.

“If you approach from a distance, it looks almost like an abstract painting and that draws people in to see, what is that?” Buehler explained. “Then you’ll see they are names of the children killed in Gaza since October 7 and there are thousands of them...

“You see these faces full of joy and hope, snapshots from graduations and birthday parties and family gatherings and knowing that these kids’ lives were just cut short.

“I hope that might lead people to think about how they might help, even if it’s just, tak[ing] a photo of the mural and pass[ing] it along on their social media or to their friends.”

Guest speakers at the moving Sydney launch included international human rights lawyer Chris Sidoti; Dr Saira Hussain, four-time volunteer doctor in Gaza; and Suzan Wahhab, president of Palestinian Christians in Australia. Other speakers included representatives of Muslim, Christian, Jewish and Hindu faiths.

Sidoti told the audience, which numbered more than 100: "The Wall of Tears is about hope, not just tears. In singling out a list of individual children who were killed in Gaza, the Wall shows the true identity of these children, not just names."

Importantly, said Sidoti, the Wall lists children who have died directly from Israeli military attacks, not those who died of starvation and disease, or whose bodies have not been recovered so far.

Dr Hussain said: "Many more Palestinians in Gaza will die unless the Israeli attacks are stopped. This exhibition is part of the essential movement to end the Israeli genocide in Palestine.”

[Visit the Amnesty Internation Pennant Hills Action Group's website for opening hours.]

author: Sonali Kolhatkar
title: New Mexico’s Challenges Hold Lessons for the Struggle for Universal Child Care
content:
New Mexico is finding out that successfully providing universal child care requires giving teachers a living wage.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The state of New Mexico in 2025 made headlines for being the first in the nation to enact free universal child care. A 12-year-long grassroots push by advocacy groups and activists to address the dismal state of child well-being resulted in Gov. Michele Lujan Grisham signing a bill to expand eligibility for no-cost, government-provided child care to all the state’s residents, regardless of income.

It was a historic bill, one that paved the way for New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani to enact a similar program.

According to the Santa Fe New Mexican, enrollment in New Mexico’s government-provided child care centers jumped over the past year, with 15,000 new enrollees recorded since the program was launched. But waitlists are also growing as demand rapidly outpaces supply. And dire stories are emerging, such as Vox Media’s June 2026 story headlined “How to Screw Up Universal Childcare.”

Expanding free child care to meet growing need isn’t as simple as opening new facilities and enrolling families. Early childhood education requires well-trained staff who are paid generously enough to remain on the job. And that appears to be the biggest obstacle to fully realizing New Mexico’s pioneering program and ensuring that all those who need child care get it.

A June 2026 report by the child advocacy group New Mexico Voices for Children (NM Voices), examined every aspect of child well-being in the state including “early childhood education” — which is the term preferred by advocates to describe child care. The report concluded that, in spite of great strides, New Mexico was falling short in serving the families who need most help, and urged policy makers to “build on recent progress by strengthening the early childhood workforce, expanding access to high-quality programs and ensuring students receive the academic and social supports they need to succeed.”

Enrollment in New Mexico’s government-provided child care centers jumped over the past year, with 15,000 new enrollees recorded.

Matthew Henderson, executive director of OLÉ Education Fund, which helps organize child care workers, underscored how “the universal child care system is definitely something to celebrate, and we do celebrate it because it has given thousands of parents free child care, saving them tens of thousands of dollars.” And Gov. Lujan Grisham, who leaves office at the end of the year, has pinned her legacy to New Mexico’s early childhood education program and hopes it offers a model for the rest of the nation. She told the Associated Press, “My hope is, as we watch elections take hold around the country, that our congressional candidates are talking about these investments, our gubernatorial candidates are talking about these investments” in child care.

And yet, according to Henderson, “there are still parents who can’t access [the program] because the administration has not been smart about how to grow the state’s capacity.”

Child care workers, who are disproportionately low-income women of color, and who are charged with caring for the most vulnerable members of society, are also egregiously underpaid. Although New Mexico’s early educators are now compensated as much as $16-$19 an hour — which is higher than the state’s $12-an-hour minimum wage — it’s not nearly enough to prevent constant turnover and worker shortages.

The New Mexico Early Childhood Education and Care Department (ECECD), which is the government agency overseeing the state’s child care centers, announced a “wage and career lattice” for employees “to support long-term recruitment and retention.” Henderson lauded the approach as “really excellent,” but accused the administration of “slow-walking any attempts to implement professional compensation for the workforce.”

Teresa Madrid, executive director of a New Mexico-based advocacy organization called Partnership for Community Action agreed, telling the Santa Fe New Mexican that the “wage and career lattice is something that has been part of ECECD’s strategic plan for the last several years, and we are now in 2026 with no implementation, no action and no dollars committed to that wage and career lattice.”

The goal is to reach pay parity with K-12 teachers, because, as Henderson asked, “how can you create tons of new early educators if you’re paying poverty wages?”

It’s hard to answer why exactly the state is delaying pay raises for child care workers other than the fact that any major state-based program takes time and effort to properly manage and roll out. “I don’t know if it is a lack of respect for workers,” said Henderson. But “that’s certainly how a lot of our members are taking it.”

By delaying implementation of salary raises for child care workers, the state risks undermining one of the few programs that has made it past austerity arguments and the prevailing conservative desire to cut government-funded social programs.

Critics are applying the same arguments against New Mexico’s child care system as they do against things like health care for all: that making the program universal means some people who can afford to pay out-of-pocket could potentially benefit. New Mexico’s Republican Party refers to universal child care as “Nannies for Millionaires.”

But removing all income requirements is precisely what makes the program so attractive. Even families who were eligible for state-funded child care years ago did not apply for it until the program was expanded to everyone. “Only when it was announced that it was a universal program did it really change how people thought of it as a benefit for all, not just for lower-income people,” said Henderson. He attributed this to “perhaps a welfare stigma” around programs that require proof of income eligibility.

Instead, he suggested people begin thinking of early childhood education as part of what advocates call “the cradle to college system.” If K-12 public education is a state-funded right, one that ensures equity, access, and quality, then why not early childhood education?

And, just as K-12 education in New Mexico does not discriminate against immigrants, neither does the newly enacted child care program. “Universal,” means everyone, regardless of income or immigration status.

The sharp demand for child care is a clear indication of what families desperately need, especially at a time of ongoing economic insecurity. “We have people in our movement who are middle-class and say how their two young children getting free child care is now saving them $40,000 a year,” said Henderson.

States and cities looking to launch a similar program must plan for proper compensation of child care workers at the outset, and not as an afterthought.

The challenge for advocacy organizations like NM Voices and OLÉ Education Fund is to maintain strong pressure on the state to preserve and strengthen the universal child care program while countering arguments such as ballooning government costs. Any program delivering high-quality and necessary services for families will incur a significant price tag. And that, according to Henderson, is something people need to accept.

The child care program is currently about 10 percent of the state budget and growing, which Henderson said is “wonderful.” Still, he said, “it has created from more austerity-minded legislators, the sense that it’s too much, the budget can’t grow any further.” But in order to be properly enacted, more funding is needed to pay workers professional-level wages.

“It is not about logic with some people, it’s about power,” said Henderson. He affirmed that OLÉ Education Fund will “continue to organize early educators to have a strong, united voice so that they can really demand and get what they want.”

Advocates of universal child care all over the country are eyeing New Mexico’s rollout. Henderson advised that other states and cities looking to launch a similar program must plan for proper compensation of child care workers at the outset, and not as an afterthought. And if that raises the price tag, so be it.

“When you’re talking about hundreds of millions of dollars, people are going to fight about it,” said Henderson. “Even when it’s something that seems like an obvious public good, like child care, people are going to fight about it.”

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

title: Resistance against geothermal project in Varto: Court schedules site inspection for November
content:
Resistance against a planned geothermal power plant in the village of Xwarik in the Varto district of Muş province continues. For 165 days, local residents have maintained a protest vigil against the project proposed by the US-based company IGNIS H2 Energy. As the protests continue, the Administrative Court in Bingöl has set a new date for a court-ordered expert inspection of the project site.




Local residents filed a lawsuit against the power plant project on April 9, requesting a suspension of its implementation. On July 21, the court ordered an on-site inspection and the preparation of an expert report. After objections were raised to the inspection initially scheduled for October 8 over the need for a suitably qualified geophysicist, the inspection was postponed to November 2. The project site in the neighboring district of Karlıova is also scheduled to be examined on the same day.




DBP joins protest vigil




The protest vigil, initiated by the Youth Council of the Varto Ecology Platform, is being supported by different groups on a rotating basis. On the 164th day of protests, the local branch of the Democratic Regions Party (DBP) took over the vigil. A banner displayed by the protesters reads: “The people of Varto do not want a geothermal power plant. Hands off our water and our land.”




Aziz Oral, co-chair of the DBP district branch in Varto, welcomed the upcoming court inspection and reaffirmed his party’s support for the resistance. He said the ongoing destruction of nature was the result of policies pursued for years at the expense of ecological livelihoods.




“For us, ecology is not an issue that can be postponed. It concerns not only the future but also the present. When nature is damaged, it affects every aspect of our lives,” Oral stated.




“The struggle against the power plant project is therefore not merely a local issue. It also concerns people who have moved from Varto to major cities. We do not see the ecological struggle as separate from the struggle for life,” Oral said, announcing that the DBP would continue to actively participate in the protests. Meanwhile, the protest vigil in Xwarik continues, with supporters visiting in solidarity.

title: Lahur Şêx Cengî Talabanî sentenced to more than five years in prison
content:
Kurdish politician and former co-chair of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), Lahur Şêx Cengî Talabanî (Lahur Sheikh Jangi Talabani), has been sentenced to five years and three months in prison by a court in Sulaymaniyah. His lawyer confirmed the verdict to the news outlet The New Region on Thursday. Talabanî’s brother Polad was also sentenced to three years and six months in prison. The court handed down a two-year prison sentence to their close associate Rebwar Hamid Haci Gali.




Power struggle within the PUK




The case stems from a long-running power struggle within the PUK, one of the two dominant governing parties in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI). Lahur Şêx Cengî Talabanî led the party alongside Bafel Talabanî until he was removed from power in 2021. The two are cousins, and Bafel Talabanî remains the leader of the PUK. Another cousin, Qubad Talabanî, serves as deputy prime minister of the Kurdistan Region.




Following his removal from the party leadership, Lahur Şêx Cengî Talabanî founded the opposition People’s Front (Bereyî Gel). In August 2025, PUK-affiliated security forces deployed tanks and drones to arrest the politician at his residence in the Lalezar Hotel in Sulaymaniyah. The operation triggered hours of heavy fighting in a residential area of the city. According to official figures, two members of Talabanî’s staff and three members of the PUK security forces were killed. Other reports indicate a higher death toll.




Defense calls for an independent trial




Following the clashes, Lahur Şêx Cengî Talabanî, his brother Polad, and numerous others were arrested. A total of 27 people detained in connection with the fighting remain in prison. The trial had been repeatedly postponed since then.




Talabanî’s defense team had requested that the proceedings be transferred to Hewlêr (Erbil), where they believed a more transparent and fair trial could be held. His lawyers also criticized alleged human rights violations against detained members of his security team.
