title: Devrim Demir: Our relations with Rojava will continue
content:
The visits by a delegation of women traveling from North Kurdistan (Bakûrê Kurdistan) to Rojava are continuing.




On 7 October, the delegation crossed from North Kurdistan to Rojava and visited the Democratic Union Party (PYD) in the city of Kobanê. After being welcomed at the PYD headquarters, the delegation proceeded to the city municipality. This morning, the delegation first visited the Kongra Star headquarters, followed by visits to the university in Kobanê, the Kobanê Museum, the families of martyrs, the Martyrs’ Cemetery, and Miştenûr Hill.




The delegation consists of Devrim Demir, co-mayor of Mardin Metropolitan Municipality and co-spokesperson of the Diplomacy Committee for Local Administrations; Safiye Aladağ, co-mayor of Amed’s Yenişehir Municipality; Sevim Bîçîçî, co-mayor of Silvan (Farqîn) Municipality; Belkize Beştaş Epözdemir, co-mayor of Tatvan Municipality; and Ruken Demir, a member of the Diplomacy Committee.




Rojava needs support




Devrim Demir, co-mayor of Mardin Metropolitan Municipality and co-spokesperson of the Diplomacy Committee for Local Administrations, stated that they would further develop their relations with Rojava in the coming period.




Explaining that, as a delegation of women working in local government, they had visited Qamishlo, Amûdê, Kobanê, and Dêrik, as well as many other cities, Demir said: “Our aim is to further strengthen relations between North Kurdistan and Rojava and, through these relations, develop joint initiatives. The issue of integration is currently on the agenda in Rojava, and institutions are being integrated. The situation is the same in Bakûr. As a result of this visit, it became clear that strong support is needed, particularly in the field of local government. Everything in this city, from infrastructure to construction and urban development, needs to be reorganized.”




Emphasizing that they would turn the notes taken during the visit into a report, Demir continued: “Everything was noted down: what is needed and which areas are experiencing difficulties. In the plans we have prepared for the coming period, we intend to maintain our relations and continue mutual visits. This was our first visit, and it was very meaningful, but it will not be our last. So far, we have held meetings with approximately 30 institutions. We hope to help establish a support network, and we will make every effort to provide this support. In addition to relations between Bakûr and Rojava, we can also bring Rojava to the attention of the international community through our international connections.”




Concluding her remarks, Devrim Demir stressed that Rojava needs support in every possible form and that this support must also be provided at the international level. She stated that they would work to fulfill this responsibility.

title: Provocations in Hesekê and the importance of self-defence
content:
Hesekê (al-Hasakah) is one of Syria's most diverse cities, home to Kurds, Arabs, Syriacs/Assyrians, Armenians and other communities living side by side. Kurds are concentrated mainly in the Mufti and Salihiyê neighbourhoods, while Arabs predominantly live in Xiwêran, Neşva and Tel Hacer. Different communities live together in Aziziyê and parts of the city centre.




The question of how the city is governed is directly linked to how this multi-ethnic population is represented. The Autonomous Administration model, established in Rojava and regarded as an example for the world, is based on shared governance in which different sections of society have a say. The current Syrian Interim Government in Damascus, however, advocates a return to the mentality of the Ba'ath regime. Although the 29 January Agreement initiated an integration process between Damascus and the Autonomous Administration, the current government continues to refuse to recognise the political will, identity and cultural rights of the Kurds. The murders, attacks on symbols, attempts to occupy Kurdish neighbourhoods and armed incidents witnessed in Hesekê recently have reflected this mentality in the city.




Attacks have continued




One of the first concrete steps in the integration process was the appointment of Nureddin Isa Ahmed as Governor of Hesekê. The Damascus administration appointed Brigadier General Ziyad al-Ayesh as Special Presidential Representative to oversee the implementation of the agreement.




It was agreed that three brigades formed from fighters of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) would be incorporated into the Syrian army's 60th Division. In May, integrated brigade structures were established under the 60th and 72nd Divisions, with new arrangements introduced in Hesekê, Qamishlo, Dêrik and Kobanê. Procedures were also initiated to bring the Internal Security Forces (Asayish) under the Syrian Ministry of Interior.




However, these military and administrative arrangements did not eliminate political tensions in the city. Anti-Kurdish rhetoric and attacks on Kurdish symbols continued, while Damascus's direct involvement in managing developments provoked criticism.




Murders and armed attacks




One of the most serious attacks against Kurds took place on 10 September, when Sîpan Hiznî, a fighter with the Hesekê Brigade, was abducted and murdered. His killing heightened concerns about the safety of fighters integrated into the army and Kurds living in the city.




On 20 September, an Asayish patrol escorting oil tankers near Qurtuba University on the Qamishlo–Hesekê road came under armed attack. Two people on a motorcycle opened fire, killing Abdulaziz Faysal Hasan and injuring two employees of an oil company. Developments during the first two weeks of October provided the clearest example of Damascus directly organising provocations.




Provocation involving flags




Calls were made through television channels and social media for all Arabs in Hesekê to join a march against Kurds after Friday prayers on 2 October.




A march subsequently took place in the Xiwêran and Neşva neighbourhoods after prayers. A Kurdish flag was burned in the city centre, while Kurdish symbols, signs and security cameras were targeted. The attacks thus escalated into a direct assault on Kurdish identity and the presence of Kurds in public spaces. In the following days, marches were organised in Raqqa (Reqa) and Serêkaniyê, calling on Damascus to take "full control" of Hesekê.




Provocations involving flags had also been planned in Kobanê and Afrin (Efrîn) before the incidents in Hesekê. Footage circulated showing the Syrian flag being taken down during Newroz celebrations in Kobanê. Asayish announced that one person involved in the incident had been detained and referred to the judicial authorities. It was pointed out that the footage was being used to heighten tensions in other areas. Around the same time, Kurds returning from Newroz celebrations in Afrin were also attacked.




ISIS's secret haven: Xiwêran




Over the past 15 years, Xiwêran has emerged as a neighbourhood that actively supported ISIS. It is predominantly inhabited by Arabs. The neighbourhood also occupies a significant place in Hesekê's security concerns because of the presence of ISIS cells, the arrest of numerous ISIS members and the fact that nearly 3,000 ISIS members were previously held in prisons in the area. The fact that the provocations were planned in this neighbourhood is therefore particularly noteworthy.




On 8 October, jihadist groups once again gathered in Peace Square in the city centre, damaging Kurdish symbols, the square's information sign and security cameras. Public and private property was damaged during the provocation that began in Xiwêran. Asayish intervened to prevent the attacks from spreading to northern Hesekê and neighbourhoods inhabited by Kurds.




The background to the 9 October march




On 9 October, the city was effectively confronted with the mentality of ISIS. Preparations for the jihadist march showed that the mobilisation was not simply the result of a call issued that day. The failure to attract the expected turnout at the march held a week earlier, on 2 October, prompted preparations for another demonstration. Arabs from Hesekê, Shaddadi (Şeddadê), Serêkaniyê, Deir ez-Zor (Dêrazor), Mount Kizwan (Çiyayê Kizwan), Raqqa, Til Temir and villages around Til Birak were mobilised to travel to Hesekê. Pressure and threats were also used to secure participation in the march.




Damascus was directly responsible for planning the provocation. Between 1,000 and 1,200 soldiers were transferred to Hesekê from Serêkaniyê, Homs, Hama and Raqqa under the pretext of "defending the city". However, once the attacks began, they withdrew, waiting for a Kurdish-Arab war to break out.




The march was organised under the name "Syrian Flag Friday". However, the slogans chanted, the targeting of Kurdish symbols and attempts to enter Kurdish neighbourhoods demonstrated that the issue went far beyond demands concerning the flag. The coexistence of different peoples in Hesekê was rejected, while masked militants with long beards and turbans issued threats with swords and knives. They attacked Kurdish-owned homes and businesses in the market area. The organisers had planned for one million people to participate in the march, but reports indicated that approximately 2,000 people attended. Furthermore, the display of ISIS flags during the demonstration and the deliberate choice of Friday strongly evoked the ideology and practices of ISIS. Ultimately, the aim was to enter and occupy neighbourhoods inhabited by Kurds.




Damascus's monolithic mentality




The Turkish state and the Damascus government have long opposed the administration of Hesekê by institutions developed under Kurdish leadership. They are seeking to establish central government control over the whole of Rojava. This monolithic and undemocratic approach reveals an intention to eliminate the gains achieved by the Kurds rather than recognise them within a shared political structure.




Security concerns




The attacks were not limited to demonstrations. Three Kurdish brothers travelling in a vehicle displaying a Kurdish flag were targeted in an armed attack near the Industrial Junction. Sixteen-year-old Diyar Muhammed Sirac and his 20-year-old brother Nezir Muhammed Sirac were seriously injured and remain in life-threatening condition.




On 10 October, the Rojava FM team came under armed attack in the Salihiyê neighbourhood. One radio worker was injured, and the attackers fled the scene in the team's vehicle. Asayish launched an investigation to establish the circumstances of the attack and apprehend those responsible.




Threats against Kurdish neighbourhoods, attacks on Kurdish symbols and armed incidents have further heightened security concerns in the city. Nevertheless, residents are reportedly remaining vigilant and alert to these provocations.




Historical repression of mother tongue and identity




The attacks in Hesekê are a continuation of the policies of denial that Kurds have faced in the past. For many years, Kurds in Syria experienced restrictions on citizenship rights, denial of their identity and limitations on the public use of the Kurdish language. Measures prohibiting the use of Kurdish in education and public life were central elements of these policies.




The targeting of Kurdish symbols and threats to occupy Kurdish neighbourhoods today have brought these historical experiences back into focus.




Memories of 2004




The historical background to the developments in Hesekê also includes the attacks targeting Kurds in 2004. Incidents that began during a football match in Qamishlo on 12 March 2004 quickly developed into widespread protests centred on demands for Kurdish political and cultural rights. The protests spread to other cities, including Hesekê.




Kurdish-owned homes and businesses in Hesekê were targeted at the time. Homes and shops in the Xiwêran and Neşva neighbourhoods were looted, forcing many Kurds to move to other neighbourhoods.




Self-defence is essential




The murders, armed attacks, targeting of symbols and threats against neighbourhoods in Hesekê have once again brought the importance of self-defence to the forefront. The right of Kurds to protect their lives, identity and political gains has become a central issue in discussions about the city's current security situation.




Self-defence encompasses not only the protection of people's own living environments but also the defence of social solidarity and coexistence. Developing democratic and legitimate resistance against the mentality of the Syrian Interim Government, which refuses to recognise the will of the peoples and rejects their legitimate demands, remains a central aspect of the political struggle in Rojava. Ultimately, the future of Hesekê will be shaped by how the will of its peoples is recognised and how the political gains achieved in Rojava are addressed. Self-defence and solidarity therefore remain important elements of this political struggle.

title: Kurdish Conference at the European Parliament: The current opening creates an opportunity
content:
The second day of the Kurdish Conference held at the European Parliament began with opening speeches. Kariane Westrheim of the University of Bergen in Norway, Chair of the EU Turkey Civic Commission (EUTCC), which organized the 20th conference, delivered the first speech.




EUTCC 20 years: A voice for Kurdish rights, peace and democracy




Speaking via live video link during the first session, moderated by EUTCC Board Member Dersim Dağdeviren, Kariane Westrheim thanked everyone who had contributed to the conference, saying: “When EUTCC was founded in 2004, Turkey was at an important crossroads. Discussions regarding Turkey's European Union membership had begun, yet the resolution of the Kurdish issue—a central matter of democracy—had not been addressed. We acted with the awareness that this political initiative, detached from reality, would neither democratize Turkey nor resolve the Kurdish issue.”




After outlining the political changes and forms of participation since the conference’s inception, Kariane Westrheim also addressed the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process in Turkey.




Drawing attention to the progress made, the EUTCC Chair said, “Mr. Öcalan's name is openly discussed in European institutions today in connection with peace and a political settlement. His 2025 call for peace and a democratic society has been discussed by the European Parliament, which described the developments that followed as a historic opportunity.”




Westrheim further stated the following:




“We should not claim that EUTCC caused this transformation. The history is much larger than any one organisation. Kurdish political movements, Turkish political actors, human-rights organisations, European institutions and, above all, those directly involved in the conflict and peace initiatives have shaped it.




But EUTCC has been part of that history, and its contribution deserves recognition. EUTCC was founded around a simple but far-reaching idea: Turkey's relationship with Europe could not be separated from the Kurdish question. If Turkey was seeking membership of the European Union, then democracy, human rights, the rule of law and political freedoms could not stop at the Kurdish question.




From the beginning, EUTCC brought together European parliamentarians, lawyers, academics, human-rights defenders, journalists and representatives of civil society. Its annual conferences in Brussels created a European meeting place where people could exchange views, challenge each other and, importantly, continue the discussion when the political climate was difficult.




Over twenty years, governments changed. EU-Turkey relations changed. The conflict went through escalation and ceasefire. A peace process began and collapsed.




But EUTCC remained a constant European forum for discussing the Kurdish question. In the early years, much of the work focused on human rights and European standards.




The message was that Kurdish cultural and political rights were not simply an internal Turkish matter. They were connected to the democratic values and obligations Turkey had accepted through its relationship with Europe. But the question inevitably became larger: How can the conflict itself be ended?




That meant political dialogue. And it meant addressing the role of Mr. Öcalan. For many years, the idea that Mr. Öcalan could participate in a political solution was highly controversial. EUTCC increasingly argued that a sustainable settlement required dialogue with the relevant political actors.




This became particularly significant during the Oslo process 2009-2011 and later during the Imrali process 2013–2015 peace process. That process collapsed, and conflict returned. But the experience demonstrated something important: a conflict of this depth cannot be resolved through security measures alone. It requires a political dimension. That principle remains central today.




There is another aspect of EUTCC's history that deserves emphasis. EUTCC has never viewed the Kurdish question only through the borders of Turkey. Its conferences and networks have brought together voices and perspectives from all four parts of Kurdistan -Turkey, Syria, Iraq and Iran. This has given European audiences a broader understanding of the Kurdish experience, while recognising that each part of Kurdistan has its own political circumstances, history and challenges.




It has also helped strengthen a sense of Kurdish solidarity across borders. That is particularly important today. Because some of the most significant Kurdish achievements of recent decades are under pressure.




The Autonomous Administration of Northern and Eastern Syria (AANES) is a clear example. The Kurdish-led administration and the Syrian Democratic Forces played a major role in the defeat of ISIS and developed institutions of local self-government and political organisation. The experience has also placed women's political participation, women’s rights and equality at the center of public life, while seeking to include the region's Kurdish, Arab, Syriac, Armenian and other communities.




Today, many of those achievements face serious challenges. Territorial control and autonomous institutions have come under severe pressure, while the future of Kurdish self-rule and rights, political representation and decentralisation in Syria remains uncertain.




Whatever one's political position, the lesson is clear: Political achievements that take years to build can be lost very quickly. This is why Kurdish solidarity (or unity) matters—not as uniformity, and not as the disappearance of political differences, but as the ability to defend Kurdish fundamental rights and democratic achievements through dialogue and political cooperation.




The current opening creates an opportunity, but an opportunity is not yet a peace agreement.




When EUTCC was founded, few could have imagined the political language we hear today. We should approach this moment with hope, but also with realism. Peace cannot be taken for granted. The Kurdish achievements of recent decades cannot be taken for granted either.




That is why EUTCC still has a role. Today, the task is to help ensure that Europe supports the conditions for a democratic and lasting peace - and that hard-won rights and achievements are protected. Let us continue to build bridges. Let us defend dialogue when dialogue is difficult. Let us look ahead with determination.




And let us continue to believe that conflicts lasting generations can be transformed through political courage, democratic participation and peace.




Twenty years ago, EUTCC was founded because people believed that Europe had a responsibility. That responsibility remains. Twenty years behind us - and, hopefully, a new chapter of peace ahead of us.”




Öcalan’s message read out




Following Kariane Westrheim’s speech, a video presentation highlighting the past 20 years of Kurdish conferences at the European Parliament was screened. Afterward, a 

message

 sent by Abdullah Öcalan to the conference was read out.




Leyla Zana: Denial must now give way to recognition and acceptance




Leyla Zana, recipient of the European Parliament’s Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought, who was unable to attend the conference, sent a message. In the message read out by Kariane Westrheim, Zana stated: “A rare opportunity of historic significance has emerged for the peaceful resolution of the Kurdish question in Turkey. A powerful light of hope for the future has appeared at the end of the tunnel. Turning this light into reality is the shared responsibility of all political parties involved. It is also in everyone’s common interest. This responsibility rests with all sides.”




Stating that the process could become an unprecedented model of transformation if a just solution is achieved, Leyla Zana said: “The Kurdish people are not an instrument of the day-to-day interests of any institution, organization, or state. Nor can they be held hostage to relationships based on self-interest.




The political and legal issues that gave rise to the Kurdish question and have caused it to persist to this day must be addressed comprehensively, taking into account the relationship between cause and effect.”




“The policy of denial must end and be replaced by a policy of acceptance and recognition,” Leyla Zana said, drawing attention to the situation of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan, who has been incarcerated in İmralı Island Prison since 1999.




“In resolving an issue as complex as the Kurdish question, the role of an actor who has been deprived of the opportunity to meet and consult even with his own people for 28 years cannot be ignored. Mr. Öcalan must be able to communicate with his own people, and this longstanding issue must be resolved without further delay,” Zana underlined.




Shirin Ebadi: Mr. Öcalan showed great courage




The third speaker at the opening session, Nobel laureate and Iranian human rights activist Shirin Ebadi, who is also a patron of the conference, said, “First of all, I would like to express my gratitude and appreciation to Mr. Öcalan for his contributions to the organization of this conference.”




Expressing her hope that Kurdish rights would be recognized not only in Turkey but throughout the Middle East, Shirin Ebadi stated: “I would like to draw your attention to the following point: Politics is a constantly ever-changing science. This means that a method that works and is appropriate in politics today may no longer be suitable five years from now. Circumstances can change. Therefore, methods and decisions must also change in accordance with those circumstances.”




Emphasizing that Öcalan had demonstrated the courage to recognize these changes, Shirin Ebadi said: “I commend Mr. Öcalan for having the courage to recognize this change. Realizing that circumstances no longer allow for armed struggle, he decided to pursue the struggle with the pen rather than with weapons. In my opinion, this is an entirely correct decision.”




Drawing attention to the situation in Iran, Shirin Ebadi said: “Our country is home to different communities, including Kurds, Baloch, Azerbaijanis, and Arabs. Unfortunately, the Islamic Republic of Iran does not officially recognize the languages of these peoples.




These communities, including the Kurds, should be able to learn, read, and write in their own languages alongside Persian. Persian may be our common language, but every community must have the right to learn and use their own language in the country where they live.”




Addressing human rights violations in Iran, Shirin Ebadi emphasized that the number of executions was far higher than reflected in official reports and that a large proportion of those executed belonged to ethnic minorities.




“The reason for this is that ethnic minorities are treated with suspicion. When I was there, people even used to joke that every baby born in Kurdistan was born with a five- or six-year prison sentence,” Ebadi said, highlighting the severity of the situation in Iran and the repression faced by Kurds.




Finally, Shirin Ebadi expressed her hope that Abdullah Öcalan would also attend next year’s conference, stating: “By releasing Abdullah Öcalan, the state would take an important step, and the EU accession process would also be shortened.”




UN mediator: Peace is possible




Mark Muller KC, a senior mediation adviser to the United Nations and Director of the International Norms Project at the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE), from the United Kingdom, said that he had worked in many parts of the world and could now speak openly about these issues, having stepped away from his official role.




Muller said: “For the past 10 years, I have served as a senior mediation adviser to the United Nations. I have helped facilitate peace processes in Syria, Yemen, Sudan, and many other places.




Due to the nature of my position, I was not free to speak publicly about the conflicts concerned. However, as I am currently taking a break from my duties, I can now speak more freely in public.




Over the past 10 years, I have witnessed firsthand how peace can be achieved and why, in some cases, it cannot. Today, I have a few observations I would like to share with you.




First, I would like to say this: Whether in Syria or Turkey, the Kurdish conflicts are not intractable or beyond reconciliation. Solutions do exist.




Both the Turkish government and the Kurdish side have put forward their political and constitutional demands. Although there are serious obstacles to overcome in the peace process, none of these demands appear incompatible with those of the other side or impossible to reconcile.




The parties came very close to reaching an agreement in 2011 and again in 2015. The outlines of an agreement existed then, and they still exist today.




There is much work to be done in the current peace process, as there was in previous initiatives. Greater efforts are needed.




Moreover, both political leaders in Turkey and Kurdish political leaders have the ability to bring their constituencies on board and ensure that such an agreement is implemented.




I also believe that those who support peace constitute a majority in both Turkish and Kurdish societies. I think there is also strong support for peace within the Turkish Parliament.




The first message I want to convey to you today is this: Peace is possible. We can achieve peace not only within our lifetimes but also within this decade. For this to happen, all parties must demonstrate political will.




My second message is this: Over the past 40 years, we human rights defenders and mediators have learned that there can be no military solution to this conflict. However, a peaceful solution will also remain impossible unless all parties address one another’s concerns and open the door to a new era.




Negotiating peace is never easy. It requires all parties to understand one another and be willing to compromise. But there is no greater achievement than the peace that can be attained.”




'Abdullah Öcalan’s role is critical'




Muller pointed out that: “Whether the public authorities wish to acknowledge it or not, the role played by Abdullah Öcalan is critical not only in promoting disarmament and reintegration into society but also in fostering reconciliation and renewal.




“It is not my place to tell Turkey how it should approach this issue. However, as one of Abdullah Öcalan’s former lawyers before the European Court of Human Rights, it is my duty to point out that the court’s ruling concerning his conditions of detention has yet to be implemented,” he said.




Drawing particular attention to the Right to Hope, Muller concluded his remarks by stating, “Peace is possible; all that is needed is the political will to achieve it.”




Jongerden: For now, we are only talking about a process




Speaking at the same session, Professor Joost Jongerden of Wageningen University in the Netherlands delivered a presentation titled “Twenty years of dialogue and debate: EUTCC conferences in the context of developments in Europe and the Middle East.”




Jongerden noted that the PKK’s decision to lay down and burn its weapons was a symbolic step, emphasizing that legal arrangements were also needed from the other side.




Jongerden said: “There is hope that the process will ultimately produce concrete results. However, unfulfilled promises and repeatedly deferred hopes have created a state of limbo in which neither peace nor war fully prevails.




Perhaps this is why many people do not yet describe what is happening as a ‘peace process’, but simply as a ‘process’. Because there is still no definitive adjective to describe it. For now, we are only talking about a process.




To understand the uncertainty we find ourselves in, it would be useful to look beyond the present and examine the long history of previous initiatives aimed at finding a peaceful solution to the Kurdish question in Turkey.”




Recalling the steps previously taken by the PKK, its ceasefire declarations, and efforts to find a solution, Jongerden recalled that the initiatives undertaken so far had been unsuccessful.




“I believe there are two obstacles to a political solution,” Jongerden said, identifying them as the framing of the issue as “terrorism” and the Turkish state’s historical preference for military approaches in dealing with the Kurdish movement. He noted that these factors had contributed to the failure of previous processes.




Jongerden emphasized that Turkey must undergo comprehensive democratization for the current process to succeed.

title: KJAR calls for freedom for Varisheh Moradi and international action against executions in Iran
content:
The Community of Free Women of East Kurdistan (KJAR) condemned the renewed death sentence against Kurdish political prisoner Varisheh Moradi as a deliberate act of revenge by the Iranian regime against the women’s movement. In a statement on Thursday, the organization described the decision as a continuation of state repression against women fighting for freedom and self-determination. It also demanded the immediate annulment of all death sentences and the release of political prisoners sentenced to death.




“The renewed death sentence against Varisheh Moradi reflects the regime’s fear of women’s political will and the ‘Jin, Jiyan, Azadî’ [Woman, Life, Freedom] movement,” KJAR stated, stressing that this determination would not bow to oppression, repression, or inhumane sentences such as the death penalty.




Resistance against the Iranian judiciary




Moradi, herself a member of KJAR, appeared again on Wednesday before Branch 15 of the Revolutionary Court in Tehran, presided over by the notorious judge Abolqasem Salavati, and was sentenced to death for alleged membership in an “insurgent group.” The women’s movement of Rojhilat views this as an attempt to suppress the political struggles of women resisting oppression through repeated court proceedings and death sentences.




Moradi has been imprisoned in Iran for more than three years. During this time, she has been subjected to severe physical and psychological torture. She has also been denied access to medical treatment and contact with her family. Despite the conditions of her imprisonment and the threat of execution, Moradi has remained steadfast in her convictions. She does not recognize Iran’s Revolutionary Courts as legitimate institutions, thereby also challenging the legality of the proceedings against her. KJAR praised her stance as an expression of revolutionary resistance that cannot be broken even by death sentences.




Call for international action




KJAR holds the Iranian judiciary and the regime’s security forces directly responsible for Moradi’s life and her physical and psychological well-being. It remarked that the repeated summonses and renewed imposition of the death penalty are part of a systematic policy of intimidation and retaliation against politically active women.




KJAR also issued an urgent appeal to international human rights organizations, women’s movements, and the democratic public: “We call on all international human rights organizations, women’s organizations, freedom-oriented forces, and the public not to remain silent in the face of the machinery of repression and executions, but to raise their voices to demand the immediate annulment of all death sentences and the unconditional release of Varisheh Moradi and all political prisoners sentenced to death.”




Background




Varisheh (also Warisha) Moradi, also known as Ciwana Sine, a member of the East Kurdistan Free Women’s Society (KJAR) from Sanandaj, Kurdistan Province, was arrested by the Ministry of Intelligence on 1 August 2023 at the entrance to Sanandaj upon her return from Kermanshah, Kermanshah Province, where she had been involved in political and organisational activities.




She spent the first 13 days of her detention in the detention centre of this security institution in Sanandaj, and was then transferred to Ward 209 of Evin Prison in Tehran.




During this period, she was subjected to pressure and threats to make forced confessions, and on 26 December 2023, after five months of solitary confinement, she was transferred to the women’s ward of Evin Prison.




On 10 October 2024, coinciding with the World Day Against the Death Penalty, Moradi went on a 20-day hunger strike in Tehran’s Evin Prison to protest the issuing and execution of death sentences by the Islamic Republic of Iran.




Due to digestive complications following the hunger strike, she was transferred to a medical facility outside the prison, and returned after spending one night under care.




The death penalty, handed down by Judge Abolghassem Salavati, followed two court hearings on 16 June and 5 October 2024, and the death sentence was formally notified to Moradi’s lawyers on 10 November 2024.




During the court hearings, Moradi was denied the right to defend herself, and the judge barred her lawyers from presenting a defence.




Additionally, the lawyers, who had previously been prevented from reviewing the case file, were only allowed a few hours to review the case after the second hearing.




Moradi’s death sentence contradicts an earlier indictment that referred to Article 288 of the Islamic Penal Code, which provides for a maximum sentence of 15 years’ imprisonment. However, in an illegal ruling, Judge Salavati cited Article 287, which allows for the imposition of the death penalty in cases where individuals are involved in armed rebellion against the Islamic Republic.




Additionally, in October 2024, Moradi and several other female political prisoners in Evin’s women’s ward were sentenced

 

to six months in prison by the Second Criminal Court of the Qods Judicial Complex in Tehran, presided over by Judge Abolfazl Ameri, on charges of “disturbing prison order”.




Moradi’s case has been referred to Branch Nine of the Supreme Court and is currently under review following her appeal against the death sentence.




Moradi is being denied access to vital medical care despite suffering from serious health conditions, including a herniated cervical disc and spinal canal stenosis.




In March 2024, Moradi was examined by a neurologist and both the specialist and the medical team at Evin Prison recommended immediate surgery. However, prison authorities have so far refused to allow her transfer to a hospital. Her condition has since worsened, leading to numbness and chronic pain in her right hand.




The political prisoner also developed gastrointestinal issues following a 20-day hunger strike in October 2024, for which she received no medical care for several months. It was only after mounting pressure from international human rights organisations that she was taken to a medical centre outside the prison for examination and treatment about two months ago.

title: U.S. Sanctions ICC in a Bid to Avoid "Criminal Liability": War Crimes Prosecutor Reed Brody
content:
The Trump administration on Friday placed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court that target the institution as a whole. This comes on top of earlier sanctions against individual 

ICC

 judges and personnel. The administration has been escalating attacks on the 

ICC

 since the court issued arrest warrants in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant. It announced the sanctions just hours after former 

ICC

 Judge Navi Pillay — the South African jurist who led the United Nations commission of inquiry that concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza — was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.




“This is really an insurance policy against accountability for crimes that the United States and its ally Israel are committing in plain sight,” says war crimes prosecutor Reed Brody, a member of the International Commission of Jurists. The sanctions, which prevent U.S.-based banks and companies from transacting with the 

ICC

, constitute an “existential attack” on the court, he says.

title: A Massa Carrara maxi-corteo: 15mila in piazza contro l’ondata di denunce, “si cerca di limitare il dissenso impedendo le manifestazioni”
content:
Almeno 15mila persone

 hanno sfilato per le strade di Massa Carrara nella giornata di mercoledì 15 ottobre, giorno in cui si sarebbe dovuta tenere la 

prima udienza

 a carico dei manifestanti colpiti dall’andata repressiva contro il movimento per la Palestina.




Da Radio Onda d’Urto




Il governo Meloni, a botte di 

decreti sicurezza

, ha cercato di mettere un freno alla straordinaria partecipazione alle proteste che hanno attraversato in particolare l’autunno 2025 in Italia. A Massa uno 

spropositato numero di denunce

 – almeno 37 – sono state comminate contro altrettanti attivisti e attiviste massesi. La prima udienza a carico dei manifestanti, che si sarebbe dovuta tenere ieri, è slittata a marzo 2027:




Quella di ieri, afferma il segretario generale della Cgil di Massa Carrara 

Nicola Del Vecchio ai microfoni di Radio Onda d’Urto

, “è stata una manifestazione non solo per esprimere solidarietà agli indagati, ma anche per denunciare quello che sta accadendo nel paese. 

Si cerca di limitare il dissenso impedendo le manifestazioni

. Dobbiamo continuare ad indignarci di fronte alle ingiustizie esattamente come facemmo lo scorso ottobre”. Di fronte a un genocidio, dice dalla piazza, “non possiamo voltarci dall’altra parte”.




“Viviamo in un contesto gravissimo, 

un contesto segnato dalle disuguaglianze che stanno sempre più aumentando

”, e “c’è una deriva bellicista che toglie risorse alla sanità, ai trasporti, alla scuola per buttarle via nelle armi. Se di fronte a tutto questo le persone vogliono dissentire, vogliono manifestare pacificamente come previsto dalla Costituzione, ecco i Decreti Sicurezza: questo è inaccettabile”, ha detto Rossano Rossi, segretario generale della Cgil Toscana, alla partenza del corteo nell’ambito della giornata di sciopero generale regionale indetta dal sindacato.




Ai sindacati, si sono uniti migliaia di giovani, studenti e studentesse, organizzazioni e singoli cittadini. 

L’intervista a Nicola Del Vecchio, segretario generale della Cgil Massa Carrara.

author: Unknown
title: Mobilitazioni studentesche in Albania
content:
Raccogliamo alcune testimonianze inviateci dall’Albania riguardo alle recenti mobilitazioni studentesche.




Ieri, a Tirana, il conflitto è proseguito non solo come il martedì, ma con un’intensità ancora maggiore. Fiamme e barricate. La giornata è iniziata con il boicottaggio delle lezioni da parte di studenti delle scuole superiori e universitari per scendere in strada. L’appuntamento studentesco per la manifestazione era fissato alle 14, ma spontaneamente la giornata è cominciata molto prima. Barricate, tentativi di sabotare i mezzi della repressione, ruote degli idranti lacerate. Prima tappa al Ministero dell’Istruzione, con un tentativo di incendiarlo. Scontri. L’atmosfera è elettrizzante, piena di entusiasmo, travolgente. Ragazze e ragazzi travisati salutano, in segno di rispetto, donne anziane che li sostengono.




Arrivano le 14. Vengono incendiate le sedi di istituti di credito privati che hanno rovinato famiglie intere, portando a suicidi. Si fa irruzione, a spinta, nei palazzi governativi, usando pali sradicati e improvvisati come arieti. Divampano incendi nel Ministero dell’Economia, nel palazzo del Primo ministro e in Parlamento: principi d’incendio, poi spenti. Fa eccezione il palazzo del Ministero della Giustizia, incendiato, tra video virali e una folla che esulta.




La protesta continua anche al calar del sole. Telecamere divelte. Nei quartieri popolari viene devastata la sede di Intesa Sanpaolo, che opera, né più né meno, come un istituto di credito oppressivo e neocoloniale. Distrutta la sede centrale della Banca di Tirana. Gli arresti vengono impediti. Ragazze con passamontagna che ballano con anziani in abito tradizionale. Scontri con le guardie: chi le dà, chi le prende. Scudi rubati, auto della polizia incendiate. Distrutto un commissariato, uno dei tanti in cui, in questi mesi, i manifestanti venivano portati senza alcun motivo né spiegazione. Trattenuti per ore, malmenati, mentre fuori li aspettavano amiche, solidali, compagni, gruppi di riferimento, familiari.




Gli studenti, che l’altro ieri hanno deciso di irrompere in questo modo sulla scena, hanno continuato a ripeterlo: hanno costretto il nostro popolo a fare così. E il popolo, anziché dissociarsi, sostiene la protesta e si unisce al livello di scontro o, quantomeno, lo sostiene. «Abbiamo manifestato pacificamente per oltre 130 giorni. Siamo stati sbeffeggiati dai poteri, mentre continuavano a emergere scandali di corruzione durante le proteste. Siamo stati totalmente silenziati dai media internazionali. Umiliati per anni. Il ricatto tra l’emigrazione all’estero, da stranieri, e gli abusi e le angherie nella propria terra. Il ricatto si spezza. Anche con il fuoco.» Ci tengono a dirlo: non siamo stati noi a volerlo. È conflitto, non violenza fine a sé stessa. Gente buttata in strada senza più una casa, morta nelle corsie degli ospedali, rimasta senza paga dopo mesi di lavoro per padroncini stranieri, costretta a emigrare. I palazzi istituzionali sono assediati. Un amico e compagno, oggi, mi ha detto: «Per forza, poi, fate i ministri AI!» Tirana, da ieri, è ingovernabile. Letteralmente.




Da Roberto Hajadari

 
















136esimo giorno di protesta consecutiva oggi a Tirana. Oggi, però, con un’enorme novità: gli studenti avevano chiamato un grande sciopero con lo slogan “Istruzione, non emigrazione”. Sin dalla mattina, folle si sono riversate nelle strade. Ben presto il conflitto si è alzato a livelli altissimi: scontri, barricate, cassonetti incendiati. E’ andato virale un giovane che, da solo, ha affrontato sei guardie come un pugile, finchè non è stato fermato e massacrato. Idranti della polizia e cariche violentissime, ma i giovani, a ogni attacco, controattaccavano e controcaricavano. Così fino alle 18, quando la canonica protesta pomeridiana e serale, è scesa in strada convergendo con gli studenti. Il livello del conflitto, già altissimo nel corso della giornata, è rimasto tale, anzi, si è ulteriormente alzato. 




Fin’ora la protesta, questi 100 e passa giorni, è stata pacifica e determinata, conflittuale ma entro i perimetri della resistenza agli abusi e alle angherie di guardie private e statali. Oggi Tirana è un’enorme barricata illuminata dalle fiamme da stamattina, e la notte è lunga, e la situazione è ingovernabile. Egli studenti hanno chiamato, per domani, un enorme boicottaggio delle lezioni.




Come detto, sin dall’inizio è una protesta ambientalista e di classe, decoloniale e per l’autonomia. Auto organizzata e senza partiti. E oggi, in autonomia, la gioventù e gli studenti sono scesi in strada, chiamando la loro protesta mattutin, dopo essere stati in prima linea fin dall’inizio. Ela piazza serale, anzichè dissociarsi, si è unita a loro. Tutto il paese che si contrappone al governo e al sistema bipartitico trentennale sta solidarizzando con gli studenti e con il conflitto. Viva viva!




Da Elon Miloti

title: Mahir Çayan’ı anlatan kitap hakkında toplatılma kararı
content:
Türkiye Halk Kurtuluş Partisi-Cephesi (THKP-C) kurucusu Mahir Çayan’ın fikir ve görüşlerinin yanı sıra Abdullah Öcalan başta olmak üzere pek çok ismin Çayan ile ilgili anı ve duruşuna dair yaptığı değerlendirmelerden oluşan kitap hakkında toplatılma kararı alındı. 




Dipnot Yayınları’nın Haziran’da yayımladığı “Mahir Çayan Kitabı: Toplu yazılar ve üzerine yazılar” isimli kitap hakkında Ankara 8’inci Sulh Ceza Hâkimliği toplatma kararı aldı. Kararda, “örgüt propagandası” yapıldığı ileri sürüldü. 




Dipnot Yayınları Genel Yayın Yönetmeni Emirali Türkmen hakkında da “örgüt propagandası” gerekçesiyle dava açıldı. Duruşma 23 Şubat 2027'de. 




"Kitaplar suç aleti, düşünceler suç delili değildir"




Dipnot Yayınları da konuya dair açıklama yaptı. Şöyle dedi:




“Bir kitabın toplatılması, yalnızca basılı bir eserin okurla buluşmasının engellenmesi değil, aynı zamanda düşüncenin dolaşımına, tarihte olan bitenlerin tartışılmasına ve toplumun kendi geçmişiyle yüzleşme hakkına yönelik bir müdahaledir. Oysa kitaplar suç aleti, düşünceler suç delili değildir.”




  “Ülkemiz tarihinin belli bir dönemine damgasını vuran toplumsal ve siyasal hareketleri yasaklarla unutturmaya çalışmak, bu hareketlerin bugüne uzanan tarihsel sonuçlarını toplatma kararlarıyla ortadan kaldırmak mümkün değildir. Hiçbir yasak, fikirlerin toplum içinde dolaşımını ve tartışılmasını bütünüyle engelleyemez; hiçbir baskı, hakikat arayışını durduramaz. Halkın eleştirel ve muhalif fikirlere erişiminin engellenmesine, kitapların suç unsuru gibi gösterilmesine ve yayıncılığın baskı altına alınmasına sessiz kalmayacağız. Biz, kitapların ve fikirlerin yasaklanmadığı, özgürce tartışıldığı bir toplumdan yanayız. Geçmişi sorgulayan, bugünü anlamaya çalışan ve özgürlükçü/eşitlikçi/ barışçıl bir toplumun ancak fikirlerin özgürce tartışılması temelinde kurulabileceğine inanıyoruz.”



















Mahir Çayan'ın mirası bugün ne söylüyor?

title: Анархиста Алексея Григорьева избили во время этапа в Верхнеуральскую тюрьму
content:
Он ждал осмотра врача полгода и это время похудел на 20 килограммов. Ему нужна помощь адвоката, сообщает проект «Огни Свободы».

Григорьев осужден на 20 лет лишения свободы по обвинению в приготовлении к поджогу релейного шкафа и расклейку в Новотроицке Оренбургской области листовок с призывом к российским солдатам сдаваться в плен. В марте 2026 года Григорьева избили во время этапа из СИЗО-5 Екатеринбурга в Верхнеуральскую тюрьму (Т-1) — предположительно, за разговор с военнопленными на украинском языке. После этого у Григорьева образовалась паховая грыжа.

Осмотра хирурга в Т-1 анархист дожидался полгода. По его словам, за это время он похудел на 20 килограммов. Григорьев говорит о «вываливающемся кишечнике» (при паховой грыже содержимое брюшной полости выпячивается через паховый канал или рядом с ним) и постоянных болях в животе. Ему трудно есть и ходить в туалет. В Т-1 Григорьева поместили на строгие условия. С самого прибытия в тюрьму ему ограничивают переписку.

После осмотра 1 октября хирург выдал Алексею направление в тюремную больницу. Чтобы добиться лечения, ему нужны юридические консультации по вопросам условий содержания и оказания медицинской помощи. На работу адвоката, который будет посещать Алексея в тюрьме, нужно собрать 70 тысяч рублей.

title: Babil Kuleleri 19 Ekim’de Maltepe’de sahnelenecek: Sınıf eşitsizliğini sahneye taşıyor
content:
Babil Kuleleri adlı oyundan bir sahne.

Bakırköy Belediye Tiyatroları (BBT), yeni sezonun ilk turnesinde 8. Uluslararası Maltepe Tiyatro Festivali’ne katılacak. Ebru Nihan Celkan’ın yazdığı, Fidan Tek Koşar’ın yönettiği Babil Kuleleri, 19 Ekim’de Maltepe Belediyesi Türkan Saylan Kültür Merkezi’nde sahnelenecek.

Bakırköy Belediye Tiyatroları, yeni sezonda yenilenen görsel kimliği ve repertuvarıyla seyirci karşısına çıkıyor. 8 Ekim’de sezonu açan tiyatronun yeni sezondaki ilk turne durağı, 8. Uluslararası Maltepe Tiyatro Festivali olacak.

Genel Sanat Yönetmeni Ragıp Savaş yönetiminde çalışmalarını sürdüren BBT, festival kapsamında Babil Kuleleri oyununu sahneleyecek. Ebru Nihan Celkan’ın kaleme aldığı, Fidan Tek Koşar’ın yönettiği oyun, 19 Ekim Pazartesi günü saat 20.00’de Maltepe Belediyesi Türkan Saylan Kültür Merkezi’nde izleyiciyle buluşacak.

Bir şantiye alanından lüks bir gökdelenin satış ofisine uzanan Babil Kuleleri, iş cinayetlerini ve farklı toplumsal sınıflar arasındaki görünmez ilişkileri ele alıyor. Yükselen binaların gölgesinde kalan emekçilerin yaşamlarını odağına alan oyun, modern kent yaşamındaki eşitsizlikleri ve sınıfsal çelişkileri sorguluyor.

Genel Sanat Yönetmeni Ragıp Savaş, tiyatronun yeni sezonuyla ilgili değerlendirmesinde dönüşümün yalnızca görsel bir değişiklik olmadığını belirtti. Savaş, amaçlarının tiyatronun sesini, enerjisini ve sahnede ele aldığı meseleleri sanatseverlerle buluşturmak olduğunu ifade ederek, geçmişten gelen birikimi çağdaş bir kimlikle sürdürmeyi hedeflediklerini söyledi.

Oyunun dekor tasarımını Ali Yenel, ışık tasarımını İlker Dursun, müziğini Melih Yüzer, ses tasarımını ise Uğur Çerkezoğlu üstleniyor. Yapımda Alper Altuner, Burak Dur, Çetin Etili, Doğuş Can Uzun, Gözde Ayar, İrem Sultan Cengiz ve Özge Çatak rol alıyor.

title: İspanya'dan AB bütçesine itiraz: ‘Kabul edilemez’
content:
İspanya Başbakanı Pedro Sanchez, Avrupa Konseyi'nin Brüksel’deki toplantısı öncesinde yaptığı açıklamada, İrlanda tarafından sunulan AB bütçe teklifine karşı çıktı.

Teklifi açıkça yetersiz bulduğunu belirten Sanchez, “Bu, İspanya hükümeti açısından ne sürdürülebilir ne de kabul edilebilirdir” dedi.

Sanchez, büyük enerji şirketlerine yönelik AB çapında vergiler getirilmesi gibi yeni öz kaynakların oluşturulması konusunda ise AB kurumları ve diğer üye ülkelerle müzakereye açık olduklarını söyledi.

İspanya’nın ekonomik performansı sayesinde AB bütçesine net katkı sağlayan ülkeler arasına girmeye doğru ilerlediğini belirten Sanchez, bunun ülkesine sorumluluk yüklediğini ve Avrupa projesine katkıda bulunmaktan gurur duyduklarını ifade etti.

AB Komisyonu, 2028-2034 dönemini kapsayan yeni bütçe için yaklaşık 2 trilyon avroluk teklif sunmuştu. Komisyon, güvenlik ve savunma, rekabet gücü, göç, enerji ve iklim dayanıklılığı gibi alanlardaki ihtiyaçlar doğrultusunda kaynakların artırılmasını ve bütçenin daha esnek hale getirilmesini hedefliyor.

AB bütçesi, harcamaların üst sınırlarının belirlendiği yedi yıllık dönemler için hazırlanıyor. Yeni bütçenin 1 Ocak 2028’de yürürlüğe girebilmesi için üye ülkeler arasında siyasi anlaşmaya varılması gerekiyor.

Uzun vadeli bütçenin kabulü için Avrupa Parlamentosu'nun onayı ve AB Konseyi'nde üye ülkelerin oy birliği gerekiyor. Müzakerelerde ülkelerin bütçeye yapacağı katkıların yanı sıra kaynakların hangi alanlara ve ne ölçüde ayrılacağı da tartışılıyor.

title: Aile Bakanlığı “Devlet korumasında değiller” demişti: Edirne'de kayıp 13 mülteci çocuk bulundu
content:
Edirne'de, İlk Kabul Arda Çocuk Evleri Sitesi Müdürlüğü'nden izne çıktıktan sonra geri dönmeyen 13 mülteci çocuk bulundu.

Yurt dışına çıkış yapmak isterken yakalanan ve İlk Kabul Arda Çocuk Evleri Sitesi Müdürlüğü'ne teslim edilen çocuklardan 14'ü, 11 Ekim'de, kendilerine verilen market izninin ardından kuruluşa dönmedi. Çocuklar dönmeyince görevliler, emniyete gidip kayıp başvurusunda bulundu. Bu sırada çocuklardan 1'i kuruma döndü.

Güvenlik güçleri, çocukları için kapsamlı arama çalışması başlattı. Çocuklardan 11'i Edirne kent merkezi ve Yunanistan sınırına yakın bölgede, 2'si de gittikleri İstanbul'da bulundu. 13 çocuk yeniden kuruma teslim edildi.

Çocukların kaybolması sonrasında hiçbir kurum sorumluluk kabul etmemiş, Aile ve Sosyal Hizmetler Bakanlığı yaptığı açıklamayla çocukların ‘devlet koruması’ altında olmadığını söylemişti.

author: Aoife Doran
title: Ceuta: Spain must protect trans asylum seekers, not return them to danger
content:
More than two months after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, many remain in precarious conditions, with inadequate access to shelter, essential services and international protection. Among them are trans asylum applicants who have fled persecution, only to face further violence, insecurity and the threat of being returned to danger. Their situation is part of a wider humanitarian crisis affecting people on the move in Ceuta, all of whom deserve safety, dignity and access to protection.




We are deeply concerned by reports of physical assaults, harassment and mistreatment of people seeking protection in Ceuta. A 

report by Border Resistance

, a grassroots collective working at the border, documents at least seven alleged incidents of violence against LGBTI people between 21 August and 6 September. One trans woman described being assaulted by police officers after being expelled from a reception centre, stating, 

“We are trans, we cannot live on the street because we are attacked.”

 Another described fleeing Morocco after receiving death threats from her family. These testimonies expose the grave risks facing trans and other LGBTI people who seek protection in Ceuta, only to encounter further violence and insecurity. We also reject the racist and dehumanising portrayal of people arriving in Ceuta as an 

‘invasion’

, language that fuels discrimination and hostility and undermines the right to seek asylum.




“Trans people in Ceuta face specific and severe risks within a wider humanitarian crisis. Our solidarity is with all migrants in Ceuta: everyone deserves safety, dignity and real access to asylum.”




– Tayri Fadil (she/her), TGEU Board member




For people fleeing persecution because of their gender identity, access to asylum can be a matter of life or death. Morocco continues to criminalise consensual same sex sexual activity, and trans people face serious risks of violence, discrimination and exclusion. Court documents indicate that seven LGBTI people arrested in Fès in August 2026 were each sentenced to eight months in prison, to be served immediately, and fined, while another person received a three-month suspended sentence. Yet Morocco’s inclusion on the EU list of so-called 

‘

safe countries of origin’

 risks obscuring these dangers and exposing people with legitimate protection needs to accelerated procedures and removal. As 

we warned in February

, treating a country as safe based on general assessments can conceal the specific and sometimes life-threatening persecution experienced by trans people.




“Seeking asylum is already one of the most painful journeys a person can undertake. When you are a BPOC trans person, you may not even make it to safety alive, but to see Spain forcibly return asylum seekers across its borders is unconscionable and constitutes a gross violation of human rights that should alarm all of us.”

 




–  Purity Tumukwasibwe (she/her), TGEU Board member 




These concerns are particularly urgent following reports of proposed changes to Spain’s asylum procedures that would further restrict safeguards for applicants from countries considered safe. Such proposals reflect the wider shift towards accelerated removals and weakened protection safeguards seen in the EU Returns Regulation, which 

we condemned in July

. Any measure that allows applicants to be removed before an effective assessment of the risks they face, including while challenging a negative asylum decision, would expose trans applicants to irreversible harm.




Spain has an obligation under European and international law to ensure effective access to asylum, assess each claim on its individual merits and uphold the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning people to places where they face persecution or other serious harm. These obligations apply regardless of how someone entered the country or whether their country of origin has been designated safe.




We call on the Spanish authorities, with the support and oversight of the European Commission, to take immediate action to:







Guarantee immediate safety and protection for trans and other LGBI asylum seekers in Ceuta, including safe and dignified accommodation, access to essential services and urgent transfers to mainland Spain for those at risk, in coordination with specialist civil society organisations.




Ensure fair and accessible asylum procedures, including confidential identification of protection needs, independent legal assistance, qualified interpreters and individual assessments that fully consider persecution based on gender identity.




Prevent unsafe returns, reject any measures that undermine effective legal remedies and ensure that no one is removed to a country where they face persecution, violence or other serious harm.




Investigate reported violence and mistreatment, ensure independent and impartial investigations into allegations involving security personnel, hold those responsible accountable and provide effective protection and remedies for survivors.







Spain and the European Union must act now. No one seeking safety should be forced to choose between violence at Europe’s borders and persecution in the country they fled. The right to asylum must be protected in practice, not sacrificed to political pressure or administrative expediency.
