title: Taksitli satışlara yeni düzenleme: Ticaret Bakanlığı ek sınırlama getirebilecek
content:
Duygu Ayber Gültekin [email protected]

Ticaret Bakanlığının perakende ticarette taksitli satışlara ilişkin düzenlemesinde değişiklik yapıldı. Resmi Gazete’de yayımlanarak yürürlüğe giren yönetmelik değişikliğiyle Bakanlığın, konut satışları dışındaki mal ve hizmet satışlarında taksit sürelerini belirleme ve ek sınırlamalar getirme yetkisinin kapsamı genişletildi.

Ticaret Bakanlığı tarafından hazırlanan Perakende Ticarette Uygulanacak İlke ve Kurallar Hakkında Yönetmelikte Değişiklik Yapılmasına Dair Yönetmelik, 15 Ekim 2026 tarihli Resmi Gazete'de yayımlandı. Değişiklikle, 6 Ağustos 2016 tarihli ve 29793 sayılı Resmi Gazete’de yayımlanan yönetmeliğin 12/B maddesinin birinci ve ikinci fıkraları yeniden düzenlenirken üçüncü, dördüncü ve beşinci fıkraları yürürlükten kaldırıldı.

Yeni düzenlemeye göre Ticaret Bakanlığı, konut satışları dışındaki taksitli mal ve hizmet satışlarında taksitlendirme sürelerini belirleyebilecek ve bu konuda ilave sınırlamalar getirilmesine yönelik kararlar alabilecek.

Bakanlığın yetkisi yalnızca satış sırasında yapılan taksitlendirmelerle sınırlı kalmayacak. Satışın ardından belirli bir ücret karşılığında borcun taksitlere bölünmesi ve ödemenin ertelendiği dönemler de düzenleme kapsamında değerlendirilecek.

Satışın kıymetli evrak düzenlenerek ya da düzenlenmeden gerçekleştirilmesi, söz konusu hükümlerin uygulanması bakımından farklılık yaratmayacak.

Bakanlığın taksit süreleri ve ek sınırlamalara ilişkin kararları, Bakanlığın internet sitesinde ilan edilecek ve üst meslek kuruluşlarına gönderilecek.

Yönetmelik değişikliğiyle yeni bir taksit sayısı ya da süre sınırı belirlenmedi. Bu konularda karar alma yetkisi Bakanlığa verildi. Konut satışlarını kapsam dışında bırakan düzenleme, yayımlandığı 15 Ekim 2026 tarihinde yürürlüğe girdi. Yönetmelik hükümlerini Ticaret Bakanı yürütecek.

author: Unknown
title: Telif gelirlerini "Palestine Action" grubuna aktaracağını duyurmuştu: İrlandalı yazar Sally Rooney'nin kitapları, İngiltere'de satıştan kaldırılıyor
content:
Fotoğraf: Frank Barat/Wikimedia Commons CC BY 4.0

"The Guardian" gazetesinin haberine göre, "Normal İnsanlar" ve "Arkadaşlarla Sohbetler" adlı eserleriyle tanınan İrlandalı yazar Sally Rooney, Palestine Action'a kamuoyu önünde verdiği destek nedeniyle İngiltere'deki kitap satışlarından telif ücreti alamadığını belirtti.

Yazar Rooney, "Palestine Action"ın Temmuz 2025'te İngiltere'de terör örgütü ilan edildiğini, ertesi ay ise gruba desteğini sürdüreceğini belirten görüş yazısı kaleme aldığını hatırlattı.

Rooney, "Eserlerimin İngiltere'de yayımlanmasına yönelik sözleşmelerin yerine getirilmesi artık ciddi suç teşkil edebilir. İstişare ve değerlendirme sürecinin ardından, benim de tam onayımla, yayınevim Faber eserlerimi artık İngiltere'de satışa sunamayacağına karar verdi." ifadelerini kullandı.

Yazar, inançları ve niyetleri konusunda kamuoyuna karşı dürüst olmak için elinden geleni yaptığını dile getirerek, "Bunun sonuçlarını kabul etmeye tamamen hazırım." ifadesine yer verdi.

Rooney'nin İngiltere ve İrlanda'daki yayınevi Faber de yaptığı açıklamada, mevcut İngiltere mevzuatı nedeniyle yazarın ülkedeki kitap satışlarından elde ettiği gelirin kendisine aktarılamadığını bildirdi.

Açıklamada, "Bir yazarın eserlerini satıp kazancını kendisine aktaramamak, bir yayınevi açısından kabul edilemez bir durumdur." ifadesine yer verildi.

Yayınevinin açıklamasında, bu nedenle, Rooney'nin tam onayıyla eserlerinin İngiltere'de hiçbir formatta satışa sunulmaması kararı alındığı belirtildi.

Ayrıca, açıklamada, yayınevinin, Rooney'nin eserlerini yayımlamaktan gurur duyduğu ve kitaplarının diğer ülkelerde satışına devam edileceği kaydedildi.

İrlandalı yazar Rooney, geçen yıl iki romanının İngiliz yayın kuruluşu BBC'deki uyarlamalarından elde ettiği telif gelirlerini, "Palestine Action" grubunu desteklemeye devam etmek için kullanacağını bildirmişti.

Rooney, İngiltere'nin Palestine Action'ı yasaklamasına rağmen gruba desteğini sürdüreceğini vurgulayarak, "Eğer İngiltere devleti bunu terörizm olarak görüyorsa, belki de faaliyetlerimi finanse eden WH Smith ve BBC gibi kuruluşları da incelemeli." ifadesini kullanmıştı.

Yazar Rooney, gözaltına alınma endişesi nedeniyle ödül almak üzere İngiltere'ye yapmayı planladığı ziyareti de iptal etmişti.

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: ‘Dropping 3 impeachment articles vs Duterte compromises accountability’
content:
Photo by Carlo Manalansan/Bulatlat

The Senate impeachment court granted the prosecution’s manifestation to drop three articles of impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte as it wanted to focus “on what is necessary.” For progressive groups, however, this move undermines calls for accountability.

“Ultimately, the prosecution chose political convenience over true accountability,” said human rights lawyer and former Bayan Muna Party-list Rep. Carlos Isagani Zarate in a statement.

After its earlier manifestation to drop Article III, which accused Sara of bribery, on October 13, the prosecution decided to also drop Article I (alleged misuse of confidential funds) and Article IV (assassination threats). Lead prosecutor Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro told the impeachment court that they would only focus on Article II which accuses the Vice President of having alleged unexplained wealth, false statements of assets, liabilities, and net worth (SALNs), and prohibited business interests.

Luistro said that the prosecution has presented sufficient evidence on Article II “to stand on its own.”

Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison, on the other hand, acknowledged the prosecution’s power to withdraw its allegations but she said that the prerogative should not affect how they would counter the accusations against Duterte.

Senate impeachment presiding officer Sen. Chiz Escudero accepted the prosecution’s withdrawal of three articles, ruling that the defense panel could no longer present its evidence to the said articles as they would no longer be subject to voting.

Read: VP Sara impeachment: ‘It is now about how evidence will be used’

For anti-corruption advocate Renato Reyes Jr., this move by the prosecution is “a great disservice to the Filipino people and a huge missed opportunity,” stressing that the evidence presented on the accusation of misuse of confidential funds, for him, sufficiently established corruption.

“It is high time that we teach a lesson to those who continue to abuse their confidential and intelligence funds through fabricated reports and fictitious beneficiaries,” Reyes, who currently serves as president of the Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan), wrote in a Facebook post.

Former ACT Teachers Party-list Rep. France Castro, who exposed the alleged misuse of Duterte’s confidential funds in 2023, echoed Reyes’ statement, raising questions if the prosecution’s manifestation has something to do with protecting other high-ranking officials. “Are they worried that this issue would boomerang to President Marcos?” she asked.

The Office of the President (OP) was the one that approved P125 million of the P250 million in confidential funds requested by the Office of the Vice President (OVP) to the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) in 2022, of which P73 million—part of the secret funds spent by the OVP in just 11 days—was disallowed by the Commission on Audit (COA) with finality.

Under the proposed 2027 national budget recently approved by the House of Representatives on October 12, the office of Marcos Jr. has a proposal of P4.56 billion in confidential and intelligence funds.

Human rights lawyer Ephraim Cortez viewed the prosecution’s withdrawal as a deemed acquittal of Sara. “In essence, the prosecution has given the Vice President a favor by absolving her of accountability for Articles I and IV despite overwhelming evidence that she misappropriated confidential funds amounting to hundreds of millions of pesos and made a mockery of accounting and audit procedures,” he wrote in a Facebook post. (DAA, RTS)

author: Shannia Cabuello
title: On the Fringes | Days in a life as a daughter of a farmer
content:
When I was told that we were going to visit a peasant community in San Jose Del Monte, Bulacan, I spent an entire day preparing for the rural work. I slept early for almost a week trying to fix my body clock and walked for hours to condition my legs. 




We were required to bring boots, blankets, tumblers, tupperware, and our own utensils. We were oriented to eat what’s laid on the table and to not be choosy about where we would sleep. 




I did not expect that there would be host families that would allow strangers in their homes and feed them for three days. It was surprising because these families are not wealthy people. 




They are the ones who consider 5 a.m. as late for farm work and 9 pm. for a good night’s sleep. They are the ones guarding their crops and plants from landlords and business elites. They are the ones being displaced to make way for state-funded infrastructure. 




Yet, they are also the ones that would greet you with a contagious smile, a warm meal, and a welcoming home. Unlike the landlords, they believe that land is not something to be owned but to be nurtured, loved, and shared. 




True enough, I didn’t even need the things I brought. 




Our host family, Nanay Linda, guided us to the paths where we wouldn’t slip. She offered us pillows and blankets we comfortably slept on. She would buy ice and soft drinks, offer us coffee and chocolate drinks, and provide water we can directly drink from their mugs and glasses. She would gladly cook freshly harvested vegetables and lay it on their printed plate for us. 




The things we were required to bring were stuck inside my bag, watching Nanay take care of us. When she started sharing their history of resistance, I wondered how they remained gentle. 




Sunrise




Nanay Linda’s household begins their day at 5 a.m. She will prepare coffee for Tatay then spend a short time chatting with her neighbors. When we were there, they treated us as if we were her own children. Even if that’s the first time she met us, she genuinely called us “anak.” 




“Kain na kayo, mga anak. Si Tatay n’yo ayaw pa kumain. Mamaya na raw siya.” 

(Go eat now, my children. Your father still doesn’t want to eat. He says he will eat later.)




“

Sama kayo kay Ate Analyn niyo. Pupunta siya mamaya sa uma para mag-ani ng tanglad.” 

(Come with your Ate Analyn later. She will go to the farm to harvest lemongrass.)




Every time she referred to her family, she made us feel as if we were part of it. 




That morning, I witnessed their bond with each other. They love to joke around and laugh. 




When one of them had a vegetable harvest, all of them would scramble for excess. The one who didn’t get any would be mocked. But none of the jokes would be taken seriously. 




They would still happily eat pandesal together partnered with the coffee they got from Nanay Linda’s kitchen. 




At 7 a.m., we joined Ate Analyn to the farm they call “uma.” We were tasked to harvest an order of 70 kilos of lemongrass. We walked for about 10 minutes before arriving at the sloped farm lands of Tungkong Mangga.




The terrain was slippery, especially when wet, and hard to climb up upon when one is not used to it. Some areas have this kind of plant called 

“kalmot pusa”

 that scratches one’s skin like a cat. Most of the area was open land, with few trees they use as a shed. 




So, Ate Analyn wore long sleeves, a hat, pants, and boots. When we got there, she cut the lemongrass from the soil, dragged it down under the shed of trees, then told us the life she has been living in for decades. 




She and her cousin cut the leaves of a banana tree for us to sit on. She shook off the remaining dirt from the lemongrass, cut the dried ends, removed some roots and worms, then tossed it to a pile. She warned us to be careful, as the lemongrass can irritate and cut the skin, while easily doing all of that with a sickle and a cutter on her hands. 




We did exactly as she taught us. We encountered different bugs such as ants, worms, spiders, butterflies, and caterpillars. We experienced going back and forth through slopes carrying bunches of lemongrass. Wearing our long sleeves, we still got scratches and cuts from it. We felt thirsty but their house is nowhere near. 




At last, our pile of lemongrass reached at least 15 out of 70 kilos. 




Ate Analyn told us to take a short rest before she accompanied us to their house. I was happy because I would finally be able to take a bath. At about 10 a.m., we got home. 




I felt relieved while also carrying the guilt of not helping them finish the remaining 55 kilos.




That morning alone felt like a whole day, but Ate Analyn would still return to 

uma

 until afternoon to complete the order. 




Just imagine how many itches, cuts, and scratches they had to endure for a kilo of lemongrass they sell for 25 pesos. And imagine if they return home with no water left in their drums. 




Noon




Before we ate the lunch prepared by Nanay, we took the time to shower. Tungkong Mangga does not have water systems they pay every month. 




The water in the drum outside was collected from rain. The water in their kitchen and comfort room was delivered by a truck that roams around their village. It costs about 40 pesos per gallon. 




I learned how to make do with a small pail of water to wash the dishes. I tried to use only five dippers of water when I took a bath. For more than land, water for them is also life. 




That’s why it’s understandable when Nanay wishes to have a water supply in their area. They said that the PrimeWater is near yet they do not feel its benefits. 




In their 

uma

, they need to fetch pails of water from a well and pour it into drums near their 

kubo

. Despite their age, Nanay and Tatay are still forced to carry heavy pails of water for their supply. 




After cleaning ourselves, we enjoyed the fried fish and soup with vegetables Nanay prepared for us. She kept apologizing, saying that it was all they could offer. 




She didn’t know that in my four years of living in Manila, I could only eat warm and home-cooked meals from carinderias. And that eating beside them felt like a hug from a parent. 




Sunset




After lunch, Nanay and Tatay will have their afternoon naps. Once they are done with farm work, most farmers would go home to rest shortly. 




While many were taking a break, I cannot help but think of all the farmers that I have encountered and how their experiences are similar. 




It is every October that their calls are amplified. The October peasant month allows me as a writer to hear different stories from peasant communities. 




In Tungkong Mangga, the community suffers from harassment, redtagging, and violence from landgrabber and business tycoon Greggy Araneta III. Private army and security guards were being deployed to intimidate its residents as well as those who visit the community. 




To defend their rights, they formed an association called Samahan at Sandigan ng mga Magsasaka sa San Isidro (SASAMAG). Nanay Linda was one of its founders.




They defended their right to continue farming. The slope-nature of Tungkong Mangga has been productive for decades. The vegetables sold during the pandemic came from their harvest. The MRT-7 station changed its route because they resisted.




Nanay Conching, one of the host families during our visit, recalled that guards of Araneta used to destroy their plants. Their land is being run over by large vehicles and the banana trees were being cut into two. 




One time, they chased the guards, wrecking their land. “After that, they never came back,” added Nanay Conching. “The more they cut the bananas, the more they grow a new one and bear more fruit. They just gave up destroying them.” 




Just like those banana trees, I know their resistance is as tough. Despite enduring a lot, it never stopped sustaining generations of families in Tungkong Mangga. 




It can be seen when Nanay Linda uses its trunk to feed their ducks, when her children use its leaves in making 

nilupak

, and when her grandchildren share the bananas with their neighbors and employers. 




They see the plants that grew from their lands as sustenance, so they selflessly share them with others. Maybe that is why they never run out of something to harvest. 




When I asked Nanay Linda about why she always shares what she has, even allowing strangers to live with and learn from them for days, she just told me that knowing their situation as farmers is really a big help. 




Night




That’s when I understood why and how peasant communities stayed gentle, loving, and nurturing. I reflected on my first assignment as a Bulatlat intern, which was also to cover the rice farmer’s forum as a buildup for the month-long peasant protest held every October. 




Last year, the peasant sector was demanding accountability as the flood control funds could have irrigated agricultural lands, provided machinery for local production, and fed millions of Filipino families. 




I remember crying with Tatay Alfonso, a farmer from Guimba, as he shared how they feel neglected by the government even if they are the ones producing food to the table. It was the first time that I heard from a rice farmer, Tatay Narcing, how farmlands should not be sold to foreign investors as land is life. Both of them do not ask for much, just enough to sustain their families. 




My next coverage at the time mostly revolved around the activities of peasant month. I was able to talk with a peasant woman from Negros Occidental, camping out of the Department of Agrarian Reform, to have a dialogue with the agrarian reform secretary. I also got a chance to meet the author of the first poetry book written by a peasant mother, Nanay Tess. Both mothers also do farm work while managing their expenses and taking care of the family.




I realized that all of them have one thing in common: they all continue fighting for land ownership. As fathers and mothers, they nurture the land so they can pass it down to the next generations. 




It is known that parents are responsible for providing shelter and food for their children. And from what I learned, these farmers I have met work so hard not just for their own families, but for the future of every Filipino youth. 




When they choose to spend their entire day working at the fields, they are ensuring the entire country’s food security. When they risk their lives to defend their land, they are hoping to sustain the future of agriculture. All their actions are never just for their own sake.




What’s sad is that these selflessness are often abused by those in power. They were being harassed, threatened, displaced, and killed. They are being treated as if the land is never theirs, as well as their lives. 




In the Philippines, they are directly affected by imperialism as the US-Marcos administration opens agricultural and ancestral land for land-use conversions, foreign control, and renewable energy projects. They suffer loss from import-dependent and export-oriented policies.




They are the target of bureaucrat capitalists who want to grab their land for selfish gains. They endure calamities destroying the fields while the government steals from public funds. 




They are suffering from deep poverty, debt, and exploitation due to feudal and semi-feudal systems that also leave them landless. 




The more I became aware of these, the more I grasped the essence of visiting rural areas. I learned about how rice, vegetables, and crops grow despite harsh conditions. I witnessed their situation. I understood why they continue planting anyway: for love, for what is right, and for collective future.




So now, when I see food being neglected on the table, I can share the process of conditioning the soil, planting the seeds, caring for, and harvesting it. When I go to the market and see that vegetables are costly, I can question how much goes to the farmers who grew them. When I discover that this was cheaply bought from farmers, I can demand justice and accountability to the very system that allows it on October Peasant Month protests. 




Now that I know why they remain gentle, loving, and nurturing, I can firmly fight for what they truly deserve: genuine agrarian reform and national industrialization.

On the Fringes | Days in a life as a daughter of a farmer

author: CNT Sierra Norte
title: 16 de octubre. Reunión abierta para preparar los Comités de Huelga
content:
En la sierra también nos organizamos para la Huelga General del próximo 11 de noviembre. Y lo hacemos de forma coordinada: CNT Colmenar Viejo, CNT Sierra Norte en la Cabrera y del CS Peña Hueca, Bustarviejo.




Nos repartimos este difícil pero maravilloso territorio de nuestra sierra dónde la vivienda también se ha convertido en un negocio a pesar de ser un derecho básico difícil de alcanzar para muchas personas con unos salarios que no llegan para cubrir el coste de la vida. Queremos coordinarnos en comités y organizar nuestro derecho a la protesta.




Lo más elemental se vuelve incomprensiblemente un imposible y por eso la gente trabajadora ha despertado. Pensionistas, estudiantes, trabajadores, jóvenes y mayores han dicho basta.




Este próximo viernes nos reunimos para que todas las personas de esta zona organicemos comités de huelga para llegar a los centros de trabajo y explicar nuestras reivindicaciones. Y lo haremos sin siglas, desde abajo y sin banderas.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Workers win illegal dismissal case vs Lazada, manpower agencies
content:
In two separate cases, the National Labor Relations Commission (NLRC) has ruled in favor of platform workers in illegal dismissal cases against manpower companies and leading Southeast Asian e-commerce platform Lazada.

Both cases involve illegal dismissal and non-payment of the 13th month pay.

Josiah David Quising, legal representative of the platform workers in two separate cases, declared that “these victories are important because of the evolving nature of the workplace.”

“We are no longer traditional wherein workers are situated in one physical space, it also extends to the digital space,” Quising told Bulatlat in Filipino.

NLRC is an attached quasi-judicial agency of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) mandated to resolve labor and management disputes involving Filipino workers.

“These winning cases are mere reaffirmation of the rights of platform workers, particularly riders, based on the Supreme Court (decision),” Quising added.

The first case was an illegal dismissal with claims for non-payment of the 13th month pay, cash bond deposit, damages and attorney’s fees by a platform rider against Metro Courier Inc. (MCI) and Lazada.

The NLRC stated that the rider is a “regular employee of respondent Lazada and that he was illegally dismissed by the latter.”

The rider was employed by the manpower services MCI for Lazada. His regular work routine was described as follows: he would wait for his assigned delivery schedule early in the morning, between 4 am to 7 am, which he would proceed to the designated hub, wait for the parcels to arrive, and proceed to sorting to delivery.

Even before completing all deliveries, the complainant was required to deposit the payments collected from customers between 2 p.m. and 4 p.m. He would return to work to complete his remaining deliveries, often working until 8 p.m. to 10 pm, depending on the volume of parcels.

The rider received an email informing him of the termination of his contract on March 26, 2025, without any hearing or prior notice of dismissal. The termination letter alleged that the rider committed following violations: false delivery, commission of a crime, and tampering with parcels.

The impact of the rider’s sudden termination was severe, since it transpired when his youngest child was hospitalized.

“As a result of the loss of his employment, Complainant (rider) and his family incurred substantial debts, and his three children were unable to attend school due to lack of money for daily expenses,” the NLRC statement of facts read. “The complainant and his family also struggled to meet basic needs, including food and housing, and eventually lost their rented residence due to their inability to pay rent.”

Lazada said that there was no employer-employee relationship between the rider and the company as he was engaged by MCI to provide services. MCI also said that it does not have an employment relationship with the rider, insisting that the NLRC does not have jurisdiction over the illegal dismissal case.

However, the NLRC cited the 2023 Supreme Court ruling that declared that Lazada platform riders are regular employees and that all four factors in the four-fold test were present: (a) the employer’s selection and engagement of the employee; (b) the payment of wages; (c) the power to dismiss; and (d) the power to control the employee’s conduct.

Read: Outdated labor policies in app-based employment

“As respondent companies Metro Courier Inc. and Lazada were engaged in the prohibited labor-only contracting scheme, they are jointly and severally ordered to pay complainant his separation pay, backwages, 13th month pay, service incentive leave pay, holiday pay, damages and attorney’s fees,” the NLRC ruling added.

The second case was filed by three platform workers against J. Alcabasa Enterprises and General Services, a manpower company that provided services for shipping company J&T Express. The three workers were deployed to the latter company.

They were illegally dismissed on January 31, 2026, without valid cause, notice to explain, nor “genuine” hearing prior to their dismissal. They were barred from entering the premises of J&T Express a day before their last day, January 30, 2026.

The notice of conferences only started in February 2026 onwards, by the J. Alcabasa Enterprises and General Services, when their illegal dismissal was already in effect.

J&T Express said that they were issued a directive not to accept or allow the redeployment of the three workers to their company because they filed a DOLE complaint.

This DOLE complaint was about the assistance the three workers sought, concerning the nonpayment of their 13th month pay. DOLE ruled in favor of the workers and the 13th month pay was released on January 27, 2026. A day after, the workers were informed that their deployment at J&T Express would end on January 31, 2026.

“This Office finds that complainants (workers) have sufficiently established dismissal by substantial evidence,” the NLRC ruling stated, emphasizing that the workers prove that they were informed and prevented from entering the workplace, reinforced by documentary trail from the companies.

The NLRC further noted that the procedural due process in termination requires the employee to be informed first of the charges, and be given a meaningful opportunity to answer, before their termination.

“An employer cannot first terminate an employee and thereafter conduct an administrative investigation for the purpose of supplying a cause for an already completed dismissal,” the NLRC ruling added.

Moreover, the workers said that they were regular employees while the company characterized them as seasonal workers.

The arbitration office clarified that the designation given by an employer is not controlling. Employment status of the workers is determined by the nature of the work and the applicable law and jurisprudence.

Article 295 of the Labor Code provides that employment is regular when the employee has been engaged to perform activities that are usually necessary or desirable in the usual business or trade of the employer, subject to recognized exceptions such as project and seasonal employment.

But the workers were repeatedly engaged since 2024, which the NLRC ruled inconsistent with the definition of seasonal work wherein workers were hired for a definite project with a predetermined completion date. Thus, the NLRC declared that the three workers were regular employees.

Due to the finding that illegal dismissal was committed in the case, payment of moral damages, attorney’s fees, and other benefits were compelled to be given to the three workers.

“The granting of moral and exemplary damages are important developments because these are usually denied in labor cases, including those cases against Lazada that reached the Supreme Court,” Quising said.

The International Labour Organization (ILO) adopted the Decent Work in the Platform Economy Convention, 2026 (No. 193) this year, marking a historic victory for platform workers around the world as it is the first legally binding international treaty to regulate gig work and establish global standards for platform workers.

ILO recorded that there are around 150 million platform workers that are employed globally. In the Philippines alone, there are 11 million recorded workers in the digital economy.

Read: ILO to negotiate binding standards for 150 million platform workers

Among the convention’s key provisions are the protection of workers’ freedom of association and collective bargaining rights, access to social security, occupational safety and health standards, fair and transparent remuneration systems, and safeguards against the misclassification of employees as self-employed contractors.

The Philippine government has been urged to ratify the ILO Convention No. 193 to reinforce international obligation for the protection of millions of platform workers in the country.

Read: Labor group urges PHL ratification of ILO convention

“It is also encouraging to see the law keeping pace with developments in these areas. We hope this will not be our last victory on this front,” Quising added.

“As a regular employee of Lazada, complainant can only be terminated based on valid grounds and that he cannot be merely dismissed on the ground of ‘Termination of Service Partner Agreement’, as the latter is not one of the just or authorized cause for termination as provided by the Labor Code and jurisprudence,” the NLRC ruling stated.

“Lazada failed to successfully discharge the burden of proof to establish valid cause for complainant’s dismissal, and that he was afforded due process prior to his termination,” the NLRC ruling added. (RTS, RVO)

Disclosure: Josiah David Quising is also a columnist and contributor for Bulatlat.

title: 18 de octubre. Comedor Popular: ¡El capitalismo nos quiere a la parrilla!
content:
El capitalismo tiene una receta infalible: convertir nuestros derechos en negocio, poner la educación y la vivienda a la parrilla y servirnos precariedad como plato principal.




Y mientras todo arde, sus gestores políticos, las personas más entusiastas defensoras, siguen vendiéndonos las bondades de su menú de mercado. ¡Eso sí que es cocinar para unos pocos!




Pero en 

CNT Sierra Norte tenemos otra receta: apoyo mutuo, solidaridad y lucha colectiva.




Este domingo 18 de octubre, a partir de las 14:00 h, vuelve nuestro Comedor Popular.

 Nos reuniremos para compartir mesa, encontrarnos y coger fuerzas para las huelgas que se avecinan.




Dónde:

 C/ Luis Fernández Urosa, 7. La Cabrera (Madrid).

Menú vegano.

Bono ayuda: 8 €.




 

Todo lo recaudado irá íntegramente a la caja de resistencia para las personas huelguistas.




Porque frente a quienes hacen negocio con nuestras necesidades, seguimos apostando por la organización, la solidaridad y el apoyo mutuo.




¡Que arda el negocio, no nuestros derechos!




¡Nos vemos en el comedor!

This zine was adapted from the French, CHAOS DANS L’ARCHIPEL DE FEU: Sur l’insurrection d’août 2025 en Indonésie et sa répression, (Infokiosques, 2026). Only a few articles were translated from the French, the majority were accessed in English from Dark Nights. A few minor edits for readability were made.

Since this zine was compiled in July 2026, the list of prisoners may be outdated, check in with counter-info resources for updated information.

Other texts on anarchism in Indonesia:

— The Parade of Rebellion against Indonesia: A Conversation between Warzone Distro & Anarcho-Nihilist Insurgents in so-called Indonesia (Warzone Distro, 2025)

— Voices from the Uprising in Indonesia (Crimethinc, 2025)

— Interview with Comrades on the Situation in Indonesia (Aniketanamag, 2025)

— We Are All Puppeteers: 42 People from Anti-Authoritarian Networks Named as Suspects After Demonstrations #bubarkanDPR (Abolish Parliament) (Serikat Tahanan, 2025)

In August and September 2025, an insurrection struck the Indonesian archipelago, engulfing in its flames many police stations, cop cars, both national and local government buildings, parliament members’ homes, businesses, and more. This revolt notably involved many anarchists, insurrectionary and direct action-oriented tendencies being particularly common.

To avenge itself, the Indonesian State launched a grand hunt for anarchists all throughout the country, after which several dozen anarchist comrades have been arrested and imprisoned. Two cases in particular have been at the center of attention: that of 16 anarchists suspected of Molotov cocktail attacks in Jakarta, and that against 44 anarchists suspected of direct actions and attempts at insurrection in an organization created by the State from scratch, called “Chaos Star,” in reference to the strong anarcho-nihilist tendency in the country.

This zine compiles many texts published online about the situation of anarchist prisoners in recent months in order to give them all our solidarity wherever we are. Spread information, write them letters, organize financial solidarity.

An uprising of angry youth, triggered by rising taxes for the general public and a repressive military. There’s no organization, the insurrection is spearheaded by young anarchists, nihilists, and the uncontrollables. Many young anarchists from high school groups are arrested. The high schoolers carry the energy. Around 400 students were arrested on August 25 according to reports. Most of the action is coordinated live on social media. Usually, some liberal union or opposition party controls the narrative, but not this time. Even mainstream media acknowledges that social media is the main source of information. Politicians cannot control the narrative any longer. It’s been a tradition for decades that student bodies are normally the stewards for these kind of demos, but each year these mediators get ousted—by the students themselves. That’s why NGOs, unions, “civil anarchists,” and student associations on the left and the right hate the anti-organizational factions.

Fuck them all. We incite the youngsters to act for themselves. Individuals are no longer afraid of ideological duty, norms, and all those external values…

Last night, August 28, police shot and killed a demonstrator [Affan Kurniawan, a 21 year old motorcycle taxi driver, was struck and killed by an armored police vehicle in Jakarta, ed.]. Nationwide riots against the tax continue to escalate. In several cities, riots are organic and self-organized. The public image of the police continues to crumble, as the people supports the rioters. Anarchist cells coordinate other actions, and most of the nihilist-insurrectionary calls to action dominate the narrative. Anonymous social media accounts on Instagram with thousands of followers call for an anti-political insurgency. Everyday, they make calls to action and give good explanations for why.

The union mediators announce that they’ll be in the streets and “there will be no riot,” but the youngsters and rioters mock them right away on social media. We give it up to the youngsters. We can only incite them to be more uncontrollable. At night, the internet goes down. While “civil anarchists” call for a people’s council, we call for fuck everything. We never really organize people, only provide a coordination of networks and technical info about street action.

Friday, August 29. Basically, anarchists control the narrative. People respond to the nationwide call to attack police stations and the police themselves. They attack the government, and the mass media loses control over information and news. Our network continues to call for revenge after the police murder last night, and shit’s getting hot. Anarchist cells are in the streets.

You can see the uprising on various news sites, though all the good videos are only on social media.

Jakarta no longer belongs to the rotten elites. Thousands of people from every corner of the land storm the capital. This is not just a protest—it’s a collective eruption of rage against rising housing taxes, endless corruption, and the military-police dogs of the state.

From dawn til’ midnight, the streets turn into a battlefield of defiance. Screams, fire, and stones become the people’s language of fury.

This is not some puppet show led by the elites. This is raw, untamed, leaderless anger, impossible to control.

The following statement by Palang Hitam / Anarchist Black Cross (ABC) Indonesia was broadcast live on air Monday, December 9, between 11am-1pm CET on Radio Blackout. The name of the show is “Bello come una prigione che brucia” (Beautiful as a Burning Prison), a show broadcast for 20 years against prisons, repression, surveillance, military tech, and AI. Radio Blackout is an autonomous radio (FM in Turin, Italy, and streaming elsewhere) born in 1992 as common project self-managed by local squats, social centers, and various collectives and individuals (anti-fascists, anti-authoritarians, anticapitalists, anti-lots of things, with comrades from different currents of anarchism and communism).

From August to early September 2025, Indonesia was struck by demonstrations and riots triggered by public anger over government policies that were considered detrimental to the people. The main triggers of these protests were drastic increases in the cost of living, including food prices and education costs, as well as mass layoffs that affected many workers. In addition, increases in land and building taxes imposed by local governments as a result of funding cuts from the federal government further exacerbated the situation. Public frustration peaked when there were proposals to increase the allowances and salaries of members of the House of Representatives (DPR), which seemed to ignore the suffering of the people.

Initially, public anger was only expressed on social media with calls to dissolve the House of Representatives. However, the response from members of the House of Representatives, especially Ahmad Sahroni, who called critics “the dumbest people in the world,” only worsened the situation. On August 25, anger erupted in the form of a massive demonstration in front of the House of Representatives office, which ended in chaos with clashes between demonstrators and the police.

This first demonstration was attended by various elements of society, such as online motorcycle taxi drivers, vocational school students, and members of the general public who were not affiliated with any particular organization. Although the posters they made were ridiculed by some pro-democracy activists for being poorly designed and therefore likely to have been “made by intelligence agents,” the protests continued. Their demands focused on the elimination of allowances for members of the House of Representatives, which were considered too wasteful, the passing of the Asset Seizure Bill, and the rejection of a number of other controversial bills.

On August 26, demonstrations continued despite a decline in the number of participants. Many students began to hold open discussions, showing that the issue of the House of Representatives was gaining public attention. However, riots broke out again on August 28, when labor demonstrations in various major cities demanded an increase in the minimum wage, the abolition of the job outsourcing system, and changes to the Labor Act. In Jakarta, labor protests in front of the House of Representatives building and the State Palace ended in riots, which escalated after an online motorcycle taxi driver named Affan Kurniawan was killed after he was hit by an armored police vehicle in Pejompongan, Central Jakarta. This incident was captured on video and went viral, sparking further outrage.

Since early August 29, online motorcycle taxi drivers have gathered at the Kwitang Mobile Brigade Headquarters, demanding justice for Affan’s death and holding the police accountable for the violence against demonstrators. The crowd grew, including students, and the demonstration shifted to police stations and government buildings. However, despite negotiations, the crowd was dissatisfied with the results, and riots broke out again, causing public transportation to come to a standstill and several police stations to close.

The riots spread to various major cities outside Jakarta. There were 34 other flashpoints outside Jakarta where public facilities, police stations, and local council buildings were set on fire by the crowds. On August 30, tensions escalated after it was revealed that several members of the House of Representatives, including Ahmad Sahroni, had travelled abroad. This news further fueled public anger, which led to the storming of the homes of Sahroni and several other members of the House of Representatives, as well as government officials such as Finance Minister Sri Mulyani. Their homes were looted by a crowd that could no longer contain their anger.

That night, the power went out around the Mobile Brigade Headquarters, and police forces deployed to control the riots used tear gas and gunfire to disperse the crowd. The armed forces and police conducted sweeps in various areas to crack down on the rioters. This crackdown continued in the following days, causing tensions to rise throughout Indonesia. The Indonesian government targeted the demonstrators with accusations ranging from terrorism to treason. Instead of meeting the demands of the demonstrations, the Indonesian government responded with continued repression and a retreat from democratization.

This popular uprising was essentially driven by ordinary people, particularly high school students, the unemployed, and the online motorcycle taxi community—forces that had been underestimated and considered “politically unaware” by middle-class activists and most leftists. These rebels are not people who act based on their reading of Marxist or anarchist books. They are in the streets because the information circulating on social media has provoked their anger; anger that is then moderated by the middle class who shout, “Don’t destroy public facilities,” “Don’t be anarchists,” “Don’t be provoked,” and who finally make a series of long-winded demands called “17+8” on September 1, just to extinguish the fires and anger (today, these demands have still not been realized). It is true that the crowds still lack practical intelligence. But of course that is not their fault. Since they are the people who have always been sacrificed by the state and even by the opposition elites who claim to be “revolutionaries”—they have grown up with the understanding that anger must find an outlet.

Then, when the fires stopped burning everywhere, when the rulers and political elites apologized in public, no one could say for sure how it all began. There had been a lot of consolidation, discussion, cross-ideological networking, political campaigns, etc., but what happened in August 2025 was a festival of insurrection that no one could have predicted. Even when the demonstrations first began, until the death of Affan Kurniawan as the boiling point of public anger, these demonstrations were still seen as “staged demonstrations” for the benefit of those in power, which, ironically, were promoted massively by most middle-class pro-democracy activists and their followers.

Now, after the riots, the police have arrested many people, including anarchist egoists/nihilists, but most of them are victims of wrongful arrest who did not even participate in the demonstrations. They are accused of being masterminds, provocateurs, intellectual agents, and are labeled as the “Chaos Star” group. Meanwhile, members of DPR such as Ahmad Sahroni, who sparked public outrage, remain in office and have not been dismissed. Recently, the DPR passed a revision to the Criminal Procedure Code that allows police officers to arrest people without evidence and to secretly wiretap, record, and tamper with digital devices.

Since August 25, the flames of rebellion have scorched the oppressive forces in Indonesia, igniting a fierce uprising against a regime that thrives on violence and subjugation. This is no fleeting moment; it is the throbbing heartbeat of resistance from those long denied their rights. The loss of ten lives in this struggle only deepens our resolve to confront the state and its henchmen.

As the government unleashes military brutality, kidnaps activists, and engages in sinister cyber warfare, we are reminded: “Insurrection is the most logical weapon of the masses.” It is time to act—our fury must unite as a force beyond borders!

Comrades across the globe, rise up! Attack Indonesian interests wherever they are found. Disrupt the machinery of oppression with every act of defiance. Join the clash, amplify the voices of the oppressed, and make it clear: our resistance knows no bounds.

Together, we can dismantle techno-industrial civilization!

Federasi Informal Anarkis/ Informal Anarchist Federation

Palang Hitam / ABC Indonesia asks if possible for the organization of solidarity demonstrations / actions at Indonesian embassies in foreign countries. We are asking international comrades for support.

The mass uprising in Indonesia is facing severe repression. Dozens of people are confirmed missing, at least 6 people have been killed. Many are injured. Thousands of people have been arrested. Police have been attacking the universities. Police and army check-points have been set up everywhere. Many people are being arrested for live streaming and counter-info blogs, and social media accounts are being tracked and comrades arrested. NGOs, liberal/left unions and student union stewards are assisting the repression.

Several multi-national companies operate and invest in Indonesia, such as Shell, BP, Unilever, Rolls Royce and GlaxoSmithKline, which have a large presence. The largest multinational bank operating in Indonesia is HSBC, which is a suitable target for coordinated action since it has branches and offices across the globe. We propose that, where appropriate, individuals in each territory and region research which companies are operating in Indonesia, circulate and make that information known, and take direct action in solidarity with the prisoners of the anti-authoritarian mass uprising.

Against torture — For social war.

A comrade in Java was arrested a few days ago, accused of administrating “Black Bloc Zone,” an Indonesian focused anarchist website. The comrade is still being detained. The media scum have been up to their old tricks of denigrating our comrades’ name. Fire to the prisons! Free the comrade!

Extensive raids in Java, Jakarta, Bandung, and Makassar. There are still clashes and conflicts taking place across the archipelago. Media scum parade the hostages on television as they try to regain the narrative but it just fuels the hatred and rebellion by the population.

In short, 5,444 people have been reported arrested from the uprising nationally. 583 are involved in further investigations. That is the recent report from a legal aid institution. On September 3, the same leftist legal organization released info that 3,337 people had been arrested, so we can see that the repression is gaining momentum. Hundreds of anarchists have been reported arrested.

The Indonesian anti-terrorist unit ‘Densus 88’, basically a death squad, have been activated by the government. ‘Densus 88’ are now hunting the insurrectionary anarchist, nihilist, and egoist circles, and they focus on the arrested. They will try to charge the comrades already arrested and those still wanted with terrorism, which will be hard to prove in court, but the repression could be bloody, so we ask for international attention and revolutionary solidarity. The anti-terrorist unit is officially hunting the same circle in Makassar. This is the way that the Indonesian state tries to spread a paranoid climate, which ultimately has not really been that successful.

16 prisoners held at the Jakarta metropolitan police station (Polda Metro Jaya) in connection with the revolt from August 25 to September 3, 2025 launched a hunger strike on Tuesday, September 16, 2025.

The strike was launched by Syahdan Husein, administrator of the Instagram account Gejayan Memanggil, who has been on hunger strike since September 11 in the Jakarta metropolitan police station. His protest was against the detention of all prisoners. He announced that he would continue the hunger strike until all political prisoners are released. From the hunger strikers:

We [the 16 prisoners signing this letter] have launched a hunger strike on September 16, 2025. We are all held in the Jakarta metropolitan police station.

We want our freedom! We are fighting for democracy!

In response to this hunger strike, we are calling for support and solidarity from all of the anti-authoritarian movement to participate in the campaign for the freedom of the 16 political prisoners in Jakarta, the 42 in Bandung, as well as in Samarinda, Pontianak, Makassar, and other cities after the “Disband DPR” demonstrations between August 25 and September 3. There are hundreds of other prisoners in cities who are reviving less attention. Support them! No one is free until all are free!

After the mass action that took place at the end of August and early September, a wave of mass arrests followed, with thousands of people being detained across various cities in Indonesia—both post-action arrests and sweeps from those already arrested. Even now, various anti-authoritarian groups in Indonesia are experiencing widespread paranoia, which is understandable for some people due to the state’s cyber operations aimed at mapping both formal and informal anti-authoritarian cells. Several collective and individual names have already been collected, which only adds to the paranoid climate that continues to persist. Some refer to this as “going underground,” or even as an individual safety method, to later continue efforts for solidarity with comrades who have been designated as suspects. The state has labeled anarchists as the masterminds behind all the mass actions that took place in various cities. For example, in Bandung, the authorities have designated 42 protesters as suspects, and in Jakarta, 16 people have been labeled as suspects. This doesn’t even account for other cities that have not yet been verified. All those who are detained face obstacles in accessing legal assistance, and torture is not spared during interrogation and examination.

In a press conference held by the authorities some time ago, they stated that there is a connection between anarchists in Indonesia and international anarchist networks. They also raised concerns about the flow of funds traced from digital wallets as money for chaos, even reporting amounts up to tens or even hundreds of millions of rupiahs — a figure that seems quite unreasonable. They have also used various books, zines, and pamphlets as evidence of anarchist actions. All of this has been criminalized under a new form of anti-terrorism in Indonesia. However, logically speaking, the state is openly the true terrorist to the oppressed people of Indonesia, through land grabs, low wages, unequal education, media suppression, killings of activists, and so on. These criminalization efforts are also efforts to scapegoat alternative methods for sustaining life without the grip of the state and its apparatuses.

Today, in Indonesia, we have entered a new phase—after the ghosts of communism and the Jakarta method—in hunting anarchists, or any movements that are seen as disturbing the stability and interests of the state. Everyone is an individual with the potential to be criminalized by the state. Therefore, to anyone reading this, continue to raise solidarity for the political prisoners of August-September so they know they are not alone. Long live resistance, long live anarchy!

After some time, following the large-scale demonstrations across various parts of the archipelago, the lack of information from our comrades who have been arrested for their actions has been a difficult challenge for us.

Firstly, the lack of communication from our comrades who have been arrested and charged stems from communication restrictions imposed by the pigs. They were even denied legal assistance and communication with their families for approximately two weeks. This was confirmed as part of the effort to investigate the motives behind the charges.

Then, suddenly, the pigs held a press conference and invited various local media outlets to cover everything, even releasing the names of those who had been charged to the public.

In the information released, particularly regarding those arrested by the West Java Police Headquarters, our comrades are being processed by two divisions: general crime (26 people) and cybercrime (16 people). These pigs have identified anarchist-egoist-nihilist subjects as a new source of threat in Indonesia, especially due to their alleged connection to international networks.

For everyone’s safety, if anyone has had, or is still in correspondence with Black Bloc Zone or Contemplative Publishing, we recommend stopping this immediately, as these two names have been identified as key actors by the pigs. It is highly likely that their websites, Instagram accounts, or even their Signal accounts are still under investigation.

Stay safe and don’t be deceived!

1. Trigger Event — The group round Comrade Acil (Itenas / University of Bandung, West Java). Acil was arrested after posting on social media about an Indonesian flag burning.

2. First Link — From Acil’s case, police traced and arrested 8 people from the Kiara Condong area where they had uploaded content showing them making and throwing Molotovs.

3. Expanding the Network — Adit (UIN / University of Bandung) and Opal (Cijerah / Ciparay area) were also arrested. It’s unclear if they were directly linked to Acil, but their arrest opened a new line of investigation.

4. Start of the Manhunt — Through Instagram communications between Adit and Opal, police began mapping further connections.

5. Initial Mapping — Authorities identified links between Egoist accounts, funding sources, and physical evidence (Molotovs, etc). From this chain, Pem (who lives in Ciamis, West Java) was arrested.

6. Next Wave — Arrests continued with Katong Press (Komar, East Java), followed by Dana and Herdi (Palang Hitam / ABC), and Abu from Makassar. Katong Press is the name of an anarchist collective.

7. Shift in Legal Framing — Investigators begin applying the Anti-Terrorism Law, citing: suspected foreign funding, acts of arson, confessions from detainees admitting to destruction during protests.

8. Information Leak — From Dana’s case, additional leads emerged, targeting networks in Bogor and Tangerang (West Java).

Preliminary Notes for Mitigating the Scope of Repression:

So far, only the “Egoist wave” is clearly mapped, but further arrest waves remain uncertain. The ages of those arrested are predominantly teenagers and those in their 20’s so far. It is impossible for our group to count all the anarchists arrested. There’s no one big organization, just loose cells and individuals. But those universities mentioned are sanctuaries for many anarchists. These universities were attacked and raided by police during the clashes. At the moment, there are many anarchists concentrated in the central police station in Bandung.

According to corporate media dated September 15, 2025, 16 people were arrested almost simultaneously in various places around Jakarta and accused of Molotov attacks. The scale of the operation and the evidence gathered (CCTV footage, phone conversations, looted items, etc) are very serious.

— Banten Police (Polda Banten) Total Arrests: 15 People

— Metro Jaya Police (Jakarta) Total Arrests: 1,240 People Total Suspects: 43 People

— West Java Police (Polda Jawa Barat) Total Arrests: 147 People Total Suspects: 42 People

— Yogyakarta Police (Polda DIY) Total Arrests: 60 People

— Central Java Police (Polda Jawa Tengah) Total Arrests: 1,240 People Total Suspects: 118 People

— East Java Police (Polda Jawa Timur) Total Arrests: 709 People Total Suspects: 51 People

Note: 56 of the 118 arrested by Central Java Police are minors.

— Bali Police (Polda Bali) Total Arrests: 138 People Total Suspects: 14 People

— West Celebes Police (Polda Sulawesi Barat) Total Arrests: 6 People

— South Celebes Police (Polda Sulawesi Selatan) Total Arrests: 53 People

— Central Celebes Police (Polda Sulawesi Tengah) Total Arrests: 1 Person

Sumatra — North Sumatera Police (Polda Sumatera Utara) Total Arrests: 50 People — South Sumatra Police (Polda Sumatera Selatan) Total Arrests: 25 People

FREE ALL POLITICAL PRISONERS FROM THE AUGUST–SEPTEMBER 2025 UPRISING!

NO ONE IS FREE UNTIL EVERYONE IS FREE!

Following the initial repression of the protests in August–September 2025, the police have documented a total of 16 police reports and arrested individuals, both adults and minors, across 16 police regions in Indonesia.

Note: The total 959 people arrested or wanted represents the largest number civilians following the largest demonstrations since the 1998 tragedy [more than 1,000 people were killed by the state during riots and demonstrations against Suharto’s regime in May 1998], making this one of the largest repressive operations in Indonesia’s history.

Below is the breakdown of the reports and the number of suspects involved:

1. Polda Metro Jaya (Jakarta Metropolitan Police) — Police Reports: 36 — Adult Suspects: 200 — Minor Suspects: 32

2. Polda Jambi (Jamba Police) — Police Reports: 6 — Adult Suspects: 3

3. Polda Lampung (Lampung Police) — Police Reports: 1 — Adult Suspects: 1 — Minor Suspects: 7

4. Polda Sumsel (South Sumatra Police) — Police Reports: 12 — Adult Suspects: 23 — Minor Suspects: 3

5. Polda Banten (Banten Police) — Police Reports: 1 — Adult Suspects: 2

6. Polda Jawa Barat (West Java Police) — Police Reports: 30 — Adult Suspects: 80 — Minor Suspects: 31

7. Polda Jawa Tengah (Central Java Police) — Police Reports: 40 — Adult Suspects: 80 — Minor Suspects: 56

8. Polda Jawa Timur (East Java Police) — Police Reports: 85 — Adult Suspects: 185 — Minor Suspects: 140

9. Polda DIY (Yogyakarta Police) — Police Reports: 9 — Adult Suspects: 4 — Minor Suspects: 1

10. Polda Bali (Bali Police) — Police Reports: 4 — Adult Suspects: 10 — Minor Suspects: 4

11. Polda NTB (West Nusa Tenggara Police) — Police Reports: 2 — Adult Suspects: 15 — Minor Suspects: 6

12. Polda Kalbar (West Kalimantan Police) — Police Reports: 3 — Adult Suspects: 1 — Minor Suspects: 3

13. Polda Kaltim (East Kalimantan Police) — Police Reports: 1 — Adult Suspects: 7

14. Polda Sulbar (West Sulawesi Police) — Police Reports: 2 — Adult Suspects: 2

15. Polda Sulsel (South Sulawesi Police) — Police Reports: 10 — Adult Suspects: 46 — Minor Suspects: 12

16. Bareskrim Polri (Criminal Investigation Agency, a central agency of the Indonesian National Police) — Police Reports: 4 — Adult Suspects: 5

The data presented here is the latest available information gathered from various sources. As of now, authorities are continuing to arrest individuals they believe were involved in the protests that took place from late August to early September. This is a clear abuse of power, aimed not only at suppressing subsequent mass actions but also at spreading fear and paranoia throughout Indonesia. Several charges have been levied against the suspects, including Articles 160 and 161 of the Criminal Code (KUHP) on incitement, Article 170 KUHP on mob violence, Article 187 KUHP on arson, and Articles 212 to 214 KUHP on resisting law enforcement. Other charges include Article 351 KUHP on assault, Articles 362–363 KUHP on theft, Article 406 KUHP on property damage, and Emergency Law No. 12 of 1951 regarding the possession of bladed weapons, Molotov cocktails, and fireworks. Additionally, some individuals have been charged under the ITE Law (Information and Electronic Transactions). This reflects the clear and varied attempts to criminalize those arrested. We will continue to report the news regarding political prisoners in Indonesia.

After the uprising in August 2025, the Indonesian state is weak and looking for scapegoats. On September 23, the bastards claimed another one and kidnapped comrade Eat. Eat is a well-known anarchist who had spent time in prison on several occasions, such as for armed robbery and an incendiary attacks against a bank. His ex-girlfriend, Anzi Matta, snitched on him, and that’s why he got caught, according to police. The cops seized his laptop and phone, so that will be part of building his case. The police bastards are holding him incommunicado, like the rest of the anarchists. Right now, he’s being held at the West Java Regional Police Station in Bandung. That’s where many comrades are held. We don’t know what official charges and accusations they will hit him with. We do know that he was publicly accused of being the leader of the anarchist “Chaos Star” network in Indonesia, in connection with the riots last August. We have not heard about such a leader of anarchists, let alone nihilists, before. Nor have we heard of any such formal network of “chaotics” before.

In many cases, the evidence used by the cops to legitimize the use of the anti-terrorist laws ranges from simple possession of a flag or zines, music, social media profile, not necessarily participation in the riots. At first sight, this seems like another absurd and fantastical concoction of the anti-terrorist unit, just like the lie that international funding of $500,000 was what created the revolt. This is part of how the Indonesian state is trying to change the narrative. Across the region our currents and tendencies are growing. Their future is finished, anarchism is the predominant narrative.

We know that according to the news circulating in Indonesia, after arresting 42 people accused of being part of egoist/insurrectionist cells, the police pursued Eat because he was also suspected of raising funds, working on prisoner solidarity and connections with international anarchists, that is, maintaining friendships across borders. The police are trying to weaken anarchists’ resolve by blaming snitches and creating anarcho-phantasms, but we know they are lying and using torture. What we know is that the police are spreading the news that the former partner of Eat, Anzi Matta, helped them with information that lead to the arrest of Eat in Makassar, and he was brought to the West Java Regional Police in Bandung on 23rd September, where he remains.

Direct Action at Indonesian embassies, corporate

interests, and related businesses.

Freedom for the Prisoners — Death to the State.

The West Java paramilitary police have submitted the first part of accused anarchist comrade Eat’s case to the court. The details are not reported yet, but it is known that the comrade is being made into a ‘leadership’ scapegoat for the fabricated “Chaos Star” frame-up and he is also accused of ‘leadership’ of the mass insurrection which happened in August 2025. Parts of the legal case are still being held back, because the Special Detachment for Anti-Terrorism (Densus 88) is handling the “Chaos Star” case, especially concerning Eat. There’s an effort to charge Eat under the terrorism law. This is also why the investigation period against Eat was extended until November 20, 2025. The Prabowo Subianto regime has reopened the old documents about the FAI-IRF attack in Yogyakarta in 2011 [in 2010, the Long Live Luciano Tortuga Cell of the Indonesian Informal Anarchist Federation — International Revolutionary Front attacked a BRI Bank]. What is certain is that Eat was tortured, like other detained comrades. We don’t have enough information to confirm the severity of his injuries. What we can confirm is that despite being tortured Eat did not give up anyone’s name. Eat is already paralyzed in one arm and also suffering from serious health conditions. The paramilitary police and the Densus anti-terrorist unit are cowards who beat and torture young people in handcuffs. All over the world we are rising up against police bastards, politicians, jailers, banks, and corporations!

We demand the freedom of Eat and all the other prisoners!

Torturer’s hands off the prisoners!

After the mass revolts in August 2025, where a large section of the population rose up and attacked state corruption and inequality, 43 anarchist comrades are imprisoned at the West Java paramilitary police compound in Bandung. There is no access for anyone but the families, and even this is minimal. The prisoners have been cut off, and they are being used for a mainstream media manipulation campaign by the Indonesian state. Many of the imprisoned comrades are very young. They are all accused of being part of the individualist-nihilist “Chaos Star” network, which is a fabrication created by the police for the purpose of their prosecution. The police claim that the imprisoned comrades were radicalized by ‘leaders’ and funded by foreign anarchist organizations. The cops point to the existence of banners, flags, books, pamphlets, and music in the possession of the prisoners as commonly held items denoting membership in this “Chaos Star” organization.

Some of the comrades are accused of serious direct actions such as molotov attacks, arson, riot, property destruction, etc. Lastly, some of the comrades are accused of instigation, either online, for their blogs or social media accounts, or for their ‘prominent’ role. They are isolated in the paramilitary compound, and the Legal Aid Institute (LBH) in Bandung has been blocked from representing them. One option is to hire a private lawyer, but that would cost tens of millions of rupiah. We ask for heightened attention to this dangerous situation. Torture and abuse are being widely used on the detainees, confirmed by the families. The young comrades were injured and hurt until they gave false confessions that they were even at the demonstrations and/or part of specific organizations, as they were subjected to the brutality of the paramilitary police. This is a known fact and a reality that we have to confront. In the wake of the insurrection across Indonesia against the right-wing ex-military Prabowo Subianto regime, young people and the anarchist movement have been severely repressed by the regime. Many young people have been caught up in the police assaults and regardless of their supposed “guilt” or “innocence”, we extend our solidarity with them, and to all those who struggle against social oppression, prisons, police, and the state.

We are publishing the names of our imprisoned comrades and the prison address of the West Java paramilitary police compound where our friends are held. Let’s not leave these comrades alone and let’s send them solidarity letters, postcards, and our message of fire. Even if the solidarity mail is stolen and blocked by the administrators of abuse, they will know that we will hold them all responsible for what is taking place in Bandung.

Let’s shine a light on what the hated police torturers and the regime of Prabowo Subianto are doing to our young comrades, where it is taking place, and by whom, and let’s fight back against the police and all prisons everywhere.

Eight anarchist detainees from the “Chaos Star” case have had their first court date on November 18, 2025. This means they have now been transferred to the prosecutor’s detention facility. They are accused of throwing stones at police officers, allegedly causing around 2 billion rupiahs in damages [around 100,000 USD] during the August 30, 2025 demonstration. All eight have been charged under multiple articles: Article 170 (public violence), Article 214 (collective resistance), and Article 406 (destruction of private property) of the Indonesian Criminal Code. They are: Muhamad Subhan (M.S), Eli Yana (E.Y), Muhamad Vansa Alfarisi (M.V.A), Muhamad Rifa Aditya (M.R.A), Veri Kurniawan Kusuma (V.K.K), Joy Erlando Pandiangan (J.E.P), Muhamad Jalaludin Mukhlis (M.J.M), Jatnika Alang Ramdani Septiawan (J.A.R.S). All eight were tortured to force them into confessing to the alleged offenses.

Conditions inside police detention:

— From the very beginning, this case hasn’t been handled only by regular police and the Cyber Crime unit, but also by Densus 88, the special anti-terrorism / anti-makar unit (“makar” is the Indonesian term for “inciting an action or planning to overthrow the government).

— Most of the arrested anarchists have already started going to trial and have been moved to Kebon Waru prison.

— Eat (Reyhard Rumbayan) still has zero info about when his trial will happen. He’s the only one who’s been interrogated by Densus 88 — they see him as the “mastermind” behind everything related to anarchism.

— There are basically three types of charges being thrown at the detainees: (1) the brains behind the scenes, (2) the instigators, (3) the ones who got instigated. Of course, that’s because the state can’t wrap its head around the idea that spontaneous actions can happen without any leader — that concept just doesn’t exist in the state’s logic.

— The anarchist detainees don’t have access to lawyers. Some of them were thrown straight into solitary confinement for a month or even longer. By Indonesian law, a lawyer has to be appointed by family members. The problem is, quite a few of these anarchists don’t have family who are willing to help. A couple who finally got family support are now starting to work with lawyers. Some lawyers are already being lined up for those who haven’t gone to trial yet.

— Health conditions of several detainees are getting worse. Two people were badly physically tortured, one was psychologically tortured to the point of severe depression so bad he can barely speak, one is in critical condition and was taken to a military hospital, and Eat’s health is deteriorating because they won’t let him get the regular medication he needs for his medical condition.

— The initial amount of money donated has mostly been used to cover medical treatment so far.

— Latest news: 12 anarchists were arrested in Bali and transferred to police detention in West Java.

General situation in Indonesia:

— Densus 88 has started infiltrating anarchist circles, including scenes that are considered close to anarchists, like the punk scene.

— These infiltrators are using imagery and symbols that anarchists (especially insurrectionary ones) normally use, so others will think they’re legit. They’re actively pushing for riots like the ones that happened last August, hoping to scoop up young anarchists who join in.

— Bad news: some of these infiltrators have actually succeeded.

— This is going to turn into a massive witch-hunt against anarchists all over Indonesia.

Palang Hitam / ABC: This letter is from a section of the Chaos Star defendants in the West Java Paramilitary police compound. The reference to FAAF is the Free Association of Autonomous Fires. Fire To The Prisons!

Greetings to friends and to enemies alike,

Even now, the structures of power—ancient, rigid, and towering—continue to stand. Yet last August, people cracked the illusion of their invincibility. They showed that nothing is beyond transformation when our desires converge into a force capable of opening pathways toward the worlds we long to create.

We are individualists because we refuse the ideological fantasies of withered anarchists who preach like missionaries of a fading religion.

We are individualists because we believe in an anarchy of imagination—creative, diverse, unbound.

We are individualists who hold that nihilism is a concrete passage toward self-actualization, beyond the messianic dead-ends of dividing reality into “good” and “evil,” knowing full well the complexity of life cannot be squeezed into the decaying relics of Judeo-Christian doctrine—relics that should be buried like the myths of prophets and their fading gods.

We are individualists because we believe in the absolute autonomy of each person to shape the life they desire—yet we also believe in cooperation, in the equality of individuals who pursue their desires together. Our anti-social anarchy is an active refusal of the old values reproduced endlessly in everyday life.

At the same time, we are bewildered, amused, and entertained by the foolish accusations hurled by some social anarchists who label us as “purists,” as if our rejection of organization were born of loyalty to some classical anarchist canon—an ideology drenched in Eurocentrism, streaked with the colonial residue of Western civilization, and infused with the Enlightenment’s humanism, the very root of authoritarian democracy. We reject all ideologies. The rebels of Paris Commune in 1871, the revolutionaries of Spain in 1936, the dreamers of Paris in 1968, and those of August 2025—all remind us of brief lives that were truly worth living beyond any ideologies.

From behind these walls and bars, we send a sharp wind to every wild soul, reminding them that they are not alone against the repulsive realities engineered by the powerful.

The compass of anarchy draws us together at the threshold between free will and the will to power. We belong to no formal anarchist organization (spare us).

We are not part of impotent collectives like the PRISONERS’ UNION (Serikat Tahanan), nor any group that claims us as their own—much less the so-called anarchist movement with its church-like rigidity and archaic morality.

Toward the fusion of social and individual anarchy, and toward the negation of every radical movement that mirrors—or even surpasses—the mental and physical prisons of the state and capitalism!

This is an open letter to all anarchist of praxis. Fuck all idols, burn all radical bibles, and attack the enemy on all fronts.

FAAF & Individualist Prisoners, West Java Police Prison, December 1, 2025.

Anarchists in Indonesia are confronting an enormous storm. More than a dozen anarchists have been imprisoned and tortured, and the State is trying to discipline us and scare us. But this is nothing to us. Because we are the storm, their catastrophe incarnate. Here we have comrades from Black Bloc Zone, Palang Hitam Anarkis (Anarchist Black Cross) Indonesia, Contemplative, Katong Press, and other collectives.

Our comrades take the form of storms enveloped in flames. Some of us consider this moment as the culmination, but this is neither the beginning nor the end. We are gathering all the flames around us, the flames that the State has tried to extinguish.

How many times must we repeat ourselves? “We can live without the State!” Fuck society! Society is the most precious tool of the State to preserve its own existence. We hate society with all our hearts.

We believe that the dawn of hunger will rise sooner or later, and this will mark the beginning of the era of the State’s destruction.

For those on the outside: be steadfast, gather all the sparks that you can. And for those behind bars, or feel imprisoned, you are not alone.

Struggle! Struggle! Fuck winning or losing. What’s important is that our eyes continue to shine in each fight.

Warm greetings from anarchist prisoners in Indonesia

We must ensure our comrades aren’t alone! Send letters of solidarity, love, and rage. Out of the approximately 650 people still detained (either imprisoned or awaiting court decisions) from the August 2025 insurrection, here are two anarchist prisoners who can read English.

Other texts on anarchism in Indonesia:
