author: Leanne Sanders
title: Advocate says chiefs, grassroots working to get 145,000 registered First Nations to vote in Alberta referendum
content:
An Indigenous political activist and advocate says chiefs in Alberta, along with grassroots organizers says they’re doing everything they can to get First Nations people out to vote in the Oct. 19 referendum which could open a path for Alberta to pursue a formal separation process.

With the vote less than a week away, a key strategist says mobilization has been underway since Premier Danielle Smith introduced legislation making it easier for separatists to mount a successful petition to force a referendum.

“It really started in May 2025 when the chiefs called an emergency meeting, and the response back then was to her first legislative piece, Bill 54. The chiefs came in very firm 100 per cent opposed to separation prepared to fight. They ordered her by letter, and they all signed off on the letter to cease and desist on her separation intention,” Cara Currie Hall told APTN News in an interview.

Bill 54 was an omnibus bill that received Royal Assent in May, 2025. It included a number of changes related to the electoral process in Alberta including lifting the ban on corporate and union political donations for provincial elections and direct democracy processes like referendums and introduced a $5,000 annual contribution limit and a $5 million general election spending limit for political parties.

The separation question is number 10 on the ballot. It reads: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”

Voters are then given two options to choose from: Option 1: Alberta should remain a province of Canada or Option 2: The Government of Alberta should commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.

Currie Hall was a key figure in the Rock the Indigenous Vote movement in Canada in 2015 and helped organize Indigenous voters in the United States to back Barack Obama in his presidential run. She’s lending her considerable political savvy to the chiefs in Alberta and contends it was easy to see what Smith’s intentions were in making legislative changes.

“Because by then, [Smith] already lowered the threshold of signatures required to advance a referendum, and she lowered it from 60 per cent required signatures… to only 10 per cent, which is how she got away with only needing a hundred and seventy seven thousand signatures to push forward for a referendum. So, she accommodated that right from the get go.”

Currie Hall has been working alongside chiefs and grassroots people at her home First Nation of Maskwacis, 96 km south of Edmonton, to inform members of the importance of this vote. That work follows legal challenges mounted by several First Nations against Alberta over the constitutionality of the referendum.

Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation and the Blackfoot Confederacy (including Siksika Nation, Piikani Nation, and Blood Tribe with a total of at least five to six distinct First Nations/groups) brought successful judicial reviews and legal challenges that led the Court of King’s Bench to quash the separation petition and rule that the province breached its constitutional duty to consult.

Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation is suing the Alberta government, the chief electoral officer, and the federal attorney general in a separate lawsuit over Bill 14 and the separation petition process. Sturgeon Lake Cree said the referendum breached the treaties which pre-dated the province of Alberta.

APTN requested an interview with the chief but were advised he is not giving interviews at this time. Instead, in an emailed statement Sunshine said they’ve been informing and educating members “ever since Danielle Smith announced there would be an unconstitutional, expensive, and divisive referendum…”

“We hope that when all votes are counted Albertans will have repudiated this farcical anti -Treaty, anti-immigrant, and anti-democratic process,” Sunshine said.

Onion Lake Cree Nation which straddles the Alberta-Saskatchewan boundary also revived a separate lawsuit against Alberta’s broader Sovereignty Within a United Canada Act over related constitutional and treaty concerns. It claimed the provincial legislation infringes on constitutionally protected treaty rights.

The Alberta Court of Appeal ruled that the province failed its duty to consult Treaty First Nations regarding a separatist referendum question and petition drive. The court affirmed that pre-existing treaty agreements supersede provincial political efforts.

Currie Hall said the chiefs have stood firm united against the referendum since the former chief of Mikisew Cree Nation, Billy-Joe Tuccaro threw a copy of Bill 54 in the air at a news conference.

“And he said, ‘this is what we think of your bill. It’s garbage. You’re on treaty land.’ So, the chiefs are very steady and very firm in the pushback and the rejection of any efforts for referendum. And, so the chiefs united…they did the cease and desist. They went to court. They won in court. And, the courts determined that the referendum was unconstitutional,” Currie Hall said.

Currie Hall likens the chiefs’ fight against separation to what the Crees of Quebec did in turning back that separation initiative during the 1995 Quebec referendum.

“And it was the Crees under the leadership of Matthew Coon Come, who was the grand chief at the time, that defeated Quebec and saved Canada,” Currie Hall said.

Coon Come lent his voice and support to Alberta chiefs at the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) Annual General Assembly on July 16, where chiefs passed a landmark resolution put forward by Confederacy of Treaty No. 6 First Nations Grand Chief Joey Pete, alongside Coon Come who was appearing as a proxy from the Cree Nation of Nemaska, Que.

“No province has the legal authority to alter, diminish, or extinguish Treaty Rights or the constitutional relationship between First Nations and the Crown,” the resolution said.

Grassroots boots on the ground getting the vote out

Meanwhile, Currie Hall has been getting help on the ground in Maskwacis from her sister Shelli Yellowbird.

“In Alberta, we only have 145,000 First Nations that are registered (to vote), that’s small” Yellowbird shared in an interview with APTN.

“On the ground, [there are] a lot of uncertainties and not understanding the real purpose and intention of the October 19 vote, but also to a lot of misconceptions about why should we vote. But a lot of it is actually pretty good. The boots on the ground initiative is working really well in terms of getting to the grassroots people, where everybody’s got an assignment to do. Mine is strictly social media blitz,” she said.

Yellowbird has been creating TikTok videos with some getting shared more than 30,000 times.

“And then it works by going door to door. We are using every means that we have in the community, the radio, social media, and word-of-mouth-signage,” Yellowbird said.

Yellowbird described their efforts as “a four nation initiative” at Makwacis primarily at Sampson Cree the biggest nation in Maskwacis. Ermineskin Cree Nation is also doing its own work alongside Montana First Nation and Louis Bull Tribe, the smaller nations that make up Maskwacis.

Yellowbird is hosting a rally at the nation on Saturday, Oct. 17 which will coincide with rallies and protests by First Nations across Alberta. There will also be a rally at the Alberta legislature on Sunday, a day ahead of the referendum.

Advance polls open through Friday

Advance polls opened Monday with some voting locations having to stay open extended hours on Tuesday, “to reflect late location openings,” according to Elections Alberta. It was to afford voters the fully advertised number of hours to vote.

“Late openings were due to various and separate technology issues that have been resolved,” it said.

Of the 311 total advance voting locations open Tuesday, 17 were affected.

author: Hope Pisoni
title: Meta Has Paid Far Right Accounts for Their Posts Ahead of the Midterms
content:
An invite-only program for content creators has accounts promoting white supremacy, anti-LGBTQ, and neo-Nazi rhetoric.

An invite-only program for content creators has accounts promoting white supremacy, anti-LGBTQ, and neo-Nazi rhetoric.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

On September 14, far-right influencer Chaya Raichik, known online as Libs of Tiktok, attacked a Washington state high school on Facebook for displaying a Pride flag. “Hey Mercer Island High School, why does your profile photo display a mutilation flag??” she wrote, tagging the school’s account in the post and attaching a photo of the entrance.

A few weeks before, on August 27, neo-Nazi webcomic artist StoneToss posted a strip that used Tim Curry’s death to mock transgender suicide rates. And earlier this month, right-wing political commentator Benny Johnson shared claims that Democrats will “transition your kids while you’re at work” and “hand out gas cards to illegal aliens.”

Meta pays these creators for making posts like these. In 2024, the tech giant unveiled a new invite-only program called Facebook Content Monetization, designed to streamline earnings for creators. Many creators celebrated the move, with some reporting a major increase in their earnings through the program.

However, that program has recently come under scrutiny. In August, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported that Meta invited accounts promoting white supremacist and neo-Nazi ideologies. And after reviewing Meta’s monetization data, Uncloseted Media identified 29 accounts with histories of anti-LGBTQ+ rhetoric that have been invited to the program. These include the three aforementioned accounts as well as podcaster Candace Owens, who has blamed gay men for child abuse in the Catholic church, and Turning Point USA, which has been connected to an assault on a queer Arizona State University professor. Meta did not respond to Uncloseted Media and The 19th’s requests for an interview or for comment.

With the midterm elections looming, some of the accounts Meta pays through the program have been spreading political misinformation. In the first week of October, for example, Benny Johnson made 14 separate Facebook posts connecting the Democratic Party to election fraud.

Courtney Radsch, director of the Center for Media and Digital Governance at Open Markets Institute, said that promoting hateful rhetoric and misinformation like this is especially dangerous during an election season where the increasingly authoritarian Trump administration, which Meta has courted since its inauguration, has openly discussed attempts to interfere.

“Amplifying and enabling harassment campaigns and centering fringe conspiracy theories through algorithmic curation and monetization opportunities has led to a dissolution of democracy in America,” Radsch told Uncloseted Media and The 19th. “This administration is dismantling democratic oversight and increasing authoritarian control. … You can’t look at your platform policies on monetization without looking at the context in which this is occurring in the U.S. with rising technofascism.”

Meta launched its Facebook Content Monetization program to incentivize more creators to post on Facebook, which has faced an aging user base and competition from newer apps. Those incentives can be substantial — within the program’s first year, content creators who accepted Meta’s invitation to join reported huge increases in their payouts, with some calling it their most lucrative platform. One creator told The Hollywood Reporter that she consistently earned $20,000 to $30,000 per month, while another said his monthly earnings often hit six figures.

While most accounts aren’t big enough to rake in that amount of money, Meta also motivates smaller accounts to join. Starting in 2025, they launched a side program called “breakthrough bonus” that advertises up to $5,000 and an automatic onboarding into Content Monetization for creators from other platforms if they start posting regularly on Facebook.

SK Smigiel, a content creator who posts about LGBTQ+ education and activism under the username justsaysk, joined the program through the breakthrough bonus initiative in April. They say Meta would offer them payouts for completing certain “missions.” For example, Smigiel says they earned $500 a month for posting 10 reels. They say other missions included using trending hashtags and audio or cross-posting to relevant groups. These incentives initially convinced them to post on Facebook due to their poor earnings on Instagram, but they didn’t stick around.

“When I post on Facebook, I don’t even open the post that I’ve made because I already know that … probably 99 percent of the engagement is negative towards me,” Smigiel told Uncloseted Media and The 19th.

Uncloseted Media identified accounts enrolled in the program via data compiled by What To Fix (WTF), a Dutch nonprofit focused on tech accountability. The Meta Monetization Archive is a searchable database of information collected from disclosures released by Meta.

Belén Luna Sanz, policy manager at WTF, said the program represents a broader shift in industry practices. While advertisers once paid content creators directly with companies like Meta taking a cut, platforms now collect all ad revenue and pay creators themselves.

“They’re only paying you royalties depending on how much engagement you are creating on your content,” Sanz told Uncloseted Media and The 19th. Jason Hong, a professor of computer science at Carnegie Mellon University, says that while inflammatory and misleading content may go against Meta’s policies, both the company and the people posting it are financially incentivized to promote it. “We know that things that get people really angry get a lot of engagement, we know that disinformation and misinformation … also gets lots of engagement,” Hong told Uncloseted Media and The 19th. “[Meta is] at a fork in the road, and one path is about the morals and ethics and well-being of society and democracy, and on the other path is a really big pile of money.”

Since Meta launched the program two years ago, WTF has identified over 18 million accounts in the program. But Sanz says the selection process has been opaque and describes the program’s rollout as “reckless.”

“[The program requires] little to no verification of their identity, there are not enough safeguards and their monetization policies are enforced in a very non-transparent way, so it’s hard to tell whether they are enforcing it properly or not,” Sanz said.

Uncloseted Media found numerous posts that seemingly violate Facebook’s content monetization policies, which state that “content may be subject to reduced or disabled monetization if it depicts or discusses [debated social issues] in a polarizing or inflammatory manner.” Those issues include race, religion, sexual orientation, political affiliation and more.

Libs of TikTok, for example, has called the organizers of an LGBTQ+ pride event “sick sick freaks,” accused pro-LGBTQ+ teachers of wanting to “indoctrinate your children” and decried the “lgbtq groomer cult.” Other posts may violate content monetization policies forbidding “derogatory words” and “hateful conduct,” including Raichik using a slur to describe the usage of the term “sex assigned at birth.”

Meta also states that misinformation, which they define as “content that has been rated false by a third-party fact checker,” is “ineligible to monetize,” even though the company ended its third-party fact-checking last year, leaving no clear mechanism to enforce the prohibition. Meta states that “repeated violations of [content monetization policies] could lead to a temporary or permanent ban on your Page or profile’s ability to use our monetization tools.” However, as of the Monetization Archive’s most recent update on September 15, all of the accounts discussed above are actively enrolled in the program. The Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC) has designated several individuals in Meta’s program as extremists. These include Tucker Carlson, who has agreed with claims that gender-affirming care allows adults to “basically molest and abuse children”; James Lindsay and Jack Posobiec, who helped popularize “groomer” rhetoric against LGBTQ+ people; and Alex Jones, whose infamous conspiracy show InfoWars received an invitation prior to its acquisition by The Onion. It also includes Libs of TikTok, which is known for stoking anti-LGBTQ+ harassment — 2024 reports by NBC News and The Washington Post cumulatively found over 80 instances of violent threats against institutions like schools and businesses connected to its posts.

“There does need to be discussion and diversity of opinion allowed in the public sphere,” Radsch said. “However, there is a difference between rational debate and harassment.”

Reports from WTF suggest that Meta doesn’t consistently uphold the program’s other rules either. Despite Meta’s policies stating that “political and government entities are ineligible for monetization,” including “current elected and appointed government officials” and “political parties,” WTF found hundreds enrolled. In addition, Uncloseted Media confirmed membership of at least 8 official Republican Party pages, including the Republican Party of Georgia.

In recent years, Meta has courted the Trump administration and its far-right allies, including influencers. Last August, the company hired Robby Starbuck, an anti-DEI campaigner who has promoted conspiracy theories claiming that pesticides turn children gay, as an adviser on preventing “political bias” in its AI systems. And in April, Meta sponsored a party celebrating Isabel Brown, a Daily Wire host who has advocated for people to leave their LGBTQ+ “lifestyles.” Brown and Starbuck are both enrolled in the content monetization program.

Radsch said that being able to control who gets monetized grants Meta significant power over political narratives.

“That can be problematic because it means that they can pick winners and losers, they can pick ideologies, they can discriminate at will, and we have very little way to know whether that’s happening,” Radsch said.

The stakes are high given the upcoming midterms. Misinformation that the 2020 presidential election was rigged inspired the Jan. 6 insurrection. Still, Meta monetizes accounts which spread similar claims. Libs of TikTok has said, “Democrats want to cheat,” and Johnson responded to reports of new plague cases in Russia by implying that Democrats would use them to rig the election.

“There’s a level of commitment with trying to preserve electoral integrity that needs to be present, especially when there are very delicate elections coming up,” Sanz said. “Disinformation should not be rewarded financially — this is something that even they have in their own policies for monetization.”

Sanz has a “wish list” of new accountability policies that could push back against the anti-LGBTQ+ rhetoric and political disinformation being disseminated through this program. These include labeling monetized accounts and adding mechanisms for users to report monetization policy violations.

Hong added that platforms should restructure their algorithms and monetization systems to consider factors other than engagement.

“I wish that Facebook would have more kinds of metrics, like societal or individual well-being,” Hong said. “These are kinds of things that would be far better for society, but it is a corporation and this is what they’re trying to do because this is the mandate from the top.”

While Meta is protected from many forms of legal action in the United States, there may be a path to legal accountability in other jurisdictions. In 2022, the European Union passed the Digital Services Act (DSA), which, among other provisions, requires large online platforms like Facebook to mitigate the potential harms of content disseminated on their platforms. WTF filed a complaint against Meta in European courts last month arguing that by monetizing 11 accounts sanctioned by the E.U. for alleged involvement in pro-Russia propaganda campaigns, the company failed to meet the DSA’s risk mitigation obligations.

Perhaps most importantly, Sanz emphasizes that social media monetization needs more public attention.

“Creator monetization is a very ill-explored area,” she said. “Although there is a good amount of legislation here in the E.U. that gives us a playground to try to incorporate much more responsibility when it comes to monetization, I do think that globally this needs to be the case.”

Note: Jones and Raichik did not respond to requests for comment.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

title: As Inflation Goes Up, New Poll Shows 4 in 10 Struggle to Pay Basic Necessities
content:
The latest Consumer Price Index report shows that inflation has gone up 3.7 percent over the past year.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows inflation has increased over the past month (and the year overall), as millions of Americans say they are struggling to make ends meet or pay for basic necessities.

According to the CPI report, which was published on Wednesday, consumer prices shot up by 0.6 percent from August to September. Year-over-year prices have increased by 3.7 percent.

That yearly rate is higher than previous reports in 2026. On average, the annual inflation rate, which is included in each monthly report, has been around 3.3 percent since the start of the year. The latest CPI numbers are also higher than they were immediately before Trump returned to the White House in 2025 — according to the December 2024 CPI, the inflation rate was 2.9 percent.

Costs for staple food items have increased over the past year, with ground beef prices up 5.4 percent, fruits and vegetables up 3.7 percent, bread up 3.3 percent, and fish/seafood up 6.9 percent. Energy costs are also markedly higher than they were last year, increasing by 10.9 percent overall, including a 21.5 percent increase in gas prices compared to September 2025.

Analysts largely attribute higher energy prices to Trump’s war against Iran, which began in late February and resulted in the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil is normally transported. The week before the war began, gas prices across the U.S. averaged around $2.937 per gallon. As of Wednesday, prices are $4.333 per gallon on average, a 47 percent increase over the past seven months.

While prices for gasoline have been higher in the past, those increased costs were temporary. This week, the U.S. broke a record set in 2022 for the most days in a calendar year where average prices for regular gasoline have been above $4 per gallon: 158 days total since the start of 2026.

On gas costs, the Trump administration has promised throughout the war that higher prices would be short-lived.

“Rest assured, to the American people, the recent increase in oil and ​gas prices is temporary, and this operation will result in lower gas prices in the long term,” former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said in March.

Asked by reporters about continuing high costs for fuel, Trump said in April that “gas will go down” and will “drop like a rock” as soon as the war is over. In June, he made a similar statement on Truth Social, writing that “Gas prices will plummet, and Affordability will be far better” than in the Biden years.

Earlier this week, Trump appeared to ignore entirely the fact that most Americans are feeling economic pinches, falsely stating during one of his campaign speeches that “prices are coming down very fast” right now.

The president promised on the 2024 presidential campaign trail to lower prices for groceries and other consumer goods, and to produce $2 per gallon gasoline shortly after entering office.

New polling demonstrates Americans are struggling, despite Trump’s rosy assessments.

According to a recently published Pew Research Center survey, 60 percent of Americans say they don’t have enough income to lead the life they desire. The poll also showed that 53 percent say they don’t have emergency savings that could help pay expenses for three months, and a third of respondents (32 percent) say they worry every day or almost every day about health care and debt costs.

Seventy percent of Americans have had to cut back their spending habits for “extras” — going out to eat or streaming services, for example. And 44 percent say they have had trouble paying for at least one basic necessity over the past year.

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister and the Terms of Freedom
content:
Something changes when a woman occupies an office men have treated as their natural inheritance. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri’s 

appointment

 on 29 September 2026 makes that change visible in Morocco. For women whose competence is routinely scrutinised, the pleasure is neither naïve nor trivial.




But the woman forming a government and the woman labouring in the fields, raising children without pay and denied an equal share of her inheritance encounter power differently. Representation changes who governs; emancipation changes what all women have the power to do. That distinction shifts our attention from PM Mansouri’s gender to the politics of the centre-right

 Party of Authenticity and Modernity (PAM

)

, which she leads. Will its programme redistribute the resources and rights on which women’s freedom depends?




The history beneath the headline




Calling women’s leadership foreign to Morocco requires forgetting its history. Historian Osire Glacier 

documents

 women’s authority long before the contemporary premiership. Kenza al Awrabiya, the Amazigh mother of Idris II, helped secure the Idrisid dynasty, founded in the late eighth century in what is now Morocco. Zaynab al Nafzawiyya influenced eleventh-century Almoravid politics around Aghmat, near Marrakech. Sayyida al Hurra governed Tétouan, a city in northern Morocco, during the sixteenth century. Khnata bint Bakkar intervened in eighteenth-century dynastic politics.




Across the region, 

Dihya

 is remembered as an Amazigh queen who led resistance to the Arab conquest in the Aurès, in present-day Algeria, during the late seventh century. Tuareg oral tradition remembers 

Tin Hinan

 as a queen and founding ancestress of noble lineages in the Ahaggar, in present-day southern Algeria.




These histories expose how male authority is made to appear natural. Fatima Mernissi’s 

The Forgotten Queens of Islam

 

challenges that selective memory. Colonialism also reorganised authority: French Protectorate administrators 

reshaped

 customary courts around imperial priorities. What survives as tradition can carry the history of political intervention. 




Religious interpretation can give exclusion another claim to permanence. Islamist and other conservative opponents invoke this 

hadith

 against women’s political authority:




«لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً»




Usually translated as saying that a people governed by a woman will not prosper, it becomes a prohibition irrespective of her competence. Asma Lamrabet, a 

Moroccan Islamic feminist thinker

, questions turning a 

narration linked

 to Persia’s dynastic succession into a universal ban. She reads it against the Qur’anic Queen of Sheba, whose judgement demonstrates capable leadership. Her argument contests male authority’s claim to divine necessity.




PAM’s promises and its record




Women have long contested how authority is distributed within the family. Fatima Sadiqi 

documents 

the Union de l’Action Féminine’s 1992 million-signature campaign to reform the Moudawana, Morocco’s family code. The 2004 reform abolished wives’ duty of obedience but retained unequal inheritance and exceptions to the marriage age of eighteen. Proposals announced in December 2024 left fundamental equality demands unresolved. In October 2025, more than sixty civil society organisations and public figures 

joined to call for comprehensive reform

. Rights in Morocco have advanced through organised demands, not the gender of an officeholder.




PAM, a centre-right party founded in 2008, 

advocates

 social modernisation and positions itself against the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD). It entered government in 2021 alongside the National Rally of Independents and conservative nationalist Istiqlal. Opposition to Islamist conservatism, however, does not itself entail reforming the laws and economic conditions that subordinate women.




PAM’s 

2026 programme

 promises improved widow pensions, childcare, safe transport, a women’s enterprise fund and labour inspection. The commitments leave inheritance equality, abortion reform and decriminalisation of consensual same sex relations unaddressed. Mansouri called for 

banning child marriage

 without exceptions in 2024, yet PAM’s electoral programme 

omits that commitment

. Employment can support independence, but a wage does not cancel criminalisation or unequal property rights. The programme leaves those constraints intact.




Even PAM’s narrow promise to increase women’s access to paid work confronts a record of failure. The government 

promised to raise women’s economic activity rate above 30 

per cent. Morocco’s statistics agency, HCP, recorded 

20.9 percent in 2021

 and 

19 percent in 2025

. That leaves 81 per cent of women aged 15 and over outside the labour force, compared with 31.5 per cent of men. Women’s unpaid work nevertheless sustains households. As a governing coalition since 2021, PAM shares responsibility for the policies that failed to reverse this decline. Promising 21.2 percent by 2031 requires explaining what will change beyond the deadline.




Women in traditional Moroccan attire exploring a bustling outdoor market in Tiznit. Photo by 

YOUSSEF elbelghiti

 /Pexels 




Mansouri’s housing record reveals the distance between reconstruction and recovery. As Marrakech mayor and national housing minister, her 

portfolio included 

earthquake reconstructio

n

. Yet in June 2026, 

Al Haouz survivors protesting 

in Marrakech reported still living in damaged homes at risk of collapse, nearly three years after the earthquake devastated the High Atlas. For women managing care in unsafe housing, delay narrows possibilities for work or study. An unfinished house can become an unfinished independence.




Moreover, PAM must form a coalition government because it lacks a parliamentary majority. Istiqlal’s 

conditions for joining

 the PAM-led government include defending a socially conservative conception of the family and its values. Such alliances protect established family hierarchies. Protection must include a woman’s ability to leave a marriage, raise children independently or refuse the family’s expectations. Support must not entrench dependence. PAM could also govern with parties from the established left, including the Socialist Union of Popular Forces (USFP) and the Party of Progress and Socialism (PPS). Both have participated in previous governments. Their participation would not itself guarantee a feminist programme: the question is which commitments Mansouri’s government would adopt




Within Morocco’s political landscape, the Alliance de la Gauche offers a substantive point of comparison because of its explicit commitments to legal equality and social justice. The Alliance brings together the Unified Socialist Party (PSU) and the Federation of the Democratic Left. Its programme

 

pledges to abolish child marriage without exceptions, eliminate ta’sib

 (which can assign residual inheritance to male relatives) and comprehensively reform inheritance law. These commitments would challenge legal mechanisms that sustain women’s dependence. Whatever coalition Mansouri forms, advancing equality requires confronting those mechanisms, rather than merely broadening the government’s political composition.




For left parties to make a substantive difference, their commitments must extend to how care is funded and shared. Nancy Fraser’s

 

analysis of capitalism’s care contradiction

 shows how economies depend on care while undermining the resources sustaining it. Cuts and inadequate services transfer obligations into households, often onto women. A feminist left must confront that transfer and defend bodily autonomy, rather than expect class justice automatically to produce it. 




When representation preserves hierarchy




Morocco’s first female prime minister follows earlier examples of women’s leadership in other Muslim-majority countries, including 

Pakistan

, 

Bangladesh

 and 

Tunisia

. Their experience challenges religious arguments against women’s leadership, but also the assumption that representation guarantees emancipation. In 2025, 

women’s labour force 

participation in Pakistan stood at 24 percent and 38.6 percent in Bangladesh, against roughly 80 percent for men. In Tunisia, Najla Bouden’s 2021 appointment accompanied 

an authoritarian concentration of power

. Patriarchy can accommodate a woman at the summit while preserving the laws, economic dependencies and hierarchies that subordinate women below. 




Emancipation requires changing how power is organised, exercised and distributed.




Women’s leadership can also lend credibility to conservative projects. Italy’s Giorgia Meloni government 

allowed anti-abortion

 groups access to counselling centres. This risks exposing women seeking abortions to pressure against their decision. Japan’s Sanae Takaichi 

defends 

compulsory shared marital surnames and male imperial succession. Their ascent to power leaves those constraints on other women intact. 




And the rise of Germany’s Alice Weidel, who raises two sons with a Sri Lankan-born female partner while 

leading the far-right AfD

, which opposes same sex marriage and expanded adoption rights and demands tighter immigration restrictions, is another example. Her presence makes the party appear more open than the freedoms it would extend to others. Rwanda’s former Minister of Family and Women’s Development 

under the interim government in 1994

, Pauline Nyiramasuhuko, 

was convicted of genocidal crimes,

 including responsibility for rape. Together, these cases expose the danger of treating gender as a guarantee of solidarity.




Patriarchy survives through the incentives and penalties that organise social life. 




Feminist sociologist Deniz Kandiyoti’s

 

concept of “patriarchal bargains”

 explains how women seek security within patriarchal systems, sometimes enforcing the restrictions they navigate. A mother may limit her daughter’s choices because she fears the consequences of disobedience. For women in political office, the question is whether they use their authority to dismantle the conditions that make obedience a price of security.




What freedom requires




Which women are recognised as entitled to freedom? Kimberlé Crenshaw’s 

intersectionality

 challenges separating gender from racialisation. Class, disability, sexuality and citizenship shape whether a woman can exercise a right. A professional’s independence may depend on another woman’s underpaid domestic labour. 




Feminism must confront that unequal distribution of freedom.




Poverty makes institutional failure harder to escape. In 2025, nine 

maternal deaths

 at Agadir’s Hassan II Regional Hospital prompted demands for accountability. Women unable to purchase private care depend on public provision. In Morocco, rural Amazigh women 

face barriers 

to services and information in their language; agricultural workers have 

described

 low pay and sexual violence. Celebrating Amazigh queens means little if living Amazigh women cannot reach a hospital or work safely.




Dependence is also enforced through law. Morocco’s article 490 

criminalises sex outside marriage

, exposing sexually active unmarried women, including single mothers, to prosecution. Single and divorced mothers need independent parental rights, 

children born outside marriage

 can be denied paternal maintenance and inheritance. Article 489 

criminalises same sex relations

, threatening lesbian, bisexual and queer women’s intimacy. Transgender women lack

 

legal gender recognition

 and face

 

policing of their gender expression

 under Article 483, whose prohibition of public indecency can be applied even when no nudity is involved.




Safety requires rights that survive disapproval. 




Rights also require that institutions be accessible for women. In its 

2017 review of Morocco

, the UN disability committee identified inaccessible courts and healthcare, and restrictions on legal capacity. Disabled and neurodivergent women need accessible services, bodily autonomy and the means to live independently with dignity.




Migration status creates another fault line in women’s access to protection. Political theorist Françoise Vergès’s

 

A Decolonial Feminism

 insists that feminism must confront racism and capitalism together. This shifts the question from whether women gain power to which women that acquired power protect. A 

2023 study of 151 migrant women

 attending healthcare facilities in Rabat found that 76.2 per cent reported gender based violence during migration, while only 9 per cent of survivors had filed a complaint. Pan-African feminism must make access to protection a measure of political progress. 




Women’s advancement cannot be measured only among those the nation recognises as its own.




I want equality that dismantles the arrangements through which patriarchy makes obedience a condition of survival. A woman needs a home she can keep, an income she controls and laws that recognise her authority over her own body. Inheritance, abortion, housing, the right to love and collective labour rights belong together because freedom requires power over the conditions of one’s life.




For girls, that begins with accessible schools, protection against violence and child marriage, and a future they can choose. A right that poverty renders unusable remains, in practice, a privilege.




PM Mansouri’s appointment enlarges what women can imagine. Its feminist significance depends on whether power becomes less concentrated and freedom more accessible to women still impoverished, marginalised or criminalised. Patriarchy can accommodate exceptional women; emancipation must reach those it keeps expendable. Women’s liberation cannot rest on the hierarchies that decide which women can be sacrificed.




 




Ayah Kareem is a Moroccan feminist researcher, writer and activist whose work connects political analysis with collective organising. She has an academic background in political science and human rights and is a Thomson Reuters Foundation mentee. Drawing on decolonial and intersectional feminism, she examines the patriarchal institutions that make inequality ordinary and the struggles that make it contestable.

title: Indigenous Just Transition in The Arctic
content:
This is going to be a collaborative event between Ungeirr Umkveraasenaar, or the Icelandic Young Environmentalists, and the Indigenous Environmental Network. Maybe we can go around and you guys can give a little introduction about yourselves. Sure.

Huang’a a’ka, pang’a’anang naka pang’a’u yu, huang’a a’taka, a’anatirma, naka kirstinuga pás, huang’a sivunga rumi. I come from St. Lawrence Island. I’ve been with IEN since 2021, and I work on organizing against climate geoengineering.

Kweyanaipaplusi maunga, huang’a a’akaluk, ungelaksirmiu runga, angayukang maktaklu Charlie. I a’anukwa’apu’a makigaklu anaktiyuk asii, janililu Charlie, chinirmiu, ungelaksirmiu. Thank you everyone for welcoming us here today.

I’m Adrienne A’akaluk Blatchford. I’m from Unalakleet, Alaska, which is up on the Northwest Coast in the passageway to the Arctic. We’re right on the coast of the Bering Sea in the heart of the Norton Sound.

And I work with Indigenous Environmental Network as a geoengineering outreach organizer with a focus on Alaska and the Arctic. Hello, thank you for having us as the host.

My name is Thomas Joseph. I’m a Hoopa Valley tribal member from the Six Rivers National Forest in Northern California. I am also Shoshone Paiute from the Sierra Nevadas. Paiute is what we call it, the land of flowing water.

I’m down there by Yosemite and the Half Dome area. I am here with the Indigenous Environmental Network as their carbon pricing educator. And again, thanks for having us.

Yá’át’ééh. My name is Talia Boyd. Older women from my community who love to have the time of their lives shared with me.

Greetings, everyone. My name is Talia Boyd. I’m the mining organizer for IEN.

I’m based in New Mexico, originally from Arizona, and I hail from the Navajo Nation in the Southwest. And I’m very honored to be here with y’all and share this space and time. Thank you.

Awesome. And a little bit about me for any of you who don’t know me. My name is Isla.

I’m originally from Wales and I’ve been living here in Iceland for over five years and I’m the education representative for the Icelandic Young Environmentalists. So how about we just go straight into things and you guys can give us a little bit of an oral presentation about your work and everything that you do and then we’ll get started with the panel Q&A afterwards. Sounds good.

Thank you. So I want to kind of do a little bit of an introduction on who is the Indigenous Environmental Network. Over 30 years ago the United States, we’re kind of seeing that return back to that, was having a really hard time addressing the mining operations of uranium in the southwest and the Indigenous people came together as they were the ones that were being directly affected by these mining operations that was being used for the production of uranium for the purpose of war.

And so the Indigenous peoples from that region rallied together to try to protect their communities against the high rates of cancers and other issues that was plaguing their communities to no avail. The state governments wouldn’t listen to them. The national governments wouldn’t listen to them and so they seen that it was in their best interest to take this fight to the international space of the United Nations and that’s when the Indigenous Environmental Network was formed with the purpose and intent of taking the struggles of the mining and the struggles of the health impacts of mining to a global positioning.

The Indigenous Environmental Network has been active in the United Nations space since then and in various different causes pertaining to the Paris Climate Agreement, water issues, mining issues, also very active in the Convention on Biological Diversity and we continue to play a role of Indigenous networks across Turtle Island. So we come from impacted communities of Indigenous peoples. Frontline community is another term that’s often used from across Turtle Island of communities that are faced with deforestation, faced with dams, faced with any type of harm that we see against our Mother Earth.

In these past 30 years IEN has now expanded its network to be globally and so we have Indigenous organizations that we work with across the globe and in North America we have a strong positioning on mining operations which is Talia Leeds and geoengineering and carbon pricing which I do but we also do a lot of other work pertaining to just transition and many other things that you can find on our website at IENEarth.org. Thank you. Great. I wanted to share a little bit about the two histories Thomas talked about.

The duality that we have to keep in mind, the recognition that the history of why we are in this work and what our priorities are in terms of the Arctic and climate change and then the history and the purpose behind the Arctic Assembly which is the meetings that we are attending. So I come from St. Lawrence Island and Akula comes from very nearby and their community also experienced a lot of the same things we did. The history that we carry is around colonization and how the purpose behind colonization was always resource extraction, resource extraction happening from Indigenous people’s lands and waters and to the detriment of our health, our welfare, the health of our ecosystems and as a violation of the sacred or the original instructions that we have carried forward through millennia.

And particularly this was done through military tactics and the military has also harmed our communities by creating bases on or near our communities or where we practice subsistence activities and other cultural activities and those bases have contaminated our lands and contaminated our waters and so we suffer the health effects and so we see all of these as connected because the military was used to colonize and the purpose behind colonizing was resource extraction. So we always come back to that and we see those issues like permeating throughout all of the issues that we’ll talk about today including carbon markets, carbon pricing, geoengineering, mining, even in the energy transition. But I was going back as I do whenever I come to the Arctic Assembly and looking at the web archives of when they first formed and some of the stuff on here is interesting.

I just wanted to read some of the wording. The Arctic is the fastest warming place on earth. This is from their website in 2013.

As a result it is moving to the center of the geopolitical stage and is playing an increasingly important role in globalization, economic development, energy exploration, environmental protection, and international security. So it’s just kind of environmental protection is just kind of sprinkled in there a little bit but the priority is clearly economic development. And if you look at the articles like I could go you can go and look at who created it, who was on their first board, who was on their first panel, but some of the articles that they attached.

Could Western Alaska become the new Panama Canal? Energy, indigenous communities, and the Arctic Council. Arctic climate change opens new shipping routes. So these are the articles that they cited as the foundation of the initial meetings that they were having and I wanted to read one excerpt just to kind of give the context of what the purpose was behind this meeting and like holding that reality in the messages that they appear to be spreading versus what is actually being done.

Owing to the vast economic opportunities and environmental, social, and geopolitical challenges it presents, the Arctic is an emerging as an important topic of debate. With an estimated 25 percent of the world’s undiscovered oil and gas reserves, and with climate change making shorter maritime routes through Arctic waters possible, the rewards of successful economic development are plentiful. Like that’s how they started out.

And then this is really interesting. They say, however, the remote pristine frontier is home to some of the world’s harshest conditions making energy development, maritime trade, and tourism increasingly difficult and dangerous. The Arctic is also home to indigenous communities whose livelihoods are likely to be challenged by both the effects of climate change and increasing external human activity in the region.

So those are just, yeah, a couple of things that I wanted you to keep in mind and I wanted to hand it back to Thomas to look at the history of carbon pricing. Thank you, Pananga. I remember my first time here in the Arctic region.

I was invited up here by Pananga Pagawi and other indigenous peoples from Greenland and the Alaska region because they told me, they came the year before, and they told me that there is a lot of talk and dialogue that’s being discussed in this Arctic circle pertaining to carbon markets and the continued commodification of our Mother Earth. And this is something that I have specialized with the Indigenous Environmental Network for quite a few years now. And when we look at the CDMs on where carbon markets came from, which is the Clean Development Mechanism, which was created out of the Kyoto Protocols, which is basically the foundation of the Paris Climate Agreement.

And so when we go that far back, we have to also understand that it was the strong arm of Al Gore at the time, who was the Vice President of the United States, that really forced these governmental nations into accepting a clean development mechanism or a carbon market mechanism, which we see as indigenous peoples is just the continuation of commodifying our Mother Earth for the profitable gain of the elite few. We also see it as a mechanism to continue colonization and white supremacy, as that’s what these northern global nations are pushing and addressing. The world did not want clean development mechanisms.

They didn’t want to put a price tag on carbon because they didn’t think that that was the route to go. But because of the strong arm of the United States, they were able to get clean development mechanisms into the Kyoto Protocols. And so we see a shift now, how the United States is not even a signer of the Paris Climate Agreement, and they have pulled out.

So their influence in that space has dramatically changed, but yet it is the foundation of how the world is addressing climate change. We now see in Article 6 of the Paris Climate Agreement and market mechanisms as a way to, how they see in their eyes, bring carbon out of the air, because we know that greenhouse gases are real. We know that that’s what’s warming our planet, and that is what is causing climate change.

But instead of reducing gases at source, or reducing the burning of fossil fuel, they’re simply offsetting it. So they’re saying that they could do offsets through RED, which is reducing emissions through deforestation and forest degradation, and RED Plus, which even expands that into nature-based solutions and other products. But that’s still just a continuation of commodifying our Mother Earth.

And now if we look at climate change, one of the root causes of climate change is capitalism, is that we continue to see our Mother Earth as something that we can make profit of, that we can continue to separate ourselves from, and think that it is here just for the profitable gain of a select few, and not that we’re in relationship with our Mother Earth, not that that relationship is reciprocal, like Indigenous peoples believe. And so when we look into even biodiversity offsets that are now being pushed, it calls that relationship into question. As humanity, are we going to continue to move forward with the desire of just raping and plaguing our Mother Earth? Are we going to try to find some type of balance and reciprocal relationship with her, so that she can heal, and that we may be able to move forward and not experience this climate chaos that’s coming our way? We see that in Nepal.

We see that with the mega El Nino that’s going on right now in California. So we will continue to experience this. Even the Secretariat has said, we have reached 1.5, we will start experiencing mega catastrophes with climate change.

But yet, what we’re seeing is just us doubling down on mechanisms that has caused climate change. I brought up colonization earlier. When we look at the world’s biodiversity, 80% of the world’s biodiversity is in the tenure of Indigenous peoples.

And so for these global elite countries to be able to maintain their economic growth, to be able to maintain their markets, they need to gain access to these unceded territories of Indigenous peoples. And that’s how they do it, is through carbon markets, through biodiversity offsets, through the 30 by 30 initiative, which is being pushed through the CBD, the Convention on Biological Diversity. And so, you know, this is just continuating the ability to access unceded Indigenous lands and further colonize Indigenous peoples, and move us away from an understanding that what we really need to do is rebuild our relationship with our Mother Earth, not to see her as a commodity just to be used, but understand that our reciprocal relationship with her is vital, and not just the humanity of humans, but in all things living.

And so when I came up here to my first Arctic gathering, I seen what they were telling me about. I seen how these Arctic nations were lifting up examples from all across the world, not even the Arctic, from New Zealand, on mangroves that are being introduced as carbon offsets in the New Zealand area. And we see how Nepal and that region is being considered the third Arctic for the purpose of offset projects on sprinkling, these guys will get more into that, but sprinkling basically fiberglass on top of the ice.

And so it’s just a continuation of us continuing to commodify our Mother Earth and not understand that we really need to address root causes, which is capitalism, which is colonization and patriarchy, and the continuation that we always need to develop new market mechanisms or new systems to gain wealth. So we need to have that system change. But when we keep on focusing on false solutions like direct air capture, which is alive and well here in Iceland, we’re not going to be able to really focus on keeping the fossil fuels in the ground, and making sure that we’re limiting the amount of carbon that’s being burnt and not simply offsetting it.

Thank you. I’m just going to snowball off of what Thomas said, because before I get into what I’m going to talk about with geoengineering, he said something really profound one time that just kind of made carbon markets and these schemes that they are implementing within our governance systems, these colonial governance systems. When you think about the world’s forest and the oceans and the rivers and Mother Earth, and we see these climate disasters, she’s already struggling to breathe, right? We already know that.

We’ve exceeded 1.5. And these carbon market schemes and these false solutions make it sound like they’re putting a new forest, or there’s a new emerging ocean, or there’s these rivers that are already leaching things like mercury, because of the melting permafrost in them, that all of a sudden they’re appearing out of nowhere for these carbon markets, right? And that’s not what’s happening. We’re seeing extractivism continue to grow. We’re seeing this sort of monetary wealth through this extractive industry pile more, right, to do business as usual on top of all of it.

And that’s led us into from fossil fuel dependency into a tech regime that has emerged from false solutions like geoengineering. And when we think about geoengineering, it’s such a far-fetched concept when you’re first learning about it, right? It’s like a sci-fi movie. There’s two different types that are really focused on, especially in the Arctic, with solar radiation management and carbon dioxide removal.

And Thomas had just mentioned, you know, we have the facility right out here, just out of town. And when these false solutions first started popping up here in the Arctic, we seen a lot of the focus on the Arctic is melting, we need to save the Arctic, because we know that the rest of the world depends on this ice cap and this old ice, right? When you think about the Arctic Ocean and where the passageway comes up through and the world perceives it as this frozen place all the time, well, it took a millennia for that ice to form, and it’s taken a hundred years for it to melt because of extractivism, because of colonialism, because of after imaginary wealth, when you think of money and the way that it is focused in our lives. The villagers have been speaking from us.

They feed us all these lies about you need daycare, you need childcare, you need education. We’ve always had those systems within our communities, within our social systems of wherever we come from, right? And so this colonial practice has led us to these false solutions, saying that if we can introduce a way to control the climate, then we can keep the world at a critical level. And so that’s when folks that started doing these carbon capture projects, the marine carbon dioxide removal, the solar radiation management, I’m sorry, is there a T-next in here anywhere? Sorry, guys, I’ve been really sniffly all day.

I went from the latitudes to the seas, and the Arctic has caught me again. But geoengineering has been a huge focus at Arctic Assembly for years. The first year that we had attended, we had gone in and they were talking about a solar aerosol injection project, and they have this huge, beautiful display, and PhD candidates, so much PhD candidates, doctorates, scientists, renowned university folks that had come in, and they’re from Ivy League colleges that are standing there saying, yeah, we’re going to spray sulfur dioxide over the Arctic, and once we deploy, it’s going to have to happen for 100 years, and 5% of the world’s population is going to perish doing it, but it’s going to be a sacrifice to the rest of the world.

And we’re sitting there, and you’re saying, and by the way, the 5% will be Indigenous people, marginalized communities, and the majority of it will be in the Arctic. Not even a blink of an eye. And this is an international platform where there are decision makers from the pan-Arctic coming here to talk about saving the world by spraying toxic chemicals into the atmosphere to literally kill people, animals, ecosystems, so they’re well synthesized.

And then we see projects like the Arctic Ice Project, which was formerly known as Ice 9-11, which is a, the idea was to increase the surface albedo of the ice by sprinkling glass beads, microscopic glass beads, which were formed by scientists at 3M who had previously worked for Chevron, and NHP as an engineer, and she has over 300 patents, came up to the Arctic, and without required consent, without proper processes processes to assess the environment that she was going to be introducing huge amounts of new substances to, had no connection to anybody in the Arctic, just came in and started doing it on their own free will, and hiring local Indigenous students at a college up north. And when we got wind of this project, we immediately saw red flags. We started pushing back, but we found that a lot of these geoengineering projects, these fossil solutions that are rooted in extractivism, are crowd-funded and have huge hedge funds that come in as a guide, as nature, they’re going to conserve nature by introducing these projects in the world to keep being, continue doing business as usual.

And so the science is rooted in all of the things that Thomas has talked about, and the foundation of the Arctic Assembly is been based on the sacrifice zone, creating new sacrifice zones, not only in Arctic Indigenous lands, but lands worldwide, because what happens in the north is going to impact the rest of the world. And so once we started organizing around, pushing back on these projects, Thomas’ family had joined us all the way down in California in Menlo Park, where Leslie Fields, one of the founders of the Arctic Ice Project, had organized a fundraiser and a golf course, a very prestigious golf course in Menlo Park. And so a group of Alaska Native folks had gone down, a delegation that IAN Kavanaugh had put together with IAN and Thomas’ family joined us.

Yeah, yeah, so we bought this, we spent thousands of dollars on purchasing a VIP ticket, and immediately they denied our entrance and said that it was still, that it was already at capacity. So we got some folks that we were working with down there, and they also applied and got in immediately. And so they went in and were able to infiltrate this fundraiser.

But it didn’t last long, and they caught on with the folks that were with us outside when we were picketing and protesting. And they came out and wanted to try to see, so the police showed up and said, sorry, we can’t do anything, this is legal here, and tried to have us removed. So we continued that, but it brought attention, right? That’s where we started, and we continued for five years.

No, 19 to 25, yeah, six years. 24. So yeah, five years, we continued to push back against this project that had moved, started in the Bay Area and then Minnesota on Indigenous lands, on a lake there, and all the way up to a camp which we had deployed, and then we started attacking on Arctic, like Arctic species of fish, and yeah, and birds, and was doing false reporting.

And it comes here to the Arctic Assembly without false reporting. And the guys, of course, that were giving this case to the Arctic, I watched Al Gore’s, her claim was, I watched Al Gore’s documentary, touched my heart, it made me want to save the world. So these projects continue to not only allow them to do business as usual, but create sacrifice zones in other Indigenous communities, not only in the Arctic, but the rest of the world.

And so geoengineering is another dangerous way for the elite to continue doing what they do, by extracting, and stealing, and killing Indigenous people throughout the world. We see that within our communities. And it isn’t only the impacts of the introduction of all of these foreign substances, but it also is our mental health, right? Without our connection to the land, and without our way of being, since we always have our mental health struggles, we have suicide clusters, we have cancer clusters, we have autoimmune diseases that are unexplained.

We have experiences at such a high level that we’re in a constant state of grief as Indigenous people. And so it isn’t only what we’re seeing on the surface, but also the subsurface of who we are. And so this geoengineering, these fossil solutions, these carbon market mechanisms, all of these different ways that they’re claiming a way to advance science, to save the world, is a shield and almost like a blind for them to continue doing what they want to do in our land.

And so we recognize that, and we continue to push for free pirate consent, and meaningful government-to-government consultation. And when we say that, we’re not talking about these colonial governments that we see, but also our traditional government systems, because that’s how we function within our community. So I’m going to leave it there, below air, if she wants to.

Yeah, just add a couple things. So as we feel continued, she left our fifth ice project. I think they figured her out because she had done the experiments outdoors.

And so then they changed their company name and said, we’re not doing outdoor experiments. And they started doing like all those experiments on those species. And then she formed her other, another company, called Wheel.

title: Le hussard noir tombe du toit / une émission de Minuit Décousu
content:
Après notre émission sur le début du mouvement lycéen à Lyon, on continue à suivre la mobilisation en passant cette fois la porte des établissements actuellement vides pour voir ce qu'il reste des fameux hussards noirs de la République et comprendre l'origine du malaise qui a poussé autant de jeunes dans les rues.




Cette semaine, cela fait déjà près d'une vingtaine de jours que le mouvement lycéen et désormais également étudiant s'est emparé des rues lyonnaises quasi quotidiennement. Partout, les lycées ont encore leurs portes solidement fermées voire barricadées de peur de la résurgence des rassemblement lycéens aux portes des établissements, malgré la répression inédite menée conjointement par la préfecture et le rectorat. Depuis notre dernière émission, où l'on écoutait dans des entretiens fleuves des lycéen-nes lyonnais-es nous parler de leurs premiers blocages, de l'organisation et des perspectives du mouvement, la répression a tenté de dégager la mobilisation des abords des établissements pour lui faire gagner la respectabilité des mobilisation sociales traditionnelles. Pourtant, la jeunesse continue de prouver jour après jour sa détermination à poursuivre le mouvement, selon son propre agenda.




Pour cette émission, on voulait aller voir ce qu'il se passait en interne dans les établissements scolaires pour comprendre l'origine du malaise qui a poussé autant de jeunes dans la rue. On est donc allés tourner dans la manifestation du 13 octobre à Lyon, où l'on écoute à nouveau des lycéen-nes, mais aussi des étudiant-es nous parler de l'avancée de leur mobilisation et la manière dont les établissements du second degré et du supérieur tentent coûte que coûte de mater la révolte en interne en gardant leurs portes fermées. Dans cette même manif', on s'est entretenu avec des profs de lycées de quartiers populaires ayant connu de nombreux blocages qui nous expliquent concrètement ce qu'il se passe dans les établissements fantômatiques depuis ces 20 derniers jours. . On écoute aussi une camarade prof de lettre en réseau d'éducation prioritaire renforcé (REP+) de banlieue lyonnaise, qui revient à notre micro sur les évolutions de l'éducation ces 10 dernières années, sur l'absence complète de démocratie dans les bahuts et sur le fossé grandissant entre l'ordre et la morale pronés par les adultes et les désirs de révolution des jeunes. Pour saupoudrer le tout d'un peu d'histoire, on est allés repiquer les archives du mouvement lycéen de 1971 à Villeurbanne dans le 2ème numéro des 

Informations Rassemblées à Lyon

 (IRL).




L'émission s'écoute sur notre 

audioblog

, ici, et un peu partout en podcast. Bonne écoute !




 

 

 

 

 

 










Minuit Décousu, c'est un fanzine radiophonique nocturne sur 

Radio Canut

 (Lyon et alentours), 

Radio Vassivière

 (Limousin) et 

Cause Commune

 (Paris/IDF). Semaine après semaine pendant une heure, on en découd avec la nuit et on tire les fils de sons, de textes, d'archives et de voix qui s'entremêlent.

author: labor4pal
title: Universities fire dozens amid pressure from Zionist billionaires (Electronic Intifada)
content:
Ali Abunimah Rights and Accountability 14 October 2026

Universities in the United States and Canada have fired, suspended and harassed employees for speaking out against Israel’s genocide in Gaza, often using ostensibly neutral disciplinary procedures to conceal politically motivated retaliation.

That is the finding of a new report from the Academic Freedom Initiative, a project of the Middle East Studies Association (MESA).

“Lessons in Repression: Silencing Campus Workers on Palestine Since October 7, 2023” is the first systematic study of retaliation against university employees for their Palestine-related speech and activism in the two countries.

The report draws on a database of 196 incidents recorded through 20 August 2026 and in-depth interviews with 31 targeted employees.

Of those incidents, 76 – nearly 40 percent – resulted in termination, while 59 involved suspension or campus bans.

Both tenured professors and precariously employed instructors and staff have been targeted. Of 134 cases in which racial or ethnic identity was known, nearly two-thirds involved people of color. Some 16.5 percent of those targeted identified as Jewish.

Most retaliation had nothing to do with classroom teaching. More than half the incidents stemmed from other on-campus activities, including protests, while only 11 percent concerned alleged classroom interactions.

Another 16 percent of cases arose from off-campus speech and 12 percent from social media posts, “suggesting that teaching is a relatively less common context provoking punishment.”

Major drivers of the repression include pressure from wealthy pro-Israel donors, government interference and the political loyalties of university administrators and trustees, the report says.

Growing financial dependence of universities on wealthy benefactors, alongside austerity and the widespread use of precariously employed workers, also makes institutions more vulnerable to political pressure.

At the University of Pennsylvania, for example, trustee Cheryl Peisach is married to the treasurer of a family foundation that donated $100,000 to Canary Mission in 2023.

The notorious pro-Israel blacklisting website publishes dossiers attacking students and academics who support Palestinian rights.

US immigration authorities have admitted to using its dossiers to target Palestine activists.

In another case at Penn, a tenured professor faced a vicious online harassment campaign over her support for Palestine, including hundreds of messages containing rape and death threats.

The donor funding her endowed chair withdrew support. According to the professor, a dean told her that donor pressure had led the university to encourage her retirement. She retired in June 2026.

Billionaire Bill Ackman demanded a blacklist of Harvard students who disagreed with his views, while billionaire Leon Cooperman threatened to stop donating to Columbia University following a Palestine solidarity walkout.

Pressure from the Trump administration has reinforced the crackdown.

During the last two months of 2023, the US government opened more federal “anti-Semitism” investigations against universities than in all previous years combined.

Dozens of institutions agreed to government monitoring, including sharing the names of students and employees accused of anti-Semitism, to close investigations.

Harvard provided a notable example of such cowardice. Even as it fought a Trump administration lawsuit falsely portraying Gaza solidarity protests as anti-Jewish terror, the university boasted of its own crackdown on alleged anti-Semitism rather than defend its students’ right to protest Israel’s genocide.

A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit in August, finding that the government had failed to plausibly allege any ongoing violation of civil rights law.

Six congressional hearings between December 2023 and July 2025 subjected university leaders to McCarthyite interrogations over alleged failures to combat anti-Semitism.

In Illinois, Northwestern University journalism professor Steven Thrasher was suspended shortly after being singled out during one of these hearings and was later denied tenure and terminated. He is currently suing the university for discrimination and violations of his First Amendment rights.

The repression has also affected Canada, where provincial ministers have publicly accused academic staff and students of anti-Semitism, attacked discussions of Palestine and genocide, and demanded the removal of pro-Palestinian statements from university websites.

The crackdown has often been brutally overt.

More than 3,000 anti-genocide protesters, mostly students, were arrested or detained on US campuses by July 2024. Faculty and staff were affected by police violence.

At Indiana University, seven faculty members were arrested while trying to protect protesting students from government forces.

One professor recalled stepping between students and state troopers armed with assault rifles.

“I was arrested trying to preserve the safety of those students,” he said. He was banned from campus for a year and has received death threats.

The university itself pushed for criminal charges against the arrested faculty, but, according to the report, the county prosecutor “refused to press any charges, believing the constitutionality of the arrests was dubious at best.”

In January 2026, a federal court ruled that Indiana University had violated the First Amendment rights of Palestine solidarity protesters it banned from campus in 2024, including students and faculty.

The court also found the university’s ban on overnight expressive activity unconstitutional and ordered related disciplinary reprimands expunged from their records.

But MESA finds that much of the repression has taken less visible forms.

University administrators have relied on lengthy investigations, vague allegations, fabricated policy violations, non-renewal of contracts and non-disclosure agreements to punish employees while concealing their political motivations.

In many cases, the investigation itself is a form of repression.

“The complaints themselves have been the punishment, have been the intimidation and were designed to be,” Judith Norman, a professor at Trinity University in Texas, said of the repeated, baseless anti-Semitism accusations she faced.

Some allegations were astoundingly petty.

One professor was summoned to an anti-discrimination office after two students complained that the professor’s use of the term “state of Israel,” rather than simply “Israel,” supposedly made them feel alienated from the learning process.

In another case, a professor had to attend a meeting to face questions about a class he had taught two years earlier. The “accusations” included his use of the term “Jewish settlers” to refer to Israeli settlers, who, as the report notes, “due to Israel’s discriminatory laws, are by definition nearly always Jews.”

Investigations frequently drag on for months or years, with employees denied basic information about the accusations against them or meaningful opportunities to defend themselves.

Some investigators displayed open hostility or political bias, conflating criticism of Israel with hatred of Jews, or themselves expressing pro-Israel, anti-Arab, anti-Muslim views.

Universities have also increasingly subjected teaching materials to political surveillance.

By August 2026, seven US states had mandated public access to course syllabi, exposing instructors to scrutiny and complaints from political activists with no connection to their classrooms.

Another prominent tactic is what the report calls “networked harassment.”

Pro-Israel social media accounts and activists generate outrage against academics, sometimes unleashing torrents of racist abuse, doxxing and violent threats.

In one striking case at the University of Pennsylvania, a tenured professor faced a vicious campaign of online harassment after declining to participate in a documentary produced by a Zionist student activist.

Targeted over her personal social media posts about Palestine, she received hundreds of hate emails, most demanding that she be raped, along with death threats and other abuse.

“Because if somebody says, ‘you should be raped’ enough, you do watch your back a little bit,” she told MESA.

The harassment was followed by demands from donors, university trustees, alumni and outside groups that she be fired.

Rather than defend their employees, university administrators often capitulate to the harassers’ demands, even amplifying the attacks themselves.

None of MESA’s interviewees reported that their universities took action to protect them from online incitement.

The personal consequences have been devastating.

Nearly half of the documented incidents involved financial harm. Employees lost jobs, health insurance, housing and career prospects, while accusations of anti-Semitism inflicted lasting damage on reputations.

Amid intensified kidnappings and deportations by ICE, the US immigration agency, the risks for international scholars are even greater.

A tenure-track professor facing retaliation feared that losing her job would also mean losing her immigration status.

“Without my work visa, then I don’t have a status in the country. I have two kids here and a [non-citizen] husband,” she explained.

A professor who had been arrested and suspended described the continuing fear he experienced simply going to work.

“Every morning I come to my office, and I put my key in the door. I wonder if it’s going to work. Did they change the lock? Did they fire me and not tell me?”

“I don’t feel safe at this university,” he said, opining that if the institution’s president decided he had to go, “I don’t feel that there is even one level or layer that would try to stop them from firing me.”

The damage extended far beyond those directly punished.

The report documents pervasive self-censorship, with academics increasingly reluctant to discuss Palestine or criticize Israel – effectively fulfilling a key goal of the repression campaign.

Targeted employees also described profound disappointment with colleagues who refused to defend them.

Some condemned the “abject cowardice” of tenured professors who were the least likely to speak out, or provide moral and material support.

Interviewees also criticized faculty and administrators who privately expressed sympathy but remained publicly silent.

“Notably, pre-tenure faculty and students were more likely to provide support, despite being in a more precarious position than their tenured colleagues,” the report states.

Yet the report also offers lessons for resisting repression.

MESA urges workers to document everything, understand their rights, build alliances and join unions and professional associations. It calls on university administrators to defend academic freedom rather than merely proclaim their commitment to it.

It also recommends that institutions reject the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s so-called definition of anti-Semitism, which conflates criticism of Israel and its Zionist state ideology with anti-Jewish bigotry.

Far from impartial, the IHRA is a self-selected group of countries including Israel, the United States and other Western states that are Israel’s principal allies and arms suppliers.

Israel’s lobby has aggressively pushed for widespread adoption of the IHRA definition as a way to muzzle and smear supporters of Palestinian rights.

One significant victory came at the City University of New York, where a coordinated campaign involving unions and Palestine solidarity activists secured the rehiring of three of four contingent instructors dismissed after participating in a pro-Palestine demonstration.

The experience highlighted the importance of openly confronting the pro-Israel motivations behind the repression rather than treating it solely as a matter of employment rights.

As one professor involved in the organizing explained, “the more direct the political message about Palestine was, the more powerful the movement became.”
