author: James Green
title: Trumponaro: como um governo de Flávio pode imitar a presidência de Trump no Brasil?
content:
Enquanto apoiadores do presidente Lula se 

mobilizam

 para reverter os resultados do primeiro turno da disputa presidencial e garantir um quarto mandato liderado pelo Partido dos Trabalhadores, acho importante considerar que tipo de presidência o Brasil teria caso Flávio Bolsonaro fosse eleito em 25 de outubro.




Obviamente, todo cenário político nacional é único. Um eventual futuro governo Bolsonaro poderia ser bem diferente da forma como Donald Trump tem governado desde que retornou à presidência em 2025. 

No entanto, dada a afinidade declarada da família Bolsonaro com o clã Trump — bem como com suas políticas e práticas —, vale a pena considerar em que medida um novo presidente, governando com uma forte base de extrema-direita no Congresso, poderia adotar elementos da cartilha política de Trump, caso suba a rampa em 1º de janeiro de 2027.




Observadores políticos vêm notando uma defasagem de dois anos entre os eventos políticos recentes nos Estados Unidos e no Brasil. Trump assumiu o poder em 2016; Jair foi eleito dois anos depois. Biden derrotou Trump em 2020; Lula venceu as eleições de 2022. Apoiadores de Trump invadiram o Capitólio em 2021; o exército de defensores de Bolsonaro invadiu Brasília dois anos depois, em 2023. Trump retornou ao poder em 2025; o Brasil poderá enfrentar uma nova presidência de Bolsonaro em 2027. Embora processos históricos distintos raramente apresentem uma relação de causa e efeito tão nítida, parece que os dois campos de extrema-direita mantêm um diálogo constante sobre a melhor forma de conquistar e consolidar o poder.




Trump rapidamente celebrou a vitória de Bolsonaro por uma margem de 1,9% em 4 de outubro, embora, 

na mensagem publicada nas redes sociais

, tenha confundido o Brasil com a Índia: “125 milhões de pessoas votaram hoje no primeiro turno da eleição presidencial da Índia. Os resultados saíram logo após o encerramento da votação, no MESMO DIA!” Ele também aproveitou a ocasião para fazer comentários bombásticos sobre uma de suas principais obsessões: “Em Detroit, Filadélfia, Califórnia e em inúmeras outras cidades e estados dos EUA, os resultados — com números muito menores — frequentemente levam semanas para serem fraudados… digo, calculados. A votação na América é CORRUPTA!!!”




Enquanto Jair Bolsonaro baseou parte de sua campanha eleitoral de 2022 em críticas à confiabilidade do sistema brasileiro de votação eletrônica, o campo da direita manteve-se em silêncio sobre o processo de votação desta vez. Parece haver fraude eleitoral quando se perde, mas não quando se ganha. Ironicamente, Trump elogiou as eleições brasileiras por utilizarem procedimentos de votação que o próprio presidente dos EUA classificou como fraudulentos em seu próprio país.




Se os apoiadores de Lula reverterem o resultado do primeiro turno e vencerem por uma margem estreita no segundo turno, tanto Bolsonaro quanto Trump contestarão o resultado.

 A Casa Branca poderia insistir que o segundo turno das eleições brasileiras foi fraudulento e que Bolsonaro foi legitimamente eleito presidente, o que provocaria uma crise nacional e internacional sobre a legitimidade do novo governo de Lula.




Já se Flávio Bolsonaro derrotar o presidente Lula, provavelmente seguirá o exemplo de Trump, revertendo quase todas as políticas e programas do governo atual.

 A exemplo da ordem executiva de Trump emitida em 20 de janeiro de 2025 — seu primeiro dia no cargo —, concedendo perdão aos apoiadores que invadiram o Capitólio dos EUA na tentativa de anular os resultados da eleição presidencial americana de 2022, Flávio prometeu um perdão presidencial para seu pai (condenado por organizar uma insurreição contra o novo governo Lula) e para aqueles que invadiram a Praça dos Três Poderes em apoio ao plano de Bolsonaro.




Embora um perdão presidencial possa extinguir a pena de prisão restante de Jair Bolsonaro, ele não anularia a condenação do Supremo Tribunal Federal nem restauraria seus direitos políticos. Portanto, os aliados políticos de Bolsonaro poderiam buscar uma anistia legislativa que restaure plenamente a elegibilidade de Jair Bolsonaro.




Flávio pode governar pela vingança, assim como Trump 




Logo no primeiro dia de sua presidência, Trump anunciou uma campanha de vingança contra seus oponentes políticos, por meio de ações judiciais retaliatórias e de outras medidas administrativas. Flávio pode repetir essa estratégia.




Alvo 1: Moraes




No Brasil, sem dúvida, o primeiro alvo seria Alexandre de Moraes, que conduziu o julgamento e condenação de Jair Bolsonaro. Como o ministro — juntamente com outros membros do Supremo, incluindo dois indicados pelo pai de Flávio — está envolvido no escândalo do Banco Master, Flávio pode utilizar esse cenário para pressionar um movimento de impeachment contra Moraes. 




O ministro já é um alvo declarado da família. O irmão de Flávio Bolsonaro, Eduardo — atualmente foragido da Justiça brasileira e vivendo nos Estados Unidos —, juntamente com Paulo Figueiredo, pressionou com sucesso a Casa Branca de Trump para que impusesse tarifas de 50% ao Brasil, condicionadas à retirada das acusações contra Jair Bolsonaro. Eles também convenceram o governo dos EUA a aplicar a Lei Magnitsky ao ministro da Suprema Corte, impondo-lhe sanções financeiras severas por supostas violações de direitos humanos, embora 

Jim McGovern

 — o congressista americano autor da legislação — tenha declarado nas redes sociais que a lei não se aplica a este caso.




Alvo 2: movimentos sociais




Outro alvo da ofensiva direta de Trump tem sido as organizações da sociedade civil que criticam as políticas do presidente. Flávio pode repetir esse ataque aqui no Brasil.




Durante o mandato de Jair Bolsonaro, o presidente já atacou movimentos sociais ambientalistas, que chamou de organizações terroristas. Devemos esperar que essa investida se intensifique significativamente caso Flávio chegue ao poder.




Alvo 3: Constituição




Desde o seu retorno à Casa Branca, a estratégia política de Trump tem sido adotar medidas que parecem violar flagrantemente a Constituição dos EUA: tentativas de negar a cidadania a pessoas nascidas nos Estados Unidos, a imposição de tarifas de 50% em 2025 sem aprovação do Congresso e o congelamento de verbas autorizadas pelo Legislativo, entre outras medidas.




Flávio Bolsonaro declarou que pretende alterar a Constituição e mencionou algumas possíveis medidas legislativas, embora mantenha seus planos gerais em termos vagos.

 Diante da tentativa de insurreição de 2023, que violou os princípios fundamentais da Constituição de 1988, resta saber se ele respeitará o Estado de Direito, especialmente tendo um grande bloco de apoio de extrema-direita no Congresso. 




Alvo 4: Imprensa




A liberdade de imprensa também pode sofrer ataques, visto que Trump baniu veículos de comunicação cuja cobertura de seu governo lhe desagradava.

 Até o momento, a grande mídia brasileira não parece muito preocupada com essa ameaça à liberdade de expressão e à liberdade de imprensa, e vários grandes conglomerados de mídia demonstraram preferir Flávio a Lula.




Mas se o primeiro for eleito e decidir perseguir quem faz reportagens desfavoráveis, quem o impedirá? Com a maioria no Congresso e uma Suprema Corte em desordem, não há mecanismos de controle do sistema capazes de impedir que o possível futuro presidente desfira um ataque frontal à liberdade de imprensa ou aos críticos mais contundentes da extrema-direita no país. 




Alvo 5: Programas sociais




Quando Trump retornou ao poder nos Estados Unidos, trouxe consigo um plano detalhado, o Projeto 2025, concebido para reduzir o tamanho do governo federal e eliminar programas que os conservadores consideravam incompatíveis com sua agenda. Trump convocou Elon Musk para realizar o “trabalho sujo”, e o trilionário obteve grande êxito ao cortar drasticamente programas governamentais e os empregos das pessoas que garantiam o sucesso dessas iniciativas. O grupo político de Bolsonaro anunciou a intenção de cortar gastos públicos, mas apresentou poucos detalhes sobre seus planos. No entanto, dada a postura ideológica de que “menos Estado é melhor”, pode-se esperar cortes severos semelhantes no Brasil. 




Sem dúvida, um dos primeiros alvos serão as universidades públicas brasileiras. 

Os ataques de Trump a Columbia, Harvard e outras universidades de renome mundial — sob a alegação de que os administradores haviam falhado em conter o antissemitismo nos campi — serviram de pretexto para forçar essas instituições a eliminar todos os programas de diversidade, equidade e inclusão.

 Tais programas eram mecanismos importantes para garantir que o ensino superior de qualidade fosse verdadeiramente acessível a todos os segmentos sociais, e não apenas aos brancos de classe média.




Não há absolutamente nenhuma garantia de que um novo governo de extrema-direita em Brasília manteria os atuais programas de ação afirmativa, sob o argumento de que são discriminatórios, racistas e parte de uma conspiração de esquerda para controlar as mentes dos estudantes universitários. Nenhum programa estará imune a tentativas de desmantelamento. 




Alvo 6: Soberania




A soberania brasileira também estará em jogo. Em todo o mundo, observadores que acompanham os Estados Unidos consideram muitas das declarações de Trump meras fantasias delirantes de uma pessoa instável. Propor a anexação do Canadá e da Groenlândia, ou mudar o nome do Golfo do México para Golfo da América e do Lago Ontário para Lago América, parecem iniciativas nacionalistas absurdas para agradar à sua base.




No entanto, a ideia de Trump de invadir a Venezuela e a declaração de que organizações criminosas brasileiras são grupos terroristas — que o governo dos EUA teria o direito divino de destruir — refletem, na verdade, o desejo de consolidar a América Latina e o Caribe como um quintal neocolonial dos Estados Unidos. 

Um acordo sobre terras raras favorável aos EUA, mas com poucos benefícios para o Brasil, é claramente uma das primeiras prioridades na agenda de um presidente brasileiro que se considera 100% alinhado ao atual governo norte-americano. 




Mais alvos: Itamaraty, direitos LGBTQIAPN+ e meio ambiente




A lista é interminável: expurgos no Itamaraty, processos administrativos contra funcionários públicos, ataques aos direitos LGBT+, a continuidade das privatizações de empresas estatais, o desmantelamento da proteção às terras indígenas e o fim da preservação ambiental. Com uma vitória eleitoral — por menor que seja —, Bolsonaro, assim como Trump, declarará ter recebido um mandato popular para implementar seu programa, ignorando a vontade da outra metade do país que não apoia seus planos para o futuro do Brasil. 




As 

pesquisas mais recentes

 nos Estados Unidos indicam que os Democratas conquistarão o controle da Câmara dos Representantes e, possivelmente, até do Senado, formando uma frente para conter as piores intenções de Trump nos próximos dois anos. Enquanto o Congresso dos EUA se inclina à esquerda em repúdio às políticas do atual presidente, o Brasil pode enfrentar quatro anos piores que a gestão de Jair Bolsonaro. Embora uma rejeição generalizada a um possível novo governo Bolsonaro possa surgir após cerca de um ano de mandato, não há cenário plausível que preveja um freio semelhante ao que a extrema-direita pretende impor nos próximos quatro anos, caso os apoiadores de Lula não consigam reverter o resultado das urnas. 




O destino do país pode depender de algumas centenas de milhares de votos.

title: Kurdish literature and cultural memory meet at Frankfurt Book Fair
content:
The 78th Frankfurt International Book Fair, which opened on 7 October in Frankfurt, Germany, concluded on Sunday evening, 11 October. The fair brought together publishing houses, writers, cultural institutions, journalists, academics and representatives of the publishing industry from around the world.




A total of 4,131 exhibitors participated in the fair, which hosted more than 3,600 events.




As one of the international meeting points for the book and publishing industry, the fair also provided a platform for discussions on literature, culture, freedom of expression, democracy, human rights and the future of technology.




‘Czechia was the guest of honour’




Czechia was this year's guest of honour at the Frankfurt Book Fair.




Under the theme “Ein Land an der Küste” (A Country on the Coast), Czechia established a 2,300-square-metre exhibition space at the fair. The Guest of Honour Pavilion hosted events covering various literary genres, with the participation of 75 writers.




The pavilion showcased Czech literature and the country's cultural heritage, incorporating artificial intelligence and interactive technologies. Visitors engaged with digital installations, while a live-drawing robot and interactive poetry applications attracted particular attention.




More than 40 publishing houses took part in Czechia's national presentation, showcasing their books and holding international publishing rights negotiations.




‘An international meeting point for publishers’




Publishing houses, literary agencies, distribution companies, cultural organisations and media representatives from around the world gathered across the Frankfurt Book Fair's exhibition halls.




Hall 3.0 stood out as one of the main areas for independent publishers and international literary circles. The hall also featured dedicated reading and event spaces for independent publishers.




Publishers not only presented their books but also discussed the future of the publishing industry through meetings with authors, rights negotiations, translation agreements and international partnerships.




‘Turkish publishing industry also represented in Frankfurt’




The fair also hosted events focusing on the publishing industry in Turkey.




A session titled “Publishing and Reading Habits in Türkiye” examined the current state of publishing in Turkey, changing reading habits and literary relations between Turkey and Europe.




‘Kurdish literature finds a place at Frankfurt Book Fair’




The fair's programme also featured works on Kurdish literature and history.




Writer Hasan Hayri Ateş presented his novel Şer Zamanıydı to readers at the Frankfurt Book Fair at the invitation of the Frankfurt Foreigners' Advisory Council.




The event was moderated by Hüseyin Çatal and attended by Rainer Vollmar, Chair of the Board of Darmstadt Literaturhaus, editor Jutta von Freyberg, and Gudrun Wörsdörfer and Marianne Koester, representatives of the Frankfurt Association for Solidarity with Rojava.




Discussions also addressed efforts to translate Ateş's novel into German and introduce it to German-speaking readers.




Kurdish politician and writer İdris Baluken gave a seminar on Kurdish literature at the fair, while Kurdish writer Musa Karbadağ also participated in events dedicated to Kurdish literature.




‘Baluken: I see politics and art as parts of the same resistance’




Kurdish politician and writer Idris Baluken emphasised the significance of his participation in the Frankfurt Book Fair, drawing attention to the repression faced by the Kurdish people in relation to their language, identity and culture.




Baluken said: “I consider it very important to be here at the Frankfurt Book Fair, one of the world's largest book fairs, as a Kurdish writer from Turkey.




We can say that this is a place where the pulse of the world's cultural, artistic and literary activities beats strongly. I am the son of a people whose language, identity and culture have been banned, who have been deprived of education in their mother tongue and whose very existence has been denied. I spent nearly seven years under conditions of aggravated isolation because I defended the rights of this people. I therefore find it significant to participate, through the literary works I produced during that time, in an event that brings together other peoples of the world and is hosted by important figures in the cultural sphere.




This is valuable both in literary and cultural terms and because it provides an opportunity to make the rights denied to our people until now visible through a different platform.




I see politics and art as parts of the same objection to the existing disorder. Sometimes the power of political action comes to the fore, while at other times we need the creative power of art. As people pursuing a just, legitimate, conscientious and humane cause, we are striving to correct the wrongs committed against our people using every means available to us.”




‘All living beings in nature have the right to life’




Baluken also discussed his novel Oko at the fair, explaining that the book focuses on the animal massacre that took place on Hayırsızada in 1910.




Baluken continued: “In this respect, I believe the subject of the work I am presenting today is also very important. My novel Oko was written to expose a mentality that seeks to revive the mass slaughter of animals carried out on Hayırsızada in 1910, and to call for greater awareness and opposition to it.




Following the great animal massacre of 1910, the Armenian people were targeted, then the Kurds and non-Muslims. For this reason, we must also examine the current legal regulations in Turkey that deny stray animals the right to life in the context of the state's approach to the country, to people, to individuals and to society, and recognise the connection between them.




This is why I call on everyone to abandon the mentality that regards nature as a commodity belonging exclusively to humankind, to be used however people wish. I urge everyone to develop ecological awareness, respect nature and recognise that all living beings have as much right to exist in nature as human beings do.”




‘Karbadağ: Kurdish literature lacks visibility on international platforms’




Kurdish writer Musa Karbadağ, who attended the Frankfurt Book Fair, also discussed the impact of living in exile on his literary work.




Karbadağ said he had been forced to leave Turkey for political reasons but had continued his literary activities despite the difficulties of exile.




Karbadağ said: “My name is Musa Karbadağ. Like many Kurds, I have been living in exile for a long time. I became a wanted person in Turkey because of my political activities, so I was forced to leave the country.




“Of course, life in the diaspora comes with profound difficulties, including the disadvantages of being a refugee. However, I have tried to continue producing literary work without allowing these difficulties to hold me back too much, and I was invited to the Frankfurt Book Fair. My works include Su Karadan Güvenli Anne, Pêpûk and Cemse, and I am continuing to work on other projects.




What I want to say is this: You can achieve the liberation of a people or a society through military and political means, but it is art and literature that will carry them towards a strong future. This is why platforms like these are so important and valuable. They provide an invaluable opportunity for a culture and its collective memory to be shared and carried forward on a universal scale.




Unfortunately, however, we are not sufficiently visible on this platform. Kurdish literature and Kurdish art do not have enough visibility. Perhaps the general perception is that book fairs are commercial spaces where books are exhibited. Yet they are also extremely valuable platforms where many cultures, from Latin America to China, from Asia to the Middle East and Europe, come together to share their experiences and bring them into a common cultural space.”




‘Translation carries cultural memory to other societies’




Karbadağ stressed that Kurdish literature needed greater visibility internationally and drew attention to the importance of translation in building connections between different cultures.




Karbadağ continued: “For example, these platforms offer certain opportunities, one of which is translation. When a work is translated from Kurdish, it becomes part of another country, another society and another collective memory. It carries our historical experiences and the lessons we have learned into that society.




Unfortunately, we have very little visibility on platforms like these. There are reasons for this, and there are consequences. These can be discussed, but unfortunately, this is the reality we face today.”




‘Ateş: Bringing Dersim’s memory to the international stage is important’




Writer Hasan Hayri Ateş, who attended the fair at the invitation of the Frankfurt Foreigners' Advisory Council, drew attention to the historical memory of Dersim through his novel Şer Zamanıydı.




Ateş said the Frankfurt Book Fair was an important gathering for world literature and stressed the significance of Kurdish literature being included in the fair's main programme.




Ateş said: “We are here today at the Frankfurt Book Fair, the Frankfurter Buchmesse. It is, of course, a very important platform, bringing together the international literary community, publishers and editors.




Our participation in this programme at the invitation of the Frankfurt Foreigners' Advisory Council is therefore significant. I am taking part, along with our former MP Idris Baluken and our friend Musa Karbadağ. I believe this may be the first time we have been included in the Frankfurt Book Fair's main catalogue. Of course, many of our friends have participated in these activities before, but as far as I have seen, very few have been included in the main catalogue.




For us, the significance goes beyond our individual participation. What matters is that Kurdish literature and the issues addressed in Kurdish literary works have found a place in the main catalogue of the Frankfurt Book Fair. My own work deals with genocide, specifically the Dersim genocide. But we know very well that genocide is not simply the concern of one people; it is a concern for all humanity.




It is therefore extremely important to bring these issues to international platforms, to make the suffering experienced by peoples visible and, on that basis, to develop a shared memory, a common culture of resistance and an understanding of collective action. I hope and wish that the Frankfurt Book Fair will help make this possible.”




‘More Kurdish writers should take part in these platforms’




Ateş said his novel Şer Zamanıydı explores the events in Dersim and the destruction of coexistence with Armenians, adding that efforts were underway to translate the book into German.




Ateş concluded: “Şer Zamanıydı is a novel about the Dersim genocide, but it also deals with how coexistence with Armenians was completely destroyed and how, following the genocide of the Armenians, genocide was carried out against Kurdish Alevis and Kurds more broadly. I want these events to become widely known.




We are working on translating the book into German. I hope we will achieve a significant result. The Book Fair is important, and I believe and hope that many more Kurdish writers will participate in these platforms in the future, bringing their subjects and stories with them.”




‘A wide-ranging programme from culture to politics’




This year's Frankfurt Book Fair addressed not only literature but also democracy, human rights, freedom of expression, disinformation, artificial intelligence and social change.




Numerous events were held at different venues as part of the “Frankfurt Calling” programme. International organisations, including Amnesty International, ARTE, Institut français, PEN International, UNESCO-affiliated organisations, United Nations agencies and Wikimedia, also participated in various programmes at the fair.




Many prominent figures from literature, academia, politics, cinema and the cultural world met with readers at the fair.




Jill Lepore, Colson Whitehead, Jenny Erpenbeck, Robert Habeck, Gisèle Pelicot, Mariana Mazzucato, Volker Schlöndorff and Wolf Biermann were among the fair's notable guests.




Literary programmes produced by ARD, ZDF and 3sat also featured Sven Regener, Susan Neiman, Cornelia Funke, Robert Habeck and Gisèle Pelicot, who participated in various events.




‘From books to the screen’




The relationship between books and cinema was another major focus of the fair.




As part of Book-to-Screen Day on 9 October, publishing houses, literary agencies, producers and screenwriters came together to discuss film and television adaptations of books, new projects and international collaborations.

title: Tosun: The case is not over until the third attacker is punished
content:
One year has passed since journalist, documentary filmmaker and environmental activist Hakan Tosun was beaten to death in the street in Esenyurt.




Tosun died after suffering a brain haemorrhage at the scene when he was assaulted by two people on the night of 10–11 October 2025 while on his way to visit his mother in the Mehmet Akif Ersoy neighbourhood of Esenyurt district.




Abdurrahman Murat and Adnan Şahin, responsible for Hakan Tosun's death, were summoned to the Esenyurt Mevlana Police Station to give statements and were arrested on charges of intentional injury. However, it was notable that Yusuf Özakdağ, a third person who had also participated in the attack, was questioned as a witness by the same police station.




Although a report by the Council of Forensic Medicine confirmed that Hakan Tosun had been severely beaten, the 17th High Criminal Court accepted the indictment for intentional injury prepared by the Büyükçekmece Chief Public Prosecutor's Office. Following months of proceedings, Abdurrahman Murat and Adnan Şahin were sentenced to life imprisonment for intentional killing. However, the verdict brought no sense of relief to the Tosun family.




Hakan Tosun's sister, Öznur Tosun, spoke to ANF and stressed that the case would not be over until Yusuf Özakdağ, who also participated in the fatal attack on her brother and has openly posed with firearms on social media while tagging gang names, is brought to trial and punished.




Continuing her brother’s legacy in the struggle for justice




Öznur Tosun joined the front ranks of the commemoration of the 10 October Massacre, an event her brother, journalist Hakan Tosun, had covered every year, and marched to demand justice for him, one year after he was beaten to death in the street.







Tosun, who experienced first-hand the difficulties of seeking justice in Turkey through the trial over her brother's murder, said: “I have always been someone who speaks out against injustice and unfairness, but the period following my brother Hakan's death made my sense of justice even more pronounced.”




Öznur Tosun, who experienced first-hand how far cruelty could go on the night of 10–11 October a year ago, recounted the events leading up to her brother's disappearance: “That day, my brother Hakan attended the commemoration of the 10 October Ankara Train Station Massacre in Kadıköy. At around 7 pm, he called my mother and told her he was coming home. She even asked him whether he was hungry. When Hakan did not arrive, my mother called him again. He told her, ‘I'm on my way, I'm coming.’ My brother was on the metrobus when he spoke to my mother. It was around 10 pm. My mother waited for a while, but when he still did not arrive, she called him again and realised she could not reach him. She did not tell me immediately because she did not want me to panic. At first, she thought his phone battery might have died. However, when Hakan still had not arrived by morning, she called one of his friends. After learning that his friend could not reach him either, she called me and told me what had happened.”




‘Mevlana Police Station concealed evidence with the killer’s family’




Öznur Tosun said she initially did not suspect anything serious but went to the nearest police station in Kağıthane to file a missing person report as a precaution. She said, “I thought perhaps my brother had been detained, or maybe he was exhausted because he had recently returned from the earthquake-hit region where he had gone to report.”




Tosun continued: “I was told that 24 hours had to pass before my missing person report could be processed. Even before those 24 hours had passed, Kağıthane Police Station checked hospital records but could not find any record of Hakan. I then contacted Esenyurt Mevlana Police Station, which was closest to where my mother lived, and filed another missing person report.




My brother's photograph was sent to them at 8 pm on Saturday. They knew that we, as his family, had been unable to reach him. Despite this, it was not until around 4 am that a police officer from Mevlana Police Station called me and informed me that Hakan was at Başakşehir Çam and Sakura City Hospital.




The incident took place on Friday evening. They knew by Saturday that we were searching for Hakan, yet they did not inform us. They had the documents and the missing person report in their possession, but they waited a full eight hours before notifying us.




During those eight hours, the killers were summoned by telephone to give statements at the same Mevlana Police Station, while footage of the attack was erased by the killer's family. At 11 am on Saturday, the family of the killer, Abdurrahman Murat, took possession of footage that the police had viewed but failed to secure.




They informed us of Hakan's whereabouts a full 27 hours after the incident, and eight hours after they had officially received the information. Instead of notifying us, as it should have done, Mevlana Police Station was concealing evidence together with the killer's family.




Mevlana Police Station did not stop at summoning the killers by telephone to give statements. It also questioned Yusuf Özakdağ, who personally participated in the attack that caused Hakan's death, as a witness rather than a suspect.




We filed criminal complaints against both the third person involved and Mevlana Police Station, but decisions not to prosecute were issued in both cases.”




‘Defence lawyers and the killer’s family tried to discredit my brother with lies’




Öznur Tosun said the Büyükçekmece Chief Public Prosecutor initially attempted to classify the incident as “intentional injury” in the preliminary investigation report and sought a reduction in the defendants’ sentences on the grounds of provocation. However, the Bakırköy 17th High Criminal Court subsequently opened a murder trial.




Tosun pointed out that witnesses gave false statements throughout the proceedings, while the defence lawyers attempted to manipulate the circumstances surrounding her brother's death.




Tosun said: “Throughout the investigation and trial, the defence lawyers and the family of the killer, Abdurrahman Murat, tried to discredit my brother by claiming that he used drugs and was a sexual harasser. They also tried to portray Hakan as an aggressive person by exploiting an incident on the metrobus. All these lies were disproved by CCTV footage.




I personally believe that the incident on the metrobus was also staged and planned. The footage from that incident was examined and submitted to the court. There is absolutely nothing in those recordings resembling what they claimed had happened. They tried to create an image of my brother, Hakan Tosun, as an aggressive, foul-mouthed man and a sexual harasser. Through these lies, they sought to lead the public to the conclusion that he somehow ‘deserved to die’. We saw this both in the slanderous statements made by the defence lawyers in court and in social media posts by the killer's family, who said things like, ‘Who are you defending? This is the kind of man he was.’ They tried to shape public opinion in that direction. Until the very end, the defence lawyers continued making these accusations against a dead man. Even this clearly shows us that the attack was planned. There is a history behind this incident.




To avoid examining what happened before the attack, they tried to attribute the cause of his death to his lifestyle and manipulate public perception accordingly. I will never forget the first hearing. Hasan Kocabay, the lawyer representing Abdurrahman Murat, said about my brother, ‘As you can see from the way he dresses and his appearance, he is clearly someone who lives that kind of life.’ Now I ask him: Does wearing a suit make you a decent human being? Who are you to pass judgement on Hakan Tosun's life? Despite the report by the Council of Forensic Medicine, they shamelessly claimed that he used drugs. Despite the footage, they alleged that he had sexually harassed a woman on the metrobus and pulled down his trousers in the neighbourhood. I have never witnessed such cruelty. Despite all the vile things they did, we continued to stand by him. Now, if this was such an ordinary street fight, why did you try so hard to divert attention elsewhere? Who are you protecting behind all this?”




‘I believe Yusuf Özakdağ was the instigator of the attack’




Öznur Tosun stressed that although the two defendants were sentenced to life imprisonment in the trial that concluded a week ago, justice had not been fully served. She said the case would not be over for the family until Yusuf Özakdağ, the third person involved in the attack, was brought to trial and punished.




Tosun said she believed Yusuf Özakdağ had not merely participated in the attack but had personally instigated it. Tosun also said: “Before my brother arrived on that street, Yusuf Özakdağ was riding around on a motorcycle. He was the first person to see my brother, and he was also the one who eventually took the killer, Abdurrahman Murat, to where my brother was sitting on his motorcycle. Yet, for some reason, Yusuf Özakdağ remains untouched, almost as though he is being protected. The third person was never made part of this case. The reason my brother was sitting there was that he was already aware he was being followed.




My brother was a journalist. He was someone who was aware of what was happening around him and lived with a journalist's instincts. He chose to sit there because it was a busy street. Otherwise, he would have sat near my mother's house, which was just one street behind. But that street was dark. He knew he was being followed and did not want anyone to know where the house was. He had not travelled all that way just to sit there for no reason. It was a busy street, and he was trying to ensure that if anything happened to him, it would be seen and known, leaving behind evidence. There is a background to this murder.”




‘A year after his murder, his ID and wallet are still missing’




Tosun continued: “Look, it has been exactly one year since my brother was murdered, yet his identity card and wallet are still missing. There is no possibility that he did not have them with him. He boarded the metrobus and used his travel card. We obtained the records of that card. But neither his identity card nor his wallet has been found. They took his identity card from him because the intention was to make him disappear without any identification. They wanted to present it as an unsolved murder. The court did not pay much attention to this issue either. It has been suggested that his identity card might have fallen out when he was thrown off the metrobus. We believe the third person played a key role in the murder, and this case will not be over for us until he is included in the proceedings. We have filed another criminal complaint against him with the Büyükçekmece Courthouse, and we will continue to pursue the matter.”




‘He was not just my brother, he was my confidant’




Öznur Tosun said the life sentences handed down to the two defendants at the final hearing had brought the family no sense of joy. Tosun  said, “Throughout this trial, I kept thinking about one thing: My brother had been slandered and accused, and by the end of the trial, we would prove that he was in the right. Somehow, I imagined that winning the case would mean we could bring him out of prison with us. But we walked out, and he did not.”




Öznur Tosun described her brother Hakan as more than a brother, saying he had been her friend and confidant and said: “I never saw Hakan simply as an older brother. He was always more like a friend to me. He was someone I could talk to about anything, share everything with and confide in. We would spend hours discussing philosophy, politics, people and life. He never put pressure on me. He always respected my opinions. He loved nature deeply. His dream was to settle in Çanakkale, build a life surrounded by nature and work in agriculture. He was always extremely sensitive to injustice. I never experienced the conventional idea of an older brother with him. He was incredibly understanding.




When I got divorced and returned home, it was as though I had never left. He said, ‘Yes, now we're starting again,’ and always stood by me. He was the same with my mother. No matter how busy he was, he never forgot her hospital appointments. Wherever he happened to be, he would come, take her to the hospital and then return to his work. We have lost a truly wonderful person. It is an enormous loss for this country, for us, for those who loved him, for his family, for nature and for everyone who defends life. Nothing will ever bring him back. It should not be this easy. I will continue fighting until every aspect of this murder is brought to light and everyone responsible is held accountable.”




‘I realised I had been living in a world built on lies’




Öznur Tosun said her life had changed profoundly since her brother's murder, revealing both those who offered genuine solidarity and those who turned their backs on her.




Tosun said she had been dismissed from her job at Hummel Sportswear, where she had worked as a manager for nine years, because of her public visibility during the trial over her brother's murder. Tosun concluded: “On 31 August, a month ago, I was dismissed from Hummel Sportswear in Kağıthane, where I had worked for nine years. They told me the company was downsizing, but gave me no further explanation. An accountant had stolen around 200 million. TV100 reported the incident, and the police became involved. Because I had been visible in the media, they assumed I was responsible for getting the story published and dismissed me. They offered to pay my severance entitlements to prevent me from taking legal action, but I refused. I have now filed a lawsuit against Hummel's management in Turkey.




They did this to me at a time when I was already fighting for justice. But on the other hand, through my brother's friends and the people around him, I learned what genuine solidarity means. My brother is gone, but he left me surrounded by wonderful people. I saw how people could stand together without expecting anything material in return, how they could struggle wholeheartedly for one another. Now I am part of that struggle too. Looking back, I realised that I had been living a meaningless life. I had actually been living in a world built on lies. My brother used to say this all the time. He would talk about how companies destroyed nature and people's lives just to make more money, and how their only concerns were their own interests and profits. Today, I find myself saying exactly the same thing. Like my brother Hakan Tosun, I will continue to stand against every form of injustice.”

author: Unknown
title: BaBa Zula: We stand for peace, the government must act
content:
Artists continue to share messages of peace through ANF. Members of the music group BaBa Zula said artists should take a political stance and called for Kurdish and all other languages spoken in the country to be free.




The musicians said: “The Justice and Development Party (AKP) does not inspire confidence. For peace to come, democracy, rights and the rule of law must come first. Thousands of our people from Anatolia and Mesopotamia have lost their lives. Peace is not a concession granted from above or a political favour. It means people being able to live freely, with their fundamental rights, mother tongues and cultures protected under a fair legal system.”




Murat Ertel, Esma Ertel and Levent Akman of the music group BaBa Zula answered ANF's questions.




‘Artists are being prevented from taking political positions’




Members of BaBa Zula said the group seeks to preserve the multicultural and multilingual heritage of Anatolia, Mesopotamia and Istanbul through its music. They said: “We are living under a cultural bombardment. There is a situation being created, particularly in the virtual world. It is as though the world is being shaped not by its seven billion people, but by the leaders of a population of just one billion. They are also trying to shape culture, but we are interested in the culture of the geography we live in. We eat the food of this region, listen to its music and try to reflect these influences honestly. Of course, we are also open to music from around the world. But what matters most to us is the music of our own geography. Istanbul is actually a beautiful example of this. It connects Asia and Europe, embraces Anatolia and has ties with the Balkans, Greece, the Mediterranean and Turkey. We find this much more appealing. For example, when we look at America, we see great power, but we also see distance.”




The group members stressed that artists should take political positions and shared the following views: “Unfortunately, efforts are being made today to prevent artists from being political and expressing political views. This is happening both in Turkey and abroad. Countries that present themselves as champions of democracy are doing this too. In Germany, for example, speaking about the massacre of Palestinians or criticising Israel provokes a strong backlash. In Britain, artists are also being prevented from speaking about these issues and are expected to remain apolitical. For example, the director Wim Wenders, who was in charge of this year's Berlin Film Festival, made the absurd claim that artists should not be political and should simply do their jobs. We also try to be political. We have our own style, which we have maintained from the very beginning, and we have no intention of ever abandoning it. Artists are very powerful because art and artists are among the most important forces shaping society.”




‘Mother tongues must be free’




The group members also defended freedom of the mother tongue, saying that while a common language could exist, different languages must be preserved. The group members said: “Different peoples have their own languages, and as long as those languages are spoken, they continue to live and their hearts continue to beat in those regions. But as a country, I think we are creating divisions over this issue too. When you look at Turkey, you are talking about a society that grew up with the idea of ‘72 nations’ in Anatolia and Mesopotamia. We believe that seven distinct ethnic communities live across the country's seven regions and that each of their languages should be able to survive.”




The musicians stressed that Kurdish should be free, but that linguistic freedom should not be limited to Kurdish alone. For example, when you travel to the east, you encounter Azerbaijanis. Azerbaijani should also be taught to their children. You go to Mardin (Mêrdîn) and encounter Assyrians; they should be able to receive education in their own language. Or you visit Arab Alevis in Adana; they should be able to continue learning Arabic as a second language. Laz should also be taught. Different languages enrich this country and make us more beautiful. We are very colourful, and we are beautiful together. Our beauty lies in multilingualism and multiculturalism. That is what makes us who we are. Children are taught English and Spanish, but they could also learn these languages. These are languages that should be integrated into our children's lives.”




‘We should be discussing steps towards democracy’




Members of BaBa Zula also shared their views on the silencing of weapons, welcoming the end of the loss of life while criticising the government for failing to take concrete steps.




They said: “The Justice and Development Party (AKP) does not inspire confidence. For peace to come, democracy, rights and the rule of law must come first. There must be justice for there to be peace. We are still talking about the silencing of weapons. We should be discussing steps towards democracy. For example, we should be talking about the release of Selahattin Demirtaş. We should be talking about the release of Osman Kavala. Demirtaş and others from that political movement must be freed from those houses of oppression, from prisons. Yet nobody is discussing these issues any further. Blood was shed for years. Mothers and fathers wept, children lost their lives and families were devastated. It is wonderful that these things are no longer happening. We are very happy about that. Because when you lose a child, when that child is buried, there is no bringing them back. You devote so much love and effort to raising them, and they will never return. Thousands of our people from Anatolia and Mesopotamia have died. Yes, the guns have fallen silent, but I do not think you can make a man whose ideas they fear so deeply, or the people who love him, part of this peace while, unfortunately, continuing to keep him in prison.”




‘Peace will last if rights are recognised’




Members of BaBa Zula said that a system based on equality and the recognition of everyone's rights could provide a solution.




The members said: “As artists, we naturally strive to promote the language of peace and bring people together. But as long as those in power continue to use the law as a weapon, you cannot build trust in society. That is why justice must first be ensured for every section of society. Social peace is not a concession handed down from above or a political favour. It means people being able to live freely, with their fundamental rights, mother tongues and cultures, under a fair legal system. Once this is achieved, peace will naturally take root throughout society and become lasting.”




The musicians also criticised the appointment of government trustees to replace elected local authorities and said: “Then they should not hold elections! Why are they holding elections if they are going to appoint trustees anyway? This is happening in Mardin, Diyarbakır (Amed) and elsewhere. We stand for peace, but what we need first and foremost is justice.”




The group members said justice could also provide a remedy for social degeneration, just as it could pave the way for peace. They said: “There is a 13-year-old girl going to school with a pump-action shotgun. There are femicides. We cannot stop them. We are still debating the Istanbul Convention. These are the wounds that continue to bleed in our society. We need to heal them profoundly, and that can only happen through justice and the rule of law. If you tell those men, ‘He is your husband, he can do what he wants. He may beat you, but he also loves you,’ this is the result. A man puts on a suit, goes to court and gets a reduced sentence. He calls it an ‘honour killing’ and is acquitted.”

title: The people of Shengal must decide their own future
content:
More than 6,000 people were abducted during the attack on Shengal by ISIS mercenaries on 3 August 2014, and around 2,500 remain missing. The Yazidis refer to the attack, in which thousands of people were massacred and abducted, as the 74th Ferman in their history.




Shengal was liberated from ISIS in 2015. In the aftermath of the Ferman (Shengal genocide), the Yazidis established their own administrative and defence mechanisms, forming a People's Council and defence forces such as the Shengal Resistance Units (YBŞ) and Shengal Women's Units (YJŞ). The autonomous administration, which has operated in practice in Shengal ever since, continues to exist as an expression of the people's determination to govern and defend themselves.




Turkey-Iraq trade-off in New York




Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Zeydi met in New York on 23 September 2026 while attending the United Nations (UN) General Assembly. The joint statement issued after the meeting highlighted two main points: the full restoration of state authority in Shengal and the elimination of forces described in the statement as “prohibited foreign armed elements”, and the gradual transfer of the Turkish army's Bashiqa (Zilkan) base to the Iraqi federal government. The transfer process was made conditional on security measures to be taken by Iraq and a timetable to be agreed upon by both sides. However, no timetable has yet been announced.




The Turkish army established a presence at the Bashiqa base, approximately 30 kilometres northeast of Mosul, in December 2015. Around 600 Turkish soldiers are stationed at the base. Turkey's military presence in Iraq consists of five main bases, more than 2,000 soldiers and nearly 100 military positions. The transfer of the Bashiqa base, which accommodates fewer than a third of Turkey's total troops in Iraq, does not mean an end to Turkey's military presence in the country. Its other bases and military positions remain operational.




The agreement was interpreted in the Turkish press as an arrangement under which the Turkish army would end its presence at Bashiqa in exchange for the establishment of Iraqi state authority in Shengal. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan also said at a press conference that these steps would be taken “after the terrorist group's presence in Shengal has been eliminated”.




Through this agreement, the Turkish state is seeking to position itself as a direct party to the Shengal issue. However, the administration and defence of a strategically important region such as Shengal have become a bargaining issue, traded against another state's military base in talks that excluded representatives of the people living there.




‘The solution lies in the constitution’




A meeting concerning the Yazidis was held in Baghdad on 1 September on the instructions of Ali Zeydi. All those attending the meeting on Shengal, which the Iraqi government held without Yazidi representatives, were military and security officials. Not a single Yazidi representative was invited. The appointment of a military district governor to Shengal was subsequently raised. However, the people of Shengal rejected the decision, stating that it had been made without their consent.




Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Zeydi later met with representatives of the YBŞ and the Yazidi community on 11 September. Sources familiar with the meeting reported that the Iraqi side had raised no serious objections to the Shengal delegation's demand to preserve its self-defence force, while the details of integration were left to a joint committee. The Iraqi Chief of General Staff visited Shengal with a military delegation on 22 September. The outcome of the visit was not disclosed, and the New York agreement was announced the following day.




This series of meetings demonstrates that Ankara was subsequently brought into the direct dialogue that Baghdad had established with Shengal. Baghdad has not ruled out the possibility of Shengal's self-defence forces continuing to operate within the Iraqi army under a recognised status. Keeping this possibility open, however, depends on continuing negotiations directly with Shengal.




Shengal's autonomy is, of course, another central issue in these discussions. Articles 122 and 123 of the Iraqi Constitution allow for extensive local autonomy without the establishment of a federal region. The constitution already provides for a degree of autonomy that would enable cultural and religious communities to preserve their existence, yet this fundamental right has not been recognised for the Yazidi community or Shengal. This demonstrates that Shengal's demands can be met within the framework of Iraq's existing constitution.




The women's dimension of the debate over self-defence in Shengal must not be overlooked. For women, this issue represents far more than a security arrangement. Leaving the YJŞ without recognised status carries the risk of returning women to the defencelessness they faced in 2014.




‘The future of Shengal and Rojava is being discussed at tables where they have no representation’




The process of military integration is also progressing in Rojava, but issues concerning mother-tongue education, local government institutions and the status of the Women's Protection Units (YPJ) remain unresolved. This experience demonstrates that integration involving the handover of weapons without recognition of local democracy would leave society without guarantees.




The Turkish state is also known to be seeking a say in the integration process and holding various talks with other countries on the issue. It appears that efforts are being made to determine the future of Shengal and Rojava at negotiating tables where their peoples have no representation.




‘The vacuum created by the lack of unity in Başûr’




Parliamentary elections in the Kurdistan Region were held on 20 October 2024. The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), which together hold approximately two-thirds of the parliamentary seats, failed to reach an agreement on the distribution of government positions. As a result, no government has been formed despite the passage of nearly two years. Delegations from the two parties held at least 31 meetings during this period.




The mission of the International Coalition Against ISIS in Iraq ended on 30 September 2026, including its air defence systems in the Kurdistan Region. More than 1,000 drone and missile attacks have targeted Başûr since the war between the US, Israel and Iran began on 28 February 2026. Iran continued its attacks against Rojhilat parties in the Kurdistan Region even after the coalition's withdrawal.




In the wake of these developments, Peshmerga forces affiliated with the KDP and PUK were brought under a single ministry at a ceremony held in Erbil (Hewlêr) on 21 September. However, although the defence structure has been unified on paper, the forces remain under the control of the two parties on the ground.




‘Unity based on local democracy’




Abdullah Öcalan's proposal for Başûr has remained consistent for more than a year. At a meeting on Imrali in June 2025, Öcalan called on KDP President Masoud Barzani to take the lead in convening a National Congress. He also proposed to PUK President Bafel Talabani that the protocol agreed with Jalal Talabani in 1993 be renewed on the basis of democratic unity.




In a letter sent to the DEM Party Local Governments Conference held in Diyarbakır (Amed) on 8 June 2026, Öcalan also identified local democracy as the formula for a solution. He stressed that this approach should not be limited to Turkey but should serve as a formula for overcoming crises throughout the Middle East, particularly in Iraq and Syria, pointing to the need to establish a common political will and defence mechanism.




‘The will of the people of Shengal must be recognised’




Any unity that excludes Shengal cannot heal one of the deepest wounds within Başûr itself. Baghdad must therefore continue the talks it initiated on 11 September with the Shengal People's Council and the Autonomous Administration, without conditions imposed by a third state. The Shengal Resistance Units (YBŞ) and Shengal Women's Units (YJŞ) must be recognised within the Iraqi army under a status that allows them to remain in Shengal. The KDP and PUK must establish a unity government based on local democracy. The Turkish state, for its part, must withdraw not only from Bashiqa but also from its other military bases in Iraq.




The validity of any agreement concerning Shengal must depend on the consent and signature of the people of Shengal.
