author: Publicación Abierta
title: El 15/10 al Congreso contra el Decreto 70/23, por la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario, por la prórroga en discapacidad y una solución a las familias endeudadas
content:
Del escandaloso fallo de la Corte Suprema que reactivó la Ley de Tierras a la marcha atrás que el viernes devolvió la vigencia ala normativa sin resolver la cuestión de fondo, para desactivar el tratamiento del DNU 70/2023 el jueves en Diputados. En paralelo, el Ejecutivo apeló el fallo que ordenaba cumplir con la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario, votada ocho veces en el Congreso. En medio, las convocatorias a la 5ª Marcha Federal Universitaria y a movilizarse cuando Diputados trate el Decreto 70/2023 que cambió la esencia de cientos de leyes.




Foto: 

Mat ((i))




“Ninguna conquista empezó con la resignación”




Por Mario Hernandez




 




Los reclamos son varios: el financiamiento universitario, la prórroga de la emergencia en discapacidad y una solución para las familias endeudadas. Las convocatorias comenzarán desde la mañana del jueves y se extenderán a las plazas de todo el país.


La 5ª Marcha Federal Universitaria, impulsada por el Consejo Universitario Nacional (CIN), la Federación Universitaria Argentina (FUA), el Frente Sindical de Universidades Nacionales (que nuclea a gremios docentes y no docentes) y Centros de estudiantes reclamará el cumplimiento de la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario que viene desconociendo el gobierno de Javier Milei. A esta convocatoria se suman sectores sindicales y sociales que promueven la derogación del DNU 70/2023 y políticas para los sectores más atacados por el modelo libertario como movimientos campesinos y de trabajadores y trabajadoras rurales, organizaciones ambientalistas, movimientos sociales y partidos políticos donde confluyen el Observatorio de Tierras, Inquilinos Agrupados y el movimiento de personas endeudadas.


Desde la mañana convocarán personas con discapacidad para reclamar por la prórroga de la emergencia del sector. Después habrá una convocatoria general y de algunos sectores, desde las 14:00, cuando comienza la sesión, para movilizarse al Congreso de la Nación.


A esa convocatoria es plegaron casi todos los partidos políticos del campo popular y agrupaciones políticas, además de las dos CTA y la CGT.


Además de reclamar la derogación del DNU, los sectores participantes reclaman financiamiento universitario, la prórroga de la emergencia en discapacidad y una solución para las familias endeudadas.


Matías Oberlin, del Observatorio de Tierras, afirmó que la movilización “viene muy grande” porque convoca a numerosos sectores afectados por el DNU 70/2023: personas endeudadas, inquilinos y personas afectadas por el Instituto de la Yerba Mate y la Ley de Tierras, entre otros. Consideró importante que la Plaza de los Dos Congresos esté llena desde temprano para ejercer presión sobre los diputados y que se sienten a dar el debate.


El integrante del Observatorio de Tierras indicó que hasta “la Iglesia se pronunció”. Junto con Inquilinos Agrupados y Movida Ciudad convocarán desde las 12:00 “hasta que caiga el DNU”.




Jugada gubernamental




Los diputados opositores necesitan 129 para el quórum, pero probablemente la convocatoria termine en una sesión en minoría. Mientras tanto, el oficialismo oficializó su convocatoria para el 21 de octubre. De todos modos, entre los opositores gana la idea de seguir adelante, aunque tampoco se pondrán en tratamiento los dictámenes en torno a discapacidad y endeudamiento familiar, que incluía el temario.


Martín Menem, titular de la Cámara Baja, negocia con los espacios aliados modificar el proyecto de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada (que tiene sanción del Senado) en el marco de un debate que comenzará a darse este miércoles en el plenario de comisiones.


La jugada sería proponer a los aliados un Proyecto de ley que establezca la eliminación del artículo 154 del DNU 70/23 para reponer las restricciones a la venta de tierras a extranjeros que rigen desde 2012. De esta manera, se caerían todos los amparos por la Ley de Tierras y la Corte no debería volver a fallar en el tema.


En el caso de discapacidad se firmaron dos dictámenes. El del oficialismo, que no contempla la emergencia, pero sí gran parte de las garantías de las prestaciones, en un giro de 180º a lo propuesto en el Presupuesto 2027. El de la oposición va por la prórroga por un año de la emergencia dispuesta por la ley.


En cuanto al endeudamiento hay tres dictámenes. El del oficialismo que prevé educación financiera (sic) y exigencias de información transparente a la hora de tomar créditos. Y dos opositores que son similares ya que proponen una emergencia, planes de pagos para morosos, tope de tasas y quita de intereses punitorios, entre otros puntos.




Malvinas




En la convocatoria del 21, el oficialismo decidió postergar la inclusión del proyecto de Defensa de la Soberanía Nacional, por falta de consenso político con los aliados.


Unión por la Patria y otros bloques exigen separar el reclamo por Malvinas de la creación del nuevo Consejo de Seguridad Nacional, acusando al gobierno de Milei de usar una causa nacional para aprobar superpoderes y reformas de seguridad interior.


Entre los principales cuestionamientos, apuntan a la eliminación del artículo 11, que establece penas de prisión por “manipular la opinión pública mediante campañas de desinformación masiva” bajo financiamiento extranjero.


Por otro lado, se rechazan las amplias facultades delegadas en el nuevo Consejo de Seguridad Nacional, que permitiría tomar decisiones militares extremas, sin la intervención obligatoria del Congreso.




La entrada 

El 15/10 al Congreso contra el Decreto 70/23, por la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario, por la prórroga en discapacidad y una solución a las familias endeudadas

 se publicó primero en 

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: "Musk": Alex Gibney on New Film, Legal Threats & Elon Musk Spending $366M to Help GOP in Midterms
content:
We speak with the Academy Award-winning director Alex Gibney about his new documentary 

Musk

, an expansive, nearly four-hour examination of the world’s first trillionaire and how he has amassed unprecedented power in business, technology and politics. The film traces Elon Musk’s early ventures and the rise of SpaceX and Tesla, examining the role of government support in their growth. It also explores his acquisition of Twitter, now X; his alliance with President Donald Trump and the 

MAGA

 movement; and his role in the Department of Government Efficiency, or 

DOGE

, whose cuts devastated federal programs, including 

USAID

.




Gibney says Musk has carefully crafted an image of a “polymath” who can solve the world’s most pressing problems, but that he is really “kind of a ruthless businessman” willing to do whatever it takes to succeed, including “a series of elaborate cons” to win government support for his companies.

author: Roaa Reda
title: From journalists’ pursuit to protection? Bid to ban jail sentences for publishing gets boost from syndicate, MPs
content:
Parliamentarians, legal advocates and representatives of the Journalists Syndicate gathered on Saturday at the Cairo syndicate headquarters for an open seminar to discuss practical steps to curb the use of detention against journalists in lawsuits related to the act of publishing.




Participants noted that, despite an explicit constitutional protection against the practice, there is a lack of mechanisms to support a change — a situation which prompted the drafting, almost a decade ago, of a law to prevent imprisonment in publishing crimes.




In an attempt to activate the dormant draft law, Tagammu Party MP Atef Maghawry told Mada Masr that he began on Monday to gather lawmakers’ support for the bill, telling Mada Masr he will seek to complete the effort over the coming weeks to secure the bill’s presentation in Parliament’s general session.




The discussion came on the back of the ongoing detention of six journalists from independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh, whose arrests earlier this month brought the number of journalists detained in relation to their work to 26.




Multiple voices at the seminar highlighted the risks facing both journalists and citizens alike given the expansion of legal grounds for the arrest of journalists over recent years.




Among the attendees was the father of cartoonist and translator Ashraf Omar, who spoke of his son’s imprisonment since 2024 for actions that fall within his duties as a journalist and expressing his opinion. Omar, who has been held in remand for nearly two years to date, is currently facing trial on terrorism charges, his father said. A due-date in his trial this week was postponed until December.




Omar’s case is a typical instance of what frequently happens to journalists facing prosecution for their work, according to defense lawyer Nabih al-Genady.




In most publication-related cases, journalists are not charged with crimes linked to the specifics of content they published, but authorities instead often rely on a range of other laws and statutes that ultimately lead to their imprisonment, said Genady.




This “legislative arsenal” constraining the work of journalists has grown over recent years, according to  Journalists Syndicate deputy head Mohamed Abdel Hafiz, who pointed to the enactment since 2015 of the counterterrorism and cybercrime laws, both of which have been used on multiple occasions as grounds for prosecution and custodial sentences for publishing acts.




Amr Abdel Rahman, the head of the civil freedoms unit at the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, added to these the telecommunications law, which includes an article on the misuse of social media platforms, while Iman Ouf, the Journalists Syndicate Freedoms Committee head, highlighted Law 180/2018 regulating the press and media, in which 

Article 12

 requires journalists to obtain security clearance before filming in public places.




It is only journalists who are subject to restrictions prohibiting photography in public spaces, said Ouf, citing the recent lawsuit filed by the Qena Governorate’s sanitation company against a journalist who had photographed a sewage on a local street.




She attributed the instance to an “expansion in the understanding of national security,” noting that most measures taken against journalists are justified under the banner of protecting national security — even when the alleged threat is indirect or undefined.




The current approach to handling journalists, said Abdel Rahman, stands in stark contrast to the good faith that originally underpinned 

Article 71

 of the 2014 Constitution.




The article was designed to protect journalists practicing their profession, and it explicitly prohibits the use of custodial sanctions as punishment for crimes committed by way of publication, except in cases of incitement to violence or discrimination.




But Abdel Rahman emphasized that the law is not merely a written text but a matter of application.




Issues surrounding publication-related offenses are a battle for everyone, not just journalists, he added. The same point was echoed by multiple attendees, who stressed that weakening the practice of journalism compromises access to information for citizens, as well as for politicians themselves, with former Egyptian Social Democratic Party MP Samira al-Gazzar stressing the difficulty of MPs’ work in light of compromised access to information, even regarding key items of legislation for which they are responsible. She pointed specifically to the 

law abolishing old rent

 and the new law on 

asylum

, which were passed while she was a sitting MP.




The pursuit of journalists by authorities holds long-term implications for the practice, said lawyer Asmaa Naeem, one of the several lawyers who represented Omnia Sweidan, who was 

sentenced

 over a Facebook post describing instances of obstetric abuse.




Journalists should be protected from imprisonment in order to pursue their work, said Naeem, stressing that journalists who make errors should correct them, while those publishing correct information are merely fulfilling their role.




It was in a bid to offer concrete protections to journalists that the syndicate began in 2014 its effort to draft a law banning imprisonment in publishing cases, said Khaled al-Balshy, the Journalists Syndicate head, who called in via phone to speak at Saturday’s seminar.




Though steps were never taken toward the law’s enactment, it was revived in 2024 by the syndicate committee tasked with drafting media legislation.




Steps to activate and introduce better legal cover could support a better atmosphere for the practice of journalism, several of the attendees said, with Balshy gesturing to the initiative, spearheaded by Egyptian Social Democratic Party MP Maha Abdel Nasser, for a freedom of information act and Maghawry, likewise, calling for the activation of limits on the widespread use of remand detention in the new 

Criminal Procedure Code

, the enactment of which is now 

postponed

 until October, 2027.




Maghawry, who pledged at the seminar to rally support for the draft law, told Mada Masr on Tuesday that he had collected during 75 percent of the 60 signatures required to present a bill to Parliament during Monday’s general session at the House of Representatives, without specifying the exact number of signatories so far.




He said he would resume his campaign for backing in the coming weeks when the general sessions 

resume

 in November.




Speaking on Saturday, Balshy acknowledged the limits of the step for new legislation prohibiting incarceration for publication-related offenses. Even if enacted, he said, imprisonment might not cease immediately.




But the principle, he said, is that legislation of this kind would serve as a vital instrument for advocacy and legal recourse to defend journalists in need.

The post 

From journalists’ pursuit to protection? Bid to ban jail sentences for publishing gets boost from syndicate, MPs

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: Yemen Plunges Back into "Full-Scale Civil War," Houthis Trade Strikes with Saudi Arabia
content:
Yemen’s Ansar Allah, also known as the Houthis, have repeatedly attacked the Saudi capital of Riyadh in recent days. On Saturday, a missile strike on the airport in Riyadh killed at least 12 and injured over 300 in the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in over a decade. President Trump is now weighing whether to join the Saudi fight against the Houthis in Yemen.




This latest escalation comes after Ansar Allah captured key areas along Yemen’s Red Sea coastline in recent weeks, driving back the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government and taking control of the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.




“Yes, the Houthis are attacking Saudi Arabia with airstrikes, but there is now, actively, a real ground war going on within Yemen, and that is a far more relevant and important issue for the Yemenis on a day-to-day basis because they are now back into a full-scale civil war,” says Middle East scholar Helen Lackner.

author: Amina Khan
title: Beware of spyware: Access Now urges pension funds to scrutinize investments for spyware exposure
content:
On September 28, 2026, Access Now wrote to four pension funds — 

Los Angeles County Employees Retirement Association

, 

Houston Firefighters’ Relief and Retirement Fund

, 

New Mexico Educational Retirement Board

, and  

Hampshire Pension Fund

 — regarding their investment in AE Industrial Partners (AEI). AEI 

purchased

 spyware technology vendor Paragon Solutions in 2024 and merged the company with its holding company REDLattice. The letters urge pension fund managers to use their leverage with AEI to ensure the fund “provide[s] remedy where warranted, and implement robust safeguards” to prevent any contribution to human rights breaches.













Investors have a responsibility to identify and address human rights risks in their portfolios. Paragon presents a clear risk given its appalling human rights record, and these pension funds should avoid exposure to such spyware in their portfolios and demand answers from AE Industrial Partners.




Isedua Oribhabor, Business & Human Rights Manager at Access Now
















A 

well-documented history

 demonstrates Paragon’s  spyware tool, Graphite, being used to target 

journalists

 and 

activists

. A 

2025 report

 confirmed the use of Graphite spyware against journalists, adding to 

previous findings

 revealing that the company’s tech was used to target civil society actors in Italy. Coupled with the 

disclosures by Meta

 and 

Apple

, an Italian parliamentary 

report

, and 

forensic confirmation

 by the Italian prosecutor, these findings raise urgent concerns regarding Paragon’s due diligence practices, post-sale oversight mechanisms, and provision of access to remedy for affected individuals.




Paragon has also sparked concerns in the U.S. given the company’s 

$2 million contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)

. Though a notice on a federal procurement website indicates that the 

contract’s “close out” date

 was January 20, 2026, and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) stated that ICE has “

no relationship

” with Paragon, DHS has not clarified whether ICE still has access to Paragon’s tools. 




Access Now previously requested information from AEI and Paragon Solutions on what steps they will take to prevent future uses such those documented in Italy, and how they will respond to those harmed, in an 

open letter

 addressed to both entities on June 19, 2025. Neither AEI nor Paragon 

responded

. The Business and Human Rights Centre (BHRC) also contacted both 

AEI

 and 

Paragon

 regarding allegations and is still awaiting a response.




Failure to comply with international human rights norms can also have substantial legal and financial repercussions for Paragon, as well as its corporate investors — who risk financial and reputational costs as backers of a firm linked to high-profile cases of human rights abuses. 




Hampshire Pension Fund confirmed on October 9, 2026, that it is not invested in Paragon through AEI. Access Now has yet to receive public responses from the other funds.




The post 

Beware of spyware: Access Now urges pension funds to scrutinize investments for spyware exposure

 appeared first on 

Access Now

.

author: ACG
title: NON-VIOLENCE DOES NOT EXIST
content:
The text below appeared in the  journal of the Organisation Communiste Libertaire (OCL) of France, Courant Alternatif. Whilst specific French instances are referred to, we feel that this is a useful general article on the question of “non-violence.”




For ages, the debate between non-violence and violence has permeated social movements. Violence is not only physical, but also institutional, symbolic, psychological, and so on. This opposition is largely fuelled by the state. It criminalises our mobilisations by accusing them of being violent, even going so far as to accuse them of terrorism or of glorifying it. It is imperative to move beyond this opposition and try to act by taking into account and articulating the multiple forms, actions, and initiatives that social movements take.




The primary function of the state is to maintain social order: capitalist society. It is founded on exploitation, the maintenance of a social hierarchy, patriarchy, and the division of the dominated among themselves, through racialisation, the subjugation of certain genders, criminalisation, and the creation of artificial competition. All of this generates daily violent conflict. Faced with challenges to these various aspects, the state has no choice but to respond violently. In this context, the debate between non-violence and violence is sterile. It only serves to perpetuate divisions within social movements.




This violence takes many forms. The first, and most visible, is physical violence, for which only the state is deemed legitimate. This requires police forces, and even military personnel if necessary. The judicial system is one of the tools of this violence. The goal is to crush by force any form of social protest and to imprison anyone who does not submit to this social order.




Politically, the bourgeoisie can turn to the most authoritarian governments when it deems the situation too perilous. Thus, in the 1930s, some capitalists declared, “Better Hitler than the Popular Front” (for example, de Wendel, a steelworks owner and member of the Comité des Forges). To analyse the interwar period, the focus is primarily on the rise of authoritarian regimes in Europe, the most well-known being fascism in Italy and Nazism in Germany.




From February 1917 until 1939, a revolutionary wave swept across much of the globe. It began with the Russian Revolution in 1917, followed by the German Revolution in 1918. This process spread to Italy with the creation of workers’ and peasants’ councils and to Central Europe. From 1936 to 1939, Spain experienced the most significant revolutionary upheaval that challenged capitalist society. The United States was also affected by this social unrest: numerous factories were occupied by proletarians who could no longer bear the consequences of the 1929 crisis. This inspired workers in France during the Popular Front, who also occupied their workplaces. This greatly worried the capitalists. In France, after initially condemning the Popular Front, they appealed to Léon Blum, the Prime Minister, to resolve the conflict so that the workers could “liberate” the factories and return to work.




Governing through fear




Currently in France, entire segments of the population are subjected to this physical violence. Residents of working-class neighbourhoods are subjected to it daily. This results in numerous injuries and deaths. Special police units are assigned to maintain order in these areas. The State, through the justice system, the administration, and the mainstream media, attempts to conceal this violence, either by minimising it or by discrediting the victims and those who express their solidarity. Legal proceedings can be initiated when individuals, political groups, or artistic groups declare that the police are killing people. The State must absolutely normalise this police violence to maintain fear in these neighbourhoods, keeping residents silent about their increasingly degraded living conditions. It is a veritable government by fear that is being established. When some residents revolt, the repression is extremely violent.




This form of government by fear has been used for several years to repress social movements (the movement against the El Khomri law, the Yellow Vests, the pension reforms, etc.). The mobilisations can be large (involving several million people), but the state responds only with violence, seeking to crush them by force. It refuses any questioning of its political choices. Macron clearly demonstrates the purpose of the state. He governs to satisfy the wealthiest few percentages of the population and large corporations, primarily multinationals. The rest of the population must endure the deterioration of public services (education, healthcare, etc.) and pay for an increasingly unequal budget. Similarly, the distribution of wealth is becoming increasingly unequal.

Under these conditions, the state must equip itself to be even more repressive. Given the deterioration of living and working conditions, he cannot rule out the possibility that people will organise to oppose these societal choices, leading to the impoverishment of increasingly large segments of the population.




But since the state alone holds the legitimacy of physical violence, any form of popular physical and violent opposition is condemned. Social movements are delegitimised in order to depoliticise them. They are often labelled as terrorists. Thus, new categories are invented, such as ecoterrorism, and more recently, movements denouncing the massacre of the Palestinian population in Gaza and the West Bank by the Israeli state are denounced as antisemitic and as glorifying terrorism.




It’s only a matter of time before any protest or mobilisation becomes an act of terrorism! Neoliberalism must prevail at all costs. Thatcher declared there was no other choice. Clearly, she has descendants! Challenging this form of capitalism is synonymous with “lèse-bourgeoisie” (a crime against the bourgeoisie). All means are justified to maintain the hegemony of the bourgeois class, even if it means killing people, massacring populations, refusing to eradicate genocidal processes, even if it means destroying the planet by refusing to question productivism and thus the creation of ever-increasing profits…




This unconditional support for the apartheid and colonisation policies of the Zionist state serves to criminalise all Muslims, and by extension, immigrants of Arab origin. They are portrayed as backward, wanting to impose Sharia law and challenge “democracy,” “equality between men and women,” and even, for some, to “replace” whites with Arabs, etc. But do we live in a truly democratic country? Are elections a democratic guarantee? Can we truly take control of our own affairs within the current institutional framework? Can we collectively determine what we produce, how, with what means, and for what purposes? Can we reclaim these questions (currently answered exclusively by capitalists according to their own interests) to prioritise socially useful work? Has patriarchy disappeared? Has racism vanished?




Social, institutional, symbolic, psychological violence…




The state and those in power exert other forms of violence. Who hasn’t experienced institutional violence from administrative services, for example? These services often receive us with suspicion. An unemployed person is frequently perceived as a fraudster who must be subjected to increasingly strict controls. A person of foreign origin often faces racism, contempt, and, again, suspicion. It is becoming increasingly difficult to assert one’s rights, even though these rights are regularly curtailed by laws.




Providing answers is very difficult due to the isolation of individuals, while the person they are speaking to relies on the institution for which they work. In fact, we are confronted with our own solitude in the face of these state machines. At times, revolts are expressed individually or collectively. Here again, we are met with authoritarian responses (police, justice system).




Psychological violence can also be perpetrated, for example, in the workplace. Employers generally receive state support when employees oppose them by occupying the company. The police, acting on the prefect’s orders, usually violently remove them, even though they are fighting, for instance, for their dignity.

Increasingly degraded working conditions are also experienced as violence against workers. Concretely opposing them can also lead to repression, often violent. And what about evictions? Finding oneself suddenly on the street can only be an act of extreme violence. Being locked up in a detention centre, then forcibly put on a plane while tied up to be “deported” to a country from which it was deemed vital to distance oneself, is an act of extreme violence.




We could continue this list of examples of everyday experiences.




This shows how difficult it is to separate all these forms of violence. Some mutilate bodies, others cause psychological pain. Some inflict physical blows, others leave no trace on the body. But all are expressions of a desire to dominate us, to impose the capitalist social order on us, to humiliate us, to remind us of our status as commoners.




A sterile opposition




We cannot accept the division imposed by the State. On one side, physical violence, for which only the State has the legitimacy; on the other, symbolic, institutional, psychological, and other forms of violence that can be exercised by many, as long as, in certain situations or thanks to a social status (like a boss, for example, or a zealous civil servant with a high opinion of their position, etc.), a person is in a dominant position.

Faced with violent situations, it is difficult to distinguish between violent and non-violent responses. Faced with violence, all responses are violent. Whatever responses we give to thugs or directly to oppressors, they will always be experienced as violent. Whether we go on strike peacefully (railway workers on strike: that’s a hostage situation!) or hold a boss hostage to obtain a pay raise; Whether we prevent the deportation of an undocumented immigrant through a sit-in or by forcing our way through a police barricade, it will always be perceived as violence on our part.




Rejecting the violence/non-violence dichotomy means rejecting the categories into which the State seeks to confine us; it means rejecting the separation between so-called responsible citizens (that is, those who ultimately accept state violence or violence supported by the state) and supposed terrorists, to use the vocabulary currently in vogue within the corridors of power. This allows us to move beyond this sterile debate, which ultimately only those in political power hold a monopoly on. The act of mobilising inevitably provokes aggression against those against whom we mobilise, regardless of the form of mobilisation. The struggle against exploitation and domination is always violent! The construction of power relations (doesn’t this common expression contain a form of violence?) requires diverse and complementary modes of action to impose our demands, but also to envision imaginaries both in everyday life and to build futures that break with capitalism: creative utopias.




J Christophe




Comment from OCL:




We wish to reiterate that, beyond what the author states, the capitalist state, whatever its form, is not the only vector of oppression. In capitalist society, and with Macron’s neoliberal policies, which normalise the state of exception (Article 49.3, state of emergency, etc.), class violence is experienced daily. It is structural violence, theorised by Johan Galtung, that produces oppression and inequalities in access to common goods (healthcare, education, resources, etc.). This can manifest as joblessness or being trapped in low-paying jobs that deprive workers of a portion of production for the benefit of the wealthy. It is also the domination and suffering of the most vulnerable that the productivist world of work engenders, as developed by Michel Foucault. It is worth recalling that one of the characteristics of this structural violence is that it renders the lives of the proletariat “uncertain” at the intersection of social reproduction, patriarchy, downward mobility, racism, and class-based racism. In the current context of radicalised anti-social policies and repression, we are publishing this perspective on state violence because, in our view, it reflects questions raised in demonstrations and shared feelings of both isolation and hope for finding the strength to act. Ultimately, this text addresses, in its own words, the fact that the state has succeeded in imposing the “collective belief” of Max Weber’s “monopoly on legitimate physical violence”, but also the symbolic violence so dear to Pierre Bourdieu. This text also questions the notion of non-violence and moves towards the notion of counter-violence, which liberates, as opposed to the oppressive, dominating violence of Herbert Marcuse . Questioning these concepts seems to us a necessary step to re-establish more solidarity, which in our view can only be revolutionary.

title: «Milei, cumplí la ley»: con tomas, cortes y vigilias, estudiantes preparan la quinta Marcha Federal Universitaria
content:
Imagen: El Destape




La comunidad universitaria vuelve a organizarse en las calles frente al incumplimiento de la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario por parte de Javier Milei. Con la toma de la Facultad de Filosofía y Letras de la UBA este martes 13, clases públicas, cortes de calles, asambleas y vigilias, estudiantes universitarios comenzarán este martes una serie de acciones en la previa de la quinta Marcha Federal Universitaria, convocada para este jueves 15 de octubre. La agenda continuará el miércoles 14 con nuevas actividades en distintas facultades de la UBA, entre ellas Ingeniería, Ciencias Exactas, Psicología y Ciencias Sociales. La movilización del jueves será nacional y reunirá a estudiantes, docentes, nodocentes, autoridades universitarias y organizaciones gremiales en defensa del presupuesto, los salarios y el funcionamiento de las universidades públicas. También confluirá con el reclamo al Congreso de la derogación del DNU 70/23, la defensa de la Ley de Tierras y de la soberanía sobre los bienes comunes y los territorios indígenas. Conocé la agenda de acciones. 

Por ANRed.







Con la 

toma de la Facultad de Filosofía y Letras de la UBA

, 

clases públicas, cortes de calle, asambleas y vigilias

, estudiantes universitarios comenzaron este martes una serie de acciones para preparar la 

quinta Marcha Federal Universitaria, convocada para este jueves 15 de octubre y que se prevé será masiva.

 Las medidas buscan fortalecer el reclamo para que el gobierno de Javier Milei cumpla la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario y garantizar el presupuesto necesario para sostener el funcionamiento de las casas de estudio.




La agenda difundida para este martes incluye 

clases públicas durante toda la jornada en la Facultad de Filosofía y Letras de la UBA

, una 

asamblea de la UNA-Movimiento a las 14

 para definir medidas de lucha, 

cortes de calle en Puan y Rivadavia y en la Facultad de Derecho

, ambos anunciados para las 18.30, y la 

toma de Filosofía y Letras

. La asamblea estudiantil de esa facultad resolvió ocupar la sede de Puan 480 desde el martes hasta el jueves, con actividades de visibilización y organización de cara a la movilización.










 


































Ver esta publicación en Instagram






































































 




Una publicación compartida por @cefyl













En tanto, el miércoles 14 continuará el plan de lucha con un 

semaforazo en Ingeniería

, junto a trabajadores de la facultad, 

a las 17

; un 

corte en Plaza Houssay a la misma hora

; y una 

asamblea en Ciencias Exactas para debatir la toma

. También habrá una 

asamblea en Psicología a las 18

 y una 

asamblea con vigilia en Ciencias Sociales a las 19

. Las distintas medidas buscan involucrar a más unidades académicas y llegar a la marcha federal con una mayor organización estudiantil.




La decisión de tomar Filosofía y Letras surgió de una asamblea que resolvió profundizar las medidas durante los días previos a la movilización: “acabamos de terminar la asamblea de la facultad de Filosofía y Letras y resolvimos tomar la facultad el próximo martes, para preparar una huelga general el jueves 15. Durante las jornadas vamos a hacer un corte de calle en Puan y Rivadavia, con clases públicas y jornadas de visibilización durante todo el día”, expresaron desde el movimiento estudiantil.




Imagen: NA




La quinta Marcha Federal Universitaria fue convocada por el 

Consejo Interuniversitario Nacional (CIN)

, la 

Federación Universitaria Argentina (FUA)

 y el 

Frente Sindical de Universidades Nacionales

. La concentración central está prevista frente al Congreso de la Nación el jueves 15, con convocatoria a las 13.30. Los principales reclamos son 

el cumplimiento de la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario, la recomposición salarial para docentes y nodocentes, los recursos para el funcionamiento de las instituciones y el sostenimiento del sistema científico nacional

.




El conflicto tiene un nuevo capítulo judicial: 

el 6 de octubre, el juez federal Martín Cormick declaró inconstitucional el tramo del Decreto 759/2025 con el que el Gobierno había condicionado la aplicación de la Ley 27.795 y ordenó su cumplimiento inmediato

. La norma contempla recursos para las universidades públicas y medidas de recomposición salarial. 

El Ejecutivo anunció que apelaría la resolución y, el 9 de octubre, la Justicia concedió el recurso, aunque la medida cautelar que exige cumplir la ley continuó vigente

.




Imagen: TV Pública




La disputa se desarrolla en un escenario de 

deterioro de los salarios y de los presupuestos universitarios

, mientras los gremios sostienen medidas de fuerza y reclaman respuestas en las negociaciones paritarias. El Gobierno argumenta que el Congreso debe definir de dónde saldrán los recursos para financiar las obligaciones de la ley, mientras 

las autoridades universitarias y los sindicatos insisten en que el Poder Ejecutivo no puede suspender por decreto una norma sancionada y ratificada por el Congreso

.




Las actividades previas buscan convertir el reclamo institucional en una nueva demostración de fuerza en las calles. 

Con facultades tomadas, clases públicas, cortes y vigilias, el movimiento estudiantil intenta recuperar la iniciativa y sumar a docentes, nodocentes y a la sociedad en general

 a una disputa que excede los números del presupuesto: 

está en juego la continuidad de la educación superior pública, las condiciones de trabajo de quienes la sostienen y el derecho de las futuras generaciones a acceder a ella

.




Imagen: TN




Agenda de acciones previas a la marcha del jueves 15




➤ 

Martes 13/10 







Clases públicas todo el día en Filosofía y Letras.




14 hs – Asamblea en UNA para discutir corte y toma.




18.30 hs – Corte en Facultad de Derecho.




18.30 hs – Corte en Puan y Rivadavia.




18.30 hs – Toma en Filosofia y Letras.







➤ 

Miércoles 14/10







17 hs – Semaforazo en Ingeniería UBA.




17 hs – Corte en Plaza Houssay.




17 hs – Asamblea para discutir la posible vigilia y toma en la Facultad de Ciencias Exactas UBA.




18 hs – Asamblea y vigilia en Psicologia UBA.




19 hs – Asamblea y vigilia en Sociales UBA.




Posible Toma en la Facultad Movimiento UNA.







➤ 

Jueves 15/10 – MARCHA FEDERAL UNIVERSITARIA




La Marcha Federal Universitaria confluirá con los reclamos en defensa de la soberanía territorial y contra el DNU 70/2023




La quinta Marcha Federal Universitaria del jueves 15 de octubre buscará expresar una confluencia que excede el reclamo educativo: además de las organizaciones universitarias, sindicales y estudiantiles que convocan a la movilización nacional, 

distintos sectores sociales, políticos, ambientales, de derechos humanos y comunidades originarias impulsan para ese mismo día acciones y reclamos en defensa de la soberanía territorial y contra el DNU 70/2023

. En ese sentido, desde el sector gremial docente señalaron que las causas convergen y convocaron a exigir al Congreso que derogue el DNU 70/23 y defienda la Ley de Tierras y la soberanía sobre los recursos naturales.




La confluencia se producirá después de que 

el fallo de la Corte Suprema del 29 de septiembre desatara un amplio rechazo político y social, al dejar sin efecto la sentencia que frenaba la derogación de la Ley de Tierras Rurales y reabrir la posibilidad de comprar tierras sin los límites que establecía esa norma

. 

La reacción obligó al máximo tribunal a dictar, el 9 de octubre, una medida cautelar interina que restableció provisionalmente esas restricciones, a partir de una presentación de la organización ambiental Árbol de Pie

.




Imagen: La Política Ambiental.




Pero la marcha atrás del máximo tribunal judicial del páis no cerró la disputa y dejó expuesta 

la fuerza del rechazo popular y mantuvo en agenda la derogación del DNU 70/23, cuyo tratamiento fue incorporado a la sesión especial de Diputados prevista para el 15 de octubre

. Así, la defensa de la universidad pública, de la educación y la ciencia, de los territorios indígenas y de los bienes comunes empieza a confluir en una misma jornada, frente a un modelo que las organizaciones denuncian como un avance sobre derechos sociales y soberanía nacional.




 




En este marco, además de la confluencia en el Congreso Nacional, habrá acciones en diferentes puntos del país, como es el caso de 

Bariloche

, donde 

más de 60 representantes de organizaciones y comunidades mapuche se reunieron para coordinar una movilización simultánea

, con participación de sindicatos, trabajadores del CONICET y de Parques Nacionales, la Asamblea del Agua, estudiantes, partidos políticos y organizaciones territoriales.

title: Israels Krieg gegen kritische Berichterstattung
content:
Dossier




„… 

Dass mißliebige ausländische Medien, mit dem Fernsehsender“Al-Jazeera“ an der Spitze, in Israel verboten werden sollen, war der „Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung“ vor einigen Tagen nur eine kurze Meldung im hinteren Teil des Feuilliton wert. (…) Noch weniger Erwähnung findet die Tatsache, dass die Armee von Benjamin Netanjahu, seinem neuen Kompagnon und Ex-General Benny Gantz sowie ihren rechtsextremen Kameraden Ben-Gvir, Smotrich & Co. bei ihren massiven Bombardements bislang 21 Journalisten umgebracht und etliche andere verletzt hat. Weitere Medienschaffende werden im Gazastreifen vermisst oder wurden verhaftet. Außerdem wurden die Büros und Gebäude mehrerer palästinensischer Medien in Gaza durch israelische Bomben dem Erdboden gleichgemacht oder schwer beschädigt

…“ Aus dem 

Überblick des Gewerkschaftsforum Hannover vom 25.10.2023

, den wir nachfolgend komplett und dankend dokumentieren und ergänzen:







taz-Korrespondentin darf nicht in Israel einreisen: Kritik an rechtswidriger Besiedlung und der Not in Gaza gilt Israels Behörden als Boykottaufruf 







taz-Korrespondentin darf nicht in Israel einreisen




„

Kritik an rechtswidriger Besiedlung und der Not in Gaza gilt Israels Behörden als Boykottaufruf. Die taz fordert Einsatz für die Einreise.


Die israelische Regierung hat der taz-Korrespondentin Serena Bilanceri die Einreise verweigert. Wir werten dies als erheblichen Eingriff in die Pressefreiheit. Die Regierung Netanjahu verlässt damit den Boden der demokratischen Rechtsstaatlichkeit. Wir kennen solch ein Vorgehen sonst nur von autoritären Regimes.


Schon in der Vergangenheit hatte Bilanceri schwer nachvollziehbare Schwierigkeiten bei der Einreise nach und Ausreise aus Israel bekommen: Ihr Laptop wurde im vergangenen Jahr am Flughafen Tel Aviv angeblich zur Sprengstoff-Untersuchung zurückgehalten, sie erhielt ihn zerstört zurück.


Eine Begründung für die Entscheidung wurde Bilanceri nicht mitgeteilt. Konkret wirft die israelische Bevölkerungs- und Einwanderungsbehörde laut der Website Israel National News – Arutz Sheva unserer Korrespondentin Bilanceri indes vor, in zwei Texten im September und November 2025 Sanktionen gegen Israel gefordert zu haben. In den beiden Beiträgen kommentierte Bilanceri die rechtswidrige Besiedlung des Westjordanlands und die humanitäre Notlage im Gazastreifen. Dies deuten die israelischen Behörden offensichtlich als Boykottaufforderung. (…)


Die Chefredaktion der taz stellt klar: Serena Bilanceri hat an keiner Stelle zum Boykott des Staates Israel aufgefordert. Es ist nicht hinnehmbar, dass die israelische Regierung eine legitime und auch von der EU vorgetragene Kritik am Vorgehen Israels im Westjordanland und im Gazastreifen als Begründung nimmt, um die Pressefreiheit einzuschränken

…“ 

Mitteilung der chefinnenredaktion vom 12.10.2026 in der taz online

 




taz-Journalistin von israelischer Regierung an Einreise gehindert




„

Die israelische Regierung greift mit der Einreiseverweigerung für die taz-Korrespondentin Serena Bilanceri die Pressefreiheit an. Wenn Journalist*innen wegen kritischer Berichterstattung oder Kommentaren an ihrer Arbeit gehindert werden, ist das mit demokratischen Grundsätzen und der Verpflichtung zum Schutz der Pressefreiheit unvereinbar. Kritik an der israelischen Regierung, an der Besatzung des Westjordanlands oder an der humanitären Lage in Gaza ist kein Beleg für fehlende journalistische Unabhängigkeit. Sie darf nicht zum Vorwand werden, um Korrespondent*innen an ihrer Arbeit zu hindern. Wer journalistische Arbeit an politische Loyalität knüpft, gefährdet die freie und unabhängige Berichterstattung

…“ 

Pressemitteilung vom 12.10.2026 von ROG

 










Israel: Kritik unerwünscht. Die Regierung will den Machern des Dokumentarfilms »Naza« – in Venedig mit dem Spezialpreis der Jury ausgezeichnet – die Staatsbürgerschaft entziehen  







Netanyahus Drohungen gegen die RegisseurInnen des Dokumentarfilms „Naza“ sind Teil seines Angriffs auf das Recht auf Information im Vorfeld der Wahlen


„

Die Hetzkampagne gegen Yuval Abraham und Rachel Szor, Journalisten des israelischen Medienunternehmens +972 und Regisseure des Dokumentarfilms „Naza“, hält weiter an. Zusätzlich zu den Morddrohungen und Einschüchterungsversuchen seitens der Demonstranten droht die Regierung damit, ihnen die israelische Staatsbürgerschaft zu entziehen. Reporter ohne Grenzen (RSF) bekundet seine Solidarität mit den Journalisten, deren Film Augenzeugenberichte israelischer Soldaten über Verbrechen der Armee im Gazastreifen enthält. Die Nichtregierungsorganisation warnt vor einer Verschärfung der Repressionen gegen die israelische Presse im Vorfeld der bevorstehenden Parlamentswahlen.




Nur wenige Wochen vor den für den 27. Oktober angesetzten Parlamentswahlen bekräftigte Benjamin Netanjahu seine Drohung, den Journalisten Yuval Abraham und Rachel Szor, den Machern des Dokumentarfilms „Naza“, die Staatsbürgerschaft zu entziehen – eine Drohung, die er erstmals Mitte September nach der Vorführung des Films bei den Filmfestspielen von Venedig ausgesprochen hatte. In einem Interview mit der nationalistischen israelischen Nachrichtenseite „Makor Rishon“ am 25. September betonte der israelische Ministerpräsident, dass „die Darstellung der Offiziere und Kommandeure der israelischen Armee als Kriegsverbrecher uns unermesslichen Schaden zufügt […] Wenn dies aus den eigenen Reihen kommt, ist es schlichtweg unerträglich.“ Gegen Benjamin Netanjahu liegt ein vom Internationalen Strafgerichtshof (IStGH) ausgestellter Haftbefehl wegen Kriegsverbrechen vor, und laut RSF trägt er die Verantwortung für die Tötung von mehr als 200 Journalisten durch die israelische Armee, darunter mindestens 63, die im Rahmen ihrer Arbeit getötet wurden – Taten, die Kriegsverbrechen darstellen. „Es ist, als wären Dutzende ballistischer Raketen auf uns abgefeuert worden. Wenn wir dafür nicht die Staatsbürgerschaft entziehen, wofür dann?“, fügte er hinzu und wiederholte damit erneut seine gefährliche Gleichsetzung von Journalisten – diesmal israelischen Journalisten – mit Kombattanten.




Seit seinem Kinostart im September hat der Film, der Augenzeugenberichte israelischer Soldaten über Kriegsverbrechen im Gazastreifen enthält, in der israelischen Öffentlichkeit für Aufruhr gesorgt. Die Regisseure Yuval Abraham und Rachel Szor sind zur Zielscheibe beispielloser Angriffe und Drohungen aus allen Teilen der israelischen Gesellschaft geworden. Der israelische Ministerpräsident bezeichnete den Film als „globale antisemitische Hetze“ und versprach die Verabschiedung zweier absurder Gesetze: Das erste würde Israelis im Ausland, die die Armee „verleumden“, die Staatsbürgerschaft entziehen, während das zweite die gegen sie verhängten Geldstrafen erhöhen würde

…“ engl. 

Meldung vom 2.10.2026 von RSF

 

 (maschinenübersetzt), siehe auch:







„#

Israel: Die Hetzkampagne gegen Yuval Abraham und Rachel Szor, die den Dokumentarfilm „Naza“ gedreht haben, geht weiter. Wir drücken unsere Solidarität mit den Journalist*innen aus und warnen zugleich vor einem immer repressiveren Vorgehen gegen die Medien in Israel kurz vor der Parlamentswahl

…“ 

Post von Reporter ohne Grenzen vom 01.10.2026 auf bsky

 

 mit Fotos










Israel: Kritik unerwünscht. Hetzjagd auf Regisseure geht weiter. Netanjahu kündigt Gesetz an, nach dem »Schmähung« der Armee mit Ausbürgerung geahndet wird




„In Venedig mit dem Spezialpreis der Jury für ihren Dokumentarfilm »Naza« über die mörderische israelische Kriegführung im Gazastreifen ausgezeichnet, in ihrem eigenen Land wegen genau dieses Films Ziel einer hemmungslosen Treibjagd: Juval Abraham und Rachel Szor. Vor dem Haus von Szors Eltern in der nur 4.500 Einwohner zählenden israelischen Gemeinde Savjon randalierten am Mittwoch mehrere Dutzend Ultrarechte, die der berüchtigte Organisator solcher Einschüchterungsversuche, Mordechai David, zusammengetrommelt hatte. Es ist an der Zeit, dass die Journalisten des Gazastreifens wie die Helden behandelt werden, die sie sind




„

Sie berichten unter unvorstellbaren Schwierigkeiten und werden in Rekordzahlen getötet. Die journalistische Gemeinschaft sollte sie jeden Tag ehren. (…)




Lokale Journalisten haben während der beispiellosen Gewalt aus erster Hand über die Bedingungen vor Ort im Gazastreifen berichtet. Die wenigen bestehenden Gaza-Büros der großen internationalen Medien (Reuters, BBC, Associated Press, Al-Jazeera, Agence France-Presse und andere) sind überwiegend mit Einwohnern des Gazastreifens besetzt.




Als Bewohner der Gemeinde, über die sie berichten, haben diese Journalisten Zugang, der anderen Reportern verwehrt ist. Vor fast einem Monat appellierte eine Koalition großer Nachrichtenorganisationen an die Regierungen Israels und Ägyptens (das die Südgrenze des Gazastreifens unter israelischer Leitung verwaltet), ihnen Zugang zu gewähren. Diese Agenturen sind praktisch nicht in der Lage, ihre Mitarbeiter zur Berichterstattung vor Ort zu entsenden. Viele von ihnen haben in Israel gearbeitet und wurden von palästinensischen Strippenziehern, Fixern und Freiberuflern unterstützt, die im Kriegsgebiet leben. Dieselbe Identität setzt sie einer komplizierten Kombination von Zwängen aus: den Anforderungen ihrer ausländischen Arbeitgeber, den Risiken der Wahrheitssuche und -darstellung unter einer autoritären Regierung und dem erhöhten Risiko, wegen ihrer Arbeit der Gewalt der IDF ausgesetzt zu sein. Maalish.




Die Tatsache, dass die internationalen Journalisten, die für kurze Zeit in den Gazastreifen einreisen, um zu berichten, sich der Zensur der israelischen Regierung beugen müssen, macht die Arbeit der palästinensischen Journalisten als Strippenzieher und freie Mitarbeiter für internationale Nachrichtenagenturen besonders wertvoll. Bei ihrer Arbeit in einer humanitären Krise beweisen diese Journalisten die bemerkenswerte Hartnäckigkeit und Anpassungsfähigkeit, die von jedem Kriegsberichterstatter verlangt wird, allerdings mit dem zusätzlichen Nachteil, dass sie zusammen mit ihren Familien im Kriegsgebiet leben. Die Zahl der getöteten Journalisten zeigt, dass vor allem die Palästinenser gefährdet sind. Von den 63 Journalisten, die seit dem 7. Oktober getötet wurden, sind bis auf sieben alle Palästinenser. (…)




Es ist schwer vorstellbar, wie diese Atmosphäre noch feindseliger oder repressiver sein könnte. In seinem jüngsten Bericht stellt das CPJ fest, dass der Ausbruch des Krieges den tödlichsten Monat seit Beginn der Aufzeichnungen im Jahr 1992 für Medienschaffende bedeutet. Die Gesamtzahl der getöteten Journalisten wird bald die Zahl der im letzten Jahr weltweit getöteten Journalisten übertreffen, wobei die höchste Zahl mit 15 Journalisten in der Ukraine und 13 in Mexiko zu beklagen war.




Folglich wird es weniger Journalismus geben. Es gibt weniger Journalisten, die zuverlässige und genaue Daten sammeln und Fakten von Desinformation unterscheiden. Es gibt weniger Stimmen, die dem Rest der Welt beharrlich die Realität im Gazastreifen vor Augen führen. Es gibt weniger Stimmen, weil so viele der Menschen, die diese Arbeit geleistet haben, tot sind, und so viele von denen, die nicht getötet wurden, einen täglichen Kampf ums Überleben mit ihren Familien führen

…“ 12.12.2023 NADIA TAHA The Nation – 

am 15.12. dokumentiert in Portside

 

 („It’s Time for Gaza’s Journalists To Be Treated Like the Heroes They Are“, maschinenübersetzt)










Der gefährlichste Krieg für Journalist*innen im 21. Jahrhundert: Bisher wurden in dem Krieg in Nahost 46 Medienschaffende getötet 




„

Kein anderer Krieg im 21. Jahrhundert hat für Journalistinnen und Journalisten so gefährlich begonnen wie der zwischen Israel und der Hamas. Insgesamt beklagt Reporter ohne Grenzen (RSF) derzeit bereits 55 getötete Medienschaffende, die meisten starben durch israelisches Bombardement. Warum ist das so? Können Medien im Gazastreifen überhaupt noch sicher berichten, und wie glaubwürdig sind ihre Informationen? Wie setzt sich RSF für die Sicherheit der Medienschaffenden ein? Fragen und Antworten gibt es in diesem regelmäßig aktualisierten Beitrag

…“ 

FAQ vom 23.11.2023 der Reporter ohne Grenzen

 

 zur Situation der Medien im Gazastreifen




Angriffe, Verhaftungen, Drohungen, Zensur: Die hohen Risiken der Berichterstattung über den Krieg zwischen Israel und Gaza – auch ARD-Team von israelischem Militär bedroht 







ARD-Team von israelischem Militär festgehalten und bedroht




„

Vorfall im palästinensischen Westjordanland: Ein ARD-Team ist dort von israelischen Soldaten festgehalten und bedroht worden. Die Reporter wollten über die Gewalt radikaler Siedler berichten. Der BR sieht die Pressefreiheit bedroht.


Ein Team der ARD ist im palästinensischen Westjordanland von Soldaten des israelischen Militärs (IDF) festgehalten und bedroht worden. Nach Angaben des ARD-Studios Tel Aviv, das vom Bayerischen Rundfunk (BR) betrieben wird, war Korrespondent Jan-Christoph Kitzler am Samstag, 4. November mit einem palästinensischen Mitarbeiter sowie einer deutschen Mitarbeiterin bereits auf dem Rückweg von einem Interview, als sie von israelischen Soldaten südlich der palästinensischen Stadt Hebron gestoppt wurden.


Wie Kitzler berichtet und Handyvideos des Teams belegen, verhielten sich die Soldaten gegenüber dem ARD-Team überaus aggressiv, mehrfach wurden Waffen in das Teamfahrzeug gehalten. Immer wieder filmten die Soldaten das ARD-Team aus nächster Nähe. Für Kitzler und das Team ein klarer Versuch der Einschüchterung. Bei den Soldaten handelte es sich nach Angaben des Teams vermutlich um Siedler aus der Gegend, die nun als Reservisten eingezogen wurden. Sie waren mit einem Privatfahrzeug unterwegs und trugen zivile Kopfbedeckungen. (…)


Für Christian Limpert, Leiter des ARD-Studios Tel Aviv, handelt es sich dabei um Versuche, die Berichterstattung aus dem palästinensischen Westjordanland massiv zu behindern, auch andere internationale Medien seien betroffen. „Für uns ist es der zweite Vorfall innerhalb einer Woche. Unser Team hat sich klar als akkreditierte Pressevertreter ausgewiesen und war fernab militärischer Sicherheitsbereiche. Wir können das Vorgehen des israelischen Militärs nicht akzeptieren

.“…“ 

Meldung vom 05.11.2023 beim BR

 




Angriffe, Verhaftungen, Drohungen, Zensur: Die hohen Risiken der Berichterstattung über den Krieg zwischen Israel und Gaza




„

Seit Beginn des Krieges zwischen Israel und dem Gazastreifen am 7. Oktober sehen sich Journalisten und Medien in der gesamten Region mit einem feindseligen Umfeld konfrontiert, das die Berichterstattung über den Krieg zu einer besonderen Herausforderung macht.  Das CPJ hat nicht nur die steigende Zahl der getöteten und verletzten Journalisten dokumentiert, sondern auch 18 Vorfälle festgestellt, in denen Journalisten bei ihrer Arbeit in Israel und den beiden palästinensischen Gebieten Gaza und Westjordanland angegriffen wurden. Dazu gehören acht Verhaftungen sowie Angriffe, Drohungen, Cyberattacken und Zensur. (Anmerkung der Redaktion: Diese Zahlen werden aktualisiert, sobald weitere Informationen vorliegen.) Mehrere Journalisten haben während ihrer Berichterstattung über den Konflikt auch Familienangehörige verloren. Am 25. Oktober verlor Wael Al Dahdouh, Leiter des Al-Jazeera-Büros in Gaza, seine Frau, seinen Sohn, seine Tochter und seinen Enkel, als ein israelischer Luftangriff das Flüchtlingslager Nuseirat im Zentrum des Gazastreifens traf, so eine Erklärung von Al-Jazeera und Politico. In Gaza sind die Risiken akut. Israel hat auf den Angriff der Hamas auf sein Gebiet am 7. Oktober mit Luftangriffen und einem Bodenangriff auf den Gazastreifen reagiert, der von der militanten Palästinensergruppe kontrolliert wird

…“ engl. 

Beitrag von Mohamed Mandour am 3. November 2023 bei CPJ

 

 („Attacks, arrests, threats, censorship: The high risks of reporting the Israel-Gaza war“, maschinenübersetzt)

CPJ auf Twitter

 
















Mögliche Kriegsverbrechen: RSF stellt Strafanzeige




„

Reporter ohne Grenzen (RSF) hat vor dem Internationalen Strafgerichtshof (IStGH) Strafanzeige eingereicht, damit dieser mögliche Kriegsverbrechen gegen Medienschaffende im Gazastreifen und Israel untersucht. Am 7. Oktober hatte die Hamas aus dem Gazastreifen heraus brutalste terroristische Attacken auf israelisches Gebiet gestartet. Seitdem bombardieren die israelischen Streitkräfte das abgeschottete Gebiet massiv. Die Strafanzeige ist vom 31. Oktober und nennt acht palästinensische Journalisten, die bei der Bombardierung ziviler Gebiete in Gaza durch Israel getötet wurden, sowie einen israelischen Journalisten, der am 7. Oktober bei der Berichterstattung über einen Angriff der Hamas auf seinen Kibbuz ermordet wurde. Ebenfalls genannt werden zwei weitere palästinensische Medienschaffende, die während ihrer Berichterstattung verwundet wurden. Diese elf Personen wurden Opfer von Angriffen, die nach Ansicht von RSF Kriegsverbrechen darstellen und eine Untersuchung durch den IStGH rechtfertigen. In der Strafanzeige wird auch die vorsätzliche vollständige oder teilweise Zerstörung der Gebäude von mehr als 50 Medieneinrichtungen im Gazastreifen aufgeführt

…“

Israel, das nach westlicher Ansicht bekanntlich

author: Λουκάς Σταμέλλος
title: Νέοι εκτελεστές, παλιοί υποκινητές
content:
Σύνδεσμος δημοσίευσης: 

Νέοι εκτελεστές, παλιοί υποκινητές




«2 στενά απτό μνημείο σας μένω… Μάντεψε που κατουραω τα βράδια….άντε φλωροι»

 είναι μια από τις απαντήσεις του Ιωάννη Καζαντζόγλου σε σχόλια που τον ειρωνεύονται, σε ανάρτηση μιας εθνικιστικής σελίδας η οποία υπερασπίζεται τους μαχαιροβγάλτες της Ελευσίνας που 

οι ίδιοι δήλωσαν φασίστες

. Σε άλλο σχόλιο απειλεί ευθέως: 

«θα τα πούμε σύντομα»

.













Ο Καζαντζόγλου εννοεί βέβαια το μνημείο του Παύλου Φύσσα στο σημείο όπου ο αντιφασίστας μουσικός δολοφονήθηκε στις 18/9/2013 από τάγμα εφόδου της τοπικής οργάνωσης Νίκαιας της Χ.Α., στην οποία 

επιχειρησιακός επικεφαλής («Υπεύθυνος Ασφάλειας») ήταν ο Καζαντζόγλου

.







Ο Ιωάννης Καζαντζόγλου στο δημόσιο προφίλ του με φωτογραφία όπου διακρίνεται το τατουάζ στον αγκώνα με τον ναζιστικό «Μαύρο Ήλιο».







Η συγκεκριμένη σελίδα εθνικιστικού οχετού φαίνεται να ενεργοποιήθηκε μόλις τον περασμένο Αύγουστο και έχει ελάχιστους ακολούθους, αλλά έχει τη σημασία του το γεγονός ότι ο Καζαντζόγλου είναι ένας από τους πρώτους που την γνωρίζουν και την ακολουθούν.




Σε συνδυασμό με το γεγονός ότι το μαχαίρωμα αντιφασίστα στην Ελευσίνα πραγματοποιήθηκε μόλις λίγες μέρες μετά από τη μαζική διαφήμιση που παρείχαν τα ΜΜΕ της χώρας σε καθοδηγητικό στέλεχος του ελληνικού ναζισμού, αυτό το «ξεμύτισμα» ενός από τους συνεργούς της δολοφονίας Φύσσα δείχνει – εκτός του ότι είναι αμετανόητοι για τις ιδέες τους – ότι είναι αμετανόητοι και για τα μαχαίρια τους.




Επιπλέον, ο ίδιος ο Καζαντζόγλου έχει δημοσιεύσει την παρακάτω φωτογραφία από συνάντησή του με άλλο ένα από τα μέλη του παλιού τάγματος εφόδου χρυσαυγιτών της Νίκαιας, τον Ν. Τσορβά, επίσης συνεργό στη δολοφονία Φύσσα. Με την εύγλωττη περιγραφή 

«Κάποιοι άνθρωποι αν θέλουν δε χάνονται ποτέ.!!!»













Αυτά τα στοιχεία ενισχύουν την υποψία ότι οι μαχαιροβγάλτες που είχαν συσπειρωθεί παλιότερα στο οργανωτικό πλαίσιο της Χ.Α. σήμερα πλέκουν ένα πιο υπόγειο δίκτυο, το οποίο ενδεχομένως λειτουργεί πίσω από διάφορες ομάδες «αυτόνομων εθνικιστών», χωρίς να εκτίθεται σε μια επίσημη κεντρική δομή.




Νέοι εκτελεστές, παλιοί υποκινητές

author: Cas Smith
title: Responding to the far-right threat in Ireland
content:
It’s no secret that the far right is on the rise in several European countries, capitalising on the rising cost of living, health and education and lack of access to housing — largely laying the blame on immigration and the “failure” of multiculturalism.

In Ireland, a wave of far-right protests in 2022 targeting refugee and asylum-seeker accommodation sites was followed by a racist riot in Dublin in November 2023, in the aftermath of a stabbing attack. More recently, pogroms targeting refugees and migrants in Belfast took place between June and September this year.

Paul Murphy – Teachta Dála (a member of the Irish parliament, TD) for Dublin South-West, representing the People Before Profit-Solidarity (PBP-S) alliance, has played a leading role in building the movement against this tendency in Ireland.

Murphy recently spoke to Green Left, explaining that the Irish far right started gaining traction in online spaces during the COVID-19 pandemic, before taking a significant step forward during Europe’s refugee crisis in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

This allowed far-right figures and groups to grow in influence as asylum cases rose, going from “an entirely marginal, entirely peripheral almost entirely irrelevant force in Ireland” to one that had a notable presence on the ground in some communities, being able to elect some councillors and influence populist national parliamentarians.

As the number of Ukrainian refugees arriving in Ireland has declined since its 2023 peak, these groups have maintained their narrative through the targeting of International Protection Accommodation Services (IPAS) centres, which host asylum seekers from various backgrounds.

“They employed very racist rhetoric — suggesting that these people were a danger, tapping into fears that people have,” Murphy said.

Along with scaremongering, the far-right suggested that these centres were “luxury accommodations that homeless Irish people weren't getting — when in fact, they're terrible and overcrowded”.

Murphy said that in response to the scapegoating of refugees, “the government ended up adopting a lot of effectively far-right policies, forcibly making people homeless”, including deciding not to open any more IPAS centres. “Any single man who arrived here was made homeless. Not just homeless, made to rough sleep.”

Murphy said the far right then turned towards a feigned concern for the cost-of-living crisis, which – alongside housing – has been a key challenge in Irish society since the 2010s.

However, although far-right activism around immigration has slowed, it has continued to influence how people understand rising costs and the lack of housing supply.

“If you asked a random person in the street four or five years ago: ‘Why do we have this housing crisis?’, they would have said that this is about the developers, the landlords, the political parties that represent those interests,” Murphy said.

“People would have put forward a basic class analysis of the housing crisis.

“Whereas now, there's a chance that if you ask a random person [this question], they would attribute it to ‘so many people coming in’.”

Murphy said the government “is delighted for this narrative to emerge” and “adds to it significantly because it distracts from its own responsibility”.

Recent protests around the cost of “green” diesel, which is used widely in agriculture and taxed at a different rate, were widely supported, but all of the identified leaders had connections with the far right and or spouted far right ideas, said Murphy.

“They blockaded ports and they won considerable concessions in the context of a generally passive working class and an absence of social movements — with the exception of Palestine,” Murphy said.

“We supported it, [but] we said ‘there's a problem with this leadership, and the trade union movement needs to take the lead’,” said Murphy. Regarding the demand for cheaper diesel, “It can't just be about bringing the price of fossil fuels down, we need free public transport, we need to have retrofitting, we need to get away from reliance on fossil fuels...”

Murphy said that a “big positive” is that the trade unions are now “stepping onto the pitch in terms of the cost-of-living crisis” and there have been “unprecedented turnouts and votes for strike action across the public sector”, in pursuit of demands around cost-of-living protections and wages.

Far-right electoral formations — such as the quasi-fascist National Party, the Irish Freedom Party and a smaller outfit, Ireland First – have been hindered by internal squabbles and disorganisation. However, Murphy said the dominance of far-right narratives has grown the populist right, which now attracts 12–13% of the vote, shared between Independent Ireland and Aontú (Unity), according to opinion polls.

One cultural expression of this is the shifting meaning connected to the Irish tricolour flag. In the past, Murphy said the flying of this flag signified an attachment to the Irish revolutionary tradition, but recently, this has changed.

“There was a campaign linked to the ‘Raise the Colours’ movement in Britain, where people were putting up union jacks in working-class communities, in public streets or lamp posts, but also in people's houses.

“Now, you go into any work class community, you'll still see some of these flags. Definitely some of them may have been to do with sporting events, or maybe put up by old republicans.

“But a significant amount of it is about sending a message, an anti-immigrant message and about making people feel unwelcome in their community.”

In spite of these trends, Murphy contends that there is a growing movement against the far right, with large mobilisations occurring in response to racist attacks and rallies.

“There’s an international phenomenon whereby the pendulum has moved to the right, and that in turn is radicalising a lot of people to the left, who are saying, this is not the type of society I want to live in.

“There have been good mobilisations in response to the upsurge in the far right. In Belfast it was 20,000 people, in Derry there was a big protest, and in the south we’ve also had similar.

“At our biggest, we’ve been able to significantly outnumber them, although our protests happen on different days: the far-right [protest] happens on a Saturday, and the counter protest is called a few weeks later.”

However, Murphy said it was important for the left to try and organise counter protests on the same day, to have the opportunity to speak to working-class people who might be convinced away from far-right talking points.

Murphy said the PBP-S alliance has a three-stage process for addressing the far-right.

“One is building broad, anti-racist, anti-far-right alliances locally and nationally — a broad section of people on a very broad basis,” he said.

“Two, try and build a harder core of anti-racists and anti-fascists who are prepared, for example, to counterprotest against the far-right.

“Three – and this is a really crucial bit – continue to deepen our connections in the working-class communities where the far-right is leading things. That’s essential, to keep open the possibility of discussions with people.”

Murphy said upcoming mobilisations show the left and the unions taking a stand on the cost of living and other social issues and PBP-S is leading the opposition to attempts by South Dublin Council to raise council rates by an average of 25%.

“We’re putting a huge amount of energy into organising street meetings and protests. It’s mainly about countering this increase, and responding to an attack on the more vulnerable parts of the working class.

“But it’s also an opportunity to talk to people about the far right. When you bring people into activities, you enable them to feel more powerful than powerless, and you have the chance of winning the argument that the problem is ‘up there’ as opposed to ‘down here’.”

A full public sector strike is also happening on October 14 – the first in several years. And then there is the movement in solidarity with Palestine, which has “played a role in the past few years in holding the line on things sliding further to the right,” Murphy said.

“It’s the biggest social movement we’ve had over the past three years, [with] thousands of people involved in activism for Palestine. And the far-right clearly doesn’t know how to deal with that.”

author: John Lost
title: Anarcho-syndicalist politics of autonomy - Jonathan Eibisch
content:
Selection from Eibisch, Jonathan (2024): Politische Theorie des Anarchismus, transcript Verlag: Bielefeld, S. 208-233. (open access: https://www.transcript-verlag.de/978-3-8376-7183-4) machined translated text from German to American English.

“Syndicalism arose in France as a revolt against political socialism, and to understand it, we must provide a brief overview of the position that the socialist parties had attained in various countries” (Russell 1971: 57), wrote Bertrand Russell, a prominent advocate of the autonomous labor union movement, in 1918. Following a historical account, he makes a case for recognizing the significance of anarcho-syndicalism, particularly because of its pursuit of a fundamental reorganization of society (ibid.: 75).[1] Similarly, Noam Chomsky, a public intellectual sympathetic to anarchism, emphasized the significance of anarcho-syndicalism, citing the model of the Israeli kibbutzim (Chomsky 1976/2005: 134). Chomsky is particularly fascinated by the large-scale Spanish Revolution, through which successful self-managed structures were created (ibid.: 135). Similarly, in an influential work, Daniel Guérin advocates for anarcho-syndicalism as a practical and constructive implementation of anarchist ideas (Guérin 1969: 41). Guérin makes it clear that Bakunin had already advocated for the proto-trade union organizations—which were still amorphous at the time—conceived in connection with the concept of decentralized, autonomous communes (ibid.: 57–62). However, as rapid social developments overwhelmed the once-influential anarchists, social democracy gained the upper hand in the socialist movement and increasingly oriented it toward parliamentary and party politics. Consequently, the anarchists found themselves

“the 1890s […] into a dead end […]. They were isolated from the world of the working class, where Social Democrats held a monopoly. They huddled in small groups and barricaded themselves in ivory towers to reproduce an unrealistic ideology; or they devoted themselves to (and applauded) individual acts of violence, allowing themselves to be drawn into the cycle of repression and reprisals. […] In order to free the working masses from the influence of the socialists, who were merely deceiving them, the anarchists had to infiltrate the trade unions. […] The workers’ unions were to be reconnected to the “libertarian-communist” society, which remained the ultimate goal of the anarchists” (ibid.: 77f.).

Finally, Guérin sees the revolutionary councils developed during the Russian Revolution of 1905 as the organizational cornerstones of a “libertarian revolution,” precisely because they took places of production as their starting points (Ibid.: 83ff.) and regards the “apolitical” revolution in Spain beginning in 1936 as the most striking example of a radical social transformation based on anarcho-syndicalist ideas, one that was able to build upon a strong tradition (Ibid.: 118–128). For Guérin, self-management remains the key concept of libertarian socialism through which the relevance of anarcho-syndicalism can be revitalized (ibid.: 145–155). This concept is also viewed in the most recent German-language book on anarcho-syndicalism as an essential point of reference, one that must be understood in light of its historical origins. Thus, syndicalism

“starts fundamentally with the material basis. […] Contrary to its materialist worldview, however, the Marxist current did not focus primarily on the economic sphere as the basis of social existence and social change. Ironically, they saw their revolutionary battlefield precisely in the political sphere—which they derived from this and which belongs to the ‘superstructure.’ They sought to participate in the state and ultimately take it over, which was consistent with their centralist orientation. In contrast, the anarchist-oriented wing of the ‘International’ adhered to the premise of overturning the foundations of society through economic struggles; the intermediate goal was direct workers’ self-management, without taking over the structures of the state. This was possible only on a federalist basis, since the state was viewed as an expression of political and military centralism” (Döhring 2017: 20).

More so than other socialist currents, its theory of transformation is derived from practical struggles within class society. Despite some successes in union organizing and labor struggles, the theory of anarcho-syndicalism, at least, seems outdated. Consequently, the substance of the anarcho-syndicalist quest for autonomy must be reconstructed in the following primarily on the basis of historical sources. Thanks to works by, for example, Jule Ehms (2023) and Theresa Adamski, however, historical scholarship on this topic has been brought up to date, including for the German context. The schematic three-step process will be outlined here using the keywords: secession of the autonomous labor movement, strike, and direct action to empower the working class and achieve self-management of production and social functions. This, in turn, involves analysis, distanced criticism, self-organized and empowering social struggles, and finally, the prefigurative path toward the transformation of society as a whole. The sources for this include various texts by Pouget (1903–1907/2014), Cornelissen (1907–1926/2015), Peiró (1931/1986), and Santillán (1936/1986), Rocker (1900–1945), Marcks (2018a, 2018b, 2019), and Schmidt/van der Walt (2009).[2]

One of the defining figures of the second wave of the syndicalist labor movement—which adopted this self-designation with the founding of the French CGT—was Fernand Pelloutier, who was elected secretary of the Federation of Labor Exchanges in 1895 (Cornelissen 2015c: 65). He describes the emergence of anarcho-syndicalism as an eminent quest for autonomy in the sense of actively breaking away from the confined position of the labor movement. It began in 1892 with a critique of social legislation, which, from the syndicalist perspective, essentially represented a shift and a cover-up of exploitation. At its core, this entails a critique of the mode of political reform (Pelloutier 1895/1972: 317). This strategic development was accompanied by an increasing disengagement from politics. Pelloutier writes: “In light of ‘their increasing weakness and their unsuccessful efforts to link politics—which is primarily of interest to the individual—with the economy, which is of social interest,’ the unions finally realized […] that their division had a deeper cause than the conflicts between politicians, and that both […] stemmed from politics” (Ibid.: 320). Due to the perceived ineffectiveness of socialist party politics and its integration into bourgeois parliamentarism, as well as the aforementioned inadequacy of social legislation

“the unions resolved to refrain from any political agitation henceforth, to ruthlessly banish any discussion not purely economic from their educational programs, and to devote themselves exclusively to resistance against capital. The uproar accompanying this shift, however, reached the public. The new motto—“No more politics!”—spread throughout the workplaces […] The unions now seemed sufficiently prepared to the anarchists to embrace and enrich their teachings, and they came to the aid of those who, finally freed from political paternalism, sought to direct their attention—and that of their comrades—toward the study of economic laws” (Ibid.: 321).

Insofar as “pure anarchism” would not be realized in the anticipated socialist revolution, there was all the more need for organization and action in the current historical situation, rather than expecting a “total upheaval.” Therefore, the Federal Committee of the Labor Exchanges has the task of “enlightening the proletariat about the futility of a revolution that is content to replace one form of government with another, even if it were a socialist state” (ibid.: 324). A specific theoretical foundation of the novel autonomous labor movement lay in the dual function of the syndicates as organizations for the working class’s struggle and as the seeds of a new society. This goes far beyond the function of conventional labor unions in aggregating interests and representation. Émile Pouget was the first to articulate this innovative claim, from which the organizational and strategic orientations of anarcho-syndicalist groups were further derived: The syndicate is

“a group such as the ‘reformists’ envision: capable of waging the daily struggle against the employers to secure limited improvements and demands. But beyond that, it is also the appropriate organization for carrying out the expropriation of the capitalists and the reorganization of society—goals that socialists, in their illusory faith in the state, hope to achieve through the seizure of political power” (Pouget 2014a: 53f., cf. Rocker 1947: 25).

In this sense, the trade unions explicitly do not constitute political organizations and combine everyday struggles with a long-term strategy. This is intended to productively resolve the contradiction between reform and revolution that exists in socialist politics, thereby predestining the trade unions as social-revolutionary associations. Through this “dual task” of the trade unions, the overarching goal of social transformation—for which the expropriation of the capitalists is a decisive step—is already being gradually realized through the specific focus of labor struggles on better living conditions (Pouget 2014b: 86ff.). However, what is decisive is “social transformation” achieved “by direct means” (ibid.: 95). According to Pouget, the “group of producers”

“be the nucleus of the new society. It is unthinkable that a genuine social transformation could take place on any other basis. It is therefore essential that the producers prepare themselves for the appropriation and reorganization that lies ahead, because they are the only ones who can carry it out successfully. What we want is a social, not a political, revolution. These are two entirely different phenomena, and the tactics that lead to one take us further away from the other” (Pouget 2014b: 97f., cf. Pouget 2014a: 63).

Rocker later agrees with this (Rocker 1947: 25) and also uses the term “germ cell” (Rocker 1919, Rocker 1924c). Even with a socialist majority, a political path would not make a reorganization of society possible. Starting with the economic base, this must be undertaken by the unions themselves in order to eventually take over production and distribution, as FAUD activist Fritz Kater (1926) also describes. This line of reasoning appears consistent with the assumption that the capitalist class must be completely stripped of power and expropriated, for which the (sometimes idealized) general strike in syndicalism is regarded as a turning point.
