Class Struggle and Policy Disputes




The progress of the cooperative movement in the DDR was shaped both by internal conditions and by the political conditions across Europe in the 1950s. In the DDR and Eastern Europe, the development of socialism was still in its infancy. At the same time, the Cold War waged by the US and its Western allies against the socialist camp intensified. There were many attempts to exploit uncertainties and contradictions in socialist countries and their political leadership, especially following the death of Joseph Stalin in March 1953. The violent political crises and anti-government protests in the DDR in 1953, Poland in 1956, and Hungary that same year can be understood in this context.




As late as March 1952, Heinrich von Brentano, then chairman of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group in West Germany’s Bundestag, openly stated his intentions to regain control of East Germany

: ‘We will do anything and everything – and I say explicitly: anything and everything – to get the Soviet Occupation Zone back’.

57

 In particular, the open border between West and East Berlin offered the West a wide range of opportunities for disruptive actions, including espionage, sabotage, and establishing terrorist organisations. For instance, the West Berlin radio station, Rundfunk im amerikanischen Sektor (Broadcasting in the American Sector), used manipulative, negative reporting to increase farmers’ doubts about the prospects of the socialist perspective.

58




The West exploited existing challenges and discontent in the DDR, which mainly stemmed from the population’s struggle to overcome the consequences of the war, and weaponised them against its government. Seeing how tense the political situation was becoming at the beginning of June 1953, the DDR’s leadership implemented comprehensive relief measures for the population. Nevertheless, protests broke out weeks later on 17 June 1953, which were incited into a counter-revolutionary coup attempt with the help of the West.




In the aftermath of the unrest, the SED leadership reflected critically and publicly on its policy mistakes, including in regard to the cooperative movement that had begun one year earlier. In a newspaper article, the SED Central Committee wrote:




The party, which had taken the right course towards building the foundations of socialism in the DDR, took the wrong path of accelerating the solution of this task without taking into account the real internal and external conditions. This… had detrimental consequences for the population’s food supply and to a certain extent led to the disruption of proper relations between the party and the working masses. Administrative methods were employed where broad and diligent educational work amongst the masses should have taken place.


It was right for the party organisations to support the movement to form agricultural production cooperatives that emerged in the DDR following the initiative of working farmers. However, in some circles, party organisations tolerated the violation of the strict principle of voluntariness and tried to increase the number of cooperatives without devoting the necessary attention to the organisational and economic consolidation of the existing cooperatives, which is the main task of the party when advancing the development of cooperatives in the villages.

59




Eventually, the effort required to establish new LPGs made further expansion difficult, leading the state to shift toward consolidating existing LPGs, supporting their efforts to raise production capacity, and integrating additional farmers, while also providing greater support to private farms whose productivity was still essential to meeting overall agricultural targets.




During this period, there was a renewed debate about the future of agriculture in the DDR, which largely revolved around the extent to which the state should continue to promote cooperatives. In the mid-1950s, most cooperatives were still less productive than medium and privately owned large-scale farms and had to be supported by state subsidies. Some politicians and analysts used this as an opportunity to campaign against state support for ‘unproductive’ cooperatives and for strengthening privately owned farms. These proposals were sharply rejected by the SED leadership under Walter Ulbricht, who declared in 1957 at a conference of the Central Committee:




It is being said that the orderly development of agriculture and the systematic promotion of socialist agriculture should be abandoned… Priority, they say, should be given to the development of [private] family farms… This proposal paves the path back to a capitalist economy, whereby the large farmers would become the main economic force in the village.

60




These disputes reveal that, throughout the entire period of the cooperative movement, there were deep conflicts and debates about how to balance the relationship between voluntariness and the active and determined promotion of cooperatives by the state. Administrative exaggerations by government agencies and political leaders that violated the principle of voluntariness were criticised and opposed. Yet so too were ideas of a self-sustaining process that assigned the state a passive role towards the farmers. There was also an active struggle against the forces that set out to sabotage the development of socialist agriculture.




Socialist Springtime: The Height of the Cooperative Movement




By 1958, six years after the first LPG was founded, there had been a gradual consolidation and stabilisation of productive capacity within the cooperative movement, though state support remained necessary in most cases. Yet, as long as private farms existed alongside the cooperative sector, the socialist transformation of the countryside remained incomplete. The coexistence of different socioeconomic structures in agriculture – cooperative production and individual farming – was bound to hold back the growth of productivity. At the same time, the mere existence of private enterprises in the countryside gave political opponents ammunition to argue against the project of socialist agriculture as a whole. Pressure increased to bring private enterprises into the cooperative movement and create a unified system.




From 1958 to 1960, commonly referred to as ‘socialist springtime’, almost all remaining private farmers were brought into LPGs through initiatives led by bloc parties,

61

 mass organisations, the Democratic Farmers’ Party of Germany, the Peasants’ Mutual Aid Association, and MTSs. This consolidation was reinforced by economic measures that strengthened the sector’s technical capacity, such a marked increase in the agricultural machinery available. As the LPGs’ productivity visibly rose and state support became more effective, medium- and large-scale farmers who had long held reservations began to




By the time the campaign was declared complete in the spring of 1960, its scale was visible in the statistics: the predominantly small, privately owned farms that had characterised agriculture in 1950 had given way to over 19,000 LPGs, each cultivating an average of around 280 hectares. Eighty-four percent of all agricultural land was now farmed

 cooperatively.

62







Image 18. Industrial workers help with the potato harvest. Cooperatives were assigned industrial enterprises at an early stage to provide support and workers helped with the harvest and repairs.







Women farmers played a key role in the expansion and consolidation of the cooperative movement, as they were often the key actors winning their families over. Women, who had traditionally worked in the time-consuming and physically taxing field of animal husbandry while also managing their households and childcare, certainly stood to gain the most from joining LPGs and the social benefits granted to their members.




Though the vast majority of farmers had agreed to join LPGs by the spring of 1960, in some cases, they only came to truly appreciate the benefits of cooperative production in the years that followed. One farmer, Elli I., reflected on her scepticism towards the cooperative in the early years:




As individual farmers, we had to work from dawn to dusk. In 1957, my daughter was born prematurely because I had to help my husband load thirty sacks of fertiliser. In the cooperative, we no longer had to worry about such things. We had joined the cooperative quite late and, after years, I thought to myself, my goodness, how stupid had we been? You can’t live any better than here. The work got easier. We had medical care, every woman could go to the doctor, we had housekeeping days, and vacations. When I think back, … those were my best years.

Cooperatives Drive Social and Cultural Progress




From their origin, the tasks of LPGs were not limited to agricultural production but to the improvement of rural life in general. Over time, they developed into hubs of social, communal, cultural-political, and economic development in rural communities. In coordination with the municipalities and urban enterprises, LPGs built apartments, cultural centres, kindergartens, and sports facilities. They improved roads and constructed new ones, installed water pipes and sewage systems, dug drainage ditches, and opened stores and restaurants. LPGs built on and expanded the cultural work of MTSs. Performances by theatre groups, dance nights for the youth, sporting events, and film screenings brought a new level of cultural life to the villages.




Hans Luft, an agronomist and former employee of the DDR’s Ministry of Agriculture, reflects on the cultural transformation brought about by the new production relations of the LPG system:




The joint work in the cooperative and [resolving] the emerging problems such as the use of complex machinery to bring in the harvest as quickly as possible, difficulties with repairs and procuring spare parts for agricultural machinery, completion of construction and irrigation systems, [and] epidemic-free management of large livestock quickly broke down generations of enmity in the villages. The farmers’ children grew into the new forms of production with new knowledge, experience, and, above all, higher levels of qualification.

64




Cooperatives vastly improved the rural population’s living conditions, reducing the physical strain on farmers through communal work and the use of machinery.

65

 In addition to national programmes that guaranteed access to national social, health, and insurance systems and so on, the LPGs achieved a number of important social advances for their members, which were impossible for previous generations of farmers to even dream of and still unavailable to the few remaining private farms, such as:







Equal pay for equal work




Special remuneration for work on Sundays and public holidays




Sick pay




Child benefits, such as monthly cash payments and birth grants




Paid vacation, with the option of spending it in a subsidised LPG-owned vacation site




Fixed and predictable work hours, except during the harvest months




The inclusion of all cooperative farmers in a uniform social insurance system that covered benefits such as healthcare, pensions, and accident insurance




‘Exemption’ from income tax contributions

66







In addition, child labour, which had been a common practice on family-run farms, disappeared with the advent of LPGs. Central schools replaced the single-class schools in the villages. Children and young people had access to the DDR’s polytechnic education system, which enabled them to choose an independent career and provided a foundation for agricultural studies. Comprehensive education and training opportunities were created for cooperative farmers, from which female farmers benefited significantly as they were able to gain professional qualifications and take on managerial roles in the cooperative farms for the first time.




Margarete Müller, an agronomist and SED politician, described the progress that her village achieved:




I have lived in Kotelow since 1960. Back then, at the age of 29, I was elected LPG chairwoman. When we started, there were no paved roads and our boots got stuck deep in the mud. Bit by bit, we modernised the village and improved it. We were happy about every new house, every new stable, every new barn, about the dairy farm and the pigsties that we built together. We celebrated together and also got frustrated together when things didn’t go the way we wanted them to. We were a community. Even in the summer, farmers could go on holiday, and youth who qualified at universities and technical colleges sometimes moved back because they saw a future for themselves and their families in little Kotelow.

67




From 1960, the height of the cooperative movement, until the dissolution of the DDR in 1990, women accounted for roughly 40–45% of LPG members.

68

 While only 8.5% of women working in agriculture had a degree or vocational training in 1963, compared to 18.1% of men, by 1984 this figure had reached 88.6% in the field of agriculture, compared to 90.2% of the general population.

69

 In 1966, 26% of all board members of the LPGs were women.

70

 Concrete structures such as the Women’s Committees and Women’s Development Plans were set up comprehensively in the LPGs and intended to strengthen the role of women, advocate for their interests, and increase their leadership positions. By 1978, the proportion of women in leadership positions had reached 35%, in part due to the increase in their professional and educational qualifications. However, the process of increasing the number of women in leadership stagnated in the late 1980s and women remained underrepresented among LPG chairs until the end of the DDR. 

71

Anti-Imperialist Solidarity in Agriculture




As the DDR sought to bring the quality of life in rural and urban areas closer together, another pillar of socialist construction was cultivated among farmers: international solidarity.




On 1 September 1960, the Institute for Tropical Agriculture was founded at the Karl Marx University in Leipzig. Why was such an institute established in Germany, a country situated in a cool temperate climate zone? After losing its colonies at the end of the First World War, there was no longer any state interest in research and education relating to tropical agriculture. This changed with the DDR, albeit with an altogether different premise: young nation states that had emerged from anti-colonial struggles were to be actively supported on their path to economic liberation. Thousands of students from over sixty countries in the Global South were trained to develop agriculture in their home countries at the Leipzig Institute and a handful of other educational establishments, such as the School of Agricultural Engineering for Tropical Agriculture in Altenburg and the VEB Interagrarkooperation.




DDR citizens also attended courses and seminars designed specifically to prepare them for agricultural assignments abroad. Groups of DDR specialists, working in close collaboration with local experts and officials, supported the complex and protracted process of transforming feudal, colonially distorted, and backward agricultural structures into sovereign, state-controlled agricultural production.




Examples include pig specialists in Vietnam attempting to combine the fertility of the Vietnamese pot-bellied pig with the fattening capacity of German breeds, a tropical farmer in the People’s Democratic Republic of Yemen who, together with local officials, carried out the first thorough statistical surveys of livestock production, or a group of thirty-eight DDR specialists who, on the basis of a friendship treaty between the DDR and Mozambique and in close cooperation with local forces, helped to establish a state farm – eight of whom were killed by counter-revolutionary forces in 1984.

72

 Furthermore, the development of the first coffee-growing regions in Dak Lak, Vietnam – supported by 32 million roubles

73

 – enabled the country to become the world’s second-largest coffee producer.

74




The dispatch of tractors and agricultural machinery, as well as the setting up of repair workshops, was financed by donations from DDR citizens, including contributions from farmers. In thousands of cooperatives, farmers in the DDR set up solidarity groups and supported campaigns such as ‘Farmers Help the Farmers of Vietnam’, which sent spraying equipment to Vietnam to rehabilitate crops poisoned by the US chemical attacks.

The Path to Large-Scale Agricultural Production




In the late 1960s, when land reform had been fully implemented and the cooperative movement had reached its height, a third central phase of agricultural development began. During this phase, strategic goals were established that would guide agricultural planning until the beginning of the 1980s: the consolidation of small- and mid-sized farms into larger cooperatives, specialisation in parts of the production process, and collaboration with processing industries as prerequisites for large-scale industrial-like production in the countryside. Hans Reichelt, long-time minister of agriculture, explained the necessity of industrial agricultural production under the conditions of a socialist society:




This was the path towards creating larger economic units in agriculture – small-scale farming is as ineffective as keeping livestock in small stables. Some may object here: ‘Yikes, large-scale livestock farming!’ But industrial-like production in agriculture is not bad 

per se

. It is objectively necessary to feed humanity – this is not possible with nineteenth-century production methods. What is bad is when all moral and ethical rules, including animal welfare, are ignored for the sake of profit. However, this stems from the character of the society. When corporate wholesale buyers force farmers to sell their produce below the production price, and when shareholders and banks speculate with food on the stock exchanges, this inevitably has an impact on production.

75




As a result of the increased investment capacities and efficiency that came with years of accumulated experience in cooperative-style production, all LPGs gradually developed into Type III LPGs (the most advanced cooperative structure, through which farmers incorporated all of their land and homestead into the cooperative, which functioned as an independent enterprise). Through a 1963 decree of the Council of Ministers, most MTS machinery was handed over to the Type III LPGs free of charge while the Type I and Type II LPGs were able to purchase it at a low price and in instalments.

76

 Many MTS workers, tractor drivers, and technicians became members of cooperatives. This meant that the use of technology could be coordinated more effectively and integrated into the work of LPGs. Finally, LPGs also merged to form larger ‘joint LPGs’. The total number of cooperatives decreased, while the agricultural area farmed by each cooperative increased. Where previously there were 19,313 LPGs working roughly 5.4 million hectares of land in 1960, in 1988 3,855 LPGs worked the same amount of land.

77




Data from a collective of authors, 40 Jahre erfolgreiche Entwicklung zu einer leistungsfähigen sozialistischen Landwirtschaft in der DDR [40 Years of Successful Development Towards Efficient Socialist Agriculture in the DDR] (Eggersdorf: agrabuch, 1989), 58.




This increase in agricultural productivity was driven by the need to meet the growing demand for food and raw materials, which were necessary inputs in a number of industries, such as the textile, leather and fur, pulp and paper, chemical and pharmaceutical, woodworking, and cultural industries. In 1988, almost 65% of the DDR’s primary raw materials were produced in the agricultural sector.

78

 This increase in agricultural productivity also freed up urgently needed labour that could be deployed to other sectors of the economy; promoted the efficient use of agricultural machinery; and created the conditions to increase the level of training that farmers and agricultural workers received – all factors that in turn further increased productivity.

Agricultural planning took place at the central, local, and farm levels. Until then, LPGs had been relatively self-contained, now they become increasingly integrated into the overall social planning and management of the DDR’s economy. The Agricultural-Industrial Associations (Agrar-Industrie-Vereinigungen, AIVs) that emerged in the mid-1970s were the culmination of this process. AIVs were an institutionalised form of cooperation between various LPGs, Publicly Owned Estates, inter-enterprise facilities used by more than one organisation also known by their German acronym VEGs, and the upstream and downstream enterprises in the service, processing, and manufacturing sectors. By 1989, thirteen such production complexes (AIVs) had formed in the DDR, which together farmed 6.6% of the DDR’s total agricultural land.

79




By the early 1980s, concrete problems arising from the trend towards specialisation and excesses in large-scale production led to course corrections and debates. For example, the specialisation and separation of plant and animal production disrupted the direct exchange of natural fertiliser and animal feed and led to logistical difficulties. Increased transport expenditures and costs for large estates strained production. In animal production, the effort to tend to veterinary hygiene and disease prevention noticeably increased. Ecological issues caused by the excessive use of mineral fertilisers rather than environmentally friendlier options were corrected over time. Energy-intensive machine systems were susceptible to energy price spikes on the global market, which had a particularly severe impact on the DDR, especially in the beginning of the 1980s.




The effort to improve the integration of LPGs into the DDR’s social and economic plans through AIVs did not signal a plan to change the ownership structure of the land. As an official information brochure on agriculture explained:




Time and again, visitors to our republic ask if and when land will be nationalised. This question is not on the table, because nobody is thinking of changing the forms of property in the countryside. Most of the land is the private property of the farmers. Its cooperative use, and the distribution of its yield to the LPG members according to their share of the work performed, creates every opportunity to further advance the [DDR’s] developed socialist society.

80




Though private ownership undoubtedly had an influence on the consciousness of individual farmers, on the whole, the increasing integration of the LPGs into the unitary structures of economic planning and democracy in the DDR prevented private land ownership from developing economic or political significance. The relationship between the different actors in rural areas and agricultural production was not without friction. As Klaus Schmidt, former director of the DDR’s Institute for Agroeconomics, pointed out:




Particularly where the AIVs managed the territory of an entire municipality or where their sphere of influence even extended beyond the municipality’s boundaries, there was a tendency for them to increasingly take on the official duties that had hitherto been managed by state organs. A fundamental problem that arose with the development of the AIVs was the question of the prospects and opportunities of individual units within the AIV, specifically to what extent they could maintain their independence.

81




Such contradictions and problems, alongside the misguided separation of plant and animal production in the 1970s, should have resulted in lively debate about the future of agriculture. The issue of balancing land ownership and independence with the further integration and centralisation of LPGs would certainly have remained the subject of political debate had the DDR continued to exist. As long as the SED and the wide-ranging democratic structures in rural areas – from the agricultural councils from the municipal to central levels to the farmers’ organisations, and numerous scientific institutions and agriculture publications of the time – responded to these contradictions and tasks in an agile, self-critical and proactive manner, they were able to drive development forward.




5. Conclusion




The development of socialist agricultural relations was brought to an abrupt end with the dissolution of the DDR in October 1990. Structural changes were imposed at breakneck speed, transforming the social and economic reality of farmers.




At the time of the DDR’s dissolution, 55% of the land cultivated by the LPGs was owned by individual LPG members. The remaining 45% was owned by the state or leased to the LPG by private owners. After 1990, this 45% was rapidly privatised, removing land from the LPGs’ existing economic structures and providing a lever for their dissolution in favour of private farming. LPGs seeking to continue to produce had to lease or purchase this land, often at additional cost, while completing the transition to a new legal form used for cooperatives in the West by the end of 1991. The transformation process placed considerable pressure on existing LPG structures.

82




This and other policy shifts in the post-1990 period created a rural exodus, especially of young and qualified workers. Of the former 923,000 agricultural workers in the DDR, 743,900 were laid off by 1993 and 4 out of 5 were pushed to leave the countryside.

83

 The social and cultural infrastructure was destroyed. Although the transformation in land ownership established by land reform was legally protected by the so-called reunification treaties signed by the last DDR government, the landowning elite that had controlled the countryside before 1945 was able to use loopholes to reclaim parts of their expropriated land.




Yet, despite the radical capitalist turnaround, the history of the DDR has left a visible mark on agricultural structures in Germany. On average, farms in East Germany cultivate much larger areas than those in West Germany and have maintained elements of the structures established by LPGs, such as machine sharing under the new legal categories of the market economy.

84




In less than fifty years, revolutionary ruptures in the living and economic relations of the countryside were seen in East Germany, from the remnants of a semi-feudal, hierarchical social and property order to a collective way of working and living based on cooperation. The land reform that began in 1945 created the conditions for the transformation in the countryside and the dismantling of the political and economic monopoly of the landowning classes. Only by ending their rule was it possible to establish and develop new economic and social relations in East Germany. With the expropriation of the large Junker estates, land reform in the DDR ended the rule of the feudal aristocracy and agrarian capitalist classes. Agricultural workers, landless and smallholder peasants, and the general village population were liberated from the system of economic exploitation and semi-feudal disenfranchisement that had been in place for centuries. Under the conditions created by the reality of Soviet occupation after the Second World War and the leadership of the workers’ movement and parties, land reform was achieved in this part of Germany, and the oppressed became the protagonists shaping agriculture and village life.




The phase of collectivisation in the post-war years (approximately 1952–1960) illustrates the complexity of social development when a change in the thinking of those involved is crucial to its success. The SED had to manoeuvre between the strategic goals of socialist construction and the adverse conditions on the ground. Between retreat and advance, external and internal contradictions, and the necessities and prospects of economic development, the SED constantly reassessed the speed and force of its leadership in this comprehensive development process.




The complexity of the path to socialism, the protracted nature of some processes, especially in people’s consciousness, and the influence and sabotage of political opponents had to be taken into account and counteracted. This required agility and clarity of purpose, but also the ability to be self-critical, which the political leadership generally demonstrated over long periods of time.




While social hardship and individual cases of injustice cannot be denied, it is necessary to understand such instances in the contradictory and complex context of post-war East Germany and to understand that they represent exceptions, not the rule. Without the leading role of the peasantry, the transition towards cooperatives would have failed. Naturally, from the bourgeois perspective, the transition away from the dominance of private property is to be condemned on principle. Narratives of ‘forced collectivisation’ that dominate the public discourse in Germany today do not seek to understand the processes in the DDR but rather to promote anti-communist prejudices. Individual fates, in which there were also tragic conflicts and entanglements, are used to obscure the view of the broader development and prevent a serious examination based on historical facts. This method of framing can be seen over and over in narratives about socialist states.




Cooperative forms of agricultural production were a cornerstone of East Germany and a decisive building block for the development of the DDR as a socialist state. Existential financial angst, which is inevitable under the ‘freedom’ of private property and competition, was overcome in the DDR through mutual aid among peasants and their integration into state planning. While some see the continued existence of cooperative ownership alongside state ownership as a major obstacle to the deepening of planned economic relations, this was not the case in the DDR. The experiences of the AIVs certainly pointed to contradictions between the different forms of ownership that needed to be resolved, but the cooperatives were already deeply integrated into the overall economic processes of the DDR through jointly developed plans and thus binding agreements on the distribution of funds as well as the fixed-price system. While the LPGs could exercise some economic autonomy regarding their internal workings, there would be no significant effect of these autonomous decisions on the broader economy.




The cooperative way of thinking, working, and living in the DDR democratised the villages by eroding social hierarchies, expanding leisure time, and promoting extensive opportunities for cultural, sporting, and social activities. Cultural centres, kindergartens, village stores, cafeterias, comprehensive medical care, continuing education opportunities, vacation sites, sports teams, music groups, and much more were an integral part of village and community infrastructure. It was the rural population itself that played a key role in building these structures and sustaining them.




The DDR was largely able to produce its own agricultural products, and hunger and poverty became things of the past. Today, in view of soaring rates of global hunger, the omnipresent overexploitation of nature, and the market dominance of agricultural multinational corporations, some political movements seek the solution in small-scale production. The DDR followed a different path, which – despite a decreasing workforce – was able to avoid the negative effects of capitalist farming while increasing yields by industrialising large-scale agricultural production on the basis of socialist relations.




The abrupt termination of this project in 1990 and the developments in the years since elucidate the essential characteristics of capitalist transformation: privatisation, the dismantling of ‘unprofitable’ social and cultural infrastructure, land speculation, and rural exodus. Farmers had and still have to fight their own way through the chaos of liquidation, privatisation, and fierce competition, pitted against a constructed false enemy/scapegoat of ‘cheap’ labour provided mostly by migrants.




The dismantling of socialist infrastructure in the countryside furthered the tendency towards isolation among rural populations. While the renewed reign of private property postured itself as offering increased freedom of choice to farmers, this ‘freedom’ is inherently limited by constraints of the market and comes at the expense of farmers’ roles as co-creators of society. Along with it came a new rule of order: profit as the determining factor in agriculture. While the conditions today differ greatly from those in 1945, the slogan ‘The land to those who work it’ is yet again on the agenda in East Germany and across the world.

author: Joel Mukisa
title: Jumuiya’s Arts Censorship and Resistance in East Africa
content:
Introduction | Coordinated Jumuiya transnational repression 




In the recent past, our Jumuiya’s democracy scales have been trembling with the impunity of human rights abuses and a worrying trend of 

transnational repression

. One incident that chilled the conscience of all freedom-loving East Africans was the 

brazen abduction

 of Ugandan opposition politician, Kizza Besigye, on 16 November 2024 in Kenya by unidentified assailants who bundled him into a vehicle together with FDC (Forum for Democratic Change) member Haji Obeid Lutale, and drove him across the border to Uganda without any formal extradition process. After suffering the ordeal of being held in incommunicado detention, Besigye was arraigned before the General Court Martial and charged with offences relating to security and the unlawful possession of firearms and ammunition, which could attract the death penalty. In July of the same year, 36 other members of the FDC party had been 

arrested in Kisumu, Kenya,

 and forcibly deported to Uganda where they were charged with terrorism despite having lawfully entered Kenya with the necessary immigration permissions. 




The Boniface Mwangi and Agather Atuhaire Torture and Deportation




Six months after the kidnapping of Kizza Besigye from Kenya, 

Boniface Mwangi and Agather Atuhaire

, who are prominent Kenyan and Ugandan human rights activists respectively, were abducted in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, while expressing solidarity with opposition leader Tundu Lissu. There is a thread of consistency in the way all these major East African nations (mis)treat their opposition politicians and Activists. Like Besigye, Tundu Lissu faces treason charges ahead of contentious elections in Tanzania. Agather and Boniface not only endured days of incommunicado detention just like Besigye, but also reported suffering 

severe sexual torture

, including rape and beatings by Tanzanian security forces. 




Since the cross-border snatch-and-transfer operation happened almost a year ago, Besigye and his counterpart Haji Obeid have not received due process contrary to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights. Similarly, the enforced disappearances and ill-treatment of Agather and Boniface breached the human rights protocols of the East African Community and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, to which all three countries are signatories.




There is a complex historical origin of artistic censorship in Africa, partly stemming from colonial policy. The post-independence African states did not shake off the institutional legacy of colonialism, including the suppression of critical artistic expression.  Through the use of draconian laws, censorship boards, and internet restrictions, more East African countries have registered excesses against the freedom of artists. 




Across the region, from the early 2000s to the mid-2010s, there was a fusion of different forms of art, from graffiti and mural paintings to subversive visuals and performances by creative artists who defied authoritarianism. 




Art Meets Gen Z Maandamano




 In April 2025, the 

Kenyan police fired tear gas

 to disperse the audience that had gathered to watch Kenya’s national high-school drama competition. This followed the staging of a play, 

Echoes of War,

 by Butere Girls High School. Kenyan authorities could not stomach a play, produced by students, set in a fictional kingdom where the youth have lost faith in their leaders. The play’s author, Cleophas Malala, was also briefly detained by police. 




Additionally, Kenya published the 

Statute Law (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill 2020

 in June 2020, with proposed amendments to the

 

Film and Stage Plays Act 1962 (Cap 222)

. The intention behind this move is to increase the reach and grasp of the 

Kenya Films and Classification Board (KFCB)

 to bolster its capacity for censorship of artistic works deemed critical of the regime. The following month in the same year, Tanzania passed a new law, the 

Electronic and Postal Communications Act (EPOCA), on Online Content Regulations 2020

, to tighten state restrictions on freedom of expression under the pretext of “morality” and national security. What the foregoing laws do is impose criminal prosecutions against grassroots satirists and online artists, further curbing dissent. 




Although digital media provided a platform for 

political participation

 and democratic expression in the recent #GenZ protests in Kenya, when young people challenged the retrogressive Finance Bill 2024, it did not come without challenges. There were reports of the Kenyan government colluding with some of the digital platforms to use automated moderation and limit the visibility of protest art amid the Gen Z-led demonstrations.




Dictator Mama Samia 




In Tanzania, although Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM), the ruling party, enjoys support from several prominent artists who compose praise songs for party leaders, it remains intolerant of any ounce of criticism from other critical artists. One of these is 

Nay Wa Mitego

, a rapper who has been persecuted several times for his creative work. In September 2024, he was arrested after the Tanzania National Arts Council accused him of inciting against government abductions and slandering the president in his song, 

Nitasema

 (I Shall Speak). During President Magufuli’s tenure, he had also faced arrests, charges, threats, and bans due to producing music deemed critical of the government.




Into the bargain, in October 2023, three of Tanzania’s leading newspapers – 

The Citizen

, 

Mwananchi

 and 

Mwanaspoti

 – were proscribed from publishing their online editions and had their 

licences suspended for 30 days

 after they ran an animation deemed critical of President Samia Suluhu Hassan. This followed the publishing of a video clip which highlighted the increasing cases of abductions and disappearances in the country.




BASATA’s Overreach 




In November 2018, Tanzania’s national arts council, Baraza la Sanaa Tanzania (BASATA) 

banned

 Diamond Platnumz and Rayvanny’s popular song, “Mwanza,” and slapped the artists with a hefty fine, claiming the song was “too vulgar” to be played in the country. The board ordered the label Wasafi Records to remove the track from all digital platforms and ensure it is never played again on the radio or in clubs in Tanzania.




In 2023, Tanzanian music sensations 

Whozu, Mbosso, and Billnass

 were heavily fined and banned from participating in artistic activities for a three-month period, starting from November 4, 2023, over a controversial music video, 

Ameyatimba

.




Maria Sarungi’s Abduction




Having left Tanzania for Kenya four years earlier following threats of arrest and the 

banning

 of her

 media outlet

, Maria was 

abducted

 in Kenya in January 2025 and feared her assailants planned to force her back to Tanzania because of her critical social media posts. Ironically, The road where Maria’s kidnapping occurred is named after 

Charles Argwings Kodhek

 (1923-1969), the first native lawyer in Kenya and East Africa who was also an early nationalist figure and a member of the labour movement. Maria was 

freed

 and left on a “rough road, in a dark place”.




Mange Kimambi’s Activism and Exile




Another prominent Tanzanian activist, Mange Kimambi, who had been enlisted by the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party in 2015 to push for John Magufuli’s presidential bid, was later forced into exile after weaponising her platform against Magufuli’s regime for its crackdown on press freedoms. With over 2.1 million followers now, Mange’s Road to exile began around 2016-2017 amid escalating backlash for her determination to 

criticise

 the Tanzanian government’s corruption and service failures, culminating in her forced exile the United States.




Historical Roots of Artistic Censorship in Uganda




Some Ugandan artists may feel that the increased restrictions against their work today are due to the political emergence of Bobi Wine, a vibrant and disruptive opposition politician whose key to fame was music. However, they would be remiss to forget that some of the laws providing the pretext for 

blocking Bobi Wine’s concerts

 were passed during the British colonial rule! The government can ban performances, censure artworks, revoke work permits of creatives, arrest artists, and even shut down venues where artists are scheduled to perform by relying on a 

law

 passed in September 1943 by the British colonial authorities. The British also 

prosecuted

 any artist who practised their traditional dances and culture, which were deemed satanic and obscene.




However, this had not always been the case. Whereas some precolonial African societies had patronage systems and centralised censorship, whereby artistic works were commissioned and controlled by royal courts, artists enjoyed a considerable degree of freedom because art was integrated into daily life and was at the centre of spirituality and identity. Therefore, the limitations against artistic expression that were registered widely in the post-colonial era were largely inherited from the colonial legacy, which had weaponised politics against art. 




Abuse of Artistic Freedom in Post-Independence Uganda




And so, it happened that in 1965, 

Wycliffe Kiyingi

 and the entire cast of his artistic radio show, 

Wokulira,

 were arrested, and the show was banned by Milton Obote’s government. For writing an article critical of the government in their literary magazine, 

Transition

,

 Abu Mayanja and Rajat Neogy were arrested in 1968. For writing 

The Burdens

 and 

Covenant with Death,

 the playwright 

John Ruganda

 was forced into exile in 1973, fearing for his life. For producing his cryptic play, 

Amayirikiti,

 

Robert Serumaga

, another playwright of great stature in Ugandan literature, was also forced into exile following negative interpretations of the play by the Idi Amin regime. For staging the play, 

Oluyimba lwa Wankoko,

 

Byron Kawadwa

 became a martyr of Ugandan literature at the hands of Amin’s rogue agents in 1977, because the play was interpreted as mocking the Amin regime through its depiction of a tyrannical rooster-king.




The Hybrid State of Artistic Freedom Under the NRM




Beyond combat, the National Resistance Army (NRA) War that shot President Museveni into power was 

cheered up by artists

, some of whom formed higher and lower ranks of the guerrilla force, including 

Gen. Elly Tumwine

 and 

Sergeant Steven Kifulugunyu,

 respectively. 




Outside of the NRA ranks, civilian artists also composed songs that decried the breakdown of social order and public service delivery under the Obote II regime, and supported the liberation struggle with songs of praise and encouragement for the fighters and their leader, Yoweri Museveni. One of these artists was 

Peter Baligidde

, who composed 

Agawalajana Mulukoola

, a popular song in the 1980s which President Obote’s regime had banned due to interpretations of its message that alluded to the degradation of political stability under the regime and applauded the struggle by the NRA guerrillas.  




Upon taking power, there was widespread hope that Museveni’s National Resistance Movement (NRM) would respect human rights, especially the right to freedom of expression, since it was one of the reasons they had launched a protracted war five years earlier. According to 

Eckhard Breitinger

, in 1986, more than 400 theatrical groups registered as members of the Ugandan Theatrical Groups Association, signalling the optimism with which cultural activists perceived this new era of unprecedented freedom of expression.




In its early days, the NRM seemed committed to protecting and empowering the freedom of artistic expression. It illustrated this by, among other ways, returning Wycliffe Kiyingi’s 

Wokulira

 radio serial. Through the Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development, and statutory bodies like the 

Uganda National Cultural Centre (UNCC

, the government seemed to encourage and support the development of cultural and artistic activities. Through teaching Music, Dance and Drama (MDD), schools were also vibrant nurseries for artistic talent. 




Creative arts also played a significant role in mobilising the Ugandan population to contain major national challenges, especially the HIV/AIDS pandemic and the restoration of peace and reconciliation in areas ravaged by civil war, especially in northern Uganda. Poems and songs were written and performed regularly by pupils and students about all those challenges. Therefore, the government had a direct benefit and critical incentive to promote the freedom of artistic expression. 




However, over time, the NRM government has increasingly constrained the space for artistic expression in Uganda. Today, cartoonists like 

Jimmy Spire Ssentongo

, a Ugandan academic who employs art to campaign against the widespread corruption in government, have reported 

threats against their lives

. In the past, the government used to charge editors of newspapers that critically caricatured the president with 

sedition

. In 2017, musician David Mugema and his producer Jonathan Muwanguzi were arrested and charged with 

offensive communication

 for disturbing the peace of President Museveni. This followed their release of a song, 

Wummula,

 which was interpreted as demanding that the president retire from his long stay in power. 




In 2012, the 

Uganda Media Council suspended performances

 of 

State of the Nation

, a play that highlighted corruption and poor governance in Uganda under President Museveni. The play had been produced to coincide with the 50th anniversary of Uganda’s independence, on 9 October.




Several artists have been arrested or suffered in some way due to the interference of the state against their freedom of artistic expression. One of the bright careers that were ended by the misapplication of the law by the state prosecutors was 

Producer Didi

, who was arrested in 2014, and his studio equipment was forfeited by the government on account of producing the song 

Panadol Wa Basajja

, which was claimed to contain pornographic content. Although Didi was eventually found innocent, his life has been 

ruined

 since. 




Artistic Resistance and Innovation in the Face of Jumuiya Repression




Nevertheless, the high-handed and imperious abuse of artistic freedom by East African states has not gone without incident. Young, vibrant artists have evolved to invent new and bold forms of expression to surmount state censorship. 




Leila Babirye

, a queer Ugandan, is one of those young East Africans blending creative expression with political critique and human rights activism. When she realised that the space for sexual minorities to freely express themselves had been further constrained by the passing of the anti-homosexuality bill in Uganda in 2023, she ingeniously found ways to address the realities of being gay in Uganda and Africa in general through art. Her sculpture artwork turns everyday materials into objects that address issues surrounding identity, sexuality, and human rights. Leila collects debris from the streets of New York that has been whittled, welded, burned, and burnished, and chisels it into beautiful sculptures, symbolising the reclamation of the disgraceful treatment of LGBTQI identities in Africa. Through her artwork, she expresses herself in ways that the government cannot restrict, furthering the cause of human rights.




When the Ugandan government denied Bobi Wine access to any public venues for his concerts, limiting his right as an artist to perform and earn, he innovatively held 

digital concerts

 at his private beach and home, further escaping state limitations. 




When Tanzanian authorities 

banned bloggers

 recently ahead of the 2025 national elections, Maxence Melo’s platform, 

Jamii Forums,

 resisted the blogger shutdowns. In Kenya, a subculture has evolved for self-expression and 

social commentary on matatus

 (public mini-buses), which are avenues for integrating hip-hop, graffiti, and reggae music that address socioeconomic, political, and cultural themes relevant to urban youth. Tanzanian youth creatives and initiatives like Wachata Collective’s urban murals have also adopted 

street art

 as an avenue for socio-political expression. Luta Ferdinand was a member of the Alternative Social Movement, a Ugandan pressure group. In February 2021, he 

publicly flogged an effigy,

 which came to be widely referred to as a makeshift dummy of the Ugandan President, Yoweri Museveni. Armed with a loudspeaker and a stick, he accused the effigy of electoral malpractice and punished it with disfiguring whips. Arrested, the police charged him with common nuisance under the Penal Code Act. A year later, Luta revealed to the media that upon arrest, he was 

tortured

 and later charged in a military court with having military stores before being remanded to Kitalya prison. 




The law and politics are often weaponised against artistic freedom because art is rich with the capacity to express issues vividly and seriously, yet with creative entertainment. With his life-size effigy sculpture, Luta made a spectacle of a powerful political figure, rendering justice to a perpetrator that the formal justice system could not apprehend.




It is easy for Luta, the creative artist, to be overshadowed by his political activism. But in truth, it is his art that has the power to socially shame a public figure and bring them to account in the court of public opinion. However, African artists and activists persist in their pursuit of artistic freedom, recognising the transformative power of art in shaping societies. We should recognise the power of art to provoke thought, challenge conventions, and ignite social change. Africa is one of the most culturally diverse continents, and our artistic talents must be supported to continue vibrantly expressing our identity, history, and contemporary realities. Art is therefore political.




The post 

Jumuiya’s Arts Censorship and Resistance in East Africa

 first appeared on 

The Elephant

.

title: Botan: Disarmament is a precondition for peace, not peace itself - Part Two
content:
Politician Lezgin Botan spoke to ANF about how the process is viewed by the Kurdish public, political and legal expectations, the relationship between disarmament and democratisation, and possible developments in the coming period.




The first part of this interview can be read 

here

. 




Botan said strengthening local governments and ending the practice of appointing trustees were among the important issues in the process. He stressed that strengthening local democracy should be considered not only in relation to the Kurdish question but also in the context of Turkey's overall democratisation.




Botan also said: “Local democracy is an important issue in the democratic resolution of the Kurdish question. The constant supervision of local governments by the central administration, and their being rendered ineffective when deemed necessary, create serious problems for the political will of the people. The practice of appointing trustees, in particular, means that the central administration appoints officials to replace elected representatives. Overriding the will expressed by the people through elections poses a serious problem for democratic representation. Strengthening local governments should not be seen solely as a demand of Kurds. This is an issue concerning Turkey's overall democratisation. The European Charter of Local Self-Government, which Turkey has signed, should also be reconsidered in this context.”




‘Freedom of expression and association is essential for democratic politics’




Lezgin Botan said a democratic solution cannot be achieved without freedom of expression and association, stressing that political normalisation requires guarantees for these rights. Botan said: “If we are talking about political normalisation, people must be able to express their views, organise and engage in political activities. Democratic politics cannot be strengthened as long as restrictions on political party activities, the right to assembly and demonstration, freedom of expression and freedom of association remain in place. The implementation of rulings by the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) and the Constitutional Court is also important. Under Article 90 of the Constitution, implementing international conventions and relevant court rulings is essential to strengthening the rule of law.”




‘Lasting social peace cannot be achieved without confronting the past’




Botan said the current dimensions of the Kurdish question cannot be considered separately from the past, drawing attention to the consequences of previous policies for collective memory.




Lezgin Botan continued: “We cannot assess the Kurdish question solely in terms of what is happening today. In the past, policies were implemented restricting the use of Kurdish identity and language in the public sphere. These policies had serious consequences for collective memory. The period of the Law on the Maintenance of Order must also be examined from this perspective. The Law on the Maintenance of Order was essentially a typical system of ethnic cleansing, particularly through demographic change. It is not easy to establish lasting social peace without confronting what happened in the past. A democratic solution also requires confronting historical memory.”




Botan said that alongside high expectations, a cautious approach persists among the Kurdish public, adding that this is also reflected in opinion polls. He said: “There are both considerable expectations and caution among the Kurdish public. People attach importance to the beginning of a process, but they do not want it to remain at the level of rhetoric, as happened in the past. A survey conducted by SAMER between 14 and 21 June 2026 among 908 people in 18 provinces found that 84 percent of respondents expected legal measures. This finding shows us that expectations among the Kurdish public are not limited to ending the conflict.




The findings of KONDA's 2025 surveys are also important to this discussion. We see that perceptions and expectations concerning the Kurdish question have changed among different sections of society. However, high expectations also increase the risk of disappointment. For this reason, concrete steps rather than rhetoric are needed in the process.”




‘Disarmament and democratisation must advance together’




Botan said one of the most important debates surrounding the process concerns the order in which steps should be taken, stressing that disarmament and democratic and legal reforms must proceed simultaneously. He said the agenda of Kurdish politics in the coming period would also take shape within this framework.




Botan also said: “On the state side, there is an approach that prioritises disarmament. However, a significant section of Kurdish politics and the Kurdish public believes that disarmament and democratic and legal reforms should proceed simultaneously. The fundamental issue here is trust. If one side expects the other to take all the steps first, the process could very easily reach a deadlock.




Disarmament is important, but it would be wrong to postpone democratisation in return. Likewise, an approach that completely disregards security concerns could create anxieties on the other side of the process. Therefore, a mechanism capable of building mutual trust is needed. Legal and political guarantees must advance alongside the disarmament process.”




Botan said the agenda of Kurdish politics in the coming period would include the status of Kurds, education in the mother tongue, local democracy, the appointment of trustees, political representation, freedom of expression, constitutional citizenship and a democratic constitution. He added that implementing ECtHR and Constitutional Court rulings, reviewing political cases and expanding the space for democratic politics were also important.




Botan said: “It would be wrong to think that the Kurdish question can be resolved through a few legal reforms. A more comprehensive constitutional and political transformation is needed. For the process to function properly, the Imrali system must be abolished entirely. Abdullah Öcalan must be granted the right to hope and his freedom must be secured.




Mr. Öcalan's role in the process must not be reduced solely to disarmament. There is also a legal issue here. The necessary legal arrangements must be made to ensure that the process becomes lasting. Reconsidering the existing system on Imrali is important for enabling the political process to advance on a democratic basis.”




‘The real issue is the transition from a security paradigm to a democratic solution paradigm’




Botan said there were four possible scenarios for the future of the process: the continuation of a security-centred approach, a controlled democratic opening, the strengthening of the democratic solution paradigm, or a renewed deadlock in the process.




Botan continued: “There are four main possibilities before us. The first is that the security-centred approach continues and the process is conducted primarily through disarmament. In such a situation, democratic and legal reforms may remain limited. The second possibility is a controlled democratic opening. In this case, certain legal and political steps would be taken, but a comprehensive constitutional transformation might not come onto the agenda.




The third possibility is the strengthening of the democratic solution paradigm. In this case, disarmament and democratisation would be treated as two complementary processes. Issues such as the status of the Kurdish language, local governments, constitutional citizenship, political representation, freedom of expression and a democratic constitution would be addressed more comprehensively.




The fourth possibility is that the process reaches another deadlock. Postponing political and legal steps could lead to continued political tensions between the state and Kurds and leave expectations unmet. Therefore, the coming period must be assessed not only in terms of its security outcomes but also its political consequences.”




Botan said one of the fundamental questions of the process was not so much how Kurds would be integrated into the existing state structure, but how the state structure itself could be democratised.




Botan also said: “There is an important theoretical question here: Are we going to integrate Kurds into the existing state structure, or are we going to make the state structure more pluralistic? If the issue is seen as Kurds adapting to the existing state model, the fundamental problem will persist. This is because we need to discuss the very relationship between the state and different identities.




A democratic solution requires restructuring the state to include different identities and social groups. Recognising certain rights of Kurds is, of course, important, but the issue goes beyond that. The relationship between the state and society in Turkey needs to be reconsidered as a whole. A pluralistic democratic system must be established in which different identities can freely express themselves and participate in political decision-making mechanisms.”




‘Political normalisation cannot be achieved simply by ending the conflict’




Botan stressed that political normalisation could not be achieved solely by ending the conflict and that the space for democratic politics needed to be expanded.




He said: “Political normalisation is not simply the end of armed conflict. The political sphere must expand, people must be able to express themselves freely, and mechanisms of political representation must be guaranteed. As long as elected representatives continue to be removed from office, trustees are appointed, political activities are restricted, legal proceedings over freedom of expression continue, and local governments face interference, it is difficult to speak of genuine political normalisation.




For this reason, the process must expand the space for democratic politics. The ability of the Kurdish political movement and Kurdish voters to express themselves through democratic politics must be guaranteed.” Lezgin Botan said concrete legal and political steps would determine the next stage of the process.




Botan concluded: “In the coming period, the main debate will focus less on the concepts used to define the process and more on the results it produces. Disarmament is important, but it is not sufficient on its own. The measure of a democratic solution is the extent to which the political, cultural and legal rights of Kurds and all sections of society living in Turkey are guaranteed.




Kurds must be able to express their identities, languages, cultures and collective existence through democratic politics. Legal and constitutional guarantees must be established for this. Disarmament is not peace itself, but a precondition for peace. Democratisation, in turn, is the guarantee of lasting peace.




Therefore, the fundamental issue facing Turkey is the transition from a security paradigm to a democratic solution paradigm. If this transition is achieved, it will open up new possibilities not only for resolving the Kurdish question but also for addressing Turkey's broader democratisation problem.




The real question is not how to keep Kurds within the existing state structure, but how Turkey can become a democratic system in which all different identities can express themselves equally and freely.”

title: Whereabouts of 5 Kurdish men arrested in Baneh remain unknown
content:
The fate of Hesen Mistefayî, Şerzad Çawşînî, Şahîn Reşîdzade, Xusrew Kerempûrî, and Muhyedîn Banerîzî, who were arrested by Iranian intelligence forces in Baneh, in Kurdistan Province, remains unknown.




According to information reported by the Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN), Iranian intelligence forces raided the family home of Muhyedîn Banerîzî, a resident of Baneh, in the early hours of 9 October 2026, and arrested him.




Xusrew Kerempûrî, who also lives in Baneh, was detained on October 7 during a raid on his family’s home.




Hesen Mistefayî, a well-known philanthropist in the city, was arrested by Iranian intelligence forces on October 6 while taking his child to the hospital. It was reported that, following Mistefayî’s arrest, intelligence agents left his child alone on the street.




Şerzad Çawşînî, originally from Sardasht and residing in Baneh, and Şahîn Reşîdzade were also arrested by Iranian intelligence forces on October 3 and September 26, 2026, respectively.




According to the KHRN, all five men were arrested without court warrants. Since their arrests, no information has been made available regarding their whereabouts, health conditions, or legal proceedings.

title: Kariane Westrheim: A democratic solution to the Kurdish question would also benefit Turkish society
content:
Prof. Kariane Westrheim, President of the European Union Turkey Civic Commission (EUTCC), said that one of the most critical issues to be addressed at the 20th Kurdish Conference at the European Parliament this year would be the ongoing process in Turkey, stressing that this opportunity must not be missed.




We spoke with Prof. Kariane Westrheim of the University of Bergen in Norway about the 20th Kurdish Conference, which will take place at the European Parliament on 14–15 October. Westrheim explained the need that led to the establishment of the conference and reflected on developments over the past two decades. She also outlined the main topics of the 20th conference, identifying the Peace and Democratic Society Process underway in Turkey as the most critical issue. “We need to make use of this process. We must not miss this opportunity,” the EUTCC President said.




Drawing attention to Europe’s declining influence on and interest in Turkey, Westrheim emphasised: “Europe has often refrained from using its influence consistently on issues of democracy, human rights and the rule of law. This is regrettable.”




Professor Westrheim, this year you are organizing the 20th Kurdish Conference in Europe. Why and how did you feel the need to initiate and sustain such a conference?




First, I am not organising the conference alone, we are a good team of volunteers and friends who have been working all these years to keep the Kurdish question on the international agenda and particularly within the EU system and Europe. The idea came in 2004 with the foundation of the EU Turkey Civic Commission (EUTCC), four organisations decided to organise an international conference which became the annual International Conference on EU Turkey and the Kurds held in the European Parliament. It emerged from an obvious conviction: the Kurdish question is not only a question of human rights, democracy, and peace in the Middle East; it is also a European question. For decades, the situation of the Kurdish people has been characterised by conflict, repression, displacement, and political exclusion. At the same time, there has been a serious lack of understanding of the historical and political dimensions of the Kurdish question in Europe.




We felt that there was a need for a forum or a platform where politicians, academics, journalists, human rights defenders, and representatives of Kurdish civil society could meet, exchange views and discuss the situation openly. With these conferences we wanted to bring the Kurdish question into the European political debate. 




The fact that we have now reached the 20th conference is significant. It shows that the need for such a platform has not disappeared. On the contrary, despite all the changes in Turkey, Europe and the wider Middle East, the fundamental questions concerning democracy, human rights and a peaceful solution to the Kurdish question remain unresolved.




Since we are touching on this subject, what is the source of your own commitment to the Kurdish cause? How did you first become acquainted with the Kurdish people and their struggle?




My commitment to the Kurdish cause developed through my first encounters with the Kurdish freedom movement in 2002. Through that experience, I began to understand more deeply the complexity of the Kurdish question.




This eventually also became an academic subject for me. I wrote my PhD thesis on PKK and education, under the title 

Education in a Political Context: a study of knowledge processes and learning sites in the PKK

. Through this work, I had the opportunity to study not only the political context in which the movement developed, but also the importance it placed on education, political consciousness through transformation and change, the development of individuals and society.




Over the years, I have worked closely with the movement and with people connected to it. That has given me an opportunity to learn a great deal - not only about the Kurdish question itself, but also about politics, education, organisation and the experiences of a people, in particular women, who have struggled for recognition and democratic rights under extremely difficult circumstances. 




My commitment has therefore developed through both academic work and personal experience. I have not simply studied the Kurdish question from a distance; I have had the opportunity to meet people, listen to their experiences, and follow their political and social struggle over the years. On a personal level, I have learned a lot from the movement and from the people within it. I witnessed their immense efforts and self-sacrifice despite all the political setbacks and losses; I encountered impressive resilience. What I experienced as the glue holding it all together was the importance of friendship and solidarity among them. As an outsider eager to learn and understand, I found every door open to me. Even though the PKK has disbanded, the values ​​it stood for remain alive.




This overall experience has strengthened my conviction that the Kurdish question is not only a security issue. It has important political, democratic, social, and cultural dimensions. And I believe that a sustainable solution can only be found through dialogue, democratic participation, and recognition of fundamental rights within a fair legal framework. 




Over the past decades, you have organized broad-based conferences almost every year in order to raise awareness of the Kurdish issue, explain the situation and contribute to finding a solution. Have these conferences produced the results you hoped for? Or, to put it another way, what kind of achievements do you believe have been made through these efforts?




One must be realistic. Conferences alone cannot resolve a conflict of this magnitude. The history is much larger than any one organisation. Different factors come into play here, and often, in the end, the decisions are made by political actors, governments and societies. So, I would not claim that our conferences have solved the problems or achieved everything we hoped for. 




But I do believe our conferences have contributed significantly. One important achievement has been to keep the Kurdish question visible in European political and academic circles. We have brought together people who otherwise might not have met; members of the European Parliament, national politicians, academics, journalists, lawyers, human rights defenders, and representatives of Kurdish society.




Another achievement is continuity. Political attention can be very short-lived. There are periods when the Kurdish question receives considerable attention and other periods when it almost disappears from the European and international agenda. Through these annual conferences, we have tried to ensure that the issue is not forgotten but remains on the agenda. 




In addition, the conferences have created opportunities for dialogue. We have always striven not only to discuss problems but also to seek workable solutions. If all the conversations we have had over the years have contributed to a better understanding of the Kurdish question and to strengthening the democratic forces working for peace, I consider them valuable.




Compared with previous years, has the European Parliament and the European Union more broadly become less effective in relation to Turkey, or have they simply lost interest in the issue?




It is a combination of both. The European Union holds significant political and economic influence in its relationship with Turkey, yet it has often shied away from exercising this influence consistently regarding democracy, human rights, and the rule of law - a regrettable situation. There has also been a gradual shift in priorities; issues such as migration, security, the war in Ukraine, energy, and geopolitical dynamics - including the 2016 migration agreement - have granted Turkey geopolitical leverage over the EU. This has become increasingly significant for the EU-Turkey relationship and has come at the expense of fundamental rights and democratic principles.




The European Parliament has been more outspoken than many governments and EU institutions. Strong resolutions have been adopted, and clear statements issued regarding human rights, democratic backsliding, and the plight of Kurdish politicians and civil society. On the other side, political statements have limited impact unless followed by concrete policy measures - and frequently, they are not.




It is important that Europe not solely view Turkey through the lens of strategic interests. Turkey is a European neighbor. Supporting democracy and a peaceful resolution to the Kurdish issue does not constitute interference in Turkey’s internal affairs; it is part of Europe’s responsibility to uphold the values ​​the Union stands for.




Looking back over the past 20 years, and considering all the conferences you have organized and the circumstances in which they took place, how do you assess the situation in Turkey today? Has the situation deteriorated further?




There have been periods of hope as well as periods of setbacks and regression and setbacks. There have been times when the prospect of a political solution seemed closer. There were periods characterised by dialogue, democratic reforms, and a willingness to discuss the Kurdish issue in political rather than purely security-related terms.




Unfortunately, many of these windows of opportunity subsequently closed. The concentration of political power, restrictions on freedom of speech and assembly, pressure on independent media and civil society, and the imprisonment or removal from office of elected Kurdish politicians have all contributed to a serious democratic deficit.




At the same time, I am not willing to view the situation in a negative light. A strong democratic movement still exists in Turkey, driven notably by Kurdish political actors, civil society organisations, women’s and youth movements, journalists, academics, and human rights defenders. The desire for democracy and peace has not vanished; indeed, it is stronger than ever.




Political circumstances can change. What matters is whether there is a willingness to learn from the past and create a new political framework based on equality, democratic participation, and peaceful dialogue.




Finally, what will be the main agenda of your 20th conference, and what issues will you focus on?




The 20th anniversary conference will naturally be a moment for reflection. We will look back at the developments of the past two decades, but we do not want the conference to become simply a historical exercise. The central question must be: where do we go from here?




We will therefore focus on the current political situation in Turkey, the Kurdish question, democracy and human rights, and the possibilities for a peaceful political solution. We also want to examine the role that Europe can and should play.




Another important theme will be the broader regional context. The Kurdish question cannot be understood entirely within the borders of one state. Developments in Turkey, Syria, Iraq and Iran are interconnected, and the Kurdish people are affected by regional as well as international politics.




We want the conference to look forward. After 20 conferences, we have accumulated considerable experience and knowledge. The challenge now is to ask how that knowledge can contribute more effectively to peace, democracy, and a political solution in the future.




In addition, there is currently an ongoing process in Turkey concerning peace and the building of a democratic society. Is this process among the issues on the conference agenda? If so, what message would you like to convey regarding this process?




Yes, this is clearly one of the most critical issues we will discuss. Whenever there is an opening for peace and democratic dialogue, it must be taken seriously. The history of the Kurdish question also includes missed opportunities. If there is a possibility of a new process, the international community, and particularly Europe, should encourage it rather than remain passive.




But a genuine peace process cannot be based only on declarations. It requires trust, political courage, and concrete steps. I must be based on fair legal principles. It must address the underlying political problems and create conditions in which all citizens can participate equally in democratic life. 




My message would therefore be that we make use of the ongoing process. We must not miss that opportunity. A democratic solution to the Kurdish question will benefit the Kurdish people, but it will also benefit Turkish society. A Turkey where political disagreements can be resolved through democratic institutions rather than repression will be a stronger, more stable, and more peaceful country-making it a stronger partner for Europe.




The process must be inclusive, involving relevant political and societal actors, and sufficiently open to build public trust. Peace requires more than an agreement between political leaders; it requires a shift in the political climate and a willingness to recognize the equal - yet also distinct - rights and dignity of all citizens.




After twenty years of conferences, my conclusion is that we must not abandon dialogue. The alternative to a peaceful solution is conflict and instability. If an opportunity for a fresh start exists, given how the situation is currently unfolding, we should seize it and do everything in our power to ensure its success.
