author: Ian Angus
title: Ecosocialist Bookshelf — October 2026
content:
Climate and Capitalism editor Ian Angus introduces eight left-wing books on the rise, ideas and goals of the new far right.

First, an apology: I’ve been working flat out on my next book — Social Murder: Capitalism’s Assault on Human Health in the Anthropocene — so this the first Ecosocialist Bookshelf since July. I will try not to miss any more.

Second, an explanation: Usually I include titles on a variety of subjects in science, politics, theory, history etc. But recently, my shelf has been crowded with new books on the rise and nature of the radical right, so I am introducing eight of them at once. I’ll return to the normal mix next month.

End Times Fascism and the Fight for the Living World By Naomi Klein and Astrid Taylor Farrar, Straus and Giroux A new iteration of the far right is on the march. Klein and Taylor explore the alliance of religious fundamentalists, Silicon Valley technologists and ethno-nationalists that aims to make the world unliveable while protecting themselves from the consequences by hiding on luxurious private islands, rocketing to Mars, or deploying massive military force to keep the ‘bad’ people out.

Backlash: The Global Rise of the Radical Right Edited by Don Kalb and Walden Bello Pluto Press We live in an age of counterrevolution. Liberal elites around the world are weaponising their fascistic narratives, creating political enemies and consolidating even more power and wealth. This collection of essays from leading researchers reveals new forms of the radical right, neo-nationalism, authoritarian neoliberalism, illiberalism and democratic backsliding.

Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed By Quinn Slobodian and Ben Tarnoff Harper Collins Elon Musk promises sovereignty through technology: plug in, power up and become self-reliant. Slobodian and Tarnoff cut through the hype to reveal what Musk really represents: a new political economy, where to be “free” means to serve a Techno-king. Muskism isn’t about the man. It’s about the machine that made him — and the world he’s trying to make.

Country of Lords: Neo-Aristocrats, Social Darwinists, Tech Utopians, and the Long Fight Against Equality in America By Kim Phillips-Klein WW Norton United States history is often told as a hard-won march toward the promise of equality, but there has always been a countertrend. Again and again, influential Americans have argued that the social, economic and racial hierarchies in which some groups of people rule over others are not only natural but good.

The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy By Gil Durán Simon & Schuster Durán explains the origins, strategies and ambitions of Silicon Valley’s war on democracy. From San Francisco’s weaponised elections and secret billionaire projects to the White House, Durán exposes how the world’s richest men aim to replace elected governments with corporate rule.

The Right-Wing Idea Factory: From Traditionalism to Trumpism By Donald F Kettl Oxford University Press Kettl traces the rise of a revolutionary political force that has redefined the United States right. Fuelled by soft money and amplified by social media, a network of determined activists and organisations aims to dismantle traditional free-market conservatism and replace it with a populist agenda rooted in cultural and social issues.

Gilded Rage: Elon Musk and the Radicalization of Silicon Valley By Jacob Silverman Bloomsbury An essential dispatch from the frontlines of the billionaire revolution in which Musk is just the beginning. Silverman maps a sprawling network of radicalised elites — from Peter Thiel and JD Vance to the financiers bankrolling Donald Trump — who are using their power and their money to drive a political revolution.

The Cultural Marxism Conspiracy: Why the Right Blames the Frankfurt School for the Decline of the West By AJA Woods Verso “Cultural Marxism” is one of the far right’s favorite buzzwords. Woods uncovers the bizarre story of the cult leaders, right-wing intellectuals and White House officials who believe a coterie of left-wing scholars and students is plotting to undermine Western civilisation.

[Reprinted from Climate and Capitalism. Inclusion of a book does not imply endorsement.]

author: Kerry Smith
title: Three years of genocide: Nationwide support shown for justice for Palestinians
content:
At least 30 major cities and regional centres across Australia joined the global day of action for Gaza on October 11 to mark three years of genocide and Palestinian resistance.

Protesters condemned Labor’s refusal to cut ties with Israel or to stop the two-way arms trade.

About 1500 people joined the Boorloo/Perth protest, which was organised by Friends of Palestine WA, to demand an end to Australia’s complicity and to place sanctions on Israel.

Greens MLC Sophie McNeil, Palestinian-Australian Dr Lama Al Ramahi and Helen O’Sullivan, a Freedom flotilla participant addressed the rally.

About 100 people joined the Gimuy/Cairns rally, where speakers also highlighted Australia’s complicity in supplying parts for military weapons to Israel.

Around 10,000 people joined the Naarm/Melbourne protest to hear from Gunnai, Gunditjmara and Djab Wurrung independent Senator Lidia Thorpe; Palestinian writer and lawyer Sara Saleh; Australian Palestinian Advocacy Network Vice President Hiba Farra; Palestinian activist Nour Salman; Sarah Schwartz from Jewish Council of Australia; and Greens MP Gabrielle De Vietri. Palestinian educator and activist Noura Mansour MCed the rally.

The protest marched from the State Library to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade head office on Collins Street.

About 70 people gathered in Bathurst, on Wiradjuri Country, to fly kites and raise funds for a medical clinic in Gaza.

Mountains for Palestine organised a protest in Springwood, in the Blue Mountains.

More than 1000 people joined the rally in Tarntanya/Adelaide, reports Markela Panegyres.

Speakers included Sawsan Zadeh from Health Care Workers for Palestine; lawyer and activist Beljana Dally; Ahmed Azhar from SA Socialists; Mike Khizam, Deputy Chairperson of Adelaide Friends of Palestine Association; Greens Senator Barbara Pocock; and year 11 high school activist Sam Ats. The Palestine Choir and drumming group added a special musical element to the rally.

The rally in Nipaluna/Hobart, was organised by the Tasmanian Palestine Action Network (TPAN). Philip Bohle reports from Nipaluna/Hobart that around 350 people attended. Speakers included MC Feras Shaheen from the TPAN, Nala Mansell, Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre, Ayda Issa Abu Daoud, from TPAN and “Potto” from Grassroots Action Network Tasmania.

The protest, which started on on Davey Street, attracted enthusiastic honks from passing motorists, and marched to the Parliamentary Lawns. Handmade placards declared: “What if it was your kid?”, “Stop the slaughter”, ‘Israel is a sick, genocidal nation” and “Zionism is Nazism”. Others deplored the deaths of Shireen Abu Akleh and more than 240 other journalists.

TPAN spokesperson Feras Shaheen said: “Three years on, Palestinians are still being killed while the institutions that claim to defend international law fail to stop it. What has been presented to the world as a ceasefire has not ended the destruction of Palestinian lives, homes and families.”

From Cavanbah/Byron Bay, Troy Tutaki reports that more than 350 people took part. Speakers included Cate Coorey, Subhi Awad, Cass Lills from Palestinian Australian New Zealand Medical Association and Chels Hood Withey from House You. Mandy Nolan, who is standing for the Greens in 2027, MCed the protest.

Several speakers highlighted the farcical nature of the “ceasefire”, when Palestinians are still being killed. About 94% of Gaza’s population remain in urgent need of shelter and basic household assistance. Ninety-one percent of assessed households experienced moderate-to-high water insecurity, 93% of all schools need to be completely rebuilt.

Nolan criticised Australia’s sovereign wealth fund for investing in tools to murder children in Gaza. She said Australia Super Funds have $2.2 billion invested in war crimes and that Australia’s Future Fund has invested $160 million on Palantir providing AI to Israel for war-related missions.

Lills, a nurse who has been to Gaza, said its healthcare facilities are still be targeted repeatedly. She said 36 hospitals had been bombed or burned by the Israeli Defense Forces since the start of the war. The targeting of health facilities, medical personnel and patients is a war crime under the 1949 Geneva Convention.

All the speakers reinforced the need to continue to build solidarity, build stronger unions and build a stronger activist movement to ensure justice for Palestinians.

Between 5000–6000 protested in Gadigal Country/Sydney. Grace Tame, NSW Greens Senator Mehreen Faruqi, and anti-Zionist Jewish journalist Yakhov Aharon were among the speakers.

The Jews Against the Occupation ‘48 also organised a vigil on October 7.

3000 people marched through the streets of Magan-djin/Brisbane on October 11 to mark the third anniversary of the beginning of Israel's genocide against the people of Gaza. It was the biggest pro-Palestine rally in the city in some time.

Two people were arrested at the rally - one of the more aggressive postures by police at a Palestine rally in Magan-djin/Brisbane - although they were both subsequently released without charge.

Organisers promoted the November 15 national day of action against Queensland's pro-genocide/anti-free speech laws as the next major action.

Hundreds marched the day before at Kombumerri/Gold Coast to mark the anniversary and to promote ongoing actions in the region.

2023–26 Israeli genocide on Gaza

En una decisión histórica, el Encuentro volverá después de cuatro décadas a la ciudad donde se fundó.

Después de 

una primera jornada de gran actividad el sábado 10

, durante el domingo 11 continuaron funcionando los más de 100 talleres organizados en 13 ejes: 1. Movimientos y activismos, 2. Soberanía, 3. Identidades y sexualidades, 4. Niñeces, juventudes y vejeces, 6. Violencias patriarcales, 6. Violencias estatales, 7. Pueblos preexistentes y afro, 8. Derechos Humanos y democracia, 9. Cuidados y crianzas, 10. Salud, educación, trabajo, cultura, deporte y ciencia, 11. ESI y aborto, 12. Horizontes emancipatorios, 13. Movimientos sociales y barrios.




Seguimos dialogando durante el domingo con las protagonistas de este masivo Encuentro Plurinacional:

Luego de los talleres y asambleas, el 39° Encuentro Plurinacional continuó con una enorme, casi infinita movilización que colmó las calles de Córdoba.

title: #39EncuentroPlurinacional: “Aunque nos quieran destruir, va a ser imposible”
content:
En el marco del 39 Encuentro Plurinacional hablamos con Camila Alvarez Barale, Secretaria de Género de la Asociación del Personal Aeronáutico (APA) Seccional Córdoba y trabajadora de FADEA (Fábrica Argentina de Aviones).




Camila Alvarez Barale




La dirigenta sindical nos dijo “que estos Encuentros nos fortalecen, nos dan mucha más energía, nos cargan para después estar en el día a día hasta volvernos a encontrar el año que viene con muchas experiencias de mujeres, diversidades. Es muy enriquecedor participar del Encuentro”.







 

 


































Ver esta publicación en Instagram









































































Una publicación compartida por Indymedia Argentina (@indymedia.argentina)













Sobre FADEA, Camila contó que “es una fábrica superestratégica para la provincia y para la Nación, porque fue pensada para desarrollar soberanía, para desarrollar aviones con con capacidad propia, sin depender ni de otras potencias ni de otros sectores que tengan interés, y la Argentina demostró que fue posible. Córdoba demostró, y los trabajadores de la fábrica demostraron que fue posible construir una industria nacional de altísima calidad, de muchísimo prestigio”.




“Aunque nos quieran destruir y que muchas veces nos bombardean, donde nos bajan el precio a los trabajadores, creo que demostramos que eso, por más que lo intenten, va a ser imposible”, aseguró Camila.




#Mujeres #Diversidades

title: #39EncuentroPlurinacional: “merecemos poder existir en la diversidad de cuerpos que somos”
content:
Entre los más de cien talleres del 39° Encuentro estuvo el de Activismos gordes, que se realizó en la Escuela Francisco Ortiz de Ocampo.







Mercedes Estruch, socióloga, del Colectivo Gordes Activistas de Argentina (CGA) y presidenta de la Fundación AnyBody Argentina, nos dijo que “el activismo gordo nace de la necesidad de defender los derechos de las personas gordas y denunciar la violencia, la discriminación y el odio hacia la gordura, y, por ende, hacia las personas gordas. Lo que reclamamos es la despatologización de la gordura para poder romper con el odio y el estigma a la gordura”.




“Creemos que las personas gordas y las mujeres, sobre todo, merecemos poder existir en la diversidad de cuerpos que somos, y sin tener que cumplir con un modelo único de cuerpo y de belleza, que está perpetuado por una cultura de la dieta, de las farmacéuticas, de la belleza, del fit”, agregó.







https://argentina.indymedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Activismos-gordes-01.ogg




Audio: Mercedes Estruch







Con respecto al acceso al trabajo, “también es un derecho que se vulnera”, nos contó Mercedes Estruch. “Nuestra aspecto físico y nuestra corporalidad se vuelve una barrera discriminatoria”.




“En una situación como la que estamos, de crueldad absoluta y de crisis económica y social, las personas gordas estamos completamente vulneradas porque solemos tener acceso a trabajos más precarios e incluso también se vive mucho, cuando uno entra a trabajar, en la imposibilidad de que te brinden un uniforme como corresponde o mobiliario cómodo para la diversidad de cuerpos”.




“También vivimos muchas cuestiones que tienen que ver con la convivencia en los espacios de trabajo, donde nuestro nuestro cuerpo se pone en cuestión, se nos señala como algo que nos hace ser víctimas de desmerecimientos o malos tratos”.




https://argentina.indymedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Activismos-gordes-02.ogg




Audio: Mercedes Estruch




Mercedes comentó que además, desde el Colectivo Gordes Activistas de Argentina organizan “los encuentros plurinacionales gordes. El último se realizó en CABA. Nos pueden seguir en las redes sociales, 

@gordesactivando

, o 

@encuentrogorde

. También pueden seguir a 

@anybodyargentina

 y saber más sobre nuestro laburo”.

#39EncuentroPlurinacional: “merecemos poder existir en la diversidad de cuerpos que somos”

 se publicó primero en 

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

author: CMI Argentina
title: #39EncuentroPlurinacional: “El que avala a un compañero que violó se convierte en un cómplice”
content:
En el marco de la Asamblea Abya Yala, dos compañeras integrantes de Jubiladas Insurgentes realizaron importantes intervenciones.







“Nosotras, como jubiladas, que estamos luchando todos los miércoles desde hace tantos años, queremos luchar, decirles que luchamos por la jubilación de todos los trabajadores, que no se van a poder jubilar, y menos las nuevas generaciones, y que nuestra lucha es la lucha de todos. Por eso tenemos que darla unidos”, dijo una de las integrantes de Jubiladas Insurgentes.







 

 


































Ver esta publicación en Instagram









































































Una publicación compartida por Indymedia Argentina (@indymedia.argentina)













“Y queremos saludar también, porque queremos decir que el feminismo es nuestra causa, porque el feminismo une. En momentos en que muchas organizaciones se ven partidas, el feminismo une, porque saca todos los males de raíz, que es el patriarcado y es la violencia machista. Así que luchamos con todos hasta el último día de nuestra vida. Gracias, compañeras”.




Por su parte, la segunda integrante de Jubiladas Insurgentes hizo énfasis en el silenciamiento y la invisibilización de la violencia de género y abusos dentro de las organizaciones: “Entre los grupos, sobre todo, jubilados y otros grupos y otros colectivos, hay muchísima violencia machista”.







 

 


































Ver esta publicación en Instagram









































































Una publicación compartida por Indymedia Argentina (@indymedia.argentina)













“Quiero que lo sepan”, señalaron, “porque hay un montón de compañeras, chicas, adolescentes que están acusando a hombres adultos que realmente se zarpan ya porque fueron violadas, fueron violentadas, y están dentro de todos los grupos metidos. Por eso necesitamos, porque las chicas lo denuncian, pero ¿saben qué? ‘Hay que hablar con ellos’. ¿Qué hay que hablar con ellos? No tenemos nada que hablar con ellos. Porque tenemos que creerles a las chicas, no queremos más violentas y violentos dentro de los grupos”.




“Digo violentas también, porque hay mujeres que realmente nos dicen, ‘hay que ver si es así’. No tenemos nada que ver, no queremos más que las chicas queden afuera, que las mujeres queden afuera. Que queden ellos afuera, no nosotres”.




“El que avala a un compañero que violó se convierte en un cómplice”, apuntaron las Jubiladas Insurgentes, y reafirmaron: “No hay más vueltas que darle a eso, y nosotras ni por omisión queremos ser cómplices de eso”.







 

 


































Ver esta publicación en Instagram









































































Una publicación compartida por Indymedia Argentina (@indymedia.argentina)

Sol Laje

title: #39EncuentroPlurinacional: “Cuidar es un trabajo, se tiene que pagar”
content:
Marina Joski de Barrios de Pie e integrante de la mesa ejecutiva de la UTEP, nos contó que se hicieron presentes en el 39° Encuentro “con nuestras cuidadoras comunitarias, compañeras que vienen peleando desde el 11 de diciembre de 2023. Que fueron perseguidas, que fueron judicializadas, que les sacaron los alimentos de sus espacios comunitarios y que luego les sacaron sus salarios, nuestros salarios”.




Foto: Indymedia Argentina




Y continuó afirmando que “seguimos reivindicando y exigiendo el reconocimiento del trabajo comunitario como trabajo, un reconocimiento que no solo tiene que ser simbólico, sino real, efectivo y económico. Y somos parte del Acuerdo Nacional de los Cuidados”.










 


































Ver esta publicación en Instagram






































































 




Una publicación compartida por Indymedia Argentina (@indymedia.argentina)













Por su parte, Norma Morales, Secretaria General Adjunta de la UTEP y también parte de Barrios de Pie, agregó que “el reconocimiento salarial es muy amplio. No es solamente ese sueldo asegurado a fin de mes, es mucho más amplio. Nuestras compañeras son compañeras que vienen sosteniendo la vida en nuestros espacios de cuidado comunitario en los barrios populares de todo el país. Y son compañeras que están grandes, ¿no? Compañeras que no van a tener la posibilidad de jubilarse, compañeras que hoy no son monotributistas, porque este gobierno se ha encargado de desmantelar todas esas políticas públicas que fortalecían, que nos fortalecían a nosotras mismas”.




“Entonces, también les ponemos en desafío a la sociedad, a la política, a los estados y a quien sea, quién nos cuida ahora a nosotras, ¿no? Somos nosotras las que nos ponemos siempre en primera línea cuando nuestro país atraviesa situaciones de crisis. Pero ¿y ahora? Nosotras ya estamos grandes, estamos en una generación ya en donde queremos empezar a disfrutar de nuestra vida. Pero, bueno, no tenemos nada asegurado”.




“Por eso estamos acá, visibilizando este reconocimiento salarial, reconocimiento social y reconocimiento político”, reafirmó Norma Morales.

author: Fareeha Ali Yahya
title: Beyond legislation: What does it take to make child marriage laws work?
content:
13th October 2026










Beyond legislation: What does it take to make child marriage laws work?
















8 min read



















Policy & Practice




End harmful practices




Global


























































Every year, 

12 million girls are married before the age of 18

. While progress towards ending child marriage remains too slow, legal and policy reforms around the world offer important lessons about what works and how change can happen.




This 

International Day of the Girl Child

, we are looking at what it takes to turn legal commitments into meaningful protection for girls. 

Setting 18 as the minimum age of marriage without exceptions is critical, but it is only the beginning.




Ending child marriage requires comprehensive laws and policies that prevent marriages from happening, protect girls at risk and support their rights to education, bodily autonomy and a future of their own choosing.




Learning from legal reform around the world




In the United States, 

California’s recent ban on child marriage

 offers a timely example of progress, following years of advocacy.




“California’s ban demonstrates that progress is possible, even after years of advocacy. The next step is to build on that momentum. With child marriage still legal in 32 states, we need to learn from reforms that have worked and ensure that strong legal protections reach every child,” says 

Anastasia Law

, Equality Now’s Legal Advisor for North America.




Understanding why some reforms succeed, how they are achieved and what makes them effective is essential to strengthening legal protections elsewhere.




Working with the

 UNFPA-UNICEF Global Programme to End Child Marriage

, our legal experts set out to identify good practices from across the globe and examine how these approaches could inform future law and policy reform.




The resulting report,

 

Towards effective laws: An analytical framework and compendium of good practices on laws and policies to address child marriage

, draws on legal analysis, lived experiences and consultations with experts, practitioners, lawmakers and civil society.




Rather than presenting a single model for countries to replicate, it brings together practical examples that can be adapted to different national contexts, while recognising gaps in implementation and contradictions that may remain.




What can we learn from the research?




The compendium

 examines how countries can move beyond setting a minimum age of marriage to develop comprehensive legal and policy responses. It offers practical learning on:







Why setting 18 as the minimum age of marriage without exceptions must be accompanied by harmonisation

 across related laws and legal frameworks.




How prevention, protection and response measures can be built into child marriage laws and policies

 to address risks before harm occurs and support those already affected.




How accountability mechanisms, clear responsibilities and multi-sectoral coordination

 can support effective implementation.




What meaningful routes to remedies

 can protect and support children already in marriages.




How criminal provisions can be designed and applied

 without unintentionally harming survivors and children.




How legal reform can strengthen access

 to education, sexual and reproductive health and rights and other essential services.







These lessons are particularly relevant for lawmakers, legislative drafters, government ministries, legal practitioners and advocates seeking to strengthen legal protections and ensure they work in practice.




What successful reform processes can teach us




Two recent reforms in Latin America illustrate how the process of changing a law can be just as important as the legal provisions themselves.




A non-punitive, root causes approach helped advance legal reform in Colombia




After 17 years and eight unsuccessful attempts, 

Colombia raised the minimum age of marriage to 18 without exceptions in 2024

.




The reform rejected a punitive approach, focusing instead on children’s rights and the root causes of child marriage. Strategic alliances between legislators, government and civil society, alongside public campaigning and efforts to challenge misconceptions, helped build broad support for reform.




The lesson:

 Legal reform can be strengthened by combining strong legal protections with approaches that address the drivers of child marriage and build support across sectors and communities.




Extensive consultation helped shape and build support for legal reform in Cuba




Cuba’s 2022 Family Code set 18 as the minimum age of marriage

 without exceptions following an extensive consultation process.




The Drafting Commission engaged 47 institutions and expert groups and received 389 expert submissions, while 6.48 million people participated in nationwide consultations. This input resulted in changes to 60% of the initial draft before the Code was approved by referendum.




The lesson:

 Meaningful public and expert participation can help shape legislation that reflects diverse perspectives while building wider understanding and support for reform.




Together, these examples demonstrate the value of looking beyond the final legislation to understand the advocacy, consultation and collaboration that make legal reform possible.




From laws on paper to protection in practice




We know from decades of work to end child marriage that passing a law is step one. Making it work is the real test.




Effective legal reform requires more than legislation. Governments must invest in implementation, coordinate across education, health, social protection and justice systems and ensure that girls can access protection and support when they need it.




Our new compendium

 brings together practical lessons from around the world to help policymakers, legal practitioners and advocates turn legal commitments into meaningful protection for girls.

 on child marriage, including legislative reform, implementation, survivor protection and multi-sectoral approaches to ending the practice.

title: Edirne'de devlet korumasındaki çocuklar kayıp iddiası
content:
Edirne’de Çocuk İlk Kabul Merkezi’nde koruma altında tutulan çok sayıda çocuğun, kendilerine verilen ihtiyaç izni süresinin dolmasına rağmen merkeze geri dönmediği bildirildi.

Eğitimden Haberler’in aktardığına göre olay, 11 Ekim günü saat 14.30 sıralarında emniyet kayıtlarına geçti. Kurumda görevli İ.K., merkezde kalan çok sayıda çocuğun ihtiyaç iznine çıktıktan sonra belirlenen süre içerisinde kuruma dönmediğini belirterek yetkililere başvuruda bulundu.

Kurum görevlisi İ.K., Selimiye Polis Merkezi Amirliği’ne giderek durumu polise bildirdi. Görevli, çocukların bulunarak güvenli bir şekilde merkeze teslim edilmesini talep etti.

Başvuru sırasında çocukların güvenliğine ilişkin endişeler dile getirilirken, herhangi bir olumsuzluk yaşanması durumunda sorumlular hakkında kurum adına hukuki yollara başvurulacağı ifade edildi.

İhbar üzerine ekiplerin çalışma başlattığı belirtilirken, izin süresi dolmasına rağmen kuruma dönmeyen çocukların nerede olduğuna dair henüz net bir bilgi bulunmuyor. Emniyet birimlerinin incelemesi sürerken, resmi kurumlardan henüz bir bilgi gelmedi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: Ephéméride des luttes : 13 octobre
content:
L'éphéméride des luttes du 13 octobre est d'humeur émeutière, parfois incendiaire. Elle exige la libération des camarades prisonniers et s'insurge contre la condamnation d'autres.




1883 :

 Naissance de l'anarchiste italien Mario Buda, "inventeur de la voiture piégée". C'est en effet lui qui expérimente pour la première fois ce type de bombe, en en plaçant une devant la banque J.P.Morgan et la Bourse de Wall Street le 

16 septembre

 1920.




1894 :

 Arrestation de Alfred Dreyfus, ce qui donne le coup d'envoi de la célèbre affaire du même nom.




1909 :

 - A Montjuïc en Catalogne, Francisco Ferrer, pédagogue anarchiste (et 'père spirituel' des écoles Ferrer) est fusillé pour sa participation à la grève générale insurrectionnelle de juillet.




 A Paris, des émeutes se déclenchent suite à cette annonce : de violents affrontements ont lieu avec la police, devant l'ambassade d'Espagne, des kiosques sont abattus des tramways renversés, des coups de feu claquent, une dizaine de manifestants sont blessés, mais également le préfet Lépine et un agent qui décèdera à l'hôpital.

 Ailleurs, des meetings et manifestations auront lieu à Bruxelles, Gand, Anvers, Liège, Londres, Milan, Naples, New York (avec échauffourées à Madison) etc. Drapeau en berne sur l'Hôtel de Ville de Lisbonne, campagne de protestation à Rome, Turin, Vienne, Genève, Prague, Chicago, etc.


En Argentine, un meeting improvisé par la F.O.R.A, réunis 20 000 ouvriers qui appellent à la grève générale, elle sera effective le lendemain et durera jusqu'au 17 octobre.


A Montevideo, (Uruguay) tous les corps de métier abandonnent solennellement le travail.




1977 :

 - Détournement du vol Palma de Majorque-Francfort de la compagnie Lufthansa par le commando palestinien Martyr Halimeh, qui formule les mêmes exigences que le le commando Siegfried Hausner de la Fraction Armée Rouge (RAF), qui avait enlevé à Cologne le 

5 septembre

 le président du syndicat des patrons ouest-allemands Hans-Martin Schleyer, qui s'avérait également être un ancien officier de la S.S., pour exiger la libération de onze prisonniers politiques. C'est la première fois que des combattants du Tiers-Monde soutiennent directement les révolutionnaires de la métropole. La prise d'otage prend fin le 17 octobre, presque tous les membres du commando sont tués.




 A Naples, un groupe de Prima Linea (PL) occupe et incendie les centres d'études entrepreneuriales Cenzato.

 A Rome, un molotov est lancé sur l'ambassade du Brésil (alors soumis à la dictature) de piazza Navona.




1990 :

 Dans le centre de Belfast, deux membres du RUC (Royal Ulster Constabulary, les troupes irlandaises armées loyales à la couronne britannique) sont abattus par l'IRA.




2009 :

 A Santiago du Chili, une pelleteuse est incendiée en solidarité avec les prisonniers révolutionnaires.




2014 :

 A Linden Rd. Cunningar en Australie, le Front de Libération Animale / Front de Libération de la Terre (ALF / ELF) incendient trois engins de chantier d'une entreprise avicole.




2016 :

 A Athènes, la Conspiration des Cellules de Feu place un engin explosif au domicile d'une magistrate, Georgia Tsatani, impliquée dans la répression des militant-e-s révolutionnaires.




Voir 

l'éphéméride anarchiste

 du 13 octobre.

author: Unknown
title: Fransa: Öğrenciler geri adım atmıyor: Bugün ülke çapında grev var
content:
Fransa'da eğitim koşullarının iyileştirilmesini isteyen öğrenciler, 13 Ekim Salı günü yapılacak grev öncesinde okul ve üniversiteleri durdurmaya devam ediyor. Paris-Nanterre Üniversitesinde pazartesi sabahı binaların büyük bölümü kapatıldı, dersler aksadı. Öğretmen sendikaları ve veli örgütleri de öğrencilere destek verdi.




Paris, Lyon, Marsilya, Lille, Nantes ve Bordeaux'nun aralarında bulunduğu en az 30 kentte gösteri çağrıları yapıldı. Paris'teki yürüyüş TSİ 15:00'te Place d'Italie'den başlayacak Hareket, öğretmen açığı ve kalabalık sınıflarla başlayan itirazı eğitim bütçesine ve fırsat eşitsizliğine doğru taşıdı. 




Yoksul banliyölerden seçkin üniversitelere




Protestolar Paris çevresindeki Créteil'de, Saint-Exupéry Lisesinden yükselen itirazlarla başlamıştı. Öğretmen bulunamadığı için boş geçen dersler, bakımsız binalar ve kalabalık sınıflar üstesinden gelinmesi beklenen ilk taleplerdi.




Reuters'ın haberine göre devlet liselerindeki derslerin yaklaşık yüzde 10'u öğretmen yokluğu nedeniyle boş geçiyor. Varlıklı ailelerin çocuklarını bu sorunların yaşanmadığı özel okullara yönlendirebilmesi, eğitimdeki eşitsizliğe ilişkin tartışmanın sınıfsal boyutunu gözle görünür hale getiriyor. 




Eylemler sonraki günlerde Paris-Panthéon-Assas Üniversitesi ve Mines Paris gibi seçkin kurumlara da ulaştı. Polis, Assas'taki ablukayı 9 Ekim'de kaldırdı. Paris-Nanterre Üniversitesinin 12 Ekim'deki  açıklamasına göre kampüsteki binaların neredeyse tamamı sabah dersleri durdurmuştu. Ancak protestolar eşitsiz gelişiyor. Ülkenin her yerinde aynı yoğunlukta değil; bazı okullarda dersler yeniden başladı.




Hükümetin öğretmen takviyesi yeterli bulunmadı




Eğitim Bakanı Édouard Geffray, 8 Ekim'de 3 bin 24 yedek öğretmenin ihtiyaç duyulan okullara gönderileceğini açıkladı. Hükümet 12 Ekim'de görevlendirmelerin başladığını duyurdu. Sendikalar geçici takviyenin yıllardır süren personel açığını kapatmayacağını, bazı öğretmenlerin uzmanlıkları dışındaki derslere yönlendirildiğini bildirerek itirazlarını sürdürüyor. 




Bakanlığın verilerine göre cuma günü 172 olan kapalı okul sayısı pazartesi 130'a düştü. Hükümet bunu hareketin yavaşlamasına dair bir işaret sayarken öğrenci örgütleri, bazı okulların açılmasının eylemlerin bittiği anlamına gelmediğini vurguladı. 




Sendikalar 2027 bütçesine de karşı çıkıyor




Birleşik Sendikalar Federasyonu (FSU), Özerk Sendikalar Ulusal Birliği Eğitim Federasyonu (UNSA Éducation),  İşçi Gücü Ulusal Eğitim, Kültür ve Mesleki Eğitim Federasyonu (FNEC FP-FO), Fransız Demokratik Emek Konfederasyonu Eğitim, Mesleki Eğitim ve Kamu Araştırmaları Federasyonu (CFDT Éducation), Genel Emek Konfederasyonu Ulusal Eğitim Sendikaları Birliği (CGT Éduc'action) ve Dayanışmacı, Birleşik ve Demokratik Eğitim Sendikaları Federasyonu (SUD Éducation), 13 Ekim için ortak grev çağrısı yaptı. Başlıca talepler yeni öğretmen kadroları, daha küçük sınıflar, okul binalarına yatırım ve çalışma koşullarının iyileştirilmesi.




FSU'ya göre 2017'den beri ortaöğretimde 10 bini aşkın kadro kaldırıldı. Sendika, 2027 bütçe tasarısında 1.250 öğretmen kadrosunun daha kaldırılmasının öngörüldüğünü, bunların 800'ünün devlet ortaöğretim kurumlarında olduğunu belirtiyor. FSU, okul binalarının yenilenmesi için on yıl boyunca her yıl 5 milyar avro ayrılmasını istiyor. Sendikalar, geçici öğretmen takviyesi yapılırken kalıcı kadroların azaltılmasına itiraz ediyor.




Öğrenci örgütlerinin talepleri arasında üniversiteye giriş sistemi Parcoursup'un kaldırılması, ders programlarının hafifletilmesi ve eşitsizliklerin giderilmesi de var. Öğrenci Velileri Konseyleri Federasyonu (FCPE), velileri salı günkü gösterilere katılmaya çağırdı.




Paris'te gözaltına alınanların çoğu çocuk




Paris Cumhuriyet Başsavcısı Laure Beccuau, 12 Ekim'de, 29 Eylül-8 Ekim arasındaki öğrenci protestolarında başkentte 273 kişinin gözaltına alındığını açıkladı. Bunların 188'i 18 yaşından küçük. Başsavcılığın verilerine göre 195 gözaltıyla ilgili adli işlem başlatıldı.




Gösteriler sırasında ağır yaralanmalar da yaşandı. Lens'te 15 yaşındaki bir öğrencinin eli patlayan mühimmat nedeniyle ağır hasar gördü. Reuters'ın haberine göre 14 yaşındaki bir başka öğrencinin çenesi ve dişleri, yakın mesafeden atılan gaz kapsülünün isabetiyle parçalandı; ailesi suç duyurusunda bulundu. Reuters, iki haftadan kısa sürede en az dört çocuğun kalıcı sakatlık riski taşıyan yaralar aldığını bildirdi.




İçişleri Bakanlığı, gösterilerde bazı patlayıcı ses mühimmatının kullanımını askıya aldı. Polis müdahaleleriyle ilgili ülke genelinde 24 soruşturma açıldı; 8'i Paris'teki olayları konu alıyor. Uluslararası Af Örgütü ve BM insan hakları uzmanları bazı müdahale silahlarına itiraz ederken, polis sendikaları şiddet olaylarını ölümcül silahlara başvurmadan kontrol etmek için bunlara ihtiyaç duyulduğunu savunuyor. 




Okullarda güvenlik ve öğrencilerin talepleri




Le Monde'un haberine göre bazı okul yöneticileri maskeli grupların saldırılarından ve binalara verilen zarardan yakındı. Hükümet eğitim çalışanlarına yönelik şiddeti kınadı; öğrenci örgütleri ise barışçıl gösterilerle şiddet eylemlerinin birbirinden ayrılmasını istedi.




Eğitim Bakanlığı'nın açtığı danışma platformuna 67 bin başvuru yapıldı. Öğrenciler uzun okul günlerinden, düzensiz ders programlarından, bakımsız binalardan ve öğretmen eksikliğinden yakındı. Bu şikâyetler, krizin yalnızca boş kadrolara geçici öğretmen yerleştirilmesiyle giderilemeyeceğine işaret ediyor.




13 Ekim hareketin yeni sınavı




Resmî rakamlara göre 8 Ekim'deki gösterilere yaklaşık 71 bin 500 kişi katıldı. Hükümet hareketin ivme kaybettiğini savunuyor; öğrenci örgütleri ve sendikalar ise 13 Ekim eylemleriyle baskıyı artırmayı hedefliyor. Hükümetin 3 bin 024 öğretmenlik takviyesi, kalıcı kadro ve bütçe taleplerini karşılamış değil. Bugün Fransa saatiyle 14:00'te başlayacak gösteriler, öğrencilerle eğitim çalışanlarının ortak eyleminin gücünü ve hükümetin hangi yeni adımlara hazırlandığını gösterecek.




(AEK)

author: Unknown
title: Walter White'ın oğlunu canlandırmıştı: RJ Mitte 34 yaşında hayatını kaybetti
content:
Fotoğraf: Gage Skidmore from Peoria, AZ, United States of America/Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 2.0

Breaking Bad dizisinde Walter White’ın oğlunu canlandırmasıyla tanınan ABD’li oyuncu RJ Mitte, 34 yaşında hayatını kaybetti.

Serebral palsiyle yaşayan Mitte'nin ölüm nedenine dair bilgi verilmedi. Temsilcisi Sean Reilly tarafından BBC'ye yapılan açıklamada “Sevilen oyuncu, hayırsever ve engelli haklarının tutkulu savunucusu RJ Mitte’nin trajik ölümünü derin bir üzüntüyle paylaşıyoruz” denildi.

Reilly, “Mitte, rolüne sahicilik kattı ve engellilik konusunda farkındalığı ve kapsayıcılığı destekleyen bir platform oluşturdu” dedi. United Cerebral Palsy ve Shriners Children’s kuruluşlarının elçiliğini üstlenen Mitte, “kalıp yargılara meydan okumak ve engelli bireylerin daha fazla temsil edilmesini sağlamak için” The Mitte Foundation’ı kurmuştu.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: Trabzonspor net borcunu 2,9 milyar TL olarak açıkladı
content:
Trabzonspor, 1 Haziran-31 Ağustos 2026 dönemine ilişkin mali tablolarını Kamuyu Aydınlatma Platformu’nda yayımladı. Kulüp, yapılan netleştirmeler sonrasında 31 Ağustos 2026 itibarıyla net borcun 2,9 milyar TL olduğunu bildirdi.

Kulüpten yapılan açıklama şu şekilde:

"Şirketimizin 1 Haziran - 31 Ağustos 2026 dönemine ilişkin mali tabloları, bugün itibarıyla Kamuyu Aydınlatma Platformu’nda (KAP) açıklanmıştır. Mali tablolarımız incelendiğinde, kısa ve uzun vadeli borçlar toplamından, 6,7 milyar TL tutarındaki dönen varlıklar toplamı, kamulaştırma gelirlerimizden Trabzonspor Kulübü uhdesinde olan Sportif A.Ş. konsolide mali tablolarında yer almayan 2,6 milyar TL tutarındaki alacağımız ve 1,8 milyar TL tutarındaki enflasyon muhasebesi kaynaklı herhangi bir nakit çıkışı yaratmayacak işlemler netleştirildiğinde, kulübümüzün 31.08.2026 tarihi itibari ile net borcu 2,9 milyar TL olduğu görülecektir. Açıklamamızda görüleceği üzere, kamuoyumuzun da malumu olan 4,9 milyar TL tutarındaki kamulaştırma alacağımız toplam borçlarımızdan düşülmüştür. Bununla birlikte rapor tarihimiz itibari ile gerçekleşmiş olan bonservis borçlarımızın ileriye dönük tüm tutarları bu borçlarımız içerisinde yer almaktadır."

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: Trump: Enerji ateşkesini Rusya da Ukrayna da ihlal ediyor
content:
ABD Başkanı Donald Trump, Rusya ile Ukrayna arasında varılan enerji ateşkesi anlaşmasının "her iki taraftan da" ihlal edildiğini, ancak anlaşmanın geçerli olduğunu savundu.

Seçim mitingi için Ohio'ya hareketinden önce Beyaz Saray'ın çıkışında basın mensuplarının sorularını yanıtlayan Trump, Moskova ile Kiev arasındaki enerji ateşkesi anlaşmasının halen geçerli olup olmadığı sorusuna, "Evet (anlaşmayı) kabul ettiler. Neden biliyor musun? Çünkü kabul ettiklerini ben söyledim. İşte bu yüzden kabul ettiler; çünkü onların kabul ettiğini söyledim. Artık bu meselenin çözülmesi gerekiyor. Bu savaş tam bir felaket" yanıtını verdi.

ABD Başkanı, Ukrayna Devlet Başkanı Zelenskiy'nin, "Rusya'nın anlaşmayı ihlal ettiği" yönündeki açıklamasının hatırlatılması üzerine, "Buna bakmamız lazım, çünkü her iki taraftan da ihlaller oldu" değerlendirmesini yaptı.

Trump, sadece Putin'in anlaşmayı desteklediği, ancak Zelenskiy'nin desteklemediği yönündeki haberlere katılmadığını kaydederek, iki liderin de anlaşmaya destek verdiğini savundu.

Daha sonra iki ülke arasındaki son duruma ilişkin de açıklamalarda bulunan Trump, "Bence Putin bir anlaşma yapmak istiyor, Zelenskiy'nin de anlaşma yapmasını istemesini sağlamalıyız. Bence Putin, anlaşma yapmayı Zelenskiy'den daha fazla istiyor" değerlendirmesini yaptı.

İki liderin de anlaşma yapmak istediğini, ancak nasıl anlaşacaklarını bilmediklerini savunan ABD Başkanı, Putin ve Zelenskiy'nin anlaşmasını sağlamaları gerektiğini ifade etti.

ABD Başkanı ayrıca, Rusya ile yaptıkları dizel anlaşmasının sadece ABD için değil, tüm dünya için önemli bir anlaşma olduğunu ve bunu tüm ülkeler için yaptığını dile getirdi.

ABD Başkanı Donald Trump, Suudi Arabistan'a yönelik saldırılara dair, "Husiler yanlış işler yapıyorlar hem de çok yanlış. Bu durum hiç iyi değil" değerlendirmesini yaptı.

AA muhabirinin, "Husilerin son dönemde saldırılarını artırması ile ABD'deki Kongre ara seçimleri arasında bir ilişki görüp görmediği" şeklindeki sorusunu da cevaplayan Trump, şunları söyledi: "Bunun seçimleri nasıl etkileyeceğini bilmiyorum. Bunu hesaba katmıyorum. Tek bildiğim, İran’ın asla nükleer silaha sahip olmayacağı ve bu durumun artık gerçekleşmiş olduğu. Asla nükleer silaha sahip olmayacaklar. Ancak Husiler yanlış davranıyorlar."

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Tings Chak
title: How Brazil’s Election Could Reshape Relations with China
content:
On 25 October, Brazilians will return to the polls to choose between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in an attempted coup. The first round gave Flávio 47.03 per cent of valid votes against Lula’s 45.16 per cent, revealing the enduring strength of the far right four years after its electoral defeat. The runoff takes place as Donald Trump seeks to restore US domination over Latin America, with Brazil emerging as a consequential battleground in Washington’s campaign to contain China’s growing relations with the region.

Over the past two decades, Brazil and China have built a political partnership that has expanded the space for independent action among countries of the Global South. Under Lula and Xi Jinping, this relationship has deepened through cooperation in industrial development, infrastructure, science, and technology. The election will determine whether this project advances or Brazil’s international orientation is subordinated to Washington’s renewed Monroe Doctrine as part of the continent’s rightward shift.

Since Lula’s return to the presidency in 2023, the two governments have connected Chinese cooperation with Brazil’s development programmes, including Nova Indústria Brasil, the Growth Acceleration Programme (PAC), and the Ecological Transformation Plan. Lula’s May 2025 visit to Beijing produced 36 agreements covering infrastructure, finance, artificial intelligence, public health, and industrial cooperation. Behind these agreements is a long-standing challenge: overcoming Brazil’s dependent position in the international division of labour, where commodity exports continue to outweigh advanced industrial and technological development.

This cooperation has also reached Brazilian popular movements. Through the International Association for Popular Cooperation (Baobab), Brazil’s Landless Rural Workers’ Movement (MST) and other organisations have worked with Chinese institutions on agricultural mechanisation, bioinputs, and digital technologies for family farming. These initiatives include the Digital Family Farming and Agroecology Laboratoryand IARAA, an artificial intelligence project for agroecology and agrarian reform developed by Brazilian popular movements using Chinese open-source models. In a countryside marked by extreme concentrations of land, machinery, and capital, such cooperation offers new tools to peasant organisations fighting for agrarian reform and the production of healthy food.

Brazil’s relationship with China also reveals the different class interests at work in the country, with contradictions particularly visible in the countryside. Massive exports of soybeans, meat, and minerals have continued under both Bolsonaro and Lula, but their governments have pursued very different political relationships with Beijing. While Jair Bolsonaro attacked China and aligned himself with Washington, Lula has sought to deepen strategic cooperation, including in industrial development, technology, and agrarian reform. Flávio Bolsonaro now promises an ‘economically pragmatic‘ relationship with China while cultivating close ties with Trump. For sectors of Brazil’s ruling classes that profit from commodity exports, continuing to sell to China while embracing Washington’s political agenda presents little contradiction. For Brazil’s efforts to rebuild its industry and develop technological sovereignty, the consequences are far greater.

The Return of the Monroe Doctrine

Washington’s ambitions were made explicit in its December 2025 National Security Strategy, which announced a ‘Trump Corollary’ to the Monroe Doctrine, seeking to restore US pre-eminence in the Western Hemisphere and deny outside powers control over strategic resources and infrastructure. Five days later, China published its third Latin America policy paper, reaffirming sovereignty, non-interference, regional integration, technological cooperation, and support for the region as a Zone of Peace. The two documents reveal fundamentally different approachesto the political future of the continent.

Brazil’s position is decisive. As Latin America’s largest economy, a founding BRICS member, and a leading participant in Mercosur, it possesses industrial, scientific, and political capacities that could strengthen independent development across Latin America and beyond.

The emergence of a new technological era makes this struggle particularly consequential. Brazil is among the few countries of the Global South capable of pursuing digital and technological sovereignty that could benefit its neighbours and parts of Africa. Its roughly 23 per cent share of global rare earth reserves is an important starting point, but control over minerals alone is insufficient. The greater challenge is developing the capacity to process them, manufacture advanced components, and build the digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence systems, and technologies that will shape future production.

Flávio has made his orientation clear. Speaking at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in the United States in March 2026, he offered Brazil as the ‘solution’ to Washington’s dependence on China for critical minerals, explicitly linking rare earths to artificial intelligence and US military superiority. Chinese economic reporting has also described proposals from his team to exclude China from rare-earth supply chains. Rather than using Brazil’s resources to develop its own industrial and technological capacities, this agenda would place them at the service of US technological and military power.

The same political orientation extends to digital sovereignty. In July 2026, Flávio’s campaign submitted proposals to US trade authoritiesthat included preventing Brazil’s Pix payment system from connecting to non-Western international payment networks and loosening commitments within Mercosur. These proposals converge with a wider US campaign involving tariffs, digital regulation, strategic minerals, and attempts to influence Brazil’s electoral process. Meanwhile, Washington’s January 2026 bombing on Venezuela and kidnapping of Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores demonstrated how far it is prepared to go to impose its will on the continent.

The BRICS and the Struggle for an Independent Foreign Policy

Brazil, particularly under Lula, has helped build institutions through which countries of the Global South can reduce their dependence on Western-dominated structures. At the July 2025 BRICS summit in Rio de Janeiro, the group advanced cooperation on development finance, local-currency transactions, and international institutional reform. The New Development Bank, headed by former Brazilian president Dilma Rousseff, is an important expression of this effort.

The BRICS cannot automatically overcome economic dependency or guarantee sovereignty for working people. Yet its expansion offers greater room for independent development, provided that participating governments have the political commitment to use these possibilities.

Brazil’s history reveals how difficult that independence has been to defend. In 1961, vice-president João Goulart became the first high-ranking representative of a Latin American government to visit the People’s Republic of China, meeting Mao Zedong when revolutionary China remained diplomatically isolated and subjected to US sanctions. Three years later, Goulart was overthrown in a US-backed civil-military coup that inaugurated a twenty-one-year dictatorship. The early history of China–Brazil friendshipwas inseparable from struggles over national sovereignty, agrarian reform, and the forces determined to suppress them.

The international material conditions for South–South cooperation are considerably more favourable today, but political direction remains decisive. Jair Bolsonaro hosted the 2019 BRICS summit in Brasília while pursuing close alignment with Washington. A government can weaken institutions from within by abandoning the commitments that give them political substance.

The far right’s resurgence also reflects the enduring power of Brazil’s own ruling classes. Bolsonarismo has a domestic base among sections of agribusiness, finance, the security apparatus, militias, conservative religious networks, and major media. These forces, whose electoral and institutional advances have continued, were strengthened by the 2016 parliamentary coup against Dilma Rousseff and the judicial persecution of Lula. They possess their own organisations, material interests, and sources of power, which do not disappear when an election is lost. Their economic dependence on Chinese markets has not prevented their support for Washington’s political agenda.

Beijing has followed the Brazilian election closely, reflecting the importance of the political relationship built between Lula and Xi over years of cooperation. In July, Xi reaffirmed China’s support for Brazil against external interference during a conversation with Lula, which also covered cooperation in artificial intelligence, satellites, mineral processing, and relations between China and Mercosur. In September, Foreign Minister Wang Yi received Lula’s adviser and former foreign minister Celso Amorim in Beijing, reaffirming the bilateral strategic partnership.

China’s principle of non-interference means that the choice of Brazil’s government belongs to the Brazilian people, but Beijing’s diplomatic restraint should not be confused with an absence of political interests or an assumption that all governments would pursue the same relationship. Chinese analysts have described the possible outlook under Flávio as one of ‘cold politics, hot economics’: commodity trade would likely continue, but the political relationship and cooperation in strategic sectors could deteriorate. The experience of Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency has already shown the limits of commercial interests in sustaining a broader political partnership.

For the Brazilian people, the consequences extend well beyond foreign policy. The election will also shape the struggles over labour rights, public services, agrarian reform, and the defence of democratic space. Brazil’s renewed role in South–South cooperation under Lula has opened possibilities for a development project that responds to the needs of its working people, but realising those possibilities depends on the political and social forces capable of carrying it forward.

The Brazilian people have fought through dictatorship, neoliberal restructuring, parliamentary coups, and the rise of the far right to defend their political and social gains. This election is another moment in that longer struggle, now unfolding amid renewed US imperial intervention and a transformation of the world’s technological foundations. The future of China–Brazil cooperation will depend on the capacity of organised popular forces to build a sovereign national project and turn international cooperation into lasting changes in people’s lives.

This article was produced by Globetrotter.

Tings Chak 翟庭君 is the Asia Co-Coordinator of Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research and an editor of the international edition of Wenhua Zongheng: A Journal of Contemporary Chinese Thought.

author: Michael Albert
title: Liberating Theory: Vision and Strategy
content:
[This article ends the sequence from the seven author book Liberating Theory—by myself, Leslie Cagan, Noam Chomsky, Robin Hahnel, Mel King, Lydia Sargent, and Holly Sklar—published in 1986. This time the collective discussed vision and strategy. We here excerpt two chapters and their dialogues.]

So far, four sources of definition for society, not one or even two. A human center and institutional boundary, not an economic base and social superstructure. Accommodation, co-definition, and even co-reproduction between components all within an encompassing ecology and international relations. Social stability and/or social transformation. Three potential ruling classes, not two. Is all that and more just academic complex-ification or does it have simplifying implications for actual, worthy, workable vision and strategy?

Definitive evidence about the worth of these new concepts can only come from applying them to three critical questions: What features and dynamics characterize our society now? What is our vision of a more desirable future society? How do we expect to get from “here” to “there”?

Much has been written about the first question. While we hope that our holist principles will inform further analyses of contemporary conditions, we now focus our attention on the latter two questions.

Having argued so strenuously that societies are rarely if ever predominately determined by the characteristics of but one sphere, it follows that we should not limit our goals by visualizing a desirable future embracing less than all four spheres. Moreover, we should not label our vision for all of society with a concept that historically resonates with an emphasis on only one sphere.

“Socialism,” “feminism,” “intercommunalism,” and “participatory democracy” are appropriate names for different aspects of a desirable future society, but why use an economic concept to describe all of society unless one is economistic? And why use a kinship concept to describe all of society unless one is “kinshipist”? People justifiably distrust labels that reduce any of their priorities to peripheral concern. Thus, we will use the familiar labels as names for desirable ways of organizing particular spheres of social activity but we will use the more encompassing term—“humanist”—to describe the overall society we envision.

I interject from 2026: Names weren’t a strong suit for Liberating Theory. If you prefer, for the whole new society, perhaps the label “participatory society” would be better? Or maybe the name picked forty years ago will resonate? In any case it is the substance behind names that mainly matters.

The chapter continues: How does one elaborate a humanist vision? First, we need to decide what core characteristics we want in both the human center and institutional boundary. Second, we need to develop a vision of how social activity could be organized in each sphere so that our favored core characteristics would be generated. For example, what major governing institutions and decision-making systems could be expected to generate the core characteristics we desire? What community institutions and rules for community inter-relations would generate these desirable core characteristics? Third, we need to refine our vision of all spheres in light of an analysis of how the dynamics of each will affect the dynamics and characteristics of all the others. Here, we only outline approaches that will hopefully serve as a basis for further work by ourselves and others.

How does one justify the superiority of one set of core characteristics compared to another? Where do humanist values come from? What core characteristics embody humanist values? We know that human potentials are sufficiently broad that a number of different reasonably stable societal alternatives to our own are feasible. Moreover, since the behavior patterns, desires, and values of citizens in any society are in large part formed by the core characteristics of the institutional structures they encounter, we know that reproductive dynamics between any society’s center and boundary will promote values in their citizens that will tend to justify whatever core characteristics they daily encounter. It follows that if we ask merely whether people get what they seek in some society we will get a yes answer in many cases where the society is, nonetheless, oppressive. To have confidence in our evaluations we must ask, instead, in what society will people seek and attain the most. Unlike philosophical nihilists who reject value statements or moral judgments and wonder only whether citizens in a society support the society, we have to wonder whether citizens also maximally develop and fulfill themselves. Thus, while many different social core characteristics are possible, not all equally fulfill human potentials. And while all sets of core characteristics fulfill at least some aspects of human potential, not all sets equally promote all aspects or foster all forms of human development.

For example, while a competitive, authoritarian system may display a degree of stability, indicating that human beings can adapt even to these conditions, this does not mean that there are no aspects of human potential that are denied by such circumstances. If needs for social solidarity and self-management cannot be fully satisfied for large numbers of people under competitive, authoritarian systems, such systems contradict these needs even if people are not loudly proclaiming them. Other systems with different core characteristics that do as well by human fulfillment and development on other counts and better on this count, are superior.

To argue for the desirability of a particular set of core characteristics it follows that we must show that they are compatible with the full expression of all important aspects of human potential and that they do not thwart meeting any justifiable human needs for some groups because of how efforts to meet the needs of other groups are organized. That is, we should determine which core characteristics allow for the fullest development of all important human potentials for all of society’s citizens, and which core characteristics provide for the greatest fulfillment of all important human needs for all. As we see it, therefore, a general understanding of basic human needs and potentials combined with a more specific understanding of how these historically develop can justify those core characteristics that best promote all people’s human fulfillment and development. We also believe that no other logic can fulfill this kind of “ethical imperative.” Most simply, a humanist must ask: What characteristics must a society have for all people to freely develop to their fullest potentials?

Of course, no one can fully answer this question. No one knows enough about human nature or the ways it manifests itself in social circumstances to give a comprehensive answer reaching into all sides of moral, spiritual, intellectual, and material life. The best we can do—without additional knowledge gained through the experience of actually building humanist alternatives—is to summarize the collective lessons of radical movements to date in order to elaborate a few straightforward aims so profound that they can provide at least the rough contours of a humanist vision.

We reject prejudiced notions which go against all that is known about human genetics to assert that all people are innately anti-social, or that men are misogynist, women passive, non-whites witless, some people born to lead and most to follow, etc. Needs we focus on instead are: 1) social solidarity, 2) diversity of life options and outcomes, and 3) collective self-management that allows each person to partake in decisions in proportion to the degree she or he is affected by the outcome. We believe these aims promote human potentials, reflect lessons from radical historical experience, and include many other more specific goals that different humanists might wish to promote: peace, equity, trust, respect, material well-being, democracy, etc.

How can equity, self-management, solidarity, and diversity become the characteristics that permeate every sphere of social life? What institutions have furthered these aims in the past and how might we alter old forms to enhance their ability to do so in the future? What entirely new institutions are needed? Our vision must inform as well as inspire.

We know economic forms are required to allow for production, consumption, and allocation, and we know that in most past societies these functions have been accomplished in ways that divided people into conflicting classes causing great inequalities and hierarchies. To define a humanist alternative we need to examine existing economic forms—markets, central planning, private and public ownership, and hierarchical divisions of labor—to see how they preclude solidarity, diversity, and collective self-management. In light of these lessons, we need to elaborate alternative economic forms better suited to organizing production, consumption, and allocation in ways consistent with humanist goals.

In earlier chapters we made many claims regarding the ways capitalist and coordinator forms elevate either capitalists or coordinators, but not workers, to ruling economic status, by compelling competition and destroying solidarity, and by centralizing decision making instead of allowing workers and consumers to self-manage their own economic activities.

A humanist alternative requires collective self-management which organizes production to involve all workers in jobs that empower them equally in decision-making, develop their potentials freely and fully, and allocate difficult and dangerous tasks equitably. Decision-making by producers and consumers must be participatory as well as democratic.

To these ends, we will also have to overcome the division of work roles so it no longer holds that some people primarily conceive tasks others perform, while other people primarily execute tasks they do not conceive. Job descriptions need to be flexible, maximizing creative opportunities while simultaneously and equitably minimizing the monotonous, unhealthy and dangerous work everyone has to do. A primary role of automation under these circumstances must be to constantly eliminate monotonous and dangerous production tasks, though jobs people want to do could be preserved. While no one would be discouraged from specializing in any area of work (whether health care, teaching, woodworking, or whatever) the economy would be fluid enough to allow people to change jobs and develop new and varied skills. Whatever the focus of people’s labors, a critical point is that they will have job complexes such that the range of tasks they do will be comparable in its combination of empowering and rote, conceptual and executionary skills to those of other workers.

Second, workplace dynamics must promote solidarity by helping workers make decisions not only in light of their own needs and capacities, but in light of those of other workers and consumers. By the same token, consumers must evolve their preferences not only according to their personal needs but also in light of implications for other consumers and for workers who produce what they consume. Allocation mechanisms must not centralize decision-making in the hands of capitalists, managers, technocrats, or a handful of central planners. Nor can allocation be carried out via a system that competitively divides economic actors, pitting each against all others. Not only private ownership of the means of production, but both markets and central planning will be ruled out as destructive of humanist goals. Some type of participatory planning will have to be developed and perfected.

Third, since unequal income distribution sustains class divisions, income will have to be allocated equitably even though individuals consume different goods and work at different job complexes according to different time schedules. The economy would provide equitable balanced job complexes for all who want work; a shorter standard work week; comparable income for all; and free comprehensive human services.

Though the task will be difficult, why aim for less than humanist institutional forms designed to allow society to effectively produce, allocate, and consume goods and services in ways fostering solidarity, diversity, and collective participatory self-management?

I interject: the seven authors obviously settled on a quite succinct summary of participatory economics as the book’s economic vision. I wish I could remember and convey how that occurred, but forty years is a long time and I cannot. The vision has deepened and refined over the years to clarify essential aspects and why they are together worthy and would be viable, but the essence is present here, albeit very loosely. I was particularly surprised that there seems to have been some squeamishness about addressing income or remuneration, but that no doubt reflected author differences about that matter. At any rate, the chapter continues:

Kinship institutions are necessary for people to fulfill their sexual and emotional needs and raise new generations of children. But most societies have elevated men above women and children, oppressed homosexuals, and warped human sexual and emotional potentials. In a humanist society we will have to eliminate socially-imposed gender definitions so that individuals can freely pursue their lives as they choose whatever their biological sex, sexuality, and (within reason) chronological age. But how?

In earlier discussions we attributed the maintenance of patriarchy to several causes including (but not limited to) the division of childrearing roles along male-female, mother-father, axes. Reproductive freedom—the right to have children without fear of sterilization, economic oppression, or other injustices and the right not to have children through unhindered access to birth control and abortion—is a fundamental precondition of equality between women and men. But more is necessary.

First, a critical characteristic of feminist kinship will be childrearing roles that do not divide tasks by sex. There must be support for single parents, couples, and multiple parenting arrangements, including lesbian and gay parenting. Parents must have easy access to diverse child-care options including high-quality personalized day care, afterschool programs, workplace day-care, flexible work hours and parental leave options. But the point is not to free parents by turning over the next generation to uncaring agencies. Instead, sustained highly personalized and rich interaction between children and adults must be enhanced while distributing the responsibilities for these interactions as equitably as possible.

Second, though there will continue to be great variations in how people organize their time and see themselves at different periods of their lives, ageism would have no place in a humanist society. Adults will certainly exert guiding influence over vulnerable children, since to be a child means, in part, to be incapable of completely governing one’s life. But even while protected and taught, children will also be respected and encouraged to voice their perspectives which they will have freedom to develop with their peers and without undue interference. Likewise, seniors will be encouraged to maintain an active life, with full or partial retirement from work guided by personal considerations and abilities, not economic dictates. The interface of perspectives molded in different times as seniors, the middle aged, and children encounter each other will become one more vehicle for each to learn from the different experiences of others.

Third, a humanist vision will embrace a liberated sexuality which respects people’s (often changing) choices and inclinations, whether homosexual, bisexual or heterosexual; monogamous or nonmonogamous. Moreover, beyond respecting rights, the exercise and exploration of different forms of sexuality by consenting partners provides a variety of experiences that can benefit all. In a humanist society without oppressive hierarchies, sex will presumably be pursued for emotional, physical, and spiritual pleasure and development. Experimentation to these ends is not something merely to be tolerated, but to be appreciated.

In general, to offer a viable attractive vision, feminists and humanists will have to elaborate liberatory visions of primary living groups, child rearing, and sexuality. But while such a vision will have to be comprehensive enough to provide compelling images and attractive possibilities, it should also leave room for experimentation and growth as we move into a new kind of future.

I interject: I am surprised the kinship vision we offered, back then, didn’t explicitly address mothering and fathering even if by implication it did make clear that parenting should not be predicated on sex or procreation only. I am guessing again, as with economics, that among the seven authors there were differences on this issue. The chapter continues:

We know that community forms give people a sense of who they are and where they fit in society and history. However, most community forms have also imposed the heavy prices of genocide, racism, jingoism, religious persecution, and ethnocentrism. The seemingly simplest alternative to the existence of many communities which confront one another with racial, national, religious, and ethnic hostility might be to integrate everyone into one comprehensive community group. Likewise, the simplest solution to communities having internal attributes destructive of solidarity, diversity, and collective self-management, would seemingly be to redefine the culture of this one large community to make it satisfactory. But reacting to the negative interaction of diverse historical communities by attempting to eliminate those communities and their cultures through cultural homogenization is a disastrous policy. It is not only internally inconsistent, since it heightens exactly the community antagonisms it seeks to overcome, but even if it could be implemented such a vision offers little variety and cultural self-

management. In fact cultural homogenization is an Orwellian nightmare.

What then is a truly humanist alternative? First, promoting diversity requires that a humanist approach to community relations emphasizes the need to respect the multiplicity of community forms by guaranteeing each sufficient material and social resources to reproduce itself indefinitely. Reversing the homogenist agenda, humanist community policies will identify cultural subgroups and help them preserve and develop their own particular solutions to life’s quandaries, not by imposing on them, but by ensuring their access to means of expression and the opportunity for free development.

Second, a humanist approach to community will emphasize that communities are not genetic or biological, but social and historical. Their forms will be diverse and memberships variable depending upon people’s commitments, not on skin color or parentage. This is not to say that there will not be Italian, black, or Jewish communities. It merely clarifies that such communities will be cultural forms whose members belong by virtue of their beliefs and practices, not their “lineage.” Of course being from Italy, or having had an Italian upbringing, or having immersed oneself in things Italian are the practices that give one an Italian culture and Italian community membership. But this is not due to genes; it is due to choice. And the same will hold for religious, ethnic, and racial community affiliation. To be black implies having been immersed in black culture. Someone whose skin is black but who has never experienced black culture is not necessarily a member of the black community. Nor will having black skin elicit a presumption about one’s culture (or hostility) from nonblacks. Moreover, someone whose skin is white but who was brought up in and has adopted the cultural allegiances of the black community could be a member of that community. These recognitions will greatly facilitate the potential for mutual respect and for mutual learning among communities.

Third, at the same time that a humanist approach to community will recognize and preserve the integrity of diverse community definitions, a humanist approach will also be sensitive to the need for community definitions to be internally humane and supportive of individual and group freedoms. People will be free to enter and leave cultural communities in accord with their own best understandings and desires. Moreover, cultures could be subject to criticism (but not intervention) from without, though the right of their members to dissent and leave will be socially protected. Spirituality will likely flourish though in many new forms as a result of changes both in our approaches to religion and in the character of the society in which our communities will be embedded. But atheists will retain their right to criticize religious believers and vice versa, though neither atheists nor the religious will be able to deny the others’ cultural rights. But if a religious community denied a member the opportunity to leave and practice atheism, or vice versa, there would be intervention to protect that individual’s right of cultural dissent and choice.

In short, under humanist intercommunalism different cultural and spiritual institutions will be preserved and the right for them to persist will be respected. Each will alter, no doubt, owing to changing understandings of the role and character of culture that evolve from liberatory internal dynamics, as well as influences from other social spheres which help erode sexist, classist, and authoritarian definitions. At the international level, as a direct extension, intercommunalism will mean respect for self-determination and commitment to nonintervention.

We know that the political sphere is a necessary means of providing overall social coherence and mediating social disagreements. But we also know that most governments to date have created hierarchies, imposed regimentation, repressed freedom, and inflicted harsh crimes against their citizens. When we think about a humanist alternative we must think in terms of new institutions which not only respect democratic advances that have occurred to date, but expand upon this base to promote a still higher degree of social participation in decision-making. We must go beyond electoral forms in which participation is brief and episodic to conceive of structures in which popular oversight and participation is continuous.

Further, we have to think not only in terms of a pluralism of contesting options, but also in terms of a pluralism of chosen outcomes. Expanding democracy means recognizing that there is no single right way to conduct social life since various alternatives can all embody valid goals and whenever possible diverse options should be implemented. We will not always automatically presume a single best way to do every imaginable task, but will instead experiment with diverse options.

We will also have to pay attention to the obvious but often neglected fact that participatory democratic decision-making forms are useless unless all citizens have access to information and means of voicing, arguing for, and organizing around their ideas and social proposals. Democratic decision-making is impossible if what people can propose is determined by a few who control access to information and ideas thereby molding even what it is possible for people to think about. We must develop rich means for information dissemination, popular debate, and sharing of new ideas.

To discover how best to attain such ends, we must analyze the dynamics of information flow and debate as well as related structures of decision-making to see how existing forms of each impede (and propel) true democracy. We must then develop alternative forms which overcome traditional obstacles to greater participation while getting the decision-making job done in an effective fashion.

A humanist vision of governing forms must therefore incorporate many dimensions of institutional life if it is not to risk undermining itself by ignoring the full array of variables that affect whether people can really manifest their wills in social decision-making.

I interject: I believe, reading all this visionary material, that the authors were in sum being quite cautious to not over-propose details which could be perceived as over-prescribing a vision that needs to largely emerge from collective practice. On the one hand, we didn’t then nor does anyone now know nearly enough to propose a full blueprint which, in any event, can’t even exist because so much of a future revolutionized society will differ from country to country, time to time, and preference to preference. On the other hand, even if it was possible, it was not the place of actors then, or now, to arrive at detailed decisions instead of future people developing and deciding their own diverse circumstances. The visionary task, instead, was and remains to propose core institutions that would not prevent and would instead facilitate people self managing their own future circumstances. After forty years, I would now want to add some commentary about how to refine the offered core features sufficiently to usefully guide practice able to arrive where participants intend—but not more. The chapter continues:

A Program For Developing A Humanist Vision

If we take all these insights simultaneously, we have a kind of research program for developing a humanist vision. First, develop detailed images of possible economic, kinship, community, and core governing forms which escape the classist, sexist, racist, and authoritarian norms of the past to accomplish their essential social functions in ways that instead promote social diversity, human solidarity, and collective self-management. We have discussed some means of accomplishing this much already.

Second, refine these separate images into a whole social picture in which the parts overlap in a consistent and mutually reinforcing fashion. The idea here is a bit more subtle.
