author: Javier Moreno Zacarés
title: Fifteen Years Later
content:
Fifteen years after the indignados occupied the Puerta del Sol, Madrid’s central plaza is once again the locus of a mass movement that has brought Spain to a political impasse. How are we back here again? The immediate trigger was the eviction of an elderly tenant. Maricarmen Abascal, who had occupied her rent-capped apartment in central Madrid since 1956, was expelled from her home on 23 September after the investment fund Urbagestión acquired the property and exploited a legal loophole to quintuple her rent. Maricarmen’s age and vulnerability – the 87-year-old was removed on a hospital bed and has since died – made it a particularly egregious breach of the moral economy. The case struck a nerve, prompting a political storm; the government has now announced a snap election. As protests spread nationwide, the encampment at Puerta del Sol consolidated under the leadership of the Sindicato de Inquilinas, Madrid’s tenant union. Media outlets are reporting on the motions passed at the open-air general assembly. One decision has been of particular public interest: a general strike for the right to housing, announced for 11 November, a few weeks before the election.

The political elite faces a reckoning. At the outset of the current parliamentary term in 2023, the progressive coalition headed by Sánchez’s centre-left Socialist Party (PSOE) placed housing at the top of the agenda. The promises were ambitious: the provision of mass social housing, the imposition of rent controls, the reassertion of the public interest against rentier logics. Yet these commitments yielded little. This was partly due to the obstruction of the right, both in parliament and in the regional governments under its control. But a share of the blame lies in the ambivalence of the Socialist Party itself, whose ministers have repeatedly expressed discomfort with what they regard as excessive regulation of housing. The junior coalition partner Sumar, a nebulous alliance of progressive parties, has proven feeble in holding the Socialists to account. They are now also a target of the protests, who charge the entire governing alliance of complicity with the rentiers. Amid the fury in the streets, Sumar’s cabinet members hastened to pressure the Socialist housing minister, Isabel Rodríguez – herself a landlord who owns multiple properties – to approve emergency measures to block evictions and institute permanent rolling contracts, both key demands of the tenant unions. Last Friday, both measures were struck down in parliament, to the anger of the masses gathered outside.

That a recalcitrant right-wing opposition – comprising the conservative People’s Party (PP) and the far-right Vox – would block the measures was entirely predictable. What was less so was that the deciding vote would be cast by an ally of the government: the centre-right Junts, party of the Catalan-nationalist bourgeoisie. The vote revealed a peculiarity of the Spanish conjuncture. Though the right-wing bloc is the largest in parliament, it is divided along nationalist lines, fractures the government has exploited – drawing support from the Catalan right to keep the Spanish unionist right out of power. It was always an unstable arrangement, premised on nation trumping class. On the housing question, the plurinational right voted in alignment with its shared interests (Junts has the largest proportion of landlords in parliament).

The Spanish right now enjoys a comfortable lead in the polls, which point to a PP–Vox coalition if elections were held tomorrow. But the wind is blowing in an uncomfortable direction for them. Over the past week, public opinion has swung massively in favour of regulating house prices, even among a slim majority of right-wing voters. In a matter of days, the protests have shifted the national conversation away from the right’s preferred talking points of crime and migration, overwriting a summer of hysteria around the border crisis in Ceuta. They have also deflected attention from the corruption scandals afflicting PSOE: only last June, a former minister in Sánchez’s cabinet was sentenced to twenty-four years in prison for influence-peddling related to substandard Covid-19 face masks. Ever the survivor, Sánchez has seized the moment with a characteristically audacious move. He has framed the election on 29 November as a plebiscite on the housing question, shifting the blame for it onto the right and boldly appealing to the electorate to ‘subdue the elites’, hoping to ride the wave of unrest that is also aimed against him.

Housing has been a political flashpoint in Spain ever since a giant real estate bubble crashed the economy between 2007–14. The circumstances in many ways paralleled those that led to the Great Recession: financial liberalization; easy credit supercharged by cross-border flows; homeowners mortgaged to the hilt; skyrocketing house prices stoked by reckless speculation. What stood out in the Spanish case was the extent to which growth and employment came to depend on a hypertrophied construction sector, rendering broad sections of the economy highly exposed to the inevitable crash. In the 2000s, as rapid population growth and the arrival of Eurozone capital accelerated house-price increases, Spain built more homes than the UK, Italy and Germany combined. At the peak of the boom in 2006, when annual housing construction reached 700,000 units, reports from the property sector estimated that ‘structural demand’ – that is, demand for housing to live in – was only 400,000 homes a year. The resulting surplus, built on a purely self-referential, speculative demand, was the substance of the bubble. When household indebtedness hit its ceiling in 2007 and transactions slowed, it burst: prices stagnated and then plummeted. Speculative developers ceased building, grinding the engine of the economy to a halt and releasing shockwaves of job destruction. At the height of the crisis in 2013, unemployment reached a historic high of 26 per cent (56 per cent among the young). Developers, banks and the state rushed to expel families who could not meet rent or mortgage payments. Between 2008 and 2015 there were roughly half a million evictions, half of them foreclosures. The bitter irony was that hundreds of thousands lost their homes because there were hundreds of thousands of homes too many.

In a series of costly bailouts, the state absorbed the losses of the property-financial complex, bringing it to the edge of insolvency. Successive administrations – of both the PSOE and the PP – passed the cost to the masses, inflicting punitive austerity under the watchful eye of Europe’s fiscal hawks. The usual sanctimony about belt-tightening and living beyond one’s means fell flat. Political parties were plagued by relentless corruption scandals, the majority involving dealings with developers and builders no less. Bankers, meanwhile, flaunted their rapacity by paying themselves obscene bonuses as their banks were being nationalized, leaving the state to foot the bill.

The ensuing crisis of legitimacy set the scene for the rise of the indignados, or the 15-M movement as it is more often referred to in Spain. On 15 May 2011, a series of mass protests descended on city squares, taking aim at austerity measures and the oligarchic bent of the political system. The movement radiated out from Puerta del Sol, where protesters emulated the camp then ongoing in Tahrir Square in Cairo. Though the social composition of the protest was broad, it was led by downwardly mobile middle-class youths, many of whom became politicized for the first time at the movement’s assemblies. The memorable yellow T-shirts of the activist group Juventud Sin Futuro captured the feeling with a defiant slogan: ‘no home, no job, no pension, no fear’. Eventually, the 15-M’s occupations dispersed into neighbourhood councils, where a wave of radicalized youngsters flooded into a myriad of militant groups. A cycle of mass unrest and civil disobedience followed. The most prominent organization was the Plataforma de Afectados por la Hipoteca (PAH), whose activists acted as the shock troops of the anti-austerity movement. Sabotaging eviction procedures was their staple practice: they confronted bailiffs and their riot police escorts on arrival, barricaded themselves with the families being expelled, occupied repossessed homes, or squatted entire tower blocks to provide accommodation for the dispossessed. The extra-parliamentary struggles of these years proved extremely successful in repoliticizing questions previously regarded as shameful personal failures – unemployment, debt, eviction – turning them into vectors of mass resistance.

Yet they were much less successful in bringing the state to heel. Ironically, the first major electoral outcome of the 15-M protests was a crushing landslide for the right in November 2011. Though the movement had wide public support, its injunction to abstain from voting for the neoliberal uniparty – ‘PPSOE’ – was followed more by the left than the right. PSOE’s vote collapsed while PP’s remained stable, translating into an absolute parliamentary majority for the neoliberal conservatives of Mariano Rajoy, who proceeded to further slash public spending, introduce a draconian labour market reform, and sell off the real estate assets acquired from the banks to global corporate landlords. With its dominance in parliament, the new administration was able to invoke the support of a ‘silent majority’ to rule by decree while cracking down on protest. At the behest of its Interior Minister, Jorge Fernández Díaz – an ultra-Catholic in the habit of praying in Franco’s mausoleum – the government introduced the notorious ‘Gag Law’ tailored to the new social movements, which included punitively high fines for blocking evictions. Meanwhile, in a perfect visual metaphor for the dissociation of the elite from the masses, parliament was fenced off from the public and fortified with a permanent detachment of riot police.

After years of being stonewalled, street-fighting fatigue began to set in around 2014. The gigantic March for Dignity that year – demanding ‘bread, work and a roof’ and culminating in riots in Madrid – was the final flashpoint of this insurrectionary cycle. Seeing the tide turning, activists previously committed to the extra-parliamentary ethos of the 15-M began to form political parties, and probe strategic entry points into the state. One approach was to capitalize on the anti-establishment mood to mount a broad, left-populist offensive aimed at capturing state power ‘from above’; the path taken by Podemos, founded in 2014 with the priority of ‘storming the heavens’ in a general election. Another was the formation of electoral coalitions between urban activists and pre-existing left-wing parties to wrest state power at the local level; a route explored by the multitude of municipalist platforms that in 2015 won office in the country’s largest cities, including Cádiz, Santiago, Zaragoza, Valencia, Madrid and of course, Barcelona, where PAH’s charismatic spokeswoman, Ada Colau, was elected mayor with housing at the top of her agenda.

Both strategies ran into the trouble of operating in the inhospitable terrain of the state. Barcelona’s Right to Housing Plan of 2016 was fairly successful in blocking evictions and expanding the social housing stock through a combination of public construction, aggressive acquisition campaigns and the imposition of social housing quotas on developers. But this was the most advanced expression of a municipalist strategy that faced severe challenges from the start. Local reformers ran up against the austerity imposed by the central government; encountered entrenched resistance at all levels of the state bureaucracy; and were forced to water down their policy proposals to navigate the political fragmentation of local councils and/or of their own electoral alliances. Frustration set in among activists and voters as the grinding pace of reform failed to live up to the revolutionary rhetoric. Most of the administrations in the ‘cities of change’ proved short-lived, voted out of office in 2019. Barcelona followed suit in 2023.

Podemos faced a different set of challenges. Upon its founding, the party quickly drew in hundreds of thousands, swelling new branches in what promised to be a participatory party-movement. However, the leadership – a group of academics sceptical of the potential of grassroots activism – quickly centralized power and reduced internal democracy to a plebiscitary exercise in which the membership merely ratified decisions handed down from above. Such behaviour followed logically from a left-populist strategy that soon became familiar in Europe and North America, one that revolved around charismatic leadership and disciplined media messaging. This strategy did not require a vibrant, independent grassroots layer, but rather the subordination of the whole organization to an ‘electoral war machine’ commanded from the top. The party’s branches withered away as its members were largely reduced to passive clicktivists. What the party gained in short-term agility from this strategy, it lost in long-term resilience: without organized cadres, it became vulnerable to media attacks and personality-driven factionalism.

Meanwhile, Podemos’s appeal waned as its electoral assaults on the central state were successively repealed. However, in the general elections of 2019 it was able to clinch enough seats to enter coalition with a reluctant PSOE, locking both parties into a fraught partnership. Podemos’s main legislative achievement was the Housing Law of 2023, which introduced a nationwide framework for rent controls. Passed as the municipalist wave died out, it seemed to confirm that the strategic entry point into the state was ‘from above’. Yet the gap between law and practice became apparent soon enough. In control of most regional administrations, the People’s Party and their far-right allies Vox have simply refused to implement it. To this day, the law is only in force in Catalonia and in areas of the Basque Country. The bill also left a glaring loophole around short-term tourist rentals, letting the hollowing out of cities through platforms like Airbnb continue unabated.

That rent controls have become a burning issue in a society in which 73.3 per cent of households are owner-occupiers reflects the permutations of the Spanish housing system since the crash. When the bubble burst, the state nationalized a huge pool of ‘toxic assets’. This devalued property could have been used to create a public housing system, badly needed at a time of rampant evictions. Instead, starting in 2013, the state opted to sell them off at fire-sale prices to investment funds. Blackstone became the country’s biggest landlord. In order to relaunch the property market as quickly as possible the state incentivized the business of the ‘mega-landlords’ with tax advantages and tailored regulations, which also benefited a broader swathe of middle-class landlords. Meanwhile, the share of the tenant population has increased for the first time since the 1950s (+7 per cent of households since 2011). Those homeowners expelled from their homes during the crisis returned to the market as tenants. There, they were joined by a new generation excluded from the mortgage market, more strictly regulated in the wake of the crisis. Credit restrictions have suppressed the leveraged purchases of the 2000s, which allowed many to ride the bubble by borrowing against the rising value of their homes or ‘flip’ them for profit.

Meanwhile, residential accumulation has reoriented itself around squeezing the growing captive market of tenants or, failing that, the exploitation of tourist rentals. Economically, the new housing regime is more stable than the previous one. Rents rise more or less in line with wages, devouring the disposable income of tenants, but without the debt-fuelled speculative excesses of the bubble. Politically, however, the present arrangement is far more unstable and more prone to social explosions, owing to the greater prominence of rent tenure, where the conflict between the residential and rent-bearing functions of housing is more transparent than in a mass market of ‘petty-rentier’ speculative homeowners.

Since 2017, Spain has witnessed the emergence of militant tenant unions, which have gained prominence for defeating Blackstone in court and for employing an old tactic of working-class struggle: the rent strike. Although tenants remain a small minority (17 per cent of households), they are demonstrating a capacity to punch far above their weight politically, as their demands mobilize broader strata around the right to housing. A rentier bloc has been taking shape in opposition, headed by large investment funds but sustained by a substantial layer of middle-class landlords, who act as its electoral base. The political frontier of this bloc is difficult to determine, but it clearly runs through the heart of the coalition government. This has been demonstrated by successive PSOE ministers, whose reluctance to regulate rents or openly support the right to housing has repeatedly given them away. With Podemos diminished, since 2023 the Socialists have governed alongside its more cooperative successor, Sumar; an entente cordiale that has failed to bear fruit on housing matters. (Perhaps for this reason Sumar is now floating Colau, former mayor of Barcelona, as a presidential candidate.)

As the left-populist wave recedes, a younger generation of activists is coming to terms with the limits of the electoral experiments of the previous decade – as well as the horizontalism that immediately preceded them. In Puerta del Sol today, formal similarities with 15-M conceal differences of substance. The encampment is once again a plural space – it is populated by three dozen organizations – where successive generations converge and where previously apolitical youngsters are acquiring a new radical consciousness. But in the assemblies there is less blue-sky philosophizing and more strategic discussion; less spontaneity and more coordination of an agreed calendar of escalation. The festive mood of the first iteration has given way to one of discipline, reflecting the maturing of a radical civil society with organizational memory and political experience. The initiative for a general strike came from the Sindicato de Inquilinas; the anarcho-syndicalist unions, which have a presence in the square, promptly joined. The major trade unions – otherwise docile and cooperative with the government – have followed suit. In recent days, the Sindicato has gradually shifted its activity away from the square toward its ‘nodes’ or neighbourhood councils, in preparation for the strike. The vacuum has been increasingly filled by the Movimiento Socialista, a Marxist youth movement highly sceptical of reformist politics, upon which a number of political currents have converged in recent years.

If Sánchez pulls off a comeback in the November election and manages to cobble together another progressive coalition, the balance of parliamentary forces will likely resemble that of today, as will the pace and scale of reform – which is increasingly intolerable to swathes of the population. But if the election plays out as it did almost fifteen years ago, and the right wins a comfortable majority, we can expect a replay of brutal austerity and police crackdown. Only this time, a government more overt in its fascist sympathies will have to face down a hardened and more disciplined extra-parliamentary left – one that will have to come to terms, sooner or later, with how to influence the state and find a fresh synthesis of the dialectic between revolution and reform. Whether this takes the form of new political vehicles contesting state power directly, or of an antagonistic yet tacit division of labour with reformist forces, remains a critical question.

Read on: Ekaitz Cancel & Pedro M. Rey-Araújo, ‘Lessons of the Podemos Experiment’, NLR 138.

Javier Moreno Zacarés is an Assistant Professor in International Political Economy in the School of Government and International Affairs at Durham University.

title: Παράσταση διαμαρτυρίας εκπαιδευτικών αισθητικής αγωγής και ΣΕΠΕ – ΕΛΜΕ, πραγματοποιήθηκε σήμερα στη Θεσσαλονίκη – ΦΩΤΟ
content:
Παράσταση διαμαρτυρίας πραγματοποίησαν σήμερα, Δευτέρα 12 Οκτωβρίου 2026, οι εκπαιδευτικοί Αισθητικής Αγωγής (Μουσικής – Θεάτρου -Εικαστικών), μαζί με Συλλόγους Εκπαιδευτικών Πρωτοβάθμιας και Δευτεροβάθμιας Εκπαίδευσης, στην Περιφερειακή Διεύθυνση Εκπαίδευσης Κεντρικής Μακεδονίας. Βασικό αίτημα της κινητοποίησης ήταν η 

ΑΜΕΣΗ 

πρόσληψη εκπαιδευτικών Αισθητικής Αγωγής, προκειμένου να καλυφθούν 

ΟΛΑ 

τα εκπαιδευτικά κενά

, 

Διαφάνεια

 καταγραφής των κενών και 

Κατάργηση

 των αναθέσεων των καλλιτεχνικών μαθημάτων. Η πλήρης απαλλαγή όλων των εκπαιδευτικών που έχουν κληθεί σε απολογία, καθώς και η οριστική αρχειοθέτηση όλων των εκκρεμών πειθαρχικών που σχετίζονται με τη συμμετοχή των εκπαιδευτικών στην Απεργία–Αποχή από την αξιολόγηση.




Ιδιαίτερα αρνητική εντύπωση προκάλεσε η απουσία τόσο του Περιφερειακού Διευθυντή Εκπαίδευσης όσο και του αναπληρωτή του

, παρότι η παράσταση διαμαρτυρίας ήταν γνωστή. Η απουσία τους δεν συνέβαλε στην ουσιαστική επικοινωνία με τους εκπαιδευτικούς και τους εκπροσώπους των Συλλόγων, οι οποίοι προσήλθαν για να θέσουν τα προβλήματα και να διεκδικήσουν άμεσες λύσεις.




Για το λόγο αυτό πραγματοποιούμε:




NEA

 ΠΑΡΑΣΤΑΣΗ ΔΙΑΜΑΡΤΥΡΙΑΣ των κλάδων ΑΙΣΘΗΤΙΚΗΣ ΑΓΩΓΗΣ (ΜΟΥΣΙΚΗΣ-ΘΕΑΤΡΟΥ-ΕΙΚΑΣΤΙΚΩΝ)




Την Τετάρτη 14/10/2026 και ώρα 14:00 στην Π.Δ.Ε.Κεντ. Μακεδονίας (Κτίριο 

ZEDA

)




Καλούμε τους Συλλόγους Εκπαιδευτικών Πρωτοβάθμιας Εκπαίδευσης, τις ΕΛΜΕ, τους Συλλόγους Γονέων και Κηδεμόνων, τους φοιτητικούς συλλόγους, τους εκπαιδευτικούς όλων των κλάδων και κάθε πολίτη που υπερασπίζεται το δημόσιο σχολείο να στηρίξει την κινητοποίηση.




Εκπαιδευτικοί μουσικής, θεάτρου και εικαστικών ζητούμε διαφάνεια και άμεση στελέχωση των σχολείων




Η σχολική χρονιά έχει ήδη προχωρήσει και όμως σε σχολεία εξακολουθούν να υπάρχουν ώρες μουσικής, θεατρικής αγωγής και εικαστικών 

χωρίς

 τον αντίστοιχο 

εκπαιδευτικό ειδικότητας.

 Την ίδια στιγμή, εκπαιδευτικοί των συγκεκριμένων κλάδων

 παραμένουμε διαθέσιμοι στους πίνακες αναπληρωτών, περιμένοντας να προσληφθούμε.




Απτό παράδειγμα συρρίκνωσης των εκπαιδευτικών αισθητικής αγωγής αποτελούντα στοιχεία των προσλήψεων των Μουσικών ΠΕ79.01.




Στην Κεντρική Μακεδονία, οι προσλήψεις ΠΕ79.01 στην Α΄ φάση της Γενικής Παιδείας μειώθηκαν από 107 το 2022-23 σε μόλις 9 το 2026-27, δηλαδή κατά 91,6%. Η πορεία είναι συνεχής: 78 προσλήψεις το 2023-24, 54 το 2024-25, 20 το 2025-26 και 9 φέτος. Στην Α΄ και Β΄ Θεσσαλονίκης μαζί, οι 58 προσλήψεις της Α΄ φάσης του 2022-23 περιορίστηκαν σε μόλις 4 φέτος.




Τα στοιχεία προκύπτουν από τους επίσημους ονομαστικούς πίνακες προσλήψεων του Υπουργείου Παιδείας και έχουν καταγραφεί με κοινή μεθοδολογία για όλα τα έτη.




Το πρόβλημα, όμως, δεν περιορίζεται μόνο στον αριθμό των προσλήψεων.




Θέτουμε ένα βασικό ερώτημα:




Πόσες είναι πραγματικά οι ανάγκες των σχολείων και πόσες από αυτές φτάνουν τελικά να καταγραφούν, να εγκριθούν και να καλυφθούν ως κενά;




Υπάρχουν ώρες μουσικής, θεάτρου και εικαστικών στα ωρολόγια προγράμματα. Υπάρχουν εκπαιδευτικοί των αντίστοιχων ειδικοτήτων διαθέσιμοι στους πίνακες. Παρ’ όλα αυτά, ανάγκες παραμένουν χωρίς κάλυψη.




Γι’ αυτό ζητούμε πλήρη και δημόσια εικόνα για ολόκληρη τη διαδρομή ενός κενού: από τη στιγμή που διαπιστώνεται μέσα στη σχολική μονάδα έως τη δήλωσή του από τις αρμόδιες υπηρεσίες, την έγκρισή του και, τελικά, την πρόσληψη του εκπαιδευτικού που θα το καλύψει.




Πόσες ανάγκες καταγράφηκαν; Πόσα κενά ζητήθηκαν; Πόσα προωθήθηκαν; Πόσα εγκρίθηκαν; Πόσα καλύφθηκαν και πόσα παραμένουν σήμερα ακάλυπτα;




Δεν πρόκειται για γραφειοκρατικές λεπτομέρειες. Χωρίς αυτά τα στοιχεία δεν μπορεί να υπάρχει πραγματική εικόνα της στελέχωσης των σχολείων.




Γιατί το γεγονός ότι ένα κενό δεν εμφανίζεται τελικά στις προσλήψεις δεν σημαίνει ότι η εκπαιδευτική ανάγκη έπαψε να υπάρχει.




Ιδιαίτερο προβληματισμό προκαλεί το τι συμβαίνει όταν ώρες καλλιτεχνικών μαθημάτων παραμένουν ακάλυπτες ή αντιμετωπίζονται μέσω αναθέσεων σε άλλους κλάδους και άλλων διοικητικών λύσεων. Ζητούμε να αποσαφηνιστεί αν και σε ποιο βαθμό αυτές οι πρακτικές επηρεάζουν την καταγραφή των πραγματικών κενών.




Εάν πραγματικές ανάγκες δεν αποτυπώνονται ως κενά της αντίστοιχης ειδικότητας, υπάρχει κίνδυνος να δημιουργείται ένας μόνιμος κύκλος συρρίκνωσης: λιγότερα καταγεγραμμένα κενά, λιγότερα αιτήματα για προσωπικό, λιγότερες προσλήψεις και τελικά ακόμη μικρότερη παρουσία των καλλιτεχνικών ειδικοτήτων στα σχολεία.




Δεν ζητούμε να δημιουργηθούν τεχνητές θέσεις. Ζητούμε να αποτυπωθούν οι ανάγκες που ήδη υπάρχουν μέσα στα σχολεία και να γνωρίζουμε γιατί κάποιες από αυτές δεν καταλήγουν σε πρόσληψη.




Το ζήτημα δεν αφορά μόνο την εργασία των εκπαιδευτικών. 

Αφορά πρωτίστως τους μαθητές.




Η μουσική, τα εικαστικά και το θέατρο

 δεν είναι μαθήματα δεύτερης κατηγορίας 

ούτε ώρες που απλώς πρέπει να «καλυφθούν». Είναι αυτοτελή γνωστικά αντικείμενα με συγκεκριμένο 

επιστημονικό και παιδαγωγικό περιεχόμενο.




Για πολλά παιδιά το δημόσιο σχολείο είναι η μοναδική οργανωμένη δυνατότητα επαφής με τη μουσική, το θέατρο και τις εικαστικές τέχνες. Η καλλιτεχνική εκπαίδευση δεν μπορεί να αποτελεί προνόμιο μόνο όσων μπορούν να την αναζητήσουν εκτός δημόσιου σχολείου.




Αντίστοιχη ανάγκη υπάρχει και για την ουσιαστική στελέχωση του Ολοήμερου προγράμματος. Το Ολοήμερο δεν μπορεί να θεωρείται πλήρως λειτουργικό όταν προβλεπόμενες εκπαιδευτικές ανάγκες παραμένουν χωρίς το αναγκαίο προσωπικό.




Ζητούμε




* πλήρη και διαφανή καταγραφή και δημοσιοποίηση 

των πραγματικών κενών 

μουσικής, θεάτρου και εικαστικών,




* στοιχεία για τις ανάγκες που δηλώθηκαν, προωθήθηκαν, εγκρίθηκαν και τελικά καλύφθηκαν,




* άμεσες προσλήψεις για την κάλυψη των πραγματικών αναγκών και ουσιαστική στελέχωση πρωινού και Ολοήμερου προγράμματος,




* σαφή εικόνα για τις 

αναθέσεις

 των συγκεκριμένων μαθημάτων σε άλλους κλάδους και για το κατά πόσο αυτές επηρεάζουν την αποτύπωση των κενών.




Ζητούμε, τελικά, μια 

καθαρή απάντηση

 από τις αρμόδιες υπηρεσίες και το Υπουργείο Παιδείας:




Αν οι ανάγκες των σχολείων υπάρχουν και οι διαθέσιμοι εκπαιδευτικοί υπάρχουν, σε ποιο στάδιο της διαδικασίας οι ανάγκες αυτές μένουν χωρίς κάλυψη;




Καλούμε τους Συλλόγους Εκπαιδευτικών Πρωτοβάθμιας Εκπαίδευσης, τις ΕΛΜΕ, τους Συλλόγους Γονέων και Κηδεμόνων, τους φοιτητικούς συλλόγους, τους εκπαιδευτικούς όλων των κλάδων και κάθε πολίτη που υπερασπίζεται το δημόσιο σχολείο να στηρίξει την κινητοποίηση.




Τετάρτη 14 Οκτωβρίου 2026 – 14:00




Περιφερειακή Διεύθυνση Εκπαίδευσης Κεντρικής Μακεδονίας – κτίριο ZEDA




Η τέχνη στο σχολείο δεν είναι πολυτέλεια. Είναι μέρος της μόρφωσης και δικαίωμα κάθε παιδιού.




Εκπαιδευτικοί Μουσικής 

– 

Θεάτρου

 – 

Εικαστικών

Παράσταση διαμαρτυρίας εκπαιδευτικών αισθητικής αγωγής και ΣΕΠΕ – ΕΛΜΕ, πραγματοποιήθηκε σήμερα στη Θεσσαλονίκη – ΦΩΤΟ

author: By Camilla Donzelli, Contributor
title: Greek Trials Turn Migrants Into ‘Smugglers’ and Minors Into Adults
content:
Crete, Greece — Crete’s courts are convicting shipwrecked people on the move as “smugglers” in trials lasting minutes, with lawyers documenting minors registered as adults and sentences reaching hundreds of years.




Eleftheria Iatraki lets her gaze wander along the walls of the room as she tells the story of Thalassa of Solidarity. The shelves are crowded with books, sewing machines, toys, and other objects. “We created this place as a space to meet each other through learning activities — sewing classes, language classes, computer classes,” she explains. She wears a black T-shirt reading “no one is illegal,” her elbows resting on the table that fills the small room where the collective carries out its activities.







Eleftheria Iatraki speaks with Unicorn Riot in the space where Thalassa of Solidarity holds its activities. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.







Through the glass door facing the street, the white facades of the buildings in central Heraklion, Crete’s regional capital, are visible.




Thalassa of Solidarity was founded in 2019 by local activists as an independent, self-funded space. Even then, Crete was a secondary destination for people on the move and refugees who had arrived in Greece 

through Turkey

, but there were no real spaces where local residents and communities on the move could meet each other. “The idea was to create situations where people could communicate with one another and identify common problems and struggles,” continues Eleftheria — a name that, fittingly, means “freedom” in Greek.




The collective has always provided social and legal support too, helping people navigate an often labyrinthine bureaucratic system. Consequently, as the migration route that has progressively made Crete Greece’s 

main entry point

 since 

2023

 became established, Thalassa of Solidarity expanded its scope of work.







The entrance to the Thalassa of Solidarity collective’s headquarters in central Heraklion, Crete. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.







Faced with the 

lack of adequate reception facilities

 on the island and authorities’ often repressive handling of arrivals, the collective began monitoring the informal centers where people are effectively detained upon landing. This work has brought into focus increasingly troubling mechanisms of criminalization.




“From the moment they arrive, people are isolated and all contact with the outside world is blocked,” Eleftheria says. “Everything is under the control of the police and the Coast Guard. Human needs, basic rights, and asylum requests are all completely subordinated to one absolute priority: finding the boat drivers, and charging them as smugglers.”







Eleftheria Iatraki, Michalis Markodimitrakis, and two other activists from the Thalassa of Solidarity collective speak with Unicorn Riot. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.







Activists from the collective Steki Metanaston, who are monitoring the situation in Chania, a city in the western part of the island, confirm this pattern. They describe how the search for boat drivers takes place during the custody phase at Agya, a former exhibition center used as a first-reception site.




“The very first step is the confiscation of cell phones,” they explain. “After that comes the so-called preliminary investigation, which consists of interrogations almost always conducted without interpreters and with extremely rough methods of communication.”




In this context, stripped of legal safeguards, police ultimately make an arbitrary designation: anyone who so much as touched the tiller or held a map is labeled a “smuggler,” with no verification of whether they drove the boat under threat or simply in an attempt to bring the group to safety — a charge that, once filed, can carry sentences of years or even decades in Greek courts.




Read Part 1

 |  

Read Part 2










People on the move who landed in Crete are transferred by the authorities to camps on mainland Greece for checks and registration in October 2025. On the ferry, they are cordoned off by police. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.










People on the move are transferred by the authorities from Crete to camps on mainland Greece in October 2025. On the ferry, they are surrounded by police and wear identification wristbands. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.













A group of people on the move who recently landed are transferred by ferry from Crete to camps on mainland Greece in October 2025, as a large number of police officers guard the perimeter. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.







A Legal Shield That Exists Only on Paper




“We have never seen this scale of mass criminalization before in Greece,” says Iliana Bompou, a lawyer with Equal Rights Beyond Borders, which has been providing free legal support to defendants in Crete’s courts since late 2025. “Not even during the daily landings on the Aegean islands during the 2015 so-called refugee crisis did we see numbers like this. Today in Crete, for every single boat that arrives, at least one so-called smuggler is identified.”




Alongside Equal Rights Beyond Borders’ work, Thalassa of Solidarity and other collectives and organizations have spent the past few years building a network that tracks the criminal proceedings against everyone arrested on arrival in Crete on smuggling charges.




Under Article 31 of the 1951 

Refugee Convention

, which Greece has ratified, signatory states cannot impose criminal penalties for irregular entry or stay on people coming from countries where their life or freedom is at risk. That provision was written into Greek national law as an 

exemption from criminal liability

 for those who facilitate their own entry, or that of family members, in seeking protection. But this safeguard appears to be systematically ignored in practice, and the scale of that failure is difficult to quantify.




According to the Border Violence Monitoring Network, an independent organization that spoke to Unicorn Riot, no official data is currently available on the number of people held in Greek prisons on people smuggling charges.







The Greek Coast Guard headquarters in Chania, Crete. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.







However, a 

report

 published in late 2025 by Legal Centre Lesvos and the Human Rights Legal Project Samos stated that more than 2,400 people were imprisoned on such charges as of September 2025 — a figure that made smuggling the second most common charge among Greece’s prison population.




“The most shocking thing is how the trials are conducted. It’s a farce,” says Ioanna Pavlou, another lawyer with Equal Rights Beyond Borders. Reports published by the 

Border Violence Monitoring Network

 and the collective 

50outofmany

 paint a stark picture of summary justice.







Ioanna Pavlou and Christina Svana, lawyers with Equal Rights Beyond Borders, speak with Unicorn Riot at the organization’s office in Athens, Greece.







In Chania, for instance, in a sample of roughly 120 cases monitored in 2025, 

96% of defendants

 had access only to court-appointed lawyers, who are frequently assigned just five minutes before the hearing begins. With no time to review the case file or consult with their client, the defense is almost always reduced to pushing for a plea deal — signed without the long-term consequences ever being made clear, including the automatic waiver of the right to appeal and to seek asylum.




Compounding this defense-side fragility is the sheer brevity of the hearings: trials last on average just seven to eight minutes, reducing criminal adjudication to a mere administrative formality.




That speed also translates into the total absence of any real evidentiary process. As detailed in the reports and confirmed by the Equal Rights Beyond Borders lawyers themselves, the boats’ passengers are almost never summoned to testify. Their initial statements are read into the record as nothing more than paper testimony, stripping the defense of its fundamental right to cross-examination. The result is “copy-paste” verdicts, in which the prosecution’s case is accepted uncritically while mitigating circumstances — or a state of necessity driven by survival or coercion — are systematically dismissed.




The outcome of this judicial machinery is reflected in the sheer severity of the sentences imposed. “If the consequence were a criminal record or a year in prison, that would already be serious. But here we’re talking about something very different,” Ioanna explains.




Because the Greek penal code multiplies the base sentence by the number of people transported, cumulative sentences on paper reach astronomical figures, with documented cases reaching 

300 years in prison

. Under Greek law, such sentences are capped at an effective maximum of 25 years. But the impact remains devastating: “People are barred from applying for asylum, with no alternative path to the documents needed to stay in Greece legally. The predictable outcome is that they end up arrested again for irregular stay.”




The Youngest Targets of the System




Another troubling element is the involvement of minors in these criminal proceedings. Out of a sample of 

102 cases

 monitored in 2025 by 50outofmany, 13 involved people under 18. And the same Equal Rights Beyond Borders lawyers report that, at present, they are handling exclusively cases involving minors.




The organization’s work on this front began after reports received while monitoring the Malakasa reception center near Athens, where the lawyers started hearing from guardians of several unaccompanied minors. The boys were stuck inside the camp because of a restraining order issued by a Crete court that blocked their transfer to dedicated protective facilities.




When the lawyers traveled to Chania to access the criminal case files, something disturbing emerged: minors are frequently registered as adults and funneled into criminal proceedings with none of the safeguards their age should trigger.




Among the most serious distortions found at the point of landing is authorities’ practice of ignoring or confiscating minors’ identity documents. The Equal Rights Beyond Borders lawyers describe the case of a young man whose ID was seized by the Coast Guard at the time of his arrest, with no confiscation record ever issued.




“He told every authority he encountered that the Coast Guard had taken his ID, and it was even entered into the court record,” they explain. “But the judge never ordered the document returned. He just moved on to the next question and ordered a radiological age assessment.”







A Greek Coast Guard patrol boat docked in the port of Heraklion on the Greek island of Crete. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.







The age-assessment procedure represents a further flaw in the system, since the practice adopted by Crete’s courts appears to rely almost exclusively on wrist X-rays — a method medical and human rights bodies 

have long criticized

 for its wide margin of error. Equal Rights Beyond Borders lawyers have raised serious doubts about the impartiality and rigor of the local forensic doctor, whose reports are routinely reduced to a single line — “the patient is over 19 years old” — with no methodology or margin of error specified, even when the judge explicitly requests this information.




Demonstrating just how unreliable these assessments are, in one case the organization followed, a radiological exam that had declared a young man an adult in Chania was repeated six months later at a hospital in Athens — this time showing he was just 16 years old.




According to the lawyers, the choice to prosecute the youngest is no accident. Instead, it conceals a deliberate strategy. “These are the people who are most alone, who have often already been victims of trafficking and forced labor for years in Libya before ever boarding a boat,” they explain. With no family members traveling alongside them and no knowledge of their own rights, minors become the ideal scapegoats for a propaganda machine that needs to produce a culprit at every landing.




According to local activists, this mass criminalization responds above all to political calculation and a deliberate strategy of deterrence.




Crete — an island of 

crucial economic weight

, with a major tourism sector and close political ties to Athens — categorically refuses to allow the construction of reception and identification centers, to avoid “reputational damage.” In this sense, the systematic arrests and trials send a clear message outward: anyone who tries to reach the island will find prison waiting.




This punitive approach seeps, unfiltered, into the courtrooms themselves, where the presumption of innocence gives way to openly ideological positions, and criminal justice becomes the operational arm of an ostentatious policy of deterrence.




Equal Rights Beyond Borders lawyers report that in a written opinion filed to justify the pretrial detention of a minor — not yet convicted — a prosecutor in Chania went so far as to put in writing that the boy had to face the consequences of his own actions: “He should have thought about that before coming to Greece. This is what happens when you cross the border.”







A group of people on the move who recently landed are transferred by ferry from Crete to camps on mainland Greece by bus as a large number of police officers guard the perimeter. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Tens of Thousands Protest in India Against Modi Government’s Voter Roll Purges
content:
At least 7,000 people in New Delhi were detained on Saturday.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Tens of thousands of people in India have taken to the streets in recent days to protest the deletion of 130 million names from the voter rolls, a large majority of which are believed to be opposed to Narendra Modi’s ruling BJP party. The demonstrations, joined by leaders from India’s opposition parties, are being led by students and the youth-led “Cockroach” movement. Tens of thousands of security forces, including paramilitary and police, were out on the streets over the weekend cracking down on the uprising, detaining protesters en masse, including lawyers, journalists and protest leaders.

The demonstrations “represent an outpouring of anger, of frustration at what many Indians feel is the fact that their democracy has been taken away,” says Shoaib Daniyal, political editor of Scroll, who was arrested on Saturday along with 7,000 other protesters. He points out that “the deletions have affected Muslims far more than they have affected other Indians.”

On Monday, in one of largest recent protests in India’s capital of New Delhi, India’s main opposition leader, Rahul Gandhi of the Congress Party, led a march to the Supreme Court of India. “This march has become a people’s march, with all of them heading towards this constitutional authority, which they feel should safeguard the rights of Indian people, especially this very basic right to vote,” says Jahnavi Sen, managing editor of The Wire.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

ANJALI KAMAT: In India, the right-wing government of Narendra Modi is facing its biggest challenge yet in 12 years in power, as tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets to protest what they call vote theft. At issue is the deletion of 130 million names from the voter rolls, and the vast majority of those deletions are believed to be opposed to Prime Minister Modi’s ruling BJP party.

The protests are being led by students and the youth Cockroach movement and joined by leaders from the opposition parties. They’re demanding the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, and an overhaul of the electoral system. The Cockroach movement started after the chief justice of India’s Supreme Court compared unemployed youth to cockroaches earlier this year.

Today, in one of largest recent protests in India’s capital of New Delhi, India’s main opposition leader, Rahul Gandhi of the Congress Party, is leading a march to the Supreme Court of India. Speaking to reporters earlier today, Gandhi reiterated the call for the election commissioner to resign.

RAHUL GANDHI: Narendra Modi is blocking the whole town, is putting 30,000-40,000 police people outside. For what? Because the opposition is asking one question: Prove to us that you have not cheated in the election. Prove to us that you’ve not cheated in the election.

AMY GOODMAN: The Modi government put New Delhi in lockdown ahead of Saturday’s protests, canceling trains to the city, shutting down metro stations, even suspending mobile internet in large parts of Delhi. Tens of thousands of security forces, including paramilitary and police, were mobilized across the city, and at least 7,000 people were detained Saturday alone, including protest leaders, lawyers and journalists. This is a protester speaking to reporters from inside a van where he was detained.

PROTESTER: [translated] The Modi government is scared of us. That is why we have been picked up from halfway. We didn’t even know where they were trying to bring us. [in English] This is just fear. And they are afraid of us because they have done something wrong, and you cannot do something wrong with the people of this country, man.

AMY GOODMAN: Several Cockroach movement leaders were also arrested right off the plane as they arrived in Delhi for the protest Saturday morning. After being released the next morning, Saurav Das, one of the leaders of the Cockroach People’s Party, vowed protests would continue.

SAURAV DAS: The protests are on. The protests will go on. [translated] The youth of the country have woken up. The youth of the country are asking for accountability. The peaceful protests will go on until they fix accountability. And now the protests will not only happen in Delhi, but in the whole country.

ANJALI KAMAT: On Saturday, the United Nations human rights spokesperson expressed concern over the mass detentions in India. In response, the Indian Mission in Geneva responded on X that the U.N.’s concerns were, quote, “misplaced and constitute an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India,” asserting that “India is the world’s largest democracy.”

AMY GOODMAN: For more, we’re joined by two guests in Delhi. Jahnavi Sen is the managing editor of The Wire, an independent news website in India. And joining us from the streets of New Delhi, Shoaib Daniyal, political editor of Scroll, another Indian independent news website.

Shoaib, you were arrested on Saturday. You are out now. Describe what’s happening in the streets and why these massive protests are happening, and also the response to thousands being arrested.

SHOAIB DANIYAL: The protests are happening over one issue, Amy, which is the rigging of the voter rolls that Anjali pointed out. A hundred and thirty million Indians have got kicked off the voter rolls in a process that could, at best, be described as arbitrary. The deletions have affected Muslims far more than they have affected other Indians, so there is a very, very racial element in what this program represents. And these protests are coming after months of this exercise going on, and they represent an outpouring of anger, of frustration at what many Indians feel is the fact that their democracy has been taken away. We fought really hard for our democracy in 1947, and it feels like the right to vote has been taken away, and really everything else is downstream from that.

On Saturday, we saw something unprecedented in India. Delhi was locked down, as you very correctly phrased it. There were tens of thousands of policemen, paramilitary forces on the streets. The entire city was barricaded. The entire city center was barricaded. Internet was shut off. The police unleashed violence on these — you know, most of the protesters are actually kids. It’s very much a Gen Z protest in many ways. The bulk of the protesters are young kids. I just met a couple of kids who are 18, who are in first year in college. They’ve come here. And again, they were brutalized. They were arrested. This happened yesterday and the day before.

And today, we’ve had a kind of turning of the tide, so to speak, where the Congress Party, which is in the main opposition, has actually put its bulk, has actually put its strength, got its strength out onto the street. And we’ve seen some pretty remarkable scenes of — the very same parts of Delhi which were completely barricaded, which were completely blocked off, which were completely empty, they’re filled with protesters today. And the police today have not or cannot do anything about it.

ANJALI KAMAT: I want to bring Jahnavi Sen into the conversation, managing editor of The Wire, another independent news website in India. Jahnavi, you’ve also been out in the streets. Can you explain why protesters are marching to the Supreme Court of India right now?

JAHNAVI SEN: This began by a call from the leaders of the opposition who wanted to submit a memorandum to the chief justice of India about their concerns with what’s happening within the Election Commission of India. And as you were mentioning earlier, you know, one of the chief demands — though, of course, not the only demand — has been the resignation of the chief election commissioner, and the opposition has been trying to go to different constitutional authorities about this. They first tried to meet the Election Commission itself. They were underway. They have had a meeting with the president of India, Droupadi Murmu. And then they wanted to go to the chief justice of India, who sits in the Supreme Court, to submit a memorandum to him. He has denied them a meeting. And that is why now this march has become a people’s march, with all of them heading towards this constitutional authority, which they feel should safeguard the rights of Indian people, especially this very basic right to vote.

ANJALI KAMAT: And, Jahnavi, there’s also concerns about excessive brutality from police and other security forces who were on the streets over the weekend, particularly on Saturday. Can you talk a little bit about this? And you were on the streets, as well. What you witnessed?

JAHNAVI SEN: No, absolutely. I think it was, in fact, both on Saturday and Sunday, very heavy-handed behavior from the police, police and the paramilitary of different kinds, detaining people, putting them into police buses. And then, they were — several people were hit. They were mistreated. Women were manhandled. There were also allegation — not even not just allegations; we saw this happen — women protesters being taken into buses where there were no women constables, which is illegal, women protesters being detained after dark, which is also illegal. And then, another tactic that the police has now perfected is to detain protesters and then to drive them around in these buses for hours and drop them off in extremely far-flung corners of the city, from where it’s very difficult to make it back. Often it’s difficult to contact people that you know. They have also tried to take people’s phones and make them delete footage.

One of the very concerning things that we’ve been seeing is also the detentions of journalists. You were mentioning how Shoaib, too, was detained. On Saturday, my colleagues and I almost faced a similar situation. And so many journalists, both yesterday and today, despite wearing press cards, saying again and again that they’re from the media and they’re here to cover what’s happening, have been treated in this way, as have senior leaders of opposition parties. There were very stark and troubling visuals yesterday of a member of Parliament from one of the left parties, the CPIM, John Brittas, who was — who said he was pinned down by paramilitary personnel inside one of these detention buses, and then had trouble breathing. He had to be taken to the hospital.

So, really, yes, we have been seeing very heavy-handed behavior on the side of the police and the paramilitary forces. And they seem to be able to do this despite the Supreme Court having a hearing early yesterday morning, where they said that, you know, no illegal detentions should take place; journalists and lawyers doing their job should not be detained. Despite that, we have not seen a change in that behavior over Sunday, as well.

ANJALI KAMAT: Shoaib, I wanted to get your reaction to what the Indian Mission in Geneva posted on X in response to criticism from the U.N. Human Rights Office expressing concern over the mass detention of protesters. And the response began by saying, “India is the world’s largest democracy,” and “the right to peaceful assembly is guaranteed by our Constitution and safeguarded by robust institutions, an independent judiciary and a free media.” Do the people on the streets agree with this?

SHOAIB DANIYAL: I think now increasingly, what was a banal fact about India is now not true. And this is exactly what the protest’s about. We’re seeing, I think — and I think this is true for democracies across the world. We have — India still maintains a veneer of democracy. We’re still wearing the clothes of democracy. But inside, there is something rotten. So, elections are held. The elections are multiparty elections. On paper, everybody has a right to contest. But, of course, we are seeing right from things which are actually legal, which I think are there in other democracies, like the U.S. also, the fact that the BJP has so much money. So, even if everything were above the board, the BJP just starts, you know, a hundred meters ahead on the starting line when the race starts, just on money. They have so much money. But they also now have institutions.

You know, you asked why people are marching to the Supreme Court today. Now, these voter roll deletions were contested in the Supreme Court as they were happening, and the Supreme Court just did not do anything. It spun this incredibly legal, complex lawyer’s web, but eventually it did not do anything to stop it. It gave a carte blanche to the Modi government. And there is a lot of anger actually on the streets against the Supreme Court. As you pointed out, you know, this is one of the greatest ironies, is that the Cockroach movement actually arises from a stray comment made by the chief justice of India. So, there is anger against the Supreme Court for not doing its job. The Supreme Court is the guardian of the Constitution. It’s meant to protect our rights. And again, like in other democracies — I think American viewers would also empathize — the Supreme Court is just not seen to be doing their job. And the SIR, the voter roll revision, is seen to be a really egregious part of that. So, in a way, this march to the Supreme Court is really, really interesting, because Rahul Gandhi and other protesters are trying to politicize the Supreme Court’s role in this matter.

AMY GOODMAN: You know, it’s really interesting, what’s happening around the world, Jahnavi. You have these mass protests in France, led by the youth, around issues of affordability and education. You have mass protests in Spain that have led the prime minister to call for a snap election November 29th, and he’s dissolved the parliament. And now you have these mass protests in India. I’m wondering what you think this means for the Modi government.

JAHNAVI SEN: I think these protests are going to be impossible for the government to ignore, even though it seems to be trying really hard. All the messaging we’ve seen coming from leaders of Modi’s party — that’s the Bharatiya Janata Party — have been attempts to show that this is just the opposition trying to get — trying to make this an anarchic situation, that they don’t have an agenda, that they’re just, you know, trying to create chaos. But it’s not sitting. And I think one of the reasons why we also saw the targeting of journalists was that they realized that building that narrative is not working.

We have a chief election commissioner who faced some pretty damning — a pretty damning exposé in a very big newspaper about the way he was functioning. And since then, we have heard absolutely nothing from him. We don’t know where he is. And, of course, this is in a country where the prime minister has not given a press conference ever since he was elected as the prime minister of this country, so perhaps the chief election commissioner is simply following in his footsteps by quickly disappearing from public sight when things become a little difficult.

But I think, yes, this tactic of ignoring, this tactic of trying to suppress narratives and suppress people has not been working. We are seeing how today so many more people have gathered. The rally that Shoaib is at right now is —

AMY GOODMAN: We have 10 seconds.

JAHNAVI SEN: — very, very large. And so, I think, you know, no matter what narrative they try to build, this is not going to go away.

AMY GOODMAN: Jahnavi Sen of The Wire, Shoaib Daniyal from the Scroll, both independent news websites in India. Daniyal was one of those thousands arrested on Saturday. And we’ll continue to cover these protests.

Coming up, it’s Indigenous Peoples’ Day. We’ll speak with the Native American activist Leonard Peltier, who spent almost 50 years behind bars. Stay with us.

AMY GOODMAN: Sonny Singh in our Democracy Now! studio.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: labor4pal
title: Trump Wanted Minnesota 15 Case to Be Another Prairieland. Instead, Twin Cities Rallied Behind Anti-ICE Activists. (The Intercept)
content:
The mainstream of Minnesota’s left-of-center politics — including unions, the backbone of Democratic power — are behind the radical left.

Demonstrators rally and march during an “ICE Out” day of protest on Jan. 23, 2026, in Minneapolis.Photo: Brandon Bell/Getty Images

As the Trump administration unveiled an indictment earlier this year against 15 anti-ICE activists, many of whom identify as radicals, for purportedly tormenting federal agents last winter, a top U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement official took the podium.

There were two types of protests, said Homeland Security Investigations special agent in charge Michael McCarthy, who oversaw the ICE agents in a St. Paul, Minnesota, field office who conducted the investigation.

“Peaceful protest is a protected right, and a cornerstone of our democracy,” said McCarthy. “When protest turns into rioting, violence or criminal activity, it becomes unlawful and it will not be tolerated.”

McCarthy’s comments stood in stark contrast with ICE’s record in Minneapolis, where a federal judge had been forced to issue an injunction to stop federal agents from pepper-spraying and arresting peaceful protesters during their enforcement blitz, dubbed Operation Metro Surge.

Legal experts, too, had criticisms of the indictment: The Justice Department, one pointed out, had concocted a federal conspiracy out of what would normally be misdemeanor charges.

In the months since, criticisms of the case have only grown louder. Court filings revealed that McCarthy’s agents secretly infiltrated groups that preach nonviolence, including labor unions and nonprofits. They also wielded subpoenas in a fruitless hunt for financiers of “domestic terrorism,” taking a cue from President Donald Trump’s National Security Presidential Memorandum-7 labeling swaths of the far left as terrorists.

The Trump administration has won some success in going after left-wing protesters under NSPM-7, but the Minneapolis case is proving to be more challenging.

In other prosecutions targeting activists, like the Prairieland case in Texas, mainstream groups have shied away from supporting the defendants. In Minnesota, though, groups once wary of being associated with the 15 defendants, many of whom are self-described anarchists, have rallied to their side.

Powerful labor unions that make up the backbone of the state’s progressive movement have raised funds on behalf of the defendants, incensed at the infiltration from federal undercover agents. Rather than dividing and conquering the left, the case has united it.

“They’re trying to split the movement and absolutely failing.”

Supporters of the defendants, who have collectively come to be known as the Minneapolis or Minnesota 15, recently packed a bowling alley for a fundraiser. On October 3, hundreds of labor union members marched through downtown Minneapolis, demanding that the charges against the activists be dropped.

Meanwhile, the defendants themselves have so far mounted a unified, joint defense; none of them have taken a plea deal.

“They’re trying to split the movement and absolutely failing,” said Emmett James Doyle, a defendant in the case. “There’s been just complete solidarity behind us from basically every sector of Twin Cities life.”

ICE Shooting in NYC Inflames Mamdani’s Policing Problem

ICE Raid on Ilhan Omar Shows How Dangerous Two Years of Flailing Trump Could Get

Susan Collins-Aligned Super PAC Buys Attack Ads in Portland… Oregon

Doyle’s ruddy face and wild beard would have been at home in Big Bill Haywood’s Industrial Workers of the World a century ago. By day he’s a union carpenter, by night he plucks a banjo and sings songs about America’s radical past.

Federal prosecutors allege that he brought those songs to life on the streets of Minneapolis.

In a 94-page indictment, prosecutors claim that Doyle and the other 14 defendants were members or associates of a group called Direct Action Minnesota that “infiltrated and exploited lawful protests” to target ICE.

Prosecutors painted a dark picture of DAMN. Their tactics allegedly included blocking access to a federal building used by ICE with disabled cars or trailers, bringing shields and gas masks to protests, and, in one instance, following an ICE agent across state lines to his home in Wisconsin.

Government attorneys also leaned heavily on the defendants’ comments to each other in private messages about their frustration with more mainstream protesters and the need for “militant” action.

Despite the prosecutors’ claims about rioting and violence at the June press conference, however, the top federal prosecutor in Minnesota, U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen, was unable to identify injuries to federal officers when reporters pressed him.

There are committed anarchists among the defendants charged in the indictment, several defendants told The Intercept, but there was little difference between what they did and what thousands of Minneapolis residents did during the federal immigration crackdown.

Ordinary Minnesotans walked frigid streets with whistles dangling from their necks to alert their neighbors about ICE raids. They sent license plate numbers of federal vehicles to Signal group chats. Members of rapid-response networks trailed suspected agents in their cars.

The indictment is replete with examples of protesters trailing agents in vehicles, a tactic known as “commuting.” Yet that was a tactic so widely employed by rapid-response groups in Minneapolis that it was even adopted by a congressional candidate in a suburban district who recently won his Democratic primary.

“I think there are people in the government who really do believe that there is like a small cabal of people who are fomenting all the dissent, and if you get rid of them, that everyone will be quiet,” Doyle said. “And that’s fundamentally wrong.”

Doyle, like the four other defendants interviewed by The Intercept, declined to discuss the specific allegations in the indictment, citing advice from his attorney.

“They’re just trying to find people to make examples of.”

Still, another defendant, Treasure Thoreson, was adamant that none of the defendants ever used violence. Thoreson is a special education teacher whose elementary school’s lanyard was still dangling from her neck during a recent interview. She believes the group was targeted because of its radical views.

“They clearly had people that they had identified as problematic in some way and have been trying to tie these people to leading the resistance,” Thoreson said. “They can’t indict 100,000 people, so really, they’re just trying to find people to make examples of.”Read our complete coverageChilling Dissent

Thoreson said she has received steady support from her teachers union since the indictment.

She and many other defendants believe the charges against them are a way of attacking Minnesota’s powerful labor movement. By the count of defendants who spoke to The Intercept, at least 11 of the 15 have been involved in union organizing.

The internal Homeland Security Investigations files unearthed by the defense team lend credibility to this theory. Undercover agents attended an organizing meeting at the United Labor Centre, a building that houses multiple unions. HSI, the investigative wing of ICE, also subpoenaed the financial records of the SEIU and the Communications Workers of America as part of an overlapping probe into “domestic terror financing.”

Several defendants interviewed by The Intercept were amused at the idea that they were receiving funding from mainstream organizations. They have long lobbed critiques at the labor movement’s institutional core from its fringes.

After some initial hesitance, unions and nonprofit groups responded in force to the case. Days after the indictment, some labor groups signed onto a joint statement denouncing the charges. After a court filing from the defendants revealed the subpoenas of the unions’ financing, more labor organizations raised their voices.

“Generally speaking, the labor movement is awfully conservative — too conservative — on issues like this, and can sometimes be scared out of solidarity with people who are fighting back,” said Kieran Knutson, the president of CWA Local 7250 in Minneapolis.

More unions rallied, Knutson said, as it became clear that prosecutors could not point to examples of physical harm, as union locals pressured statewide organizations, and as the defendants themselves articulated why the case was important.

“These are active people in the labor movement, and I think in many ways people see them as an expression of the movement as a whole,” Knutson said. “And these charges were an attack on the movement as a whole.”

Knutson said he knows the value of solidarity: In 1993, he was charged with assaulting a man wearing neo-Nazi patches during an antiracist demonstration on the University of Minnesota campus, according to news reports from the time. He was acquitted with the help of attorney Keith Ellison, who later went on to win election as the state’s attorney general.

“I know what it’s like to have the weight of the charges just hanging over you,” Knutson said.

The leading candidate in the Hennepin County Attorney race, state Rep. Cedrick Frazier, who also works as a lawyer for labor union Education Minnesota, told The Intercept in a recent interview that the charges should be dismissed.

“I think they’re trying to, for lack of a better word, ‘Trump’ up some charges to continue his pursuit of retribution against Minnesota,” said Frazier. “I mean, look, they don’t like labor groups.”

A broad coalition of labor groups including the state AFL-CIO endorsed an October 3 rally and march in support of the defendants, another sign that skepticism of the case has gone mainstream.

Hundreds of janitors, teachers, public employees, and hospitality workers joined the march, said Isaac Sant, a defendant and longtime labor organizer. He said seeing them on the streets was “humbling.”

Sant recently joined defendants from other cases with political overtones, including Prairieland, to form what they are dubbing the NSPM-7 Defendants Union.

“I can only speak for myself, but I don’t have any problem linking my case to the Prairieland cases. I think what happened to them was a travesty and a miscarriage of justice,” Sant said. “I think it’s very important that we stand in solidarity with people who are in that position, and especially with people who are getting railroaded even worse than we are.”

author: Mada Masr
title: Scores killed, Sudan announces an investigation, Egypt a new phase of anti-illegal gold mining campaign
content:
In the first official comment since a mine near the Sudanese-Egyptian border was bombed on Saturday killing scores of miners, Sudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council 

issued

 a statement on Monday to mourn the souls of “Sudanese citizens who lost their lives in the painful incident involving a number of Sudanese miners in the border area between Sudan and the Arab Republic of Egypt.”

 




Without providing further details on when, how or where the Sudanese nationals died, the executive authority that has ruled Sudan since 2019 announced that a fact-finding committee composed of members of the Sudanese Public Prosecution as well as relevant judicial and security authorities would be formed to investigate the matter. 




The council underlined that “leadership in both brotherly countries,” referring to Egypt, have “remained in continuous communication immediately after the incident occurred, ensuring the protection of lives, preserving the relationship between the two brotherly peoples, understanding the details of the incident and sharing the facts with public opinion.” 




Later on Monday evening, the Egyptian Armed Forces spokesperson released a statement announcing the implementation of the “third phase of the large-scale campaign to confront illegal gold mining in the Eastern Desert, after dropping warning leaflets on criminal elements to impose full sovereignty within the borders of the Egyptian state and protect its national resources and wealth.” 




The spokesperson similarly underlined “the depth of ties” that unite the Egyptian and Sudanese nations. 




Since the incident occurred on Saturday, Mada Masr has spoken to miners, paramedics, security officials and traders at the mining camp, which they say sits just inside the northern border of the Halayeb and Shalateen Triangle, to understand what happened. 




One of them is Abdel Bagy Nour Eddin, a shift worker at the Jabal al-Uqaydat gold mines in the Shamal al-Wadi area, north of the Halayeb Triangle. 

He told Mada Masr he was at his work site when he heard warplanes flying at low altitude on Saturday morning

.




Then the mining site began to be bombed. Missiles struck the mine’s drilling sites, ore processing areas and the miners’ living quarters, triggering panic and a stampede among the miners at the site, he said.




Nour Eddin’s account was corroborated by three other eyewitnesses: Al-Taher Mohamed Ahmed, a generator technician working in the area; Al-Haj Idriss Yagoub, a trader that supplies water and food to miners from the Ansary market, in Sudan’s Ratag locality south of Halayeb; and Osman al-Gassem, a site supervisor and owner of a drilling well. 




They describe “successive waves” of strikes that made it difficult to find cover. 




The site of the strikes. Courtesy: Al-Fadel al-Rifaey’s mobile phone. Picture taken by his friend.




While many of the miners fled in panic, causing a near stampede, according to Nour Eddin, several others rushed toward the tunnels in order to rescue those injured.




Among them was Yagoub. As he approached the blast site, he saw burning machinery and people among the rubble, some dead and others in need of urgent medical help.




Ahmed, the generator operator, said a power outage in the tunnels after the explosion made movement to provide first aid to the injured and the transport of bodies to higher ground difficult.




The attack, Gassem said, came without warning, leaving workers no time to evacuate before the missiles hit.




While repeated campaigns have been carried out in recent months to push back miners in the area, which include people from Sudan, the Central African Republic and Chad, all of the sources that spoke to Mada Masr said that the scale of this attack goes far beyond anything that has happened before. 




The final toll of dead and wounded remains unclear. Miners in the area say some workers fled to the mountains after the strikes. The dispersal of workers across widely separated sites makes it harder to account for the missing and determine how many people remained within the strike zone.




However, Al-Fadel al-Rifaey, a paramedic who helped count the dead and prepare their bodies for burial at the mine, put the death toll at over 100 and added that initial estimates of the number of wounded stands at between 95 and 115 people.




Preparations for burials.

 Courtesy: Al-Fadel al-Rifaey’s mobile phone. Picture taken by his friend on October 10, between 12 pm and 1 pm




Rifaey told Mada Masr that most of the bodies recovered at the site of the attack had been disfigured by the strikes and some could not be identified by their facial features. Those involved in counting the dead had to rely on personal belongings found, including mobile phones, ID cards and pieces of clothing, to establish their identities and record their names.




Volunteers from among the workers and miners helped prepare the bodies and the burial site, which is on the outskirts of the area near the mine. They recorded their names, burial locations and grave markers to preserve their identities and prevent information about them from being lost, Rifaey added.




The counting and burial operations unfolded amid grief and shock among workers as the number of injured continued to be monitored and as more injured miners arrived at assembly points around the mine for medical care, he said. The death toll could still rise as efforts continue to account for the victims, verify their identities and establish the fate of workers who were inside the extractions sites when the raid hit.




In the wake of the attack, miners tried to transport the injured to the nearest facilities that would serve them for treatment. That meant a seven-hour drive across the border to the Ansary Mining Market. 




Adam Ismail, a lorry driver who transports stone, was one of those who pitched in. He told Mada Masr that he transferred around 40 wounded people away from the mine immediately after the airstrikes. Those he transported had lost limbs and sustained shrapnel wounds in the attack.




Nour Eddin told Mada Masr he drove some of the injured to reach the Ansary Mining Market in Sudan, navigating through desert tracks and mountainous terrain interspersed with valleys and mining sites, routes used by trucks and vehicles traveling between the mining sites and the markets. 




A medical source on the Sudanese side of the border monitoring the reception, at Ansary market, of casualties from the strike told Mada Masr that 96 injured people had been documented by medical staff in the area as of Sunday afternoon. Some sustained critical injuries and were transferred to medical facilities in River Nile State’s Abu Hamad and Atbara, and Red Sea State’s Oseif, depending on the severity of their conditions and the capacity of the facilities to provide treatment. Several require urgent blood transfusions because of severe bleeding and injuries caused by shrapnel and projectiles, the source added. Emergency response efforts were hampered by the site’s remoteness, the sheer scale of casualties and the need to treat multiple cases all requiring immediate intervention.




Some of the injured died while being transported for initial treatment because of the severity of their wounds, the source said. 




Medical tallies continue to change based on the arrival of additional casualties and on updates to records of the injured and dead, he said, adding that critically injured patients continue to be transferred to medical facilities in nearby towns, while first aid is being provided to those who could be reached at the site.




A Sudanese security source told Mada Masr an initial assessment indicates that warplanes carried out an airstrike on the mine, damaging mining infrastructure and equipment at the site.




This is not the first time the area has been targeted. 

In June, warplanes 

targeted

 the Jabal al-Uqaydat and the nearby Jabal al-Ahmar mining sites in Egypt, which was followed by the deployment of ground forces and the closure of mining sites, according to eyewitnesses.

 A Sudanese medical source told Mada Masr at the time that 23 people were killed as a result of the strikes.




Jabal al-Uqaydat and Jabal al-Ahmar have drawn thousands of Sudanese and Egyptian miners, traders and laborers over the years. They are part of a wider border region whose sphere of movement, economic influence and point at which mining activity begins starts inside Sudanese territory and extends into Egypt by around 50-70 km. 




The area has witnessed a gold rush in recent years, most clearly seen in the Sudanese border locality of Ratag, which has turned into a sprawling commercial hub as a result of the gold trade flowing through the area. 




But the area also suffers from lack of infrastructure, medical supplies and security presence. This has given way to competition among tribal communities seeking to control access to mines, trade routes and markets, which has prompted Sudanese authorities at points to step in to calm tensions. 




While Egypt has worked to formalize its control over the surge 

in informal mining

, which followed the 2011 revolution, in the deserts around Aswan by carrying out repeated security raids on artisanal mines, it has also pointed to the lax security presence on the border with Sudan as a national security issue.

 




But for Nour Eddin, there was no security rationale for Saturday’s strikes. 




“The site had no signs of a military presence or targets,” Nour Eddin says. “What happened was a direct strike on civilian workers looking to earn a living.”

The post 

Scores killed, Sudan announces an investigation, Egypt a new phase of anti-illegal gold mining campaign

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

.
