author: JoEllen Chernow
title: What If We Organized Survivors of Sexual Violence?
content:
Every few months America discovers another “monster.” A celebrity. A billionaire. A politician. A religious leader. A professor. A CEO.

The details differ, but the story doesn’t: rape survivors risk everything revealing years of abuse, followed by a burst of public outrage and demands for accountability.

Survivors of Jeffrey Epstein told us about a global rape and sex-trafficking network in which young people were abused and exploited by some of the world’s wealthiest and most influential men. For decades, survivors were ignored, disbelieved, and failed by the institutions around them. Newly released files corroborating their horror stories have resulted in zero US criminal arrests and little tangible accountability.

The #MeToo movement was supposed to interrupt this cycle. For a brief moment in 2017, it seemed possible that we could stop treating each “scandal” as an isolated incident and confront the systems connecting them. Instead, less than three months after the hashtag went viral, the press was full of opinion pieces about how it had all “gone too far.” The backlash flipped #MeToo into #NotAllMen. Outrage faded into fatalism, denial, and eventually business as usual.

As a rape survivor, community activist, and labor organizer, I call bullshit.

The problem isn’t that we keep “discovering” abusive men. It’s that we keep refusing to look at the underlying systems that reproduce sexual violence. Instead, we focus on finding, exposing, and punishing the monster du jour (or not) and then wait for the next one.

What we haven’t built is survivor power. Survivors are a constituency with the potential to change the social, political, and material conditions that enable violence and produce abuses of power.

Survivor power is not simply inviting us to the table or ensuring we are represented in leadership. It begins when we invite survivors to bring their full selves. Survivor power is built in the movement by moving from isolation to connection, from private shame to shared analysis, and from shared analysis to collective action. And because sexual violence is enabled by unequal distributions of power, survivor power means changing the basic conditions that make people vulnerable to violence in the first place: economic precarity, workplace exploitation, racism, misogyny, housing insecurity, and isolation.

We use the term power-based violence more than gender-based or sexual violence with survivors. It shifts our focus from seemingly separate forms of harm toward the throughline that links rape and domestic violence to workplace sexual harassment and coercion to the daily intimidation of strangers shouting obscenities and catcalls.

Survivor power is the power to imagine and build what does not yet exist.

More than 90 percent of adult rape victims are women and over 80 percent of survivors under the age of 18 are girls. Of every 100 survivors, 98 of them are raped by men. The vast majority of male survivors are also assaulted by men. Abusers are almost never strangers.

Sexual abuse and harassment aren’t isolated incidents just because they happen behind closed doors (or on private islands). They are expressions of ideology–a structural pattern of male power and control that reproduces itself from the intimate to the institutional and beyond.

Violence–and the ever-present threat of it–shapes where women go, whom they trust, what jobs they take, how they move through public space, and hundreds of other daily micro-calculations about their bodies and lives. Criminalized survivor and Chicago abolitionist organizer Monica Cosby maps out these similarities in the reframing of State Power and Control Wheel tracing how dynamics familiar from domestic violence–coercion, isolation, surveillance, economic control, threats, and violence–are also wielded through institutions and the state.

Yet we continue funding systems designed primarily to (inadequately) respond to violence while dramatically underinvesting in the people and strategies capable of changing the conditions that produce it. In 2026, the Violence Against Women Act and related sexual and gender-based violence programs received roughly $720 million–less than the cost of the White House renovation. Within these limited resources, funding overwhelmingly flows toward what happens after the harm is done.

The state’s narrow mandate to identify, prosecute and remove the “monster” has failed to make us safe. Only a tiny fraction of sexual assaults result in prosecution, while an estimated 95% of incarcerated women have themselves experienced interpersonal violence. That is not an argument for putting more people in prison. It is an indictment of a system that has made punishment our primary measure of prevention and accountability while doing remarkably little to change the societal conditions that produce violence in the first place.

And, survivors are already in your organizing spaces. The question is whether they can bring their full selves and experiences.

What we’re left with is a collective shrug and a wearied acceptance that maybe misogyny is just too big to fail. The carousel of “scandals” spins so fast it begins to feel inevitable – too vast to confront, too entrenched to interrupt, too powerful to stop. That sense of inevitability is part of what keeps us spinning. We are stuck because we have invested so deeply in systems organized around individual perpetrators that we struggle to imagine how to build systems organized around survivors and collective safety. What would it actually mean to center survivors–not symbolically, not after we have been harmed, but structurally?

A basic organizing tenet is that power protects itself, unless and until it is forced not to. Three decades as a labor and community organizer shaped how I understood my assault and healing. Organizing taught me to ask questions like: How does power operate? Who benefits from the status quo? What systems allow harm to continue?

I benefited from privilege and access very few survivors experience. My father was friends with a senior Chicago detective, so word spread to “treat me like their daughter.” DNA from my rape kit was tested within ten days. Investigators returned my calls, kept me informed, and prioritized my case. Ultimately, a serial rapist went to prison. By conventional measures, justice was served. At the time, I understood this as the system working.

Years later, I understand it differently. I was watching the state unevenly distribute protection, deciding implicitly and explicitly whose safety mattered. As a college-educated white woman raped by a Black stranger on a dark, empty street, I fit neatly into the mythology of the “perfect victim,” while my rapist fit just as neatly into its racist counterpart.

At Survivors Know, we start by talking about power. Treating sexual violence as a private burden obscures its root causes and purpose. That narrows our response to managing symptoms by helping people survive violence rather than changing the systems that produce it.

We use the term power-based violence more than gender-based or sexual violence with survivors. It shifts our focus from seemingly separate forms of harm toward the throughline that links rape and domestic violence to workplace sexual harassment and coercion to the daily intimidation of strangers shouting obscenities and catcalls. By listening to and centering survivors, we’ve built on a framework that examines how power and control are asserted, maintained, justified, and normalized. When we extend this understanding beyond interpersonal harm we can see those same dynamics of power and control operating at a structural level.

The circumstances and scale are different, but the mechanisms can be hauntingly familiar: fear, isolation, coercion, forced dependence, surveillance, and impunity. That lens helps us understand what is happening around us now–from the expansion of ICE and its enforcement power to the broader authoritarian project reshaping our policies and public life.

When violence is understood as a problem of power rather than individual pathology, survivors can move from carrying private shame to building collective change.

One place where we are experimenting with what that looks like is the Reimagining Safety & Justice Cohort. The cohort brings together frontline anti-violence workers (social workers, hotline responders, case managers, circle keepers, advocates and survivors themselves) to develop and launch non-carceral responses to power-based violence. Over several months, they learn from one another, map systems of power, explore healing-centered and abolitionist frameworks, and transform their ideas into tangible projects.

This August, they presented what they had built over four months:

Grief circles created by and for Black trans survivors; youth-led sex education responding to community violence; young men organizing other young men to interrupt gender-based violence; a survivor-designed fund treating money as a question of power and redistribution; a project using pop culture and music to challenge the normalization of rape culture; survivor-led evaluation of programs serving queer survivors of childhood sexual assault; and nail sets for survivors, pairing one-on-one connection with the idea that survival and “luxury” belong together.

This is the transformative power of organizing survivors to come together and create forms of safety that our existing systems have conditioned us not to imagine.

As Cierra Olivia Thomas Williams, Survivors Know board member and Director of Nothing Without Us Collective, puts it:

Conflict, when held with purpose, becomes the uplift. When systems tighten around us, we rise through collective resistance. We have been here before, and before, and before. Together, we create the conditions for transformation, even when the process feels impossibly slow or invisible. The unseen labor of your care work is snowmelt. A trickle becomes a river. A river becomes an ocean. From an ocean comes life. Every story circle, every person now safe is an act of creation. As the political storm rages and policies strip our communities bare, rise slowly, carry memory. Our work takes disruption, pressure, and persistence. It takes time measured in layers. To survivors, to movement makers, my message to you is to remember we are tectonic. Be the Mountain.

Our progressive movement has a lot of catching up to do.

A lasting and welcome impact of #MeToo has been a shift toward believing survivors. Now we need to build survivor power.

Collective advocacy by Epstein survivors helped force rare bipartisan congressional action after years of reporting and political pressure. That matters. But much of the public attention remains fixated on who is “on the list”–individual perpetrators, celebrities, and political scandal–rather than the systems of wealth, access, institutional protection, and impunity that allowed abuse to continue for decades. Survivor testimony can expose power without redistributing it.

Survivors are not a niche group. We are one of the largest–and least organized–constituencies in America. More than half of women and nearly one in three men have experienced sexual violence. That does not mean survivors share a political analysis–or even the same understanding of what happened to us. That is precisely why organizing matters.

And, survivors are already in your organizing spaces. The question is whether they can bring their full selves and experiences. Organizing survivors does not always mean creating a separate survivor space. It means creating opportunities for people already in our movements to name how violence and power have shaped their lives, connect those experiences to broader systems, and act together to change them.

There is something powerful about connecting personal transformation to structural organizing. Survivor organizing addresses what we need now while connecting those needs to the systems and conditions that produced them. It allows the wholeness of our experiences to be present. And when that happens, something begins to shift. We can loosen our dependency on oppressive systems that have taught us they are our only source of safety and begin to imagine together what we actually need to be safe, connected, and able to thrive.

That possibility must extend beyond the anti-violence movement and requires bringing a deeper analysis of power into anti-violence work and a deeper analysis of violence into organizing spaces.

It requires our movements to change the typical response to allegations of sexual harassment and abuse that often emerge during elections. Every time, instead of relying on clear, survivor-centered processes established before the allegations surface, there is a default to the familiar pattern. Political operatives, surrogates, and the media interrogate the survivor. Their credibility, mental health, sexual history, and motivations are matters of public scrutiny, while calculations about viability, electability, party loyalty, and political consequences shape the response by parties, politicians and organizations..

A structural, meaningful response would look very different. It would establish transparent standards and independent processes before allegations arise. Believing survivors would be a starting point for taking allegations seriously, not a predetermined conclusion. Investigations would be insulated from political interference. Survivors would be protected from retaliation and proxy attacks. And those principles would apply consistently, regardless of the political affiliation, popularity, or perceived “winnability” of the candidate.

Beyond a fair process, we need to strengthen our collective muscle to recognize abuses of power, intervene meaningfully, and support those that come forward. And commit to changing the cultures and power structures that incentivize silence and enable abuse to take root and thrive.

The upcoming elections offer a glimpse into what could be possible if and when we decide that organizing matters. Political spending in the 2026 midterms is projected to top $11.6 billion. Campaigns, PACs, unions and big donors are pouring resources into reaching, persuading, and mobilizing voters. Winning elections matters enormously–especially now. But mobilizing people to win an election is not the same as organizing them to build solidarity, develop leadership, and wield collective power over the conditions of their lives. Imagine bringing even a fraction of that seriousness (and money) to organizing survivors. Imagine treating survivors not as victims, clients, voters, storytellers, or recipients of care, but as a mass constituency with knowledge, ideas, leadership, and power worth investing in.

We can keep mistaking outrage for transformation. Or we can organize. Survivors are already part of our movements and our communities. It’s time to support the infrastructure for us to find one another. It’s time to give us the resources to take what we know and turn that knowledge into collective power. The next time we discover another monster, we can demand accountability–and refuse to stop there.

In the moments when I have felt most untethered, it has been through my relationships with fellow survivors that I’ve regained myself. This essay is for you. You remind me that healing–like liberation–is something we create together, in community, through collective care for one another.

Acknowledgements: This essay was a labor of love, grief, hope, and, yes, rage. It took shape over many months through countless conversations, wordsmithing, and revisions. Thank you to the many survivors and anti-violence workers whose insights, organizing, and care continue to shape how I understand power, healing, and what it takes to build a world beyond violence. A special thank you to Timi Gerson, whose clarity, generosity, and extraordinary gift for words made this piece immeasurably stronger. Your thoughtful questions, careful edits, and unwavering belief in this work helped transform my scattered ideas into something far more coherent and courageous. Thanks also to Rebecca Wilson Bretz, Ebony Thornton, Meher Rehman, Sara Ogawa, Maurice BP-Weeks, and Ann Russo .

Jo Chernow is a survivor, organizer, and Co-Director of Survivors Know. For 30 years, she has organized workers, built grassroots power, and led campaigns advancing survivor justice, labor rights, and progressive policy at the local, state, and national levels. Survivors Know is a Midwest-based organization that works to transform the systems, culture, and conditions that enable power-based violence through survivor-led organizing and non-carceral approaches to community safety, accountability, and collective care.

author: Roxanne D. Brown
title: The Inspiration That Leads Workers to Unionize
content:
Davion Johnson long realized that they and their colleagues deserved higher pay, fairer treatment, and greater respect at the Corning plant in Hemlock, Michigan.

But nothing drove home the need for change more than a supervisor’s callous response when a coworker fell from a ladder.

Instead of calling an ambulance, Johnson recalled, the supervisor threatened to dock the injured man a sick day if he left to seek care on his own.

An angry Johnson subsequently helped to lead 1,400 coworkers in a successful union drive with the United Steelworkers (USW). Now, they wield a collective voice on safety, pay, and other issues as they do the important work of manufacturing components for the nation’s solar industry.

Rampant inequality continues to fuel record support for unions nationwide. In all, 71 percent of Americans now approve of unions, and a growing number want organized labor to have more influence in American life, a new Gallup poll found.

Johnson’s experience shows why.

With costs of groceries, healthcare, utilities, and mortgages all skyrocketing, everyday families are falling further behind in today’s economy than they did during the pandemic.

Banding together empowers workers to fight for the higher wages they need to survive an affordability crisis that’s battering everyone except the uberwealthy. Studies show that union workers make higher wages, on average, than nonunion peers while also narrowing wage- and gender-based pay gaps.

But as Johnson came to understand, inequality isn’t solely measured in money. It isn’t only working people struggling to make ends meet while the rich get richer at our expense.

It’s just as pernicious in how bosses view workers with disdain, deny them a seat at the table, and even put their lives at risk, treating them as expendable machine parts rather than the skilled people responsible for a company’s prosperity.

The Occupational Safety and Health Administration repeatedly cited an Ohio contractor for failing to protect its nonunion workers from falls before a teenager on a company construction site in Pittsburgh plunged three stories, sustaining a serious head injury, in September.

Four times, the National Council for Occupational Safety and Health put Amazon—founded by Jeff Bezos, one of the world’s richest people—on its annual list of unsafe employers because of deaths, injuries and intimidation of nonunion workers at company warehouses.

Residents of Ascension Parish, Louisiana, grew so alarmed about reports of child and prison labor in Hyundai’s supply chain that they’re pushing for unionization of workers at a steel mill the company is building there.

Corning’s mistreatment of the worker who fell off the ladder fits right into the pattern.

As workers there battled safety issues, however, they also faced arbitrary scheduling changes, favoritism, and other indignities. Attempts to discuss these problems with management got the workers nowhere.

Amid mounting frustration, Johnson sometimes thought about the previous generations of workers who powered the nation’s manufacturing economy. No one pushed them around. They raised middle-class families, owned their own homes, bought cars, took vacations, and retired in dignity.

“What are we missing?” Johnson asked, comparing workers at Corning with those who came before them.

The answer, Johnson realized, was a union.

Corning attempted to thwart the workers’ union drive, as corporations often do when workers decide to exercise collective power. Johnson expressed surprise at “how hard they pushed back with their anti-union messaging and how much effort they put into making sure those messages were heard.”

“They put TVs in all the breakrooms and a projector up on the wall of my department within probably three days of us filing for a union election,” they said, noting the anti-union propaganda played on a loop.

The harder Corning fought against the union drive, the more workers knew they had chosen the right path.

“It felt like a boys’ club,” Johnson said, referring to management before workers joined the USW. “Having a union will undercut that.”

This article was produced by the Independent Media Institute.

Roxanne D. Brown is the international president of the United Steelworkers Union (USW).

author: Steve Ellner
title: Delcy Rodríguez is Bending Over Backward to Accommodate Washington
content:
Venezuelan provisional president Delcy Rodríguez’s all-smiles photo op with Trump in a Manhattan hotel on September 22 proved too much for some of her erstwhile supporters. For the Spanish leftist Juan Carlos Monedero, a staunch defender of Hugo Chávez, Maduro and at first Rodríguez, her New York appearance “clashed with the previous socialist and anti-imperialist discourse” of her movement.

Shortly before the encounter, Rodríguez evaded a reporter’s question about whether she would visit jailed Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro in Brooklyn. Her decision to stay clear of Maduro is consistent with her attempt to chart a new course for Venezuela.

Rodríguez became interim president following the bloody U.S. military incursion on January 3, 2026 that resulted in the kidnapping of Maduro and the First Lady Cilia Flores. Facing the prospect of a second, more devastating military attack, Rodríguez shifted sharply toward Washington on foreign and oil policy while reshuffling the public administration and military at the expense of hardline pro-Chávez (Chavista) loyalists.

Rodriguez’s strategy goes too far

Rodríguez’s strategy from the outset was to demonstrate that she was not cowardly submitting to Washington’s dictates or acting as a collaborationist a la Vichy France. Her wholehearted embrace of policies pushed by Washington is designed to dispel any impression that she is bowing to U.S. pressure. On many key issues, she has become as Catholic as the Pope with regard to Trump, while retaining the Chavista label. Shortly after January 3, Rodríguez affirmed “there is no foreign agent” governing Venezuela, a claim unconvincingly echoed by the second in command Diosdado Cabello who alleged “we don’t depend on anyone.”

In a different vein, pro-Rodríguez analysts argue that the interim president has zero options given the U.S. threats. Either submit to Washington or expect massive bombardment and/or a return of the old regime.

But there is clear evidence that Rodríguez has some latitude, albeit limited, which she has declined to fully exercise. That’s because Trump is fully wedded to his partnership with her.

Trump decided to recognize Rodríguez rather than right-wing leader María Corina Machado – much to the disappointment of Miami-based anti-Communist hawks – for good reasons. A confidential CIA report requested by the Trump administration prior to January 3 warned that the Venezuelan opposition lacked support within the pro-Chavista armed forces as well as the police force. The conclusion was obvious: turning power over to Machado was a recipe for chaos, if not civil war.

Trump has assimilated the Pentagon’s assessment of “de-Baathification” following the U.S. invasion of Iraq as a “complete disaster,” responsible for the endless internecine conflict in that nation. Trump has repeatedly invoked the Iraq fiasco when discussing the Rodríguez government. At one press conference he noted with reference to Venezuela “We had, as you remember, Iraq, where everybody got fired…And you know what they turned into? ISIS. And we don’t want that.”

Moreover, the decision to recognize Rodríguez rather than Machado was not taken on a whim but rather followed months of careful deliberation at the highest level of the Trump administration. He now touts his partnership with Rodríguez as a major success at a time in which he has very few of them to tout. It is thus unlikely that Trump will readily turn his back on Rodríguez. The upshot is that Rodríguez has some room to maneuver.

The Chavista movement under Rodríguez has retreated from its defining banner: the uncompromising defense of national sovereignty. To its credit, the movement’s leadership continues to cast itself as an opponent of the traditional elite and a defender of the collective production units known as “communes.” But these positive features fall short for a movement that once raised such high expectations. While retaining a sense of realism, Rodríguez could have at least maintained a more neutral position on issues that compromised national sovereignty.

One of the most troubling examples was Venezuela’s collaboration in the extrajudicial killing of Niño Guerrero, leader of the criminal Tren de Aragua, in a U.S. Southern Command missile strike in the state of Bolívar in June 2026. The Venezuelan government, which provided intelligence information to the Southern Command, issued a statement in which it “congratulated” all participants in the operation. In doing so, Caracas lent credence to Trump’s false narrative that drug traffickers are terrorists. At the very least, the Rodríguez government could have stayed out of the operation while maintaining a neutral public posture.

Equally striking was the marked presence of Israeli military officers, including senior army officer Brigadier General Elad Edri, at a formal farewell meeting on July 21 in which Rodríguez thanked Israel for its earthquake relief efforts. U.S. and Israeli military involvement in the recovery operations drew objections from Chavista social movements, such as the famed Caracas barrio-based Coordinadora Simón Bolívar. They especially resented the conspicuousness of the presence of military personnel of both nations, symbolized by a controversial photograph of a beaming Diosdado Cabello shaking hands with U.S. Southern Command chief Francis L. Donovan, who had overseen the January 3 incursion. This, then, was another instance in which the Chavista leadership offered Washington a level of support that went well beyond what was necessary given the circumstances.

Still another example of the lengths to which Rodríguez has gone in accommodating Washington is her willingness to accept the Pentagon’s participation in the Venezuelan oil industry. The mega oil deal reached between Washington and Caracas in late August gives the Pentagon 35 percent ownership of the operating company that is to exploit 17 Venezuelan oil fields representing nearly 150 percent of U.S. proven reserves. But there is no precedent for the Pentagon’s equity ownership of this nature which is of dubious legality. Venezuelan analyst Phil Gunson, who has been briefed on the deal, told the Guardian that the major oil companies “are concerned about the irregularities.” From Venezuela’s viewpoint, the involvement of the Pentagon in the nation’s oil business makes little sense.

From the perspective of the Pentagon and its Israeli counterpart, Rodríguez’s conciliatory stance appears to be a vindication and a reversal of Chavista defiance – if not a payback for past grievances. In January 2000 Chávez turned back a sizable relief operation that the same U.S. Southern Command was in the process of sending in response to catastrophic floods, which had devastated the state of Vargas the previous month. Chávez’s decision was an embarrassing rebuff for the Pentagon, if not humiliating.

Along similar lines, Roni Kaplan, spokesperson for the Israeli armed forces and a member of his nation’s aid mission, told CE Noticias Financieras-English on July 22, “it’s like when you fight with someone and they come to apologize, and when they say they’re sorry, you say, “‘I’ve already forgotten all about it.’” Kaplan’s statement puts in sharp relief the extent to which Rodríguez’s posture breaks with the Chavista past.

The pro-Chavista think tank Misión Verdad puts a positive spin on Rodríguez’s strategy. According to its take, the Manhattan meeting with Trump marked the point at which “Washington’s asymmetric coercion and the strategic adaptation deployed by the Chavista movement converge.” For both Trump and Rodríguez, the aim was the same: “stabilization… to reduce political costs by sacrificing ideological orthodoxy.” The asymmetry according to the Misión Verdad statement “does not erase the agency of the quantitatively weaker actor; it alters its tactics, shifting it from open confrontation toward strategic adaptation.”

The adaptation demanded by the asymmetry is captured in a slogan championed by Diosdado Cabello: “Venezuela: Reborn United.” Strip away the Misión’s lofty language, and the message is that the Chavista movement needs to make a fundamental break with its past in important ways.

Adaption is understandable given the circumstances of January 3. But if Chavismo abandons the banner of defense of national sovereignty, little remains of what defined the movement. And that is precisely where the strategy of being “as Catholic as the Pope” in accommodating Washington has led.

That’s not to say there are easy answers or that an alternative strategy would necessarily succeed, particularly given Trump’s notorious unpredictability. Nor does it mean that Rodríguez deserves to be demonized as a sellout as so many on the left are doing. Such demonization underestimates the challenges and uniqueness of the situation, at the same time that it divides the solidarity movement. The relative unity of the Chavista leadership has been one of its strengths ever since Chávez’s death in 2013, and the same needs to be preserved in the solidarity movement.

The problem is that the options available to Rodríguez are scarce, whereas Trump has many. He need not pull off another January 3. Nearly all Venezuela’s oil-derived revenue is in a U.S. account handled by Marco Rubio. All Rubio has to do is to withhold it or scale it back whenever Rodríguez steps out of line with Washington.

Even with this reality hanging over her, Rodríguez and other Chavista leaders have put forward two major demands: free Maduro and Flores and an end to the sanctions, which remain largely intact. Rodríguez, however, has not put these two demands front and center in her dialogue with the Trump administration – not by a long shot.

As pressure from Miami grows for Venezuela to set an electoral timetable, the position that elections and harsh sanctions are incompatible would shift responsibility for any delay onto Washington. Last Spring, Chavista leader Ernesto Villegas, who headed the government’s Program for Peace and Democratic Coexistence, called for “elections free of sanctions.” Linking elections explicitly to the lifting of sanctions would allow the Rodríguez government to reclaim some distance from Washington, even as U.S. blackmail severely limits its ability to fully assert national sovereignty.

title: Weiße Nationalisten raus aus dem Gebiet der Secwépemc
content:
Es gibt eine wachsende Bewegung weißer Supremacisten, die den Völkermord im sogenannten Kanada leugnet.


Am 27. September marschierten Mitglieder der „Second Sons“, einer weiß-nationalistischen Miliz, durch das Gebiet der Secwépemc und trugen rassistische Transparente in der Nähe einer ehemaligen Internatsschule, wo Massengräber indigener Kinder entdeckt worden waren.




Am 27. September marschierten Mitglieder der „Second Sons“, einer weiß-nationalistischen Miliz, auf nicht abgetretenem Secwépemc-Gebiet und trugen rassistische Transparente in der Nähe einer ehemaligen Internatsschule, wo Massengräber indigener Kinder entdeckt worden waren.


Die „Second Sons“ stehen in enger Verbindung zur sogenannten „Active Clubs“-Bewegung und haben nicht-weiße Menschen in Kanada mit Waffen bedroht, um sie aus dem Land zu vertreiben.




Diese Aktion war zeitlich so gelegt, dass sie drei Tage vor dem Nationalen Tag der Wahrheit und Versöhnung stattfand – einem mangelhaften und begrenzten Versuch, Kanadas Völkermord an indigenen Völkern anzuerkennen.


Weiße Vorherrschaft ist im Siedlerkolonialismus verankert.

Die Secwépemc blicken auf eine lange Geschichte des Widerstands gegen den kanadischen Kolonialismus zurück, darunter die Auseinandersetzung am Gustaffson Lake im Jahr 1995 und in jüngerer Zeit die „Tiny House Warrior“-Bewegung, die als Widerstand gegen das TransMountain-Pipeline-Projekt ins Leben gerufen wurde. Weiße Vorherrschaft ist untrennbar mit dem Siedlerkolonialismus verbunden. title: Message from the mountains of Kurdistan to the 39th International Women’s Gathering in Argentina
content:
The 39th International Women’s Gathering, bringing together thousands of women from different regions of Abya Yala, has begun in Córdoba, Argentina. During the three-day gathering, women will share their experiences through meetings and various activities and discuss strategies for advancing their struggles.




Ahead of the opening, members of the Kurdish Women’s Movement conveyed their greetings to the participants and also to Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan, who has been incarcerated in İmralı Island since 1999. A video message sent from the mountains of Kurdistan was then screened.




Speaking on behalf of KJAR (The Community of Free Women of Eastern Kurdistan) and the Kurdish Women’s Movement, Zîlan Vejîn greeted the 39th International Women’s Gathering and emphasized the importance of the common struggle.




Zîlan Vejîn stressed that Abdullah Öcalan’s philosophy offers an answer for peoples and women around the world.







 








The video message was enthusiastically received by the participants with great enthusiasm and slogans such as “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” [Woman, Life, Freedom].




Before the beginning of the three-day gathering, a ritual, according to the traditions of different original people of Abya Yaha, was held. The gathering’s activities will continue over the next two days, with the participation of women from across Abya Yala, representing various feminist movements, including indigenous ones. Workshops, demonstrations, film screenings, and various other activities are also scheduled as part of the event.

title: Unknown assailants vandalize the facility of the Families of Martyrs in Til Temir
content:
In the northeastern Syrian town of Til Temir, a facility belonging to the Council of Families of Martyrs was attacked and damaged by unknown assailants. The perpetrators tore down the sign bearing the council’s name and set a fire on the roof of the building. It is not yet known who was behind the attack.




The Council of Families of Martyrs, which organizes the relatives of members of the Kurdish freedom movement and the YPG/YPJ defense forces who have fallen in combat, issued a statement condemning the attack.




The Council stated that the attack violated the sanctity of the site and its moral and humanitarian significance. It called for the circumstances surrounding the incident to be clarified, those responsible to be identified and held accountable under the law.




The Council also called for the necessary measures to be taken to protect civil and social institutions in order to prevent such attacks from recurring.

title: Mehmed Uzun commemorated in Amed on 19th anniversary of his death
content:
On Sunday, relatives, companions, and representatives of political parties and civil society organizations gathered at the grave of Kurdish writer Mehmed Uzun in Mardinkapı Cemetery in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) to mark the 19th anniversary of his death on October 11, 2007. The commemoration, organized by the Association of Kurdish Writers, paid tribute to Uzun’s contribution to the development of modern Kurdish literature and his commitment to the Kurdish language.




His brother, Mustafa Uzun, thanked those present for attending. Mehmet Ildoğan, who had met the writer in Adıyaman, recalled how Uzun had inspired him and many others to develop a passion for literature. “We have only one Mehmed Uzun, not twenty,” Ildoğan said. “His works will light our way like a torch.”




Writing against language bans and cultural oppression




Herdem Merwani, co-chair of the Association of Kurdish Writers, described Uzun as one of the pillars of Kurdish literature. He said the association would continue its efforts to preserve and further develop this literary heritage.




Adem Avcı, the doctor who cared for Uzun during his battle with cancer, also paid tribute to his life’s work. He recalled that Uzun had fallen ill while in exile and had wanted to spend the final years of his life in his homeland. Avcı called on Kurdish writers to preserve Uzun’s legacy.




Lawyer and politician Serhat Bucak highlighted the significance of exile in Uzun’s literary development. “Mehmed Uzun was an immensely valuable writer. He had to go to Sweden. I wish he had not been forced to leave. But perhaps without that exile, he would not have become the Mehmed Uzun we know today,” Bucak said. He added that one day Uzun’s works would be taught at universities.




“He left behind timeless works”




Serra Bucak, co-mayor of Amed, emphasized that Uzun had transformed the painful experiences of his people into literature and had continued to write in Kurdish despite the bans. In doing so, she said, he made a significant contribution to Kurdish literature. “Mehmed Uzun left behind timeless works. I hope that many more Mehmed Uzuns will emerge,” Bucak said.




The commemoration will continue with a panel discussion at Sümerpark.

The victim who is able to articulate the situation of the victim has ceased to be a victim: he or she has become a threat.




 James Baldwin, 

The Devil Finds Work










Raise your hand, bite your tongue Conversation is over and done




We let ‘em out, we let ‘em in




We’ll let ‘em know when it’s the tipping point, the tipping point

 Tears for Fears,

Author’s note:




 This is a section of my book, 

What is to Be Undone

. 




 And it is not necessarily easy reading. 




 The book has a singular focus: we face an impossible moment in this global, dying civilization. In the violent fits of fascistic might, we see the old colonial apparatus showing itself in full light. For many of those held captive by it, the reality of its systemic brutality has been kept at bay. And for the rest, that brutality has been a lived experience. 




 The veneer is quickly fading, and the costs of this technological nightmare are exponentially impossible. We face a world where climate instability has shaken every facet of life as our species has known it. 




 Everywhere, the consequences of this Empire flood our lives, and that will only continue. 




 The point is this: civilization is dying, but we don’t need to share its fate. 




 It is never too late to fight the Leviathan. And I don’t say this in a way to instill false hope or naivety: there is no guarantee we survive this. 

That is all the more reason to fight

. 




 How the book unfolds is meant to identify the falsehoods civilization is built upon: to lay waste to ideas that History has led the victor by divine right. Civilization is a willingness to brutality, and it has advanced, not by ingenuity, but by opportunism and cruelty. 




 This chapter is a plea to understand how deeply civilization’s narratives burrow, showing how vital it is to divest from this horror by facing our own. 




 The path of the book is a series of challenges to the way we view and interact with this world, culminating in a plea to understand that the fires have come for this Empire, and they inevitably will again. 




 We need to understand what we face, because all life depends upon it. 




 By dragging it into the light, we free ourselves to act in kind. 




 This section draws me in as a character because it had to. I did not intend for that to be the case, but it came out this way. As such, there are content warnings for triggering sections. 




 If necessary, please heed them. 




 I’ve been struggling to write this. I really have. 




 I keep asking myself why, but it’s because I’m dancing around it all. I know why. 




 What I had planned to write and what I need to write are two different things. 




 There are many aspects about this book, in particular, that kind of hedge me out of my own comfort zone. There is no doubt that’s important, especially when the book is ultimately about seeing civilization and its realities from literally any other perspective than that which civilization sells us. 




 I know how hard that can be. Because these things unfold infinitely, don’t they? We’re moving from the artificial safety of preordained boundaries. We want to believe that there’s an adult in the room, for all the horrors that civilization can throw at the world. We want to believe that there’s a bottom for how much evil individuals and organizations are capable of unleashing. 




 The truth is that there isn’t. 




 You and I might have boundaries and limits, but those that seek power and control just do not have those things. You see, civilization didn’t invent horror. It didn’t invent the capability of doing terrible things to other living beings. It didn’t invent cruelty. 




 Those things all existed. To a large degree, egalitarian societies function because they saw this from the outset. They don’t hide from cruelty. They make tales of it. They put energy into conflict resolution. They dealt with these things before they could become endemic. 




 They were capable of having hard conversations, of doing hard things. And all the better for it. 




 What civilization did, stretching back into the origins of domestication, was different. 




 It 

rewarded

 cruelty. It took nightmares and gave them forms. 




 It birthed institutions of barbarity. 




 Civilization gave the tools of abuse, and coerced a social order which granted power to abusers. 




 Every single step of the way, the worst things imaginable were empowered and encouraged. 




 It took time. It took atrocities. It took the tiering of society, and the suppression of many at the hand of the increasingly fewer. Every step, it just gets worse, and it grows larger. 




 Then it spreads, by force. 




 It conquers. It colonizes. It steals what it needs to grow. It becomes the war machine. It becomes the police. They build the fortress, and all of its walls have two sides. It exports its brutality. It imports its spoils of war. It standardizes and compartmentalizes itself. It becomes industrialized. Capitalists create a measure for it. Socialists respond in kind. 




 Of all the possible routes life could take, we end here every time. Not because it was inevitable, but because no amount of hindsight will change the fact that we live in a world haunted by the means of its own extermination, thousands of times over. And every single threat was constructed from within it.

LA DISTANZA DALLE ABITAZIONI

IL PAESAGGIO E LA BIODIVERSITÀ

LA TUTELA DEI TERRENI AGRICOLI




NON È SOLO UNA QUESTIONE DI ENERGIA.

 

È UNA QUESTIONE DI 

COME, DOVE E A QUALE PREZZO

 PRODUCIAMO ENERGIA.

Diciamo no a un modello in cui i nostri territori diventano terreno di speculazione e le comunità locali restano con i costi dal punto di vista del territorio, dell’ambiente, della qualità della vita, mentre i profitti prendono altre strade.




Vogliamo investimenti che portino 

lavoro, servizi, opportunità e benefici concreti per chi vive questi territori

.




Il territorio non è una merce da sfruttare. È la nostra casa, la nostra storia, il nostro futuro.




Il Comitato dei Cittadini di Piano di Mommio







La chiamata da parte di Freedom Flottilla Viareggio 




Anche Viareggio e la Versilia parteciperanno alla giornata di mobilitazione nazionale contro il sionismo e il genocidio.




Abbiamo scelto di farlo iniziando una lotta contro la presenza dei capitali israeliani nel commercio del fotovoltaico nelle nostre terre.




Boicottare, disinvestire e sanzionare Israele è oggi la pratica più concreta che possiamo attuare per fermare uno Stato genocida come Israele. Per questo invitiamo tutti a prendere parte al presidio con conferenza stampa che faremo al campo del fotovoltaico a Massarosa.







e il 

comunicato

: 




Stamani, nella giornata di mobilitazione nazionale contro il genocidio in Palestina e il sionismo, siamo scesi in piazza insieme al 

Coordinamento Versilia per la Palestina

 e il Comitato cittadino di Pian di Mommio (Massarosa) per una giornata di boicottaggio contro i capitali delle aziende israeliane nel fotovoltaico locale e regionale. Abbiamo manifestato davanti all’impianto di Pian di Mommio costruito attraverso scatole cinesi di holdings che fanno capo al maggior fondo di investimento israeliano nel fotovoltaico e ad una società multinazionale israeliana. Se i governi non sono in grado di sanzionare e fermare il genocidio deve essere la mobilitazione popolare che attraverso il boicottaggio, sanzionamento e disinvestimento devono costringere Israele a non colonizzare le nostre economie e le nostre terre.







Della giornata di presidio organizzato davanti al campo fotovoltaico ne ha parlato anche un 

quotidiano locale

. 







Sempre sullo stesso tema il collettivo Diritti per la Palestina di Ribolla ha organizzato un presidio che si terrà venerdì 16 ottobre. Di seguito l’indizione: 




16 ottobre: Presidio sotto la Regione per dire NO all’Autorizzazione Unica Energetica all’impianto agrivoltaico “Ribolla” dell’azienda genocidaria Shikun&Binui, inserita nella Black list ONU per violazione dei diritti umani in Palestina. Sembra assurdo ma è così, la Regione Toscana è ad un passo dal concedere l’autorizzazione. Ma c’è di più, Shikun&Binui ha presentato progetti per 5 impianti tra la provincia di Grosseto, Livorno e Pisa che, se fossero autorizzati, frutterebbero all’azienda israeliana oltre 100MW e 180 000 pannelli su un latifondo multicentrico di 150 ettari complessivi che sarebbero così completamente deturpati e colonizzati. La transizione ecologica che vogliamo dev’essere etica, giusta e democratica, e lo ribadiremo insieme nel giorno del Climate Strike. Dopo due mesi di resistenza, 17 000 firme raccolte, l’appoggio di Francesca Albanese e Moni Ovadia, ci troveremo per rammentare alla Regione Toscana che ha l’obbligo morale di rispettare i diritti umani, come sancito dall’art 3 dello Statuto Regionale e di onorare il Riconoscimento – avvenuto l’11 febbraio 2026 – dello Stato di Palestina da parte della stessa Regione Toscana.




Come cittadini, non abbiamo intenzione di accettare che il nostro sole produca alcun MW che alimenti il genocidio a Gaza e in Cisgiordania, nemmeno se dovessero esserci vantaggi per il territorio. Non solo non accetteremo ulteriori complicità con Israele, ma chiediamo l’interruzione di ogni rapporto con Israele, perché finora è stata la mancanza di azioni concrete per interrompere il ciclo di impunità che ha permesso ad Israele di portare avanti il genocidio.




Se passa Ribolla, è probabile che anche gli altri impianti passino. Se non passa Ribolla, avremo fatto quello che ci chiedono i Palestinesi quando ci dicono “Grazie di tutto, ma fate qualcosa dove siete voi per fermare il sistema economico finanziario di Israele, altrimenti questo inferno non finirà mai”




Ci vediamo il 16 ottobre, via Cavour ore 11!

title: Hein Htet Kyaw - On the Question of Ethno-Nationalist Burmese Federal State
content:
Author

: Hein Htet Kyaw

Title

: On the Question of Ethno-Nationalist Burmese Federal State

Subtitle

: In Favor of Geographical Multicultural Federalism

Date

: 10 Oct 2026

Notes

: English Version of 

https://sea.theanarchistlibrary.org/library/hein-htet-kyaw-on-burma-ethnostate?__language=en

Source

: 

redandblackanarchists.com.au




Regarding "Bamar State"




 Today, the political and federalist demand for a "Bamar State" has become a preliminary political and federal roadmap for a third-way coalition outside the NLD/NUG factions. 




Why is a "Bamar State" Needed?




 The political and federal demand for a "Bamar State" has emerged due to several reasons. 




 In the article 

"The Eight-State Principle Must Be Fundamental"

 published in the May 2022 issue of 

New Society Journal

 (Vol. 3, No. 10), the author Lun Nway Nyein from Democratic Party for a New Society wrote: 




 · "It is completely unacceptable for any single ethnic group to hold disproportionate rights or powers under any pretext. To be precise, it is unacceptable that the Bamar ethnic group has taken 7 units while other ethnic groups have taken less." 




 Similarly, quoting an interview on Federal FM titled 

"Why a Bamar State Should Exist"

 with Maung Saungkha, commander of the Bamar People's Liberation Army (BPLA): 










 To establish an equal state-structure, a Bamar State must be included. This will foster an understanding of ethnic fraternity between Bamar and non-Bamar groups. 










 The term "Pyi-ma" (Mainland) should no longer be used as it implies greater importance; instead, it should simply be called the "Bamar region." 










 Thus, I understand the political and federal demand for a "Bamar State" as an effort by other ethnic minority groups to check the political overreach and excess federal units claimed by successive rulers—from U Nu to U Ne Win, down to present-day leaders—who claimed to represent the majority Bamar ethnic group. 




 At the same time, when discussing the federal structure of the state alongside the "Bamar State," we can observe ongoing debates over whether the design should be purely ethnic-based, geographic-based, or an ethno-geographic hybrid model. 




 In an excerpt from 

Essential Interim Constitution in 2022 (Part 10)

 broadcast by NST, U Aung Htoo, an influential intellectual regarding the law (especially the constitutional laws) and the founder of the Legal Aid Network stated: 










 “States flying a nationalist flag should be designated as "National States." 










 “New states can be formed if other existing states accept them (e.g., Kachin, Shan).” 










 “States inhabited by a diverse mix of different ethnic groups should be designated as ‘Multi-National States’ (e.g., Yangon Region).” 










 In a September 21, 2022 interview with CNI News, Saya Than Soe Naing, a former member of Communist Party of Burma who currently is a heterodox political commentator remarked: 




 · "Our country cannot be organized purely along ethnic lines, nor can it easily be divided purely by geography. We need to consider both factors together." 




The Historical Concept of a "Bamar State"




 To trace the concept of a "Bamar State" back through history, we must start with the Eight-State Shan Federal Proposal. 




 Around 1960, when the Shan Proposal was first presented to the public, U Tin Aye, a lecturer at the Yangon University Translation Department, was among its key proponents. 




 I also recall reading from past interviews that in 2013, Dr. Aye Maung, chairperson of the Rakhine Nationalities Development Party, discussed the eight-state concept at the Taunggyi Conference of the Nationalities Brotherhood Federation (NBF) in Shan State. 




 Furthermore, the concept of a "Bamar State" was reportedly deliberated during the first session of the Union Peace Conference held in Naypyidaw in 2016 (pro-military agenda). 




"Bamar State and the Eight-State Model"




 In the article 

"The Eight-State Principle Must Be Fundamental"

 in the May 2022 issue of 

New Society Journal

 (Vol. 3, No. 10), author Lun Nway Nyein wrote: 




 · "No ethnic group should hold excessive rights, power, or territorial units, whether formally or substantively. The Bamar ethnic group must take a single Bamar State, just like the other ethnic nationalities. This is what it means to base our system on the Eight-State principle." 




 Similarly, Dr. Aye Maung, chairperson of the Rakhine Nationalities Development Party, once remarked regarding the Eight-State Model: 




 · "To shape a genuine Union, the Amyotha Hluttaw (House of Nationalities) must function as an Ethnic Chamber. The seven administrative divisions should be merged into a single Mainland State." 




Unpacking Bamar Chauvinism




 We can approach majority Bamar oppression through three distinct lenses: 




1. State-Based Bamar Oppression




 This is straightforward. Successive military leaders who seized state power—from U Ne Win to U Than Shwe—forcefully claimed to represent the Bamar majority through the barrel of a gun. Consequently, Bamar people themselves have struggled under the banner of the pro-democracy movement to reclaim their representation from this military-bureaucratic apparatus. From this perspective, the genocides, atrocities, and human rights violations committed by consecutive military dictatorships were not carried out by the Bamar people, but rather by a military-bureaucratic class operating under the label of "Bamar," while the Bamar population itself was oppressed, suffered violence, and resisted.

title: Gustave Lefrançais: A Link to The Past
content:
A short biography of Gustave Lefrançais, pioneering French libertarian communist

The text below is an article in the book by Nick Heath, The Idea: Anarchist Communism, Past, Present and Future.

Gustave Adolphe Lefrançais was born in 1826 in Angers. He became a teacher, was sacked for his progressive views in 1847 and took part in the 1848 events in France. He was subsequently sentenced to several months’ imprisonment for his activities with two different sentences. A communist influenced by Fourier and Pierre Leroux, he fled to England with the coup d’état by Louis Napoleon in 1851. Here he met with Déjacque “an old acquaintance of the 1848 clubs” who showed him around the London of the French exiles. This encounter was to radicalise his ideas considerably. Together with Déjacque and a dozen other exiles he set up a mutual aid association, La Sociale. As he wrote: 'All in the same precarious situation, with so thin resources, so thin that remaining isolated, we would surely die of hunger, and by associating our miseries, perhaps they will be less insupportable for each one'. He lived in poverty, teaching when he could, but also weaving baskets and selling tobacco at theatres during the Christmas season.

Returning to Paris in 1853, he associated with Proudhonists like Alfred Darimon and Georges Duchene and took part in militant activity with Alfred Briosne who advanced a theory of collectivism as a synthesis of individualism and communism. Lefrançais was critical of the mystical communists like Cabet and his followers, and the latter day Babouvists and Blanquists. According to police reports, he developed his ideas on collective property and the suppression of inheritance, as well as attacking marriage and advocating free union.

An active participant in the Paris Commune of 1871, he fought on some of the last barricades at the Bastille and Arsenal. He managed to escape and was condemned to death in his absence.

In exile in Switzerland, he immediately joined the Central Section of the International in Geneva, and found himself in the midst of a war between the Marxists and Bakuninists there. It did not take long for him to take sides. He attended the Sonvillier congress and took part in the “anti-authoritarian International. He chaired the Internal Congress of the Anti-Authoritarian International at St Imier on September 15th, 1872. He contributed to various anti-authoritarian Swiss papers and helped Reclus with his geographical work.

Returning to France with the amnesty, he stayed outside of the different political groupings, whilst speaking at many political meetings. He consistently criticised universal suffrage, and when he ran as a candidate in the 1889 elections this was just a protest against Boulangism and not a move towards electoralism.

Speaking of himself in the third person, he wrote: “He is very convinced that the future is with communism, that is to say with the complete disappearance of any individual property as instrument of production [...]. Only, while admitting as exact the communist formula: "To each according to his needs and each according to his abilities", he recognizes that the applications proposed by Gracchus Babeuf, Étienne Cabet and Louis Blanc do not respond sufficiently to the legitimate demands of individual liberty.” Memoirs, p318-319).

In an article written in the paper La Commune in 1874 he wrote that the revolution” can be nothing else than the incessant demand for the individual of his autonomy, that is to say, the absolute government of his faculties." In order for this to come about, it was necessary for "The suppression of government - of power - in the political order; that of wage labour, in the economic order. Now this double suppression can only be accomplished by the triumph of the communalist idea which is incarnated in the social revolution - the only legitimate one, the only one that interests us ".

Nettlau, in his Bibliography of Anarchy, describes the text by Lefrançais “Where are The Anarchists Going” of 1887, as one of the authoritarian critiques of anarchism. But in fact, Lefrançais, like Saverio Merlino after him in his Individualism in Anarchism, criticises both selfish individualism, in terms of anti-organisationalism and the dangers of illegalism and individual propaganda by deed. He remained a libertarian communist, who defended the ideas of the Paris Commune to the end, and who rejected “the evolution of a movement which privileged both philosophical individualism and ideological communism to the detriment of revolutionary anti-authoritarian socialism which had been its origin” (Frejaville).

Biographical notice on Lefrançais: http://maitron-en-ligne.univ-paris1.fr/spip.php?article33693

Frejaville, Claude. Gustave Lefrançais et les malentendues de l’histoire. In Le Monde Libertaire, 30th May-5th June 2013.

title: Küçükçekmece'de yıkımı yapılan 7 katlı bina çöktü
content:
İstanbul'un Küçükçekmece ilçesinde kentsel dönüşüm kapsamında yıkımına başlanan 7 katlı bina, çalışmalar sırasında çöktü. Çökmenin etkisiyle çevredeki binalar, doğal gaz ve su tesisatları ile aydınlatma direği zarar gördü. Binanın çökme anı cep telefonu kamerasıyla kaydedildi.

Olay, dün öğle saatlerinde İnönü Mahallesi 2'nci Yıldız Sokak'ta meydana geldi. Kentsel dönüşüm kapsamında bitişik nizamda bulunan 7'şer katlı iki binanın yıkımına başlandı. Ekiplerin binalardan birinde yürüttüğü çalışmalar sırasında diğer bina aniden çöktü.

İhbar üzerine olay yerine polis, sağlık ve itfaiye ekipleri sevk edildi. Çöken binadan kopan parçalar çevredeki yapılara ve tesisatlara zarar verirken, ekiplerin incelemesinde enkaz altında kimsenin kalmadığı belirlendi.

Mahalleli Kibar Yıldırım, binanın yıkım sırasında çöktüğünü belirterek, "Dün kentsel dönüşüm kapsamında bu binanın yıkımı gerçekleşti. Yanlış yıkımdan dolayı bina bir anda çöktü. Bizim en büyük sevincimiz, binanın aynı yere çökmesi. Çünkü 7 katlı bir binaydı. Bina da değil, site şeklinde bir bloktu. Yaklaşık 54-55 daireli olabilen bir blok. Bir anda durduğu yere çöktü, yan yatsaydı karşıdaki bütün binaların hepsini götürürdü" dedi.

Yıkım çalışmalarına ilişkin daha önce yetkili kurumlara başvurduğunu söyleyen Yıldırım, gerekli önlemlerin alınmadığını öne sürdü.

Yıldırım, "Ben defalarca belediyeyi aramama rağmen, Çevre ve Şehircilik Bakanlığı'nı aramama rağmen, hatta dün bütün kurumları aradım. Çoğu bana cevap vermediği halde ben dün 112 Acil'i aradım. Oradan emniyete bağlandım. 'Bakın, bizim bu sokakta kentsel dönüşüm sebebiyle yıkım var ama yıkım çok yanlış yapılıyor. Burada bir facia olacak, gelip müdahale edin' dedim. Oradan birkaç arkadaş da geldi. Hatta emniyetten birkaç arkadaş da geldi ama 'Burada bizim yapacağımız bir şey yok, sadece güvenlik önlemi alabiliriz' dediler. Ancak belediyeden ve diğer kurumlardan kimse yıkım sırasında burada değildi" ifadelerini kullandı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: Milano: un migliaio di persone in piazza della Scala contro lo sviluppo incontrollato dei data center
content:
Un migliaio di persone si sono radunate sabato 10 ottobre in Piazza della Scala a Milano hanno risposto all’

appello lanciato dalla Rete nazionale dei Comitati Stop Data Center 

e manifestato nel pomeriggio per esprimere preoccupazioni e denunciare le criticità che lo sviluppo di questi impianti hanno sul territorio, in primis lombardo

. 




Chiedono in particolare una 

moratoria sulle nuove autorizzazioni fino alla definizione di regole più precise 

su impatti ambientali, urbanistica e un coinvolgimento reale dei cittadini nelle scelte rispetto a questi impianti.




Sollevano diverse criticità, tra le quali la mancanza di una valutazione complessiva: in Lombardia,  nell’area milanese in particolare, sono molti i progetti che insistono sul territorio, spesso a pochi chilometri di distanza. Servirebbe, secondo i rappresentanti della rete, analizzarli con uno sguardo d’insieme e non singolarmente.




Da piazza della Sacala la corrispondenza di 

Giulia della redazione

. 







L’intervento in piazza di 

Enrico Duranti, della rete dei comitati stop data Center e di Sergio Manera, professore di Fisica all’università di Pavia







da 

Radio Onda d’urto 




Di seguito il comunicato della 

rete nazionale Stop Data Center 




𝐂𝐄 𝐋’𝐀𝐁𝐁𝐈𝐀𝐌𝐎 𝐅𝐀𝐓𝐓𝐀! 𝐆𝐑𝐀𝐙𝐈𝐄 𝐀 𝐓𝐔𝐓𝐓𝐄 𝐄 𝐀 𝐓𝐔𝐓𝐓𝐈!




Un immenso e di cuore 𝐆𝐑𝐀𝐙𝐈𝐄 𝐚 𝐭𝐮𝐭𝐭𝐢 𝐢 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢 𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐥𝐢, vera anima della nostra Rete e insostituibili sentinelle dei territori! E un grazie gigantesco a ciascuna persona, associazione e realtà che oggi è scesa in piazza, ci ha sostenuto e ha fatto sentire la propria voce. È grazie alla tenacia, al presidio costante e all’impegno di tutti noi se la manifestazione di oggi, 10 ottobre, è stata un 𝐒𝐔𝐂𝐂𝐄𝐒𝐒𝐎 𝐒𝐓𝐑𝐀𝐎𝐑𝐃𝐈𝐍𝐀𝐑𝐈𝐎!




La 𝐑𝐞𝐭𝐞 𝐍𝐚𝐳𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐝𝐞𝐢 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐩 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐂𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 ha fatto sentire un urlo forte, chiaro e inarrestabile: il nostro territorio non si svende!




Ribadiamo a gran voce che la 𝐌𝐎𝐑𝐀𝐓𝐎𝐑𝐈𝐀 è la chiave di volta per fermare questa colonizzazione! Serve uno 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐩 𝐢𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐨 ai progetti devastanti per tutelare i beni comuni.




Vedere così tante persone unite, fianco a fianco con la stessa passione e determinazione, ci riempie di orgoglio e ci carica di un’energia incredibile. Abbiamo dimostrato che di fronte al consumo scriteriato di risorse e alla cementificazione selvaggia dei mega data center, le comunità sanno organizzarsi e lottare insieme!




𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐨 𝟏𝟎 𝐨𝐭𝐭𝐨𝐛𝐫𝐞 𝐬𝐞𝐠𝐧𝐚 𝐮𝐧 𝐩𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐝𝐢 𝐬𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐭𝐚: 𝐧𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐢𝐚𝐦𝐨 𝐩𝐢𝐮̀ 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐨𝐥𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐚̀ 𝐢𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐞, 𝐬𝐢𝐚𝐦𝐨 𝐮𝐧 𝐦𝐨𝐯𝐢𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐧𝐚𝐳𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐞, 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐨 𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐚𝐩𝐞𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐞!




UN GRAZIE INFINITO A TUTTE E TUTTI: a chi ha sfilato in piazza, a chi ha organizzato ogni dettaglio, a chi ha diffuso la voce sui social e nei quartieri, e 𝐚 𝐜𝐡𝐢 𝐨𝐠𝐧𝐢 𝐠𝐢𝐨𝐫𝐧𝐨 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞 𝐥𝐚 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐚 𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐚.




Non ci fermeremo qui. 𝐋𝐚 𝐥𝐨𝐭𝐭𝐚 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐮𝐚, ma oggi abbiamo dimostrato a tutti la forza e la determinazione della nostra rete!

title: İstanbul Modern’de “Panorama: Hayaller ve Yerler” sergisi sona eriyor
content:
İstanbul Modern’de farklı kuşaklardan 18 sanatçının çalışmalarını bir araya getiren “Panorama: Hayaller ve Yerler” sergisi, 18 Ekim’de sona eriyor. Sergi, düşsel manzaralar, kurgusal portreler ve alternatif mekân tasarımları üzerinden izleyiciyi dünyayla kurduğu ilişkiyi yeniden düşünmeye çağırıyor.

İstanbul Modern’in birinci kat galerilerine yayılan sergi, sanatçıların 2010’lu yıllardan bu yana ürettiği çalışmalardan oluşuyor. Yerleştirmelerden hareketli görüntülere, yapay zekâ uygulamalarından arşivsel malzemelere uzanan seçki, farklı sanatsal üretim biçimlerini bir araya getiriyor.

Sergide Larissa Araz, İlgen Arzık, Emre Baykal, Silva Bingaz, Hasan Deniz, Umut Erbaş, Cem Ersavcı, Ece Gökalp, Cemre Yeşil Gönenli, Ege Kanar, Zeynep Kayan, Metehan Özcan, Yusuf Sevinçli, İrem Sözen, Selim Süme, Kerem Uzel, Begüm Yamanlar ve Cansu Yıldıran’ın çalışmaları yer alıyor.

Küratörlüğünü İstanbul Modern Artistik Direktörü Çelenk Bafra ile Fotoğraf Küratörü Demet Yıldız Dinçer’in üstlendiği serginin küratöryel ekibinde Selen Erkal ve Şevval Yürüten de bulunuyor.

“Panorama: Hayaller ve Yerler” sergisine eşlik eden Türkçe ve İngilizce katalog, serginin çerçevesini farklı yazılarla ele alıyor. İstanbul Modern Fotoğraf Danışma Kurulu üyeleri Refik Akyüz, Serdar Darendeliler ve Orhan Cem Çetin’in yanı sıra Çelenk Bafra ve Demet Yıldız Dinçer’in yazılarını içeren katalog, İstanbul Modern Mağaza’dan edinilebiliyor.

“Panorama: Hayaller ve Yerler” sergisi, 18 Ekim’e kadar İstanbul Modern’de ziyaret edilebilir.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: Gian Piero Godio: «Il “nuovo nucleare” è uguale al veccho. Meloni ha scelto un sistema energetico centralizzato»
content:
Il cosiddetto “nuovo nucleare” ricorre ancora alla fissione dell’atomo e continua a produrre scorie radioattive che si accumulano sul nostro territorio. Da quarant’anni, i rifiuti liquidi ad alta attività dell’impianto Eurex di Saluggia sono sempre nello stesso posto nel Vercellese e non sono state neanche solidificate. Del deposito nazionale non c’è neanche l’ombra e, anche per questo, l’Italia è sotto procedura di infrazione europea. Come se non bastasse, il Maxi Data Center “Cavour Hyperscale Campus” previsto a Trino (Vc), come tutti i grandi Data Center, suscita forti preoccupazioni energetiche, ambientali ed etiche. Per funzionare, limitandoci al solo aspetto energetico, richiede di essere alimentato con 400 MW continuativi di energia elettrica, pari a 3 miliardi e mezzo di chilowattora: più del triplo del consumo di tutti i settori della intera provincia di Vercelli (1 miliardo di kWh/anno). Questi nuovi enormi consumi vanificheranno la transizione energetica, essendo persino superiori alla produzione di tutto il fotovoltaico installato in Piemonte (3 miliardi di kWh). E a Trino rispunterà una nuova centrale atomica







Ripubblichiamo ’intervista di FABIO BALOCCO con GIAN PIERO GODIO, 

ambientalista

, apparsa su 

Italia Libera.




Segnaliamo anche che a proposito di questi temi si terrà un incontro pubblico promosso da 

Legambiente del Vercellese e della Valsesia

 a Trino, stretto tra data center e nucleare.







Gian Piero Godio in una manifestazione ambientalista




► 

Gian Piero Godio ha lavorato per molti anni al Comitato Nazionale per l’Energia Nucleare (Cnen) come responsabile della unità di Automazione e Calcolo scientifico dell’impianto nucleare di riprocessamento Eurex

 di Saluggia, in Piemonte. È proprio facendo quel lavoro che ha constatato quanto il nucleare fosse pericoloso per i lavoratori, per l’ambiente e per il suo legame con le guerre, e così si è sentito in dovere di far conoscere a tutti questi aspetti poco pubblicizzati, entrando a far parte attiva, già negli anni ’80, dei movimenti ecopacifisti e successivamente delle associazioni ambientaliste Pro Natura e Legambiente, delle quali fa parte tuttora, oltre ad essere referente dell’Osservatorio dei Cittadini sul nucleare [

nota

].




— 

Tanto tuonò che piovve: dopo anni che si parla del ritorno all’energia nucleare, pare che ci siamo, il governo ha approvato il Ddl delega per la realizzazione di nuove centrali. Si parla di nucleare sostenibile: è così? E in cosa le nuove centrali si differenzierebbero dalle vecchie?







«Può mai esistere il nucleare sostenibile, può esistere la guerra giusta? Sono una contraddizione, un ossimoro. In ogni caso, persino formalmente, il Regolamento Delegato (Ue) 1214 del 2022 prevede che un impianto nucleare possa ritenersi sostenibile se:




– lo Stato dispone di impianti di smaltimento finale in esercizio per tutti i rifiuti radioattivi a più bassa radioattività; 




– di un piano per l’entrata in funzione, entro il 2050, di un impianto di smaltimento di rifiuti radioattivi ad alta attività; 




e mi risulta che l’Italia su questi temi sia addirittura in procedura di infrazione. Per quanto riguarda le “nuove” centrali non potrebbero che essere del tutto simili alle “vecchie” che in Italia già conosciamo bene: innanzitutto continueranno ad utilizzare la fissione nucleare e, conseguentemente, a produrre ulteriore plutonio e ulteriori scorie radioattive; poi viene detto che saranno “più piccole” delle precedenti, cioè tra i 100 e i 200 MW, ma le ex centrali nucleari di Latina e del Garigliano erano rispettivamente da 200 e da 150 MW … e poi, se saranno da 100 MW, per fare anche solo il 10% dell’energia elettrica necessaria al 2050 ne occorreranno quasi un centinaio, allegria!».







Il ministro dell’Ambiente e Sicurezza energetica Gilberto Pichetto Fratin “abbracciato” dai nuclearisti italiani




— 

Dato che dietro ogni scelta di carattere economico c’è una lobby che spinge, nel caso di specie ti chiedo: quale business c’è dietro? Si sa o si può ipotizzare?







«

A mio parere il Governo più che il nucleare in sé, vuole scegliere quello che definirei il “modello nucleare”, cioè non una singola tecnologia, ma un sistema energetico centralizzato e a favore dei grandi interessi industriali, evitando i processi di democrazia partecipativa e le autonomie locali attraverso decreti d’urgenza o procedure autorizzative speciali. Infatti la nuova legge prevede che ad autorizzare tutti i vari impianti nucleari sarà esclusivamente il Mase (ministero per l’Ambiente e la Sicurezza energetica), e non è neppure una novità, se pensiamo a Ponte sullo stretto, Tav, mega Data Center, ecc.».







— 

Debbono ancora essere smaltite le scorie lasciate dal nucleare “insostenibile” e in futuro si uniranno quelle del sostenibile…







Foto storica dell’impianto di riprocessamento Eurex di Saluggia (Vc), credit Sogin




«I rifiuti radioattivi del nucleare pregresso non sono stati sistemati. Appare innanzitutto evidente la vergognosa incapacità dimostrata per l’indispensabile e urgente solidificazione dei rifiuti liquidi ad alta attività giacenti da oltre 40 anni presso l’impianto Eurex di Saluggia: l’impianto di solidificazione Cemex. Nei serbatoi del sito nucleare Eurex – gestito prima da Cnen-Enea e, dal 2003, da Sogin – sono tuttora presenti complessivamente circa 270 metri cubi di rifiuti liquidi radioattivi prodotti nel corso delle campagne, condotte negli anni ‘70 e ‘80 in questo sito, campagne di riprocessamento degli elementi di combustibile irraggiato, provenienti da varie centrali nucleari italiane ed estere. La solidificazione di questi rifiuti è stata richiesta più volte dagli organi di controllo fin dal 1977, quando il ministero dell’Industria prescrisse al Cnen la realizzazione dell’impianto entro cinque anni. Ma dopo oltre quarant’anni e innumerevoli proroghe della prescrizione l’impianto non è ancora pronto e la solidificazione non è ancora iniziata. I rifiuti liquidi poi, una volta cementati, andranno portati in depositi che ancora non si sa dove e quando verranno realizzati. Siamo quindi in buone mani! Ed ora il Governo vorrebbe ripartire daccapo con nuove centrali nuovi impianti di fabbricazione e di riprocessamento e ulteriori depositi di scorie?».







— 

Come giustifica il governo questa scelta a fronte del fatto che in passato gli elettori con ben due referendum si sono dichiarati compattamente contrari all’energia nucleare?







Sondaggio Demopolis dopo l’approvazione del disegno di legge sul nucleare alla Camera, giugno 2026




«

Nella relazione che accompagnava il Disegno di Legge, definitivamente approvato il 23 settembre, si giustificava il mancato rispetto del risultato del referendum del 2011 sostenendo che vi era nel frattempo stato un cambiamento dello scenario tecnologico e politico. Invece il risultato del referendum del 2011 risulta ancora valido in quanto, per lo meno in un primo periodo, secondo la proposta governativa, si tratterà inevitabilmente dello stesso tipo di reattori oggetto dello scorso referendum (terza generazione), quindi, lo scenario tecnologico è lo stesso del 2011. Inoltre il Governo del secondo referendum del 2011 era presieduto da Silvio Berlusconi; quindi, oggi, anche lo scenario politico è approssimativamente lo stesso di allora (Centrodestra)».







— 

Un tema scottante e attuale: qual è il rapporto tra il nucleare e i data center?










«

Effettivamente centrali nucleari e mega data center sembrano fatti apposta per un matrimonio di interessi e di potere, mentre l’Intelligenza Artificiale dovrebbe essere considerata un Bene Comune ed essere sottratta ad applicazioni belliche, speculative o antidemocratiche. Il suo sviluppo dovrebbe essere aperto e graduale, ed il suo addestramento nei data center dovrebbe avvenire in modo flessibile, così da adattarsi alle disponibilità orarie e stagionali delle fonti rinnovabili che devono rappresentare da subito l’unica fonte energetica utilizzabile, e devono derivare da nuovi impianti e nuovi accumuli a questo specificamente destinati, per evitare che venga cannibalizzata la quantità di energia rinnovabile tuttora prodotta. Questo sviluppo potrebbe essere preventivamente pianificato a livello statale e regionale, ma così non è, tant’è che il Maxi Data Center “Cavour Hyperscale Campus” previsto a Trino (Vc) è stato riconosciuto “strategico” dal Consiglio dei ministri, anche se, come tutti di grandi Data Center, suscita forti preoccupazioni energetiche, ambientali ed etiche. Intanto ci si dovrebbe chiedere a cosa serve questo gigantismo dei data center? Alla speculazione, al controllo sociale, alla guerra? Ma, limitandosi ai soli aspetti energetici, dato che richiede di essere alimentato con 400 MW continuativi di energia elettrica, significa che ogni anno in Data Center di Trino consumerà 3 miliardi e mezzo di chilowattora di energia elettrica, più del triplo del consumo di tutti i settori della intera provincia di Vercelli (1 miliardo di kWh/anno). Questi nuovi enormi consumi vanificheranno la transizione energetica, dato che sono persino superiori alla produzione di tutto il fotovoltaico installato in Piemonte (3 miliardi di kWh nel 2024). Se dovesse alimentarsi con solo agrivoltaico, per avere un funzionamento continuo servirebbero impianti per almeno 35 chilometri quadrati (3.500 ettari) di superficie, e una quantità impressionante di batterie (400 MW, 4 milioni di kWh). Allora lo dicano chiaramente che pensano di mettere a Trino una nuova centrale nucleare per alimentarlo! Riguardo al tema, Legambiente del Vercellese e della Valsesia e Pro Natura del Vercellese, Valsesia e Vco organizzano a Trino, per venerdì 16 ottobre 2026, alle ore 20,45, presso l’Auditorium delle Scuole Medie “Famiglia Tricerri” in via Vittime di Bologna 5, una serata dal titolo: “Trino – tra Data center e nucleare. È questo il futuro che ci spetta?”».
