author: Rizomatica
title: Mesa Nacional de Hogares Indígenas se manifiesta contra cancelación de presupuestos por parte de Junaeb
content:
En Temuco, durante la mañana de ayer 8 de octubrelos estudiantes se manifestaron en las oficinas de Junaeb en el centro de la ciudad y en TVN red araucanía, para dar visibilidad a sus problemáticas.




En palabras de su voceria desde la Toma de TVN red Araucania, la Mesa Nacional De Hogares Indígenas declara el inicio de sus acciones de movilización en defensa de sus presupuestos y garantías del programa.




Tras el término de la jornada de movilización levantada por los estudiantes mapuche de la Mesa nacional de hogares indígenas, Carabineros realizó un control de identidad deteniendo una micro de la locomoción colectiva.

























Esta información se publicó en 

Radio Kurruf

.

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Mashair Idris
title: RSF preps new front from Ethiopia, pummels Blue Nile; In Kordofan, RSF conducts ‘field’ executions, digs in heels at Nuhud; Dagris prison dispute stalls registry; Gov’t criticizes UN fact-finding renewal
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter

 

here

.




With all eyes turned toward the escalating conflict in Ethiopia that is teetering on the brink of becoming a wider regional war, the Rapid Support Forces stepped up their attacks on the Sudan war’s southeastern front this week. 




Blue Nile’s 

Wad al-Mahi

 locality in the east of the state bore the brunt of the escalation. The RSF launched an attack from Ethiopia on Saturday and seized the Kadalo mountains area, which sits near the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and Roseires Dam reservoir. This coincided with a drone campaign against Damazin, which included strikes on the homes of Blue Nile Governor Ahmed Badry and Regional Finance Minister Abbas Kara, fuel stations, military sites, universities and mosques. 




The military has hit back, launching airstrikes on RSF positions in 

Wad al-Mahi and tried to reassure residents. As of Sunday, about 

2,800 people are estimated to have been displaced from 10 villages in Wad al-Mahi.




But action in the southeastern front wasn’t limited to the Blue Nile. Large numbers of RSF fighters have been moved from Darfur to Addis Ababa in recent weeks in preparation to transfer them toward Sudan’s eastern border, where they are expected to gear up for an attack on the Fashaga border strip in Gadarif State, according to an RSF source and another source informed of the mobilization arrangements who spoke to Mada Masr. 




In anticipation of escalating attacks on the border, the Sudanese military has reinforced its positions in the east, military sources tell Mada Masr. And on Wednesday, military chief and Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan visited the 11th Infantry Division in Khashm al-Gerba, Kassala State, which borders Gadarif to the north.




On the western front, the military is preparing to attack the remaining RSF-held areas in North Kordofan and advance into West Kordofan, with eyes set on Um Bader and Hamra al-Sheikh in northwestern North Kordofan. Meanwhile, the RSF is digging its heels in West Kordofan, with the group having dug trenches and built earth berms around the strategic city of Nuhud to guard against surprise attacks, an activist in the state told Mada Masr.




West Kordofan also saw yet another attack on an aid truck this week, with Khartoum laying blame for the strike at the feet of the RSF and the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (Abdel Aziz al-Hilu faction). 




In Um Bader, a social media video of the execution of 23 detainees is raising concern. While the RSF-led Tasis government tried to pin the executions on the military, three sources from the paramilitary group confirmed that the RSF had carried out the ‘field’ executions. As to why, the RSF sources’ accounts conflicted with those of medical sources and relatives of one of the men killed who spoke to Mada Masr. 

But both Tasis and officials in Khartoum are keen to pursue justice, even if a Tasis official continued to dismiss the RSF’s implications when presented with what sources from the paramilitary told Mada Masr. 




In Darfur, the joint forces push toward Geneina continues to stall, with territory swapping hands. The US’s politicking over the Darfur arms embargo — which has done next to nothing to stop the flow of weapons through Darfur or seen the provider of those arms in the United Arab Emirates face international criticism — got kicked down the road for another two months, as DC continues its push to extend the embargo across the whole country. The UN’s fact-finding committee on Sudan did get its mandate renewed, much to the chagrin of the government in Khartoum, which sees any form of international intervention as an infringement on its sovereignty. And opacity around the infamous Dagris prison, where an estimated 20,000 people are being detained, has posed a roadblock in the government-RSF prisoner exchange registry process. 




In yet another senior defection from the paramilitary group, Mohamed Azrag al-Fanjary, the commander of an RSF special operations group, announced on Thursday that he and around 300 officers and soldiers with 30 combat vehicles would join the military. You can read all about how the defections are symptomatic of a larger contradiction at the core of the RSF project in a Mada Masr investigation 

published 

earlier this week. 




***




RSF executes 23 detainees in North Kordofan’s Um Bader, sources say




RSF troops prepare to shoot a group of blindfolded men in Um Bader in North Kordofan, September 24. Courtesy: Journalist Ahmed Albalal via X.




Twenty-three people were executed in the RSF-held town of Um Bader in western North Kordofan on September 24 after being detained by the paramilitary group, according to three RSF sources, a medical source, a source with the military-allied joint force and a relative of one of the 23. 




All of them agree that the RSF executed the group, but their accounts differ over their affiliation, what they had been accused of and what happened before they were killed.




The killings follow a longstanding pattern of violence and reprisals in the area, which has intensified since the military launched its campaign across the state in July. 

The RSF forces operating along this axis are commanded by Abdel Rahman Jumaa Barakallah, who was 

sanctioned 

by the UN Security Council for human rights abuses committed while commanding RSF forces in West Darfur in 2023.




A video circulating over the past week shows the execution. A group of blindfolded men are made to lie face down with their hands bound behind their backs as armed men in RSF uniforms stand near them. The person filming the video says the men had looted Um Bader’s market and identifies an RSF field commander, Ali al-Balla Gabbara, as being in charge of the execution. The men are ordered shot in groups.




The RSF-led Tasis alliance, which heads the parallel government in western Sudan, sought to distance itself from the incident on October 2, 

saying

 the group was killed by the military and its allies in Sodary, a town captured by the military the previous week.

 In a statement, Tasis accused the forces of carrying out a “heinous massacre,” saying they executed “innocent citizens in cold blood in a public square” after taking control of Sodary, on the pretext that they had stolen from the markets.




But accounts from multiple sides confirm Um Bader as the site of the killings. Mutawakkel Abu Gaa, the spokesperson for the military-allied joint force, confirmed to Mada Masr that the 23 civilians were killed there by the RSF, citing information the force received from the area.




A RSF source likewise confirmed that an execution was carried out by the group, saying the victims were killed at Jabal Um Bader, north of the town, in the presence of RSF military police officers. The source said the bodies were later buried in a mass grave near the site.




The circumstances surrounding their detention remain contested. According to a source in the Sudan Doctors Network, the 23 had been held in RSF custody after being accused of siding with the military and of theft — charges the source said were also driven by ethnic bias. Some of those detained denied the accusations and demanded a trial, according to information gathered by the medical group.




A relative of one of the men told Mada Masr that his family has been trying to establish what happened to him. Several families, he said, have been searching for their relatives since the incident and maintain that the men had no ties to either the RSF or the military. He said they were civilians who worked in the gold market.




Two RSF sources disputed that account. They said the group had arrived in Um Bader from Nyala, in South Darfur, and had been detained after committing thefts and killing civilians. They said an internal investigation found them to be affiliated with the RSF, after which they were subjected to a “field trial” that ended in their execution.




A source in the Tasis government said the administration was prepared to open an investigation if evidence emerged of RSF involvement, dismissing the accounts provided by the RSF sources to Mada Masr as unreliable, and saying Tasis would summon the commander of the Um Bader force. 




So far, however, the evidence available points to RSF involvement in both detaining the group and killing its members, based on corroborating accounts from the field, an informed judicial source with Khartoum state authorities, who is based in North Kordofan, told Mada Masr. 




Whatever the circumstances of their detention, killing people in custody constitutes a grave breach of international humanitarian law, the source added. The law prohibits the killing of detainees and people who are no longer taking part in hostilities outside of the scope of judicial proceedings. State investigators are now documenting the incident, working to identify the victims and establish the chain of command behind the killings — including who carried them out and who ordered them — before determining criminal responsibility on the basis of the evidence, he said.




The Um Bader killings came against a backdrop of repeated violence across western North Kordofan. Over the past months, in Murra, Um Saadoun, Rada, Um Kiredam, Shag al-Nom and elsewhere, civilians have been killed, wounded, displaced from their homes and had their property looted, according to a source in North Kordofan state government appointed by Khartoum who spoke to Mada Masr. Local authorities have attributed the incidents to RSF forces deployed across the area.




Information gathered by the state government on RSF troop deployments places the units involved within the command of Abdel Rahman Jumaa Barakallah, the source said.




Barakallah took charge of the area after the RSF’s withdrawal from Khartoum in early 2025. He had initially been appointed commander of the group’s Omdurman sector, which borders North Kordofan. But after the RSF was driven from Omdurman weeks later, he was reassigned to North Kordofan, a former member of the RSF’s operations authority in North Kordofan, who defected to the military, told Mada Masr. From there, he remained responsible for the commanders leading operations on the North Kordofan and West Bara axis.




The RSF’s presence in the area came under increasing pressure in July, when the military 

launched

 

a sweeping campaign against its strongholds across North Kordofan.

 The military captured Bara, Um Sayala and Gabra al-Sheikh, among other areas, forcing the RSF to fall back toward positions in the West Bara and Sodary localities.




The withdrawal was followed by a new wave of retaliatory attacks, according to a notable from the Majaneen tribe, whose nazirate is based in Mazroub, which was under RSF control until last week. The attacks struck Mazroub, Um Bader, Sodary, Abu Zaeima and Hamra al-Sheikh, the tribal notable said, with withdrawing RSF forces looting markets and homes and detaining dozens of residents accused of passing information to the military. 




The Sudan Doctors Network accused the RSF of killing at least five civilians and displacing thousands of residents in attacks across West Bara between July 25 and 26, as forces withdrawing from Bara redeployed through the area.




Barakallah’s responsibility for the axis carries added significance because of his earlier record in West Darfur, where he commanded RSF forces during some of the war’s worst violence.




The UN Security Council 

sanctioned 

Barakallah in November 2024, identifying him as an RSF major general and commander of the group’s forces in West Darfur.

 The council said he was listed over acts and policies threatening peace, security and stability in Darfur, including violence and human rights abuses. It also linked him to the killing of West Darfur governor Khamis Abakar, who was last seen in Barakallah’s company before his death, as well as to RSF and allied attacks in Geneina and Ardamata that killed thousands of people. 




***




Khartoum presses Red Cross on detainee exchange, RSF’s Dagris prison at center of registry challenges




Sudan’s Foreign Ministry has asked the International Committee of the Red Cross to step up its work on the exchange of civilian and military detainees held by the Sudanese military and the RSF, as the government works to build a verified registry of people held by the two sides. 




The RSF’s Dagris prison in Nyala, where the government estimates that more than 20,000 people are being held, has emerged as one of the most difficult parts of that effort, according to sources in the government, with little access to the facility and limited information available about many of those detained there.




The request came during an October 2 

meeting 

between Deputy Foreign Minister Muawiya Othman Khaled, who was in New York for the UN General Assembly, and Elyse Nicole Mosquini, the head of the ICRC’s New York office.




The meeting focused on moving the detainee file beyond scattered humanitarian contacts toward a more structured process for identifying detainees, verifying their whereabouts and conditions, releasing civilians and arranging the exchange of military prisoners, according to a Foreign Ministry source who spoke to Mada Masr. 




The government’s push to compile a registry followed a June proposal by Pekka Haavisto, the UN secretary-general’s personal envoy for Sudan, to work toward a prisoner exchange in coordination with the ICRC. 

In July, the TSC 

established 

a preparatory committee tasked with compiling and verifying detainee lists and called on families who had not previously reported detained or missing relatives to register their cases.

 




Senior sources from both the military and the RSF told Mada Masr at the time that they supported the proposal on humanitarian grounds, while stressing that any exchange would require internationally monitored safeguards against military manipulation.




For the government, the ICRC could provide a channel through which the parties can exchange information about detainees, their places of detention and their conditions, the Foreign Ministry source said.




A TSC source said the government is seeking to know the fate of people the RSF transferred from areas it previously controlled in Khartoum, Gezira, Sennar and White Nile states to Darfur. Families have often been unable to reach the detention sites and, in some cases, have lost contact with their relatives altogether, the source added. 




Dagris is the largest known detention site in that network. A government source serving on the preparatory committee estimates that more than 20,500 people are held there and in surrounding military garrisons, including members of the armed forces, police and intelligence services, civilians, medical workers and women. 




The estimate includes 5,000 civilians transferred from Fasher, 3,795 members of the armed forces, 4,670 police officers, 564 intelligence personnel, 83 medical workers and 720 women, the source said. The number could grow as families continue to report missing relatives and receive information about people inside the prison through intermediaries.




The figures cannot be independently verified. Human rights and humanitarian organizations have been unable to gain access to Dagris, according to a human rights source monitoring detainees in Darfur. Accounts collected from former detainees and families of people still being held point to sharply deteriorating conditions, including shortages of food, water and medical care, the source said.




The Committee for Justice, a Geneva-based human rights organization, 

documented 

the deaths of more than 215 detainees at Dagris in May and June.

 It attributed the deaths to what it described as deteriorating detention conditions and the spread of disease, and reported repeated allegations of ill-treatment and denial of medical care.




In May, the committee also 

documented

 what it described as a “troubling pattern” in which civilian detainees were released after their families paid money.

 The organization said the cases amount to exploitation of families’ suffering.




As for their legal status, some detainees have spent prolonged periods in custody without their families receiving clear information about the charges against them or the judicial proceedings, the human rights source said.




For rights groups, those concerns mean that any future exchange would need to go beyond compiling names. It would require an independent mechanism to verify detainees’ conditions, gain access to detention sites, document deaths in custody and establish the fate of people whose whereabouts remain unknown, the source said.




Dagris makes humanitarian access and independent monitoring an essential part of any process for dealing with detainees and prisoners, the source added.




***




New attack on WFP aid convoy in South Kordofan




A World Food Programme convoy of aid trucks were hit by an airstrike on Saturday while traveling between Dalang and Kadugli in South Kordofan. 




The trucks were “clearly marked as humanitarian vehicles,” according to the WFP, which 

called 

for an independent investigation to identify those responsible and hold them accountable.

 




Two government sources, one in the Foreign Ministry and the other in the South Kordofan administration, told Mada Masr that the strike was carried out by the RSF and its ally the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, citing investigation findings and information the authorities had received.




In a 

statement 

condemning the strike, the United Nations Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown, noted that the convoy, which she said was carrying lifesaving assistance, was hit in an area “that has been under continued attack by the RSF and the SPLM-N.”




The attack took place along the same route where two WFP trucks carrying food aid to Kadugli were 

struck 

outside Dalang just weeks before.




The latest convoy was hit by the allies’ drones, killing one driver and injuring others, the source in the state government said. Two trucks were damaged, he added.




Humanitarian shipments between cities in South Kordofan rely heavily on road transport, making the Dalang-Kadugli road a crucial route for moving food and other supplies, the source said. Local authorities are trying to secure convoy movements, he added, but threats linked to fighting, shelling and drone attacks have made such efforts an increasingly complex task.




Drivers now weigh the threat before every trip. One who regularly uses the Dalang-Kadugli road told Mada Masr that drivers now assess the situation before setting out, exchanging information about clashes, military movements and conditions along the route. Those conditions can change quickly, he said, sometimes forcing drivers to delay or reschedule journeys.




The danger is not confined to areas of direct fighting, the driver added. Vehicles can come under shelling or attack while passing through areas that appear far from the frontlines.




The recurrent attacks on aid trucks have raised the stakes for transport workers more broadly, the driver said. The killing of one driver sends a message of fear to everyone who relies on the same routes to move food, fuel and other essential goods between South Kordofan’s cities.




The attack on the WFP trucks comes as fighting and restricted access leave roads as a critical lifeline for communities across the state, particularly as local markets in conflict-affected areas become less able to provide basic goods. Targeting these roads also drives up the cost of aid and commercial goods, with organizations and traders paying more to secure vehicles and staff and to reroute convoys.




***




UN’s Sudan fact finding mission renewed, Darfur arms embargo extended for 2 months




The international investigation into abuses committed during Sudan’s war will continue for another year after the UN Human Rights Council voted on Monday to renew the mandate of its independent fact-finding mission, with 28 countries voting in favor, 10 against and nine abstaining. 




The renewal put the council 

again 

at odds with Sudan’s government, which has argued that accountability for crimes committed during the war should remain primarily in the hands of national institutions.

 Khartoum has also objected to what it sees as the mission’s tendency to place the Sudanese military and the RSF on the same legal and political footing.




The resolution nonetheless 

draws 

a distinction on one issue the Sudanese government has made central. It calls for respect for Sudan’s unity and territorial integrity and rejects attempts to establish a parallel governing authority in areas controlled by the RSF. At the same time, it condemns military support to all warring parties and holds both sides responsible for violations committed during the war.




The renewal comes as international attention has increasingly focused on the role of drones in expanding the war’s impact on civilians. 

In its latest report, 

released 

September 1 and titled “Fueling Sudan’s conflict: weapons, fighters and external support networks,” the fact-finding mission documented drone attacks by both sides and said their growing range and operational capabilities had allowed the military and RSF to strike far beyond the frontlines, including in places where civilians had sought refuge.




“Drone warfare conducted by both the RSF and the Sudanese Armed Forces has extended the geographical reach of hostilities,” the United Kingdom representative said in presenting the draft resolution on Monday.




The UK, which led the group of countries behind the resolution, defended the mission as “the only independent investigative body documenting and reporting on these violations and abuses across Sudan,” the representative said.




He also sought to answer Sudan’s objections by pointing to the negotiations over the text. “We have held consultations and discussed this draft extensively with all delegations, starting with Sudan,” he said, adding that the sponsors had incorporated a number of proposals from the Sudanese side. “Yet, despite our best efforts, it is regretful that these changes were not enough for the Sudanese authorities.”




During the negotiations, the Sudanese delegation argued that the mandate itself should not be extended and that investigations and accountability should remain primarily within the jurisdiction of national institutions, according to a source in the Sudanese mission in Geneva who spoke to Mada Masr. The delegation also objected to what it viewed as an equivalence between the military and the RSF, the source said, and argued that the mission has consistently disregarded abuses attributed to the RSF in several parts of the country.




A Foreign Ministry source likewise framed the disagreement as one of sovereignty, saying the government sees the resolution as reflecting the position of some countries that treat the military and RSF as equivalent parties despite their different constitutional and legal status. Khartoum does not oppose international cooperation, the source said, but wants it to operate alongside Sudanese institutions rather than in ways that supersede them. The ministry will continue engaging with states and international organizations over the war, the source added, particularly on the role of external actors in sustaining the flow of weapons, fighters and military support into Sudan.




That distinction — between international involvement and international jurisdiction — was echoed by Sudan’s judicial institutions. The Public Prosecution maintains that crimes committed during the war should be investigated and prosecuted by national courts, while allowing international cooperation where cases require the exchange of evidence or information, a source in the Sudanese prosecution told Mada Masr. The prosecution is collecting and documenting reports of violations, the source said, but the existence of an international fact-finding mechanism does not remove the jurisdiction of Sudanese courts over crimes within their remit.




For the prosecution, documentation and criminal accountability are separate stages. Establishing individual responsibility requires verifiable evidence linking specific people to crimes, whether as direct perpetrators, those who issued orders or others who contributed to their commission, the source said. International findings can therefore contribute to the evidentiary record, he added, but insisted that they do not by themselves constitute a judicial determination of criminal responsibility.




The Justice Ministry similarly regards the council’s resolution as an international political and human rights decision whose implementation inside Sudan remains subject to national law and the jurisdiction of state institutions, a ministry source told Mada Masr. International investigations and accountability mechanisms should operate in complementarity with those institutions, while investigations should cover violations by all parties without exception or selectivity, the source stressed. The government will review the resolution’s recommendations in light of those principles, the source added.




Egypt and Qatar were among those voting against the resolution, echoing Sudan’s objections over the treatment of the two sides and the extension of the mission’s mandate.




Egypt’s representative told the council that equating the Sudanese military with the RSF sends “the wrong political message at a time when Sudan needs safeguarding its unity.” He also objected to extending the mandate despite what he described as “the non-consent of the concerned country,” and called instead for greater cooperation between the Sudanese government and UN human rights mechanisms.




Qatar similarly reaffirmed its support for Sudan’s unity and territorial integrity, while condemning violations committed during the war and foreign interference. Its representative said Qatar rejected equating “an illegal militia with a legitimate, recognized government.”




The fact-finding mission was 

established

 by the Human Rights Council in October 2023, months after the war began, to investigate the human rights and humanitarian crisis.

 Its mandate includes identifying individuals and entities responsible for human rights abuses and violations of international humanitarian law, with the aim of supporting accountability and access to justice for victims.




A US push to bring drones acquired by all parties to the war, including the Sudanese state, under a nationwide arms embargo has faltered for a second time on Thursday, as Russia and China continued to oppose expanding the existing restrictions beyond Darfur.




The UN Security Council instead voted unanimously to extend the Darfur arms embargo until December 11, following the expiry of a one-month technical rollover. 

The extension had been expected to give Washington more time to lobby council members and negotiate changes, after the initial draft failed to secure the votes needed without risking a Russian veto, an informed UN source 

told

 Mada Masr at the time.




US Senior Advisor on African and Arab Affairs Massad Boulos 

said Washington’s decision to support the second rollover

 does not constitute “a lapse in our resolve.”

 Boulous stressed that Washington remains committed to expanding the embargo.




Khartoum has staunchly opposed the US proposal on the grounds that it equates state institutions with a militia.




***




RSF eyes new front in eastern Sudan as military reinforces positions, sources say




Military chief and Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan visits the 11th Infantry Division in Kassala, October 7. Courtesy: The TSC.




Large numbers of RSF fighters have been moved from Darfur to Addis Ababa as preparations begin to transfer them toward Sudan’s eastern border, where they are expected to prepare for an attack on the Fashaga border strip in Gadarif State, according to an RSF source and another source informed of the arrangements for moving the fighters who spoke to Mada Masr. 




The RSF source said specialized drone units are among the forces currently undergoing training in Addis Ababa. During his unannounced visit to Addis Ababa in August, RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo delegated a number of RSF leaders to follow the forces’ situation on the ground and make operational decisions, the source added.




Over the past week, hundreds of fighters were moved from Darfur to Addis Ababa via an air bridge from Nyala and then transferred to areas near Fashaga in Gadarif, according to the source informed of the transfer operation.




The movements are intended to open a new front toward Gadarif, the source said, potentially allowing the RSF, which already controls significant areas in the bordering Blue Nile region, to push deeper into other parts of eastern Sudan.




Such a move would be highly sensitive given Fashaga’s strategic location along Sudan’s border with Ethiopia and its proximity to Eritrea, the source warned, and could open the door to a wider escalation along the Sudan-Ethiopia border.




The region is already facing a particularly complex security environment, with fighting intensifying between Ethiopia’s federal government and opposition forces in the north, including in 

Tigray

, which borders Sudan, while diplomatic tensions between Addis Ababa and Asmara continue to mount.

 At the same time, Sudan’s Blue Nile region remains one of the key flashpoints in the country’s civil war, with the RSF and its allies fighting there and with Ethiopia playing a significant role in the movement of military supplies to them.




The Sudanese military has been responding to this web of threats by reinforcing its positions in the east. On Wednesday, military chief and Transitional Sovereignty Council chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan visited the 11th Infantry Division in Khashm al-Gerba, Kassala State, which borders Gadarif to the north, “to review the overall security and operational situation in the area,” according to a military statement.




Over the past week, the armed forces have sent additional troops to a number of positions in Gadarif and Kassala, part of broader security measures involving military divisions and units across eastern Sudan, according to a military source in the Second Infantry Division in Gadarif. Commanders across both states have been instructed to raise readiness and prepare for any developments along the border, the source said.




Military commanders are coordinating on border surveillance and the protection of key facilities and strategic sites, with particular attention to Fashaga and Khashm al-Gerba, as well as the Upper Atbara and Setit Dam Complex on the Tekeze River, near the Ethiopian border, and Wad Zayed Airport, in Gadarif, according to the source.




The airport has been undergoing expansion since the beginning of the year as the armed forces seek to strengthen aerial surveillance in Gadarif, and has recently received reinforcements, the source added.




A senior Sudanese military officer, who spoke to Mada Masr, maintained that the border on the Gadarif side was fully secured, stressing that the military has strengthened its presence in the area over the past several months. He added that Popular Resistance forces — civilians who volunteer to fight alongside the military — have received advanced training to respond to any potential attack.




***




RSF expands in eastern Blue Nile, launches drone campaign on Damazin




Aftermath of an RSF drone attack on Damazin in Blue Nile, October 3. Courtesy: Press Office of the Governor of Blue Nile via Facebook.




The RSF advanced into a new locality in Blue Nile on the Ethiopian border, expanding its ground offensive in the region, which coincided with a wave of drone strikes on officials’ homes and civilian infrastructure in the regional capital Damazin.




On Saturday, RSF 

troops

, including fighters under the command of Obeid Mohamed “Abu Shotal” Solaiman, who hails from Blue Nile, seized the Kadalo mountains area in 

Wad al-Mahi

 locality in eastern Blue Nile after launching an attack from inside Ethiopia, a 

military source told Mada Masr.




The area includes the villages of 

Jabal al-Nimr, Bashkarkad and Minza al-Nimr

 along the Ethiopian border.




The attacking forces had amassed large numbers of fighters inside Ethiopian territory before advancing on military positions under heavy drone cover and taking control of the area, the military source said. 




The military responded by deploying an additional brigade to Balgwa south of Roseires town to secure the eastern axis and halt their advance, he added.




The Kadalo mountains are strategically important because of their location along the Ethiopian border, near the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and the expanded reservoir of the Roseires Dam. The area also is also home to the Dinder National Park and has substantial mineral deposits and extensive agricultural land.




The advance displaced thousands of families amid severe shortages of shelter, food and medicine. 

The International Organization for Migration 

said

 that 2,800 people were displaced on Sunday from 10 villages in Wad al-Mahi as the security situation deteriorated.




The military has since stepped up its response along the eastern axis. 

Airstrikes against RSF concentrations intensified, with the heaviest attack coming on Tuesday in 

Abu Gaddaf

, also in Wad al-Mahi, where the air force destroyed 12 combat vehicles and killed several fighters, according to the military source.

 Some fighters withdrew toward 

Makla

, the source added.




The Fourth Infantry Division in Damazin sought to reassure residents, 

saying 

the RSF was attempting to create anxiety and uncertainty by spreading “rumors” and exaggerating events.

 Reinforcement and support forces were on full alert to protect civilians and respond to threats, it said.




The ground offensive in Wad al-Mahi coincided with the start of a drone campaign against Damazin. The RSF began targeting the regional capital on Saturday, striking the home of Blue Nile Governor Ahmed Badry. The house was damaged, but no casualties were reported, an official in Blue Nile told Mada Masr. Fuel stations and other civilian and military sites were also hit, the official said.




The attacks continued over the week, targeting government officials’ homes and civilian infrastructure. At around 1 am on Wednesday, RSF drones struck the Hijra neighborhood and Sudan Technical College, damaging classrooms, administrative offices and labs. 

A mosque was destroyed and the headquarters of the 

Islamic Appeal Organization

’s branch came under fire, according to a medical source and a resident in Damazin who spoke to Mada Masr.




Regional Finance Minister Abbas Kara, meanwhile, survived a simultaneous strike on his home along with his family and security detail, the two sources said. 

Kara 

said 

in a statement that his house had been hit four times by an RSF strategic drone, but that no one was injured.




The Wednesday attacks killed four civilians and wounded 12.




In a 

statement

 issued on the same day, the Blue Nile governor described the attacks as a systematic campaign against the region’s residents and “a blatant assault on their lives and security.”

 




Targeting civilians and the families of officials and political leaders, and terrorizing people in their homes “would not achieve the aggressors’ aims or weaken the resolve of the people of Blue Nile,” he said.




A former military officer told Mada Masr that the simultaneous attack on 

Wad al-Mahi’s Minza and Bashkarkad

 and the escalation of drone strikes against Damazin pointed to a widening campaign of military pressure on the capital and its supply routes.




But the attacks could also be intended to keep the military occupied and stretch its forces thin ahead of an attempt to seize its most important bases in southern Blue Nile, including 

Keili, Baraka, Sali and Dandaro

, he added.




On the Kurmuk axis, where much of the fighting over the past year has been concentrated, the RSF has deployed additional forces, a second military source said, suggesting they may launch renewed attacks on military positions in Baraka and Keili in the coming days.




***




RSF fortifies West Kordofan’s Nuhud as military readies final push in North Kordofan




After clearing the last major RSF defensive positions in western North Kordofan last week, the military is preparing to attack the remaining RSF-held areas in the state and advance into West Kordofan, a field source told Mada Masr.




The next offensive is expected to target Um Bader and Hamra al-Sheikh in northwestern North Kordofan, with preparations already complete, the source said.




Military forces have been repositioned along several fronts, with units expected to advance from Sodary and Mazroub, near the West Kordofan border, both of which the military took control of last week.




North Kordofan Governor Abdel Khaleq Abdel Latif said in a press release that the military now controls 96 percent of the state.




The military’s gains have come largely through a strategy of sustained pressure rather than direct assaults, a retired officer told Mada Masr. By surrounding RSF positions, cutting off supply lines and wearing down fighters with airstrikes, the military has weakened the group’s ability to hold territory and forced it to withdraw, he explained.




With Mazroub now under its control, the military has greater room to maneuver, the retired officer said. 

It can use the area as a base to strike RSF positions in Um Bader, advance southeast toward 

Khawi

 in West Kordofan, or push southwest toward Nuhud.




As the military prepares for what is intended to be the final offensive to secure North Kordofan, Mohamed Didan, the spokesperson for the special operations forces in West Kordofan, 

said 

the air force had carried out more than 150 airstrikes between Sunday and Tuesday, destroying 100 military vehicles and dozens of other targets.




Anticipating a military advance into West Kordofan, the RSF has been reinforcing its positions in Nuhud. Additional forces have arrived in the city, and the group has dug trenches and built earth berms around it to guard against surprise attacks, an activist in the state told Mada Masr.




Nuhud is considered the western gateway to North Kordofan’s capital, Obeid, and the northwestern corner in West Kordofan’s strategic triangle, alongside Babanusa and 

Heglig.

 Whoever holds it controls a staging point between West Kordofan and North Darfur.




The Dar Hamar emergency room 

said

 on Wednesday that the RSF was also conducting forced recruitment campaigns in the city.




In its statement, the emergency room said the RSF cut Starlink satellite communications in Nuhud and surrounding areas for the third consecutive day, as security restrictions on residents intensified. The group was also cutting tree branches to cover its vehicles and conceal them from aerial surveillance, the statement added.




The RSF has also turned Nuhud’s main referral hospital into a base for jamming equipment and taken over West Kordofan University to house foreign fighters, according to the emergency room.




These measures come as humanitarian and security conditions in Nuhud continue to deteriorate, with communications disrupted and residents facing restrictions on their movement, the emergency room said.




***




Control shifts again along West Darfur border areas




Border areas in West Darfur, near the Chadian border and the state capital Geneina, continue to change hands, with the military and its allied joint force of armed movements on one side and the RSF on the other vying for control.




The joint force 

said 

its troops clashed with the RSF on Monday along the Bir Saliba and Abu Sorug fronts, retaking Bir Saliba and consolidating their presence in the area.

 The alliance also announced it destroyed seven RSF combat vehicles and inflicted heavy casualties during the operation.




The latest fighting follows repeated shifts in control of the two areas, which lie about 30 and 36 km north of Geneina, which is held by the paramilitary group. 

In 

August

, the joint force seized the area before pulling back to avoid being outflanked as the RSF deployed large numbers of troops and vehicles to retake it.




Monday’s operation began with a surprise attack on RSF positions from several directions, inflicting casualties and destroying equipment before the joint force secured Bir Saliba, a field source in the joint force told Mada Masr.




Abu Sorug is more difficult to hold because of its exposed terrain, the source said, predicting that the joint force might withdraw again toward Bir Saliba and Hajar Marfain. 




The two areas have remained a challenge for the RSF since the military launched a surprise offensive in West Darfur in July, advancing from North Darfur and bringing military and allied forces within reach of Geneina. The RSF has since 

launched

 several 

attacks

 in an effort to 

retake

 lost ground and ease pressure on the capital.




The border location, rugged terrain and open routes toward Tina in North Darfur, which is held by the military, have made these areas particularly difficult to secure.




***




RSF special operations commander defects




Former RSF commander Mohamed Azrag al-Fanjary announces his defection in a video statement, October 8. Courtesy: AlArabiya Screen via YouTube.




Mohamed Azrag al-Fanjary, the commander of an RSF special operations group, 

announced 

on Thursday that he defected with around 300 officers and soldiers and 30 combat vehicles, in the latest of a series of senior departures from the paramilitary group in recent months.

 




The group included commanders and officers from units that had operated under Al-Nour “Gubba” Adam, the former senior RSF commander and Mahamid tribal leader who defected to the military earlier this year, according to a source close to Fanjary who is a member of Gubba’s defected forces. The decision followed contacts with military commanders and arrangements that had been underway for some time, the source told Mada Masr.




In a video statement, Fanjary 

said 

he was relinquishing his military duties and responsibilities within the RSF, describing his decision as the result of “an honest review of oneself and deep reflection” on the state of Sudan due to the war.

 He disavowed abuses against civilians and their property and called on other RSF members to follow his lead.




The defection is significant because of the nature of the unit that left with him, according to both the source close to Fanjary and a former RSF source who had worked in the group’s operations authority. The officers’ roles gave them knowledge of RSF deployments and operational arrangements, the sources said.




According to the source close to him, Fanjary and his group decided to leave after reviewing the state of the RSF and the course of military operations in recent months. The source did not disclose where the group had been stationed or where it ultimately went.




The departure involved an organized unit that kept its internal hierarchy, with officers still in command of their men and equipment, rather than individuals leaving the RSF separately, the source added. Several of the officers had been involved in field operations, giving them direct knowledge of how the RSF was deployed and operated.




The source close to Fanjary placed the defection within a broader pattern among forces that had served under Gubba before his departure from the RSF. Several members of those forces, particularly field commanders, have begun holding separate discussions about leaving, the source said, adding that Fanjary was among them before he made his decision public.




The former RSF operations source cautioned against interpreting the departures as evidence that the paramilitary group was collapsing. The RSF still has large units and retains significant military capabilities spread across several fronts, the source said.




What Fanjary’s departure means for the RSF may become clearer in the coming days, particularly if other units that operated on the same fronts follow suit, the source close to him said. The fact that groups have been discussing their departure with military commanders makes it harder to view each case in isolation, the source added, while drawing a distinction between units that leave with their equipment and individual fighters who depart on their own.




***

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: JAWS Reception Celebrates Legacy of Women in Journalism
content:
The Journalism and Women Symposium (JAWS) celebrated the legacy of women journalists at a reception on October 2 hosted at the Ms. office. The gathering brought together journalists, longtime JAWS members, and feminist advocates to recognize the women who helped shape media and discuss the importance of preserving their work for future generations.

The reception highlighted the connections between JAWS, Ms. and the Feminist Majority Foundation (FMF), publisher of Ms. magazine. Kathy Bonk, a longtime feminist advocate and leader, recalled how Ms. founder Gloria Steinem reached out to ask FMF to keep the magazine alive. With the support of Ellie Smeal, Katherine Spillar, Peg Yorkin, and others, FMF committed to sustaining Ms. feminist journalism.

Bonk also reflected on the role of feminist journalism in advancing the women’s movement, arguing that the journalists who documented the movement helped make its progress possible. Bonk shared, “It’s no longer just news coverage. It’s looking for an impact. It’s looking at how we change people’s lives.”

A central focus of the reception was JAWS’ Legacy Fund and its efforts to preserve the history of women in journalism. Pam Morland, a former JAWS president and longtime journalist, described donating decades of professional and personal materials to archive her materials going back to 1985.

Morland encouraged fellow journalists to preserve their own work rather than discard it, explaining that materials that may seem unremarkable today can become valuable historical records. The archives offer researchers an opportunity to explore the experiences and contributions of women journalists and document the development of organizations such as JAWS.

The reception highlighted the importance of preserving women’s experiences in journalism, particularly as the profession continues to confront challenges. JAWS is helping ensure the future generations can study their work and understand the history of feminist media.

As Ms. approaches its 55th anniversary in December, marking 25 years with the Feminist Majority Foundation as publisher, the gathering celebrated the relationships, reporting and feminist organizing that have sustained the magazine and the broader movement. Speakers closed by celebrating Ms., Gloria Steinem, and the community of women journalists whose work continues to shape feminist media.

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Martin Soto, Organizer of Delaney Hall Hunger Strike, Released After 8 Months
content:
Soto was abducted by ICE in February while buying diapers for his son.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Martin Soto, who helped lead a hunger strike at Delaney Hall immigration jail in Newark, New Jersey, earlier this year, was released from detention with an ankle monitor on Tuesday evening.

Martin was released after U.S. District Court Judge Jamel Semper ruled that his detention was illegal, citing the conditions of his confinement, his deteriorating mental health, and lack of sufficient reason to continue his detention.

Martin was abducted by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) while buying diapers for his 11-month-old son in February, and was central to organizing the hunger strike at Delaney Hall that began in May. The strike lasted for a month and put a national spotlight on the inhumane conditions at the for-profit immigration jail — including medical neglect, deprivation of legal counsel, and coerced deportation of people being detained.

Martin faced retaliation at the ICE detention center almost immediately.

From the first day of the hunger strike, Martin’s wife, Gabriela Soto, protested outside of Delaney Hall with other family members of hunger striking detainees, translating calls from Martin and others inside who described the conditions they were facing. Guards at Delaney retaliated by cutting phone access for those detained.

ICE agents and staff at Delaney Hall reportedly singled out Martin as the leader of the strike on the first day, asking him, “If we release you right now, will you tell your wife to stop the protest outside?”

ICE agents then transferred Martin from Delaney to New Jersey’s Elizabeth Detention Center in an attempt to crush the hunger strike. But instead of stopping the hunger strike, his transfer led to sustained mass protests outside of Delaney Hall. Activists attempted to block his transfer by forming a blockade, which led to daily protests as well as clashes with ICE followed by the state police.

During the protests, Gabriela regularly spoke about the squalid conditions at Delaney Hall, where three immigrants have died since it was reopened as a detention center run by GEO Group in May 2025. More than 50 people have died in ICE custody across the U.S. throughout President Donald Trump’s second term.

In an article for Truthout, Gabriela wrote that she “learned about the abuses firsthand. Martin told me that in May, all detainees in Unit 2 were fed food infested with worms, and when they refused to eat the worm-ridden food, the guards told them either eat or you will starve until the next day.”

“Meanwhile, when Martin got sick, he would go three or four weeks without getting seen, much less treated.”

After his transfer to Elizabeth Detention Center, Martin was held in solitary confinement for four months, from mid-May to mid-September. During this time, Gabriela experienced a miscarriage, which she says was due to the stress of her husband being detained.

In late June, ICE transferred the hunger strikers out of Delaney Hall en masse — forcibly moving some 200 of the 300 hunger strikers and effectively ending the strike.

But the hunger strike and solidarity protests, as well as Gabriela’s continued agitation, eventually led to Martin’s release — though he remains in an ankle monitor pending the outcome of his immigration case.

“I am so thankful for everybody that has helped me,” Gabriela said in a comment after Martin’s release. “These months have been very, very difficult. Not only did I lose our home, not only did I lose our child, but it made me — this experience made me stronger to keep fighting to have the reunitement of our family.”

author: Gwynne Hogan
title: Protests Erupt in New York City After ICE Agent Shoots Father in the Bronx
content:
The man, who is still being detained, had his 5-year-old child in his car at the time of the shooting.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

A federal immigration officer shot a man Thursday afternoon in New York’s Marble Hill neighborhood, according to police, eyewitnesses and the Department of Homeland Security, in an incident that drew swift rebuke from elected officials and a crowd of spontaneous protesters late Thursday night.

The man was treated at a nearby hospital for a gunshot wound to the neck, officials said.

Eyewitnesses described a chaotic scene unfurling on a busy street in Marble Hill — a neighborhood that is legally in Manhattan but connected to The Bronx — around 4 p.m., as a slew of New Yorkers were getting home from work and school. As shots rang out, bystanders sheltered in neighboring businesses, the eyewitnesses said.

New York City officials said the ICE agents were in plainclothes wearing masks and construction vests at the time of the shooting, and video and photos of the moments after showed one agent brandishing an assault rifle, as passersby ducked for cover.

Crowds of protesters and elected officials arrived at the scene in the hours after the shooting and outside the nearby NewYork—Presbyterian Allen Hospital, where the wounded man was taken.

“What happened today was an outrage,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a press conference at the scene late Thursday night. Mamdani confirmed the man’s 5-year-old son was in the car at the time of the shooting.

“When ICE agents opened fire, a 5-year-old child — a 5-year-old child — was in the back seat of that car,” he said. “Thank god that child is physically unharmed.”

The mayor said he spent two hours on the phone with President Donald Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in a failed attempt to get the shooting victim — identified as 28-year-old Oscar Belgal — released. Instead, Mamdani said, ICE agents “whisked him away” from the hospital in Upper Manhattan. “During the incident, an ICE officer discharged his weapon and the criminal illegal alien was injured,” the statement read. “ICE officers immediately rendered aid. The individual is alive and at a local hospital. The FBI and HSI are on the scene. The incident remains under investigation.”

Belgal was identified by Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch late Thursday. Court records showed he pleaded guilty in 2025 to grand larceny in the fourth degree and had an open charge for criminal possession of a controlled substance stemming from an arrest in 2025.

Eyewitnesses to the shooting spoke to The City Reporter and Documented in the hours after the shooting, recalling the commotion as gunfire erupted in the middle of a residential neighborhood. Iris Rosa, a school therapist, said after she emerged from a nearby shop, she saw a man bleeding on the ground in front of a car, while agents milled around, one holding a small child.

“He was all full of blood,” she said, while the child an agent held was quiet. “How could you do this? What is going on? And then I’m looking at the baby.”

Stephanie Ferrer, 30, who lives in Marble Hill, said she heard multiple shots and called 911. She watched the scene from one of her bedroom windows until agents carried the man away by his arms and legs.

“He was disoriented, I think because one of the guys that was holding him next to him was trying to keep him aware, trying to keep him awake by just doing some taps on the cheek,” she said. “You know, like, ‘hey buddy,’ like ‘stay awake, don’t fall asleep.’”

A video posted to social media appeared to show the chaotic aftermath, with a crowd gathered as NYPD officers rushed to a car and carried a man, seemingly unconscious, out of it and into the back of a law enforcement vehicle.

“Put pressure,” one officer is heard to say as they load the man into the back seat.

In a statement posted to X, the NYPD confirmed federal agents were behind the shooting and took the victim to the hospital. “The NYPD was not involved in the incident and was not on scene at the time of the shooting,” they said.

By Thursday evening a crowd of protesters had gathered at the scene, while NYPD officers and caution tape blocked off the street. The dented car Belgal was driving could still be seen blocking West 225th Street at Marble Hill Avenue. Two agents in plainclothes from the Department of Homeland Security were canvassing the area for video footage.

At an impromptu protest at the scene Thursday night elected officials and immigrant advocates gathered to denounce the shooting.

Rep. Adriano Espaillat told the crowd the child was safe with other family members and that he had tried to visit the wounded man in a nearby hospital and been barred from talking with him by ICE agents.

“The family is shaken…by this terrible horrible shooting,” he said.

Another crowd of protesters gathered outside the nearby NewYork-Presbyterian Allen Hospital where the man was said to have been taken, as police and officials from Mamdani’s office stood at the perimeter.

Protesters tried to block a car of federal agents leaving the hospital, and police officers pushed demonstrators aside to clear the way, making several arrests.

The shooting occurred not far from the rooftop parking deck of a Target store where, Bronx Borough President Vanessa Gibson said later that night, federal immigration agents sometimes muster, before heading into The Bronx to make arrests.

Jumaane Williams, the city’s public advocate, told Documented and The City Reporter that he spoke with the family of the shooting victim.

“Thankfully, the father is alert, from what I understand. Shot in the neck, but alive, which I’m thankful for, and his child is with the family,” said Williams. “But I don’t trust the investigation that the federal government is going to try to do.”

Mamdani called for ICE to be abolished and, referring to striking images of one of the agents standing at the shooting scene in a yellow construction vest and holding a rifle.

“Residents have no idea if these are law enforcement agents or if they are simply attacking someone on the street,” he said. “When it comes to ICE it begs the question, ‘What’s the difference?’”

Gov. Kathy Hochul said she had talked with President Donald Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin about the shooting.

“I expressed outrage on behalf of New Yorkers and urged them to halt ICE enforcement operations in New York,” she said in a statement. “I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public so we can establish the facts and get to the truth.”

title: ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᕕᒃ ᐱᒋᐊᕐᐳᖅ ᐊᕐᕕᐊᓂᑦ
content:
For the English version of this story, please see 

Modular home factory begins production in Arviat

.







ᒪᑐᐃᖅᑕᐅᓂᖓᓄᑦ ᖁᕕᐊᓲᑎᖃᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᑭᐱᓯᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᒪᑐᐊᕈᑎᖓᓂ ᐅᓇ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᕕᒃᓴᖅ ᒪᑐᐃᖅᑕᐅᓪᓚᕆᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᓯᑎᐱᕆ 29-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




ᐅᓇ $75-ᒥᓕᐊᓐᑖᓚᑐᕐᑐᖅ, ᐊᖏᓂᖃᖅᖢᓂ 64,500-ᑭᑉᐹᕆᒃᑎᓯᒪᔪᓂ ᕘᑦᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᒃᓴᖅ ᐱᒋᐊᕈᑎᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ 60 ᐳᓴᓐᑎᒥ ᐱᒋᐊᕈᑎᖃᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᓯᑎᐱᕆ 23-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ, ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᓴᒃᑯᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᑐᑭᒧᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᔨᖓ ᔭᐃᓴᓐ ᒋᐸᓐᔅ ᐊᐱᕐᓱᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ. ᑕᖅᑭᑦ 18 ᐃᓗᐊᒍᑦ ᐅᓇ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᕕᒃ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖏᓐᓂᑦ ᑕᒪᒃᑮᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᐊᕐᑐᖅ ᓴᓇᕙᒡᓗᑎᒃ 40-ᓂ ᐃᓚᒌᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑲᑎᕐᖓᐅᖅᑐᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒥ.




ᐃᓄᖕᓄᑦ ᓇᖕᒥᓂᕆᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᕕᒃ ᐊᕐᕕᐊᓂᒃ ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᔪᖅ ᐅᕘᓇ ᓴᒃᑯ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕈᑎᓄᑦ, ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᖃᕐᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᓴᒃᑯ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᓕᕆᔨᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑯᐸᐃᒃᒥ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᖅᑎᓄᑦ (ᐊᔾᔨᙳᐊᖅ ᐅᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᑕᓃᔅ ᑯᓱᒐᖅ/ᓴᒃᑯ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᓕᕆᔨᓄᑦ ᑯᐊᐳᕇᓴᓐᑯᓐᓂᑦ)




ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᕕᒃ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᖃᕐᑐᖅ 15-ᓂ, 14 ᐃᓅᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᑭᐅᕈᓕᓐ ᓅᑦ, ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᔨ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᖅ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᓴᒃᑯ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕈᑎᒃᑯᑦ, ᐱᓕᕆᐊᕆᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᓴᒃᑯ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᓕᕆᔨᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑯᐸᒃᒥᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᖅᑎᓄᑦ RG Solution-ᑯᓐᓄᑦ, ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐃᓄᖕᓄᑦ ᓇᖕᒥᓂᕆᔭᐅᔪᒧᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᒃᒥ. ᑖᒃᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᖁᓕᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᖅᐸᒃᑐᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᕕᒃᒥ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᓂᒃᑰᖓᙱᖢᑎᒃ.




“ᐊᑕᐅᓯᑐᐊᕐᒥ ᐃᓅᙱᑦᑐᒥ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᖃᕐᑐᑦ, ᐅᕙᓐᓂ,” ᓅᑦ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᐊᐱᕐᓱᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




2028 ᐊᕐᕌᒍ ᑎᑭᑉᐸᑦ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑐᑦ 40-ᐅᓕᕐᓂᐊᖅᑐᑦ ᐃᓚᖃᕐᓗᑎᒃ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔮᖃᓪᓚᕆᒃᐸᒃᑐᓂᑦ, ᕿᔪᓕᕆᔨᓂᒃ, ᓱᓪᓗᓕᕆᔨᓂᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᐊᔭᓕᕆᔨᓂᒃ, ᒋᐸᓐᔅ ᐅᖃᕐᒥᔪᖅ.
















ᐱᔪᓐᓇᐅᑎᖃᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᖅ ᒪᑯᓂᖓ ᕿᔪᓕᕆᔨᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᓪᓚᕆᒃᑐᓂᒃ ᐅᓇ ᑲᒻᐸᓂᐅᔪᖅ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᖅᓴᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᐊᖅᑐᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᖃᕐᓗᑎᒃ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᓯᓚᑦᑐᖅᓴᕐᕕᒃᒥ ᓇᓗᓇᐃᒃᑯᑎᑖᖅᑎᑕᐅᓇᓱᒡᓗᑎᒃ ᓴᓇᔨᐅᔪᑦ, ᓅᑦ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᓴᒃᑯᑯᑦ ᐃᓱᒪᔪᑦ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔮᒃᓴᓂ ᑕᒪᐅᖔᕐᓯᒪᙱᑦᑐᓂ ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᓂᐊᕋᓱᒋᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᒪᐅᓇ ᐃᖏᕐᕋᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᓂᒃᑯᑦ, ᐋᖄᖅᑭᒃᓱᐃᕙᓪᓕᐊᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᐊᓂᒃᑕᐅᑎᑦᑎᔾᔪᑎᒃᑯᑦ.




ᒫᓂ ᐊᑕᐅᓯᖅ ᐱᖓᓲᓕᖓᓪᓗᒍ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᒃ, ᑖᓐᓇᓗ ᓴᓇᔭᐅᓕᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᖅ 2023-ᒥ ᐊᐅᓚᔾᔪᑎᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᒫᓂᒃ $50 ᒥᓕᐊᓐ ᑖᓚᓂ ᐅᖅᑰᑕᐅᑎᖃᑦᑎᐊᑦᑐᑦ ᓯᕐᓗᐊᖅ. ᓂᒡᓕᓇᖅᑐᓂᒃ ᐃᓂᖃᕐᕕᐅᓂᐊᖅᑐᖅ ᓯᕐᓗᐊᖅ ᓴᓂᑦᑎᐊᖓᓃᓐᓂᐊᖅᑐᖅ ᐱᐊᓂᒃᑕᐅᓂᐊᕋᓱᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᓄᕕᐱᕆᐅᓕᕐᐸᑦ. ᐃᓂᖃᕐᕕᐅᑎᑕᐅᓂᐊᖅᖢᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒧᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᓂᐊᖅᑐᓂᒃ ᐃᒡᓗᒃᓴᕆᔭᐅᓂᐊᖅᑐᓂᒃ.




ᐅᓇ 6-ᓄᑦ ᐃᓚᒌᓄᑦ ᑲᖏᖅᖠᓂᖅᒥ ᓴᓇᔭᐅᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᕆᔭᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᓴᒃᑯ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕈᑎᒃᑯᑦ, ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᒌᖕᓂᒃᑰᖓᔪᖅ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᓴᒃᑯ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᓕᕆᔨᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑯᐸᐃᒃᒥ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᖅᑎᓄᑦ RG Solution. (ᐊᔾᔨᙳᐊᖅ ᐅᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᑕᓃᔅ ᑯᓱᒐᖅ/ᓴᒃᑯ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᓕᕆᔨᓄᑦ ᑯᐊᐳᕇᓴᓐᑯᓐᓂᑦ)




ᓴᒃᑯ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᒃᓴᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᖃᖅᑎᑦᑎᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᕕᒃᒥ ᐊᑐᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᐃᓄᖕᓅᖓᔪᓄᑦ ᐱᖁᑎᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᒌᖕᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖏᓐᓂᒃ, ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᐅᑭᐅᕐᑕᖅᑐᕐᒥ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂ, ᐃᓛᒌᓄᑦ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓕᕆᔨᓄᑦ, ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᕆᔨᕐᔪᐊᓄᑦ, ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᓐᓄᑦ.




ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᕕᐅᔪᖅ ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᕙᓪᓕᐊᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᓂᐊᖅᑐᓂ ᑕᖅᑭᐅᓵᖅᑐᒥ 9-ᓂ ᐱᖓᓱᓂ ᐃᒡᓗᕈᓯᖃᖅᑐᓂ ᐃᒡᓗᒃᓴᓂᒃ, ᑖᒃᑯᐊᓗ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᑕᐅᓯᒪᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓄᑦ ᐃᓕᐅᖃᖅᑕᐅᓂᐊᕐᓗᑎᒃ ᐅᐱᕐᖔᙳᖅᐸᑦ, ᓅᑦ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ. ᑲᒻᐸᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐸᕐᓇᒃᐸᓪᓕᐊᔪᑦ ᒪᕐᕈᐃᓂ 12-ᓂ ᑲᑎᕐᖓᐅᖅᑐᓂᒃ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᓂᐊᕐᓗᑎᒃ ᑲᖏᖅᖠᓂᖅᒥᓐ.
















ᓯᕗᓂᐊᒍᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᑕᐅᔪᑦ ᐱᐊᓂᒃᑕᐅᓚᐅᖅᑎᓐᓇᒋᑦ ᑯᐸᐃᒃᒥ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᕕᒃᓴᓂᑦ, ᑲᒻᐸᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓯᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᒪᕐᕈᐃᓂ ᑕᓪᓕᒪᐅᓕᖓᔪᓂᒃ ᐃᒡᓗᒃᓴᓂᒃ ᐊᕐᕕᐊᓂᑦ, ᒪᕐᕈᐃᓄᑦ ᐃᓚᒌᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᒃᓴᓂ ᓴᓪᓕᓂᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑎᓴᒪᓂᒃ ᖁᓕᕇᓕᖕᓂ ᐃᒡᓗᒃᓴᓂᒃ, 6-ᓄᑦ ᐃᓚᒌᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᒃᓴᒥᑦ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᒪᕐᕈᐃᓕᖓᔪᒥᑦ ᑲᖏᖅᖠᓂᖅᒥᓐ.




ᐃᒡᓗᐃᑦ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᑕᐅᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᐅᑭᐅᕐᑕᖅᑐᕐᒥ ᐃᓅᓯᕐᒧᑦ, ᐃᒻᒥᒃᑳᖓᔪᓂᒃ ᐃᓯᕐᕕᖃᐅᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᐃᓚᒌᓅᖓᔪᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓂ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᑐᕐᓲᖃᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᓯᕗᓂᐊᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑐᓄᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᑕᐅᓯᐅᓈᕐᓯᒪᔪᓂᒃ ᐃᒡᓗᒃᓴᓂᒃ, ᓅᑦ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᐊᓂᐊᕐᕕᖃᑦᑎᐊᖕᓂᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐅᖁᔭᔾᔮᖏᑦᑐᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᒍᑎᖃᙱᓐᓂᕐᓴᐅᓗᑎᒃ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᒪᑐᐃᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᖁᕕᐊᓲᑎᖃᕐᓂᖅ ᐅᐸᒃᑕᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐅᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᑭᕙᓪᓕᖅᒥᑦ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᑦ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᖓᓄ ᑯᓄ ᑕᑦᑎᐃᓂᕐᒧᑦ, ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᑐᙵᕕᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᖓᓄᑦ ᒍᓘᕆᐊ ᐅᓗᕐᓯᒧᑦ, ᔮᓐ ᒪᐃᓐᒧᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᒪᓕᒐᓕᐅᖅᑎ ᓘᕆ ᐃᓪᓚᐅᕐᒧᑦ.

author: newsroom
title: «Το κίνητρο της επίθεσης συνδέεται με τη ναζιστική ιδεολογία των δραστών»
content:
Σύνδεσμος δημοσίευσης: 

«Το κίνητρο της επίθεσης συνδέεται με τη ναζιστική ιδεολογία των δραστών»




Δελτίο Τύπου εξέδωσαν 

οι συνήγοροι

 του αντιφασίστα που μαχαιρώθηκε στην Ελευσίνα, ξεκαθαρίζοντας ότι δεν υπάρχει βάση για τις φήμες που διασπείρονται από κάποια ΜΜΕ σχετικά με ύπαρξη άλλου κινήτρου για την δολοφονική επίθεση.







ΔΕΛΤΙΟ ΤΥΠΟΥ




Την 8η Οκτωβρίου 2026 και περί ώρα 16:10, ο εντολέας μας δέχθηκε επίθεση με χαρακτηριστικά ενέδρας και ανθρωποκτόνο πρόθεση, έξω από την οικία του, στην περιοχή της Ελευσίνας.




Οι δράστες έχουν ήδη ταυτοποιηθεί από τις αστυνομικές αρχές.




Το κίνητρο της επίθεσης γνωστοποιήθηκε στον εντολέα μας από έναν εκ των δραστών, πριν από την έναρξή της. Σύμφωνα με όσα του δηλώθηκαν, η επίθεση συνδέεται με τη ναζιστική ιδεολογία των δραστών και με τις αντιρατσιστικές ιδέες και την κοινωνική δράση του θύματος.




Της επίθεσης είχε προηγηθεί η παρακολούθηση και ο εντοπισμός του εντολέα μας, ενώ ακολούθησαν απειλές σε βάρος του, απόπειρα ανθρωποκτονίας με τρεις μαχαιριές — δύο εκ των οποίων τον έπληξαν, ενώ η τρίτη του προκάλεσε εκδορά στην περιοχή της κοιλίας — καθώς και απόπειρα ληστείας σε βάρος του.




Ο εντολέας μας νοσηλεύεται στο Τζάνειο Νοσοκομείο. Η κατάσταση της υγείας του έχει σταθεροποιηθεί και η ζωή του δεν βρίσκεται πλέον σε κίνδυνο. Οι δράστες εξακολουθούν μέχρι στιγμής να διαφεύγουν της σύλληψης.




Στο σημείο της επίθεσης υπήρχαν αυτόπτες μάρτυρες, οι οποίοι πρέπει να αναζητηθούν και να εξεταστούν από τις αρμόδιες αρχές.




Καθώς ο εντολέας μας και η οικογένειά του βιώνουν ιδιαίτερα δύσκολες στιγμές, παρακαλούμε τα μέσα ενημέρωσης να επιδείξουν τον αναγκαίο σεβασμό και διακριτικότητα, προστατεύοντας την ιδιωτικότητα του ίδιου και των οικείων του.




Αθήνα, 9 Οκτωβρίου 2026




Οι συνήγοροι




Ελευθερία Τομπατζόγλου




Βασίλης Τσίλης




Αργύρης Συρίγος







Νωρίτερα εξέδωσε σχετική ανακοίνωση και ο 

Σύλλογος Πολιτισμού «Παύλος Killah P Φύσσας»

:







Η δολοφονική επίθεση γνωστών οργανωμένων νεοναζί εναντίον ακτιβιστή του αντιφασιστικού κινήματος στην Ελευσίνα είναι κομβικής σημασίας για την πορεία του φασισμού στην Ελλάδα.




Αν οι φασίστες αφεθούν ξανά ελεύθεροι να επιτίθονται σε όποιον δεν τους αρέσει, σε αντιφασίστες, συνδικαλιστές και μετανάστες, με μαθηματική ακρίβεια θα φτάσουν ξανά στις δολοφονίες.




Είναι άκρως ανησυχητική η αρχική στάση της αστυνομίας που διέρρευσε (και μέρους των ΜΜΕ που αναπαρήγαγαν) το σενάριο της υποτιθέμενης “ληστείας” ενώ ήταν εξ αρχής γνωστά και επιβεβαιωμένα τα κίνητρα των νεοναζί.




Καλούμε όλους τους φορείς, τις οργανώσεις και τις συλλογικότητες από κάθε κοινωνικό και πολιτικό χώρο, σε άμεση κινητοποίηση πριν να είναι ξανά αργά.




Καλούμε κάθε αρμόδιο θεσμικό φορέα να αναλάβει τις ευθύνες του.




Δε θα επιτρέψουμε ξανά τη θεσμική ανοχή ή και συγκάλυψη των ναζιστικών εγκλημάτων.




Να δράσουμε τώρα!




Σύλλογος Πολιτισμού




«Παύλος Killah P Φύσσας»




9.10.2026







«Το κίνητρο της επίθεσης συνδέεται με τη ναζιστική ιδεολογία των δραστών»

author: Sarah Lane
title: Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize is a victory for the power of human rights law
content:
9th October 2026










Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize is a victory for the power of human rights law
















6 min read



















From S. Mona Sinha – our CEO


























































Navi Pillay grew up under laws designed to deny her equality. Born into a Tamil family in apartheid South Africa, she knew that injustice could be written into a statute and defended from a judge’s bench. She devoted her career to proving the law could be a force for justice instead making legal equality into lived equality.




Today, the Norwegian Nobel Committee has awarded her the 2026 

Nobel Peace Prize

 

for her efforts to promote peace and international law. It recognises a career spanning the struggle against apartheid, international criminal justice and her service as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. Throughout, Navi has demonstrated an unwavering belief in the power of international law and the institutions created to uphold it, not as abstract ideals, but as essential protections against abuse, persecution and impunity.




For us at Equality Now, this is a moment of immense pride. Navi 

co-founded our organisation in 1992

 with Jessica Neuwirth and Feryal Gharahi. Together, they challenged a deeply entrenched hierarchy: violence and discrimination against women were human rights violations, not private matters or cultural practices beyond the reach of justice. Governments had a duty to deliver gender equality under the law.




Over her lifetime, Navi has defended justice across the world. She helped secure a landmark legal breakthrough as a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda where she was instrumental in the Akayesu judgement establishing that rape could constitute genocide. It transformed the recognition of sexual violence in international law, acknowledging its deliberate use in the destruction of a people.




Navi’s career is a testament to what these legal mechanisms can achieve when they are respected, utilised and given the authority to act.




That conviction runs through the work of Equality Now. We are global because injustice is global, and we share Navi’s determination to confront it wherever it exists. We use international law to help reform discriminatory laws and turn legal commitments into lived reality. In Africa, as Secretariat of the 

SOAWR Coalition

, we support women to use the 

Maputo Protocol

, one of the world’s most progressive women’s rights treaties, to demand equality and protection. Around the world, we work with partners to strengthen laws on sexual violence, expand access to survivor-centred justice, end child marriage and challenge systemic discrimination. In every region, the principle is the same: justice must reach those whom power, prejudice and politics too often leave behind. 




The Nobel Committee’s announcement comes at a critical moment. International human rights institutions, courts, and the principles they uphold are under growing attack. We cannot forget why they exist. They were built from humanity’s darkest lessons knowing what happens when power goes unchecked and human dignity becomes expendable. They exist not only to reckon with the past, but to stop us from repeating it. 




That conviction remains at the heart of Equality Now. Since Navi helped found us, we and our partners have helped 

reform more than 140 discriminatory laws

 around the world. But Navi’s example reminds us that changing the law is never the end of the work. Justice only becomes real when the law reaches the people it was meant to protect. Her Nobel Peace Prize is an affirmation of their enduring importance, and of the people who devote their lives to making them work.




At Equality Now, defending international human rights law and enforcement mechanisms is central to our work. Alongside partners worldwide, we are challenging attempts to weaken human rights protections, strengthening accountability through UN and regional mechanisms, and working to ensure that international legal obligations and commitments become a reality and provide justice in people’s lives. We share Navi’s conviction that international law must be more than a promise on paper. It must be upheld, defended and made real for the people who depend upon it.




From confronting the injustices of apartheid to helping establish new standards of international accountability, Navi has shown what becomes possible when we refuse to accept that power should prevail over principle. I celebrate Navi today not only with immense pride, but with gratitude. To lead an organisation she helped build is to inherit both an extraordinary gift and a responsibility: to keep asking whether the law is serving those with the least power, and to keep challenging it when it does not.




Her Nobel Peace Prize honours a lifetime of making justice possible. It also reminds us that the institutions she has helped shape are worth defending because the people they exist to protect are worth defending. Every one of us.




The honour is hers. The responsibility to uphold what she stands for belongs to us all.
