author: Nahuel Lag
title: Mucha tierra en muy pocas manos: un plan para favorecer a las grandes empresas globales
content:
Por Nahuel Lag 




La decisión del gobierno de Javier Milei de buscar estrategias jurídicas —DNU 70/2023, Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada— para derogar la Ley de Tierras y la decisión de la Corte Suprema de validar la derogación sin revisar su constitucionalidad, no son un fenómeno aislado. Carlos Duarte, relator por América Latina del Grupo de Trabajo de la Declaración de las Naciones Unidas sobre los Derechos de los Campesinos (Undrop, por sus siglas en inglés), lo identifica dentro de una “arquitectura jurídica transnacional que se difunde por mimetismo legislativo y presión multilateral” en el informe 

“Contrarreformas agrarias: anatomía de un despojo en progreso”

. 




El trabajo da un a

nálisis minucioso, con particular foco en América Latina, en el que establece cuatro lógicas contemporáneas de despojo

 que se repiten en todos los continentes: ingeniería legal, 

financiarización, acaparamiento verde y el rol del Estado como promotor corporativo

. El objetivo: avanzar sobre las tierras campesinas, indígenas y de pequeños productores para trastocar el derecho de acceso a la tierra y ponerla al servicio de los intereses corporativos.  




El informe, publicado este año, continúa actualizándose de manera vertiginosa en los últimos meses ante cada nuevo paso de los sectores políticas de la derecha regional: el 

debate del capítulo de tierras en la Argentina

, el 

decreto de “fortalecimiento del agronegocio” en la Honduras

 del presidente Nasry Asfura y 

la Colombia del flamante mandatario Abelardo de la Espriella

, cuya primera acción fue prohibir la palabra “campesino” en documentos oficiales.    




“

Con la llegada de gobiernos de ultra derecha hay un proceso muy agresivo

 de intentar romper todas las salvaguardas sobre la propiedad de la tierra y reinterpretar los marcos regulatorios para generar procesos de concentración”, sentencia Duarte en diálogo con Tierra Viva y contrapone que el problema tampoco logró pasar de 

tímidos reformismos durante los gobiernos progresistas

 por la imposibilidad de romper con las élites terratenientes.  




Foto: Luciana Fernández




Seguir concentrando lo ya concentrado




América Latina, advierte Duarte, es el laboratorio primordial de estas estrategias que tienen como objetivo pasar de “la tierra como base material de proyectos de vida” a “su consolidación definitiva como un simple activo financiero líquido” y como consecuencia la 

“concentración acelerada, desplazamiento de los sujetos vulnerables y ruptura del relevo generacional campesino”

.




Al contextualizar esta arquitectura jurídica global, el profesor e investigador del Instituto de Estudios Interculturales Javeriana de Cali (Colombia) contrapone llamamientos a la redistribución de la tierra como la 

Declaración de Derechos Campesinos

, en 2018, y los acuerdos alcanzados en la última 

Conferencia Internacional sobre Reforma Agraria y Desarrollo Rural

 (Ciradr+20) con un mundo en regresión normativa y en proceso de concentración. El dato más reciente del informe “La situación de la tenencia de la tierra y la gobernanza” —publicado por la FAO, la Coalición Internacional por la Tierra y el Cirad— ubicó la distribución de la tierra entre países en un 0,95 en el coeficiente de Gini, siendo 1 el mayor nivel de concentración. 




Tres datos permiten realizar un repaso rápido de cómo esa situación se refleja en la Argentina. Según el informe 

"Los señores de la tierra"

 —FIAN Internacional y Focus on the Global South, 2025—, 

diez terratenientes transnacionales controlan 40 millones de hectáreas y tres de ellos operan en Argentina: Arauco, Benetton y Cresud

. Según datos del Registro de Tierras —creado por la Ley en disputa—, el 

Observatorio de Tierras

 señaló que Argentina el cinco por ciento de la tierra está en manos extranjeros y en 36 municipios con recursos estratégicos superan hasta el 50 por ciento. Según el 

Censo Nacional Agropecuario 2018

, 

el 55 por ciento de las chacras solo tiene el dos por ciento de la tierra y el uno por ciento de las grandes explotaciones agropecuarias controla el 36 por ciento de la tierra

. 




La ingeniería legal para los negocios corporativos con la tierra 




El trabajo de “Contrarreformas agrarias” del relator de la Undrop toma dimensión para entender qué lugar ocupa la Argentina en un proceso de orden mundial. De las cuatro lógicas de despojo descritas en su trabajo, el Decreto 70/2023 es uno de los mayores ejemplos de la primera de ellas: la “ingeniería legal”. “Es uno de los excesos más graves de los últimos veinte años en la región. Tres líneas de motivación no pueden justificar la abrogación de un régimen que el Congreso sancionó para proteger un bien colectivo indivisible”, señala sobre 

la derogación de la Ley de Tierras que validó la Corte Suprema

.  




—¿Cómo analizás el caso de Argentina dentro de la lógica de “ingeniería legal” del despojo?




—El caso Argentina se enmarca en una serie de procedimientos de despojo al 

hacer pasar por “interés público” lo que son intereses corporativos

 y operó en distintos países a partir de “leyes ómnibus”. El objetivo de estos mecanismos es hacer prevalecer la función productiva del territorio y quitarle el basamento social. Porque, normalmente, la función del territorio debe ser social, es así como se entiende el valor de la propiedad en términos liberales. ¿Por qué se valida que un territorio rural exista? Porque cumple una función social: alimenta, produce, etcétera. Pero lo que se está haciendo es, sobre todo, hacer prevalecer más que lo social la función productiva del territorio. Si la función es social, es para que la tierra se redistribuya, para que disminuya la pobreza. Pero si la prioridad es su productividad, entonces se puede abrir la compuerta para que ese mismo territorio sea vendido a intereses extranjeros. La ingeniería legal que se está utilizando reinterpreta las normas de tierras rurales o agrarias no para la redistribución sino para la explotación, para profundizar la privatización a contramano de los pequeños productores y las personas más vulnerables de la ruralidad. 




El informe ofrece algunos otros ejemplos de leyes ómnibus que a nivel global avanzaron con esta “ingeniera legal” para desplazar los derechos sobre la tierra y dejarlos disponibles para el mercado: 







En Brasil, impulsada por la bancada ruralista del agronegocio, la Ley 14.701, de 2023, introdujo el llamado “marco temporal” a partir del cual solo los pueblos que puedan demostrar ocupación al 5 de octubre de 1988 tienen derecho a la demarcación de sus tierras, obviando el desplazamiento forzado por la dictadura, por ejemplo, y a contramano de la Constitución. En diciembre de 2025, el Supremo Tribunal Federal declaró inconstitucional el “marco temporal”, pero dejó en pie el resto de la “ley ómnibus” que sostiene otros tantos aspectos regresivos denunciados por la Articulación de los Pueblos Indígenas de Brasil.




En Indonesia, a partir de una ley laboral en 2020, se reunieron decenas de regímenes sectoriales: ambiental, laboral, forestal y agrario. Esto debilitó, como denunció Amnistía Internacional, el consentimiento previo, libre e informado sobre las tierras comunitarias y permitió expandir sobre ellas el monocultivo de plantaciones de palma. 




En Vietnam, la Ley de Tierras de 2024 incorporó 31 supuestos a través de los cuales el Estado puede “recuperar” tierras y reasignarlas a desarrolladores privados bajo la rúbrica del desarrollo socioeconómico.  




Ucrania, en 2020, levantó una moratoria de casi dos décadas y habilitó desde el 1 de enero de 2024 la adquisición corporativa de hasta 10.000 hectáreas. Esto en plena guerra y con el campesinado descapitalizado o desplazado abrió paso a la compra de las tierras más fértiles del continente europeo para los capitales que sí pueden esperar al final de la guerra para hacer negocios. 




En Bolivia ocurrió el caso de la 

Ley 1720 de Conversión de la Pequeña Propiedad a Mediana Propiedad

, con la que se habilitaba al Instituto Nacional de Reforma Agraria a reclasificar, mediante trámite voluntario, la condición jurídica de los pequeños predios. Esto habilitaba a acceder al crédito al tiempo que rompía con la inembargabilidad de esas tierras, protegidas por la Constitución. De esta manera, las tierras quedaban dispuestas para ingresar al mercado. La norma sancionada en abril fue derogada en mayo tras masivas movilizaciones de las organizaciones campesino-indígenas bolivianas. 







“Esta disputa no es solo por la tierra, sino que son los recursos naturales, en general, el acaparamiento también de los recursos marítimos, del agua o de las semillas también hacen parte de un mismo proceso. 

La tierra está cada vez en menos manos, los recursos naturales están privatizados y la comida se produce en cada vez porciones más pequeñas de territorio

”, explica Duarte con mirada global.  




Foto: Plaga Colectiva




—Marcás este quiebre legal con la función social de la tierra a favor de una mirada totalmente productivista. El debate sería la tierra para qué en un mundo que aún padece un alto déficit alimentario…  




—Sí, totalmente. Todos los estudios muestran que el nivel de hambre se sigue manteniendo desde la pandemia con 

2.000 millones de personas que sufren hambre

. Si tenemos en cuenta los mismos estudios de la FAO, el 60 o 

el 55 por ciento de la alimentación que se consume en el mundo viene de los predios menores de dos hectáreas

 y si tenemos en cuenta que los predios menores de dos hectáreas apenas llegan al inco por ciento de las superficie global es que estamos muy mal. 

El acaparamiento de tierras se ha incrementado para el monocultivo, la producción de commodities, destinados a la exportación

, a la alimentación del ganado o para producir energía: biocombustibles, parques solares o eólicos. Pero la canasta familiar de alimentos que se consume todos los días aún proviene de esa pequeña agricultura campesina. Y vivimos dentro de una paradoja en la que la gente en la ruralidad no tiene los suficientes alimentos para sus dietas, mientras que en las ciudades hay una sobrealimentación porque la alimentación no es la adecuada. Entonces, ahí tenemos un desbalance alimentario a doble nivel a nivel rural y a nivel urbano. 




—¿Y cómo opera el dogma de la “productividad” frente a esta realidad de tierras que no producen alimentos suficientes ni nutritivos? 




—El dogma pareciera que es productividad en términos de empleo. El empleo en sí trae toda una serie de visiones sobre el territorio. Cuando estamos hablando de empleo ya, de una o otra manera, quiere decir que tú no eres el propietario o que el territorio no es tuyo, sino que es de otro y tú trabajas para algo. La segunda noción es que no importa para qué se utiliza la tierra porque lo alimentario lo resuelvo por vía monetaria, por vía del salario. Y esa vía monetaria, claramente, hace que la soberanía nacional de los alimentos, en muchos países, sea puesta en cuestión, porque necesitan importar sus alimentos, porque en sus tierras se producen más commodities. En un contexto que, quizás sea lo más alarmante, los países hegemónicos buscan, sobre todas las cosas, asegurar su propia soberanía alimentaria. 




—¿Cómo está ocurriendo?




—Está el caso de Donal Trump con la suba de aranceles o de China que debe salir a buscar tierras para abastecer su propia demanda. 

Las potencias económicas protegen su soberanía alimentaria

 porque el dogma liberal de las commodities, del comercio y de los grandes desplazamientos de la comida se puso en cuestión con la pandemia y con las últimas guerras, que han incrementado el valor del combustible y de los alimentos. Sin embargo, el plan que están implementando no es el de protegerla a través de los que producen los alimentos, que son los pequeños productores, sino a través de la financiarización, a través de la gran producción. 




Financiarización, desalojos y expropiaciones exprés 




—La financiarización es otra de las lógicas de despojo que encontraste como un patrón a nivel global que prioriza el activo financiero sobre los derechos territoriales campesinos

.




—Hay tierras que son el activo más importante de una familia por muchas generaciones. Para que eso pueda ser así en muchos países o regiones se crean salvaguardas para que la tierra se mantenga en un círculo familiar. Pero, por ejemplo, en Francia, la Ley 

Sempastous

 rompió esa prevalencia de los herederos para tener la tierra. La Confédération Paysanne denunció, con razón, que la ley terminó legalizando el acaparamiento al sustituir el control sobre la transacción inmobiliaria por una simple compensación económica o ambiental. En Bolivia ocurrió con la Ley 1720. En Estados Unidos ocurrió con salvaguardas que se rompieron para poner las tierras en el mercado accionario. Otra estrategia es desvincular la tierra de los recursos naturales como ocurrió en Australia con el 

Water Act

, que desvinculó los derechos hídricos de los derechos de la tierra. Vos podés conservar la tierra, pero para ponerla a producir, tenés que pagar aparte un arriendo sobre los derechos del agua. Es un despojo por sed administrada. Al final, son los fondos financieros especulativos los que se mueven casi como autónomos buscando su propia ganancia e invierten donde hay oportunidad de crecer sin importar lo que eso signifique socialmente.




—Otra lógica de despojo es el “acaparamiento verde” a partir de proyectos de conservación o mercados de carbono. El Senado de Argentina está debatiendo un proyecto para regular estos mercados, mientras en Misiones

 

familias campesinas denuncian agresiones por parte de la forestal Arauco para expulsarlos

. 

¿Qué ocurre con este fenómeno a nivel global?

 




—Bajo estas modalidades se crean parques nacionales como figuras de reserva, pero que funcionan como parques turísticos o se crean proyectos forestales para la emisión de bonos de carbono que son intermediados y usufructuados por las propias empresas como acciones y terminan desplazando a las comunidades ancestrales. En Tanzania las expulsiones de las tribus Maasai se ejecutaron mediante decisiones ejecutivas que rezonificaron territorios de uso múltiple como reservas exclusivas. Hay muchos ejemplos que muestran cómo esos derechos de protección ambiental, reconocidos internacionalmente, son usufructuados sobre el mismo ambiente por terceros y no son las mismas comunidades que están en el territorio las que reciben los beneficios.  




Foto: CLOC - La Vía Campesina




El análisis de Duarte no solo se posa en la ley ómnibus que implicó el Decreto 70/2023 —o la Ley Bases en la que también se intentó derogar la Ley de Tierras— sino que apunta a la Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada, que avanzó en una modificación del Código Civil para 

habilitar los desalojos exprés

 (y consiguió media sanción en el Senado).    




“En muchos lugares de América Latina estamos viendo el choque entre la defensa de la propiedad y la defensa de tierras en las que la propiedad no tiene certeza: propiedades estatales, tierras fiscales, territorios comunales, en los que se tilda de ‘invasores’ a los campesino e indígenas que habitan allí”, indica Duarte y pone como ejemplos a la criminalización agraria que ocurre en Honduras y Guatemala, a través de leyes antiterroristas, o la revocatoria de adjudicaciones que ocurren en Ecuador, vía el Poder Judicial.




“Hay mucha minucia legal, muchos estudios de abogados pensando cuáles son las fisuras que tienen las leyes agrarias y cambiando sus artículos para reinterpretar la legislación a favor de los intereses corporativos y de 

las élites que mantienen relaciones con el Poder Judicial

”, indica Duarte. 




El caso de Honduras se actualizó con el reciente decreto 107-2026, cuyo nombre no deja lugar a dudas sobre el orden del prioridades de las reformas que atraviesan los procesos de despojo: “Fortalecimiento y Protección del Sector Agroindustrial, Proyectos de Energía, Turismo, Ganadería y Pequeños Productores Agrícolas”. “Nunca habíamos visto algo como el caso de Honduras, porque anula la discusión desde el inicio. No importa qué legislación previa haya existido, las tierras son inafectables para otro uso que no sea el de la explotación con fines productivos de las corporaciones. No hay discusión sobre la posesión ancestral o sobre adjudicaciones de tierras anteriores. Aquí dicen, de facto, que la tierra queda inafectada para el uso campesino-indígena”, alerta Duarte.  




Esa fuerte decisión estatal de despejar el camino para los negocios se vincula con la cuarta lógica señalada por Duarte: 

el rol del Estado como promotor corporativo

. Si el otro capítulo que obtuvo media sanción en la Argentina busca modificar la Ley de Expropiación para restringir el sentido de utilidad pública, en El Salvador, donde gobierna el ultraderechista Nayib Bukele, el proceso descrito por Duarte es el de “expropiación exprés”.  




Bukele avanzó con ese dispositivo jurídico, en 2021, a través de la Ley de Dominio Eminente, que ordena procesos de expropiación sobre adjudicaciones de tierras campesinas para megaproyectos como el Tren del Pacífico, el Aeropuerto del Pacífico o Bitcoin City o para entregarlas a plantaciones de monocultivo mediante un procedimiento expedito.  




Foto: Vía Campesina




Hacia una arquitectura para el derecho del acceso a la tierra




Frente a estos dispositivos jurídicos desplegados por los Estados, el relator recupera la declaración de la primera conferencia de reforma agraria ocurrida en Porto Alegre, en 2006, que contrapone cuatro principios irrenunciables para la distribución de la tierra:  







La reforma agraria como instrumento de redistribución del poder territorial. 




La diversidad de modelos de tenencia, incluida la consuetudinaria y comunitaria.




La centralidad de la agricultura familiar y campesina en la seguridad alimentaria.




La responsabilidad del Estado sobre la gobernanza de la tierra. 







Esos principios fueron reforzados, veinte años después en la conferencia de reforma agraria ocurrida en febrero pasado en Colombia, promovida por el saliente gobierno de Gustavo Petro. El caso colombiano muestra fortalezas y debilidades en la correlación de fuerzas: el gobierno de Petro reconoció el derecho campesino, reforzó los Territorios Agrarios Campesinos (Tecam) con la entrega de 700.000 hectáreas, pero ahora el violento viraje político del país amenaza el proceso.  




—¿Cómo queda amenazado el proceso de redistribución de tierras con la llegada de Abelardo de la Espriella a la presidencia, quien tuvo como primer gesto prohibir la palabra “campesino” en los documentos oficiales?   




—El tejido social de Colombia no es el mismo que el de algunos otros países de América Central, que son más pequeños. No va a ser tan fácil revertir lo conseguido porque hay territorialidades campesinas y colectivas muy robustas, constituidas. Que un ministro diga que la palabra campesino no le parece, no cambia la Constitución colombiana que dice que el campesinado es un sujeto de especial protección. Esta semana un juez le dijo al ministro que no puede decir eso, que tiene que pedir disculpas. De todas maneras, sí se va a buscar detener la reforma agraria para pequeños productores, que era lo que venía fuerte en términos de Constitución, de figuras como las zonas de reserva campesina y los Tecam, pero el gobierno actual en Colombia cometería un error quitándole tierra a la gente y al pequeño productor porque las movilizaciones son muy potentes.




—¿La movilización, como ocurrió en Argentina contra la Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada y en Bolivia contra la 1720, es el punto clave para la defensa de los derechos de la tierra?




—Como diría la máxima maoísta, los derechos no se regalan. Se consiguen al calor de la lucha. Ningún derecho ha sido, digamos, realmente ofrecido. Vienen de procesos de movilización, de lucha, y, obviamente, los derechos por la tierra o de los campesinos para nada son una excepción. Al mismo tiempo existe una paradoja que ocurrió en Colombia, en Argentina, en Ecuador, que es que 

cuando hay un gobierno progresista, mucha gente del movimiento social va a ocupar puestos de gestión. Y cuando hay un cambio de gobierno y vuelven a territorio, muchas organizaciones están fragmentadas, divididas.

 Toma un tiempo reconstruir el tejido social, paradójicamente, después de haber salido el gobierno progresista. 




—En relación a los gobiernos progresistas de la primera década de este siglo, que convivieron con los principios de Porto Alegre, y el avance de las lógicas de despojo, ¿por qué esos gobiernos no pudieron profundizar la redistribución de la tierra?




—Es muy complicado. Son gobiernos progresistas, pero no son revoluciones. Desde un punto de vista democrático, llegan al poder a través de alianzas y esas alianzas, definitivamente, construyen bordes muy claros en cuanto a qué se puede hacer y qué no. Y uno de los bordes clásicos ha sido la propiedad o la estructura de la propiedad de la tierra. Se mantuvo un statu quo con marcos regulatorios liberales que reconocían la función social de la tierra, pero con procesos tímidos de reformismo. En el informe cito a Michael Albertus, uno de los teóricos de los reformismos agrarios en América Latina, quien ha mostrado que 

en el camino democrático es difícil que se desconcentre la propiedad

, porque es necesario intervenir sobre la concentración con mecanismos de expropiación, como los más efectivos. Y en muchos países, como Argentina, se dice: "No, ni siquiera lo vamos a pensar".




—Frente a la arquitectura del despojo, proponés crear una arquitectura al servicio de los derechos territoriales. ¿Qué herramientas jurídicas deben debatirse para ello? 




—Hay una discusión grande que el movimiento social tiene que dar, siento que no está saldada. Muchas personas y organizaciones con las que dialogué son críticos con la misma idea de propiedad. Esto se debe a que cuando un campesino lleva mucho tiempo en la tierra y, finalmente, obtiene su título de propiedad, si no hay salvaguardas, si no hay normas que lo impidan, es posible que frente a tantas dificultades venda la tierra. Es lo que se intentó en Bolivia con la Ley 1720, habilitar la disponibilidad de las tierras para el mercado y se rechazó. Por eso, en muchos países de América Latina, las organizaciones no están convencidas de que la formalización sea el único camino, por temor a que esas tierras comunitarias se introduzcan al mercado. La paradoja es que esta andanada de agresión y contrarreformismo agrarios demuestran que si los derechos de propiedad no están ciertos, entonces las tierras se vuelven muy vulnerables para que otros las acaparen. Es una paradoja que hay que analizarla país por país, caso por caso. En algunos lados es indudable que es mejor tener el derecho de propiedad que no tenerlo, mientras que en otros, cuando el manejo de la tierra es más consuetudinario, ancestral, se salvaguarda más si no hay un derecho que permita su venta. 




—

¿Y qué rol juega la

 

Declaración de Derechos Campesinos

 

para favorecer la creación de esta otra arquitectura? 




—La declaración permite apoyarse en la discusión legal a partir del artículo 17, que habla específicamente del acceso a la tierra y de las salvaguardas que habría que tener por parte de los Estados. Muchas de estas discusiones siempre se van a peleas legales y es importante que, cada vez más, en los países se invoque la Undrop como un derecho internacional existente, votado y reconocido en la ONU. Puede servir como un insumo de hacia dónde debería cabalgar la arquitectura del acceso a la tierra, pero la declaración por sí misma no tiene un poder mágico, tiene que ser invocada para poder transformarla en jurisprudencia como ocurrió, por ejemplo, con el Convenio 169 la OIT y los pueblos indígenas. Hay que dar la discusión legal para que se construya un corpus de los derechos del campesinado.







La entrada 

Mucha tierra en muy pocas manos: un plan para favorecer a las grandes empresas globales

 se publicó primero en 

Agencia de Noticias Tierra Viva

.

author: Chris Walker
title: FBI Adds Torture Charges Against Maduro as US Faces Questions Over Its Abuses
content:
New torture charges against Maduro come as the US faces scrutiny over its treatment of migrants.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

FBI Director Kash Patel announced additional charges against ousted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, alleging that both have committed crimes relating to torture.

Patel announced the new charges in a post on X on Thursday. The two were already indicted on separate charges relating to drug trafficking and firearms shortly after the U.S. invasion of Venezuela that resulted in their capture earlier this year.

Both Maduro and Flores are now facing an additional count of Conspiracy to Commit Torture, Patel said. Flores is also charged with one more count of narcoterrorism.

“They will now answer for their crimes,” Patel promised.

The 30-page indictment alleges that Maduro and Flores tortured opposition party members and dissenters to his presidency from around 1999 through 2025, including some U.S. citizens. The couple have not yet entered a plea on the new charges, but pleaded “not guilty” to the original ones.

“President Maduro ⁠denies the charges in the new indictment and looks forward to his day in court,” Barry Pollack, Maduro’s lawyer, said in a statement.

Aspects of the charges against Maduro and Flores may prove difficult for the Department of Justice (DOJ) to prosecute. The “narcoterrorism” statute has rarely been used at trial, and has only resulted in four trial convictions since it was enacted in 2006. Even then, two of those four convictions were later overturned due to concerns about witness statements.

Much of the evidence against Maduro relies on witness statements from less-than-reputable sources, The Washington Sun reported after his capture.

The January invasion resulted in over 100 people killed, including civilians, with at least one United Nations expert decrying it as a likely violation of international law and the sovereignty of Venezuela. After Maduro’s removal, the U.S. began seizing Venezuela’s oil reserves, and this past summer, a “deal” between the countries was brokered, which includes the U.S. taking control of 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s oil reserves, and 100-year leases to 17 oil fields.

Trump reportedly sought advice on his decision to invade Venezuela and capture Maduro, in part, from the AI chatbot Grok.

The charges against Maduro come as the Trump administration has also been accused of employing torture techniques.

For example, as part of the administration’s mass deportation campaign, the White House is sending refugees and other immigrants to countries known for torturing incarcerated people, including to El Salvador, where immigrants have been incarcerated at the notorious CECOT prison, which critics contend is in violation of U.S. and international law.

Within the U.S., the administration has tortured immigrants in detention facilities across the country, such as at the now-closed “Alligator Alcatraz,” where incarcerated people were subjected to a device known as “the box” — a 2×2 foot cage-like structure that was used to punish people.

The U.S. has also sent immigrants (some of whom were legally permitted to live in the country) to Guantánamo Bay Naval Base in Cuba, where individuals have been subjected to horrendous, unsanitary conditions and kept in isolated confinement for up to 23 hours per day.

author: Daron Letts
title: Crosswalk crash stalls Iqaluit traffic
content:
A downed crosswalk pole on Niaqungusiariaq Rd., across from Iqaluit’s Qikiqtani General Hospital clinic entrance, slowed traffic for 90 minutes, following a two-car collision at around noon on Thursday.




“Everyone was checked at the scene, and one person went to the hospital on their own afterwards for further assessment,” said city spokesperson Geoff Byrne in an email.




The city warned drivers of the traffic disruption in a public service announcement issued shortly after 12 p.m.




Two RCMP vehicles blocked Niaqungusiariaq Rd. about two hundred metres past the Sailijaaqvik boarding home at the southeast corner of the intersection. An RCMP truck also blocked Queen Elizabeth Way about 100 metres from the entrance to Astro Hill.




Traffic was backed up on Niaqungusiariaq Road all the way up to Joamie School for approximately 90 minutes while city workers removed the pole, broken in two places, with heavy equipment. The crew also filled-in the hole left behind.




The intersection is the site of Iqaluit’s first controlled 

crosswalk

, which was installed in fall 2024.

author: Brittany Boschman, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: A century after it was taken, ancestral tipi cover returns to Kawacatoose First Nation
content:
Using wooden pins and great care, Kawacatoose First Nation members fasten an Ancestor’s painted tipi cover on Aug. 28, after it was finally returned to their Saskatchewan community from ‘Washington, D.C.’ 

Photo by Brittany Boschman




“We’re gonna take you home now.”




Those were okimâw (Chief) Cory Dustyhorn’s words when he first touched the tipi cover connected to his great-great-great-grandfather, sîpiskwêsîkan.




After a century away from 

Kawacatoose First Nation

, the ancestral item has returned to the Cree community.




Community and family members gathered around the tipi cover after it was brought back from the 

Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of the American Indian

 in “Washington, D.C.” 




They prayed over it and welcomed it home.




“When I first touched it, I just felt so emotional,” Dustyhorn said. 




“I was thinking of all those that are gone on before me.”




He thought about his parents, grandparents and ancestors — who preserved the history of the item through generations.




He prayed for them to be present as the community finally brought home a piece of their history. 




“I told all of them, ‘Come with us, come and attend with us,” Dustyhorn recalled. 




“I know they were in between all of us — and they were here, too.”




Members of the Dustyhorn family and supporters celebrate the return of their Ancestor sîpiskwêsîkan’s painted tipi cover. From left: Oral Dustyhorn, Joyce Pratt, Philip Dustyhorn, okimâw (Chief) Cory Dustyhorn, Vanessa Dustyhorn, and researcher Andrew Miller. 

Photo by Brittany Boschman




Colonizers’ ‘vanishing Indian’ narrative




The tipi cover remained in the community for four nights before being temporarily housed at the 

Royal Saskatchewan Museum

 in 

oskana kâ-asastêki

 (Regina). 




Until the First Nation can build a permanent museum or cultural centre to house it safely, they plan to bring it home each year.




The return followed a reparation process that lasted almost three years. 




Andrew Miller, an associate professor at the First Nations University of Canada, helped the Dustyhorn family locate the item and communicate with the Smithsonian.




Miller described the tipi cover’s return as a meaningful example of reconciliation in action. 




“One of my friends from the Royal Saskatchewan Museum said, ‘Congratulations, you’ve just realized reconciliation,’” Miller said. “That’s what this is.”




But for Miller, reconciliation means more than merely acknowledging past injustices. It also requires returning ancestral belongings and supporting communities as they restore cultural teachings.







READ MORE:

 

Indigenous leaders celebrate belongings returned from the Vatican: ‘We welcome them home’







Dustyhorn said the return also highlights the need for stronger support from governments and museums — for all Indigenous communities hoping to recover what was taken away from them. 




“They talk about truth and reconciliation,” he said. “They splash that all over the news for a few years. 




“But where’s their help? How can we get the stuff back that was taken from us, too?”




Miller and Dustyhorn said the tipi cover was taken during an era when museums and governments declared that Indigenous cultures were disappearing and needed to be archived. That view justified an urgent push to collect ceremonial belongings and other ancestral items from Indigenous communities worldwide.




“They were wanting to capture the disappearing Indian,” Dustyhorn said.




Miller said museums particularly sought items connected to regalia, ceremonies, and other cultural practices as part of that colonial narrative.




“They were targets,” Miller said, describing sacred belongings as part of the “vanishing Indian culture” narrative.




But, Dustyhorn emphasized, “We’re still here.”




Kawacatoose First Nation members look at and touch the sacred tipi cover painted in the early 1920s by sîpiskwêsîkan — before a collector from the Smithsonian Institution took it to ‘Washington, D.C.’ — promising payment that never came. 

Photo by Brittany Boschman




‘Let’s get it back’




Miller first learned about the tipi cover from a former student, Andrea Dustyhorn. Years later, while researching 

ethno-ornithology

 — the relationships between people and birds — he found the tipi cover in the Smithsonian’s catalogue.




So he reached out to Dustyhorn.




“You should see this,” he told the chief. “What do you want to do?”




“And he said, ‘Well, let’s get it back.’”




Together they began an arduous process to bring the cover home. 







READ MORE:

 

Honouring my ancestor’s remains — at a Smithsonian warehouse







Dustyhorn’s family provided genealogical information and oral histories connecting it to his great-great-great-grandfather.




During one meeting, he recounted Smithsonian representatives asking how he knew the tipi cover actually belonged to his community. 




Their question, he said, reflected what he called a big difference between written museum records and Cree ways of preserving history: through oral stories, saved for generations.




“Everything is handed down orally,” Dustyhorn told them. “Let me tell you a story.” 













sîpiskwêsîkan’s painted tipi cover before and after it was taken into the Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Indian collections in ‘Washington, D.C.’ 

Photo courtesy Smithsonian Institution (Item NMAI-159004)










A collector, remembered




Dustyhorn began sharing the history passed down through his family about the tipi cover — and the person who took it. 




As he described the collector’s journey from Alaska through Saskatchewan, the Smithsonian representatives recognized details that matched their own written archival records.




“They said, ‘Did you know he started in Alaska?’” Dustyhorn recalled them asking about information he already knew. “And I’m like, ‘Really?!’”




The exchange connected the community’s oral history with the Smithsonian’s documentation, which to the museum established the family’s claim to the cover.




According to archival records, the item was taken in Saskatchewan in 1926. 




Although the National Museum of the American Indian has since deleted its record of the tipi cover, an 

archived version

 of its webpage states it was obtained by museum staffperson Donald Cadzow — who it notes was a “non-Indian.”




“Collected from Dusty Horn (sîpiskwêsîkan, Plains Cree, b. ca. 1863),” the record states.




Cadzow was 

hired

 seven years before he took sîpiskwêsîkan’s painted fabric, promising payment the community says never came.




“He made four field trips north,” the Smithsonian Institution states, “and collected over 2,000 objects from northern Athapaskan and Plains peoples.”




It was later transported through Winnipeg, “Toronto” and “New York City”— before finally reaching “Washington, D.C.”




A century later, last June, the Smithsonian notified the family it had deemed the cover was ready to return. At the time he was travelling to “Regina” when he got the email.




“I just started pumping my fist,” he remembered. 




His wife asked, “What?! Is it the tipi?”




“Yeah, it’s the tipi,” he replied. “It’s ready to come home.“




Chief Cory Dustyhorn and other Kawacatoose First Nation members touch the painted tipi cover in the Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Indian in ‘Washington, D.C.’ 

Photo courtesy Andrew Miller/First Nations University




The ‘unbelievable’ journey home




In August, a group from Kawacatoose First Nation finally travelled to “Washington, D.C.” to repatriate the tipi cover.




On the journey back, Dustyhorn said the weather changed as they approached the border. Rain, hail and lightning surrounded the vehicle.




“It started raining really hard,” Dustyhorn said. “It was raining and lightning happening all around us… it started hailing.”




He saw the weather as a sign that the tipi cover was leaving behind the painful history connected to its removal.




“It’s washing the negativity — the 100 years of negativity that it is carrying … leaving it in the States,” he said.




Miller also remembered that storm — but also the clear skies that emerged soon after they crossed into “Canada.” 




The travelers placed tobacco down, seeing the brightening weather as a meaningful part of the tipi cover’s return journey home.




Kawacatoose First Nation Chief Cory Dustyhorn (left), four members of his community, and First Nations University associate professor Andrew Miller (right) drove to ‘Washington, D.C.’ to recover their sacred painted tipi cover from the Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Indian. 

Photo courtesy Andrew Miller/First Nations University




Yolanda Dustyhorn, the community’s cultural co-ordinator, described the item’s return as an emotional and historic moment.




“Words can’t describe,” she said. “It’s very touching to have it come [back home]. 




“I shed a tear. It’s unbelievable.“




She also spoke about the item’s condition after so many decades away.




“The way it’s preserved, it’s 100 years old … yet we were able to still erect it,” she said. “It’s amazing.”




She hopes having the tipi cover available in Saskatchewan will help younger generations learn about their history, culture and traditional teachings.




“We gotta bring our culture back,” she said. “I want them to see this and to realize we gotta bring our culture back.”




She plans to incorporate the returned tipi cover into programs for Youth. Her work includes teaching traditional medicines, ribbon skirts, belts and other cultural practices.




“I’m targeting the Youth and the children,” she said. “We are gonna start bringing culture back.“




Generations of the Dustyhorn family stand in front of the tipi cover — painted by their Ancestor in the early 1920s — erected in Kawacatoose First Nation on Aug. 28. 

Photo by Brittany Boschman




‘One foot in front of the other’




Miller said the loss of cultural belongings continues to impact many Indigenous communities a century later.




“It impacts the present generation to this day.”




He said the removal of ceremonial belongings like the tipi cover significantly disrupted cultural education, language and traditional practices.




“This was involved in ceremony,” Miller said. 




But there are countless more ancestral belongings from Indigenous Peoples still held in museums and archives around the world. 




“There’s a lot out there,” he said. “Pipes, rattles, regalia, medicine bundles.”




Reflecting on his correspondence with the Smithsonian, Dustyhorn said he felt there were unnecessary delays throughout the repatriation process.




“We’d wait months for a reply,” he said, and they kept setting up more and more meetings.




Although they were ultimately successful, Miller argued that museums should be willing to participate more proactively in repatriating communities’ cultural belongings — “to give back the things that are requested,” he said.




For Kawacatoose’s leader, despite the hurdles he had to jump through, the return of his great-great-great-grandfather’s tipi cover proved what communities can accomplish when they keep fighting for their belongings.







READ MORE:

 

This Salish woolly dog pelt has returned to ‘B.C.’ after over 100 years







He encouraged other First Nations hoping to recover ancestral belongings to be persistent.




“Start the process and finish the process,” Dustyhorn recommended. “Keep going forward — one foot in front of the other everyday — until they get it home.




“I want all the other communities to get their stuff, to bring pride back to their Nations.”




His First Nation is now working to bring home additional belongings, he said, estimating that about 900 artifacts connected to the community are held at the 

Glenbow Museum

 in 

otôskwanihk

 (Calgary).




The community is also preparing for the return of objects from the 

Field Museum

 in “Chicago.” Miller said that collection could include roughly 60 items.




For the Nation and the Dustyhorn family, the return of sîpiskwêsîkan’s tipi cover is both a homecoming — and a renewal of their profound cultural pride.




“I want all our kids to be proud,” the chief said. “Walk with your head held high.”




sîpiskwêsîkan’s early-1920s tipi cover once again stands tall on Kawacatoose First Nation, with logs for a fire and community members nearby to take in the moment beneath the afternoon sun on Aug. 28. 

Photo by Brittany Boschman




The post 

A century after it was taken, ancestral tipi cover returns to Kawacatoose First Nation 

 appeared first on 

Indiginews

.

title: ICC Arrest Warrants Challenge the Normalization of Taliban Rule and Gender Persecution
content:
On October 5, the International Criminal Court (ICC) unsealed arrest warrants for four senior Taliban officials. They include Taliban Supreme Leader Haibatullah Akhundzada, Chief Justice Abdul Hakim Haqqani, Education Minister Habibullah Agha, and Higher Education Minister Neda Mohammad Nadim. The warrants were issued in July 2025 but had remained sealed.

The ICC says there are reasonable grounds to believe the four are criminally responsible for the “crime against humanity of persecution on gender grounds against girls, women, and others who do not conform to the Taliban’s policies on gender, gender identity, or expression.” The crimes include conduct involving murder, imprisonment, torture, rape, and enforced disappearance.

The Court also found that Taliban decrees and edicts have severely deprived women and girls of fundamental rights, including education, privacy and family life, as well as freedoms of movement, expression, thought, conscience, and religion. Importantly, the Court recognized that gender persecution can encompass not only direct acts of violence, but also systemic and institutionalized forms of harm.

What does the arrest warrant mean for the four Taliban officials?

The warrants do not mean that the four Taliban leaders will suddenly be arrested. The ICC has no police force of its own and relies on states to execute its arrest warrants. The 125 countries that are parties to the Rome Statute have obligations to cooperate with the Court, including complying with requests for arrest and surrender.

That puts a significant question before those countries: What does it mean to engage with or recognize a regime whose senior leaders are subject to ICC arrest warrants for alleged crimes against humanity?

As governments continue to weigh whether to recognize the Taliban, the warrants create an unavoidable diplomatic and legal question, especially for countries that are members of the ICC: Will you recognize and legitimize a regime whose senior leaders are wanted by the International Criminal Court?

The question is particularly significant in a region where several countries maintain relationships with the Taliban but are not parties to the Rome Statute. Pakistan, India, Iran, Qatar, China, Uzbekistan, Turkiye, and Russia are not ICC States Parties.

That distinction matters. Non-States Parties generally have no obligation under the Rome Statute to arrest and surrender ICC suspects, although the ICC can request their cooperation and countries can choose to assist.

And these are precisely the kinds of countries where Taliban officials have been able to travel and engage diplomatically. Russia, for example, recognized the Taliban government in 2025 and hosted a high-level Afghanistan meeting in Moscow this week attended by Taliban officials and representatives from countries including Iran and Pakistan.

A warrant can be difficult to enforce and still matter

The lack of an immediate mechanism to arrest the Taliban leaders does not make the warrants meaningless.

They establish an important record of international accountability and put governments on notice about the allegations against senior Taliban officials. They also make it harder to treat the Taliban’s systematic restrictions on women and girls as merely an internal matter, a cultural difference, or a set of domestic policies.

The ICC has identified the persecution of women and girls under the Taliban as a crime against humanity.

For governments considering recognition, diplomatic engagement, or deeper ties with the Taliban, the warrants leave a clear question:

How do you recognize a regime while its senior leaders face ICC arrest warrants for alleged crimes against humanity?

For Afghan women and girls, the warrants represent something more fundamental: a recognition that what has happened to them is not simply policy. It is not cultural and it is not religious. Their persecution is a matter of international criminal accountability.

The warrants may not immediately bring the Taliban leaders to The Hague, but they put accountability on the table and leave every government deciding how to engage with the Taliban with a choice to make.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: JD Vance Defines Socialism in US as Replacing Americans “With Foreign Workers”
content:
When asked to define the term, the vice president stuttered, saying, “it’s a hard term to define these days.”

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

When asked to define socialism on Thursday, Vice President JD Vance said that the rising left-wing ideology means a desire to “replace American workers with foreign workers” — a bizarre response coming from an administration that has made anti-socialist policies one of its central priorities.

Vance spoke to the press about the Trump administration’s announcement on Thursday that it is suspending Microsoft, Adobe, and other firms from a program that grants green cards to workers who work in the U.S. under H-1B visas.

Following his press conference, Vance was asked to give his definition of socialism in response to the growing number of socialist candidates running for office across the U.S. this election cycle.

Vance stuttered, saying “it’s a hard term to define these days” and that “I don’t know what the term means anymore.”

“Classically, you would think socialism is about prioritizing workers, and yet in reality I guarantee that most of the self-described socialists running across the United States of America are going to howl about this announcement today, which is prioritizing American workers over foreign workers,” he said, using a racist definition of “Americans” that excludes people who move from other countries.

H-1B visas are issued for highly skilled jobs, typically in science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) fields, that people already in the U.S. aren’t likely to fill. Because of that, H1-B visas are already highly limited, though research has found that such workers are a boon to the U.S. economy and can even help raise other U.S. workers’ salaries.

“I think in reality, what it actually means in the American context is that you want to replace American workers with foreign workers and you want boys to play in girls’ sports. That’s what unites the socialists I see running across the United States of America today,” Vance said.

“They love the idea of replacing American workers with foreign workers, which suggests to me it’s not really about the working class, it’s about their hatred of native-born citizens,” he went on.

It’s unclear what socialist proposals Vance is referring to.

Many left-wing candidates are opposed to the Trump administration’s mass deportation policies, which, along with being horrific and abusive, harm the economy. Time and again, research has found that immigration contributes to the growth of the economy, contributing to tax revenue and helping to bolster welfare programs and the labor market in the U.S.

As Vance suggests, labor is indeed a central tenet of socialism. Democratic socialist candidates and socialist organizations and activists in the U.S. have a strong focus on worker rights and the labor movement, which is a major source of power and unity on the left. Recent polls have found that democratic socialist candidates outpoll those who back Trump.

Additionally, there isn’t evidence of left-wing candidates for office saying that they have a “hatred of native-born citizens.” In fact, it is the Trump administration that has been endangering U.S. citizens with its fascist anti-immigration policies. President Donald Trump has famously sought to drastically upend birthright citizenship, and his Department of Homeland Security has detained at least 500 U.S. citizens in its mass deportation campaign across the U.S.

title: La oposición en Diputados convocó a excombatientes para darles voz por el proyecto del gobierno sobre Malvinas
content:
Después de que el gobierno enviara a la secretaria legal y técnica a defender el proyecto de Ley de Defensa de Soberanía Nacional, el peronismo convocó a organizaciones de ex combatientes. La sesión del 15 de octubre por la Ley de Tierras y las maniobras oficialistas.







Por Verónica Benaim @VeBenaim




 


La agenda Malvinas copó toda la semana legislativa en la Cámara de Diputados de la Nación. El día 

después de la presentación de María Ibarzabal Murphy

, funcionaria clave del gobierno de Javier Milei, el peronismo abrió este jueves la Comisión de Asuntos Cooperativos, Mutuales y ONG para darle voz a representantes de organizaciones de excombatientes de Malvinas en el marco del debate sobre el proyecto de ley de Defensa de la Soberanía Nacional.




Mientras el oficialismo prepara una estrategia para desactivar la sesión convocada por la oposición para la semana que viene, que tiene como fin principal voltear el DNU 70/23 que deroga la ley de venta de tierras rurales a extranjeros, el diputado de Unión por la Patria, Aldo Leiva, convocó a un batallón de representantes de asociaciones civiles nucleadas en la Mesa de Coincidencia Malvinas (MECOMA). Y es que, tras el fallo de la Corte Suprema, el peronismo buscar sumar rechazos a la decisión judicial por facilitar la extranjerización de tierras nacionales.




Del encuentro, que tuvo una fuerte presencia de dirigentes y expertos de Malvinas de la provincia de Buenos Aires -sobre todo de la ciudad de La Plata- participó el diputado Máximo Kirchner que no forma parte de la comisión y que suele participar de las actividades cotidianas del parlamento.







Los que estuvieron ausentes fueron los diputados del bloque de La Libertad Avanza que, según pudo saber Tiempo, tomaron la reunión como una forma de “oportunismo político” por parte de los opositores. Es más, enviaron una carta, en donde expresaron su rechazo al encuentro bajo el argumento de que “se propuso un temario que no se condice con la comisión. Se desvirtúa el objeto de una comisión permanente de esta Cámara”.




Durante el encuentro, 

Tiempo

 dialogó con Leiva quien explicó los motivos de la convocatoria. “En mi doble rol como diputado y veterano de Malvinas, creemos que estamos viendo una situación muy compleja donde la Corte dice que el planteo de una de nuestras organizaciones es ilegitima, y por otra parte en lo que se viene debatiendo del proyecto enviado por el gobierno ha habido muchas limitaciones para escuchar nuestras voces por lo que creemos oportuno hacer esta convocatoria para escucharnos y generar propuestas”.




El diputado y veterano de Malvinas, Aldo Leiva.




Ante la consulta sobre qué le dejo la defensa que hizo Ibarzabal, la secretaria de Legal y Técnica de la Casa Rosada, respondió que fue “insulsa”. “Ha sido pésimo, nos faltan el respeto al no venir responsables como el canciller (Pablo Quirno), pero este gobierno rehúye al debate y pretende llevarnos de las narices a votar algo que nada tiene que ver con Malvinas, sólo un tercio se refiere a la cuestión Malvinas y el resto se nos quiere meter por la ventana”.




De todas formas, detalló que para Unión por la Patria se debe dar el debate, aunque fragmentando el tratamiento del proyecto de ley con el fin de desvincular el endurecimiento de las penas relativas a Malvinas de los artículos referidos a la seguridad interior y modificaciones en los servicios de inteligencia.




El excombatiente, escritor y periodista, Edgardo Esteban.




La sesión del 15 y las maniobras oficialistas




En paralelo al desarrollo de la reunión de la comisión convocada por el mayor bloque opositor al Gobierno, circuló que la Libertad Avanza prepara una convocatoria de comisiones para el miércoles a las 16 con el fin de revivir el proyecto de ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada que aprobó el Senado. Es el día anterior de la sesión convocada por los opositores. La estrategia del bloque violeta es incluir en ese proyecto un apartado de Ley de Tierras y convencer a los legisladores provinciales que están en duda de no dar quorum al día siguiente.




Frente a este escenario, la diputada camporista Paula Penacca manifestó: “Nos van a querer engañar y confundir. Desde hoy hasta el jueves 15, ellos van a intentar confundir. El miércoles que viene van a querer poner en tratamiento la sanción del proyecto de inviolabilidad privada que viene del Senado y que fue el que logramos hacer pelota el 6 de agosto porque era en contra de la soberanía y a favor de los grandes intereses. Entonces van a querer construir una trampa”.




En ese sentido, Penacca expresó: “Nosotros tenemos que estar claros y por eso el jueves nos vamos a encontrar en la calle o algunos adentro cumpliendo con nuestras tareas. No quiero invitarlos a que vengan, porque si muchos de ustedes empuñaron un arma y bancaron las peores condiciones por parte de un gobierno de facto, por lo que no tengo ninguna duda de que van a poner el cuerpo también el jueves 15”.




“Si ustedes están ahí afuera nosotros nos vamos a sentir más fortalecidos y esperemos construir una victoria”, finalizó.







Fuente: 

https://www.tiempoar.com.ar/ta_article/oposicion-en-diputados-convoco-a-ex-combatientes-proyecto-del-gobierno-sobre-malvinas/

title: RCMP arrest suspect in Pangnirtung shooting
content:
The RCMP has arrested a 21-year-old man in relation to a shooting in Pangnirtung on Tuesday afternoon.




Police received reports of gunshots at around 4:03 p.m. Tuesday. Ten minutes later, they arrested Jonah Kuniliusie, according to a news release issued by Sgt. George Henrie on Thursday.




Kuniliusie faces two counts of endangering life, two counts of pointing a firearm, two counts of aggravated assault, and the unlawful possession of a weapon in public. He also faces three counts for breach of probation.




The RCMP was not immediately available to answer questions about the incident.




Deputy mayor Markus Wilcke said the event harmed everyone in the community, either directly or indirectly, including children who were nearby 

when the shooting happened

.




Kuniliusie remains in custody and will have his next court appearance on Oct. 20 in Iqaluit.

author: Victoria Law
title: Mississippi Is in Danger of Executing Woman on Death Row, Despite Key Evidence
content:
Lisa Jo Chamberlin’s co-defendant confessed to coercing her into their crime. Will that be enough to stop her execution?

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Lisa Jo Chamberlin’s life has always been a tangle of drug use, abuse, and extreme violence. Her mother drank and used Sudafed heavily during her pregnancy. As a result, Chamberlin was born with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD), a group of medical conditions, including poor reasoning and judgment skills, learning disabilities, and intellectual disability, that occur when a fetus is exposed to alcohol.People with FASD are more vulnerable to manipulation by others. For Chamberlin, that vulnerability led to a death sentence.

The 45 women on death row across the country make up 2 percent of the total number of Americans sentenced to death. The vast majority of women behind bars have experienced abuse before arrest. Ninety-six percent of women on death row had experienced gender-based violence before arrest, 80 percenthave intellectual or psychosocial disabilities, and 90 percent have no prior conviction for a violent felony. Chamberlin checked all of these boxes.

As a child, she suffered constant physical and sexual abuse from her father, her mother, her stepfather, her brother, and even her fourth-grade teacher. Her mother beat her with whatever was on hand, sometimes whipping her with a wooden spoon until it broke. When she was six, her 11-year-old brother put her into a closet with three neighborhood children, instructing them to touch her sexually. He also sexually abused her for years. Chamberlin told her mother, who dismissed her complaints.

When she was 12, Chamberlin began using drugs to numb the constant violence and abuse.

As an adult, her boyfriends used her substance dependency to exert control. They also physically and sexually abused her. Roger Gillett, who would become her co-defendant, strangled her, attempted to drown her, and raped her. He ordered her to move with him from Oregon, where her family lived, first to Kansas and then Mississippi in 2004. That was where Gillett killed two people.

Now 53, Chamberlin is the sole woman on Mississippi’s death row. If her appeals fail, she will be the first woman the state executes since 1944.

“In capital cases, women who have experienced some of the most extreme forms of gender-based violence and oppression are also among those who have received the least support from the legal system, from their communities, from their families, and from society,” Sandra Babcock, founder and director of the Cornell Center on the Death Penalty Worldwide, told Truthout. “There are two dynamics: One is that these women are among the most damaged and vulnerable survivors to become involved in the criminal legal system. But their experiences of violence and trauma go unrecognized by the legal system when they are charged with a capital crime.”

In Mississippi, Chamberlin and Gillett stayed with Gillett’s cousin, Vernon Hulett, and his cousin’s girlfriend, Linda Heintzelman. At first, they all got along. Then, after an auto accident between the two couples, they hatched a plan for Heintzelman to report the accident, collect insurance, and split it with Gillett and Chamberlin.

Heintzelman never filed the insurance claim, leading to tension between the two couples. When their hosts suggested that they move out, Gillett tortured and killed them. He and Chamberlin then placed their bodies into a freezer, loaded it into Heintzelman’s truck, and drove to an abandoned Kansas farm owned by Gillett’s grandfather.

There, police conducted a drug raid, arresting both. They later found the freezer and charged the couple with the deaths of Hulett and Heintzelman.

The pair were tried separately. Both were convicted and sentenced to death.

Chamberlin’s trial was marked by demonizing gender stereotypes. The prosecutor painted her as the mastermind behind the murders. He introduced testimony about Chamberlin’s sex life, including testimony from two jailhouse informants. Jailhouse informants’ testimonies, commonly motivated by law enforcement, are inherently unreliable and have been the leading cause in 46 percent of death row exonerations. Even the Mississippi Supreme Court recognized the problematic nature of relying on jailhouse informants, stating in 1989, “The testimony of jail-house informants, or ‘snitches,’ is becoming an increasing problem in this state, as well as throughout the American criminal justice system.”

“It is much easier to conclude that this is simply an evil person, that this is not someone who is herself damaged, who is herself a crime victim.”

Nonetheless, the informants’ testimony was not contested. One of the informants, Marsha Petrofsky, already on probation for five fraudulent checks, had been jailed for arson. A year after she testified, she pled guilty to first-degree arson and was sentenced to five years’ probation and $4000 restitution even though Mississippi law requires a 5-to-20-year sentence and restitution of triple the amount of damages. The other, Vanessa Stringfellow, was contacted by the state in 2006, the year of the trial. She testified that she overheard Chamberlin tell other women that she and Gillett had sex in front of the corpse and it was the best sex she ever had.

Their testimonies painted Chamberlin as an immoral and hyper-sexualized woman, a portrait that the prosecutor drew upon to inflame the jury. Additionally, Chamberlin’s attorney did not present testimony about FASD and how it made her more easily dominated by Gillett.

A psychologist for the defense testified about her abuse history, but the prosecutor dismissed her testimony, suggesting that Chamberlin was not a victim of repeated gender-based violence but instead a “sociopath” or “psychopath.” The jury believed his version and sentenced her to death.

That’s not unusual, said Babcock. “Prosecutors will minimize, distort, dismiss women’s accounts of sexual violence, whether they come via women’s testimony or through an expert.”

During the penalty phase, the prosecution painted Chamberlin not only as a sexually promiscuous woman, but also a bad mother, stating that she “abandoned [her children] like a reptile.”

In Mississippi, the jury, not the judge, makes the decision on whether to impose the death penalty. Chamberlin’s jury returned a sentence of death.

“When somebody is charged with a capital crime, particularly offenses that make people recoil, it is much easier to conclude that this is simply an evil person, that this is not someone who is herself damaged, who is herself a crime victim, but that [her actions] are attributable to her depraved character,” said Babcock.

It is a tragic irony that it often takes a death sentence appeal for a person to receive better legal help — help that in many cases could have prevented the sentence in the first place. In Chamberlin’s case, that help came in the form of the Mississippi Office of Capital Post-Conviction Counsel. The office also representedGillett when he appealed his death sentence. The Mississippi Supreme Court vacated his sentence because the jury heard inadmissible evidence of an invalid sentencing factor (a previous felony for escaping from a Kansas jail). In 2018, he was resentenced to life without parole.

In 2022, the Mississippi Office of Post-Conviction Counsel began representing Chamberlin. None of her legal team had represented Gillett, avoiding any conflict of interest. They found three experts to attest to the effects of FASD. They also approached Gillett who, in 2023, submitted an affidavit admitting that he had “complete control over her.” He also stated, “When my attorney told me Lisa was painted as the mastermind behind the homicide, I almost didn’t believe him. It is laughable to think that Lisa is the mastermind behind anything. Her involvement was minor, and she would not have participated had I not clearly been in control.”

Chamberlin has been the only woman on Mississippi’s death row for the past decade. The isolation has impacted her mental health — in 2025, she was placed on suicide watch at least twice.

The Mississippi Supreme Court ruled that this new evidence was time-barred (or not filed within a certain timeframe) and was contradicted by evidence presented at trial. The court denied her appeal.

In 2025, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Andrew v White that the Due Process Clause forbids the introduction of evidence that is so unduly prejudicial as it renders a criminal trial fundamentally unfair. In the case of Brenda Andrew, sentenced to death in Oklahoma for her husband’s death, the prosecutor’s inclusion of her sex life, her dress and demeanor (complete with holding her lacy bra and thong up in court), and closing comments painting her as a bad mother were so prejudicial that they violated the Due Process Clause. The court sent her case back to the Tenth Circuit Court, which declined a re-hearing. Andrew remains on death row while her legal team plans to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Given that ruling, Chamberlin’s attorneys again appealed to the Mississippi Supreme Court for a rehearing. The court denied it.

“In 2006, Lisa Jo’s jury only heard one side of the story,” her attorneys told Truthout. “They did not hear that Lisa Jo was born with FASD, and organic brain damage. They did not hear that Lisa Jo’s actions are shaped by Battered Woman Syndrome. They did not hear that Roger Gillett was primarily responsible for the crime and that Lisa Jo believed Roger would kill her if she did not participate.”

Should the state supreme court strike her petition, she can petition the U.S. Supreme Court. Should it decline to hear her petition, she can turn to the federal district court, which has already granted a Rhines stay (or a pause on the strict timeline for federal filing). Should that court deny her petition, Mississippi will set an execution date. If the state-sponsored killing is carried out, Chamberlin will be the first woman executed since the state executed 23-year-old Mildred Johnson in 1944.

Chamberlin has been the only woman on Mississippi’s death row for the past decade. The isolation has impacted her mental health — in 2025, she was placed on suicide watch at least twice. At one point, she considered signing papers allowing her execution to proceed but later decided against it. After she spoke about her conditions with Mississippi Today, prison officials retaliated. She spent up to 48 hours confined to her cell, was denied access to showers, and was given less outdoor time than men on death row. Friends, family, and Chamberlin herself told Mother Jones that her communication with the outside world was blocked for months.

In 1999, Michelle Byrom’s husband was found shot at home with a pistol that was a family heirloom. Byrom was medicated and recovering from pneumonia at a local hospital when the sheriff questioned her. She said that she was responsible for the murder.

Her son, Edward Byrom Jr., testified at trial that Byrom had hired his friend Joey Gillis as a hit man. Both Edward Byrom Jr. and Gillis were convicted of lesser charges and were released from prison in 2013 and 2009, respectively.

Michelle Byrom was convicted and sentenced to death. When the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear her case in 2014, Mississippi set an execution date. But media scrutiny into her conviction uncovered a pretrial confession from Edward Jr. to his mother, a letter that she had never seen. That attention sparked outrage. People called the governor, demanding he halt the execution.

The Mississippi Supreme Court — the same court where Chamberlin is now appealing — vacated Byrom’s conviction after her new legal team presented evidence that jurors had never seen, including the confession letter and a separate confession by Edward Byrom Jr. to a court-appointed psychiatrist. Gillis submitted an affidavit admitting that Byrom did not hire him to kill her husband.

Opposition to Chamberlin’s execution has also come from an unexpected source — Vernon Hulett’s mother

The court granted her a new trial.

Byrom was taken to the local jail to await a new trial. In 2015, she agreed to an Alford plea, which allowed her to maintain her innocence while accepting a felony charge on the record. The judge sentenced her to time served and Byrom, after 16 years behind bars, left the courthouse. She moved to Tennessee, where she died in 2019 at age 62.

“Mitigating evidence and new evidence can really put a case in a different light and a different perspective,” Krissy Nobile, one of Chamberlin’s attorneys, told Truthout. “In this post-conviction process, we are now learning of the new evidence,” she said. “Anyone and everyone that has seen her case, especially after Roger’s affidavit, has been outraged. The more the public knows, the more outraged people will be about [her death sentence].”

Opposition to Chamberlin’s execution has also come from an unexpected source — Vernon Hulett’s mother, Caroline Hester.

In 2019, Hester sent a letter to then-governor Phil Bryant. “As I told our local DA for years, I do not need for Lisa Chamberlin to be put to death,” she wrote. Hester clarified that she does not want Chamberlin freed, but said that life imprisonment was enough. She ended her letter stating, “I need for this to be over!”

In 2022, Chamberlin connected with a sister she never knew she had. Yvonne, born 10 years earlier to the same father, had been abandoned by her biological parents at eight months old. She was adopted by what she described as a loving family. But she never stopped searching for her history. (Yvonne asked that only her first name be published to protect her privacy.)

In 2022, an organization that helps adoptees connected her with her oldest sister, who told her about Chamberlin. She wrote her a letter. “Now, we talk on the phone once or twice a month,” Yvonne told Truthout.

“The life she had could easily have been my life,” Yvonnereflected.

Yvonne has watched true crime shows about her sister. But, she said, Chamberlin is not the monster they portray. The sister she knows is warm, compassionate, and, at times, funny. She cares for baby birds that fall out of trees. She ministers to others in the prison. Once, during a cold night, she gave her only blanket to a woman who had none. Knowing her has also pushed Yvonne to become more active in fighting for her beliefs.

“She has profound remorse for her participation,” noted Chamberlin’s attorneys. “She found faith in prison and stopped using drugs. Now she seeks to help other women in prison struggling with addiction. Lisa Jo can be a force for good in prison if she is no longer under a sentence of death.”

Even with execution hanging over her head, Chamberlin has helped others in the prison. Laykin Bordelon met Chamberlin when she was 19 years old and placed in the behavior modification unit at Central Mississippi Correctional Facility. Chamberlin, as the only woman on death row, was also on that unit.

“Lisa Jo saved my life,” Bordelon, now 36, told Truthout. “I spent 13 years incarcerated. I felt so forgotten.”

She and Chamberlin talked through the tray slots of their cells, never having the opportunity for face-to-face or physical contact. After Bordelon was transferred to general population, she would sometimes go on suicide watch just to talk to Chamberlin. “That was laying butt naked on a concrete floor, no clothes, no blanket, nothing, just so I could talk to her.”

Bordelon is now home, but she hasn’t forgotten the woman she calls her godmother. Earlier this year, she attempted to draw official attention to Chamberlin’s extreme isolation, sending letters to legal organizations and the Department of Justice’s Office of Civil Rights Division requesting an investigation into her godmother’s conditions.

“I have completely turned my life around,” Bordelon reflected. She’s a manager at a local business and plans to get involved with advocacy for incarcerated people. “It’s because of her.”

“I have always been against the death penalty,” Yvonne said. “Now that it’s personal it brings a deeper perspective into my feelings on the subject.” She has offered to help Chamberlin’s attorneys in any way possible. She’s also become involved in advocacy to stop the execution of Christa Pike, whose lifetime of abuse mirrors Chamberlin’s.

On September 30, which was Chamberlin’s 54th birthday, Pike survived the horrific experience of Tennessee’s attempt to execute her. After two doses of lethal pentobarbital, Pike was still breathing and sent to the hospital.

“I’m hoping that this leads other states to change their death penalty sentencing. There are so many things that can go wrong and these two cases are so similar,” Yvonne said. “When I see [Christa Pike’s] case, my mind is on her.”

This story has been updated to note that the Mississippi Supreme Court denied Chamberlin’s latest motion for a rehearing on October 8.
