:

There are many people who don’t share this sentiment, but I have an appreciation for when a fanfic is so separated from canon that it could’ve easily been its own original novel, and yet the author was only ever going to put that much energy into it if their favourite characters got to be there

I think there’s a difference between “the author stripped the media of everything it had to replace it with something easy” and “the author thought up a concept they really really like and are bestowing it upon the character like a medal”

For most of human history, you could say “I am going to take Gilgamesj / Odysseus / King Arthur / Laosheng* /etc” and give him a completely new story, maybe in a completely different setting" and it would be considered just as valuable as a work of fiction with ‘original’ characters. That wasn’t 'fan’ fiction, that was just fiction. 

The idea of the individual genius that has to build a completely new setting with new characters and a new plot from scratch is a very recent invention and a very European invention and it has greatly reduced the spectrum of what can be considered 'real’ art. 

(*ok, a character archetype isn’t exactly the same as a character, but it’s another example where taking cues from a pre-established story telling tradition is appreciated and encouraged)

The very idea of “intellectual property” is and always has been antithetical to the way we communicate and share knowledge. No one can own a character or a setting or an idea, and we all know that. Copyright laws don’t exist to protect you or your unique ideas, they exist to enforce the existing power structure.

YES! And so is the idea of the individual genius.

Every time I see a post on here about how difficult it is to write and how it’s hard to write dialogue when you only want to do world building or it’s hard to write world building when you only want to do dialogue or it’s hard to see where the story should go next I want to shake people and go IMAGINE IF YOU DID NOT NEED TO DO THIS ALONE.

Because you really. do not. need to. do this. alone! And not just writing either. Painting, pottery, sculpture, everything. Art can be collaborative and it will usually be better art and more fun to make. 

I am asking genuinely and without ulterior motive. This is not a trap, and any informed answer will be welcomed:

Does the use of the word 'novel’ (which simply means “new,” of course) to describe a particular format of written fiction - does that have anything to do with the advent of the expectation of originality described above?




I’m not an etymologist so I had to look this up and it looks like the word 'novel’ for a story is very old, 500-ish years, and from what I can find it does come from the word for news and used to mean something like 'a short story’. 

But the idea that such a story should be 

entirely

 original in all aspects (characters, plot, dialogue, etc) and could not borrow anything substantial from previous stories, is much more recent.

Though copyright law is probably the biggest culprit, literacy probably does have something to do with this too. When most people could not read, most stories were read aloud or performed as plays. Familiar characters or familiar plots are useful in such a setting because you can skip some of the set up and get right to the storytelling. 

Shakespeare plays are obvious examples. They’re full of historical characters and often used a familiar plot from an existing play that Shakespear did not invent. The fun for the audience was often not in a completely new story, but in Shakespeares’ twist on a familiar character and/or the plot. (This is also how good fan fiction works.)

It’s worth noting that our current cultural idea of a 'new’ story is genre specific and has culturally accepted exceptions. Putting familiar characters in movies and TV series is considered more socially acceptable, especially if they’ve been recycled before. If you choose a public-domain character like Sherlock Holmes, you can put him in new adventures and make a successful TV show out of it without being side lined as 'fan fiction’. 

But your Sherlock Holmes work is unlikely to be considered high art, no matter how good the story, because our modern concept of high art requires an entirely new creation, new plot, new characters, etc. Shakespeare is only considered high art because he’s not held to today’s standards. 

The tradition of using existing character in opera is another thing worth analysis but I’m not knowledgeable enough about opera to do that.

author: Austin Corona
title: The bipartisan energy bill tearing the climate movement apart
content:
In order to solve climate change, you have to do two things — stop burning fossil fuels, and build clean energy to replace them. The last few decades in the United States have witnessed a long back-and-forth over which of the two goals is more important, and over how to achieve either of them. Is it more important to pass a carbon tax, or subsidize electric vehicles? To block a new oil pipeline, or build a lot of solar and wind? 




On this question, the coalition known as the climate movement has fractured into two broad groups. On one side, there are activists, lawyers, and environmentalists, who tend to focus on blocking and reducing fossil fuel use. On the other, there are renewable energy companies and policy wonks, who tend to focus on building more clean energy.




These factions have clashed in the past, but over the past week a kind of civil war has erupted between the different elements of the climate movement. The inciting incident was the release of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, a long-awaited Senate bill that is designed to enable the construction of more power plants, transmission lines, and gas pipelines. The bill does this by weakening some of the nation’s bedrock environmental laws, speeding up the timeline for government agencies to issue permits, and making it harder to cancel projects that have already gotten federal approval. 




For climate-conscious supporters of the bill, it’s better for the planet to build a lot of clean energy even if it means some fossil fuels get built as well, and even if they cause some damage to the environment on the way. Supporters of the effort argue that if the U.S. builds out new clean capacity, it will be easier to wean off fossil fuels, which are the primary cause of global warming and all its myriad consequences. Opponents say that’s a Faustian bargain, one that will jeopardize tribal nations, other marginalized communities, and endangered species.




“It is definitely exposing a potential fault line between the environmental community and clean energy interests,” said Representative Jared Huffman, a Democrat who represents Northern California, in an interview with Grist. 




Representative Jared Huffman, a Democrat from California, is skeptical of the Senate permitting reform bill.
 

Photo by Andrew Harnik / Getty Images




BAAJA is the product of months of bipartisan negotiation between four members of the Senate committees focused on energy and the environment. The two Democrats in the talks were Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who are both climate hawks and clean energy advocates. The Republicans were Mike Lee of Utah and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, who are advocates of fossil fuels and critics of environmental regulation. Despite their ideological differences, the four senators managed to reach a compromise on a 

sprawling 400-page bill

 with hundreds of individual provisions. 




The so-called “four corners” reached a deal just before Congress left for its fall recess, and the Senate will not return to take up the bill until after the midterm elections. The bill has not even made it through committee yet, and it also faces an uncertain fate in the House of Representatives. The next few weeks will see a scramble of lobbying as supporters and opponents of the bill try to sway senators and representatives for or away from the bill.




So far, at least, the builders seem to have more influence than the blockers, at least within the climate movement. President Donald Trump has spent the last two years 

repealing

 

most

 

federal

 

climate policy

 and blocking the development of new clean energy, and many climate advocates seem willing to accept an imperfect deal rather than hold out hope of fixing Trump’s damage after he leaves office.




“It’s a lot easier to prevent things from being built than to build things, and that applies both to fossil fuels and to renewables,” said Zeke Hausfather, a climate expert at the science nonprofit Berkeley Earth, who also directs climate research for the tech company Stripe. “I don’t want us to run roughshod over any community, but we also can’t give everyone a veto for an issue as important as climate change. So ultimately, we need to strike a balance there.”




The case in favor: Build more




A big challenge with building clean energy is that it takes up a lot of space. Solar farms and wind farms can cover thousands of acres of land, and the transmission lines that carry their power to cities can extend for hundreds of miles, covering far more territory than coal and natural gas plants do. This large footprint makes these projects more likely to touch federal lands or waters, which triggers a series of obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act, the foundational environmental protection law also known as NEPA, and other laws that protect endangered species and historical artifacts. Under NEPA, federal agencies must carry out an extensive analysis of a project’s environmental impacts before issuing or denying a permit for it.




That review process often inspires time-consuming litigation. Opponents can bring lawsuits against an agency even years after a review is complete, arguing the review wasn’t comprehensive enough, and they can ask courts to halt the project until the agency redoes the analysis. A 

2025 study

 found that 64 percent of solar projects, 38 percent of wind projects, and 31 percent of transmission line projects face NEPA lawsuits.  




This litigation can come from almost anyone, and can cover almost any conceivable impact from a project. On one end of the spectrum, a coalition of tribes and environmental groups sued the developer of the SunZia transmission line. The line carries much-needed wind power to Arizona and California, but the plaintiffs wanted the developer to reroute the wires away from a holy cultural site, an effort that was 

ultimately unsuccessful

. On the other hand, opponents of a wind project in California 

delayed development for years

 by suing on the grounds that a federal agency had failed to consider pseudoscientific theories about wind turbines creating dangerous electromagnetic fields. Both projects were ultimately completed, but years behind schedule.




A group of wind turbines generate electricity at the Block Island Wind Farm off the coast of Rhode island. The clean energy industry has pushed for provisions that would prevent President Donald Trump from canceling future offshore wind permits.

 

Photo by John Moore / Getty Images




The bill would make it much harder to file this kind of lawsuit. Litigation would need to be brought within 150 days of the end of the NEPA review process, rather than six years, and the plaintiff must have already described the issue of their suit during a public comment period. Even then, a court could only order the agency to redo its analysis while a project moves forward, rather than pausing a project altogether. The agency could then only revoke the permit under limited circumstances, including a violation of law or the risk of immediate or substantial harm to “life, property, national security, or defense.”  




“This is a great bill, and it’s a huge step in the right direction,” said Ray Long, the president of ACORE, a trade group representing the solar and wind industry. “We need to really put this in reality. We need to build a ton of stuff over the next four years, or else we’re gonna have higher [electricity] prices.”




A related set of provisions makes it harder for the government itself to block projects, providing developers with “permitting certainty.” Here, both the Republicans and Democrats believe they have won — Republicans resent President Joe Biden’s decisions to 

block the Keystone XL oil pipeline

 and to 

pause the construction of new liquefied-natural gas terminals

 on the Gulf Coast, while Democrats have watched the second Trump administration 

use dubious executive authorities

 to halt the construction of solar and wind farms on federal lands and waters. One provision in the bill would help developers seek compensation if they can establish that the government has discriminated against a specific project type, like offshore wind, through delayed and canceled permits.




“This president has found ways to skirt the edges of every law that we have, and his attacks will continue,” said Kris Ohleth, executive director of Special Initiative on Offshore Wind, a pro-offshore wind nonprofit research group. “But at least if developers know they can recoup some of their development costs, as this bill might allow, it’s more appealing for them to return to the market.”




What’s arguably the most important thing in the bill doesn’t have to do with permitting per se. It’s about the massive transmission lines that carry electricity from region to region. The United States has built very few of these interstate lines in recent years. This dearth of new wires 

has made it infeasible

 for developers to build more solar and wind. 




“Historically, it didn’t matter too much where power plants were located, so we built them close to where the power was needed,” said Chirag Lala, vice president of research and chief economist at the Center for Public Enterprise, a think tank. “But we don’t have that same luxury with clean energy, which can be very location-specific. If you’re going to rely on those resources, you have to ship the power over long distances.”




High-voltage transmission lines run through the Central Valley of California. The bipartisan permitting bill would overhaul federal rules for transmission, requiring utilities to plan for more lines that move clean energy around the country.
 

Photo by Jay L. Clendenin / Getty Images




BAAJA would force utilities and regional grid operators to plan for interregional transmission lines, and would let private developers (like the one behind SunZia) come in and build lines themselves if utilities don’t build enough. The bill would also clear away a number of procedural roadblocks that have allowed utilities to block interregional transmission. 




The Democrats who negotiated the bill and the climate experts who support it see these provisions as a sea change for clean energy. If the bill passes, it could unleash solar in Nevada and wind in the Dakotas, and then bring that power to places like Appalachia that have little solar or wind potential of their own.




The case against: Stop the damage




But while the clean energy industry has celebrated the bill’s effort to speed up permitting for new power plants, many environmental groups have condemned it. These groups argue that the changes would allow for a surge of new development near disadvantaged communities, and will leave residents with no legal recourse to stop that development. 




These groups argue, in essence, that the bill sacrifices many communities in places like the Gulf South in order to achieve an overall nationwide increase in the supply of clean energy. 




“That battle between fossil fuels and renewables is not going to necessarily go well for the people of our region, especially if you take those regular protections that we’ve relied on for years away,” said Liz Zepeda, the director of federal policy at the Southern Environmental Law Center, an environmental law group that represents six states in the Southeast. 




The permitting changes have also drawn intense criticism from Indigenous groups, who say that the narrowing of historic preservation law would deprive tribal nations of a voice in development decisions. By the time that tribes learned about a company’s plans for a new transmission line or solar farm, it could be too late for them to protect culturally important sites.




“These changes will reduce opportunities for Tribal Nations to learn that an infrastructure project is occurring or to participate before decisions are made, all but guaranteeing that construction or other activities affecting sacred places can proceed without meaningful Tribal involvement,” said Valerie Grussing, the executive director of the National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers, a group representing tribal officials who advise federal agencies on protecting Indigenous historic sites during project development.




The bill would constrain litigation on behalf of endangered species and would also weaken states’ power to stop development under the Clean Water Act. This latter state power has been used in the past to take down old hydropower dams, like the 

ones on the Klamath River

, and that would now be harder.




BAAJA would also allow mines on public lands to unload excavated rock and waste materials on adjacent land. Mining is essential for clean energy development — solar panels, wind turbines, and EV batteries all need metals and minerals — but some environmental groups worry about the impact on local ecosystems.




Indigenous youth and climate activists hold a protest against pipeline projects in Washington, D.C., in 2021. A new bipartisan permitting reform bill in the Senate would make it easier to build many pipelines.

 

Photo By Bill Clark / CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images




In addition to raising concerns about environmental and social impacts, opponents argue that the bill would lock in future development of fossil fuels, which could negate the climate benefit of building clean energy. Among the biggest concessions to Republicans is a broad environmental exemption for natural gas pipelines, which, along with the Clean Water Act changes, would make it much harder for states on the East Coast to block new pipelines. Hausfather, who is supportive of the bill, allows that more gas reaching the Northeast would likely cause emissions to go up, though he believes that increased clean energy development elsewhere would more than offset those increases.




The bills’ opponents are also extremely skeptical of the “permitting certainty” provisions that the offshore wind industry welcomed. The bill would prohibit the president and federal agencies from discriminating against any specific energy source, but that prohibition would apply to fossil fuels as well as renewables. It would in theory make it almost impossible for a future president to undertake an LNG pause like the one Biden pursued, or to block offshore oil development. 




“If you have a dominant industry right now, which is the fossil fuel industry, you are creating a structure that makes it possible for them to lock in their dominance forever,” said Brett Hartl, the government affairs director at the Center for Biological Diversity, the environmental protection nonprofit that has led the opposition to the bill.




Opponents argue that by trading away their ability to stop new oil and gas production, the bill would hamstring the climate fight, no matter how much solar and wind gets built.




“Do we just ignore the political and economic power of the fossil fuel industry, and just hope and pray we can deploy renewable energy fast enough to reduce emissions?” asked Erich Pica, president of Friends of the Earth, a nonprofit environmental group. “That’s what this bill does.” 




Builders vs. blockers




BAAJA’s fate is far from guaranteed. In addition to the opposition from influential groups like the Center for Biological Diversity, there are a number of House members who have expressed uncertainty about the bill. At least one senior Republican, Brett Guthrie, has said 

he opposes the effort to force new transmission lines

, and major utilities will likely oppose that provision as well. On the Democratic side, Huffman, the representative from California, told Grist that he thinks Democrats can likely get a better deal after the midterms.




“The idea that this is this once-in-a-lifetime great opportunity that will never come again and has to be accepted without any scrutiny or questions is pretty silly,” he told Grist. Huffman said he believes the bill is a “Trojan horse” with “giveaways” for the fossil fuel industry, and said he believes he could negotiate a bill without significant environmental rollbacks should the Democrats take control of the House. 




But even if Democrats retake the House and the Senate, they will need some Republican votes to pass a major transmission reform, so some kind of compromise is inevitable. Many supporters say they doubt that Republicans would negotiate a bill when in the minority, or that Trump would sign a Democratically-led bill.




For now, the bill seems to have split the climate movement down the middle. While hundreds of small environmental groups 

signed a letter

 urging Democratic senators not to pass the bill, most major green groups did not sign. The list of absences includes the Sierra Club, the Environmental Defense Fund, the Nature Conservancy, and the Natural Resources Defense Council, arguably the nation’s most influential climate nonprofit, whose leader 

said in a public statement

 the bill raises “hard questions” but could be “good for clean energy — really good. ” Others, like Citizen’s Climate Lobby, have offered their 

unequivocal support

. Even the environmental opponents seem somewhat fractured — when a group of opposing nonprofits held a Zoom call to coordinate their strategy, someone 

leaked the transcript

 to Punchbowl News.




The fact that the bill has a chance of passing with some support from green groups and climate hawks like Whitehouse reflects a shift in the American climate movement. The movement took off during the fracking boom with protests against pipeline projects like Keystone XL, but efforts to phase out fossil fuels have been stymied by 

court

 

decisions

 and administration changes. During that time, solar and wind have both experienced dramatic growth as they’ve gotten cheaper to build, but they are now hitting bottlenecks thanks to transmission constraints and environmental review. 




The fact that Whitehouse and Heinrich came to the table with Republicans, and that so many green groups aren’t fighting their compromise, may be a sign about how climate advocates have come to see fossil fuels: If you can’t beat ‘em, build something that can replace ‘em.







This story was originally published by 

Grist

 with the headline 

The bipartisan energy bill tearing the climate movement apart

 on Oct 8, 2026.

author: Grist staff
title: Trump’s Gutting of the Endangered Species Act Will Imperil Hundreds of Species
content:
Razing the habitat of an endangered or threatened species will no longer come with federal penalties.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The Supreme Court once billed the Endangered Species Act as “the most comprehensive legislation for the preservation of endangered species ever enacted by any nation.” Federal protections have been key to saving nearly 300 U.S. species — including the bald eagle, American alligator, and grizzly bear — from permanent extinction.

Each year, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, which is primarily responsible for implementing the law, evaluates species and lists them as “endangered” or “threatened.” When federal activity or private development has the potential to harm a listed species or its habitat, project developers are required to consult with the Service or obtain a permit prior to construction.

For the last several decades, the interpretation of two words in particular — “take” and “harm” — have formed the backbone of the Nixon-era law. Its prohibition of “taking” an animal criminalized any attempts to “harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect” at-risk species. And the provision on “harm” ensured that degrading a listed species’ habitat could be penalized. These definitions have been key to the success of the law.

But that all changed last month when the Trump administration determined that razing the habitat where endangered or threatened species breed, feed, and shelter would no longer face federal penalties. In a separate internal memo, the administration also reinterpreted the definition of “take,” limiting it to instances of intentional killing of an endangered species. (Nearly two dozen attorneys general have sued over some of these changes.)

“These rule changes, when you zoom out, are an assault on threatened and endangered species unlike we’ve ever seen before,” said Elizabeth Forsyth, a senior attorney in the biodiversity defense program with Earthjustice, a nonprofit environmental law organization. “It’s an effort to eliminate habitat protections, eliminate automatic protections for threatened species, and give industry power.”

Climate change is making matters worse, as species struggle to adapt to warming temperatures and changing ecosystems. Below, Grist reporters look at how 10 species — from lovable sea otters to a misunderstood snake — might fare as the regulatory framework that has kept them afloat is weakened.

North Atlantic right whales got their name perversely. Because they stick close to shore and to the surface, and float when killed, they were the “right whale” to hunt. So right that humans hunted them nearly to extinction before the practice was banned in the 1930s.

That’s not why right whales are dying today.

“Nobody goes out and says, ‘I’m gonna hit a right whale with my ship,’” said Delcianna Winders, director of the Animal Law and Policy Institute at Vermont Law and Graduate School. But it happens anyway.

Though it’s not always possible to determine the cause of death for a whale, research shows that the leading cause is human activity: Ships strike the whales and fishing gear ensnares them, leading to injury and death. It happens often enough that North Atlantic right whales have been experiencing an unusual mortality event since 2017, in which 43 have died and 133 have been spotted injured or in poor health. About 380 whales remain, only 70 of whom are breeding females.

Well before the latest changes to the Endangered Species Act, the Trump administration had already begun rolling back protections for right whales. In March, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration announced plans to rescind ocean speed restrictions designed to reduce the risk of vessel strikes. The agency later declined to expand the whales’ designated critical habitat to include their migratory route.

The administration will likely use its new definition of “take” to bolster those actions, Winders said. “Now they can point to this and say, ‘Look, we can’t have speed limits under the law because it only applies to intentional direct activities.’”

Right whales are “particularly vulnerable” to the changes, Winders said, both because of their critically low population figures and because their primary causes of death are incidental takes.

“Right whales don’t have two years or four years” to wait for a new president or Congress to restore their protections, Winders said. “This is going to impact them immediately.”

Admirers of the only venomous snake species in Michigan call the creature misunderstood. The eastern massasauga rattlesnake — which grows up to 3 feet long, with a rattle at the end of its sandy, brown-speckled body — is often vilified in rare accounts of snake bites and has been the subject of state advisories to stop harassing the animal.

These snakes are actually “very shy, pretty calm,” said Adam Austin, a wildlife biologist who leads the conservation nonprofit Midwest Friends of Wildlife. They prefer to hide in the wetlands that they call home, and their name is a nod to their swampy abodes; massasauga means “great river mouth” in Anishinaabemowin, the Indigenous language spoken across the Great Lakes.

In recent years, as wetland acreage has shrunk across the Midwest — due to development, drainage, and climate change — the massasauga’s habitats have become fragmented. The resulting isolation makes it difficult for them to breed with other populations, diminishing genetic diversity and leaving them less resistant to new diseases. More than a third of the roughly 260 sites where the snake has been surveyed across the Midwest are at risk of habitat loss, according to the Fish and Wildlife Service.

As a result, federal officials listed the snake as threatened under the Endangered Species Act in 2016. The move has helped conserve millions of acres of wetlands in the region, Austin said, but recent changes to federal protections are likely to spell trouble for the rattlesnake.

Snake advocates worry that under the Trump administration, razing wetlands the massasauga roam in or accidentally killing them during construction may not be a violation of federal law. While Michigan has its own endangered species laws — eastern massasaugas are considered state-threatened — protections are narrower than the federal Endangered Species Act. The state also has strong legal protections for wetlands, but the loss of a federal backstop could shift more responsibility to the state to fill regulatory gaps, said Tara Zuardo, a senior advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity.

“Michigan’s law and the federal Endangered Species Act would suddenly be operating under the same words, but radically different legal meanings,” Zuardo said.

Bull trout, native to Montana and recognizable by their large heads and white-tipped fins, are the alpine equivalent of a canary in a coal mine. They rely on cold, clean water, and as warmer temperatures, invasive species, and sediment runoff have degraded their habitat, Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks, the state’s wildlife management agency, has documented significant declines across half of the population. Road construction, particularly for industrial logging, poses one of the greatest threats to bull trout spawning habitat. The fish are particularly sensitive to sediment buildup, which can coat the gravelly bottom of a river and smother their eggs.

“I could list off 10 streams right now that 15, 20 years ago had bull trout in them, and they don’t anymore,” said Brian Riggers, a retired fisheries biologist with the U.S. Forest Service who spent decades documenting bull trout in streams across western Montana. “That’s a sad thing.”

Bull trout are listed as “threatened” by the Fish and Wildlife Service in recognition that they’re likely to become endangered and at risk of extinction without protection. The listing ensures that anglers are not allowed to catch and release them like other species of trout, and it’s not legal to fish for them in most of their habitat.

The Trump administration’s proposed policy changes to weaken the Endangered Species Act, as well as rescind protections for roadless areas in national forests and allow more motorized recreation, are the latest blows to these imperiled fish.

Riggers said that without protections for their remaining habitat, bull trout will continue to face steep declines. The need to preserve their habitat has been a key component of legal challenges against large-scale logging projects in the state. Without the explicit federal protections to prevent harm to a listed species’ habitat, it could become nearly impossible to stop development projects that degrade spawning streams and block the bull trout’s ability to move through rivers.

Florida panthers once roamed much of the American Southeast. But then settlers arrived and hunted them until just a few dozen remained. Their range dwindled to a small area in southern Florida — a state that, until 1950, paid a $5 bounty to any hunter who turned in a panther scalp. Today, the panthers, among the first species protected by the Endangered Species Act, are recovering, with an estimated 200 thought to live in the state.

“It’s been a tremendous effort over the years,” said Elizabeth Fleming, a career expert on the species at Defenders of Wildlife, a conservation nonprofit that helps protect panthers. Because most Floridians haven’t lived with panthers for more than a century, recovery depends on helping people coexist with them as they spread, often through educational programs or compensating ranchers who lose livestock to panthers. Without public acceptance, “we can kiss panthers goodbye,” she said.

But now, nearly 60 years after panthers were first federally protected, the Trump administration’s new interpretation of the law could undermine this progress.

This is particularly worrisome for Florida panthers, which were listed in the law’s early days and don’t have the additional habitat protections that became mandatory later on. Florida’s population is also booming faster than nearly any other state. That means more housing developments and highways that fragment panther habitat, and more traffic that can kill them. Vehicle collisions are the leading cause of panther deaths, Fleming said. One of the most quickly developing parts of the state directly abuts its only panther refuge. Under the new federal rules, developers may no longer need to contend with how their projects could harm panthers.

“People don’t understand that these animals need so much more,” Fleming said. “They need a connected system in which to travel and live their lives, and with every single instance of weakened laws, regulations, and protections, it’s just another thing going against them.”

Thousands of sea otters spend their lives weaving through the towering emerald ribbons of kelp forest found around California’s central coast. Lucky kayakers might spot one taking a moment to float belly-up, perhaps cracking open a tasty sea urchin with its favorite rock. They also rest this way when they sleep, sometimes holding hands to stay together while trusting their ultra-buoyant and water-resistant fur to keep them above the waves.

These lovable marine mammals were once thought to be extinct in California, after intensive pelt hunting in the 19th and 18th centuries culled their population down from some 16,000 individuals. But a small number of otters survived and repopulated. Today, some 3,000 otters live in the Big Sur region, just south of San Francisco.

That recovery was largely possible through Endangered Species Act protections that the Trump administration has repeatedly weakened. The latest changes, which gut habitat protections, could leave sea otters especially at risk. Much like the Florida panther, they also do not have a “critical habitat designation,” an additional safeguard that only became mandatory after sea otters were already added to the list.

When it comes to protecting otters, habitat is everything, said Sean Bothwell, the executive director of the California Coastkeeper Alliance. In the past, conservationists rallied to fight against oil spills in otter habitat. Today, they’re turning their attention to fertilizers used for farming, which can cause algae blooms and make the shellfish that otters eat toxic. “We’re so concerned about otters because they live in the tidal zone; they are directly impacted by anything that runs off of the land,” he said.

The Trump administration’s changes to habitat protections will make it much harder to hold companies accountable for this kind of pollution, Bothwell said. His organization recently decided to pause a lawsuit against a dam that was threatening a number of endangered species, like fish and toads, because the case partly rested on the legal definition of “harming” an animal that the administration rescinded this summer.

Without these safeguards, he said, lawsuits that focus on habitat protections could lose their teeth. “We are worried there will be some kind of backsliding,” Bothwell said.

Like the nearly 50 other bumble bees native to North America, the rusty patched bumble bee is a fuzzy, mostly yellow-and-black insect that buzzes between plants gathering nectar and pollen. Unlike its cousins, and as its name suggests, the rare bee sports a distinctive amber spot near the middle of its back.

When Libby Shafer, now an urban ecologist and PhD Candidate in plant biology at Northwestern University, was a biological technician with the United States Geological Survey and tried to track down the bee over the course of a three-month search that spanned Illinois, Indiana, and Wisconsin, she had very little luck. “I personally only saw one,” she said.

The bee, once common in 28 states including Illinois and the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec, has declined by nearly 90 percent over the past 30 years. Today, it occupies just 0.1 percent of its historic range.

The pollinator was listed as federally endangered in 2017, becoming the first bee species listed under the Endangered Species Act. Experts have pointed to a number of stressors that explain the bees’ dramatic decline, including habitat loss, pesticide use, disease, and climate change. For example, warmer temperatures can set off a mismatch between when bees emerge from hibernation and when native plants bloom and provide food.

This past summer, conservationists celebrated the Fish and Wildlife Service’s designation of approximately 1.5 million acres of occupied critical habitat for the rusty patched bumble bee, which protects it from projects funded or permitted by federal agencies but not from private landowners — approximately 83 percent of the bees’ critical habitat is privately held.

“The rusty patched bumble bee is better positioned than many listed species since critical habitat has finally been designated,” said Delcianna Winders, of the Animal Law and Policy Institute at Vermont Law and Graduate School. But she added that the Trump administration’s rescission of the regulatory definition of “harm” to exclude habitat destruction and reinterpretation of “take” pose serious threats to the species. Bumblebees are small, can easily go unnoticed, and spend about half the year in the soil, making them difficult to spot for an expert, let alone a developer building a service road over a prairie.

“This is bad news for the rusty patched bumble bee,” Schafer said.

Wildlife advocates with the Center for Biological Diversity and other organizations have been trying to get the eastern hellbender listed for more than a decade. In 2024, they came close. After Hurricane Helene felled trees and kicked up sediment, disturbing the sensitive salamander’s habitat, the Fish and Wildlife Service finally proposed the hellbender for protection, with a decision expected at the end of 2025. But the decision never came. In fact, not a single endangered species has been listed since Trump took office.

The eastern hellbender has enjoyed state protection in places like New York and North Carolina. However, unlike other species that have been federally designated as “endangered” or “threatened,” the hellbender has had no federal protection, even as its population has dwindled dramatically. The salamander is a homebody — once it finds a place it likes to live, it often stays there its entire life. An ancient remnant of the Ice Age, it has lived in the same streams and rivers for just about 160 million years and has been called a living fossil.

According to the Fish and Wildlife Service, its roughly 600 known historical populations have endured narrowing margins over the past few decades. More than 40 percent of those populations have vanished, and another 36 percent are in active decline. The hellbender breathes through its skin, meaning water pollution and sedimentation can cause disease and death. It thrives best in the cold, clear streams of the higher mountains in the Appalachian region, and shade cover is vital.

The Center for Biological Diversity filed a lawsuit in February, demanding the Fish and Wildlife Service complete its decisionmaking process. Since then, though, there’s been no movement, with the next regulatory step listed as “to be determined,” along with hundreds of other endangered species whose protections have been similarly delayed.

According to Michael Gangloff, who studies freshwater life at Appalachian State University, human development is the biggest threat to hellbenders. But, he said, they’re also fighters.

“These things are tough, and the fact that they’re still here attests to their toughness,” he said. “They’re an ancient, ancient group of salamanders.”

The southeastern United States used to be a red-cockaded woodpecker’s paradise, with longleaf pine forest stretching across much of the region. Unlike many other woodpeckers that hollow out dead trees to nest, these black-and-white-spotted birds live exclusively in the trunks of living pine trees. They spend months or years hollowing out a suitable cavity, and they prefer to do it in mature trees.

But finding suitable trees has become much harder than it was a century ago. Much of the South’s longleaf pine forest was clear-cut for timber and replaced by faster-growing species of pine. Management practices vary, but commercial timber operations often cut and replant pines before the trees are mature enough for a red-cockaded woodpecker’s liking, according to Joe Burnham, a wildlife biologist with the Georgia Department of Natural Resources.

“They have pretty specific habitat requirements,” Burnham said. “There are a whole suite of species, both plant and animal, that evolved with this ecosystem over time that really have a hard time surviving elsewhere.”

Development is booming in Georgia, with much of the state’s forested land at risk of conversion to housing or more profitable forms of agriculture. The Trump administration’s policy changes, particularly its new definition of “harm,” could put red-cockaded woodpeckers at greater risk by removing protections for their habitat. As a result, more forests could become vulnerable to conversion, further shrinking the mature pine forests they rely on.

Still, red-cockaded woodpeckers have made substantial strides since their 1973 Endangered Species Act listing, thanks in large part to efforts to restore longleaf pine habitat and transplant birds to suitable forests so they can reestablish themselves. In 2024, the federal Fish and Wildlife Service downlisted them from endangered to threatened. Despite the change, state- and region-level restoration efforts continue, Burnham said, because the woodpeckers need them — as do the long list of other endangered and threatened species that rely on the same habitat, including gopher tortoises and indigo snakes.

“We’re managing these stands for a multitude of species,” he said. “We’ve invested a lot of conservation effort into these species.”

Hawaiʻi is losing its lush and unique biodiversity at a rate seen hardly anywhere else, earning it the depressing distinction of being known as the “extinction capital of the world.” It may be no surprise, then, that the palila — a small, yellow-capped parrot native to the Big Island — is a poster child of the Endangered Species Act.

The palila was on the very first list of animals that the federal law protected. But conservationists soon discovered that protecting the bird itself was not enough; goats and sheep released on the island were denuding the high-elevation māmane forest that the parrot lives in. When they took the issue to court in 1979, federal courts agreed that allowing the palila’s habitat to be damaged was a violation of the Endangered Species Act and ordered the state to protect the forest from sheep and goats. The decision set a historic precedent and led to habitat protections for listed animals from industries — like mining, logging, and farming — across the United States. (The Supreme Court later cemented these protections.)

But the Trump administration is now upending the legal precedent that the palila once set. The court decisions meant that the Hawaiʻi government had an obligation to continually remove the feral sheep and goats that still roam in palila habitat. When a company or the state wants to build through these areas, it is often required to help offset that lost habitat by reforesting old ranch land with māmane trees. Under the Trump administration’s interpretations, however, damaging an animal’s habitat no longer counts as harming it. And killing an animal no longer counts as violating the law unless it was done on purpose.

That means, in the administration’s view, it may now be legal to build a road through māmane forest without considering how it affects palilas. And the state may no longer be required to continue eradicating the remaining feral sheep and goats, which would hasten the bird’s demise.

Only 600 palila still remain on the island. For a bird on the brink, the latest policy changes may accelerate its decline.

Every year, across Washington’s rivers and tributaries, hundreds of thousands of Chinook salmon sacrifice their lives for the next generation. They swim upstream for weeks, battling currents, starvation, and a flood of hormones that wreck their organs. Then they spawn — often in the river where they were born — and die.

The completion of this journey is critical for tribal communities, commercial fisheries, and the wildlife of the Pacific Northwest that depend on salmon. But in the last century, salmon populations have plummeted. Humans have built dams and developed the land, degrading river ecosystems and blocking salmon from migrating. And recently, Washington has become the epicenter of another threat: 6PPD, a chemical used in vehicle tires that washes off roads into waterways and harms several fish species, including Chinook salmon.

The Endangered Species Act protects several area-specific populations of salmon found in Washington’s rivers, like Chinook, coho, sockeye, and chum. Environmental advocates have had success leveraging the law to protect these habitats. Dozens of dams in Washington and other Pacific Northwest states have recently been removed, and salmon populations seem to be bouncing back quickly as a result.

But this recovery is still nascent and, as the Trump administration upends federal protections, it may be cut short. The government recently rescinded the law’s “harm” rule, which previously said modifying a habitat could be considered harming a species. Now, it only prohibits activities that kill salmon on purpose.

The change could devastate efforts to protect salmon, said Sean Bothwell, the executive director of the California Coastkeeper Alliance. His organization recently began tackling 6PPD contamination in Northern California, but has had to pause these efforts because their legal strategy relied on the rescinded “harm” rule. The change may also mean dam operators can no longer be pressured to maintain adequate flows for salmon, a particular concern as climate change makes downstream areas too warm for spawning.

“People aren’t going out there and stabbing salmon, but they are putting a chemical into the habitat that is directly killing them” or modifying their habitat by blocking the flow of rivers, Bothwell said. “That’s why this rule was so important.”

author: Mike Ludwig
title: Border Patrol Unleashes Violence on Protesters Over Trump’s Border Wall
content:
Activists say federal agents dragged protesters across a barbed wire and used “extreme pain compliance” tactics.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Since construction began on President Donald Trump’s border wall in haste on October 5, federal agents have clashed with land defenders and arrested roughly two dozen activists who camped out on private land to protest the destruction of fragile desert ecosystems on both sides of the imaginary line that separates Mexico from the tiny town of Lochiel, Arizona.

The protest received media attention after Border Patrol agents extracted and arrested a tree sitter and cut down the “Grandmother Tree,” an ancient cottonwood in a grove of several trees that stood in the way of contractors building the border wall. Estimated to be around 200 years old — older than the current border — the grove’s branches reached from the United States to Mexico, a symbol of international solidarity for the protesters.

The felling of the Grandmother Tree may have also symbolized the Trump administration’s disregard for nature and public opinion, but it did not mark the end of the protests, as construction continues. Video captured by journalist Max Granger shows land defenders climbing into a tree on the Mexican side Tuesday morning and setting up another tree-sit style blockade in a renewed attempt to halt construction. Clashes with Border Patrol continued throughout that day, with activists accusing federal agents of dragging protesters across a barbed wire fence during a chaotic confrontation that was caught on video.

On Wednesday afternoon, a protester locked themselves to moving construction machinery, according to a statement from activists. Border Patrol agents attempted to remove the protester with “extreme pain compliance” and pepper sprayed the surrounding crowd, the activists said. Protester continued to lock themselves down after construction came to a halt and construction crews left, the activists noted. “We do not intend to back down,” said Adriana, a Tierra Libre activist identified only by first name, in a statement on Wednesday. “Our resolve only grows with their violence.”

Jason, an activist from the Tierra Libre protest camp in Lochiel who declined to use his last name due to concerns over state repression, said roughly two dozen people have been arrested. Some received citations on the spot, and others were taken into custody and released onto the streets of Nogales or Tucson hours later, he noted.

Among the police presence is an elite unit known as the Border Patrol Tactical Unit (BORTAC). BORTAC was also deployed to Operation Metro Surge, the now-defunct federal invasion of Minnesota’s Twin Cities launched in December 2025 as part of the Trump administration’s violent immigration crackdown.

Activists say the tactics that the unit are using now in Arizona are similar to the ones deployed in Minnesota. “BORTAC was kind of one of the units famous for their brutality in Operation Metro Surge,” Jason said. “We are seeing a lot of the same tactics on the ground that they started to use during Metro Surge and some of these other large mobilizations against various cities like Chicago and Los Angeles.”

“A lesson from past attempts at a fascistic regime is that, if they are able to [abuse] one population of people that is easy to ‘other,’ what they are doing to that population will always expand out to other populations,” said Jason. “It’s all the more reason to take what they are doing to immigrants seriously, and what they are doing in Lochiel seriously.”

In their statement on Wednesday, protesters said Border Patrol and BORTAC have “beaten, detained, arrested, and maced activists engaged in morning prayer,” and “kidnapped” fellow protesters who faced further abuse while in custody for about 24 hours. Jason said arrestees were released at random public places such as a fast-food restaurant, mirroring stories about people swept up in Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Jessica Turner, a spokesperson for Customs and Border Patrol, said Border Patrol conducted an “enforcement operation” in Lochiel to protect personnel and the federally managed area around the border line. While most activity remained peaceful, Turner said agents took appropriate action in response to “alleged violations” and an “alleged assault on a federal officer.”

“U.S. Border Patrol respects the public’s right to lawfully express their views,” Turner said in an email. “Individuals are expected to comply with lawful orders and avoid conduct that endangers others or interferes with authorized federal operations.”

Based in El Paso, Texas, BORTAC is a specially trained “rapid-response force” that was typically deployed for “high risk” missions involving “terrorism and drug enforcement, sometimes abroad,” before Trump took office, according to Human Rights Watch. Under Trump, BORTAC and other militarized immigration enforcement units have also been deployed in immigration policing operations like the one in Minneapolis.

Despite violent arrests, more than 2,300 deportations, and the killing of two U.S. citizens by federal agents during Operation Metro Surge, the people of Minnesota famously continued to protest and provide for immigrant families. Operation Metro Surge was called off amid widespread public outcry on February 12.

The land defenders in Lochiel initially set up their protest camp shortly after contractors began clearing the area in late August. From Arizona’s Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument to southern Texas, a secondary 30-foot wall is being built 100 feet from the existing border wall. Flush with more than $46 billion in funding from Congress, Customs and Border Protection is building a “border barrier system” that includes a “primary and secondary wall” with a road between them, as well as “waterborne barriers, patrol roads, and the technology required to tie it all together, such as cameras, lights, and other detection technology.”

The area around Lochiel is historically Yaqui and Tohono O’odham territory, and Indigenous activists are protesting construction at multiple points along the border in and around the Tohono O’odham Nation. Jason said activists regularly gather to pray as a form of protest at the Quitobaquito Springs, a rare oasis ecosystem a few miles from Lochiel that has served as a sacred ceremonial site for generations of Tohono O’odham and Hia-Ced O’odham.

In May, federal border wall contractors clearing land in the nearby Cabeza Prieta National Wildlife Refuge damaged Las Playas Intaglio, a fish-shaped geoglyph made by human hands 1,000 years ago. Lorraine Marquez Eiler, a Hia-Ced O’odham elder, told High Country News in September that the Quitobaquito Springs are also a direct connection to their ancestors.

“All of my lifetime of work has been for the memories of my ancestors, of what they went through,” Marquez Eiler said. “With the incoming wall, should it be disrupted?” she asked. “That’s just another slap in the face, as far as I’m concerned, to my ancestors. And so, I ask: Why?”

The border wall also disrupts wildlife by blocking off migration routes and hunting grounds for species such as the endangered desert jaguar. As contractors began clearing and damaging areas near the spring to make way for border wall construction, conservationists removed endangered mud turtles from the springs to prevent the species from being lost forever.

“The water runs just a couple dozen feet from the border; if they put a second wall there, they will destroy the hydrology,” Russ McSpadden with the Center for Biological Diversity told Truthout in August.

While the Tohono O’odham Nation has for years allowed Border Patrol onto its territory to chase after a dwindling number of migrants and smugglers, the tribe sued the Trump administration in July over construction of border wall infrastructure along 62 miles of border that bisects the nation. However, a federal judge refused to issue an injunction to temporarily block construction, ruling in July that that government’s purported national security interests outweigh the tribe’s claims of sovereignty. To defend their sovereignty, the Tohono O’odham also put up “no trespassing” signs warning contractors to stay off their land or risk legal consequences.

Jason said the Trump administration has ignored the warnings and rushed to build as much of the “border barrier system” as possible before residents and federal courts have a chance to step in and start asking questions. “It all comes down to wanting to assert their control without any checks or balances and just do what they want, and anyone who stands in the way be damned,” Jason said.

Jason said contractors are working quickly, but the protest camps are located on private property and not going anywhere. A tree-sitter in the last remaining cottonwood on the Mexican side of the border was still blocking construction as of Wednesday evening, and activists on the ground say the fight is far from over.

“The tree has saplings already planted in several places, and the symbol of the tree has become more than the individual tree herself,” Jason said. “She lives through everyone’s actions and determination to defeat the border wall.”

There are many people who don’t share this sentiment, but I have an appreciation for when a fanfic is so separated from canon that it could’ve easily been its own original novel, and yet the author was only ever going to put that much energy into it if their favourite characters got to be there

I think there’s a difference between “the author stripped the media of everything it had to replace it with something easy” and “the author thought up a concept they really really like and are bestowing it upon the character like a medal”

For most of human history, you could say “I am going to take Gilgamesj / Odysseus / King Arthur / Laosheng* /etc” and give him a completely new story, maybe in a completely different setting" and it would be considered just as valuable as a work of fiction with ‘original’ characters. That wasn’t 'fan’ fiction, that was just fiction. 

The idea of the individual genius that has to build a completely new setting with new characters and a new plot from scratch is a very recent invention and a very European invention and it has greatly reduced the spectrum of what can be considered 'real’ art. 

(*ok, a character archetype isn’t exactly the same as a character, but it’s another example where taking cues from a pre-established story telling tradition is appreciated and encouraged)

The very idea of “intellectual property” is and always has been antithetical to the way we communicate and share knowledge. No one can own a character or a setting or an idea, and we all know that. Copyright laws don’t exist to protect you or your unique ideas, they exist to enforce the existing power structure.

YES! And so is the idea of the individual genius.

Every time I see a post on here about how difficult it is to write and how it’s hard to write dialogue when you only want to do world building or it’s hard to write world building when you only want to do dialogue or it’s hard to see where the story should go next I want to shake people and go IMAGINE IF YOU DID NOT NEED TO DO THIS ALONE.

Because you really. do not. need to. do this. alone! And not just writing either. Painting, pottery, sculpture, everything. Art can be collaborative and it will usually be better art and more fun to make. 

Sure. Fanfic in general sucks ass though

write better books and your medium won’t be seen as shit




I think you’re probably just being rude and annoying on purpose but on the small chance that you generally don’t know this: you’ve got the chicken and the egg backwards. 

Most fan fiction spaces are very welcoming to new inexperienced writers. So it is where a lot of people learn to write. Of course there’s going to be a lot of work that isn’t great yet in a place where a lot of people are still learning and where their imperfections are allowed to exist without shame or mockery. 

A lot of fan fiction writers with real talent eventually move away from fan fiction because writing fully 'original’ works is the only thing that gets them money and status. As a result there’s a constant talent drain on the community. 

Books are curated. There are a LOT of shitty books out there that you’ve never read because libraries and bookshops already filtered them out so they never reached you. There are A LOT A LOT of terrible drafts of books that you’ve never read because publishes already filtered them out.

Result: because fan fiction spaces are uncurated or much less curated, you need to put more effort into finding the good works and you will encounter more bad works in your search for good works. 

If fan fiction was not curtailed by copyright and more respected as a medium, then high quality works would be printed by publishers, sold by book stores and reviewed by newspapers and you could easily read only high quality works and never encounter a bad piece of fan fiction. 

Shakespeare wrote fully new plays about familiar historical characters (tons of British kings, Antony and Cleopatra, Julius Caesar, etc) and borrowed characters from other works of fiction, such as Romeo and Juliet. In other plays he invented new characters but put them in a familiar plot from an existing play. The fun for the audience was in his twist on a familiar character and/or plot. This is how good fan fiction works.

author: Jillian C. York
title: When No ID Means No Internet: Age Verification and the Right to Access Information
content:
This post was co-authored by 

Sheila B. Lalwani

, a doctorate student and recent 

COMPASS Fellow

 hosted by EFF.




Age verification proposals are 

often presented

 as a simple tradeoff: sacrifice a little privacy to better safeguard children online. But that framing overlooks a more fundamental question. What happens to people who cannot verify their age at all? This is particularly a problem when users are required to prove their age with identity documents.




Age-related restrictions are developing quickly around the world. While they differ radically across jurisdictions, in the past year, we’ve witnessed a sharp uptick toward mandatory age assurance for social media access but also for other high-risk digital services.




For example:







In late 2025,

 Australia 

became the first country

 to implement a minimum age requirement for prohibiting children under age 16 from creating or holding social media accounts. 




India 

passed the 

Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act

 that includes mandatory verifiable parental consent and has undertaken ongoing discussions for social media restriction.




The United Kingdom 

passed the 

Online Safety Act

 

requiring age verification

 across a swath of services hosting content considered harmful to users under 18. More than half the states across the 

U.S.

 

have enacted age verification laws

. 




An 

EU Commission

’s expert 

report

 recommends a ban on social media access for users under 13. It also recommends mandatory age verification for platforms to ensure that users are ‘age appropriate.’ 







The Access Problem 




Age verification laws that 

are predicated on the necessity of

 users possessing a current passport, driver’s license, credit card, or similar documents proving their identity exclude critical sections of populations.  And this problem is global in nature: 

Millions of people lack government-issued identification

 or encounter regular challenges to obtaining or updating it. 




Roughly 

15 million adult U.S. citizens

 lack a driver’s license, and a further 

2.6 million lack any government photo ID

; leaving large groups blocked from online content or services. The UK has a similar predicament: proof-of-age checks are often reliant on passports, driver’s licenses, or other recognized alternatives, which can pose unique challenges to people without these documents.




Much of the advocacy around age verification discusses the 

privacy harms

 of age verification. Yet these measures also threaten something more fundamental: equal access to information and the ability to exercise the right to freedom of expression. 




Unfortunately, age verification systems foster unequal access to information and provide an asymmetric solution to find essential information, build community, and weigh in on public discourse. As governments and companies increasingly require users to prove their age before accessing online services, these individuals risk being excluded from large parts of the internet altogether. 




Effects on Global Majority Countries 




Age verification laws reshape who can speak, who can access information, and who gets excluded from the digital public sphere. In other words, age verification is not a neutral safety measure: it presents a structural barrier to disproportionately exclude certain groups—particularly those in the global majority—and alters the architecture of global online expression. Some of these groups are already marginalized offline, and age verification extends that exclusion into digital spaces.




For instance, 

850 million people globally do not have ID

. Most of these individuals exist in primarily low and middle income countries in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. The World Bank 

points out

 that many are members of marginalized groups and more than half of those lacking access to identity documentation also have children whose births have not been registered. Women are particularly vulnerable and are 8% less likely than men to have an ID. Other vulnerable groups, such as adults in low income countries, are less likely to have an ID when they fall below 25 years, as are those with a primary school education or less or those in rural areas. 




A 

policy paper

 from EDRi points out that age verification laws provide quick tech solutions but overlook longstanding structural challenges and undermine the universality of the internet. The analysis finds that age verification laws have serious human rights implications and ironically harm the very individuals they deem to protect. Moreover, these laws depend on the collection of harmful mass data that human rights organizations, including EFF, is 

fighting against

—and 

has for decades

. 




For example:







In 

Morocco

, a push to restrict children’s access would ban under-13s from creating accounts on gaming platforms. This could potentially create challenges for those with IDs that have incomplete information concerning the year of birth. In addition, this push would also 

impact those who attempt to leave

 Morocco.




In 

Egypt

, the 

lack of ID cards

 has created challenges for minority groups such as the Baha’i.




Stateless individuals would also struggle under age verification laws. The 

Rohingya

, 

the world’s largest population of stateless people

, often 

lack IDs

. 




Kuwait’s 

Bidoon

 population

 also lacks proper identification materials. According to 

Amnesty International

, this leads many to rely on standard civil identity cards, which can be restrictive.  




Nigeria 

launched a national program

 to provide ID cards to its population in 2007. Since then, 64.4 million have registered, but that represents just over 30% of the national population. 




The Kafala system, a practice in several countries across the 

Middle East

, also introduces challenges for age verification laws. Under this legal framework, 

migrant workers’ legal residency

 and employment status are bound to a specific employer. This potentially leaves stateless persons or migrant workers vulnerable to forced labor and restricted movements. 







No ID, No Access




Age verification laws are less about confirming the age

 of a user and more about creating barriers to online participation that many people cannot reliably scale. The net result is reduced access, more data collection, and an increased chance of unequal or mistaken exclusion from accessing information online. 




Nobody doubts the importance of protecting children online. While proponents assert that age verification laws protect minors from harmful material, online harassment, and digital addiction, these laws are not the solution. They subvert fundamental freedom of expression rights and pose significant privacy risks.  




EFF has long warned against age-gating the internet. Age verification technology itself is often

 

inaccurate

 and

 

privacy-invasive

,

 and 

as more countries considering implementing ID-based checks

, 

the risks move beyond 

censorship

 and 

surveillance

 toward excluding some people entirely. That’s why we’re working with groups in the U.S. and around the world to push back against these laws, and why we hope you join our effort.




For more information on how to fight back against dangerous age verification laws, visit our resource hub at 

eff.org/age

author: Daron Letts
title: Nunavut Sport and Recreation awards gala honours leaders, volunteers
content:
Leadership and volunteerism were recognized during the Nunavut Sport and Recreation awards gala at Iqaluit’s Aqsarniit hotel on Saturday.




The Recreation and Parks Association of Nunavut co-hosted the event in partnership with the NU Sport Federation and the territorial government’s sport and recreation division.




Novoalia Carriere of Kinngait earned the Calm Air Youth Leader of the Year award for his work as a summer camp supervisor and now as head of the hamlet’s after-school program.




“Sport is important for young people because it promotes healthy physical growth, builds mental resilience, and teaches essential life and social skills,” said Carriere over Facebook Thursday.




The 18-year-old athlete cares for up to 40 children aged five through 12 from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. weekdays at the youth centre.




With the music of Black Eyed Peas and other pop artists filling the background at low volume, Carriere tries to create an atmosphere that’s distinct from school and home.




He cycles through creative indoor activities to foster social connection without any concern for “competition or adult expectations.”
















“When activities feel less like school and more like an unfolding adventure, kids naturally stay hooked,” he said.




The non-profit association also honoured the Kinngait Youth Group with its Volunteers of the Year award.




“Volunteers really are the heart of their communities,” said association executive director Aaron Robinson in a phone interview Thursday.




Made up of 10 youths aged 13 to 19, the group offers a safe, welcoming space for younger children, he said.




In February, the teens served more than 200 residents at a Valentine’s Day breakfast, Robinson said.




“These youth have led with heart, teamwork and pride, and it’s still going,” he said. “They are inspiring others, building community and showing us what volunteerism and leadership truly looks like.”
















City of Iqaluit recreation director Breton McNeil received the Recreation Leader of the Year award.




During the gala, the NU Sport Federation inducted former NHL player Jordin Tootoo and the late Arctic sports athlete and organizer Attima Hadlari into its newly established Nunavut Sports and Recreation 

Hall of Fame

.




The federation and the Government of Nunavut also handed out awards to athletes, officials, and administrators from throughout the territory.




The audience included more than 100 recreation professionals who participated in the association’s weekend summit.




Organizations that included Nunavut Basketball, Volleyball Nunavut, Nunavut Soccer, Nunavut Table Tennis, Cambridge Bay Wrestling and Nunavut Badminton hosted coaching sessions in Iqaluit school gyms on Saturday and Sunday.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Throughout US War on Afghanistan, “We Could Clearly See Failure Was Coming”
content:
The “war on terror” is still ongoing in Afghanistan despite US withdrawal, journalist Emran Feroz says.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

This week marks 25 years since the U.S.-led invasion of Afghanistan, the beginning of what would become the longest war in U.S. history. After installing a pro-Western government in Kabul in December 2001, U.S. and other NATO troops would remain in the country for the next two decades battling a stubborn insurgency — until a chaotic U.S. withdrawal in August 2021 that saw the Taliban return to power.

“During the 20 years of America’s longest war in Afghanistan, we could clearly see that failure was coming,” says journalist Emran Feroz, just back from a month of reporting in Afghanistan. He says the relative economic and political gains under the Western-backed government were undercut by widespread corruption and violence, particularly in rural Afghanistan. “You had torture prisons next to Burger King and KFC and Starbucks.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Nermeen Shaikh.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: This week marks 25 years since the U.S.-led invasion of Afghanistan, the beginning of what would become the longest war in U.S. history. Less than a month after the September 11th World Trade Center attacks, the United States launched airstrikes against Afghanistan. The Taliban government was ousted within months, but the U.S.-led war and occupation would continue for nearly two decades, during which more than 100,000 Afghan civilians were killed, according to the U.N. More than 2,300 U.S. service members died. The U.S. spent trillions of dollars on the war and efforts to build an Afghan government and military, that ultimately collapsed with stunning speed in August 2021.

Today, Afghanistan is facing a deepening humanitarian crisis. Women and girls have been shut out of higher education and face sweeping restrictions on their work, movement and participation in public life.

AMY GOODMAN: Our next guest, Austrian Afghan journalist Emran Feroz, is just back from a month reporting in Afghanistan. His new piece for Truthout is headlined “The War on Afghanistan Was Launched 25 Years Ago. It Still Hasn’t Ended.” He’s joining us from Stuttgart, Germany.

Emran, welcome back to Democracy Now! Why don’t you lay out what you found, as you’ve just returned from Afghanistan? The U.S. bombed Afghanistan when the Taliban were in power, and the Taliban are back a quarter of a century later.

EMRAN FEROZ: Hi. Thanks for having me.

So, yes, I spent almost a whole month in Afghanistan, and the thing is that, as I wrote in this piece, I believe the “war on terror” is not over, especially because since the U.S. withdrawal, a lot of airstrikes are still taking place, especially in the last weeks and months. And all these airstrikes are being conducted by the Pakistani military regime, which kind of took over America’s role and is now using the same “war on terror” arguments that we heard for 20 years, again to hit Afghan civilians. And the recent strike just took place a few days ago in the south of the country, close to the Pakistani border. And again, most of the victims were civilians, especially children.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: So, Emran, if you could say — you know, a lot of people were surprised by the fact that the Taliban came back to power so quickly. Who was supporting the Taliban in all those years?

EMRAN FEROZ: I mean, during the 20 years of America’s longest war in Afghanistan, we could clearly see that failure was coming. The Afghan regime in Kabul, the pro-Western Afghan regime in Kabul, was highly corrupt and was engaging in a war that seemed to be endless because too many people were profiting from it. And this war actually made a lot of people angry and, you know, left them frustrating, and a lot of these people, actually, especially in Afghanistan rural sites, started to support the Taliban again.

But I also want to highlight that a lot of the places that I visited during the last weeks, for example, Bagram Air Base, close to Kabul, were in fact breeding grounds for America’s enemies, because you had this huge prison complex in the middle of the country, which became kind of a Little America. You had torture prisons next to Burger King and KFC and Starbucks, and a lot of young men who vanished there and who never came out, or a lot of people, including Taliban fighters, who were brought there and, in fact, became even more radicalized through the things that happened there.

AMY GOODMAN: In fact, you wrote this piece, just out, headlined “Why Bagram Air Base Remains a Target Five Years After U.S. Exited Afghanistan.” If you can talk about what’s happened to women and girls there now?

EMRAN FEROZ: The situation of women and girls is pretty bad in Afghanistan. I mean, it’s — as already mentioned, they have no access to higher education. Also, there is a lot of — like, you know, a lot of problems when it comes to letting them work, allowing them work. And you could clearly see that girls and women in Afghanistan are facing these repressions, and that, actually, unfortunately, the Taliban themselves declared war against them. That’s what at least a lot of Afghan girls and women are going to tell you.

And you see that also a lot of people, for that reason, still try to leave the country. Afghanistan is still producing a lot of refugees, tens of thousands of people who want to leave the country. And especially in the cities, when you talk to people, including my own relatives and friends, they say, “OK, what should we do here? Especially when it comes to the future of our daughters, there is no future here. So we are forced to leave, even if we don’t want to do that.”

And this is, unfortunately, the harsh reality that everyone knows about, including a lot of Taliban officials. And if you talk to them, you will also hear different things. For example, there is kind of a discrepancy between the Taliban leadership in Kabul and the one in Kandahar, which is making the laws. And it seems that, especially in my case, like the things that I experienced, is that a lot of Taliban themselves do not really support these repressions, but they are forced to do it because there is a strict hierarchy, and they fear that they’re going to be split if they start to fight about this.

AMY GOODMAN: Emran Feroz, we want to thank you so much for being with us, Austrian Afghan journalist, author of Graveyard Empire: Four Decades of Wars and Intervention in Afghanistan.

That does it for today’s show. The conversation will be moderated by the Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Maria Hinojosa. To find out more, you can go to StealThisStory.org.
