title: Συγκέντρωση αλληλεγγύης στους εξεγερμένους μαθητές στη Γαλλία, Πέμπτη 8/10, στις 19.00, στα Προπύλαια
content:
Συσπείρωση Αναρχικών




Συγκέντρωση αλληλεγγύης στους εξεγερμένους μαθητές στη Γαλλία







ΣΥΓΚΕΝΤΡΩΣΗ ΣΤΑ ΠΡΟΠΥΛΑΙΑ ΠΕΜΠΤΗ 8 ΟΚΤΩΒΡΙΟΥ 2026, στις 19.00. – ΑΛΛΗΛΕΓΓΥΗ ΣΤΟΥΣ ΕΞΕΓΕΡΜΕΝΟΥΣ ΜΑΘΗΤΕΣ ΣΤΗ ΓΑΛΛΙΑ




Η εξέγερση των μαθητών με αφορμή διάφορα εκπαιδευτικά αιτήματα σε δεκάδες πόλεις της Γαλλίας και ενώ 500 Γυμνάσια και Λύκεια παραμένουν κατειλημμένα, αντιμετωπίζεται από το γαλλικό κράτος με άγρια καταστολή, εκατοντάδες τραυματίες και τουλάχιστον 5.000 συλλήψεις, κυρίως ανήλικων διαδηλωτών.




Οι εξεγερμένοι μαθητές στήνουν οδοφράγματα, πυρπολούν σχολεία, αυτοκίνητα, επιτίθενται σε αστυνομικά τμήματα και συγκρούονται με τις δυνάμεις καταστολής δίχως να υποχωρούν.




Τα παιδιά της «κρίσης» κραυγάζουν για το παρόν και το μέλλον και πυροδοτούν μια ακόμη κοινωνική εξέγερση, όπως έγινε στον ελλαδικό χώρο το 2008, δίχως να έχουν ψευδαισθήσεις για όσα υπόσχονται οι εξουσιαστές, χωρίς να έχουν αυταπάτες για τους λόγους για τους οποίους τα πράγματα θα χειροτερέψουν.




Η «κρίση» χρέους, οι «απαραίτητες» μεταρρυθμίσεις, η προετοιμασία των ευρωπαϊκών κοινωνιών για πόλεμο, η έκρηξη του πληθωρισμού, η ενεργειακή ή πολιτική «κρίση» σημαίνουν ένα και μόνο πράγμα για τους καταπιεσμένους και εκμεταλλευόμενους: οι ζωές μας δεν έχουν την παραμικρή αξία για τους δυνάστες μας.




Να σπάσουμε τις αλυσίδες της παραίτησης,


του φόβου και της ανάθεσης.


Να πιστέψουμε, ότι το μόνο αδύνατον,


είναι να ζούμε με σκυμμένο το κεφάλι.













Η καταστολή δεν θα κάμψει τους αγώνες μας




Το τελευταίο διάστημα, στη Γαλλία έχει πυροδοτηθεί ένα εκτεταμένο κύμα κοινωνικών και μαθητικών κινητοποιήσεων. Μαθητές και μαθήτριες σε ολόκληρη τη χώρα προχωρούν σε καταλήψεις, αποκλεισμούς σχολείων, διαδηλώσεις και συγκρούσεις με τα όργανα καταστολής, διεκδικώντας αξιοπρεπείς συνθήκες εκπαίδευσης και εναντιώνονται στην ολοένα εντεινόμενη υποβάθμιση της δημόσιας παιδείας. Οι κινητοποιήσεις αυτές δεν αποτελούν ένα μεμονωμένο ξέσπασμα δυσαρέσκειας, αλλά αναδεικνύουν τις βαθύτερες αντιφάσεις ενός εκπαιδευτικού συστήματος που αντιμετωπίζει τις ανάγκες των μαθητών ως κόστος και τις κοινωνικές διεκδικήσεις ως απειλή προς καταστολή.




Υπερπλήρη τμήματα, χρόνια υποστελέχωση, ελλείψεις σε εκπαιδευτικούς, σχολικούς νοσηλευτές και προσωπικό υποστήριξης, ανεπαρκείς υποδομές και εξαντλητικά ωράρια συνθέτουν την καθημερινότητα χιλιάδων μαθητών. Πρόκειται για συνθήκες που δεν είναι καθόλου άγνωστες και στην ελληνική εκπαιδευτική πραγματικότητα. Η υποχρηματοδότηση, η απαξίωση των δημόσιων σχολείων και η μετακύλιση των ευθυνών στις ίδιες τις σχολικές κοινότητες αποτελούν όψεις μιας ευρύτερης πολιτικής που υποτάσσει την εκπαίδευση σε δημοσιονομικούς περιορισμούς, αποκλείοντας σταδιακά όλο και περισσότερα κομμάτια της κοινωνίας από την ισότιμη πρόσβαση στη γνώση.




Την ίδια στιγμή, απέναντι στις μαθητικές διεκδικήσεις, το γαλλικό κράτος επιστρατεύει την αστυνομική καταστολή, τις συλλήψεις και τη βία, επιχειρώντας να επιβάλει την πειθάρχηση και να ανακόψει την εξάπλωση των κινητοποιήσεων. Περισσότερες από 5.000 συλλήψεις έχουν καταγραφεί από την έναρξη των κινητοποιήσεων, ενώ σύμφωνα με τις γαλλικές αρχές πάνω από 170 μαθητές έχουν τραυματιστεί.

 

Ωστόσο η κρατική καταστολή

 

στις 5 Οκτωβρίου, πήρε μια ιδιαίτερα σοβαρή διάσταση. Στη Λανς, ένας 15χρονος μαθητής τραυματίστηκε σοβαρά κατά τη διάρκεια κινητοποίησης έξω από σχολείο, χάνοντας το χέρι του μετά την έκρηξη αστυνομικής χειροβομβίδας.




Η αντιμετώπιση των μαθητών ως απειλή, αντί ως υποκειμένων που διεκδικούν τα δικαιώματά τους, αποκαλύπτει τον τρόπο με τον οποίο η κρατική εξουσία αντιμετωπίζει κάθε συλλογική αμφισβήτηση της κυρίαρχης πολιτικής. Όταν οι διεκδικήσεις δεν χωρούν στα θεσμικά όρια που τίθενται από τα πάνω, η καταστολή επιστρατεύεται για να επιβάλει τη σιωπή και την επιστροφή στην κανονικότητα.




Ωστόσο, η κανονικότητα που υπερασπίζεται το κράτος είναι η ίδια που γεννά τις ελλείψεις, την ανασφάλεια και την υποβάθμιση της καθημερινότητάς μας. Είναι η κανονικότητα που απαιτεί από τους μαθητές να αποδέχονται παθητικά τις αποφάσεις που καθορίζουν τη ζωή τους, να προσαρμόζονται σε ένα σχολείο που αδυνατεί να καλύψει τις ανάγκες τους και να αντιμετωπίζουν ως αυτονόητη την αστυνομική παρουσία όταν επιλέγουν να αντισταθούν. Απέναντι σε αυτή τη συνθήκη, οι μαθητικοί αγώνες αναδεικνύουν τη δυνατότητα συλλογικής οργάνωσης, αυτοοργάνωσης και διεκδίκησης από τα κάτω, έξω από τη λογική της ανάθεσης και της παθητικής αναμονής λύσεων από τους εκάστοτε διαχειριστές της εξουσίας.




Για εμάς, η αλληλεγγύη στους αγωνιζόμενους μαθητές και μαθήτριες της Γαλλίας δεν αποτελεί μια συμβολική χειρονομία συμπαράστασης σε έναν αγώνα που διεξάγεται μακριά μας. Αποτελεί αναπόσπαστο κομμάτι της κοινής μας αντίστασης απέναντι στις πολιτικές που υποβαθμίζουν τη δημόσια παιδεία, εντείνουν τους κοινωνικούς αποκλεισμούς και επιχειρούν να πειθαρχήσουν κάθε φωνή αμφισβήτησης. Οι αγώνες των μαθητών

 

οπως και γενικότερα δεν περιορίζονται από εθνικά σύνορα, καθώς οι συνθήκες που τους γεννούν συνδέονται με ευρύτερες κοινωνικές και πολιτικές επιλογές.




Από τα σχολεία της Ελλάδας μέχρι τους δρόμους της Γαλλίας, οι μαθητικοί αγώνες είναι κοινοί.




Αλληλεγγύη στους αγωνιζόμενους μαθητές και μαθήτριες της Γαλλίας.




Κανένας αγώνας δεν είναι μεμονωμένος

title: Istigazione alla cura. La medicina sotto l’attacco razzista del governo
content:
Con questo articolo le Collettive Brigate Basaglia mostrano la totale solidarietà a colleghi, colleghe e altre persone indagate per aver fatto quello che dovrebbe essere il gesto più semplice e naturale della medicina: guardare una persona prima ancora del suo documento, ascoltare una sofferenza prima ancora della sua posizione amministrativa, riconoscere un essere umano prima ancora di una categoria giuridica. Già, proprio così: 

la Procura di Ravenna ha indagato di recente oltre 20 professionisti sanitari in tutta Italia (circa 23-24 medici) con l’accusa di aver emesso 

falsi certificati di non idoneità

 per impedire il trattenimento di migranti irregolari nei 

CPR 

(Centro di Permanenza per il Rimpatrio)

.




Forse mancava solo questo. Dopo il reato di solidarietà, dopo il reato di soccorso in mare, o a chi attraversa un confine senza il permesso o senza un conto in banca abbastanza consistente, arriva finalmente il nuovo grande pericolo per l’ordine pubblico italiano: l’istigazione alla cura!




Perché se il personale medico osa fare quello per cui dovrebbe esistere la medicina — guardare una persona, ascoltare la sua sofferenza, valutare la sua vulnerabilità — allora forse, qualcosa nella macchina istituzionale “democratica” si è inceppato..




Ma forse la questione più profonda non riguarda soltanto i CPR, il personale medico o un singolo procedimento giudiziario. La questione riguarda un problema ancora più grande, l’esistenza stessa di strutture amministrative o detentive costruite attorno all’assurda idea che alcuni esseri umani possano trovarsi fuori posto (soprattutto se poveri).




Ma fuori posto rispetto a cosa? Rispetto a una linea tracciata su una mappa da quattro burocrati. Rispetto a un confine deciso nella storia. Rispetto a un documento che stabilisce chi può muoversi liberamente (soprattutto se pieno di soldi) e chi invece deve dimostrare continuamente di avere il diritto di stare da qualche parte. La guerra ai migranti poveri agita dai governi ad ogni latitudine è realtà anche per la “democrazia europea”, non un errore di percorso!




Il problema non è soltanto il modo disumano con cui questi lager, definiti strutture “amministrative”, vengono gestiti e su cui abbiamo già detto abbastanza. Il problema è proprio il principio stesso secondo cui un essere umano possa diventare irregolare, invisibile, sospeso, semplicemente perché nato dall’altra parte di una frontiera, o perché “povero”, o perché non bianco abbastanza, o non cristiano abbastanza.




Prima ancora dei CPR esiste questa maledetta dottrina: quella secondo cui il mondo sia diviso in territori appartenenti a Stati-nazione e che dentro questi territori alcune persone siano considerate legittime e altre temporaneamente tollerate, controllabili, espellibili.




È proprio dentro questa logica disumana che nasce la contraddizione più profonda, dove la medicina viene chiamata a certificare non la salute, ma la capacità di una persona di sopportare una condizione che può danneggiare la salute. Infatti, come viene affermato ampiamente anche dalla rete “Mai più lager- NO ai CPR”, di cui fanno parte alcuni dei medici accusati, è riconosciuta ormai la patogenicità, ovvero la capacità di questi centri di detenzione, di creare malattie e danni. La sola permanenza in un CPR, a causa delle condizioni profondamente dannose documentate e testimoniate, può portare infatti a gravi compromissioni della salute. Ciò è tristemente ironico, se si pensa che per definizione legislativa, in questi centri “lo straniero deve essere trattenuto con modalità tali da assicurare la necessaria assistenza ed il pieno rispetto della sua dignità”.




Ormai non è più sufficiente che una persona venga privata della libertà dentro un CPR. Non è più sufficiente che il suo corpo venga inserito dentro un dispositivo amministrativo costruito per rendere possibile l’espulsione. Ora quel corpo deve anche essere dichiarato compatibile con quella condizione assurda e disumana, la repressione chiama dunque la medicina ad essere collaborazionista di tutto ciò.




E qui emerge il paradosso. La medicina dovrebbe porsi una semplicissima domanda clinica: di cosa ha bisogno questa persona per stare meglio?




E invece non basta! In questi contesti la stessa medicina è chiamata anche a porsi ulteriori domande, domande di natura politica: questa persona può essere ficcata dentro l’ingranaggio disumano che lo Stato centrale ha deciso per lei senza che crei troppi problemi?; la possiamo rendere invisibile e farla morire dentro la democrazia istituzionale della fortezza Europa senza che alzi troppa polvere, e anzi, raccattando pure qualche voto sul suo corpo?




La recente vicenda, che vede altri clinici indagati su tutta Italia (che si aggiungono a quelli di Ravenna di inizio anno) per aver certificato la non idoneità di alcune persone migranti destinate ai CPR, non riguarda soltanto un procedimento giudiziario. Riguarda bensì una questione molto più ampia: quale ruolo viene assegnato alla medicina dentro una società che si definisce democratica?




Il medico deve essere un garante della persona oppure un ingranaggio amministrativo incaricato di rendere funzionale un sistema di detenzione?




Dati ufficiali dell’Organizzazione Mondiale della Sanità hanno più volte evidenziato come la detenzione amministrativa delle persone migranti rappresenti un fattore di rischio per la salute mentale e fisica, soprattutto quando si combina con isolamento, incertezza sul futuro, esperienze traumatiche precedenti e condizioni ambientali difficili.




La medicina non può essere chiamata soltanto a verificare se un corpo sia abbastanza resistente da sopportare una condizione patologica. Altrimenti il medico non cura più il danno: certifica la capacità del corpo di subirlo.




Ed è proprio qui che il problema diventa politico. Perché se un luogo è fonte di sofferenza, la risposta sanitaria non dovrebbe essere aumentare la capacità delle persone di resistere dentro quel luogo. La risposta sanitaria dovrebbe interrogarsi sull’esistenza stessa di quel luogo.




I CPR non sono ospedali. Non sono strutture terapeutiche. Sono luoghi di privazione della libertà. La loro particolarità è proprio questa: una persona può essere privata della libertà senza aver commesso un reato penale, ma perché si trova in una condizione amministrativa considerata irregolare. Eppure, il corpo umano non distingue tra una cella chiamata carcere e una stanza chiusa chiamata centro di permanenza. Il corpo conosce soltanto l’esperienza concreta, cioè il maledetto isolamento da tutti e da tutto, la perdita di controllo sulla propria vita, l’impossibilità di scegliere, la paura dell’espulsione, la sospensione del futuro.




Negli anni sono emersi numerosi episodi di autolesionismo, tentativi suicidari e suicidi compiuti all’interno dei CPR. Il caso di Ousmane Sylla, morto suicida nel CPR di Ponte Galeria nel 2024, è diventato uno dei simboli delle criticità legate alla salute mentale nei centri. Non è un dettaglio marginale.





In medicina detentiva, il gesto autolesivo non è semplicemente un comportamento individuale, ma spesso rappresenta un chiaro segnale comunicativo di un contesto che sta producendo sofferenza. Quando molte, tantissime persone, dentro lo stesso ambiente manifestano disperazione, la questione non ha alibi, e non può essere ancora e soltanto sul “come controllare queste persone”. La questione dovrebbe essere: che cosa sta facendo questo ambiente alle persone che vi vengono inserite?




Un altro elemento inquietante riguarda il fiume di psicofarmaci dentro i CPR. Diverse relazioni e osservazioni indipendenti hanno segnalato nei CPR un utilizzo significativo di farmaci sedativi e psicofarmaci. Naturalmente, ogni trattamento farmacologico dovrebbe essere valutato caso per caso e può rendersi effettivamente necessario, se in presenza di specifiche condizioni cliniche.




Ma esiste una questione più generale: quando una persona soffre perché è inserita in un ambiente che produce angoscia, paura e perdita di controllo, la risposta è sedare la persona, oppure modificare tutto l’ambiente che genera quella sofferenza?




La storia della psichiatria ci ha insegnato proprio questo: per decenni abbiamo chiamato “malattia individuale” ciò che spesso era anche e soprattutto prodotto di istituzioni, rapporti sociali e condizioni di vita disumane e opprimenti.




Basaglia lo aveva mostrato con chiarezza. Il problema non era soltanto la sofferenza mentale, ma il modo in cui una società decideva di organizzare la risposta a quella sofferenza.




La questione dei medici dei CPR è quindi una questione deontologica, prima ancora che giudiziaria. Il medico non è chiamato a certificare che un sistema funzioni, è chiamato a valutare una persona. La differenza sembra piccola, ma cambia tutto. Quando la logica amministrativa diventa dominante, il rischio è che la salute venga trasformata in un semplice requisito tecnico: un timbro necessario affinché una procedura burocratica possa continuare.




Ma la medicina non dovrebbe essere una pratica di adattamento dei corpi alle maledette esigenze delle istituzioni. La medicina dovrebbe ricordare alle istituzioni che esistono limiti che nessuna procedura amministrativa può cancellare. La medicina non è mai stata neutrale, lo sappiamo. Nel corso della Storia è diventata più volte strumento di classificazione, esclusione, controllo e violenza, soprattutto verso categorie oppresse socialmente, come donne e persone razzializzate. Al contrario, ci sono stati momenti in cui invece ha scelto la parte della persona contro l’apparato.




Medici che durante il fascismo falsificarono documenti per salvare vite. Medici che denunciarono la violenza dei manicomi. Operatori sanitari che durante il G8 di Genova curarono persone colpite durante le proteste, a prescindere da qualsiasi altra valutazione, proprio perché nella deontologia medica è da sempre presente il diritto alla cura della persona, chiunque essa sia.




Forse un giorno il problema non sarà ricordato come “il caso dei medici che ostacolavano i CPR”. Forse verrà ricordato come il momento in cui una società ha dovuto scegliere se la medicina dovesse servire i corpi, oppure i dispositivi europei “democratici e attenti ai diritti umani” costruiti per governare i corpi.




Ed è qui che sta il paradosso. In un sistema in cui la sofferenza viene amministrata e somministrati, chi prova a curarla rischia di diventare il problema. E allora sì, forse arriverà davvero il giorno in cui dovremo difenderci dal nuovo reato di istigazione alla cura. Anzi, è già arrivato.




La colpa? Aver continuato a vedere esseri umani dove altri vedevano pratiche da smaltire. Ma la nostra sopportazione finisce qui!




Siamo stanc* di assistere all’ennesimo abuso di logiche autoritarie dentro strutture che si definiscono democratiche, ma che continuano a permettere e a promuovere forme di violenza, controllo e oppressione sulle persone più vulnerabili.




E allora la cura, da sola, non basta! Curare non può significare soltanto intervenire sul dolore quando il dolore è già stato prodotto. Curare significa anche riconoscere insieme ciò che quel dolore lo genera, nominarlo, contrastarlo, costruire legami capaci di impedire che venga continuamente riprodotto. Per questo la cura deve diventare azione collettiva.




Oggi non basta più al personale medico dire 

“e mi no firmo”

 come disse Basaglia in occasione del suo 

primo giorno come direttore del manicomio di Gorizia nel 1961.

 La responsabilità non può essere lasciata al singolo medico/a che si trova davanti a un certificato da firmare. Se il problema è strutturale, anche la risposta deve esserlo.




Chiediamo a tutte le cliniche e a tutti i clinici, alle attiviste e agli attivisti e a chiunque continui a credere nella dignità umana, di rompere queste gabbie burocratiche nel modo che ritiene più giusto.




Mettiamo bombe di cura dappertutto. Bombe che non esplodono, ma che aprono crepe nei muri dell’indifferenza. Bombe fatte di solidarietà, presenza, mutuo aiuto, disobbedienza professionale e responsabilità condivisa. Bombe che bruciano simbolicamente i documenti inutili, quelle categorie e quelle procedure che non proteggono le persone, ma servono soltanto a separarle, classificarle, renderle espellibili e meno umane. Bombe che facciano saltare in aria simbolicamente quelle catene burocratiche che servono soltanto a creare confini artificiali tra gli esseri umani.




Non dobbiamo distruggere nulla, se non l’idea, propinata dalle istituzioni, che una persona possa essere considerata meno umana di qualcun’altra.




Ciò che dovrebbe esplodere è l’amore che abbiamo dentro di noi, che ci permetta di riconoscere nell’altra persona non un problema amministrativo, ma una vita, un cuore che ama, e che invece si sta spegnendo dentro una cella a due passi da casa nostra.




La cura non è soltanto ciò che accade tra un professionista e una persona. La cura accade anche quando una comunità decide che nessuno debba essere lasciato solo davanti al potere oppressivo. Accade quando un medico rifiuta di firmare ciò che ritiene ingiusto e altri medici gli stanno accanto. Accade quando un’attivista denuncia un abuso e altre persone fanno in modo che quella denuncia non venga soffocata. Accade quando trasformiamo la solidarietà da sentimento privato a pratica organizzata.




Non dobbiamo far esplodere nulla, se non il silenzio opprimente, la rinuncia devastante che ci circonda e ci uccide da dentro.




Quello che deve esplodere è la capacità collettiva di prenderci cura gli uni degli altri. Perché, quando la cura diventa collettiva, smette di essere soltanto assistenza e diventa resistenza e quando quest’ultima pulsa, vibrante di un diffuso sentimento di libertà, diventa rivoluzione!




Non lasciamo che queste parole finiscano solo su questa carta!




Scriviamo lettere ai nostri ordini professionali, se questo è lo strumento che abbiamo a disposizione. Scriviamo su milioni di altri fogli, scriviamo sul corpo, sui muri, sulle strade, sulle porte e sui portoni! Facciamo sentire la nostra voce, gridiamo, ma gridiamo forte! Facciamo uscire il dolore, facciamo uscire l’umanità repressa dalla burocrazia delle istituzioni totalitarie. Organizziamoci nei luoghi di lavoro. Costruiamo reti tra professionisti e amici. Rendiamo pubbliche le contraddizioni. Sosteniamo chi si espone. Non lasciamo solu chi rifiuta di trasformare la propria professione in un ingranaggio amministrativo. Ma facciamolo con il cuore e con la calma rabbia! Non siamo sole! Solidarietà.




Brigate Basaglia




L'articolo 

Istigazione alla cura. La medicina sotto l’attacco razzista del governo

 proviene da 

.

author: Marina Amaral
title: O saldo do 1º turno para a Amazônia
content:
Já temos os resultados do primeiro turno das eleições, e com um Senado dominado pela extrema direita e um STF fragilizado, as perspectivas pro meio ambiente não são boas. Isabel Seta, Marina Amaral e Ricardo Terto analisam o cenário pós primeiro turno, com foco nos impactos para a Amazônia, para os povos indígenas e para o clima – o que impacta a todos.




O episódio traz a dimensão geopolítica, em que os Estados Unidos se tornaram uma ameaça a nossa democracia, o crescimento de Flávio Bolsonaro justamente no arco do desmatamento, e também os senadores e governadores eleitos na região. Ouça agora.







E MAIS:




Uma Trombeta negacionista. E no quadro “Se é pra falar de economia…”, Clara Marinho mostra que nem sempre os indicadores econômicos se refletem no resultado das eleições.

author: Unknown
title: 12 prisoners begin hunger strike at Bukan prison
content:
The Kurdistan Human Rights Network reported that at least 12 Kurdish prisoners being held at Bukan Prison for political and religious reasons began a hunger strike on October 5 to protest pressure exerted by Iranian regime forces in prisons.




The prisoners announced in a letter to Bukan Prison authorities on 5 October that they had begun a hunger strike. They are reportedly protesting restrictions on their access to leave permits and the open-prison placement program, as well as restrictions imposed on them under prison conditions.




The prisoners whose names have been identified as participating in the hunger strike are: Ardalan Mineh, Behrouz Barakhas, Esmail Atash-Mard, Kaveh Rahimi, Hamed Maroufi, Ali Mohammadi, Mahmoud Jafari, Ali Faroughi, Arsalan Minaei, Aziz Banehei, Ghader Salimi, and Mullah Davoud.




It was reported that on the second day of the hunger strike, the 12 prisoners were transferred to the quarantine section on the orders of the director of Bukan Prison. Their phone calls and family visits are reportedly still being restricted.




A Kurd detained 




Meanwhile, Faramarz Seîdî, from the city of Dehgolan in Kurdistan Province, was detained by forces from the Ministry of Intelligence using violence and taken to a detention facility operated by the ministry. It was reported that Ministry of Intelligence forces arrested Seîdî on 6 October on Esteghlal Street in Dehgolan, without a court order.

author: Unknown
title: Women murdered in Amed: A common story of violence, complaints, and failed protection
content:
In the first eight months of 2026, 197 women were killed by men in Kurdistan and Turkey. The same period also saw suspicious deaths of women and cases in which women were driven to suicide.




In Diyarbakır (Amed), one woman has died under suspicious circumstances since June, while the body of another woman who disappeared years ago was also found. Four women were also killed by men during this period.




Similar circumstances emerged behind the suspicious deaths and femicides in the city, while the families of the women killed shared a common demand: penalties must be sufficiently deterrent.




Four women killed




Interviews with the families of the women killed during this period revealed that the women had been subjected to systematic violence and were not adequately protected despite reporting the abuse to the police.




Sultan Karadağ was killed on 10 August. Sultan Kara was killed on 26 August by Ersan Akdemir, whom she wanted to divorce. Mizgin Kılıç was killed on 18 September by her former husband, and Ayfer Çakmak was killed on 27 September by her husband Orhan Çakmak, after reportedly enduring systematic violence for years.




The names and number of the women killed are more than mere statistics. Although their stories differed, they shared a common experience: they were subjected to violence, and their requests for protection went unanswered.




Mizgin Kılıç and Sultan Kara wanted to build new lives despite the violence they had endured, but they were not protected despite filing complaints. According to information provided by her relatives, Gülistan Karadağ was killed by people who had subjected her to violence and were reportedly using drugs.




Ayfer Çakmak was shot dead by her husband Orhan Çakmak, who had reportedly prevented her from even leaving the house for years. Following the killing, Çakmak claimed that her death was a suicide, saying, “The gun suddenly went off.”




Gülistan was targeted with violence and drugs




The family of Gülistan Karadağ said their daughter had been subjected to violence and threats for a long time and demanded that those responsible be held accountable. The family said: “Gülistan suffered violence and had been beaten again before she died. Who is bringing in these drugs, and how are they getting here? She constantly wanted a new beginning, a life of her own. But they never allowed her to have one. She was constantly beaten and threatened. Whoever did this must be held accountable. Our only demand is justice. We want nothing else.”




Sultan was not protected despite requesting a restraining order




The family of Sultan Kara, who was killed in front of her three-year-old daughter, said numerous complaints had previously been filed against the perpetrator. The family said Sultan had endured threats and violence for a long time: “The state is doing nothing. We lost our sister. Sultan had been married for four years. Every morning, my sister would say, ‘He is going to kill me.’ Twice, he beat her almost to death. He threatened and assaulted her. Even when Sultan was pregnant, he grabbed her by the throat and tried to kill her. His family threatened her to prevent her from filing a complaint.




Sultan had requested a restraining order when she filed for divorce. Following the decision to divorce, the perpetrator threatened both my older sister and Sultan with death. My sister is dead, while that man is walking around freely. Women are being killed and no one is taking it seriously. I want justice. Enough is enough.”




Sultan’s family said she had been subjected to violence not only by the man she wanted to divorce but also by his mother: “Sultan suffered violence both from him and from his mother. When she went to file a complaint, they sent her away, saying, ‘They are not the kind of people who would kill someone.’ Our only demand is that he receive the harshest possible sentence.”




The electronic tag was removed after the divorce




Mizgin Kılıç, who was killed by Ömer Kırıcı a year after divorcing him, had also endured violence and threats for a long time. According to her family, Mizgin left the house several times because of the violence but was forced to return after “family elders” intervened.




Ömer Kırıcı reportedly continued to stalk and threaten Mizgin even after their divorce. Mizgin was shot dead, and Kırıcı died by suicide following the killing.




Mizgin’s family said she had gone to the police while experiencing violence and that an electronic monitoring tag had been imposed on Kırıcı: “Mizgin went to the police. She was being followed, but she hadn’t told us. Mizgin was suffering violence. They put an electronic tag on him at the time. They removed it after the divorce.”




Calling for an end to femicides, Mizgin’s family said: “Women are being killed every day. We want these killings to end. The state arrests these men and then releases them. If there were genuinely deterrent consequences, this would not happen. Not one more woman should be killed.”




He would not even allow Ayfer to leave the house




Ayfer Çakmak, who was killed by Orhan Çakmak, had been married for 14 years. According to her neighbours, Ayfer had been subjected to physical and psychological violence from the first day of her marriage.




Neighbours who saw Ayfer’s body said it was covered in bruises and that her arm was broken: “Ayfer had been married for 14 years. Even when her body was being washed for burial, it was covered in bruises and her arm was broken. He constantly threatened Ayfer, including with death. He would not even allow her to leave the house. Ayfer was so afraid that she could not even go outside. She had suffered violence from the first day of her marriage. There was no end to the torture she endured.”




Ayfer’s neighbours said she was shot while trying to escape: “That day, Ayfer was trying to escape when she was shot from behind and killed. We want justice. We want not only him but his entire family to be punished.”




Violence cannot be explained solely by individual behaviour







 







Tevgera Jinên Azad (TJA) activist Suzan Işbilen spoke about the femicides in the city, saying that killings of women were increasing and becoming normalised in society. Işbilen argued that violence against women could not be explained solely by the individual behaviour of men: “Violence against women has increased to such an extent in society that this is now our greatest concern. It has become something people are accustomed to. This is unacceptable. I believe the main reason for the increase in these killings of women is linked to those in power. Just as the patriarchal mentality regarded women’s system as a threat to its own power and established its authority by dismantling that system and excluding women from society, I believe we are seeing something similar today.




Since 2015, women have been the main section of society taking to the streets and exposing the government’s anti-democratic, repressive policies and practices of torture. Naturally, this is something that disturbs those in power.”




Impunity has brought us to this point




Işbilen referred to the Istanbul Convention and Law No. 6284, arguing that femicides were linked to impunity and the absence of deterrent penalties: “There are already very few legal provisions that protect women. The Istanbul Convention was the one instrument that provided comprehensive protection for women. By withdrawing from that convention, you allow men who kill women to go unpunished. Law No. 6284 is another law, and now the only one remaining, that protects women. The policies of the state and the system can be seen behind femicides. It is absolutely correct to say that femicides are political.




Violence against women is political. If it were not, men who kill women would at least receive deterrent sentences. But we see that such sentences are not imposed. We have seen many men leave prison and then kill their wives. We have seen men released from prison who went on to kill their mothers and sisters. There are men who spend only two months or two years in prison for killing someone. Such practices only encourage further violence.”




Perceptions of gender roles must change




Işbilen said entrenched gender roles contributed to the normalisation of femicides, adding that questioning the behaviour of women who had been killed further reinforced this attitude.




Işbilen also said: “When a woman is killed, the reaction is often, ‘Why? What did the woman do?’ The conventional ideas of womanhood and manhood created by these gender norms make women who struggle for their own freedom targets. Then, when a woman is killed, people try to normalise the murder with remarks such as, ‘She deserved it. Why couldn’t she just stay in her place?’




When so many women are being killed, when five women are killed in a single day in Turkey, all women need to stand up against it. This is unacceptable. Perceptions of gender roles need to change completely. Men must confront themselves and challenge this mentality. This mindset has to change.”

author: Unknown
title: KDP seeks permission from Turkey to use roads in its own territory
content:
Organizers of the Berwarî Bala Festival in Amêdiyê, linked to the KDP, and the KDP’s 18th Branch obtained permission from the Turkish state to use the roads for the event.




A source who spoke to Rojnews about the issue said that although the decision provides some relief to citizens and festival participants, it has also raised serious concerns and questions among local residents. The source said: “This is a public and tourist road within the Kurdistan Region. However, it has become an occupied and military road. Citizens have to obtain permission from the Turkish state to travel on this road in their own territory, and their passage is subject to conditions. This permission has been granted for only three days for the festival.”




According to information obtained, the road normally used to reach these areas is 35 kilometers long. However, for the past three days, people coming from outside the city who need to travel to Kanîmasî have been forced to use a route more than 80 kilometers long that is designated for local residents and villages. This situation places a significant burden on tourists and the local population.

author: Fozzie
title: Chapter 23: Simple Reproduction
content:
Harry Cleaver's study guide to Marx's Capital volume one, chapter 23.

Production must be continuous, i.e., repeat itself, as such it is also reproduction. In capitalism reproduction is also reproduction of value advanced as capital, i.e., "self-valorizing value." (p. 711)

Reproduction requires all of the elements of production be replaced, i.e., the means of production and labor power.

Reproduction of means of production = replacement of used up raw materials and worn-out machinery, buildings, etc.(MP) (p. 711)

Reproduction of labor power = reproduction of workers and their labor power requires production of necessary means of subsistence (MS). (p. 712)

Both MP and MS are produced by workers.

the means of subsistence required for reproduction of labor power (p. 712),

variable capital (under capitalism); rare, 1/4 world's workers) (p. 714, footnote 4),

product of peasants own land/labor (under feudalism) (p. 713).

... is the "mere continuity of the production process" (p. 715)

... "converts all capital into accumulated capital" (p. 715)

=alienation of workers' labor, sold by them to capitalist (p. 716)

=alienation of workers' product, owned by capitalist, an "alien power that dominates and exploits him." (p. 716)

Worker's consumption is of two kinds:

Productive consumption of MP during work - allows capital to live

Individual consumption of MS outside work - allows worker to live

Abusive consumption: where individual consumption is merely the means to "keep his [the worker's] labor-power in motion, just as coal and water are supplied to the steam-engine." (p. 717)

At the aggregate level of the classes:

Investment of variable capital = "reconversion of the means of subsistence . . . into fresh labor power which capital is then able to exploit."

As such, "individual consumption" . . . remains an aspect of of the production and reproduction of capital."

But, "the capitalist may safely leave this [individual consumption] to the worker's drives for self-preservation and propagation." (p. 718)

With some exceptions, e.g., South American mine owners who force their workers to eat beans to increase their strength and work. (p. 718, footnote 9)

Workers' consumption above what is needed for reproduction of labor power is unproductive consumption - from capitalist point of view.

Reproduction of workers is also "transmission and accumulation of skills from one generation to another." (p. 719)

Marx gives a series of quotes from a spokesperson for English cotton textile industry who objects to any government subsidy to worker emmigration during cotton famine and high unemployment caused by American Civil War.

workers are machines that should be kept on hand and in order

if they left, it would take a generation to replace them with a new batch of skilled workers

therefore the cotton industry and other, related industries would suffer

therefore the workers should be kept via forced public works (pp. 720-22)

The Times newspaper editorial also worried:

that "human machinery will rust under inaction"

that "human machinery will, as we have just seen, get the steam up of its own accord, and burst or run amuck in our great towns" (p. 722)

Marx concludes his example by noting Parliament passed an Act "empowering the municipal corportations to keep the workers in a state of semi-starvation, i.e., to exploit them without paying the normal wages." (p. 723)

As Marx pointed out in a two-page introduction to this section of Capital, pp. 709-710, his analysis in this and the subsequent two chapters is based on a number of simplifying assumptions. The most important one in this chapter, and the one that differentiates this chapter and its discussion of simple reproduction from the discussion of expanded reproduction in the next two chapters, is that capitalists consume all of the value that their operations generate over and above that which is necessary to replace the used up means of production, e.g., raw materials, tools, and to replace their living workers. In other words this chapter deals with how production is also reproduction of all of the elements of the capitalist organization of production in abstraction from investment that generates growth, i.e., accumulation.

This said, most of what Marx writes in this chapter should already be familiar from the study of preceeding ones, especially chapter 6 that deals explicitly with the reproduction of labor power, and indeed he often refers back to previous discussions. There are, however, a couple of points, one minor and another major, that are worthy of examination.

As discussed in my commentary on chapter 7 on the labor process, there has been a debate as to whether there was a fundamental change in Marx's analysis of capitalism from his discussion of alienation in the 1844 Manuscripts to the theory laid out in Capital. I have argued that there was no fundamental change and what we have in Capital includes an essentially a detailed elaboration of his earlier discussion of four forms of alienation, e.g., of how capital controls workers on the job thus alienating them from their labor, of how capital controls their product and uses it against them, of how capital pits workers against each other alienating them from each other and of how capital, by imposing its will, alienates them from their very species-being.

For the most part, the substantiation of this argument involves showing how the various moments of Marx's analysis in Capital are elaborations of these themes despite the absence of any explicit use of the term "alienation." In this chapter, however, he does use the term and his use deserves some attention.

On page 716 we find the following passage:

Here we find two uses of the term "alienation." The first use clearly refers simply to the sale of labor power; sold, the labor power and its use value now belongs to the capitalist "before" production begins. This is a fairly vernacular use of the term "alienation", just meaning to go away from or be taken away from. Even though what is being described is integral to the creation of alienation, and indeed if the worker's labor becomes "incorporated with capital" then all forms of alienation obtain, the use of the term here does not seem to refer to any of the four forms that Marx discussed in the 1844 Manuscripts. The second use, however, refers to what happens "in the course of the [labor] process", i.e., during production: the capitalist utilization of the use value of the worker's labor power results in a product that belongs to the capitalist. This is the alienation of the product, the second form of alienation mentioned above. When Marx goes on to point out how that product is converted into "capital, i.e., into value that sucks up the the worker's value-creating power" and thereby becomes "an alien power that dominates and exploits him," we have, explicitly, all the elements of the second form of alienation discussed in the Manuscripts.

The second, and more important issue raised in this chapter, concerns the reproduction of workers and their labor power as an integral part of capitalist reproduction as a whole. The key passage concerns the reproduction of capital as a whole, i.e., "the capitalist class and the working class":

"The capital given in return for labour-power is converted into means of subsistence which have to be consumed to reproduce the muscles, nerves, bones and brains of existing workers, and to bring new workers into existence. Within the limits of what is absolutely necessary, therefore, the individual consumption of the working class is the reconversion of the means of subsistence given by capital in return for labour-power into fresh labour-power which capital is then again able to exploit. It is the production and reproduction of the capitalist's most indispensible means of production: the worker. The individual consumption of the worker, whether it occurs inside or outside the workshop, inside or outside the labour process, remains as aspect of the production and reproduction of capital, just as the cleaning of machinery does, whether it is done during the labour proces, or when intervals in that process permit. The fact that the worker performs acts of individual consumption in his own interest, and not to please the capitalist, is something entirely irrelevant to the matter." (pp. 717-718)

Let us examine this passage in some detail. First, "the capital given in return for labour-power" is the wage, the variable capital invested in the hiring of workers. As we have seen before, this can be represented, from the capitalist point of view, as M-LP, the exchange of money for labor power. Or, from the workers' point of view as LP-M, the sale of labor power for money. Second, the "conversion" of the wage into "the means of subsistence" refers to all those expenditures workers make on everything necessary to reproduce their labor power, e.g., food, clothing, music, transportation, housing, and so on. Third, all of those things are not just bought, but they "must be consumed" in order "to reproduce the muscles, nerves, bones and brains of existing workers, and to bring new workers into existence." In other words, individual consumption must reproduce the labor power of existing workers and produce the next generation and its labor power. That individual consumption can include everything from cooking and eating to learning a skill to various amusements that re-creates the ability and willingness to return to work for the capitalist. The key point is that their consumption is, from the capitalist point of view, production - the production of labor power.

Now as we have seen, the industrial circuit of capital can be represented by the following sequence, what Marx calls the circuit of money capital:

where ...P... stands for the production process. Nowhere in Marx's writings, not even in Part I of Volume II of Capital where he sketches a detailed analysis of that circuit and also analyses it from two other points of view, is there a parallel symbolic representation for consumption qua production of labor power, but there is nothing to prevent us from using his same notation to represent a parallel process. Thus, I have suggested in my comments on chapter one (in Reading Capital Politically) that we can represent what Marx is saying in the above passage by:

where ...P... represents consumption as production of labor power and LP* is the labor power produced. The sense of this "circuit of the reproduction of labor power" is the same as his circuits of industrial capital: it represents a sequence of processes through which a key element of capital is reproduced: labor power. [I have given the final LP* an asterisk instead of a prime (e.g., LP') because in Marx's notation primes are used to designate increases in value but the impact of the work of consuming in ways that produce labor power has ambiguous effects, e.g., procreation by generating new workers may increase the value of labor power, but more housework that substitutes for purchased goods or services may reduce the value of labor power.]

Now Marx's final comment in this passage notes that "The fact that the worker performs acts of individual consumption in his own interest, and not to please the capitalist, is something entirely irrelevant to the matter." In other words, from the workers' point of view we could represent their entry into the labor market as merely a means toward their "own interest", i.e., the elaboration of their own lives, as LP-M-C(MS). Here consumption is not production, it is simply living! Here is the passage from Chapter 1, Volume II of Capital:

"It is also the sale of labour-power - we may here say of labour, since the form of wages is assumed - by the laborer who owns it. What is M-C(= M-L) for the buyer is here, as in every other purchase, L-M(= C-M) for the seller (the laborer). It is the sale of his labour-power. This is the first stage of circulation, or the first metamorphosis, of the commodity (Buch I, Kap. III, 2a).[English edition: Ch. III, 2a-Ed.] It is for the seller of labour a transformation of his commodity into the money-form. The laborer spends the money so obtained gradually for a number of commodities required for the satisfaction of his needs, for articles of consumption. The complete circulation of his commodity therefore appears as L-M-C, that is to say first as L-M(= C-M) and secondly as M-C; hence in the general form of the simple circulation of commodities, C-M-C. Money is in this case merely a passing means of circulation, a mere medium in the exchange of one commodity for another."

But this "little circuit" fails to capture the central point of this part of chapter 23: from the capitalist point of view working class consumption must involve the production of labor power.

This brings us to another important issue. A few lines after the passage quoted above Marx comments that "the capitalist may safely leave this [consumption qua production of labor power] to the worker's drives for self-preservation and propagation." (p. 718) Almost immediately, however, he gives a counter-example of South American mine-owners who force their workers to eat beans as well as bread to increase their strength and productivity. What are we to make of this contradiction?

On the one hand, Marx's comments here reflect what he was seeing around him in England in the years that he was writing, and what he was reading in the reports of the Factory Acts inspectors: a general tendency on the part of capital to minimize wages and all other costs related to the reproduction of the working class. Engels' book The Condition of the English Working Class upon which Marx drew repeatedly gave many vivid illustrations of such minimization and of the misery it imposed on British workers.

On the other hand, although Marx calls the South American mine-owner's oversight of the diet of their workers "crude", in historical retrospect we can see that they were actually harbringers of the capitalist future. That is to say, as those workers' struggles to reduce the working day, that Marx analyzed in chapter 10, were successful in driving the working day to 12 hrs, then to 10 hrs and then to 8 hrs, they were simultaneously successful in freeing more and more time from production under the eyes (and control) of the capitalists and gaining more and more time for living, i.e., for consumption that was not production of labor power. That working class success made the capitalist class more and more reliant upon two strategies, one that Marx analyzed extensively and one that he did not. The two strategies were those of relative surplus value and the management of working class consumption and free time to make sure that they resulted in the production and reproduction of labor power. We have already seen, in chapters 12-15, how detailed Marx's analysis of the former strategy became. The sketchiness of this chapter shows how limited was the attention he paid to the latter strategy.

As I suggested in my commentary on Chapter 10, today we must analyze not only capitalist strategies in the sphere of production, but also its strategies in the sphere of reproduction, indeed throughout the social factory. At the same time, we must also analyse workers struggles in both spheres to see how they rupture and force changes in capitalist methods and repeatedly repose the possibilities of revolutionary ruptures that capital can not handle and which lead to its replacement.

Carrying out such analyses requires study that goes well beyond what is provided in this chapter. First, it requires applying to capitalist strategies in the sphere of reproduction the same kind of close, analytical examination that Marx brought to production in chapters 7, 12-15, that is to say where he examined the basic outlines of the labor process (Chapter 7), some forms of co-operation (chapter 13), the division of labor in industry (Chapter 14) and the dynamics of technological change (in Chapter 15). We need to replicate this kind of analysis in all of the spheres of reproduction. Second, beyond such basic analytical theorizing, we need to examine all those concrete forms of such relationships that currently obtain and are relevant to our struggles, not just as "examples" to illustrate the theory, but as contributions to our understanding of those struggles and as one basis of deciding what future directions those struggles should take. Third, as the last point might suggest, our point of departure for such studies can be theoretical but current struggles should provide focus to our efforts because, as Marx said "the point is not to understand the world but to change it."

This is obviously not the place to undertake any systematic investigation of the sort outlined above, but just to illustrate a bit, let's recall the application of Marx's analysis of the labor process to the sphere of reproduction. In his analysis there were three elements: the workers, their tools and the raw materials upon which they worked to fabricate commodities. In the case of reproduction where the commodity being fabricated is labor power how are we to understand these elements? The workers include all kinds of people beginning with housewives and children-in-school and continuing through waged workers on and off the job, prostitutes, teachers, and so on. The tools would include everything used by those people to produce and reproduce labor power: kitchen and dining equipment, washing machines, irons, beds, computers, school books, training manuals, self-help books, playgrounds, footballs, condoms & sex paraphernalia, music cd's, film DVD's and so on. And the raw materials? Those are the people themselves: from ovulation, fertilization and conception through children to adults. As in Marx's very enlightenment view where the active, willing worker uses tools to transform passive, will-less, nature, the labor process that produces and reproduces labor power treats human beings as objects to be created and shaped according to the needs of capital. Procreation, child rearing, education and training are not shared activities of socially interactive human beings, they are alienated relations of power as some people are used to craft other people into useful tools of capitalist production and social control.

He'd make his moves with no regard for feeling she might have 'til in resistance she would claim the headache everyone laughs at.

And it's Yes. No. Yes. No. Sorry I got a headache.

Oh for the day when women get free. Oh for the day when men accept it. No more shames No more games Just yes, yes, yes!

Women's liberation came along said men can't have all thesay of if and how and where and when at the end of a weary day.

For woman wants her fair share too in pleasure as in pay but he still wants to be the boss so he turns away.

With No. Yes. No. Yes. Damn it , woman, I've got a headache.

Oh for the day when women get free. Oh for the day when men accept it. No more shames No more games Just yes, yes, yes!

Carol Hanisch, Fight on sisters... and other songs for liberation,1978?.

Once we understand this we can see how so many of the nasty aspects of the patriarchal dimension of capitalist reproduction have the character that they do. Feminists have for years critized such things as the imposition of gender roles wherein, for example, in the absence of women's struggles, men dominate women sexually, e.g., they satify their desires for control and sexual release (orgasm) with no regard to the pleasure, or lack of it, experienced by women. One of the discoveries by feminists in the 1970s was how few of their mothers ever experienced any real pleasure in sex and mostly viewed it as an onerous obligation - sometimes tolerated and sometimes rejected (via appeals to fatigue, headache or nervous breakdown). Thus the labor process of reproduction involves dehumanization of people as they become passive, will-less objects of manipulation, and, of course, the alienation of those who are doing the manipulating because their manipulation prevents them from having any healthy human contact with those they are manipulating. The particular concrete forms of such dehumanization and alienation naturally vary with the many, many different labor processes included in the sphere of reproduction.

In chapters 23 through 25 as Marx distinguishes between simple and expanded reproduction, his exposition is largely verbal. In Volume II of Capital, however, he reworks the French economiste Francois Quesnay's Tableau Economique to both model the requirements of reproduction and to distinguish between simple and expanded reproduction. Quesnay, the main theorist of the "Physiocrat" school of economics in the 18th Century, developed his Tableau to trace/demonstrate the interlinkages of the economy and to argue how, in his view, all expansion could be traced back to the work of farmers on the land - the only truly productive workers.

Like Adam Smith before him, Marx found Quesnay's approach to analyzing the "circular flows" of the economy useful, while disagreeing with his interpretation, especially his privileging of land/farming as the unique source of value. So, in Volume II of Capital, Marx suggests his own formulation of those flows, first for simple reproduction and then for expanded reproduction. In what follows I will only sketch his analysis of simple reproduction, holding a discussion of his parallel treatment of expanded reproduction over for chapter 25 that deals with that subject.

Marx's analysis breaks the economy down into two sectors, or "departments". All those circuits of industrial capital that produce the means of production are regrouped, or aggregated, into "Department I"; all those circuits of industrial capital that produce the means of subistence are aggegated into "Department II." Using his value theory, the value of the output of each department can then be represented by C+V+S such that we have:

Now, in order for the present organization of capitalist society - represented above - to reproduce itself, certain conditions must be met. First, Department I must produce enough of the means of production to replace those used up in its own activities plus enough of the means of production to replace those used up in the activities of Department II. Second, Department II must produce enough of the means of subsistence to sustain/reproduce the labor power employed in its own activities, plus enough means of subsistence to sustain/reproduce the labor power employed in Department I. Third, given the assumption that none of the surplus value is reinvested, but all is consumed by the capitalists, Department II must also produce enough consumer goods to sustain the capitalists of both departments. These conditions can be represented in the following manner:

If, and only if, these conditions are met can simple reproduction take place, i.e., can the system reproduce itself from period to period.

In the language of Chapter 23, what this says is simply that not only must capital organize its productive activities to maintain its raw materials, tools, machines at the current level of effectiveness, but it must also make sure that enough food, clothing, housing, etc. are produced to make possible the reproduction of the current number (and effectiveness) of workers. Meeting these requirements necessitates an appropriate balance between the activities of the two departments; failure to achieve that balance creates a crisis in the ability of the system to reproduce itself. Indeed, some Marxists have leaned heavily on these schemes in advancing the thesis that capitalist crises originate in such "disproportionalities."

For our purposes, this scheme of simple reproduction is useful merely to highlight the necessity for capital to organize itself to guarantee not only the means of production it uses to put people to work, but also the necessity for it to meet the needs of those people in so far as those needs result in the reproduction of them and their labor power.

We should note in passing a couple of the limits of this schema: first, there is no discussion of the labor processes in either Department, only their outcomes in terms of value. Nor is there any discussion of the labor processes of converting the output into functioning components of on-going production, neither the processes of replacing depreciated physical capital, nor the processes of maintaining labor power. These processes, and the parallels between them, are touched on in Chapter 23 but not in these schemas. Second, as Marx will make clear in Chapter 25, the ability of capital to keep its currently employed workers working (at profitable wages) also requires that it produce and reproduce what he calls the "reserve army" of the unemployed - unemployed workers whose demands for jobs and wages keep pressure on those with jobs to accept wages and working conditions that they might refuse in the absence of such pressure. Now what this is true whether we are talking about expanded reproduction (chapter 25) or simple reproduction (chapter 23), in both cases capital must reproduce not only those who are waged, but also those who are unwaged. Therefore, the output of the means of subsistence in Department II destined for the working class, i.e., V1 + V2 must be sufficient to feed, cloth etc. (to greatly varying degrees, of course) not only the waged but also the unwaged. But nowhere is this explicit in the schema. I will return to this in my discussion of Chapter 25.

Marx insists, pp. 718 - 719, on how both capitalits and their "ideologists", the political economists, have differentiated between working class consumption necessary to capital and any consumption that goes beyond that and only benefits the workers themselves. He sites James Mill, David Ricardo and Thomas Malthus as all considering any working class consumption over and above what capital requires as "unproductive." Their concepts of what constitutes "productive" vs "unproductive" consumption, whether of the means of subsistence or of capital itself, frankly express the view point of capital itself.

Adam Smith had insisted in distinguishing between the unproductive use of money, e.g., rich landlords hiring large numbers of retainers, and the productive use of money as capital, i.e., hiring workers who produced products upon which a profit could be earned. Marx, in Volume III of Capital retained a similar distinction between investments of money in mere mercantile buying and selling vs investments in industrial production.

Here in this discussion of working class consumption Marx accepts the economists' useage, even embracing Thomas Malthus' assertion (in footnote 12, p. 719) that workers' consumption is not even productive to themselves:

Malthus: "The workman . . . is a productive consumer to the person who employs him, and to the state, but not, strictly speaking, to himself." Marx: "In reality, the individual consumption of the worker is unproductive even from his own point of view, for it simply reproduces the needy individual . . . "

However, in the very next sentence after the one quoted above, Marx also says "Even its [the working class'] individual consumption is, within limits, a mere aspect of the process of capital's reproduction." The caveat "within limits" refers, of course, to the degree to which workers are able to achieve some degree of life autnomous from capital over and beyond the simple reproduction of their labor power. This was the worry of the capitalists and of their economists: they knew that in periods of upturn and tight labor markets workers were sometimes able to achieve increases in wages from which they alone benefited, at the expense of the capitalists. Marx was well aware of this phenomenon, not only because the economists that he read were aware, but because such increases in wages were occurring around him during upswings in the business cycle and because there was debate among working class strategists about the importance of struggles that won such gains. Marx himself argued against those who thought that such struggles were a waste of time because downturns in the business cycle and rising unemployment would eventually hammer wages back down.

The important point here, I think, has nothing to do with the periodic fluctuations in the wage, and hence variations in the degree to which working class consumption became "unproductive" for their employers, but rather the simple fact that such consumption could, and has, occurred and that therefore, there is something like a counter-concept of "productivity" from our (the workers') point of view! To the degree that we are able to consume in ways that escape or go beyond simply reproducing our labor power, that consumption is "productive" from our point of view, even if "unproductive" from the point of view of capital. I am speaking, obviously, of what I have elsewhere referred to as "self-valorization".

Now, as I have also argued elsewhere, such terms as "productive", "unproductive", "self-valorization", as well as their roots (production, valorization) and even "consumption" are all terms derived from the vocabulary of capital, even if we use them in an inverse sense to express our own point of view. We do better, I think, to seek out, and use, a vocabulary untainted by such vile origins and associations. Capital may find it convenient to reduce our various life activities to the single category of "consumption" on the one hand, and to that of "production" etc. on the other hand, but we will find it more enlightening to break out of such reductionism and to contemplate our activities as irreducible and complex variety.

When we prepare food, serve food and eat food, especially in a social setting, we are not merely "consuming" - something the fast-food industry is organized to make quick and efficient, from capital's point of view. On the contrary, we can be engaged in a creative search for (as the ancient Chinese said) the harmonious combination of tastes, shapes, smells, colors, and textures; we can be engaged in the preparation of gifts for our friends and/or families, (in the language of Marx's 1844 Manuscripts) gifts of ourselves objectified in our dishes ; we can be engaged in cooperation and collaboration in that preparation, mutual aid (in the language of Kropotkin); in eating together we can be sharing the pleasures of food laced with love and the benefits of cooperation; our mealtimes can be moments of the sharing of our lives through conversation, stories, body language and facial expressions; eating together may have collective spiritual significance, and so on, and so forth. Let not the economist's reductionism (which is capital's) guide our language and our lives, but rather let us learn from poets and artists how to talk about and appreciate all the dimensions of every human experience, both individual and social.

The chapter largely comes to an end with a discussion of how the reproduction of workers and their labor power must necessarily include "the transmission and accumulation of skills [especially] from one generation to another." (p. 719) This was already touched upon in chapter 6 on the buying and selling of labor power but here Marx takes the opportunity to illustrate how acutely aware capitalists are of this necessity. He quotes, at some length from one Edmund Potter who argues against allowing cotton mill workers to emmigrate away from English mills during the downturn in employment brought on by the cotton famine caused by the American Civil War. In his arguments he emphasizes that such workers "are the mental and trained power which cannot be replaced for a generation." Better than allowing them to emmigrate, Potter argues, for the state to spend the money necessary to force them locally to accept "some occupation or labour". While, in response, the Times of London mocks Mr. Potter's proposal to "sustain them by alms" and, most likely, "to keep down their discontent by force", it too worries about the loss of skill due to unemployment - "Human machinery will rust under inaction, oil and rub it as you may." - and the possibilities of such workers running "amuck in our great towns."

Over time, the protests of workers against the immiseration brought on by increases in unemployment and the kinds of concerns of capital laid out above led to increasing state intervention in the "the transmission and accumulation of skills [especially] from one generation to another." Whereas from pre-capitalist times well into the capitalist epoch, the transmission of skills was primarily accomplished by institutions such as apprenticeships, the state would gradually become more and more involved in the training of workers for jobs. As workers fought for an achieved (at least to some degree) the exclusion of child labor, the state would, as discussed in commentary on earlier chapters) reincarcerate them in schools of various sorts, schools that the state, generally under the influence of business and its needs, structure as to primarily produce, not enlightenment or the knowledge and skills needed for citizenship and political participation, but labor power of various sorts. There would also, of course, be private schools but in the United States widespread public schooling would become the norm in the 20th Century. Today part of the crisis of the school brought on by both student struggles and capitalist efforts to reoganize its labor force for better control has been a fierce debate over the relative role of private vs public schools. In that debate capitalists have sought to frame the debate, not surprisingly, primarily in terms of which kind of school, private or public, can best prepare young people for the labor market. That is a framing that obviously seeks to exclude other questions that we might well consider more important: such as which kind of school, if either, provides a better terrain for fighting to liberate learning from its subordination to "skill transmission" and the capitalist world of work?

For some commentary on Francois Quesnay and his Tableau Economique you might look at my notes on the physiocrats (together with the links included in those notes) written up for my course on The History of Economic Thought, Eco 368.

You can examine Marx's treatment of simple reproduction in Volume II of Capital by going to the four sections covering Chapter 20 at the Marx-Engels Archive Webpage for Volume II.

My previous remarks on the need for new language to think about, and talk about, post-capitalist relationships mainly concerned "labor" and "work". Those remarks can be found in an essay titled "Work is Still the Central Issue!" (1999).

productive consumption individual consumption unproductive consumption skill transmission

1. What is the key assumption that Marx makes that differentiates his concept of simple reproduction from his concept of expanded reproduction?

2. Which of the four forms of alienation that Marx analyses in the 1844 Manuscripts shows up in this chapter?

3. In what ways is the "individual consumption of the worker" an integral and necessary part of capitalism's self-reproduction?

4. To what degree might you argue that Marx's comment that capitalists can "safely leave" individual consumption to the workers still true? To what degree, and in what ways, is it no longer true?

5. Why do you think Marx divides the economy into the two "departments" that he does in his reproduction schemas? Why not more departments, say, the way Leontief's "input-output" tables are constructed with up to a 100 sectors?

6. According to the schema of simple reproduction what criteria must be met for reproduction to be succssful? If you presented this schema to mainstream economists as a two-sector growth model, what forces do you think they would evoke as the means by which that criteria would normally be met?

7. To what degree, and in what way does Marx agree with the classical economists that working class consumption that goes beyond the reproduction of the workers' ability to work is "unproductive"?

8. The commentary offers some alternative ways of talking about "consumption". Suggest some alternative vocabulary for talking about the kinds of things that in capital are regrouped under the rubric "production."

9. How does an elementary and secondary school education differ from more traditional forms of training such as apprenticeships?

10. To what degree do you think elementary and secondary school education actually involves the "transmission of skills"? If you think that degree is not very high, then what do you think is/are the primary purpose(s) of those levels of education in contemporary society?

author: Joseph Lee
title: From the farm to your door: How our global food system exploits workers
content:
Like many big cities, New York teems with delivery workers who bring takeout, groceries, and any number of other things to anyone with a cellphone. They work at all hours and in all conditions, often without job security, health insurance, or even 

access to safe restrooms

. They are often hit by cars, assaulted, or robbed. Many of them are Indigenous people from Guatemala and Mexico who left home to escape violence and the impacts of climate change.




The worst impacts of that global crisis 

add to the risks

 those 

workers face

.




“When the city is hit with with massive snowstorms, floodings, or the recent smoke fires, many deliveristas are the ones who are on the front lines doing this work and responding to the climate crisis in order to take care of New Yorkers,” said Ligia Guallpa, who is Kichwa and the co-founder and executive director of the Worker’s Justice Project and Los Deliveristas Unidos. The organization organizes app-based delivery workers and advocates on their behalf. “But the reality is that often they cannot even take care of themselves.”




A report released Monday says that exploitation is deeply embedded in the global food system, leaving many of the 1.4 billion people who produce, process, distribute, and deliver food poorly paid, 

inadequately protected

, and vulnerable to abuse. Climate change and a global affordability crisis are intensifying those pressures, according to the International Panel of Experts on Sustainable Food Systems, or IPES-Food, an international food policy research organization.




Although the document does not specifically focus on Indigenous peoples, it finds that many of the forces driving that exploitation have roots in the colonialism, land dispossession, forced labor, and racialized labor systems that have long harmed Indigenous communities worldwide. 




“Here we are in the United States, a country that’s founded on stealing land and the import of enslaved people to be able to make agriculture and agricultural labor possible and cheap,” said Raj Patel, an IPES-Food expert and a professor at the University of Texas at Austin. “And the legacy of that is still with us.”




The report notes that Indigenous peoples remain 

particularly vulnerable to displacement

, and pressures from industrial agriculture and climate change that can undermine traditional livelihoods. For people who have been 

forced off their land

 and are disconnected from those livelihoods, exploitative, low-paying work is often the only option. 




“If you put yourself in a situation of a woman who needs to feed her children, they can go to any extreme,” said Teresa Chemosop, who is Ogiek from Mount Elgon, Kenya, and the coordinator for the East Africa Indigenous Women-Led Assembly, which advocates for Indigenous women across the region. 










Read Next




























The people who feed America are going hungry













Ayurella Horn-Muller

 



















Chemosop said that Indigenous workers face severe discrimination and abuse, such as being compared to baboons and not being given utensils to eat with while working. That’s on top of low wages and long, difficult hours. 




Indigenous and intergenerational 

agricultural knowledge

 is routinely minimized or dismissed as “unskilled,” the report notes, obscuring valuable expertise and helping to justify lower wages. That knowledge, which often goes back millenia, includes skills like cultivating plant medicines and drought-resistant crops. The authors call for formally recognizing that expertise alongside broader efforts to strengthen worker rights and protections.




The people who keep the global food system running do far more than grow and harvest food. They distribute it to markets and restaurants, deliver it to homes and offices, and provide care work like cooking and feeding families, often in seasonal or subcontracted jobs. Between 60 and 80 percent of food workers are informally employed — a higher share than in any other industry — and they earn about half as much as those with conventional employment. About 30 percent of food system workers, or more than 400 million people, 

earn less than a living wage

. 




An estimated 2.1 million people in agriculture work under forced-labor conditions, the report estimates. Migrants, who account for about a quarter of all farmworkers worldwide, are three times as likely to experience such conditions and are more likely than their peers to die on the job.




Despite their importance in feeding the world, these workers do not receive the respect or protection other essential workers enjoy. Guallpa pointed to the pandemic, when nurses and doctors were widely praised even as food service workers remained largely anonymous. “Immigrant workers, who do some of the most dangerous, dirtiest jobs, often go unseen and often are invisibilized,” she said.




The report argues that valuing food work in all its forms, from the field to the table, is just one part of building a more just system. It also calls for building worker power, establishing and sustaining workplace protections, ensuring equal rights for migrant workers, and reining in corporate power. And it makes clear that there is a false choice between affordability and worker rights, arguing that better working conditions do not have to mean higher food prices.




“We can manage all of this, and we will have to manage all of this because climate change isn’t getting better,” Patel said. “But we have choices about protecting workers, and we’re choosing not to do any of those things.”




In New York, Los Deliveristas Unidos’ organizing provides a glimpse of what workers can accomplish. It has established mutual aid chat groups and helped win minimum wages and 

other protections

. “It is possible to give gig workers or independent contractors the ability to earn better pay, to ensure that workers have better working conditions. It is possible to regulate multi-billion-dollar corporations,” Guallpa said. “There’s a lot more to do, but I think it can be applied in every city.”




This story was originally published by 

Grist
