author: Andrea DiP
title: Há três anos os palestinos pagam pelo 7 de outubro
content:
Quis o destino que eu estivesse na Cisjordânia neste 07 de outubro, e que essa coluna fosse publicada no exato dia em que, 

3 anos atrás, o ataque terrorista do Hamas que resultou na morte de cerca 1000 pessoas entre civis e militares, deu início a um massacre cometido pelo 

Estado de Israel

 que, até agora, somente na 

Faixa de Gaza, já matou mais de 75 mil e feriu mais de 170 mil palestinos. 




Eu sei que o Brasil pega fogo neste momento e é difícil falar em outra coisa ou pensar em um povo que está tão longe geograficamente. Mas talvez nós possamos aprender uma coisa ou duas sobre resistência e resiliência

 com um povo que vem sendo oprimido, colonizado e sofre tentativas reiteradas de apagamento há mais de 100 anos. 




Meus avós são sobreviventes do Holocausto. Minha avó polonesa e meu avô romeno passaram por campos de concentração e tinham números tatuados neles. Ainda jovens migraram para o Brasil, onde se conheceram e formaram família. E é também por respeito a essa história que não posso me calar diante de um genocídio étnico que acontece 

live stream

 nos celulares na palma de nossas mãos. 




Nos últimos dias estive rodando pela Cisjordânia, visitando comunidades palestinas que estão sendo despejadas, torturad

as, roubadas e dizimadas por milícias israelenses formadas por colonos e por militares.

 A Cisjordânia é um território palestino que fica no Oriente Médio, situado na margem ocidental do rio Jordão, entre Israel e a Jordânia. É dividida em três zonas administrativas – zonas A, B e C –  segundo os Acordos de Oslo, assinados na década de 1990, que previam transferir gradualmente o controle do território para a Autoridade Palestina. A área teoricamente estaria sob controle total da Palestina. A área B teria um controle misto entre Israel e Palestina e a área C, cerca de 60% da Cisjordânia, está sob controle israelense total, tanto para administração civil quanto para segurança. 




Mas atualmente esses contornos estão cada vez mais borrados, com colonos israelenses tomando cada vez mais áreas.




Tudo isso ainda vai virar reportagem e indico o Pauta Pública desta sexta-feira (09/10) com o diretor geral do Centro de Assistência Jurídica e Direitos Humanos de Jerusalém (JLAC) e membro do Conselho de Comissários da Comissão Independente de Direitos Humanos da Palestina (ICHR), Issam Aruri, que traz uma verdadeira aula sobre o conflito na região. 




Mas queria contar aqui na coluna uma

 

das histórias que mais me marcou até agora: A de uma mulher de 67 anos, moradora de um vilarejo em Masafer Yatta

, que fica nas colinas ao sul da cidade de Hebrom, cerca de 70km ao sul de Ramallah – capital administrativa da Cisjordânia. Não vou revelar seu nome por motivos óbvios. Mas 

sua vila está totalmente cercada por

 

assentamentos israelenses, que tentam a custo de barbárie expulsar os palestinos que estão ali há dezenas de gerações, vivendo da colheita de azeitonas e do pastoreio de ovelhas e cabras. 




Sua vila não tem água encanada nem luz. Se vê apenas pedras, areia, pequenas casas e barracões. Os cabos de energia passam por cima da comunidade, de um lado a outro, para os assentamentos israelenses, mas os palestinos não podem usar. Foi instalado um portão na estrada, que pode ser fechado pelos soldados a qualquer momento e por tempo indeterminado, impedindo os moradores de entrar ou sair, mesmo que em emergência médica.

 Essa é uma prática bastante comum na região. Até mesmo ruas dentro de comunidades são fechadas indiscriminadamente pelas forças israelenses. 




“Foi aqui que um colono israelense matou meu filho”. A senhora aponta para um ponto do centro de convivência, que já foi destruído e reconstruído várias vezes e que abriga o único banheiro disponível para a comunidade.

 As casas tinham banheiro. Mas eles foram destruídos ou absurdamente declarados como zonas militares, tornando-se inacessíveis aos moradores. Sua filha mora em uma casa há poucos metros dali e não pode usar o próprio banheiro nem construir outro sem permissão. Mais: o celeiro, que fica no quintal da casa, foi declarado “zona militar” e trancado, então a família não pode levar os animais para o pasto ou mesmo chegar perto do pequeno barracão. O exército israelense passa por lá uma vez na semana (quando muito) para alimentar as ovelhas e cabras, que estão obviamente morrendo paulatinamente. 




“Um colono entrou na comunidade e atirou na cabeça do meu filho. Meu neto, aquele ali  – aponta para um gurizinho de uns 3 anos – estava no colo dele. Entrou e atirou. Assim. Na frente de todo mundo. Chamamos a polícia que veio, levou o corpo e não puniu o colono. Alguns dias depois ele estava caminhando por aqui normalmente e eu perguntei: ‘Por que você matou o meu filho’? Ele me empurrou ali, eu caí de cabeça em uma pedra e desmaiei. O portão estava fechado e só pude ser levada ao hospital dias depois. Sofri uma concussão e perdi a visão. Quebrei ossos do corpo. Mas nenhuma dor foi igual a de não poder enterrar meu filho.

 A polícia levou o corpo e não nos deixou velar ou enterrar”, contou. Ela enxugava os olhos no hijab preto, que contornava seu rosto e se fundia ao vestido também preto. Uma mãe em luto há três anos.




Não faltam provas. 

Todas as comunidades que visitei me mostraram dezenas de vídeos de colonos invadindo, cortando as oliveiras centenárias, subindo à noite nos telhados das casas batendo os pés e cantando músicas, ameaçando botar fogo, e todo o tipo de humilhações e torturas inimagináveis.

 Em todas as vilas, ouvi que os moradores fazem turnos durante a noite, para que não morram queimados enquanto dormem. 




As violações também são amplamente registradas por organizações de direitos humanos na região. Eu vi as árvores cortadas. Eu vi os animais mortos. Eu fiquei do lado de fora dos portões e levei 4 horas para atravessar poucos quilômetros, porque no caminho havia pontos de checagem com soldados pesadamente armados que me fizeram descer do carro, mostrar meus documentos e passar minha bolsa em detectores. 

Eu visitei uma escola de crianças palestinas que era proibida de pôr o lixo pra fora e tinha que manter todo ele dentro das classes – não no pátio, dentro das salas – por semanas. 




Enquanto caminhava por um mercado árabe a céu aberto em Hebrom e ouvia histórias de porque os corredores estreitos haviam sido cobertos por grades – para evitar que pedras fossem jogadas do alto, 

fui cercada, junto a colegas jornalistas e guias palestinos, por um grupo de soldados israelenses usando roupas camufladas e rosto coberto, mais novos que meu filho. Um deles apontou sua metralhadora para nós. 




Ouvi de moradores que a Cisjordânia está virando Gaza. Mas também ouvi que eles não pretendem ir a lugar nenhum, que ali é sua terra há dezenas de gerações, que eles têm resistido.

 Que uma hora esse massacre vai ter que acabar. “O que eles vão fazer? Matar 7 milhões de nós? Nós não temos para onde ir, aqui é nossa casa”, me disse um senhor, diante das suas oliveiras centenárias queimadas por colonos israelenses.




Há três anos a Palestina é punida pelo 7 de outubro. Todos os dias. Mas teve uma frase que ouvi de uma mulher que conheci pelo caminho que acho que serve pra nós também, nesse momento da nossa história: 




“O mais difícil é não se tornar um monstro. Não desejar a morte deles como eles desejam as nossas. Enquanto eles passam com tanques sobre bebês em Gaza, eu quero o bem das crianças deles. Esse é um desafio e um exercício diário. Que a indignação nos fortaleça em nossa resistência, mas que não nos torne monstros”.

author: Steven Methven
title: How Labour Put Big Property Above Camden’s Local Residents
content:
A little more than a week before Thursday’s crucial byelection in the London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras, prime minister Andy Burnham laid out 

a radical social and economic programme

 at Labour’s party conference in Liverpool. If the ideas were big, the shift in Labour’s direction was even bigger. Words not heard in years peppered the speech: 

the working class

, 

public control

, and apologies for political failures. Beginning with a curt acknowledgement that former prime minister Keir Starmer won a general election he could hardly lose, Burnham spent the rest of his speech slamming the door on Starmerism. 




Not in Holborn and St Pancras, though, Starmer’s old parliamentary seat.




Labour’s candidate in the byelection, Sagal Abdi-Wali, has been 

a fixture of Camden council

 (the London borough in which the constituency falls) since the 2022 local elections. She quickly rose to prominence, appointed cabinet member for the council’s Better Homes programme in 2024, before being voted council leader in May this year.




But sources close to Camden council have described it as a stronghold of the Labour right. Characterised by purges of dissenters, cosiness to corporate interests and a lack of vision, the Labour group running the council, Novara Media was told, is ground-zero for Starmerism. 




That empty philosophy is epitomised in the council’s approach to housing, a topic – especially in the form of social housing – 

at the heart of Burnham’s national plans

. While the new prime minister has promised a generational transformation in building council home capacity, Camden council has repeatedly sided with wealthy corporate developers when they’ve requested massive cuts to promised affordable and social housing allotments in new developments. Described as a “weak touch” by one source, another was more blunt: “They are fucking aroused by private developers.”




One example is the redevelopment of the O2 centre on north-west London’s Finchley Road. The three-phase plans, drawn up by Landsec, Britain’s largest commercial property developer, were originally approved by the council in 2023. Involving the demolition of an existing shopping centre, cinema and leisure centre, Landsec promised that 570 of the 1,796 new flats would be a mix of social and affordable housing. At a meeting last month, Camden council 

approved an enormous reduction

: now, just 330 flats will meet those criteria, a drop from 32% to 18%. In the first phase of the construction, the slash has been even deeper, with 

barely 15%

 of the total being classed as affordable. (A council spokesperson told Novara Media that the permission granted includes 20% affordable housing across the whole site, and that the development also supports the delivery of other community benefits, including funding for step-free access at West Hampstead Station.)




If the prime minister is to be believed, neoliberalism is on its way out of Burnham’s Britain. But in Camden, it appears in rosy health.




In the O2 centre case, Landsec took advantage of a Starmerite innovation. In October last year, then-housing secretary and 

self-proclaimed Starmer-loyalist

 Steve Reed (since returned to the backbenches) announced a two-year window in which developers who promised a 20%, rather than the previous 35%, affordable housing quota 

would have their plans fast-tracked

. This didn’t require Camden to accept Landsec’s changes. But the council rolled over anyway. 




The council’s approach to private development has also raised questions over future social housing. Approved in January, the Camley Street development near King’s Cross currently promises 401 new homes of which 

almost half will be for social rents

. History suggests this too may be revised downwards before the first completions – and several longstanding businesses have already been 

forced out, they say without council support

 (the council 

denied this

). In the constituency’s northern-most area, the Labour stronghold of Kentish Town, 

residents were perturbed

 by the permission granted for the construction of a £1bn Film Quarter. Promising 11 purpose-built sound stages, production suites and workspaces, developer Yoo Capital has also committed to 

243 affordable homes

 – 50% of the sites’ planned 485 flats. Asked in a recent profile whether the developer could be trusted not to slash those figures, Abdi-Wali refused to consider that highly-plausible possibility. “I don’t want to talk like that,” 

she said

. “We’re in a place now where it’s 50% affordable housing – secured. We want to make sure they do that. Having conversations about ‘what if they do this or that’ isn’t helpful.”




Affordable housing means rents capped at 80% of market value – a price still out of reach for most in a borough where the average monthly private rent is 

over £2,800

. What matters in Holborn and St Pancras (and apparently to Burnham too) are secure social rents. Camden’s council’s housing waiting list now stands at over 8,000 individuals and families desperate for homes in an already densely populated borough. The National Housing Federation has said that, at current rates, it would take 

82 years to clear the backlog

. A baby born today might be more likely to find herself in a casket, having expired from old age, before being housed in Camden. And yet in 2025-26, the borough completed 

just 56 social rent homes

, amongst the lowest number in London.




Growing Camden’s housing stock is funded through the council’s Community Investment Programme (CIP), a £2.3bn fund that claims to have delivered 1,780 new homes, 70% of them affordable, since CIP’s inception in 2010. 

Just 677 homes for social rent

 have been completed. That figure, however, doesn’t take into account reductions in the borough’s social housing stock through demolition. When subtracted, that figure could easily halve. Take, for example, a 

contested development at One Museum Street

 in Holborn, approved in 2023. That plan promised just 11 social rents out of 44 new homes (and space for 1,600 office workers). But to make way for it, 

councillors at the time

 reported that 26 “perfectly sound homes” would be destroyed – having been allowed to go to ruin. Not a social housing record to boast about, and yet Abdi-Wali was 

doing just that

 last week with housing secretary Angela Rayner.




Camden’s housing shortages – the result of a decade and half, some might argue, of mismanagement by the Labour-led council – could be having very real social effects. The borough is depopulating. In 2025, Camden’s population 

shrank by 1.8%

, the largest decrease of any area in England and Wales apart from the Isles of Scilly. Since 2019, 

30% fewer children

 have been born in Camden. And of the children who do live in the borough, around 

40% live in poverty

 after housing costs.




Those lucky enough to have a council home in Camden may also be unlucky enough to have to deal with its repairs service. In November 2024, six months after Abdi-Wali took responsibility for Camden’s housing stock, the independent housing ombudsman released 

a damning report

 on her department. It found maladministration in 90% of complaints involving repairs (the national average is 73%). The scope of the report was, however, long, covering complaints raised by tenants from before Abdi-Wali’s cabinet position. While in post, 

Abdi-Wali reduced the repairs backlog

 from over 10,000 to 5,600, though, still under her tenure, it 

grew once more in 2025

. 




Still, issues abound. Novara Media has been told of unchecked cases of black mould, damp, and intermittent heating. Elderly and arthritic tenants have been left in the cold, 

their heaters torn off the walls by cowboy contractors

. In May last year, after a 15-year stint, Labour councillor Awale Olad resigned his position. In addition to standing alone on Gaza in the party’s group, he blamed the overwhelming neglect of tenants’ repairs for his departure. “I find myself engaged in a sort of tragic farce,” 

he wrote

, “endlessly pursuing the same missed repair appointments, often dealing with miserable residents at the end of their tether.” At one point, he added, “I wrote to a senior officer that ‘I was losing the will to live’.”




A source close to the council told Novara Media that the state of affairs is due to a lack of ideas, commitment and enthusiasm for making lives better amongst the Labour group. And certainly, previous Labour councillors appear to have had their eyes on a different prize: parliament. 




The 2024 general election saw three recent councillors elevated from the then-prime minister’s seat to parliament. Georgia Gould, daughter of Tony Blair adviser Philip Gould and who’s 

reported to count Alastair Campbell as her mentor

, was handed the Labour-stronghold of Queen’s Park and Maida Vale. Lloyd Hatton, who served just two years as a councillor before being selected by Labour in South Dorset, won by barely 1,000 votes. Finally, there’s Danny Beales. Elected a Camden councillor in 2014, Beales was selected to fight for Boris Johnson’s recently-resigned Uxbridge and South Ruislip in a late 2022 by-election. He lost, but won it for Starmer’s Labour in 2024 with the slightest margin: a little under 600 seats.




The Labour council, it’s said, has for years adopted what’s been called 

Camden’s “north sea oil” approach to development

. According to that strategy, Camden should leverage the wealth of its land via corporate developers in order to plug the holes in its budget. Drill, baby, drill – except it’s not spurts of oil rising into the sky, but blocks of glass and steel encasing foreign-owned luxury flats (thought to be 

worth several billions

 in Camden alone). 




That north sea oil approach is often blamed for Camden Labour’s neglect of its housing stock. Speaking at an event organised by then-London Assembly member Zoë Garbett (now Green mayor for Hackney) in February this year, 

one Camden council home resident said

: “The land under our homes is viewed as an asset too valuable for working-class people to live on.” A source close to Camden council concurred, accusing the leadership of allowing homes to go into disrepair, neglecting them to the point of irreparability, then taking the opportunity to sell. 




Private home owners in Camden have also struggled to get help from the borough’s Labour figures when things go wrong. In 2019, a seven-flat new build was completed at 53 Agar Grove in Camden Town. Dan Bruce bought his first home in the block, telling Novara Media he was “dead excited” to have the keys to a place of his own. But within days of moving in, water began to enter the apartment from its terrace. The excavation that followed revealed further shoddiness: structural cracking in the brickwork. 




There began, for Bruce and two of his neighbours, an almost decade-long process of trying to get justice from the developers and the insurers, while fearing the potentially imminent collapse of the building. After a period in which it looked like then-MP Starmer might come to the rescue, nothing happened. Abdi-Wali, in her earlier role as Camden council’s housing lead, also did not reply to Bruce’s letters. And when Bruce tried to organise a housing hustings ahead of this week’s byelection, the Labour candidate declined an invitation to attend.




Bruce, following the dream, paid his life savings for a flat that may well be worthless. Others, less fortunate, depend, if they’re lucky, on Camden council for a roof over their heads. Those even worse off languish on a list it’ll take a generation to clear. Meanwhile, corporations have grown richer on human misery and hope in this borough. Not all of that is Sagal Abdi-Wali’s individual fault. But neither, Novara was told, has she used her powers to move the dial. 




Asked for comment on Novara Media’s findings, a Camden council spokesperson said: “We want all our residents to be safe and feel safe in their homes. 




“Over the past year, we have resolved more than 6,000 damp and mould cases and responded to 100% of emergency cases within 24 hours. We have robust compliance regimes and are working to ensure all aspects of our council homes are frequently checked so they are as safe as possible. 




“We have built 1,780 new homes so far – 70% of these are affordable and this includes 677 homes at social rent, in addition to intermediate rent homes, assisted living, sheltered housing and temporary housing. The council is also buying back former social housing and changing properties originally intended for private sale into affordable homes where possible. We are building larger and high-quality homes to address overcrowding.”




A Labour spokesperson said: “London has acutely felt the long-term consequences of a national housing crisis. Local authorities including Camden had their budgets slashed by the previous Tory government, forcing them away from preventing homelessness and into crisis management mode. 




“From 2010-2023 the Conservative government cut Camden’s budget by around £200m, along with reducing other public sector budgets, resulting in increasing numbers of people seeking help.




“As a councillor, Sagal Abdi-Wali secured £670m to improve social housing. She also supports the Camley Street brownfield regeneration project, which will deliver 401 new homes where there were previously none, and nearly half will be genuinely affordable. These homes will be made available as social rents for families on Camden’s housing register, and at intermediate rents for key workers. 




“We know there is lots of work to be done, and that Camden needs more homes. As a local champion working with a Labour government, Sagal is best-placed to deliver on that need.”

author: Hassan Alnaser
title: How the Dagalos’ ever tightening hold on power destabilized the RSF project
content:
Daein. Amid the rain showers veiling the city in the first week of August, the fourth August of the war, four-wheel-drive vehicles pull up one after another. Out of them come men who know the villages and firgan that have sent fighters into the Rapid Support Forces, who know the families who have been giving up their sons to war since April 2023.




Abdel Rahim Dagalo sits opposite the Rizeigat tribal omdas who have come from across Darfur’s different localities. Trees ring the meeting place, shielding it from the eyes of drones. He wants one thing from them: to mobilize again.




The tribal leaders begin by talking about the soldiers wounded in battle, about fighters who came home missing limbs, a source who attended the meeting tells Mada Masr. They speak of families who lost their sons, of men who went to the front and never came back, and of communities that, for more than three years, have borne the cost of a war whose military and political decisions they have no hand in.




Then the conversation turns to the men the leadership still wants to send to fight. The omdas say they can no longer persuade their tribes to mobilize as they did in the first years of the war. The war has dragged on, and the losses have piled up. People have begun asking about the sons they sent to the front, about treatment for the wounded, asking what place these communities that gave up their men will hold in the political order being talked about.




At one point, one of the tribal leaders breaks with the language usually upheld in official gatherings. He tells Abdel Rahim that the leadership has left them and their tribes alone to deal with the consequences of the war. He asks him to go with them to the villages and speak to the women and families, to persuade them himself to send their sons.




The remark angers Abdel Rahim. He accuses the tribal leaders of colluding with the military and threatens to send them to Nyala’s Dagris prison. Several cut him off. “You don’t threaten us with prison,” one of the leaders says. The nazir and his deputy step in to contain the situation, and Abdel Rahim Dagalo leaves Daein angry.




But the problem is bigger than one angry meeting, than one rainy day in Daein.




No, that meeting in the first week of August was the culmination of a slowly building tension at the core of the RSF’s political project.




Since the start of the war, over successive battlefronts, successive planning meetings, in the administrative halls that the paramilitary group hastily erected, the RSF had circled around the same issue: how can they mount a formidable challenge to the historic government in Khartoum?




The question couldn’t be merely thought about as a military challenge. For the RSF’s leaders, it was a totalizing question that required a complete recasting of social relations and a transcending of the historical archetype of the rebel group from the state’s margins, sources inside the RSF’s leadership and former advisors who have spoken to Mada Masr over the last six months say.




To pull off such a feat has required a consistent push for greater and greater centralization of power, the sources say.




Two tracks emerged within the tangle the war’s continuation has produced. Abdel Rahim represents the military track — the belief that the answer comes with the sound of Land Cruiser engines, that military power dictates its own terms. He is the one who mobilized fighters from every corner, whose strategy succeeded in securing the RSF political influence.




The other track holds that a parallel civilian authority must be built with enough political capacity to exert negotiating pressure and impose its terms, represented by Hemedti, the younger and most trusted Dagalo brother in the RSF’s leadership. He is the godfather of the RSF project, going back to the days when they were rovers in Nyala’s plains, eating manasees in the shade of Cruisers paid for with ousted-President Omar al-Bashir’s money.




But if centralization could save the project, it could also undo it.




With every passing month, the state casts the “rebels” back into its sacred shadow. One military defection here, one political defection there. Each proving the failure of the RSF’s attempt at centralization — the kind of centralization that Hemedti once broke with the state over, when he 

cast 

himself as the son of the margins against the center, and is now trying to restore in the form of a project whose capital is Nyala. The other, out in the field, has failed to mobilize his fighters or even hold on to the ones still there. Between the meeting rooms and the battlefield, the seeds of further splits are taking root inside the military and political body of this difficult Sudan war — the war that sparked the country’s great fire.




RSF Commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo gives a speech casting himself at the margins of the state against the center, February 2023. Courtesy: Al Jazeera Mubasher




***




The seeds of the RSF project began to germinate during the early days of the war. Inside the group’s closed meetings during the second half of 2023, a term began to circulate: “sovereign system.”




A former political advisor who participated in planning meetings during the first months of the war recalls it as part of a “mental transition” within the leadership. Until then, there had been little room for anything beyond the fighting. The meetings had been about keeping the RSF moving and supplied. But as Darfur’s capitals fell to the RSF one after another, discussions began turning toward what authority in the territory it was taking might look like.




On one of the maps used during those meetings, the advisor says, the boundaries between areas stopped being lines marking the direction of operations and became questions of who could keep the authority in place after the frontlines moved past. The “sovereign system,” according to the advisor, envisioned administration, economy, political decision-making and foreign relations being brought together under a single center.




But the same expansion that raised the ambition of building an administration for the project also meant that the overwhelming majority of resources were still going to the fighting, and thus any dreams of a full state system needed to be deferred. “Control over land was faster than the ability to manage it,” the former advisor says, and the gap between the two became a permanent and stormy subject of debate in the closed meetings.




The RSF nevertheless had ways of holding its ground that did not depend on a fully developed administrative system.




Its strength in Darfur had been built through commanders and local networks that connected the group to communities; relationships that let it recruit and retain territory.




And when the RSF took the step out of Darfur, it looked to replicate this model. That meant finding local intermediaries, understanding who held influence, opening channels with community leaders and turning military gains into a presence that could hold on the ground, the former advisor says.




Gezira was the first test of whether the way the Dagalos had built and exercised power in Darfur could work outside it. And one of the commanders through whom the RSF tried to make that transition was Abu Agla Keikel.




Keikel had a strong social base in eastern Gezira and commanded the Sudan Shield Forces, a local force he founded in 2022 that knew the area intimately. His public profile was associated with the Butana plain and eastern Sudan and had a presence in the region’s civil space.




In August 2023, Keikel came out to pledge allegiance to Hemedti and announce that the Sudan Shield Forces had joined the RSF “in support of the rights of the marginalized.” What came with the group was relationships formed before the war and the knowledge of the social and geographic terrain its forces later operated in.




Four months later, Wad Madani fell to the RSF, and Keikel was central to its capture.




According to three residents of eastern Gezira, Keikel used his strong social presence in the region to recruit local communities and Arab tribes. A community that knows the commander before the fighting, they say, becomes an easier space to reach fighters, unlike a commander that reaches an unfamiliar area through the chain of command. Keikel knew the figures that confer social weight, the locations of influential families and even the rivalries that obstruct deployment.




After Wad Madani’s fall in December, Keikel’s units became part of the advance across Gezira, bringing large swathes of territory under RSF control.




As accusations of widespread abuses by the RSF and Keikel’s forces mounted, the leadership began separating military and administrative responsibilities in the state, according to a former RSF field source in Gezira. In March 2024, the RSF 

established 

a civilian administration led by Gezira locals from political forces aligned with the RSF, which it presented as a response to a security and administrative vacuum and a way to “protect civilians.”




The new arrangement offered a way to manage the growing consequences of the military campaign.“Whenever the political and human rights cost of the Gezira State’s file grew higher, having a local leadership that shoulders the public face became more useful and advantageous for the leadership center,” the former field source says.




Keikel’s military and political usefulness continued to grow, and he carried that influence into the next front. His forces moved into Sennar and took part in the advance toward Singa in mid-2024, extending his reach into a new battlefield and adding another set of men, relationships and local knowledge to the network around him.




In one sense, the experiment worked. Keikel had done exactly what was required. But the Dagalo project wanted two things at once — to expand beyond Darfur and to keep its military and political structure centralized, a former official in the RSF’s operations sector says. A commander who could reproduce the Darfur model on his own, wherever he went, satisfied the first ambition but undercut the second.




According to the former official, this was becoming a source of extreme caution and concern inside the organization. “The war was continuously producing new centers of influence and power,” he says. The RSF needed commanders like Keikel because they could do things the center could not do from a distance. But the longer they remained successful, the more they acquired a power of their own, he adds.




The killing of Abdel Rahman al-Bishi in July 2024 was a turning point. Bishi had emerged as one of the RSF’s most influential commanders in Sennar and Blue Nile. After intelligence on his whereabouts reached the military, its air force 

killed 

him and hundreds of fighters with him, according to a military source who spoke to Mada Masr at the time.




The former RSF operations official says internal accounts connected the flow of information and movements to units associated with Keikel, fueling suspicions within the leadership about information leaks and competing loyalties.




A few months later, Keikel 

defected

. And hundreds of his forces left with him.




That was 10 months after the fall of Wad Madani, a period in which the state had shifted from being a new military front to a space where the RSF was trying to establish durable control.




With his departure, the RSF lost a commander who knew its forces from the inside and understood the local networks through which they moved, recruited and supplied themselves. Gezira’s population, in turn, came to be read as a potential source of alignment with Keikel.




The alliance broke down into conflict, and the RSF 

launched 

a wave of retaliatory violence against communities associated with Keikel. Within the organization, it restricted sensitive information, reduced the circle attending key meetings and concentrated major decisions among fewer people, the former political advisor says.




Former RSF commander and Sudan Shield Forces commander Abu Agla Keikel, along with several of his troops, surrender to the Sudanese military in Jabal Lebitor, Gezira state, October 2024. Courtesy: Dabanga




***




While holding ground outside Darfur was proving difficult, inside it, state capitals had fallen to the RSF in turn as the group steadily consolidated control over the whole region.




By 2024, only one city remained outside RSF control: Fasher. For 18 months, its forces laid siege to the city, held by the military and allied Darfuri armed movements — the final gap in the RSF’s military control of the region.




But Fasher’s importance extended beyond being the last city standing. It was a place where another political reality in Darfur could survive.




The city had long been the administrative center of the region, connecting state institutions to tribal administrations, armed movements and communities shaped by decades of war. The movements that defended it had spent years fighting and negotiating for a place in Sudan’s political system and in Darfur’s own political arrangements.




In the Darfuri armed movements’ calculations, Fasher’s importance stemmed from its position as “the city that embodies the very idea of Darfur, politically, administratively and socially,” according to a figure who previously worked in the political and advisory circle around Minni Arko Minnawi, Darfur’s governor and the Sudan Liberation Movement’s Darfuri head. As long as it remained outside RSF control, he says, Darfur’s post-war arrangements still had a chance of being negotiated through the institutions and political space the movements had spent decades building rather than determined by whoever controlled the region on the ground.




It was that possibility Abdel Rahim wanted closed off. A source who worked in the RSF’s advisory office in Nairobi during the siege says that for the RSF deputy commander, the presence of the military and armed movements in Fasher allowed forces opposed to the RSF to rally around it and sustain an alternative political and social order. Capturing it was not just about breaking the last military defense in the region. It was about preventing a rival authority from taking shape alongside the one the RSF was building, the source says.




Within RSF circles, the source says, the aim was referred to as “reshaping the terms of governance.” The RSF had emerged outside the traditional structure of the armed forces and central state institutions. Abdel Rahim was looking to change the terms that define power itself — so that Khartoum’s institutions would not be the sole route to legitimacy and influence, and Darfur would no longer seek a share of power from the center but would become a center capable of producing power itself, he adds.




Fasher, however, did not fall quickly, and this posed problems for the RSF’s goal.




From a purely military calculation, the fact that the siege stretched on for 18 months created pressure on the RSF’s supply lines.




But the real problem was that the complex logistical tasks of maintaining such a long siege created an opening for middle ranks to begin sharing in decision making.




A former RSF training official in Darfur says that “every passing week without resolution created a confusing new reality for leadership. Ammunition needs multiplied shockingly, fuel required safer alternative supply lines, fighting units needed continuous reorganization and new blood, and military decisions became tied to minute field details impossible to manage from afar.”




The commanders and units holding the axes began making more of the decisions themselves, he says. Field supply officers determined when and how much could be moved, communications officers controlled the flow of information, and reconnaissance and drone teams became part of the daily decisions. The operation rooms around the battlefront were becoming decision-making centers in their own right, according to the former training official.




The official in the RSF operations office says the change was being observed with suspicion inside the central command. “Before Fasher, military rank and proximity to the Dagalo family determined influence and standing within the organization. After long months of siege, field expertise and resilience on the axes forged new stature. A person managing a complex, burning front for months becomes a strong actor participating in shaping and issuing military decisions,” he says.




When Fasher finally fell, the RSF completed its military takeover of Darfur, a takeover that would hand it a territorial fait accompli, something that would transform the group from a militia with strongholds into the ruler of an entire region — for that reason, Abdel Rahim refused to let go of Fasher, even as its military and humanitarian cost mounted, the former advisory office source says.




But the long siege showed that a prolonged war could create commanders whose authority was produced on the battlefield, rather than handed down by the center.




For those who had carried the battle, the victory came with expectations — a place in whatever military and political structure would govern the territory they helped take. Instead, the leadership pulled the organization in.




Among those caught in the post-Fasher shift was Al-Nour “Gubba” Adam, one of the RSF’s most important commanders in North Darfur and a central figure in the battle for Fasher. He had helped design and direct operations, while also playing an important mobilization role through his standing among the Mahamid tribe and his relationships with tribal leaders across the region and its borders. After the fall of Fasher, however, Geddo “Abu Shouk” Hamdan, a commander from the Mahariya clan of the Rizeigat tribe, to which the Dagalos belong, was appointed to lead North Darfur over him. A source close to Gubba previously 

told 

Mada Masr that the move drew his ire, and the rift with the RSF leadership deepened from there.




As a Mahamid figure in North Darfur and a commander of an armed formation in Darfur, Gubba had relationships with local leaders and communities that he carried with him into the war, and, in a way, he represented the kind of pragmatic way of doing politics that the RSF intended to transcend in taking Fasher




In December 2023, Gubba sat in the home of Al-Malek Adam Nour, the Dar Berri administration head and Kutum locality’s tribal administration office head, alongside a number of tribal administration figures, local notables and youth, says a former RSF official and relative of Gubba who accompanied him and worked with him during the siege of Fasher. It was a time when the RSF had become the dominant military power around the locality.




In that meeting, the commander who held a foot in both the military and the community’s traditional structures discussed the affairs of the locality.




According to his relative, Gubba moved between meetings with notables and tours of the villages surrounding Kutum.




In Kassab al-Hilla, he spoke to people about living conditions and security, asked them to cooperate with his forces in combating bandits and smugglers and tied the success of the security force to the information it received from residents. In Abdel Shakur, he directed his forces to secure the roads and protect residents, and he called on people to cooperate with the forces in “eliminating negative phenomena,” the relative says.




He attended the Sudanese Secondary School Certificate exams in Kutum alongside the North Darfur security committee, where the relative says he spoke about arranging food and security for students. And at a sporting event in Kutum town, he spoke about the forces’ role in protecting civilians and backing youth.




And when the agricultural season turned, his forces helped in the delicate business of moving herders’ livestock past farmers’ fields at the end of the harvest, while the tribal administration kept its formal place in the arrangement, according to the relative.




A military commander turning up deliberately at the road, the exam hall and the football pitch makes his presence attached to every strand of public life. And the same social standing that allowed Gubba to mobilize men had also made him more capable of influencing the community.




If Gubba showed how far a single commander’s local standing could reach, Musa Hilal showed what happens when that same kind of standing exists at the scale of an entire tribe across Darfur. Hilal, the military-aligned Mahamid tribal leader and the Revolutionary Awakening Council head, had a network built over decades, answerable to him, and not something the RSF had ever really absorbed so much as borrowed.




This is what made Hilal a figure capable of doing something Abdel Rahim could not: reach directly into tribal networks across Darfur and speak to fighters not as their commanding officer but as the head of their own people. In mid-February, he 

appealed 

to Mahamid civilians and fighters inside the RSF, calling them “misled” and urging the tribe to unite behind the military. He announced plans to convene a conference to politically and militarily unify the Mahamid under his group’s umbrella — a project that he said would eventually produce a political party not limited to the Mahamid alone.




It was an old kind of appeal, the kind Abdel Rahim had been trying to foreclose. And faced with a rival network, he tried to burn it down.




Abdel Rahim 

ordered 

an attack on Hilal’s stronghold in North Darfur’s Mostariha. When the area was stormed days after the speech, Gubba left the RSF with many of his forces and moved toward military-held areas. What had started as a dispute over Gubba’s place in the reorganized RSF had brought to the forefront something much older: a network of tribal authority that the central leadership could use when it needed men but could not fold into its own chain of command.




Navigating a fragile balance between military loyalties and tribal allegiances in the aftermath of Gubba’s defection, Hemedti’s choice was another turn toward centralization. He held lengthy meetings with sector commanders and security officials in Nyala in May, after which the command structure was reorganized, and the authority and movement of field commanders was significantly restricted. Decisions over troop deployments, finances and logistics were concentrated in a five-member committee directly tied to the Dagalo leadership, 

according 

to a commander in the RSF’s First Shield Brigade who spoke to Mada Masr at the time.




The restructuring was meant to prevent further dissent in the post-Fasher Darfur. Instead, another influential Mahamid commander, Ali “Savanna” Rizgallah, defected, followed by waves of Mahamids leaving the RSF.




Former RSF commander Al-Nour “Gubba” Adam shakes hands with TSC Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan in Dongla, Northern state, April 19. Courtesy: Sudan Tribune




***




Abdel Rahim understood that taking territory changes the people who live on it and the relationships between them, according to the source who worked in the RSF advisory office in Nairobi. Displacement alters where communities are concentrated. Changes in control over roads and markets alter how people move and trade. Over time, these shifts produce a social reality that could look very different from the one that existed before the war.




The source describes this as recomposition. The term, he says, does not necessarily refer to a written plan to redistribute the population. It describes what fighting could produce in practice. For Abdel Rahim, the political significance was clear — whoever controls this new social composition would have greater influence over the authority that emerges after the war, he adds.




But trying to rule over and make use of the social reality produced by the war has not gone entirely according to plan. And the changes it has set off could reach a breaking point, one that defections bring closer, faster.




When a top commander who had once been a reliable intermediary changes sides, communities watch and “the questions begin: Why did he leave? And who is with him? ” a notable in North Darfur’s tribal administration says.




A defection could travel through councils and villages, becoming a question about the next request for fighters. “If the man who used to ask the tribe for fighters on behalf of one side starts fighting for another side, people begin to reconsider,” the notable says.




In Darfur, mobilization has long been a negotiation, a bargain. Requests from the military leadership pass through local commanders, who in turn work through the omda, sheikh or nazir and from there through families, villages and tribes. The local commander is the link to the military leadership, and the tribal leader is the person who could speak for the community and negotiate what could be delivered by each side. Fighters are mobilized in exchange for something: protection, resources, status, money.




And the relationship between the two middle men is not necessarily one of alignment. Tribal leaders could be pressured or intimidated into compliance. And even short of coercion, there was the risk of allegiance to weigh, since a leader too closely identified with the RSF could find himself exposed when the balance of power shifts. As one member of the tribal administration put it, they had to “keep a door open to more than one side.”




The war put greater pressure on this system. Communities were dealing with kidnappings, displacement, resource disputes and disrupted markets and roads, and the bargain had to expand to cover the costs the war was imposing on them.




“We ended up dealing with people’s problems on the ground,” says Aboul Qassim Omar Gandoul, the tribal administration head in the Shataya locality in South Darfur — pulled, he says, into problems far beyond the tribal authorities’ traditional responsibilities.




The longer the fighting continued, the more the benefits of cooperation mattered and the more closely communities watched whether commanders kept their promises.




A commander with genuine roots in the community has something to lose when he abuses his power or breaks his word. His reputation is bound up with the families. His own children and the children of those he recruits live in the same place. Social capital can become a constraint on military conduct, the former political advisor says.




A field commander who relies mainly on his relationship with the higher command is different — his legitimacy comes from the center, from weaponry rank and command over a group of fighters rather than a standing in the community. The longer the war drags, the more this commander leans on force to offset a weakening relationship with the community, the former advisor says.




In North Darfur’s Shangil Tobay, the former advisor describes dozens of displaced people being detained and taken to Nyala for training. In Nyala itself, young men have been pursued in markets and other public spaces for forced recruitment.




These practices change the terms of the relationship. The people who negotiate between commanders and communities have little to no room to do so when fighters are taken by force.




The same is true of payments. Community leaders negotiate with commanders over what fighters would receive and what would be provided for their families. The sons being sent to the battlefield are also needed at home to farm and herd, and that need has become greater as the war drags on and resources for families and communities dwindle, according to the former advisor. When promised payments do not arrive, some community leaders face growing anger from the families they had asked to provide fighters. That anger turns into resistance to further recruitment, he says.




Communities also expect something in return at a collective level — protection of tribal land for when the displaced return to their villages and a stronger hand when it comes time to settle land disputes.




In Darfur, the hakura, the tribal landholdings, occupies a place that goes far beyond land ownership in the narrow legal sense. It is a social arrangement that ties a community to its land. When people demand protection of the hakura, they are simultaneously demanding protection of an entire system of relationships. They need an authority that recognizes the right to land itself, protects the rightful owner when they return, prevents damage to crops, regulates the movement of livestock, adjudicates disputes and determines compensation when losses occur.




“The military leadership sees land as a space to move through, while the community sees it as a right, a memory and a relationship between groups,” a member of South Darfur’s tribal administration says. A commander can move a base within hours, while a village may need years to rebuild its relationship with the land after displacement, he adds.




By then, however, the land may have changed. A returning family may find that others have farmed its fields, grazed animals across them or settled on them. The family may carry documents, testimonies or collective memory to establish its claim, but those who arrived during its absence may have claims of their own, according to several tribal administration members.




Protecting return, therefore, requires an institution capable of managing this tangle of competing claims, they say.




For all the state’s failures in Darfur, its institutions remain recognizable. A former member of the tribal administration says that, despite the weakness of its institutions during the war, the state remained present in communities’ memory in the form of courts, records and civil and tribal administrations. A sheikh or omda needs an entity capable of recording rights, settling disputes and managing the return of displaced people. “After the battle is over,” he says, “the land will still be there, the dispute will still be there, the displaced person will still be there, and the family that lost its son will still be there.”




According to the former administration member, this has led some local leaders to see state institutions as a framework capable of accommodating society over the longer term, even when the state itself is unable to perform all of its functions.




That does not mean communities automatically choose the state or that a commander who defects could automatically bring them with him, a Darfur notable says. Their choices depend on the balance of power, the position of local leaders and whether an authority could actually protect people and make good on its promises.




Gandoul says the tribal administration will continue dealing with the consequences of the war, whichever force controls the area. “We have people who want to return and land that needs to be returned to its owners. We have families that have lost their sons. We have a community that wants to live,” he says.




Displaced people flee Darfur to Chad, August 2023. Courtesy: Zohra Bensemra/Reuters




***




It wasn’t just military defections. Inside the RSF, the structures built for the “sovereign system,” built to carry its authority beyond military control, started to lose people.




Fares al-Nour, Hemedti’s confidant and close political advisor since the start of the war, defected in June, at a time when Tasis and its Government of Peace was trying to present itself as a political structure capable of engaging the outside world and administering areas under RSF influence.




“If a project wants to govern Sudan, it needs people who can speak to society, politicians and foreign governments,” says a tribal administration notable who took part in Tasis’s political meetings over the past period. “So when the people at the political center start leaving, the question becomes whether the project can continue, not how many vehicles it has on the battlefield,” he says.




Two months later, the fracture reached the administrative side. Tasis Kordofan Governor Hamad Khalifa, who had been part of the structure intended to translate RSF control into administration outside Darfur, also defected.




But Kordofan is not just another area in which the RSF has tried to establish itself. It is the hinge that connects Darfur to the rest of Sudan, where the military and social networks operating across the two regions overlap. Commanders who have built their influence in Darfur have operated there. For the RSF, the region has been the route out of Darfur and an extension of its Darfuri power.




“If commanders [who have defected to the military] start heading [to Kordofan], it could become the front where the internal retreat begins,” the Darfur notable says.




The prospect of the fighting moving back toward Darfur would carry a significance beyond the loss of territory. “When the war drags on, people start seeing the movement through the region where it is fighting,” says the notable in North Darfur’s tribal administration. Continued fighting within the same region, the notable says, makes the national project more vulnerable to shrinking into demands for local protection and control.




Darfur had already taught this lesson. The armed movements that arose there in the early 2000s began as broader political projects but fractured over the years — through disputes over leadership, negotiating positions and access to resources and power. What had been framed as unified projects speaking for the region’s marginalization and the redistribution of power and wealth had come to be known instead by the names of their individual leaders, their strongholds and their local bases.




Hemedti had entered the war already aware of where that path had led others before him, the North Darfur notable says. That is why the efforts to expand the RSF beyond the region became part of a longer attempt to transform it from a structure with regional roots into a national force. The expansion into Khartoum, the building of an economic network, involvement in transitional government arrangements, the expansion of regional ties and, eventually, the creation of a political front such as Tasis can all be read as attempts to break the geographic constraint that had been attached to the RSF since its inception, he says.




If the RSF is pushed back into Darfur, that could give it the capacity to survive militarily, the Darfur notable says, but it would weaken its ability to present itself as a national alternative. The region would change from a launch base into a border of the project. It would become the place where the RSF can take cover in and the space it may find increasingly difficult to move beyond politically and socially, he adds.




“The real fear is not that the [RSF] loses a city,” the notable says. “It is that it loses the idea that made people believe it could govern Sudan.”

The post 

How the Dagalos’ ever tightening hold on power destabilized the RSF project

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

.

content:
Abahlali was formed at a meeting of 34 people held in Durban on 4 October 2005. When the movement celebrated its 21st anniversary in Durban on 4 October 2026 it had more than 200 000 members across five of South Africa's nine provinces. 




In 21 years of struggle it has won large tracts of urban land, extracted significant policy concessions and resolutely opposed the xenophobia that is systemically used to divided impoverished and working class people in South Africa. It has also built strong connections with radical movements around the world and has, in recent years, moved towards building communes.




The struggle has come at a high cost. As of 4 October 2026 26 lives have been lost in the course of the struggle.




This archive runs from the movement's formation in 2005 till 4 October 2026 and includes a complete list of all the statements it has issued, memoranda delivered at marches as well as the articles and speeches by its members which are archived on the movement's website.

author: Fozzie
title: Part VII: The Process of Accumulation of Capital
content:
From October 7 to the Present: States at War with Human Beings


The Israeli–Palestinian conflict cannot be said to have begun on October 7, 2023, just as it cannot simply be reduced to a war between “two nations.”


































Author







Hasse-Nima Golkar


























    Submitted by 

heinhtetkyaw

 on October 8, 2026
  
















































































































































































































The roots of this catastrophe go back decades: to the end of the British Mandate, the 1948 war, the establishment of the State of Israel, the displacement and expulsion of more than 700,000 Palestinians, and the emergence of what Palestinians call the Nakba — the catastrophe. Following the 1967 war, the occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza, the expansion of Israeli settlements, and extensive restrictions on Palestinians’ lives and freedom of movement further entrenched structures of inequality and domination.


 


Today, nearly 5.9 million Palestinian refugees are eligible for services provided by UNRWA.From an anarchist perspective, the question is not simply: “Which state has the right to govern which territory?” The more fundamental question is:


Why should human beings have to submit to states, armies, borders, and military institutions in order to live, enjoy freedom, and secure their safety?


 


 

October 7: A Crime That Cannot Be Justified


On October 7, 2023, Hamas forces and several other Palestinian armed groups attacked southern Israel. Approximately 1,200 people were killed, and 251 were abducted and taken to Gaza. Civilians were among those targeted in the assault. According to the findings of the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry, hostage-taking, murder, torture, and other acts against civilians constituted war crimes. From an anarchist standpoint, no occupation, repression, or historical injustice can justify the deliberate killing of civilians or the taking of hostages. But this principle must be applied consistently, without exception. If killing an Israeli child is a crime, killing a Palestinian child is equally a crime. If taking an Israeli civilian hostage is a crime, depriving an entire civilian population of water, food, medicine, and security cannot be justified as a “right to self-defence” either.


 




From “Revenge” to Collective Punishment


Following October 7, the Israeli government launched a large-scale war in Gaza. The scale of killing, destruction, displacement, and deprivation of basic necessities went far beyond a limited military operation against armed groups.In 2024, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry reported that Israeli operations in Gaza involved war crimes and crimes against humanity, including murder, extermination, forcible transfer, torture, and the use of starvation as a method of warfare. The same Commission also identified Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups as responsible for war crimes committed during the October 7 attack. In September 2025, the same Commission went a step further, concluding that, based on its investigation, Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. This is a finding by a UN Commission of Inquiry; it is not the same as a final ruling by the International Court of Justice in the genocide case, and the two should not be conflated. South Africa's case against Israel remains before the International Court of Justice. In November 2024, the International Criminal Court also issued arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity. These decisions, however, do not constitute final convictions; they are part of an ongoing international judicial process.


 


 

An Anarchist Is Neither a Supporter of the Israeli State nor of a Palestinian State


This is where the difference between an anarchist perspective and many prevailing narratives becomes clear. Anarchism fundamentally opposes turning human beings into soldiers serving a state. From this perspective:







The State of Israel, even if it regards the protection of its citizens as its responsibility, has no right to pursue security through mass killing and military domination over another people.




Hamas, even if it describes itself as a resistance movement, has no right to kill civilians or take hostages in the name of the Palestinian people. No state, army, or armed organization owns human lives.




“National security” cannot be used to justify depriving millions of people of their freedom and dignity.




The suffering of one community must never become an excuse for repressing another.




Victims must not be turned into soldiers serving state ideologies.From this perspective, the binary choice between “Israel or Hamas” is fundamentally incomplete.







 


The anarchist questions are:







What does an Israeli living in fear of rockets and attacks want?




What does a Palestinian living under siege, occupation, and displacement want?







 Before belonging to any community, both are human beings.


 


 

After the Ceasefire: Has the War Really Ended?


The October 2025 ceasefire brought an end to the large-scale war, but it did not put an end to violence. A September 2026 UN report states that the ceasefire remains fragile, Israeli attacks continue, large parts of Gaza remain subject to severe access restrictions, and reconstruction is proceeding on a scale far below what the population needs. According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), between the announcement of the ceasefire on October 10, 2025, and September 2026, at least 1,402 Palestinians were killed and 4,881 injured in Gaza. These figures are attributed to Gaza's Ministry of Health and do not encompass all the consequences of the war and the destruction it has caused. The situation in the West Bank is no different. Settler violence, home demolitions, restrictions on movement, settlement expansion, and the forced displacement of Palestinians continue. The United Nations has reported that in 2026, an average of approximately 17 Palestinians were displaced every day as a result of settler violence and demolitions — twice the average recorded in previous years.


Therefore, a “ceasefire” does not necessarily mean “freedom” or “peace.”


The sound of bombardment may diminish, but as long as domination, occupation, discrimination, siege, settlement expansion, imprisonment, military borders, and structural poverty remain in place, the conditions that reproduce violence will remain as well.


 


 

The Problem Is Not Just War; It Is the Structure of Power

Anarchism compels us to take a step back and examine the bigger picture.


States usually say:







“We need an army to protect your security.”







The military says:







“We need more weapons to defend you.”







Politicians say:







“You must give the state more power to confront the enemy.”







And ultimately, ordinary people, both Israeli and Palestinian, pay the price of this cycle with their lives, homes, freedom, and future.


 Under such circumstances, each side can present the other side’s crimes as evidence that it needs even more power.Hamas says: Occupation and repression exist; therefore, armed resistance is necessary.The Israeli government says: Hamas and other armed groups exist; therefore, a military and military control are necessary.And this cycle can continue for generations. Power justifies its own violence through the violence of the opposing side.This is one of the most fundamental lessons that an anarchist perspective can draw from this catastrophe.


 


 




A Third Way: Beyond States

Anarchism does not necessarily mean indifference to the security of Israelis or the rights of Palestinians. On the contrary, it can demand security for both, but a form of security that is not built upon the domination of one group by another.The path that deserves serious consideration is one based on direct cooperation among people, democratic local councils, trade unions, mutual-aid networks, women's groups, peace activists, human rights defenders, anti-war movements, and all those who refuse to reduce human beings merely to “Israeli,” “Palestinian,” “Jewish,” “Muslim,” or “enemy.”Movements for Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions — BDS — can also be examined from this perspective: as efforts to exert pressure from below rather than send human beings onto battlefields. However, even these movements are compatible with anarchist ethics only as long as they do not turn into hatred of Jews, Palestinians, or any ethnic or religious group.If the cycle of violence is ever to be genuinely broken, the demand must go beyond “Israel's victory” or “Palestine's victory.” It must be something much deeper:







An end to the killing of civilians.




The release of hostages and prisoners, with their rights respected.




An end to occupation and military domination.




An end to the siege and collective punishment.




An end to settlement expansion and forced displacement.




The right of return or fair compensation for displaced people, within a framework that recognizes the rights of all inhabitants.




Full legal and political equality for all human beings, regardless of ethnicity or religion.







And, most importantly:







The right of people to determine their own destiny, without states, armies, or armed organizations deciding that destiny on their behalf.







From an anarchist perspective, the issue is not to prove that “these people are good and those people are bad.”


The issue is to understand how states, armies, nationalist ideologies, and armed organizations trap ordinary people in a cycle in which every death becomes an excuse for the next. October 7 cannot be separated from the history of occupation, displacement, and repression. But the history of occupation cannot justify the deliberate killing of civilians or hostage-taking either. Likewise, the crimes of October 7 cannot justify the killing, starvation, displacement, and collective punishment of millions of Palestinians.


If we are to escape the cycle of revenge, we must also move beyond the logic of “the enemy of my enemy is my friend.” A peace achieved solely through the victory of one army over another is not the peace of the people. Real peace begins when no child has to be sacrificed so that another can live freely.


And perhaps the fundamental question here is this:







How can we build a society in which people's security comes not from the barrels of state guns, but from freedom, equality, mutual aid, solidarity, and the organized collective power of the people themselves?







 




 




Conclusion: No to States, Yes to Human Beings


From an anarchist perspective, choosing between Israel and Hamas means choosing between two armed powers; it does not necessarily mean choosing between two paths to liberation.


We can:







Condemn the killing of civilians on October 7.




Condemn hostage-taking.




Condemn occupation and settlement expansion.




Condemn the collective punishment of Gaza's population.




Condemn violence against Palestinian and Israeli civilians.




And, at the same time, refuse to turn any state or armed organization into an idol.




No to antisemitism.




No to hatred of Palestinians.




No to extreme nationalism.




No to terrorism.




No to occupation.




No to apartheid and discrimination.




No to collective punishment.




No to the glorification of armies and war.







And yes to:







Freedom, equality, solidarity, self-determination, and the equal dignity of all human beings.







Anarchism has never sought to replace one flag with another. Instead, it asks us to consider: Why should a human being have to possess a state in order to be free? Perhaps the way out of this cycle is not the victory of one community over another, but the creation of a society in which no state, army, armed organization, or ideology can turn human beings into instruments of its own power.







An Israeli life lost is no less human than a Palestinian life lost.




And as long as human lives are not valued equally, no victory can truly be a victory for humanity.

content:
Türkiye Görme Engelliler Spor Federasyonunun ev sahipliğinde, Türkiye Futbol Federasyonu Hasan Doğan Milli Takımlar Kamp ve Eğitim Tesisleri'nde düzenlenen turnuvanın finalinde ay-yıldızlı takım, Polonya ile karşı karşıya geldi.

Kaptan Gülşah Aktürk ve Kevser Ökmen'in golleriyle rakibini 2-0 mağlup eden Türkiye, böylece tarihinde ilk kez katıldığı Avrupa Şampiyonası'nda namağlup altın madalyanın sahibi oldu.

title: Eylül ayında 28 kadın cinayeti: Kadınlar en çok evlerinde öldürüldü!
content:
Kadın Cinayetlerini Durduracağız Platformu raporuna göre, 2026 Eylül ayında erkekler tarafından 28 kadın öldürüldü, 19 kadın şüpheli şekilde ölü bulundu. Kadın cinayetleri oranı bir önceki aya göre yüzde 21 arttı.

Öldürülen 28 kadından 2’si ekonomik bahanelerle, 2’si hayatına dair karar alma bahanesiyle öldürüldü. 23’ünün hangi bahaneyle öldürüldüğü tespit edilemedi.

Platformda yer alan bilgilere binaen, “23 kadının hangi bahaneyle öldürüldüğünün tespit edilememesi, kadına yönelik şiddetin ve kadın cinayetlerinin görünmez kılınmasının bir sonucudur. Kadınların kim tarafından, neden öldürüldüğü tespit edilmedikçe; adil yargılama yapılmayıp şüpheli, sanık ve katiller caydırıcı cezalar almadıkça, önleyici tedbirler uygulanmadıkça şiddet boyut değiştirerek sürmeye devam ediyor.” ifadelerine yer verildi.

Eylül ayında öldürülen 28 kadından 5’i evli olduğu erkek, 3’ü birlikte olduğu erkek, 2’si tanıdığı biri, 2’si babası, 1’i oğlu, 1’i kardeşi, 1’i eskiden evli olduğu erkek, 1’i eskiden birlikte olduğu erkek, 1’i akrabası, 1’i eski damadı tarafından öldürüldü. 4 kadının öldüren kişi ile yakınlığı tespit edilemedi. Eylül ayında öldürülen kadınların yüzde 23’ü evli olduğu erkek tarafından öldürüldü.

Kadınların 4’ü evde, 6’sı sokakta, 2’si iş yerinde, 1’i arabada, 1’i arazide, 1’i diğer bir kamusal alanda öldürüldü. 3 kadının öldürüldüğü yer tespit edilemedi. Bu ay öldürülen kadınların yüzde 50’si evde öldürüldü, öldürülen kadınların yüzde 54’ü ateşli silah ile öldürüldü.

Öldürülen kadınların yüzde 4’ü, 6284 kapsamındaki koruma kararına rağmen öldürüldü, öldürülen kadınların yüzde 68’i evliydi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: Smart’ta direniş çadırı kuruldu
content:
Smart Solar Aliağa Fabrikası'nda işçiler taleplerinin karşılanmaması nedeniyle fabrika önüne direniş çadırı kurdu. İşçilerin Tes İş Sendikası'ndan DİSK Enerji-Sen'e geçiş yapmasının ardından 7 işçi işten çıkarılmış, işçiler işten atmalara karşı 4 gün üretimi durdurarak eyleme geçmişti. Patronun işçilerin taleplerini kabul ederek görüşmeler yürütüleceğini iletmesinin ardından işçiler eylemi sonlandırmıştı.

15 Eylül'de bitirilen eylemlerin ardından patron ve sendika yöneticileri toplamda üç görüşme gerçekleştirdi. İlk iki görüşmeden taleplere ilişkin somut adımların atılmaması ve yeni görüşme tarihine dair dönüş yapılmaması nedeniyle, Enerji Sen 29 Eylül Salı günü eylemlerin yeniden başlayacağını duyurmuştu. Eylem duyurusunun ardından hızla görüşme talebi ileten patron yeni görüşme için tarih vermek zorunda kaldı.

Yapılan bu son görüşmede ise; patron atılan işçiler için kıdem ve ihbar tazminatlarına ek olarak 2 brüt maaş vererek işe geri almamayı, temmuz ayından beri yatırılmayan enflasyon zammını Ocak ayından itibaren 12 taksit şeklinde yatırmayı, gelecek olan Ocak enflasyon zammını ise bir sene sonra vermeyi teklif etmişti. İşçilerin taleplerinin karşılanmadığı bu son görüşmenin ardından işçiler fabrika önünde direniş çadır kurarak her gün eylemlerine devam edeceğini ilan etti.

İşçilerin eylem kararının ardından şirket tarafından işçilere mesaj atılarak 16-24 vardiyasının iptal edildiği, servis gönderilmeyeceği iletildi. Henüz net olmayan bilgilere göre patronun fabrikada makina tamiri ve hammadde eksikliği nedeniyle 10 günlük üretim durdurma gerçekleştireceği söyleniyor. İşçiler bu durumu patronun eylemleri baltalamak için yaptığı yönünde değerlendirmeler de bulunurken eylemlerine vazgeçmeden devam edeceklerini dile getirdi.
