author: rti_admin
title: Why do we Protest? A Moral and Philosophical Basis
content:
The protests that have sparked in most South Asian countries in the last few years have sparked hope for socio-political, economic, and cultural change. Bangladesh’s protest over the job crisis in 2024, Nepal’s Gen Z protest (2025), and Sri Lanka’s protest of 2022 shocked the nations and their corrupt political systems. The Gen Z protest forced ruling BJP minister Dharmendra Pradhan in India to resign and raised demands for educational reform and accountability in 2026. The growing unrest of youths and their protests demand an objective analysis. This article asks some fundamental questions on the moral, philosophical, existential, and political basis of protest. More than answering the question of why we protest, this article is about why we should protest. While the outward manifestation and result of protest are obvious, the inward changes that protest brings are pertinent in shaping the morale of individuals in particular and society in general.

Let us ask, therefore, why shall we protest? Do we protest because we are bad? Bad as citizens, bad as human beings, bad daughters, and sons? Why do our youth protest? Why does this act of protest arouse so much fear? Fear from society and the state. Aristotle writes that “young men (and women) have strong passions and tend to gratify them indiscriminately” (Aristotle 2012). The younger generation possesses tremendous energy, creative force, and potential. More importantly, they are full of life, and life, to thrive, needs proper conditions that the current regime has failed to provide. However, it is the nature of life to expand itself. Hence, the protest of the youths. The old society, religion, and state use force to serve their purpose, and they try to control the boundless possibilities of youths. When any social and political structure downplays human nature and the necessities of life, we can no longer contain ourselves and remain silent. There is a limit to the control of the inner nature of humanity. Family, society, religion, and political power have always been terrified of human nature. They are forever trying to control, subjugate, and overpower the true potential of humanity.

Gods came, religion came, and then came the state! But is it possible to contain our boundless humanity that runs in our veins? History has proven again and again that it has never been, and never will be, able to suppress the beauty of humanity. The way religion, society, and the state forever wish to control individuals, individuals, in return, have forever rebelled and protested in every way possible. No god, no religion, no society, or no state can contain our boundless humanity. Is it possible to contain a forever-flowing river? We might try to control and put a brake on its flow for a temporary period of time, or it may dry out in a particular season. But for how many days? For how many seasons and years? It will return in the next season; it will return next time; eventually, with more vigorous force, it will make its own course. Nothing can stop it from reaching its destination.

In the same way, human beings possess immense potentiality. Hence, their free actions, thinking, and will cannot be stopped. Protest and rebellion can manifest in different ways. It may not always be political in nature. Sometimes it is chaotic, enigmatic, mysterious, decadent, and even in the form of telling the truth. When politics reduces to a level of tyranny, we rebel not only in the political domain but also in art, literature, science, and even in philosophy. Rebellion is a part of human life and its very existence. Reducing everyone who reads, thinks, and creates to the level of ‘Dimagi Naxal’ by none other than Narendra Modi, PM of India, is absurd and brands basic human nature and constitutional rights as criminality. His comments came in the wake of the Gen Z protest that was led by highly educated minds of India. Hence, delegitimising them while branding them with various tags is an act unbecoming of a leader of the nation. It must have been an act of rebellion that attracted people in power. All of these are various forms of negotiation with the existing socio-political structure. When we refuse the dictates of family, society, religion, or the state, that act of refusal becomes a site of protest. The protest must be understood as an act of negation. Camus rightly asked, “What is a rebel? A man who says no” (Camus 2013). While saying ‘no’ to negative politics, organisations, and beliefs, we say yes to what is desirable and good. By negating something, we claim our agency and nature. We own ourselves once again. It is an act of fighting for ourselves.

When we refuse and abandon ourselves, we become bad and ugly—not only to ourselves but also to others. What happens when we endure injustice? First, we hate the one who causes it; second, we allow him to continue to violate others; third, we hate ourselves because of our incapacity to defend what is right; and finally, the outcome of the process, i.e., resentment. Resentment toward self is resentment toward everyone. Hate and resentment are negative psychological states. Due to this kind of psychological state, we hardly find peace and cannot settle down. In an act of protest, first we refuse the violator. Protest against the violators means not only putting a full stop to their act of violation but also allowing them to be good. Only by doing that can we become good. We will not resent ourselves, we will not hate them forever, and finally, we will not resent everyone around us. In the long run, protest allows us peace and space to be good. This is the process of creating a good society where individuals are not suppressed but given space to thrive along with the larger society.

Control and subjugation started at the basic level, in the family. The family is the basic unit of the caste structure. When Indian parents control their daughters and manipulate their sons, either through the ideology of love, caste, rules, regulations, or force, it disables them. Since control never erodes, our children never grow up to be truly independent. Blind obedience becomes their first nature. The same obedient children later obey authority without questioning it. They become good slaves. They can hardly believe that power can be corrupt and questioned. Further, parental control over girl children makes it difficult for them to survive and navigate the world all alone. Their right to survive with dignity is snatched away by parents.

Their capacity to become an individual and develop their true individuality was crippled at the very door of their freedom. First, they depend on their parents, and later on their husbands. The family, and later society, first disables their daughter and then declares her a burden. The act of declaring girls a burden turns South Asian parents into murderers and criminals for either killing girl children, otherwise known as female infanticide, or disabling their daughters. This social process creates bad parents. Secondly, a woman who cannot survive on her own starts despising herself, hates herself, and leads a life of resentment and humiliation under a man. In this process, she becomes bad. Men are controlled as well and forced into society and family. Parental control over young men never wanes. It is not enough to blame the parents. We must also blame ourselves. It is our incapacity, silence, endurance, and unwillingness to take our own responsibility that allow parental, societal, and casteist abuse. We have allowed that to happen. Hence, merely protesting against the government or society or religion is not enough. We must protest against ourselves as well; we must denounce our weak, pathetic, and powerless conditions. Youth not only need to rebel against the government; they also need to rebel against the family that wishes to impose a casteist, patriarchal way of life. The question of rebellion is not merely political but existential as well. We protest because we no longer can exist in the current socio-political and religious climate. We imagine, we have vision, we doubt, and that makes us rebels in the eyes of the state.

Women are subjugated from childhood, while men become lovers and husbands and wish to become supermen! Heroes only exist when a large number of people remain helpless. However, they are merely men. Their unexpressed emotions, desires, and anger turn ugly with time. They emerge as toxic masculine figures. They grow up despising themselves and their toxic parents. This toxic masculinity enables them to perpetuate crime, demand dowry, and abuse their parents, wives, and children. Dowry death has been one of the horrific crimes that is taking place to this day. Instead of raising financially empowered women, parents search for men for their daughters. Men in our society treat women as their private property and themselves as the owners of them. Hence, they perpetuate violence with impunity. In this cycle of toxicity, the man becomes a criminal.

In a Brahmanical society, everyone becomes bad, controlling, and manipulative. The greatest creation of Brahmanism is not merely evil but legitimising it and glorifying it as dharma, culture, and tradition. Brahmanism has deeply destroyed the moral values of society. Brahmanical organisations are poisoning our young generations with hate against minorities, women, and marginalised communities. Ambedkar rightly observed that “the effect of caste on the ethics of the Hindus is simply deplorable… virtue has become caste-ridden, and morality has become caste-bound” (Ambedkar 1936). When our youths protest, they wish, should, and must annihilate caste-ridden ethics to create universal morality. When young generations refuse their parents, claim their own agency, and protest, they liberate not only themselves but others as well. We need not fight for others. We have to fight for ourselves, for our rights. Every protest is a creation of universal moral and egalitarian values.

A young woman, by fighting for herself, fights for others. Her liberation is liberation for everyone. Her fight is to make herself good. Her becoming good is everyone becoming good. Hence, every fight we fight for ourselves is a fight for everyone. The act of protest and rebellion is an act of morality. Aristotle writes in the context of youths that “their lives are regulated more by moral feeling than by reasoning; and whereas reasoning leads us to choose what is useful, moral goodness leads us to choose what is noble.” Hence, the act of protest is an act of nobility and virtue. To fight for ourselves is good, and to be good is to be beautiful. German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche asked, “What is good?”… “To be brave is to be good.” The protest that has aroused our youth across India is about them becoming good, just, moral, and beautiful. It is a protest to make others moral as well. It does not tolerate weakness, corruption, or mediocrity. They wish to take their destiny into their own hands. They do not wish to depend on others anymore. They want to be accountable and, at the same time, hold others accountable. More than that, it is a protest against a society and a system that treats young people as irrelevant—as pawns in the hands of old people, systems, and tradition. It is us chasing our destiny. We will never be stopped. We have no bounds, no limits. Nothing can stop us from expanding our inner qualities, agency, and humanity.

Old age, social relations, and traditions should be discarded. They should perish with time. The young have arrived, and they should take the destiny of India into their hands. The old people have ruined India with the ugliness of caste, gender, and all forms of corruption. And the old politicians despise the new age, new life, and new generations. Under the current regime, they wish to reverse time. The old are living in ‘memory’ while the young are in hope (Aristotle 2012). And hence, the old long for the past while the young long for the future. However, the older generations have possessed our young minds like ghosts possessing their victims; in doing so, they have contaminated their hearts, minds, and souls. A substantial portion of the young population is contaminated by the virus of Brahmanism. Ambedkar foresaw this ‘sickness’ long before, in 1936 (Ambedkar 2014). They are suffering through outdated thinking, traditions, and social relations. We must cure them through compassion, humanism, and radicalism. More importantly, we have to let them know their true potential, the beauty of their body and mind. These young bodies possessed by the old are the vanguards of the ‘ancient regime’; they forgot their own well-being and that of fellow beings. With the help of these victims, the old are on the path of destruction of every democratic institution and law because they wish to “go back to the Vedas.” They love the backward conditions of existence. They disregard change and despise the beauty of democracy. They hate the rhythm and unity of life, and they resent youthfulness. They say India is youthful, and yet when they find our youths loving, sitting, or walking, they are beaten down by anyone as if they have committed a crime. Crimes are forgivable in India, but love is not. They kill their daughters and sons of other mothers in the name of honour and now in the name of love jihad. That tells us the conditions of the youth in India. Love is a very basic thing; forget about demanding jobs and accountability. Alas! They deployed an army battalion with sticks, tear gas, water cannons, guns, and goons.

The kind of condition we are in now needs more than protest, more than becoming good, and more than a revolution. Everything India needs is more, and it must be in every field, every aspect of our lives. The youth have to be organised and start scrutinising everything old, ugly, and outdated. They should long to be good, just, moral, beautiful, and dangerous. They should hate corruption and mediocrity. That is the only door to the future. That will save our corrupt and mediocre souls. With hope, let us protest, revolt, and participate in this dangerous festival so that we can reclaim our “human personality” and become good citizens of the nation and the world. The dead are forcefully creating our world in their own image. That is why India has become ugly, stinking, and a ‘hellhole.’ It is time to kill the dead, the past. It is time not only to “create dangerously,” beautifully, and radically, but also to act and live dangerously (Camus 2019).

Albert Camus, Create Dangerously: The Power and Responsibility of the Artist, Translated from the French by Sandra Smith, Vintage International, New York, 2019.

Albert Camus, The Rebel, Penguin Books, New Delhi, 2013.

Aristotle, The Art of Rhetoric, Harper Collins, London, 2012.

B.R. Ambedkar, “Annihilation of Caste,” in Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 1, Government of Maharashtra, Bombay, 2014.

Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil, Wilco International, 2023.

Will Durant, The Story of Philosophy, Replika Press, 2006.

Dr. Jitendra Suna is an Ambedkarite activist and intellectual. He is one of the founding members of the Birsa Ambedkar Phule Student Association (BAPSA), and was a presidential candidate for the JNUSU election in 2019. He is currently teaching history at Rama Devi Women’s University, Bhubaneswar, Odisha.

author: asn
title: Debate on the Australian United Workers Union  Election & Industrial Strategy
content:
Article from Rebel Worker Paper of Anarcho-Syndicalist Network www.rebelworker.org Vol. 44 No.2 (243) Sept. - Oct. 2026

Debate on Australian United Workers Union Election & Industrial Strategy

The United Workers Union leadership election (and why it didn't really matter)

11/9/26 Back in June, the United Workers Union (UWU) wrapped up a hotly contested election for its National Convention. The UWU is one of the biggest unions in the country, with 150,000 members in dozens of industries, including warehousing, hospitality, aged care, and early childhood education.

Two tickets pitched themselves to members. 'United for You', led by union president Jo Schofield, ended up winning with a slim majority. But they faced a serious challenge from a group calling itself 'Members First'.

Members First had a slick campaign and some of what they had to say sounded pretty good: Less focus on the Labor Party, no back room deals without delegates present, and more money for strike funds and organisers.

But despite its name, and what some on the Left claimed during the campaign, Members First was no rank-and-file movement. The ticket was the project of UWU's national secretary, Tim Kennedy, and was run with very little member involvement.

The election, then, was a factional battle between sections of the officialdom, and the parts of the Labor Party they align themselves with.

Two sides, same coin The UWU was founded as a merger between the National Union of Workers (NUW) and United Voice (UV) in 2019. The forces behind the two election tickets can be traced back to the separate unions.

United for You represented the UV wing. The ticket's campaign carried on their faction's tradition of prioritising political lobbying over industrial organising. Under their model, unionism is a kind of 'service' that members sign up for: legal advice and other perks are provided by the staff of the union in exchange for dues.

The NUW, on the other hand, placed more emphasis on traditional industrial organising, in industries like warehousing, logistics and food manufacturing. The leadership of the Members First campaign came from the NUW faction, and their election promises - more organisers, support for delegates, the occasional serious strike - reflect their own priorities.

The NUW approach, and the promises of Members First, might look pretty good at first glance. But the two strategies aren't as far apart as they seem.

The empowerment of members promised by Members First was incredibly limited, and largely focussed on 'transparency'. Even the promised strike funds were a fraction of the union's actual resources. Members weren't engaged in democratic structures as part of the campaign, and very few attended election events.

Members First wasn't an example of organisation from below-it was an advertising campaign, controlled from above.

Power to the rank-and-file? Despite the hundreds of thousands spent on campaigning by both sides, only 31% of members actually voted. Neither ticket mobilised members in a genuinely democratic or militant way, because, ultimately, both want to maintain the power of the officials and their links with the Labor Party.

Throwing money at an election isn't how you build the confidence, militancy, or participation of members. On paper, Members First may have been a marginally more militant ticket. But had they somehow managed to win, they would still be in the exact same position as their United For You opponents.

Without a real, well-organised rank-and-file movement, with power based in workplaces, the officials are left balancing between members, the bosses, and their mates in the ALP. With all the power on the bosses side, and pressure from the government to keep members in line, they have every reason to settle for bad deals.

The only people that can really put members first are the members themselves. To win democratic control over our union, we have to get organised at the level of the rank-and-file.

The UWU election was a fight for control of the National Convention, a body of 500 which then elects the day-to-day managers of the union. Rather than elect Convention delegates by industry or workplace, members are grouped together by the electorate they live in.

This system was designed to entrench the power of the Executive and prevent an alternative base of power forming among specific groups of workers on the shop floor.

Still, there are industry specific structures for parts of UWU's coverage (farms, early childhood education, logistics etc.) Delegates and other members should use these to make connections with each other and facilitate democratic decision making. These structures can be used to pull the leadership in behind members' actual demands, or push beyond the leadership entirely.

Connections between workers elected from the shop floor would be the basis for genuine member control. Where these structures don't function democratically, or in industries like hospitality, where they don't exist, we have to build them: shop by shop, street by street, suburb by suburb.

Only a real rank-and-file movement, based on democratic rank-and-file groups, can make a clean break from the Labor Party and embrace militant industrial action. This would have been true even if Members First had won.

No faction fight is going to bring the change we need, because saviours never come from above. We, the members, are the union. And it's our job to make it a fighting one.

Comment: The article fails to grasp the nature of corporate unionism which the UWU is a leading example. In particular, its integration into the Corporate set up/ALP Octopus tentacles/Corporate media/Deep State. Through UWU officials' contacts with the ALP Godfathers/Deep State/ASIO and associated networks in the AEC (Australian Electoral Commission) the officials would be able to rig any election in their collegiate electoral system. As part of this scam deep state infiltrators or those who made a deal with the ALP Godfathers would be “allowed” to be elected. As a result of the officials' Deep State/CIA training/Corporate connections, etc, they would have the capacity to engage in sophisticated manipulation in the case of a crisis. If pressured to take seeming militant action and achieving victories, they would give it a demoralising swing for workers and take advantage of it for their bureaucratic/ALP machinations.(1)

The UWU officials would have long experience like the officials of other corporate unions in co-opting/corrupting union reps making them part of their machines. If this doesn't work in certain cases, the union officials would conspire with managements to get the union rep sacked or attend their union meetings to disrupt them. In the case of the RTBU(Rail Tram & Bus Union) in the late 1990's at Central Station in Sydney, the RTBU sub branch meetings where militants had influence and held the Secretary position, these meetings were constantly attacked/disrupted by groups of union officials. In the case of Leichhardt bus depot in Sydney some years back, a militant was elected as union rep and immediately led a wild cat strike involving 70 or so drivers in a mass sickie over speed up issues. Subsequently, he was quietened down by the officials, going along with them and the bosses. At Port Botany bus depot in Sydney some years back prior to privatisation, a militant was assisted by the ASN to be elected as union rep. He was a trainee so the union officials and the bosses conspired to frame him up for the sack and replace him with one of their stooges.

The article is basically grasping at straws regarding “democratising” the UWU. A more realistic strategy would be a focus on transport industries so as to launch a strike/direct action wave movement across industry. In this context of raised morale of workers in industries covered by the UWU, syndicalist education and networking of militants in which Rebel Worker distribution would play a useful role and the industrial solidarity of a breakaway syndicalist transport union, major syndicalist breakaway unions in various sectors of the UWU would be possible. Leading to the establishment of a new syndicalist union confederation based on direct action, ultra democratic processes and opposition to all political parties. M. Notes (1) See “RTBU Elections 2018: Were They Rigged?” In RW Dec.2018 – Jan. 2019 Vol.36 No.3 (223) on www.rebelworker.org & “From Corporate Bureaucratic Unionism to Grass Roots Controlled Direct Action Unionism: Perspectives for Strategy & Activity in Australia, Today” in RW No.41 No.3 (235) Dec. 2023 – Jan. 2024 on Libcom.org and www.rebelworker.org & “Spotlight on Rorts in the Union Office” in RW Vol.36 No.2(231) Aug.-Sept. 2018 on www.rebelworker.org

title: Torino è contro il riarmo: corteo 24 ottobre “Noi la guerra non la paghiamo”
content:
Nasce dal percorso cittadino che ha visto una 

tappa il 19-20 settembre

 scorso una data di mobilitazione cittadina con respiro regionale per sabato 24 ottobre: contro il riarmo, contro il caro-benzina, contro i data center e per rivendicare risorse per salute, formazione e casa. Sulla pagina 

torinocontroilriarmo

 si trovano il lancio e gli appuntamenti in avvicinamento. 




Di seguito ripubblichiamo l’indizione.







La crisi della città di Torino e della regione Piemonte non vedrà alcuna possibilità di fuoriuscita con la conversione dei territori, delle industrie, delle scuole e della ricerca in chiave bellica. 

Le poche risorse esistenti oggi non devono andare alle armi ma a sanità, formazione, casa e reale presa in carico e gestione dei territori a livello energetico e ecologico. 




Assenza di pianificazione, processo di privatizzazione, consumo di suolo e speculazione energetica, oltre alla 

svendita a big tech americane

 di intere porzioni di territorio cittadino e piemontese per la corsa all’oro dei data center, sono le questioni da contrastare. Non pagheremo i costi della cosiddetta transizione green, che impone 

il ritorno al nucleare, truffa del governo

, insostenibile sia economicamente che ecologicamente. 

Basta con grandi opere inutili come il tav

, vogliamo investimenti nella cura e manutenzione del territorio oltre che per il trasporto pubblico. Non vogliamo la 

militarizzazione dei quartieri

, da Barriera di Milano a Vanchiglia. Quest’ultimo  segnato dalla presenza costante e inutile di forze dell’ordine a seguito dello sgombero del centro sociale Askatasuna, spazio che vogliamo venga restituito al quartiere e che possa ritornare a vivere. Così come rifiutiamo  la svendita di pezzi di città a fondi speculativi come BlackRock e patrimonio abitativo pubblico ridotto in briciole, sono dinamiche da fermare immediatamente. 




Le scuole e le università diventano il terreno di propaganda militarista, bellica e patriottica, contaminando saperi e trasformando gli istituti scolastici in caserme. Mentre le scuole crollano, le Università cullano la rivoluzione tecnologica utile ad alimentare il complesso accademico-militare-industriale. 

Il riarmo erode le briciole destinate alla formazione e a una sanità in completa crisi

: liste d’attesa, privatizzazione, chiusura di poliambulatori in favore di case di comunità inesistenti, aumento del ticket sanitario a seguito della cancellazione del bollo auto, sono solo alcuni aspetti. Ma i soldi per la costruzione di mega ospedali come quello che dovrebbe sorgere nel parco della Pellerina si trovano, mettendo in contrapposizione ambiente-salute.




Oggi 

la propaganda dell’amministrazione si piega alle necessità delle industrie belliche e dei capitali privati

, unici investitori nella crisi perché è proprio nel processo di finanziarizzazione che i grandi fondi o monopoli possono ancora fare profitto. Il lavoro non è in crisi soltanto perché a Torino non esiste più la FIAT, ma perché si muore per lavorare, perché chi studia e si forma non ha alcuna garanzia e lavora in condizioni pessime, perché il lavoro è organizzato in funzione di rendere la popolazione disponibile e ricattabile. 

La fuoriuscita dalla crisi è possibile solo se insieme ci si organizza dal basso per riappropriarsi di ciò che è utile ad una vita dignitosa, senza guerra e in cui le nostre poche ricchezze non vengano espropriate. 




In questa città abbiamo saputo porre delle questioni fondamentali sul piatto: 

il terreno del dibattito pubblico lo vogliamo dettare noi a partire da un percorso di partecipazione collettiva e dal basso, a partire dalle esigenze delle lotte.

 La vivacità dei giovani, il riscatto collettivo che la Palestina ci ha dato, la possibilità di vivere bloccando la logistica di guerra di una città dove ogni arteria è complice di un futuro di morte e genocidio, la vittoria di essere in piazza ogni giorno liberandosi dal lavoro e di riconoscersi nelle dimensioni di confronto e di incontro è un patrimonio prezioso che sarà la bussola per andare avanti. 




Torino è partigiana perché ha saputo e continuerà a schierarsi dalla parte giusta della storia.

title: Chapter 21: Piece Wages
content:
Harry Cleaver's study guide to Karl Marx's Capital volume 1, chapter 21.

Piece wages seem as if workers sell their embodied labor in each piece. Piece wages seem as if the wage is not determined by the value of labor power.

Piece wages and time wages often exist side-by-side:

Marx gives us an example as a point of departure:

1) Setting of piece rates is a source of struggle between workers and capitalists

2) With piece work the need for direct "superindendence" is reduced or even eliminated; workers are forced to work fast and well to meet the going standard of production under the threat of not being fully paid, or losing their job.

3) Piece wages tend to produce hierarchies of wages

4)Piece wages result in workers being willing, or even desirous, of longer working hours.

"Piece-work", to the experienced worker whether in home, factory or field always carries the flavor of exploitation. The subtlety that Marx insists upon - how the form of payment leads workers to drive themselves to high intensity and long hours - is not always immediately apparent to new and naive workers. To them piece-work may seem to provide an opportunity for great achievement: the more you work, the more you get paid. They don't realize at first that the piece rates have been set so that even with their greatest efforts they will earn little in relation to what they produce. They don't realize, because they haven't had the experience, that if they outperform past standards, the piece-rates will be adjusted downward so that their income rises but little, even with increased effort.

In the passage below, from his story "The Apostate", Jack London describes some of this psychological dynamic as well as the physical costs workers may bear under such conditions of exploitation.

After he recovered, he got work in a glass factory. The pay was better, and the work demanded skill. It was piece-work, and the more skilful he was, the bigger wages he earned. Here was incentive. And under this incentive he developed into a remarkable worker.

It was simple work, the tying of glass stoppers into small bottles. At his waist he carried a bundle of twine. He held the bottles between his knees so that he might work with both hands. Thus, in a sitting position and bending over his own knees, his narrow shoulders grew humped and his chest was contracted for ten hours each day. This was not good for the lungs, but he tied three hundred dozen bottles a day.

The superindendent was very proud of him, and brought visitors to look at him. In ten hours three hundred dozen bottles passed through his hands. This meant that he had attained machine-like perfection. All waste movements were eliminated. Every motion of his thin arms, every movement of a muscle in the thin fingers, was swift and accurate. He worked at high tension, and the result was that he grew nervous. At night his muscles twitched in his sleep, and in the daytime he could not relax and rest. He remained keyed up and his muscles continued to twitch. Also he grew sallow and his lint-cough grew worse. Then pneumonia laid hold of the feeble lungs within the contracted chest, and he lost his job in the glass-works.

(Jack London, "The Apostate', in Jack London, Novels & Stories, New York: The Library of America, 1982.

One of the great attractions of piece work and piece wages to capitalists is that with piece rates set low enough, very little supervision is required. In order to earn a living wage workers must work hard, fast and well to produce enough pieces - quite irrespective of whether anyone is looking over their shoulder. The costs of supervision are essentially passed from the capitalist to the workers as they internalize the discipline of piece work and impose work on themselves. This self-imposition of work, of course, goes against workers' instinctive ressentment and resistance to suffering the indignities of alienating work - doing what some one else says to do, they way they say to do it, for their profit and enrichment, and so on. The piece workers, therefore, pay the psychological costs not only of alienation but of the hour-to-hour experience of imposing that alienation on themselves.

In reaction to the unpleasantnesses of piece-work exploitation, workers often band together in self-defense. On the one hand, they often fight for hourly wages instead of piece wages to improve their situation. But if that doesn't seem feasible and they must remain on the terrain of piece work then their primary objective is to avoid being drawn into the cruel dynamic of more work - lower rates - more work - lower rates, etc. One way they avoid this is to cooperate to make sure that they not be pitted against each other; that everyone works at about the same speed and no-one outperforms the others. They know that if this happens the fastest worker's time will be used to set the pace for everyone else, and that the rates will be lowered so even the fastest worker will make little more than before. The following example, taken from another of London's tales "South of the Slot" about a conservative sociologist who got a factory job in order to study "labor", describes the kind of conflict that would sometimes emerge between the cooperating workers and an individual who either didn't understand the dangers, or refused to go along with the collective strategy. In this case the violence of the piece-rate system was resisted by a cooperation which was willing to use violence to preserve itself. This situation was undoubtedly one London knew well, since he had worked in just such a cannery himself.

One of his first experiences was in the great Wilmax Cannery, where he was put on piece-work making small packing cases. A box factory supplied the parts, and all Freddie Drummond had to do was to fit the parts into a form and drive in the wire nails with a light hammer.

It was not skilled labor, but it was piece work. The ordinary laborers in the cannery got a dollar and a half a day. Freddie Drummond found the other men on the same job with him jogging along and earning a dollar and seventy-five cents a day. By the third day he was able to earn the same. But he was ambitious. He did not care to jog along and being unusually able and fit, on the fourth day earned two dollars. The next day, having keyed himself up to an exhausting tension, he earned two dollars and a half. His fellow workers favored him with scowls and black looks, and made remarks, slangily witty and which he did not understand, about sucking up to the boss and pace-making and holding her down when the rains set in. He was astonished at their malingering on piece-work, generalized about the inherent laziness of the unskilled laborer, and proceeded next day to hammer out three dollars' worth of boxes.

And that night coming out of the cannery, he was interviewed by his fellow workmen, who were very angry and incoherently slangy. He failed to comprehend the motive behind their action. The action itself was strenuous. When he refused to ease down his pace and bleated about freedom of contract, independent Americanism, and the dignity of toil, they proceeded to spoil his pace-making ability. It was a fierce battle, for Drummond was a large man and an athlete, but the crowd finally jumped on his ribs, walked on his face, and stamped on his fingers, so that it was only after lying in bed for a week that he was able to get up and look for another job.

(Jack London, "South of the Slot," in Jack London, Novels & Stories, New York: Library of America, 1982.)
