We demand that handicraft production be authorized, provided it does not utilize wage labor.

Two weeks later, on the 50-year anniversary of the Paris Commune, 60,000 Red Army troops captured Kronstadt, murdering and imprisoning thousands. Just as the bourgeois republic that came to power in France in 1870 stabilized its reign by slaughtering the rebels of the Paris Commune, the Bolsheviks stabilized their reactionary seizure of the Russian revolution with the bloodbath at Kronstadt.

Apologists for the Bolsheviks have argued that it was necessary to slaughter the Kronstadt rebels to consolidate power for the Soviet state. Perhaps so, but that is no argument in favor of any state! If it was admirable and appropriate for the Kronstadt sailors to rise against the Tsar, it was equally admirable and appropriate for them to rise against the new tyrants.

The failure of the Kronstadt upris-ing is above all a lesson in solidarity: if the Kronstadt rebels had asserted themselves in April 1918 when the Bolsheviks were carrying out their first attacks against anarchists in Moscow, the entire story might have ended differently. What is done to the least of us will be done to the rest of us sooner or later. This is why solidarity is such an important value to anarchists.

“Since you are from Kronstadt with which they frighten us all the time, and you want to know the truth, here it is: we are starving. We have no shoes and no clothes. We are physically and morally terrorized. Each and every one of our requests and demands is met by the authorities with terror, terror, endless terror. Look at the prisons of Petrograd and you will see how many of our comrades sit there after being arrested in the last three days. No, comrades, the time has come to tell the Communists openly—you have spoken enough on our behalf. Down with your dictatorship, which has landed us in this blind alley. Make way for non-party men. Long live freely elected Soviets! They alone can take us out of this mess!”

—A worker in a factory in St. Petersburg addressing a delegation of 32 sailors from Kronstadt on February 27, 1921, as recorded by Stepan Petrichenko in O prichinakh Kronshtadtskogo vosstaniia. Revelations like these motivated the rebels of Kronstadt to rise up and call for a “third revolution.”

“Today is a worldwide holiday, the Day of Working Women. We the people of Kronstadt, under the thunder of cannons, under the explosions of shells sent at us by the enemies of the laboring people, the Communists, send our fraternal greetings to you, the working women of the world. We send greetings from Red Kronstadt, from the Kingdom of Liberty. Let our enemies try to destroy us. We are strong; we are undefeatable.”

—From a statement commemorating Inter-national Women’s Day on March 8, 1921. This appeared in issue 6 of Kronstadt Izvestia, a paper published by the Provisional Revolutionary Committee, the day after the bombardment of Kronstadt began under the orders of Leon Trotsky.

Alexander Berkman, an anar-chist who served 14 years in prison in the US for an act of vengeance against the union-busting industrialist Henry Clay Frick, set out enthusiastically for Russia after the Bolshevik revolution, only to discover that the state was just as authoritarian under Lenin as it had been under the Tsar. He was fortunate to escape alive. He summarized his experiences in The Bolshevik Myth, and also assisted with Letters from Russian Prisons, documenting Bolshevik oppression.

“Grey are the passing days. One by one the embers of hope have died out. Terror and despotism have crushed the life born in October. The slogans of the Revolution are forsworn, its ideals stifled in the blood of the people. The breath of yesterday is dooming millions to death; the shadow of today hangs like a black pall over the country. Dictatorship is trampling the masses under foot. The Revolution is dead; its spirit cries in the wilderness... I have decided to leave Russia.”

– The Bolshevik Myth (Diary 1920–22), Alexander Berkman

Emma Goldman shared Alexander Berkman’s enthusiasm for the initial apparent triumph of the October Revolution and his dismay at its dismal results. She traveled with him to Russia, witnessed the first years of the revolution firsthand, and afterwards shared his conviction that Bolshevik authoritarianism was responsible for the results.

“Lenin had very little concern in the Revolution... Communism to him was a very remote thing. The centralized political State was Lenin’s deity, to which everything else was to be sacrificed. Someone said that Lenin would sacrifice the Revolution to save Russia. Lenin’s policies, however, have proven that he was willing to sacrifice both the Revolution and the country, or at least part of the latter, in order to realize his political scheme with what was left of Russia.”

– My Disillusionment in Russia, Emma Goldman

Malatesta began his career as a revolutionary in Italy in the 1870s, working with Bakunin within the famously insurrectionist Italian section of the First International—arguably the first properly anarchist movement on record. From the start, he opposed statist models for social change, having seen how republican nationalism had only brought a new regime to power in Italy and reinforced existing social inequalities. He went to jail and prison again and again in the course of his efforts to open the way to freedom.

In the 1880s, when Malatesta’s former comrade Andrea Costa renounced anarchism, entered the Italian Parliament, and set out to convince the movement that electoral politics were the best way to seek social change, Malatesta sneaked back into Italy, despite facing a variety of unresolved criminal charges in his homeland, and challenged Costa to a public debate. Costa attempted to weasel his way out of it, but was ultimately compelled to meet with Malatesta, then fled the city after being trounced in the discussion. Having won the argument, Malatesta went directly to jail.

Later, after escaping Italy concealed in a box of sewing machines, surviving an assassin’s bullet in New Jersey, and organizing one clandestine newspaper and uprising after another, Malatesta witnessed the 1917 revolution and the mass defection of anarchists to the Communist Party when the state communist model suddenly appeared more “effective” and “pragmatic.” If not for these wrongheaded conversions, there might still have been hope for emancipatory revolutions in the 20th century.

“It seems unbelievable that even today, after everything that has happened & is happening in Russia, there are people who still imagine that the difference between socialists & anarchists is only that of wanting revolution gradually or quickly.”

–Errico Malatesta in Umanita Nova, September 3, 1921

Born in 1897, in a Russian village, Mollie Steimer immigrated to the United States in 1913 with her parents and siblings. At fifteen, she went to work in a garment factory to support her family. In 1917, while still a teenager, she became an anarchist, and soon joined a collective that published a clandestine journal called Frayhayt (Freedom).

In 1918, when US troops were landed on Russian soil to intervene in the Russian Civil War, their collective published a leaflet calling for workers to launch a general strike in protest. After a violent police raid, Steimer and five of her colleagues were arrested and indicted on charges of conspiracy to violate the Sedition Act; one of her codefendants died during the trial, most likely as a consequence of the brutal beating inflicted by the police.

Steimer was convicted and sentenced to fifteen years in prison, but lawyers appealed the conviction to the Supreme Court. Released on bail while awaiting the ruling, she was arrested eight more times over the next eleven months and ultimately deported to Russia. She arrived in December 1921, when anarchist organizing in Russia had been all but destroyed.

She met Semya Fleshin, who had been active in the Golos Truda group in St. Petersburg and the Nabat Confederation in the Ukraine and had been incarcerated under the Bolsheviks alongside Voline and Aron and Fanny Baron. The two organized a Society to Help Anarchist Prisoners. On November 1, 1922, they were themselves arrested on charges of aiding criminal elements in Russia and maintaining ties with anarchists abroad—they had been corresponding with Alexander Berkman and Emma Goldman, who had already left Russia. Sentenced to two years’ exile in Siberia, they declared a hunger strike and were released the next day, on the condition that they check in with the authorities every 48 hours.

On July 9, 1923, they were arrested again, and declared a hunger strike once more. This time, they were expelled from the Soviet Union, departing for Berlin on September 27, 1923. For the next 25 years, they lived without citizenship in any country, utilizing the passports that the Norwegian arctic explorer Fridtjof Nansen arranged for stateless people.

“On March 5, 1923, the Central Government Clothing Factory in Petrograd reduced the wages of its employees 30 per cent, without giving notice or making any explanation to any of them. When the salaries were handed out, each of the workers was under the impression that it was a clerical mistake, and went for an explanation to the office, with the result that 1200 employees went simultaneously to ask why so much of their pay was missing. To this the factory director replied that the people ought to be satisfied with what they get and ought to thank them (the directors and the government) for supplying them with work at all. Amazed at such an answer and boiling with indignation, they decided not to resume work until they got a satisfactory explanation. Union representatives were thereupon called, but those officials refused to come until the workers went back to their machines. The factory manager told them also that if they dared to strike, all of them would be considered counter-revolutionists and dealt with accordingly. Immediately the workers called a meeting. While they were discussing their grievances, the union representatives entered. But instead of sympathizing with the workers, one of these ‘defenders of labor’ pounded on the table with his fist and called in a thundering voice: ‘I order you back towork.’

“Naturally, such behavior only aroused all present to the highest pitch of excitement. The order was bitterly resented and the meeting continued. An old workingman got up and related the conditions under which he and his family were forced to live, and asked how on earth he could keep from starvation with the miserable wages he received. The description of his own life being the very mirror of the life they all led, resulted in the most pitiful scene. Everybody suddenly burst into tears. Young and old, men and women, all were crying, and several in the audiencefainted.

“A few hours after this came several chiefs representing the GPU, the Union and together with the head director of the Petrograd Clothing factories, announced that the wages would be reduced only 18 per cent instead of 30 per cent. The workers, thereupon decided to resume work and quietude prevailed in the factory. But at the end of the next week 120 workers, who were considered to be more outspoken and determined than the others, were discharged from the factory, thrown out of the Union, and put on the blacklist; that is, on their passports were written: ‘Citizen... discharged from the Central Government Clothing Factory for mutiny against the Workers and Peasants Government, with the purpose of taking over thefactory.’[...] “No, I am NOT happy to be out of Russia. I would rather be there helping the workers combat the tyrannical deeds of the hypocritical Communists.”

—Mollie Steimer, in a letter written from Berlin in 1923, published in Freedom, January 1924

Victor Serge started adulthood as an anarchist. However, after the Bolshevik seizure of power, he joined the Party and served them as a journalist, dutifully excusing the imprisonment of honest anarchists, the butchery of the Kronstadt rebels,[7] and many other steps in the Bolshevik counterrevolution. In this regard, he is an example of the millions of rebels and common laborers shifted their allegiance from anarchists to statists after the apparent victory of the Bolsheviks in Russia. Once more, so much for pragmatism.

How did it work out for Serge? A few years later, he was expelled from the Communist Party, thrown in jail, sentenced to internal exile, and in the end barely managed to escape the Soviet Union with his life. Had he remained faithful to his anarchist politics, he might have saved himself a lot of grief—and above all, he would not have been complicit in setting the stage for the slaughter and imprisonment of millions.

“When [Victor Serge] was asked why he, as a party member, did not raise his voice in protest [against the attack on Kronstadt] in the party session, his reply was that that would not help the sailors and would mark him for the Cheka and even for silent disappearance. The only excuse for Victor Serge at the time was a young wife and a small baby. But for him to state now, after seventeen years, that ‘the Bolsheviki once confronted with the mutiny had no other recourse except to crush it,’ is, to say the least, inexcusable. Victor Serge knows as well as I do that there was no mutiny in Kronstadt, that the sailors actually did not use their arms in any shape or form until the bombardment of Kronstadt began.”

—“Trotsky Protests Too Much,” Emma Goldman, 1938

“On one of these black days [during the Kronstadt uprising], Lenin said to a friend of mine (I use his exact words): ‘This is Thermidor. But we shall not let ourselves be guillotined. We’ll be our own Thermidor.’”

— Memoirs of a Revolutionary, Victor Serge. Thermidor was the11th month ofthe calendar introduced under the French Revolution in 1793. In 1794, during Thermidor, a reactionary backlash overthrew the radical Jacobins and guillotined their leader, Robespierre.

Peter Arshinov participated in the anarchist uprising in the Ukraine alongside Nestor Makhno between 1919 and 1921, at which point he narrowly escaped the Bolshevik counterrevolution with his life. Fleeing west into Germany, he authored the History of the Makhnovist Movement (1918–1921) and co-authored the “Organizational Platform of the Libertarian Communists.” Eventually, he renounced anarchism and returned to the Soviet Union to join the Communist Party, only to be purged and executed. If not even the original Bolsheviks were safe from Stalin’s Terror, it was foolish to imagine a former anarchist might be.

“Prisons are the symbol of the servitude of the people. They are always built only to subjugate the people, the workers and peasants. Throughout the centuries, the bourgeoisie in all countries crushed the spirit of rebellion or resistance of the masses by means of execution and imprisonment. And in our time, in the Communist and Socialist State, prisons devour mainly the proletariat of the city and the countryside. Free people have no use for prisons. Wherever prisons exist, the people are not free.”

— History of the Makhnovist Movement (1918–1921) , Peter Arshinov.

Once the Bolshevik Terror was underway, it became increasingly difficult to get information about what was happening to anarchists and other rebels behind the borders of the Soviet Union. Fedor Mochanovsky was one of countless anarchists who vanished in the course of this repression. By 1928, the Soviet authorities had moved Mochanovsky from the Butyrka prison in order to cut off international support, effectively disappearing him. He almost certainly died in the hands of the Stalinist state.

“The real antagonism between the anarchists and the Bolshevists is nothing new as far as anarchists are concerned. That antagonism has existed since the days when Karl Marx and Mikhail Bakunin set out their ideas. The former embraced the State and government whereas the latter rejected them, even in embryo. That antagonism became very clear at the congress of Marxists chaired by Engels and Liebknecht and held in The Hague [September 2–7, 1872], at which they pledged to string up anarchists as soon as they camepower.

“In which all they were doing was talking in the same terms as the Bolshevists talk in Russiatoday.

“In 1918, the Bolshevists organized an anti-anarchist front to seek the destruction of the anarchists in Russia. Throughout the land and in every sphere of life across the territory of the soviet republic, they took up arms against the anarchists. They shut down their presses and their literature. They shut down anarchist clubs and bookshops. They resorted to all sorts of means in order to undo the organization of their congresses and they arrested the anarchists. And when the opportunity presented itself, they shot them down on one pretext or another.”

–Speech of the anarchist Fedor Mochanovsky before the Petrograd Revolutionary Court on December 13, 1922, published in La Antorcha (Argentina), September 23, 1923. Translated by Paul Sharkey.

Born in Russia, Voline dropped out of the university in 1904. He participated in the uprising of 1905 as a member of the Socialist-Revolutionary Party and an organizer of the Soviet of Workers and Peasants; sentenced to internal exile afterwards, he escaped from Russia and joined the anarchist movement in France. When the First World War began, the French government intended to put him in a concentration camp, but he escaped to New York, where he joined the staff of Golos Truda. After the Revolution, he returned to St. Petersburg with the rest of the staff.

In fall 1918, following the Bolshevik crackdown on Golos Truda, he traveled the Ukraine, where he helped to organize the Anarchist Federation of the Ukraine and the editorial group Nabat (Tocsin). Nabat published several papers throughout the region. Nabat entrusted him with the responsibility of drafting a Synthetic Declaration of Principles that would enable anarchists and libertarian socialists of all stripes to work together throughout the Soviet Union. Later on, along with Mollie Steimer and Senya Fleshin and several other longtime anarchists, he published a critical response to Arshinov’s “Organizational Platform of the Libertarian Communists,” arguing that it had too much in common with Bolshevism.

Organizing alongside Makhno’s insurgents in the Ukraine, he was captured by Bolsheviks; Trotsky had already ordered his execution, but Makhno was eventually able to broker his release as part of a treaty with the Bolsheviks—which they violated almost immediately afterwards. Voline organized a Congress of Russian Anarchists; the Bolsheviks pretended to offer permission for it, then interrupted it and arrested the participants. They languished in the Taganka prison in Moscow until an international labor congress furnished them the opportunity to go on hunger strike. In the end, they were deported to Germany.

Voline spent the rest of his life in France, where he worked with anarchists in the CNT during the Spanish Civil War and published his exhaustive work, The Unknown Revolution, 1917–1921.

“Any school of thought that countenances dictatorship—be it of all-out or kid-glove, ‘right wing’ or ‘left wing’ variety—is, deep down, objectively and essentially fascist. In my eyes, fascism is primarily the notion of the masses being led by some ‘minority,’ some political party, some dictator. In terms of psychology and ideology, fascism is the idea of dictatorship. That idea articulated, spread or implemented by the propertied classes is readily understood. But when that same idea is taken up and implemented by ideologues from the working class as the road to emancipation, that should be deemed a poisonous aberration, a shortsighted, silly nonsense, a dangerous deviation. For, being essentially fascist, that idea, if put into effect, leads inevitably to a profoundly fascist social organization.“This truth has been comprehensibly—and incontrovertibly—borne out by the ‘Russian experience.’ The notion of dictatorship as a means of emancipating the working class has been put into practice there. Well, its implementation has inevitably brought forth an effect which these days is becoming plainer and plainer and which soon even the most ignorant, short-sighted and pig-headed will be forced to acknowledge:instead of leading to the emancipation of the working class, the victorious revolution actually and despite all the theorizing of the dictator-liberators, brought forth the most comprehensive, ghastliest enslavement and exploitation of that working class at the hands of a privileged ruling class.”

Near the end of his life, Max Nettlau, one of the greatest historians of the classical anarchist movement, having witnessed the Bolshevik victory and the subsequent nightmares of Leninism and Stalinism, summarized the essence of Marx’s political incoherence in a letter to a friend. This little-known excerpt casts considerable light on the contradictions within Marx’s thought, which have been the cause of so much misfortune:

“I call Marx ‘triple-faced,’ because with his particularly grasping spirit he laid a claim on exactly three tactics and his originality no doubt resides in these pan-grasping gests. He encouraged electoral socialism, the conquest of parliaments, social democracy and, though he often sneered at it, the People’s State and State Socialism. He encouraged revolutionary dictatorship. He encouraged simple confidence and abiding, letting ‘evolution’ do the work, self-reduction, almost self-evaporation of the capitalists until the pyramid tumbled over by mathematical laws of his own growth, as if triangular bodies automatically turned somersaults. He copied the first tactics from Louis Blanc, the second from Blanqui,[8] whilst the third correspond to his feeling of being somehow the economic dictator of the universe, as Hegel had been its spiritual dictator. His grasping went further. He hated instinctively libertarian thought and tried to destroy the free thinkers wherever he met them, from Feuerbach and Max Stirner to Proudhon, Bakunin and others. But he wished to add the essence of their teaching as spoils to his other borrowed feathers, and so he relegated at the end of days, after all dictatorship, the prospect of a Stateless, an Anarchist world. The Economic Cagliostro hunted thus with all hounds and ran with all hares, and imposed thus—and his followers after him—an incredible confusion on socialism which, almost a century after 1844, has not yet ended. The social-democrats pray by him; the dictatorial socialists swear by him; the evolutionary socialists sit still and listen to hear evolution evolve, as others listen to the growing of the grass; and some very frugal people drink weak tea and are glad, that at the end of days by Marx’s ipse dixit Anarchy will at last be permitted to unfold. Marx has been like a blight that creeps in and kills everything it touches to European socialism, an immense power for evil, numbing self-thought, insinuating false confidence, stirring up animosity, hatred, absolute intolerance, beginning with his own arrogant literary squabbles and leading to inter-murdering socialism as in Russia, since 1917, which has so very soon permitted reaction to galvanize the undeveloped strata and to cultivate the ‘Reinkulturen’ of such authoritarianism, the Fascists and their followers. There was, in spite of their personal enmity, some monstrous ‘inter-breeding’ between the two most fatal men of the 19th century, Marx and Mazzini,[9] and their issue are Mussolini and all the others who disgrace this poor 20th century.”

–correspondence with a comrade, c. 1936.

The tragedies brought about by the Bolshevik seizure of power in 1917 did not end in Russia. Once there was a state that supposedly represented the revolutionary socialist agenda, revolutions and revolutionaries all around the world were sacrificed in cold blood to advance the imperatives that drive all states. As his temporary pact with Hitler illustrates, “Stalinism” was not a coherent ideology but a mishmash of all the things Stalin had to do to continuously pursue power for himself and the Soviet Union.

Not wishing any revolutionary movement to triumph that did not answer to his Comintern, Stalin made sure to undermine the anarchist and Republican forces in the Spanish Civil War. The Stalinist faction within the struggle against Franco was small, but because they controlled access to resources from outside Spain and did not shrink from open betrayal, they were able to centralize control of the defense in their hands. In the end, many Spanish anarchists were murdered by Stalinists rather than by the fascists they were supposedly fighting together.

An associate of Malatesta and fierce critic of Trotsky as well as Stalin, Luigi Berneri was a well-known Italian anarchist organizer who traveled to Spain to fight in the Spanish Civil War. He was offered a position in the Council of the Economy, but refused to participate in the government on principle.

When clashes between anarchists and the Stalin-controlled Communist Party broke out in Republican Spain, the house Bern-eri shared with several other anarchists was attacked. He and his comrades were labeled “counter-revolutionaries,” disarmed, deprived of their papers, and forbidden to go out into the street. On May 5, 1937, Stalinists murdered Bernerialong with another Italian anarchist, Francisco Barbieri.

What evil the Communists are doing here too! It is almost 2 o’clock and I am going to bed. The house is on its guard tonight. I offered to stay awake to let the others go to sleep, and everyone laughed, saying that I would not even hear the cannon! But afterwards, one by one, they fell asleep, and I am watchful over all of them, while working for those who are to come. It is the only completely beautiful thing.”

—Berneri’s last letter to his family, May 3–4, 1937; translation published in The Cienfuegos Press Anarchist Review #4, 1978

When proponents of state socialism accuse anarchists of being sectarian for not desiring to work together for common ends, we have to ask:dowe share the same goals, really? What can we have in common with those who believe that guillotines, courts, judges, prisons, gulags, and firing squads can do the work of liberation?

If history is any guide, partisans of the state will not hesitate to use those against any-one who hinders their pursuit of centralized power. Tens of millions murdered by the state cry out to us from the 20th century, urging us to heed their warnings so their deaths might not be in vain.

[1] It was published at segadores.alscarrers.org as “A cent anys de la contrarevolució Bolxevic: memòria històrica a prop de la destrucció de les nostres lluites.”

[2] It leaves off at the opening of the Second World War, when most of the anarchists had been exterminated. For the rest of the story, we are forced to rely on conservatives like Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn—himself a twice-decorated war veteran and adherent of Marxism before his stint in the gulags embittered him. To those who celebrate Stalin for his part in defeating Hitler, we answer that the struggle against fascism would surely have gone better if all the anarchists and other anti-fascists Stalin and his cronies killed, incarcerated, or undermined had been able to participate. The fact that fascism was defeated by superpowers rather than by grassroots social movements took revolutionary social change off the table for several decades.

[3] Even the name, Bolshevik, is derived from a historical misrepresentation. It derives from a vote that took place in 1903 at the second congress of the Russian Social Democratic Labor Party. Lenin’s faction of the party was calling for a more exclusive membership policy; they lost the vote 28 to 23, but later, after the Jewish Labor Bund and other participants walked out, Lenin described his faction as “the majority.”

[4] For example, V. D. Bonc-Brujevic, who included a highly suspect account of Kropotkin’s meeting with Lenin in his Reminiscences of Lenin 1917–24.

[5] Throughout 1918, Makhno and his comrades fought alone against the capitalist class and the German occupation, after the Bolsheviks had abandoned the revolution in the Ukraine for the sake of statecraft. In the end, the Bolsheviks only reentered Ukraine in order to seize it from anarchists and other Ukrainian revolutionaries.

[6] Official newspaper of the Soviet government.

[7] Two decades afterwards, in his memoirs, Serge acknowledged that at the time of the Kronstadt uprising, he had written, “In spite of its faults, in spite of its abuses, in spite of everything, the Bolshevik party, because of its size, its insight, its stability, is the organized force to which we must pin our faith. The Revolution has at its disposal no other weapon, and it is no longer capable of genuine renewal from within.”

[8] Throughout half a century, Louis-Auguste Blanqui was imprisoned by one government after another for his efforts to overthrow the French government and institute communism by means of revolutionary dictatorship. Bakunin borrowed some of Blanqui’s framework of organizing in conspiratorial groups, but asserted that the only proper activity for such groups is to seek to render government impossible, not to institute a new one.

[9] Before “Italy” existed as a single nation, Mazzini founded Young Italy, a group demanding the uni-fication of all Italian-speaking countries under a Republican government, and Young Europe, a coalition of analogous groups around Europe. (The expression “Young Turk” is derived from the equiva-lent Turkish group.) Revolutionary republicans like Giuseppe Garibaldi bore the brunt of the bloody work of bringing about Italian unification, but King Victor Emmanuel took control of the new nation of Italy: Mazzinian nationalism did not pro-duce a democratic republic but a monarchy. Victor Emmanuel’s successor put Mussolini in power. As so often occurs, nationalism was initially associated with Left movements for “liberation,” yet ultimately became a reactionary phenomenon. This explains the outcome of “national liberation” movements throughout the 20th century that op-posed European colonialism in order to establish nation-states according to the European model, of-ten producing bloody ethnic conflicts like the ones in India and Pakistan. From its origins as a social movement, anarchism distinguished itself from authoritarian socialism, as represented by Marx, and from nationalism, as rep-resented by Mazzini. Marx and Mazzini were the most influential figures associated with the forma-tion of the International, though Marx swiftly forced Mazzini out. Early Italian anarchists like Malatesta started their careers as disciples of Mazzini, then rejected his thinking after the Paris Commune.

Anarchism and Insurrectionary Anarchism

Hacktivism as Digital Insurrection

Examples of Hacktivist Resistance

The essay you are about to read was written in the past when I was an early grad student still becoming a realized writer of anarchism’s ideas. Some of the information may be overly moralistic and other points may be overly empirical. Some of the writing may be overly casual while other areas may be overly academic. Some information that should be cited may not be, and some information that is cited may not have to be. My standpoints and interpretations of ideas throughout this piece may have changed since its writing, but it was my analysis at the time that I stood behind and defended. For any questions on the information presented, my updated perspectives and beliefs, or anything of the like, feel free to message me directly. If you believe the question you are asking is of good faith and may encourage a fruitful conversation including others, feel free to comment below to start the conversation. Be kind.

On December 29, 2025, a hacker known as Martha Root took the stage at an annual hacking convention in Hamburg, Germany. Dressed in a pink Power Rangers outfit, she shared how for months, she had been infiltrating three white supremacist dating websites by creating AI chatbots to interact with users while collecting their personal information. In the panel’s final fifteen minutes, she remotely accessed and deleted all three websites, much to the neo-Nazi website creator’s disapproval, which he described in a tweet as “cyberterrorism.” Root noted how easy it was to hack into the websites, citing “poor cybersecurity hygiene that would make even your grandma’s AOL account blush.”[1] Root’s actions can arguably show how the principles of insurrectionary anarchism, such as direct, autonomous, and disruptive intervention, can extend from physical spaces into the digital realm. Such actions can include Root’s hacking/hacktivism as well as DDoS attacks and the targeted takedowns of extremist, corporate, or state-controlled websites. Cyberspace itself can be seen as a loosely-governed libertarian space that offers hackers near-total freedom to translate traditional anarchist tactics into digital actions. Insurrectionary anarchism can take form in contemporary digital spaces through autonomous hacktivism, the disruption or removal of oppressive online networks, and decentralized digital interventions.

Anarchism can be defined as a sociopolitical philosophy that is against hierarchies wherever they may be found. Such hierarchies can include political ones such as the state and representative democracy, economic ones such as capitalism and wage labor, and social ones such as patriarchy, homophobia, and organized religion.[2] It is widely seen as one of the only ideologies that fully confronts and wishes to dismantle all forms of capitalism along with the state and its power without utilizing either for personal benefit. Although anarchistic ideas can be found throughout history and cultures, the modern anarchist movement developed in Western Europe after the Enlightenment period in the 18th century. Subsequent developments in the field of anarchism led to many variants, including but not limited to anarcho-communism, eco-anarchism, anarcho-syndicalism, and more. While anarchism largely began as an anti-capitalist and self-determinist philosophy, today, it has greatly expanded to include anti-racism, environmentalism, feminism, Black, Indigenous, and Queer liberation, and other intersecting struggles that reproduce domination of the many by the few.

The philosophies of anarchism vastly predate the advent of the anarchist movement in Europe. In other words, anti-authoritarian thought did not originate with the creation of a European society built around industrialism and the centralized modern state. Ancient Greek writers wrote of characters navigating conflicts brought on by the state, and Socrates himself posited that the only way to oppose Athenian authority was to encourage individuals to be able to make their own decisions. Cultures that operated for thousands of years prior to the creation of the state, and therefore private property, are anarchistic in the sense that they are non-state. Anarchists famously point towards the decision-making processes of Native and Indigenous groups around the world as existence of a complex life prior to a state. As expected, the classical anarchist movement was a response to fierce European industrialization and not a solidarity with colonized people around the world. After all, the state that European anarchists wanted dissolved was the same state that acquired wealth upon colonization of the Global South.

In 1866, European working class activists came together to discuss the material conditions of the working class. This meeting became known as the First International, which sought to bring together left-wing groups and trade unions around the idea of class struggle. The organization is remembered for the divide that formed between two major factions, Marxists and anarchists. Karl Marx, the German philosopher and economist, led the “statist” faction. His supporters argued that a temporary worker-run state would be necessary to abolish capitalism and foster socialism. The opposing faction, guided by Russian philosopher Mikhail Bakunin, identified themselves as mutualists and collectivists. They shared Marx’s desire of ending capitalism, but rejected the idea of establishing a workers’ state. Their standpoint grew from their belief that a state run by workers would not resolve their concerns and would only replace one group of rulers, and therefore oppressors, with another.[3] While both groups agreed on opposing capitalism, abolishing the private ownership of production, and criticizing liberal capitalism, they both disagreed fundamentally on the role of the state, control, and authority. Visually, this means both groups share the same far-left point on the x-axis of the left and right spectrum, but are on opposing ends of the y-axis separating authoritarianism and libertarianism. Fierce debates erupted, eventually leading Marx to famously expel Bakunin and his supporters from the International entirely.[4]

It is from this point where anarchism splintered into its many variants and interpretations. While all anarchists believe that the state is unnecessary, their strategies and tactics for why and how it should be dissolved greatly varied. Anarcha-feminists wanted an end to the state that perpetuated the patriarchy, green anarchists desired ends to states that caused environmental degradation, and anarcho-syndicalists wished to replace corporatism and unchecked monopolies with worker-controlled systems of production. The most popular, or widely accepted, strategy within many anarchist branches is a concept called dual power, which is defined as the creation of alternative institutions that coexist with and ultimately seek to replace existing authority. Those who believe in dual power do not wish for “their authority” to replace the state’s, but to build structures to enable as many people as possible to reduce their reliance on hierarchical institutions, the market, and centralized systems of power. Rotational leadership, horizontal structures, and direct democracy are some of the core values of how these bottom-up structures would function. It is through this standpoint where insurrectionary anarchism, also known as insurrectionism, splinters from the concept of dual power.

By the 1930s, anarcho-syndicalism’s methods of trade unionism had proven to be one of the more popular forms of anarchism. Earlier decades saw extensive syndicalist action in Uruguay, Brazil, and Argentina culminating in state crackdowns and massacres of thousands. Insurrectionary anarchism has its roots in the Italian anarchist tradition which largely took form the 1870’s. Growing out of a larger discontent with the anarchist movement, it remains one of the more controversial variants of anarchism with many devaluing it due to its structure and desires. Rather than engaging in dual power to offset reliance on state structures, insurrectionary anarchists reject dual power entirely and even syndicalism’s labor unions.[5] They believe that building up a counterpower to challenge the state is more defensive than offensive and is not removing the oppressor in the relationship, which still is the state. Insurrectionists believe in mass spontaneous actions that can spread unrest across regions faster than the state can contain it. To the countless martyred Italian insurrectionists, dismantling the state was the immediate goal and not building a dual power to counter it. In an inclusive effort to not alienate insurrectionism from the larger anarchist movement, non-insurrectionists have redeemed the current by framing the practice simply as a mode of attack and not a model for a society. This in turn means that anarchists of any variant, with exception to syndicalists, can identify as insurrectionists.

Anarchism is situated opposite to authoritarianism, which inherently makes anarchism a libertarian ideology. Libertarianism is defined as a philosophy that holds freedom and personal sovereignty as primary values. American society often incorrectly views it in its entirety as a right-wing ideology, typically shown through images of the Gadsden “Don’t Tread On Me” flag, individualist approaches to advocacy of the Second Amendment, and slogans such as “Live Free or Die.” These individuals also strongly support capitalist property rights and lobby against wealth redistribution. However, these are all aspects of the libertarian right and not libertarianism as a whole. Libertarianism is home to both left and right currents, similar to authoritarianism. The libertarian left is often referred to as libertarian socialism, which was historically used by anarchists at times when they could not openly identify as such.

In 1958, the Advanced Research Projects Agency (known today as DARPA) created a technology called ARPANET. Operating as a branch of the United States’ Department of Defense, this technology was the predecessor for what would become the internet which was used to connect two computers for the first time in 1970.[6] By the end of the next year, around fifteen locations were connected to ARPANET in a decentralized fashion, yet still only at military bases and remote government centers. Without diving into a deep history of the internet, the point here is to show that the internet originally began as a military technology. The internet itself is used by nearly all entities in technological societies whether it be in private, public, business, or academic sectors. Primarily used as a communication network, older forms of media such as television, radio, and newspapers have greatly been impacted, giving rise to newer technologies such as email and video streaming websites. The internet also has physical points of measure, the most popular of which can be physical brick-and-mortar stores to respond to high activity of online shopping. This can include more mundane products such as Warby Parker selling eyeglasses, but also Google selling phones, watches, and home devices, both of which strictly began as online services. The development of the internet has also led to ecommerce, which can be simplified as digital transactions for digital or real-world products.

Aside from money-making ventures, digital communication is utilized for actions that manifest in the real world whether they are text invites for birthday parties or for coordinating mass shootings. These examples show that the digital world is not entirely unlinked from the real world. Even before the digital world was created, ARPANET itself was built due to there being a physical necessity for an encrypted form of communication by the U.S. military. Overall, the creation and development of the internet gave people new places to want to be free in, which was and continues to be an especially important desire as freedoms are often being curtailed in the physical world. As more users joined the internet upon commercialization in 1994, it felt to be a very libertarian promise as users could quite literally do whatever they wanted.[7] The reason why anarchism and anti-authoritarian thought is deeply embedded in conversations of early digital freedoms is due to one of anarchism’s key conditions: finding or building an area where power cannot settle.

This line of anarchist logic is not new to technology nor is it new to conversations regarding the internet. The role of the internet and digital technology led to extensive anarchist theorization including crypto-anarchism, cyberstates, “pirate utopias,” and more.[8] Cyberlibertarians, as they would come to call themselves, fused the earlier mentioned ideas of freedom and liberty with these new developing technologies. Similarly to their desires in the physical world, these cyberlibertarians wanted less governmental regulation, and overall, less of anything that got in the way of a “free World Wide Web.”[9] Over time, as the internet became larger and larger, individuals recognized there was no efficient or practical method of searching for information. Historically, librarianism was a very respected profession in which an individual was required to be able to skillfully navigate vast collections of knowledge. In the digital world, librarians manifested as search engines, the first of which was Archie in 1990.[10]

To cyberlibertarians, search engines were critically theorized to hold similar amounts of power that early global empires held regarding control. The power of later sites such as “Yahoo!” and “Google” were not required to own entire websites in ways people may think historic empires controlled entire seas. Whether it was empires controlling the exit/entry ports, or search engines handpicking information to show up as top results, it was enough to shape how individuals navigated the world. Although the web itself was expanding at a very high rate, access to it increasingly depended on these centralized points, which today have evolved to become some of the largest corporations in history. The fear was not necessarily that governments alone would, or could, dominate the internet, but that new private technological creations could accumulate influence comparable to states by controlling information itself. The “anarchist fear” of the internet being ruled by corporations, some could argue, has come true. Personalized advertising, user-activity being tracked, and mass adoption of paywalls prove that the internet is no longer the open and decentralized space it was once imagined to be.

While this could be a “philosophical betrayal” of the internet’s role, it is also important to recognize that the desires of cyberlibertarians for the internet was just that, desires. The internet was not originally built “by the people,” it was built by and for the military. Even after the creation of Instagram and Facebook, governments recognized that these creations “by the people” could still be used for surveillance and data extraction. What fuels the anarchist fire in America is that of the top fifty wealthiest businesses in the world, exactly half of them are located within the United States.[11] Each and every one of those companies are not state-owned while few others are, which directly means that large scale corporations have single-handedly accumulated levels of power that previously could only be reached by governments.[12] This inherently allows private wealth to shape society, labor, and even policies on a global scale. From an insurrectionist perspective, the concentration of digital power within corporate and state institutions transforms cyberspace into a terrain of conflict. In this context, the very act of hacking becomes not only a possibly justified action, but one that understands the different roles these corporations play. Ultimately, it shows centralized entities that all of their data can be extracted, leaked, or stolen if hackers can enter via a “single point of failure.”

Since cyberspace has become an increasingly centralized space flooded with corporate and governmental power, hacking has emerged as one of the clearest expressions of resistance within the digital sphere. Much like anti-authoritarians who targeted state and capitalist authorities through sabotage, expropriation, and direct action, hackers disrupt digital infrastructures that sustain systems of domination. Rather than seeking reform through institutional channels such as elections, lobbying, or corporate accountability campaigns, anarchists have fully recognized that reforms are structurally constrained and will never destabilize systems. Regarding the internet, most congressional policies deal with information access, regulation, and privacy as it extends to youth, but never anything that hurts algorithmic governance and the dependence of everyday social existence on corporate-controlled networks. Even the 2020–2025 anti-trust federal court case of Federal Trade Commission v. Meta Platforms, Inc. (formerly known as Federal Trade Commission v. Facebook, Inc.) ruled in favor of billionaire-CEO Mark Zuckerberg. The U.S. District Court ruled that Meta, already in charge of Facebook, had not accumulated a social media monopoly power upon obtaining social media platforms Instagram and WhatsApp.[13] As institutional methods of “regulation” continue to fail to meaningfully challenge digital monopolies, hacking increasingly functions as a quick and decentralized form of resistance.

“Hacking” is simply described as an action utilizing information technology to achieve goals and solutions by non-standard means. However, a “hacker” is someone with knowledge of bugs or exploits who can access information within computer systems that otherwise would not be accessible. Corporations and companies get hacked fairly often, with the most popular ones typically entering popular news coverage. The public largely thinks that less-secure companies are “easier” to hack than larger ones, but the same public does not mentally distinguish if some hackers can simply be better than others. The difference in skill levels among hackers often comes down to their experience and knowledge of systems, but as it concerns anarchism, their personal and political motivations. Around three, but oftentimes more, types of hackers have been identified and are referred to as black hat, white hat, and gray hat hackers. Black hat hackers utilize objectively illegal methods, white hat hackers protect systems and largely work in cybersecurity, and gray hat hackers often do both. This inherently means there are distinguishable differences between cybercrime and plain hacking.

For example, the Russian invasion of Ukraine warranted the creation of Ukrainian “hacker armies.” One of these individuals, who BBC published an article on, is 32-years old Oleksandr who has “...disabled hundreds of Russian websites, disrupted services at dozens of banks, and defaced websites with pro-Ukraine messages.”[14] The “hacker army” at hand was identified by BBC as a volunteer group active with a Telegram group consisting of more than 200,000 people.[15] Almost immediately, there are glaring contradictions regarding the role of these hackers and anarchism. The contradiction at hand is how a hacker group can be resituated as having anarchist tendencies if they are very clearly being utilized by Ukraine against the Russian state. National wartime goals have very clearly been established by the Ukrainians, and alignment of any group with Ukrainian defense efforts could be labeled as nationalist. In this case, would Oleksandr and the Ukrainian hackers be state-directed or even state-compatible? On top of this, does the volunteer status of the group even matter if they are still serving state strategy? Do the prior concepts of black, white, and gray hat hackers matter if Oleksandr’s illegal actions could be aligned politically with the state?

The key characteristic that sets the hackers apart from other groups is that they are defending the Ukrainian state. The only reason why their motives and interests align with the state is due to Russia declaring war on all parts of Ukraine. Had these hackers truly been anti-authoritarian to the bone, their nationalist behavior would never have been questioned. While there may be anarchists or even anarchist-adjacent members within the Ukrainian hackers, they very clearly are aiming their cannons towards the Russian state and not the Ukrainian. This ties back into the blurred lines between the different types of hackers, and if illegal hacking is inherently bad even if the state is using it as an offensive measure. Perhaps this ties back into German philosopher Max Weber’s definition of the state as one that has a monopoly on violence. Outside of hacking and cyberspace, this undoubtedly is the case even if it is not a descriptive nor analytical definition of the state, which too can be defined in a multitude of different ways. As it pertains to Weber’s analysis, if murder is illegal, why are soldiers allowed to do it? Similarly, if black hat specifically engages in illegalism, why does the Ukrainian state not arrest their hackers if they are disrupting Russian banks? The state is allowed to do what it wants to do and does not seek any entity’s permission. The anarchist analysis is that it both deploys violence and “prevents” violence, proving to be one of its many contradictions regarding social organizing and control. To make matters more complicated, the same BBC source shares that Viktor Zhora, deputy chairman of the State Service of Special Communications, claims that the cyber section of the Russian army is actively recruiting hackers.[16] BBC managed to interview Russia’s top hacking group’s leader, going simply by the name Killmilk, who shared that he was determined to disrupt Ukraine and its allies.[17]

Perhaps the best way to differentiate between hacker groups outside of their motivations is to investigate their strategy. Ultimately, what is the difference between anarchist sabotage and digital sabotage? Our answers may lie in the overall relationships between violence, authority, and organization as it deals with the individual and/or the group. Anarchist sabotage, ideally by definition, pays no allegiance to a nation state if it is adhering to itself. In other words, the definitions and interpretations of anarchism themselves are the motivation for those who act within it, not an exterior relationship with one’s own country or even personal motivations. This provides us with an analytical framework to investigate an anarchist hacker’s mind and not a moralistic one. If a hacker collective coordinates with the national military or smears the enemy sites with patriotic rhetoric, its actions are less anti-authoritarian resistance and more a form of digital warfare. This would mean that digital sabotages are not neutral, which insurrectionists would agree with, but instead further says that the form of sabotage ultimately does not matter as much as what it is intended to do. Hackers could still be seen as revolutionaries, because revolutionaries do not have to be anti-state to be considered as such.

Early ideologies of anarchist hackers in the late 1980s pushed a narrative that the only entity to fear was the government.[18] However, dystopian sci-fi literature like Mona Lisa Overdrive and Neuromancer pushed these hackers to also oppose corporate power since these private companies sought to extend their reach into cyberspace.[19] Aesthetic movements such as cyberpunk and crypto-anarchism solidified the idea that anarchist hackers were not just overlapping identities, but entirely distinct identities forming out of punk music, the rise of technology, and arts movements. The 2011 release of “The AnarchoHacker Manifesto” showed to the world that anarchists were more than just physical threats.[20] The creations of Riseup, AntiSec, and Noisebridge told anarchists that basic knowledge of computer science and hardware/software engineering were necessary skills to protect oneself against surveillance.

One of the earliest groups of anarchist hackers were Electronic Disturbance Theater (EDT) who became active in the mid-1990s. Launched by four members, EDT’s goal was to deploy computer software to spread propaganda, display their anti-military views, and most importantly, provide a home to FloodNet.[21] On December 22nd, 1997, the Mexican government surrounded a Catholic church in the Chiapas region of Mexico, a region which is famously home to the Zapatistas, an autonomous Indigenous network of communes home to more than 300,000 people. The Mexican government has consistently been attempting to reabsorb the regions into the state, which have been resisted continuously since 1994 advocating for autonomy, liberation, forms of libertarian socialism and anarchism, and more. The Mexican government that day shot and killed 45 Indigenous men, pregnant women, and children, which today is known as the Acteal Massacre. EDT responded by creating a browser-based window that, when opened by thousands of protestors, would crash several websites belonging to the Mexican and American governments. Websites belonging to the Mexican presidency, military, and PRI (Mexico’s main political party) were “flooded” with protestors around the world taking part.[22] Advertised as a “digital sit-in” but functioning as a DDoS attack, protestors were instructed to input the names of the murdered victims, with the crash page updating with their names. Both governments implemented anti-FloodNet software as countermeasures against further and similar attacks. In 2007, EDT created a similar software that would transmit poetry along with water and safehouse sites to migrants along the Mexico-America border.[23] They were one of the first groups to explicitly frame hacking-style disruption as political protest rather than cybercrime.

Another group named LulzSec notoriously entered the media in 2011, which was active for a mere month. They repeatedly shared that their motivation was simply to have fun, cause mayhem, and quite literally, do things “for the lulz.”[24] This was confirmed in the group’s multiple manifestos where they explicitly say they are not interested in financial profit and found the attacking of certain targets to be pure entertainment. This group, which famously claimed responsibility for taking down the CIA and Sony Playstation’s website, are an example of theatrical hacking. This sort of hacking still does all other forms of hacking and is not limited to interpretations or definitions of the aforementioned black, gray, or white hatted hackers. Theatrical hacking willingly chooses to “annoy” power, which can be in the form of embarrassing authority figures, demonstrating technical dominance, or also in the case of EDT, turning hacks into performance-like protests. For example, a thief stealing money from a bank would be financially motivated. Yet a punk spraypainting a large message and livestreaming it to social media would be closer to theatrical disruption. In both cases there was a subject and an action, but the differences involve both of their motivation, intent, and operational goals. As it pertains to LulzSec, their choice to do things “for the lulz” shows that they have more in common with the spraypainters than with other hacker groups who are profit-seeking or attempting to directly challenge institutional authority. LulzSec member “Whirlpool” AKA “Topiary” shared with BBC that “politically motivated ethical hacking is more fulfilling.”[25] However, not all politically motivated hacking is actually changing anything. Pressing keys from a bedroom is not the same as materially transforming social conditions. This asks one of the largest questions throughout this whole topic, does hacking actually frighten power or does it simply annoy it?

Hacking, in my research, has proven to exist in a space between genuine disruption and symbolic defiance. Genuine disruption could be equated to the black hats, symbolic defiance could be the tamer white hats, and the entire field of hacking could be nestled in between the both as a gray hat. Successful hacks regardless of legality can expose vulnerabilities within institutions, systems, or websites that falsely present themselves as secure. This proves that even some of the most powerful corporate and state systems remain susceptible to decentralized intervention; after all, everything is digital. Data leaks, website defacements, and service disruptions can force organizations to spend considerable amounts of financial and technical resources repairing damage. This suggests that hacking can, at least temporarily or for a single instance, unsettle structures of authority. However, websites are restored, systems are patched, and institutions often emerge with stronger defenses than before, as seen with anti-FloodNet measures both the United States and Mexico took. What appears as a rupture at first just may ultimately be another routine challenge for those who defend the systems. Insurrectionary anarchism demands immediate confrontation with systems of domination, yet digital confrontation, as seen in the examples, was lacking the permanence that a physical insurrection seeks. However, this is not only a digital problem, or a problem that only exists with the translation of anarchist tactics to cyberspace. Workers sabotaging the factory floor cannot simply be restored with a software patch, nor can digital hacks be resolved with a declaration of war. The creation of cyberspace has allowed for unprecedented and new forms of resistance, but it also allows authority to recover with equal speed assuming the hack had no physical or material losses. This creates a unique relationship between resistance and power where disruption can be both significant but also never enough. However, to dismiss all of hacking as insignificant or online foolishness would be incorrect. Every successful hack, breach, leak, or takedown reminds institutions that being technologically dominating does not mean they are immune. Whether carried out by decentralized Ukrainian hackers, EDT, or LulzSec, each group agrees that digital power only exists due to human built systems, which are therefore vulnerable to human interventions. If insurrectionary anarchism is only concerned with attacking power wherever it settles, then hacktivism remains one of the best modern examples of this struggle being translated into a new terrain. It is from this point that the final analysis is achieved.

Philosophically, an uncontested fusion of hacktivism and insurrectionary anarchism would require an updated analysis of what power looks like in the twenty-first century. Sabotaging factories, railways, and exploding banks are physical points of resistance, but are those the only points of resistance? As mentioned before, one of the key conditions of anarchism is finding or building an area where power cannot settle. Unfortunately, the internet has absolutely been settled and some may even argue it has been colonized by corporations. The more hacking only becomes a point of technical disruption of inconvenience is what makes it fall within anarchist Peter Gelderloos’ concept of nonviolence protecting the state. Anything that is not directly affecting the functioning of the state must and should not be considered insurrectionary. It still may be anarchist, as nearly all non-insurrectionists will agree, but it would not remain comfortably under the insurrectionary umbrella. One of the things digital algorithms, and even artificial intelligence, set out to do is create conclusions based on predictability. In that sense, the only way for people to reclaim their autonomy is to be completely unpredictable. This is not only a way to counter form and “decency,” but to remind people that guerilla tactics, horizontalism, and asymmetric warfare too are examples of resistance the physical state does not know how to counter. The ways of organizing and thinking are completely different, which more often than not, has repeatedly proven to be one of the most effective ways of countering entrenched structures.

If “digital insurrectionary anarchism” is only inconveniencing authority and failing to create widespread antagonism, then much of contemporary hacktivism should not be considered insurrectionist. However, even if these hackers make the headlines, publicly embarrass elected officials, or temporarily pause operations, they still do have a justifiable place in society. Even if their results or effects were limited, it crushes the manufactured image of institutional invulnerability. In other words, no system or government’s dominance is uncontested. The question is not whether hacktivism has overthrown states or dismantled corporate monopolies, but whether it has revealed the instability beneath the systems that present themselves as permanent. In this sense, hacktivism has proven itself by demonstrating that digital authority, exactly like physical authority, depends heavily on perception. Institutions derive power not only from law, capital, and force, but from the belief that their systems are untouchable. These moments of institutional embarrassment may not constitute revolution, but they reflect the same anti-authoritarian impulse that has defined the insurrectionary struggle for generations. If nothing else, hacktivism proves that cyberspace has become one of the newest battlegrounds where the legitimacy of power can be contested. As Spanish insurrectionist Miguel Amorós writes, “our criticisms do not prevent us from recognizing their courage and our disagreements do not constitute an obstacle to our demand for their liberation.”[26]

Så kom Bresa-Litovsk-freden. Två månader förut, i december 1917, hade Trotzky tillbakavisat med en fin gest av nobel indignation den av Tyskland erbjudna freden på villkor som voro mycket fördelaktigare för Ryssland. "Vi föra intet krig, vi underskriva ingen fred!" hade han sagt, och det revolutionära Ryssland applåderade honom. "Ingen kompromiss med den tyska imperialismen, inga medgivanden" ekade det genom landet; och folket stod färdigt att försvara sin revolution ända till döds. Men nu fordrade Lenin ratificeringen av en fred som innebar det mest modlösa förräderi mot den större delen av Ryssland, Finland, Lettland, Lithauen, Vitryssland, Bessarabien - alla gingo över till den tyska inkräktaren och deras egen bourgeoisis förtryck och exploatering.

Lenins inflytande var starkt. Han segrade. Brest-Litovsk-freden ratificerades av den 4:de sovjetkongressen.

Det var Trotzky, vilken först försäkrade under avvisande av den tyska freden på de erbjudna villkoren i december 1917 att arbetarna och bönderna, inspirerade och beväpnade av revolutionen, skullem edelst guerillakrig besegra en invasionsarmé. Vänstersocialrevolutionärerna kallade nu till bonderesningar, till kamp mot tyskarna, övertygade att ingen skulle kunna besegra den revolutionära glöden hos ett folk som kämpade för bevarande av dess stora revolutions frukter! Arbetare och bönder, lyssnade till detta upprop, bildade militärdetachement och störtade till Ukrainas och Vitrysslands hjälp, tappert skridande mot de tyska inkräktarna. Trotzky befallde ryska armén att förfölja och undertrycka dessa friskaror.

Mordet på Mirbach följde härefter.

Det var det vänstersocialrevolutionära partiets protest och utmaning mot den preussiska imperialismen i Ryssland. Bolsjevikregeringen började vidta åtgärder till deras underkuvande, den hade nu en känsla av att stå i obligation till Tyskland. Dzerzhinsky, allryska utomordentliga kommissionens ledare, fordrade terroristernas utlämnande.

Det var en unik situation i revolutionsannalerna: ett revolutionärt parti med makt krävande av ett annat revolutionärt parti, med vilket det samarbetat, arrestering och bestraffning av en revolutionär för avdagatagandet av en imperialistisk regerings representant. Brest-Litovsk-freden hade ställt bolsjevikerna i den onaturliga ställningen av en gendarm för Tyskland. Vänstersocialrevolutionärerna besvarade Dzerzhinskys fordran med den senares arrestering. Denna handling och de väpnade skärmytslingarna, som följde därpå, (ehuru obetydliga i sig själva) voro helt och hållet utförda av de bolsjevikiska politikerna. De förklarade att det var ett försök av vänstersocialrevolutionära partiet att bemäktiga sig regeringstömmarna. De förklarade detta parti fågelfritt och dess utrotning började.

Denna bolsjevikiska metod och taktik var icke av tillfällig natur. Snart blev det klart att det är den kommunistiska statens ständiga politik att krossa varje slags yttring som icke var i överensstämmelse med regeringen. Efter ratificeringen av Brest-Litovsk-freden återkallade vänstersocialrevolutionärerna sina representanter i folkkommissariernas sovjet. Bolsjevikerna voro i besittning av den ensamma kontrollen över regeringen.

Under en och annan förevändning fullföljde de den mest godtyckliga och grymma undertryckning av alla de andra politiska partierna och rörelserna. Mensjevikerna och högersocialrevolutionärerna hade "likviderats" långt förut, tillsammans med den ryska bourgeoisin.

Nu var det de revolutionära elementens tur - vänstersocialrevolutionärerna, anarkisterna, de partilösa revolutionärerna.

Men dessas "likvidation" inbegrep mycket mer än undertryckandet av små politiska grupper. Dessa revolutionära element hade strängt förföljts, vänstersocialrevolutionärerna bland bönderna, anarkisterna huvudsakligen bland stadsproletariatet. Den nya bolsjeviktaktiken inneslöt systematisk utrotning av varje tecken till missnöje, förkvävandet av all kritik och tillintetgörandet av all självständig opinion eller ansträngning.

Med denna fas inträdde bolsjevikernas diktatur över proletariatet, såsom det populärt karaktäriserades i Ryssland.

author: Luis Feliz Leon
title: Film Review: A Portrait of How Workers Build a Strike
content:
“Who Moves America” is touring the U.S., with upcoming screenings across the West Coast, Northeast, and South. See when it’s coming to your town, or request a screening, 

here

.




In the new documentary 

“Who Moves America,”

 filmmaker Yael Bridge offers a window into the working-class culture of one of the country’s largest unions, the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, at United Parcel Service (UPS) in 2023.




It’s a rare and moving portrait of a massive, diverse group of workers building themselves into a fighting force, who then must wrestle with a different version of victory than they expected.


We watch as 340,000 Teamsters gear up for a potential strike against package giant United Parcel Service, the largest private-sector union contract in North America. Behind the wheel in brown trucks and along conveyor belts in warehouses, their working conditions are grueling and dangerous: at the time, two drivers had died in the past year from sweltering heat.




If they strike, their market leverage from moving 6 percent of the country’s gross domestic product means they can cripple the company’s profits and send shock waves across the economy.




The last time UPS Teamsters struck was in 1997; grainy home video and archival footage from that strike is interspersed throughout the documentary. The film’s contemporary subjects—from strike veterans to workers who weren’t even born yet—reference that walkoff as a touchstone in their lives, Teamsters history, and the American labor movement.




‘REPLACE YOU WITH A HAND TRUCK’




Spoiler alert: A 2023 strike isn’t called. Members all across the country are chomping at the bit to walk off the job, but after the union reaches a tentative agreement that even the most strike-ready militants acknowledge is a much stronger pact than previous ones, the members ratify the contract 5 to 1. (The five-year contract is set to expire on July 31, 2028.)




So the film is deprived of the sexy stuff of massive picket lines and physical confrontations with strikebreakers. A simpler narrative of heroic workers taking on greedy bosses gives way instead to a thornier one, as workers who were charged up to strike wrestle with what it means to win these gains without walking off the job.




From covering the campaign, I recall workers seething in anger from the pandemic-era abuses and risks they were exposed to and wanting to stick it to management. “I can still vividly remember getting my drivers together outside the building when the pandemic first started and the fear on their faces that somehow they could bring the virus to their children,” delivery driver Greg Kerwood, a steward in Somerville, Massachusetts, told 

Labor Notes

 at the time. 




“Part of what happened when people got out there with the practice pickets was they started to feel a sense of their own power,” Kerwood said. “The shackles were beginning to break. And they were starting to stand up and hold their shoulders straight and put their heads high and start to take some pride in their own self-respect in the workplace.”




That pent-up anger meant high expectations that a strike could temporarily rebalance workers’ relationships to their management tormentors. “This company hates you,” Teamsters Local 804 President Vinnie Perone says in the documentary. “If they could, they would replace you with a hand-truck.”




REAL ORGANIZING, ON SCREEN




Like the 2024 documentary “Union,” which chronicled the stunning organizing victory of Amazon workers at a fulfillment center on Staten Island in New York City  (producer Mars Verrone was involved in both films), “Who Moves America” shows what organizing looks like in practice in the buildup to a potential strike.




Teamsters President Sean O’Brien makes a number of appearances, deploying tough talk against UPS that gets under corporate investors’ and executives’ skins. He’s recorded at his stately desk at Teamsters headquarters in Washington, D.C., relating an anecdote of how a fellow union leader was surprised by the size of the UPS National Negotiating Committee, which was expanded by appointing rank-and-file members.




But the film spends the bulk of its time tracking not the moves at the union’s top but the ferment below. O’Brien is on screen less than the Teamsters discussing the contract and developing working-class leadership across locales, from a beach in Southern California to the streets of Louisville, Kentucky, and Brooklyn, New York.




We see fellow Teamsters talking at a diner across generations, dipping French fries in ketchup while chatting about how the contract could change their lives (including, one part-timer half-jokingly hopes, being able to afford a ticket to a Beyoncé concert). We see them shifting in their chairs during trainings at union halls and local sandwich shops, debating how to engage part-time package sorters in the contract campaign and where best to position picketers if and when the strike comes, and then whether the contract is good enough to warrant a yes vote.




LOWER FREQUENCIES




None of that happens spontaneously. The work of working-class organization involves weaving relationships into dense knots across lines of race and immigration status and age and job type, over and over again, forming a rank-and-file network that can take action. As shown in the film, that’s largely the work of the rank-and-file movement Teamsters for a Democratic Union.




TDU members and staff led online and in-person meetings for tens of thousands of UPS Teamsters across the country. Member leaders are seen collecting strike pledge cards, explaining contract demands, answering questions, and training co-workers to carry out workplace actions to put pressure on the company.




We meet Tim Peppers, a veteran of the 1997 strike, and Justin Alo from San Marcos, California, who is classified as a “22.4” worker, a reference to a section of a previously ratified UPS contract that created a classification of drivers who deliver packages for less pay than regular drivers with fewer contractual protections.




Alo has banded together with his co-workers to hold meetings at a local coffee shop to learn about their contract and prepare for the fight with UPS. We watch him and his wife talk with quiet anxiety about saving money in case he goes on strike, and their decision to pause their autistic son’s daily therapy sessions if Alo strikes because they won’t be able to afford them. That’s the stuff of real sacrifice, multiplied an untold number of times over by every worker considering a strike.




Alo is among the newbies, but he has helped organize these social gatherings alongside other UPS Teamsters with experience in the 15-day 1997 strike. That strike was transformative, reducing the reliance on subcontractors and boosting wages. But it also contained a concession: a five-year contract term, instead of three or four years. Now that the contract terms are longer, workers have fewer opportunities to strike than earlier generations did.




As workers debate whether to ratify their tentative agreement, a worker in California compares the momentum they built up to a wind-up toy car whose wheels are charged up but never allowed to take off. Workers wonder if, by not striking, they’ll miss out on the transformative experience their co-workers had in 1997, especially as the institutional memory fades once veterans of that strike begin to retire.




As A. J. Muste once wrote, “the trade union seeks to combine within itself two extremely divergent types of social structure, that of an army and that of a democratic town meeting.” In the lead-up to a strike, these divergent forms can temporarily work together through the picket line discipline of the union as a combat organization and the union hall as a democratic town meeting where workers deliberate about their contract demands. “Who Moves America” takes us to the lower frequencies where workers educate each other on what it means to move like a class.




A longer version of this review appeared on 

Lower Frequencies

 and 

Jacobin
