author: Unknown
title: Kevin Carson - Juneteenth, and the Right-Wing Conception of “Freedom”
content:
Author

: Kevin Carson

Title

: Juneteenth, and the Right-Wing Conception of “Freedom”

Date

: November 18th, 2024

Source

: https://c4ss.org/content/59964




 Billy Binion (“

Juneteenth is a Celebration of Freedom

,” 

Reason

, June 19) writes that, despite widespread right-wing aversion to Juneteenth as a holiday, the GOP “in some sense still fashions itself as the party of freedom.” 




 Matt Yglesias is most famous these days for his almost daily garbage takes; but years ago, back when the Republican progression toward fascism had gone no further than the Tea Party stage, he aptly commented on the 

incoherence

 of right-wing conceptions of freedom: 







 I continue to be fascinated by the way in which the rhetoric of “freedom” is always so closely associated with authoritarian populist nationalist movements. Absolutely nothing in the imagery of the video or the policy agenda of the Republican Party is suggestive of freedom. It’s full of flags and grim-faced folks and bourgeois respectability and military jets flying in tight formation. It’s an ad from a conservative politician that’s about exactly what an ad from a conservative politician ought to be about — about preserving a way of life against Muslims, freeloaders, sexual deviants, and other threats. 







 Whenever the white, right-wing, and Evangelical demographic talks about its “freedoms,” you can get a good sense of what they mean by “freedoms” by translating it into “white folkways.” Whatever substantive content “freedom” has for them is wrapped up in a haze of 90s CMT video imagery about little white frame churches, porch swings, pickups, checkered picnic table cloths, gingham, flags, guns, and Murca HOO-raw! 




 And the “threats” to these “freedoms” — i.e. white folkways — all boil down in one way or another to anything that undermines their status as the American cultural default by allowing people who are unlike them to exist in public: e.g. the very sight of multiracial commercials or TV sitcoms, trans people on beer cans, people speaking Spanish or same-sex couples holding hands in public, or schools teaching the actual history of slavery and acknowledging the existence of LGBT people. 




 In short, their idea of “freedom” has about the same substantive content as “Freiheit” in Nazi ideology. Remember when Sarah Palin talked about the “pro-America parts of America”? Just change “the people” to “Volk,” and we’re getting into some serious 

deja vu

. 




 This is true as well for much of the “libertarian” right. Witness, for example, 

this tweet

 from the Libertarian Party of New Hampshire’s Twitter account: “Anyone who celebrates Juneteenth should be deported from America.” This is far from atypical for them. They subsequently 

tweeted

: “Degenerates must be expelled in order to maintain a libertarian social order.” 




 You might think “libertarian” is an odd self-designation for people who object to a holiday celebrating the end of slavery, and who call for physically removing “degenerates” from society. The Mises Caucus, which controls both the national and New Hampshire Libertarian Party organisations, has about as much to do with actual liberty as the crossed-hammer stormtroopers in “

Waiting for the Worms

” (a song which LPNH probably has on repeat — probably only a matter of time until they adopt “final solution to strengthen the strain” as an official motto). But it’s nothing new. 




 There has long been an authoritarian strain on the “libertarian” right. This was true at least as long ago as 1969, when Walter Block enthusiastically defended “

voluntary slavery

” — along with the implied right of the slave owner to 

beat, torture, and mutilate

 the person who “voluntarily” sold themselves into slavery — as a logical implication of self-ownership and freedom of contract. 




 And this has become even more true in recent years, starting with the rise of the so-called “paleolibertarian” movement of Ron Paul and Lew Rockwell in the 90s. The intellectual gray eminence — or Joseph Goebbels, if you prefer — of this movement is Hans Hermann Hoppe, and its primary institutional home is the Ludwig von Mises Institute. Unsurprisingly, the Hoppean/paleo community includes under its umbrella the ruling Mises Caucus of the Libertarian Party, and Walter Block (who continues to 

advocate “voluntary slavery”

 

to this day

). 




 The essence of the Hoppean project is to create an authoritarian society — their ideal society is one in which every square foot of land is privately appropriated by predominantly white, Christian owners, no one can exist anywhere without permission from the land-owners, and “degenerates” and socialists are “physically removed” or “helicoptered” in order to purge the society of those who are incompatible with its “libertarian” character — but to do so entirely in ways that are fully consistent with self-ownership and the non-aggression principle. 




 It’s odd that people whose substantive values are thoroughly authoritarian, and who have no have no sympathy whatsoever with human agency or human flourishing, even care about consistency with formal “libertarian” principles… but here we are. 




 And here’s where we also are: If you want to know anything about actual human freedom and liberty, don’t listen to right-wingers.

title: Historic Trees Demolished, Land Defenders Arrested and New Treesit at US-Mexico Border
content:
Lochiel, AZ – In the early hours of October 5, Border Patrol agents raided the anti-border camp called “Tierra Libre” on the U.S.-Mexico Border near Lochiel, Arizona. An estimated 200 Border Patrol Agents invaded camp — entering the tracts of private property along the border that had long-shielded land defenders from the authority of the federal agents — and cut down the ancient Grandmother tree that campers had attempted to protect. Less than 24 hours later, land defenders established a new treesit in the immediate path of construction, this time on the Mexican side of the border. 




Although Border Patrol agents were parked along the easement throughout the night, a masked land defender snuck past them and scrambled up into the 50-foot-tall Grandmother tree and into the platform already built there. “This brave warrior climbed right up there,” said Pablo, a land defender who was at camp Tuesday morning. “The new treesit is very much blocking construction, as long as someone is in that tree they will not be able to build their wall.”




Past Coverage: 

Treesit Blocks US-Mexico Border Wall Construction for Six Weeks in Arizona




According to multiple sources on the ground who spoke with Unicorn Riot, Border Patrol agents entered private property Monday morning, refusing to show evidence of a warrant allowing them to do so, and refusing to explain what authority granted them that right. 




Agents shoved and tackled campers, pointed guns at them, stomped on their necks, and pushed several campers into the barbed wire fence that marks the private property line. One land defender who goes by the name Hoops showed wounds on her hands and wrist to members of the media that she said resulted from agents twice her size tackling her into the barbed wire fence. 




“Border Patrol has been coming onto private property since yesterday morning,” said Rachel, a land defender who spoke with Unicorn Riot about the raids. “No warrants are shown, as far as we can tell there’s no legal ground for them to come onto private property. It seems like they’re pushing through the construction process quickly and will deal with the law later.” 




Construction workers protected by Border Patrol agents used a cherrypicker to cut branches off of the 200-year-old cottonwood Grandmother tree, in which a treesit had been sustained for 71 days. Agents then removed a treesitter stationed to protect the tree from border wall construction. 




Within minutes, the Grandmother tree was felled and the treesit destroyed. Ten land defenders were arrested, including the treesitter. Ten more were cited and released. 













BREAKING: For Trump’s wall, Border Patrol cut down the sacred Grandmother Tree, a more than 200-year-old Cottonwood on private property + Indigenous territory.

The tree sitter and many others have been arrested, according to activists @ Tierra Libre anti-border wall camp in AZ https://t.co/oYbG1fasNH

— Mike Ludwig / @mludwig.bsky.social (@ludwig_mike) 

October 5, 2026













“The Grandmothers live inside us now,” said an anonymous land defender who spoke on behalf of those at camp. “We make this promise: this wall will not be built! We will tear down what has already severed the land and our peoples, piece by piece.” 




Land defenders established the new treesit in the tall cottonwood tree that land defenders had briefly occupied in August, early on in the campaign. Facing pressure from Border Patrol and Mexican State Police, the treesit had been vacated. It remained unoccupied for over six weeks – until today. 













 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

View this post on Instagram

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

A post shared by Max Granger (@mxgrxngxr)
















Shortly after the treesit was reoccupied Tuesday morning, Border Patrol responded in force, confronting land defenders and attempting to push them back off the easement road that runs along the border. 




In the midst of that confrontation, at least five protesters were arrested and taken into custody and five more were charged and released. The situation is actively developing. 




“We stand strong and will not be deterred by state violence or intimidation,” said an unnamed spokesperson for Tierra Libre in a press release emailed to media. “We call on all people of ceremony, all people of conscience, to come join us now in La Noria and Lochiel, to protect the land, to protect the sacred.”













 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

View this post on Instagram

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

A post shared by Tierra Libre Lochiel (@tierralibre_noborders)
















The raids came just a week after notices posted near the camp announced that the U.S. Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management had issued a new order, restricting “all forms of access and entry” to the designated areas and making it illegal for civilians to enter areas owned by those federal agencies adjacent to the border wall. 




The order was effective as of September 29 and remains in effect until January 20, 2029. The restricted areas include the entire Roosevelt Reservation in the Tucson sector, the 60-foot-wide stretch of land that runs along the entire U.S.-Mexico border. 




The order also deputizes Border Patrol to make arrests enforcing the order.




Camp, however, is on private property, not on federally managed land. Land defenders have permission to use the land, and have been in friendly negotiations for months with the families who have owned these parcels of land for generations. 




“If they can come onto private property here, they can come onto private property anywhere,” said Rachel. “If we’re not safe here, if masked federal agents can act with impunity here, then no one is safe anywhere in this country.” 




One family member, Belicia Lynch, expressed her solidarity with the land defenders in the midst of the raid on her family’s property. “As a De La Ossa family member, I just want to thank you guys for being out there to not only protect the Grandmother tree, but the land itself that many animals and bugs inhabit,” she said in a message on Signal, a private messaging app. 







“No matter what has happened today, they can’t erase the history you all have created and contributed to. Whatever propaganda they decide to spew will not compare to the coverage that you have witnessed firsthand and showcased to the world. Continue to spread truth and fight for what you believe in no matter the outcome.”







Cover image by Niko Georgiades for Unicorn Riot with images from Sonoran Desert Press Office.

author: Christoph Morich
title: Theodor W. Adorno – Studien zum autoritären Charakter
content:
(Teil 1): Die Entwicklung der F-Skala zur Untersuchung des potentiell faschistischen Individuums




„Die Erfahrung aber und die Geschichte lehren, ist dieses, daß Völker und Regierungen niemals etwas aus der Geschichte gelernt und nach Lehren, die aus derselben zu ziehen gewesen wären, gehandelt haben.“ resümiert Hegel in seinen Vorlesungen zur Philosophie der Geschichte über das Verhältnis der gegenwärtigen Praxis zur eigenen Vergangenheit. Das gilt nicht nur für jenen Teil der Gesellschaft, der sein Glück nun wieder in der Hingabe an die deutsche Volksgemeinschaft zu suchen scheint, sondern lässt sich auch an den Reaktionen der bürgerlichen Öffentlichkeit beobachten, die einmal mehr nicht verstehen kann, warum um alles in der Welt nun schon wieder der Faschismus um die Ecke kommt. Die AFD scheint plötzlich vom Himmel gefallen zu sein und bedroht nun unsere demokratische Gesellschaft, in der doch bisher im Groben und Ganzen immer alles gut lief. Monchi, der Sänger einer Punk-Band, erinnert die deutsche Bevölkerung daran, dass wir schließlich nicht in Bangladesch leben, während Friedrich Merz darüber sinniert, wie er die Menschen emotional besser mitnehmen könnte, wenn er ihren Lebensstandard dem von Bangladesch annähert. Insgeheim haben sich längst alle politischen Akteure darauf geeinigt, dass die Geflüchteten selbst das ursächliche „Problem“ sind und die Lösung scheint nun darin zu bestehen, die rassistischen Forderungen der AFD einfach selbst umzusetzen. Zwischen Olaf Scholz‘ Ankündigung im Jahr 2023, nun endlich im großen Stil abzuschieben, bis zum Wahlslogan der AFD – „Wir werden abschieben, bis die Startbahn glüht.“ -, der ihr zum Wahlsieg verhalf, passt kaum ein Blatt Papier. „Migration steuern, bevor es die Falschen tun.“ brachte die FDP diese Politik in ihrem Europawahlkampf 2024 sehr prägnant auf den Punkt, die kaum deutlicher machen könnte, dass die qualitative Differenz zwischen Faschismus und bürgerlicher Gesellschaft relativ ist – die Faschisierung ist ein Prozess. „Der Schoß ist fruchtbar noch aus dem das kroch.“, heißt es dazu in einem Theaterstück von Bertolt Brecht. Die umfassendste Untersuchung zum sozialpsychologischen Schoß des Faschismus in der bürgerlichen Gesellschaft sind wohl die Studien zum autoritären Charakter, die als Reaktion auf den deutschen Nationalsozialismus in den USA durchgeführt wurden. Kein Weg führt an ihnen vorbei, wenn wir das sozialpsychologische Fundament unserer Gegenwart wirklich begreifen wollen.




Die Studien zum autoritären Charakter




Die Studien zum autoritären Charakter sind in ihrer Systematik ein Meisterwerk dialektischen Denkens, das einen bei der Lektüre verstehen lässt, was es bedeutet, einen Gegenstand analytisch zu erfassen, anstatt bei einer oberflächlichen Betrachtung zu verweilen. Sie heben sich in ihrer systematischen Ausarbeitung auch von den sonstigen Schriften Adornos zur Psychoanalyse ab, in denen er sonst oft recht eklektisch auf die Schriften Freuds Bezug nimmt. Das mag vor allem der Zusammenarbeit mit den drei weiteren Autoren der Studie geschuldet sein, deren Mitwirkung an der Studie in der heutigen Rezeption meist unter den Tisch fällt. Die Studien wurden unter der Leitung von Else Frenkel-Brunswik, Daniel J. Levinson, R. Nevitt Sanford und Theodor W. Adorno in einem mehrstufigen Verfahren, das Fragebögen, empirische Erhebungen, ausführliche Interviews und psychoanalytische Deutungsverfahren miteinander verknüpfte, zwischen 1944 und 1949 in Kalifornien durchgeführt. Entgegen eines sehr weit verbreiteten Vorurteils gegenüber dem Konzept des „autoritären Charakters“ geht es in den Studien ebenso wenig wie bei Reich oder Fromm darum, das Bewusstsein der Individuen zum eigentlichen Motor der Geschichte zu erklären. Von einer solchen Psychologisierung grenzen sich die Autoren in der Einleitung unmissverständlich ab: „Man scheint sich heute wohl bewusst, dass es in erster Linie von der Situation der mächtigen ökonomischen Interessengemeinschaften abhängt, ob antidemokratische Propaganda hierzulande eine beherrschende Rolle spielen wird oder nicht, ob jene, mit Vorbedacht oder nicht, sich dieses Instrumentes bedienen, um ihre Machtstellung aufrechtzuerhalten.“ (Adorno et al.) Auch heute dient die Faschisierung der herrschenden Klasse dazu, ihre Interessen gegen einen Großteil der Bevölkerung durchzusetzen. Daran lässt die mächtige ökonomische Interessensgemeinschaft des Silicon Valley, verkörpert von Wahnsinnigen wie Elon Musk und Peter Thiel, nicht den geringsten Zweifel. Dass die Studien sich auf die Analyse der individuellen Psychologie beschränken, um zu erklären, wie der Faschismus zum Massenphänomen werden konnte, heißt nicht, dass die vorrangige Bedeutung der in der Geschichte wirkenden Kräfte geleugnet wird.




Ein weiteres Missverständnis, das über lange Zeit vor allem in der antideutschen Rezeption kultiviert wurde, liegt in der Einengung des Untersuchungsgegenstandes der Studien auf die Frage des Antisemitismus. Das Forschungsinteresse gilt „dem potentiell faschistische[n] Individuum, ein Individuum, dessen Struktur es besonders empfänglich für antidemokratische Propaganda macht“ (Adorno et al.). Es geht in den Studien also nicht darum, lediglich jene Personen zu untersuchen, die offen antisemitische Positionen vertreten, sondern darum, die Aspekte der Charakterstruktur zu begreifen, die Individuen empfänglich für faschistische Positionen machen, die in einer feindseligen Haltung gegenüber allen Minderheiten ihren Ausdruck findet. Es geht um die Untersuchung des fremdenfeindlichen Subjekts, dessen Objekt über den Verlauf der Geschichte variabel ist. „Die Bereitschaft, feindselige Äußerungen gegenüber Minoritäten zu akzeptieren, kann sehr wohl als mehr oder weniger einheitlicher Zug angesehen werden.“ (Adorno et al.) Auch rassistische Ideologien haben einen Zeitkern. Da die Untersuchungen in den 40er Jahren durchgeführt wurden, nimmt der Antisemitismus natürlich eine zentrale Rolle in den Studien ein. Auch der Ort der Befragungen ist ein spezifischer. Da die Untersuchungen an einer US-amerikanischen Population durchgeführt wurden, ist die Frage des Antisemitismus eng mit der Frage nach der Aufnahme von Geflüchteten verknüpft. Die ablehnende Haltung gegenüber jüdischen Geflüchteten, die von vielen Beteiligten geäußert wurde, war dabei durchaus in Einklang mit der US-amerikanischen Einwanderungspolitik. Nach Angaben des US-Holocaust Memorial Museum wurde hunderttausenden jüdischen Menschen während des Nationalsozialismus die Einreise in die USA verweigert. Ein großer Teil von ihnen wurde später in deutschen Konzentrationslagern ermordet. „Migration steuern“ würden wir diese US-amerikanische Praxis heute wohl nennen.




Die Methode der Studie




Die Autoren der Studie gingen in ihren Untersuchungen davon aus, dass autoritäre Charakterzüge in der US-amerikanischen Gesellschaft, entsprechend dem Selbstverständnis einer freiheitlichen Gesellschaft, nur in den wenigsten Fällen durch ein offenes Bekenntnis zu faschistischen Positionen zum Ausdruck kommen. Der Raum dessen, was gesagt werden darf, wird durch das gesellschaftliche Klima abgesteckt, das in den USA der Nachkriegszeit ein anderes war als auf dem letzten Reichsparteitag in Deutschland. Es war daher davon auszugehen, dass die Teilnehmenden sich in ihren Aussagen entsprechend der gesellschaftlichen Konventionen selbst zensieren. Daher „waren spezielle Techniken erforderlich, um Oberflächenmeinungen, -attitüden und -wertvorstellungen beobachten zu können, um ideologische Trends offenzulegen, die nur in indirekten Manifestationen an die Oberfläche gelangen, die im Unbewussten wirkenden Charakterkräfte ans Licht zu bringen.“ (Adorno et al.) Um das „potentiell faschistische Individuum“ zu erfassen, wurde die psychoanalytische Deutung zum essentiellen Instrumentarium der Untersuchung. Dafür wurden zunächst Fragebögen entwickelt, die Antisemitismus, Ethnozentrismus, politisch-wirtschaftlichen Konservatismus erfassen sollten, um den Pool an geeigneten Personen für ausführliche Interviews einzugrenzen.




In klinischen Interviews wurden später Teilnehmer:innen ausgewählt, die auf der Ethnozentrismus-Skala zu den 25 % mit den höchsten und den 25 % mit den niedrigsten Punktwerten gehörten. Diese Interviews wurden mit der Absicht durchgeführt, die Psychodynamik der Teilnehmenden mit stark ausgeprägten autoritären Charakterzügen genauer zu erfassen, die Teilnehmenden mit niedrigen Punktwerten galt daher als geeignetste Vergleichsgruppe. „Das Interview wurde so geführt, dass das erworbene Material Rückschlüsse auf die tieferen Schichten in der Charakterstruktur des Befragten erlaubte.“ (Adorno et al.) Im ideologischen Teil des Interviews sollten die Teilnehmenden dazu bewegt werden, sich möglichst spontan und im freien Gespräch zu Themen wie Politik, Religion, Minderheiten, Einkommen und Beruf zu äußern. Im klinisch-genetischen Teil des Interviews sollte dann genauere Informationen über die gegenwärtige Situation und die Vergangenheit der Teilnehmer:innen erfragt werden. Außerdem erhielten sie die Gelegenheit, sich in freier Darstellung über eigene Gefühle, Wünsche und Ängste, ihre Beziehungen zu Eltern und Mitmenschen sowie über Vorstellungen zur eigenen Kindheit und Umweltbedingungen zu äußern.




Die F-Skala




Aus den Fragebögen und den Interviews wurde schließlich die berühmte F-Skala als Instrument zur Messung des potentiell antidemokratischen Charakters entwickelt. Sie misst die Charakterstruktur, die den Ausprägungen auf der Antisemitismus-, Ethnozentrismus und politisch-wirtschaftlichen Konservatismus-Skala genetisch zugrunde liegt, also auf einer tieferliegenden Ebene der Charakterstruktur zu finden ist. Die Autoren betonen, „dass von einer Charakterstruktur nur insoweit gesprochen werden kann, als die Kohärenz der Skalensätze sich besser auf der Grundlage einer inneren Struktur als auf der äußerer Assoziation erklären lässt.“ (Adorno et al.). Unter Charakter wird dabei „eine mehr oder weniger beständige Organisation von Kräften im Individuum, die in den verschiedenen Situationen dessen Reaktionen und damit weitgehend das konsistente Verhalten – ob verbal oder physisch – bestimmen“ (Adorno et al.) verstanden. Die Charakterstruktur bildet sich in der Kindheit heraus und bleibt im Erwachsenenalter weitgehend resistent gegenüber Veränderungen.

Die F-Skala definiert sich durch insgesamt neun Variablen, mit denen „ein in der Charakterstruktur verborgener Trend“ (Adorno et al.) gemessen werden kann, die einen empirisch eindeutig nachweisbaren Zusammenhang mit der Übernahme antisemitischer, rassistischer und faschistischer Positionen aufweisen. Entsprechend der psychoanalytischen Theorie über die Bedeutung frühkindlicher Erfahrungen, werden diese Charakterzüge durch die familiäre Erziehung und die Erfahrungen mit wichtigen Bezugspersonen im Laufe der Entwicklung des Kindes erworben. Die Autoren knüpfen dabei an die Erkenntnisse der marxistischen Sozialpsychologie zur Familie als „Struktur- und Ideologiefabrik“ (Wilhelm Reich) bzw. „psychologische Agentur der Gesellschaft“ (Erich Fromm) an. Die patriarchale Familienstruktur ist die „Keimzelle des Faschismus“ (Max Horkheimer), in der die autoritären Charakterzüge heranreifen.




Konventionalismus, Anti-Intrazeption, Stereotypie und Aberglaube




Die Weltwahrnehmung des autoritären Charakters ist einfach, der des Kleinkindes verwandt. Er verfügt nur über eine gering ausgebildete Instanz des Gewissens, die in der Lage wäre, nach ausdifferenzierten internen Normen die Realität zu prüfen und ein kritisches Verhältnis zur eigenen Umwelt zu entwickeln. Stattdessen klammert er sich an die konventionellen Normen der Gesellschaft, denen er sich bedingungslos anpasst. Wer davon abweicht, ist ihm verdächtig. „[D]ie am stärksten Angepassten hegen demzufolge die stärksten Vorurteile“ (Adorno et al.) Das ist insbesondere „charakteristisch für den Mittelstand“ (Adorno et al.). Die Beschäftigung mit dem eigenen Gefühlsleben, Emotionen, Phantasien und Sehnsüchten lehnt er ab, da sie die starren Kategorien seiner Wahrnehmung der Welt gefährden könnten. „Daher mag er ‚Neugier‘ nicht, will er nicht wissen, was die Menschen fühlen und denken und lehnt er unnötiges ‚Geschwätz‘ ab.“ (Adorno et al.) Alles Menschliche wird entwertet. In der Forderung, „im großen Stil abschieben“ (Olaf Scholz) zu wollen, wird die Verdinglichung alles Menschlichen zur Manövriermasse deutlich, die für den autoritären Charakter typisch ist. Die AFD und die „bürgerliche Mitte“ streiten derzeit nur noch über die Quantitäten ihrer Remigrationsphantasien, nicht über eine qualitative Differenz in der Frage, wie das zwischenmenschliche Zusammenleben nach moralischen Maßstäben zu organisieren sei. Die mangelnde Fähigkeit, über das eigene Innenleben zu reflektieren, wird oft durch einen Hang zu Stereotypie und Aberglauben kompensiert. „Stereotypie ist eine Form von Beschränktheit besonders in psychologischen und sozialen Fragen.“ (Adorno et al.) Was nicht in dieses Schema passt, muss aus dem Innenleben verdrängt werden und wird oftmals in die Außenwelt projiziert. Im Aberglauben entsteht so „eine Quelle der bizarren Vorstellungen zum Verhalten der anderen und zur Ableitung von Ereignissen aus Naturgegebenheiten.“ (Adorno et al.) Auch heute erfahren äußerst bizarre Vorstellungen von Religion weltweit ein sehr beängstigendes Comeback.




Sexualität, Destruktivität und Zynismus, Projektivität




In den Ergebnissen der Studien wurde deutlich, dass der autoritäre Charakter sich übermäßig mit bestimmten Fragen der Sexualität beschäftigte. Die Variable wird von den Autoren als ich-fremde Sexualität verstanden, die im Prinzip das Gegenteil eines aufgeklärten Verhältnisses zu Sexualität darstellt. „In dem starken Trieb, Übertreter des Sexualkodex zu züchtigen (Homosexuelle, Sittlichkeitsverbrecher) kann sich eine allgemeine Strafsucht äußern, die auf der Identifikation mit Autoritäten der Eigengruppe basiert, die aber auch darauf schließen lässt, dass die eigenen sexuellen Triebe des Individuums unterdrückt werden und in Gefahr sind, seiner Kontrolle zu entgleiten.“ (Adorno et al.)




Die heutige Obsession der Rechten mit den angeblichen Perversionen der queeren Community spricht Bände bezüglich der Aktualität dieses Syndroms. Die Unterdrückung der eigenen Triebbefriedigung führt entsprechend der psychoanalytischen Theorie zu starken aggressiven Impulsen. Diese führen einerseits zu einem zynischen Verhältnis zur Welt, durch die sich der autoritäre Charakter einer gewissen Verantwortung für die Konsequenzen seines Handelns entledigt. Andererseits ist diese Aggression der Ursprung der Destruktivität des menschlichen Handelns, deren Weg unter der autoritären Herrschaft bereitet wird. Was unterdrückt werden muss, wird projiziert. Die Projektion ist „ein Mittel, Es-Triebe ich-fremd zu halten, und kann als Zeichen der Unzulänglichkeit des Ichs betrachtet werden, seine Funktionen zu erfüllen.“ Sie ist der Ursprung jeder genozidalen Politik.




Machtdenken und „Kraftmeierei“, Autoritäre Unterwürfigkeit, Autoritäre Aggression




Die vereinfachte Wahrnehmung der Welt erfolgt für den autoritären Charakter anhand des Prinzips der Macht. „Nach unten treten, nach oben buckeln“ ist die geläufige Charakterisierung seines Verhältnisses zu seinen Mitmenschen. Die zwischenmenschlichen Beziehungen sind für ihn durch einen permanenten Kampf um Macht gekennzeichnet und werden „unter Kategorien wie stark – schwach, überlegen – unterlegen, Führer – Gefolgschaft, ‚Hammer und Amboß‘“ (Adorno et al.) betrachtet. So wie er die Macht verehrt, verachtet er die Schwäche. Sein Ich ist bis ins Erwachsenenalter schwach geblieben. Entsprechend den eigenen Erfahrungen mit züchtigenden Erziehungspersonen findet er in Führern und anderen Autoritäten die Möglichkeit, dieses Beziehungsmuster zu wiederholen. So wie einst dem Herrn Papa, kann er sich im Erwachsenenalter daran machen, nun Volk und Führer zu dienen. Die masochistische Unterwerfung wird durch den Sadismus gegenüber den Schwächeren kompensiert. Hierbei geht es, wie die Autoren der Studie betonen, nicht bloß um eine oberflächliche „Suche nach dem Sündenbock“, sondern um eine tieferliegende Dynamik in der Charakterstruktur. „[D]er Theorie der Verdrängung zufolge 

muss

 der Autoritäre seine Aggression aus innerer Notwendigkeit gegen die Fremdgruppe richten.“ (Adorno et al.) Da diese Dynamik in der Regel unbewusst bleibt, wird sie durch die moralisch verkümmerte Instanz des Gewissens oberflächlich rationalisiert. „Hat das Individuum erst einmal die Überzeugung gewonnen, dass es Menschen gibt, die bestraft werden sollten, hat es eine Bahn gefunden, in die es seine tiefsten aggressiven Triebe leiten und sich dennoch für durchaus moralisch halten kann.“ (Adorno et al.) Darin besteht der funktionale Charakter der Projektion. Die Deutschen töteten demnach in den Konzentrationslagern keine Unschuldigen, sondern die „Brunnenvergifter“ und „Volksschädlinge“. Soldaten töten in Kriegen keine Kinder, sondern „zukünftige Terroristen“. Die in Deutschland lebenden Afghanen wurden innerhalb weniger Jahre von den zu schützenden Opfern des Taliban-Regimes zu potentiellen „Messermördern“. Die eigenen Aggressionen werden rationalisiert, indem sie auf die Opfer projiziert werden. Die Täter imaginieren sich als die wahren Opfer.




Die Bedeutung der Potenzialität für die innere Dynamik der Faschisierung




Die Erkenntnisse, die sich aus den Studien zum autoritären Charakter ergeben, lassen sich in ihrer Bedeutung für eine Analyse der Faschisierung unserer Zeit kaum überschätzen. In Reaktion auf den Wahlsieg der AFD fanden auf Social Media verschiedene Statistiken Verbreitung, die darauf hinwiesen, dass ein Großteil der Deutschen bis heute 

nicht

 die AFD gewählt hat und damit immer noch zum „guten“ Teil der Gesellschaft gehören würde. Abgesehen von dieser recht willkürlichen Bestimmung des „guten“ Teils der Gesellschaft, sollte – und das scheint eine der zentralen Erkenntnisse der Studien zum autoritären Charakter – weniger Anlass zur Beruhigung geben, als wir es uns heute wünschen. Die Verbreitung autoritärer Charakterstrukturen lässt sich weder umfassend daran bemessen, wie viele Menschen eine faschistische Partei wählen, noch daran, wie viele Menschen offen rassistischen Positionen zustimmen. In den Studien zum autoritären Charakter geht es darum, mittels der F-Skala das „

potentiell

 faschistische Individuum“ ausfindig zu machen, also jene Menschen, die in der Zukunft leicht dazu bereit wären, faschistische und rassistische Positionen zu vertreten, wenn aufgrund eines geänderten politischen Klimas kein eigener Nachteil daraus mehr zu befürchten ist. Nur unter bestimmten politischen Bedingungen finden die autoritären Charakterzüge ihren Ausdruck in offen rassistischen Positionen. Auf unsere Zeit übertragen geht es also nicht nur um den bekennenden Neonazi des 3. Wegs, sondern um eine autoritäre Charakterstruktur, die auch heute in der „bürgerlichen Mitte“ weit verbreitet sein dürfte, deren Schoß, um mit Brecht zu sprechen, täglich fruchtbarer wird.




Der Migrant ist parteiübergreifend als Feindbild markiert und die wesentlichen Forderungen der AFD wurden in die eigenen Programme übernommen. Ulrich Siegmund stellt derweil offen zur Debatte, ob die Unvereinbarkeitsbeschlüsse der AFD mit irgendwelchen Neonazi-Gruppierungen wirklich noch zeitgemäß sind. Martin Sellners Buch zur „Remigration“ ist ganz bewusst als „Vorschlag“ formuliert, der durchaus Türen offenlässt, die eigene Politik zu brutalisieren, falls es mit der „freiwilligen Rückkehr“ und den Abschiebungen der „Asylanten“ und sonstigen Nicht-Deutschen in die „Musterstadt“ in Nordafrika, die er gerne bauen würde, überraschenderweise Komplikationen geben sollte. Die von Götz Kubitschek vorgegebene Taktik der „Provokation“, die darin besteht, den Raum des Sagbaren ständig zu erweitern, geht auf, weil sie in Teilen der Charakterstruktur der Bevölkerung Anklang findet, die durch die dauerhafte Propaganda über kriminelle Ausländer seitens der Massenmedien in den letzten Jahren täglich genährt wird. Die Potenzialität birgt die Gefahr einer inneren Dynamik der Eskalation, die auf beiden Seiten der Brandmauer in vollem Gange zu sein scheint. Dank der Politik der herrschenden Parteien der „Zeitenwende“ wird die AFD im Falle ihres Erfolgs nicht nur einen vollkommen militarisierten Staatsapparat, sondern auch eine zwangsrekrutierte Jugend und eine ideologisch kriegstüchtig indoktrinierte Bevölkerung vorfinden, die für die damit einhergehende Verarmung die Ausländer verantwortlich machen soll. In einer moralischen Niedertracht, die ihresgleichen sucht, befeuert die herrschende Klasse unter dem Deckmantel des Kampfes gegen Antisemitismus den antimuslimischen Rassismus, der der AFD zu ihren Wahlsiegen verhilft. Die öffentlichen Reaktionen auf den Wahlsieg der Linken in Berlin, von der Vorsitzenden der Grünen bis zu Ulf Poschardt, sprechen Bände über die geistige Verrohung des Bürgertums. Der Kampf gegen den Faschismus verläuft nicht entlang der „Brandmauer“, sondern entlang der realen politischen Fragen unserer Zeit, letztendlich an der Frage, ob wir unser Zusammenleben nach Maßstäben von Moral und Vernunft oder denen von Konkurrenz, Ausschluss und Gewalt organisieren wollen. Sozialismus oder Barbarei. Die Erkenntnisse der Sozialpsychologie gilt es für diese Kämpfe fruchtbar zu machen, denn entschieden werden sie letztendlich in den Schulen, Fabriken und auf der Straße und das machten Wilhelm Reich, Erich Fromm und Theodor W. Adorno immer wieder deutlich: nicht auf der Couch.

author: Vashti Fox
title: Three years of Palestine solidarity
content:
In mid-October 2023, after the first major march against Israel’s attacks on Gaza, the director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign UK, Ben Jamal, said to his staff: “We are probably going to need to be responding to this through marches until potentially Christmas”. He was wrong. The protests did not abate. As Israel’s offensive in Gaza continued, the number of actions across the world multiplied rapidly, eventually blossoming into one of the largest and most sustained antiwar movements in generations. From the world’s largest cities to the smallest hamlets, millions of voices rose in the same chant, with the same cadence: “Free, free Palestine!” 

The numbers tell part of the story. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), an international monitor, estimated that, in the three weeks after 7 October, some 3,700 demonstrations calling for a ceasefire and showing solidarity with Palestine took place in almost 100 countries and territories. In the first months of the genocide, most were in the Middle East and North Africa and were especially frequent in Yemen, Iran, Turkey and Morocco. In several of these countries, major government or religious institutions backed the demonstrations. 

In the West, however, governments were overwhelmingly hostile. In France, for instance, pro-Israel demonstrations were legal and encouraged. But the Macron government banned all Palestine solidarity demonstrations on 12 October, Interior Minister Gérald Darmanin determining that they were “likely to generate public disorder”. Nevertheless, on 22 October, 15,000 people took to the streets chanting “Gaza, Paris is with you!”

Two years after 7 October, ACLED provided data to SBS Australia showing 50,122 Gaza-related protests, the overwhelming majority in support of Palestinians—more than 40,000 Palestine solidarity events took place between 7 October 2023 and 5 September 2025. In contrast, just 3,120 pro-Israel demonstrations took place, more than two-thirds of them (2,159) held in Israel. 

What was striking about these actions was not simply their geographic breadth but their regularity. While the movement against the Iraq war in 2003 organised the largest single set of coordinated antiwar demonstrations in history, attracting an estimated 12 to 14 million people on 14 and 15 February, it did not sustain such mass mobilisations. The Palestine solidarity movement, by contrast, mobilised consistently over three years. London, for example, hosted the largest demonstrations in the UK, with 100,000 on 21 October, 70,000 on 28 October, 30,000 on 4 November, and 300,000 on 11 November 2003. Then, in 2024, 400,000 attended a demonstration on 9 March, followed by 200,000 again in March, April and October. 

Israel is a major participant in US-dominated imperial capitalist networks, and governments across the world (of all political colours) have been reluctant to break economically, politically or even symbolically from the Israeli-US coalition. Mass mobilisations, regardless of how mass and how determined they are, are unlikely on their own to force a government to break these relationships, especially in this new era of intensifying imperial competition. The stakes are simply too high. 

Nevertheless, the Palestine demonstrations were important for several reasons. They aimed not just to express moral outrage at Israel’s brutality but also to push their own governments for a change of policy. The demonstrations first demanded (with many local specificities) a ceasefire, and then, the longer the genocide continued, that their own governments break militarily, economically and diplomatically from Israel itself. 

Furthermore, the size and consistency of the demonstrations forced the issue of Gaza into the public debate. Governments responded differently to these protest movements, but most Western countries (with the notable exception of the USA) eventually backed the call for a ceasefire. (Of course, it was too late to stop the murder of tens of thousands of Gazans.). Some European governments, such as Spain and Ireland, moved more significantly in the direction of breaking ties with Israel, while others enacted more symbolic changes such as the recognition of Palestine and increased measures against Israeli settlements in the West Bank. None of these stances was anywhere near enough, but they likely would not have happened without the protest movement.

While protest movements’ impact on governments matters, the mobilisations were important for several other reasons: they helped build collective sensibilities and broke down the atomisation and sense of powerlessness that capitalism engenders. Of course, it is impossible to measure the exact impact of the mass demonstrations on each individual, but it doesn’t take much imagination to understand how transformative participation can be. 

From the Palestinian refugee discovering a sense of solidarity, to the young person attending a demonstration for the first time, to the older activists who had shouldered years of isolation, to the Muslims vilified by racist societies, the rallies offered a space to express collective social grievance. The demonstrations also helped, for a time, to politicise a section of society. People’s involvement in mass action inevitably raises political questions. Namely, why and how Israel could do what it did and get away with it. There were many answers offered to these questions, but the fact that they were asked at all was important and gave some space to socialists to offer answers and attempt to build a stronger and more radical anticapitalist movement. 

The forcing of Gaza into the centre of political life in many countries via mass demonstrations also compelled those not at the rallies to take a position on what was happening. The rallies made a visible, public and embodied argument about what attitudes should be taken. In this instance, the realities of the genocide and the mass demonstrations, and their flow-on effects, had an effect on broader attitudes toward Israel and Palestine. 

A YouGov poll in 2025 found that public support and sympathy for Israel in Western Europe had hit a record low, “with fewer than a fifth of respondents in six countries holding a favourable opinion of the country”. Similar attitudinal changes were recorded in many other countries. 

Changes in thinking were especially dramatic among Jewish populations in the US, the UK and Europe, particularly among the young. The shifts predated the genocide but accelerated during it. In 2020, 48 percent of Jewish Americans aged 18-29 said they were emotionally attached to Israel; by 2025, the figure had fallen to 36 percent of Jewish Americans aged 18-34. In 2024, 52 percent of Jews under 35 considered Israel’s military conduct acceptable; by 2025, half of Jewish Americans in this age group said Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Similar developments occurred in many Western countries. 

Jewish criticism of Israeli conduct in Gaza was expressed in the form of visible and often defiant campaigning. In the United States, Jewish Voice for Peace organised a range of public direct actions. For example, on 19 October 2023, 5,000 people attended a Jews Against Genocide rally in Washington, D.C. Organisers claimed this was the biggest ever mobilisation of Jews in support of Palestine in the US. The protest was followed by two dozen rabbis leading a sit-down of around 500 people in the Capitol rotunda. These defiant interventions in the political debate mattered. Jewish people protesting, and sometimes getting arrested, to oppose the genocide played a role in undermining the lie that to oppose Israel means hating Jews. 

The Australian movement simultaneously reflected global patterns and stood out for its size and consistency. On 8 October 2023, the New South Wales state Labor government lit up the Sydney Opera House in the colours of the Israeli flag. Just one day later, the Palestine Action Group (PAG), a coalition of left-wing Palestinians and socialists, organised a rally to march on the Opera House. In what would become a pattern, the demonstration provoked an almost universally hostile response from Australia’s political class. Labor Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the demonstration should not go ahead; opposition leader Peter Dutton described the protest as “despicable” and “unimaginable in modern Australia”. 

Despite the establishment ideological offensive, demonstrations in support of Palestine spread. By the next weekend, protests had spread to all the capital cities. In most cities, there had been preexisting Palestine solidarity groups, coalitions of socialists, Palestinians and Muslims, many of whom had been organising for years together. In Melbourne and Sydney, the protests against the Gaza genocide became weekly and ran for approximately 71 weeks before shifting to a monthly schedule in February 2025. Organisers in Victoria claimed Melbourne was the only city in the world to hold weekly rallies for so long. 

ACLED found that between October 2023 and September 2025, almost 906 pro-Palestinian protests took place in Australia. Thirty-four pro-Israel protests and another 31 protests that were either neutral or supported both sides also occurred during this time. Australia ranked ninth globally for pro-Palestinian protests and was fourth among non-Muslim majority countries. “When it comes to large-scale protests—those attracting more than 10,000 people—Australia is second only to Yemen in terms of the number of pro-Palestinian protests held”, SBS reported. 

Of course, the global movement for Palestine comprised much more than mass rallies. For more than two-and-a-half years, in country after country, local organising hubs, reading groups, film screenings, speaking tours, direct action groups, union fractions and school and university groups proliferated. 

To briefly detail a few of the many hundreds of such initiatives in Australia. Families for Palestine organised a 24/7 camp of hundreds outside the prime minister’s office in Marrickville, Sydney, in response to the government’s failure to break ties with Israel. “We have done everything that we could—we have sent emails, we did phone calls, we have sat outside weekly for four months, and we haven’t seen attention from Anthony to our demands”, one of the organisers told SBS. These families spent weeks sleeping, eating and educating people about Palestine. 

In Victoria, a movement of local groups emerged to force local councils to take a stand against the genocide and, in some cases, divest from Israel. An article in 

Red Flag

 reported that seven councils, representing more than one-fifth of Melbourne’s population, passed motions calling for an end to the Israeli onslaught. Socialist councillors played a key role in putting and then fighting for these motions. 

In the NSW city of Wollongong, hundreds of people regularly picketed Bisalloy, a steel company that manufactures steel plating used in tank armour used by the Israeli military. The longest of these pickets lasted 72 hours and was backed by the local teachers’ union. Similar pickets of docks and other Israeli-linked weapons manufacturers also occurred regularly.

Some in the cultural industries also joined the fight. In November 2023, cast members working for the Sydney Theatre Company wore keffiyeh scarves while taking their bows for their performances in Chekhov’s play 

The Seagull

. Board members claimed such actions were offensive, and the play was cancelled the next night. Similarly, in August 2024, during a recital with the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, classical pianist Jason Gilham introduced a piece called “Witness” by dedicating it to Palestinian journalists killed in Gaza. He said killing journalists to prevent them from reporting war crimes was a war crime itself. Following complaints, the MSO cancelled his next performance.

Many Australians also attempted to go to Gaza. Doctors, nurses, anaesthetists and others quit their jobs and joined convoys to help treat people in the Strip. They would spend weeks without much sleep in the living nightmare of broken and bloodied bodies to try and help. Others participated in the Global Sumud Flotillas, boats filled with activists determined to break the siege on Gaza. 

Students led some of the most defiant actions. At 4am on 17 April 2024, under a Spring moon, hundreds of students at Columbia University in New York unrolled tents, pushed pegs into damp lawns and established the first encampment for Palestine. The demand of the students was simple: their university should divest from the genocidal state of Israel. In the long tradition of student protests having an outsized influence, the spark lit at Columbia spread in the weeks that followed across the United States and then the world. Around 133 encampments were set up across the United States and over 100 more across Europe, Australia, the UK, Asia and Latin America. 

The Australian student encampments, inspired by the movement in the US, began at Sydney University five days after the students at Columbia pitched their tents. The initial and main organising force at Sydney University was students from Socialist Alternative. Our national spread allowed camps to rapidly spring up at many universities. The encampments became hubs of protest, education and debate. Students faced down university administrations, technocratic opposition and, in some instances, open Zionist aggression. Hundreds of students devoted over a month of their lives to the encampments. 

Student and youth mobilising, particularly those on the flotillas, had a particular impact in Italy. There, they helped to inspire an important section of the working class to initiate the 

blocchiamo tutto

 (“let’s block everything”) movement. On 22 September 2025, around half a million workers, students and activists mobilised across more than 80 cities, with dockworkers blocking ports, railway workers disrupting transport, students occupying universities and protesters shutting roads and highways. The action was initiated by grassroots unions and built around the demand to end Italy’s military and commercial cooperation with Israel. It was the first and most significant industrial action workers took against the genocide, and Italian unions were joined by other port workers across the Mediterranean. 

The movement against the genocide in Gaza has not won. The Israeli armed forces still occupy the territory. The ceasefire in Gaza has not brought liberation and the Strip remains rubble and dust. The Israeli state marches on in the West Bank. 

The genocide in Gaza and the war in Ukraine are the most visible expressions of a broader drive to militarisation and war, and this drive will not be stopped easily. Nevertheless, the Palestine solidarity movement should be remembered. More, it should be treasured. Millions of people across the world—students, workers, migrants, activists old and new—saw what our rulers find acceptable and said “no”. Millions saw the bodies wrapped in white, the children’s faces tattooed with tears and found it in themselves to stand against media slander, police aggression, legal restrictions and the weight of everyday life, to protest and campaign.

author: Editors
title: The world since 7 October
content:
Gaza is a generational touchstone and the key dividing line of politics in the West. It has laid bare the lies of the society we live in. It has exposed the genocidal bloodlust of the political right. And it has tested official “progressive” liberal politics, which has so often shown itself to be utterly hollow or cowardly. 

Anyone can now use Google Maps’ satellite view to see for themselves the apocalypse wrought by Israel and its allies over the past three years. Gaza City, once home to around 700,000 people, is a mostly bombed-out hellscape of ruins. The same is true of Beit Hanoun, Jabalia and other major centres. 

Rafah was a city thousands of years old, first recorded in an inscription from 1303 BCE. It has now been wiped off the face of the earth. Google still displays location markers for what once existed: “Kamal Adwan School”, “Playground”, “Musab bin Amir Western Mosque”, now a pile of rubble—“temporarily closed”, according to Google.

About 80 percent of structures in the Gaza Strip have been damaged; two-thirds of those are destroyed, according to the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees. Israel has used the so-called ceasefire since last December to systematically demolish remaining structures in the 60 percent of the Strip occupied by its forces, while killing another 1,200 Palestinians and herding around 2 million into unliveable tent cities in an ever-shrinking concentration camp.

When millions around the world poured into the streets to take a stand against this barbarism, they were viciously attacked and slandered by the institutions of our “democracy”, which have cried about “social cohesion” while turning a blind eye to the genocide and the growth of fascism they are helping to stoke.

The ruling class and the political establishment want to go after not just the Palestine movement, but the left more generally, which has naturally been at the centre of that movement. Hence the persistent effort to define antisemitism as a problem of the left rather than the far right, to ban the word “genocide”, and to criminalise opposition to the state carrying it out. 

This is not because loyalty to Israel itself is so important to the establishment, but because this loyalty test is a proxy for loyalty to Australian capitalism; a test of subservience to Australian billionaires, bosses and bureaucrats. 

Will you keep your mouth shut? Will you force that student to remove their keffiyeh? Will you cancel that author? Will you censor that article? Your answer will determine your place in Australian society. With troublemakers pilloried and purged, the apparatus can be hardened, ready to oversee the next war, the next genocide, the next round of cutbacks and layoffs, the next racist campaign against immigrants and refugees, as capitalism lurches towards its next crisis.

Despite the establishment’s intimidation and slander, and partly because of it, a seismic shift in attitudes has occurred. A July Pew Research poll found that 79 percent of Australians have a negative view of Israel, and just 4 percent have a strongly positive view. Hundreds of thousands have taken to the streets. The movement globally has been big, defiant, and defining for so many people who have thrown themselves into it. 

Yet it has not produced a widespread radicalisation or a sizable new left committed to confronting and overthrowing the capitalist system more broadly. There are many reasons for this, from the relative weakness of far-left organisations going into this period, to the weakness of the workers’ movement and spinelessness of trade union leaders.

The depth of feeling and moral commitment to the cause of Palestinian liberation is palpable, but the general political level remains low. Instead of generalising from the atrocity in Gaza to develop a critique of capitalism and imperialism, there is an obsession with the pro-Israel lobby, and there are illusions in reactionary opponents of the US and Israel such as the Iranian regime. Instead of open debate about the best strategies and tactics of resistance, recriminations focus on who is qualified to lead campaigns against the Australian government—not based on ideas or organisational skills, but on individuals’ identities. 

While our side sustained the largest anti-war movement in Australian history, the far right, rather than the left, has emerged as the most organised political force and is making all the running to push society in its desired direction: more racism, more militarism, more exploitation and fewer democratic rights.

We must continue to demand a free Palestine, while also throwing ourselves into the urgent fight against One Nation and the disgusting extreme right movement they are building. Ultimately, we must build a socialist left that offers a vision of hope, solidarity and a challenge to the whole system that underlies these horrors.

author: Nick Everett
title: How the media sold the Gaza genocide
content:
When 700,000 Rohingya were forced to flee Myanmar for Bangladesh amid widespread killings, sexual violence and village burnings in late 2017, an 

Age 

editorial pleaded for Australian government action: 

“There is a genocide happening today in Myanmar. Our government should urgently, repeatedly and loudly call for international intervention, and lead in imposing sanctions. We should send bountiful aid to the victims, and halt economic and diplomatic relations with Myanmar unless and until the savagery is stopped. All of us, as Australians, should shun travel to Myanmar for tourism or business. And our government should, as it did with the Syrian refugee crisis a few years ago, rapidly engineer an intake of Rohingya refugees.”

The 

Age

 didn’t wait for an International Court of Justice ruling before issuing its dire warning. It repeatedly used the term “genocide” to describe the Myanmar state’s atrocities despite no case of genocide having been brought before the ICJ at the time (it wasn’t until late 2019 that Gambia brought such a case and the ICJ still hasn’t ruled on it).

After three years of Israeli genocide in Gaza, no similar editorial can be found in the 

Age

, nor in any of the mainstream media in Australia. That is despite Israel having killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, including over 21,280 children who, 

according to

 a UN Commission of inquiry, have been targeted as “part of a deliberate strategy to destroy the future of the Palestinians in Gaza”. 

Indeed, “genocide” is a term that journalists—at the behest of their editors—routinely shun, despite the ICJ’s preliminary ruling back in January 2024 that there is a plausible case Israel is committing genocide. And when the term is used, we are reminded that Israel denies such claims, despite the UN Human Rights Council, the International Association of Genocide Scholars and numerous international human rights organisations having all concluded that Israel is indeed committing genocide in Gaza.

It is not just that the media fail to acknowledge this simple fact. For the past three years, they have been accessories to Israel’s crimes: dehumanising Palestinians, sanitising Israel’s atrocities, and silencing its critics. 

In his groundbreaking book 

How to Sell a Genocide

, author Adam Johnson sets out to “prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the genocide in Gaza was enabled, facilitated, and cheered by establishment US media providing cover for months of a nihilistic campaign of starvation, bombing, arbitrary detention, shooting and sexual violence”.  

Johnson’s approach is methodical and meticulous. His research draws on more than 12,000 articles and 5,000 TV clips from nine major outlets during the first year of the genocide, including the 

New York Times,

 the 

Washington Post, 

CNN

 

and

 

MSNBC

 

(now MSNOW

)

. He focuses on the liberal media because “there was a Democratic president in office when the genocide began in earnest, and support from Democrats in Congress and in the think-tank and media world was dispositive [decisive] in continuing said genocide during the given time of my study”.

Johnson argues that the “centre-left” (i.e., liberal) media engaged in “an elaborate framework of excuse-making, deflection, faux-savvy realpolitik, orientalist tropes, and glaring double standards … to justify the White House’s lockstep support for producing carnage everyone could easily witness across their social media timeline on a daily basis”.

“The primary role of [US liberal] media”, he argues, “was to rationalise, negotiate, obscure and ultimately, deny the most inconvenient of truths: a genocide carried out, defended and authorised by elite liberals and liberal institutions”.

Johnson demonstrates how the media were willing accomplices to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s efforts to portray 7 October as Israel’s “9/11 moment”, and to equate Hamas violence with that of ISIS, despite the two Islamist groups being implacable enemies. They did so by repeating and perpetuating a series of lies that emanated from Israeli media spokespeople: that Hamas beheaded 40 babies on 7 October 2023, that they targeted children and that they systematically used rape as a weapon of war.

Johnson cites evidence that the first claim was repeated, “without evidence of skepticism”, by more than a dozen journalists from outlets such as CNN, the 

New York Post

, CBS, Reuters, Sky News, MSNBC and NBC in the days following 7 October. The claim first appeared on an Israel-based i24NEWS 

report

, having been made by Israeli military personnel, but was soon debunked as false. So pervasive was this lie that President Biden felt comfortable 

telling

 a meeting of Jewish community leaders four days later that he had seen “confirmed pictures of terrorists beheading children”.  

A Biden spokesperson later walked back the claim, but only after footage of the meeting received global coverage. 

Reviewing the first month of US print and online media after 7 October, Johnson observes that Hamas was equated with ISIS 149 times, frequently accompanied by uncritical quotes from Israeli and US officials. The same group of publications mentioned “beheadings” ten times. Cable news outlets went further: Hamas was equated with ISIS on air by CNN commentators 350 times and by MSNBC 369 times. CNN mentioned “beheadings”, including non-existent beheadings of babies and infants, 77 times, while MSNBC did so 82 times.

On 13 October 2023, NBC ran a nightly news 

report

 revealing “chilling new details on how Hamas terrorists deliberately targeted Israeli schools and youth centers in their hunt for hostages”. In total, 36 Israeli children were killed on 7 October, making up 3 percent of the 1,195 victims. While this was certainly a war crime, it contrasts with Israel’s deliberate targeting of schools and densely populated apartment blocks in Gaza, where 30 percent of Palestinian victims have been children. 

Similarly, allegations of systematic rape as part of Hamas’ “terror strategy” were evoked ad nauseam by US media, and repeated by President Biden, without evidence. In contrast, when news broke in mid-2024 of Israeli 

sexual abuse

 of Palestinian prisoners, there was a marked silence. In Johnson’s study of reporting during the first three months of the Gaza genocide, and again during three months in late 2024, he observes 502 on-air mentions of Palestinians engaging in mass rape of Israelis by CNN and MSNBC, compared with just two mentions of Israel committing acts of rape against Palestinians. Similarly, while the 

New York T

imes, 

Washington Post

, 

Politico

 and 

Axios

 made mention of Palestinian rapes of Israelis 128 times, the same mastheads mentioned Israelis sexually abusing Palestinians just nine times.

This coverage served a discrete purpose, argues Johnston. It bought time for Israel and took pressure off the Biden administration when demands were increasing for a ceasefire in Gaza. The above examples formed part of a broader picture in which Palestinian violence was held up as something different and more threatening than years of Israeli military occupation and bombardment of Gaza to justify an unprecedented “military response”.

That the “military response” deliberately targeted schools, homes and hospitals did not matter, as a picture was well-established that Palestinians were less human, or “human animals” to use the pejorative terminology of Israeli spokespeople. Johnson cites examples of “Israeli children” versus “Palestinian minors” (sometimes in the same sentence), as well as emotive terminology such as “murderous,” “vicious” or “brutal” to describe the actions of Hamas, while such terminology was absent from reporting on Israel’s massive destruction of Palestinian lives, limbs and infrastructure. 

Alongside Palestinians’ dehumanisation, the media portrayed the White House and the US President as unable to shape Israel’s actions, let alone stop the war on Gaza. In his 2023 biography of Biden, 

The Last Politician

, Franklin Foer 

reported

 that, in May 2021, Biden put an end to Israel’s bombardment of Gaza with a single phone call. Netanyahu was obliged to accept an Egyptian-brokered ceasefire.

Israeli officials have been well aware of their dependence on US military hardware, which has flowed without interruption during the genocide. In a November 2023 

interview

, retired Israeli Major General Yitzhak Brik acknowledged: 

“All of our missiles, the ammunition, the precision-guided bombs, all the airplanes and bombs, it’s all from the US. The minute they turn off the tap, you can’t keep fighting. You have no capability … Everyone understands that we can’t fight this war without the United States. Period.”

So why couldn’t (or wouldn’t) Biden threaten to turn off the tap this time around? In part, because the media helped him get away with it. Johnson cites ten examples across US print media in which feature articles present Biden as “helpless” to effect a ceasefire, and another ten where Biden is painted as “secretly upset, outraged … or anguished about civilian casualties”. 

As pressure mounted, the White House adopted another PR tactic: presenting Hamas as the obstacle to a ceasefire. Establishment media obligingly followed suit. Johnson cites eight 

New York Times

 headlines in which an intransigent Hamas is pitted against a willing and earnest Biden. 

The White House’s definition of a ceasefire was deliberately vague. While expressing a desire to “end the war”, Biden insisted that Hamas could have no role in a post-conflict Gaza. This amounted to support for what Netanyahu termed a “total victory”, or a complete surrender by Hamas. At other times, a “ceasefire” meant a temporary pause in fighting to facilitate hostage exchanges, followed by Israel’s resumption of its war on Gaza. 

Johnson also cites numerous cases of how the US media parroted Israeli propaganda. In October 2023, the Israeli military’s social media accounts shared a 3D-rendered video supposedly showing a “Hamas command and control center” underneath Al Shifa Hospital, connected via a series of tunnels. 

At the time, Israel was determined to ethnically cleanse northern Gaza, and Al Shifa stood in its way. The 

Washington Post

 

debunked

 the “command centre” myth on 21 December. However, not before Israel’s siege and raid of the hospital, which resulted in the deaths of at least 100 of the hospital’s 1,500 patients.

During the siege, the US media danced to Israel’s tune. On 10 November, five days before the raid, the 

New York Times

 

reported

 that wounded patients and displaced people were “stranded on hospital grounds as intense, close-quarters combat between Israeli troops and Hamas fighters raged around them”.

This and other reports sought to create a false impression that heavily armed Hamas fighters were inside the hospital trying to repel Israeli troops. The 

New York Times

 did report Hamas denials that a command centre operated under the hospital, but it failed to report credible evidence from hospital doctors and medical staff that Israel’s claim did not stack up.

Much like Australian media, US media echoed and amplified Zionist claims that those who alleged Israel was committing genocide were antisemites. In late November 2023, as campus protests spread, a narrative developed that the primary victims were not bombed and starved Palestinians, but rather Jewish college students who were being made to “feel unsafe” by anti-genocide protests. That many of the protesters were Jewish did not warrant a mention. 

While no comparable study has been undertaken of Australian media, the same bias has clearly been evident. The royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion has been nothing short of a show trial of Palestine solidarity activists, with the media joining the witch hunt.

Consider the sole occasion when a Palestine solidarity activist appeared before the commission. When Yasmine Johnson, a Jewish student, socialist and national co-coordinator of Students for Palestine, gave testimony, she was attacked not only by the Murdoch media but also by the 

Age

.

“Violence a legitimate tactic in freedom movements, pro-Palestine student leader tells royal commission”, declared an 

Age

 headline, deliberately conflating Johnson’s reference to the tactics of anti-apartheid and anti-colonial movements with the peaceful student encampments that took place across Australian campuses in 2024.

For journalists who stray from the path, there are consequences. Antoinette Lattouf’s contract as an ABC radio presenter was cut short for the crime of sharing a Human Rights Watch post that accused Israel of war crimes. Australian cricket reporter Peter Lalor was similarly dropped by the broadcaster SEN for reposts on X critical of Israel. And former SBS World News Australia presenter Mary Kostakidis was pursued through the courts for two years, accused by the Zionist Federation of Australia of breaching the Racial Discrimination Act for sharing allegedly “antisemitic” posts on X. 

Despite three years of media lies, public support for Israel has collapsed. Seventy-nine percent of Australians have an unfavourable view of Israel, according to a recent Pew Research 

survey

. Even among American Jews—historically a bulwark of support for Israel—a generational shift is occurring. A recent 

poll

 found a narrow majority favour cutting US military aid to Israel, while 

another

 found half of American Jews under 35 favour replacing apartheid Israel with a democratic binational state.

But a collapse in support for Israel hasn’t ended Israel’s crimes, nor curbed the flow of weapons from Western states. For that we need something much more profound: a revolutionary movement that can shake up the whole logic of capitalism’s drive to war.

Nick Everett chairs Friends of Palestine Western Australia.

title: Two separate armed attacks in Aleppo: 2 people killed
content:
Two people were killed in two separate armed attacks that took place in different parts of Aleppo.




On Kelas Street in Aleppo’s Sulaymaniyah (Silêmanî) neighborhood, a person on a motorcycle opened fire on a shop owner. The seriously wounded business owner died at the hospital where he was taken. The identity of the attacker and the motive for the attack have not yet been determined.




In Aleppo’s Nêreb neighborhood, a young man was killed when unidentified armed individuals opened fire on the vehicle he was traveling in.




According to data from the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR), 408 murder cases have been recorded across Syria since the beginning of 2026. A total of 448 people have lost their lives in these incidents.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Report: Trump Admin Is Deporting LGBTQ Asylum Seekers to Hostile Third Countries
content:
Officials have deported LGBTQ people to Sierra Leone, where they could face life in prison for same-sex activity.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The Trump administration has reportedly deported dozens of LGBTQ immigrants who sought or were granted asylum for their sexuality and gender to third countries where they face danger of persecution and criminalization, a new report says.

In an investigation published this week, Reuters identified 40 cases where these LGBTQ individuals were sent to countries that either criminalize same-sex relations or have been designated by the State Department as dangerous for LGBTQ people.

All of these people were granted legal protection in the U.S. for fleeing persecution for their LGBTQ status in their countries of origin, per Reuters. However, more than half of them were ineligible for asylum because of a restrictive Biden-era transit ban on asylum seekers.

Individuals tracked in the report have been deported to countries including Sierra Leone, Cameroon and Eswatini, three countries where same-sex acts are criminalized. In Sierra Leone, same sex acts carry a punishment of up to life in prison. Other countries that have signed deportation agreements with the U.S. have seen abuses against LGBTQ people like conversion therapy and “corrective rape,” the report notes.

The Trump administration has signed third country deportation agreements with at least 35 countries, and has deported over 25,000 people this way, sending them to places that they have no affiliation with. Many governments in Africa and central and South America have signed agreements to receive such deportees, often in exchange for direct funding or other financial incentives.

Reuters noted the story of one man, identified as Abdou Latifou, who fled his home country of Togo after a mob assaulted him and threatened to kill him after he kissed a man. A U.S. immigration judge decided last year that it was too unsafe for him to return home; he recalled thinking, “From this day on, I’m entering a world where I’m free to live as myself.”

But amid its mass deportation campaign, and while knowing that Latifou was gay, the Trump administration deported him to Sierra Leone, where he was held for two weeks under police surveillance before being put on a flight to Togo. Fleeing danger yet again, he went to the Ivory Coast, where he lives in fear of being recognized.

“When an individual is no longer in ICE custody then ICE will no longer be responsible for them,” Department of Homeland Security spokesperson ​Chandler Rebel told Reuters.

The report is the latest documenting the Trump administration’s deportations of people to places where they may be endangered. Other reports this week found that the Trump administration deported a former political prisoner back to the place he was imprisoned and tortured last week. Jeffrey Jarquín, who led pro-democracy protests against the Nicaraguan government, was reportedly taken directly from the deportation flight to the capital of Managua to a notorious Nicaraguan prison.

The Trump administration is facing a lawsuit from Iranian asylum seekers who say that U.S. officials secretly shared sensitive information, including LGBTQ status, about them with the Iranian government — as it’s tried to deport them into a country where they may face persecution.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration has terminated Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitians in the U.S., and has deported hundreds of immigrants back to Haiti, which has experienced a surge of violence and hunger.
