author: Camila Borges
title: Regra de 1968, ano do AI-5, embasa exonerações de professoras na rede estadual paulista
content:
Em janeiro deste ano, Veruschka de Sales Azevedo passou pouco mais de uma hora contando à 

Agência Pública

 como perdera o cargo de professora na rede estadual de ensino de São Paulo. Ela chorou algumas vezes durante o encontro que foi finalizado com certa esperança: “O meu retorno será triunfante”, disse. Enquanto aguardava o desfecho do seu caso, ela organizava um livro com relatos de professores também investigados por meio de Processos Administrativos Disciplinares (PAD) na Secretaria de Educação de São Paulo (SEDUC). “A gente precisa registrar isso em tudo quanto é lugar.” 

Doutora em história, Veruschka tinha 24 anos de magistério, cerca de vinte deles na mesma escola de Guarulhos onde estudara antes de ser exonerada em maio de 2024 num PAD que se iniciou em 2017.

 Entre a abertura do processo e a exoneração, passaram-se sete anos e seis meses.




Em março deste ano, num artigo no 

Le Monde Diplomatique

, Veruschka escreveu que o trauma da exoneração lhe causara uma doença crônica. Ela viria a falecer em julho, seis meses após a entrevista para a reportagem.

 A família não divulgou a causa da morte, mas a filha, Rayssa Sales, não tem dúvida sobre a origem da doença: “Antes, a imunidade da minha mãe era perfeita, mas, depois da exoneração, ela começou a ficar doente.”




As acusações contra a professora na SEDUC apontam falta de comprometimento com os estudantes, tumulto em reuniões pedagógicas, incitação de alunos contra a direção e excesso de atenção a temas raciais e de empoderamento feminino nas aulas. 

 




Três dias antes da demissão de Veruschka, também a professora Fabiana de Abreu, que ensinava história na mesma escola, fora exonerada. Em agosto de 2025, chegaria a vez de Maitée Nogueira, professora de sociologia em São Sebastião, no Litoral Norte paulista. As três contestaram as acusações em entrevista à 

Pública

. 

Os processos se apoiam em um estatuto anterior à Constituição de 1988: o dos servidores civis do estado, de 1968, ano do AI-5.

 Para Salomão Ximenes, professor da Faculdade de Educação da USP e pesquisador do Observatório Nacional da Violência contra Educadores (Onve), 

os estatutos escritos durante o período ditatorial têm sido “ressignificados com o objetivo de dar mote a processos administrativos de perseguição a educadores”. 




Ele fala em 

“lawfare educacional”: o uso de instrumentos jurídicos e burocráticos para conter a mobilização de professores, a luta sindical e os avanços no currículo.

 Além de São Paulo, outros estados regulamentam o magistério por meio de normativas elaboradas durante o regime de exceção como Rio Grande do Sul, Pernambuco, Paraná, Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais, Acre e Ceará, conforme Ximenes identifica no artigo “

Os anos que não acabaram; o uso de estatutos jurídicos da ditadura militar na perseguição a educadores(as) no Brasil

”, que publicou na metade deste ano com a jurista Ligia Ziggiotti de Oliveira.
















Veruschka de Sales Azevedo e Fabiana de Abreu (centro), professoras exoneradas via PAD




Sarau criado por Veruschka incomodava a direção




Veruschka nasceu em Sanharó, no interior de Pernambuco, e chegou a Guarulhos ainda criança, com seis irmãos. A mãe era empregada doméstica; o pai, caminhoneiro. Ela estudou na Escola Estadual Professora Maria Aparecida Rodrigues, no bairro Pimentas, em Guarulhos, e cursou história na Unesp. Concursada em 2000, deu aulas na cidade de Sertãozinho até pedir, em 2004, transferência para a escola onde estudara. “Lá, havia professores que incentivaram os alunos a buscar a universidade pública”, disse a filha Rayssa. “Daí ela veio com o sonho de fazer o mesmo que fizeram por ela.” Ficou lá mesmo depois do doutorado, concluído em 2016 na PUC-SP.




Nas aulas, discutia desigualdades, feminismo, direitos humanos e identidade negra, e aplicava a Lei 10.639, de 2003, que tornou obrigatório o ensino de história e cultura afro-brasileira. Militava na Associação Nacional de História (Anpuh), no sindicato e na Marcha Antirracista do Bairro dos Pimentas. Na escola, conduzia o Sarau Resistência: ao longo do ano, os alunos pesquisavam personalidades negras e as homenageavam com apresentações.

 “No sarau do Milton Nascimento, fizemos o Milton de açúcar, porque ele é uma pessoa doce”, lembrou o ex-aluno Thiago Gomes, hoje estudante de filosofia na USP. “Eu via alunos racistas mudarem de opinião depois do sarau.” No cursinho popular da UNEafro Brasil que Veruschka coordenou na Unifesp, Thiago ouvia dela que era “um menino de ouro”. Para ele, a professora Veruschka morreu duas vezes. A primeira foi quando sofreu a exoneração. “Foi ali que perdi o brilho nos olhos. Eu continuava tendo aula com a Veruschka no cursinho da UneAfro, mas não era a mesma coisa”, afirma.





































Veruschka conduzia o Sarau Resistência: ao longo do ano, os alunos pesquisavam personalidades negras e as homenageavam com apresentações




Os atritos com a direção da escola começaram em 2008, segundo Veruschka, quando, ainda no governo de José Serra, passaram a exigir o uso de apostilas. O material, disse ela, “não tinha respaldo na diversidade das minhas salas de aula, na realidade dos alunos”. 

Depois vieram suas cobranças por transparência no uso das verbas e as queixas da gestão contra o sarau. “Esse projeto incomodou tanto a gestão que, a todo momento, queriam acabar com ele, porque os alunos começaram a se sentir parte desse movimento.” 




Salomão Ximenes, do Onve, diz que os estatutos preservam princípios como “a proibição de manifestação e uma lógica hierárquica em relação às autoridades administrativas”, incompatíveis com a democracia, que “continuam a persistir e a servir de mote para processos de punição”.




O advogado de Veruschka, Roberto Parahyba, chama a demissão de “arbitrária” e “antissindical”: “não tenho dúvida de que o principal ponto foi ter participado do ato sindical.”

 A defesa sustenta, ainda, que o caso estava prescrito com base no próprio estatuto de 1968, que fixa em cinco anos o prazo para a pena de demissão. 




O Procurador do Estado havia pedido a suspensão da professora por 90 dias, mas o Secretário de Educação do Estado de São Paulo, Renato Feder, aplicou a pena de demissão em maio de 2024, por considerar que Veruschka “teve conduta incompatível com o cargo de professora, principalmente no aspecto da moralidade” e agiu “de maneira desrespeitosa perante a gestão escolar”.




Para o Sindicato dos Professores do Ensino Oficial do Estado de São Paulo (Apeoesp), “se o professor tem uma atuação mínima que seja de defesa da escola pública é perseguido. Se for sindicalista então, a situação é ainda pior”

, diz Roberto Guido, presidente interino do sindicato.




Exoneração fez Veruschka perder o acesso ao hospital




Com a demissão, Veruschka perdeu o acesso ao hospital dos servidores estaduais. “A gente sabe como o SUS é demorado e que ir buscar uma consulta particular é caro”, disse a amiga Vera Aparecida dos Santos, assistente social. Em janeiro, a professora contou ter uma úlcera gástrica e o intestino inflamado. 

“Eu quero meu cargo de volta. Quero os meus 25 anos de contribuição. A gente nunca espera parar de trabalhar”

, disse, emocionada, à 

Pública

.




Numa pesquisa da Apeoesp divulgada em maio de 2026, 97,6% dos professores ouvidos associaram o adoecimento mental às condições de trabalho na rede; 24,8% precisaram se afastar da escola por esse motivo. Segundo Guido, depressão e burnout já superam as doenças físicas, em razão da superlotação das salas, das jornadas duplas ou triplas, dos conflitos e, mais recentemente, da plataformização do ensino. A SEDUC afirma que, desde dezembro de 2024, oferece atendimento psicológico e psiquiátrico aos servidores por meio do programa Viva Bem.




Segundo a mentora espiritual de Veruschka, a Iyalorixá Cláudia de Oyá,  a demissão causou um sentimento de abandono na professora diante de toda uma vida dedicada à educação: “ela começou a perder muito peso e tinha um sentimento de solidão. Se sentiu muito perdida em meio a todo o esforço de uma vida”, explicou. 
















Veruschka e a Iyalorixá Cláudia de Oyá durante aula na UNEAfro




Fabiana tratou “repetidamente” de pautas raciais e indígenas




Fabiana de Abreu foi exonerada em maio de 2024, também durante a gestão do governador Tarcísio de Freitas. Em 2017, ela foi afastada por 90 dias, sem salário, após conflitos com a direção da mesma escola de Veruschka em Guarulhos. A suspensão de 2017 foi anulada e Fabiana voltou à escola após 39 dias. Segundo ela, o prazo para punição já havia prescrito. “Mas quando eu retornei, começou outro processo.” Nele, 

Fabiana foi acusada de falta de urbanidade, insubordinação, tumulto em reuniões pedagógicas, falhas no lançamento de notas e de incitar alunos a atos contra a direção. O processo registra ainda que ela trabalhava “repetidamente questões sobre índios, negros e movimentos sociais para todas as turmas, sob a justificativa de que tem liberdade de cátedra”. 




A defesa da professora considera as acusações “comprovadamente distorcidas”

 e alega também a prescrição. A SEDUC diz que os processos de Fabiana e Veruschka apontam interrupções reiteradas nas reuniões pedagógicas e conflitos com a gestão, e que houve tentativas prévias de mediação.



















Fabiana de Abreu foi exonerada em maio de 2024, também durante a gestão do governador Tarcísio de Freitas







Com o avanço conservador sobre a educação, diz Ximenes, o estatuto que embasou as demissões “passa a ser cada vez mais reivindicado como possibilidade de contenção de educadores que propõem ações de educação democrática, antidiscriminatória e mobilizações no âmbito da escola pública”.




Fabiana diz que estaria “um pouco mais tranquila” se tivesse sido demitida sozinha. Por causa do afastamento dela, em 2017, outros professores que foram ao ato sindical, como Veruschka, passaram também a responder a processos. Com a exoneração, ela também perdeu o direito de tratar o câncer da mãe no hospital dos servidores. “Esses processos atrasam toda a nossa condição de existência. A cabeça adoece”, afirma a docente, que recorreu à justiça sobre a demissão.




Fabiana liga o caso dela à adoção de plataformas digitais nas escolas estaduais, a partir de 2024: professoras como ela e Veruschka, diz, foram afastadas para que as dirigentes pudessem “de maneira mais sossegada implantar o projeto do governo”. Diego de Freitas, professor de filosofia que trabalhou com Veruschka, vê o modelo como “uma educação enlatada, ultraprocessada”, na qual a colega não se encaixaria. “Ela sempre estava defendendo uma educação democrática, a liberdade de cátedra e isso causava tensão no ambiente.”




Para Ximenes, o controle do currículo, a obrigação de alimentar as plataformas e a cobrança de metas nas avaliações eliminaram a pluralidade pedagógica nas escolas paulistas. “Tudo já vem dado, plataformizado e construído”, diz. “Aqueles que não se plataformizam ou não performam se colocam em risco.” Uma nota técnica da Rede Escola Pública e Universidade (Repu), de julho de 2025, aponta que o tempo de uso das plataformas é monitorado, com possibilidade de punição a professores e diretores.




Caso Maitée: “debates polêmicos” sobre sexualidade e religião




Maitée Nogueira dava aulas há mais de vinte anos quando entrou em conflito com a direção da Escola Estadual Walkir Vergani, em São Sebastião, em 2023. O processo a acusa de descumprir o horário de trabalho, de falta de urbanidade, de condutas discriminatórias e de insubordinação grave, e menciona “debates polêmicos” sobre sexualidade e religião.

 A Procuradoria-Geral do Estado reconheceu não haver documentação oficial que comprovasse o descumprimento da jornada de trabalho. A demissão foi determinada em agosto de 2025, também na gestão de Tarcísio de Freitas.




“Está na ordem do dia da Secretaria de Educação exonerar, pois qualquer investigação séria teria parado quando comprovei que cumpri meus deveres como professora”, afirma Maitée. Ela também explica que os supostos “debates polêmicos” são inerentes à disciplina e que sempre seguiu o currículo. Os conflitos, diz, deveriam ter sido mediados pela coordenação. 

Sua advogada considera as acusações “frágeis” e “contraditórias” e afirma que a professora “era perseguida, veladamente, pela gestão, tendo ainda de lidar com o preconceito decorrente de sua orientação sexual”.




A SEDUC afirmou à reportagem que o processo apurou agressões verbais contra estudantes e servidores, linguagem ofensiva, intimidação de alunos, recusa em usar o nome social de uma estudante e comentários discriminatórios, além de abandono de atividades, atrasos frequentes e descumprimento de obrigações pedagógicas. Demitida, Maitée não pode assumir outro cargo público, mesmo que aprovada em concurso. “Não posso mais exercer a profissão em que atuei por 20 anos, na qual estudei e me preparei”, desabafa. 
















Exonerada em agosto de 2025, a defesa de Maitée Nogueira afirma que a professora “era perseguida veladamente pela gestão”




A SEDUC diz que os processos das três professoras citadas na reportagem garantiram o contraditório e a ampla defesa, que os recursos das professoras foram rejeitados e que nenhuma delas levou o caso à Justiça, o que contradiz as informações das defesas das professoras enviadas à 

Pública

. Nos três casos, as professoras estão recorrendo contra as exonerações. 




Ximenes defende que os estatutos anteriores à Constituição de 1988 sejam atualizados para incorporar as premissas de uma educação democrática. “Para mim é escandaloso que a gente continue usando uma legislação do período da ditadura”

, diz. “Assim, é muito mais fácil para as perspectivas autoritárias se desenvolverem, com essa infraestrutura jurídica à disposição.”




No velório de Veruschka, decidiu-se que o Sarau Resistência passaria a se chamar Sarau Veruschka de Sales Azevedo. Ela foi homenageada pela Associação Nacional de História (Anpuh) e recebeu uma moção de aplauso na Assembleia Legislativa de São Paulo (Alesp). A família tenta anular a exoneração, mesmo após o falecimento. “Como filha, eu gostaria de algo impossível: ter minha mãe de volta e que ela pudesse usufruir do cargo dela”, disse Rayssa: “O que a gente gostaria é que, pelo menos, o caso dela se revertesse.”

author: ACG
title: French High School Students Rise Up
content:
From September 17

th

, high school students and staff staged blockades throughout France. This was to protest deteriorating educational conditions. The tempo of these blockades and demonstrations increased on September 29

th

 and 30

th

.




Lack of teachers, teaching assistants, special needs assistants, and nurses; poorly insulated and unrenovated facilities; and untenable class schedules… All high school students in France are suffering the consequences of insufficient funding for the national education system. This has sparked a nationwide mobilisation that is shaking the media and the government.

The national education budget has increased by 30% since 2017, so why is the situation in high schools deteriorating? For the start of the 2026 school year, approximately 4,000 teaching positions were eliminated in both public and private schools across France. Then there is Parcoursup (1) and its unfair selection system, which relies on “digital filters”. Then, in higher education, the freeze on housing benefits will prevent the most vulnerable from finding accommodation. Not to mention the “Welcome to France” decree imposed by the government before the summer, a blatantly anti-immigration project that aims to increase tuition fees for non-European international students. In short, for all high school students, stress is mounting regarding their future studies, all while enduring gruelling schedules and conditions that make optimal learning impossible.




A mass movement emerged. But on October 1

st

, the government sent in its riot cop attack dogs, and there was brutal repression, particularly in working class neighbourhoods. There were mass arrests of students, more than 5,000 in one week. Beatings, injuries, flashball shots, tear gas, mutilations—the number of injured is high.  This has not, so far, deterred the movement, with huge demonstrations across France on October 6

th

.




From the Union Communiste Libertaire website:




“Parcoursup is blocking lives.” With these words, a high school student summed up on Tuesday the reasons for the blockade of his school, a blockade that was part of the widespread student movement that has been mobilizing for a week to demand resources for education. Understaffed personnel, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded classrooms 

“We lack everything”

 cry the students exposed daily to the stress of constant selection.




In working class neighbourhoods, students are sent to programs they didn’t choose, programs whose curricula are sometimes very opaque. Year after year, educational policies are reduced to managing a workforce in training and increasingly restrictive regulations. Student mobilisations in these neighbourhoods can take on more violent forms and are less like traditional demonstrations. How can we be surprised when we know the social and racial violence they endure daily? And let’s not be mistaken: when students take revenge on their schools, they are symbolically rebelling against this entire system of oppression and selection. We therefore warn staff against the knee-jerk moral condemnation that would dismiss this movement out of hand.




All these young people, who refuse to let their gaze towards the future be fixed only on catastrophe, make us proud.




This generation is aware of the systematic dismantling of its schools, the budget cuts being made at its expense, and the hostility directed towards it. In recent years, it has mobilsed against police brutality, for climate justice, and so on. This high school student movement is therefore not an isolated phenomenon. Its expansion across France since the initial blockades in the Paris region, and its alignment with the public sector strike on September 29th, is not a coincidence but rather the result of conditions shared throughout the country.




There’s plenty of money: let’s take it all! 450 billion: that’s the public money from the French rearmament plan, a windfall for the arms industry to maintain French imperialism. 655 million: that’s the funding allocated to developing AI in the public sector, without any consultation with employees on the usefulness of this tool, but simply to create opportunities for speculation. 1,400 positions: that’s the planned creation for the police and gendarmerie to continue the repression of our legitimate protests. No one can call this a technical problem; it’s a political choice. 

It’s a class struggle

 .




The Macron regime is increasingly concerned about this uprising, remembering the days of May-June 1968. It notes the frequent attacks on high schools by angry students, inflicting millions of euros damage. It fears the increasing possibility of workers joining in the movement. This accounts for its increasingly brutal repression. The most recent horrific incident was on October 6

th

, when a 15 year old student had a hand blown off by a stun grenade.







Parcoursup is a web portal designed by the 

French Ministry of Education

 and the

, which manages the balance between undergraduate places in French universities and other higher education institutions, and the application of candidates with a high school diploma. (From Wikipedia).

author: Clara Saliba
title: Por que a proibição das Bets é tão importante
content:
Na sexta-feira, dia 25 de setembro, às vésperas do primeiro turno das eleições, o presidente Lula assinou a 

Medida Provisória (MP) 1394

, que proíbe a atuação das bets no país. A MP é uma vitória, ainda que venha tarde.




É apenas o começo de uma batalha jurídica e regulatória que irá se desenrolar no próximo mandato eleitoral, com papel central tanto do presidente eleito quanto dos demais parlamentares.

 Afinal, deputados e senadores compõem as comissões mistas que analisam as medidas provisórias, e, para virar lei, uma MP também precisa ser aprovada pela Câmara e pelo Senado. 




Aqui, quero enaltecer o papel fundamental que 

a cobertura jornalística da 

Agência

 

Pública

 teve nessa decisão, e que minha colega Natália Viana detalha 

em sua coluna da semana passada

.  




Que o vício em apostas – a ludopatia – tem um impacto grande na saúde da população, já está estabelecido, tanto em termos psicológicos quanto financeiros. Não são poucos os casos de pessoas que perdem bens materiais, se endividam e quebram relações familiares por causa das apostas.




O marido de uma amiga não tem celular desde o ano passado: foi a condição para que seguissem o relacionamento, depois de ele perder tudo o que tinham guardado e até vender o carro para seguir jogando. 




Rafael Borges Amaral, de 26 anos, perdeu a vida na batalha contra a ludopatia. A carta escrita por sua mãe, Vânia de Souza Borges, não foi ouvida pela CPI das Bets, 

mas alcançou o Brasil

 e ajudou a levantar a bandeira de muitas outras famílias pela proibição das apostas online.




A saúde das pessoas é muito mais importante do que qualquer impacto econômico. 

Antes de pensar no PIB ou na arrecadação tributária, é a vida que precisa ser colocada em primeiro plano

. 




Então, mesmo se proibir as bets fosse ruim para a economia, seria a decisão acertada.




Mas este não é o caso. Para a economia do país, acabar com esses jogos é bastante benéfico.




Isso porque a renda que é absorvida pelas bets não retorna em mesmo volume para a economia do país. Ela é tirada de circulação, em grande parte apropriada pelas casas de aposta, muitas das quais nem no Brasil estão.




Então, além da renda que sai do bolso das famílias e prejudica suas contas diárias, a economia do país como um todo é afetada. 




Isso porque, quando alguém vai ao mercado e gasta dinheiro comprando um produto ou contratando um serviço, esse valor retorna em maior escala para a economia. É o que chamamos de efeito multiplicador. 




Por exemplo, se eu compro R$ 100 no mercadinho, estes R$ 100 viram a renda do comerciante. Ele, por sua vez, vai gastá-la, o que gera renda para outra pessoa, que também vai gastar, e assim por diante. No final, R$100 viram muito mais em atividade econômica. A roda da economia gira.  




Mas, se eu perco estes mesmos R$ 100 num cassino online, este dinheiro não comprou nada, não gerou demanda nenhuma. E a maior parte dele não vai retornar em prêmios, vai ser retida na casa de apostas.




Um 

estudo

 conduzido pelo professor Guilherme Klein para o Centro de Estudos de Macroeconomia das Desigualdades da Universidade de São Paulo (Made/USP) dimensionou o impacto das bets nesse movimento. 




A conta é a seguinte. 

O Centro Celso Furtado estimou que, em 2025, houve uma transferência bruta de R$ 62,5 bilhões para as plataformas de apostas.

 Ou seja, somando tudo o que foi apostado e redistribuído em prêmios, as bets ficaram com mais de 60 bilhões para si. 




Com esse número, o professor estimou alguns cenários diferentes, com hipóteses mais ou menos otimistas sobre o papel econômico do setor de apostas, e chegou numa perda total para a economia brasileira de algo entre R$ 90,9 bi e R$ 141 bilhões de reais – ou de 0,7 a 1,1% do PIB do nosso país.




De um terço a metade do crescimento da economia brasileira em 2025. Até cinco vezes mais do que o impacto estimado para o tarifaço americano. 




A própria 

Confederação Nacional do Comércio de Bens, Serviços e Turismo (CNC)

 estimou que o varejo sozinho deixou de faturar cerca de R$ 103 bilhões em 2024, devido ao direcionamento de recursos das pessoas para as bets.




Mesmo quando consideramos o ganho de arrecadação que a regulamentação das apostas trouxe, regular sai mais caro para o país do que proibir.

 No Estudo do Made, o efeito final é de uma redução entre R$ 14,6 bilhões e R$ 35,6 bilhões na arrecadação de impostos.




Isso sem nem considerar a elevação dos gastos em saúde pública para tratamento do vício em apostas. Conforme o 

Instituto de Estudos para Políticas de Saúde (IEPS)

, 

as bets geram um custo anual para o SUS de R$ 30,6 bilhões.

 




No fim, a soma do jogo é clara. Com a proibição, ganham as pessoas, sua saúde mental e financeira, e a economia do país. Só perdem, mesmo, as casas de apostas – e os influenciadores que elas remuneram.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Police Violence Causes Serious Injuries as French High School Students Protest
content:
Students protest teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, and dilapidated school buildings beset by rats and debris.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Nearly 2,000 French high schools are blockaded or closed today amid massive student-led protests over school funding and inequality. The demonstrations began in September at a single school in the economically deprived suburbs of Paris, where students protested teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and dilapidated school buildings beset by rats, falling debris and more. But the scope of the protests has widened amid a violent crackdown by French police. French authorities have arrested more than 5,000 people, largely underage students, since the movement began. Violent police tactics have led to serious injuries. One protester lost an eye after being hit by a rubber bullet, while another lost a hand when he picked up a police stun grenade.

We hear from an anonymous protester who describes the violence meted out on students, who “aren’t even adults yet,” and from Claire Vigneau, general secretary of Fédération Syndicale Étudiante, the French student union, who reports from a protest in Rennes, Brittany, “where we are trying to escape from the policemen that are chasing us with tear gas and with water cannon[s].”

“The amount of spending that France has done on education has stagnated, if not declined,” explains French American journalist Cole Stangler. “The critiques that high school students are making are actually very similar to what teachers’ unions have been saying for quite some time.”

“Everyone is deeply, deeply angry. We are completely fed up [with] the living conditions, the school conditions, the work conditions that we have,” says Alys Rowlands, a university student in Lille and also a member of Fédération Syndicale Étudiante. “The true violence is the violence of the state that we are being faced with all day, every day, all year. That’s the true violence: having no money, having difficulty finishing the month, having less and less help from the state, having to choose between eating and putting your heating on during the winter.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: Nearly 2,000 French high schools are blockaded or closed today as massive student-led protests spread over France over school funding and inequality. The demonstration began in September at a single school outside Paris, where students protested teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and crumbling school buildings. But the scope of the protests has widened amidst a violent crackdown by French police. French authorities have arrested more than 5,000 people since the movement began, about 85% of them high schoolers.

These are the voices of two students protesting in Paris earlier today.

HUGO VETZEL: [translated] For us, it’s, first of all, in support of the high school students who started blockades a few days ago. I think we all have a role to play in this movement, and the more we are, the more we will be heard. And I think this is not a fight of a few handful of people, but a more global fight for the youth. …

We feel despised, because when the answer is violence, that means, in a way, democracy is no longer working. But we feel especially that there is such a gap between the elites and us, and we feel we are creating unease, because we are disrupting so much that they are using force to shut us up.

MONA FALLACARA: [translated] I am quite happy because, for once, we see a real movement of the youth everywhere, and we hear about it. But then, what I deplore is that the media is showing more of the violence done by the students before their demands, which are vital. And yes, there is a bit of violence, but it’s not everywhere. …

France’s budget will come to a vote soon, so we hope there will be a higher budget for education. And for the presidential election next year, as well, we hope for a bit of change after 10 years of President Macron heading the country.

AMY GOODMAN: France’s official independent national human rights body has expressed deep concern over what it called the state’s disproportionate use of force in response to the protests. On Monday, Democracy Now! reached a French student who described the violent police crackdown. For her safety, she asked not to be identified.

PROTESTER: During the protests, people, students receive tear gas, receive — like, get hit, get attacked, get charged by policemen, by the CRS, which is a police institution. And yes, basically it has been really violent. Many people have been wounded. Many people have been arrested. Someone lost an eye. Someone lost a hand. And this is happening to literal teens, literal children. We even — most of us aren’t even adults yet. And this is terrible, because literal adult people, adult policemen, adult policewomen, with weapons and tear gas and shields and helmets, are attacking literal students with some — some cardboard with messages on it. Like, we’re pacifists, and our movement is nonviolent, and yet we receive so much violence, violence from the government.

AMY GOODMAN: That was a French high school student afraid to be named or shown.

We go now to France. We begin with Claire Vigneau, the general secretary of the French student union, the FSE. She’s at a protest in Rennes, in northwestern France.

Thanks so much for joining us, Claire. If you can start off by talking about how these protests began? When people hear “suburbs,” they think more middle-class, but in France, it’s basically the opposite, where more poverty is concentrated. Talk about the schools, the high school students and how this has grown.

CLAIRE VIGNEAU: Yeah, so, it started like a few days ago, and maybe 10 days ago, something like that. And now it’s getting bigger and bigger every day. Yes, it started in Saint-Denis, which is a suburbs near Paris, but very poor suburbs. And it started because class conditions, like studying conditions, are really getting worse and worse. And, like, there is water in their class. They have rats in their class. The roof is falling out. And yeah, so it’s getting harder and harder to study for these high school students. And so they started to block their high schools.

And now it’s widened out to most of the high schools in France. Actually, today, the state decided to close 500 high schools, because they didn’t want them to be blocked. But even with that precaution, 500 more high schools are blocked. And for now, we are — for now we are — we have also like 90% of the universities, the campuses that are blocked. And we are going to keep on going yet, keep on going to block.

Today, we were on a protest in Rennes, yes. We are trying to escape from the policemen that are chasing us with tear gas and with cannon, water cannon. And so, yes, it was a very big protest in Rennes. There was actually like 16,000 people in Rennes, which is not a big city. And one thing to note is that the minister of the interior told today the head of the biggest trade union in France that Rennes was going to be an example of repression, of violence, and to show all the rest of the movement that we can’t do what we are doing now, which is protest for our living conditions.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Claire, could you talk more about what the demands of the students are, and especially their concerns about so many of these schools having no air conditioning in warm weather, that the heat gets up to 35 degrees Celsius, or 95 degrees Fahrenheit, especially given that France has had so many people die during heat waves this past year?

CLAIRE VIGNEAU: Yeah, yeah, because we have seen a lot of classes, even in classes for like really young child, starting from 6 years old, being in classrooms where there were like 35 students with temperatures attaining 35 degrees and even more — some of them attained 40 degrees. And we are concerned, because you can’t learn, really, in a really good way when you are under this weather. And we are fighting, of course, for the weather conditions, like the stunning conditions, but not only.

And obviously, we are struggling for more budgets in school and less budgets in the Army, because in France the financement for the Army doubled in 10 years, and when they — at the same time, the budgets for education is getting lower and lower every day. And so, that’s like — the air conditioning is, of course, one of the goals, but not only. And before even having air conditioning, we would like to have safe classrooms with no bad products for our health in the buildings. And we would like, if it rains outside, we don’t want rain in our classrooms, etc., etc.

AMY GOODMAN: We’re going to go right now to southern France, where we’re joined by Cole Stangler, a journalist in France covering politics and labor. The significance of this protest call? I mean, we see Claire in the streets of Rennes. There are protests in Lille, a nationwide day of protests, the college unions and other labor unions joining in these protests right now, thousands of people arrested, about 5,000, over 87% of them kids in high school.

COLE STANGLER: Yeah, that’s right. And I think maybe just to complement some of what we’ve been — already been hearing, you know, those issues have been absolutely at the forefront of what I’ve been hearing on the ground here. I was just at a protest in Aix-en-Provence, just in the south of France, just north of Marseille, where students were telling me their own stories of the dilapidated conditions of some of their buildings, which, to be fair, aren’t nearly as bad as when we talk about the suburbs of Paris, where you have, you know, rats in the hallways, but still, people talking about dilapidated buildings, having to install nets around their — around the buildings to make sure there’s not falling debris. That’s an issue I heard about.

And, you know, another issue people talk a lot about here is the staff shortages, the lack of teachers. This has been an issue that’s been bubbling up for years, in fact. And we heard it mentioned, France’s — the amount of spending that France has done on education has stagnated, if not declined. You know, if you go back to the late ’90s, 1997, France was spending over 7% of its GDP on education. That’s declined about nearly a percentage point. So, the government is spending less, and the salaries are quite low, as well. That might be shocking to some viewers in the United States. You know, a starting salary for a public school teacher in France is around 2,000 euros. Even mid-career professionals are making less than the OECD average, less than the European Union average. And so, when you have low salaries, you know, and you have dilapidated buildings, it’s easy to maybe understand why you have these staff shortages. And so, this is an interesting issue where the critiques that high school students are making are actually very similar to what teachers’ unions have been saying for quite some time. So, there’s that issue of the shortages.

And I think another key issue that’s emerged — and again, students were talking about it, both the high school students I talked to earlier today and the university students who joined the protests — was the issue of what in France they call Parcoursup, which is the new platform that was introduced a few years ago, which is basically an application platform for high school students to get into universities, that is not very transparent. There’s a lot of critiques about how this sort of seemingly mysterious system will offer university spots to students. So, students aren’t getting to go to the universities they want to go to that are close to them. They might have to move halfway across the country. That means more money that they’re spending on rent; they can’t live with their parents. And so, that critique of the university application process is something that unites, again, both high school students and university students.

And that’s what’s been interesting when you’re talking to people on the streets here, is to see to what extent the high school student issues actually resonate beyond just high schools. Right? It’s university students. It’s also trade unions. Today, at the protest I was at, you had a lot of trade union support from, you know, the main labor unions in France. And I think the movement is really resonating because it’s really hit a nerve here on a lot of issues that are important to French society.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Cole, I wanted to ask you — the French government has accused the left-wing political party France Unbowed of stoking the violence at the — or, some violence at these protests. Can you talk about the significance of this, especially as France is preparing for next year’s presidential elections?

COLE STANGLER: Yeah. You know, I was talking about this earlier, and I think that this line that we’ve indeed heard from the government — I think it is both a great exaggeration of the mobilizing power of that party, La France Insoumise, led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, and it’s also, I think, an insult to the collective intelligence of the high school students who are protesting. I mean, I don’t think it’s physically possible for a political party to have this broad of a reach. So, I think that’s sort of an easy excuse. But that’s — you know, that’s indicative of the approach the government has taken so far.

And, you know, this question of police repression and police violence, which we heard about just earlier, has also been something that’s been kind of pushing the movement forward. A lot of French people, I think, have been shocked by the degree of the police violence. You know, we heard there was a 15-year-old who had his hand basically blown off by picking up a stun grenade that the police use here. We had another student who lost the use of his eye because he was hit by a rubber bullet. These are like, you know, low-grade, almost military kind of technologies that the police use in France. And it’s part of a policing strategy that has been in place for several years now. Many of your viewers might remember the yellow vest movement back in late 2018, where we had, you know, decentralized mass protests and a huge amount of violence, where you had protesters having — you know, losing their eyes, losing their hands.

The difference here — and this is what makes it frightening — is we’re not talking about adults. We’re talking about literal high schoolers. We’re talking about 15-, 14-year-olds who are being beaten by police. And, you know, there have been incidents. We should just be clear: There have been incidents of, you know, people attacking police officers, at some points firefighters. But that is the extreme minority. And I think the much bigger story here, we’re talking about a democratic country where the police have been attacking high school students. And I think it’s — again, it’s documented. There’s been hundreds of complaints that have been filed with the French government to this effect. This French policing strategy that was used during the yellow vests is now being directed against high schoolers. And that’s also energizing this movement. A lot of people think it’s unacceptable.

AMY GOODMAN: We’re going to go from Aix-en-Provence, where Cole Stangler is, to Lille, France, from the south to the north of France. Alys Rowlands is a university student and member of the national board of the French student union, also just at a protest. Alys, thanks so much for joining us. As we wrap up, what do you think it’s most important for us to understand about this mass protest that’s taking place in France, and what you’re demanding, and how this might even affect the national elections that are coming up next year in France?

ALYS ROWLANDS: Yeah, absolutely. I think the most important thing here is that it started with the high schoolers. Today, it’s also university students, but we’ve seen also teachers. We’ve seen farmers. We’ve seen the yellow vesters who want to join again. We’ve seen everyone want to join this mobilization, because I think what’s very interesting about this one here is that everyone is deeply, deeply angry. We are completely fed up of the living conditions, the school conditions, the work conditions that we have, and everyone is really, really deeply angry. And that’s what’s really interesting at the moment.

So, the students, like they’ve said, are being faced with really strong repression from the police forces. So, as they said before, there are many kids. This is children who are being shot at with rubber bullets and tear gas and water cannons, who are being chased, who are being, you know, arrested massively. And this is completely unheard of before. It’s only been a week of this mobilization with the different protests and schools being blocked, etc., and it’s already over 5,000 people arrested, and, as you said, mostly children. And so, this is completely different from things that we’ve seen before.

And because France, it’s — quite often there are mobilizations and things, but this is completely a different proportion, because people are really deeply angry about what’s going on and the conditions that we are living in. And I think this will have an impact, because we’re already seeing things changing. But what people want right now, it’s not one reform. It’s not one thing. It’s a deep change in the system and more budgets for the public services in France, which is behind all of this.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Alys, what is your sense of the — excuse me — the response of adults, of the parents of these children, of the general society to the way that the government has reacted to the student protests?

ALYS ROWLANDS: Yeah, that’s an interesting question, because we can see in protests loads of parents. And we’ve seen online, on TikTok and the different apps, that the teachers and parents have been joining the protests, because they understand that the students, the high schoolers especially, are really deeply angry and they are completely fed up of going to school and then there being rats and the ceiling falling down and chemical products in the ceiling that are giving us cancer. Like, it’s completely — it’s completely insane. And so, the parents and teachers, but also, much wider, the general population are completely with the mobilizations.

But the media are only showing violence and this and that. But the true violence is the violence of the police, the violence of the repression. How is it possible that children, 14-year-olds, are having their eyes being blown off, their hands being blown off, their teeth being completely ripped out by these rubber bullets and tear gas? How is it possible that this is happening in France today? Five thousand people arrested, mostly children, how is this possible? The true violence is the violence of the state that we are being faced with all day, every day, all year. That’s the true violence: having no money, having difficulty finishing the month, having less and less help from the state, having to choose between eating and putting your heating on during the winter. It’s that kind of violence that we are faced with all year. And so, you know, the parents and the teachers and, wider, the general population are completely agreeing with the —everything that they want, the students, the high schoolers, the university students, but also much wider. Everyone has things they want to change.

AMY GOODMAN: Alys Rowlands, we want to thank you for being with us from Lille, from the north of France, university student, member of the national board of the FSU, French student union. I also want to thank Cole Stangler, journalist based in France, covering politics and labor issues, joining us from Aix-en-Provence in the south, and Claire Vigneau, general secretary of the French student union, joining us from the streets of Rennes, where the massive protest also is taking place today, as it is across the country. And just to underscore something Juan said about the heat and the lack of air conditioning, this isn’t just a luxury. We’re talking about 8,000 people in France this summer died from heat.

Coming up, we go to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where the death toll from Ebola has topped 4,000. Stay with us.

AMY GOODMAN: “Freedom Is Free” by Chicano Batman.

We now have three full months of data since Google changed its search to feature AI results. The numbers are worse than we anticipated. Overall readership that comes to Truthout through Google is down 54 percent against last year. The number of new readers who discover Truthout via Google searches is down 49 percent, and returning users from Google are down 51 percent.

We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We anticipate a loss of roughly $500,000 in online revenue as a result of this massive traffic plunge in the next year alone.

The only way we can keep publishing is with strong reader support. We are asking you to start a monthly donation to Truthout today — anything you can do, whether $5 or $25, makes a difference.

title: Fundamental ideological consciousness
content:
The most fundamental characteristic of today’s world system is that it is hostile to nature and women. These represent the greatest deviation from nature and from social life. Women object to this; they rebel and struggle. But what about nature? Who will stand up for nature? Undoubtedly, nature also has a form of objection and rebellion. This rebellion can reach such a point that the links in nature’s evolutionary chain are broken. When several of the evolutionary links that created humanity are broken, human life itself may disappear; indeed, many species may become extinct. Scientists are already discussing the consequences that the destruction of nature will bring to the world. It is said that the consequences will be extremely grave. If those who say these things are dismissed as pessimistic prophets of doom, what they predict may actually come to pass.




Seeing the harm that human beings have inflicted on nature, one could argue that the greatest deviation nature has experienced is the emergence of this human being. The fact that a part of nature evolved into this state and became nature’s greatest enemy naturally leads one to such an assessment. In the holy scriptures, God’s wrath is presented as a response to the deterioration of social life. The wrath brought about by the deterioration taking place in nature could completely destroy humanity.




Humanity’s first fundamental consciousness is its approach to nature. The Kurdish People’s Leader called this the first ideological consciousness. Human beings showed respect for nature that created and sustained them. Early humans respected nature. They saw nature as alive, just like themselves. Through the figure of the totem, they both recognized the value of nature and became aware of their own social power. This is called animism. The fact that many elements of nature are regarded as sacred in Dersim has such a historical background.




Today, human beings have lost all respect for nature. In fact, this means treating oneself without respect. The most fundamental moral corruption in human beings is also this disrespect toward nature. Such disrespect toward nature is incomprehensible. It is a condition created by humanity’s failure to know itself. Human beings have become alienated from nature. If people truly knew themselves, could they ever behave this way?




A person who approaches nature in this way can have neither conscience nor morality. Anything can be expected from someone who treats nature this way. Therefore, one’s approach to nature is a philosophical approach. To regard the approach to nature as something secondary opens the door to all kinds of disasters. From this perspective, in order to understand the character of a political movement or an individual, one must look at their approach to nature. Today, too, the approach to nature should be regarded as a fundamental form of consciousness. Although it is formally different from the ecological consciousness of early humans, in essence it is the same. Just as early humans’ consciousness was philosophical and moral, so it is today.




There are many contradictions in the world today. The contradiction between women and the male-dominated system is very important. We can now understand what social life, and even the political system, is by looking at the position of women. Marx attributed the determining character of a social and political system to relations of production. While this remains important, in order to concretely understand what a society and political system are, we must look at the position of women. In one respect, this has come to take precedence over understanding what the relations of production are when it comes to recognizing political and social relations.




Today, the contradiction between the existing political system and nature is the most fundamental contradiction. This assault on nature is the greatest problem facing the world and humanity. Because it does not concern only a part of humanity; nor does it concern humanity alone. It concerns all nature, both living and non-living. In this respect, it has surpassed all other contradictions. Without being sensitive to this issue, one cannot truly be sensitive to anything else. Because nature, and therefore humanity as well, is sending out an S.O.S. In other words, it is calling for help. From this perspective, it is not enough simply to be sensitive to this issue; action must also be taken. And urgently!




Undoubtedly, this is an ideological and political issue. It is necessary not only to engage in practical and activist efforts, but also to intensify the ideological and political struggle. Priority must also be given to this issue. Just as a genuine ideological and theoretical struggle has been waged around the line of women’s liberation, it has now become extremely important to wage such a struggle in the ecological sphere as well. Socialist forces, in particular, must wage this struggle.




Anti-nature industrialism was turned into a theory. It was transformed into a mentality. Socialists also bear great responsibility for this mistake. In the Soviet Union, industrialism was elevated to the theoretical level. Socialism was even equated with electrification. Of course, electricity and energy were not unimportant. However, pursuing them in a manner hostile to nature was a major mistake of actually existing socialism. Indeed, this understanding strengthened capitalism. In essence, industrialism developed as a major deviation from the socialist line.




From this perspective, socialist forces need to wage the struggle against the destruction of nature both ideologically and theoretically, as well as practically. At present, the greatest harm the AKP government is inflicting on the peoples is its assault on nature. The assault on nature in Turkey and Kurdistan has become not merely an attack on nature, but an attack against the entire population. From this perspective, the struggle against this assault on nature must be intensified everywhere. If the fragmented struggles are brought together into a unified whole, a major ecological movement can develop. The ecological situation is an emergency. Alongside an ideological and theoretical initiative on this issue, practical struggle must also be developed. If this struggle develops, it will also pave the way for struggles on every other issue. In this respect, all political forces need to put this issue on their agendas.




Source: Yeni Yaşam Newspaper

title: Black Sea musicians call on artists to promote peace
content:
Black Sea musicians Ismail Hakkı Demircioğlu and Fuat Saka spoke to ANF about the Peace and Democratic Society Process.




Fuat Saka said there was nothing wrong with wanting peace or standing up for it: “It is called ‘peace’ for a reason. If peace is going to bring tranquillity to everyone, then that is how it should be. Peace is welcome, more than welcome. It is not something to fear, but something to embrace.”




Saka stressed that everyone living in these lands was part of the same fraternity, saying that great suffering had been endured in the past but that it was now time to put an end to it. He called for stronger steps towards building a democratic society and urged political actors to take responsibility.




Saka said: “I believe those who seek to govern this country need to approach this issue with greater sensitivity, just as they should with every other issue. I hope the days when friendship and fraternity are strengthened in these lands, when we can stand shoulder to shoulder, are not far away. Politicians have a major role to play here. The responsibility lies first with them, and then with all of us.”




Saka said one of the most fundamental functions of art was to break down prejudices. He stressed that art could bring people together and that this power would emerge as long as the intention behind it was positive.




Saka said artists had a responsibility to defend peace and added: “Of course, artists can actively contribute to this process. We should make films and music about fraternity, friendship, solidarity and peace. Such works are already being produced, but is it enough? I don’t think so. We need to put much more effort into this. Making our voices heard more strongly should also be one of our responsibilities.”




‘People should be able to express themselves in their mother tongue’




Fuat Saka also stressed the importance of freedom for Kurdish musicians and the Kurdish language: “People should, of course, be able to express themselves in their mother tongue, in every sphere of life. Nothing could be more natural. When we speak of ‘freedom’, the question is: what kind of freedom? We need to look for the answer within the system, identify what is not working and correct it. Sincerity is essential here, and the institutions responsible for making these changes must act with care.”




‘Let us defend peace and fraternity through our work’




Musician Ismail Hakkı Demircioğlu stressed that artists should defend peace and fraternity both through their words and the works they create, saying that conflict would bring nothing but bloodshed and tears to all peoples.




Demircioğlu said: “Music with lyrics is easier to understand, so it can reach and connect with people more easily,” adding: “Credibility is, of course, very important here. If decisions are made at the top, disconnected from the people, they can leave deep wounds in people’s conscience. People need to understand and care for one another. Unfortunately, those who rule the world harm all of us by turning people against each other.”




Demircioğlu said the economic crisis and current conditions had distanced people from artistic and cultural activities: “People have been left without hope or enthusiasm. Harsh economic conditions mean that people cannot attend events. They have been cut off from artistic activities. If we cannot overcome this situation, things will become very difficult.”




Demircioğlu said he also experienced the power of music through the connection it created with audiences, stressing that there was no problem between peoples and that people could find their own ways of overcoming divisions. He recalled an experience at a concert in Diyarbakır (Amed) in the early 2000s: “At an open-air concert in Diyarbakır in the early 2000s, we were walking through the crowd towards the stage when security wanted to take us by another route. But the people lovingly made way for us, and we reached the stage through the crowd. There is no problem between peoples. People will always find a way if they are left to themselves.”




‘Kurdish and art will be freer’




Demircioğlu said folk songs and traditional verses had for centuries served as a form of collective memory and healing in these lands in the aftermath of wars, displacement and suffering: “Folk songs have this quality. They are like medicine. They both diagnose and heal. For those who understand them, they are a refuge. There is a saying that ‘the power of folk songs is greater than that of weapons’. That is why governments are afraid of folk songs. Pir Sultan, Dadaloğlu, Nesimi and Ruhi Su were all targeted by those in power who wanted to silence them. Although interest may have declined in today’s industrial society, folk songs will continue in other forms. There is a folk song for every pain.”




Demircioğlu stressed that both Kurdish and art would become freer if the Peace and Democratic Society Process were successfully completed, saying that bards should also be free to express society’s problems in Kurdish: “Musicians will be able to perform concerts more freely. The same applies to Kurdish. My mother, for example, is Laz and my father is Hemshin, but I was never taught Laz. If I knew Laz, I would sing folk songs in Laz too, and that would be wonderful. I would like to see bards like Aşık Veysel and Muharrem Ertaş playing and singing in Kurdish about society’s problems. I feel the same way about the kemençe (a traditional Black Sea bowed string instrument). As peoples, we live one way, but unfortunately those who govern us think in another.”




‘Democratisation is crucial’




Ismail Hakkı Demircioğlu also stressed the importance of democratisation and criticised the continuing violations of rights. Demircioğlu was also asked whether he had a message for politicians and responded: “Democratisation is crucial. The rule of law is not functioning, and there are many other problems that need to be resolved. Many of the rights and gains we had have disappeared. There are innocent people who have paid an extremely heavy price. More important than politicians is for the people to understand what is happening. There is little point in me telling politicians anything. I cannot tell them to use reason; they all have that. What I can ask for is conscience.”

title: DEM Party: Events of October 6–8 must be fully investigated
content:
The Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) commemorated those who lost their lives during the protests of October 6–8, 2014, on the twelfth anniversary of the events and called for a full investigation into what happened. The party also demanded the immediate release of the politicians convicted in the Kobanê case.




The protests erupted in October 2014 during the attack on Kobanê by the terrorist organization Islamic State (ISIS). People took to the streets in numerous cities across the country in solidarity with the resistance of Kobanê’s population against ISIS and to protest against the Turkish government’s support for the jihadist group. The demonstrations and the violent events that followed resulted in numerous deaths.




According to various human rights organizations, 54 people were killed during the protests and violent clashes involving demonstrators, police, the military and organizations affiliated with ISIS, including 47 HDP members. “We respectfully commemorate our citizens who lost their lives during the protests of October 6–8,” the DEM Party stated. Even twelve years later, demands for a comprehensive investigation into the events remain unanswered, it added.




Instead of investigating the circumstances surrounding the events, the truth was obscured and proceedings that the DEM Party describes as the “Kobanê conspiracy trial” were brought against leading politicians of the then-HDP. The defendants included former HDP co-chairs Selahattin Demirtaş and Figen Yüksekdağ, as well as members of the party executive at the time. Some were sentenced to decades in prison, while an appeal remains pending.




The DEM Party explicitly linked its demand for their release to the ongoing peace and democratic society process aimed at resolving the Kurdish question. Social peace, the party said, also requires an end to unjust and unlawful judicial proceedings. “The rulings of the European Court of Human Rights must be implemented, and our friends who were prosecuted in the Kobanê conspiracy case must regain their freedom without delay,” the party stated.




Clarifying the events of October 6–8 and ensuring justice are crucial for social peace and a democratic future, the party said. “We will continue our struggle for truth, justice and freedom,” the statement concluded.

title: YRK announces the death of guerrilla fighter Çekdar Paytext
content:
The Eastern Kurdistan Defense Units (YRK) announced the death of their fighter Çekdar Paytext, who lost his life in an accident in the Pêncewîn region of Southern Kurdistan (Northern Iraq) on September 2, 2026. In a statement released by its Press and Communications Center, the YRK extended their condolences to the Akan family and the people of Kurdistan and commended his life and path within the movement.




Çekdar Paytext’s birth name was Barış Akan. He was born into a patriotic family in the province of Amed (Diyarbakır) in Northern Kurdistan and grew up in an environment closely connected to the Kurdish freedom movement. His older brother, Nizam Akan, who used the nom de guerre Çekdar, had lost his life in 1994. When Çekdar Paytext joined the guerrilla ranks in 2023, he adopted his brother’s name in his memory.




The YRK paid tribute to him as a committed fighter whose life, it said, was marked by a deep bond with his comrades, his homeland and the philosophy of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan. Quoting his own writings, the YRK cited a passage reflecting his understanding of guerrilla life: “What matters is the organization. All comrades are prepared to give their lives for one another.”




“Çekdar Paytext will remain in our memory as a symbol of comradeship,” the YRK stated. “Realizing our fallen comrades’ dreams of a free life is our most fundamental task. Our commitment is to the promise of carrying the flag entrusted to us by the martyrs to victory,” the statement said.




The identity details of the fallen YRK fighter is as follows:




First-Last Name: Barış Akan




Nom de Guerre: Çekdar Paytext




Birthplace: Amed




Date and Place of Martyrdom: 2 September 2026, Pêncewîn

title: Iraqi Prime Minister: Agreement reached on the withdrawal of Turkish troops
content:
Iraqi media have reported details of a meeting between Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Zeydi and tribal leaders.




According to the reports, the Iraqi Prime Minister said that funds recovered through corruption investigations would be transferred to the “Development Fund.” He emphasized that the rule of law and Iraq’s independence in decision-making would be safeguarded.




Zeydi reportedly praised the tribes for supporting the government and drawing attention to the country’s most sensitive issues. He announced that five armed groups were prepared to hand over their weapons, describing the move as a practical step.




Addressing the presence of the Turkish military on Iraqi territory, the Iraqi Prime Minister reportedly said that talks had been held with Turkish officials on a number of issues and that an agreement had been reached on the withdrawal of Turkish forces from Iraqi territory.

title: Bakırhan calls for work to begin under Öcalan’s coordination
content:
DEM Party co-chair Tuncer Bakırhan has called for concrete steps in the peace and democratic society process as the new parliamentary year begins. The Council for Disarmament and Strategic Coordination must begin its work under the coordination of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan. At the same time, he said, necessary conditions must be created for Öcalan to work freely, hold talks and communicate.




Bakırhan made the remarks at the DEM Party’s first parliamentary group meeting of the new legislative year. He devoted a substantial part of his speech to the peace process and the political and legal steps he believes must now be taken. “One concrete action is better than a thousand words,” Bakırhan said. Mutual trust, he added, can only be established if the developments so far are now followed by practical steps.




‘Disarmament requires a legal counterpart’




Bakırhan described the peace process as a scale with two sides. Disarmament, he said, must be matched by legal safeguards. “If the laying down of arms has been placed on one side of the scale, the law must be placed on the other. Because disarmament is a matter that requires a legal counterpart,” the Kurdish politician said. The same, he said, applies to the dissolution of the PKK (Kurdistan Workers’ Party). “Obstacles to the recognition of democratic rights and legal guarantees must be removed. If dissolution is on one side, legal guarantees and politics must be on the other. The political and legal dimensions of the process must therefore now become as concrete as the steps already taken by the Kurdish freedom movement.




‘Coordination Council must work under Öcalan’s leadership’




Bakırhan attributed a central role to the Council for Disarmament and Strategic Coordination, stating that the bodies and commissions established for the process must now begin carrying out their responsibilities in practice. “This council must begin its work under Mr. Öcalan’s coordination as soon as possible,” Bakırhan said. “To make this possible, the conditions necessary for Öcalan to work freely, hold talks and communicate must be ensured. At the same time, he must be able to maintain regular contact with the parties relevant to the process.”




The demand for appropriate working and communication conditions for Öcalan has long been one of the DEM Party’s central demands in the peace process. His role, the party argues, must not merely be recognized without also creating the conditions necessary for him to exercise it in practice.




‘Monitoring Commission must begin its work’




Bakırhan also called on parliament to assume responsibility and said that the Monitoring Commission provided for under the framework law must be established without delay. Its role will be to monitor the implementation of the process, address problems that arise, hold talks with the parties involved and initiate the necessary legislative measures. “We, as the DEM Party, are ready to assume responsibility,” Bakırhan said. He also called on all other parties to take responsibility in this historic process.




“No one has the right to exhaust the hope for peace”




Bakırhan also addressed the twelfth anniversary of the events of October 6–8, 2014. He described the period as a “very dark chapter” and called for those responsible for the deaths at the time to be identified. Twelve years later, he said, the events have still not been fully investigated. At the same time, he called for the politicians imprisoned in the Kobanê case to be released. “Our friends who were prosecuted in the Kobanê conspiracy case must finally regain their freedom.”




Bakırhan also criticized the government over allegations of corruption, access restrictions imposed on media outlets, the imprisonment of journalists, femicides and the continuing injustices resulting from emergency decrees (KHK). What matters now, he said, is advancing the peace process in a way that meets society’s expectations. Bakırhan warned against allowing the current phase to remain mired in uncertainty: “No one has the right to exhaust the hope for peace through uncertainty and keep postponing society’s expectations.”
