author: Julius Gavroche
title: French Youth Take the Streets against a Bleak Future
content:
from the 

CrimethInc.

 collective, 06/10/2026







A Report




This past week, thousands of teenagers have taken the streets of France, clashing with police as they demonstrate against the deplorable conditions in their high schools and a rapidly collapsing future. This is a promising sign, shifting attention from the seemingly unstoppable rise of the extreme right to the question of what people can do on a grassroots basis to defend themselves. Our correspondents in Paris explore the situation in detail.










Another unprecedented summer of record 

heatwaves

, 

droughts

, and 

wildfires

 throughout Europe underlines the desperate situation we are all facing today, while politicians of all stripes and their techno-industrial sponsors continue to turn a blind eye, forcing us down the path to catastrophe in the name of progress.




Hoping to turn the page on these environmental disasters, the French government has hurriedly shifted focus to other priorities. The coming months represent a crucial transition for Emmanuel Macron and his government, as they will bring Macron’s second term to a close, opening a new political era in France. Candidates are already battling to succeed Macron in power at the beginning of May 2027.




In the midst of this political spectacle, during an increasingly 

menacing surge

 in the popularity of the National Rally (formerly, the National Front), the extreme-right party, it is especially meaningful that teenagers have started to organize at a grassroots level to defend themselves. This organizing gained momentum last week, when blockades of high schools, demonstrations, and riots erupted across France, taking everyone by surprise.




Students clash with police forces in Montpellier on October 2, 2026.







Licensed to Kill?




Since Macron was elected President for the first time in May 2017, the political discourse in France has been even more dominated by an emphasis on authoritarian and far-right ideologies in terms of security, immigration, and economic and social issues.




This political shift towards an even more aggressive form of governance has led to increasing state violence targeting the social movements and uprisings that have emerged since. From the eviction of the 

ZAD

 at Notre-Dame-des-Landes in 2017 to the 

riots

 following the murder of Nahel in 2023, not forgetting the 

Yellow Vest

 sequence and the COVID-19 pandemic lockdown experimental 

doctrines

, we have experienced a headlong plunge into a world of surveillance, repression, and loss of individual freedoms. This has become today’s new normal.




It was in this already suffocating context that last July, the French government decided to vote on a new bill giving police officers more latitude to use their firearms without consequences—a demand that the far right has promoted for years. If voted through, this legislation could set a 

dangerous precedent

, as it would establish “a presumption of ‘legitimate use of arms’ by police and gendarmes ‘in the exercise of their duty’.”




Police arrest a student in Lyons on October 1, 2026.




In other words, not only will police officers be able to freely use their weapons if in any situation they claim to fear for their lives or the lives of others, but authorities will no longer have to prove that the officers acted within the framework of the law, as they are required to do today. It will be up to the victims and their families to provide evidence that the use of firearms was not justified. We can already see how this new law represents a legislative tool enabling law enforcement agents, and therefore, the state, to cover up future murders.




Unwilling to let such a law pass without resistance, political opponents and radicals, who had rightly rebranded this law the “license to kill,” decided to organize massive demonstrations and events throughout France on the weekend of September 18 to 20. 

Thousands

 of people took part in these protests in different major cities alongside traditional leftist politicians, rights groups such as Amnesty International and the League of Human Rights, and various lawyers and magistrates’ unions.




In the meantime, another call for action reusing all the codes of the Yellow Vest movement spread online. The origins of this call remain obscure, as some national 

newspapers

 have raised the possibility that AI-generated accounts had flooded social media platforms with this rumor on purpose. Nevertheless, media and politicians began commenting on this potential resurgence of the Yellow Vest movement due to the rise of fuel prices and the overall increase of living costs. Rumor or not, the call to take the streets on October 17, 2026 has spread and only the future will tell us if people’s desperation and anger will be able to give birth to another inspiring moment.




Police forces welcome students blocking their high school with clouds of tear gas in Lille on September 30, 2026.




Growing Frustrations…




Since mid-September, another form of discontent has been slowly spreading within another part of society. Tired of their working conditions, some high-school students decided to block access to their schools in order to make their voices heard. During the early stages of what became a national movement a few days later, only a few high schools were blocked here and there. This did not create any real impact or worry the authorities.




Among the students’ various demands, we can summarize the following points:







Reduce the number of students per class.







For years now, the number of students per class has gradually increased to the point that it is not unusual for a teacher to have an average of between 30 to 35 students in a classroom. This is impacting the capacity for every single student to learn at their own pace.







Reduce the number of school hours per week.







Even if France is known for having numerous and long school breaks throughout the year, students usually spend a long day at school—sometimes from 8 am until 6 pm—adding up to 28 or 35 hours of teaching per week, depending on the high school level and options.







Improve high school infrastructure.







Just like the state’s territorial management, high schools reproduce social inequalities. Some high schools located in rich districts have no infrastructure issues, while high schools located in low-income areas are falling apart. For example, some high schools have constant bathroom issues, some have no heat during winter and no proper insulation, some have roofs that leak when it rains.







Put an end to “ParcourSup.”







“ParcourSup” is the name of an online platform that students have to use during their final year to list what they would like to do after the school year. Created in 2018, this platform allows students to list their “wishes” and apply to different post-secondary education options such as universities, colleges, vocational and trade schools, and the like. Run by algorithms, this platform has been criticized since its implementation for the opacity of the criteria according to which it fulfills or thwarts students’ wishes. The platform creates considerable stress and competition among students, as those with better grades can be accepted more easily while the others might find no options whatsoever after high school, proving once more that this form of computerized selection increases social disparities and inequalities.







Engage more substitute teachers to maintain continuity in learning.







Students have been complaining that when one of their teachers is sick, there is often no substitute teacher available to take over in order to assist them in continuing to learn. This creates situations in which students sometimes don’t have a teacher for weeks in a specific discipline, even if it will be part of their national high school diploma exam.




Students burning trash bins in front of a high school in Lille on October 1, 2026.




All the 

previous points

 made by students are the direct result of years of educational restructuring, public spending cuts, and neo-liberal reforms. More and more, public schools are managed like private companies and forced to compete with one another to be more efficient.




This is not to say that without public spending cuts and neo-liberal reforms, the school system would be desirable. Under capitalism, the school system is a tool for the state to coerce us, to crush our individuality, to subdue our rebellious spirits and desires in order to reduce us to a docile workforce that can be exploited for the rest of our lives.




Police forces moving towards a burning barricade in Saint-Denis on October 1, 2026.




…Burst into Flames




By Monday, September 28, word had finally spread among students to coordinate actions on a larger scale. Early that morning, students started blocking the entrances of their schools, creating makeshift barricades out of whatever they could find nearby and in some cases by setting trash containers ablaze. Some of these blockades might have been the initiative of student unions or small political organizations, but in other cases, these actions were clearly personal initiatives on the part of small groups of highly motivated individuals. Viral images on social media likely helped to spread the word, creating a domino effect among teenagers: “Look at what the other high school is doing. Let’s do it, too!” This first day of action set the tone for the rest of the week as the movement spread beyond Paris and its suburbs.




The following day, while teachers, health care workers, firefighters, and other people from the public sector went on strike and 

demonstrated by the thousands

 in various cities against the next government budget cuts and in favor of better wages and working conditions, high-school students increased the pressure by protesting in front of some 400 schools throughout France, fully blockading approximately 40 of them.




Without hesitating, Laurent Nuñez, the current Interior Minister and former Prefect of Police of Paris from 2022 to 2025, decided to repress this emerging movement via brute force. Police were sent to high schools to crush the blockades and disperse the crowds of teenagers. Unsurprisingly, this strategy provoked confrontations between high-school students and heavily equipped police forces.




During the clashes, police used numerous tear gas canisters and shot rubber bullets at students while groups of teenagers and young adults resisted by throwing stones, bottles, fireworks, and other projectiles. By the end of the second day of actions, more than 400 individuals had been arrested across France, with two thirds of those arrests leading to police custody, according to 

official sources

.




Police forces in front of a burning barricade in Lille on September 30, 2026.




Nevertheless, the brutal repression didn’t undermine the determination of the students, who decided to continue the movement, blocking the schools on a massive scale on Wednesday, September 30. Clashes with law enforcement continued to escalate while blockades and other actions spread to numerous major cities, forcing the Interior Minister to officially recognize that same night that despite his repressive strategy, the student movement was gaining momentum and expanding. On September 30, police arrested 

625 individuals

 during the clashes. The first evidence of police brutality circulated online, as at least three students were severely injured by police ammunition.




On Thursday, October 1, the students continued to organize. For the first time since the beginning of the movement, some university students decided to join the struggle—even if they were not as numerous and determined to act as their younger accomplices. Fully 900 demonstrations, riots, and blockades took place 

all around France

. Authorities reported arson attempts both outside and inside some buildings; due to some extensive fire damage, a high school in Nantes will remain closed for a whole month. That day, students were able to shut down at least 160 high schools and to block access to 30 universities. This intense day of action resulted in almost 2000 new arrests, raising the total number of students arrested and detained since the beginning of the week to nearly 3000.




The Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes on October 1, 2026. After the arson, the high school will remain closed for at least a month.




Defending Power at Any Cost




That night, the government realized that its inability to control student unrest was drawing it towards another political crisis.




In order to regain control of the situation, the authorities made several hasty decisions:







The current Prime Minister called a crisis cabinet meeting for the following day to discuss possible plans and strategies to put an end to this unrest, on the grounds that the situation had shifted from a student movement characterized by school blockades to an unruly situation of urban violence.




The Minister of Education announced publicly that 400 high schools would be closed on Friday for “safety reasons,” either because the safety of the working personnel and students could not be assured, or simply on account of property damage. Students who can’t go to their schools will be following their classes online. In doing this, the government is reusing some of the strategies implemented during the COVID-19 pandemic in a different context.




The Minister of Education also announced that, the following day, he would meet with student unions and political organizations to hear their demands and find collective solutions in order to end the crisis. By meeting so-called spokespersons, the government wants to weaken the movement by dividing “good” students with legitimate requests from “rioters” and “violent individuals.”




The Interior Minister presented law enforcement agencies with an official list of all the high schools considered “high risk” by its intelligence services. In Paris alone, there were 13 high schools on this list. This suggests that the government has identified potential threats to the reigning order and is preparing to do everything in its power to neutralize these threats.




The Minister of Justice gathered attorneys general in order to discuss the proper legal response to adopt in order to prosecute all the students in custody. It is highly possible that the government will try to process these cases as fast as possible in courts, requesting harsh legal repercussions in order to make an example of these brave young individuals.







Nonetheless, all these announcements barely curbed the momentum of student unrest. Actions, blockades, and clashes with police continued across the country on Friday, October 2 before a well-deserved weekend.




A police officer attempts to destroy a burning barricade in Aubagne on October 2, 2026.




After a full week of political unrest involving intense property destruction, confrontations with law enforcement, and repression, and while the first trials were getting underway, political leaders of every stripe sought to use this situation to their own advantage, reaffirming their various positions.




While Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right party National Rally, emphasized the supposed need to create a new “anti-rioter” law in order to repress those who commit property destruction and resist police, the Macron government criticized the “violence” that took place and played on the classic dichotomy between “good ways of protesting” and “unforgivable ways of protesting”—while at the same time accusing the so-called “far-left” statist party of being responsible of all these events.




Clashes between students and police forces in Brest on October 2, 2026.




On Sunday, October 4, the 

government officially announced

 that the following day, more than 400 high schools in France would remain closed as security conditions still could not be assured. The Minister of Education declared that “24 schools had been burnt or ransacked and 78 education staff members injured” since the beginning of the movement.




Riot police arrest a demonstrator in front of a high school in Toulouse on October 2, 2026.




Students running away from tear gas in the streets of Lyons on October 2, 2026.




What Now?




Right now, information is flooding 

media outlets

 about the events of Monday, October 5. So far, it is estimated that almost 1000 individuals were arrested today, 589 schools experienced protests or blockades—240 schools in the Paris region alone—and 65 law enforcement agents were injured during confrontations with demonstrators. This suggests that the movement is not slowing down.




We are deeply saddened to learn that on October 5, in Lens, a 15-year-old boy 

lost his hand

 after picking up a stun grenade that law enforcement officers used to attack protesters. One of the three teenagers injured last week suffers from a broken jaw, having been shot point blank with a grenade launcher. Currently, the 14-year-old boy can’t open his mouth, as all his bottom teeth were knocked out by the impact and all his upper teeth are broken. Another 16-year-old teenager injured last week lost an eye after an officer shot him in the face with a rubber bullet.




Unfortunately, as the government is not willing to back down and wants to regain control by any means necessary, police violence will only continue to escalate. More and more serious injuries are likely to occur in the next days of confrontations. So far, according to official sources, 215 students have been injured since the beginning of the movement, as well as 85 educational staff members and—supposedly—715 law enforcement officers. These figures are skewed to over-represent police: the state does not distinguish “offensive” injuries such as bruised knuckles from inflicted injuries, while most demonstrators who are injured do not dare to seek treatment for their wounds or, if they do, conceal the fact that they were injured by police violence. Injuring and mutilating people both physically and psychologically is the only solution the state has found to preserve the fragile illusion of order. The police and the government are not here to protect us.




Since the beginning of the student unrest, 5060 people have been arrested, including 4406 minors and 654 adults. As of today, 1802 individuals are facing charges: 1483 minors and 319 adults. Of those, 14 are in pre-trial detention—10 adults and 4 minors.




A burning barricade in Aubervilliers on October 2, 2026.




Right now, people are holding their breath on the eve of the Third Act of this high school movement. On Tuesday, October 6, there is 

another call

 to 

join students in the streets

. Several sectors are already planning a variety of blockades elsewhere in France in solidarity.




No one can predict what will happen next or if the current political unrest will continue to gain momentum, reinventing and extending itself until October 17, the next day that there is a national call to take the streets. No one knows if the movement will find its resources to survive the brutal state and police repression that it is experiencing.




All we know for certain is that nothing is written in advance. The courage of the students taking part of this movement should inspire all of us to act now and to continue to push forward in order to fight against all odds for a better world!




Confrontations in Cran-Gevrier between students and police forces on October 1, 2026.




Further Reading




These articles, written in French, explore these events further:







À nos enfants et lycéens




La jeunesse emmerde l’État policier




L’ordre contre la jeunesse




Des cauchemars et des rêves




La mobilisation lycéenne à travers les yeux d’une professeur du 93




Brûle ton lycée










A makeshift barricade in the streets of Paris on October 2, 2026. The graffiti refers to the extreme-right National Rally party.

author: Folashade Roberts
title: Old Nollywood 2.0
content:
Scroll to the comments under the movie 

Love in Every Word

 on YouTube, and you will find viewers from Lagos to London, Accra, Houston, and beyond, tagging sisters to “come and watch this.” Even though the movie had no cinema release and no streaming deal, it reached 15 million views within a week of its March 2025 release on the Omoni Oboli TV YouTube channel. It reached roughly 30 million by year’s end. Actress and filmmaker Omoni Oboli and her business partner, Tomi Adeoye, launched Omoni Oboli TV in December 2023. Since then, the channel has gained more than two million subscribers. The success of 

Love in Every Word

 and its sequel pushed their YouTube television channel past 182 million total views across 550 videos, and it was named YouTube Nigeria’s Top Creator Channel of 2025.

The story and style of 

Love in Every Word

 are typical of Nollywood cinema, but there is something about the success of its format that raises questions. Is it an example of a new paradigm for how we understand the present-day movie industry in Nigeria? Or is it marking a return to the spirit of the original Nollywood? Does this format’s mix of “New Nollywood” and “Old Nollywood” betoken a new concept? Perhaps we could call it “Old Nollywood 2.0.”

Sometimes journalists and scholars like to divide film history into neat periods of succession. But looking at the history of Nollywood cinema, the reality is that there have been overlapping industrial formations. For the past three decades, the Nollywood phenomenon and its global impact have been described, analyzed, and debated, and the storyline goes something like this. Once upon a time, in the late 1980s, in the street markets of Onitsha and Lagos, movie theaters were declining because the cost of production and distribution of celluloid films was prohibitive. Independent producers were shooting television drama on video, working with Nigerian television networks, while the Yoruba traveling theater troupes were experimenting with video. Alongside this development, traders and marketers, who were already distributing imported and pirated Hollywood and Bollywood films, began to make and market their own cheaply produced melodrama on VHS.

Before Nollywood, there was a politically Pan-Africanist movie industry across Africa into which the recently liberated postcolonial nation-states enthusiastically invested. In the 1970s, the Nigerian government expanded its involvement in film and cultural production when it hosted FESTAC ’77 and repositioned the existing Nigerian Film Unit (formerly Colonial Film Unit) into the Nigerian Film Corporation, with a mandate to broaden its responsibilities and foster development of the national film industry. Filmmakers such as Ola Balogun and Adamu Halilu made artistically stunning films, sometimes collaborating with Black artists from across the world.

With the onset of structural adjustment policies imposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), alongside the devastation of civil wars and repressive regimes, the state’s investment in a liberated media crumbled. What some consider the “golden age” of artistically brilliant, politically progressive Nigerian cinema was diminished. Into the void stepped entrepreneurial, commercially minded filmmakers who took advantage of the straight-to-video format and what economists call the “informal market” of the street. The new “video-films” (first made on VHS and then on VCD and DVD) were quite popular for a multitude of genres, from crime (

Issakaba

, 2001), domestic melodrama (

Violated

, 1996), and family drama (

Rattlesnake

, 1995), to religion (

Agony of a Mother

, 2002), romance (

Keeping Faith: Is That Love

?, 2002), slapstick comedy (

Osuofia in London

, 2003), social mobility (

Glamour Girls

, 1994), urban aspiration (

Domitilla

, 1996), and occult and supernatural narratives (

Living in Bondage

, 1992, and 

Nneka the Pretty Serpent

, 1994). The rapid success of these movies far exceeded expectations.

Nollywood’s enormous local and global popularity attracted new investors and renewed interest in theatrical exhibition. The opening of new multiplexes from 2004 created another route to audiences and encouraged a strand of filmmaking characterized by larger budgets, improved production values, and theatrical premieres. The transformation did not stop at the cinema. The South African company MultiChoice/Africa Magic expanded its investment in Nigerian content, while digital distribution and, later, global streaming platforms created still more routes to audiences. Netflix became available in Nigeria in 2016, followed later by Amazon Prime Video’s more substantial engagement with the Nigerian market.

Journalists branded the movies and business that came from this “New Nollywood.” Champions of New Nollywood included filmmaker Kunle Afolayan with 

The Figurine

 (2009), 

Phone Swap

 (2012), and 

October 1

 (2014). Others include Chineze Anyaene with 

Ije: The Journey

 (2010); Obi Emelonye, who went transnational with 

Mirror Boy

 (2011) and also made 

Last Flight to Abuja

 (2012); Biyi Bandele, who adapted Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie’s novel 

Half of a Yellow Sun

 in 2013; Stephanie Linus, who made 

Dry

 in 2014; and Kemi Adetiba, who made 

The Wedding Party

 in 2016 for EbonyLife Productions, owned by Mo Abudu. Many of these films premiered with cinema runs and then transitioned to DVDs before streamers came around to lease them for internet consumption.

Soon, everyone was talking about the difference between “Old Nollywood” and “New Nollywood,” whether one was a professor of literature at the University of Ibadan or a taxi driver in Lagos. The salient features of the old Nollywood in the 1990s were low-budget and fast film production, direct distribution through the Alaba Market and Onitsha Market, moral and lesson-driven storytelling, familiar character types and stereotypes, family stories, and religious themes. Often, dancing and other public performances were used as marketing tools. More often than not, what sold the movie was the image and the name recognition of the actors and actresses. We see those features in the classic movies such as 

Living in Bondage

, 

Nneka the Pretty Serpent

, 

Domitilla

, and 

Glamour Girls

.

A good example of Old Nollywood is when filmmaker Amaka Igwe famously boasted back in 1995 that she made her movie 

Rattlesnake

 in just two weeks. 

Rattlesnake

 is a crime drama about the double life of its main character. It is typical of “Old Nollywood” movies in the way it interrogates the corruption behind wealth through the formal genre conventions of exaggerated melodrama. In contrast, what was called New Nollywood had much larger budgets and production quality good enough for premiering with the public pomp and fanfare of red carpets and large-screen theaters and got recognition at both local (the Africa Movie Academy Awards, or AMAA) and international film festivals (the New York African Film Festival and FESPACO, the Pan-African Film and Television Festival of Ouagadougou). For example, one of the films that ushered in New Nollywood is 

The Figurine

 by Kunle Afolayan, which brought the public back into the cinema halls. Because it matched international standards for cinematography and sound design, and because it offered audiences a morally ambiguous, complex plot and realistic acting, it premiered at prestigious international film festivals, thus marking a shift away from Old Nollywood’s grassroots style.

Love in Every Word

 is an example of what we are calling “Old Nollywood 2.0.” Beyond its impressive viewing numbers, it quickly became a social event. Viewers shared clips on WhatsApp, created memes on TikTok and Instagram, and tagged friends and family across Nigeria, Ghana, and the African diaspora, extending the film’s reach beyond YouTube itself. The movie is about the romance between Chioma and Odogwu, played respectively by the former Big Brother star Bamike Olawunmi-Adenibuyan and Uzor Arukwe. As the plot unfolds, the relationship between the two protagonists is affected by familiar Nollywood topics, such as career pressure and family matchmaking, but Chioma also has a troubled past that makes her guarded against men who in any way resemble her wealthy, distant father, whose rejection scarred her as a child. 

This story became a pop culture phenomenon when phrases and character types from the movie translated to memes across social media. For example, the phrases 

Odogwu paranran

 (a rich provider “Igbo” man who loves loudly) and 

Achalugo

 (a beautiful girl who lives softly and receives the love graciously from her Odogwu) adapt the nicknames of the characters to describe real relationships that fans of the movie might have (or fantasize about having). Some fans even made their own videos with voiceovers from the movie, where girls might recreate the story, manifesting the 

Odogwu paranran

 soft life for themselves.

The success of the movie is just one example of how filmmakers and film audiences are finding new ways to produce, distribute, promote, and consume motion picture entertainment. Other examples include 

Head of House

 (directed by Ruth Kadiri in 2024), 

My Crazy Rich Girlfriend

 (directed by Ben Cassie, 2024, for Uchenna Mbunabo TV), and 

Momiwa

 (directed by Biodun Stephen in 2025). Interestingly, although the YouTube channel owners are well-established filmmakers, they often hire directors and talented professionals to produce movies for their channels. The statistics are remarkable: 

Head of House

 reached more than 6.3 million views, 

My Crazy Rich Girlfriend

 reached more than 19 million, and the recent film, 

Momiwa

, had reached 1.3 million when we last checked. In the past, journalists and scholars had to beg theaters, producers, and streaming services for statistics about sales in order to gauge a movie’s popularity and worried that the statistics were inaccurate. But YouTube does that for us.

The apparent dominance of YouTube productions in the Nigerian market comes at an interesting moment, historically, for African cinema. Around November 2024, there were rumors that Netflix was pulling out of the Nigerian market. Netflix denied this vehemently, but there have been fewer “Netflix originals” and fewer acquisitions from Nigeria on Netflix since then. Netflix, which entered the Nigerian filmscape in 2016 and produced the first Nigerian original, Genevieve Nnaji’s 

Lionheart

 in 2018, went on to partner with many Nigerian filmmakers, including Kunle Afolayan, Kemi Adetiba, Mo Abudu, and Bolanle Austen-Peter for originals while also leasing several titles. The rumor of Netflix’s departure from Nigeria came as a shock to the industry. Amazon Prime and Showmax have since followed suit.

For the past eight years, African filmmakers and film scholars across the continent have been debating whether the involvement of Netflix, Amazon Prime, DStv, Canal+, and other multinational corporations in African film industries would positively upgrade production quality and opportunities for local talent or would negatively undermine authentic African storytelling. By the year 2025, the market of production and consumption had already shifted from Netflix and DStv to YouTube — so much so that what we are calling Old Nollywood 2.0 seems to have responded to the departures of global investors such as Netflix with a shrug of indifference, as its star filmmakers and others have moved on to YouTube, blazing a trail for sustainable production under new terms and conditions.

Does the success of these filmmakers on YouTube and the new ways of engaging with audiences suggest a paradigm shift in Africa’s movie industry? That is the argument of a new book about African cinema, 

Contemporary African Screen Worlds

 (2025), edited by Lindiwe Dovey, Añulika Agina, and Michael W. Thomas, which celebrates what they see as a grassroots, authentic relationship between artists and audiences. These scholars challenge the gatekeeping function of cineplexes, television stations, journalists, academics, and anyone who aims to be the curator of what is and what isn’t worthy of public consumption. The authors gush about the techno-utopian promise of YouTube, TikTok, WhatsApp, and other social media to bypass the film critics and enable those who were left out of the conversation to have a more active voice. Their argument is compelling, even though one might wonder if it’s mostly those with access to wealth and power that are able to bypass the critics.

We agree that social media has transformed how we watch and relate to cinema, but many of the qualities of YouTube Nollywood remind us of the “Old Nollywood” of the 1990s, and not in a bad way. The migration of Nollywood films to YouTube has created new possibilities for filmmakers, but it has not necessarily produced an entirely new cinema. In many ways, what emerges is recognizably Nollywood: familiar stories, stars, production methods, and narrative conventions, now operating within a different distribution and consumption environment. Nigerian films released on YouTube have attracted substantial audiences, but they also retain elements of the older Nollywood tradition.

The numbers also demonstrate the considerable audience available to YouTube Nollywood. Unlike Old Nollywood’s VHS and VCD circulation, however, the YouTube audience is now publicly measurable. Views and comments leave visible traces of consumption, while the channel allows filmmakers to gather audiences repeatedly around subsequent releases. In this sense, Old Nollywood 2.0 is not simply the old industry transferred online. Rather, YouTube changes the relationship between filmmaker, distributor, and audience even when some of the storytelling remains familiar. Arguably, if African cinema across the continent is entering a new era in which YouTube is the dominant form of media, then when journalists and scholars talk about cinema, they must pay attention to what is unique about YouTube — namely, its computer algorithms, its monetization structures and mechanisms for copyright control, the possibility for quick and easy cross-platform distribution and advertising from YouTube to TikTok to WhatsApp, and most importantly, the virtual spaces for audience participation.

The film 

Momiwa

 is an example. As with the majority of Biodun Stephen’s work, this movie bypassed theaters and streaming companies such as Netflix and was uploaded directly to Biodun Stephen TV on YouTube in early 2025. Stephen is known for writing strong and relatable female characters and is frequently credited as writer, director, and producer of her films. 

Momiwa

 bears some of the production characteristics of Old Nollywood: much of the action takes place indoors, with outdoor scenes largely contained within the compound and around the gate. The emphasis is therefore on story, character, and domestic conflict rather than spectacle. The actions of the selfish, absent mother are performed with exaggerated melodramatic flair by actress Iyabo Ojo, in stark contrast to the angelic, Christ-like performance of Blessing Obasi’s character Momiwa. Even the awkward gateman recalls the comic stock characters of older Nollywood, particularly Yoruba-language films where performers such as Baba Suwe often appeared across films in recognizable comic personas. The difference between movies such as 

Momiwa

 and “Old Nollywood” is partly technological: the images are cleaner and the production quality higher, even if still modest compared with Nollywood films commissioned for Netflix or Amazon Prime. It’s also a matter of distribution and the relationship to the audience, as the actors and producers are also social media personalities who reach out to audiences online.

YouTube appears to offer filmmakers greater autonomy: they can own their channels, choose their stories, determine their release schedules, and communicate directly with their audiences. But they do not own YouTube. Their visibility and earnings remain subject to the platform’s policies, monetization structures, and algorithms. Nollywood has moved from a marketer-driven distribution system to an algorithmically governed one.

Neither does the rise of YouTube mean that cinema or global streaming has disappeared. Nigerian films continue to circulate through multiple routes, sometimes moving from cinemas to streaming platforms while other films go directly to YouTube. These forms coexist and overlap rather than neatly replacing one another. Perhaps, then, Nollywood has never developed through the tidy periods that we sometimes impose on its history. Old forms persist, newer ones emerge, and practices thought to have disappeared sometimes return in altered forms. 

“Old Nollywood 2.0” is not an attempt to announce yet another neatly defined and chronologically bound era of Nigerian cinema. It is a way of naming this particular moment of return and reinvention, and of asking whether what appears strikingly new about Nollywood today may also be remarkably old.

title: Cuerpos que piensan, cuerpos que resisten: la danza tomó el Centro Cultural Universitario Paco Urondo
content:
Iara Pavanello, Dulcinea Segura Rattagan y Carolina Bergero, el equipo del IAE encargado de la curaduría del encuentro




Durante dos intensas jornadas, el Instituto de Artes del Espectáculo de la UBA reunió a decenas de investigadoras, bailarinas, creadores y docentes de distintos puntos del país y de Latinoamérica para pensar una pregunta urgente: ¿qué hacen los cuerpos cuando los poderes fácticos tienen tanto interés de desmaterializarlos? El VI Encuentro de Pensamiento sobre Danza y Prácticas Somáticas, titulado «Cuerpos en estado de resistencia» combinó ponencias académicas, talleres participativos, funciones y proyecciones de videodanza en un formato mixto que permitió seguir las actividades de manera presencial, y virtualmente. El Centro Cultural Universitario Paco Urondo fue el escenario para el despliegue artístico. Su arquitectura de estilo academicista funcionó como el cuerpo receptor del 6° enc

uentro de prácticas somáticas. 

Por ANRed.







El 1 y 2 de octubre, el Área de danza y artes del movimiento del IAE-UBA, 

que coordina la investigadora especialista en danza Dulcinea Segura Rattagan, junto al equipo que componen Iara Pavanello y Carolina Bergero

, organizó una nueva edición de su encuentro anual, que desde hace seis años viene consolidándose como uno de los espacios de reflexión sobre el cuerpo más importantes del ámbito académico porteño.




La convocatoria superó el formato de jornada universitaria tradicional: 

43 ponencias distribuidas en dos días reunieron a más de cincuenta expositores/ as

, con una variedad de voces que incluyó a estudiantes de grado y posgrado, investigadores del CONICET, docentes de conservatorios, trabajadores de la salud y representantes de escuelas de formación artística.




Taller exploratorio de investigación corporal, por Soledad Manrique




Lo federal 

fue una

 marca del encuentro

. A la participación de universidades porteñas y bonaerenses —la UBA, la UNA y la Universidad Nacional de Río Negro— se sumaron 

expositoras de Chaco, Rosario, Córdoba y Neuquén

, además de la presencia internacional: Brasil, Chile, Colombia, Uruguay y España representados a través de ponencias que pusieron en diálogo tradiciones corporales y de la danza de muy variada procedencia. Del ballet barroco al zaar sudanés; desde la danza gawazi egipcia hasta las memorias somáticas de comunidades indígenas del Chaco argentino. La amplitud geográfica se tradujo en una conversación rica, donde 

la pregunta por la resistencia se formuló desde contextos culturales y políticos diferentes

, sin perder nunca el hilo común.




«Estamos volviendo a casa» obra del grupo Bailarines toda la vida, del grupo de Danza Comunitaria dirigido por Aurelia Chimelli




La dinámica de trabajo favoreció esa multiplicidad. Las mesas temáticas, organizadas en bloques de entre cuatro y seis exposiciones breves, permitieron que cada jornada avanzara a ritmo ágil, con un diálogo rico de temas, que permitieron tender puentes entre un trabajo sobre eutonía y una reflexión sobre psicodrama, o con una investigación sobre danza y salud mental. 

El tema: la resistencia

, sumada a la cuidadosa curaduría 

fue un acierto. 




La jornada del jueves tuvo una fuerte impronta práctica y artística.

 Por la tarde, en el Paco Urondo, se desarrolló un 

taller exploratorio de investigación corporal a cargo de la Doctora e investigadora Soledad Manrique

, abierto a todo público. Allí se propuso indagar modos de habitar la crisis desde la sensopercepción y el vínculo grupal. Luego llegó el turno de la 

videodanza

, bajo la curaduría de 

Ladys González

, integrante del Circuito Argentino de Videodanza, y a cargo del Festival Internacional Corporalidad Expandida (FICE). Se seleccionaron: 

R.E.D., de Oscar Martínez

, un trabajo que indaga el vínculo entre el sonido y la ciudad, entre el ser humano y el espacio público urbano. 

DES(ARCHIVADAS), de Anahí Mariluan

, distinguida en el Festival Internacional Cámara Corporizada, y 

LONA, de Malena Martínez

, homenaje en stop-motion a los 194 muertos y más de 1400 heridos que dejó la tragedia de Cromagnon, en clave amorosa. Todos los videos pusieron en diálogo el archivo, la memoria y la resistencia a través del movimiento, y fueron seguidos de un conversatorio con sus directorxs. La jornada cerró con la función de 

«Todas las cosas que somos», de Alina Marinelli

, a cargo del Grupo de Experimentación en Artes del Movimiento de la UNA (GEAM) que dirige Valeria Martínez.




«

Todas las cosas que somos», dirigido por Alina Marinelli, a cargo del Grupo de Experimentación de Artes del Movimiento (GEAM), UNA




Si hubo un momento que condensó el espíritu político del encuentro, fue el conversatorio entre el 

Colectivo Fin de un Mundo

 y 

Danza por la Identidad

; dos espacios con historias y lenguajes distintos, pero con una misma convicción de fondo: que 

el cuerpo es territorio de memoria y lucha

. El cruce entre ambos colectivos fue una suerte de síntesis de lo que se planteó en muchas de las ponencias, desde la teoría: que todo cuerpo en movimiento es en función de la coyuntura específica, de la historia, de las instituciones y de las violencias que se hayan sufrido.




Bailarines toda la vida, Danza Comunitaria dirigida por Aurelia Chimelli




El 6° encuentro cerró con la 

conferencia performática: «Resistir para crear, crear para resistir», de 

Revista Kiné

, bajo la coordinación de Julia Pomiés, con la función de 

«Estamos volviendo a casa», de 

Bailarines Toda la Vida

, el espacio de danza comunitaria dirigido por 

Aurelia Chillemi

. Dos propuestas que confirmaron que la calidad no estuvo reñida con la accesibilidad, ya que 

todas las actividades fueron gratuitas y abiertas

. Un gesto que reafirmó desde la propuesta integral lo que variadas ponencias sostuvieron en la teoría: que 

resistir es una tarea colectiva

.




Fotos: Andrés Manrique

author: Thomas Kennedy
title: Florida City That Willingly Signed Deal With ICE Finds Itself in Crisis
content:
This story was co-published with

 

Truthout

.




The City of Doral is in crisis. Since Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, the Florida municipality has found itself in the crosshairs of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), with ongoing raids and targeted operations that seem to be intensifying in recent weeks.




Nearly half of Doral’s 

population

 is from Venezuela, the largest population of Venezuelans in any city in the United States. This is a diaspora that finds itself under constant attack by the Trump administration, as more than 

615,000

 have lost or are facing the termination of their temporary protected status (TPS) following revocations, and Venezuelans make up 59 percent of all immigrants affected by mass terminations of TPS designations. These are the same people who now find themselves in the crosshairs of enforcement operations in Doral. The recent earthquakes in Caracas that have killed thousands and destroyed critical infrastructure did nothing to stop these attacks against Venezuelan immigrants, despite the country obviously being in no condition to receive hundreds of thousands of these nationals back if they were to be deported.




Despite presiding over such a vulnerable population, Doral’s government was one of the first in the state to sign a 287(g) agreement under the second Trump administration, deputizing local police with specific federal immigration enforcement powers. The mayor and council members did this under no requirement, mandate, or obligation, as Florida statute requires only counties and sheriff’s departments operating jails or detention facilities to sign these types of agreements, and Doral operates neither. 




Doral’s government was one of the first in the state to sign a 287(g) agreement deputizing local police with specific federal immigration enforcement powers.




Now that 

public

 sentiment is turning against them, amid the draconian immigration enforcement we see across the country daily, Doral politicians are trying to have it both ways. Mayor Christi Fraga continues to mischaracterize the 287(g) agreement that the city signed under her tenure, 

falsely

 claiming that it is not a direct partnership with ICE, and that the state of Florida obligated Doral to sign on. As already established, this is simply not true, and Fraga claims that the city can’t rescind the agreement because their “responsibility as elected officials is to follow the law as it exists.” Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier has claimed that cities like Doral can’t revoke 287(g) agreements because this would create a de facto sanctuary city jurisdiction. This is nonsense, as Doral still falls under the correctional jurisdiction of Miami-Dade County, which actively funnels people from its local jails into ICE detention.




It seems Fraga, who supported the signing of the 287(g) contract in Doral, may be obfuscating in this manner because she doesn’t want to burn any political capital rescinding the agreement and would rather do 

photo ops

 with Trump. During the president’s visit to Doral for the “Shield of the Americas” Summit,  Fraga sat next to him during a meal, even as heightened levels of immigration enforcement under his administration are separating her constituents’ families. When asked for comment for this article Fraga responded by sharing a letter she sent to Florida’s Attorney General James Uthmeier asking for legal clarification on whether localities are obligated to remain in the 287(g) program, which Uthmeier has not responded to.




Similarly, Doral Councilman Rafael Pineyro, who 

voted

 in favor of Doral’s 287(g) agreement, is trying to have it both ways as a Republican who supported Trump and has not outright broken with him, but who is increasingly pushing back as hardline immigration crackdowns intensify in Doral.













The Appeal in Your Inbox




Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.
































          Sign Up
        
















Pushing back with mumbled statements and an ineffectual letter expressing disagreement with the rescinding of TPS and 

stating

 that the “law can be enforced without losing our humanity,” Pineyro exemplifies the do-nothing approach of politicians across South Florida who supported Trump, who in turn paid them back by separating families and creating chaos in our neighborhoods. Pineyro did not respond by press time when offered the chance to comment.




Residents of Doral, especially the immigrant families disproportionately targeted by ICE enforcement, deserve better than this. The damage is also spreading to business owners, who complain about the widespread fear impacting commerce as people stay home and avoid shopping. Restaurants like 

Chaguarma Grill

 have gone on the record with 

Telemundo

 to announce their closure, as they have neither clients nor workers. Other food establishments have lost up to 40 percent of their clientele. 




Doral is hardly the only municipality in Florida besieged by heightened levels of aggressive immigration enforcement and facing calls by residents to stop local cooperation with ICE. The 

City of Miami

 also needlessly signed a 287(g) agreement last summer, as three out of five commissioners ignored hours of public testimony from residents who overwhelmingly opposed deputizing their police department to conduct immigration enforcement operations. Since then, we have seen ICE agents 

indiscriminately

 stop people in Little Havana, asking for their immigration status, and Uber drivers being stopped and detained on main roads. People are being stalked and taken by ICE 

outside

 places of worship.




Will Doral’s leaders rectify their mistake in needlessly signing on to a 287(g) agreement and rescind it — something they can legally do under Florida law? 




This is occurring without the militarized-style raids seen in other parts of the country, such as Minneapolis, Chicago, and Los Angeles. Instead, Florida’s high rate of immigration arrests is driven largely by cooperation between local law enforcement and federal immigration authorities through 287(g) agreements. The result is a state where immigration enforcement has become pervasive, reaching far beyond traditional immigration agencies. The

 Florida Lottery

, the Florida Department of Financial Services, and even police departments at public universities have entered into 287(g) agreements with ICE.




The Florida Highway Patrol (FHP) has taken this role particularly far, making thousands of immigration arrests in recent months after Gov. Ron DeSantis announced a 287(g) partnership between the Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles and ICE. The agreement gives FHP troopers authority to question people about their immigration status during traffic stops, effectively turning routine encounters with state law enforcement into potential immigration-enforcement encounters.




The expansion has reached even agencies with little traditional connection to immigration enforcement. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) — whose law-enforcement mission has historically centered on hunting, fishing, boating safety, and habitat protection — has 

increasingly

 been drawn into immigration enforcement. Roughly 90 percent of its law-enforcement personnel (about 800 of nearly 890 officers) have been deputized under 287(g). The training has reportedly been so limited that one officer 

described

 feeling like a “newborn giraffe with wobbly legs trying to make its way around.” These agreements illustrate how immigration enforcement has been woven into the ordinary operations of state and local government, extending from highway traffic stops to wildlife officers, university police, professional licensing agencies, and even the state lottery.




Attorneys for the DeSantis administration acknowledged that the state does not require every municipality to enter into a 287(g) agreement with ICE.




So, the question for Mayor Fraga and Doral’s councilmembers is a simple one: Will they continue to feign empty sympathy for the plight of their immigrant constituents, the families impacted, and the businesses struggling, without doing anything to address this issue? Or will Doral’s leaders rectify their mistake in needlessly signing on to a 287(g) agreement and rescind it — something they can legally do under Florida law? While cities like Doral and Miami excuse their inaction by claiming that they fear removal from office by Governor DeSantis if they rescind the 287(g) agreements they irresponsibly signed, the City of South Miami 

provides a case study

 in successful pushback against state pressure to comply with overzealous immigration crackdowns. 




A lawsuit filed by South Miami sought to clarify whether state law required municipalities to establish police-ICE cooperation. Although the case was dismissed for lack of legal standing, attorneys for the DeSantis administration 

acknowledged

 during oral arguments that the state does not require every municipality to enter into a 287(g) agreement with ICE.




Similarly, after facing opposition from residents, Miami Shores 

deferred

 a proposed 287(g) agreement. South Miami, Miami Shores, and two-thirds of municipalities in Miami-Dade continue to operate without entering into these agreements, demonstrating that local governments retain the ability to decline this form of cooperation, and highlighting the political cowardice of officials in cities like Doral and Miami.




Will Doral officials do the right thing and stop their police coordination with ICE? Time will tell — but for many of Doral’s residents, time is something they do not have.




The post 

Florida City That Willingly Signed Deal With ICE Finds Itself in Crisis

 appeared first on 

The Appeal

.

title: "Incredible Moment for the Borderlands": Judge Blocks Border Wall Expansion in Big Bend & West Texas
content:
In a victory for environmentalists and immigration rights’ advocates, a federal judge in El Paso, Texas, has blocked further border wall construction inside Big Bend National Park. “We slammed the brakes on $7 billion worth of corrupt construction contracts,” says Laiken Jordahl, a national public lands advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity, which sued to block the expansion. “We have effectively stopped construction across West Texas, and it’s incredible.”




Jordahl also responds to the Trump administration’s excavation of a 200-year-old cottonwood tree on the Arizona-Mexico border that had been protected by activists for months. “Watching those videos of them toppling this ancient tree that was very likely older than the border itself is symbolic of how 

DHS

 has treated the border region. They see our communities, our wildlife, our nature as a sacrifice zone,” says Jordahl.

author: Andrés
title: Dos años bordando historias: memoria, identidad y comunidad
content:
Foto: Daniel Ávalos




«Bordando Historias – Construyendo Memoria» cumplió dos años y lo celebró con música, baile y encuentro entre distintas comunidades. Mujeres paraguayas y bolivianas compartieron sus danzas, la música del norte argentino acompañó la jornada y la memoria volvió a aparecer como un territorio común. A pocos días del 12 de octubre, la celebración puso en el centro la diversidad cultural y las historias de quienes construyen sus identidades lejos de los relatos oficiales. 

Por Daniel Ávalos (ANRed).







Hay memorias que se escriben con palabras y otras que se construyen con las manos. Hay historias que sobreviven en fotografías, en relatos familiares, en canciones y también en una tela atravesada por hilos de colores. Hace dos años nació Bordando Historias – Construyendo Memoria, un espacio que encontró en el bordado una herramienta para recuperar historias, encontrarse y construir memoria colectiva. Ayer, sus integrantes celebraron ese recorrido con una jornada donde el arte, la música y las distintas identidades culturales ocuparon el centro de la escena.




La celebración tuvo música y baile. Mujeres compartieron sus danzas, mientras la música del norte argentino acompañó un encuentro que reafirmó los lazos entre distintas comunidades. Porque allí donde muchas veces se construyen fronteras, el encuentro puede convertirse en una forma de resistencia.




El aniversario estuvo atravesado también por la proximidad del 12 de octubre, Día del Respeto a la Diversidad Cultural. Una fecha que invita a revisar las miradas históricas sobre los pueblos originarios y, al mismo tiempo, a reconocer las múltiples culturas que forman parte del presente. En ese sentido, la celebración de Bordando Historias tuvo algo de declaración colectiva: las identidades no están congeladas en el pasado. Se encuentran, se mezclan, se transforman y se sostienen en comunidad.




Foto: Daniel Ávalos




El espacio está vinculado además a la memoria de los trabajadores textiles, con las historias de quienes padecieron condiciones de explotación y precarización, particularmente en torno a la Masacre de Luis Viale, ocurrida en 2006.




Recuperar ese pasado es también poner en discusión las condiciones de vida y trabajo de las comunidades migrantes y de los sectores populares. Pero la memoria no apareció ayer como una pieza de museo. Apareció viva. En las manos que bordan. En las mujeres que bailan. En las canciones compartidas. En las distintas maneras de hablar, de recordar y de celebrar. En una comunidad que se reconoce diversa y que hace de esa diversidad un punto de encuentro.




Dos años de Bordando Historias son dos años de construir memoria desde abajo, de recuperar voces y de transformar el recuerdo en encuentro. Puntada a puntada, historia a historia, las distintas comunidades siguen tejiendo una trama común. Quizá allí esté la potencia de este espacio: entender que la memoria no solamente se conserva; también se construye colectivamente, se baila, se canta y se vuelve presente.

title: Organizaciones sociales marchan a Capital Humano contra el ajuste y a la Corte Suprema por la recuperación de la Ley de Tierras
content:
Más de 70 organizaciones sociales, territoriales y piqueteras se movilizarán este martes 6 de octubre contra las políticas de ajuste del gobierno de Javier Milei y en rechazo al fallo de la Corte Suprema que dejó vigente la derogación de la Ley de Tierras Rurales. La jornada comenzará a las 13.30 con una conferencia de prensa frente al histórico edificio del Ministerio de Capital Humano (ex Desarrollo Social), a cargo de Sandra Pettovello, donde denunciarán el ajuste, la pérdida de ingresos y el desmantelamiento de políticas destinadas a los sectores populares. Luego, movilizarán al Palacio de Justicia, donde confluirán con una amplio marco de organizaciones que repudiarán el fallo de la Corte Suprema de Justicia de la semana pasada, que eliminó los límites para la adquisición de campos argentinos por parte de extranjeros. La jornada de lucha de los movimientos sociales busca también preparar nuevas acciones para el jueves 15 de octubre, cuando la Cámara de Diputados tiene prevista una sesión especial para tratar el DNU 70/23.







Más de 70 organizaciones sociales, territoriales y piqueteras se movilizarán este martes 6 de octubre contra las políticas de ajuste del gobierno de Javier Milei y en rechazo al fallo de la Corte Suprema que dejó vigente la derogación de la Ley N° 279 de Tierras Rurales. La jornada comenzará a las 13.30 con una conferencia de prensa frente al histórico edificio del Ministerio de Capital Humano (ex Desarrollo Social), a cargo de Sandra Pettovello, y continuará con una movilización hacia el Palacio de Justicia.




Imagen: CTA Autónoma.




“Más de 70 organizaciones territoriales, sociales y piqueteras que venimos luchando en los barrios contra la destrucción y el ataque sistemático a las condiciones de vida de la enorme mayoría de las y los trabajadores, nos convocamos este martes 6 de octubre a las 13 en el histórico edificio del Ministerio de Desarrollo Social para realizar una conferencia de prensa”, señalan en la convocatoria.




Concentración de la UTEP frente al Ministerio de Capital Humano contra el hambre.




“Esta situación se da en un cuadro de crecimiento de la desocupación y la precarización laboral, caída del consumo y cierre de empresas, mientras la mayoría de las familias se encuentra endeudada a niveles insostenibles para poder llegar a fin de mes”, sostienen las organizaciones. En ese mismo sentido, un informe del Instituto de Investigación Social Económica y Política Ciudadana (ISEPCI) calculó que la eliminación del programa Volver al Trabajo, efectiva desde abril de 2026, dejó sin ese ingreso a cerca de 950.000 trabajadores informales y afectó a más de tres millones de personas al considerar a sus grupos familiares.




Otro de los ejes está puesto en la asistencia alimentaria: «venimos, además, de sufrir el corte abrupto e injustificado de la entrega de alimentos a más de 45.000 comedores populares, situación por la cual la ministra Sandra Pettovello ha sido llevada a juicio». El reclamo contra la política social se articula además con la eliminación del programa Volver al Trabajo: “Milei eliminó el programa Volver al Trabajo, dejando a casi un millón de trabajadores sociales, cocineras, recicladores y otros trabajadores de la economía popular sin el único ingreso que percibían por trabajar”. La medida efectivamente alcanzó a cientos de miles de titulares y, según un informe del ISEPCI, implicó el retiro de unos $74.100 millones mensuales del circuito de consumo popular.




Foto: David Briasco.




Luego de la conferencia de prensa, anuncian: “marcharemos al Palacio de Justicia en repudio al infame y cipayo fallo de la Corte Suprema, que sostiene la extranjerización de la tierra mediante la ratificación del inconstitucional Decreto 70/23”.




Para las organizaciones convocantes, la cuestión territorial forma parte de una ofensiva más amplia: “este decreto no solo habilita la entrega del territorio nacional al capital extranjero, sino que agrava la situación de tenencia precaria que padecen los pueblos originarios y la población trabajadora, amenazada permanentemente por desalojos en terrenos recuperados mediante enormes luchas para defender un pedazo de tierra donde vivir y producir”. El reclamo se produce, además, después de una jornada federal el pasado 6 de agosto en la que organizaciones indígenas, campesinas, ambientales, sociales y sindicales se movilizaron contra la extranjerización de la tierra y denunciaron el proyecto de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada.




CIUDAD DE BUENOS AIRES, ARGENTINA – 6 DE AGOSTO: Un manifestante sostiene una bandera argentina en defensa de la tierra y los recursos públicos frente al Palacio Legislativo. La jornada de protesta coincide con consignas sobre la soberanía, sumando reclamos a la movilización. (Foto: David Briasco)




El fallo del máximo tribunal, dictado el 29 de septiembre, revocó la sentencia de la Cámara Federal de La Plata que había declarado inconstitucional el artículo 154 del DNU 70/2023, que derogó la Ley 26.737, al rechazar la demanda presentada por el Centro de Ex Combatientes Islas Malvinas (CECIM) La Plata por considerar que la organización no estaba legitimada para promoverla. Aunque el tribunal aclaró que no se pronunció sobre la constitucionalidad del decreto, su decisión dejó vigente la derogación de la Ley de Tierras y, con ella, los límites que impedían superar el 15% de tierras rurales en manos extranjeras.




La movilización de hoy se produce, además, en la previa de una nueva batalla institucional, donde sectores de la oposición convocaron para el próximo jueves 15 de octubre una sesión especial en Diputados para intentar derogar el DNU 70/23. El decreto ya fue rechazado por el Senado y su derogación en Diputados permitiría recuperar las restricciones de la Ley de Tierras. Para abrir la sesión la oposición necesita reunir 129 legisladores. ATE también convocó para este martes 6 de octubre al mediodía a un cese de tareas y movilización a la Corte: Rodolfo Aguiar sostuvo que «no los votó nadie pero quieren gobernar» y denunció que el fallo pasó «por encima del Congreso».




Por eso, las organizaciones sociales convocantes buscan transformar el rechazo en una agenda común de movilización: «convocamos a las organizaciones y a los trabajadores a fortalecer una acción de lucha unitaria el 6 de octubre y la jornada del 15 de octubre, impulsando además una agenda propia de lucha unitaria por nuestras reivindicaciones». La disputa que vuelve a llevarse a las calles unirá así los reclamos conjuntos por el acceso a la tierra y la vivienda, la defensa de los territorios indígenas, el hambre, la precarización, la pérdida de ingresos y el rechazo a un modelo económico que las organizaciones caracterizan como de ajuste y entrega.




La jornada de lucha cuenta con la adhesión de más de 70 organizaciones de distintos sectores y espacios territoriales. Entre ellas se encuentran el Frente de Lucha Piquetero (Polo Obrero, MTR Votamos Luchar por el Cambio Social, CUBa MTR/MIDO, MTR 12 de Abril, Bloque Piquetero Nacional, Frente de la Resistencia-MOT y TODEL.A.C.); la Unión de Trabaajdores/as de la Economía Popular (UTEP), con Barrios de Pie, Movimiento Evita, Corriente Clasista y Combativa, Movimiento de Trabajadores Excluidos, Movimiento de Trabajadores Organizados, Frente 22 de Agosto, Movimiento Octubres, Organización 25 de Mayo, Organizaciones Libres del Pueblo, Frente Popular Darío Santillán, Movimiento Popular La Dignidad y otras organizaciones; Territorios en Lucha, integrado, entre otros por FENAT, Libres del Sur, Movimiento Argentina Rebelde, Coordinadora por el Cambio Social, MST Teresa Vive, FOL, MTD Aníbal Verón, Federación Nacional Campesina, MNCI Somos Tierra y UTT; además del MTL, Frente Transversal Nacional y Popular, Movimiento Mayo, Corriente Política Germán Abdala, Movimiento Agustín Tosco, Agrupación Envar El Kadri, FTV, CANPO, Frente Cajade, Agrupación Juana Azurduy, Las Barriadas, El Colmenar, Red Mayo, Movimiento Social Aeronáutico, Unidad de Organizaciones en Lucha y la Red de Organización Social Independiente (ROSI), entre otras.

Organizaciones sociales marchan a Capital Humano contra el ajuste y a la Corte Suprema por la recuperación de la Ley de Tierras

 se publicó primero en 

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: Ebola Death Toll in DRC Tops 4,000; Trump USAID Cuts Fuel Outbreak
content:
We go to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the site of the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. Health authorities believe the outbreak first began in January but was not detected until May, in part due to cuts in global health investments, like the dismantling of 

USAID

. Since then, over 8,000 cases have been recorded, with more than 4,000 fatalities so far. From Bunia, Ituri province, the epicenter of the outbreak, we speak to Congolese journalist Akilimali Chomachoma. Chomachoma describes the strain on the underfunded Congolese healthcare system as the disease spreads. Many frontline workers have not been paid for months.




“We are seeing this outbreak emerge, and really unfurl, in a setting of decreased global health support,” says Craig Spencer, a doctor and public health expert based in the United States who contracted Ebola while on a medical mission to Guinea in 2014. “The U.S. has not shown up in the same way that it has in previous Ebola outbreaks.” Spencer also comments on the “unprecedented” measles outbreak in the United States, which he warns is likely to continue and lead to additional deaths.

Argentinien: Dreitägiger Streik an den Universitäten Ende September bereitete den 5. Marsch zur Verteidigung und Finanzierung der Hochschulbildung am 15. Oktober vor 







Argentinien: Dreitägiger Streik an Universitäten




„

Buenos Aires. Der Widerstand der öffentlichen Universitäten gegen die Hochschulpolitik der Regierung von Javier Milei geht weiter. Nachdem die Regierung eine von einem Bundesgericht gesetzte Frist zur Begleichung der ausstehenden Zahlungen ignoriert hat, riefen die Gewerkschaften des Lehr- und Verwaltungspersonals zu einem dreitägigen Streik auf. Ihre Hauptforderung ist eine Gehaltsanpassung von 33,4 Prozent und die sofortige Umsetzung des vor knapp einem Jahr verabschiedeten Hochschulfinanzierungsgesetzes, das eine Erhöhung der Universitätsbudgets gemäß der Inflationsrate und die Wiederaufnahme von Stipendienprogrammen für Studierende  vorsieht.




An dem Streik beteiligten sich die Universität von Buenos Aires (UBA) und andere Hochschulen des Landes. Zu dem Streik hatten unter anderem die beiden größten Hochschuldozentenverbände Conadu und Conadu Histórica sowie weitere Gewerkschaften wie der Verband der Beschäftigten an nationalen Universitäten (Fatum) und die Gewerkschaft der Bildungsbeschäftigten (UTE) aufgerufen. (…) Im Rahmen der Protestaktionen öffnete die Fakultät für Wirtschaftswissenschaften der UBA ihre Türen für die Öffentlichkeit. Angeboten wurden unter anderem Tipps zur Betrugsprävention und Schuldenregulierung. An der Medizinischen Fakultät fand eine „Umarmungsaktion“ statt. Der dreitägige Streik gilt als Vorbote des für den 15. Oktober geplanten fünften Bundeshochschulmarschs

…“ 

Artikel von Stephan Hollensteiner vom 05.10.2026 in amerika21

 




Universitäten: Lehrerstreik und neues gerichtliches Ultimatum – Milei verstößt gegen das Finanzierungsgesetz




„

Richter Cormick bestätigte die Anordnung zur Gehaltsanpassung und setzte eine neue Frist von fünf Tagen für deren Umsetzung fest, unter Androhung von Geldstrafen für die Beamten. Die Gewerkschaften traten in einen 72-stündigen Streik.




Die Justiz hat den Staat erneut aufgefordert, innerhalb von fünf Tagen die beiden wichtigsten Artikel des Gesetzes zur Hochschulfinanzierung zu erfüllen; andernfalls müssten die Beamten Geldstrafen zahlen. Vom Ministerium für Humanressourcen hieß es, es handele sich um „einen angeblichen Verstoß, der als solcher gar nicht existiert“, doch Richter Martín Cormick bestätigte die Vollstreckungsanordnung, und die Hochschulgewerkschaften traten in einen 72-stündigen Streik, um den Kampf für die öffentlichen Hochschulen im Vorfeld des Fünften Bundesmarsches, der am 15. Oktober stattfinden wird, sichtbar zu machen

…“ span. 

Artikel von Camila Pace vom 1. Oktober 2026 auf Página|12

Am 15. Oktober findet der fünfte bundesweite Marsch zur Verteidigung der Hochschulbildung statt




„

Die Regierung zögert die Zahlungen hinaus, und die Universitäten gehen auf die Straße. Die Gehälter der Lehrkräfte müssen noch um 32 Prozent erhöht werden, doch die Regierung bietet lediglich 3 Prozent an. Zu allem Überfluss will sie im Haushalt 2027 4 Billionen Pesos weniger für diesen Bereich bereitstellen als gefordert

Bildungsstreik gegen Kürzungskurs in Argentinien: Zweiter, landesweiter Streik der Hochschullehrkräfte innerhalb nur einer Woche




„

Hochschulbeschäftigte wollen erneut gegen ausbleibende Finanzierung der Universitäten und niedrige Gehälter streiken




Gegen die spalterische und erpresserische Politik der Regierung, für bessere Bedingungen an Universitäten: Mit einem zweiten, landesweiten Streik innerhalb nur einer Woche wollen Hochschullehrkräfte den Universitätsbetrieb in Argentinien an diesem Dienstag landesweit zum Erliegen bringen. Ihre Forderungen sind konkret: Sie verlangen eine Erhöhung der Gehälter um 31,2 Prozent, zuzüglich der Inflationsrate vom August, und außerdem von der Regierung, die Betriebskosten aller akademischen Einrichtungen sicherzustellen – wozu sie eigentlich gesetzmäßig verpflichtet ist.




Schon am vergangenen Mittwoch waren die Hörsäle der Universitäten in Argentinien für 24 Stunden leer geblieben. Das Gewerkschaftsbündnis der Föderation der Hochschullehrenden (FEDUN) und der Föderation der Nationalen Universitätsbeschäftigten (FATUN) hatte den ersten Teil ihres Aktionsplans in Angriff genommen, nachdem die Lohnverhandlungen mit der Regierung erwartbar gescheitert waren. Zuvor waren die Gewerkschaftsspitzen schon von der ursprünglichen Forderung einer 51prozentigen Erhöhung abgerückt und hatten sich trotz verstärkter Mobilisierung und Protesten auf 21 Prozent verständigt. Doch nach drei Monaten platzte den Lehrenden schließlich der Kragen, als die Regierung eine Erhöhung der Gehälter um drei Prozent auf den Tisch legte.




Denn seit mehr als 300 Tagen ignoriert die Regierung das Gesetz zur Finanzierung der Universitäten, das ihr die Erhöhung der Dozentengehälter um 51 Prozent und eine Budgeterhöhung in Höhe von 0,36 Prozent des BIP vorschreibt. Das Gesetz war im vergangenen Jahr nur aufgrund des starken öffentlichen Drucks verabschiedet worden. Weiterhin weigert sie sich, den legislativen Rückschlag für ihren Kurs zu akzeptieren, obwohl sie bislang mit allen Einsprüchen und bereits vier juristischen Anfechtungen gescheitert ist. Selbst eine dreitägige Frist zur Vorlage eines Fortschrittsberichts, die der Oberste Gerichtshof Argentiniens in der vergangenen Woche erteilt hatte, scheint am Kabinett von Präsident Javier Milei vorbeizugehen

…“ 

Artikel von Santiago Stavale, Buenos Aires, in der jungen welt vom 08.09.2026

 

 („Bildungsstreik gegen Kürzungskurs“)




Landesweiter 24-stündiger Lehrerstreik am 3. August für Aufstockung der Mittel, das soziale Recht auf Bildung und gegen die bildungsfeindliche Offensive der Regierung Milei 







In Argentinien weiten sich Proteste gegen Milei aus: Soziale Organisationen kritisieren Sparpolitik und Arbeitsmarktreformen der rechten Regierung




„

Buenos Aires. Lehrergewerkschaften und Hafenarbeiter prägen in dieser Woche eine neue Welle von Protesten gegen Präsident Javier Milei. Sie machen die Regierung für den Verlust der Kaufkraft, die Unterfinanzierung des öffentlichen Bildungswesens, die Deregulierung des Arbeitsmarktes und Reformen verantwortlich, die nach ihrer Auffassung soziale Errungenschaften der vergangenen Jahrzehnte abbauen.


Die Eskalation der sozialen Konflikte fällt mit einer weiteren Verschärfung der Rhetorik des Präsidenten zusammen. In einem Fernsehinterview erklärte Milei, es gebe „als Studierende, Journalisten, Professoren und Wissenschaftler verkleidete Terroristen“, und löste damit scharfe Kritik der Opposition, Gewerkschaften und Hochschulverbände aus.


Einer der Schwerpunkte des Konflikts ist das Bildungswesen. Die Vereinigung der im Bildungswesen Beschäftigten CTERA rief zu einem landesweiten Streik auf und warf der Regierung vor, Tarifverhandlungen zu verweigern sowie den Lehrerfonds (FONID) nicht wieder einzuführen. Dieser Gehaltszuschuss wurde von der Regierung Milei 2024 eingestellt.


Darüber hinaus fordern die Gewerkschaften ein neues Gesetz zur Bildungsfinanzierung sowie höhere Mittel für Schulen und Schulkantinen. Sie argumentieren, dass die Lehrergehälter angesichts der Inflation erheblich an Kaufkraft verloren hätten und die Kürzungen im Bildungsbereich fortgesetzt würden. (…) Noch schärfer äußerte sich die oppositionelle Strömung Multicolor innerhalb der Lehrergewerkschaft SUTEBA. „Die Lehrkräfte im ganzen Land streiken und mobilisieren sich, um die bildungsfeindliche Offensive der Regierung Milei zurückzuschlagen (…), die das öffentliche Bildungswesen in einen Zustand absoluter Not gebracht hat“, erklärten ihre Vertreter

…“ 

Artikel von Sven Hanfstängl Reuss vom 08.08.2026 in amerika21

 

 (zu den übrigen Protesten siehe die Berichte im Dossier: 

Ultrarechter Javier Milei wird neuer Präsident von Argentinien – wenn Bolsonaro und Trump gratulieren…

)




Landesweiter Lehrerstreik in Argentinien: Lehrer fordern Dialog und angemessene Gehälter




„

Der Verband der Bildungsbeschäftigten hat für diesen Montag zu einem 24-stündigen Streik aufgerufen, nachdem sich die Regierung geweigert hatte, über Löhne zu verhandeln und den FONID wieder einzuführen. Zu den Forderungen gehören eine Aufstockung der Mittel und die Ablehnung von Reformen.


Am Montag, dem 3., beginnt in Argentinien ein landesweiter Lehrerstreik, zu dem der Verband der Bildungsbeschäftigten (CTERA) für die Vorschul-, Grundschul- und Sekundarstufe aufgerufen hat, nachdem die „anhaltende Weigerung“ der Regierung von Javier Milei , einen Dialog aufzunehmen und neue Lohnverhandlungen zu führen.


Wie von CTERA und verschiedenen Gewerkschaften angekündigt, zielt der Arbeitskampf, der zunächst 24 Stunden dauern soll, auf weitere Forderungen ab, darunter die „sofortige“ Wiedereinführung des Förderfonds für Lehrkräfte (FONID) und höhere Mittel für Schulen und Bildungsprogramme. „Die Gehälter der Lehrkräfte verlieren weiter an Kaufkraft, die Rückzahlung des FONID und der nationalen Bildungsmittel bleibt weiterhin aus, und es werden Initiativen vorangetrieben, die darauf abzielen, Arbeits- und Rentenrechte sowie das soziale Recht auf Bildung zu beschneiden“, argumentierten die Gewerkschaften in einer gemeinsamen Erklärung.


Die Forderung nach einer Lohnanpassung und einer „dringenden“ Finanzierung ist eine Reaktion auf die „Abwertung“ der Löhne unterhalb der Inflationsrate sowie auf die fehlenden Mittel für Schulen und Kantinen. Zudem forderten die Lehrkräfte die Verabschiedung eines neuen Bildungsfinanzierungsgesetzes und lehnten den Gesetzentwurf zur Bildungsfreiheit sowie mögliche Rentenreformen ab, um „das öffentliche, solidarische und umlagefinanzierte Rentensystem zu verteidigen“.


Die Maßnahme fällt mit dem geplanten Schulbeginn in der Stadt und der Provinz von Buenos Aires, Chaco und Santiago del Estero zusammen, wird sich jedoch auf das gesamte Land auswirken. Zwar betrifft sie in erster Linie staatliche Einrichtungen, doch werden sich auch einige Privatschulen daran beteiligen, je nach Entscheidung der jeweiligen Einrichtung oder den Vorgaben des Lehrkörpers und der Gewerkschaften des Sektors, wie beispielsweise der Argentinischen Gewerkschaft der Privatschullehrer (SADOP).


Parallel dazu hat auch die Gewerkschaft der Staatsbediensteten (ATE) für denselben Tag zu einem landesweiten Streik aufgerufen, weshalb der normale Betrieb verschiedener öffentlicher Einrichtungen auf Provinz- und Bundesebene eingeschränkt sein wird.“ 

span. 

Meldung vom 2. August 2026 auf teleSUR

Eindringlicher landesweiter Lehrerstreik mit extrem hoher Beteiligung und massiven Mobilisierungen der CTERA im ganzen Land




„

Der Verband der Bildungsbeschäftigten der Republik Argentinien (CTERA) teilt mit, dass der für den heutigen Tag ausgerufene landesweite Lehrerstreik im ganzen Land eine äußerst hohe Beteiligung verzeichnete, wobei sich die Beschäftigten im Bildungswesen in großer Zahl an den verschiedenen Aktionen und Demonstrationen in den einzelnen Provinzen beteiligten.


Im Mittelpunkt des Aktionstages stand die groß angelegte Kundgebung vor dem Wirtschaftsministerium, die gemeinsam mit CONADU, CONADU Histórica und ATE organisiert wurde und bei der nachdrücklich Maßnahmen gefordert wurden, die das soziale Recht auf Bildung sowie die Achtung der Arbeitnehmerinnen und Arbeitnehmer gewährleisten

…“ span.
