author: Manila Today Staff
title: The cost of US imperialism that we are fighting against
content:
with added reports from Jessica Obciana and Kline Vergara

“Homes are destroyed, livelihoods are lost, nations are lost by interests that are made far beyond our own borders. Even now, initiatives like Pax Silica, supply chains for critical minerals and semiconductors are being reordered around the needs of the US war machine, and countries like us [the Philippines] are being asked to serve as suppliers and now become their targets, rather than being allowed to decide our own development,” said Dr. Giovanni Tapang, convener of the Stop the US-Israel War on Iran Network.

Various anti-imperialist groups gathered for the webinar Updates from the Resistance: The Current Situation in Iran, Palestine, Venezuela, and Cuba, co-organized by BAYAN, the International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines, the Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association (PPFA), and the Stop the US-Israel War on Iran Campaign Network, to express people’s solidarity in lambasting US imperialism following its sanctions, blockades, military aggression, and other forms of intervention and coercion against the people.

“This is the war machine that we are fighting against. And as we listen to those who are on the front lines, we learn of their resistance, deepen our understanding, and together strengthen solidarity to defeat this war machine,” Tapang added.

“We have seen the case of Venezuela: how this warfare has been attacking the Global South, attacking the country, and in many, many aspects, not only the political one, military, economic, and cultural, and in social consciousness. Venezuela is under siege now,” said Richard Lobo, Venezuela’s Chargé d’Affaires.

Venezuela possesses the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves, estimated at around 303 billion barrels as of 2023, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Lobo noted that US intervention in Venezuela extends beyond economic sanctions to political, military, economic, and cultural intervention.

In January 2026, the US launched Operation Absolute Resolve as a large-scale military operation in Venezuela framed around drug trafficking and national security that led to the capture of President Nicolás Maduro and First Lady Cilia Flores and their transfer to the United States. Such an operation also targeted Venezuelan military infrastructure across Caracas and other locations.

Months after Maduro’s capture, the US laid out an agreement to gain access and control over an estimated 65 billion barrels of oil reserves, mineral wealth, and other resources.

Meanwhile, Lobo emphasized that the situation has only amplified the resistance among Venezuelans in defending their sovereignty and their right to determine the country’s political and economic direction.

“Even though we have been under attack […] the people there in Venezuela have been resisting and have been struggling. And one thing that I can say right now is that even with the kidnapping of our president, they believe the government is still in power,” Lobo stated.

More than 5,000 civilians have been killed in the US-Israel aggression against Iran, including 168 girls who were killed when a school was struck in March this year.

“Iran is experiencing aggression by the United States and Israel since the 1979 revolution against a very corrupt government, the Shah’s government. The United States has been trying to overthrow the revolutionary government in Iran, engaging in economic warfare for 46 years,” said Dr. Foad Izadi, associate professor at the University of Tehran.

The 1979 Iranian Revolution overthrew Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, whose government had maintained close relations with the US. The revolution fundamentally changed Iran’s relationship with the US, posing decades of diplomatic confrontation, economic sanctions, and political pressure.

“(The US) has also asked Iran to reduce its support for the Palestinian cause. As you know, Iran has been a strong supporter of Palestine. Not only with words, not only with speeches, but with military aid. Iran is the only country that is helping Palestinians with military aid,” said Dr. Izadi, noting that other governments should also learn from them by providing help to those countries fighting against aggression and genocide.

“Iran has learned that if you allow Israelis, genocidal people, the apartheid regime to get away with their crimes in Palestine, they they would want to take over the Middle East and go beyond,” he added.

Meanwhile, similar to Venezuela, Dr. Izadi noted that the US-Israel are targeting Iran not only because of its continued support for Palestine but also because of its strategic importance including its large oil and gas reserves.

Iran is one of the world’s major oil and gas producers. The Strait of Hormuz, through which a significant share of global oil shipments passes, makes Iran strategically important to international energy markets.

“Although the war is hurting Iranians, it’s also hurting people in the Philippines and basically all over the world because of this illegal aggression on Iran. Oil supplies have been disrupted, and that is affecting everybody all around the globe with higher gas prices,” said Dr. Izadi.

Dr, Izadi further observed the US-Israel aggression and colonial expansion in West Asia, pointing to the idea of “Greater Israel,” which encompasses territories in Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Iraq, and Lebanon.

He argued that Israel’s territorial expansion should be understood as an attempt to reproduce colonial practices in the present period.

“They have talked about Greater Israel, which includes Saudi territory, Egyptian territory, Jordanian territory, Syrian territory, Iraqi territory, Lebanese territory, and they have already taken over Syria and Lebanese territory,” Dr. Izadi said, calling it the “19th-century colonialism in the 21st century.”

Following the US-Israel aggression, Dr. Izadi said Iran has developed indigenous technology, including ballistic missiles and drones in response to the attacks.

“Iran has used indigenous technology to build quite sophisticated ballistic missiles and drones to hit the aggressor regimes, US-Israel,” Dr. Izadi noted, describing Iran’s ability as a non-nuclear state to resist attacks from two nuclear-armed states.

He also warned that if the US gains control over regional resources, it could use them as leverage against countries like the Philippines, among others.

“We are fighting the Epstein class. The Epstein class that likes to rape little American girls and kill little Iranian girls,” he added.

“This is a very crucial moment for our civilization,” said Republic of Cuba ambassador Yadira Ledesma Hernández, describing the worsening conditions faced by Cubans under decades of US comprehensive economic, commercial, and financial restrictions.

“The US has threatened many enterprises across the world not to sell oil to us, even the enterprises in the business of cargo and shipments. We have many containers in the islands of the Caribbean with medicines and with food, but they threaten those companies: if you bring containers of food and medicine to Cuba, we will seize your bank account,” the ambassador shared.

For more than six decades, the US maintained its restrictions and embargo against Cuba beginning after the 1959 Cuban Revolution and the subsequent nationalization of properties and realignment of Cuba’s political and economic relations. This year, the US sanctions further intensified by imposing an oil and energy blockade.

Cuba’s electricity crisis has also triggered a water crisis as prolonged blackouts disrupted water distribution across the country. Around 3.5 million people across Cuba are affected, including hospitals and clinics struggling for basic sanitation and healthcare services.

“Imagine the families are facing more than one day without electricity. We don’t have electricity. You cannot have water. And without water you cannot live,” she added.

Since the 1959 Cuban Revolution, healthcare has become one of its major social programs by transforming it into a publicly funded and universal model for free access, preventive medicine, primary healthcare, vaccination, and maternal and child health.

Meanwhile, Cuba’s infant mortality rate rose from 4.0 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2018 to 7.2 in 2022.

“The human damage, we cannot say how much it is, because it’s already claiming lives in our country that used to have an excellent healthcare system that we provide for free. Nowadays, our infant mortality rate has doubled,” Ledesma shared, describing the situation in Cuba as a “silent Gaza” following the humanitarian consequences of restrictions marred by destruction and deprivation endured by Palestinians.

“Palestine is not something I learned from textbooks. It is the place where I was raised, the place of my family, my memories, my education and my community. We are not speaking about an abstract geopolitical conflict. We are speaking about millions of human beings whose lives, homes, families, and futures have been shaped by decades of displacement, occupation, blockade, and war. The situation in Palestine must be understood within this longer historical context,” said Mahadia Abu-Dalal, a Palestinian peace advocate and educator.

Since October 2023, the scale of destruction in Gaza has been devastating. More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.

Despite the ceasefire announced in October 2025, the humanitarian crisis has continued and worsened. As of October 1, at least 1,439 Palestinians had been killed and 5,052 injured in Gaza since the ceasefire began.

Nearly two million remain displaced, scrambling for shelter in overcrowded displacement sites or damaged buildings. Access to food, clean water, medicine, and other necessities has been severely restricted.

The healthcare system also remains under extreme strain, with only 19 out of 36 hospitals in Gaza partially functioning, and essential medical supplies and equipment fall critically short. The World Health Organization also said that approved aid can currently enter Gaza only through Kerem Shalom, while other crossings remain closed.

The United Nations also reported the heightened risk of waterborne diseases among displaced communities as water and sanitation remain major concerns. Around 77% of households depend on water trucking, while all six wastewater treatment plants are non-functional and around 70 percent of sewage pumping stations are inoperable.

The peace advocate urged the people to look beyond the statistics and remember the lives and identity behind them. For Abu-Dalal, this is where solidarity must move beyond sympathy.

She further called on institutions and governments to uphold international humanitarian law, human rights, self-determination and equality.

“You cannot ask the victims to live in peace when there is no justice, because peace requires justice,” Abu-Dalal said. “It requires safety, freedom, dignity, accountability, and it requires that Palestinian lives be valued equally with every other human life.”

“We need to explain and condemn what those imperialist powers are doing,” Ledesma implored.

For her, there is a need for progressive forces around the world to continue articulating and amplifying people’s resistance against what she referred to as “new neocolonialism strategies”.

“We have businessmen that control the media. And and social media in particular, and for us, this is something really that we need to take into account from the less to try to share our views and articulate because we will not have the capacity. To put in the news what they put. But definitely we need to share our experience,” she added.

Speakers also shared that the culture of resistance is shaped by forms of democratic expression as communities come together to rally and express solidarity in support of people’s struggle in Iran, Cuba, Venezuela, and Palestine.

“People come out of their house. They go to the square near the house; they see their neighbors, and generally their speeches, messages of solidarity, patriotic songs, people waving flags and shouting against Netanyahu and Trump for all the crimes that the country Iran has suffered,” Dr. Izadi said.

“The current situation is tough, but people are resisting, and Iran’s military has been able to defend the country in a very, very serious manner,” he added.

As an artist and educator, Abu-Dalal witnessed how creativity can become a form of survival. She said that resistance takes many forms through documenting violations, teaching children, preserving language, writing poems, creating art, or simply planting an olive tree.

“This is also a struggle over memory and identity,” she said, “When a home is destroyed. What disappears is not simply concrete or stone. It is family photographs, the embroidery, the books, the memories, the olive trees, the kitchen where generations gathered, and the stories that connect one generation to another.”

“Peace is not simply the absence of bombs. It’s not the absence of war or bombs or killing. A population cannot be expected to live under permanent domination and be told that this is peace. You do not have to be Palestinian to care about Palestine. You do not have to share our history to recognize injustice. And you do not have to speak Arabic to say that every child deserves a future. Your solidarity matters. Your voice matters. Your classrooms matter. Your art and your institutions matter, and your choices as citizens matter,” she concluded.

author: Fozzie
title: Chapter 18: Different Formulae for the Rate of Surplus-value
content:
Harry Cleaver's study guide to Marx's Capital volume 1, chapter 18.

In this chapter Marx, pauses a moment before the section on wages, to juxtapose his own formulations to those of classical political economy and to critique the latter in ways that foreshadow the critiques he will make in the next three chapters.

By always comparing surplus value (or product) to the total value (or product), classical political economists portrayed the relationship between workers and capitalists in ways that 1) hid the existence of exploitation and 2) created an illusion that labor was getting its fair share. The existence of exploitation was hidden by making it appear that each factor of production, i.e., labor and capital, is rewarded according to its contribution to production. So, surplus value, s, appears to equal capital’s contribution and s/(s + v), its share, while by implication, variable capital, v, appears to equal labor’s contribution and v/(v+s), its share. Within a few decades after Capital was published, neoclassical economists, having substituted utility for labor value, would use the same trick but with fancier mathematics.

Mathematical concepts such as production functions, e.g., Q = f(K, L), permitted the use of calculus to derive marginal products for K (dQ/dK) and L (dQ/dL) and with a few more assumptions, conclude that wages = market value of dQ/dL and profits = the market value of dQ/dK. In the development of this theory of production, the labor theory of value of the classical political economists was set aside, so the only “value” left was money price determined by markets. Yet the conclusion was essentially the same, both the old formulae and the new ones hid exploitation by reducing the antagonistic social relations of production to engineering-like technical relations among things.(1)

For Marx, by formulating the value of labor as one part of the working day, the classical political economic formulation understated what was for him the essential issue: how much of workers’ time toiling produced the means of consumption they needed (or their value/money equivalent) and how much of their work time produced the means of production (or their value/money equivalent) capital needed. Clearly, both formulations of the rate of surplus-value, the classical one, s/(v+s), and his own, s/v, are possible measures of capital’s share of the total new value created. He preferred s/v because it provided a more direct representation of the division of workers’ days. When he notes how s/(v+s) is a “mode of presentation which arises, by the way, out of the capitalist mode of production itself” (2) and promises to return to the point later on, odds have it that he was thinking about the parallel between s/(v+s) and s/(c+v), the rate of profit. He did return to juxtapose the rate of profit to the rate of exploitation in material included in Volume III of Capital where he presents the rate of profit as expressing capital’s preoccupation with the rate of return on its investment (c+v) and the rate of exploitation as expressing the degree to which workers are being exploited, i.e., forced to produce products and value for someone else.(3)

Commenting on the “popular expression” that juxtaposes unpaid to paid labor, instead of surplus to necessary labor, Marx affirms the reasonableness of that way of talking about exploitation in money terms. By pretending to buy labor, rather than labor-power, capitalists argue that all labor is paid for. But as workers grasp intuitively and Marx’s analysis in Chapter 6 demonstrated, although fluctuations in supply and demand can push wages above, or drive them below the value of labor-power, on the average workers are only paid wages equivalent to the amount of work that produces the value of their labor-power and capitalists arrogate to themselves the fruits of all excess labor beyond that—with no compensation to those performing it. He concludes, “Capital, therefore, is not only command over labour, as Adam Smith thought. It is essentially the command over unpaid labor. All surplus-value . . . is in substance the materialization of unpaid labor time.” (4) But what is the importance of this command over unpaid labor time? We have seen how Marx’s focus is on one, and only one, use of surplus-value, or unpaid labor time: investment, i.e., employing it to impose more work in the future!

1 It would not be until the 1960s, when economists at Cambridge University in England, building on the work of Piero Sraffa (1898&ndash1983), attacked these formulations and forced neoclassical economists to admit that they were built on logical flaws, e.g., they pretend to derive the price of capital but to do so they must assume the price of capital in order to aggregate heterogeneous capital to come up with "K". See G. C. Harcourt, Some Cambridge Controversies in the Theory of Capital, Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1972.

3 Capital, Vol. III, Part One, Chapter 3: "The Relationship between Rate of Profit and Rate of Surplus-Value".

author: Fozzie
title: Chapter 17: Changes of Magnitude in the Price of Labour-Power and in Surplus-Value
content:
Harry Cleaver's study guide to Marx's Capital volume 1 chapter 17.

The title of this chapter announces a transition from value analysis to money by making clear that the value of labor-power will be discussed in terms of its price. Price, as we saw in Chapter 1, is the money expression of the value of a commodity, in this case of the value of labor-power. In this chapter, Marx reiterates his analysis of past chapters in terms of changes in both the value and the price of labor-power and notes how changes in price may differ from changes in value. In passing from analysis in terms of value to one in terms of money, Marx must, and does, take into account changes in the real value of money wages, e.g., caused by a change in the price of consumer goods. Therefore, the price of labor-power may not equal its value.

Throughout this analysis, the price of labor-power can be assumed to be wages, in as much as money wages were predominant over other expressions of the value of labor-power in the period in which Marx was writing. (As opposed to wages in kind, salaries, commissions or government payments to the unemployed or the poor.)

While the reiteration of previously explained material has often caused this chapter to be passed over as pure pedantry, there are two reasons for its close study. First, thinking of the value of labor-power in terms of its price, its monetary equivalent, lays the groundwork for Part VI, Chapters 19-22 on wages. Second, among familiar words and phrases there are also politically important points well worth repetition.

The first of these is his highlighting of how, in the dynamic of capitalist development, despite the existence of some zero-sum relationships where one class can benefit only at the expense of the other, there are situations in which the material situation of both can be improved. The most important of these being when a rise in the productivity of labor results, to use modern terms, in an increase in the size of the pie being produced. When the pie/output grows, it is at least possible for both workers and capitalists to get more of what they want: means of consumption and life for workers, means of production to impose more work for capitalists. Marx writes that it is “possible that owing to an increase in the productivity of labor both the worker and the capitalist may simultaneously be able to appropriate a greater quantity of means of subsistence [or of means of production] without any change in the price of labor-power or in surplus-value.”(1) The same mutual benefit is possible with increases in the length and intensity of the working day; where more is produced, more could potentially be shared. In this second case, because longer and/or more intense working hours use up workers’ energy faster, any increase in real consumption requires an excess over the necessary compensation for the accelerated wearing out of workers. But it is at least possible for the increase to be large enough.

The importance of these observations is they show how his theory is perfectly compatible with historically observed increases in standards of living among some workers, even as others are thrown into poverty and pauperism. It is also compatible with, and indeed predates, the recognition by neoclassical economists (from at least Alfred and Mary Marshall on) that increases in wages can go hand in hand with increased profits.(2) This was the reality on the basis of which John Maynard Keynes built his theory of how capitalist development could be socially progressive, i.e., one in which growing profits and investment were stimulated by growing wages and benefits.(3) In the process, he overthrew the traditional business view that any increase in wages would undermine profits and therefore had to be resisted by all means possible—including violence when necessary.

Under these circumstances, Marx also points out how the degree to which the fruits of higher productivity and more work are shared depends in large part upon the balance of class forces, i.e., on the struggle between workers seeking to share in increases in the social wealth resulting from increased productivity and the efforts by capitalists to arrogate all increases to themselves. “The new value of labor-power”, Marx writes, “depends on the relative weight thrown into the scale by the pressure of capital on the one side, and the resistance of the workers on the other.”(4) In the wake of the Russian Revolution and of World War I, Keynes pointed out that the English working class would no longer accept reductions in real wages and was well enough organized to insist on rising real wages. The alternative to provoking a general strike by trying to lower wages, he suggested, was raising productivity (either by shutting down low-productivity operations or by investing in new technology) that could make higher wages possible with no loss to capitalists.

Although Keynes’ observations and proposals were made in Britain, similar recognition in the United States underlay the acceptance and legalization by the Roosevelt Administration of industrial unions and collective bargaining. Those changes forced capitalists in major industries, such as motor vehicles and mining, to recognize unions, bargain with them collectively and cut “productivity deals” in which workers were allowed to share in the fruits of rising productivity in exchange for cooperation in the introduction of new technology that made that rise possible. Although such deals were written into union-industry contracts, how the agreements worked out in practice continued to depend on struggle and the balance of class power on the shop floor and in the pits.

Marx draws our attention to two cases. The first was during the period of the Napoleonic Wars, 1799–1815. He cites 1799 presumably because it was in November of that year that Napoléon Bonaparte (1769–1821) seized power—ten years after the French revolution. Actual war between the British and French governments began in 1803 as Bonaparte’s armies began to conquer much of Europe. He was finally defeated at Waterloo in 1815 after his disastrous withdrawal from Moscow and despite Britain’s defeat in the War of 1812 with the United States. During those years of warfare, the ability of England to import grain from the European continent was curtailed—both by the French government’s closing of its territory to British trade and by the British naval blockade of French ports.(5) As a result, the British economy was forced to rely on less productive local agriculture, especially of corn (the English term for wheat and other grains requiring grinding). The resulting increase in the price of bread for workers helped drive them to accept the longer, harder hours that Marx cites. The increased price of grain and bread not only reduced real wages, but increased ground rents profiting landlords. This situation was prolonged after the war by so-called Corn Laws, enacted in 1815, putting tariffs on imported grain. The continued high price of grain and bread intensified class conflicts and led to the famous debate between Malthus, who defended the tariffs as vital to national security and Ricardo who critiqued them as harmful to industrial development because they diverted income from profits that could be invested to rents that went largely to luxury consumption by landlords. Capitalists mounted a sustained movement, enlisting workers, to end the Corn Laws, increase wheat imports, and lower the price of bread, an effort that finally succeeded in 1846. Of course, they didn't mention to the workers their plans to lower wages once the price of bread dropped!

The second of the two cases, involving a shortening of the working day but increased intensity and productivity, became dominant in the period of the real subsumption of labor to capital once workers organized themselves effectively enough to force down their hours of work. This forced capitalists to resort to relative surplus-value strategies. In other words, the history analyzed in detail in Part IV, Chapters 12-15.

What is interesting in Marx’s treatment here, is how he draws from that analysis implications for the possibilities beckoning from a future beyond capitalism. In such a future world, he argues, those dreams of Aristotle that he evoked in Chapter 15 could finally be realized. Freed of the capitalist mandate to order society through imposed work, rising productivity could be converted into more and more free time. His brief discussion here echoes Engels’ lectures at Elberfeld two decades earlier, where he blasted all the wasteful forms of work that capitalism requires, e.g., police and juridical protection of private property, finance, a military-industrial complex, and so on, imagining all those wasting their time in such activities changing occupations and sharing a declining burden of actually useful labor.(6) No more separate leisure class, freed from work by the labor of others, but an equal sharing by all in less and less work and more and more leisure. Such a future, Marx argues, would allow “the free intellectual and social activity of the individual”.(7) Here Marx is also echoing his own words from the Grundrisse notebooks a decade before. There he wrote, “The saving of labor time [is] equal to an increase of free time, i.e., time for the full development of the individual, which in turn reacts back upon the productive power of labor as itself the greatest productive power.”(8)

A final note: in the midst of pointing out the potentialities created by raising productivity, Marx recognizes how the development of individuals, both intellectual and social, changes their aspirations and therefore their needs and desires. As a result, the amount and diversity of labor required to provide the means for satisfying those needs and desires grows. Therefore, “what is now surplus labor would then count as necessary labor, namely the labour which is necessary for the formation of a social fund for reserve and accumulation.” (9) In a post-capitalist world, clearly “accumulation” would no longer involve the expanded reproduction of antagonistic class relationships, but rather the growth in all those elements necessary to satisfying changing aspirations. Here we have an answer to an objection long posed by mainstream economists to Marx’s theory of surplus labor/value and exploitation within capitalism. “Would not”, they have argued, “people in a post-capitalist society still need to do more work than is required to meet their immediate needs in order to create the wherewithal to meet future needs?” Yes, but in such a society, as Marx says here, such extra work would not be “surplus-value” because it would not be dedicated to the expanded imposition of social control via more and more work.

1 Capital, Vol. I, p. 659. No change in nominal or money wages, but an increase in real wages because the money buys more due to lower prices of consumption goods.

2 Neoclassical microeconomics allows wage increases to be compatible with increases in profit as long as the marginal productivity of labor rises.

3 In Keynesian macroeconomics, rising wages increase consumer demand, which, ceteris paribus, induces investment and greater output.

5 For vivid fictional accounts—often based on real historical documents—of the British blockade from France's northern ports along the Channel to Gibralter and ports along the Mediterranean coast, see the Napoleonic War novels of C. S. Forester and those of Patrick O'Brian, and the films based upon them. Forester's novels provided the basis for a 1951 film Captain Horatio Hornblower starring Gregory Peck and an ITV and A&E TV series Hornblower (1998–2003) starring Ioan Gruffudd. O'Brian's Aubrey–Maturin novels provided the material for Master and Commander: The Far Side of the World (2003) starring Russell Crowe and Paul Bettany.

6 See his two speeches, delivered in February 1845 in MECW, Vol. 4, pp. 243–264.

9 Mainstream economists, apologists as they are for capitalism, argue that what is produced in capitalism is always a function of people's needs and desires, as manifested in how they spend their money. While making that argument, they completely ignore not only all the ways in which capitalists manipulate need and desire to create more opportunities for imposing more work, but also all of those kinds of work that both Engels and Marx deplored as superfluous to a society freed of capitalist domination.

title: So many things would be better if doctors could just say “yeah that is a real problem but there…
content:
vergess

:

joy-haver

:

So many things would be better if doctors could just say “yeah that is a real problem but there isn’t much we can do to treat it so our only real recommendations are other things that raise your general health level to compensate”

instead they just say “thats normal” or “oh theres nothing wrong with you”. Because in their mind “it wont kill you and i cant fix it” means its not worth mentioning. 

Affirm the problem doc, it wont kill you. Knowing that something just isnt the kind of thing doctors treat will save your patients so much time, money, and stress, all of which will improve their health. 

I was going to link to that essay about how med school beats this out of doctors, complete with clinically diagnosable PTSD in 20-40% of doctors depending on field.

But then I went to collect the link on duckduckgo since I don’t have my bookmarks at work, and oh god, there’s actually thousands of these essays, and even studies now.

So uh. I’ll synthesize a bit here:

Doctors need to stop doing this, yes. But for that to happen, med school has to stop punishing this with public humiliations, residency has to stop punishing this with extra shifts, and employers have to stop firing doctors who admit this for “malpractice liability.”

The individual doctors sending their patients home ignorant and afraid are the last leg in a long chain, basically.

author: Unknown
title: Эррико Малатеста - Наша внешняя политика
content:
Автор

: Эррико Малатеста

Название

: Наша внешняя политика

Подзаголовок

: Война и Мир

Дата

: 7 марта 1914

Дополнительная информация

: К сожалению, только первые три абзаца переведены с итальянского. Остальное - с английского.

Источник

: Volontà (Ancona), год 2-1, №10. "La nostra politica estera. Guerra e Pace"




 Строго говоря, у нас не может быть внешней политики, поскольку мы находимся и хотим находиться вне и против нынешнего раздела мира на соперничающие государства. 




 Для нас нет чужих. Мы хотим, чтобы все люди – каково бы ни было их место рождения, каков бы ни был этнический корень, из которого они происходят, каков бы ни был язык, на котором они говорят, – считали себя братьями, свободно объединялись в группы и сотрудничали вместе ради большего благосостояния, большей свободы, большей цивилизации для всех. 




 И поскольку это всеобщее братство, эта гармонизация всех интересов, всех стремлений в обширном единстве (единстве человеческого рода), которое уважало бы и благоприятствовало свободному развитию всех различий, полной автономии всех индивидов и всех групп, всё ещё остаётся идеалом, противостоящим суровой реальности сегодняшнего дня; поскольку люди всё ещё разделены на угнетённых и угнетателей, и одни живут, эксплуатируя труд других, а трудящиеся несут бремя всех общественных тягот, стеснены в своём материальном и моральном развитии и часто низведены до самой убогой и оскотинивающей нищеты, – мы стоим, какой бы ни была наша страна рождения или место жительства, на стороне угнетённых против угнетателей, трудящихся против паразитов, не считаясь ни с какими политическими группировками, на которые исторические события, интересы и амбиции хозяев – пусть даже благоприятствуемые особыми природными условиями – разделили человечество. 




 Если кто-то хочет говорить об иностранцах, то для нас иностранец – не тот, кто родился по ту сторону границы и говорит на другом языке или имеет другой цвет кожи; – иностранец, враг – это угнетатель, это эксплуататор, это всякий, в любой стране, кто подчиняет другого человека своей воле. 




 — «Но мы, несмотря на наш космополитизм, всё же должны жить в государстве, в котором находимся, и подчиняться его политическому режиму. Мы можем в идеале чувствовать солидарность как с рабочим из далёкой страны, так и с тем, кто работает рядом с нами, мы можем ненавидеть иностранные правительства так же, как национальное; но на практике именно с соседями солидарность или борьба живее, сердечнее, действеннее». 




 Так скажите же нам те, кто, не будучи в состоянии сделать нас патриотами и националистами с помощью обычных аргументов, основанных на преступной ненависти и глупом тщеславии, полагают, что могут воззвать к нашим боевым инстинктам и заставить нас принять самые реакционные теории под личиной революционности. И мы принимаем их тезис. Мы, несмотря на наши идеи, по необходимости итальянские граждане, то есть подданные правительства Италии; и потому это правительство угнетает нас и влияет на нас больше, чем могло бы, например, правительство Японии; и мы в свою очередь можем сделать против правительства Италии то, чего у нас не было бы средств сделать против правительства далёкой страны. Итак, вывод: для анархиста главный враг – тот угнетатель, который ближе всего к нему и против которого он может бороться эффективнее. Для итальянского анархиста и вообще для всякого итальянского рабочего, стремящегося к освобождению своему и своих товарищей, прежде всего необходимо бороться с правительством Италии и с хозяевами Италии, то есть с теми, кто называет себя нашими согражданами и соотечественниками и во имя нации и отечества хотел бы, чтобы мы покорно принимали их господство. Это ли вывод, к которому они хотели прийти? Если да, мы согласны. 







 *** 







 Говорят, что националистическое и патриотическое чувство – это факт, и потому его надо принять. 




 Религия, преступность, нищета, рабство и тысяча индивидуальных или коллективных отклонений – тоже факты. Неужели нам поэтому придётся принять всё и отказаться от всякого действия ради улучшения положения? 




 Патриотическое чувство, когда оно не просто шумиха, делаемая в интересах класса, и действительно существует в народном сознании, бывает хорошим или дурным в зависимости от обстоятельств: хорошим, когда оно служит тому, чтобы воодушевить на восстание против угнетателя, который оказывается иностранцем; дурным, когда оно толкает угнетать других и лучше принимать отечественное угнетение. Оно всегда остаётся чувством низшим, которое цивилизация должна будет заменить широким чувством человеческого братства, но оно почтенно и может развиваться и расширяться, если признаёт и уважает в других право на равное чувство, то есть когда, требуя родину для себя, оно умеет уважать родину других или, ещё лучше, умеет бороться, как уже делают итальянские патриоты, чтобы помочь другим отвоевать родину. Напротив, оно презренно и ведёт к самым ужасным злодеяниям и самому жалкому разложению, если служит удовлетворению преступных инстинктов грабежа и господства. 




 Правительства и правящие классы используют патриотическое чувство (как и тот другой человеческий недостаток – религиозное чувство), чтобы народ лучше принимал их власть и чтобы втягивать народ в войны и колониальные предприятия, делаемые для их, правящих классов, исключительной выгоды. И их теоретики говорят, что выше борьбы между бедными и богатыми, между пролетариями и собственниками есть национальная солидарность, объединяющая в общем чувстве и интересе весь народ одной страны, всех членов одной нации.

author: dev
title: Tout comprendre sur Parcoursup
content:
C'est l'une des revendications les plus spontanées et récurrentes du mouvement lycéen en cours : l'abolition de Parcoursup. Si personne n'est encore en mesure de savoir 

comment

 ce système de sélection opaque fonctionne, lycéens, parents et professeurs ont déjà bien compris 

à quoi il sert

.


Nous proposons ici une petite sélection de nos articles sur le sujet qui ne manqueront pas d'étayer les évidences et intuitions partagées par les élèves.




Tout comprendre sur Parcoursup


« Faire patienter, c'est dominer »




« Pour comprendre la nature de “Parcoursup”, il faut partir de l'expérience directe, sans tenter d'y plaquer des interprétations hatives ou idéologiques. Pour la plupart des lycéens — ceux que les communicants qui encombrent désormais l'appareil d'Etat appellent “nos jeunes” — le processus d'affectation dans l'enseignement supérieur se présente comme une boîte noire nimbée de brouillard, comme une obscure Machine.


Son opacité ne tient pas tant à l'interface numérique par laquelle se font les connexions que dans l'impression diffuse de ne pas connaître les règles d'un “jeu” qui s'apprête à déterminer la place sociale qui sera assignée à chaque “candidat” pour le reste de son existence. »







Parcoursup et la police prédictive


La vie, le destin, l'algorithme




« Quoi de commun entre la police prédictive et Parcoursup ? Les deux reposent sur des algorithmes, certes, mais ils sont surtout deux outils plus ou moins subtils du contrôle social assisté par ordinateur. À chaque fois, l'algorithme incarne une somme de décisions politiques dont l'importance n'a d'égale que l'opacité : tout repose alors sur l'efficacité opérationelle, l'interface, la baisse du taux de criminalité ou la répartition des élèves dans les filières en fonction de leurs choix. Une fois n'est pas coutume, les causes structurelles ou les déterminations collectives sont converties et neutralisées en décisions individuelles. »







Rejeter l'école


Un lycéen décrypte le quotidien de la génération Parcoursup




« un lycéen lecteur de lundimatin nous a transmis cette excellente analyse de son expérience d'élève. Depuis l'intérieur, il évoque avec précision et érudition les nouvelles modalités d'isolement, de contrôle, de punition et d'auto-discipline qui trament le quotidien de cette nouvelle génération Parcoursup. »







Parcoursup : conseils de désorientation


Entretien avec Aïda N'Diaye, Johan Faerber et Camille




« Si l'on peut reconnaître un seul mérite à l'opacité du dispositif Parcoursup, c'est d'avoir rendu transparent ce processus de sélection. Dans ce lundisoir, nous essayons de comprendre plus précisément ce qui se joue dans l'expérience de cette plateforme. Comment les logiques d'auto-management imprègnent désormais chaque lycéen, comment les professeurs deviennent petit à petit les supplétifs de la sélection algorithmique, comment l'angoisse continue de l'évaluation devient une norme à laquelle on ne peut plus échapper. »

title: Fuel hikes squeeze jeepney drivers, commuters dry
content:
Jeepney with signage: "No to Oil Price Hike" (Photo by Roselle Ochobillo/Bulatlat)

By Wendyl Geronimo and Roselle Ochobillo

For commuters, the recent P1 increase in jeepney fares may seem small. But for workers who rely on public transportation every day, the additional peso can add to an already tightening budget.

For jeepney drivers, meanwhile, the bigger burden is not the fare increase itself but the fuel prices behind it.

After several rounds of oil price increases, diesel prices have continued to eat into drivers’ daily earnings, leaving some struggling to provide food, pay rent and keep their children in school.

The pressure was among the reasons transport groups, including the Pagkakaisa ng mga Samahang Tsuper at Opereytor Nationwide (PISTON), held a nationwide strike on Sept. 29 and 30, calling for lower petroleum prices and relief from fuel taxes.

For 52-year-old jeepney driver Teody Bermejo, National Capital Region and Alabang Pasay President said that the additional peso in fare does little to address what drivers actually spend to keep their vehicles running.

Bermejo, who has been driving for around 30 years, said he now spends much of his working day trying to recover the cost of diesel.

He drives from around 4:00 a.m. until 9:00 p.m., or as long as 16 hours a day. When diesel was around P50 to P55 ($0.80 to $0.88) per liter, he said he could take home around P1,000 ($15.98), sometimes reaching P1,500 ($23.97).

Now, he said, his take-home income has fallen to around P500 to P600 ($7.99 to $9.59), despite the long hours on the road.

“That is really not acceptable to us because diesel prices have increased by around P52 to P55 ($0.83 to 0.88), while they only added P1 to the fare. There is a huge difference. It really won’t be enough for us.”

For Bermejo, the impact of rising fuel prices has reached his household. He has four children in school, but his income can no longer cover their needs at the same time.

One of his children who was in college had to temporarily stop studying and find work to help the family.

“My child in college had to stop studying for now. In a way, they also had to find a job to help me because my income now is not enough to support all of them in school at the same time.”

He said the family is now trying to continue the education of his other children while making ends meet with his reduced income.

The same struggle is felt by 50-year-old Janet “Arja” Tumbaga Pocsidio, a member of Piston Women who helps operate a Cubao-Divisoria route.

Pocsidio is a mother of five and helps provide for her children and grandchildren. When diesel prices reached around P140 to P145 ($2.24 to $2.32) per liter, she said their earnings from driving became too small to sustain the family.

On some days, her husband would earn only P70 to P80 ($1.12 to $1.28).

The family eventually stopped operating their jeepney for periods because the cost of fuel outweighed what they could earn from passengers.

Pocsidio then worked as a barker, earning around P250 to P400 ($3.99 to $6.39) a day, which she used for food and her children’s school expenses.

The rising cost of basic necessities also changed what the family could afford to eat.

She said they often relied on dried fish and eggs, while even small increases in food prices became noticeable in their daily budget.

Housing became another burden. Pocsidio said their family was paying P6,000 ($95.88) in monthly rent, aside from electricity and water.

Eventually, they were forced to leave their rented home because they could no longer keep up with the payments.

“We were evicted, and we ended up sleeping in our jeep. Yes, we were evicted because we couldn’t afford to pay,” Pocsidio told Bulatlat.

The family later stayed at the Piston San Juan office for about four months, where they paid for electricity.

For her, depending on the organization for shelter was difficult.

“I feel ashamed. I’m extremely ashamed. I’m quite self-conscious, but I have no other choice. I just told myself that I would leave it in the Lord’s hands.”

While drivers struggle with operating costs, commuters are also adjusting their budgets.

Bench Cuabo, a government worker, said that the P1 ($0.02) fare increase may appear minimal but still affects his daily transportation expenses.

He said his usual P15 ($0.24) fare has increased to P17 (0.27), and when drivers cannot provide change, he sometimes ends up paying P20 ($0.32).

“Although the increase is P1, it will still affect the daily budget of transportation.” He added.

Cuabo also said rising fuel prices also affect his transportation choices. When jeepneys become unavailable or drivers stop operating because of high fuel costs, he sometimes resorts to taking a taxi, which costs significantly more.

However, he highlighted that fare increase should not be treated as the only solution.

He said transportation services have not necessarily improved alongside the higher fare.

“The fare increases because of the rising cost of fuel but the transportation remains the same, no changes.”

Beyond fares, Cuabo said the government should consider measures that would reduce fuel prices and help workers cope with the rising cost of living. Among his suggestions are the temporary suspension of fuel excise taxes and an increase in workers’ wages.

His concern reflects the larger gap facing both commuters and drivers: transportation costs are rising, but household incomes do not necessarily rise at the same pace.

For Bermejo, lowering the price of diesel remains the more immediate solution.

“First and foremost, we really need the price of diesel to be rolled back. Second, if it really cannot be rolled back, perhaps the VAT and excise tax on fuel could be temporarily removed.”

The fuel crisis has also fueled continued protests from transport groups. During the September 29–30 strike, Piston members and other groups marched in Metro Manila to demand government action on petroleum prices.

On September 29, seventy-eight-year-old Piston driver Elmer “Tatay Elmer” Cordero was rushed to a hospital after suffering a heart attack during the protest, according to the group.

For drivers like Bermejo and Pocsidio, the issue goes beyond whether passengers can afford another peso in fare.

It is about whether the income from a day on the road can still cover the basic needs of the families waiting at home.

And as fuel prices continue to affect transportation, food, education and housing, the question for many jeepney families is no longer simply how much a passenger can afford to pay—but how much longer a driver’s income can keep a household afloat. (AMU, RVO)

author: ACG
title: When history accelerates: Maricarmen’s eviction
content:
We publish below the statement from the Spanish group Liza on the Maricarmen mobilisation and the need for revolutionary organisation.




Context: On Saturday, September 26, thousands of people marched through the streets of Madrid to protest the eviction of 87-year-old disabled  Maricarmen Abascal from her home. Her door was broken down by local riot police, and she was evicted on a stretcher despite the resistance of a cordon of protesters. Maricarmen, who had lived in her apartment for 70 years, instantly became a symbol of the housing crisis plaguing Spain, particularly in major cities. Whose fault is it? Rampant gentrification, in which real estate developers systematically buy up buildings in city centres, taking the opportunity to “revise” rents. Maricarmen’s rent, which was around 500 euros per month, was increased by 275% to 2,750 euros! Anger swept across Spain, withtens of thousands mobilised and fifty demonstrations,, particularly in Madrid, where the demonstrations, claimed as involving as high as 500,000, culminated in an impromptu encampment at Puerta del Sol, reminiscent of the 2011 protests that sparked the Indignados movement. This time, a few nights of occupation were enough for the real estate company that had evicted Maricarmen to reverse its decision, release her from the hospital, and reinstate her in her apartment, cancelling the rent increase it had planned to impose. While applauding this outcome, the Puerta del Sol “campers” are maintaining the pressure, as numerous other evictions are taking place daily across Spain. They are demanding that the “socialist” government enact a new, more protective law to curb rising purchase and rental prices.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez promised once more to introduce a new bill to regulate rent levels.  However, this was blocked by the conservative People’s Party (PP) and far-right Vox and the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat). Sánchez has now called a snap election.




On the political climate and the need for revolutionary organisation




“Revolutions have their own rhythm, punctuated by accelerations and decelerations. They also have their own geometry, in which the straight line breaks at the bifurcations and sharp turns of history.” Daniel Bensaid, 

Politics as a Strategic Art




There is a fundamental difference between chronological time and political time. The former unfolds in a seemingly uniform manner: days follow days, and development is linear. The latter, however, under the dialectical logic of a contradictory reality, is very different: There are historical periods in which months or even years seem to contain very few substantial transformations, while there are moments in which, in a matter of days, political reality can be radically transformed.




This means that political time cannot be understood simply as the succession of events on the calendar. It is, above all, the pace at which the relationships between social forces, institutions, organisations, and the possibilities for political action change. There are specific events that, based on the accumulation of internal contradictions, appear as turning points, making possible, in qualitative terms, what until recently was unthinkable.




A society can remain seemingly stable for years and yet be accumulating contradictions. These contradictions don’t necessarily manifest themselves immediately. They can remain separate, partially invisible, or even appear unconnected. An economic crisis, a labour dispute, a housing crisis, a particular police action, a popular mobilisation, or an institutional crisis may seem, individually, like isolated phenomena. However, they can establish connections between them: each event modifies the conditions under which the next ones occur, and each new conflict can amplify, accelerate, or transform the previous ones. It is at this point that the acceleration of political time appears, the concrete expression of latent contradictions.




It is not that an isolated event creates a revolutionary situation out of thin air. Rather, it happens that a prior accumulation of contradictions finds certain events capable of condensing them and making them politically visible. The event then acts as a catalyst for processes that were already developing in society.




“Men make their own history, but they do not make it as they please; they do not make it under self-chosen circumstances, but under circumstances directly encountered, given and transmitted from the past.” Karl Marx, 

The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte




The history of the Paris Commune can serve to illustrate this point. The Commune did not simply emerge as a consequence of a single event on March 18, 1871. Prior to this, there had been an extraordinary accumulation of conflicts: the Franco-Prussian War, the French defeat, the fall of the Second Empire, the Siege of Paris, the organisation and arming of the National Guard, the growing tension between the government in Versailles and the Parisian population, and the political radicalisation of certain sectors of the city. For months, elements had been building that altered the situation.




But there comes a point when this buildup changes pace. The government’s attempt to withdraw the National Guard’s cannons from Montmartre on March 18 triggers a rupture. Within days, what might have seemed like just another political crisis transforms into a completely different situation 

: the government loses effective control of Paris, the National Guard assumes a central role, and on March 26, elections are held for the Commune

 , which will be proclaimed two days later.




The important thing to understand is that no one could have foreseen how it would all end. For Kropotkin, the existence of the Commune began to create possibilities that previously couldn’t even be formulated in the same way. According to him, 

the idea of ​​the Commune wasn’t conceived suddenly by an individual; he presents it as something born of collective intelligence.

 Therefore, we don’t want to claim that the Commune was inevitable. It wasn’t. The important thing is to understand that a series of processes that had been developing for months were able to crystallise into 

a qualitative transformation in an extraordinarily short period

.




In January 1917, Lenin, in exile in Zurich, did not consider the Russian Revolution imminent. He spoke of it as a coming revolution that perhaps his own generation would not live to witness. In his own words: “We of the older generation may not live to see the decisive battles of this revolution.” However, he did not doubt the historical possibility of a new revolutionary wave. Just a few weeks later, the fall of Tsarism radically transformed the horizon of what was possible. 

What in January had appeared as an indeterminate historical prospect had become by March a concrete political situation that required intervention.




This allows us to understand something fundamental: 

the acceleration of political time does not mean that suddenly everything is possible. It means that the boundary of possibility can shift rapidly.

 What yesterday seemed politically unfeasible may become a concrete possibility tomorrow. And, likewise, a possibility that seemed open may quickly close.




That is why 

political acceleration is also a strategic problem.




The event and the accumulation




We can apply this reflection to a much more immediate scale. Let’s consider an eviction like Maricarmen’s. The eviction, viewed in isolation, might seem like a specific conflict between an individual and a vulture fund, a legal matter, or a particular housing claim. But certain conditions may already exist surrounding this event: organised groups, solidarity networks, prior experiences of struggle, social unrest, conflicts with institutions, and a shared awareness of a broader problem. The eviction can then become something more than the specific case that triggered it. In the words of a colleague, 

fires are unpredictable, but it is our duty to stockpile flammable material for when one appears

.




It is not about denying the particularity of each conflict, but about understanding how it can relate to other conflicts and how it can contribute to building a collective force and, of course, one capable of exceeding the predictable.




A concentration of power can produce a primary network of affinities. This network can enable further mobilisation. The institutional response can generate outrage. Outrage can increase participation. Participation can lead to a convergence of forces. Organisation can connect the conflict with other conflicts. And these conflicts, in turn, can modify other sectors’ perceptions of their own possibilities for action. In this process, feedback occurs: 

an acceleration of conditions

 and conflicts, an intensification of repression, and a primary awakening of consciousness among much broader segments of the population. There is not necessarily a straight line between the initial event and the final outcome. It is a concatenation of events that interact dialectically. One struggle modifies the conditions of another; a partial victory can generate confidence for a subsequent struggle; a defeat can produce demoralisation or, conversely, new forms of organisation; a repressive response can contain a movement or provoke a broadening of solidarity. In short, 

a regime of acceleration in which each event ceases to be merely an event and begins to modify the conditions of subsequent events.




And that is precisely where the organisational problem arises.




Getting organised when time speeds up




During periods of stability, the need for a 

revolutionary political organisation may seem abstract

. If struggles develop slowly, are subject to inertial bureaucracies, conflicts are absorbed by institutional mechanisms, and demands appear isolated from one another, it may seem sufficient to intervene in each specific conflict.




But when the political clock speeds up, a different question arises:




What do we do with the strength we’ve managed to accumulate? How do we make the fire spread?




“Because mobilising is not the same as organising” (Jane McAlevey). And winning a specific demand does not necessarily mean having built a political force capable of transforming the social relations that produce that demand.




Every struggle also generates different possible directions. A mobilisation can be channelled toward institutional negotiation, it can be limited to resolving the specific problem that originated it, it can become a broader organisational experience, or it can connect with other conflicts and produce a new form of collective power. 

Events can shift from being quantitative to being qualitative.




Deactivating or diverting the struggle doesn’t require imagining a permanent conspiracy by institutions or union bureaucracies. It’s about recognising that in every struggle there are 

actors with different interests, positions, and strategies

. Some will seek to resolve the conflict quickly; others will try to broaden its scope; others will seek to institutionalise it; others will try to keep it within certain limits acceptable to barbarity.




Therefore, a struggle does not have a predetermined political direction. 

Acceleration opens up possibilities, but it does not, in itself, determine where they will develop.

 However, this statement requires a fundamental caveat: 

intervening in a struggle does not mean appropriating it.




This issue was especially important for anarchist thought and, in particular, for Malatesta and Fontenis. Faced with the false dichotomy between absolute spontaneity and top-down direction, they defended the need for revolutionary organisations capable of intervening in social movements, but without turning that intervention into a replacement for those leading the struggles.




A revolutionary organisation can contribute analysis, coordination, experience, strategy, and a broader perspective; it can try to connect specific conflicts and help a struggle develop its full political potential. But there is a fundamental difference between 

intervening to strengthen the autonomy of a struggle

 and 

intervening to turn it into an instrument of an external organisation

.




The revolutionary should not position themselves above the struggle to dictate from the outside what it should do. Nor should they merely observe it passively in the name of spontaneity, as if there were no interests within the conflict itself seeking to co-opt or channel discontent. Their task is to 

deploy political action within it

, contributing whatever can increase its class independence and organisational capacity, without replacing the subject who leads it.




In this sense, the revolutionary organisation would be 

a mediator between the spontaneity of the struggle and the conscious construction of a political strategy. A strategic operator for emancipation.




The organisation as strategic mediation




The role of an organisation is not to artificially accelerate history or to replace those who are leading a struggle. Nor is it simply to wait passively from the couch for a revolutionary situation to arise so it can intervene. During periods of relative stability, the organisation must build the necessary capacities to take political action when the situation changes. It must pivot constantly between objective and subjective conditions, between social reality and a revolutionary program.




In other words: 

the revolutionary organisation establishes itself in periods of calm in order to develop its strategy before political time moves too quickly.




When acceleration arrives, there is no longer enough time to build a strategy, relationships, activist cadres, a political culture, coordination mechanisms, and the capacity for intervention from scratch. Everything that hasn’t been built beforehand will have to be improvised when conditions become more difficult.




The organisation is, therefore, 

a form of political accumulation, of antagonistic capital.




But this accumulation should not aim to build a 

structure separate

 from society that would later seek to govern it. Its function should be to build capacities that can be placed at the service of broader collective processes. To move from being committed militants to revolutionary cadres. In the words of Fontenis: “The class before the party.”




Therefore, we can perhaps formulate the relationship between organisation and movement in the following way:




It is not about directing the struggle from the outside, but about increasing from within its capacity to organise, understand itself and defend itself against deviations.




In fact, the false dichotomy between organisation and mass front is too often presented, when it is actually a dialectical relationship: organisations contribute to the fronts, political action within the fronts contributes to the development of activists within the organisations, organisations base their programmes on the fact that the fronts perceive or feel the progress is coherent, and the spaces improve qualitatively through constant theoretical and practical development. This is always done with honesty and activist ethics.




Organisation provides memory when the movement is subject to the urgency of the event. It provides perspective when the conflict threatens to be reduced to its immediate dimension. It provides coordination when the struggles appear fragmented. And it provides strategy when a situation arises in which decisions made in days can have consequences for years.

From individual struggle to revolutionary cadre




There is a fundamental question here: to identify the political potential inherent in a given struggle. A specific demand may contain a much broader contradiction.







Defending a home can open a discussion about property ownership.




Defending a job can open a discussion about who makes the decisions in production.




A fight against a particular institutional measure can open a discussion about who has the effective capacity to decide on the living conditions of the majority.







The organisation can help make that connection, but it cannot impose it mechanically. It has to start from concrete reality, from existing relationships, from the level of consciousness, and from the current state of the class struggle.




In this sense, the revolutionary programme should not be understood as a list of slogans applied externally to any conflict. It must be a tool for interpreting existing contradictions and guiding intervention toward transformations that expand collective capacity. From this arises another role of the revolutionary organisation, mentioned earlier only superficially: 

that of creating revolutionary cadres

 —individuals capable of applying revolutionary theory and translating it to the concrete context where the struggle is unfolding. Revolutionary politics, then, does not consist of mechanically applying a pre-constructed program to any situation. It consists of maintaining a permanent, focused yet flexible relationship between program, organisation, movement, and reality.




The notion of a revolutionary cadre is not a label for “enlightened” militants, but rather the idea that selfless and committed militancy alone is not enough, that the task is immense and, for that reason, no less inspiring. It is time to develop a program and build strategic unity. A unity founded on fraternal debate and the political will to move forward.




Not all acceleration is revolutionary




This also helps us understand why not all political acceleration is necessarily revolutionary.




A crisis can produce radicalisation, but also fear or reaction. It can generate organisation, but also retreat. It can broaden the struggle or create the very conditions for its eradication. It can open the possibility of a rupture or strengthen existing structures. In fact, we are at a moment in which the intensification of contradictions within capitalism can cause an overlap of events that accelerates the course of history in one direction or another. History neither warns nor asks permission.




Acceleration does not determine the outcome: what it does is 

reduce the time available to intervene in a field of possibilities that is still open.




For years, what seems impossible remains outside the political horizon. Until an accumulation of contradictions, an unexpected event, and a particular balance of power produce a 

qualitative transformation.

 Then, the question ceases to be whether it is possible. 

The question becomes which actors exist and what direction they want to give to the situation. Politics leaves no vacuum, and if we are not there, others will be.




We have certain sectors, after the moment of social outrage following Maricarmen’s eviction, clamoring for a new 15M movement. These sectors, with their reformist leanings, are simply seeking an accumulation of indignation that will crystallise into yet another parliamentary alternative. This will only fuel the reactionary forces due to their real inability to impose any real change on our conditions. The 15M movement was an acceleration process that caught us, at best, in a cobweb-filled basement. We lacked the effective capacity to steer that process toward more revolutionary positions. Reformist bureaucracies, the media apparatus, and the movement’s internal contradictions dissolved any possibility of change. 

The revolutionary obligation is to be prepared for the opportunities that history will open for us.




Get organised before the acceleration arrives




Therefore, a revolutionary organisation cannot be conceived solely as a structure intended for moments of crisis. It is precisely in moments when seemingly “nothing is happening” that the possibilities for intervention are built when everything starts to happen. It accumulates experiences, relationships, knowledge, tools, trust, and collective capacities that can acquire a completely different value when the situation changes.




And when political time imposes a new pace upon us, those unprepared for this acceleration may discover that, while they are still trying to grasp that the situation has changed, 

others are already intervening.

 Revolutionary organisation is, ultimately, the conscious construction of a political capacity to intervene at that moment when history ceases to unfold according to the calendar and thus ushers in historical cycles.




What would happen if Maricarmen’s eviction, as a concrete event, opened up previously unimaginable opportunities? What position would that put us revolutionaries in to contest the path these mobilisations would take? Do we have enough strength to stand up to the bureaucracies and reformist sectors? The answers, if given honestly, are bleak.




Our task is to prepare ourselves, not to replace those who make history, but to help, to the best of our ability, to clarify the interests of our class.




We can help accelerate history; events don’t happen by chance. There are always actors and subjects involved. Be that as it may, we must take sides. To navigate the waves of history, to write its lines.




Liza, Anarchist Platform




Liza is a revolutionary platform of anarchist socialists located in the cities of Madrid and Granada

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Deterioration of civic space continues under Marcos Jr — global report
content:
Activists protest in front of Department of Justice to condemn the filing of twin terror laws against activists. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat.

MANILA — Civic space in the Philippines continues to deteriorate with the Philippine government’s failure to implement human rights obligations, global civil society alliance CIVICUS reported.

“Since coming to power, the (Ferdinand Marcos Jr.) government has sustained a systematic pattern of repression against activists, harassing those who defend human rights with the use of trumped-up charges or anti-terror laws,” said Josef Benedict, Asia researcher of CIVICUS.

The Philippines has been rated “Repressed” for five consecutive years — the second worst rating a country can receive — indicating severe restrictions to the freedoms of expression, peaceful assembly, and association.

The country was included in the Monitor Watchlist last March 2026, flagging serious concerns about its crackdown on dissent, criminalizing protesters, and targeting activists.

Read: Philippines on human rights watchlist due to crackdown on dissent

“The government must reverse course to protect the rights of activists and allow them to work without fear, interference or retaliation,” Benedict added.

Such a rating was a product of failure of the Philippine government to fulfill its human rights obligations under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), which it ratified in 2007.

For example, the government failed to implement the recommendations on civic space during the fourth cycle of the Universal Periodic Review in November 2022 at the United Nations Human Rights Council. It includes the need for the Philippine government to ensure enabling space for civil society and human rights defenders, end red-tagging or the linking of activists and human rights defenders to armed insurgency.

The ICCPR mandates all state parties to respect and protect civic freedoms, including freedoms of association, expression and peaceful assembly: all of which are also enshrined in the 1987 Philippines Constitution.

Among the significant forms of attack against activists is the use of fabricated charges under the twin terror laws.

Karapatan reported as of September 2026 that at least 259 individuals had been charged with the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA) and the Terrorism Financing Prevention and Suppression Act (TFPSA).

Activists are also being charged with violations of the Public Assembly Act of 1985, a relic from the Martial Law of dictator Ferdinand Marcos Sr used against protesting activists.

The Marcos Jr. administration has been warned several times this year for its low performance on human rights and civic space. In Safety from the State metric of the Human Rights Measurement Initiative, the Philippines scored a “very bad” performance for freedom from arbitrary arrest, which is the lowest score recorded among Southeast Asian countries surveyed. Its freedom of assembly and association metric also falls under “bad” score.

Read: Philippines’ human rights record worse than average in Southeast Asia

The CIVICUS report also flagged the persistence of red-tagging and killings against activists and journalists. The Philippines remains the deadliest country for environmental and land defenders in Asia since 2012, while it maintains a low rank of 114th in the World Press Freedom Index of the Reporters Without Borders due to its press freedom violations this year.

Moreover, the impunity for the killing of 19 people in Negros Occidental this April 19, 2026, is also highlighted in the report. Not one has been held accountable for the killing of nine civilians and ten revolutionaries, with the Philippine Army maintaining that all of them died in armed encounters.

“The authorities must respect the right to protest and ensure that when arbitrary arrests occur or excessive force is used, that the perpetrators are held to account,” Benedict said.

Some of CIVICUS recommendations for the government include the abolition of the National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC), adoption of Human Rights Defenders Protection Act, decriminalization of libel and cyber-libel, and the withdrawal of the Digital Media Anti-False Information Bill.
