author: Moataz Hagag
title: State security prosecution releases journalist Rasha Azab on LE10,000 bail
content:
Journalist Rasha Azab was released on LE10,000 bail on Monday evening by the Supreme State Security Prosecution following questioning in relation to a tweet she published in recent weeks regarding the conduct of the Interior Ministry and its impact on the public mood. 




She was questioned on charges of “promoting the perpetration of terrorist acts” and using a website to promote ideas calling for doing so in Supreme State Security Prosecution Case 8025/2026, her defense lawyer, Ragia Omran, told Mada Masr. 




Azab was questioned on her reasons for publishing a tweet, in which she wrote, on September 23, “how long does it take to go from ‘the Interior Ministry are thugs’ to ‘the people want the fall of the regime.’” Azab responded that her tweet was commentary on the case of Dina Ezzat, a woman who called for her husband’s release on social media in September, after he was arrested from their Nasr City home by authorities in their local area. Ezzat herself was briefly 

taken

 into custody after she spoke out against her husband’s arrest before she was later released on bail. 




According to the case’s record, 12 people filed complaints at police stations across several governorates against Azab the day after she posted her tweet, Omran said.




The prosecution did not question her about the Matsda2sh case. Azab herself, however, pointed to what she had read on social media regarding 

the Matsda2sh journalists’ complaints of torture at National Security Agency headquarters

, when prosecutors asked her for examples of “thuggery” on the part of the Interior Minsitry. She also cited her own subjection to assault during a 2024 protest outside the United Nations Women office, after which she was briefly 

arrested

 before being released on bail, as well as threats, pursuit and the theft of her car; incidents she said her local police station had refused to allow her to file a report on.




During the investigation, Azab said that she did not know the Matsda2sh journalists previously and that she knew of them and of their arrest through the statements published by the Journalists Syndicate, and that she had heard that they were tortured in custody via published statements. 




Azab received a 

summons

 to the prosecution on Saturday, without explanation of the charges or the incidents under investigation, and was presented on Monday afternoon for questioning. 




She 

posted

 to her X account earlier on Monday that she views herself as “once again accused,” after two years of harassment which included her hounding, the theft of her car in 2024 and the “destruction of her life.” 




She added that the summons comes during a time of an ongoing push for “independent journalism and a nation without despotism,” and called for the support of her colleagues present today at the Journalists Syndicate.




The summons came in the wake of an ongoing demonstration at the syndicate, in which Azab had participated, along with dozens of other journalists, in solidarity with the six from independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh who were arrested last week. Upon receiving the summons, her lawyers inquired about the case against her and found that it predated the campaign targeting the Matsda2sh team.

The post 

State security prosecution releases journalist Rasha Azab on LE10,000 bail

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

.

author: Unknown
title: Эррико Малатеста - Как некоторые республиканцы не хотят делать Республику
content:
Автор

: Эррико Малатеста

Название

: Как некоторые республиканцы не хотят делать Республику

Дата

: 15 ноября 1924

Источник

: Pensiero e Volontà №22







КАК НЕКОТОРЫЕ РЕСПУБЛИКАНЦЫ 

НЕ ХОТЯТ ДЕЛАТЬ РЕСПУБЛИКУ







 Под заголовком «Как будет сделана республика» республиканский орган 

La Bandiera

 в Риме писал в своём первом номере: 













Республиканцы не хотят навязывать свои идеи насилием и произволом. Они хотят убедить Народ, что с Республикой будут решены главнейшие проблемы экономической, социальной и политической жизни сегодняшней Италии.




Не бесцельные бунты, не насилие против людей, не диктатуры политиканов и произвола.




Республиканцы утверждают, что Народ должен избрать

 Учредительное собрание

, составленное из представителей всех классов, всех идей, всех течений, всех интересов.




Учредительное собрание

 

решит, как должна быть устроена Италия: должна ли Италия быть

 монархией 

или

 республикой

; Учредительное собрание даст

 основные 

законы новой итальянской жизни.




Так, то есть через цивилизованную встречу всех существующих в нашей стране течений; так, цивилизованным средством принятия решений.




Так: как делали все народы, когда хотели закрыть мучительный период своей жизни.




Итальянские граждане, серьёзно озабоченные благом Нации, пусть подумают, что нет иного пути, чтобы избавить Италию от новых траурных утрат и новых разрушений.













 А мы хотели бы знать, принимают ли республиканцы – те, что в официальной партии, и те, что вне партии, старые и молодые, – эту программу или нет. 




 Вопрос будет нескромным, но он, несомненно, имеет непосредственную актуальность теперь, когда Республика представляется возможным, и несомненно не худшим, решением итальянского кризиса [речь идет об убийстве депутата Матеотти, из-за которого режим Муссолини едва не рухнул]. 




 Мы, как известно, не республиканцы; но, будучи непримиримыми антимонархистами, нам важно знать, есть ли в Италии республиканцы, которые 

хотят

 действительно сделать республику, или речь идёт только о литературных республиканцах, которые затем кончают, один за другим, как Каппа и Бардзилаи [приняли пост министра в королевском правительстве]. 




 Поскольку нам представляется очевидным, что если бы Республику пришлось делать на манер 

La Bandiera

, то не только не была бы сделана Республика, но была бы оказана благоуханная услуга Монархии. 




 И чтобы доказать это, нам было бы достаточно аргументов, которые используют сами республиканцы, когда ведут пропаганду. Тем, кто говорит, что монархия необходима, потому что народ ещё недостаточно образован, они отвечают, – и так отвечал их учитель Мадзини, – что Монархия не воспитывает, а развращает; что именно Республика создаст республиканцев; что именно со свободой приобретается потребность, вкус, способность быть свободными. И действительно, после более чем шестидесяти лет конституционной, национальной, либеральной и так далее Монархии, в Италии меньше республиканцев и особенно меньше республиканского духа, чем в десятилетие 1860–70 годов. 




 А теперь эти республиканцы открывают, или надеются, что Собрание, составленное из «представителей всех классов, всех идей, всех течений, всех интересов», даст Италии Республику!.. Готовые, впрочем, подчиниться Монархии, если так решит Учредительное собрание. 




 Не следует ли скорее предвидеть, что в собрании, составленном так, как говорит программа 

La Bandiera

, восторжествуют самые сильные интересы, те течения, которые меньше всего задевают мизонеизм [боязнь нового] и естественную любовь людей к спокойной жизни, партии, за которыми стоит вооружённая сила, классы, владеющие богатством и знанием? 




 И разве не несомненно, с другой стороны, что избранное собрание, хотя бы и без материального насилия, в тех моральных и экономических условиях, в которых находится итальянский народ, – далеко от того, чтобы представлять справедливо все идеи и все интересы, – было бы составлено в огромном большинстве из собственников, священников, адвокатов и политиканов и не представляло бы по существу ничего, кроме интересов тех, кто уже пользуется теперь всеми экономическими и политическими привилегиями? 




 И в каком же учебнике истории видели эти республиканцы, что 

народы делали всё так

, то есть «закрывали мучительные периоды своего существования через цивилизованную встречу»?... Разве что под 

цивилизованной встречей

 они не подразумевают ружейные выстрелы, покушения, военные путчи и подобные милости! 




 Нет, пусть убедятся друзья-республиканцы: если они хотят сделать республику, они должны сделать её силой, ибо ни Монархия не уйдёт спокойно, чтобы доставить им удовольствие, ни имущие классы не захотят по доброй воле, без принуждения, идти на риск радикального переворота, который мог бы поставить под угрозу их положение. 




 Но, нам кажется, мы слышим, как нам говорят: не повторяете ли вы непрестанно, вы, анархисты, что не намерены навязывать анархию силой? Значит, республику надо было бы навязать, тогда как анархия была бы основана на свободном согласии?! 




 Именно так. 




 Мы хотим силой разрушить силу, которая нас угнетает, силой хотим завоевать свободу, которая силой у нас отнята; но как только мы освободились сами и помогли другим освободиться, мы не намерены навязывать никому свои идеи и свои методы и рассчитываем, для всеобщего осуществления Анархии, на пропаганду и на пример. 




...

author: Chris Walker
title: At Ohio Campaign Rally, Trump Threatens to Withhold Aid If Democrats Get Elected
content:
“I’m not going to help” if an Ohio Democratic candidate for governor wins, Trump said.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

In a campaign speech in Vandalia, Ohio, on Saturday, President Donald Trump suggested he would withhold federal funds from the state if voters elect Democratic politicians in this year’s midterm races.

Trump appeared to conflate two different political races, discussing U.S. Sen. Jon Husted’s (R-Ohio) Senate reelection campaign and Democratic candidate Amy Acton’s campaign for governor in the same statement. (Husted is running against former U.S. Senator and Democrat Sherrod Brown, while Acton is facing off against Republican candidate for governor and Trump ally Vivek Ramaswamy.)

“Jon Husted…calls me all the time. He always wants money,” Trump said during his speech. “If Amy Acton got in, I don’t know anything about her.”

“I’m not going to help her, probably, she hates me, I guess,” Trump added.

Trump’s speech also featured vulgar attacks against Democrats in general. At one point, he encouraged those in attendance to “just get out and vote” for Republicans.

“If you do that, we’re going to win, and we’re going to win big, and we’re going to shove it up their ass,” Trump said.

The president made a number of bizarre claims during his Saturday night speech. He claimed that he has one of the highest IQs “anywhere in the world,” telling the audience it was around 1,775. Such an IQ would indeed be the highest, as no IQ test has ever measured above 300. He also said that polls are “fake,” complaining that they didn’t take into account his plans to campaign in the final weeks of the race — a statement that is technically true but misleading, as polls question respondents about their current attitudes. And he reiterated an unlikely (and legally dubious) promise to deliver $5,000 checks to every American adult if Republicans win the midterms.

Trump has already withheld disaster aid from states for seemingly political reasons. In a series of Truth Social posts in late June, Trump announced hundreds of millions of dollars in disaster aid funds going to states that backed him in 2024, while ignoring some requests from states that backed his opponent, Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris.

An analysis from the Urban Institute around that time showed that, since Trump reentered the White House, over 84 percent of requests from states that voted for him won approval, as opposed to only 41 percent of requests from states that didn’t back him. Approvals, when they did occur, happened twice as fast for red states as for blue ones.

We now have three full months of data since Google changed its search to feature AI results. The numbers are worse than we anticipated. Overall readership that comes to Truthout through Google is down 54 percent against last year. The number of new readers who discover Truthout via Google searches is down 49 percent, and returning users from Google are down 51 percent.

We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We anticipate a loss of roughly $500,000 in online revenue as a result of this massive traffic plunge in the next year alone.

The only way we can keep publishing is with strong reader support. We are asking you to start a monthly donation to Truthout today — anything you can do, whether $5 or $25, makes a difference.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Far Right Makes Gains in Brazil in First Round of Presidential Race
content:
“The momentum has been with the right since 2018,” says Brazilian philosopher Rodrigo Nunes.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Brazil’s presidential election is headed to a runoff between leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far-right Senator Flávio Bolsonaro after neither candidate cleared 50% in Sunday’s vote, in which the right made gains in Congress and in governor races across the country. Bolsonaro received 47% of the vote compared to Lula’s 45%. The second round of voting is on October 25. If elected, Flávio Bolsonaro has vowed to grant amnesty to his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest and serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup in 2022 to overturn Lula’s last victory. He has also vowed to strengthen ties to the Trump administration, which is accused of trying to influence the result in Bolsonaro’s favor.

“The momentum has been with the right since 2018,” says Brazilian philosopher Rodrigo Nunes, who explains that public disillusionment with politics is part of that shift. “Lots of people see the far right as promising them, ‘Well, if this is all there is, if all we can expect from the future is ever more dog-eat-dog conditions, an ever more competitive struggle of all against all, at least what the far right says is the state will get off our backs.’”

Nunes is author of Neither Vertical nor Horizontal: A Theory of Political Organization and the new book Anatomy of Disintegration: What Brazil Reveals About the Global Far Right. He recently wrote about the stakes of the Brazilian election for North South Notes.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: We begin today’s show in Brazil, where the presidential race between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far-right Senator Flávio Bolsonaro is headed to a runoff. During the first round of voting Sunday, Bolsonaro received 47% of the vote; Lula got 45%.

Bolsonaro is the son of Brazil’s former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, currently under house arrest serving a 27-year sentence after he was convicted of plotting a military coup in 2022 to overturn Lula’s win in that year’s election. If elected, Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged to grant amnesty to his father and others involved in the coup. Flávio has also vowed to strengthen ties to the Trump administration.

In Senate races, Bolsonaro’s party secured 19 of the 54 Senate seats up for grabs. In total, the right or far right won 34 seats. Flávio Bolsonaro spoke to supporters in the capital Brasília.

SEN. FLÁVIO BOLSONARO: [translated] I am very happy about the real possibility that three weeks from now Brazil will give a definitive answer that it wants a modern government, a government with fewer ministries, a government that will restore democracy. What I have to say is that Lula is fighting for power. He has already contested seven presidential elections. Seven presidential elections. He is concerned about power. I am concerned about Brazil’s future. I am fighting for Brazil.

AMY GOODMAN: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva addressed supporters in São Paulo.

PRESIDENT LUIZ INÁCIO LULA DA SILVA: [translated] The result is unexpected. We never get everything we want. I must admit that I was convinced that I was going to win on the first round. … But we have the second round, and the runoff is the moment of truth. It’s time to show the true Brazilian picture, because today is the Brazil we want. So, starting tomorrow, we’re launching a new campaign.

AMY GOODMAN: Ahead of the elections, a group of 31 Democratic lawmakers sent a letter to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, accusing the Trump administration of being engaged in a, quote, “sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilization in Brazil,” unquote.

We go now to Rio de Janeiro, where we’re joined by Rodrigo Nunes. His new book, out this week, Anatomy of Disintegration: What Brazil Reveals About the Global Far Right. He’s associate professor of philosophy at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, and a visiting fellow at the University of Essex, U.K.

Rodrigo Nunes, thanks so much for being with us. First, if you can respond to Flávio Bolsonaro coming out ahead, 47 to 45%, against President Lula, and Lula’s even expression of surprise, saying he expected to win this round? Of course, then it goes to the next runoff election on October 25th. Can you talk about what happened in Brazil and its significance?

RODRIGO NUNES: Well, I think anyone who’d been following closely the polls and the tendencies in this election would have thought it would be tight, both in the first and in the second round, but everyone really did expect Lula to come marginally ahead of Flávio in the first round. So that was a surprise.

Having said that, it isn’t a surprise that this is a victory for the right. Everyone could tell that they were going to have the majority in Congress, that they were going to come very close to an easy majority in the Senate, which puts them very close to being able to impeach Supreme Court justices, which is — which has been one of their main rallying points in this election.

So, yes, Flávio coming ahead is a surprise, but everything else, the Congress results, the results in the majority of states that the right has also carried, none of that is really a surprise at this point.

AMY GOODMAN: Tell us who Flávio Bolsonaro is, the son of the former far-right president.

RODRIGO NUNES: Sorry. Could you —

AMY GOODMAN: I want you to tell us —

RODRIGO NUNES: Could you come again?

AMY GOODMAN: I want you to tell us who —

RODRIGO NUNES: Because I lost you for a second.

AMY GOODMAN: I want you to tell us who Flávio Bolsonaro is. But first, let me go back to the current president, Lula, speaking last night, criticizing Flávio Bolsonaro.

PRESIDENT LUIZ INÁCIO LULA DA SILVA: [translated] We only have uncertainties, with a murky biography and a shadowy past. Nothing suggests a promising future for Brazilian society, either in the biography of the father or the son, and we do not know the details regarding other relatives’ biographies. It is a murky biography. There are publications and evidence pointing to very serious suspicions linked to militia, organized crime and Rio de Janeiro’s murders. All of this will become clear, as will his involvement in the founding of Banco Master, which led not only to the biggest corruption case in this country, but also in the biggest orgy involving this country’s authorities.

AMY GOODMAN: If you can respond, Rodrigo Nunes, to what Lula said? And give us the background of Flávio Bolsonaro.

RODRIGO NUNES: So, when Flávio was chosen by his father to be the candidate of the far right, not even people in the right expected him to catch as a candidate. Everyone thought he was too weak and inexpressive as a candidate to actually run against someone, a figure as strong, a figure of the stature of Lula. So, even for the right, it was a surprise that his candidacy did become a real thing in the course of the last months. He is the oldest son of the Bolsonaro clan, and he is the more traditional figure among his brothers, who are all also in politics. He is more of an old-style politician rather than a culture warrior like his other brothers, and even, to some extent, his father.

And in particular, whereas his dad had very strong ties to the military and dependent on — depended on the military a lot for his government, what is most worrying about Flávio Bolsonaro is that there are very well-documented stories connecting him not only to various corruption scandals, including the main corruption scandal that is being talked about in Brazil at the moment, which involves a failed bank that helped, among other things, fund a film on — a biopic of Jair Bolsonaro’s that many people suspect was actually used as a way of channeling funds into the campaign and into the lobbying operations that the Bolsonaro family has been doing alongside the U.S. government since last year, but — so, basically, not only he’s got several ties to several corruption scandals, but, more worryingly, he’s got a well-documented history of ties to organized crime in Rio, not only to the paramilitary militias that occupy several parts of Rio, but also lots of people in his political group in Rio are connected to the drug trade. So, obviously, a victory for him worries several people in Brazil that it would be a victory for organized crime, bringing organized crime to the very top of Brazilian politics.

AMY GOODMAN: And if you can talk about not only the fact that Flávio Bolsonaro came out ahead, but the fact that the far-right and right parties also came out ahead, and what this means, and where you think this runoff election will go, who the other candidates were who will now be not part of it, who might throw their support to, or simply their voters will go to, either Flávio Bolsonaro or Lula?

RODRIGO NUNES: So, another sign of how strong the right is in Brazil at the moment is that the only candidate on the left was Lula. Everyone else contesting this election is broadly in the right-wing camp, or even far right, even farther to the right of Flávio. The tendency is, of course, that most of those votes are going to go to Flávio now. Certainly, the momentum is with him at this moment. He’s leaping ahead in the first round, and I would expect him to go even farther in the first polls that will come out this week. Certainly, the momentum is all with him.

And it has to be said, in a certain way, the momentum has been with the right since 2018. The right wing has managed to — if we understand a cultural revolution to mean shaping the way in which most people understand reality, in which most people see what’s happening around them, then you could say that the far right has managed to produce a cultural revolution in Brazil, especially in the south of Brazil, in those areas in which agribusiness is strong, or what you could call the extractive frontier, where you have agribusiness, mining and so forth, and even in the south — the southeast, and even in the peripheries of Brazil, where lots of people see the far right as promising them, “Well, if things — if this is all there is, if all we can expect from the future is ever more dog-eat-dog conditions, ever more — an ever more competitive struggle of all against all, at least what the far right says is the state will get off our backs. We won’t have to — we’ll pay less taxes. There’ll be less regulations stopping us from doing what we need to do in order to survive. And even at the end of the day if I remain hyperexploited, at least there won’t be anyone telling me that I can’t make jokes about gay people, or there won’t be anyone meddling with my private life if I beat my wife up.” So, there’s a very complex portfolio, let’s say, of material and psychological compensations that the far right offers. And it has to be said, it’s a message that has been working.

And even though Lula has been in power for the last four years, he was — he was always dealing with a Congress that was in its majority of the right and far right. He didn’t manage to do anywhere near enough to counter the strength of the far right in Brazilian society. And what we see is basically a continuous growth. Even though Bolsonaro lost the last elections to Lula, what you can see is just a continuous growth from 2018 until now. And you see that in the way that they’ve carried most states, that they carried the majority of the Congress, and so on.

AMY GOODMAN: So, last week, a group of 31 U.S. Democratic lawmakers, led by Congressmembers Delia Ramirez, Pramila Jayapal, Jesús “Chuy” García, along with Senator Bernie Sanders, sent a letter to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio accusing the Trump administration of interfering in Brazil’s elections, the letter saying, “Over the course of President Trump’s second term, we have seen U.S. officials engage in a sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilization in Brazil,” and then goes on to outline the diplomatic, economic and political pressure wielded by the Trump administration leading up to the elections. What do you know of whether there was U.S. interference there? Of course, both Flávio Bolsonaro, his father Jair Bolsonaro, very close to President Trump, and you have Flávio also promising to pardon his father, who’s under house arrest for decades for involvement in the attempted coup against Lula.

RODRIGO NUNES: So, Amy, I belong to what is called in Brazil the redemocratization generation, i.e. the people who were born in the very last years of the military regime. And I have to say, I didn’t expect, in my life, to see the level of U.S. interference that we’ve seen in these elections.

If in the last elections the U.S. played a very positive role when it very clearly signaled to Jair Bolsonaro that it wasn’t going to support any coup attempts to overrule the result of the elections, in these elections and since last year, there’s been a clear pattern of U.S. interference, starting with the tariffs imposed on Brazil at the time of the coup trials that came to an end in September last year. And there was a very open, very explicit activity on the part of one of the Bolsonaro brothers to lobby the U.S. government to impose those tariffs on Brazil. So, we’ve had more tariffs imposed on Brazil this year.

But on top of that, there is another thing that was an object of lobby from the Bolsonaro family, the fact that very recently the U.S. named the two major drug factions in Brazil as terrorist organizations, which we understand from the pattern that we’ve seen in places like Colombia, Venezuela, etc., is always a first step in the direction of more intense interference, including potentially military intervention, which is supposed to be fighting the war on drugs, but, in effect, is actually interfering in domestic policy, in domestic politics, and picking sides in domestic politics in countries of the region.

Finally, there’s also been a pattern of funds being invested both from supporters of President Trump or supporters of the far right in the U.S., but also from the State Department, funds that have been directed to political activity in Brazil, which has systematically been political activity on the right, to support the candidacy of Flávio Bolsonaro and his supporters.

AMY GOODMAN: Flávio Bolsonaro asked Trump to designate two crime groups as terrorist groups. Does this open, as you’re talking about, U.S. — more of a U.S. military presence in Brazil if Bolsonaro wins? Also, Flávio Bolsonaro is vowing to build more maximum-security prisons similar to El Salvador’s CECOT prison, which the U.S. used to send hundreds of migrants to, until a judge ruled they had to be released.

RODRIGO NUNES: Yeah, absolutely. I mean, the model here — one of the models here is very clearly Nayib Bukele in El Salvador, both in the sense of the public security policies of Nayib Bukele, so, you know, an intensification of the militarization of social conflict, and with absolute disregard to human rights, but also in the sense of a policy of automatic alignment with U.S. interests. So, we could see — we could end up seeing Brazil, like El Salvador, becoming a first line of support for Trump’s migration policies in the U.S., but also Flávio Bolsonaro has spoken very openly and very clearly about the fact that he intends — and, obviously, this is part of the bargain that he’s making with the U.S., the present U.S. government — he’s spoken very openly about the fact that if he wins, Brazil’s rare earths will be — will be entirely dedicated to, and other resources, like oil and so on, will be entirely dedicated to U.S. interests, which, obviously, in the U.S.’s present situation in its competition, international competition, with China, Brazil would be a major asset. Brazil has the second-largest reserves of rare earth in the world, one of the largest reserves of oil, as well, so this would be a major asset for the U.S. in the coming years.

AMY GOODMAN: Rodrigo Nunes, I want to thank you for being with us, Brazilian philosopher, author of Anatomy of Disintegration: What Brazil Reveals About the Global Far Right, out this week from Haymarket Books.

Coming up, “I am Jane Doe.” The rallying cry of outrage grows over Cornell University’s handling of allegations of a female student who says she was raped by seven fraternity members in 2024. Stay with us.

AMY GOODMAN: The great Brazilian singer Caetano Veloso performing in New York City years ago.

author: Curtis Johnson
title: Trump’s Repeal of Roadless Rule Would Declare Open Season on Protected Forests
content:
A public policy expert described the move as “the largest evisceration of public lands protection in American history.”

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

On August 18, Donald Trump’s United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) officially proposed eliminating the national Roadless Rule. If finalized, the repeal would strip protections from 44.7 million acres of wild intact forest.

The rule, passed in 2001, protects in total 58 million acres of forest from road building, logging, fossil fuel extraction, and other development. Forests in Idaho and Colorado, which have their own state roadless laws, would be exempt, at least for now.

The USDA, which oversees the U.S. Forest Service, initially gave the public only 30 days to comment on the plan. They were forced after public pressure to allow 15 additional days, until October 6. Opponents are aiming to mobilize 1 million public comments during this short period, as well as sponsoring public events speaking out against the repeal.

One hundred and eighty environmental, conservation, and citizen’s groups have been joined by tribes, sportsmen, wildland firefighters, and businesses dedicated to tourism, in submitting a joint public comment or otherwise speaking out against this decision. A letter in support of the Roadless Rule and opposing recission has been signed by 164 congressional representatives.

The recission is “the largest evisceration of public lands protection in American history,” according to Randi Spivak, public lands policy director at the Center for Biological Diversity. Spivak told Truthout the Roadless Rule shelters “hundreds of threatened and endangered species. It provides incredible recreation opportunities — hunting, fishing, hiking. These were really the last of the forests outside of wilderness that had not been opened up to industrial development.”

The roadless-area forests contain immense old-growth trees, pristine rivers that are filled in the summer and fall with some of the last healthy salmon runs in the country, and trail through some of the U.S.’s grandest scenic beauty. These forests help protect some of the country’s remaining wild species — grizzly bears, wolverines, and endangered lynx. They host key migration corridors for antelope, elk, and mule deer. They protect headwaters of streams providing clean drinking water to 24 million people in the country.

The current protections include 9.3 million acres of the Tongass rainforest in Alaska. The Tongass contains incredible landscapes — rugged ocean coastlines, glacial fjords, snow-capped peaks, wild rivers, and old-growth forest. Concentrated in the Tongass are Earth’s largest remaining intact stands of coastal temperate rainforest, making it a vital carbon sink for curbing climate change. Its trees capture approximately 44 percent of all the carbon stored by U.S. national forests, absorbing 1.5 times more carbon than the U.S. emits annually.

Opening the Tongass and all roadless forests to destruction would be a crime against nature. And further opening the Tongass to development would be yet another crime against Native peoples. The Tongass is the ancestral homeland of the Tlingit and Haida Indigenous peoples. A joint statement from the tribes condemns the decision to rescind the rule, saying it was taken “without any prior consultation with our Tribe or other Southeast Alaska tribes. As a sovereign tribal nation, we do not recognize the validity of federal actions impacting our traditional homelands when undertaken without meaningful government-to-government consultation, as required by law and respect for our inherent sovereignty.”

The statement continues, “The Tongass is more than an ecosystem — it is our home. It is the foundation of our identify, our culture, and our way of life.”

The USDA proposal claims to “reduce regulatory burden and return decisionmaking for the management of inventoried roadless area to the land management planning process at the individual national forest level…. Recission of the national-level prohibitions provides responsible officials with flexibility to better guide management of the National Forest System lands and respond to changing local resource conditions.”

Describing these relatively untouched forests — rich with species, habitat, and natural wonders — as “resources” is a dead giveaway to the proposal’s actual intent.

Despite claims to “return decisionmaking” to local forest officials, the proposal quickly pivots to whom these officials and their management of these “resources” would be directed by — namely, the federal government under Trump and his executive orders to cut so-called “burdensome” regulations (environmental and safety protections) and expand timber extraction, leading to the “unleashing” of energy production and maximization of resource extraction in Alaska. These measures will allow for plowing roads into and decimating formerly protected public lands to expand logging, mining, oil and gas drilling, and other capitalist development.

The forest service has already been gutted by Trump and restructured to more thoroughly service resource extraction over forest protection.

“Whatever Forest Service staff is left, because they have fired so many people, they are under tremendous pressure to kick out the board feet” of timber, Spivak told Truthout. Further, forest management plans in local areas that the proposal says will now be under the aegis of local officials are already often too weak, and can be changed at a moment’s notice under an administration that Spivak points out is “stripping all of those safety valves away.”

The Center for Biological Diversity currently is in court fighting a separate new rule by the Department of the Interior (DOI) redefining “harm” to endangered species. The new rule defines harm as only directly killing or damaging a species, but allows destruction of the habitat they need for survival.

Spivak continued, “So if you are a spotted owl or marbled murrelet or any wildlife creature that depends on forest canopy and older forests, their new definition under the Endangered Species Act would make bulldozing their habitat legal.” The DOI is doing this despite scientific studies clearly demonstrating that habitat loss is the primary cause of species extinction.

Along with its new proposed rule, the USDA is required to release a draft environmental impact statement (DEIS) to elucidate the potential impacts of the change. An analysis by the Center for Western Priorities, a nonpartisan conservation and advocacy organization, stunningly reveals how the DEIS undermines many of the arguments USDA gives in favor of the proposal and explains the vast environmental damage the proposal would cause.

The DEIS found that repealing the Roadless Rule “would increase soil erosion, landslide risk, and sediment pollution in watersheds that supply drinking water to roughly 24 million Americans.” It also would expose “[o]ld-growth forest that has been off-limits for 25 years to new logging,” and open the door to new oil, gas, and coal leasing on currently protected lands. The DEIS states the new rule would be “‘likely to adversely affect’ 327 threatened and endangered species and 71 designated critical habitats,” the analysis notes.

The DEIS also admits money from timber sales “would [not] be sufficient to cover the costs of constructing and maintaining all new roads related to a project.” National forests already contain 370,000 miles of roads, enough to circle the globe 15 times. And the Forest Service can’t even maintain these existing roads, to the tune of billions of dollars.

The USDA’s rule proposal and Trump’s executive orders on logging expansion have claimed repealing the Roadless Rule and further logging under the guise of “forest management” are required to address “increasing wildfire risk.” Yet they try to obscure the overwhelming evidence that more intense wildfires are being driven primarily by temperature increases and drought brought on by climate change. The administration’s forest plans, along with its moves to expand fossil fuel production while eliminating efforts to combat climate change, will only expand dangerous wildfire.

The DEIS itself further undermines the claim that the move is about combating wildfire risk by admitting more roadbuilding in forests could mean more human-caused wildfire ignitions. It states, “ignition density is approximately four times greater” on national forest lands containing roads than on roadless and wilderness areas.

This has been confirmed by recent scientific studies. The National Interagency Fire Center says that as of 2023, the “10-year average of human-caused fires account for 88 percent of all wildfires nationally.” These fires result from a multitude of human causes such as arson, debris burning, smoking, fireworks, equipment and vehicle use. In fact, new research published in the journal Fire Ecology shows that fires are four times more likely to start near a road than in roadless areas. Environment America has found that “fewer than 1% of wildfires in the lower 48 states — and none of the costliest fires — since 2010 have started in roadless areas.”

Firefighters United for Safety, Ethics, and Ecology (FUSEE), an organization of active, former, or retired wildland firefighters, is also speaking out against the repeal. It said in a statement that more roads and human access will mean more human-caused wildfire starts, and that logging roads in backcountry areas are dangerous for attempting to stop wildfire. FUSEE argues this is best done by aviation-based tactics and other means fully allowed by the existing rule.

Molly Maguire, a representative of FUSEE and current member of an active wildfire module (a firefighting team), stated, “Wildland fires are necessary and incredibly significant ecological processes. Roadless areas lack much infrastructure or human structures, so they offer opportunities to safely, economically, and ecologically manage fire across large areas without threatening human assets.”

Kate Groetzinger of the Center for Western Priorities told Truthout the DEIS findings about wildfire risk made it clear to her that eliminating the Roadless Rule “is really about supporting the timber industry and potentially other types of infrastructure in our forests … it’s not about wildfire risk at all.”

The USDA first announced it was considering eliminating Roadless Rule protections in June 2025. Over 600,000 public comments poured in during the restricted period of 21 days allowed by the USDA. Ninety-nine percent of the comments listed on the official regulations.gov website opposed the repeal, according to an analysis by the Center for Western Priorities. Still the administration is barreling ahead, despite its claim to consider public opinion in the decision.

While Trump’s USDA claims the rule is being pushed through to return authority to local management, the administration clearly has no interest in hearing from the people. In 2001 when the rule was adopted, 600 public hearings were held and 108 days were given for the public to comment. But with this decision, the Trump regime has not held a single public hearing and cut the comment period to 45 days.

Further, the government’s decision has been made without respect for tribal sovereignty, especially regarding the Tongass. The USDA has only agreed to get “input” from tribes, not consult government-to-government as required by law. And the administration hasn’t held a single hearing with affected tribes since the decision was made and instead only set up “subsistence hearings” in Alaska in late September that occurred at the tail end of the comment period. These hearings fall far short of full consultation with Alaskan tribes. The draft environmental impact statement from the USDA itself also admits that consulted tribes overwhelmingly oppose the repeal.

Both Spivak of the Center for Biological Diversity and Tim Preso, managing attorney of the Biodiversity Defense Program at Earthjustice, told Truthout their organizations will launch lawsuits to prevent this repeal from moving forward if the USDA proposal is finalized.

“We’ve been defending the Roadless Rule against misguided attacks on it for 25 years and we’re not about to stop now,” Preso said. “This administration has taken a wrecking ball to environmental protections that have been in place for decades and that really have been the reason why we have the environmental quality that we do have today. And now this administration is tearing them down one by one.”

Groetzinger of the Center for Western Priorities said in a statement, “Despite all these negative implications and immense public opposition, the Trump administration seems to be dead set on moving forward with these rules. Western communities must rise up and oppose this change as loudly and forcefully as possible during this comment period.”

The move to wipe out roadless area protections may be the biggest and latest assault by the regime on public lands, but it’s also part of a larger picture — a relentless, many-sided war on nature conducted for capitalist development. And it’s taking place and substantially pushing forward existential climate and biodiversity crises that are confronting the entire world.

Spivak told Truthout that Trump’s stripping of 3 million acres of land from the Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monuments this summer are among countless projects she’s working on where a lot is being lost.

These areas are sacred ancestral homelands of five sovereign Indigenous nations in the Southwest. Days after ripping away these lands, the Bureau of Land Management removed tribal seals at Bears Ears that signified the joint management and stewarding of the lands between tribal nations and the U.S. government at entry locations. Then it tore down signs at both monuments. Mining companies began filing claims on these formerly protected lands rich in Native heritage, stories, foods, cultural sites, and spiritual connection within days of Trump’s announcement, despite the law requiring a 60-day waiting period. As of September 28, 72 claims have been filed by three mining companies on these sacred lands, according to the National Parks Conservation Association.

Beyond the heartbreaking losses accumulating, there is the continual erosion of what Spivak termed the “rulebook for disclosing harms,” through maneuvers like weakening the National Environmental Policy Act and gutting public comment periods.

“I think they’re doing tremendous harm to life on Earth,” Spivak said. “They have complete and utter disregard for what they’re destroying. Because all they care about is a for-profit company’s bottom line, and where they see quote ‘burdensome regulations’ to everybody else, and especially our public lands that we, the public own, those to us are protective measures.”

author: Chase Woodruff
title: Case at Supreme Court Could Have Profound Consequences for Other Climate Suits
content:
With help from the Trump administration, Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil have asked the court to quash the lawsuit.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Attorneys representing two Colorado local governments are set for a high-stakes legal showdown over climate change Monday at the U.S. Supreme Court, where they’ll ask justices to allow Boulder’s lawsuit seeking monetary damages from two fossil fuel companies to proceed in state court.

With help from the Trump administration, the two companies, Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil, have asked the court to step in and quash the lawsuit, which was filed in 2018 by Boulder County and the city of Boulder. The plaintiffs are seeking monetary damages under state tort law “for the substantial role (the companies) played and continue to play in causing, contributing to and exacerbating climate change.”

Monday’s Supreme Court hearing in the case, known as Suncor v. Boulder, follows another unprecedented summer of record heat, extreme drought conditions and destructive wildfire activity impacting communities across Colorado. Boulder’s suit is one of more than 30 similar cases filed to date by state and local governments nationwide as human-caused climate change, mostly the result of fossil-fuel combustion, pushes average global temperatures to dangerous new highs.

“This case is really about who’s going to bear the costs of all of these accelerating effects that we’re experiencing on the front lines here in Colorado,” Chris Winter, an environmental attorney and executive director of the Getches-Wilkinson Center at the University of Colorado School of Law, said in an interview. “Are those costs just going to fall on the shoulders of all of the taxpayers and citizens and our local governments? Or is the oil industry going to be at least partially responsible for their role in contributing to this crisis?”

Exxon and Suncor, a Canadian oil giant that operates Colorado’s only fossil fuel refinery, argue that federal law preempts Boulder’s efforts to hold the companies accountable in state court. The defendants have tried and failed repeatedly to have the case dismissed or removed to federal court, most recently in May 2025, when the Colorado Supreme Court issued a ruling allowing the case to proceed.

Soon after that ruling, however, the companies asked the U.S. Supreme Court, where conservatives hold a 6-3 majority, to step in. Their petition asks the nation’s highest court to rule that federal statute “precludes state-law claims seeking relief for injuries allegedly caused by the effects of interstate and international greenhouse-gas emissions on the global climate.”

In February, justices agreed to hear the case, which is set to be among the most closely watched proceedings on the court’s docket for the 2026-27 term, and one of its highest-profile climate change decisions ever. A ruling from the court could have profound consequences for the dozens of other lawsuits seeking climate-related damages from fossil fuel companies, as scientists warn that catastrophic impacts from higher temperatures will continue to accelerate.

In an unusual move, President Donald J. Trump’s administration filed an unsolicited brief in support of Suncor and Exxon’s petition shortly after it was filed, urging the court to overturn the Colorado Supreme Court’s decision, which it called “contrary to the Constitution.” Alongside petitioners and respondents, U.S. Solicitor General John Sauer will be given time during Monday’s oral arguments to represent the Trump administration’s position in support of the companies.

“We’ve seen this administration really bend over backwards to serve the interests of the fossil-fuel industry, and this case is just one of many examples,” Winter said. “A lot of us who watch the court and have studied these issues for a long time are quite troubled by some of the legal arguments this administration has used, to try to undercut the ability of the states to protect (their) citizens, and to insulate the oil industry from liability for its actions.”

In another unusual development, Justice Samuel Alito, one of the Supreme Court’s most conservative members, recused himself from further proceedings in the case last week.

Though the court’s announcement did not explain why, environmental advocates had called for Alito’s recusal because he owns stock in at least two oil companies. He previously stepped aside from a separate environmental case involving the oil industry in January of this year.

Critics say Alito’s abrupt recusal, announced just days before oral argument, raises the question of why he nonetheless participated in the court’s deliberations over whether to take up the case in the first place. Known as granting a writ of certiorari, that process requires at least four of the court’s nine justices to agree to accept a petition. The court does not release such votes publicly.

“We don’t know whether Alito’s vote made the difference, and that uncertainty is precisely the problem,” Alexandra Nagy, organizing director of the nonprofit Consumer Watchdog, said in a statement last week. “The Court is preparing to hear a case of enormous national consequence after one of the justices who participated in granting review concluded days before the hearing that he should no longer participate. If Alito was the fourth vote, this case should be dismissed.”

In their petition, Suncor and Exxon raise the specter of “potentially crushing monetary liability” imposed on fossil fuel companies for what they repeatedly refer to as the “alleged harms” of climate change.

“The requested damages in any one case could reach into the billions,” attorneys for the companies wrote. “And if claims such as Boulder’s are allowed to proceed, every political jurisdiction in the Nation could bring a similar suit against any subset of the world’s fossil-fuel producers.”

Attorneys for Boulder’s city and county governments say it’s far too early for the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case — which, despite having been filed eight years ago, has not even proceeded to the trial stage amid the protracted jurisdictional challenges made by the companies. Neither the Constitution nor any legislation passed Congress preempts the state’s authority to try the case under tort law, they argue.

“Unwilling to let either the federal legislative or the state judicial process play out, (Suncor and Exxon) have run to this Court at the case’s outset, claiming that something implicit in the Constitution resolves the debate,” Boulder’s attorneys wrote in a response to the court.

“The conservative justices, and conservative line of thinking, usually interprets the Constitution in a way that protects the authority of the states, unless there’s been a very explicit grant of limited authority to the federal government that’s found in the text of the Constitution,” Winter said. “But this case flies directly in the face of that typical way of looking at the Constitution — because there’s nothing in the text of the Constitution that says states are preempted in this field.”

We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We anticipate a loss of roughly $500,000 in online revenue as a result of this massive traffic plunge in the next year alone.

The only way we can keep publishing is with strong reader support. We are asking you to start a monthly donation to Truthout today — anything you can do, whether $5 or $25, makes a difference.

author: groundxero
title: ‘We can’t report anything against AP govt’: National media silent on Tirumala Tirupati controversy after ED and CBI probes debunk false claims of ‘beef tallow’ use
content:
In a press release on 17 September 2026, eight months after the Supreme Court-appointed CBI Special Investigation Team (SIT) explicitly ruled out the presence of animal fats in the ghee used for manufacturing the Tirumala Tirupati temple’s prasadam, the Enforcement Directorate has arrested a promoter of a private food company allegedly involved in contamination after lab forensic analysis revealed the presence of seven adulterants. Notably, none of them are animal fats, specifically ‘beef tallow’, the allegation of whose presence triggered outrage and investigation in the first place, and cemented a political upset in the state by amplifying communal tensions.




 




by

 Mouli Sharma




 




On 19 September 2024, Andhra Pradesh’s Tirumala Tirupati temple had taken over national and regional news by storm for an unsavoury reason: an allegation of the presence of animal fats in the temple’s 

prasadam

 (consumable offerings to Hindu deities given as blessed alms to devotees), specifically the accusation that ‘beef tallow’ was used in the rendering of adulterated ghee used to make the temple’s laddus. Unverified accounts of ‘lab reports confirming the allegations’, which were amplified by TDP’s CM Chandrababu Naidu himself, eventually led to an FIR about the same being registered on 25 September 2024, followed by a PIL being filed in the Supreme Court by one Dr. Subramanian Swamy.













Over a year later, the allegations were debunked by a Special Investigative Team constituted by the CBI to investigate the case, whose forensic examination categorically ruled out the use of animal fats, though the presence of synthetic adulterants was confirmed.













On 17 September 2026, almost exactly two years later, the enforcement directorate reproduced the same findings. Seven adulterants were listed in an ED press release announcing the arrest of a food promoter allegedly involved in multi-crore transactions behind the procurement of the adulterated ghee—Refined Palm Oil, Palm Kernel Oil, Palmolein, MG-90, Monoglycerides, Myvacet Soft 400 and Acetic Acid Ester—none of which are animal fats of any kind, let alone fats of particularly polarising animals, like cows.




 




On 17 September 2026, almost exactly two years later, the enforcement directorate reproduced the same findings. Seven adulterants were listed in an ED press release announcing the arrest of a food promoter allegedly involved in multi-crore transactions behind the procurement of the adulterated ghee—Refined Palm Oil, Palm Kernel Oil, Palmolein, MG-90, Monoglycerides, Myvacet Soft 400 and Acetic Acid Ester—none of which are animal fats of any kind, let alone fats of particularly polarising animals, like cows.










In the light of both revelations, the dozens of mainstream media outlets across the country who expounded the now debunked claims without any evidence of their legitimacy back when the controversy had first surfaced, fanning communal sentiments within the country’s dominant caste-Hindu population, triggering a rise in hate speech, and cementing the popularity of the then newly elected NDA government in the state, have remained conspicuously silent.







“Unfortunately, we cannot use any news content against the AP government. I cannot say more than that,” he said.













Major newspaper outlets with the largest circulation rates in India; channels with the highest viewership statistics, and websites at the top of Search Engine Optimisation and provenance score rankings—The Times Group, The Express Group, Firstpost, The Hindu, Dainik Bhaskar, NDTV, and many more—all solicit their newsdesk items from this agency. This is possibly why the only visible headlines currently in the public domain that acknowledge this debunking, are the opposition party’s own social media posts, and an article by The News Minute, an independent alternate online news portal focusing on the South.




 




A noteworthy aspect of the entire controversy was that the allegations, from the outset, were being made in retrospect. Though the Telugu Desam Party had already come to power by the time the FIR was registered, with Naidu having replaced YSRCP’s Jagan Mohan Reddy (who was then targeted for his Christian identity) during the Legislative Assembly elections in May 2024, the complainant made it clear that his accusations were about procurements made during the preceding government’s tenure.













The evidence as such was so tenuous that when the matter 

was heard

 in the Supreme Court on 30 September 2024, the 2-judge bench of Justices B.R. Gavai and K.V. Viswanathan noted that the ghee samples being used for initial testing had never been meant for use at Tirumala Tirupati—the investigation at that point was based on rejected samples. The bench thus criticised CM Naidu for making polarising speculations while investigation was still under way.




 




“We are, 

prima facie

, of the view that it was not appropriate on the part of a high constitutional functionary to go in public to make a statement which can affect the sentiment of crores of people and when investigation to find out if adulterated ghee was used to make laddus was underway,” reads the order.




 




“We expect the Gods to be kept away from politics,” Justice Gavai said during the hearing. “It is very clear from the report that this is not ghee that was used. Unless you are sure, how did you go to the public with that?” Justice Vishwanathan asked.




 




As such, it became clear that the conflict, like so many in India, was one of alleged corruption being made into one of communalism; with propaganda and disinformation taking centre stage over facts or genuine anti-corruption sentiment in the bickering battle of parliamentary politicians. The collateral damage, of course, was the nation’s sense of reality, scientific temperament, and conscience.




 




In a party statement titled, ‘ED findings expose Naidu’s false Tirumala propaganda’ published on 19 September 2026, YSRCP addressed the latest findings, stating that they have, “further exposed the false and politically motivated propaganda spread by Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu and the TDP over the sacred Tirumala Laddu.”




 




“Without waiting for a proper investigation or conclusive scientific evidence, Chandrababu Naidu publicly alleged that animal fat was used in the sacred Tirumala Laddu during the previous YSRCP government,” the release goes on to say. “He made this serious allegation while holding the responsible office of Chief Minister. His reckless statements hurt the sentiments of crores of Lord Venkateswara’s devotees. They also damaged the sanctity and worldwide reputation of the TTD. Chandrababu Naidu, his ministers, the TDP and their supportive media repeatedly promoted the animal-fat allegation and attempted to use the faith of devotees for political mileage.”




 




Party spokesperson, Karthik Yellagrappada, a self described ‘techie’ based in Amsterdam, was unavailable to comment on whether the sanctity and reputation of a religious institution in a secular nation took precedence over gross allegations of money laundering and chemical adulteration, but the aforementioned party press release says the following on the subject: “Adulteration is a serious offence, and everyone responsible must be punished. However, adulteration with vegetable oils cannot be dishonestly presented as proof that beef tallow or animal fat was used.”




 




Another concern raised by YSRCP, also seconded by the aforementioned Supreme Court bench, is regarding the veracity of the investigative process itself, which they allege leaves open the possibility of foul play. “Reports have indicated that rejected ghee stocks were allegedly repackaged and supplied again in August 2024, after the TDP-led coalition government came to power,” they said. “This raises serious questions about the quality-control and monitoring failures under the present government. Instead of explaining what happened under its own watch, the TDP tried to blame the previous YSRCP government and mislead devotees.”




 




This suggests the possibility that TDP itself had been reusing expired stock/stock that had failed quality control, and may have intentionally stirred up the controversy to have a dual effect: ensure plausible deniability in the event of this negligence becoming exposed and simultaneously malign the opposition. The Telugu Desam Party was contacted for comment on these allegations by this reporter but received no response.




 




The YSRCP ultimately demanded that CM Chandrababu Naidu immediately withdraw his false animal-fat allegation and tender an ‘unconditional public apology to Lord Venkateswara, the TTD and crores of devotees’. “Sacred faith must never be sacrificed for political mileage,” they said.




 







 




Mouli Sharma

 is a journalist based in New Delhi. She currently writes for GroundXero, and her work has appeared in various publications.

author: Sophia Sheera
title: Burnham Scraps Starmer-Era Plans to Roll Back Jury Trials
content:
Andy Burnham’s government has scrapped plans to curb jury trials, after months of outcry from lawyers, MPs and the public. 




New justice secretary Alex Norris said on Sunday that his government inherited a court system “on the brink of collapse” – but that the answer to driving down backlogs was not to roll back jury trials. 




He added that scrapping the plans, which were introduced by former justice secretary David Lammy under Keir Starmer, would enable the Ministry of Justice to find better ways of addressing the courts backlog. 




“

I have heard the strength of feeling on the proposals for increasing the number of judge-alone trials in the Crown Court and have made the decision to change course,” he said. 




The government has instead promised to invest millions in new technology to modernise the sluggish courts system and give greater resources to judges.




Campaign group Defend Our Juries said the move was “a step in the right direction”. The group has argued Lammy’s plans were a deliberate attempt to stop protesters being acquitted by juries who believe they acted on their conscience when breaking certain laws.  




But the group criticised the government for

 announcing that courts

 will “have the final say over where cases should be heard” in order to prevent “criminals accused of relatively minor crimes trying to game the system by electing a jury trial in an attempt to avoid prison.” 




“The centuries-old democratic principle of trial by a jury of one’s peers is not an attempt to ‘game the system’”, the 

group said

 on X.




The justice ministry has also said it will give magistrates the power to hand out longer sentences under the new plans. 




Last month, the Crown Court backlog reached a record high, with 81,000 cases awaiting trial and a third of them for longer than a year. 




Lammy’s plans would have meant cases where the sentence is less than three years would not be tried by jury. They also called for lengthy fraud and financial cases to be tried by only a judge, a policy that Norris will keep.




Critics of Lammy’s plans included 

39 of Starmer’s own Labour bankbenchers

 and 

Shami Chakrabarti

, former director of advocacy group Liberty Shami Chakrabarti. 




“The drastic restriction of the right to trial by jury is not a silver bullet,” the rebel MPs wrote in a letter to Starmer last December. “To limit a fundamental right for what will make a marginal difference to the backlog, if any, is madness and will cause more problems than it solves.”

author: CMI Argentina
title: Dos policías bonaerenses a juicio por apremios ilegales contra un joven
content:
La Cámara de Apelación y Garantías en lo Penal de Azul confirmó la elevación a juicio de la causa que tiene como imputados a los policías bonaerenses Brian Nahuel Ríos y Agustín Villarreal, por la violenta y desproporcionada intervención que desencadenó la muerte de Nahuel Tasori, ocurrida en julio de 2023 en la ciudad de Tandil. Los policías llegan imputados por el delito de apremios ilegales, por haber golpeado y rociado con gas pimienta a la víctima cuando ya estaba reducida y esposada. A pesar del evidente estado de excitación por el consumo de estupefacientes, Tasori fue trasladado a la comisaría donde estuvo alojado durante varias horas hasta que lo llevaron al hospital donde finalmente murió. La Comisión Provincial por la Memoria (CPM), en su carácter de Mecanismo Local de Prevención de la Tortura, participa en la causa como particular damnificado institucional (PDI).







El fallo de la Cámara de Apelación y Garantías en lo Penal de Azul –integrada por los magistrados Damián Pedro Cini, Carlos Paulino Pagliere y Gustavo Agustín Echevarría- llega como respuesta al recurso de apelación interpuesto por la defensora particular Noelia Soledad Pereyra, para quien la elevación a juicio dictada el pasado 10 de junio por el juez de garantías de Tandil José Alberto Moragas es una resolución arbitraria, infundada y lesiva de las garantías constitucionales de defensa en juicio.




El hecho que se ventila en esta causa ocurrió durante la madrugada del 28 de julio de 2023, cuando una mujer (cuya identidad no se reveló) llamó al 911 denunciando que un ladrón había saltado un paredón de un domicilio particular en la intersección de las calles Pasaje y Segundo Sombras de Tandil.




El llamado dio origen al arribo de un patrullero de servicio en el que se trasladaban Villarreal y Ríos. Cuando llegaron al lugar el presunto ladrón ya había sido reducido en el piso por los propios vecinos, que se habían alarmado con los gritos y los ruidos esa madrugada. Luego de esposar al joven, mientras intentaban introducirlo en el móvil policial uno de los agentes le dio un fuerte golpe de puño y el otro le roció la cara con gas pimienta, sin ninguna circunstancia de peligro inminente que amerite el uso de la fuerza física o la violencia.




Al momento de la aprehensión, Nahuel estaba en un estado de alteración y excitación por el consumo de estupefacientes. Pese a que sus síntomas eran evidente, los funcionarios policiales no aplicaron los protocolos para la intervención en casos de salud mental y adicciones, que consistían en convocar a personal de la salud para su intervención. Por el contrario, lo trasladaron esposado a la comisaría donde quedó alojado durante varias horas. A medida que pasaba el tiempo, el estado de Nahuel fue empeorando y cuando decidieron llevarlo al hospital ya era demasiado tarde: falleció a poco de ingresar.




Desde el comienzo, la instrucción judicial -a cargo del fiscal José Calonje- se centró en el accionar violento de Villarreal y Ríos en el momento de la aprehensión, pero sin ahondar en la responsabilidad de cuidado que tenían sobre la víctima que estaba bajo su custodia. De hecho, tanto en la elevación a juicio solicitada por el juez Moragas como en el reciente fallo de la Cámara, la muerte de la víctima apenas aparece mencionada, a pesar que ocurrió en el contexto de la aprehensión y debió considerarse que, con la atención profesional y medicación adecuada, podría haberse evitado.




Para la CPM –que participa de la causa como particular damnificado institucional (PDI)- el caso reviste mayor gravedad aún si se considera que el joven aprehendido violentamente fue llevado a una comisaría que ni siquiera tenía calabozos y allí fue mantenido durante horas en lugar de trasladarlo directamente a un centro de salud mental, considerando el notorio estado de excitación psicomotriz en que se encontraba.




Sin atender a esta responsabilidad policial por las personas que están bajo su custodia, la defensa de los policías intentó incluso recurrir la elevación a juicio por la imputación de apremios ilegales. Entre los ejes del planteo para solicitar el sobreseimiento, se destacaban una errónea valoración de la prueba, las presuntas contradicciones que afectarían la credibilidad de la única testigo de la conducta agresiva y la falta de valoración de evidencias que favorecen la posición de los policías imputados, entre otros aspectos.




Sin embargo, por mayoría de votos, los jueces Echevarría y Cini rechazaron el planteo defensista y ratificaron la elevación a juicio tras considerar que el juez de primera instancia había justificado acabadamente su decisión y alcanzado un grado de certeza suficiente para esa etapa del proceso.




Según Echevarría, de las constancias valoradas por el juez de garantías se puede acreditar con el grado de probabilidad requerido la existencia del hecho, la participación penalmente responsable de los imputados y la tipicidad legal establecida del delito de apremios ilegales: “Del testimonio de Sonia Vanesa Rivero se extrae que uno de los funcionarios policiales, quien resultaría ser Villarreal, de los dos que procedieron a la aprehensión de Brandon Nahuel Tasori, en la madrugada del 28 de julio de 2023, cuando éste ya tenía colocadas las esposas, previo ingresarlo al móvil policial, le aplicó un golpe de puño en el estómago”, describe.




“Sin desconocer el estado de excitación y la resistencia que activamente ejerció Brandon Nahuel Tasori en los distintos tramos del procedimiento, aparecen como probables en esta instancia otras alternativas menos gravosas que los funcionarios estatales tenían a su alcance en dicho momento -entre otras la aplicación del protocolo de actuación para salud mental que tienen previstos los agentes estatales para aplicar en casos de similares características-“, amplía el voto del juez Echevarría.




Y concluye: “La hipótesis fiscal aparece como probable; mientras que las objeciones de la defensa -basadas en la crítica al testimonio de uno de los testigos y en la legalidad de la actuación de sus representados- deberán ser tratadas en el debate mediante la profundización de los elementos existentes (nuevos y más exhaustivos interrogatorios a los testigos) e incluso con la incorporación de prueba adicional”.




El caso de Nahuel evidencia las graves irregularidades de la intervención policial en casos de salud mental. En su Informe Anual 2026 publicado recientemente, la CPM advirtió que durante el 2025 murieron 18 personas por intervenciones policiales violentas en aprehensiones de personas con padecimiento mental o bajo los efectos del consumo de drogas.

Dos policías bonaerenses a juicio por apremios ilegales contra un joven

 se publicó primero en 

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))
