author: Ed Wanderley
title: O tempo das bets e a hora da luta: a perda familiar que não está em jogo no STF
content:
Esta reportagem é parte de uma investigação especial da 

Agência Pública

 financiada pelos nossos Aliados, sem nenhum dinheiro de bet. Apoie mais reportagens como essa 

clicando aqui.













O tempo é uma das ferramentas mais poderosas de perspectiva. Em apenas um segundo, as plataformas de apostas online ganharam mais dinheiro do que 33 milhões de brasileiros fizeram em um mês no ano passado. Literalmente. 

Por cada segundo de 2025, as famílias brasileiras perderam para as bets R$ 1.982, mais do que o salário mínimo atual, de R$ 1.621

 – uma realidade, por exemplo, de três a cada cinco trabalhadores no Maranhão. 




Os dados são do Comitê Nacional de Secretários de Fazenda dos Estados e do Distrito Federal (Comsefaz), que, em agosto deste ano, estimou o esvaziamento do orçamento das famílias em R$ 62,5 bilhões em 2025 – um mercado cuja hora de “trabalho” ficou acima dos R$ 7 milhões. Na política, é justamente o tempo que muitas vezes dita urgência, relativização ou esquecimento.




Por quase uma hora, uma mulher se mantinha encolhida em um sofá na sala do apartamento da família em Uberlândia (MG). Era 25 de setembro. Em silêncio absoluto, cortado apenas por um respiro ansiosamente pesado. O som da TV preenchia o ambiente embalando a mulher, seu marido e sua filha mais velha. Evitavam falar, talvez até se mexer. As próprias vidas em suspenso.




O relógio marcava exatamente 19h07 quando um misto de riso, lágrimas e alívio tomou conta de seu semblante. Na tela, o presidente da República 

assinava

 a Medida Provisória (MP) 

1.394/25

, que proibia não apenas a propaganda, mas o funcionamento das plataformas de apostas em todo o território nacional. 




Ao longo dos sete minutos seguintes, viu Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, com quem havia se encontrado dias antes em Brasília, endossar o discurso que ela ajudou a popularizar, ao comparar a jogatina ao crack, e classificar a 

ludopatia

 por jogos online como um risco ainda mais invasivo. 

“O país trouxe o jogo para dentro de casa. O cassino está na sala, o cassino está na cozinha”, disse antes de citá-la “eu conversei com a ‘mãe que perdeu o filho de 26 anos’”.

 E ela sorriu, sem se incomodar com a alcunha.




“Foi uma sensação de dever cumprido”, resumiu a professora Vânia Borges do Amaral, de 54 anos, emocionada, ao ver sentido em compartilhar o luto de seu filho, Rafael Borges do Amaral, que tirou a própria vida após perder todas as economias acumuladas para as bets. É o mais recente marco na linha do tempo interrompida pela última aposta que o rapaz fez, à 1h48 de 23 de março de 2024 – um novo capítulo de sua história, agora provido de sentido.
















Professora Vânia segura a foto de seu filho Rafael




A MP das bets determinou o fim da oferta dos jogos online, tanto em ambientes físicos quanto virtuais, abrangendo concessões federais e estaduais. Loterias tradicionais não foram atingidas pela mudança.

 Na prática, os sites e aplicativos das empresas devem ser retirados do ar nesta terça-feira (6) e as publicidades, mesmo em outdoors e outros meios físicos devem ser removidos. As multas pelo descumprimento da regra podem chegar a R$ 2 bilhões.




Não há previsão de indenização para as empresas detentoras das 85 outorgas para explorar a atividade legalmente desde 2023 no país. Cada outorga custou cerca de R$ 30 milhões, o que significa um investimento de R$ 2,55 bilhões por parte das companhias para ofertar plataformas reguladas no Brasil – valor quase 25 vezes inferior ao montante gasto pelas famílias em bets apenas em 2025. 

Estudo da Universidade de São Paulo (USP) estima que as plataformas retiraram R$ 141 bilhões do Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) nacional, enquanto renderam R$ 9,9 bilhões em tributos em contrapartida.




“Eu não imaginava que chegaria a esse ponto, porque quando eu comecei essa luta, eu fui recebida com muito descaso. Primeiro pela Polícia Civil, depois pelo Ministério Público. Eu dei entrada, mas tudo foi demorando tanto… e eu sempre buscando uma resposta que nunca vinha. Eu vi ser instaurada a CPI das Bets e acabar naquela farra. Me gerou muita frustração, muita tristeza. Eu tive a impressão de estar abandonada”, pontuou Vânia sobre testemunhar a proibição, com a qual vinha sonhando há meses. “Eu me senti ouvida”, resumiu.




A história de Vânia e Rafael foi apresentada originalmente pela 

Agência Pública

, que identificou uma carta que ela enviou ao Senado durante a CPI das Bets, em que narra a tragédia familiar. Os impactos da 

reportagem

 noticiados até fora do Brasil fizeram parte do especial 

Jogo Perigoso: O Brasil das Bets

, publicado entre maio e julho de 2026 e incluíram 

dois projetos de lei

 protocolados na Câmara dos Deputados e o convite da presidência da República para que ela fosse ouvida sobre sua experiência familiar com as apostas online.




A MP 1.394 deve ser apreciada no Congresso Nacional dentro de 120 dias. Enquanto isso, o cronograma previsto na publicação se impõe para as empresas – e para um a cada três brasileiros que faziam apostas regulares nas plataformas.

 Às 23h59 desta segunda-feira (5), se encerra o prazo para que apostadores retirem os saldos mantidos em suas contas em todos os sites de bets, que saem do ar à meia-noite.

 Ainda não há certeza se o fim das apostas online será definitivo ou temporário. O futuro, mais uma vez, o tempo há de dizer.
















Em setembro, Vânia pediu diretamente ao presidente Lula, em Brasília, a proibição total das apostas online no país




Clandestinidade e Justiça: os desafios além da canetada




Mais de mil plataformas ilegais foram detectadas desde o dia 21 de setembro

 pela plataforma 

bet legal

, a partir do momento em que a possibilidade de proibição das bets formais ganhou força na imprensa – mais de 700 desde a assinatura da MP 1.394. Mas o campo da ilegalidade, que até então movimentava metade da fatia financeira desse mercado no Brasil, não é o único grande entrave para uma realidade sem apostas online no país.




No Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) uma grande frente de defesa da atividade de apostas online se formou rapidamente após a proibição das bets pelo governo federal. 

A Associação Nacional de Jogos e Loterias (CNJL) e o Instituto Brasileiro de Jogo Responsável (IBJR), que representam a maioria das empresas que detinham 85 concessões legais para operar no Brasil, entraram com pedido de suspensão da medida ainda no dia 28 de setembro.

 Dois dias depois, a Associação de Emissoras de Rádio e Televisão (Abert) fez o mesmo, alegando entre os argumentos “perdas de receita”. 




As associações receberam um reforço massivo. 

Ao menos 20 clubes de futebol entraram unidos para tentar influenciar a decisão do STF.

 Flamengo e Botafogo pediram para integrar o processo como 

amicus curiae

, uma espécie de consultoria para auxiliar as decisões da Corte com informações e perspectivas a serem consideradas, o que, no caso do Flamengo, já foi aceito. 




São Paulo, Guarani, Ponte Preta, Portuguesa e Vitória, por sua vez, pedem um prazo de transição de pelo menos um ano para que a suspensão tenha validade em território nacional, citando a possibilidade de inviabilidade da continuação do Campeonato Brasileiro – cujo nome oficial após acordo de naming rights atualmente é “Brasileirão Betano”, em menção a uma das maiores plataformas de apostas online até então em atividade, o que foi deixado de fora da peça judicial. 




Por fim, em outro processo, América, Athletic Club, Atletico Goianiense, Botafogo, Ceará, Chapeconse, Criciúma, CRB, Cruzeiro, Fluminense, Goiás, Juventude, Mirassol, Grêmio e Vila Nova pedem para que a suspensão da MP requerida pelas associações seja deferida e também solicitam que sejam ouvidos no processo. Os clubes brasileiros já haviam emitido publicação conjunta antes da publicação da MP decretando o possível “fim do futebol” em caso de proibição das apostas online.




Segundo levantamento da Bites publicado por 

O Globo

, a publicação conjunta dos clubes provocou uma 

rejeição

 de cerca de 90% do público, incluindo de seus torcedores. De acordo com a 

CNN

, os patrocínios dos clubes da Série A variam de R$ 12 milhões a R$ 268,5 milhões. À luz da polêmica, o Senado Federal abriu consulta popular em seu site e até o início desta segunda-feira, 85% dos votantes concordavam com a MP (481 mil votos contra 80,6 mil).
















Ao menos 20 clubes ingressaram com processos no STF pedindo a suspensão da MP que proíbe as bets ou prazo de adequação do setor




A judicialização do caso das bets está sob relatoria do ministro do STF Luiz Fux, que já tratava do Marco Regulatório das Apostas de Quota Fixa.

 Por isso, as ações diretas de inconstitucionalidade movidas pelas partes interessadas na volta das bets coube ao magistrado. Caberá a ele não apenas julgar a MP, mas também se havia urgência suficiente para que uma medida provisória fosse editada, já que há prazos e cenários previstos em lei para o uso desse tipo de recurso. No sábado (3), o magistrado deu um prazo de 72 horas para que o governo federal justifique a necessidade da MP.
















Ficou a cargo do ministro do STF Luiz Fux decidir sobre as ações de inconstitucionalidade propostas pelas empresas de apostas online e times de futebol 




O ministro Luiz Fux já tem um histórico de posicionamentos quanto às questões dos jogos. Foi ele, por exemplo, que, em dezembro de 2025, mandou suspender parte da norma do Ministério da Fazenda que proibia que beneficiários do Bolsa Família apostassem nas plataformas das bets – o que apenas posteriormente foi confirmado para todos os benefícios sociais. Por outro lado, em agosto deste ano, também foi o ministro que votou para manter os demais jogos de azar como contravenção penal, como a legislação prevê com base em texto legal de 1941 – na ocasião, inclusive, correlacionando as perdas nesses jogos a episódios recorrentes de violência doméstica.




Em uma frente contrária à tentativa de intervenção judicial, que só deve entrar na pauta do Congresso Nacional após o período eleitoral, deve entrar em pauta o Projeto de Lei 5.477/26,

 proposta pelo governo federal logo após a publicação da medida provisória. O PL criminaliza as atividades de apostas online prevendo multa e de 2 a 4 anos de reclusão para divulgação, oferta de meios de pagamento, captação de usuários e até o desenvolvimento de aplicativos para as bets, além de 4 a 6 anos de reclusão para quem de fato explore as apostas de quota fixa no país. 




As penas ainda podem ser agravadas em caso de uso por crianças e adolescentes ou quando o usuário conseguir burlar mecanismos de verificação de idade ou localização. O projeto será avaliado na Câmara e tem que passar pelo Senado antes de ser sancionado.
















Rafael faleceu em 2024 aos 26 anos e inspirou projeto de lei na Câmara dos Deputados




“Naquela mesa tá faltando ele”




“Você tá ganhando quanto para fazer tudo isso?”, perguntou uma colega à professora Vânia Borges do Amaral

, na semana da publicação da medida provisória que suspendeu as bets. A pergunta foi recebida como uma pancada. “Eu defendo uma causa”, conseguiu responder, sem se alongar. 




“Uma colega bolsonarista, né?”, diz Vânia em entrevista à 

Pública

. “Acho que ficou ofendida porque Lula subiu nas pesquisas depois disso [anúncio da MP]”, brinca, ainda magoada. Questionada se não se incomodava em estar sendo usada politicamente, já que sua história foi parar até no guia eleitoral do presidente petista, é categórica: “Eu provavelmente faria o mesmo. Mas tenho confiança de que ele vai ser coerente [e continuar lutando pela proibição]”. O petista avançou para o segundo turno das eleições, marcado para 25 de outubro, em busca de um quarto mandato frente à Presidência da República. 




Para lidar com as culpabilizações e ataques nas redes sociais que passou a sofrer desde que sua história ficou conhecida no Brasil e fora dele – e foram muitos –, Vânia teve que reaprender a lógica da audição seletiva, agora do outro lado da equação. Ao longo de três décadas de ensino, a professora enfrentou greves nas redes municipal e estadual de ensino, em Uberlândia, e, longe do papel de protagonismo, convivia com ganhos eventuais e uma tradicional surdez de agentes políticos. Não ser “ouvida” não seria exatamente uma novidade. Colher frutos em escala nacional, isso sim, foge de qualquer histórico.




“A gente nota a diferença, né? Mais confiante, mais positiva…”, comenta a filha, a nutricionista Aline Borges Amaral, 33. “Repercutiu muito a história da minha mãe, então a luta dela não está sendo em vão. Fico muito feliz de ver ela indo à luta, procurando, não abaixando a cabeça, porque a gente sabe que não vai ser fácil essa medida se tornar definitiva”, pontua. A segunda filha, Amanda Borges Amaral, 31, completa: “A Vânia que a gente conhece desde criança é extremamente protetora, não foge de nada e direciona, abre caminhos. E depois de tudo que aconteceu, ela foi perdendo a vontade de viver. E ela foi se recuperando, né?”




As duas irmãs de Rafael fazem aniversário no dia 23 de março, o mesmo dia em que ele faleceu. E esse é um lembrete que não passa batido na longa lista de perdas que a família contabiliza desde 2024. 










 




Eu carrego essa dor, e vou carregar para o resto da minha vida. Aqui, nós fazemos as reuniões aos domingos, sempre fomos uma família muito unida, e sempre que a gente se reúne aqui, talvez eu nem fale isso, mas olho na mesa e ‘falta um, tem uma cadeira vazia’. É dia das mães, outra comemoração… O aniversário das minhas duas filhas é uma data que a gente não comemora mais. Então, é algo difícil de descrever. Por isso, acho que essas pessoas, empresários, influenciadores, elas têm que ser punidas




Vânia Borges do Amaral

 

Mãe do Rafael

 










Rafael, segundo a família, não deixou dívidas para os parentes. O caçula vendeu uma moto de R$ 8 mil, se desfez de todas as economias e, nos seus últimos meses, saiu de casa para fugir das tentativas da mãe de salvá-lo, o que incluíam alertas e cobranças recorrentes, “chatices” daquelas que todo jovem rejeita por “saber mais que os pais”. Vânia insistiu o quanto pôde, conjugando todas as vozes e tempos de quem é mãe.
















Família vem lidando com ataques digitais desde que a história se tornou pública, mas diz que não irá se calar até que setor de apostas online seja proibido




E fez-se verbo




A professora Vânia é formada em direito e advogou por muitos anos, antes de se dedicar a ensinar português. A luta que encampa vai além da proibição do setor. 

“Eu tenho provas concretas do porquê Rafael fez isso, tenho gravação, áudio, testemunha, cópias de email, tenho tudo que comprova que ele cometeu suicídio por causa das bets, eu não vou deixar isso assim.

 Quero que quem provocou essa morte seja responsabilizado”, pontua, devagar, com a calma de quem se acostumou a esperar. 




Ela lembra que muitos enriqueceram com o lucrativo negócio que a fez perder o filho, de políticos a influenciadores. “Isso tudo foi construído à custa do sangue de muito inocente”, conclui, a professora e advogada, que promete brigar para levar o caso à esfera criminal e buscar reparação cível pelos danos causados à sua família, uma realidade que os números provam que passam longe de isolada. 




O Ministério da Saúde reconhece um crescimento dos atendimentos relacionados a jogo patológico da ordem de 140% entre 2018 e 2025

 e estimava que a marca seguisse crescendo mais 104% até 2028, caso a proibição não fosse feita. Segundo o Instituto de Estados para Política de Saúde, os custos anuais associados aos jogos são de R$ 38,8 bilhões, dos quais R$ 30,6 bilhões são apenas para gastos com saúde, incluindo 

suicídios e tratamentos de depressão

.




Até agosto de 2026, 5 milhões de brasileiros estavam impedidos de acessar as plataformas de apostas online, 1,2 milhão por iniciativa própria na plataforma de 

autoexclusão

, 800 mil por renegociarem dívidas no programa Desenrola, que tem uma edição 3.0 para lidar com as consequências das bets a partir da proibição, e outros 3 milhões por receberem benefícios sociais.




No horizonte da família de Vânia, há planos de transformar a luta num livro sobre a morte e vida de Rafael. “Falar sobre um caso assim poderia gerar ataques, chacotas pela situação… a gente sabia disso, porque a pessoa com 

vício

 é vista como uma pessoa fraca e não como uma pessoa doente, né?”, resume a filha Amanda. 




“A gente falou: ‘mãe, o nosso Rafael infelizmente não volta, mas existem outros Rafaéis’. Não dá pra se calar, né? É um dever com a sociedade que a gente abra a boca

 e que mostre o grande problema que está todo mundo vivendo e ao mesmo tempo todo mundo com vergonha, pelo julgamento”, completou.




Falar sobre o caso abriu as comportas para uma avalanche de mensagens à família com relatos diários de dificuldades semelhantes enfrentadas em lares brasileiros. Mães, parceiras, irmãs, que se inspiram na luta da professora de Uberlândia para tentar encontrar desfechos outros. E, sem querer, Vânia virou verbo: não se calar para proteger até quem nem se conhece. Vaniemos.










Precisa de ajuda ou conhece quem precisa?




O 

Centro de Valorização da Vida (CVV)

 oferece apoio emocional e prevenção ao suicídio. O serviço é voluntário e gratuito, disponível 24h pelo número 

188

 e todos os dias também por 

chat

 ou 

email

. O sigilo é garantido.

author: Publicación Abierta
title: El martes movilización a Tribunales y el jueves a la Secretaría de Industria
content:
El martes, las dos CTAs, ex combatientes de Malvinas, movimientos sociales, partidos de izquierda y organismos de Derechos Humanos marcharán al Palacio de Tribunales en rechazo del fallo de la Corte Suprema que permitió la derogación de la Ley de Tierras.




La CGT confirmó una movilización para el próximo jueves 8 a las 15:30 hacia la sede de la secretaría de Industria -antiguo ministerio de la Producción- en la avenida Roca 651, en el centro porteño, “contra la política económica” del gobierno de Javier Milei.




Foto: 

Mat ((i))




Calentando motores




Por Mario Hernandez




La ñata contra el vidrio




El secretario de DD HH del CECIM La Plata, Ernesto Alonso, denunció que la resolución de la Corte deslegitima tanto a los ex combatientes como a todo el pueblo argentino, dejando vía libre a un “plan sistemático de entrega”. Advirtió que el fallo busca dejar a la ciudadanía “con la ñata contra el vidrio” mientras corporaciones transnacionales y magnates tecnológicos se apoderan de los recursos estratégicos.




Foto: Agencia Andar/CPM




También la CTA Autónoma y la CTA de los Trabajadores acusaron a los magistrados de “complicidad cipaya” y de firmar un “cheque en blanco” al gobierno de Javier Milei. Advirtieron que eliminar las restricciones de la Ley 26.737 de 2011 que fijaba un máximo del 15% a la propiedad extranjera, límites por nacionalidad del 30% del cupo, un tope de 1.000 hectáreas en zona núcleo y la prohibición sobre cuerpos de agua, habilita la compra ilimitada de suelos, fuentes de agua dulce y zonas de frontera por parte de fondos especulativos.







En una asamblea en Parque Lezama el viernes pasado, Gabriel Solano, dirigente del Partido Obrero, reclamó “voltear todo el DNU 70/2023” señalando que la norma desregula también prepagas, alquileres y tasas financieras.




En tanto, las fuerzas con presencia en el Congreso tratan de fortalecer su posición de cara a la sesión especial del próximo jueves 15. Con su sentencia, la Corte Suprema podría generar la derogación total del DNU 70/23, lo que significaría un golpe demoledor a la gobernabilidad del presidente Javier Milei.




Foto: Indymedia Trabajadoras/es




CGT: sin paro general y con plan de lucha escalonado




Bajo el lema “Las Malvinas son argentinas, la industria también”, la CGT marchará a la secretaría de Industria el próximo jueves. Será la cuarta acción coordinada con otras organizaciones: 22/7 por los jubilados, 7/8 por San Cayetano y 20/8 por los endeudados.




Estará emparentada con la que una semana después se realizará en el Congreso convocada por los docentes y estudiantes universitarios a la que se sumó el rechazo al fallo de la Corte Suprema.




Al respecto, la CGT acusó a los jueces supremos Horacio Rosatti, Carlos Rosenkrantz y Ricardo Lorenzetti de poner en venta al país y ratificó que se sumará a la movilización del 15 de octubre.




Cristian Jerónimo




Paro pospuesto




Pese a las presiones internas, la conducción pospuso una huelga inmediata. Cristian Jerónimo, uno de los triunviros de la CGT, argumentó que un paro perjudicaría a los representados, mientras que otro, Jorge Sola, secretario general del Seguro, garantizó una huelga general antes de fin de año “si no hay respuestas”.




Sectores de izquierda sindical calificaron la movilización del jueves como una “medida raquítica de la burocracia sindical” y que la cúpula cegetista fue complaciente al convalidar contrarreformas laborales como los bancos de horas y el Fondo de Asistencia Laboral (FAL). Según este sector, la marcha busca alianzas con un empresariado liderado por Techint para pedir proteccionismo para el capital, en lugar de aumentos salariales o la derogación de la reforma laboral.

El martes movilización a Tribunales y el jueves a la Secretaría de Industria

 se publicó primero en

author: Publicación Abierta
title: Se cumplió un nuevo paro docente en las Universidades nacionales y en la PBA
content:
El personal docente y no docente de las universidades públicas realizó el 30 de septiembre, 1° y 2 de octubre un nuevo paro por 72 horas para exigir la aplicación inmediata de la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario y la recomposición salarial del 33,4%. Mientras tanto, el juez Cormick le dio un nuevo plazo de cinco días al Estado nacional para que cumpla con la ley de Financiamiento Universitario, que Milei insiste en ignorar. Paro en PBA por violencia en las escuelas y reclamo salarial.







Por Mario Hernandez




La medida fue votada por la CONADU y la CONADU Histórica, dos de las federaciones docentes más grandes del país, que se sumó a los diversos planes de lucha que organizaron la Federación Argentina del Trabajador de las Universidades Nacionales (FATUM) con paros regionales, la Asociación de Docentes de la Universidad de Buenos Aires (ADUBA), la Asociación del Personal de la Universidad de Buenos Aires (APUBA), el Sindicato de Trabajadores Docentes de la Universidad de Buenos Aires (Feduba) y con la Unión de Trabajadores de la Educación (UTE), con un esquema de paros por 24 horas en cada una de las sedes.




Asimismo, el jueves se realizó un abrazo simbólico en la Facultad de Medicina como una “acción de visibilidad”. También se organizó una radio abierta y actividades participativas para los ciudadanos.




El reclamo por la aplicación de la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario comenzó a finales del año pasado, cuando el Consejo Interuniversitario Nacional (CIN) presentó acciones de amparo debido a que el Poder Ejecutivo no ponía en práctica la norma bajo el argumento sobre falta de fondos, que aún mantiene.




Las medidas de fuerza de la semana pasada son la antesala de lo que será 

la 5ª Marcha Federal Universitaria programada para el próximo jueves 15 de octubre

.







La Justicia intimó al Gobierno

 




El Juzgado Contencioso Administrativo Federal N°11 volvió a intimar al Gobierno de Javier Milei para que cumpla con la Ley de Financiamiento de la Educación Universitaria (LFEU).




En una resolución firmada el miércoles, el juez federal Martín Cormick le dio cinco días de plazo al Estado Nacional para que cumpla con la medida cautelar dictada por él en diciembre pasado, que ordena la actualización de los salarios de docentes y no docentes de las universidades públicas y la recomposición de los programas de becas estudiantiles, “bajo apercibimiento de astreintes”, es decir, de multas.




El pasado 22 de septiembre, Cormick ya había intimado al Gobierno de Milei-también dándole un plazo de cinco días-para que cumpla con la Ley de Financiamiento Universitario. Ante esa primera intimación, el Gobierno presentó un pedido de revocatoria, que fue rechazado el miércoles.




La medida cautelar para que el Gobierno pague lo adeudado fue dictada por Cormick el 23 de diciembre del año pasado. La decisión del juez fue confirmada por la Sala III de la Cámara en lo Contencioso Administrativo Federal y ratificada por la Corte Suprema el 25 de junio pasado.




Foto: Data Trenque




Docentes bonaerenses




El miércoles, luego de un nuevo hecho de violencia en el distrito de Trenque Lauquen, las conducciones del Frente de Unidad Docente se vieron obligadas a convocar al paro para el 1° de octubre. La lista Multicolor ya había convocado a la medida, a partir de asambleas y mandatos de escuela. Es necesario imponer un plan de lucha frente a la miseria salarial y falta de respuesta del gobierno provincial de Kicillof en las paritarias, el endeudamiento y las situaciones de violencia en las escuelas.




Las y los trabajadores de la educación vienen protagonizando importantes muestras de descontento y movilización frente a una situación salarial y educativa que se vuelve cada vez más difícil de sostener.




Los paros y las convocatorias impulsadas por la Multicolor son un canal de expresión de un descontento que también aparece por diferentes vías en los distritos. En La Plata se realizó una importante movilización al Banco Provincia contra el creciente endeudamiento docente y las tasas que golpean nuestros salarios.




Mientras tanto, distintas situaciones de violencia en las escuelas dieron lugar a medidas de fuerza y movilizaciones en Ensenada, San Miguel, Hurlingham, Almirante Brown y Florencio Varela.




Luego de los graves hechos de violencia contra los docentes de la EP Nº 13 de Ensenada, la exigencia de asambleas y de una medida de fuerza se impuso desde abajo. Tras el paro de 36 horas, y en el marco de una movilización de más de 300 maestras y profesores, la Lista Multicolor que es segunda minoría en el distrito y cuenta con la fuerza de los delegados en las escuelas, realizó una asamblea en la que quedó planteado que la respuesta no podía terminar allí.




Por eso, el lunes pasado desde la Multicolor y ante la ausencia de convocatoria por parte de la conducción Celeste se impulsaron asambleas zonales abiertas a la comunidad educativa con más de 400 docentes, con suspensión de clases, para debatir colectivamente las demandas necesarias frente a estas situaciones: presupuesto, creación de cargos, jornadas institucionales y protocolos efectivos de resguardo para docentes y estudiantes. No alcanza con actuar después de cada hecho de violencia. Necesitamos recursos y políticas que permitan intervenir integralmente antes que las situaciones lleguen a esos extremos.




Frente a la masividad de las medidas que se vienen sosteniendo durante todo el año, convocadas con mandatos de escuelas, impulsados por las seccionales de conducción Multicolor y la oposición en casi 100 distritos; la respuesta del gobierno Provincial en lugar de hacerse eco de los reclamos y la insostenible situación de miseria salarial y falta de recursos en las escuelas, responde castigando a la docencia con descuento que promediaron $ 85.000 en los últimos recibos. Según el relevamiento impulsado desde la Multicolor sobre 9.327 casos, los descuentos podrían haber representado 2,5 veces el “aumento” otorgado en agosto.










 


































Ver esta publicación en Instagram






































































 




Una publicación compartida por SUTEBA.Tigre (@sutebadetigre)













Unificar las luchas




Más del 80% de la docencia son mujeres, muchas sostén de hogar, por lo que los descuentos tienen un impacto directo en el marco de magros salarios, a lo que responde el efecto disciplinador que pretende tener esta medida del gobierno provincial. En momentos en los que el gobierno nacional se embandera atacando el derecho a huelga, Kicillof elige seguir ese camino. Por eso necesitamos fortalecer la organización desde abajo y construir medidas cada vez más masivas.




Este escenario se desarrolla mientras el gobernador Axel Kicillof busca proyectarse políticamente a nivel nacional. Su reciente viaje a Nueva York incluyó reuniones con empresarios y representantes de fondos de inversión. Busca mostrarse potable para el establishment.




En la Provincia de Buenos Aires la miseria salarial, la precarización son moneda corriente. Mientras una maestra tiene que endeudarse para llegar a fin de mes y en muchas familias se decide qué gasto básico se puede pagar y cuál debe postergarse, no podemos aceptar que la respuesta sea esperar al 2027.




Para enfrentar las políticas del gobierno nacional de Javier Milei y, al mismo tiempo, reclamar al gobierno provincial de Kicillof respuestas en salarios, presupuesto educativo y condiciones de trabajo, necesitamos fortalecer la organización de las escuelas y la coordinación provincial.




Las y los docentes no pueden esperar un recambio electoral mientras sus salarios pierden poder adquisitivo, aumenta el endeudamiento y las condiciones en las escuelas son cada vez peores. Tienen la posibilidad de llevar esta pelea a cada escuela y barrio, organizando asambleas o comisiones junto con familias, estudiantes y auxiliares que también vienen sufriendo la miseria salarial y van al paro el próximo 7 de octubre que será en los hechos la continuación del paro del 1/10.




La fuerza está en las escuelas. Organicemos esa bronca, transformémosla en mandatos y construyamos desde abajo un nuevo paro provincial.

Resumen Latinoamericano, Página 12, La Izquierda Diario

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Lessons from high school students in rebellion
content:
from 

lundimatin

 #536, 05/10/2026







A surprise lesson

. It was the surprise of the start of the school year, one that no one saw coming, let alone predicted. While everyone seemed resigned to waiting for the next presidential election to hope for change, high school students burst onto the scene and shook all political agendas. Starting in a few high schools in the Paris suburbs, the revolt quickly spread throughout France. Without any leading organisation, without a party or union pulling the strings; just groups of students self-organising, blocking the entrance to their schools, and spreading the word among themselves and on social media; a sign that embers were beginning to rekindle beneath the ashes, just waiting for a spark to ignite the blaze.







This has been a spontaneous, unpredictable, and sudden revolt, like all revolts. As with the emergence of the Yellow Vest movement in the fall of 2018, and so many other social uprisings before it, in the fall of 2026, all political attention seemed destined to focus, inevitably, on the upcoming presidential elections, once again reducing aspirations for change to the bleak choice of the ballot box, to delegating power over one’s own destiny to others.




Defying all predictions, and disregarding the electoral calendar with a carefree attitude, the high school students wanted to say, first and foremost, that they existed, that their present and future lives had value. Even though, as minors, they had no right to vote and no added value for political parties.




They had reasons to revolt. Those put forward, relayed by the student unions, denounced overcrowded classrooms, fragmented and restrictive schedules, unfilled teaching positions, and dilapidated and unsanitary school buildings. They also denounced the humiliation and incongruity of the cell phone ban in schools, given that their teachers, like the parliamentarians who voted for it, were constantly glued to their phones. They were treated like children who needed to be punished and disciplined, even though they were young adults who refused to resign themselves to a bleak and undesirable future.




Clearly, behind the structural reasons for the lack of resources and the state’s disinvestment in national education, lie deeper criticisms. At its core, it is a denunciation of the school system of a so-called Republic which, under the guise of formal equality, merely reproduces and perpetuates class and racial privilege and discrimination.




A lesson in sociology

. What is entirely new in the history of student revolts, from 1968 to the present day, is that the movement of autumn 2026 is not led by students from the city center, by offspring of the bourgeoisie who have (temporarily) deviated from their social class, but by high school students from working-class neighbourhoods. Moreover, those most mobilised in the struggle appear to be students from vocational high schools, already steered toward work and excluded from higher education. Furthermore, images of the blockades show that many of the rebellious high school students have Black or brown skin. These are young French people, of course, representing this new France which, while not recognised and appreciated by white supremacists (except, marginally, for the performances of PSG football players and the national football team), embodies its history and its future.




This is very likely why the State and its government decided, from the very first blockades, not to listen to the voices, the grievances, the demands of the striking high school students, but to repress them immediately and brutally. It’s unspoken, hidden, certainly not openly displayed, but how can one not suspect that behind the (completely unnecessary) decision to immediately resort to force in response to the students’ demands, there lies a deep-seated racism embodied by the Minister-Prefect of Police and so many officers under his command? That, like 

Éric Zemmour

 and many other descendants of Oran settlers, 

Laurent Nuñez

 is consumed by resentment and a visceral hatred towards Arabs and Muslims? That the police, accustomed to hunting down young Arabs and Black people in the housing projects under the pretext of fighting drugs, do not feel justified in beating high school students who fit the same physical profile?




A grammar lesson

. To unleash the full force of the repression, ministers, police officers, and complicit journalists set up the discrediting machine. While acknowledging that high school students might have legitimate reasons to complain about their learning conditions, government officials and complicit media outlets attributed the revolt to “

LFI

 and its far-left proxies.” To the perennial denial of the autonomy of social movements, to the ritualistic conspiratorial insinuation of a deus ex maquina using poor, naive individuals for its perfidious ends, the system’s spokespeople, disguised as independent journalists, added the label “far-left proxies.” A deliberate choice of terminology: until now, this term referred to Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis, and other politico-military groups fighting against Israel and American imperialism, allegedly manipulated by Iranian devils. Just another layer of paint intended to discredit the protesters.




Faced with the inevitable reaction of the protesting high school students—beaten, tear-gassed, tackled to the ground, handcuffed, and taken into custody at police stations—the tired old trope of “rioters” was trotted out once again: masked revolutionary militants supposedly infiltrated the movement. From the very first blockades of the high schools, what we witnessed were not demonstrations by rebellious students, but rather “riots,” “urban violence,” “an outburst of hatred against the police,” who were supposedly there only to protect the population, and in particular “our children,” from the evil rioters. Thus, faced with heavily armed police officers and gendarmes protected from head to toe in body armour, the protesters allegedly used formidable weapons such as “mortars,” without mentioning that these were firework mortars, far less dangerous than any of the projectiles used by the police.




A lesson in semantics

. Drawing a distinction between good, well-behaved high school students, concerned with their studies, and “individuals, groups from outside the schools, seeking only to sow chaos and attack law enforcement,” aims to justify police repression. A fierce and massive repression: in one week there were 5,000 arrests, hundreds of people injured and brutalised, two high school students blinded in one eye and another left without a tooth; a ruthless and disproportionate crackdown that fell upon girls and boys, most of whom were minors. But the perversity of the Ministry of the Interior, echoed by the mainstream media, relentlessly focuses on the daily toll of burning garbage cans and injured police officers (where, how, and by whom is never specified) at the hands of “villainous masked rioters.”




The height of this reversal of responsibility for violence against individuals was reached in Belfort, where the Prefect of Police and the Public Prosecutor opened an investigation against protesters accused of “attempted murder of a person holding public authority.” This individual, who had been punched and kicked, was in fact a high-ranking local police officer, without a uniform, without even an armband, masked, and disguised as a black bloc member to infiltrate the protesters. Before being identified and beaten, he had assaulted a high school student, holding his head underwater in a stream for an extended period. Subsequently, the charge was reduced to “intentional violence,” two minor high school students were imprisoned, the police officer received his eight days of sick leave, and the congratulations of his superiors.




A philosophy lesson

. What do these rebellious high school students want? Their grievances, demands, and objectives are clearly written on the banners and signs displayed in front of their schools. Complaints about their study conditions, criticisms of unfair treatment between city center and suburban high schools, protests against the selection process of 

Parcoursup

 [the French university admissions platform], and the lack of resources and teachers are juxtaposed with slogans like “Free Palestine,” “ACAB,” and “Stop police brutality.” The list of objectives continues with the fight against patriarchy, gender-based violence, colonialism, racism, and all forms of discrimination and injustice; a whole program written by high school students, young people, legal minors, not taken into account by all the authorities supposedly deciding their fate.




Anti-authoritarianism, the driving force of the ’68 generation, is resurfacing. Should we be outraged if head-teachers have been booed, sometimes even mistreated, by students? Must we agree with the self-righteous moralisers that setting fire to the gate of a “public” school is unacceptable and must be severely punished? Or should we try to consider the reasons for these actions? Can we imagine the resentment, the bitterness, the hatred accumulated by a secondary school student who, throughout their schooling, has silently endured bullying, humiliation, and contempt from the adults who are supposed to educate them, not mold them into obedience to the authorities?




The revolt of French high school students this autumn of 2026 cannot be confined to the school environment. It is overflowing everywhere. This new generation of rebels seems to concentrate and amplify the legacy of many struggles, both old and new. From anti-capitalism to anti-racism, from anti-sexism to anti-authoritarianism, it embodies principles of solidarity with all the oppressed worldwide. It emerges as a social movement of free people, without imposed or constructed cages, without leaders, without the need for representatives. It makes struggles, the construction of analyses, discourses, and collective actions the means to envision a desirable future.




This nascent movement seems to bear the traces of movements that preceded it, drawing inspiration from and renewing discourses, methods, and practices. There is a certain blend of the uprisings in working-class neighbourhoods, particularly following the murder of 

Nahel

, and the 

Yellow Vest

 movement. A beautiful mix of colours, too, smiling faces, and groups of solidarity. These “young people” are demonstrating, day after day, without giving up, a courage and determination in the face of police repression that only their conviction in the justice of their struggle can sustain.




Are these “young, determined, and revolutionary” people, as they chant in unison on the barricades, opening new paths to dismantle this world ruled by a consortium of powerful men—economic, political, military, and media? Will they attract students, teachers, cleaning staff, the unemployed, precarious workers, skilled labourers, artisans, and retirees? Could the “young” teach the “old” a lesson?




Alessandro Stella

title: Trump Says Iran War “Should Help” Republicans in Midterms
content:
Recent polling shows more than 6 in 10 Americans want the war to end as soon as possible.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

In remarks to reporters at the White House on Friday, President Donald Trump conceded that it is “possible” that his continued war on Iran will drag Republicans down in the midterm elections.

But Trump also claimed the issue could be viewed positively by voters, thus helping the GOP, despite consistent polling data suggesting otherwise.

“It should help,” Trump said of the war.

The president then blamed supposed media spin for Americans’ negative views of the war, saying it could hurt the GOP in the midterms.

“When you say, ‘Is it OK for Iran to have a nuclear weapon?’ I would say 100 percent of the people say no, including worldwide,” Trump said. “So, when you say it that way, it would help. If you don’t say that, it could hurt.”

Trump has pressed the idea that the war is justified due to the nuclear issue. However, his comments ignore reality — Iran was engaging in indirect but productive negotiations with the U.S. and had already said they didn’t intend to pursue a nuclear weapons program before Trump launched the unprovoked U.S.-Israeli war effort against the country.

As talks for ending the war have stalled in recent weeks, Trump has continued to suggest that he may amp up attacks on Iran, at times using genocidal language. In a recent Time magazine interview, Trump said he might seek to “annihilate” the country in the coming weeks, showing little concern for civilians when pressed by interviewers.

In the same interview, Trump complained that Americans are only upset about him breaking his initial promise that the war would last weeks rather than months because the press keeps highlighting that point. Trump tried to justify breaking that pledge by claiming he had new objectives for the war.

Notably, Trump’s decision to launch an attack against Iran while negotiations were ongoing in late February could push more countries around the globe to pursue nuclear weapons, experts have pointed out.

Polling indicates that most Americans are opposed to the war continuing beyond its seventh month. According to an Economist/YouGov survey from last month, 63 percent of Americans want the war to end as soon as possible, with only 15 percent disagreeing.

Other data suggests that Trump is wrong when he implies the media is to blame for negative attitudes about the war. Indeed, a majority of Americans were opposed to the conflict at its very start, with polling in March showing 56 percent opposed to the war and only 36 percent supporting it.

We now have three full months of data since Google changed its search to feature AI results. The numbers are worse than we anticipated. Overall readership that comes to Truthout through Google is down 54 percent against last year. The number of new readers who discover Truthout via Google searches is down 49 percent, and returning users from Google are down 51 percent.

We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We anticipate a loss of roughly $500,000 in online revenue as a result of this massive traffic plunge in the next year alone.

The only way we can keep publishing is with strong reader support. We are asking you to start a monthly donation to Truthout today — anything you can do, whether $5 or $25, makes a difference.

title: Director Ismail Güneş: Peace should be at the heart of cinema and art - Part Two
content:
Director Ismail Güneş spoke to ANF not only about his own cinema, but also about the current state of political cinema in Turkey and the role of art in the peace process.




Part one of this interview can be read 

here

. 




Ismail Güneş' latest movie, 

One of the Unplastered Houses, 

focuses on the story of a father and mother who, because they are poor, do not want their son to remain in conflict zones. He said: “I made this film not to repeat the artificial rhetoric of heroism produced by those in power or clichéd political slogans, but to tell the raw and naked reality of people waging their own quiet struggle for existence far from front lines and macro politics, in a stagnant town in Anatolia—in other words, the invisible philosophical tragedy of the ‘unplastered houses.’ Because while the themes of homeland and life are abstract concepts on ideological platforms, inside those homes in the grip of poverty they turn into a ruthless ontological contradiction between a child’s life and the family’s bread.




The mother figure before us is the purest manifestation on earth of universal compassion and the instinct to ‘keep alive’; while the desperate father figure, who wants his son to remain in the military and complete his service so that the money he earns there can sustain the family, is a disturbing mirror of how the capitalist system and deprivation subject human dignity and a father’s conscience to a radical test.




The father does not desire his son’s death; on the contrary, while being crushed beneath the vertical pressures of life, he takes refuge in the illusion that his son will be safe within a military order and in the economic relief that this order will provide.”




The director continued: “Therefore, with this film, I saw it as a philosophical moral responsibility to shake the sanitized images of heroism presented by the system or media on glittering screens; to pull the audience away from the comfort of heroic rhetoric and confront them with the silent rupture of a human being trapped between poverty, conscience, and the desire to survive—in other words, with the true sociological cost of war and deprivation.




We can elaborate on this under three headings.




The transformation of money into an ontological threat: On a philosophical level, money is one of the most powerful instruments in the modern world for mechanizing human relationships, commodifying values, and alienating individuals from their own essence. In the film, the bag full of money is not merely a means of economic relief; in the father’s subconscious, it is the ‘price of the soul’ that he has surrendered to the system in exchange for his son’s life, existence, and future. The fact that the bag is accidentally found in a bank, a place regarded as a temple of capitalism, is a manifestation of the enormous suppressed sense of guilt within the father’s soul.




The father needs that money, but deep down he knows of its connection to his son’s blood and the risk of death, so the bag becomes an impossibly heavy burden to carry in his conscience, a philosophical curse.




The moral rupture that begins when the bag is lost: The moment the bag scatters and is lost on a snowy night is the turning point at which the character’s mask falls away and his inner tragedy becomes exposed. When the money disappears, the false balance between the father’s helplessness in the face of poverty and his instinctive love for his son collapses. Karl Marx’s notion of ‘things enslaving human beings’ is reversed here: when the money disappears, the father does not merely suffer a material loss; the refuge he had obtained at the cost of keeping his son in danger has vanished, leaving him completely exposed to his own moral choice and guilt.




The search for money is actually a session of searching for fatherhood dignity, social respect, and, most importantly, inner peace that the father has lost.




The naked truth of the ‘Unplastered House’ and purification (Catharsis): Through the image of the nylon bag, I wanted to show the audience the most dramatic contradiction of Anatolia’s voiceless poverty. Money, which in wealthy homes is merely a number, has the tragic weight of something measured against the length of a child’s life in an ‘unplastered house.’ Storing the money in a tangible nylon bag symbolizes the raw, fragile nature of poverty, stripped of aestheticization. The tension the father experiences around the bag makes the audience ask: What remains of a person’s humanity when, in order to survive and keep their family alive, they turn their child’s risk of death into a financial resource?




This moral anguish throughout the process of finding or completely losing the bag separates the father from the heroic rhetoric of the outside world, confronts him with that pure flicker of compassion deep within his soul, and pushes him toward a moving process of purification.”




It is poor people who pay the higher price




We asked Ismail Güneş about the observation by a Kurdish writer that “This peace will be between those who leave the unplastered houses and those who come from the mud-brick houses.” Güneş emphasized that peace should exist between these two groups and said: “I find this observation extremely justified and philosophically very profound. Because no matter how fiercely the artificial winds of division generated by politics, ideologies, and heroic rhetoric may blow, ultimately, in the macro struggles of these ancient lands, the people who suffer and bury their children are not those sitting in ivory towers, but precisely the poor and abandoned people in those ‘unplastered houses’ and ‘mud-brick houses.’




While conflict is an abstract matter of survival in the language of vertical centers of power, in an unplastered house in a town in Anatolia and a mud-brick house in a village in the East, it becomes the same burning, naked, raw ontological tragedy—the silent and shared cry of losing a child.




Therefore, if a real, lasting, and sincere peace is to come to these lands, that peace will not be made possible by grand, heart-wrenching texts signed at political tables; it will be made possible when the inhabitants of these two sorrowful homes, whose roofs leak and whose walls are unpainted, and who are trapped between dignity and bread, look into each other’s eyes and rediscover their shared pain and that ancient compassion they have forgotten.




When I tell the story of that unplastered house in my cinema, I am actually trying to point precisely toward this bridge: the people at the very bottom, whom mortar, plaster, and luxury cannot reach, always pay the price for violence and destruction. That is why true reckoning and reconciliation will begin on the day we can completely reject the intoxicating language of heroic rhetoric and bring together the embarrassment of the unplastered houses and the sorrow of the mud-brick houses on the same scale of human conscience.”




Our cinema has largely been used as a tool of heroic propaganda




Pointing out that cinema in Turkey has failed to approach either Kurdish characters or the war that has taken place from the right perspective, Güneş said: “Unfortunately, Turkish cinema has not fully succeeded in looking at either its Kurdish characters or this devastating war from a genuinely philosophical, ontological, authentic, pure, and truthful perspective. Because our cinema has mostly either turned this profound human tragedy into a sanitized propaganda tool for glorified heroic rhetoric, or condemned it to the sterility of political engagement, ideological ownership, and shallow emotional provocation viewed from the opposing side.




While both poles have tried to fit people, suffering, and the naked sociology of those ‘unplastered or mud-brick houses’ into their own theoretical frameworks, they have turned the Kurdish or Turkish characters in front of the camera into cardboard extras serving pre-written ideological theses or sociological objects of victimhood, rather than seeing them as flesh-and-blood human beings, as subjects left alone with their conscience and helplessness.




This selective blindness—which aestheticizes violence, demonizes the other, or, conversely, turns suffering into commercial capital—has placed the greatest obstacle in the way of our cinema confronting past traumas courageously and impartially and therefore constructing a healing and unifying language of compassion. The correct perspective, however, lies in raising the camera above all political polarization and, freeing itself from the windows blinded by ideologies, reflecting on the screen with limitless honesty that ancient flicker of conscience in the human soul and the universal commonality of the pain of losing a child.”




The director added: “To put it more clearly, to avoid ideological traps I have developed a human-centered and conscience-centered cinematography in which I try to transform my camera from a tool for proving political theses into a philosophical instrument of discovery that searches for the flickers of compassion in the human soul. In my cinematic language, characters are not cardboard extras of macro identities such as ‘right-wing-left-wing’ or ‘Turk-Kurd’; they are flesh-and-blood subjects, brought into close-up shots reminiscent of Emmanuel Levinas’s concept of the ‘Ethics of the Face,’ looking directly into the audience’s eyes, left alone with their weaknesses and moral ruptures.




I never aestheticize violence as a box-office element; on the contrary, by avoiding the trap of action, I focus on the lingering pain that violence leaves in the human soul and in those ‘unplastered houses’ the following day.




Instead of studio comfort, I use the raw reality of Anatolia, endless train tracks, and stagnant town settings. Through this journey cinematography, I distance the characters from neighborhood pressure and confront them with their own inner monsters in the simplicity of nature. Rather than epic heroic music, I use universal melodies such as the duduk and kaval that whisper humanity’s ancient sorrow, trying to tear the audience away from the numbing comfort of slogans and leave them alone with a pure conscience-centered catharsis.”




Cinema should show society that tears are of the same color




Emphasizing that cinema, and art in general, should put peace at the center, Güneş concluded: “In Turkey, cinema and art should stand at the very center of this peace process, beyond all ideological polarization, as the ‘pure defenders of humanity and conscience.’ Because the true moral duty of art is not to turn people against one another or blind them with artificial winds of heroic rhetoric, but to make them friends and kin to one another in their deepest sorrow.




An artist cannot take a comfortable position during this process by taking refuge in politicians’ sanitized peace texts or propaganda apparatuses; on the contrary, they must enter both sides’ ‘unplastered and mud-brick houses’ with the same unsettling honesty and show society that the tears shed in those homes for their children are chemically the same color and burn with the same intensity.




If our cinema can move beyond prohibitions, exclusions, and the sterile attitude of ‘if I don’t do it, you shouldn’t either’; if it can bring human beings to the screen in their simplest form without turning suffering into political capital and by completely purging the language of hatred, then it can open the door to genuine social reconciliation.




Therefore, the only stance art should take is to be a healing and unsettling mirror that whispers conscience against slogans, compassion against violence, and humanity’s ancient, indivisible ontological brotherhood against division.”

title: South Kurdistan after the Coalition: Kurdish national unity is crucial
content:
The mission of the International Coalition against ISIS in Iraq officially ended on 30 September after 12 years. The date marked not only the end of a military mission, but also the conclusion of the US military presence that had continued since the 2003 invasion and of the air defence system from which South Kurdistan (Bashur) had indirectly benefited. The withdrawal, announced by Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Zeydi, was welcomed as a victory in Baghdad and among Iran-aligned Shia groups, while it has been met with concern in Southern Kurdistan and among Sunni communities.




South Kurdistan, which has been targeted by more than a thousand drone and ballistic missile attacks since the US-Israel-Iran war began on 28 February, is entering a new period without air defences. Peshmerga forces have been unified on paper but remain affiliated with the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) on the ground. The Coalition’s financial support for the Peshmerga has also ended. Twenty-three months after the elections, a government has still not been formed in the Kurdistan Region.




The weakness of a common political will has now been compounded by the reality of a Kurdistan Region increasingly exposed to attacks.




23 years from invasion to withdrawal




US forces entered Iraq in 2003 to overthrow Saddam Hussein’s regime. US troop numbers peaked at 170,000, and approximately 4,500 US soldiers were killed. The US withdrew from the country in 2011 but returned in 2014 following the rise of ISIS. The International Coalition against ISIS was established that same year, and its forces were deployed to the country at the formal invitation of the Iraqi government.




In recent years, around 2,500 US troops have been stationed in Iraq, mainly in Erbil (Hewlêr) and near Baghdad Airport. Their number stood at around 2,000 in July before falling to several hundred as the phased withdrawal proceeded. As major bases across Iraq were evacuated, hundreds of troops and air defence systems were concentrated around Erbil. The withdrawal has seen hundreds of troops and military equipment redeployed to Jordan and other countries in the region.




The timetable for the withdrawal was finalised following Prime Minister Zeydi’s first visit to Washington in July, where he met US President Donald Trump.




Security, economic and political gaps in the Kurdistan Region




The most tangible impact of the withdrawal on Southern Kurdistan has emerged in air defence. Iraqi National Security Adviser Qasim al-Araji said the withdrawal also covered defence systems in the Kurdistan Region, explaining that the process was being carried out under an agreement signed between the previous government and the Coalition: “The US side has also made it clear that it is ready to implement the agreement and withdraw within the agreed timeframe. This withdrawal covers all defence forces and systems previously agreed upon.”




As a result, air defence systems deployed particularly in and around Erbil, including Patriot batteries and C-RAM systems, were also removed from the region.




Although Southern Kurdistan was not a party to the war between the US/Israel and Iran that began on 28 February 2026, it became one of the regions most heavily targeted by attacks. According to Community Peacemaker Teams (CPT), 196 drone and missile attacks struck the region between the beginning of the war and 8 March. Forty-three of these targeted bases belonging to Kurdish parties from Eastern Kurdistan (Rojhilat). The targets also included Erbil International Airport and the 70th Forces Command in Sulaymaniyah (Silêmanî).




CPT also recorded 751 attacks during the three months between 28 February and 28 May, in which 22 people were killed and 112 others injured.




At the end of July, the Prime Minister of the Kurdistan Region said the number of attacks had exceeded 900, with 30 people killed and 140 injured. Figures released by the Peshmerga Ministry at the end of September put the number of drone and ballistic missile attacks at more than 1,000.




Most attacks targeting Erbil had been intercepted by US air defence systems deployed to protect American assets, while Sulaymaniyah did not have comparable protection.




The Peshmerga Ministry described the US withdrawal at such a critical time, without another air defence system being put in place, as “concerning”. The ministry recalled that the Kurdistan Region’s airspace formed part of Iraqi airspace and said: “The federal government must assume responsibility for protecting the airspace of the Kurdistan Region when necessary.”




The KDP President, Masoud Barzani, and other officials in the Kurdistan Region recalled the rise of ISIS in 2014 following the US withdrawal in 2011 and warned that a similar security vacuum could emerge.




South Kurdistan is facing a significant gap not only in air defence but also in its budget. The Peshmerga Ministry announced that financial assistance provided to the Peshmerga by the Coalition under a four-year memorandum of understanding that came into effect on 21 September 2022 had ended. The ministry said the final payment was distributed on 24 September and called on the federal government to cover the resulting shortfall in salaries.




According to US budget documents, the US provided $135 million in salary support for Peshmerga forces in 2024 under the Counter-ISIS Train and Equip Fund (CTEF). The figure fell to $60 million in 2025, before the assistance ended entirely in September 2026.




The security and economic gaps accompanying the US withdrawal have coincided with a political deadlock in the Kurdistan Region. Twenty-three months after the elections held on 20 October 2024, a new government has still not been formed.




The KDP and the PUK, the two parties that together hold a parliamentary majority, have been unable to agree on the distribution of government posts, leaving parliament unable to become fully operational. The parties have met dozens of times in an effort to break the deadlock. The talks have failed to produce an agreement, however, and both sides have said they do not know how much longer the impasse will continue.




The resulting vacuum in governance is therefore being felt directly by citizens through serious shortcomings in public services and economic instability.




Those who see the withdrawal as a victory and those who are concerned




The Popular Mobilisation Forces (Hashd al-Shaabi) and Iran-aligned groups are celebrating 30 September, the date of the formal US withdrawal, as a day of victory. Abu Mujtaba al-Yasiri, a commander in Hashd al-Shaabi, said: “On 30 September, we will celebrate the closing of a dark chapter in Iraq’s history and the failure of the occupation’s attempt to impose itself on our country.”




Sunni communities, however, remain concerned, believing that Iraq is not yet fully prepared to assume responsibility for the country’s security. They say a potential security vacuum is something feared by Iraqis across the country.




Kurds also have serious concerns about the Kurdistan Region, which has been left vulnerable to possible attacks by Iran and armed groups. Kurdistan Region officials have pointed to the continuing threat posed by ISIS following the withdrawal of US forces. The removal of air defence systems has also caused concern among a population living under the persistent threat of attack.




The need for a professional and unified security force has become more apparent than ever.




Disarmament deadline postponed




The Zeydi government wants the Coalition’s withdrawal to proceed alongside efforts to bring weapons under state control. The approach has been summarised by the formula: “No foreign troops, weapons in the hands of the state.”




Prime Minister Zeydi, however, extended the deadline for armed groups from 30 September 2026 to 30 June 2027 following meetings with Trump and US officials in New York on 23 September. The plan envisages an initial 90-day phase beginning on 30 September. The government has stressed that the programme is “not optional, but mandatory”, signalling its determination to proceed.




The government’s programme to bring weapons under state control also directly concerns the Peshmerga. Kata'ib Hezbollah in Iraq set out three conditions on 18 August for laying down its arms: the complete withdrawal of US forces from Iraqi territory and airspace, the withdrawal of Turkish forces from Iraq, and the dissolution of the Peshmerga forces. Kata'ib Hezbollah described the Peshmerga as a threat to Iraq’s territorial integrity.




Sixty years of division and the drive for Peshmerga unity




The most structural weakness facing Southern Kurdistan is that its defence forces have yet to become fully independent of party control. The roots of the division between the KDP and the PUK date back to 1964, while the PUK was founded in 1975. The regional administration was established in 1992. Law No. 17, adopted in 1993, prohibited political parties from maintaining armed wings. Despite this, the two parties entered into a civil war in 1994. The agreement reached at the end of the conflict led to a power-sharing arrangement, with the Kurdistan Region effectively divided between the KDP’s “yellow” zone and the PUK’s “green” zone. The two areas remain separated by the Dêgele checkpoint today.




The 2006 administrative unification agreement, the establishment of a unified Peshmerga Ministry in 2009, the incorporation of 42,000 Peshmerga into brigades between 2010 and 2013, and the reform project drawn up with the Coalition in 2018 all failed to eliminate this dual structure.




Masrour Barzani signed Decree No. 703 on 26 February 2026, placing the KDP-affiliated 80th Unit and the PUK-affiliated 70th Unit under the Peshmerga Ministry. The unification was formally announced at a ceremony in Erbil (Hewlêr) on 21 September 2026.




Under the new structure, the former 80th Unit became the 1st Regional Command, comprising approximately 58,000 personnel under the command of Major General Nejat Ali Fatim. Its area of responsibility covers Erbil, Duhok, Mosul and north-western Kirkuk. The former 70th Unit became the 2nd Regional Command, with approximately 56,000 personnel under Major General Omar Salih. Its area of responsibility covers Sulaymaniyah, Halabja (Helebce), Kirkuk, Khanaqin (Xaneqîn) and Tuz Khurmatu (Xurmatû). The forces are being organised into 11 light infantry divisions.




Peshmerga Minister Shoresh Ismail said at the ceremony that the forces were now directly under the authority of the ministry, the government and the presidency. The Peshmerga Ministry said the process, launched in 2022 at the request of the US, could only be completed in September 2026 because of disagreements between the KDP and PUK.




Unity on paper, party divisions on the ground




The unification has largely remained nominal, with party authority continuing beyond the ministry’s control. A substantial part of the security apparatus also remains outside the reform process. There are 152,182 Peshmerga personnel in total, while 87,505 personnel under the Interior Ministry and 42,896 members of the Asayish security forces remain outside the scope of the unification. The approximately 45,000-strong KDP-affiliated Zeravani force and the 16,000-strong PUK-affiliated force also remain under the Interior Ministry.




The KDP’s Parastin intelligence organisation and the PUK’s Zanyari intelligence organisation also continue to operate along party lines. US oversight reports have likewise documented continuing party influence within units formally under the Peshmerga Ministry.




Shengal on the negotiating table




The Coalition’s withdrawal has also brought other unresolved issues in and around Southern Kurdistan back onto the agenda. Shengal stands out as one of the most critical issues concerning the gains of the Yazidi Kurds, while the future of the Shengal Resistance Units (YBŞ) and Yazidi security forces remains uncertain.




As discussions continue over the integration of Yazidi security and defence forces into the Iraqi army, a military delegation headed by Iraqi Chief of Staff Lieutenant General Abdul Amir Yarallah visited the region on 22 September. Neither side, however, issued an official statement on the outcome of the visit.




Shengal is also part of negotiations between the Turkish state and Baghdad. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Zeydi met in New York on 23 September on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. Their joint statement said Iraqi state authority would be fully established in Shengal and that the presence of “banned foreign armed elements” would be brought to an end.




Turkish military bases remain in place




According to the same statement, Turkish forces will gradually hand over the Bashiqa-Zilkan Base to the Iraqi Federal Government, in line with an agreed mechanism and timetable and depending on Iraq’s progress in the security sphere. No date has been announced for the handover.




The transfer of Bashiqa does not mean the end of the Turkish state’s military presence in Iraq and Southern Kurdistan. Around 600 Turkish troops are stationed at the Bashiqa Military Base, which was established in December 2015. The Turkish state has a total of five main bases, more than 2,000 troops and nearly 100 deployment points in Iraq. According to some figures, around 5,000 Turkish troops have occupied a 20-kilometre-wide strip along the border since 1997.




Zeydi told the New York Times on 22 September that talks with Ankara were continuing over the withdrawal of Turkish forces from Iraqi territory. A two-day visit by National Intelligence Organisation (MİT) Director İbrahim Kalın to Baghdad, Kirkuk, Erbil and Sulaymaniyah also prompted discussions about the security architecture of the Development Road Project.




The way forward: Democratic unity and collective defence




For years, the administration of Southern Kurdistan entrusted its security to external powers rather than building a defence system based on its own strength. The Peshmerga’s salaries, training and weapons, as well as the protection of the Kurdistan Region’s airspace, all became dependent on outside powers. Southern Kurdistan’s airspace being left unprotected today is therefore not simply the result of the Coalition’s departure, but of this dependency. Security that depends on an external power ends when that power withdraws.




The same dependency is now being transferred to Baghdad. Expecting the federal government to protect the region’s airspace amounts to replacing one external guarantee with another. Given Baghdad’s moves towards centralisation, this carries new risks for the status of Southern Kurdistan.




Fragmentation is undoubtedly another factor behind the current situation. The failure to achieve national unity and the persistence of a dual administration remain fundamental obstacles to Southern Kurdistan organising its own strength. Parties pursuing separate external alliances have been unable to establish a common defence structure.




Kurdish People’s Leader Abdullah Öcalan’s call on the political forces of Southern Kurdistan to establish a “Democratic Unity Government” therefore goes beyond a formula for forming a cabinet. The call seeks to build a common political will and a collective defence based on the region’s own strength.




The unification of the Peshmerga forces under a single structure on 21 September represents a critical step in this direction. A unification that remains only on paper, however, will not be enough to protect Southern Kurdistan. Neither Washington nor Baghdad can provide the guarantee Southern Kurdistan needs. That guarantee lies in Kurdish unity, self-defence rooted in the people and national unity. The Coalition’s departure may provide an opportunity to recognise this reality.
