title: DFG publishes September report on rights violations against journalists
content:
The Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG) released its “September Report on Rights Violations Against Journalists.” The report stated that, in September, access restrictions were at the forefront in terms of press and freedom of expression.




The report emphasized that access to social media accounts had been blocked and stated: “According to the September data, access to 3,492 digital media content was blocked on the internet and digital media sphere. In addition, access to 15 news reports was blocked, while 4 websites were shut down. In September, the accounts or websites of media outlets such as JINNEWS, Mezopotamya Agency, Evrensel, Kısa Dalga and T24 faced access restrictions and platform interventions. In addition, the personal X accounts of numerous journalists were made invisible in Turkey on grounds such as ‘the protection of national security and public order.’”




The DFG report also included the following points.




“In September, 15 journalists were detained, and 8 journalists were arrested. The homes of 4 journalists were raided, 3 journalists were threatened, journalists were prevented from covering the news in 5 incidents, and 2 journalists were subjected to ill-treatment. During the same period, investigations were launched against 2 journalists under freedom of thought and expression, while cases were filed against 10 journalists. There are 80 journalists involved in 25 ongoing cases. As of 4 October 2026, the number of jailed journalists is 29.




A significant portion of the interventions against journalists in September took place directly over the news reports they produced or their posts on digital media. Journalist Oya Lale Arslan was detained and arrested on the grounds of her digital media posts and YouTube broadcasts. Journalist Selahattin Günday was arrested over footage he reported on as part of the Kaşif Kozinoğlu investigation, and a second arrest warrant was subsequently issued against him. Journalist Tuğba Tekerek was arrested over a report she produced for Kaos GL, while Hüseyin Aykan, Editor-in-Chief of Bolu Gündem, was also arrested over a report he published.




In September, the interventions journalists encountered while covering the news also reached notable levels. In 5 incidents in September, journalists were prevented from covering the news, while 3 journalists were threatened and 2 journalists were subjected to ill-treatment.




One of the forms of attack faced by journalists was judicial pressure. Investigations were launched against 2 journalists in September, while investigations involving 10 journalists were turned into court cases. While the trials of 80 journalists in 25 cases are ongoing, ETHA reporter Züleyha Müldür was sentenced to 6 years and 3 months in prison.”




According to the report, 2 journalists were attacked, 1 journalist was targeted, the homes of 4 journalists were raided, 15 journalists were detained, 8 journalists were arrested, 2 journalists were subjected to ill-treatment, 3 journalists were threatened, 5 journalists were prevented from covering the news, and 1 journalist experienced rights violation in prison.




The report stated that investigations were launched against 2 journalists and cases were filed against 10 journalists; 2 journalists were sentenced to a total of 6 years, 5 months and 24 days; there were 25 ongoing journalist cases, 80 journalists were on trial, and the number of jailed journalists was 30 as of October 3.




The report stated that 10 journalists had lost their jobs and that RTÜK had imposed penalties on 14 broadcasts. It also emphasized that 4 websites had been shut down, access to 15 news reports had been blocked, and access to 3,492 social media posts had been restricted.

title: Geothermal plants and rising costs hit fig producers
content:
Fig producers in Yaykın neighbourhood in the Karacasu district of Aydın are struggling with high input costs and falling crop prices. Gülhanım Tarhan, one of the producers who spoke to ANKA News Agency, said they sorted their figs according to quality, yet the average selling price still failed to reach even 100 Turkish Lira (TL, around 1.81 euros) per kilogram. Tarhan said they were making a loss this season on figs they had sold for between 225 and 250 lira per kilogram last year, adding that their income no longer covered production costs.




Average selling price falls to 67–70 TL




Another fig producer, Yeliz Tüzyılmaz, provided details of this year’s market prices. First-grade figs are sold for around 120 TL per kilogram, second-grade figs for 60–70 TL, and third-grade figs, known among producers as “baby” figs, for around 50 TL.




Tüzyılmaz said that once all grades were taken into account, the average income per kilogram had fallen to between 67 and 70 TL. Last year, she said, first-grade figs sold for 210 TL per kilogram and second-grade figs for between 120 and 130 TL.




Twenty kilos of figs do not cover a day’s wage




Tüzyılmaz said producers were being squeezed by rising fertiliser, diesel and labor costs, while Tariş had still not announced a base price despite the season nearing its end. She said this had deepened uncertainty in the market.




Tüzyılmaz described fig production as an extremely demanding process, involving labor-intensive stages such as shaking the trees, harvesting the fruit, drying it in greenhouses, grading it and selecting the figs individually. She added that producers had to sell at least 20 kilograms of figs simply to cover the daily wage of one agricultural worker.




Producers face market pressures and geothermal plants




Aydın has been a centre of commercial fig production for thousands of years. Even the fig’s scientific name, Ficus carica, derives from Caria (Karya), the ancient name of the region.




Another problem affecting fig production in Aydın is geothermal power plants. Producers and local campaigners have linked geothermal operations to declining yields, while environmental and public health concerns associated with the plants have also intensified across the province.




An environmental impact assessment approving three new geothermal wells on land used for vegetable cultivation has been issued in the Germencik district of Aydın. Leaks and pipeline ruptures at geothermal facilities have brought agricultural production close to a standstill, while it has been reported that the cancer rate in the district has reached four times the national average.




Source: Yeni Yaşam

title: Director Ismail Güneş: Peace should be at the heart of cinema and art - Part One
content:
As the Peace and Democratic Society Process enters its second year, debates surrounding the process in Turkey continue across different social and cultural spheres. Artists share their views and criticisms of the process with the public through their statements and works.




Director Ismail Güneş, who brought the torture experienced in Turkey following the 12 September 1980 military coup to the screen with his movie 

Where the Rose Ends,

 approaches the Kurdish issue from a different perspective in his latest movie, 

One of the Unplastered Houses

. Director Güneş spoke to ANF not only about his own cinema, but also about the current state of political cinema in Turkey and the role of art in the peace process.




Discussing the socialization of violence in his movies, Güneş said that violence emerges at the point where an individual loses the ability to establish a civilized and philosophical bond with “the other,” and continued: “Because violence is a primitive form of ‘imposing truth’ that begins where an individual loses the ability to establish a civilized and philosophical bond with the other, emerging at the moment when words run out. As I have tried to show in films such as ‘Where the Rose Ends’ and ‘Where the Fire Fell,’ violence hiding behind sacred armor such as tradition, custom, or ideology is in fact a tragic manifestation of our collective social memory’s inability to confront past traumas and the vertical forms of oppression imposed by the system, and of its loss of the feeling of compassion.




Within this culture of power that flows from the top down and is sustained by impunity, people attempt to prove the agency they have lost and their shaken sense of existence only by establishing authority over an ‘other’ weaker than themselves—that is, by aestheticizing and legitimizing violence.




Therefore, the reflection of violence across every sphere is connected to society being in a state of moral and philosophical decay. The only way to break this structural vicious cycle is a cultural and artistic revolution that will confront human beings with their own brutality, reminding them not of the monster in the mirror but of that noble conscience and ontological compassion they have forgotten deep within their souls.”




Violence becomes institutionalized because of lack of education 




Güneş also addressed his decision to portray the socialization of violence in his films through poor people, explaining this choice in terms of the impact of poverty on an individual’s dignity, existential resilience, and moral values. He continued: “The reason I portray the socialization of violent tendencies, particularly through poor and conservative sections of the population is that I see poverty not merely as an economic deprivation but as the most radical ontological sphere of existence in which a person’s dignity, existential resilience, and moral values are tested. Because the poor person living under the vertical pressure of capitalist mechanisms and macro systems conducts their struggle to survive and realize themselves face-to-face with the most naked and raw reality of life, far removed from the intellectual masks of the bourgeoisie.




At this social level, violence becomes institutionalized beyond the madness brought about by economic desperation; it becomes institutionalized when an individual trapped within the narrow boundaries of lack of education, helpless anger toward the system, and traditional codes resorts to bodily domination—the last primitive language remaining to them—in order to protect their battered honor and sphere of power.




Therefore, when I tell the story of poor people, I position them not as an aestheticized form of misery or as a focus of crime, but as a mirror in which the structural injustice produced by the system turns into a spiral of violence. My aim is not to blame poverty; on the contrary, it is to seek the philosophical possibility of remaining human—to explore how that ancient conscience and compassion within a person can endure despite all the brutality and feudal oppression—and to remind society, through this unsettling reality, of the profound responsibility it has forgotten.”




Cinemas showing my movie were threatened




Director Güneş addressed torture and its psychological effects on human life in 

Where the Rose Ends

. He described the production of the film and the reactions it received as follows: “When making 

Where the Rose Ends

, I approached torture not merely as a depiction of physical pain, but as an absolute attempt to destroy a person’s sacred existence, psychological integrity, and ontological bond with ‘the other.’ The reason I designed the train on which the young man travels as a panorama of Turkey was that the carriages were actually a metaphorical projection of our collective complicity: a society afraid to confront its past traumas, closing its eyes to the suffering of those who were tortured and silently watching the tragedy unfold.




The reactions I encountered after completing the film were themselves a bureaucratic manifestation of this philosophical and social blindness. At first, the left-wing circles viewed with distance and suspicion the fact that a nationalist—literally, an idealistic—director had made a film about torture, approaching it with a sense of ideological ownership, while the state apparatus and established censorship board placed every possible obstacle in the way of preventing the film from being released and making it impossible to find theaters. I even found myself confronting members of the censorship board in uniform, their instinct to ban the film by threatening theaters, alongside the fears of cinema professionals.




In fact, this wave of exclusion and prohibition proved a painful truth that coincided with the film’s train metaphor: rather than confront themselves in the mirror with the naked truth of violence carried out by the state or through ideological blindness, society and the system chose to break the mirror. Because, like everyone traveling on that train, ignoring the pain was the most comfortable way to avoid the moral responsibility that comes with confronting it.”




The relationship between violence and poverty is not simply a cycle of material deprivation




In his film 

Where the Fire Fell

, Güneş explores the conflict between a poor Turkish villager’s inner world and the death sentence imposed on his daughter by the family council. He said he does not define the murders depicted in the movie as “honor killings,” arguing that the term softens the murder in the public perception.




Güneş said the following about the movie: “First of all, I do not describe these murders through the word ‘custom.’ Because this word also contains positive meanings that are accepted by broad sections of society. Contrary to what is intended, when an act of murder is called a ‘custom murder,’ the act becomes softened in the eyes of the public. I want to emphasize that.




In 

Where the Fire Fell

, while telling the story of a father taking his own daughter to her death in the name of ‘honor,’ I positioned poverty not as a direct, mechanical cause of violence, but as a structural and philosophical state of entrapment that paralyzes a person’s agency, conscience, and moral resilience.




The relationship between violence and poverty is not simply a cycle of material deprivation; it is established primarily when a poor person, feeling helpless in the face of the system’s vertical pressure, lack of education, and lack of social security, surrenders to collective reflexes such as ‘custom, tradition, and neighborhood pressure,’ which constitute the only refuge to which they feel they belong.”




The director added: The father in the film is not a murderous character who wants to kill his daughter; rather, he is a tragic victim who, amid the social vulnerability brought about by poverty, fears being subjected to the moral exclusion of those around him and shoulders the savage law of neighborhood pressure as a ‘duty’ in order not to lose his existential footing.




Therefore, poverty does not by itself create the tendency toward violence within a person; however, when it blocks an individual’s civilized avenues for seeking justice, it prepares a conservative ground on which violence can be justified by condemning that person to the primitive sense of justice contained in traditional codes. What my cinema tries to do is to reveal, despite this grip of poverty and custom, that ancient flicker of compassion in the father’s heart, and to seek the philosophical possibility of how the human conscience can resist this painful vicious cycle.




In our story, as long as the father (Osman) remains in his impoverished environment and alongside his family, he has no individual agency; he is playing the role of the “patriarchal figure who must cleanse his honor” imposed upon him by the social structure and “neighborhood pressure.” Violence and the order to kill are the invisible consensus of that environment.




However, from the very first moment the father sets out with his daughter (Ayşe), this static social armor begins to loosen. As the geography expands and the vertical boundaries of the places they inhabit—sometimes a village, sometimes a town, sometimes a city—are left behind, the voice of social pressure grows faint. The dynamism of the setting strips the father of his collective identity and isolates him; this isolation forces a person, in philosophical terms, to become a subject and confront the moral responsibility for their own actions.”




The director continued: “On a philosophical level, violence becomes easier when you turn the person in front of you into an object, an abstract “other,” and create distance between yourself and their suffering. In the silent room at home or in the hospital corridors, Ayşe is nothing more in the father’s eyes than “an object that has brought shame upon the family’s honor.” But the days spent together in the vehicle, on long, winding roads, force the father into uninterrupted dialogue, physical proximity, and eye contact with his daughter.




Witnessing his daughter’s childlike innocence, the physical pain caused by her illness, and her absolute trust in him along the way, the father loses the “abstract culprit” standing before him and discovers there a piece of his own flesh and blood—in other words, a naked human being.




This corresponds directly to philosopher Emmanuel Levinas’s concept of the “Ethics of the Face”; his daughter’s vulnerable face and gaze silently whisper to the father the command: “Do not kill me; you are responsible for me.” As the journey lengthens, the cold ideological anger commanded by custom melts away and gives way to humanity’s most ancient and purest emotion: compassion.




The most striking philosophical irony of this journey is that, although it was initially conceived as a “journey of death and execution,” the dynamics of the road and of life itself transform it into a “struggle to keep alive and protect.” The father is forced, instinctively, to protect his daughter and shield her from the dangers of the outside world, the difficulties of the road, and strangers who might harm her. Defending fiercely against external threats a person whose life he had planned to end with his own hands brings the division and moral rupture within the father’s inner world to their highest point.”




According to Gunes, “this paradox makes visible the battle between the “monster” within the father and his “father’s conscience.” Ultimately, this journey, serving the exact opposite of its original purpose, becomes a profound moral victory in which the father chooses not obedience to what he has been taught, but the expulsion of his violent impulse, a confrontation with guilt, and ultimately the will to remain human.




I want to show the audience that violence is not a mechanical monstrosity; it emerges when a person breaks the bond they have established with their conscience, and that rebuilding this bond requires a relentless inner journey in which one becomes immersed in the suffering of the “other.”




the movie was not released because it was not  ‘commercial enough’




With his latest movie, 

One of the Unplastered Houses

, Ismail Güneş approaches the Kurdish question from a different perspective. He spoke about why the movie was not released and about the movie itself: “In 

One of the Unplastered Houses

, I told about the burning tragedy that has marked Turkey’s last half-century not through the heat of armed conflict on the front, but by focusing on that conflict’s impact on a poor town in Anatolia, on the soul of a father caught between poverty and his conscience, and on the sociological reality of those ‘unplastered houses’ left behind by sons who have fallen in battle.




The sole reason the film was not released is that the popular cinema industry and theater operators did not find this naked truth ‘commercial enough,’ and that the capitalist machinery rejected this profound social pain. In a country of 90 million people that has been living with the sociology of ‘terror’ for more than 40 years, global and local cinema monopolies that fill screens with mafia relationships, ephemeral romances, and consumer objects that numb the conscience did not want to make room in their theaters for a morally significant work that would enable people to confront their own suffering in the mirror.




In fact, this state of being left without theaters and being obstructed is, in philosophical terms, a tragic confession of modern society: while the system pretends to glorify the enormous honor and the price paid in shrouds that it places on the backs of unplastered houses, when it comes time to confront the real human drama inside those houses and the unsettling questions posed by poverty and conscience, it hides its head behind commercial comfort and chooses not to look into that mirror.




Therefore, the fact that my film was left without theaters is not an artistic failure; it is a testament to the profound moral and philosophical blindness developed by the cinema industry and, indirectly, society toward its own deep pain.”

title: KCK commemorates Mam Jalal Talabani
content:
The Kurdistan Communities Union (KCK) commemorated Jalal Talabani, founder of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the first Kurdish president of Iraq, on the ninth anniversary of his death. In its statement, the KCK particularly highlighted Talabani’s role in the Kurdish freedom struggle, his efforts toward national unity, and his commitment to a political solution to the Kurdish question.




The KCK statement on Saturday reads as follows:




“Today marks the ninth anniversary of the death of President Mam (Uncle) Jalal Talabani, founder of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan and the first Kurdish president of the Federal Republic of Iraq. As an intellectual, revolutionary, Peshmerga, commander and accomplished Kurdish politician, President Mam Jalal Talabani shaped more than 50 years of the history of the freedom struggle of Kurdistan and the Kurdish people. Throughout numerous phases of the national and political struggle, he achieved significant gains for the Kurdish people.




Mam Jalal’s work and struggle for the freedom of Kurdistan and the Kurdish people were not limited to Southern Kurdistan. Whenever necessary, he supported and participated in the armed struggle in other parts of Kurdistan. Whenever required, he assumed a leading role in politics and diplomacy in pursuit of a solution and peace.




President Mam Jalal Talabani played an important role in the struggle and efforts for the national unity of the Kurdish people. In this regard, the close friendship and ties between Mamoste Ibrahim Ahmed, Leader Abdullah Öcalan, and President Mam Jalal developed into a significant force in efforts to achieve Kurdish national unity. The establishment of the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK) was one of the outcomes of this friendship and solidarity.




President Mam Jalal also played a significant role in efforts to resolve the Kurdish question in other parts of Kurdistan. In particular, his mediation between Leader Öcalan and then-Turkish President Turgut Özal initiated a process of dialogue with the Turkish state.




Even after Leader Öcalan was abducted and handed over to the Turkish state as a result of an international conspiracy, President Mam Jalal continued these efforts. Before falling ill in 2012, he was preparing, together and in consultation with prominent figures from Southern Kurdistan and internationally renowned personalities, a congress intended to launch an initiative for the freedom of Leader Öcalan under the name “Mandela Project.”




Today, 34 years later, we once again find ourselves in a period of dialogue between the Turkish state and Leader Öcalan and are engaged in the process for peace and a democratic society. At this particular moment, President Mam Jalal’s skills and experience are needed more than ever for the success of this process.




Therefore, to struggle for the democratic unity of the people of Kurdistan, for the freedom of Leader Öcalan, and for a democratic solution to the Kurdish question in Northern Kurdistan also means preserving the legacy of struggle left by President Mam Jalal and working to realize the hopes and goals for which he himself fought.




On the ninth anniversary of his death, we respectfully honor the memory of President Mam Jalal. We renew our promise and pledge to preserve the national legacy of Kurdistan’s freedom struggle and its aspirations for peace and freedom.”

author: Miguel Enrique Stédile
title: How Trump Tries to Decide the Elections in Brazil
content:
On the last Friday before the first round of Brazil’s presidential elections, the U.S. embassy and consulates in the country remained closed, following a generic order from the State Department regarding ‘security concerns.’ Elections in Brazil proceed peacefully; there are no civil conflicts or military threats, no records of political violence above normal levels, nor any threats to American citizens or diplomatic structures. But the decision, followed solely and inexplicably by the Australian embassy, is part of a set of actions by Washington to attempt to interfere in the Brazilian elections.

The actions began more than a year ago, when the United States linked increased tariffs on items imported from Brazil to the ongoing process to try former President Jair Bolsonaro for an attempted coup d’état. The relationship between political pressure to prevent the conviction of an ally and economic measures was publicized by the White House itself, as well as used to persecute the Supreme Court Justice responsible for the trial, blocking financial movements in the U.S. and preventing his entry into the country, and with ministers of the Lula da Silva government. A document delivered to Brazilian diplomats presented 21 demands to the Brazilian government including, among them, guaranteeing freedom for what the U.S. calls ‘political dissidents’; advantages for the U.S. in accessing Brazilian critical minerals; and not regulating big techs.

The list of demands is instructive for understanding why the Brazilian elections are so important to Trump. Brazil is rich in minerals, especially those fundamental to the technology industry, used in chip manufacturing and data centre installation; it also has numerous sources of renewable energy, especially hydroelectric and solar; it is beginning to prospect a new oil region in the Amazon area, near the blocks explored by ExxonMobil in Suriname and Guyana. Furthermore, Brazil’s largest trading partner is China, and both are part of the BRICS bloc. Brazil is also not a signatory to the Shield of the Americas, the contemporary version of Operation Condor, and chose the Chinese initiative for AI cooperation instead of the U.S. proposal. Additionally, on the map of South America, Brazil is one of the few countries not governed by a Trump ally. And it is not a small country, but a regional leader with presence in international articulations.

Therefore, one understands not only the economic and public actions, but also the clandestine ones unleashed from Washington. On 30 September, the British newspaper The Guardian revealed that Donald Trump’s government allocated US$1 million to a project called ‘Combating Weaponized Litigation and Censorship in Brazil,’ aimed at funding civil society organizations that challenge the actions of the Supreme Federal Court. The funds are part of a package of 43 grants totalling US$176.9 million, destined for conservative projects in various countries. The same State Department that remains silent about its own foreign influence scheme now sponsors the ‘defence of freedom of expression’ in Brazil. Before that, in July, Trump tried to send two State Department officials to meetings with authorities and civil society entities to question the electronic voting machines used in Brazilian elections. This is one of the main narratives of the Brazilian far-right that, despite having elected a President and most parliamentarians, insists that elections are fraudulent and illegal. This was, in fact, one of the motivations for the attacks on the Presidential Palace and Supreme Federal Court buildings on January 8, 2023, by Bolsonaro supporters, which would be the civil spark for a frustrated coup d’état.

Another common mechanism of U.S. interference is the use of non-governmental organizations. The Rockbridge Network — a network of conservative funders founded in 2019 by U.S. Vice-President J.D. Vance and businessman Chris Buskirk — tried to establish itself in Brazil with a plan that included creating a Technology Council of 23 businessmen to directly advise Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign. Of the 23 executives listed, 19 are foreigners. Brazilian law is clear: candidates and parties cannot receive, directly or indirectly, money, goods, or services from foreign entities or governments.

Funders of the Rockbridge network are the Rebekah Mercer, conservative megadonor and heiress of the Mercer hedge fund fortune, Peter Thiel, a fascist billionaire tech investor and financial supporter of Vance, as well as Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss, the cryptocurrency enterpreneurs. They see themselves as a right wing venture capitalist firm that will turn the Americas into a far right paradise for the billionaries.

It is no coincidence that in May, Flávio Bolsonaro met with Trump, Vance, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Washington. In September, Trump himself declared that he is following the Brazilian elections ‘very closely.’ Additionally, Bolsonaro’s advisors have stated in the press that they intend to carry out a ‘Marco Rubio reform’ within the Brazilian diplomatic service.

The Brazilian Intelligence Agency (ABIN), Brazil’s intelligence service, has already informed the Presidency of the Republic and the Superior Electoral Court about the possibility of U.S. interference in the electoral process. The Attorney General’s Office has also notified the Supreme Federal Court about foreign resources used in Bolsonaro’s campaign. A few days ago, President Lula da Silva, candidate for re-election, used his speech at the UN General Assembly opening to warn that interference will not be tolerated and that ‘Brazil will not be anyone’s backyard.’ At this moment, the known actions to block U.S. interference remain in the political and narrative field. But they may not be sufficient.

Latin America after 3 January 2026, is a territory surrounded and under constant threat from the Donroe Doctrine. The United States’ decision to classify two Brazilian organized crime factions, the Comando Vermelho (Red Command) and the Primeiro Comando da Capital (First Capital Command), as terrorist organizations opens precedents for U.S. force interventions on Brazilian territory. If Lula da Silva wins, it is possible to expect non-recognition or silence from Washington about the Brazilian electoral process. Minimally, this would keep Bolsonaro’s supporters cohesive and mobilized, who, at another time, already tried to retake executive power through a coup. If Lula da Silva loses, it is already known that Brazil would complete the map of subordinates, giving up its sovereignty and natural resources out of mere ideological loyalty. If Lula da Silva wins, the first years of his new government, at least until the next U.S. elections, should remain tense, threatened, and resistant to the Trump project on the continent.

Miguel Enrique Stédile holds a master's degree and a doctorate in history from the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul. He is researcher at Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research/Oficina Nuestra América and member of the coordination team at the Josué de Castro Institute of Education. He is the author or co-author of nine books, including Nadie regula América (No One Regulates America) on hybrid wars and geopolitical disputes in Latin America. He contributes to various media outlets in Brazil, such as Brasil de Fato and TV dos Trabalhadores (TVT).

author: Thomas Klikauer
title: German Car Workers Rally Against Job Cuts
content:
In September, 175,000 workers at 280 locations in Germany’s automotive and supplier industry engaged in a day of protest against the planned job cuts in the car industry. It shows that Germany’s workforce is prepared to fight for its jobs and its future. However, at several large Volkswagen (VW) locations, the true collective power of workers remained largely hidden behind factory gates.

At Volkswagen’s prime location in Wolfsburg, thousands gathered inside the factory gates. At an adjacent “public” rally only around 300 workers came. At Volkswagen’s Kassel-Baunatal location, about 850 workers took part in an “inside the factory” event, according to IGM’s Vertrauensleute, or union stewards. Representing workers in Germany’s still mighty car industry, the IGM union had planned for mostly union representatives [Vertrauensleute] to participate.

On the positive side, this might have been because IGM was unsure whether workers would follow its call to protest. On the downside, it might have been because the union wanted to confine the protest to its “controllable” union body rather than risk a true – and perhaps uncontrollable – protest by disgruntled workers against VW’s management. IGM wants to negotiate with that management and, as in the case of VW, has a relationship with it that is commonly seen as that of an assistant to management.

Worse, at another Volkswagen location, Braunschweig, union representatives – furnished with a union-developed “discussion guide” – were sent into VW’s production, even though the participation of all three shifts had been agreed beforehand.

On the whole, the “Union Day” of action has shown two things: first, the union can mobilize workers against management’s planned job cuts; and second, at the same time, local union representatives can limit or contain workers’ protest. German workers tend to follow their union. They are still more like Heinrich Mann’s rather tame Loyal Subject than anarcho-syndicalists – people who combine anarchism with revolutionary trade unionism.

Beyond that, one of the key questions isn’t just how many people took part: 175,000, or more, or fewer? It must also be asked who decided what form the “Union Day of Action” should take. Which proposals from workers about how best to challenge management were addressed, and which were eliminated by the union apparatus? Why did it appear, at several VW sites, as if management had received protection from the ever so compliant section of the union apparatus?

The reason for the “Union Day of Action” at Volkswagen was the planned removal of more than 60,000 jobs in Germany by the Volkswagen corporation. According to the most recent collective agreement between IGM and VW (from December 2024), VW’s works council – the legally elected body of workers’ representatives – and IGM accepted what is called “the socially acceptable removal” of more than 35,000 jobs at VW’s German locations by 2030. The term “socially acceptable removal” is not only the language of managerialism; it also means that workers who leave through retirement, by finding a new job, etc. are not replaced.

To make matters even more confusing, Germany’s labor relations operate with union representatives [Vertrauensleute], who have no legal support other than the strength of a local union organization, and, parallel to that, a legally elected and protected works council.

The former tends to be more progressive, while the latter tends to operate within the confines of Germany’s labor law – it operates as an offsider to management. Worse, union representatives who show compliance with Germany’s labor laws – no wildcat strikes, etc. – are selected and promoted by the union body and are often rewarded with election to the works council, which means, at VW for example, an almost lifelong job.

By splitting Germany’s workers into three institutions – an external union apparatus, a factory-based official body (the works council), and a factory-based union body – the “divide and conquer” strategy comes to life.

Volkswagen‘s management explicitly linked the collective agreement to a long-term reduction in production capacity and a reduction in annual labor costs of €1.5 billion ($1.7bn). Accordingly, redundancies are excluded until the end of 2030.

The agreed job cuts were to be achieved primarily via the so-called “demographic curve” – the retirement of workers. In 2026, Volkswagen’s top management calculated a need for further “adjustments” (meaning job cuts) of about 50,000.

According to IGM, about half of those are to occur in Germany. The additional approximately 25,000 on which management focuses are not yet on a definite management list of specific jobs to be cut. Together with the already agreed more than 35,000 jobs to be eliminated, more than 60,000 jobs are to be eliminated at various VW locations in Germany.

For workers, it is rather irrelevant whether jobs disappear through resignations, retirement, unfilled positions, the cancellation of the transition from apprenticeship to full-time positions, etc. In reality, each job that is eliminated by management increases the pressure on the remaining workforce. Beyond that, job cuts on such a massive scale will weaken Germany’s industrial regions.

It is a loss of income, health, training opportunities and family support structures, and the future of entire regions is at stake. This is capitalism – the best system, so we are made to believe. It is also about the ability of a union to shape the conversion, or transformation, of an entire industry towards sustainability instead of supporting management’s job cuts in a so-called “socially responsible manner” (read: sharpening the edges of neoliberal capitalism to make the system work better, i.e. in favor of corporations).

Since more than 35,000 jobs have already been agreed to be axed and VW’s top management eyes a further 25,000 in Germany alone, the question must be asked: what else needs to happen for car production to stop for a visible and impactful protest?

The union did not want that. Instead of a proper strike, IGM organized a day-long, nationwide action on 21 September. IGM called on workers at car manufacturers and suppliers to participate under the motto “For a Future instead of Job Cuts.” The plan was to make the protest visible to the public. The participation of 175,000 workers was a strong signal.

The 175,000 prove that the often-alleged passivity of German workers is not a sufficient explanation for the weakness of the public outcry. The decisive factor was the conditions under which workers were able to participate, and whether workers were involved in planning the union’s day of action.

In different locations, rallies were organized in front of the factory gates and other activities took place during the change of shifts. In Hanover, approximately 6,500 workers took part. Workers at Volkswagen‘s commercial vehicles division, at ZF Wabco and at other locations took their protest outside the factory gates.

The view at Volkswagen, however, shows that the relatively large workforces at VW Wolfsburg, Kassel and Braunschweig were mobilized primarily in a highly controlled way. Evil heretics might argue that controlling workers is the raison d’être of trade unions.

At VW’s HQ in Wolfsburg, for example, thousands of workers assembled at the factory while about 300 rallied in front of the union building. At VW’s main plant in Wolfsburg, thousands of workers walked to VW’s “Hall 11,” where IGM chairwoman Christiane Benner and the head of VW’s group works council, Daniela Cavallo, spoke.

The union was able to mobilize workers. A public rally in front of the union house was held on a Monday, between 10 and 11 am, with 300 workers. Anyone who worked in VW’s morning shift and was not “officially” released from work could not rally in front of the union house. It shows how such protests are organized in Germany – rather unthinkable in France, for example.

Worse, IGM segregated the relatively large mobilization of workers inside VW’s factories from the public protest. Even the media’s access to the events inside the factories was meticulously controlled and limited.

Only Germany’s state TV station, ZDF, the private channel Sat.1 and dpa – the Deutsche Presse-Agentur, or German Press Agency – were given access. Other media outlets were prevented from watching the main event. The media was not totally excluded, but access was highly restricted.

Despite this, thousands of workers came together to protest against VW management’s job cuts, but their real power remained behind the factory gate, unseen by the general public. Winning public support and solidarity for workers who fight for their jobs and against VW’s massive job cuts – which is undoubtedly strong throughout Germany – was severely hindered by IGM.

Despite the union’s best efforts to contain the public protest, a small rally outside the VW factory in Kassel is no substitute for a mass rally of thousands of workers. The union’s plan in Kassel was to limit the participation of workers. The union succeeded at Volkswagen Kassel-Baunatal, where the “Day of Action” remained an internal affair. There was an assembly for the early and late shifts in the foundry and an extraordinary meeting of union representatives. VW’s management was petrified by an “extraordinary meeting of union representatives.”

Yet 500 workers took part in the morning and 350 in the afternoon. Workers were drumming and clapping while moving from VW’s main factory gate into an internal meeting room inside the factory – and away from the public.

Meanwhile, about 200 “self-organized” workers – uncontrolled by IGM – also attended the rally. In any case, IGM and the works council had called for the rally. There were rumors that pressure was put on workers not to let “other” workers participate, as these were not elected union officials. Some workers still participated.

Limiting the rallies to the inside of the factory was criticized by many workers. Despite all this, the “officially” published report is still relevant because it describes a conflict between workers and the official union organization about the participation in, or organization of, the protest rally. The nationwide call of the union included all workers and all shifts. When participation was deliberately restricted to union representatives [Vertrauensleute], the scope and number of participants were significantly reduced before the rallies for the “Day of Action” had even started.

At the nearby Daimler Truck plant in Kassel, the “Day of Action” took place in public, in front of the factory gate, where 150 people attended. A comparison shows the weaknesses of both approaches. At Volkswagen, many more workers were included, but outside of work their protest was hardly visible. At Daimler, by contrast, the protest was open to the public, but mobilization reached only a small part of the workforce.

The alternative cannot be either a lot of people internally (behind factory gates) or a few people in front of the factory gate. Such a public “Day of Action” depends on linking broad participation inside factories with creating visible pressure from the outside.

The example of Braunschweig shows the limitations of the “Day of Action.” At the meeting on 16 September, prior to the rally, considerable discussion about the planned protest took place. During the meeting, there were 27 contributions on which form the protest should take, but the debate was stopped after the twelfth. It was to continue at a later date. A date for this was never issued. In other words, 15 contributions remained undiscussed, even though a nationwide day of action was planned only a few days later.

On 21 September, the plant’s body of union representatives and the works council issued a three-page “participation guide.” It called for the equal participation of the factory’s early, late and night shifts. After these discussions, the works council, union representatives and IGM were to inform workers which demands were accepted and how the next steps were planned.

In the end, a debate involving the works council, union representatives and interested workers was to be held. A key sentence in all this was that production should not be the sole yardstick for the duration and design of the Day of Action. In other words, whatever union representatives do, car production should continue unhindered.

On the “Day of Action,” union representatives received a “discussion guide” for debates inside the factory. Meanwhile, some union representatives wanted to take the “Day of Action” further and include a strike. Several union representatives announced that a strike would be the best way forward. Yet the feedback from many workers and union representatives did not provide an overall agreed picture.

Despite the success of the strategy of the union, the works council and many union representatives in limiting the “Day of Action” to the inside of factories, preventing visibility and broader solidarity with a German public that is hugely in favor of the workers, the “Day of Action” has shown that the willingness to resist is there. Now the works council and IGM have to decide whether to put that willingness to resist into action or to continue their strategy of supporting production and VW’s management with as few interruptions as possible – no interference.

Workers should no longer leave such decisions to the aficionados of union-management cooperation – or perhaps: complicity. Challenging this are ideas such as:

Work must not be eliminated together with people.

Existing work has to be distributed fairly, and industrial production needs to be aligned with meaningful, future-oriented tasks.

There should be no further job cuts, factory closures, or outsourcing to distant locations.

We need a reduction of working time with full pay and no cuts to personnel.

There should be socially useful products supporting public transport, energy storage facilities, small vehicles, load-carrying bicycles and cargo trams, as well as appropriate investment in all existing production sites.

All workers on temporary contracts are to be transferred into full-time positions under the principle of “one operation – one workforce.”

The current arrangement of an “on demand” workforce, management’s so-called “duty shifts” and the continuous availability of workers needs to end.

The weekend belongs to workers and their families.

There should be a democratically controlled transition towards decent, humane and sustainable mobility instead of production for the military – armament is no replacement for the destruction of jobs in the civilian industry.

Public contracts should only be issued to companies that offer job security, are part of Germany’s established system of collective agreements, and are committed to Germany as a location for production facilities.

Meanwhile, the reduction of working time at full pay must remain at the center. It distributes work fairly and offers a collective response to job cuts. Those who focus only on state subsidies and energy prices accept, in principle, the loss of jobs and only negotiate the speed at which these cuts are carried out.

Thomas Klikauer has over 1200 publications (including 16 books) and writes regularly for Cross Border Talks ( Europe), Countercurrents (India), and ZNet (USA) on global warming, labor relations, and Germany’s far right.

title: Barry Pateman - Tensions in Anarchism
content:
Author

: Barry Pateman

Title

: Tensions in Anarchism

Notes

: ‘Anarchist Tension #1-#4’ From 

Mob action against the state: collected speeches from the Bay Area Anarchist Book Fair

 (AK Press, 2002), ISBN 1902593510. Recorded by DJ Slo-Mo and Rad, compiled, edited and produced by DJ Slo-Mo of Entartete Kunst with assistance from RK of AK Press. Now out of print. 

https://web.archive.org/web/20221129074326/https://www.akpress.org/mobactionagainstthestate.html

 

 This is a transcript of a talk by Barry Pateman at the Bay Area Anarchist Bookfair in San Francisco. It shows something of his approach to anarchism, and the history of anarchism, and mentions some of the important people and experiences in his life. Barry spoke with passion and a greater concern for people than abstract ideas. As you’ll see, his humour (and swearing) were always self-deprecating: ‘Thank you for your time. I’m really sorry that you’ve got nothing else to do.’




 I just want to talk about some tensions I think that us as anarchists or people sympathetic to anarchism need to try and consider. ’Cause… I suddenly realised last night when I was laying in bed and just looking at the ceiling that I’m tending to become a bookfair groupie. There’s a bookfair in London. I go to a bookfair in London. It’s an anarchist bookfair, I sell anarchist books. I come to San Francisco. And I’m really talking, I guess, about how we as each other, as a group, as an organisation, as people who share a similar – what Galleani called the ideal, the dream – How we gonna make that real? And so, there are some tensions I think we have to face. 




 The first tension is ourselves and our history. There 

is

 a history of anarchism. But within that history of anarchism, there are things and people who have been forgotten. Now, with the Kate Sharpley Library, we have two reasons to exist. One is, yes, flowers for the fallen. We printed a pamphlet called 

Anarchists against Franco

* where there were twenty anarchists who’d been killed between 1942 and 1960 in guerrilla warfare against Franco. And Frank Torres who wrote it in Spanish says – and I couldn’t agree more – it doesn’t matter whether you think libertarian communism, anarchism will happen, it doesn’t matter whether you think it’s silly, it doesn’t even matter if you think you’re cleverer than those anarchists who went out there. What matters is how 

dare

 we forget them? How 

dare

 you and I sitting in this room not know about them? How dare we forget their bravery and their courage when they went over the mountains against stupidly impossible odds for that dream? So, any anarchist, any person sympathetic to us has to be aware of our history, not the history of ideas, that’s something I’ll talk about in a second, but simply the people who have suffered physically and emotionally for our belief. 

You’ll

 know some of them, nah? But we’ll also not know a lot of them and one of the things we must do is to revise history, to give them that dignity of that memory. 




 And the second thing of course is that if we’re canny we learn from history. We have to 

learn

. Look, I’ve been an anarchist for thirty years, so you’re not going to learn much from me because we haven’t got that far. But I do know what’ve we done wrong. I do think I’ve got an idea that what we’ve done has gone wrong. But we have to learn from our history. We can’t just pretend that we exist now and that really that those people were a bit strange or not like us because they spoke a different language. If we’re not guided by our history, we have no foundation, nothing, except living on our wits. So that I think is the first tension, how we discover and make our history come alive for all of us. 




 The second tension is, is between us as anarchists or sympathetic who are clever buggers ’cause we are… and ordinary people… who aren’t. I don’t mean racist, nasty people, I mean ordinary people who get up every morning, go to work, watch telly, watch baseball, go to bed… yeah? I mean those people. And you know what, there’s a lot more of them than us. 




 OK, so one of the things that’s disturbed me lately is there’s been a trend in anarchism to think that ordinary people are sort of fucking stupid. Yeah? They’re not clever or, really, they’re the problem. No, they’re not the problem. Look, every time there’s been some type of thing kicking off, starting, some insurrection, its come from dispossessed, poor people, ordinary people. And if we’re not there, if we don’t know them, if we’ve got no relationship with them… what’re we? Who are we? Just somebody else. It means nothing. Our relationship, surely, is with ordinary people. How we get to them. If our belief, if our dream is something that we believe in and live by and suffer by… then we have to go out there somehow. That tension is a critical one. You know, I could sit down all night and convince myself that anarchism’s tomorrow. But actually anarchism’s nothing… it’s something up here. Anarchism’s out there. 




 Let me give you some examples, two examples. Sixteen years ago in England there was the most brutal strike there’s ever been in the history of the country in many ways. It was a coal strike. One year it took. All my family as a result of that have, now have no jobs. They do not work. Secure, safe communities have become riddled with drugs and riddled with fear as a result of that huge defeat. But let’s look at the problem that we have. Sixteen years ago you could get up in Markham Main, Armthorpe Village where my family lived, and worked. They were on strike. Mutual aid, not in a fucking book, but in everyday existence was happening, yeah? None of those people had read Kropotkin, they didn’t know what it meant but it was happening. Alright? You went out, seven o’clock in the morning. ‘Who’s gonna have the wood? It’s bitter winter, it’s November. Who’s gonna have the wood? Well, those people with kids have the wood and the old people have the wood.’ That decision’s made. That decision’s made at a mass meeting a week before. So if you’ve got no kids and you’re on your own with your wife or your partner, you don’t have the wood. That – you’ve agreed on that. You’ve made that decision. You go through there – ‘who’s gonna get the food? The people – old people, kids.’ Again, that’s voted on. ‘Who’s gonna go on the picket lines today?’ ‘Well, I tell you who’s going to go on the picket lines today,’ says Brenda, ‘the women are going on the picket lines today because the fucking Metropolitan Police are here today and they’re out to get the strike leaders. So, we’ll put the women on the picket line today, so if they start swinging the truncheons at least they won’t get the men they’re looking for. We’ll protect them.’ You may disagree with that decision, we all can. I did. That didn’t matter. You had it alive. You had it living. You had something actually happening in your hand, yeah? 




...

author: Yohannes Woldemariam
title: From Tigray to the Red Sea: Ethiopia’s War in a Wider Regional Struggle
content:
I am not a military expert, but I do not read the withdrawal of Tigrayan forces from towns as straightforward evidence that their military position has weakened. An army can leave towns, roads and airports without losing its ability to move, reorganize, coordinate and strike. The more important questions are whether the force remains intact, how mobile it is, whether it can coordinate across different fronts, and whether it can still choose where and when to engage.

That is how I look at what is happening around Mekelle. Reuters reported on October 2 that federal and allied forces were moving toward the Tigrayan capital, and the following day reported that they had retaken Alula Aba Nega Airport. On a conventional military map that looks like a major federal success. But the map may be giving us a false sense of what is actually happening.

Debretsion Gebremichael who is the president of Tigray had already announced a counteroffensive and said Tigrayan forces would not fight according to the government’s dictates. I therefore do not see their movement out of Mekelle as a setback. I see an orderly and deliberate withdrawal from a fixed urban position by a force whose leadership had already told us that it intended to choose a different battlefield.

That distinction is important. Under conditions of federal air and drone superiority, concentrating fighters and equipment inside a city can make them sitting ducks. Moving out can preserve forces, stretch the opponent and create possibilities elsewhere. During the struggle against the Derg, the TPLF repeatedly relied on mobility rather than treating possession of every town as the measure of military strength. Today’s circumstances are different, especially because of drones and surveillance, but that experience should not simply be forgotten.

As I argued in The Geography of Asymmetric War, military power cannot be measured only by territory. Terrain, mobility, strategic depth and the ability to force a stronger opponent to fight differently also matter. A counteroffensive does not have to begin by immediately retaking Mekelle. It can strike supply lines, isolated units, communications systems, airfields or another front entirely.

This is why I am cautious even about the language of a federal “advance.” Federal forces are certainly moving into places Tigrayan forces have left. But that does not necessarily mean that one army is advancing while the other is simply retreating. If one side is deliberately giving up fixed positions in order to preserve mobility and shift the war elsewhere, the territorial map can create an illusion of momentum that may turn out to be temporary.

Focusing only on Mekelle also misses how much the war has changed. Fighting extends through Amhara and Afar, and armed movements that were enemies only a few years ago are now cooperating against the same federal government. Afar matters because it lies between Tigray, Eritrea and the routes toward Ethiopia’s Djibouti corridor. Amhara matters because Fano and Tigrayan forces, who recently fought a devastating war against one another, are now cooperating. These are not secondary developments. They change the political and military meaning of the war.

I began writing about this changing landscape in Tsimdo and the Changing Politics of the Horn. The creation of the seven group Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival took that process much further. The political map that existed when Pretoria was signed no longer describes Ethiopia, which is why I later argued that Pretoria Cannot Explain Ethiopia Anymore.

The map can show federal troops entering Mekelle. It cannot easily show former enemies learning to fight together. Nor can it show what has happened hundreds of miles behind the supposed front line in Bishoftu and Addis Ababa.

For years the federal government could use aircraft and drones against its opponents while assuming that its own air bases, military command and political center were safely beyond their reach. That assumption has been shattered. Drones have reportedly struck Harar Meda Air Base at Bishoftu, headquarters of the Ethiopian Air Force. Ethiopia Observer reported explosions inside the base and described considerable alarm among military personnel.

This is much more than another attack on a military installation. Drone warfare was one of the decisive advantages that helped Abiy Ahmed’s government survive when Tigrayan forces approached Addis Ababa in 2021. Now the headquarters of the air force itself is vulnerable to drones. Other aviation facilities have reportedly been attacked as well.

Then came Addis Ababa. On October 1, explosions were heard around the capital after opposition forces claimed strikes against military targets. Reuters reported the explosions and the opposition claim. Drone flights over the capital were banned, anti drone systems were deployed and security around sensitive facilities was tightened.

The significance is not simply the amount of physical damage. The attacks have brought fear into the political and military center. Abiy Ahmed and the ruling establishment can no longer behave as though war is something happening to other people hundreds of miles away. Air bases have to be defended. Military headquarters have to be defended. Officials and strategic infrastructure have to be protected. The government that once used drones to terrorize its opponents now has to worry about drones reaching its own centers of power.

That changes the psychology of the war. A drone does not have to demolish military headquarters to have an effect. It only has to demonstrate that the headquarters can be reached. The same applies to Bishoftu. An air force accustomed to projecting power outward must now devote attention to protecting its own home base.

This is another reason the territorial map may be deceptive. It can show government troops entering Mekelle at precisely the moment when insecurity is spreading into places the government once considered untouchable. What looks like strength at one end of the map can coexist with vulnerability at the other.

The situation in Mekelle itself should also make us careful about speaking casually of control. Federal forces captured the city once before, in November 2020, and its capture was presented as essentially the end of the war. Months later, Tigrayan forces returned and federal forces withdrew from much of Tigray.

Now there are reports of looting, abandoned government offices, police stations without security personnel and growing fear among residents as authority breaks down. Military entry and political control are not the same thing. An army can occupy an airport or enter a city. Governing it is something else.

Who prevents looting? Who protects homes and businesses? Who keeps hospitals running? Who provides food and medicine? Who restores electricity, banking and telecommunications? Who keeps public order?

There is also the terrible memory of the previous war. A joint investigation by the UN Human Rights Office and the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission documented unlawful killings, torture, sexual violence, displacement and other grave violations. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International documented killings, detention, torture, sexual violence, forcible displacement, pillage and denial of humanitarian assistance against Tigrayan civilians in Western Tigray.

Would Mekelle again experience the horrors civilians suffered during the previous war? Heaven forbid. But even without a repetition of those atrocities, military possession of Mekelle is not evidence that the political problem of Tigray has somehow been solved. A map can tell us who entered a city. It cannot tell us whether that city is governable, secure or politically controlled.

More importantly, territory is not the objective the opposition alliance has set for itself. When seven armed groups announced the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, their declared objective was the overthrow of Abiy Ahmed’s government and the creation of a transitional political order.

That should be the measure of success or failure.

The alliance is not fighting in order to accumulate towns on a map. Mekelle matters. Alamata matters. Afar matters. Roads, airports and military bases matter. But they matter in relation to the larger political struggle. If the alliance’s purpose is to remove the government in Addis Ababa, then territorial movements have to be judged by whether they bring either side closer to or farther from that objective.

This changes the entire interpretation of the present moment. Federal forces may enter Mekelle while the government’s strategic position worsens elsewhere. Tigrayan forces may leave Mekelle while preserving their capacity to fight. Opposition forces may lose visible territory while expanding cooperation across regions and bringing the war into Bishoftu and Addis Ababa.

The question is therefore not whether Abiy Ahmed can put his forces in Mekelle.

The question is whether Abiy Ahmed survives this war politically and militarily.

That is the scoreboard that matters.

And Tigray is not standing alone in that contest. The alliance linking Tigrayan, Amhara, Oromo, Afar and other armed movements changes the balance fundamentally. Forces that Addis Ababa could once confront separately are increasingly treating the government itself as the common problem. Their disagreements have not disappeared, but their cooperation means the federal government can no longer count on the divisions that protected it in the past.

The Eritrean dimension makes the territorial interpretation still more misleading. I have no doubt that Ethiopia’s military designs extend beyond Tigray. The repeated rhetoric surrounding Assab and Eritrea’s coastline has made that clear to me. I wrote about this before the present fighting in Ethiopia’s Imperial Ambitions Are Making the Horn of Africa Chronically Dangerous.

I have also rejected the historical arguments used to weaken Eritrean sovereignty. In There Is No Timeless Eritrea or Ethiopia, I argued that ancient kingdoms and shifting borders cannot be converted into property deeds for modern states. Eritrea is a sovereign state. Assab and Massawa are Eritrean ports.

This is why the struggle in Tigray cannot be separated from Eritrea’s security. The Ethiopian army moving through northern Ethiopia is moving toward the Eritrean frontier. If Addis Ababa believes it can first neutralize the military challenge from Tigray and then turn its attention northward, Eritrea has every reason not to wait passively for that sequence to unfold.

Many people already suspect Eritrean involvement in the present conflict. Addis Ababa accuses Eritrea of supporting its opponents; Eritrea denies it. What is clear is that Ethiopia and Eritrea have broken diplomatic relations at the same time that Ethiopian forces are moving closer to Eritrea and opposition forces inside Ethiopia are coordinating more closely.

The timing of Isaias Afwerki’s visit to Egypt therefore matters. On October 3, Abdel Fattah el Sisi met Isaias in New Alamein and publicly reaffirmed Egypt’s support for Eritrea’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. This happened not in a vacuum but while war was moving through northern Ethiopia and relations between Asmara and Addis Ababa were collapsing.

Egypt, Eritrea and Sudan have interests that increasingly converge. For Eritrea the immediate issue is sovereignty. For Egypt the Red Sea and Suez are vital, while the dispute with Ethiopia over the Nile remains unresolved. Sudan is fighting its own war and has seen its relationship with Addis Ababa deteriorate at the same time.

Somalia is more complicated. Mogadishu continues to talk to Ethiopia even after Ethiopia’s dealings with Somaliland challenged Somali sovereignty. That can look contradictory, but Ethiopia is a huge neighbor with military and political influence inside Somalia. Somalia cannot simply stop dealing with it.

At the same time, Somaliland has become increasingly important to Ethiopia, the UAE and Israel. Berbera is strategically valuable. The UAE has invested heavily in the area, while Israel’s recognition of Somaliland added another dimension to an already crowded geopolitical space. From Mogadishu’s perspective, all of this is happening on Somali territory. Somalia therefore has reasons both to keep channels open with Addis Ababa and to cooperate with Egypt, Eritrea and Sudan. Regional politics rarely divide themselves into perfect camps.

The wider Red Sea makes these connections even clearer. The recent Financial Times report on the growing relationship between the Houthis and al Shabaab reinforces an argument I have been making for some time. We cannot understand the Red Sea by looking only at Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Iran and the Gulf. Africa is not sitting on the opposite shore waiting for Middle Eastern politics to arrive.

According to the Financial Times, the Houthis and al Shabaab have developed a relationship involving weapons, personnel and training in drones and explosives. It is tempting to describe this simply as Houthi influence spreading into Africa, but that gives all the agency to the Houthis.

Why are the Houthis dealing with al Shabaab? Because al Shabaab has something they can use. It has fighters, territory, networks and an established presence in Somalia. The Houthis bring their own weapons, networks and experience. Al Shabaab brings capabilities and objectives of its own. Each sees something useful in the other.

We do not have to admire an actor to recognize its agency. Al Shabaab is an extremist organization responsible for enormous violence, but it remains an African actor making calculations of its own. It is not simply an empty container into which Middle Eastern influence is poured.

Africa is too often written out of its own geography. We hear about the UAE using African ports, China and the United States operating from Djibouti, Israel looking toward Somaliland, Saudi Arabia worrying about Bab el Mandeb and outside powers competing for strategic positions. The outsiders become the actors while Africans become ports and coastlines.

Eritrea makes choices. Djibouti makes choices. Somalia makes choices. Somaliland makes choices. Sudan makes choices. Ethiopia makes choices. African actors bargain, resist, cooperate, exploit rivalries and pursue their own interests. Sometimes those choices make the region more stable and sometimes they make it more dangerous, but they help create the regional order.

This is also why I have resisted reducing the Houthis themselves to an Iranian proxy. In To Understand the Houthis, Begin With Yemen, I argued that Yemen has its own history and politics. The same principle applies to Africa. African agency does not disappear because outside powers are involved.

Bab el Mandeb exists because Africa and Arabia face one another across a narrow body of water. Eritrea and Djibouti form one side of that chokepoint. Somalia carries that geography into the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. Farther north is Suez.

So we should stop asking only what Yemen means for Africa. We also have to ask what developments in Africa mean for Yemen, Bab el Mandeb and the wider Red Sea. Africa matters not simply because outsiders want its ports. Africa matters because Africans act.

The Red Sea is not a Middle Eastern security system with an African coastline attached to it. Africa is one of the places where Red Sea politics is made. That is what I mean when I say the Red Sea has two sides.

This brings me back to the map. One map shows Mekelle, Alamata, Amhara, Afar, Bishoftu and Addis Ababa. Another stretches through Eritrea, Assab, Massawa, Port Sudan, Berbera, Djibouti, Bab el Mandeb, Yemen and Suez. Neither can be understood without the other.

A conventional battlefield map may currently make the federal government look as though it is winning. I am not convinced that it is telling us that at all. It may instead be showing us where one side has chosen not to remain while hiding what is happening elsewhere: Tigrayan forces preserving mobility, former enemies coordinating, drones reaching Bishoftu and Addis Ababa, law and order breaking down in Mekelle, Eritrea preparing for what may come next and regional actors positioning themselves around a widening struggle.

Territorial possession is therefore not my measure of this war. The opposition alliance has told us what its objective is: the overthrow of Abiy Ahmed and the creation of a transitional political order.

If Abiy Ahmed survives that challenge and breaks the alliance’s ability to threaten his government, he will have defeated its stated purpose even if battles continue somewhere.

If the alliance remains intact, expands the war, deepens its cooperation and ultimately removes his government, then temporary federal possession of Mekelle, Alamata or any number of towns will not have meant victory.

That is why I think the present map can be deceptive.

It may look like the government is moving forward while the political foundations beneath it are becoming less secure.

The real question is not who holds Mekelle today.

It is who holds power in Addis Ababa when this war reaches its political conclusion.

And by then, what began in Tigray may have become inseparable from a much larger struggle reaching all the way to the Red Sea.

title: DFG commemorates Nagihan Akarsel on the fourth anniversary of her killing
content:
In a written statement, the Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG) commemorated Nagihan Akarsel, a journalist and member of the Jineology Research Center who was killed on 4 October 2022, and called for those responsible to be identified and brought to justice.




“This year, as her colleagues and those who have followed in her footsteps, we once again call for the real perpetrators to be exposed and prosecuted,” the statement said.




“On the fourth anniversary of the killing of Nagihan Akarsel, one of the pioneers of the Free Press, we remember her with respect, love, and an enduring sense of longing,” the DFG said, adding: “Nagihan Akarsel once said 'I am an adventurer; I do not settle in one place.'




The struggle for freedom that she began within herself has today become a path for millions of women. Women, journalists who have followed in her footsteps, and the students she taught are keeping Nagihan Akarsel’s dreams alive through the struggle for women’s freedom. Nagihan Akarsel’s pen continues to write at every level of the Free Media. We once again reaffirm our commitment to preserving the legacy she left us and keeping her dreams alive.”




Nagihan Akarsel




Nagihan Akarsel (Zîlan) was born in 1976 in the village of Gölyazı in Cihanbeyli district of Konya province in central Turkey. The Kurdish name of the village is Xelîkan. 




Between 2001 and 2007, she was imprisoned for her political activity at universities. After her release from prison, she worked as an editor and reporter at the Dicle News Agency between 2008 and 2014. During this period, she also followed the lectures of Hacettepe University Women’s Studies Department in order to deepen her understanding of women’s liberation. She took part in the establishment of the first women’s press agency, JINHA. For years, she worked as a reporter in the Kurdish press, chasing news. She was a hard worker, a teacher, a friend and comrade in the development of Kurdish women’s journalism.




She answered the call of Jineology (Women's Science), to which Abdullah Öcalan attaches great importance, at the highest level in both its academic and institutional dimensions. When the process of institutionalization of Jineology began, she took part in the work of the Jineology Academy. She worked hard during the establishment of the Jineology journal. She not only served as a member of the editorial board of the journal, but also constantly fed it with her articles.  She never stopped knocking on new doors to transform the Jineology magazine into a women’s freedom platform.




She conducted research and educational activities in many areas of Bakur, Bashur and Rojava (North, South and West Kurdistan). She educated thousands of people and wrote for many newspapers and magazines. Everywhere she went, she was a beacon of light, especially for young people. Children and mothers moved close to her. After 2018, she continued her sociological studies in Afrin and Shengal, to be published in a book. As someone in love with the culture of Hewreman and the resistance culture of Rojhilat (Eastern Kurdistan) women, she continued her research in this field, but she always felt a loss at not being able to go to Rojhilat.




From 2019 until the date of her assassination, she worked tirelessly for the development of Jineology studies in Bashur, South Kurdistan. Although she had only just learned the Sorani dialect, she gave dozens of courses and seminars on JineoJineologyoji in Bashur, and organized Jineology camps with young people.
