title: Ephéméride des luttes : 4 octobre
content:
Le 4 octobre, l'éphéméride des luttes détruit des chantiers de centrale nucléaire et s'organise radicalement contre les fascistes. Ce qui serait aussi intéressant de reproduire aujourd'hui.




1884 :

 A Chicago, parution du premier numéro du journal anarchiste '

The Alarm

'.




1893 :

 Naissance près de Milan de Francesco Ghezzi, qui mourra dans les camps de travail en Russie. Voir l'éphéméride anarchiste pour une biographie détaillée (lien en bas).




1905 :

 A Ekaterinoslav en Russie, le Groupe d'Ouvriers Anarchistes-Communistes pose une bombe dans la maison du directeur et actionnaire de l'usine Construction de Machines à Amur, qui avait fait licencier 3000 ouvriers. Lire 

le communiqué

 en français.




1930 :

 Au Brésil, début de la Révolution avec la prise du quartier général de la 3e Région Militaire.




1957 :

 Premier satellite artificiel lancé dans l'espace. C'est le Spoutnik russe.




1971 :

 A Belfast, un soldat de l'armée britannique est tué par une bombe de l'IRA 'Officielle' (OIRA).




1977 :

 A Rome, une assemblée autonome décide de continuer à mener une campagne d'actions dures contre les fascistes, dans la continuité de ce qui avait été fait les jours précédents.




1981 :

 Une manifestation de 4000 personnes envahit le site de la centrale nucléaire de Golfech en construction, provoquant beaucoup de dégâts dans le chantier, le retardant de fait pour un bon moment. Pendant 4 à 5 heures, jusqu'à la tombée de la nuit, des affrontements (grenades lacrymogènes d'un côté, jets de pierres ou de cocktails molotov de l'autre) ont lieu. Selon 

Courant Alternatif

 de novembre 1981 (extrait reproduit 

ici

), « 

Des centaines de mètres de barbelés arrachés et de nombreuses installations attaquées et incendiées, partiellement ou totalement détruites : plusieurs hangars, des engins de travaux, un poste de vigiles, les bureaux d'une agence d'intérim, le local d'EDF (bureau d'information situé le long de la RN113) ainsi que celui de l'ANPE.


Les dégâts sur le site sont conséquents

 ».




 Attaque de la prison de Frosinone, en Italie, par les COLP (Communistes Organisés pour la Libération du Prolétariat), afin de faire évader le militant des Prolétaires Armés pour le Communisme (PAC) Cesare Battisti. L'évasion réussira sans que personne ne soit blessé.




1993 :

 Dans le nord de Londres, l'IRA fait sauter cinq bombes.




2016 :

 A Munich, un véhicule de l'entreprise de sécurité privée VDH, qui travaille dans les camps pour migrants et fait ses profits avec l'enfermement, le harcèlement et le contrôle, 

est incendié

 en solidarité avec les luttes des migrant-e-s.




2018 :

 A Clermont-Ferrand, à trois heures du matin, le local néofasciste du Bastion Social est la cible d'une tentative d'incendie, peu de temps après avoir déjà été saccagé par des antifascistes.

author: Sarah Glynn
title: French lessons on authoritarianism and solidarity: The lycée student blockades
content:
For French lycée (high school) students, this week has been an important step in their education. You can study books about the role of the state and of the forces of law and order, of political deception and media bias, and of organisation and solidarity; but that is not the same as practical experience.

This week they learnt the meaning of authoritarianism, and that the official values of the French Republic — liberté, égalité, fraternité (liberty, equality, fraternity) — have to be fought for again and again. They have also provided a lesson in solidarity for us all.

As in other countries that have undergone years of neoliberal austerity, French schools suffer from chronic underfunding. This affects everything from teacher shortages to building maintenance, and is especially bad in poorer areas. The students have had enough of this undermining of their futures and are on strike.

They are protesting the lack of crucial teachers and other staff, large class sizes, overloaded timetables, badly maintained buildings, and the discriminatory system for allocating university places.

Their main form of action has been blockades of their lycées, supplemented by spontaneous marches and supported by general assemblies.

President Emmanuel Macron’s government is responding to discontent the way it always does — with violent suppression. Instead of listening to the students and acting on their concerns, they have sent in the police — riot cops armed with tear gas against teenagers demanding a better education.

Protests first erupted on September 21 at the Lycée Saint-Exupéry in Créteil, in the south-eastern suburbs of Paris, which was short of several teachers. By the end of the week, actions had spread to around 60 lycées throughout the Île de France (the Parisien basin).

The action was taken up in lycées in other parts of France, on September 28 and the following day, the Union Syndicale Lycéenne (students’ union) called for blockades everywhere. Lycée students marched with striking public sector workers. Police arrested 440 students.

Blockades and other actions continued on September 30, and students from more privileged schools came out in support of the students and the principle of equality.

The Lycée students were joined by students at a number of universities, on October 1. The Union Étudiante (University students’ union) claimed they closed 640 lycées and around 30 university campuses. Their statement read: “These blockades are an expression of young people’s anger at the contempt they face. Over nearly 10 years of anti-social and discriminatory policies, Emmanuel Macron and his successive governments have eroded our living and learning conditions.”

About 2000 people were arrested on October 1. Actions continued the following day.

Representatives of the Lycée students finally met with the Minister of Education after 10 days of protests, but reported that they had not received a “concrete announcement”. More actions are planned for October 5 and preparations are underway for major protests on October 6, supported by the trade unions.

The streets were turned into a battleground as police fired off rounds of teargas and dragged thousands of teenagers into custody, using the sortof violence that we are sadly becoming accustomed to.

A 14-year-old suffered a broken jaw and missing teeth after being hit with a teargas cylinder at point blank range. Another teenager lost an eye. A newly-emerged video shows a police officer holding a youth in water, as if to drown him.

The government could not have chosen a better way to ensure that the protests spread. The Union Étudiante said: “They think they’re putting an end to the movement, but all they’re doing is fuelling it.”

Protesters in France, including lycée students, readily take to the streets, but this time the response has exceeded expectations — in both size and determination – boosted by the aggressive behaviour of a police force that is clearly enjoying its license to terrorise.

Teachers have been supportive of the students’ demands, and also of the students themselves and their right to protest and not suffer police attacks. Trade unionists and elected representatives have tried to give the students an element of protection. And popular support is evident in the reactions of passers-by and of people watching the protests from neighbouring flats and cafés.

However, not everyone is happy to support the protests, and much of the media — which is largely owned by a handful of billionaires — is working hard to demonise them and to tell a very different story.

With thousands of angry teenagers facing attacks from the state, it would be absurd to expect the protests to cause no damage. There will always be a few individuals who want to push things further, regardless of the consequences, and there are not always others able to stop them. We must expect that agents provocateurs are active, too.

Most damage has been limited to burning bins and shattering bus-stop glazing — a gift for those looking for images to sully the students’ cause — as well as the purloining of lose items for use in constructing barricades.

However there have also been more serious destructive acts, including arson attacks on parts of the very lycée they want to see improved. A fire at the Lycée Nelson-Mandela in Nantes is said to have caused €2 million in damage.

And of course, some students have lashed out at the attacking police, and people have been hurt in the general mêlée — though the worst cases quoted by the politicians have turned out to be fabrications.

While the streets are full of heavily-protected police armed with teargas, it is student violence that has been a major theme of media reports, and interviewees sympathetic to the students are always called on to condemn this violence.

Compounding this mis-portrayal, a young man who has been interviewed on television channels as a “representative” of the lycée students has been discovered to be an employee of a Macronist communications agency and an advisor to Gabriel Attal, the presidential candidate from Macron’s Rennaisance Party. Unsurprisingly, he kept close to the government script.

The political establishment and their media friends do not simply want to dismiss and crush the protesting students. They see this as an opportunity to attack the left, and especially La France Insoumise (LFI), whose leader and presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is increasingly portrayed as a major danger to the country.

LFI deputies have been prominent in the demonstrations, showing their support for the students’ demands and helping them to get heard. They bear witness and provide a measure of protection, and help ensure that the protesters remain non-violent, despite police provocations.

The Interior Minister has talked about “urban violence” and claimed that the movement is being instrumentalised by LFI. Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen claims Mélenchon “bears a heavy responsibility for the situation our country finds itself in today”. And television debates run above headlines such as “Mélenchon a ‘firefighter who is a pyromaniac’?”

Meanwhile, Mélenchon himself insists on the importance of remaining non-violent, and stresses: “The ‘Insoumis’ movement does not lead grassroots movements. They lead themselves, through their own self-organisation and their representatives. We protect them, we help them, and then they decide.”

A particular target of the attacks against LFI is Bally Bagayoko, the popular mayor of Saint-Denis — a working-class commune where schools have been disproportionately deprived. Bagayoko was welcomed by the protesting students and videoed surrounded by students all singing the Marseillaise.

He also warned the students to be prudent, and helped extinguish a fire that had been lit. But this did not prevent the Chief of Police from reporting him to the public prosecutor, accusing him of “provocation to commit a crime”.

Establishment politicians and media have no qualms about instrumentalising the situation to discredit LFI — and no interest in the issues raised by the protesting students. They are prepared to use misrepresentation alongside physical force to divide the country and ignite fires of hatred that will long outlast burning wastebins.

The run up to April’s presidential election is set to be increasingly turbulent, but the scale of this week’s protests and the coming together of lycée students and trade unionists provides a source of hope for all to build on.

[Sarah Glynn is a writer and activist based in Strasbourg. Visit her blog at: sarahglynn.net.]

author: Cormac Mills Ritchard
title: Demolishing the idea of public housing
content:
The United Nations’ special rapporteur on adequate housing, Koldo Casla, usually deals with slum demolitions in third-world countries. Last month, he took aim at the Victorian Labor government, claiming its demolition of Melbourne’s 44 public housing towers and the “forced evictions and mass displacement of approximately 10,000 residents” could be a violation of their 

human rights

. This follows a Victorian parliamentary inquiry in December, which called for an 

immediate pause

 to the demolitions, and a class action against the demolitions filed by Inner Melbourne Community Legal (IMCL), which has been granted special leave to 

appeal

 to the High Court on 7 October.

Despite growing challenges, Premier Ben Carroll is ploughing ahead with the demolition of Melbourne’s public housing towers. Of course, Labor doesn’t characterise what it’s doing as “eviction” and “demolition”, but “renewal” and “redevelopment”, which it claims will increase the number of residents on the estates from 10,000 to 30,000, and replace towers that have “reached the end of their useful life”. There is no truth to this.

If Labor’s multi-billion-dollar project is aimed at addressing the waiting list for social housing, it’s missing a couple of zeros. Only 11,000 of the new residents will be in social housing, an increase of just 1,000. As of June this year, there were 58,021 people on the Victorian Housing Register’s 

growing waiting list

, of which 33,253 have been assessed as “priority”—mostly those who are currently homeless or experiencing family violence. The redevelopments will mean that just 1,000 more people will have places in social housing ... by 2051.

The redevelopment won’t help others affected by the housing crisis, either. The other 19,000 residents of the new mixed-tenure developments will live in a combination of build-to-rent, a model that the

 Age

 has found to be between 20 and 70 percent 

more expensive

 than the market rate, and “affordable housing”, which is not that affordable and does not provide long-term security, as exposed by a recent 

Four Corners

 

investigation

. 

The North Richmond public housing precinct is a telling example. In September, the state government briefed the City of Yarra on its plans for the tower at 139 Highett Street. The 

Age

 reported last month that the tower, which currently has 220 public housing units, will be replaced with a development that has 

only 150 social housing units

 and 650 build-to-rent units.

Simon is a former resident who grew up in the North Richmond precinct after his parents emigrated from Vietnam. After the latest announcement about the precinct, he attended a community meeting of public housing tenants who demand the towers be refurbished rather than demolished. He told 

Red Flag

 that his parents, a labourer and kindergarten worker, were both poorly paid. Living in the public housing tower allowed them to escape the anarchy of the private rental market. “We knew what the rent was next week and didn’t have to worry about eviction or not being able to afford food. I could attend school and university without many issues. That security meant you could plan your life”, he said.

“Social housing” is an umbrella term that covers both public housing, run by the government, and community housing, run by not-for-profits. When Labor talks about social housing, it usually means community housing—so its claim to be replacing 10,000 public housing places with 11,000 social ones actually represents a huge cut in public housing.

Public housing rent is capped at 25 percent of a household’s income or the market rate, whichever is lower, while community housing providers can charge up to 30 percent. However, community housing organisations (CHOs) are entitled to 100 percent of any tenant’s Commonwealth Rent Assistance and can charge extra fees on top. In its 

submission to the inquiry

, IMCL notes that some of its clients pay up to 50 percent of their income to a CHO through “rent, utilities, lift fees, concierge and management fees”. Community housing residents also have fewer rights than public housing residents; West Heidelberg Community Legal found that “long-term community housing tenants were 3 to 5 times more likely to face eviction than public housing tenants”.

Worse still, unlike the government, CHOs don’t have to allocate places based on need, which means that the more the social housing waiting list is serviced by community rather than public housing, the more that people with the greatest need who have complex problems such as alcohol and drug dependency may end up in perpetual limbo, constantly having their place in the waiting list taken by someone who will make fewer demands on the provider and will pay more rent.

The human cost of the demolitions is horrific. In 

testimonies to the parliamentary inquiry

, residents reported how the whole process has made them feel powerless. Many first learned that their homes would be demolished through the media, after then-Premier Daniel Andrews made a public announcement. “[We] heard it like everyone else on the news”, one resident said. “It was shocking.” Another said that they felt they were not being treated “as a human being”.

The towers sit at the heart of Melbourne’s most diverse and most marginalised communities, particularly those from the Horn of Africa, as well as others from Vietnam, Egypt, Iraq and elsewhere. Reem Yehdego, a resident of the North Melbourne precinct, told the inquiry that the demolitions “feel like erasure”, and that residents were being coerced into relocation “far from our doctors, our schools, our mosques and our community‑based support networks”. IMCL reported to the inquiry that, in meetings with Homes Victoria, their clients have been repeatedly told their family unit may need to split into two homes because of the small size of available homes, and that if they refuse two offers of this sort of alternative housing, they will be evicted. 

This is not the first “redevelopment” program. One woman spoke of her nan’s experience being relocated in her 80s from Huttonham Estate, Preston, which was demolished in 2011:

“She became extremely lonely. Her community was gone. Her neighbours were gone. She had lived in that house for over 40 years, raised her children there—it was sentimental, important. It was the family gathering spot, imbued with memories from three generations. My mother and her siblings all agreed that after she was relocated, her dementia symptoms worsened ... There was only so much we could do to support her—we could not hire carers; we are working class. We are working class and need to work. How did you expect us to support her?”

In January, the government announced a second tranche of public housing tower demolitions. All seven towers house people over 55. I visited Kenneth Coldicutt, a resident at 94 Ormond Street in Kensington. If Housing for the Aged Action Group hadn’t helped him get a place there, he said, he would have likely remained homeless. Sitting on a sunny bench outside the estate’s community hub, he says he is furious about Labor’s decision. 

“They want to wash their hands of public housing”, he said. But more enraging is “the way they’ve targeted the most vulnerable, the most frail, the most marginalised people”. There are three residents he knows of in his tower who are over 90, “and at least one person with terminal cancer who is in no fit condition to move”.

Ken is a member of Ormond St’s five-person residents’ committee. For months, he doorknocked his tower with help from 44 Flats United, a campaign group, to draft a list of demands and elect a committee to negotiate with Homes Victoria. They sent a letter to Homes Victoria at the end of August and have still received no response. They want Homes Victoria to begin cleaning the windows, which are so dirty that “natural light is blocked on many floors”. And they want a systemic plan to eradicate bedbug, cockroach and rat infestations that have plagued the tower. 

“A more cynical person than myself might say that they’re using the rats and the cockroaches to speed up the process of relocating people”, Ken said as he gave me a tour of the rat holes and the stained vinyl floors where they last battled the cockroach infestation. His remarks echo one of the major themes of the parliamentary inquiry—the allegation that the government has engaged in managed decline, waiting for the towers to deteriorate to justify their demolition. Ken thinks they could all live there for another couple of decades, if the towers were properly maintained, “which they haven’t been for a very long time”.

This comment takes us back to Labor’s claim that the towers have to be demolished. You would think evicting 10,000 people would be a last resort, after all other options were exhausted. But Labor didn’t even begin to investigate other options. It commissioned a 

report from MGS Architects

, investigating the possibility of refurbishing (rather than redeveloping) the towers to bring them in line with modern standards. It received this report in September 2024, a full year

 

after it announced the demolitions

.

 It then buried this report for the entire parliamentary inquiry (no doubt because it found refurbishment both possible and in the public interest), along with 146 other documents relating to its decision, claiming executive privilege over all but twelve.

So why is Labor doing this?

Speaking to 

North West City News

 in February, University of Melbourne urban geographer Kate Shaw said the government is 

trying to shift responsibility to not-for-profits

, even though “it’s becoming increasingly clear that community housing organisations are financed by large companies that expect a return on their investment”.

The redevelopments follow the latest version of Labor’s model of public-private partnerships, which are just vehicles to involve profit-seeking businesses in public projects. What does this look like? One example is the “not-for-profit” community housing provider Together Housing (Victoria), which was awarded $206 million by the federal government’s Housing Australia Future Fund as part of a consortium of developers and CHOs redeveloping and managing public housing estates. As the ABC revealed, 

Together Housing is controlled by Tetris Capital

, an investment firm with $3.7 billion in assets.

State and federal Labor governments are throwing money at developers, investment firms and dodgy charities, which get tenants’ rent assistance, subsidies and, to cap it all off, a 40-year lease of the public housing estates. Business feasts while the most vulnerable are left out in the cold.

“The government is trying to erase the idea that the state has any responsibility to meet the needs of its working class”, Simon said. “The whole point is you’re on your own.” Built between the 1950s and 1970s, Melbourne’s housing commissions have been the most visible monument to public housing in Melbourne.

Destroying the towers divests the state of its responsibility to provide, and pays dividends to Labor’s corporate mates. The result is that the most vulnerable people—migrants and asylum seekers, victims of homelessness and family violence—will be left to the vicissitudes of the private market, to rent hikes, mould and domineering landlords.

If you look past the dirt on Ormond Street’s unwashed windows, there is a magnificent, unobstructed view of the city. The eucalypt-framed skyscrapers go gold in the sunset. When Ken first arrived in his apartment, he remembers feeling it could never last—developers would look for any way to get their hands on the land and the view. It’s heartbreaking that the world has proved him right, that the working-class instinct that “this might be too good for me” has been borne out.

But it isn’t too good for Ken, or anyone else. We all deserve to be freed from the housing market. We deserve high-quality, sustainable public housing. We deserve houses next to parks and playgrounds, and we deserve the security to know where we’ll be living in one year, or ten. We all deserve a view.

author: Igor Ojeda
title: Brazil’s elections and environmental policy: A choice between continuity and dismantling
content:
Never before in the history of this country has the climate crisis been as relevant to a presidential election as it, very likely, will be in the 2026 vote. Once again deeply polarised, this year’s electoral contest between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of the Workers’ Party and Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party is taking place against a decisive climatic and geopolitical backdrop.

Less than a year ago, in November 2025, Brazil hosted the United Nations’ annual climate summit, COP, that restored the country’s status as a key player in the global climate debate. This was a particularly important development given that Brazil currently ranks among the top five contributors to greenhouse gas emissions, primarily due to agriculture, cattle ranching and deforestation.

Four years after the last Brazilian presidential election, in which Lula defeated Jair Bolsonaro by a razor-thin margin, the effects of the climate crisis have intensified. As scientists and environmental, social and civil society organisations have been warning for years, the planet is increasingly suffering the severe consequences of this reality, with a rise in the frequency and intensity of extreme natural events, in addition to the increase in average global temperatures. In Brazil, the historic drought in the Amazon in 2023 and the unprecedented floods in Rio Grande do Sul in 2024 were just a few examples.

The arrival of the El Niño weather phenomenon, forecast to last until early 2027 and once again cause severe droughts and above-average rainfall, alongside rising food prices, contributes to the growing importance of the climate debate in the electoral landscape.

In the geopolitical arena, the Brazilian presidential election will serve as yet another stage for the struggle for global hegemony between the United States and China — a contest currently focused largely on the race to control reserves of so-called critical minerals and rare earth elements. Beyond their strategic value for a clean energy transition, these resources are essential inputs for the defence industry.

“The election will reflect this struggle for hegemony,” says geographer Bruno Malheiro, a professor at the Federal University of Pará (UFPA).

“One side, Flávio Bolsonaro’s, will be clearly structured around a policy of alliance and total alignment with the United States over critical minerals and rare earth elements,” Malheiro says. “On the other side, President Lula’s, we see a more open, multifaceted diplomatic policy, yet one clearly tethered to China in terms of economic strategy.”

An analysis of both candidates’ platforms, as well as their speeches, stances and track records, including Lula’s third term and Jair Bolsonaro’s administrations alongside Flávio’s tenure in the Senate, reveals two different paths. While the incumbent president signals a continuation of policies, with equally significant advances and limitations, his rival envisions a return to his father’s administration, grounded in the dismantling of environmental policies and a disregard for the climate agenda.

Political scientist Maureen Santos is a climate justice activist and international relations professor. In terms of the Paris Agreement negotiations, she believes that the fight against deforestation and illegal mining, and other issues, President Lula’s platform for the 2026 elections “doesn’t change much” compared to the proposals from the previous election or his current administration’s policies.

“However, it seems to me there is an attempt to forge a stronger connection with other areas of the government,” she notes.

To her, however, the platform does introduce some new elements. In particular, Lula places greater emphasis on policies concerning critical minerals and rare earth elements. Yet, Santos criticises the lack of measures ensuring greater state control over the exploitation of these resources.

“Rhetoric about sovereignty obviously matters, but how can Brazil exercise sovereignty, for instance, given the new environmental licensing law, which relaxes licensing requirements, or the absence of a state-owned company for this sector?” she warns. “It is very difficult to envision sovereignty if the country continues to merely sell commodities.”

According to Santos, although Lula’s platform mentions technology transfer, processing and value addition, there are doubts about whether this will actually materialise, given the negotiations the government has been conducting on this topic.

“But this is obviously not a sell-out like the one proposed by Flávio Bolsonaro on the subject. There is a stark difference,” notes Santos. She refers to a statement made by Flávio Bolsonaro in the US this past March, that Brazil could be the solution for the US to reduce its dependence on minerals from China.

For Suely Araújo, public policy coordinator at the Climate Observatory, a network of Brazilian environmental organisations, the content of the Lula government’s platform aligns with the actions taken during his current administration on the environment and climate. In her assessment overall, the president’s third term has yielded good results in this area.

“The Lula administration rebuilt environmental and climate governance, which had been severely dismantled by the end of the Bolsonaro administration,” she said.

Other positive aspects, according to Araújo, include the drop in deforestation rates, which account for a significant share of Brazil’s greenhouse gas emissions, and the increase in resources for the Climate Fund, the primary financing tool for climate change policy.

Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research monitors Amazon deforestation by satellite. According to the agency’s figures in August, the Amazon recorded the smallest area under deforestation alerts in history, a 36% drop compared to 2025. According to the Climate Observatory, the total area under deforestation alerts in the Amazon region dropped 41% over the past four years during the Lula administration, compared to the four years prior under the Bolsonaro administration.

Meanwhile, Climate Fund resources have increased by more than 300 times since 2020, according to the figures presented in July by the Ministry of Finance. For 2026, the budget forecast is $5.3 billion, compared to $17.4 million six years earlier.

Flávio Bolsonaro’s government platform, meanwhile, is “a non-plan in this area”, observes Araújo.

“There are scattered references throughout the text making it clear that we would face very serious climate and environmental problems in general if everything he proposes were implemented. The possibility of this plan becoming reality is truly alarming,” she warns.

In Bruno Malheiro’s assessment, a Flávio Bolsonaro administration would lead us “to complete chaos, because he represents a project of violence and the total destruction of the state, of agreements, and of universities, which would become more directly tied to agribusiness, losing their autonomy”.

Malheiro also says, “we would see the destruction of the very logic of politics, turning it into an engine of destruction. We saw this clearly with the Jair Bolsonaro administration.”

While climate and environmental agendas appear repeatedly throughout Lula’s platform, Bolsonaro’s platform contains no mentions, for instance, of terms such as climate change, greenhouse gas emissions, the Paris Agreement, Nationally Determined Contributions — each country’s official plan to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, mitigation or adaptation.

Suely Araújo points out that Flávio Bolsonaro’s stance as a senator already offered a preview of what a potential administration of his might look like.

“He signed bills attempting to eliminate the legal preservation of native vegetation on rural properties, and supported the law that dismantled environmental licensing, among other measures,” she says. “As for the climate, it is a non-issue for him; his approach to the subject would likely follow along the lines of his father Jair Bolsonaro, who, in some statements, bordered on denialism.”

“At the very least, a denial of the subject’s relevance,” she adds.

Although he backed away from the promise to withdraw Brazil from the Paris Agreement, Jair Bolsonaro’s administration cut climate research funding, stalled the Amazon Fund and took a confrontational stance on international demands for deforestation and emissions reduction targets, among other issues.

According to Malheiro, a potential Flávio Bolsonaro administration would follow the denialist logic of his father’s tenure, but with certain nuances shaped by the current context.

“For instance, regarding critical minerals, he already envisions handing them over entirely [to the US], but he will logically leverage the energy transition narrative to make this somewhat more palatable. Flávio Bolsonaro might be a bit more adept than his father in this regard,” Malheiro says.

However, on international climate agreements, Malheiro believes that Flávio Bolsonaro — if elected — would indeed adopt a denialist policy.

“He might engage in opportunistic behaviour during a specific climate event, should a particular sector pressure him to accept an agreement that works to his advantage,” he says.

Santos suggests that the fact that Brazil attracts investment by playing a key role in the climate agenda might prevent a potential Flávio Bolsonaro administration from breaking away from it entirely.

“It will depend heavily on the dialogue with the United States, which withdrew not only from the Paris Agreement but also from the Climate Convention,” she points out.

In his campaign platform, Lula pledges to work toward “achieving net-zero deforestation by 2030”.

“To this end,” the document states, “all levels of government will continue to act in an integrated manner to implement deforestation control and prevention plans and to fully implement the National Integrated Fire Management Plan.”

According to the text, a fourth Lula administration would seek to ensure the effectiveness of the Forest Code and the Atlantic Forest Law, “advance the allocation of public lands for conservation units, Indigenous and quilombola territories (communities descended from Africans and Afro-Brazilians who escaped slavery), and strengthen land tenure regularisation”.

“It is crucial to truly eliminate deforestation by 2030. The policy in this area is positive, but it also needs to be reinforced by economic policies that empower the relevant stakeholders,” says Santos. However, she finds that one of the current administration’s major “bottlenecks” is the weakness of policies aimed at strengthening family and peasant farming, local food systems, the demarcation and titling of Indigenous lands, and agrarian reform.

“It falls short on these points,” she adds.

Meanwhile, Flávio Bolsonaro announces a goal of eliminating “illegal deforestation” by 2029.

“We will combat illegal burning by strengthening prevention, monitoring, enforcement, and the fight against environmental crimes, using tools enhanced by artificial intelligence, real-time databases, satellite imagery, and coordinated action among state agencies,” the text reads.

Araújo notes, however, that legalised deforestation must also be reduced, or at the very least, offset by carbon sequestration measures, such as reforestation and the restoration of degraded areas.

“None of this is in Flávio Bolsonaro’s plan,” she says.

While acknowledging that the third Lula administration has achieved positive results for the environment and climate, Araújo says those results are limited or contradicted by the low number of non-reimbursable grants from the Climate Fund, and the decision to expand fossil fuel exploration.

“Lula’s plan states that he will continue to expand climate finance. However, there are challenges, because the bulk of the funding consists of loans, meaning the government can lend the money but cannot provide it as grants,” she says. “This poses a limitation, particularly for municipalities that lack borrowing capacity. We need to increase the resources available as non-repayable grants, especially for climate change adaptation.”

Malheiro, however, criticises the logic behind the climate finance model that he believes dominated the third Lula administration’s climate and environmental policy.

“It represents the state abdicating its responsibility and outsourcing this policy to international funds controlled by major corporations,” he argues.

“You can no longer think in terms of public policy, at least in the area of climate finance, as if the problem were merely a lack of money. The real challenge is building a structured policy to combat climate change — something we fail to do because we are held hostage by the logic of the funds,” he says.

Regarding energy generation, among other points, Flávio Bolsonaro’s government program promises to “integrate” new renewable sources, “transform our oil and gas wealth into energy and jobs”, stimulate the modernisation of oil refining, encourage transport to Brazil’s centre-west region via “modes cheaper than trucking”, and favour domestic fertiliser production using gas “to reduce the foreign dependency that weakens agribusiness and our food security”.

Lula’s program, in turn, states that a new Workers’ Party administration will continue to increase the use of renewable energy and accelerate “the progressive replacement of fossil fuels with biofuels and low-carbon fuels, including hydrogen-based ones”.

It also says it will continue participating in international conversations to create a global roadmap away from fossil fuels. On the other hand, the text celebrates the resumption of investments in oil and gas and the successive production records broken by Petrobras.

For Andrea Camurça, coordinator of the Terramar Institute, an NGO defending the rights of traditional peoples and communities in Ceará’s coastal zone, the energy plan presented by the incumbent president’s campaign reflects the policies adopted during his administration.

“At the same time that we see the advance of renewable energy, we see the continuation and expansion of fossil fuel exploration, as is the case in the basin of the mouth of the Amazon River,” she says. “There is even a dispute over the area, whether it should be used for oil exploration, the installation of offshore wind turbines, or even mining.”

Camurça sees a significant contradiction between the expansion and diversification of renewable energy in Brazil, and the fact that it is largely allocated to major industrial projects. She points out that while low-income families spend a significant portion of their budgets on energy, the state subsidises it for the implementation of projects such as data centres, facilities essential for technologies like artificial intelligence.

“When we talk about the need to consider the energy transition, it cannot focus solely on replacing fossil fuels with renewable energy. We have to rethink this capitalist, consumerist society. If we continue on this path, who will actually suffer the most?” she asks.

[Republished with permission from Panamerican Dispatch. This article first appeared in Le Monde Diplomatique Brasil and can be read in its original Portuguese here.]

author: Jordan Humphreys
title: Germany’s far right surges
content:
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) made significant gains in several state elections across Germany in September. In Saxony-Anhalt, the party won a frightening 44 percent of the vote and fell just three seats short of forming government. Two weeks later, it won 38 percent in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, doubling its vote share from the previous election. Even in liberal, multicultural Berlin, the AfD vote went from 9 percent to 16 percent.

The results have sent political shockwaves across not just across Germany but the whole of Europe. It is no wonder why. The AfD is on the extreme wing of the broader far-right surge worldwide. Founded in 2013 as a Eurosceptic opposition to Chancellor Angela Merkel’s bailouts of the Greek government, the party has moved radically to the right over the last decade.

Today, the AfD calls for mass deportations and a strict blood-based concept of German citizenship, while opposing the right to political asylum. It also campaigns for separate schools for the children of migrants. The party also argues that focusing on the crimes of the Nazi period encourages national humiliation and therefore opposes Holocaust memorials. In 2023, AfD leaders attended a secret meeting in Potsdam with wealthy donors and prominent neo-Nazis to develop a plan to expel from the country millions of migrants and refugees and hundreds of thousands of German citizens of non-German background.

The AfD is riddled with veteran neo-Nazis. While the party initially placed barriers on fascists joining, these have been loosened as the AfD has moved further right. Björn Höcke, leader of the AfD in the eastern state of Thuringia, has been a key figure driving this shift. Prior to his public rise with the AfD, Höcke wrote articles under the pseudonym “Landolf Ladig” for neo-Nazi publications, praising Hitler and the Nazi regime. 

At campaign speeches, Höcke has repeatedly used the slogan “everything for Germany”, which was the official motto of the Nazi paramilitary wing (the 

Sturmabteilung

, known as the Brownshirts or Storm Troopers). In an infamous 2017 speech in Dresden, Höcke sparked outrage by calling the Holocaust Memorial in Berlin a “memorial of shame”. The AfD branches in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern are closely associated with Höcke’s faction in the party.

A 2024 investigative report by Bavarian Radio found that AfD parliamentarians employ more than 100 individuals with ties to far-right extremist organisations. Numerous former activists and staff from the National Democratic Party—an openly neo-Nazi party since renamed The Homeland—are employed as strategy writers, social media managers and advisors. The AfD’s youth wing is effectively controlled by Nazis.

The AfD is so extreme that other European far-right leaders like France’s Marine Le Pen, Italy’s Giorgia Meloni and Britain’s Nigel Farage have broken ties with the party, expelling it from their European Parliament coalition. However, the Trump administration and Elon Musk in the US and the Putin regime in Russia are all friendly with the AfD.

While the AfD has been gaining ground for some years, the latest results are a significant step forward and confirm that, despite the ebb in support for some figures like Trump, the fascist right has firmly entrenched itself as a permanent feature of contemporary capitalist politics across the globe.

That the AfD is so extreme only reinforces the seriousness of the situation. It also raises the question of why people in Germany, after the experiences of the Nazi period, would support such a filthy, bigoted party.

The primary driver behind the AfD’s rise has been the collapsing social base of the traditional parties in the German government. In a story repeated across the world, decades of support for neoliberal economics and centrist politics by the centre-right and centre-left have alienated millions of people from the establishment parties. The shift to the right in mainstream German politics in recent years has created plenty of kindling for the AfD fire to burn.

After all, it was not the AfD that invented the demonisation of Muslims and Arabs in Germany. Both the centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU) and the Social Democratic Party (SPD) have stoked racism for years, promoting harsher border control regulations and punishing refugees and migrants in the process. A key turning point came when Angela Merkel surprisingly allowed more than 1 million Syrian refugees into Germany in 2015. In the aftermath of a racist backlash, the political establishment has mostly criticised the decision, legitimising the anti-refugee rhetoric of the AfD.

The centre-right CDU has bled the most support to the AfD, losing around a million voters to the far-right party in the last two election cycles. The AfD has skilfully won over the most rabidly racist right-wing voters who feel the CDU has been too moderate. However, as the AfD has grown, it has also broken away larger numbers of non-aligned voters and supporters of other parties such as the SPD.

In Saxony-Anhalt the AfD won a large proportion of working-class voters. Sixty-one percent of manual workers and labourers voted for the party, according to a post-election analysis by Democrata. It also found that 46 percent of office workers and 65 percent of voters who self-reported as poor or being in a negative financial situation voted for the AfD. While working-class support for the AfD is higher in eastern states such as Saxony-Anhalt, the party has also made inroads into traditional SPD-voting working-class suburbs in western Germany.

The SPD’s eroding social base has undoubtedly facilitated this growth in far-right support among working-class voters. This has been fuelled by the SPD’s embrace of “economic reforms” that punished workers and enriched German corporations. In particular, the SPD’s implementation of harsh labour laws and welfare cuts in the early 2000s fractured working-class loyalty.

In the face of this social demoralisation and the fraying of left-wing working-class loyalties, the AfD can get away with the lie that it is an anti-establishment force defending the interests of ordinary people against the elites.

This is not to say that the AfD is winning support on an economically populist basis. While the AfD has undoubtedly fed off the demoralisation produced by years of neoliberalism, it has pretty stock-standard, pro-free-market conservative economic positions not dissimilar to the Liberal Party in Australia. Much of the criticism of the establishment parties focuses on their supposed abandonment of good patriotic Germans for evil Islamic foreigners.

With the retreat of class politics and organisation in Germany—a pattern repeated elsewhere—it is not surprising that many people now support parties whose electoral appeal has little to do with their class interests. This also elevates the issues related to race, migration and law and order in the popular consciousness. Many working-class voters for the AfD either support or don’t seem to mind that the party supports classical free-market, anti-working-class policies.

Germany’s 

Mittelstand

—small- and medium-sized businesses, family-owned businesses, independent tradespeople and self-employed professionals—also remains a large part of the AfD’s base. This is especially true in the eastern states, where middle-class support for the AfD often equals or exceeds working-class support. Many small business owners would classify themselves as financially struggling and attack the CDU for backing away from more extreme free-market policies.

While the AfD’s electoral breakthroughs have shocked much of the European political world, the responses are unlikely to stop its continued rise. The CDU and the SPD remain committed to corporate tax cuts, reduced social spending and other attacks on workers. They continue to chase the AfD to the right on anti-migrant racism. The CDU faces huge pressure to end its policy of refusing to work closely with the AfD.

The electoral victory of The Left party in the Berlin elections, and the recent history of anti-AfD protests involving tens of thousands, show there are opportunities to build a fightback. However, the proposals by The Left leaders for a united bloc of all non-AfD parties is a dead end. While this might block the AfD from forming government in the short term, it will likely just reinforce the AfD’s narrative that it is the only true anti-establishment opposition. If the German socialist left is going to defeat the AfD, it will have to take a radically different approach. But time is running out.

author: Deaglan Godwin
title: Student Union independence under threat at Sydney University
content:
The University of Sydney has announced its intention to intervene in the student union and potentially undermine democratic elections.

The announcement follows a controversy, concocted by the right-wing Murdoch media, about an election ticket contesting this year’s Students’ Representative Council election. The ticket, called Globalise the Intifada, drew hysterical condemnation from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, federal Education Minister Jason Clare and a spokesperson for NSW Premier Chris Minns. Albanese told Sydney’s 

Daily Telegraph

 the slogan “is an absolute outrage that has no place in Australia”. 

Vice-chancellor Mark Scott and chancellor David Thodey joined the chorus of condemnation. 

In a statement released on 29 September

, they said: “We deplore the manipulation of the recent election campaign to spread hurtful and distressing language across campus”. 

The university also said it will commission an independent review of the SRC’s “current affiliation and funding arrangements ... to ensure compliance with legal, regulatory, and psychosocial safety requirements”. The review will also focus on student and staff codes of conduct and on campus security. 

Behind closed doors, Scott and Thodey floated even more drastic measures. A source present at last week’s University Senate meeting 

told 

Honi Soit

, the student newspaper, that Scott raised the possibility of the university taking control of student elections and conducting them online. A university spokesperson refused to answer 

Honi Soit

’s questions about the discussions. 

The university’s investigation rests on the spurious claim that phrases in support of Palestine, such as “globalise the intifada” and “from the XXXX to the sea”, threaten the safety of Jewish people. 

In Arabic, “intifada” simply means “shaking off” or “uprising”. It commonly refers to the First and Second Intifadas, mass movements of Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank against Israeli apartheid and settler-colonialism. The phrase denotes the steadfast resistance of the Palestinians to decades of ethnic cleansing and apartheid. 

Governments, corporate media and university managers spend huge amounts of time and energy painting these phrases as calls to violence. Meanwhile, they turn a blind eye to the very real violence that Israel is committing in Gaza and the West Bank. New satellite imagery of the city of Rafah in Gaza illustrates the scale of Israel’s assault. Before 2023, the city looked like any other: houses, public squares, parks. Today, the city is a wasteland, all the buildings reduced to rubble. 

Our government and our universities are complicit in this violence. Many universities maintain research partnerships with weapons companies that sell arms to Israel and conduct exchange programs with Israeli universities. Yet we are expected to believe that student activists campaigning against racism and genocide are the violent actors!

These attacks on student political organising don’t come from nowhere. This confected crisis is taking place in the context of the sham royal commission into antisemitism. Vice-chancellors grovelled before the commissioner as they were grilled about why they allowed Palestine solidarity protests on their campuses. The conflation of anti-Zionism with antisemitism has been a constant of the entire affair. 

Universities are under significant pressure from both the government and pro-Israel organisations to clamp down on free speech and solidarity activism on campus. This aligns with their own self-interest in squashing mounting criticism of their complicity in Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and their desire to attract funding from arms companies and the broader corporate sector, which by and large supports Western imperialism and Israel. 

Widespread hostility to university ties to Israel among students and staff has been on display recently at Sydney University. The controversy around the ticket has distracted from the fact that the election also included a referendum on the administration’s complicity in Israel’s genocide. More than 4,000 students voted, and an overwhelming 92 percent of students voted in favour of breaking the university’s ties with arms companies and Israeli institutions.

Anyone who supports Palestine, who supports student unionism or who supports freedom of speech must speak out against Sydney University’s recent decision.

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: On the campaign trail with Victorian Socialists
content:
“We need Jasmine in parliament!”, called out Abdul. He runs Konjo, an Ethiopian cafe in Footscray. He’d just let us use the cafe as a backdrop for a promotional video we were making for the Victorian Socialists’ state election campaign. I’m running as the party’s candidate for the Western Metropolitan upper house region, and the cafe is adorned with a huge picture of Jasmine Duff, our candidate for Footscray. It is one of hundreds of campaign signs on front fences and on stakes in people’s front yards across the electorate. 

Since the last federal election, it feels like support for Victorian Socialists has grown. Back then, Jasmine was the candidate for the federal seat of Fraser—encompassing Footscray and suburbs to the west and south, including Yarraville, Sunshine and St Albans. At the booth I staffed, and have done for the last few election cycles, she received more than 20 percent of the vote. In Seddon, the booth at the scout hall recorded 18 percent for Jasmine. 

Near that scout hall, I recently met a woman who had always voted Green. She told me she had volunteered with Sea Shepherd in her youth and cared deeply about the environment, as well as sexism in our society. We talked about how society is getting worse. We talked about the fear of heading into an El Niño at the same time as the government has just fast-tracked the development of the NextDC hyperscale data centre up the road, which stores millions of litres of fuel and can act as a heat pump, warming the surrounding area by several degrees. I ended the conversation with an iced tea to quell the coughing fit I’d gotten from the surrounding plane trees. She was excited to talk to me, and ready to vote socialist for the first time. 

Conversations like this are happening not just in Footscray but across Melbourne’s west. In Braybrook, I knocked on Helena’s door. Her front yard was an oasis compared to the dry and hot suburban street. I spied orchids, ferns and other luscious plants. When I said that politics was rigged for the rich, Helena replied: “It always has been. The rich get richer and the poor get poorer”. Helena is a Maltese woman in her 70s. She arrived in Australia in the 1970s, and spoke about the trials of being a working-class migrant. She asked how she could help us. Later that week Van, the VS candidate for Laverton, went back and put a campaign sign on her front fence. 

In Sunshine West, I met a young Bangladeshi student, Julfiqar. He can’t vote because he isn’t a citizen. This is a common interaction and always feels unjust. People live and work here but are denied a basic democratic right. We chatted anyway, because he has a keen interest in politics and wanted to know what we stand for. He’s a student at Swinburne University and has interacted with the socialist club there. We talked about the campaign my comrades were involved in there to stop the university from interfering in who would be the imam for Friday prayers. The university had intervened because the imam spoke about Palestine—a step too far, apparently. Julfiqar was also passionate about the student protests in Bangladesh in 2024 that ended the sixteen-year rule of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. At the end of the conversation, despite not being able to vote for us, Julfiqar wanted to help. He agreed to put up Van’s sign on his front fence. 

In Altona, part of the Williamstown electorate, I spoke to a woman who works at Victoria University. She expressed horror at the rise of Pauline Hanson and One Nation. When I explained that our candidate, Oskar Martin, also worked at VU in the Aboriginal Archives with Gary Foley, her face lit up. It isn’t often that you get an opportunity to vote for a young Aboriginal man who wouldn’t be afraid to stand up to Hanson, and he’s also your workmate. We talked about racism, but also the way that people are just struggling to get by. The cost of everything has gone up, as have billionaires’ profits. The only thing that seems to be going backwards is our wages. 

A sense of struggling just to get by is the common denominator in most of our campaigners’ conversations. Even those who feel a bit more secure or better off are worried about those around them. 

In Seddon, I spoke to a couple, Jasmine and Tom, who said they had been discussing the Victorian Socialists’ campaign with their friends the night before. We’re impossible to ignore, as we have hundreds of signs up in the area. Among many topics, one we kept coming back to was the narrative of the inner west being pushed by the government, the opposition and the media—that Footscray is a crime hotspot and the solution is more police. 

Jasmine and Tom were appalled by the mainstream political conversation around this issue and wanted to know what we had to say. I argued that an approach of sending in more cops won’t solve any issues for people facing homelessness in Footscray. More likely it will inflame the situation. What we need instead is more housing. The Victorian Socialists’ policy is to build 150,000 new, high-quality public housing units across the state over the next ten years. We also need an injection of money into social services, like drug counselling and mental health. We don’t think we can solve these issues on an individual basis. Long-term solutions require changing how we organise society and its priorities. We think we need a society that puts people first, before business profits and the profit motive in general. 

Jasmine and Tom agreed and were happy to have had a chance to talk to me. They said they hoped Jasmine and I would be elected. Like Abdul, they thought we should be in parliament because socialist politics offers answers to our society’s problems.

People have been looking to other parties, like Labor, to do something for them. But Labor has discredited itself time and time again. Many people who have been Labor supporters for decades are jumping ship to Victorian Socialists. 

One wonderful example is Catherine, a teacher, who had been a Labor member since the 1980s. Catherine is a fighter. She has spent the last few months in a poster war with a right-winger in Seddon who keeps ripping down and defacing the posters she puts up advertising VS events. Catherine left Labor after sitting on countless committees, drafting policies that were roundly ignored by those higher up in the party, and seeing Labor’s support for Israel in its ongoing genocide in Gaza. 

Catherine is the backbone of one of the local Victorian Socialists’ groups in Footscray—dubbed “south”, taking in Yarraville and Seddon. These local groups meet every Tuesday at our campaign office in central Footscray, where we plan doorknocking, letterboxing, yard sign delivery and phone banking. Across the state, hundreds of people are giving their time to our campaign. 

We want to use this state election to do a few things. 

We want to raise people’s expectations about what is possible, and what we should expect from the government. Right now, people don’t expect much because every part of life feels difficult. It has come to seem normal that most of the time, working-class people struggle to get by. We want to convince people that we can and should demand more. 

We want to build opposition to the political “centre” of Labor and the Liberals—representatives of the status quo of neoliberal capitalism that has ravaged working-class communities for decades—as well as to the far right of Pauline Hanson and One Nation. We know the far right can’t be beaten by the “politics as usual” of a Labor government that has betrayed Victorian workers in so many ways. We need an alternative that wants to smash the status quo, fight for working-class people, and directly combat the racism of the far right. That’s what the Victorian Socialists aim to provide.

We want, finally, to get socialists elected to parliament. This would be a significant step towards rebuilding the socialist movement in Australian political life. 

Beyond potentially getting socialists elected to the Victorian parliament, a big vote for the Victorian Socialists would signal that the current slide to the right isn’t inevitable. Lately, it has seemed as if the only side in politics having any successes is the pro-capitalist and racist one. Instead, we can show that there are many people who want an anti-establishment politics that resists the bosses and fights for solidarity and against racism. We want to show that the left can grow too. 

Already, more than 2,000 people have participated in the Victorian Socialists’ election campaign. That means 2,000 people doorknocking, letterboxing, putting up yard signs, making phone calls, coming along to events and more. And of course, none of this will end with the election on 28

 

November. Whatever the result, Victorian Socialists members will continue to fight for change, as we have for years through the Palestine solidarity movement, rank-and-file organising in our unions, and many other areas of work. For us, campaigning in elections is just one part of the effort to win the kind of system change we need.

author: anred
title: Fuegos sincronizados: cientos de hornos se encendieron para construir una obra colectiva
content:
Después de una videollamada que conectó a ceramistas de distintos puntos del país y del mundo, durante la noche del 26 de septiembre cientos de hornos se encendieron al mismo tiempo. Por Manuela Wilhelm (ANRed)




Mientras en cada taller la arcilla atravesaba el calor y esperaba la transformación del fuego, quienes participaban compartían imágenes, videos y mensajes desde sus propios territorios. La propuesta había nacido casi como un juego, pero terminó convirtiéndose en una enorme experiencia colectiva.




Carlos Ovando, conocido como “Lalo”

, ceramista mendocino en Tawa Taller y constructor de hornos, todavía intenta dimensionar qué fue lo que puso en movimiento. La transmisión en vivo que habían preparado terminó borrada —“no sé qué hice y lo borré todo”, cuenta entre risas—, pero eso poco importó. La experiencia quedó registrada en cada taller, en cada grupo de WhatsApp, en cada video compartido y en una cartografía que permite imaginar la dimensión que alcanzó aquella noche.




El censo elaborado por la organización reúne 

416 registros de personas, talleres o colectivos de 18 países

. Argentina concentró la mayor parte, con 318 registros, seguida por Chile y México, con 18 cada uno; Brasil, con 17; Colombia, con 12; y Perú, con 6. También hubo participación de España, Uruguay, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Paraguay, Portugal, Francia, Suecia, Japón, Taiwán, Nueva Zelanda y Estados Unidos.




No era necesario tener un horno a leña. La convocatoria estaba abierta a hornos a leña, a gas y eléctricos. La única condición era sumarse a ese gesto común: encender, hornear y acompañarse a la distancia.




Una idea que nació casi jugando




La primera chispa apareció a partir de una horneada que se iba a realizar en La Plata, en el taller de la ceramista Aluminé Fernández. Lalo, que vive en San Carlos, Mendoza, había construido allí un horno meses antes. Le escribió a su compañera para avisarle que iba a participar y, casi jugando, se le ocurrió que podía acompañarla desde Mendoza.




“Se me ocurrió que podía acompañarla de manera sincrónica. O sea, hornear simultáneamente”, cuenta.




El equipo de 

Fuegos Sincronizados

 quedó conformado por 

Lalo, Flavia Torres, Aluminé Fernández, Fernanda Guevara, Julia Spangenberg y Silvana Ruiz Charó.




La idea tampoco era completamente nueva para él. Años atrás había realizado junto a otros ceramistas mendocinos varias horneadas sincronizadas vinculadas a una muestra de esculturas en cerámica y a la noche y la luna. Eran apenas tres personas conectadas por WhatsApp o videollamada. Esta vez, sin embargo, la propuesta podía crecer.




Primero convocó a ceramistas cuyos hornos había ayudado a construir en Córdoba y Chile. Después se sumaron otras personas conocidas. La convocatoria comenzó a circular por WhatsApp hasta que una compañera de Córdoba, Julia, le propuso hacer un video y abrirla mucho más.




“

Ahí explotó todo”, recuerda.




La comunidad ceramista respondió rápidamente. El grupo de WhatsApp llegó a superar las 600 personas y fue necesario armar un pequeño equipo de organización. De allí surgió también la idea de 

construir una cartografía

 con los lugares donde se encenderían los hornos.







La iniciativa fue creciendo al mismo tiempo que se organizaba. Se creó una cuenta de Instagram, se elaboraron placas informativas y se buscó la manera de conectar a los distintos grupos. Incluso intentaron transmitir en vivo desde la nueva cuenta, pero no pudieron hacerlo por las restricciones de antigüedad de Instagram. Finalmente utilizaron la cuenta personal de Lalo y también realizaron una transmisión por Meet y YouTube.




Y aunque ese registro terminó borrado, quedaron las huellas dispersas de la experiencia: los videos de cada taller, las fotografías, los mensajes y, sobre todo, el mapa.




Un fuego que no arrasa: une




Para Lalo, allí está una de las claves de la propuesta. El fuego ocupa un lugar central en la práctica ceramista. Es el momento en que una pieza cambia definitivamente, pero también un momento íntimo, de espera y de encuentro.




“El objetivo de la sincronización era poder conectarnos y juntarnos a través del fuego”, explica.




Por eso hace una distinción: no se trata de cualquier fuego. “

No es un fuego arrasador de esos que no queremos, sino que es un fuego que une

”, dice.







Cada horno tenía sus propias características. Había hornos grandes y pequeños, hornos a leña, a gas, eléctricos y hasta hornos en pozo. Había talleres con condiciones muy diferentes, ubicados en territorios distintos y atravesados por realidades particulares. La sincronización no buscó borrar esas diferencias, sino ponerlas en relación.




La propuesta terminó haciendo posible algo que, para Lalo, es parte fundamental de la práctica artística: conocer otros talleres, otros modos de trabajar y otros territorios sin necesidad de estar físicamente allí.




“Como que abre camino también a muchas cosas”, plantea.




La obra fue encender los hornos




Con el paso de los días, entre quienes participaron comenzó a aparecer otra manera de pensar lo sucedido. Una compañera le dijo a Lalo que lo que habían hecho podía pensarse como una obra.




La idea lo interpela: la obra no sería una pieza de cerámica determinada, sino el acto colectivo de encender cientos de hornos de manera simultánea en distintos territorios.




“El impulso fue convocar. La obra fue encender los hornos de manera sincronizada o colectiva o simultánea en diferentes lugares”, explica.







Y entonces aparece también la memoria de esa obra: todos los videos, las fotografías, las publicaciones, los mensajes que circularon después de las cocciones y la cartografía que registra los lugares donde se encendieron los fuegos.




Es una manera de entender la cerámica que va más allá del objeto terminado.




“Para mí ser ceramista no es solo hacer cerámica, hacer objeto, hacer una pieza”, sostiene.







También es generar encuentros, construir hornos en conjunto, comunicarse y producir experiencias colectivas. “

Hacer cerámica también es generar estas cosas que no tienen que ver exclusivamente con hacer una obra o un objeto

”.




Del encuentro a la construcción de una comunidad




La experiencia del 26 de septiembre no surgió en un vacío. Lalo venía de participar en encuentros y de integrar espacios colectivos de ceramistas. Es parte, entre otros, de 

Ronda Sin Cabezas

, un colectivo mendocino que organiza encuentros en distintos puntos de la provincia, muchas veces buscando llegar a lugares donde el acceso a la cultura y al arte no es sencillo.




También integra 

Crece desde el pie

, un colectivo de productores de alimentos agroecológicos del Valle de Uco.




Esa experiencia previa aparece ahora en Fuegos Sincronizados: la necesidad de construir un espacio común no desde una institución centralizada, sino desde los propios talleres, territorios y vínculos entre quienes hacen cerámica.







La convocatoria comenzó con una persona invitando a otra. Después otra invitó a otra. Un video abrió la puerta a cientos. Y esos cientos terminaron formando una comunidad que, después del 26 de septiembre, todavía permanece activa.




La pregunta que queda ahora es qué hacer con ella




“Se armó una comunidad grande de más de 600 personas, entonces yo creo que podemos hacer varias cosas”, dice Lalo. Entre las posibilidades aparece repetir la experiencia el año próximo, incorporar nuevas propuestas y seguir dándole una vuelta al encuentro para que no quede reducido a una única fecha.




Sincronizarse también para defender la cultura




Hay, además, otra dimensión que atraviesa la experiencia. Para Lalo, hacer cerámica hoy implica también preguntarse por las condiciones materiales en las que se produce cultura.




Construir un horno, conseguir materiales, producir una pieza, enseñar, organizar un encuentro o sostener un taller forman parte de una economía cultural que no siempre encuentra apoyo. En un contexto que describe como de “cero cultura, cero apoyo a la cultura”, la respuesta que imagina no es individual.




“También es un desafío para nosotros, para los artistas, para la gente que hace arte en general”, plantea. Y frente a esa situación, encuentra una herramienta concreta: “

Una manera es esta: juntarse y hacer cosas de manera colectiva”.







La discusión excede entonces a la cerámica. Se trata de qué lugar ocupa la cultura artesanal, comunitaria y territorial frente a modelos que privilegian otras formas de producción y de desarrollo, mientras las comunidades reclaman poder decidir sobre sus territorios y sostener sus propias formas de vida.




En ese sentido, la sincronización adquiere otro significado. Así como los hornos se encendieron al mismo tiempo a miles de kilómetros de distancia, también puede pensarse la necesidad de sincronizar las resistencias: conectar experiencias, compartir saberes y construir redes allí donde las políticas de ajuste, extractivismo y desmantelamiento de la cultura tienden a fragmentar.







“Esto generó mucha alegría en la gente que lo iba a hacer”, cuenta Lalo. Alegría, acompañamiento, amor, la sensación de estar haciendo algo junto a otros. Para él, eso también importa.




Casi 30 años entre el barro y el fuego




Lalo hace cerámica desde hace casi 30 años. Su acercamiento comenzó en Mendoza, cuando se trasladó desde el sur de la provincia para estudiar, en una época en la que en su zona no había universidades ni institutos terciarios.




Unos amigos que tenían un taller de cerámica y estudiaban la carrera en la Facultad de Artes de la Universidad Nacional de Cuyo lo acercaron a ese mundo. Se inscribió en la carrera, cursó durante tres o cuatro años, aunque no llegó a terminarla, y desde entonces no dejó de formarse. Más adelante estudió una tecnicatura en el instituto Condorhuasi, en Buenos Aires, y continuó aprendiendo junto a otros ceramistas.




Pero hubo un momento que marcó definitivamente su vínculo con el oficio: la crisis de 2000. “Lo que más me marcó fue la crisis del 2000. Entonces en ese momento tuve que empezar a hacer producción para vivir de la cerámica”, cuenta.







A partir de allí comenzó a hornear a leña y profundizó una formación que le permitió ganar autonomía: aprendió a construir hornos, a elaborar sus propios esmaltes y sus propias pastas y a buscar materiales disponibles cerca de los lugares donde trabajaba, en lugar de depender de comprarlos. Con el tiempo construyó hornos más eficientes, incorporó materiales refractarios y avanzó hacia cocciones de mayor temperatura. Hoy trabaja con gres y porcelana a leña.




Su práctica se fue ampliando mucho más allá de la producción de objetos. Hace vajilla, esculturas y murales; participa de muestras individuales y colectivas; construye hornos y da clases de cerámica en una escuela de arte del Valle de Uco, en Tunuyán.




También forma parte de colectivos de ceramistas y de productores de alimentos agroecológicos, espacios desde los que sostiene una idea de la cerámica vinculada al encuentro, al territorio y a la construcción colectiva. “Disfruto mucho de estar haciendo cerámica”, dice. Y en esa frase parece condensar casi tres décadas de un oficio que, para él, nunca terminó de ser solamente un trabajo: también fue una forma de aprender, producir, enseñar y construir comunidad.

title: Altın Koza’dan yükselen toplumsal muhalefet enerjisi
content:
33. Uluslararası Adana Altın Koza Film Festivali’nde ödüller sahiplerini bulurken, kapanış gecesine yalnızca yarışan filmler ve oyuncuların başarıları değil, ödül alanların ve verenlerin kürsüde  sinemanın ve sinemacıların dünyanın değişmesinde üstleneceği rolün önemini vurgulayan sözleri de damgasını vurdu.




33. Altın Koza'da büyük ödül Ali Vatansever’in yönettiği “Bir Arada Yalnız” filminin oldu. Vatansever aynı filmle En İyi Yönetmen ödülünü alırken, Fatih Al  da En İyi Erkek Oyuncu seçildi. En İyi Kadın Oyuncu ödülünü “Mutter: Bir Annenin Hatıra Defteri”ndeki oyunculuğu ile Hazar Ergüçlü aldı.




Banu Sıvacı’nın “Günyüzü” filmi Yılmaz Güney Ödülü’ne, Miraç Atabey’in “Moda Evlilik” filmi Kadir Beycioğlu Jüri Özel Ödülü’ne değer görülürken Adana İzleyici Ödülü Tunç Şahin’in “Canavar” filmine verildi. En İyi Senaryo Ödülü “Karanlıkta Islık Çalanlar” ile Pınar Yorgancıoğlu ve Emre Gülcan’ın oldu. 




Çukurova Üniversitesi Kongre Merkezi’nde yapılan Büyük Kapanış ve Ödül Töreni’ni Jülide Ateş ve Volkan Severcan sundu. Ulusal Uzun Metraj Film Yarışması jürisine Zuhal Olcay başkanlık etti. 







33. Adana Altın Koza Uluslararası Film Festivali'nde 

ödül alanlar 

kapanışta bir arada 







Ergüçlü: “Biz adaletsizlikle mi yaşayacağız?”




Ödül töreninde gecenin en güçlü konuşmalarından biri En İyi Kadın Oyuncu ödülünü alan Hazar Ergüçlü’den geldi.




Ergüçlü, “kendin olmanın böylesine tehlikeli olduğu, hatta yasaklanmaya çalışıldığı” bir dönemden geçildiğini söyledi; ardından sözü Soma’daki son maden kazasında yaşamını yitiren 37 yaşındaki Kerim Ören’in oğlu Yaşar’a getirdi.




Ergüçlü büyükannesi ve büyükbabasının madenci olduğunu aktardı ve şöyle dedi:







Benim nenem, dedem kömür işçisiydi. Dedem bakır madeninde çalıştı. Her madenci gördüğümde gözümün önüne kendi dedem, kendi nenem geliyor. İnsanca yaşayabilmek için, çocuklarını okutabilmek için verdikleri emek geliyor.




Madenci çocuklarını ağlarken gördüğümde ben yaşamaktan, aldığım nefesten utanıyorum. Bunu vicdanımı rahatlatmak veya bir şeyin sözcüsü olmak niyetiyle de yapmıyorum şu an. Sadece bu adaletsizlikler bana fazla geliyor ve ne yaparsam yapayım bu üzüntüyü içimden atamıyorum







Ergüçlü, konuşmasını umudu bırakmama çağrısıyla bitirdi: “Elimizde bir tek umudumuz kaldı. Onu da vermeyeceğiz.” 




“İçeride ve dışarıda olan dostlarımızla”




“Bir Arada Yalnız” ile Umut Veren Genç Erkek Oyuncu Ödülü’nü alan Onur Gözeten ise konuşmasını cezaevindekilere uzattı:




“İçeride ve dışarıda olan dostlarımızla film yapmaya devam ederiz.”




Ödül konuşmalarında tutuklu sinemacı Çiğdem Mater’in yanı sıra Selçuk Kozağaçlı, Can Atalay ve Berkin Elvan’ın adları da anıldı.




Festivalin toplumsal mesajları ana yarışmayla da sınırlı kalmadı. Ulusal Öğrenci Filmleri Yarışması’nda Deneysel Jüri Özel Ödülü’nü “Islak Köpekler” ile alan Metin Konar, ödülünü Filistin’de öldürülenlere ve “haksız yere gözaltında tutulan translara” adadı. Kurmaca Jüri Özel Ödülü’nü alan “Uslu”nun ödülü ise “sesi duyulmayan, yaşam hakkı elinden alınan çocuklara” ithaf edildi. 

l




Vatansever: “Yalnız olabilirsiniz ama çaresiz değilsiniz”




Geceden En İyi Film ve En İyi Yönetmen ödülleriyle ayrılan Ali Vatansever de yönetmenlik ödülünü öğrencilerine adadı.




Sinemaya yeni başlayanlara seslenen Vatansever:




“Yalnız olabilirsiniz ama çaresiz değilsiniz.”dedi.




Genç sinemacıları kendisine ulaşmaya çağıran Vatansever, En İyi Film ödülünü alırken de ödülü “tüm dünya yanarken iyi kalanlar” için aldığını söyledi.




Plastik atık ithalatı da kürsüdeydi




Sinema Yazarları Derneği (SİYAD) Cüneyt Cebenoyan En İyi Film Ödülü’nü “Ölü Köpekler Isırmaz” ile alan Nuri Cihan Özdoğan, Adana çevresindeki plastik atık sorununu gündeme getirdi:




“Dilerim ki bu atık ithalatı son bulur.”




Plastik atık sorunu festivalin önceki etkinliklerinde de gündeme gelmişti.




Olcay: “Sinema bakış açılarını değiştirir.."




Ulusal Uzun Metraj Film Yarışması Jüri Başkanı Zuhal Olcay ise yarışan filmlerin ardındaki emeğe ve cesarete dikkat çekti ve sinemanın toplumsal etkisine işaret etti:







“Sinema dünyayı değiştirmez belki ama bakış açılarını değiştirir ve bu da dünyanın değişmesi demektir; yaşasın sinema!”







Onur ve Emek Ödülleri




Festivalin açılışında verilen emek ve onur ödülleri kapanış gecesinin habercisiydi aslında. 26 Eylül’deki açılış gecesinde Orhan Kemal Emek Ödülleri Suna Selen, Macit Koper ve Aydın Sayman’ın oldu. 1 Ekim’de ayrı bir törenle Onur Ödülleri Ferzan Özpetek ve Vahide Perçin'e sunuldu.
