title: Transmisión en vivo, 18:00 horas y palabras del Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés en la reunión del 3 de octubre del 2026 a las 1100 hrs.
content:
TRANSMISIÓN EN VIVO 18:00 HORAS | SÁBADO 3 DE OCTUBRE

Sesión Informativa sobre el Viaje-Abrazo a Buscador@s, diciembre 2026-Enero 2027 CIDECI de San Cristóbal de Las Casas, Chiapas, México

Sesión Informativa sobre el Viaje-Abrazo a Buscador@s, diciembre 2026-Enero 2027 CIDECI de San Cristóbal de Las Casas, Chiapas, México Sesión 13:00 HORAS | SÁBADO 3 DE OCTUBRE

Palabras del Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés en la reunión del 3 de octubre del 2026 a las 1100 hrs.

.- El principal objetivo: el encuentro-abrazo con buscadoras. Es importante que esto se entienda bien y quede bien claro. Porque no vamos a cancelar una reunión o actividad con Buscadoras por cualquier otra cosa.

Llevamos muchos años esperando el momento de encontrarnos con ellas.

Entonces, la prioridad o lo más importante en nuestra agenda o programación son las reuniones, encuentros y actividades con las Buscadoras, el día y la hora que ellas establezcan.

Cualquiera otra propuesta de actividad o reunión, deberá ser cuando no haya encuentro o actividad con buscadoras.

Incluso la celebración del aniversario del alzamiento será dependiendo de nuestro abrazo con las Buscadoras.

.- Ya está la paga para los buses de la delegación. Se consiguió gracias al apoyo de la Europa Insumisa, que donó lo que se había juntado para el Capítulo Europa de la Gira por la Vida, y que no se usó completamente. Estas compañeras, compañeros y compañeroas nos dijeron, desde hace tiempo, que esa paga es de los zapatistas, pero, hay que decirlo, es producto de su trabajo, su esfuerzo y su dedicación, y hay que reconocerles esa solidaridad incondicional. Esperamos que ese ejemplo sea luego replicado en capítulos siguientes de la Gira por la Vida, de modo que cada capítulo apoye la realización del siguiente.

Mientras tanto, aquí reconocemos el trabajo desinteresado de todas las personas, grupo, colectivos, organizaciones y movimientos de la Europa de abajo y a la izquierda.

También ha sido fundamental el trabajo de apoyo del colectivo de la Sexta México. “Mujeres y la Sexta”, para conseguir los autobuses.

Gracias compañeras, compañeros y compañeroas. A las Buscadoras les haremos saber de su apoyo.

.- Por lo tanto, toda la campaña económica será ahora para apoyar el traslado de todos los grupos, colectivas y organizaciones posibles a la Ciudad de México, en las fechas que les parezcan más adecuadas a ellas, dentro del mes de diciembre del 2026 y la primera semana de enero del 2027.

En el caso de amenazas y peligros, se tratará de que su traslado ida y vuelta sea por vía aérea, de modo que no corran riesgos al transportarse por tierra.

.- Les vamos a quedar mal porque no vamos a ir 1,111, sino que hasta ahora van 1,509. Más los que se suben de última hora. Pero hay lugar para el Frayba por si quieren acompañarnos.

.- el segundo objetivo es reunirnos con algunos grupos, colectivos, movimientos y organizaciones de la Sexta para planear juntos, en común, lo que sea posible para la segunda etapa de la Gira por la Vida-Capítulo México.

Esto es, cuando vamos a ir a escucharles de lo que son y están haciendo, y hablarles de lo que somos y estamos haciendo, o sea del común.

.- Si hay tiempo y modo, podemos movernos a lugares cercanos geográficamente a la Ciudad de México.

Pero sólo si hay condiciones y somos invitados. Hasta ahora hemos recibido invitación a Oaxaca, Oaxaca; a Querétaro, Querétaro, y se está viendo si a Puebla, Puebla. Si es posible en otros lugares, hay que organizarse y proponer.

Las compañeras de Oaxaca empezaron a organizarse desde que se anunció la salida a la Ciudad de México. Tienen ya resuelto el hospedaje y la alimentación para un parte de la delegación zapatista.

.- Estamos organizados por equipos y podemos cubrir bien lo que se haga en el Valle de México y hacer presencia en geografías cercanas. Así, dislocados, podríamos cubrir al mismo tiempo varios lugares, y varios temas.

.- Van más de 300 teatristas con 3 obras de teatro: Bichos, Agüitas y El Común en el día después. Por si alguien quiere presentar las obras o alguna de ellas en los lugares convenientes, resolviendo lo del traslado, que en la Ciudad de México suele ser un problema.

.- la fecha de salida del CIDECI es la madrugada del domingo 29 de noviembre, dependiendo de la hora en que recomienden los hermanos choferólogos de las empresas que han tenido a bien rentarnos los más de 31 autobuses que se utilizarían. Hemos elegido ese día, por si alguien de la Ciudad de México o de puntos aledaños y de Chiapas, que quiera acompañar el trayecto de ida, no se vea afectado en su trabajo.

.- Calculamos que el regreso sería el domingo 10 de enero, aunque falta precisar más eso.

.- Los lugares a los que hay que dirigirse para participar como Buscadoras, para proponer actividades y para donar paga para el traslado de las Buscadoras, son los que ya saben del Frayba, de la RUA y la cuenta de “Llegó la Hora”.

.- La base operativa de la delegación, esto es, su lugar de hospedaje y de las reuniones que sean posibles, será en la Casa de los Pueblos Samir Flores Soberanes, con la comunidad compañera Otomí en la Ciudad de México.

.- Mucho ojo: puesto que ya se entró en el fraudulento proceso electoral del 2027, en el que un grupo de criminales se disputa el poder político con otros grupos de criminales, es de esperar que alguno o alguna de esos malandros y malandras quiera sacar provecho del dolor, la lucha y la persistencia de los encuentros con Buscadoras.

O de que se imponga un silencio mediático y el supremo gobierno recurra a su ridícula cantaleta de “conservadores”, “derechistas”, y “fuerzas extranjeras queriendo desestabilizar a la inefable 4T”.

Entonces hay que estar atentos. Debemos garantizarles a las Buscadoras que su dolor y su empeño heroico no sea usado para nada que no decidan ellas libre y voluntariamente.

Si no permitiremos que las fuerzas electorales ensucien su labor aprovechando nuestra visita y nuestro abrazo, tampoco permitiremos que, con ese motivo, causa o razón, personas, grupos, colectivos, organizaciones y movimientos de la Sexta Nacional e Internacional, y de la Declaración por la Vida, usen esos encuentros para promover agendas propias políticas y sociales.

Si algo deberíamos hacer como la Sexta en México, es pedir disculpas a las Buscadoras por poco o nada hacer en todos estos años en los que han cargado su dolor a cuestas. Y mientras tanto, algunos, algunas y algunoas de la Sexta corrieron a refugiarse en cargos gubernamentales convirtiéndose así en cómplices de ese crimen de Estado que es la desaparición forzada y el asesinato de inocentes. Su radicalidad e intransigencia duró lo que se tarda en incorporarles a la nómina gubernamental.

Mientras otras personas de la Sexta, a pesar de decirse de abajo y a la izquierda, se veían el ombligo y se consideraban demasiado revolucionarios para tender a la mano no a quien está lejos, en las montañas del sureste mexicano o en Palestina, sino a quien vive, lucha y muere en sus mismas geografías. No pocas veces en la misma ciudad, el mismo barrio, la misma calle.

Convirtieron así una posición política en una pose para consumo local o hasta familiar.

Sin embargo, también hay quien entendió que abajo y a la izquierda no es ser un grupo de apoyo o un comité de solidaridad con los pueblos zapatistas, sino un compromiso permanente en la lucha contra el sistema y en apoyo a todas las luchas que se resisten y rebelan contra las múltiples cabezas de la Hidra capitalista.

Cada quien su modo, su calendario y su geografía, así hemos dicho una y otra vez, y así vivimos como zapatistas que somos.

Quienes se dicen revolucionarios radicales o no tan radicales, al menos deberían tener la vergüenza y la dignidad de reconocer que toda esta pesadilla es en parte por nuestra responsabilidad.

Todos, todas, todoas cargamos nuestras propias pesadillas, sufrimos nuestros propios dolores, enfrentamos nuestras propias dificultades y obstáculos. Pero eso no nos da derecho a ignorar y hacer oídos sordos a los llantos, los reclamos y las exigencias de quienes pierden parte de su vida por la ausencia de una persona cercana, sin la posibilidad siquiera de saber si está viva o muerta.

No imaginamos, aunque la crueldad del sistema capitalista no tiene límites, un dolor más grande que el de la angustia de no saber; la incertidumbre y la desazón de cada día esperar la aparición y vuelta de quien falta, así sea en pedazos de huesos y ropas desgarradas.

Y aun así, de ese dolor nacer como comunidad, buscarse entre sí, buscar dolores semejantes, que es también decir esperanzas iguales.

Así sea el despojo y el desprecio que viven los pueblos originarios, la explotación que padecen trabajadores de todas las ramas, las agresiones físicas y verbales en razón de género o de no género, las injusticias cotidianas del común de la gente, la popularidad o no de causas nobles en geografías cercanas o lejanas, la necesidad indiscutible de la solidaridad con el pueblo Palestino o con el pueblo Cubano o con el pueblo en turno en las amenazas del Mandón.

O los sufrimientos y angustias de la clase política que repite la cantaleta de corrupción impune de sus antecesores.

Nada de eso iguala, así sea lo mínimo, al dolor de las Buscadoras. Y pocos, muy pocos, pueden siquiera semejarse a su empeño, su lucha, su compromiso, su persistencia.

Tenemos que hacer algo y no ya sólo el abrazo pendiente, que tiene mucho de agradecimiento y de pedir disculpas a las Buscadoras.

Tenemos que hacer algo más. Al menos, hacerles saber que estamos a su lado y de su lado, que no es lo mismo, pero es igual.

Cada quien según su calendario, su geografía, sus modos y sus ni modos, debiera encontrar la forma de que esto no sea un evento coyuntural.

Algo pasajero como pudo ser la Otra Campaña, la marcha del color de la tierra, la consulta de los 5 mil, la marcha de los 1,111, la salida de la Comandanta Ramona o el alzamiento indígena iniciado el primero de enero de 1994, gestado siglos antes, y que aún ahora, casi 33 años después, sigue buscando al otro diferente pero semejante en dolor y en resistencia y rebeldía.

Y lo seguimos buscando para echar trato, para organizarnos sin dejar de ser lo que somos cada quien, sin renunciar a la identidad, a la historia propia.

Porque eso y no otra cosa es la Gira por la Vida. No para buscar hegemonía, no para imponer homogeneidad, sino para reconocer la riqueza de nuestras diferencias y la similitud de nuestros dolores.

En los tiempos actuales, toda lucha por la vida es una lucha antisistema.

Nosotros, como pueblos zapatistas organizados que somos, hemos puesto nuestra mira doble en dos objetivos:

En lo interno, la construcción del común con el día después en el horizonte.

En lo externo, el acompañamiento, así sea a la distancia, a las buscadoras. Hacerles saber que su dolor es el nuestro, que compartimos la necia esperanza que les anima, y que el encuentro en que culminará su búsqueda será celebrado no sólo en sus hogares con sus familias, en sus grupos, colectivas, organizaciones, movimientos y redes. También será celebrado en un rincón lejano en geografía, pero cercano en humanidad. Y, así, en las comunidades zapatistas de las montañas del sureste mexicano sonreiremos con su triunfo y será también nuestro sin que deje de ser suyo.

Y esto, compas de la Sexta y de la Vida, es lo que quiere decir: “Todas las luchas y una demanda en común: Verdad y Justicia para las Ausencias”.

Ahí lo vean. Si se creen solos y pequeños, díganselo a la mujer que busca a su marido, a su hijo, a su hija, a su hermano, a su hermana. Y que busca, sola, con un pico y una pala si tiene suerte, con las uñas si no la tiene, porque siente que es su deber buscar, porque sabe que esa ausencia espera que la busquen y que la encuentren.

Si tienen lástima de sí mismos, pues claro les decimos que se equivocaron de canal y que en la Sexta y en la Vida no encontrarán lástima ni consuelo, sino compromiso.

author: Neha Madhira
title: Austin Communities Rally Around Victim of ICE Shooting as He Faces Criminal Charges
content:
Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez appeared in court in a wheelchair Wednesday, the bullet still lodged in his spine.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Federal prosecutors in Texas charged a Venezuelan national and father living in Austin on Tuesday with assaulting, resisting, and impeding a federal officer, after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) sideswiped his car and shot him in the back Sept. 20 without warning as he was turning around to park.

Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, entered the U.S. in 2024 with a valid work permit to seek asylum and provide for his son in Venezuela, who has mobility disabilities that require expensive physical therapy, through a program begun under former President Joe Biden. However, President Donald Trump ended the program on his first day in office. According to Garcés Pérez’s lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, a judge issued a deportation order after he missed an immigration court hearing because the notice was sent to a former address.

At his detention hearing on the criminal charges on Sept. 30, a judge ruled that Garcés Pérez will remain detained because he is a “flight risk” and that the government has probable cause to continue the criminal case.

Garcés Pérez was delivering for DoorDash in North Austin last week when ICE agents ran his license plate and began to follow him. He then called his wife at around 12:30 p.m. to let her know he had been shot. Community member Toast Lopez, who was walking home on the same route, told Prism that he heard gunshots and ran over to see if anyone needed assistance.

“That was when I saw them pulling [Garcés Pérez] out of the car as soon as I got over here, and when I crossed the street to help, that’s when an [ICE] agent pointed the gun at me,” Lopez said.

“Next thing I knew, the whole community had pulled up, and we were all yelling and screaming, protesting almost immediately because, you know, this is our place. These are our people.”

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Garcés Pérez was taken in an ambulance to the Dell Seton Medical Center — where his wife and Lincoln-Goldfinch were not allowed to see him — before being taken back into ICE custody. Court filings from Lincoln-Goldfinch’s team state that he was forced to sleep on a cement floor at an ICE temporary processing center that night and then was transported to the South Texas ICE Processing Facility in Pearsall at 4 a.m. on Sept. 28.

After calling into a news conference from a facility-provided tablet to say that he had not received any medication and was “losing feeling on the left side of his body,” Garcés Pérez was transported to a second hospital that night. However, Lincoln-Goldfinch said on X that after Garcés Pérez spoke in the conference, guards at the detention center “forcibly took the tablet from his hands, revoked his communication privileges, and moved him out of the infirmary into an isolated room with a flat bed that cannot be adjusted like a medical bed.” The bullet remains in his spine.

Demonstrations continue in Austin since the initial protest erupted at the site of the shooting against ICE, the Austin Police Department (APD), and the Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS) on Sept. 20, where at least six were arrested. An Austin City Council candidate was arrested after the protests on Sept. 26 while walking his dog and charged with “rioting”; DPS cited that he was identified through “a variety of records,” including social media posts, phone, and government records.

Organizers say they want Garcés Pérez to be released and receive appropriate medical care.

Texas has been steadily increasing immigration enforcement since 2021, after Gov. Greg Abbott began Operation Lone Star, an initiative that has spent more than $11 billion on border enforcement and walls. Two years later, Texas passed one of the U.S.’s most aggressive immigration enforcement laws, allowing police to arrest and deport undocumented people who crossed the Texas-Mexico border.

After the Trump administration began cracking down on immigration and sharply increased ICE raids nationwide, average daily arrests in Texas have more than doubled from 85 under Biden to 176 under Trump.

Vladimir Herrera, a member of Dare To Struggle Austin, a grassroots advocacy organization against police brutality and immigration enforcement, said he noticed more community members in Austin get detained by ICE this past February and March, with the presence of federal agents being at its largest around July.

“For months we’ve been set up at a pulga [flea market] at North Lamar and [West] Rundberg,” Herrera said. “When we first went, there were 30-plus vendors setting up in this space behind some businesses. This neighborhood was known to us as a hotbed for ICE activity, so we started going there to talk to people about the crisis.”

Emilio Verdooren, another Dare To Struggle organizer, said that masked plainclothes agents sit in unmarked cars at the local shopping plaza, banks, and parking lots within the North Austin neighborhood, surveilling community members and waiting to “pull people over, dragnet style.”

“We would see DPS stalking, be waiting behind bushes, in parking lots, waiting for people to pass by, and within five to 10 minutes of having stopped someone, ICE would show up and pick them up,” Verdooren said. “We’ve seen them pick someone up and leave their car doors open with keys inside the ignition.”

DPS did not immediately respond to Prism’s request for comment.

Other Austin nonprofits and immigrant rights coalitions, such as the Austin Sanctuary Network and La Frontera Unida, have also continued organizing community discussions and small demonstrations, as well as providing resources to impacted community members.

Garcés Pérez was brought to the Austin federal courthouse Wednesday in a wheelchair for his criminal hearing, where body camera footage was reviewed. In the video, an officer calls for DPS dispatch and shuts off his body camera before calling the other ICE agent, who investigators say shot Garcés Pérez. The agents were referred to by the initials “L.G.” and “D.F.”

“I don’t want to see him disappear into the system like I’ve seen many others,” Lopez said, adding that he does not know the whereabouts of his cousin who was taken by ICE. “That’s one of the reasons why I’ve been at [the site of the shooting] every day, making sure no one forgets Wilber’s name.”

Lincoln-Goldfinch maintains that Garcés Pérez’s criminal charge “is not an isolated case,” and “is often used against protesters and resisters against the government.”

“ We know that ICE has a pattern of trafficking people across this country and trafficking them outside of this country,” Herrera said. “More people should be thinking about what we’re seeing now as the beginning and not some climax.”

author: Sérgio Spagnuolo
title: Processos sobre desinformação e propaganda digital triplicam nas eleições de 2026
content:
O volume de reclamações judiciais sobre desinformação e publicidade digital irregular quase triplicou na Justiça Eleitoral em 2026 em relação às eleições de 2022, totalizando 9.571 processos no mesmo período até 1º.out.2026.




Esse montante corresponde a 11,4% do total de processos desse ciclo eleitoral, frente a 4,1% das eleições de 2022, de acordo com análise de dados feita pelo Núcleo.




A maioria desse tipo de processos envolve propaganda irregular em redes sociais e na internet em geral, inclusive impulsionamento de conteúdo denunciado.










Ao todo, o TSE já registrou ao menos 84,1 mil processos judiciais nesse ciclo eleitoral até 1º.out, cerca de 1% a mais do que no mesmo período em 2022.



















Como fizemos isso




O 

Núcleo

 acessou dados de processos eleitorais no 

repositório de dados abertos

 do TSE. Última data de acesso 1º.out.2026.




Esses dados possuem um campo de assunto principal do processo em questão, além de outros assuntos relacionados. O 

Núcleo

 fez a junção de duas tabelas a fim de saber todos os assuntos mencionados, a partir do seguinte filtro.







internet

 (Propaganda Política – Propaganda Eleitoral – Internet)




redes sociais

 (Propaganda Política – Propaganda Eleitoral – Redes Sociais)




impulsionamento

 (Propaganda Política – Propaganda Eleitoral – Impulsionamento)




app de mensagem

 (Propaganda Política – Propaganda Eleitoral – Aplicativo de Mensagem Instantânea)




inteligência artificial

 (Propaganda Política – Propaganda Eleitoral – Uso de Inteligência Artificial)




deep_fake

 (Propaganda Política – Propaganda Eleitoral – Deep Fake) 




fake news







Propaganda Política – Propaganda Eleitoral – Divulgação de Notícia Sabidamente Falsa (fake_news_a)




Propaganda Política – Propaganda Eleitoral – Divulgação de Notícia Sabidamente Falsa (fake_news_b, variante com caractere diferente)




Divulgação de Falsa Imputação (fake_news_c)




Desinformação sobre a Integridade do Processo Eleitoral (fake_news_d)




Divulgação de Fatos Inverídicos na Propaganda Eleitoral (fake_news_e)













Para a análise foram considerados processos únicos, levando em conta que um processo pode aparecer mais de uma vez quando muda de relator ou de instância. Vale notar que, embora a campanha oficial tenha começado em 16.ago.2026, há processos anteriores a isso sobre essas eleições na Justiça.




O 

Núcleo

 utilizou o modelo de IA Claude Fable 5.1 para checar as análises desenvolvidas por humanos e sugerir melhorias.

author: Unknown
title: Turkish companies accelerate tree cutting in the Behdînan region
content:
In recent days, Turkish companies have intensified tree cutting in the Behdînan region, encompassing Zaxo, Duhok, Berwarî Bala and Amediyê. Increasing their logging activities ahead of winter, the Turkish companies are transporting the trees across the border in trucks under military supervision. Footage shows dozens of trucks carrying felled trees from rural areas. Some of the trucks are accompanied by Turkish armored vehicles.




Over the past 10 days, felled trees have been transported by more than 250 trucks in the Berwarî Bala area of Amediyê district in Duhok.




Residents who filmed the footage protested the tree cutting, saying: “What you see here are felled trees. These trucks belong to the Turks. They are transporting trees cut down in Kurdistan. At the security checkpoint, our vehicles were stopped to facilitate the passage of the trucks loaded with trees.”




















According to information provided to Rojnews by local sources, some of the areas and villages where tree cutting has intensified include Mîska, Qumri, Hirûrê, Kêste, Tirwaniş and Nizdûrê in Berwarî Bala. The sources said that the destruction of trees in the region has accelerated particularly with the approach of winter.




The tree cutting is reportedly concentrated near the Turkish military base at Girê Biyê. Trees felled under the supervision of soldiers are being transported to Turkey through the Serzêr border crossing.




Turkish soldiers are reportedly present in the areas where tree cutting continues, and civilian access to these areas is prohibited. Hundreds of villages had been evacuated following the start of Turkey’s military operations in the region.




While the Kurdistan Regional Government and the Iraqi government remain silent over the tree cutting, residents of Behdînan have reacted to both this silence and the destruction of nature by sharing footage on social media.

author: Taya Graham
title: Maryland Used Discredited Science to Convict a Woman of Murdering Her Newborn
content:
Advocates say the case is an alarming example of the prevalence of unsubstantiated forensic science.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Moira Akers was prosecuted and convicted of the murder of a newborn in 2022. She claims to have given birth to a stillborn baby in her home in Columbia, Maryland, in 2018.

Prosecutors doubted Akers’ story, using her online searches for abortion services and lack of prenatal care as evidence of ill intent. But it was a “forensic method” devised in the 17th century that proved key to Akers’ conviction.

The method, known as a “float test,” was designed to determine if a baby was stillborn or born alive by placing the lungs of a deceased fetus in water. If the lungs float, then they are aerated, meaning the baby was breathing and alive prior to their death.

In 2018, former Maryland chief medical examiner Dr. David Fowler signed the autopsy report that, using the float test as proof, determined that Akers’ baby died after Akers asphyxiated it. Fowler also testified in Akers’ trial. Prosecutors used Fowler’s testimony and autopsy report as evidence to convict Akers of second-degree murder in 2022.

Similar to Fowler’s infamous 2021 testimony in the trial of former Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin, in which he argued that George Floyd died due to drug intoxication and inhaling fumes from a car tailpipe, Fowler’s citation of the float test in Akers’ case has elicited criticism from the medical community.

Fowler was also the subject of a scathing audit released by the Maryland Attorney General’s office last year, which found that at least 36 cases involving deaths that occurred during police restraint were improperly ruled accidents or left unclassified during his tenure

The float test has been widely discredited as imprecise and lacking methodological rigor.

In the course of our reporting on Akers’ case, we not only reviewed court transcripts and the testimony of physicians and medical experts; we also pressed Fowler’s former office for comment about whether or not the float test was still used in fetal death investigations. Just prior to publication, Maryland Department of Health spokesman David McCallister disavowed the test.

“The lung float test is not part of OCME’s current routine practice, which reflects evolving scientific evidence, National Association of Medical Examiner (NAME) guidance, and the independent medical judgment of our forensic pathologists,” McCallister wrote in an email.

“When performed historically, the test was only one component of the overall forensic assessment and was interpreted together with the investigative and autopsy findings. How an individual autopsy finding is characterized or used in criminal prosecution is separate from OCME’s medical determination of cause and manner of death.”

McCallister’s disavowal of the float test marks a stunning departure from past practices for determining causes of death in Maryland. Whether the change will affect Akers’ case remains to be seen.

But what hasn’t changed is the fact that Akers was convicted, has served three years in prison, and is facing another prosecution—all while advocates and her lawyers are still fighting against a bureaucracy wedded to Fowler’s past practices.

Akers’ fate remains in legal limbo, but her story reveals how flawed science can have real-life consequences, and how an indifferent bureaucracy can defend the mistakes of the past despite public outcry and scientific pushback in the present.

Akers’ ordeal began in November of 2018.

According to a statement she gave to police, Akers was watching TV with her daughter when she noticed she was bleeding. The Howard County resident retreated to her upstairs bedroom. There, she gave birth to what she described as a baby that was not breathing, or stillborn.

The mother of two young children told police her husband did not want another child. Finances were tight, and the couple was already struggling to care for both a toddler and an 8-year-old.

“I almost didn’t want to admit to myself that it was [a pregnancy],” she told police.

She hid the possible pregnancy from her family and did not seek prenatal care. “I just didn’t want my family [to know],” Akers said, “a stigma of them knowing that we had even contemplated the abortion part, but knowing that they wouldn’t be happy if we gave up the baby officially for adoption… that’s why I looked into the safe haven stuff.”

The birth itself was a moment of confusion and panic for Akers. When she started bleeding profusely, she thought it was possible the unexpected pregnancy could be the cause. After giving birth in her bathroom, she placed the baby’s remains in a plastic bag and put the bag in a closet.

Her husband, who had found her bleeding, called an ambulance. According to her lawyer, Akers refrained from discussing the ordeal in front of her two children when EMTs arrived at the house. But when she arrived at the hospital, she told doctors about the stillbirth.

When Akers awoke from surgery, heavily sedated with painkillers and anesthesia, she found Howard County police detectives probing her with questions, which a recording reveals she struggled to answer through the haze of drugs.

Even though the doctors told detectives not to question Akers after her surgery, they did anyway. And prosecutors were able to include statements Akers made during that interview while still heavily sedated and under the influence of multiple drugs, including fentanyl.

“The hospital physicians attending told the police who had arrived at the scene not to speak to her for at least two hours after surgery because she was put under general anesthesia,” Akers’ lawyer, Debra Saltz, told us in an interview.

“So the police, rather than wait two hours, interviewed her. I think it was approximately an hour and 20 minutes later, they began an interview.”

Saltz challenged the admissibility of the interview in court. But presiding Judge McCrone ruled that Akers “sounded okay” after reviewing a recording of the interview.

During Saltz’s cross-examination of lead medical examiner Dr. Nikki Mourtzinos, Mourtzinos made a critical admission: float tests are not performed in a uniform fashion, and the test does not call for a consistent, controlled (i.e. scientific) methodology. “Multiple people do things differently. Some people tie off the lungs, some people would clamp off the lungs and float them in water,” Mourtzinos testified.

Saltz filed motions to toss out the float test results as evidence. But Judge McCrone ruled it admissible, too.

And more unresolved questions about the efficacy of the police and OCME investigations before Akers’ trial remain.

Even though the official OCME autopsy report was not released until four months later, detectives claim Maryland’s Office of the Chief Medical Examiner (OCME) told them Akers’ baby’s death was likely a homicide.

But Saltz says OCME and Howard County detectives had already made up their minds about Akers before their investigation into her ordeal even began in earnest. “It was never going to be about science in this case. It was going to be about a determined outcome, which was going to be homicide, even though it should not have been,” Saltz told us.

Along with the float test results and her post-surgery interview with detectives, prosecutors focused on both Akers’ prior internet searches for abortion providers, as well as her lack of prenatal care, as evidence that she intended to kill her baby.

Again, Akers’ defense argued this evidence was inadmissible due to a state law that prevents drawing criminal inferences from a woman’s behavior during pregnancy. Again, Saltz was overruled. Judge McCrone allowed prosecutors to use Akers’ actions as evidence of later criminal intent.

The chief OCME pathologist who conducted the float test testified in Akers’ trial that the final mechanism of injury was asphyxiation and exposure. However, the autopsy did not find petechial hemorrhaging in the eyes or any trauma around the neck indicating strangulation. The medical examiner argued that the determination of asphyxiation was due to observed inflammation in the pancreas, a less common indicator of strangulation.

But there was also substantive evidence that the baby was stillborn.

The defense offered expert testimony that argued the detection of multiple infections in Akers’ placenta and umbilical cord was indicative of a stillbirth.

“One of the more perplexing aspects regarding the opinions of Drs. Simon and Mourtzinos [the state medical examiners who conducted the autopsy] is that they describe gross and microscopic evidence of chorioamnionitis (inflammation of the placenta and its membranes), and funisitis (an inflammation of the umbilical cord), along with inflammation of the umbilical cord’s arteries and vein,” Gregory J. Davis, a forensic pathologist and professor at the University of Kentucky, wrote in a letter to the court.

The jury convicted Akers of second-degree murder. Judge McCrone sentenced her to 30 years.

In February 2025, after she had served three years in prison, the Maryland Supreme Court granted Akers a new trial. In a 5-2 decision, Justice Brynja M. Booth wrote for the majority:

We hold that the internet searches are irrelevant and that the trial court erred as a matter of law in admitting them. We similarly hold that Ms. Akers’ bare decision to forgo 2 prenatal care was not probative of motive or an intent to kill or harm a live child… In light of our holding on the inadmissibility of the abortion searches, we reverse the judgment of the Appellate Court and remand this case to the circuit court for a new trial.

To win a conviction against Akers during the retrial of the case, prosecutors have to navigate a major evidentiary obstacle now that the Maryland Supreme Court has essentially barred them from using much of the “evidence” used to convict Akers in 2022.

But the float test will still be admissible, and Saltz says prosecutors are likely to use it. Even though Fowler’s former office has publicly repudiated the test, the shadow and influence of Fowler himself still looms large.

“Dr. Fowler had a very large impact on this case and the judge heavily credited his testimony and relied on his testimony to allow in evidence the fetal lung float test,” Saltz told us.

Saltz says the admission by Fowler’s former office that the float test is scientifically unreliable should give prosecutors pause. “I find it hard to believe that the state’s attorney’s office in Howard County would still consider using this outdated test,” she wrote in an email.

“I have always believed that they were motivated by emotion rather than science as they undertook to prosecute my client. I would hope they would dismiss the charges based on this newest information.”

For now, prosecutors are not talking. A spokesman for the Howard County State’s Attorney’s Office said they do not comment on pending cases.

“It is the policy of the Howard County State’s Attorney’s Office not to comment to the media on the facts, evidence, or litigation strategy of a pending case until the matter has concluded,” Yolanda Vazquez wrote in an email.

Akers’ fate will be decided soon; the case is set for trial in November. Saltz says she is prepared to defend Akers, float test or not.

“My client is a very, very strong person. And she always held out hope that this would go her way… she knew that she had a stillborn baby,” Saltz said. “And there are plenty of people — including myself and the actual scientists who can read scientific evidence — who believe her.”

author: Nolan Higdon
title: Corporate Media Consolidation Is What Makes Trump’s War on the Press Possible
content:
As mergers concentrate outlets in the hands of a few billionaires, the right’s grip on mainstream media grows tighter.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

“CNN, MSNOW and Politico back at the White House, hours after judge ordered Trump to lift ban,” read a September 24, 2026 Associated Press headline, published just one week after the administration had barred the three outlets from press briefings. In response to the ban, the White House press pool — a rotating group of journalists, photographers, and broadcast technicians organized by the White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) to cover the President of the United States (U.S.) — refused to participate in news conferences until the ban was lifted. Even after the federal courts put a temporary 14-day restraining order on the ban, CNN, unlike right wing media producers, was blocked from covering Trump on Air Force One. Rather than waiting for the courts to issue a permanent ruling halting the Trump administration’s punishment of CNN, the press pool abandoned its protest and returned to the White House following the restraining order. When the press pool traded collective solidarity for a rushed return to the briefing room, it laid bare a troubling structural reality: in modern journalism, the pursuit of daily access routinely overrides the defense of a free press.

President Donald Trump publicly justified the press ban on national security grounds. However, the move was more plausibly driven by political vulnerability. Facing historically low approval ratings ahead of the midterm elections — with his party underwater in 47 states and projected to lose both chambers of Congress — the administration sought to suppress widespread public discontent by censoring the press. Compounding this friction, the White House released taxpayer-funded advertisements promoting the Republican agenda that sparked bipartisan warnings of illegality, functioning essentially as state propaganda disguised as public service announcements. These spots featured dubious claims, such as pledging to dismantle the “deep state” — despite the administration’s own deep-state affiliations and ties to figures like the late Jeffrey Epstein — or promising to eliminate “warmongers” from government while simultaneously prosecuting an elective war in Iran.

The court’s decision to suspend the ban came as no surprise given that the 1977 federal appeals court ruling Sherrill v. Knight established that while the government is not strictly required to open its doors to the media, once it voluntarily establishes a public press facility or invites the press, it cannot arbitrarily ban or deny access to specific news outlets based on the content or viewpoint of their coverage. Furthermore, efforts to execute similar authoritarian bans on journalists Jim Acosta and Brian Karem during Trump’s first administration and the Associated Press in his second term failed.

Nor did it come as a surprise that other corporate-funded news outlets eventually abandoned their refusal to cover the White House, capitulating before the courts could legally invalidate the ban. The underlying reasons for this collapse are structural: contemporary media outlets are tethered above all to profit maximization. To capture market share, they routinely pander to audiences’ desires for partisan confirmation, prioritizing ideological validation over journalistic veracity. This began with Fox News Channel, which pioneered the art of hyper-partisan conservatism to attract an audience, and was subsequently copied by outlets such as MSNOW (formerly MSNBC), which soon did the same for liberals. At the same time, newspapers shifted online to a subscriber model where they, too, were caught up in ideological bias, trying to confirm the political biases of their audiences while manufacturing conflict against the “other party.”

Beyond partisan narratives, the press’s profit model remains anchored in the age-old adage that “if it bleeds, it ledes.” Consequently, corporate media outlets prioritize sensationalistic content — often described as junk food news, such as gossip, scandals, and inflammatory rhetoric — over substantive reporting. This for-profit imperative has proven uniquely detrimental in the Trump era, as his mastery of provocative staging and hyper-partisan unpredictability allows him to dictate media coverage — whether by amplifying preferred narratives, such as false claims about the Iran conflict, or by deflecting from vulnerabilities like the Epstein records. For instance, Trump consistently triggers media fixation through deliberate provocations, ranging from racist and sexist slurs and outlandish policy proposals — such as annexing Greenland or Canada — to absurd public spectacles that news organizations find impossible to ignore, including hosting a UFC fight and previewing Tesla vehicles at the White House.

Aside from relying on spectacle, corporate news media prioritizes famous figures, assuming that celebrity appeal drives viewership better than the voices of everyday citizens. This bias routinely sidelines “man-on-the-street” journalism that elevates the everyday public. Eager to preserve access to power as Trump entered his second term, prominent television figures who once built their brands on anti-Trump rhetoric — such as Joe Scarborough, Mika Brzezinski, and Bill Maher — sought to mend fences, trading uncompromised critique for public displays of sycophancy and renewed dialogue. Similarly, networks like CBS and ABC settled fraudulent lawsuits from Trump to safeguard their institutional access. By prioritizing proximity and ratings dominance over journalistic integrity, the corporate press has willingly allowed a manufactured political persona to eclipse substantive democratic discourse.

It is difficult for actual journalists to offer a counter to the corporate media given that a handful of corporate news media dominate the market. Back in 1983, Ben Bagdikian warned in The Media Monopoly that the 50 or so corporations that controlled 90% of news media were steadily dwindling. The climate of unchecked concentration was accelerated by the Telecommunications Act of 1996, which dismantled ownership caps and enabled single corporations to monopolize multiple news outlets within local markets. At the time, the internet was relentlessly promised as the ultimate solution, arguing it would magically create the diversity that antitrust laws once aimed to achieve. However, internet companies quickly followed the same path, consolidating just as legacy corporate media had. Acronyms like FAANG and GAMMAA are now used to describe the handful of monopolistic companies that control this digital traffic. Regardless, by the time that Bagdikian wrote the last edition of The Media Monopoly in 2004, there were only six corporations controlling 90% of the news media.

The corporate consolidation of U.S. news media has continued to shrink the landscape in the years since. Indeed, the very week of Trump’s press ban, state attorneys general announced a settlement clearing the path for the Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery merger, subject to final court review. This followed a 2025 arrangement in which the administration signaled it would approve Paramount’s proposed merger with Skydance Media on the condition that Paramount settle Trump’s personal lawsuit against CBS. In response, Paramount executed a $16 million settlement with Trump, and the merger was granted.

This Paramount merger saga illustrates how the profit motive at the heart of such mega-mergers consistently supersedes both journalistic integrity and the principle of an independent press. For Paramount, maximizing market control through corporate consolidation was paramount, making the $16 million settlement little more than the cost of doing business. Beyond securing this payout, Trump’s approval of the transaction paved the way for political allies — the Ellisons — to take ownership of CBS. This shift subsequently placed figures like Bari Weiss in charge of CBS News, where unfavorable coverage of the administration has reportedly been suppressed. Furthermore, industry reports suggest Weiss is positioned to take over CNN should the broader Paramount–Warner Bros. Discovery merger reach finalization.

The financial and ideological gains for Trump, Weiss, and the Ellisons come at the expense of the substantive, diverse coverage that democracy depends upon. Indeed, given press consolidation and the influence of the White House on news narratives, it is unsurprising that the United States ranks 64th out of 180 countries in Reporters Without Borders’ Press Freedom Index, and 51st out of 179 nations according to the Varieties of Democracy project. Submitting the free press — the very foundation of democratic accountability — to five decades of unbridled profit motives and corporate consolidation has yielded predictable consequences. Continuing down this path risks realizing a post-democratic landscape devoid of a substantive, independent press. Driven by political expedience and financial self-preservation, corporate media leaders appear all too willing to follow this trajectory, trading democratic integrity for short-term gain. Safeguarding U.S. democracy requires breaking up media monopolies, eradicating news deserts, funding independent press ecosystems, and demanding that journalists act as a unified front of resistance rather than isolated outlets cashing in on corporate greed at the expense of the public good.

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

author: Paul Messersmith-Glavin
title: A Lifelong Organizer Shares Lessons on Sustaining Activism for the Long Haul
content:
Organizer Chris Dixon discusses how we can sustain our collective efforts over years of social and political struggle.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Writer and organizer Chris Dixon has his fingers on the pulse of North American grassroots movement. Dixon has extensively and repeatedly traveled throughout North America, talking with people working for social change — engaging with activists concerning their successes and heartbreaks, their frustrations and dreams. His first book, Another Politics: Talking Across Today’s Transformative Movements, published in 2014, focused on antiauthoritarian organizers and politics across a range of movements of the 2000s and early 2010s, including migrant justice, prison abolitionism, and Occupy Wall Street. His new book, For the Long Haul: How to Stay in the Fight for a Better World, focuses on how we can sustain our collective efforts over years of social and political struggle.

Movement elders I am close to — now in their 70s — who maintain radical political commitments developed in their youth, benefitted from both the intense community that formed around movements for Black Power and liberation, the youthful counterculture and the New Left, and anti-war movements, as well as from their own inner convictions that served as an animating passion. For these elders, political engagement is a kind of vocation. Though they continue to maintain relationships with those comrades who are also still alive and committed to political struggle, those vibrant communities they once thrived in are gone. Only their specific commitment to the possibility of freedom and liberation keeps them going.

Coming of age politically in the 1990s, we also had strong bonds of friendship born through relentless organizing meetings, demonstrations, and coalition work. It seemed we could collectively change the world. Thirty years later, only a handful of us remain involved. Why? Why do people stop organizing, beyond and in addition to the realities of acquiring increasing responsibilities as we age? Why do people give up on the possibility of creating fundamental social and structural change together over the long term? How can we cultivate and sustain caring radical communities that support us all, while drawing new people in, or welcoming them back? These are some of the questions Chris Dixon sets out to answer in For the Long Haul: How to Stay in the Fight for a Better World. The interview that follows has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Paul Messersmith-Glavin: Who should read your book?

Chris Dixon: I wrote For the Long Haul as a practical guide with two main audiences in mind. On the one hand, I wanted to warmly welcome people who have recently become involved in radical political efforts, especially those who have joined movement upsurges since 2020. I’m particularly thinking of the Movement for Black Lives and Palestine solidarity organizing, but also renewed labor militancy and collective defense of queer and trans people. A lot of people I talk to who are newer to movements — many but not all of them younger people — are hungry for conversations about how to sustain lifelong political commitments.

On the other hand, I wanted to speak lovingly to my peers — long-time activists and organizers who have been involved in movements for decades. Many of us talk informally with our friends about the challenges we face in staying actively involved on the left. We’re working a lot to pay our bills, reckoning with disabilities and chronic health conditions, and holding significant care responsibilities for kids, elders, and others in our lives. So many of us are deeply exhausted and hungry for realistic advice about how to stay steady in the fight.

I also wanted to sympathetically address people who participated in movements of the left at one time or another and then moved away from active involvement. I know many people who have followed this trajectory. Rather than being moralistic or dismissive, I wanted to remind them that they’re always welcome back. And I wanted to suggest that perhaps, together, we can build some better structures and practices for helping people stay engaged.

You have spent a tremendous amount of time travelling around the U.S. and Canada, listening to on-the-ground organizers. What have you learned?

I have learned a lot! My most intense and sustained travel was connected to the process of writing and then sharing my first book, Another Politics: Talking Across Today’s Transformative Movements. In the late 2000s, I spent a bunch of time traveling and interviewing experienced anti-authoritarian organizers, mainly anarchists and abolitionists. That was the basis for Another Politics. In 2014 and 2015, I toured through 40 cities in North America, giving presentations and facilitating workshops based on the book. During that period, the Movement for Black Lives was picking up in significant ways, and there were still reverberations from the movement associated with Occupy Wall Street. Then, in 2016-17, I was again on the road in the U.S., and I participated in mobilizations against the far right in the wake of Trump’s election, including in my home state, Alaska.

I heard a lot about challenges that people were experiencing, especially related to the sustainability of their organizing efforts in increasingly crisis-ridden circumstances, and also in relation to the ordinary difficulties of working together collectively. Many people shared about the challenges of navigating conflict, reckoning with harm, and organizing effectively.

People of the past faced and fought in tremendously crisis-ridden circumstances, and we can too.

During that time, I learned that there are a lot of people — more than anyone knows, really — earnestly trying to figure out how to make radical change. They are mostly unsung, and sometimes they don’t even think the work they’re doing is important. But I could see that people everywhere are experimenting with modes of organization and methods of struggle motivated by a deeply felt sense that we can change the world.

The COVID pandemic significantly changed my travel practices. I also live with a chronic pain disability that limits what I can do. So, much of my learning from movements since 2020 has involved maintaining ongoing conversations with many friends across North America and an exhaustive practice of following movement-based media. Here I’d say that I’ve learned especially from migrant justice organizing, Indigenous-led fights against resource extraction projects, rank-and-file union organizing efforts, disability justice initiatives, fights for trans dignity and joy, and Palestine solidarity organizing. Key lessons coming out of these struggles have included the importance of collective care practices, of organizing expansively, and of fighting stubbornly.

Stitching all this work together, I came to the five key lessons that ended up each becoming a chapter in For the Long Haul. I put them as imperatives, or invitations, for the chapter titles: cultivate a long view, work with others, care, make plans, and stick around.

What advice do you have for those in the U.S. organizing against authoritarian consolidation and ecological collapse?

This is such a difficult time, full of unfolding catastrophes. Many people respond to these escalating crises with a lot of urgency and a sense that they have to work incredibly hard and all the time, but that they still won’t win. There’s widespread despair, and it’s not unjustified.

I take a lot of inspiration from studying social movement history. For me, it has helped to learn about how people in the past reckoned with overwhelming circumstances and persevered in collective struggle. It’s true that authoritarianism is ascendant globally right now, and it’s true that we’re facing an unprecedented ecological crisis. But people of the past faced and fought in tremendously crisis-ridden circumstances, and we can too. I think, for instance, about the original abolitionist movement fighting chattel slavery; when we organize to abolish the carceral system today, we are building on that legacy. It was a crisis then and it is a crisis now, and people persevered over decades. So, one piece of advice is for us to understand ourselves in history — to cultivate a “long view.” Let’s avoid romanticizing past struggles, but let’s see ourselves in relation to them. Let’s also study them; while there are no recipes, there are lessons.

My other piece of advice might sound kind of basic, but I think it’s crucial: Work with other people. This is both strategic and an antidote to despair. The forces we face are so big, and can be so overwhelming, that we cannot win what we need if we try to go it alone. The only way we’re going to have any hope for large-scale change is by bringing lots of people together in ways that keep growing and building power. For me, this also means intentionally building durable and functional organizations in which people can make plans together, act, build skills and capacities, and take care of one another.

Some people put their faith in the U.S. midterm elections to help stop Trump’s power grabs; to hopefully begin to chart a different course. From your perspective, what role does electoral politics play in affecting dominant power relations? And what difference do you think the midterms will make to the unfolding disaster we find ourselves in?

This is a difficult question. The theory of change that I feel the most confidence about is based on building powerful and combative social movements from below. I think that’s key for challenging and transforming dominant power relations. That’s where I put my organizing energy.

For those waking up to the realities of white supremacy, heteropatriarchy, colonialism, and the viciousness of the capitalist economy, what advice do you have to prepare those folks for the long haul that social movement organizing is? What’s your best advice to those newly radicalized to the left?

Part of what I do politically in the city where I live, Ottawa, is supporting other activist groups in building their internal practices and infrastructures. This past summer, while helping to facilitate a planning session for a local organization, I was speaking to someone who is newly politicized in just the way you describe. He initially got involved in organizing against the genocide in Palestine, and he talked about the incredible urgency he felt. He said he also now was feeling it about every new injustice he learned about. He described how overwhelming this was — to encounter these oceans of suffering and to want to struggle against oppression with every ounce of his strength. I get it! I still feel this way three decades after coming into political consciousness myself.

But he was already realizing that if he kept throwing himself into every campaign, he would burn out quickly and perhaps be unable to return. Any of us who’ve been around for a while in movements have seen this pattern, and I talk about it a lot in the book.

My best advice for people who are newly radicalized is to be as intentional as you can. I say this also to my peers who are re-joining movement activity after a period of burn out and to those who are hanging on by their fingernails.

Vibrant movements welcome the full range of contributions and capabilities that people bring, in all of their beautiful differences.

Let me be specific about this. Being intentional means setting priorities about what we’re trying to achieve, making plans for how we’re going to get there, and building structures that help us make collective decisions about workload. My partner has a framed cross-stitch that says, “You can do anything! You can’t do everything!” I think this is not a bad motto for us. Whenever we decide what we’re going to do, we are also deciding some things we’re not going to do. Saying no to some things and setting priorities isn’t actually wrong. It helps us be more focused and effective. It doesn’t guarantee our success, but it increases our chances of winning more often. And of course, often we’re not going to win. So, planning is also about how we set up to carry on and keep building even when we lose.

The other thing I want to emphasize here is that we can’t build sustained movements that assume that everyone will be available 24-7. If you’re holding care responsibilities, scheduling in advance is often necessary. One of the key lessons I take from disability justice efforts, and from my comrades who are parents, is the insight that vibrant movements welcome the full range of contributions and capabilities that people bring, in all of their beautiful differences. But we need to plan for that. This is one practical expression of collective care.

The last thing I’ll say is that in these terrible times, being part of movements really can be the most nourishing way to keep going and refuse despair. I think it’s worth it to do this work, together, for the long haul.
