author: Derek Seidman
title: A Growing Movement Is Working to Evict ICE From Its Buffalo Command Center
content:
Activists are pressuring Buffalo corporations to kick ICE out of the office building where it is imprisoning children.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A glimmering 12-story building towers over the intersection where Delaware Avenue meets Chippewa Street in downtown Buffalo. The building is owned by Uniland Development, a major Buffalo real estate developer. Surrounded by coffee shops, luxury hotels, and boutique restaurants, the building’s facade is emblazoned with the corporate logo of its anchor tenant, Delaware North, one of the world’s largest concessions corporations, headquartered in Buffalo.

But amid the daily humdrum at 250 Delaware Avenue — paper shuffling inside, cars honking outside — is, to many Buffalonians, something more shocking: The building’s seventh floor serves as the operational hub of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) machinery of detention and deportation across much of New York State, and it is a “hold room” site used to detain immigrant neighbors, including children.

For years, ICE’s Buffalo field office has lived inside the Delaware North Building. Now, an escalating campaign, Evict ICE from 250 Delaware, is determined to pressure the building’s corporate owners — Uniland Development, owned by the Montantes, a prominent Buffalo area family — and its flagship renter — the Delaware North corporation, owned by the billionaire Jacobs family — to cut ties with ICE when its current lease expires on March 31, 2027.

Backed by a broad coalition of community organizations and immigrant rights groups, and driven by dozens of volunteers, the campaign is working actively — canvassing and petitioning, protesting weekly, staging direct actions — to not only shame and compel Buffalo’s corporate class into evicting ICE from its properties, but also to use the campaign’s momentum to advance the more sweeping movement goals of kicking ICE out of Buffalo and abolishing the agency altogether.

On September 26, eight people were arrested as they sat down and occupied the intersection in front of 250 Delaware — which the campaign is now calling the “Montante Detention Center” — to protest “the Montante family’s continued profiteering from deportation,” according to a press release.

“The people of Buffalo will not allow mass deportation profiteers to hide any longer,” the arrestees said in a statement. “There can be no more business as usual at 250 Delaware Ave until the Montantes EVICT ICE.”

Buffalo is a border town — a city shaped by immigrants, past and present. The region is a focal point for Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) operations, with raids, detentions, and deportations of immigrants a constant reality. Buffalo made national headlines in February after the death — ruled a homicide by the county medical examiner — of Nurul Amin Shah Alam, a blind Rohingya refugee who Border Patrol left at a downtown coffeeshop without notifying his family of his release.

The Evict ICE campaign describes ICE’s field office in 250 Delaware as the “command center” of the agency’s operations across most of New York State — essentially all areas upstate of New York City and its vicinity. Its purview also includes the nearby Batavia holding center, the state’s only ICE federal detention facility, which is expanding its capacity to hold detainees. In Buffalo, ICE arrests have soared over the past year.

“The masked men kidnapping people off the streets — that is orchestrated out of 250 Delaware,” Jennifer Connor, the executive director of Justice for Migrant Families, told Truthout.

Additionally, the building houses the Buffalo office for Homeland Security Investigations and Buffalo’s Office of the Principal Legal Advisor. Both are arms of DHS’s machinery across New York State.

The Evict ICE campaign and numerous sources say 250 Delaware contains more than piles of paperwork and ringing phones.

The campaign’s analysis of data from the Deportation Data Project found that 237 people were held at the “Buffalo Hold Room” on the 7th floor at 250 Delaware Avenue from February 2025 to March 2026, including 18 children under the age of 12. Many people were held for multiple days, exceeding ICE’s short-term holding policies, and in overcrowded conditions.

Connor says she’s spoken to multiple people who were held in 250 Delaware and that former detainees told her there are at least two holding cells in the building.

Truthout reached out to ICE’s Buffalo office for comment but did not receive a response.

For many Buffalonians, it is jarring to discover that the gleaming Delaware North Building is a place where immigrant neighbors, including children, are detained behind walls that are in plain view of passing drivers, latte sippers, and visiting tourists.

“At first I was like, ‘Oh, it’s just an office building,’” Lena Forti, an organizer with the Evict ICE campaign, told Truthout. “Now I understand that there’s so much power coming from this building. It’s directing all of ICE’s actions for New York State outside of New York City, and it’s holding people.”

Local activists have been protesting ICE’s presence at 250 Delaware for nearly a decade. The current campaign began to take shape in 2025 among a core of local researchers and activists with mutual aid networks, immigrant rights groups, and progressive community organizations.

The Evict ICE campaign formally launched on May Day of 2026 with a rally in front of 250 Delaware Avenue. It has expanded to a coalition of nearly 60 organizations, small businesses, and elected officials, ranging from housing and environmental groups to labor unions and the Democratic Socialists of America, from bookstores and bike clubs to worker-owned bread co-ops.

The Evict ICE campaign has a clear and immediate goal: pressuring Buffalo’s corporate enablers of ICE to not renew the agency’s lease at 250 Delaware Avenue.

Two corporations — tied to two prominent Buffalo-area families — are at the center of the campaign. The first is Uniland Development, the owner and developer of the building at 250 Delaware North. Uniland is owned by the Montante family, which has a wide presence across Buffalo’s corporate structure and network of educational and cultural institutions.

Uniland rakes in over $2 million annually by renting to ICE at 250 Delaware, in addition to around $850,000 by renting to CBP at two other locations, and it has enjoyed millions in public subsidies.

The second is Delaware North, one of the world’s largest concessions corporations, which is privately owned by the billionaire Jacobs family. Delaware North is the anchor tenant at 250 Delaware Avenue, the company’s global headquarters.

The Jacobs’ have their hands all over the Buffalo area, from universities to banks to art museums. The Jacobs family has donated to politicians from Donald Trump to Kathy Hochul, whose husband, Bill Hochul, was Delaware North’s general counsel and senior vice president until 2023. Delaware North has also raked in public subsidies.

“We have to hold the Montantes and the Jacobs accountable,” said Connor. “The types of violence we’re seeing at the hands of ICE can’t happen without the support of the existing power structures.”

Uniland and Delaware North are just two of the most prominent examples of how Buffalo’s power structure — some of the city’s traditional elite families and leading names in real estate — are profiting from the machinery of detention and deportation through lease agreements with federal agencies.

“It’s really important for us to name names of people who have a responsibility to do better in the Buffalo community,” added Connor.

Since its May Day launch, the Evict ICE campaign has organized a steady stream of activities and near-weekly demonstrations.

In May and June, the campaign placed billboards across from the building shaming Uniland and Delaware North and calling for ICE’s eviction. During Mother’s Day brunch, protesters held signs in front of the building’s restaurant with names of mothers who have been detained and deported. Jeremy M. Jacobs Sr. is the recent former chairman of the NHL’s Board of Governors and owner of the Boston Bruins, so protestors crashed the National Hockey League draft in June, which took place in Buffalo.

There were around 80 people at a protest and vigil at the building that I attended on July 25, organized to honor the lives and memories of those who have been killed by ICE and DHS. Labor activists, faith leaders, poets, and representatives from refugee organizations all spoke. Dozens marched around downtown Buffalo after the rally.

“If you really care about Buffalo, you shouldn’t be putting the safety of your pocketbook over the safety of Buffalonians’ lives,” Alicia Huff, a community activist who co-facilitated the action, told Truthout.

The campaign says it has around 85 volunteers, including new organizers who have joined canvassing teams, led protests, and managed social media efforts. It has an ongoing petition that it says over 6,000 people have signed. It sent letters directly to Uniland asking it not to renew ICE’s lease and Delaware North asking it to advocate against the lease’s renewal. The campaign told Truthout it has not received any responses.

Organizers say that one indicator of the campaign’s influence came in August when the Erie County executive, Mark Poloncarz, cancelled a planned DHS job fair that was scheduled at a government-owned building. The city of Buffalo also recently ended free downtown parking for ICE officials.

Amid loud chants of “Evict ICE!” at the July 25 protest, organizers stated their commitment to see the campaign through to victory. “We’re going to show how much opposition the entire city of Buffalo has to ICE’s field office existing here,” said Tom Griffin, another rally co-facilitator.

“We’re going to continue standing in solidarity with all of Buffalo,” said Griffin.

The Buffalo campaign can also be seen as one expression of a wider strategy being deployed by movements across the U.S.: attempting to isolate and ostracize ICE by driving a wedge between the agency and the public-facing corporations and billionaires that enable its operations.

Nationally, for example, organizers across the U.S. successfully pressured Avelo Airlines to end its contract with ICE to carry out deportation flights. Additionally, activists have targeted hotels like Hilton that house ICE agents who invade localities to carry out the Trump administration’s deportation agenda.

This corporate-focused strategy has a clear logic. While movements today lack the immediate capacity to compel the abolition of ICE at the federal level, they can create friction between the agency and businesses it depends upon.

Many corporations that work with ICE have vulnerabilities. They depend on a healthy brand image or desire public subsidies. Through their sponsorships, donations, and executive and board member connections, ICE-tied corporations often have a wide presence across local and regional philanthropic, educational, and cultural institutions — all of which widen the surface area for activists to protest and confront them locally.

In Buffalo, the use of “power mapping” — researching and visualizing the relationships of entities and individuals that undergird the local power structure — has been particularly important for campaign strategy. The Evict ICE website includes visual maps of the campaign’s main corporate targets, revealing their extensive imprint across Buffalo institutions and civic and cultural life.

This power mapping, in turn, cracks open tactical possibilities for organizers to protest, shame, and isolate corporate targets.

Around 50 protesters gathered on the steps of the Montante Cultural Center at Canisius University on the afternoon of Friday, September 25, asking the Catholic and Jesuit institution, a flagship Buffalo school, to join the Evict ICE campaign, and demanding it use its longstanding relationship with the Montantes, a major university donor, to pressure the family to not renew ICE’s lease at Uniland’s 250 Delaware Avenue building.

Rush-hour traffic — insofar as it exists in Buffalo — whipped by as students and alumni spoke passionately about the need for Canisius to live up to its “social justice” Jesuit values.

“I am not here just to shame my school, but to ask them to do better,” Canisius alumnus Lauren Narbe told the crowd, adding that the Montantes “are profiting off of someone’s family being ripped apart.”

“We ask that Canisius be on the right side of history, even when their largest donor is the Montante family,” Narbe said.

Canisius told Truthout in a formal statement that “we are aware of the demonstration taking place near campus and understand people’s right to express their views peacefully.”

The campaign escalated the next day, on September 26, when eight campaign activists, supported by a hundred picketers, blocked the intersection in front of 250 Delaware for two hours.

The protesters staged the action to rechristen the 12-story building the “Montante Detention Center.”

“We are renaming the ‘Delaware North’ building to reflect its owners’ abuse and greed: Montante Detention Center,” the activists said in a statement.

The eight activists who sat down in the intersection were arrested on charges of “disorderly conduct.”

“I find it ironic that the Buffalo Police Department arrested us for ‘disorderly conduct’ for a peaceful protest, when ICE agents are allowed to brutalize and abduct our neighbors every day,” said one arrestee in the press release.

Truthout reached out to both Uniland and Delaware North for comment on this article but did not receive responses.

On September 27, the Buffalo News published a prepared statement from Uniland saying the company was “legally and contractually obligated to honor all lease agreements and abide by their terms, just as we do with every client” and that “as with all lease agreements, the lease renewal is governed by previously agreed upon contractual terms and conditions.”

The Evict ICE campaign has a ticker atop its website counting down the days until ICE’s lease in the Delaware North Building expires.

In the meantime, organizers plan to continue to ramp up protests against ICE’s corporate enablers. In a place like Buffalo, the purported “City of Good Neighbors,” this means breaking through surface-level civility and forcing powerful people — who otherwise enjoy fine local repute in polite society — to make clear which side they’re on.

“It’s very easy for Uniland to not respond,” said Forti. “To get them to evict ICE, we need to be disrupting them more and make it impossible for them to ignore us.”

I asked Harper Bishop, a key leader in the campaign, what victory would look like.

“Victory would look like ICE no longer operating its regional headquarters in downtown Buffalo,” he said, adding that this would represent an “incremental win” toward ICE’s abolition.

“Having ICE leave one building isn’t enough,” Bishop added. “This campaign is giving people the feeling that their voices and actions matter and they have the power to change material conditions on the ground.”

“It’s bringing people into the place of fighting for what we ultimately need: ICE out of Buffalo and abolished completely,” he said.

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

Truthout produces reporting you won’t see in the mainstream: journalism from the frontlines of global conflict, interviews with grassroots movement leaders, high-quality legal analysis and more.

Our work is possible thanks to reader support. Help Truthout catalyze change and social justice — make a tax-deductible monthly or one-time donation today.

author: Corey Larocque
title: An Early Inuit relocation scheme – Part 1
content:
On August 13, 1877, an unusual expedition left New London, Conn., bound for Cumberland Sound on the southeastern coast of Baffin Island. Known officially as the Howgate Preliminary Arctic Expedition, it was to be the first stage of a much grander enterprise planned by Captain Henry W. Howgate of the United States Army.




Howgate had been inspired by the recent British expedition to the High Arctic led by George Nares. With two ships, Nares had tried to reach the North Pole by way of Smith Sound, the narrow channel separating Ellesmere Island from Greenland. One ship, the Alert, had reached a point on Ellesmere Island farther north than any other ship had ever gone and wintered there.




Howgate thought that Americans should do one better than the British. He wanted to establish a permanent scientific colony at Lady Franklin Bay. For that, he would need Inuit — for he knew that none lived that far north — and dogs and skin clothing.




And so a plan was hatched that a preliminary expedition would travel to Cumberland Sound and winter there. It would be under the command of Captain George Tyson, a whaler well known to the Inuit of the sound. During the winter, Tyson would hire Inuit who were willing to relocate to Ellesmere Island and collect supplies. Two scientists would accompany the preliminary expedition. Because the entire scheme was underfunded, it was planned that Tyson would also hunt whales to support the expedition financially. The following spring, the vessel would travel across Davis Strait to Greenland where it would liaise with a larger ship from the U.S., to which the Inuit would transfer for the trip to Ellesmere Island.




The expedition, aboard the tiny vessel, Florence, reached Cumberland Sound in September. She headed first for Naujartalik (Niantilic), a popular destination for whalers on the southern coast of the sound. There, Tyson learned that four whaling ships were planning to winter there, and two others at Kekerten on the northern side of the sound. Tyson knew that both were popular wintering places because early ice breakup would allow early spring whaling.




But the competition for trade would not augur well for the success of his efforts to acquire skin clothing and encourage Inuit to join his expedition. So he decided that he would have to be farther up the sound. He put into winter quarters on Oct. 7 at the head of the sound at a place the whalers knew as Ananito Harbour, or Annanatook Harbour, the place later spelled by Franz Boas as Anarnitung — the Inuit place name Anarnituuq.




The expedition’s two scientists were Ludwig Kumlien, an ornithologist and naturalist, and Orray Taft Sherman, a meteorologist. They immediately set to work. Tyson busied himself collecting skin clothing, purchasing dogs and convincing Inuit to relocate. Three Inuit families had been living at Anarnituuq when the Florence made anchor there. But over the winter, the location became a popular destination for more Inuit coming to trade with Tyson.
















“The Cruise of the Florence” is a scarce book telling about the Inuit relocation scheme.




Tyson described his efforts to convince Inuit to relocate to Ellesmere Island: “I have had several conversations with the Esquimaux in regard to their going with us to the East Land, as they always call the coast of Greenland. Some say they will go; others fear to go. The latter are afraid of the ‘mulling’ (sea) in such a little vessel as the Florence. Others, again, have mothers who do not want them to go; then, again, brothers and sisters, uncles and aunts and cousins, and I do not know what else.”




Five men promised to go, as did several from Naujartalik. In the spring, the disadvantages of Tyson’s choice of wintering harbour became apparent. His ship was firmly locked in the grip of the ice, while the other ships which had wintered farther to the mouth of the sound had been released from their harbours and gone about the business of whaling. By the time the Florence was free, there was no time for whaling.




When the ship left harbour, it carried ten Inuit (four men, two women and four children) who had agreed to relocate to Ellesmere Island. They were Nep-e-ken and his family; Al-o-kee; a man named Ete-tun and his family; and a man nicknamed Chummy. He is also referred to as Thu-nu-ping-nar or Shu-mar-ping-uter. What this confusing agglomeration of letters was intended to represent in Inuktitut is a mystery to me.




Nep-e-ken had worked successfully for other whalers, and just the year before Captain Keeny of the Isabella had given him a whaleboat as a reward for his services. He was in his mid-40s and had adopted the name “Tyson.”




The real Tyson explained: “When the ships first commenced to winter in the gulf, some twenty-five years ago, the captains who hired the Esquimaux — and they all did so — finding it difficult to recollect their native cognomens, would give them English names; as, Tom, Charley, Dick, or Harry, and others, again, which were not quite so euphonious to the ear. This youngster… was baptized Tyson; I know not for what reason, unless it was because he was so handsome!”
















Nep-e-ken was a great hunter; Tyson called him “the Nimrod of the gulf.” American captains vied for his services, and he was the boss of a boat’s crew. His wife was O-cas-e-ak-ju and, a capable hunter of deer, seal and polar bear, she was “good with the rifle and the spear.”




The couple had two adopted children. One of them was a boy of about five, named As-see-wer – probably the Inuit name Aasivak. The whalers had nicknamed him ‘Boatswain.’ Tyson noted, “I know that he can chew and smoke equal to an old tar.” He added, “They commence young in this country. I have seen some of the little girls, not older than this boy, chewing and smoking tobacco.”




Ete-tun’s wife was Kim-ik-pak-jic, (probably Kimipiarjuk), whom the whalers called Polly. She gave birth to a baby on board the ship on May 1, 1878. Alokee was single and had expressed a desire to get a wife before he left on the expedition. Chummy was single, and trusted Tyson implicitly, having been to the United States for a winter with him in 1861. Indeed, on his return to Cumberland Sound the following year, he appears on the crew list as Chummy Tyson.




In the next instalment, the expedition leaves Cumberland Sound for Greenland.




Taissumani is an occasional column that recalls events of historical interest. Kenn Harper is a historian and writer who lived in the Arctic for over 50 years. He is the author of 

Give Me Winter, Give Me Dogs: Knud Rasmussen and the Fifth Thule Expedition

, and 

Thou Shalt Do No Murder

, among other books. Feedback? Send your comments and questions to kennharper@hotmail.com.

author: Daniel Opasinis, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Grassy Narrows River Run brings demands for mercury justice to Tkarón:to
content:
On Wednesday, Sept. 23, members of Grassy Narrows First Nation, Whitedog, and organizers in Tkarón:to came together for the annual Grassy Narrows River Run. Photo by Daniel Opasinis




On the front lawn of Queen’s Park in Tkarón:to stands a tall statue of Sir James Pliny Whitney, Ontario premier from 1905 to 1914, whose government promoted mining and forestry development in northern Ontario.




Over a century later, Glenn Cameron, councillor for Wabaseemoong First Nation (Whitedog), stood below that same statue. Holding a microphone connected to a portable sound system, he addressed a crowd gathered to demand action on the mercury contamination that continues to affect his community.




On Wednesday, Sept. 23, members of Grassy Narrows First Nation, Whitedog, and organizers in Tkarón:to came together for the annual Grassy Narrows River Run. They are calling on Ontario and “Canada” to fairly compensate people in Grassy Narrows 

for the mercury crisis and stop the Dryden mill

.




People rally for justice for Grassy Narrows in Toronto on Sept. 23. Photo by Daniel Opasinis




Between 

1962 and 1970

, Dryden Chemicals Limited discharged approximately nine tonnes of mercury into the Wabigoon River. The contamination spread through the river system, poisoning fish that people in Grassy Narrows and Wabaseemoong relied on for food and their livelihoods. 




Eating contaminated fish exposed people to methylmercury, a highly toxic form of mercury that accumulates in the food chain and can damage the brain and nervous system. Exposure during pregnancy can also harm developing children. 




People rally for justice for Grassy Narrows in Toronto on Sept. 23. Photo by Daniel Opasinis




Earlier that day, participants gathered in Grange Park in the downtown core holding signs and papier-mâché fish. Some played instruments as people got to know one another. It wasn’t long before the crowd filed along McCaul Street, led by a banner reading “Justice for Grassy.”




At the head of the march, participants carried photographs fixed to wooden dowels of loved ones from Grassy Narrows and Whitedog who had died. 




Cameron said malnutrition and mercury contamination from the Dryden Pulp and Paper Mill have been 

a constant concern

 within his community. 




People rally for justice for Grassy Narrows in Toronto on Sept. 23. Photo by Daniel Opasinis




“Now, you can actually see the effects of it — from 1970 and onward,” Cameron said. “A lot of birth defects, a lot of problems in the community, the body, nerve, eyesight, you name it.”




Research conducted with Grassy Narrows has examined how exposure before birth may affect vision decades later. A study published in the 

International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health

 compared adult retinal scans with historical measurements of mercury in participants’ umbilical-cord blood. Among the 59 participants studied, higher prenatal exposure was associated with thinner retinal layers in adulthood. 




People rally for justice for Grassy Narrows in Toronto on Sept. 23. Photo by Daniel Opasinis




Outside of the Native Canadian Centre’s 

Dodem Kanonhsa’

 — a cultural facility dedicated to Elders and knowledge preservation — the march paused to honour community members who had died, with non-Indigenous allies invited to sit in the roadway for a moment of silence. 




The march resumed along Bay Street, with protestors chanting in unison.




“What happens to the water—happens to the people!”




People chant in unison at the rally on Sept. 23.




Continuing along University Avenue, the crowd finally settled outside the Ontario Legislative Building at Queen’s Park. 




People rally for justice for Grassy Narrows in Toronto on Sept. 23. Photo by Daniel Opasinis




“We travel from afar. Whitedog and Grassy united together as one. To fight this process of getting the provincial government and the federal government on board to do something about this,” Cameron said.




Organizers in the city had been instrumental in planning the rally, Cameron added. 




“Being one, as we walked through this corridor, and we all sat down, gathered here. That was the message today.”




People rally for justice for Grassy Narrows in Toronto on Sept. 23. Photo by Daniel Opasinis




The mill’s wastewater remains central to the shutdown demand. A 2024 

study

 led by Western University researcher Brian Branfireun found that sulphate and organic matter in mill effluent increase the conversion of mercury already in contaminated river sediments into methylmercury. Eliminating those discharges would reduce the problem, the report found, although the historical contamination would still require cleanup.

IndigiNews reached out to the Dryden mill for comment but did not receive a response by publication time. 




Grassy Narrows First Nation Chief Sherry Ackabee addresses the crowd. Photo by Daniel Opasinis




Invited by organizers, Grassy Narrows First Nation Chief Sherry Ackabee stepped in front of the crowd. 




“We need their mill shut down, because that’s where all the poisoning is coming from, and it’s still open today,” Ackabee said as a chant broke out.




“Shut it down! Shut it down!”




The post 

Grassy Narrows River Run brings demands for mercury justice to Tkarón:to

 appeared first on 

Indiginews

.

author: Kate Sharpley
title: Tensions in Anarchism - Barry Pateman
content:
This is a transcript of a talk by Barry Pateman at the Bay Area Anarchist Bookfair in San Francisco. It shows something of his approach to anarchism, and the history of anarchism, and mentions some of the important people and experiences in his life. Barry spoke with passion and a greater concern for people than abstract ideas. As you’ll see, his humour (and swearing) were always self-deprecating: ‘Thank you for your time. I’m really sorry that you’ve got nothing else to do.’

I just want to talk about some tensions I think that us as anarchists or people sympathetic to anarchism need to try and consider. ’Cause… I suddenly realised last night when I was laying in bed and just looking at the ceiling that I’m tending to become a bookfair groupie. There’s a bookfair in London. I go to a bookfair in London. It’s an anarchist bookfair, I sell anarchist books. I come to San Francisco. And I’m really talking, I guess, about how we as each other, as a group, as an organisation, as people who share a similar – what Galleani called the ideal, the dream – How we gonna make that real? And so, there are some tensions I think we have to face.

The first tension is ourselves and our history. There is a history of anarchism. But within that history of anarchism, there are things and people who have been forgotten. Now, with the Kate Sharpley Library, we have two reasons to exist. One is, yes, flowers for the fallen. We printed a pamphlet called Anarchists against Franco1 where there were twenty anarchists who’d been killed between 1942 and 1960 in guerrilla warfare against Franco. And Frank Torres who wrote it in Spanish says – and I couldn’t agree more – it doesn’t matter whether you think libertarian communism, anarchism will happen, it doesn’t matter whether you think it’s silly, it doesn’t even matter if you think you’re cleverer than those anarchists who went out there. What matters is how dare we forget them? How dare you and I sitting in this room not know about them? How dare we forget their bravery and their courage when they went over the mountains against stupidly impossible odds for that dream? So, any anarchist, any person sympathetic to us has to be aware of our history, not the history of ideas, that’s something I’ll talk about in a second, but simply the people who have suffered physically and emotionally for our belief. You’ll know some of them, nah? But we’ll also not know a lot of them and one of the things we must do is to revise history, to give them that dignity of that memory.

And the second thing of course is that if we’re canny we learn from history. We have to learn. Look, I’ve been an anarchist for thirty years, so you’re not going to learn much from me because we haven’t got that far. But I do know what’ve we done wrong. I do think I’ve got an idea that what we’ve done has gone wrong. But we have to learn from our history. We can’t just pretend that we exist now and that really that those people were a bit strange or not like us because they spoke a different language. If we’re not guided by our history, we have no foundation, nothing, except living on our wits. So that I think is the first tension, how we discover and make our history come alive for all of us.

The second tension is, is between us as anarchists or sympathetic who are clever buggers ’cause we are… and ordinary people… who aren’t. I don’t mean racist, nasty people, I mean ordinary people who get up every morning, go to work, watch telly, watch baseball, go to bed… yeah? I mean those people. And you know what, there’s a lot more of them than us.

OK, so one of the things that’s disturbed me lately is there’s been a trend in anarchism to think that ordinary people are sort of fucking stupid. Yeah? They’re not clever or, really, they’re the problem. No, they’re not the problem. Look, every time there’s been some type of thing kicking off, starting, some insurrection, its come from dispossessed, poor people, ordinary people. And if we’re not there, if we don’t know them, if we’ve got no relationship with them… what’re we? Who are we? Just somebody else. It means nothing. Our relationship, surely, is with ordinary people. How we get to them. If our belief, if our dream is something that we believe in and live by and suffer by… then we have to go out there somehow. That tension is a critical one. You know, I could sit down all night and convince myself that anarchism’s tomorrow. But actually anarchism’s nothing… it’s something up here. Anarchism’s out there.

Let me give you some examples, two examples. Sixteen years ago in England there was the most brutal strike there’s ever been in the history of the country in many ways. It was a coal strike. One year it took. All my family as a result of that have, now have no jobs. They do not work. Secure, safe communities have become riddled with drugs and riddled with fear as a result of that huge defeat. But let’s look at the problem that we have.

Sixteen years ago you could get up in Markham Main, Armthorpe Village where my family lived, and worked. They were on strike. Mutual aid, not in a fucking book, but in everyday existence was happening, yeah? None of those people had read Kropotkin, they didn’t know what it meant but it was happening. Alright? You went out, seven o’clock in the morning. ‘Who’s gonna have the wood? It’s bitter winter, it’s November. Who’s gonna have the wood? Well, those people with kids have the wood and the old people have the wood.’ That decision’s made. That decision’s made at a mass meeting a week before.

So if you’ve got no kids and you’re on your own with your wife or your partner, you don’t have the wood. That – you’ve agreed on that. You’ve made that decision. You go through there – ‘who’s gonna get the food? The people – old people, kids.’ Again, that’s voted on. ‘Who’s gonna go on the picket lines today?’ ‘Well, I tell you who’s going to go on the picket lines today,’ says Brenda, ‘the women are going on the picket lines today because the fucking Metropolitan Police are here today and they’re out to get the strike leaders. So, we’ll put the women on the picket line today, so if they start swinging the truncheons at least they won’t get the men they’re looking for. We’ll protect them.’ You may disagree with that decision, we all can. I did. That didn’t matter. You had it alive. You had it living. You had something actually happening in your hand, yeah?

But here’s the downside. The tension between ourselves and ordinary people. At that time I was in a group called the Direct Action Movement, yeah? It was an anarcho-syndicalist group. And… we were very lucky. Direct Action Movement had international links and we were sending miners to Italy – to France – to Greece – to get money to support their people. They respected us. There’s lovely stories that’ve come through – you may have read David Douglass,2 a lovely anarchist miner, who talks about all the Trotskyist groups and the Communist groups at various picket lines and as the miners are running past ’cause the police are chasing them with their great big fucking great batons – the old groups are saying ‘Socialist Worker, buy your Socialist Worker…’ and the miners are running through the lines. Not so the anarchists. Respect was given to them.

A lot of anarchists did very well, were superb and courageous in many ways themselves. And a lot of the young miners’ apprentices from the Yorkshire coalfield said ‘Hey, can I join your group? Can I join the Direct Action Movement?’ And all of a sudden they went, ‘Fuckin’ ’ell, er, I dunno. I dunno really. I dunno what we’re gonna do with like twenty-five young miners’ apprentices from Markham Main Colliery.’ ’Cause like they’re not fully formed, they’re not full, full anarchists, they haven’t gone through the… Problems. No, it begs the question why there was an anarchist organisation. And so no, they never joined. But at the same time, some of those young lads are now heroin addicts, some of those young lads are into drink, and some are in prison. We couldn’t provide a platform, we couldn’t sort that tension out between joining an anarchist organisation, organising yourselves. It’s the most critical question of all.

I want to say something now which I hope is not too contentious. I think there is a problem, a tension, between middle class people who’re anarchists and working class people who’re anarchists. I said to you when I came up here this is the first time I’ve spoken at this for seventeen years when I spoke with my father on a platform to support the miners. Middle class people – and this is not an insult so please don’t say I’m insulting middle class people because I’m not – they tend to be far more fluent, articulate and they can write well. And they have more importance in a movement than maybe they deserve. And that’s not to denigrate their efforts or the superb work they do. But working class people, do not, often. Some do. And some will. But others are frankly intimidated – I’ve seen grown, fifty-year old miners intimidated at political meetings and they’ve walked away.

It also means that the comrades amongst us who are fluent in terms of writing, and in terms of oracy, tend to have far more power than maybe they should have. Again, that doesn’t denigrate them. It means that if we don’t have leaders, we have to work out ourselves about how we deal with people who are fluent and articulate who are good comrades and those comrades who aren’t. Those comrades who haven’t got that confidence and that ability. It doesn’t mean they’re worse, mebbe even the opposite I don’t know. But that problem seems to me a running one that’s been going through anarchist circles for thirty years since I’ve been involved.

It shows itself I’ve often thought about violence. I had the misfortune to grow up in an extremely violent area and I have – for whatever sins I’ve had – I’ve used violence – not for political reasons either. I find violence very messy and unpleasant and there’s nothing glorified or attractive about it. Most people I’ve known who’ve used it have had to use it reluctantly and they’ve got it over with. … We have to be careful. We have to be careful about making sure that everyone in our movement has got a say. If we ourselves – because, see, anarchism isn’t just the end, it’s the process, in’t it? We’ve got to draw people in. We’ve got to draw people in with us and play to each other’s strengths.

Miguel Garcia3 who was a, I think a very great man, he’d been in prison for eighteen years – he was with Sabate who some of you may have read about.4 He was actually working with Sabate and Sabate was going into Spain in the 1940s and 1950s. Miguel was imprisoned in the late ’forties because Miguel’s job was the forger. He counterfeited cards so Sabate and the others would have them. He was based in Barcelona and they’d come across the French border, down across the Pyrenees and they’d see Miguel and they’d get their cards and their identity papers. Now, Miguel would say to me quite seriously he’d never ever picked a gun up in his life. Never. He served eighteen years for it – but he never picked a gun up in his life. But people like Sabate who used the gun gave him as much respect as if he had’ve. We play to each other’s strengths, we encourage each other’s strengths. We don’t idolise anything except in some ways mebbe the future.

I think as well another tension, is between the whole idea of theory and practice. You can’t be a theoretical anarchist. You can’t. Well, you can I suppose. You can, you can make anarchism into an intellectual idea and play games. And fuck me, some of the magazines I’ve read, you know, I sit down with a thesaurus and try and make sense of them. (laughter) It’s like… Albert Meltzer who’s now dead once said to me ‘You know, one of the problems with anarchists is if they put their heads up their arses far enough they will talk utter shite.’ Right? And at the moment comrades, some of our, some of our heads are very near our tonsils, yeah? (laughter) Because we’re in our own world making things up. We’re making ideas up. And those ideas look great. Have you done it? I’ve woken up at four in the morning and thought ‘Fucking ’ell, yeah, that’s great. Oh yes, Descartes – we’ll put a bit of Descartes…’ Fuck off! Look – one of the problems with that is that anarchism is how you are, right? It’s a bastard. I said to you I’ve been an anarchist for thirty years. I’ve often at times wished I hadn’t been. Never mind people think you’re about to… you know… sexually intimidate their animals or something.

More importantly if you’re an anarchist you try and live by some morality that’s different. Alfredo Bonanno in his book that’s being sold round here, The Anarchist Tension,5 says you wake up and you try. You try not to be fucking selfish. You try to listen. I’ve got a ten year old son and I have a go at him awful sometimes and I fucking hate myself. I hate myself. Now I think most anarchists have been in that situation, where you actually sit there and you writhe about how you’ve been. I tell you what, you can be a Marxist and be an utter bast– well, they have been haven’t they to all of us? But we can’t be. We can’t do that. We live in practice. You can’t say ‘Ah, I’m an anarchist.’ ‘Oh, yeah? Well fucking prove it then.’ And by the way you are with people, how you talk to people and how you operate with people. And (applause) – we’ll have less of that for a start, alright – Look, what I’m saying I guess is that we all know that and sometimes all of us criticise ourselves too much… yeah?

It’s hard. It’s hard. But it is important, that link between theory and practice. No-one here demeans intellectual ideas… but what we do, is we reduce them. What does an idea mean in practice? What does it mean then, if you actually put it into practice what does it mean? And if it means shite, you don’t put it into practice. If it means turning on someone, or demeaning someone, or not thinking it through and ending up in shit, so be it. You don’t put it into practice. Any idea is clever, people tend to be difficult, yeah? They’ve got emotions and feelings. You live with people, not ideas.

I should also, I guess, say as well that my final point, mmm, second to final point, would be there ought to be ways that we discourse with each other and in the language that we use. I’ve been interested in the American term called Ranting, yeah? Where you have a rant. I don’t think we rant. You don’t rant with anybody. Anarchism isn’t about me. It’s about us, right? That’s all. It’s about us. And I’m quite important, thank you, I’d like to say that, but it’s also about how I become We. Because one of the problems that maybe I should’ve mentioned is that we need to consider our relationship to capitalism. Some of us are leading a nice life, thank you. We’re doing alright. We’re getting on alright, eh? Look at us – it’s nice, nice day, San Francisco, County State Building, here we are … it’s alright. Some of us can live, and not be challenged. But you can’t live – I mean Debs6 said it years ago, Until everybody’s free you’re not and I’m not. And ranting at me or me ranting at you gets nowhere. I’ll talk and I’ll listen and I’ll try and mebbe we ought to learn how to speak to each in a comradely fashion instead of being fuckin’ egoistic and stupid.

Final point is this, I guess, that I’m intrigued about anarchist bookfairs. I’ve noticed, and mebbe you have, that there seems to be almost a cadre of professional speakers who do the circuits. You know, like, ‘Hey, where you going the next year? I’m going to Montreal and…’ I’d like maybe to see people who aren’t like that. I like to see people who are working through things. I like to see the language of an anarchist bookfair talk being one of confusion, sometimes. As people who people who are actually doing activities, events try and work things out. I don’t really come here to be entertained, I come here to learn, I guess… whatever. Thank you for your time. I’m really sorry that you’ve got nothing else to do. (laughter)

And I would say this. Erm, for thirty years now I’ve wanted it to happen. I dunno. All I do is say, what Malatesta says, you know, what matters is that whatever we do, we judge it whether it brings anarchism closer. And we can argue forever about what anarchism is and the way to do it. But you know, and so, whatever we do, we judge it in those ways. Thanks for your time. (applause)

2David Douglass – ‘“Workers Power!” he cried, as we ran past, bleeding, sweating and laughing. Then the cavalry rode past him, to the left and right as bombards of bricks hit them from all sides. We retreated into the trees and waited till they rode back, bloody and hot. Then we crept out to dare again and found the man still unmoved in his central position. “Workers Power!” he cried.’ From 'Charge of the Left Brigade: The Left, Working Class Trade Unionism and the Experience of the Miners.’ in The Heavy Stuff, no.5 (1992). Tell us lies about the miners (1985, 1987) and Come and wet this truncheon (1986) are online: http://libcom.org/tags/dave-douglass. See also volume 3 of his autobiography Ghost dancers: the miners’ last generation (2010).

3Miguel Garcia – See Looking back after twenty years of jail (1970, 1975, 2002), Franco’s prisoner (1972), and Unknown Heroes: Biographies of Anarchist Resistance Fighters (2005).

4Francisco Sabate – see Sabaté: guerrilla extraordinary by Antonio Téllez (1974, 1985, 1998)

5Alfredo Bonanno – The anarchist tension was published (translated to English) in 1998.

6Debs – Eugene V. Debs: American socialist.

author: Corey Larocque
title: Education must continue to be the counter to denialism
content:
Education remains the best way to ensure Canadians understand the legacy of residential schools, to preserve the memories of children who died, and to care for survivors.




Earlier this week, after the Second Sons white nationalist group held an ominous demonstration just outside the Tk’emlúps te Secwépemc reserve near Kamloops, B.C., it became easier to understand the calls to criminalize residential school denialism.




A recurring theme at the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation ceremony on Parliament Hill, residential school denialism is becoming an alarming, disturbing phenomenon.




“We must … confront all forms of denialism that persist despite extensive historical records and an indisputable body of evidence, including first-hand survivor testimony,” Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour said during Wednesday’s event. “This leaves no room for doubt about the history and impact of the residential schools.”




Several speakers spoke to the harms caused by denialism, which is the belief that either children didn’t die at residential schools or that survivors’ experiences were not as bad as they have made it out to be.




In fact, over a century and a half, approximately 150,000 Indigenous people attended residential schools. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s final report notes 3,201 deaths in residential schools. Its former commissioner, Murray Sinclair, believes at least 6,000 children died as a result of their time in residential schools.




National media have reported on what appeared to be Second Sons members’ deliberately provocative acts in the days leading up to Sept. 30, the annual National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.
















On the social media platform X, Prime Minister Mark Carney called “the cowardly act” an “abhorrent” display and added it was a “stark reminder” of Canadians’ responsibility to confront the consequences of the residential school system that are felt today.




He paid tribute to the courage of survivors who have shared their stories so all Canadians can work toward reconciliation.




Nunavut survivors like Iqaluit’s Jack Anawak — once again a fixture at the city’s gathering at the cadet hall — and Cambridge Bay’s Jeannie Ehaoloak, who spoke in Ottawa, contribute to that truth-telling.




In June, Nunavut Sen. Nancy Karetak-Lindell tried unsuccessfully to criminalize residential school denialism.




She tried to amend the Liberal government’s Combatting Hate Act that would have made it a crime to “willfully promote hatred” against Indigenous Peoples by “condoning, denying or downplaying the Indian Residential Schools system.”




Karetak-Lindell’s amendment was supported by the Senate’s human rights committee but was defeated in the Senate.
















A week later, this editorial space argued that 

education

 — not jail time — is the way to counter the denial of the harmful effects of residential schools.




As abhorrent as the Second Sons’ actions were, the most effective way to counter the misinformation that deniers spread is with the spread of accurate information.




The residential school system is a horrible, dark, painful chapter in Canada’s history. But it’s one Canadians need to come to terms with.

author: rti_admin
title: Caste Denied, Gender Dismissed: Reading Literature, Love and Social Life through Selective Lenses
content:
Literature both reflects and shapes social life. This article examines how literature, people’s perspectives, and social life are deeply entangled. It asks how literary works and social relations are interpreted through selective lenses that foreground some forms of inequality while obscuring others. What readers notice in a literary work is not always separate from how they understand the social world around them. Their interpretations are shaped by what they recognise as important, what they have experienced, and what they may have learned to overlook. In this sense, reading is not simply an individual act of interpretation; it can also reveal how social inequalities are recognised, denied, or made invisible. Caste is denied in the name of progress and demanded in the name of awareness, while gender is dismissed in the name of unity. Through reflection on a poem and everyday experiences, this article shows how caste and patriarchy are intertwined rather than operating separately. Ignoring this reality reveals how easily we refuse to confront forms of inequality that do not directly affect us.

To explore this tension, we turn to the poem ଢୋଲିଆ! (Dholia/Dhulia) by the renowned poet Basudev Sunani. The poem brings together themes of love, Ganda Baja, and survival. Later circulated on social media, it offers an opportunity to consider how readers interpret literary expressions through their own social experiences and locations. The poem provides a window into how readers interpret literature through their own social locations and experiences. We should not assume that the poem has one fixed meaning. We examine how readers encounter it through their own social locations and what they see as relevant or missing. Some may respond primarily to its themes of love and connection, while others may be drawn to the social histories and inequalities that surround the lives represented in the poem. These different readings raise a question: what becomes visible when we read literature through different social experiences, and what remains invisible?

One reader asks: “Where is the caste angle?” For some readers, the question seems unnecessary: why bring caste into a poem about love and Ganda Baja? They understand the poem primarily through love, emotion, imagination, and personal expression and see these experiences as separate from social conflict. Others read the poem differently. For them, caste does not disappear simply because the poem speaks of music, intimacy, or love. Caste remains present in these experiences and shapes relationships, choices, and possibilities even when it is not explicitly named. Some feel that the poem should be read for what it expresses, without relating it to caste.

These comments therefore do more than express different opinions about the poem. They reveal how readers bring different social experiences to literature and, in doing so, make some realities visible while leaving others unseen. Reading the poem thus becomes a negotiation over not only what it means, but also whose social reality counts in making that meaning.

However, the poem can also be read through a caste angle, even though caste is not always explicitly named. The poem’s representation of intimacy makes visible the experience of being Ganda/Dom, the Dhulia’s encounter with untouchability, and the difficulty of crossing caste boundaries. The possibility of a relationship between a Dhulia and an upper-caste woman cannot be separated from these social relations. For the Dhulia, caste shapes how he is seen, approached, and touched; for the upper-caste woman, entering into an intimate relationship with him means crossing a boundary that caste has historically made difficult to cross. These realities reveal the caste dimension of the poem, even when caste itself remains unnamed.

Readers, however, respond to this poem differently. Their responses reveal the social lenses through which they approach literature. What one reader recognises as part of everyday social reality may remain invisible to another. This difference is not necessarily a limitation of the poem; it reflects the unequal social experiences that readers bring to their interpretations. Lived experience and social location shape how people understand everyday life, as caste continues to organise relationships, marriage, belonging, and social relations.

Caste shapes where people live and whom they marry. It shapes how families respond to relationships and friendships. It also shapes how communities define honour and belonging. Inter-caste love still faces resistance, social exclusion, and violence. Many people grow up hearing warnings about maintaining caste purity in marriage. These realities become part of everyday consciousness. Because of this history and lived experiences, some readers feel that caste must appear in every narrative. They want literature and public conversations to recognise the structures that shape life. They fear that ignoring caste normalises the very system that produces inequality. In their view, bringing caste into discussion is an act of political awareness. It challenges the illusion that love and personal relationships exist outside social hierarchies

Yet this reality also reveals a deeper contradiction in contemporary discussions. Many upper-caste people today claim that we are “casteless” and deny the continuing significance of caste in the present. They argue that modern education, urban life, and economic mobility have weakened caste identities. This language appears progressive. But in practice it often hides privilege. Caste still organises access to resources, opportunities, and social networks. Declaring society casteless allows privileged groups to avoid confronting their own advantages.

Similarly, many upper-caste feminists advocate gender equality but hesitate to confront caste privilege. They foreground gender while overlooking how caste structures women’s lives differently. The experiences of upper-caste women often become universal, while Dalit women’s realities remain marginal. In these cases, caste is denied in the name of progress, even as its inequalities continue to shape everyday life.

This irony is evident when some Dalit Ambedkarite men speak powerfully against caste oppression yet dismiss women who raise questions about patriarchy. Many assume that challenging caste will automatically resolve gender inequality, overlooking how power operates within their own communities and anti-caste spaces. As a result, women who question patriarchal practices are often labelled as divisive or overly sensitive. Gender is then dismissed in the name of unity, as if confronting patriarchy weakens the struggle against caste.

On the contrary, Dr B. R. Ambedkar showed that patriarchy sustains caste. In Caste in India: Their Mechanisms, Genesis, and Development, he argues that caste survives through the control of women’s sexuality, particularly through endogamy. Practices such as child marriage, sati pratha, and restrictions on women help preserve caste boundaries across generations. For Ambedkar, patriarchy is not separate from caste but one of the mechanisms through which it reproduces itself. Any discussion of caste that ignores patriarchy, therefore, remains incomplete. This insight resonates with Kimberlé Crenshaw’s concept of intersectionality, which highlights how social identities such as race, gender, and class combine to create unique experiences of discrimination.

Both upper-caste feminists and some Ambedkarite Dalit men avoid confronting the structures from which they benefit. One denies caste, while the other dismisses gender. Each position protects a form of contextual privilege while claiming a commitment to justice. The burden of this contradiction often falls on Dalit women. They confront caste oppression in society and patriarchy in everyday life, both within domestic spaces and in anti-caste organisations. They carry a complex struggle that cannot be fully understood through caste alone or gender alone.

To conclude, Dalit women stand at a difficult intersection. They confront caste hierarchy and patriarchal control at the same time, yet their voices are often sidelined when they refuse to reduce their experiences to a single narrative. Recognising caste remains essential, but demanding caste everywhere while dismissing gender creates another hierarchy of recognition. This tension forces us to ask: where do we stand in this struggle? If upper-caste society claims to be casteless while continuing to benefit from caste privilege, what happens when Ambedkarite spaces refuse to confront patriarchy? The structures differ, but the logic of selective recognition can remain similar.

The consequences of this selective recognition are most visible in the lives of Dalit women. There appears to be an ease of using Dalit women’s critiques of feminism while failing to listen harder when Dalit women speak about patriarchy within anti-caste spaces. Their voices can become uncomfortable when they challenge not only caste oppression but also gendered power within their own social and political spaces. For Dalit women, these are not separate struggles; they are lived together. Their experiences therefore challenge us to move beyond choosing which form of inequality deserves recognition and to confront the ways different structures of power shape the same life. Taking Dalit women’s experiences seriously means listening even when what we hear unsettles the spaces and positions we occupy. Refusing to recognise caste or gender does not make these structures disappear. Reality does not change because we refuse to see it.

Dr. Saraswati Suna (Swati) is a sociologist and Dalit feminist ethnographer from Odisha. Her research examines educational institutions, caste, gender, and social inequality, with a particular focus on institutional reproduction and unequal life chances.

author: Sonali Kolhatkar
title: An Abolitionist Vision for the World We Want
content:
A recent New York Times editorial by Tim Wu, a former antitrust adviser for the Biden administration, caught my eye for the criticism it leveled at Democrats for making affordability a central issue ahead of the midterm elections. Wu contends that the party needs to go further and focus not merely on the high price tags of necessities, but on the unfairness of the entire economic system.

While this is a refreshing shift in the right direction, it doesn’t go nearly far enough. It’s true that a majority of Americans across the political spectrum believe our economy is rigged in favor of the rich. But merely pointing out the obvious is unlikely to attract a huge shift in voting toward the Democratic Party.

Moreover, Wu says nothing about the racist rage that has defined President Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s decimation of our democracy, about the devastation to communities of color, immigrants, women, LGBTQ+ people, and other marginalized members of our society. Nor does he acknowledge the corporate harms that Democrats failed to tackle when they were in power and are now being accelerated under Republicans: fossil fuel emissions, tech domination, and AI, harms that disproportionately impactpoor people and people of color.

To Wu and most Democratic Party consultants, these issues are distinct and, depending on the cultural tides, are either worth tackling or anathema.

In fact, they are intimately linked. White supremacy feeds capitalism by distracting poor whites from billionaire-fueled inequality and climate devastation using immigrants and people of color as scapegoats. To take on an unfair economy without addressing the systematically racist impacts of policing, immigration, corporate oligarchy, and the climate crisis does us all a disservice. Moreover, there is an absence of a radical vision for tackling economic and racial justice risks to prevent repeating the same crises in the future.

Democratic Party leaders are falling deeply short by offering little more than undoing Trump’s worst excesses. It is a conservative position to seek a return to the “good old days,” when a predatory capitalist system was overseen by articulate, sensible-sounding statesmen who didn’t embarrass the nation on the global stage, who championed police and prisons as tools of safety, who echoed Trump’s rhetoric on “border security,” who preserved corporate profiteering in healthcare, who embraced endless war as long as it was their party’s doing, and so on.

The Democratic Party is essentially a modern-day conservative party, while Republicans are the extremist, fascist party.

No wonder Americans in general dislike both major parties at roughly the same rate. And while the Democrats’ chances of taking control of Congress appear to be surging ahead of the midterm elections, it is likely because the pendulum is swinging away from Republicans, rather than towardDemocrats and their milquetoast agenda.

So, what can Democrats do to ensure victory?

Frankly, it is not our job as voters—or for that matter, the job of newspaper editorialists—to offer advice to political parties.

Our job as voters, especially in this moment, is to seize power in a system that has rendered us powerless and articulate our demands loudly and clearly. Politicians win our votes by acceding to our agenda. Not the other way around.

Therefore, the far more important question is, what do we, the voters, want?

If we agree that the economic system is rigged against the majority of Americans, then how do we unrig it? Is it as basic as “a promise to level out a lopsided economy,” as Wu advises, while ignoring other issues? Is it as simple as a rallying cry to “tax the rich,” as some Democratic-leaning states are doing?

If we want to end the wild pendulum swings of American politics, which are veering us further into the abyss of authoritarianism with each election, we need a complete reset on all fronts, not merely a return to a more balanced economy.

We require, I would argue, an “abolitionist mindset.”

Black abolitionists, who are better versed than the rest of us on what it’s like to be on the receiving end of systemic harms, have long articulated a vision for a better world where we all can thrive: a world where we reverse the equations of how our collective wealth is spent and where we refuse to let our needs be continually defunded.

Black abolitionists like Angela Davis, Ruth Wilson Gilmore, Mariame Kaba, and Andrea J. Ritchie have already shown us the way to a better world. We only have to listen and apply their vision to all of society.

The foundations laid by these thinkers have helped countless racial justice organizations, big and small to articulate visions for a more just society. Take the Movement for Black Lives, which released a detailed plan in 2020 for a nation where Black people can thrive. Central to this vision is an invest-divest strategy: invest our tax dollars in what actually keeps all human beings safe, while divesting from things that actively cause harm.

The trouble is, we likely disagree on what keeps us safe. White Americans may have forgotten the lessons of the historic 2020 racial justice uprisings in response to George Floyd’s murder. But studies continue to show how the police have always kept whites safe at the expense of Black people. Meanwhile, local police eat up a whopping $135 billion in taxes each year to do so.

Immigration enforcement is similar. A system that disproportionately commits violence against people of color while lulling MAGA supporters into a false sense of safety currently swallows up more than $200 billion of our tax dollars.

Trump’s war on Iran has similarly vaporized $113 billion of our collective wealth. And, since October 2023, we taxpayers have financed Israel’s genocide in Gaza to the tune of nearly $18 billion. Both wars have been deadlier for Iranians and Palestinians thanks to AI-powered weapons and offered us no benefit in return.

To pay for all of this brutalization of Black, Asian, and Latino people at home and abroad, we have defunded public health, housing, food stamps, and Medicaid. We have refused to fund healthcare for all and universal childcare, and have backslid on free higher education, all while continually gifting the wealthy and corporations lower tax rates.

The cost of such violence against nonwhite people is one we all bear. We have all lost out on fully funded healthcare, childcare, education, housing, and the things that keep us safe and thriving. This has not been worth it, even for the most racist whites among us. What good is it to cheer on the barbarity against immigrants if it means you still don’t have a job or can’t afford healthcare? (In fact, the economy is worsebecause of deportations).

And, unless we stop this trend and reverse it, it will only get worse. The dystopian vision that billionaires—the greatest beneficiaries of our rigged system—are offering is a society that is violently policed by ICE agents and cops, where we are forced to live amid detention centers and data centers, in serfdom and in debt, while bracing ourselves for one climate disaster after another, all while our taxes pay for wars and corporate subsidies.

As we approach the midterm elections, the 2028 presidential race, and every election hereafter, we need to define a vision of the world we want, one that is more radical than merely rebalancing the economy, and one that does not rely on throwing some of us—specifically people of color—under the bus as Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has done.

For us all to feel safe and to thrive, we need to flip the line items on our budgets all the way from local to state to national levels. This abolitionist mindset offers a grand unifying vision of a world where we all can thrive. It can apply to local budgetary line items all the way to Congressional appropriations for immigration and war. We need to, as abolitionists have long argued, divest from death-making institutions such as the police, ICE, and military, fossil fuels, and AI, and invest in life-giving systems such as healthcare for all, housing, food, and education. And, if we run out of money, there’s plenty more at the top echelons of our economy.

Undoing the horror show that our society is becoming requires so much more than politely asking Democrats to make the economy better. It requires ending systems of harm and adopting a care-based economy. It requires imagining a better world where the entire equation of our social contract is reversed and demanding that politicians adopt this agenda in order to win our votes.

Sonali Kolhatkar is an award-winning multimedia journalist. She is the founder, host, and executive producer of “Rising Up With Sonali,” a weekly television and radio show that airs on Free Speech TV and Pacifica stations. Her most recent book is Rising Up: The Power of Narrative in Pursuing Racial Justice (City Lights Books, 2023). She is a writing fellow for the Economy for All project at the Independent Media Institute and the racial justice and civil liberties editor at Yes! Magazine. She serves as the co-director of the nonprofit solidarity organization the Afghan Women’s Mission and is a co-author of Bleeding Afghanistan. She also sits on the board of directors of Justice Action Center, an immigrant rights organization.

La propaganda no es y no puede ser más que la repetición continua, incansable, de aquellos principios que deben servirnos de guía en la conducta que debemos seguir en las varias contingencias de la vida.

Repetiremos, pues, con palabras más o menos diferentes, pero con un fondo constante, nuestro viejo programa socialista-anarquista-revolucionario.

Nosotros creemos que la mayor parte de los males que afligen a los hombres dependen de la mala organización social, y que los hombres, si quisieran y supieran cómo, podrían destruirlos.

La sociedad actual es el resultado de las luchas seculares libradas por los hombres. No comprendiendo las ventajas que podrían sacar de la cooperación y de la solidaridad, viendo en los demás hombres (excepto lo más vecinos por los vínculos de la sangre) un competidor y un enemigo, han procurado acaparar, cada uno para sí, la mayor cantidad posible de disfrutes sin preocuparse por los intereses de los demás.

Dada esta lucha, naturalmente debían salir vencedores los más fuertes o los más afortunados, y de una u otra forma, someter y oprimir a los vencidos.

Mientras el hombre no fué capaz de producir sino lo que necesitaba para su sostén, los vencedores no podían hacer otra cosa que matar al vencido y apoderarse de los alimentos por éste cosechados.

Más tarde, cuando con el descubrimiento del pastoreo y del la agricultura un hombre pudo ya producir mas de lo que necesitaba para vivir, los vencedores encontraron mas ventajoso reducir a los vencidos a esclavitud y hacerles producir para sus dueños.

Más tarde aún, los vencedores se dieron cuenta de que era más cómodo, más productivo, y más seguro explotar el trabajo ajeno con otro sistema: retener la propiedad exclusiva de la tierra y de todos los medios de trabajo, y dejar nominalmente libres a los despojados, los cuales, no teniendo ya medios con que vivir, venían obligados a recurrir a los propietarios y a trabajar para éstos en las condiciones que éstos querían.

De este modo, poquito a poco, a través de toda una red complicadísima de luchas de todo género, invasiones, guerras, rebeliones, represiones, concesiones arrancadas, asociaciones de vencidos unidos para la defensa y de vencedores unidos para la ofensa, se ha llegado al estado actual de la sociedad, en la cual unos cuantos detienen hereditariamente la tierra y toda la riqueza social, mientras la gran masa de los hombres, desheredada de todo, se ve explotada y oprimida por unos poco propietarios.

De este estado de cosas depende el estado de miseria en que generalmente se encuentran los trabajadores y por consiguiente todos los males que de la miseria derivan: ignorancia, delitos, prostitución, la abyección física causada por la desnutrición, la depresión mental, y la muerte prematura. De este modo depende la constitución de una clase especial (el gobierno), la cual, provista de medios materiales de represión, tiene la misión de legalizar y defender a los propietarios contra las reivindicaciones de los proletarios, sirviéndose, además, de esta fuerza, para crearse a sí misma ciertos privilegios y para someterse, cuando se puede, incluso hasta la misma clase propietaria. De esto depende la constitución de otra clase especial (el clero), la cual, con una serie de fábulas sobre la voluntad de Dios, sobre la vida futura, etc., procura persuadir a los oprimidos a que soporten dócilmente al opresor, y al igual que el gobierno, al propio tiempo que trabaja por el interés de los propietarios, trabaja también por sus propios intereses. De esto depende la formación de una ciencia oficial que es, en todo aquello que puede servir los intereses de la clase dominante, la negación de la verdadera ciencia. De esto, depende el espíritu patriótico, los odios raciales, las guerras, y la paz armada, más desastrosa a veces incluso que las mismas guerras. De esto depende la transformación del amor en tormento o en mercado vil. De esto depende el odio más o menos disimulado, la rivalidad, la desconfianza entre los hombres, la incertidumbre, y el miedo universal.

Es este estado de cosas lo que nosotros queremos cambiar radicalmente. Y puesto que todos estos males derivan de la lucha entre los hombres, de esta búsqueda del bienestar individual efectuada por cuenta propia y en contra de todos los demás, nosotros buscamos remediarlo, sustituyendo el odio por el amor, la competencia por la solidaridad, la búsqueda exclusiva del propio bienestar por la cooperación fraternal del bienestar de todos, la opresión y la imposición por la libertad, y la mentira religiosa y pseudo-científica por la verdad.

Abolición de la propiedad privada de la tierra, de las materias primas, y de los medios de producción, a fin de que nadie pueda subsistir mediante la explotación del trabajo ajeno, y teniendo todos los hombres garantizados los medios de producir y de vivir, puedan ser verdaderamente independientes y asociarse a los demás livremente en vista del interés común y conforme a las propias simpatías.

Abolición del gobierno y de todo poder que haga ley y la imponga a los demás, o sea: abolición de las monarquías, de las repúblicas, de los parlamentarios, de los ejércitos, de los cuerpos de policías, de las magistraturas, y de todas las demás instituciones dotadas de medios coercitivos.
